title: Israeli forces kill disabled Syrian in raid on homes in Deraa
description: Snipers deployed on rooftops in southern governorate as Damascus condemns rise in cross-border incursions
content: Israeli forces shot dead a Syrian civilian with disabilities during raids on homes in the southern governorate of Deraa, state news agency Sana reported on Thursday. Troops fired indiscriminately and snipers were positioned on roofs as the Israeli forces entered the village of Jamlah and searched homes, Sana reported. The man's body was transferred to Deraa National Hospital. On Wednesday night, Israeli forces had shelled the outskirts of Abidin in the western Deraa countryside. Two shells landed west of the town, with no reports of injuries or damage. Israeli attacks and incursions in Syria have escalated since the ousting of president Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024, with further intensification in recent months. Following the regime's fall, Israel declared the 1974 Disengagement Agreement void and moved to take control of the Syrian buffer zone, while also seizing positions beyond it. Israeli forces have continued to violate the agreement through repeated incursions into southern Syria, raids on civilian homes, arrests, land seizures and missile attacks, Sana reported. On Sunday, Syria's Foreign Ministry condemned an increase in Israeli incursions into Quneitra province and the Deraa countryside, alongside more frequent helicopter, reconnaissance and warplane flights over the south. These violations “undermine the prospects for achieving stability and security in the region in general and Syria in particular, and obstruct reconstruction and recovery efforts”, the ministry said in a statement. It called on the international community to halt the incursions and compel Israel to comply with international law and UN resolutions. In early October, the UN said Israel was holding 49 Syrians and had carried out 280 armed incursions into southern Syria in September. Released detainees alleged torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, prolonged forced standing and threats against their families, a statement by UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said.

title: F1 title race explained: What Kimi Antonelli needs to become champion at the United States Grand Prix
description: Italian teenager can clinch first place in Austin if results go his way
content: A little over two years ago, just after his 18 th birthday, Kimi Antonelli crashed at Monza in his first-ever Formula One practice session. Today, he stands on the brink of the world championship and could become the sport’s youngest title winner in Austin, Texas, this weekend. Five drivers can still beat him on paper, even if most of them are clinging to the faintest of hopes. Six races remain, and all of them are traditional grand prix weekends as Singapore was the last Sprint weekend. Each GP win is worth 25 points, second place is 18, third is 15 and so on down to a single point for finishing 10th. That leaves a maximum of 150 points on the table. If two drivers finish the season level on points, the title goes to the one with more race wins. Teammate George Russell remains Antonelli’s closest challenger, while seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, four-time champion Max Verstappen, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and defending champion Lando Norris are still technically in contention. Here is what each of the six contenders needs to finish the season as world champion. Where he stands: First on 340 points with eight GP wins. What he needs: Antonelli can win the title in Austin this Sunday if he wins the race and Russell finishes ninth or lower, and Hamilton finishes fifth or lower. Victory would take Antonelli to 365 points and nine GP wins this season. Even if Russell subsequently won all five remaining races to draw level on points, Antonelli would still prevail, as he has secured more race wins. If the Italian finishes second or lower in Austin, his next opportunity comes a week later in Mexico City, on November 1. Where he stands: Second on 238 points, 102 points behind. What he needs: Russell’s best-case scenario involves him winning all six remaining races, which would take him to 388 points. Even then, Antonelli would have to score 48 points or fewer across those six races, which is essentially finishing sixth every weekend. Russell began the year as favourite, considering his experience and the brilliance of the car, and things started brightly for the Briton, who won the opening race in Australia. Since then, reliability issues and his own style of driving have seen him usurped by his younger, more daring teammate. Where he stands: Third on 229 points, 111 behind Antonelli. What he needs: If Hamilton wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 379 points. Antonelli would then have to score 38 points or fewer. In Austin, Hamilton would be eliminated from title contention if Antonelli wins and the Brit finishes fifth or lower. He is also out if Antonelli outscores him by 14 points or more. Hamilton’s second year at Ferrari has seen him be more competitive but he has still only won once this season. He would need six wins in a row and a total collapse from the young driver who replaced him at Mercedes for him to take the crown. Realistically, the chase for a record eighth title will have to wait another year. Where he stands: Fourth on 221 points, 119 behind. What he needs: If Verstappen wins all the remaining races, he will finish on 371 points. Antonelli would then have to score 30 points or fewer, which is worse than seventh place every weekend. If Antonelli scored exactly 31 points, they would tie on 371 points with eight wins each and second places would settle it. In Austin, if Antonelli wins the race, Verstappen is eliminated from title contention wherever he finishes. There may be little hope for Verstappen. He spent most of the year struggling to get the car to compete and did not win a grand prix until October, in Sepang. Red Bull’s progress over the last few weekends has been exceptional, and the burst of form has dragged him back into the title conversation. Antonelli has admitted it unsettles him. It is a warning for next season, but it has probably come too late for this year. Where he stands: Fifth, on 215 points, 125 behind. What he needs: If Leclerc wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 365 points. Antonelli would then have to score 24 points or fewer, which is essentially finishing P8 in every remaining race. Leclerc has virtually no hope of winning the championship and his teammate Hamilton has produced better performances this season. His early exit at Monza, Ferrari’s home race, perfectly demonstrated how the season has drifted away from him. Where he stands: Sixth on 201 points, 139 behind What he needs: If Norris wins all six races, he finishes on 351 points. Antonelli would then have to score 10 points or fewer across six weekends. In Austin, Norris would need to outscore the Italian by at least 15 points just to remain in contention.

title: Gulf tour gives sombre and combative Macron platform to fight protests at home
description: Embattled French President secures diesel and LNG supplies in exchange for military support against Iran
content: A noticeable shift in mood was apparent during French President Emmanuel Macron's three-day tour of five Gulf states, from his sombre demeanour on arrival in the UAE to an upbeat, combative tone in Doha. Walking past the Emirati national guard at Abu Dhabi airport on Monday with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, Mr Macron looked stern, his brow furrowed and his steps deliberate. The next day, after his plane landed in Doha flanked by Rafale jets, he greeted Qatar's ambassador to France, Sheikh Ali bin Jassim, with a hearty handshake. “How's the family?” Mr Macron asked the ambassador with a smile, before winking, as he often does, at the journalists watching from the sidelines. Such highly choreographed moments in international diplomacy are difficult to compare, but the change in demeanour reflected a broader shift that took place between Mr Macron’s departure from Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and his arrival in Doha a few hours later. By then, the key deliverable of his trip to the Gulf, which also included stops in Kuwait, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, had been announced. In the words of his advisers, France had secured in-kind compensation for its role as a reliable security ally to Gulf states, in the form of LNG shipments from Qatar and diesel sales from Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the UAE, equivalent to 10 per cent of French consumption. “When you have shown that you are there during difficult times, it is easier to gain visibility,” Mr Macron told reporters before departing Doha on Wednesday. The energy announcements were aimed at a domestic audience as France grapples with violent social unrest, fuelled in part by high energy prices following Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . “I’ve had partners who understood that, as clients – as consumers – we have a need for this,” Mr Macron said. The Gulf gave Mr Macron a platform to regain control of the narrative at home. The President made it clear that he considered this exchange of services with Gulf states a political victory. “It was important for us,” he said. He also confirmed that defence co-operation had been high on the agenda, with an “important inter-governmental agreement” signed with the UAE to develop a joint strategy on the next generation of Dassault Rafale jets alongside deals with Qatar to upgrade its own Rafale jets. The last leg of the trip, to Saudi Arabia , was kept under wraps until his plane had departed Doha, most likely because of security concerns following Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s airport and critical infrastructure. The French presidency had adopted a similar communications strategy when Mr Macron travelled to Syria in July. An hour-long meeting with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman secured further commitments to supply diesel to France for “as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace said. Ahead of the trip, Mr Macron's advisers had brushed aside persistent questions from journalists asking why Saudi Arabia was not included in the trip. There was no need, they argued, pointing to Prince Mohammed travelling to Paris in August. But such reasoning appeared unconvincing, given that the tour aimed primarily to secure oil and gas guarantees from Gulf states and accelerate investment in alternative export routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Just before heading to the airport to fly to Riyadh, Mr Macron emerged from the Rosewood hotel in Lusail, Qatar, after taking questions from the press. He declined to answer questions about a hypothetical visit to Saudi Arabia. Yet he appeared keen to highlight French military support to the kingdom, asking The National to repeat a question that had been drowned out by the media pack. The question referred to the UK announcing on Tuesday that it would send Typhoon jets to Saudi Arabia and asked for clarification about French support. “I think it is important for talks with the Houthis to resume and, obviously, for tensions to ease, because that would contribute to the same objective,” Mr Macron said. “Saudi Arabia has a very important pipeline that runs from the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea, terminating at Yanbu. Several facilities have been destroyed by Houthi strikes. We have offered to help rehabilitate the site and, above all, secure it. For the past eight days, we have had personnel and capabilities deployed there.” This means French military support has been in Saudi Arabia since October 13. Mr Macron had said on September 24 that France would dispatch soldiers , radars and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia to protect the strategic Red Sea port of Yanbu. Contradictory information had since come out from the Foreign Ministry and the Elysee Palace about whether the mission had begun. The Defence Ministry has declined to give operational details. In March, France sent air defence systems to the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar. Yet despite the strength of France’s ties with Gulf states, its influence over continuing Iran-US negotiations remains limited. Questioned by a Qatari broadcaster on whether he had come with a concrete mediation proposal on the table in his meeting with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim, Mr Macron did not answer directly. Instead, he pointed to the French-British initiative to station an international naval mission in the Strait of Hormuz. The initiative has remained stalled since its announcement in April, as it requires a negotiated political solution to a conflict from which Europeans have been excluded. The French President said he had discussed “details and developments extensively” with Doha, and that “the coming hours and days would allow us to receive a response, particularly from Iran”. For a country that punches above its diplomatic weight and is grappling with a mounting debt crisis, France makes a point of keeping up appearances abroad. Unlike many other European presidents who travel with their entire delegations on a single plane, Mr Macron travels with three aircraft: an Airbus A330-200 for him, his ministers and senior members of his delegation, including chief executives; an Airbus A330 MRTT for more junior members of his delegation and journalists; and a Dassault Falcon for the handful of pool reporters with access to some restricted meetings. The National was part of the second group. Mr Macron took nearly a dozen questions from reporters in Doha, devoting the first half to the Middle East before switching to the French crisis. He had not spoken publicly about the violent protests that have shaken France for weeks since addressing the nation on Sunday night, before leaving for Kuwait, the first stop of his Gulf tour. His harshest words were for US President Donald Trump , who has blamed migrants for the protests. Mr Macron described his comments as “stupid”. “Does Mr Trump not like France?” Mr Macron was asked. “One cannot help but notice,” he said. “When I see leaders that are campaigning in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic and sometimes with credulity pick up AI content or relay what some spheres want to make believe is happening in France, they’re campaigning on our back, so we don’t need that.” With these comments, Mr Macron also appeared to be referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose relations with France have soured since Paris recognised Palestinian statehood alongside 10 other countries last year. The episode is a reminder that foreign policy – from relations with Israel, to the US and the Gulf – is playing an increasingly important role in French politics. What remains to be seen is whether the French public appreciates Mr Macron’s diplomatic efforts. Critics accused him of appearing disconnected from reality by pressing ahead with his Gulf tour despite the worsening situation in France. Mr Macron said he had no regrets. “What we are doing here is important for our citizens, so I decided to maintain it,” he said. More protests are planned for Saturday.

title: Abu Dhabi's M42 launches AI platform to give doctors more time with patients
description: 'Ossi', whose has four main agents work alongside the emirate's electronic medical records, will be available at seven M42 centres
content: Abu Dhabi tech-enabled healthcare company M42 has launched Ossi, an AI platform designed to help with administration and give doctors more time with patients. The platform, announced at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, will be available at seven M42 centres in the UAE and Bahrain, and is estimated to help doctors spend up to 60 per cent more time with patients. Kareem Shahin, M42’s chief executive of Digital Health Solutions Platform and group chief digital officer, told The National that Ossi, launched in partnership with Microsoft, is “an AI platform that has been built by and for people here in Abu Dhabi”. It works alongside electronic medical record systems, bringing together AI agents, voice recognition and healthcare-focused large language models to support physicians before, during and after a consultation. “Before the patient arrives, the doctor can open Ossi, where the Patient Summary Agent provides a summary of the patient’s historical details and all of their medical details,” Mr Shahin said. “So during the patient appointment there is more time between the physician and the patient, and they are focused on the patient and their needs rather than checking all of the medical summaries. “Using AI to summarise medical history leaves nothing missed, so that the physician will see everything as per the most recent data, such as medications, lab results, radiology, and all of the recent appointments that the patient has had. “It’s a cloud-based AI solution, and we’ve started implementing it across the network. We’re looking through the strategic partnership with Microsoft to host Ossi on Microsoft Azure cloud and take it globally, with many clients and many countries capitalising on the reachability of Microsoft worldwide.” The name Ossi comes from the ossicle bones in the human ear, which help to amplify and refine sound. “It listens to Arabic and English, and now we’re working even with our international partners to translate it into understanding Greek and other languages,” he said. Mr Shahin said that during the consultation with the patient, another of Ossi's AI agents listens in. “While the physician is interacting with the patient, the Scribing Agent listens to the consultation and transforms the conversation into a structured clinical note for the physician to review,” he said. “The physician can then use the Chat Agent to ask questions about the patient’s medical information and identify best practice based on available evidence and clinical guidelines. “Finally, the Coding Agent analyses the clinical documentation and suggests relevant medical codes, supporting the physician and coding workflow.” Together, the four agents work to provide AI assistance across the consultation, while keeping the physician at the centre of clinical decision-making. Mr Shahin said that Ossi is designed to sit alongside, rather than replace, a hospital’s electronic medical records (EMR). “It doesn’t interrupt the EMR,” he said. “It is beside the EMR integrated within the doctor’s workflow.” “If a patient is going to see an oncology doctor, usually the doctor spends three to four hours before the patient visit to review the file. With Ossi and AI, this can be reduced to less than 10 to 15 minutes", as the doctor receives “the relevant summary of the file”. Mr Shahin described Ossi as part of Abu Dhabi’s wider digital health ecosystem, and M42’s government healthcare platforms were hosted on the UAE’s sovereign cloud, providing privacy for medical information. “We have security measures and we have a very robust security team aligned with the UAE Cyber Security Council, applying all of the guidelines and making sure our systems are updated as per the regulatory standard," he said. “Definitely at the end of the day, who will make the final decision is the doctor himself. But it’s a tool that can help to reduce time, to be more efficient, and not miss anything.” The seven M42 centres where Ossi is available are: Amana UAE; Amana Bahrain; Healthpoint; HealthPlus; Mubadala Health Dubai; Sheikh Sultan bin Zayed Hospital and Imperial College London Diabetes and Endocrine Centre in Abu Dhabi.

title: Dayne Viernes out to cement status as Power Slap greatest in Abu Dhabi
description: 'Da Hawaiian Hitman' defends super heavyweight title against Vasilii 'Dumpling' Kamotskii at Space42 Arena
content: Dayne “Da Hawaiian Hitman” Viernes is looking to cement his status as the greatest super heavyweight of Power Slap when he defends his title against Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii in Abu Dhabi next month. Viernes made his second title defence against the man he dethroned in June 2025, taking a majority decision over Kamotskii in five rounds at Power Slap 13. Power Slap 25 takes place at Abu Dhabi’s Space42 Arena on October 23, a day before UFC 333, and Viernes said he is “locked in” ahead of his rematch. “Physically and mentally, I’m ready to make a statement. Right now I’m just perfecting my slap and ready to win the title. Training daily and excited to showcase my skills,” Viernes told The National . After beating Kamotskii, Viernes successfully defended his belt against top-ranked super heavyweight Makini “Big Mak” Manu, taking a split decision over the American. This will be his first time competing in Abu Dhabi, and Viernes is determined to put on a show. “Yes, first time in Abu Dhabi. I’m excited to put on a show for the fans at the Space42 Arena and around the world to get the win, be known as the greatest super heavyweight of Power Slap of all time and hopefully getting some knockout reactions.” The rivalry between Kamotskii and the Viernes family goes back even further and has strong ties to Abu Dhabi. “Dumpling” first faced Dayne’s older brother, Layne Viernes, in the UAE capital in October 2024, with the contest ending in a majority draw. The pair later met again, with the Russian defeating Layne to claim the super heavyweight title. The return to Abu Dhabi brings that family history back to where it began. While October 23 will mark Dayne’s first appearance in the UAE capital, it will be the third year straight Kamotskii has competed in Abu Dhabi. For Viernes, the mission is clear: “I’m expecting his best and nothing less and I’m looking for a KO win.” For former champion Kamotskii, owner of multiple high-profile first-round KOs, a return to Abu Dhabi offers a shot at redemption. “The audience and atmosphere in Abu Dhabi are really great. I love performing in Abu Dhabi. I haven't been able to win in Abu Dhabi before, but this time it'll be different,” he said. “We need to knock out Dayne to reclaim my title and for me to be the best superheavyweight of all time in Power Slap.” For Power Slap chief executive Frank Lamicella, being part of Abu Dhabi Showdown Week helps elevate Power Slap on the global stage. “In Power Slap, we always want to put the best against the best. Abu Dhabi is the world’s fight capital,” he told The National . “There is no bigger stage to hold two super heavyweights – weighing in at nearly 800 pounds together – vying to be named the best in the world in the super heavyweight division.”

title: UAE leads $39 billion global digital fraud crackdown with more than 900 arrests
description: Ministry of Interior teams up with Interpol and 30 countries to tackle AI-driven and digital plots
content: The UAE has led an international digital fraud crackdown in which hundreds of arrests were made and more than $39 billion in illicit funds and assets uncovered. Operation Confrontation Ghost – overseen by the Ministry of Interior – thwarted more than 123.7 million online fraud attempts worldwide, blocked 4,126 bank accounts, shut down 570 social media accounts and involved 29 raids on locations linked to fraud. The major crime-fighting campaign brought together law enforcement agencies from 30 countries, Interpol, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance and 13 private-sector partners specialising in technology, digital platforms and financial services. The three-month drive – conducted from July 1 to September 30 – focused on three major forms of digital crime: AI-enabled fraud, digital financial fraud and online "sextortion", state news agency Wam reported. The cross-border collaboration resulted in the arrest of more than 960 people, the identification of a further 3,500 suspects and 15,500 victims of crime and the exchange of more than 9,000 pieces of intelligence. The operation helped to secure more than four billion financial transactions made each month through tokenisation technology, bolstering user data protection and curbing fraud threats. The UAE's partners in the organised crime clampdown included the UK, Japan, Korea, Canada, Italy, France, the Netherlands, Brazil, Ecuador, Jordan and Bahrain. Private sector support in tackling wide-ranging fraudulent activity was provided by the likes of the UAE's Bayut and Dubizzle, as well as social media giants Meta and TikTok. Col Dana Al Marzouqi, director-general of the International Affairs Bureau at the Ministry of Interior, said the operation demonstrated the importance of international partnerships in addressing fraud networks that seek to exploit online platforms, financial services and emerging technologies to conduct cross-border criminal activities. She said the Ministry of Interior continued to strengthen co-operation with countries, international organisations, and technology and financial services companies to combat transnational digital fraud and protect both the public and organisations. Dr Monica Juma, executive director of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, described Operation Confrontation Ghost as a model of international co-operation in addressing emerging forms of crime. She stressed that the growing use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in fraud, alongside the exploitation of digital platforms, bank accounts and cryptocurrencies to transfer funds and conceal their origins, highlighted the need to continue to bolster counter-measures and strengthen global collaboration.

title: 'I have lived that hell': Former Iran detainee calls for release of British couple in Evin Prison
description: Anoosheh Ashoori campaigns for UK tourists Lindsay and Craig Foreman to be freed
content: More than four years after his release from an Iranian jail, Anoosheh Ashoori still wakes up with nightmares from the “dark, dark moments” he experienced there. Mr Ashoori, 72, was speaking on a dreary wet day outside the UK Parliament. The former inmate of Tehran's most notorious prison was out on the street to call on the UK government to do more to release another detained British couple, Lindsay and Craig Foreman . The British-Iranian survived more than five years in Evin Prison until the British government secured his release in a high-profile deal in 2022. “I still have my nightmares. I still have my moments of remembering all the hard times that I went through,” he told The National . “I do dream about my former inmate and friends, in different scenarios – but horrible ones. Then I wake up in the middle of the night and I have to deal with that feeling until I can manage to go back to sleep again." Mr Ashoori’s experience with Iran's hostage-taking and hopes that it can be stopped for good is what compelled him to campaign outside Parliament on Wednesday for the Foremans. "I have lived in that hell. And I know that Lindsay and Craig are going through the same thing I did, even perhaps worse. So I felt that I must participate in this campaign." The couple were arrested while on a motorcycle tour of Iran in January 2025, and have since been sentenced to 10 years in prison for espionage. Their family have repeatedly raised concerns about their health and welfare in prison. Since their arrest, a war with the US and a popular uprising against the regime have rocked Iran – leading to greater paranoia and oppression from security officials. Mr Ashoori fears the couple may be going through an incarceration that is worse than his own. “I have met a few of my former inmates who were released and it is far worse than what it was when I was there,” he said. “Diseases have intensified, food quality has diminished. The tyranny itself has intensified. My condition there is nothing compared with what we are what is happening now." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in Parliament on Wednesday that the Foremans' sentence was “appalling and unjustifiable”. “We will continue to pursue the case relentlessly until Lindsay and Craig are safely returned home to the UK and reunited with their family,” he said. Tension between the UK and Iran is at an all-time high after a suspected terror attack at a British airbase used by US bombers this month. This followed attacks on Jewish businesses and Iranian dissidents in the UK , which police suspect were ordered by Iranian officials. But the couple’s family are calling for stronger action from the UK government to secure their release. Lindsay’s son Joe Bennett and other members of the family delivered a petition to the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office, signed by about 110,000 people, calling on the UK government to call the Foremans' imprisonment “arbitrary” and “unlawful”. Richard Ratcliffe, husband of former Evin detainee Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe who was released in the same deal as Mr Ashoori in 2022, also joined the family, alongside MPs and supporters. Mr Ashoori's release in 2022 was secured by a payment of £400 million ($535 million) made by the UK government to Iran – which Tehran had claimed was debts owed over a historic arms deal. “The options are limited because we don’t understand what Iran wants. They seem to be holding them as hostages pending any demands that they may have,” Tony Vaughan, the couple’s MP, told The National . “The government has to call a spade a spade and call it unlawful and arbitrary detention. " The family will be meeting Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband next week. “We’re very thankful that he’s given us his time. But we need to make sure this isn’t another sort of meet and greet,” Mr Bennett said. “What we have to get next week is concrete answers as to [why] you’re not calling it arbitrary detention." He hopes that a declaration of arbitrary detention by the UK government would enable diplomatic protection for the couple. The family was also considering an application to the International Court of Justice in the Hague. “From there, this is a bit further down the line, we'd be looking to apply for International Court of Justice. this all takes a lot of political will and the right person to get behind it,” Mr Bennett said. UN experts have described the couple’s detention as a “state hostage-taking for political leverage”, citing “irregularities” in their trial last year. Mr Ashoori warned that the detainees' families were also victims of trauma, just as his were. "This is what I call shrapnel, because it is not only the victim who has been tyrannised, it is the family members who are hit. Shrapnel is exactly what hits the family members, and they go through the same trauma, but in a different way," he said.

title: AI power demand underestimated, say 81% of energy executives
description: Adipec survey finds growing electricity requirements could strain infrastructure as technology companies gain influence over global energy markets
content: More than eight in 10 energy industry decision-makers expect artificial intelligence to drive electricity demand beyond current forecasts, raising concerns about whether there is enough global infrastructure to power the rapid expansion of data centres. A global survey commissioned by Adipec , Abu Dhabi's annual energy conference, found that 81 per cent of energy industry insiders believe AI-driven electricity consumption will exceed existing projections, with 32 per cent expecting demand to be significantly higher. Only 3 per cent expect demand to fall below current forecasts, according to Adipec's Global Energy Report 2026, released on Thursday. Those surveyed included executives from energy companies, technology providers, investors and industry suppliers. The findings come as technology companies accelerate investment in energy-intensive data centres, creating opportunities for power producers while putting additional pressure on electricity networks. The International Energy Agency expects data centres to consume about 950 terawatt-hours of electricity by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level, according to figures cited in the report. The growth in data centre power demand has become an increasingly important consideration for energy producers and governments. At Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week in January, Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc , said global electricity requirements from data centres could increase fivefold by 2040. The report's findings build on the “power is knowledge” message that was the theme of discussions at Adipec last year, as The National reported. The relationship between AI and electricity remains a central focus of this year's event, which will take place at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi from November 2 to November 5. The expansion of AI is also expected to change the balance of influence within the energy industry. About 43 per cent of respondents believe technology and AI companies will gain the most influence over the sector, compared with 15 per cent who selected governments and regulators. Financial institutions were also selected by 15 per cent, followed by international oil companies at 14 per cent and national oil companies at 9 per cent. The findings reflect the increasingly close relationship between AI and energy , as technology companies become major drivers of investment in electricity generation and infrastructure. For oil and gas companies, the shift is creating new commercial opportunities. While gas and liquefied natural gas growth currently ranks as the biggest commercial opportunity for oil and gas insiders, AI-driven efficiency is expected to take the top position over the next decade. About 27 per cent identify AI-driven efficiency as a leading opportunity in 10 years, while 25 per cent cite supplying power for AI and data centres. The report also found that 81 per cent of oil and gas insiders believe adopting AI will become essential to remain profitable over the next decade. The findings are particularly relevant to the UAE, where Abu Dhabi is developing a 5-gigawatt AI campus that will house the Stargate UAE computing cluster, expected to cost more than $30 billion . However, a quarter of energy insiders believe the industry is unprepared for AI-driven electricity demand, with grid delays among the biggest obstacles. At Adipec last year, Dr Al Jaber called for “massive” energy investment to meet growing requirements. The Adipec report, conducted by global strategic communications consultancy Kekst CNC between August and October 2026, surveyed 1,832 energy industry decision-makers across 78 countries and included 17 executive interviews. Its findings reflect industry expectations rather than independently verified demand forecasts.

title: UFC Abu Dhabi: Merab Dvalishvili has new plan for Petr Yan and promises ‘domination’
description: Bitter rivals to settle trilogy at Etihad Arena on Saturday with bantamweight title on the line
content: For a former UFC champion, the fighter with the most takedowns in company history and a man whose face is plastered across billboards around Abu Dhabi advertising UFC 333, Merab Dvalishvili hardly needed to introduce himself to the assembled media. He did it anyway. “Hello everybody. My name is Merab Dvalishvili.” The Georgian cut a suave figure in a brown tailored suit, an expensive watch and a permanent smile. He was jovial and playful, joking about riding motorcycles and horses with Sean Strickland. It was in stark contrast to his opponent. If Dvalishvili’s vibe was light, Petr Yan’s was heavy. Dressed in a black baseball cap and UFC apparel, Yan exuded a brooding, smouldering intensity. He said Dvalishvili should not even be in line to face him this Saturday for a shot at his UFC bantamweight belt. “Song Yadong is really more deserving of a title fight, to be honest,” the Russian champion said through a translator. “I do not choose my opponents. Whoever the company gives me, that's who I fight.” Make no mistake, Dvalishvili and Yan do not like each other. One does a passable job of disguising his disdain; the other wears it like a badge of honour. If all fights are personal, in the sense that both combatants are trying to inflict maximum pain and damage on each other, this one carries an extra edge. The two meet for the third time in their careers at Etihad Arena on Saturday , with one win apiece. It is billed as the co-main event but could easily headline the card, with no disrespect intended to Alexander Volkanovski and Movsar Evloev. Trash talk dominated the build-up to their first two encounters, and there have been plenty of barbs fired this time around, too, mostly from Yan. “I'm really excited to fight Petr Yan; the title is secondary,” said Dvalishvili. “His trash talk and his disrespect doesn't bother me because the most important thing is to get the win against him and answer that way. “I'm not here to show who is the better person. I'm here to show who is the better fighter.” Abu Dhabi will bring the trilogy - which began three years ago - to a close. Back then, Dvalishvili took a unanimous decision over Yan, a result the Russian heavily disputed. Before that bout, Dvalishvili had made the extreme claim that he would kill himself if he lost to Yan. Having suffered defeat the last time the two met, the Georgian has adopted a much more measured approach this time around. “No, the first fight was very important; it was really personal. But right now I'm a different person, at a different stage [in life]. That time it was a different situation,” Dvalishvili said. “But right now, I just want to win the fight. I can see now if I lose, it's gonna just be a loss. And it's possible, of course. Petr Yan is a dangerous guy. “Even when we fought the last time, I was the one who said he deserved the fight with me. He's the most dangerous guy. “And of course, I knew I could lose this fight, but I still take this risk. I'm not saying that I'm not gonna lose. Every time I fight, there is a chance that I lose. It's possible. But I'm not gonna kill myself.” Yan produced the performance of a lifetime when the two met last December at UFC 323. He literally took the breath away from Dvalishvili with crunching body shots and broke his opponent's spirit by repeatedly denying his takedown attempts. Dvalishvili had taken that bout just two months after beating Corey Sandhagen. It was his third successful title defence, bringing him level with his good friend Aljamain Sterling, who was in attendance to support him and will also corner Dvalishvili on Saturday. The Yan rematch was Dvalishvili's fourth fight of 2025. Most champions defend their belts no more than twice a year. Dvalishvili admitted in an earlier interview with The National that it had been a mistake to take on Yan so soon after his win over Sandhagen. A fighter renowned for his cardio and work ethic simply ran out of steam. Dvalishvili conceded that he knew he was losing the fight after the second round. He said he would take a different approach to Saturday's contest. “I'm not really focused on the takedown. I have a different strategy. I think it's gonna be domination this time, like it was the first time. I have a different game plan, and I can't wait to show everyone, and I can't wait to raise my hand.” Yan said that, regardless of what Dvalishvili brings to the octagon, he will emerge victorious. “He has his own thoughts, his own ideas, his own plan,” he said. “I'm not really interested in what he has to do. I have a plan, and my plan is to come out there and win.” Yan underwent major back surgery in January following his win over Dvalishvili. Sean O'Malley, who knows both fighters well having faced Dvalishvili twice and Yan once, believes Yan has made a mistake by taking the fight and needs more time to recover. “If I am here, I am 100 per cent ready to fight,” Yan snapped when asked for his thoughts. There is no need for either man to raise the stakes. They have already fought twice, shared one victory apiece and spent the best part of three years trading blows and barbs. On Saturday, at Etihad Arena, there will be nowhere left to hide.

title: Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open to celebrate fifth anniversary as 2027 tournament is announced
description: WTA 500 to take place from January 30 to February 6 at Zayed Sports City
content: Preparations are in full swing for the fifth edition of the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open at Zayed Sports City. The tournament will run from January 30 to February 6, 2027, at the International Tennis Centre. Last season, the WTA 500 tournament welcomed more than 60,000 supporters, further cementing its status as an elite event on the international tennis calendar. The 2027 tournament will once again feature 28 singles players and 16 doubles teams competing across eight days, with a $1.2 million prize fund and WTA ranking points on offer. Aref Hamad Al Awani, Secretary General of Abu Dhabi Sports Council, said: “The fifth edition of the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open is another important milestone for Abu Dhabi’s sporting journey. The tournament has grown significantly in just a few years, while its impact reaches beyond the court through its engagement with young players, schools and the wider community. Through these initiatives, we aim to support the development of tennis, strengthen sporting culture and encourage people to make sport a way of life." Homaid Al Shimmari, deputy group CEO, Mubadala Investment Company, said: “The Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open reflects our long-standing commitment to tennis and to creating a positive impact in our community. Beyond bringing the world’s best players to Abu Dhabi , the tournament serves as a platform to inspire young people, encourage greater participation in sport, and bring families and communities together.” Nigel Gupta, tournament director at MARI, the tournament’s organiser, said: “The fifth edition is a significant milestone for the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open, but what is most exciting is how much the tournament has grown in such a short space of time. Seeing over 60,000 in attendance in 2026 was remarkable and a real testament to the appetite for world-class tennis in Abu Dhabi and the kind of fan experience we have tried to build.” Earlier this year, Czech qualifier Sara Bejlek won her first ever WTA Tour title by defeating Ekaterina Alexandrova in the 2026 Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open final. For the 2027 edition, the tournament will introduce a new Village pass, giving fans of all ages access to the 15,000-sqm Mubadala Village. A programme of live entertainment, tennis clinics, player Q&As, food and beverage, sponsor activations, children's activities and merchandise will be on offer for both Village pass and Stadium ticket holders. On January 30-31, the Village pass will also include access to all qualifying matches taking place across both days. Adult Village passes will be available for Dh10 per day, while children under the age of 12 can attend free of charge throughout the opening weekend. The event has also made its mark on the wider sporting landscape, becoming the first WTA-only event to stage a wheelchair tennis tournament and reinforcing its commitment to inclusion and growing opportunities to engage with the sport. Attendees will require a valid ticket for entry and/or participation in the Mubadala Village activities. For ticket information, visit www.mubadalaabudhabiopen.com.

title: Oil tops $110 as Houthi drone strike near Saudi Shaybah field rattles markets
description: Attacks on the kingdom's energy infrastructure and airports raise supply risks as key crude export routes remain under pressure
content: Oil extended gains above $110 a barrel on Thursday after a Houthi drone attack near Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield heightened concerns over supply disruptions as Yemen's rebels stepped up strikes on the kingdom's energy infrastructure. Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent, or $1.81, to $110.63 a barrel as of 7.36am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate gained 1.4 per cent, or $1.37, to $98.52. Two people were killed and two injured on Wednesday when debris from a drone intercepted by Saudi air defences fell near a processing plant at Shaybah, one of the kingdom's largest oilfields. The drone targeted the plant, but its debris struck a contractor's vehicle outside and caused a fire, the Saudi Energy Ministry said. Operations were unaffected. Shaybah, deep in the Empty Quarter near the UAE border, produces about one million barrels of crude a day. The strike came hours before another attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one person and injured eight, according to Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority. The Houthis have not commented on the airport attack. The latest strikes follow an attack on Riyadh's main international airport earlier this month, the deadliest on the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline , a critical alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, has also come under attack. Crude flows were reportedly halted on October 5 after a Houthi strike damaged a pumping station east of Riyadh. The pipeline, which has a capacity of about seven million barrels a day, carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oilfields to Red Sea export terminals, allowing shipments to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Washington has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure. The widening campaign is adding to the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices as attacks threaten Saudi production facilities and alternative export routes already strained by the Iran war.

title: Ballon d'Or 2026 predictions: Who will be crowned the world's best footballer?
description: Awards to be given out in London on Monday – here's who we think will win each category
content: All eyes will turn to London on Monday evening when the 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be announced. Paris Saint-Germain attacker Ousmanne Dembele took the honours last year with the Frenchman finishing ahead of Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, who was second, and third-placed Vitinha, also of Uefa Champions League winners PSG. The women's prize was claimed by Barcelona's Aitana Bonmati for the third year running, with other award winners including Yamal in the men's under-21 section and England's Sarina Wiegman as best women's coach. Below, we give our predictions about who will be walking away from the 2026 ceremony at the London Palladium with a prize. 1) Harry Kane (Bayern Munich and England): The stage is surely set for the Three Lions captain to lift the prize on home turf. And what better timing for Kane to become the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001. He smashed a remarkable 61 goals in 51 games last season as the 33-year-old striker spearheaded Bayern Munich to the domestic double, while also scoring six times at the Fifa World Cup, helping England finish in third place. 2) Lamine Yamal (Barcelona and Spain): Could be runner-up for the second year running is only a matter of timer of time before Yamal takes first prize. The 19-year-old provided 24 goals and 18 assists in 45 Barca matches as the Catalan side retained the La Liga title . Helped Spain become world champions but a pre-tournament injury seemed to hinder his impact as he registered only one goal and one assist in North America. 3) Kylian Mbappe (Real Madrid and France): For Los Blancos, the 27-year-old striker ended last season with 42 goals in 44 appearances, securing the Spanish Golden Boot award for a second consecutive campaign. For Les Bleus, Mbappe also won the World Cup Golden Boot award with 10 goals and became the all-time tournament top-scorer with 22 goals, overtaking Lionel Messi. But neither Real nor France won a trophy, most likely scuppering his Ballon d'Or chances. 1) Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses and Spain): In what was her final season in Spain before moving to London, two-time Ballon d’Or winner Putellas helped Barcelona power to a stunning quadruple with 26 goals and 15 assists. Spain also retained the Uefa Nations League title last October, while the 32-year-old also scored twice as La Roja hammered England 4-0 to seal World Cup qualification. Ballon d’Or hat-trick should be safely in the bag. 2) Ewa Pajor (Barcelona and Poland): Pajor should seal a Barca one-two after scoring 33 goals and assisting a further seven to her club's quadruple cause. The 29-year-old top-scored in the Champions League with 11, while her 16 Liga F goals was only bettered by teammate Claudia Pina's 21. Pajor also ended her miserable run of five Champions League final defeats in a row as she scored twice in the 4-0 final win over OL Lyonnes. 3) Khadija Shaw (Manchester City and Jamaica): A stunning season in front of goal for City as her 21 goals in 22 games helped her club secure the league and FA Cup double. The 29-year-old dominated the individual awards, winning a third consecutive Women’s Super League Golden Boot as well as the PFA and FWA Player of the Year awards. Shaw also scored nine goals in this year’s Concacaf Women’s Championship qualification, helping her country reach the finals. 1) Lamine Yamal (Barcelona and Spain): For second year running, winger Yamal might have to make do with the consolation of winning the best young player prize. 2) Pau Cubarsi (Barcelona and Spain): A rock at centre-back for club and country. The 19-year-old played 48 games across all competitions as Barca claimed another La Liga title, then played every minute of every match as Spain lifted the World Cup, earning the tournament's best young player award. 3) Warren Zaire-Emery (PSG and France): The 20-year-old midfielder played a key role in PSG retaining their Champions League crown, while making 54 appearances across all competitions as the French side secured four trophies. Only a World Cup spent warming the bench and playing just 109 minutes can take a little shine off an impressive campaign. 1) Vicky Lopez (Barcelona and Spain): The winner of last year's inaugural award for women is favourite to triumph again this time round. The 20-year-old attacker contributed 17 goals and 15 assists in 53 matches as Barca lifted four trophies. She earned her first senior title when Spain won the Nations League. 2) Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes and United States): An excellent first season in France, after moving from Dutch side Ajax, saw the 19-year-old contribute six goals and 10 assists in 48 appearances playing in midfield as OL Lyonnes won the treble and reached the Champions League final. 3) Clara Serrajordi (Barcelona and Spain): Has established herself in the Barca midfield at the age of just 18, making 48 appearances in the quadruple-winning campaign, and already has four senior Spanish caps. 1) David Raya (Arsenal and Spain): A magnificent season for Arsenal which saw him win a third consecutive Golden Glove for keeping 19 clean sheets in 37 Premier League games, helping the Gunners end their title drought . Also produced nine clean sheets in 14 Champions League games as Arsenal finished runners-up to PSG. The 31-year-old just beats Spanish teammate Simon for the top prize. 2) Unai Simon (Athletic Club and Spain): Preferred between the sticks by Spain manager Luis de la Fuente ahead of Raya, Simon proved it was a good call by winning the World Cup Golden Glove award after keeping seven clean sheets and conceding just one goal in eight matches, as La Roja beat Argentina in the final. The 29-year-old also started 37 out of 38 La Liga games for his club, keeping six clean sheets. 3) Joan Garcia (Barcelona and Spain): Completes a Spanish clean sweep of the top three after a stellar season for Barca, where he kept 15 clean sheets in 30 La Liga appearances, conceding only 21. The 25-year-old earned the Zamora Trophy for having the lowest goals-to-games ratio in the Spanish top-flight in what was his first season at the club following his move from Espanyol. 1) Cata Coll (Barcelona and Spain) Barcelona and Spain's domination of the women's awards goes on. Coll kept 23 clean sheets in 39 matches for club and country, with the 25-year-old conceding just 18 goals. 2) Ayaka Yamashita (Manchester City and Japan): Earned the domestic double with City, keeping eight clean sheets across 20 matches. The 31-year-old was also named best goalkeeperthe Asian Cup, which Japan won after beating Australia in the finalinal. 3) Lorena (Kansas City Current and Brazil): Enjoyed a remarkable debut season in the NWSL which saw her set a league record for not conceding a goal in 900 minutes. The 29-year-old set another league record by keeping 14 clean sheets in 24 games, helping Kansas win the NWSL Shield. 1) Luis Enrique (Paris Saint-Germain): The Spaniard has guided PSG to a second consecutive Champions League crown and five trophies in all and will retain his coach of the year crown. PSG look on course to become only the fourth club to win three or more consecutive European Cups. 2) Luis de la Fuente (Spain): Spain produced a devastating performance on the way to lifting the World Cup for a second time, with De la Fuente's side winning seven out of eight matches, drawing the other. Spain are now a record 42 games unbeaten and are the reigning European and world champions. 3) Vincent Kompany (Bayern Munich): Belgian led Bayern to a domestic double and the Champions League semi-finals. Followed that up by winning the German Super Cup in August. 1) Pere Romeu (Barcelona): The 32-year-old Spaniard masterminded Barca's domination of the women's game in Europe. Lost just once across all competitions last season. 2) Jonatan Giraldez (OL Lyonnes): Another Spaniard who achieved great things, leading Lyon to the Premiere Ligue title without losing a single game. But were swept aside in the Champions League final by Barca. 3) Andree Jeglertz (Manchester City): Swede's first season in charge saw City win their first WSL title in a decade while also thrashing Brighton in the FA Cup final.

title: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed begins official visit to Greece
description: Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi greeted on arrival in Athens by Minister of Foreign Affairs
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed , Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, has begun an official visit to Greece primed to further bolster growing ties between the nations. Sheikh Khaled was greeted on arrival at Athens International Airport by George Gerapetritis, the Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs, state news agency Wam reported early on Thursday. Sheikh Khaled's visit comes at the invitation of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis , with whom he is expected to hold key talks during the trip. The visit holds particular significance as the two allies mark 50 years since diplomatic ties were formally established. UAE-Greece relations have expanded greatly in the decades since, underpinned by a comprehensive strategic partnership encompassing vital sectors such as the economy, investment, energy and technology. President Sheikh Mohamed has held a series of phone calls with Mr Mitsotakis this year in a further demonstration of the flourishing friendship between the countries. In May, Sheikh Mohamed hosted Mr Mitsotakis for high-level talks in Abu Dhabi, centred on co-operation across the economic, investment, technology, artificial intelligence, renewable energy, sustainability, infrastructure and cultural sectors. Sheikh Khaled is accompanied by a high-level delegation, which includes Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc, Reem Al Hashimy, Minister of State for International Co-operation, Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi, Minister of Foreign Trade, and Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment.

title: Give people who stutter the time to be heard
description: We should make classrooms and workplaces more inclusive for those who have this condition
content: When I was in Grade 7, I raised my hand and volunteered to read aloud in class. After a few words, I began to stutter. My teacher stopped me and told me to raise my hand again when I could “speak properly”. I still remember those words. I had done what children are encouraged to do: participate. I knew how to read. I knew the words. But in a few seconds, I learnt something about participation: I could speak up, but only if my words came out the “right way”. For a child who stutters, experiences like these can influence whether they raise their hand the next time, volunteer to speak, ask a question, or decide that staying quiet feels safer. Although the classroom may change, the assumption can remain. About one in 100 adults stutter, across languages and dialects. Up to one in 10 children experience stuttering at some point during childhood. Fluency is often mistaken for confidence. A quick answer can seem more prepared. A smooth presentation can appear more persuasive. A block, that is when a word gets stuck and no sound comes out, can be mistaken for nervousness. However, stuttering is not caused by anxiety. Research points to differences in how the brain produces speech , and it often runs in families. A pause does not mean someone does not know the answer. A repetition does not mean they are unprepared. Taking longer to say something does not make the thought behind it any less valuable. Yet many people who stutter learn to manage other people’s reactions to their speech. That can mean changing a word before anyone notices it is difficult to say, avoiding a phone call, rehearsing an introduction repeatedly, or staying quiet in a meeting because finding the right moment to enter the conversation feels harder than letting the idea go. These behaviors are often invisible. The listener may never know how much planning went into a sentence before it was spoken, or how many sentences were never spoken at all. This is where it becomes important to separate fluency from competence. Nowhere is that distinction more consequential than in the places where participation shapes opportunity: schools, recruitment and the workplace. Consider a typical job interview. An interviewer may unconsciously interpret hesitation as a lack of preparation or favour the candidate who responds quickly and smoothly. But what is the interview actually trying to measure? Is it the candidate’s knowledge, judgment, experience and ability to do the job? Or is it how fluently they can deliver an answer under pressure? Sometimes the changes needed are remarkably small. Give someone time to finish. Do not complete their sentence unless they ask you to. When someone takes longer to speak, resist filling the pause simply because the silence feels uncomfortable. At home, the same patience matters: listen to what a child says, not how smoothly they say it. But individual behaviour is only part of the answer. Inclusion should not depend on whether a child happens to have an understanding teacher or an employee happens to have an considerate manager. We can build better defaults into the places where people speak. In Abu Dhabi, Department of Education and Knowledge policies already provide a framework for supporting students with additional learning needs and providing assessment accommodations. The next step is for schools to make sure stuttering is understood within that framework, including when children are reading aloud, giving presentations or participating in class. Teachers should give advance notice before oral work, ask what helps and provide appropriate flexibility. The goal should not be to remove speaking opportunities, but to make sure participation does not become a test of fluency. Recruitment processes deserve the same scrutiny. Employers should build flexibility into recruitment from the start. Interview invitations should make clear what options are available, such as sufficient time to answer, the opportunity to supplement an answer in writing, or alternatives to phone-only screening where spontaneous speech is not essential to the role. Crucially, the process should build in basic flexibility rather than making it available only after someone discloses a stutter. Job descriptions also matter. Employers should define communication according to what a role genuinely requires, rather than using terms such as “articulate” as shorthand for ability. In addition, inclusion should continue once someone is hired. Meetings should not reward the fastest speaker only. Sharing agendas in advance, limiting interruptions, providing more than one way to contribute and helping managers understand that a block is not a sign of nervousness are simple changes that can benefit far more people than those who stutter. None of this lowers standards – it makes them clearer. Assess knowledge when knowledge is what matters. Assess ideas when ideas are what matter. Assess fluency only when fluency is genuinely relevant. This is not special treatment, it is better design. For more than a decade, The Stutter Community has created spaces where people with speech impediments can connect and speak without first proving they can articulate fluently. Yet most of life happens outside those spaces, in classrooms, interviews and offices. That is why our work also extends into schools and workplaces, helping those environments become more inclusive. When I think back to that classroom, what I needed was simple: I needed time to finish. In that spirit, inclusion begins not by asking people who stutter to sound more like everyone else, but by creating classrooms, recruitment processes and workplaces where different ways of speaking have the same opportunity to be heard. A moment costs the listener nothing. For someone who stutters, it can be the difference between speaking and staying silent. Give us one.

title: US pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia but denies wider Gulf withdrawal
description: Oil surges after attack on Dammam airport and fears of new escalation
content: The US has ordered non-essential employees and their families out of Saudi Arabia over a surge in Houthi attacks. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott announced the order in a post on X. It covers “non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”, he said. He denied the move was extended to US diplomatic families in the wider region. That was in response to wire agencies claiming diplomatic relatives in UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain were to leave. Saudi Arabia ’s civil aviation authority reported an attack late on Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. One person was killed and eight were injured, it said. Earlier on Wednesday, two people died when air defences intercepted a drone aimed at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield, the Energy Ministry said. Oil advanced on news of the airport attack. Brent climbed above $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate traded at about $98. Mr Pigott said the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen had “increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia”, including strikes on civilian airports that caused deaths and “severe travel disruptions”. The General Authority of Civil Aviation said the airport had been attacked. Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reported that operations at the airport had been halted since about 11.15pm local time. Mr Pigott called reports of a Gulf-wide order “inaccurate”. But four US officials told Reuters that missions in other Gulf states would also order family members to depart. A diplomatic source told AFP that families in the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain had been told to leave. The US mission in the UAE warned on Sunday that the hostilities “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area”. The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday warning of possible further Houthi attacks. It followed recent deadly strikes, including one on Riyadh’s airport, according to the report. Washington had sent some diplomatic staff back to the region in recent months. Many were pulled out after Iran attacked US sites when the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, including the Riyadh embassy and a CIA station in the Saudi capital. The latest departures follow an escalation of fighting in Yemen. That has opened another front in a regional conflict that has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies.

title: From borrower to lender: How Louvre Abu Dhabi is sharing its masterpieces with the world
description: New book Birth of a Collection reveals how museum built its permanent collection over the past decade
content: More than five centuries ago, the workshops of Mamluk Cairo produced an elaborate wool carpet decorated with three medallions. Prized across the Mediterranean, such carpets were coveted by Europe's wealthy and powerful, commissioned by popes and exchanged as diplomatic gifts. The rare carpet, now part of Louvre Abu Dhabi 's permanent collection, returned to Europe last year to be displayed at the Louvre in Paris in a major exhibition examining the Mamluk dynasty and its artistic legacy. The loan may seem like a routine exchange between museums , but it reflects how far Louvre Abu Dhabi has come since opening in 2017, when many of the artworks in its galleries were borrowed from international institutions and collectors. “We were originally a borrowing institution, but we are moving towards a lending institution as well,” Guilhem Andre tells The National . “Since the opening, we've lent many of our masterpieces abroad.” Andre, who joined Louvre Abu Dhabi project in 2012 and helped to build its collection and Asian art programme, is now the museum's director of scientific, curatorial and collections management. As editor of Birth of a Collection , an elegant coffee table book documenting much of the work he has witnessed and helped to oversee, Andre brings together contributions from 42 scholars, curators and historians who examine 240 objects, from ancient artefacts to modern and contemporary artworks. The book is available online and select bookstores in English, Arabic and French. But the artworks seen at Louvre Abu Dhabi tell only part of the story. Andre recalls how the museum began lending works even before the building opened in 2017, with that activity expanding considerably in recent years. Since opening, it has lent 42 works to exhibitions in the UAE, the Gulf and internationally, including at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, Musee d'Orsay in Paris and the Galleria Borghese in Rome. Outgoing loans have more than tripled since 2021, he adds. Meanwhile, visitors to Louvre Abu Dhabi are also seeing more works that belong to the museum itself. Andre says that when it opened, approximately 30 per cent of the artworks in its permanent galleries came from its own collection. By 2021, owned works outnumbered loans for the first time, with their share reaching 56.8 per cent in 2025. The collection has expanded from around 600 works at opening to more than 6,000 today, including those held in storage or conservation rather than displayed. The growth is documented in Birth of a Collection , a successor to Birth of a Museum , published in 2013 to introduce the founding collection and plans for a universal museum in the Arab world. The new book arrives nine years after Louvre Abu Dhabi opened, with a much larger collection to examine and a decade of curatorial work to draw upon. “The more you move forward, the more you notice that you have gaps, in fact. So that's an unending process, collecting,” Andre says. “Private collector know this as well. But as a museum, of course, we are acting at a very high level, and it's slightly different because we focus on masterpieces at Louvre Abu Dhabi. That's why the book is so important, because it shows the process of collecting.” Some of those gaps have been addressed through acquisitions of Asian, African and Oceanian art , which Andre says were underrepresented in the museum's earlier holdings. He stresses, however, that the museum's ambitions go beyond expanding its holdings. “We are not there to unfold in our galleries endless lists and piles of artworks. We are there to feature the cross-cultural relations, to show the artistic production across time during more than 10,000 years of history .” Among the acquisitions noted in the book is an ornate ivory casket made around 1543 in the Kingdom of Kotte, in what is now Sri Lanka. Decorated with gold, rubies and sapphires, it belongs to a small group of objects sent by the rulers of Kotte to the Portuguese royal court as diplomatic gifts. Acquired by Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2024, the casket is an example of the interesting stories Andre wants the museum's collection to tell, with galleries bringing together artworks from different civilisations to examine artistic and cultural connections that might otherwise be overlooked. “Of course, you could think about collecting everything when you see the word universal museum. In fact, it's very different because we have a specific mandate of featuring the diversity, the cross-cultural relationships across time, the encounters,” he says. “We not only focus on the artworks themselves, but on the relationship between them, because we put them in dialogue. So this is also the immaterial relationship between them.” Looking ahead, Andre is already imagining what a follow-up to Birth of a Collection might reveal in another decade. “We have to dream that one day we can present our permanent galleries entirely through our own collection, allowing the museum to achieve full autonomy,” he adds. “And not only that, but also to lend more of our masterpieces to museums internationally and share our story with audiences abroad.”

title: Abu Dhabi Finance Week to make half of 2026 sessions private to drive deals
description: New format aims to connect senior leaders to encourage candid dialogue and advance business opportunities
content: Abu Dhabi Finance Week will hold about half of its sessions behind closed doors this year, as organisers seek to encourage more candid discussions among global financial leaders and generate tangible business outcomes. The event to be held from December 7 to 10 is expected to draw more than 40,000 attendees, including 8,000 senior executives, with financial leaders representing about $70 trillion in assets under management. Chris Hughes, editor-in-chief of ADFW, said private meetings enable senior executives to exchange information more openly than on public stages, potentially influencing investment decisions and corporate strategies. "I find that when they are in the private rooms there's a little bit more openness, a little bit more dialogue," he told ADGM's Global Media Forum on Tuesday. "It's not just monologue, it's dialogue," he added, which is physically represented by attendees and speakers alike being seated face-to-face rather than shoulder-to-shoulder. The shift towards invitation-only discussions, he said, reflects growing demand among executives for meetings that deliver practical outcomes rather than simply provide networking opportunities or public exposure. ADFW recorded 82 memorandums of understanding and partnerships in 2025, according to the organiser, Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM, which was almost double the 44 agreements and announcements in 2024. The agreements involved major financial institutions and businesses including BlackRock, Franklin Templeton, Mubadala, Mastercard and Swiss Re. While the figures demonstrate the event's growing role as a platform for forging partnerships, ADGM has not disclosed how many resulted directly from private meetings or their combined monetary value. Private meetings could allow investors, regulators and executives to discuss commercially sensitive issues, identify investment opportunities and advance potential transactions without the scrutiny of a public audience. Mr Hughes referred to a closed-door leadership meeting involving the International Monetary Fund during last year's ADFW, attended by chief executives of major financial institutions. He recalled watching senior executives take handwritten notes throughout the discussions, which suggested that information exchanged in such settings could influence decisions within large organisations that aren't directly seen, but have major implications. "That extra grain of information they didn't usually have, that can change the economy of... a city or town, or company, or country, just by a tiny little 0.1 degree." The growing emphasis on private engagement comes as Abu Dhabi attracts more international financial institutions. Fourteen global financial firms managing more than $5 trillion announced plans to establish a presence in ADGM during the first half of this year, according to figures disclosed by ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi this week. ADFW is also expected to host more than 80 events and 400 content sessions this year, compared with more than 70 events and 350 sessions in 2025, according to organisers' projections. The preparations come amid regional uncertainty as the Iran war continues to disrupt business activity, energy markets and travel across the Middle East. Saudi Arabia this week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26 to 29 in Riyadh, until 2027, after a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The attacks, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, have raised security concerns among international executives and investors. Asked about contingency plans for ADFW amid the regional tension, Mr Hughes expressed confidence in Abu Dhabi's security and preparations to welcome international delegates in December.

title: Bruno Fernandes turns on Michael Carrick as Manchester United crisis deepens
description: Captain criticises tactics after 4-1 thrashing in Como leaves boss fighting for his future
content: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes publicly criticised head coach Michael Carrick's tactics after their 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como. The humiliating defeat has left Carrick fighting for his future after a run of seven games without a win in all competitions. He apologised to the 700 travelling fans and ignored his beaten players after the final whistle in scenes reminiscent of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in 2021, which preceded his dismissal 24 hours later. Fernandes, who has made a poor start to the season and performed badly in Italy, took aim at Carrick's setup after Wednesday's game. “It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence,” he said. Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: “That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.” Carrick offered a rebuke when told of the comment, as he said: “There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win.” Fernandes's comments come just weeks after defender Lisandro Martinez laid into the club's board over a lack of investment in the squad. Elsewhere, Declan Rice rescued Arsenal with a late equaliser in an ⁠electric 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich. Arsenal's ​evening in Germany began ominously when Bukayo Saka limped out of the contest in the 10th minute, clutching his knee after falling while attempting a pass. Fifteen minutes later, ⁠however, Eberechi Eze raced on to Martin Odegaard's long ball and fired an angled shot past Manuel Neuer. Initially flagged offside, the goal was awarded following a VAR review. Bayern replied in the 35th minute when Harry Kane released Alphonso Davies down the left with a through ball from halfway, the Canadian breaking clear before beating David Raya with a ⁠composed right-footed finish. Kane put the hosts ahead from the penalty spot in the 61st minute after his shot struck Jurrien Timber's raised hand, blasting his 58th ​Champions League ⁠goal into the roof of the net. But Rice had ‌the final say eight minutes from time, exchanging passes with Viktor Gyokeres inside the box before slotting past Neuer. At the Santiago Bernabeu, Real's emphatic ​4-1 scoreline owed much to goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who denied Romulo's close-range volley and thwarted Christopher Nkunku one-on-one before the hosts found their rhythm. Bernardo Silva broke the deadlock in the 43rd minute, pouncing to tap home almost on the goalline after Leipzig goalkeeper Maarten Vandevoordt spilt Federico Valverde's shot. Arda Guler doubled the lead seven minutes after halftime, beating a defender to Kylian Mbappe's goalbound header from Jude Bellingham's cross. Mbappe curled a shot into the top corner in the 83rd minute before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back a minute later. Substitute Yan Diomande capped Real's victory with a spectacular volley from Brahim Diaz's cross. Elsewhere, Galatasaray won 4-2 at Lille, Inter Milan edged Shakhtar Donetsk 1-0, Aston Villa beat Viking Stavanger 3-1 and Real Betis beat Feyenoord 1-0, while LASK stunned Sporting 3-2 in Lisbon.

title: Como v Manchester United player ratings: Who got a three on disastrous night for Michael Carrick?
description: Italian side produce superb performance to win 4-0 and pile pressure on Red Devils manager
content: Serie A side Como secured the biggest result in their history when they thrashed Manchester United 4-1 in the Uefa Champions League on Wednesday night. Cesc Fabregas's side , who are playing in the tournament for the first time, produced a sensational performance, dominating the three-time European champions from start to finish. Argentine attacker Nico Paz scored two and assisted another in a man-of-the-match performance, with the other goals coming from Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon. Substitute Joshua Zirkzee grabbed United's late consolation. It was a dismal night for United manager Michael Carrick who is now under intense pressure after going seven matches without victory – their worst run since 2015 – as his side became the first English team to concede in the first two minutes of consecutive major European games. Como are now on six points, having won two and lost one of their opening three Champions League matches. United are on three points and have not tasted victory in any competition since beating Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on September 10. Como boss Cesc Fabregas: “It's a special night, but we are still at the beginning for everything we have in our minds. The team played well this evening, but we need to keep our feet on the ground and remember there is another match coming up on Saturday.” Man United captain Bruno Fernandes: “It's not the first time, we started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early. Not much pressure on the ball, not many good movements with the ball, not many things going our way. “Conceding early makes us go into game with a mood of defeat, it's difficult to get out of that, trying to be brave, to have the ball and make something happen. If we are not able to do that, it is going to be very difficult to get out of this situation. “It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.” Jean Butez – 7/10: Not much to do in first half as United failed to register shot on target. First save came in 65th minute when he tipped Diallo shot over bar. Missed out on clean sheet when Zirkzee beat offside trap to score late on. Yan Couto – 8/10: Brazilian full-back was full of energy up and down right after being rested for weekend win at Fiorentina. Lovely pass through to set-up first-half chance for Douvikas.
