Marc-Oliver Kempf – 8/10: Como's defence was so cool in and out of possession at the back with the German a key part of that. Late booking for foul on edge of box on Diallo. Jacobo Ramon – 8/10: Spanish under-21 defender headed home Como's fourth goal. Fantastic in defence as Como kept United's attack very quiet. Alex Valle – 8/10: Like Yan Couto on other flank, left back Valle was excellent defensively and always looked to push forward and help Como attack. Luis Milla – 8/10: United had no answer to Como's midfield dominance with the 32-year-old Spaniard superb at Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia. Fabregas has his team so well drilled from front to back. Maximo Perrone – 8/10: Helped home side dominate possession in middle of park alongside Milla with slick, intricate passing. A masterclass performance from the boys in blue, albeit against woefully passive opponent. Lucas Da Cunha – 8/10: The captain earned an assist for first goal after cutting inside from right and playing ball into Paz's feet. Involved in build-up for second goal. Almost made it 3-0 but sent shot wide. Nico Paz – 9/10: Young Argentine curled home his first Champions League goal from Como's first attack in some style. Supplied perfectly weighted pass to set up second goal. Took advantage of Baleba error and open defence to finish superbly and make it 3-0. Came close to a hat-trick on several occasions. Martin Baturina – 8/10: One lovely flash of skill early on when he flicked the ball through legs of Dalot on the turn. Croatian midfielder hit shot straight at keeper just before break. Another who was involved in slick move ahead of Douvikas goal. Tasos Douvikas – 8/10: Saw his first effort, a low shot in the 35th minute, saved at near post. Should have scored a few minutes later but sliced wild effort over bar. Did score straight after break with clinical finish following slick Como move Maxence Caqueret (on for Baturina, 64') – 7/10: First touch in penalty area let him down or Como might have been on for another goal. Kaiki Bruno (on for Da Cunha, 69') – 7/10: Supplied perfect cross for Como's fourth goal from Ramon. Samuele Ricci (on for Paz, 80') – N/A . Ivan Smolcic (on for Yan Couto, 80') – N/A . Senne Lammens – 5/10: Just three minutes before Como went ahead through Paz’s excellent finish, Lammens stretched but couldn’t reach the ball. He saved from Douvikas on 35 minutes and Baturina on 42 minutes, although the latter was offside. Three minutes into the second half, he conceded a second to Douvikas, followed by Paz’s second on 56 minutes. Como scored a fourth, but Lammens was not at fault for any of the goals. Diogo Dalot – 4/10: Back at right back and fired wide in the first minute. Switched to left back for the second half for no discernible reason. Poor, like the rest of them. Matthijs De Ligt – 5/10: First start since last November – and how he was needed with all the other injuries. Extended a leg to turn away an 11 th minute attack. A fragment of positivity on a wretched night that he’s back, but he couldn’t have expected to be up to speed. And he wasn’t. Harry Maguire – 4/10: Couldn’t close down Paz for the first. Headed wide on 18, then made a diving challenge at the other end which saw some appeals for a penalty. It wasn’t. Noussair Mazraoui – 3/10: Left back at the start and stretched by a team who kept the ball well and passed patiently left to right. It was the worst combination for United, who couldn’t contain their extreme possession and diagonal balls. The Moroccan was too slow on the ball. Andrey Santos – 3/10: Booked on 22 after catching Paz, who’d easily bested him on a night where United found little peace. Off at half-time. Poor performance from the Brazilian. Mason Mount – 4/10: Left side of United’s attack and picked up ball in tight areas. Dropped back more in second half, shot well over on 50. It’s hard to come into a game like this against such a good team and playing for a team with so many injuries and have a positive outcome. Youri Tielemans – 4/10: Played behind Fernandes in the middle, but United have struggled to press all season and struggled in Como. Linked with Mbeumo a couple of times on a desperate night for United. Bruno Fernandes – 3/10: Tried to thread tricky balls to Mbeumo, whom he alternated with. Shot miles over, like every other United effort on goal. Smart ball towards Amad on 65. Subbed off early. Said after it was the decision of the staff not to press man to man and leave space behind, which Como exploited. Dire season for United’s best player. Matheus Cunha – 4/10: Started where he prefers on the left. Good early header from a Lammens ball, but nobody around him to get it. Turned and shot well over on 44. Off at half-time. Bryan Mbeumo – 4/10: Drove down the right, shot well over on 78 – as was the norm from his teammates. Not a good night. He had a couple of half chances, but it was an awful night for United. Carlos Baleba (on for Santos, 46') – 4/10: I mmediately into the fray, but lost the ball to Paz who ran forward and scored the third. Amad Diallo (on for Cunha, 46') – 5/10: Made a lovely run into the box on 63 and shot pushed over two minutes later, but it was all too late. United were 3-0 down. His free-kick on target on 86 and crossed for Zirkzee to score a consolation on 90. Joshua Zirkzee (on for Fernandes, 66') – 5/10: A bit of pace, a bit of energy, but the damage was done. Still, he scored after bringing the ball down beautifully, which is something United had failed to do. Harry Amas (on for De Ligt, 79') – N/A: Another youngster who should be enjoying Champions League minutes. Shea Lacey (on for Mbeumo, 85') – N/A: Deserves minutes, it’s such a shame he had to be introduced in these circumstances.

title: Two UAE scientists recognised in programme to support female researchers
description: L’Oreal-Unesco scheme has recognised 25 women in the UAE since its 2014 launch
content: A programme to support women scientists in the Arab world has selected two female researchers in the UAE for grants. The L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme has awarded Dr Marieh Al Handawi, of New York University Abu Dhabi , and Jawaher Al Hammadi, of Khalifa University, for its 2026 iteration. They are among half a dozen female researchers in the Arab world, working in fields including pandemic preparedness, water security and personalised medicine, recognised in this round of the scheme. Ms Al Hammadi, an Emirati PhD student from Sharjah who grew up in Abu Dhabi, works on lab-based models of cell membranes. She told The National that recognition from the programme provided “a valuable opportunity to increase the visibility of my research”, forge connections with researchers internationally and potentially create collaborations. “I think these opportunities are incredibly important especially for young researchers, because science thrives when we exchange knowledge and learn from one another,” she said. Her research focuses on developing customisable cell membrane models that could lead to ways to test personalised treatments for patients. “The cell membrane surrounds every cell in our body and plays an essential role in how cells communicate, recognise signals, and respond to their surroundings,” she said. “By recreating these membranes in the laboratory, we can study these interactions in a more controlled environment.” Conventional cell membrane models are often made from synthetic materials, which, Ms Al Hammadi said, meant that they could not fully replicate the complexity of real cell membranes. “To address this, I combine synthetic components with tiny particles derived from cells, known as extracellular vesicles, which carry characteristics of the cells they originate from,” she said. “I then integrate these membranes with electronic sensors that allow us to detect and monitor changes in the membrane through electrical signals. “Ultimately, my goal is to develop a technology that can help researchers better understand diseases and evaluate how cells respond to different treatments.” She said that, with her method, it may be possible to recreate cell membranes that represent specific cell types, diseases or even particular patients. It is, Ms Al Hammadi said, “a very exciting time” to be a woman working in her field in the UAE, adding that the country “places great importance on science, innovation and empowering women”. “Over the years we have seen more women entering Stem [Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics] fields, taking on leadership positions, and making important contributions to scientific research, and that is something I am very proud to witness,” she said. In total, 69 female scientists, including 25 in the UAE, have been supported by the L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme, which was launched in 2014. In total the programme has In total, the programme has awarded Dh4 million to support research in the region. Six women in the Arabian Peninsula have been recognised in the programme’s latest edition. According to Unesco, 41 per cent of scientists in the Arab world are female, behind only Central Asia, where the figure is 50 per cent, and Latin America and the Caribbean, where it is 44 per cent. In East Asia and the Pacific, for example, only 27 per cent of scientists are female, while in sub-Saharan Africa the figure is 32 per cent and in western Europe, 34 per cent. Dr Al Handawi, a Syrian born and raised in the UAE, has been working at NYU Abu Dhabi after completing master’s and doctoral degrees at NYU in New York. She looks at how plants adapt to salty and dry conditions, in the hope this may highlight ways in which people can extract water from their environment. Among the plants she has analysed is the native tree Tamarix aphylla , which lives in salty sabkha habitats. The plant excretes a salt solution that evaporates, forming salt crystals. “These crystals act as magnets, capturing moisture directly from the air, even at relatively low humidity and condensing it on the plant,” she said. “This showed me that desert plants can provide us with natural solutions to the same problems we are trying to solve: how to access and manage water under extremely dry and challenging conditions. “My research explores whether we can use the significant amount of water already present in the UAE’s atmosphere as humidity and extract it with much lower energy requirements.” She said there were many more plants in the region waiting to be studied that “may offer completely different strategies for water harvesting”. Ultimately she would like to establish an independent research programme focused on “bioinspiration” and learning from natural systems, especially those adapted to the Middle East’s harsh environments, and on translating those mechanisms into practical solutions. “I want my research to go beyond discovery and ultimately lead to materials and technologies that can be tested and used to support communities,” she said. Sarah Al Amiri, Minister of Education, said in a statement that in the UAE women were “playing an increasingly prominent role in research” and in fields including advanced technology, health care, sustainability and aerospace. “Our focus is on strengthening the journey from education to research, and from research to real-world impact, so that young people have the skills, confidence, mentorship and opportunities to shape the future,” she said. “The L’Oreal-Unesco For Women in Science Middle East Programme advances this ambition by recognising women researchers, supporting their careers and giving the next generation visible examples of what scientific leadership can achieve.” Other programme recipients are Alaa Al Mushaikeh, a Saudi physicist at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (Kaust), and Qatar University’s Hadeel Zedan, who researches antiviral medications against, for example, coronaviruses. Also awarded were Dr Aljawharah Al Rubayyi, a Syrian scientist at Kaust who works on vaccines and immunotherapies, and Dr Sara Al Araimi, who researches ways to turn waste into water and useful materials at Oman’s University of Technology and Applied Sciences. Laurent Duffier, managing director of L’Oreal Middle East, said the scientific talent emerging across the region was “remarkable”. “Women are increasingly at the heart of that progress,” he said. “Our responsibility is not only to recognise that talent, but to help create the visibility, networks and opportunities that allow it to thrive."
