Reports that dropping the mansion tax threshold from £2m to £1.5m is not going ahead would probably be welcomed by a market seeking certainty, he said. “The £5 million-plus market continues to be most impacted by uncertainty and weaker sentiment, with a higher proportion of discretionary buyers and sellers meaning less urgency to do deals,” he said. Knight Frank’s latest Residence Report highlighted the growing scarcity of larger new build apartments, with fewer than 3 per cent of completed homes across Westminster and Kensington & Chelsea exceeding 200 sq m, making super prime residences rare. One of the luxury properties released on to the market in recent weeks is a £15.5 million, 3,100 square foot, four-bedroom duplex penthouse with a private roof terrace at 100 George Street in Marylebone. Developers Native Land said the 41-residence development was one of the fastest-selling in prime central London. The trophy penthouse has been designed by Eloisa Cuturi of design studio Cuturi Cameto. It includes bespoke furniture and commissioned artwork including paintings by Joanne Yulan inspired by the neighbouring Regent’s Park. Nicholas Gray, executive director at Native Land, said: “Opportunities to acquire a newly built home in Marylebone of this calibre, with this quality of interior design and scale of private outdoor space, are exceptionally limited.” Rupert des Forges, head of prime central London developments at Knight Frank, said: “We are seeing sustained demand from buyers for larger, turnkey homes in prime central London.” A £20 million ($26.4 million) penthouse has also gone on sale at Southbank Place , the final launch of a £1 billion development delivered by Braeburn Estates, a joint venture by Qatari Diar and Canary Wharf Group. The development is on the site of the former Festival of Britain, and has taken more than 10 years to complete.

title: UK orders dozens of official websites offline after flaw warnings
description: BBC and municipalities join rush to protect services from new defect
content: British government official websites were taken down on Thursday as administrators rushed to safeguard against two critical ​security flaws in PHP, ​a programming language that powers a large share of the internet. Baroness Lloyd, parliamentary undersecretary of state at the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, told the House of Lords the decision to protect data was made after the flaws emerged. “The principle impact on government digital services has arisen from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates are applied,” she said. “The government continues to monitor the situation closely and work with departments to maintain the security, resilience and availability of public services.” Government, school and hospital websites across Europe and beyond were taken offline on Wednesday as cybersecurity ⁠agencies across the world warned fixes were needed. Organisations unable to apply fixes in ⁠time were told to consider taking affected sites offline. PHP's developers said a ​set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was available. The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand. "I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, ⁠saying the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex. "It was a long day and a long night, I ​know, for all ⁠the IT and security folks." Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, said the discovery appeared to be the most serious vulnerability detected for five years. Felix Kuhlenkamp, head of security at German digital industry association Bitkom, said that many larger operators had already carried out updates, but that for complex IT systems and smaller organisations it could ​take longer. "They may run a website using PHP but don't really keep a close eye on it," he said. "If a website is based on an old version of PHP for which there is no security update, the entire system must be updated." More than 30 government services in the UK remained offline by Thursday afternoon. The British public service broadcaster BBC said it had taken down some web portals on Wednesday. The broadcaster also reported several municipalities taking down their web services, including the city of Edinburgh. A representative for the German Digital Ministry said on Wednesday the federal IT service provider ITZBund had taken several websites offline due to the discovery of PHP vulnerabilities. The temporary deactivation was purely preventive and no security incidents were known to have occurred, they said. The Interior Ministry said it ⁠had temporarily taken offline the websites of prefectures, which are local government administrative offices, while awaiting a security fix for ​the PHP framework ⁠they use. It said the move was ‌a precaution pending a patch from the framework's publisher. Belgium's Foreign Ministry said it had temporarily taken its websites offline after reports ​of cyber attacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, although the country's cybersecurity centre said it had not recorded any attacks on Belgian websites. Many organisations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and preventively took their public-facing sites offline. They included the Port of Rotterdam, government site Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites of the five largest political parties and numerous hospital websites across the country. State IT centre Valtori shut down the government's public web services on Wednesday as “a precautionary measure”. Valtori said it had not identified any attempt to exploit the flaws and that the services being taken down was not the result of a data breach. The Czech government took its website offline on Wednesday at 7pm (1700 GMT) at the recommendation of the country's cyber watchdog to “allow for the implementation of necessary security patches”. “The measure aims to ensure the secure operation of the website. During the shutdown, the site and its content will not be accessible to the public. Services will be restored once the recommended security updates have been applied,” the government office said. Japan's Ministry of Finance and Meteorological Agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan's National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service. Several Japanese companies, including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway said ​on Thursday they were also temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures. The French telecoms group temporarily suspended access to a number of websites ⁠and applications using the PHP programming language as a precaution. The measure affects websites, services and applications across several subsidiaries and entities.

title: Two Syrian security personnel killed in anti-ISIS raid
description: Five more injured in the clash west of Damascus
content: Two members of Syria’s Internal Security Forces were killed and five others injured during a raid against an ISIS -linked cell near Damascus, authorities said on Thursday. Clashes broke out during the raid in the town of Rankous, in the western countryside of Damascus, resulting in the deaths and injuries, the forces said. The operation was carried out with Syria's General Intelligence Service. ISIS attacks against Syrian government forces have risen sharply in 2026 – from 16 last year to 52 in the first half of this year, the monitor Armed Conflict Location and Event Data said in August. The increase is linked to an anti-ISIS campaign launched by the government, triggered by an attack on US troops in Palmyra in December last year, in which a member of the Syrian security forces opened fire during a joint patrol. Two US soldiers and an interpreter were killed. Attacks have hit checkpoints, patrols and security centres. The Syrian government that took over in late 2024 after the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime has made assurances to world powers that it can keep extremists at bay, despite the militant background of President Ahmad Al Shara and the wider leadership cadre. The Syrian leadership has its origins in the country’s Islamist insurgency. It evolved from Al Nusra front, Al Qaeda’s former affiliate in Syria, to Hayat Tahrir Al Sham (HTS). Mr Al Shara has sought to demonstrate that his government is a reliable security partner, particularly in the fight against ISIS. Syria has been co-operating with a US-led coalition against ISIS, reaching an agreement late last year when Mr Al Shara visited the White House. ISIS used to control large areas of land in Syria and neighbouring Iraq. While the group has been largely territorially defeated, pockets of fighters continue to launch attacks.

title: France brings in police reinforcements as luxury boutique owners brace for new protests
description: Businesses fear more riots this weekend as President Macron tries to improve security
content: Businesses across France were boarding up on Thursday and bracing for more protests as the government promised new security measures to protect them and avoid a repeat of last week's destruction. President Emmanuel Macron, returning from a tour of the Gulf, said he would ban public protests unless they were organised by unions that respected alternative routes avoiding city centres. “The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days,” Mr Macron said after a meeting with intelligence services at the Elysee Palace in Paris. Protests organised by those with “no legitimacy” will be outlawed because “we want a return to calm”, the President said. There had been “failures to anticipate” the violence of last week's protests, he added, and the government is now working on making sure city centres stay safe over the coming weekend despite the expectation that further protests will take place. “The goal is to ensure calm, to protect businesses and to safeguard public buildings,” Mr Macron said. Far-left groups aiming to provoke the “fall of the Republic” were behind last week's violence, the President said, as he condemned what he called “acts of delinquency”. “I can assure the French people listening to us that … everything is being done to ensure that what we experienced last Saturday cannot happen again next Saturday,” government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon said, speaking shortly after Mr Macron. The number of police officers on the streets will be 20 per cent higher than last weekend, according to Jean-Didier Berger, minister delegate to the Minister of the Interior. Protests are planned for Paris on Saturday. “We have cancelled some vacations. We have called back people who were supposed to be on vacation but will not be,” he told BFMTV. He said officers had been given permission to use weapons such as stun grenades, which had been questioned after a teenager lost his hand while picking one up during a previous demonstration. Businesses in Paris were urged by the police chief, Patrice Faure, to increase their own security by hiring private guards, potentially with dog units, and use alarm systems. Rallies are planned for Thursday in several cities including Lille. Across Paris’s shopping districts, luxury boutiques bear the scars of a weekend of rioting that filled social media feeds around the world. Now they are bracing for the possibility of another round. On the Champs-Elysees , Louis Vuitton’s flagship store now has metallic grates protecting its window, as does the Christian Dior Couture emporium on Avenue Montaigne, a nexus of high-end shopping in Paris’s eighth arrondissement. Both stores escaped serious damage last weekend, even as shops elsewhere were less fortunate. Windows and doors are boarded up along the Rue Saint-Honore, not far from France’s presidential palace. Mobs on Saturday broke into and looted shops along the street, including those of Burberry, Christian Dior perfumes and Guerlain. Those three boutiques have remained closed, as has a Salomon sportswear store on the nearby Boulevard de la Madeleine that was similarly ravaged. The Hermes boutique on Avenue George V, close to the Champs-Elysees, suffered broken windows. The brand’s store in Marseille fared far worse, and “won’t reopen any time soon”, after being ransacked by rioters, chief financial officer Eric du Halgouet said on Thursday. Hermes has beefed up its security measures, he said. The violence followed protests last Saturday that drew more than half a million people across France. As night fell, roving bands of hooded and masked rioters hit hundreds of shops, smashing windows, destroying equipment and running off with merchandise. The turmoil abated after curfews and transport restrictions were imposed on Monday, but the protesters’ call for another day of unrest this Saturday has residents, authorities and shopkeepers on edge. The brazen attacks and ineffectual police response prompted an outcry from retailers, among others, and led to a profit warning from Carrefour SA, one of the country’s largest grocers. About 50 of its stores were hit on the first day of rioting, with many looted and damaged, chief executive Alexandre Bompard told financial analysts on Tuesday. The unrest is hurting consumer confidence, dissuading shoppers and driving up costs for security and logistics, Mr Bompard said. Carrefour expects a hit to profitability of as much as €200 million ($225 million). Laurent Milchior, who heads lingerie brand Etam, told BFM Business that the destruction at the weekend represented €1 million in lost sales and another €500,000 from stolen goods and damage to its outlets. “If it’s a one-off, it’ll work out, but the issue is if it lasts,” he said, referring to repeated days of protests that degenerate into violence. Mr Milchior called on President Macron to mobilise the army to deal with the incidents, saying anti-riot police and other forces were outmatched. Thierry Guibert, the chief executive of Lacoste owner Maus Freres SA, urged the state in a LinkedIn post “to mobilise without delay all legal means it has to put an end to the violence, protect our citizens, our police officers, our workers and our companies”. Galeries Lafayette, after suffering damage and looting at locations including Boulevard Haussmann in Paris and in Bordeaux, said the material and economic consequences would be significant. In response to the attacks, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised “massive” security measures around this Saturday’s protests in remarks to the National Assembly. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez is scheduled to give further details later on Thursday. The impact of the rioting is likely to ripple across the tourism industry, particularly if it carries on. Images of violence have led to cancellations at high-end Paris hotels, according to Christophe Laure, who heads UMIH Prestige, which represents four-star and five-star hotels. Well-heeled guests of those establishments often shop at the local luxury shops. “It’s too early today to assess whether this will have an impact on foreign tourist clientele in coming weeks,” said Mr du Halgouet of Hermes. With demand for luxury goods in China already weak and the wider industry in a slump, an extended drop in tourist purchases in France would come at a difficult moment. That is especially the case with the Christmas shopping season now getting under way. Milan, another European luxury shopping destination, has also experienced looting in the past few days. Two prominent events set to lure foreign visitors are still going ahead this weekend. The Art Basel Paris fair, at the Grand Palais, said it “has extensive protocols in place” for the show and “works closely with a private security company and, where necessary, the Paris police”. On Sunday, the National Football League will hold a game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the New Orleans Saints at Stade de France, the stadium in the suburbs of Paris where a Champions League final in 2022 ended in scenes of chaos and violence as local individuals assaulted football fans. Security will be heightened for the game. Agencies contributed to this report

title: WGES 2026: Dubai’s green economy summit puts waste, water and AI on the agenda
description: The World Green Economy Summit opened on Wednesday, allowing policymakers and industry leaders to discuss how to build an economy that does not consume faster than the planet can replenish
content: Thousands of delegates gathered at Dubai's World Trade Centre on Wednesday for the opening day of the World Green Economy Summit (WGES), with speakers pressing the case that the transition to a green economy requires change not just from governments and industries but from every individual consumer. The summit brought together figures from waste management, artificial intelligence and environmental finance, among many other sectors. The conversations ranged from the contents of a Dubai rubbish chute to the future of AI-powered desalination, and most confirmed that solutions exist, but we still need incentive structures and out-of-the-box thinking from entrepreneurs looking to scale them. For Timothy Clarke, chief executive of Dubai's Warsan Waste Management Centre (WWMC), the single most important shift in thinking is linguistic. "We need to stop talking about ‘waste’," he said. "It is a hugely valuable ‘resource’. We have a resource which, at the moment, we destroy, we throw away. But actually what we need is for people to look at that and say, ‘I can use that part of it for something else’." WWMC receives 6,000 tonnes of unsorted waste every day from Dubai Municipality, burning it to generate electricity. The plant works, but Mr Clarke argues it is the last resort, not the goal. "If nothing comes to the energy-from-waste plant, that is a success for me, because it means we are recycling everything." Getting there requires a policy environment that makes recycled materials economically competitive with virgin ones. "Everybody always goes for the cheapest product that meets their requirements," he said. "If cost is a major driver, we have got to make sure that the green alternatives are economic, so that people make the wiser, sustainable, recycling choice." Sitting alongside Mr Clarke on a morning panel about driving the circular economy was Anssi Mikola, co-founder of River Recycle, a company that operates cleaning and recycling operations on rivers in the developing world. He argues that the ocean plastic crisis starts inland, where inadequate waste infrastructure leaves communities with rivers as their only disposal option. "The rivers are the only place where nobody comes after you," Mr Mikola said. "It is out of sight, out of mind. Nobody is responsible for it. Once you get it in the river, it moves to the next municipality." River Recycle is now operational on 20 rivers and is expanding to 30, a milestone Mr Mikola described as significant because it opens the door to larger, city-scale solutions rather than individual waterway interventions. "It has taken a long time to prove that the cleaning works and that the recycling part works." The company's challenge – and its reason for attending WGES – is funding. Scaling a circular economy in developing nations requires capital those nations do not have. "We exist to save the oceans," Mr Mikola said, "and the oceans have been destroyed by developing countries. You need funding to scale up a circular economy in those countries." Blended finance instruments – combining philanthropic seed funding with impact investment – are the vehicle he is seeking. The connections made at events like WGES, he said, matter as much as the panel discussions. AI was also, naturally, integral to the conversation. Darren Kimura, chief executive of AISquared, delivered one of the morning's keynote addresses. "A summit, by nature, brings together leaders in an area – people that can actually create policy, laws, guidance, thought leadership," Mr Kimura told The National . "And then it allows you to bring different perspectives in and hopefully change the way people are thinking or what they are doing." His keynote included what he called the Dubai AI Challenge: a call for the UAE's technology community to stop measuring AI by headline-grabbing capabilities and start measuring it by concrete environmental outcomes. "Rather than having AI just create interesting things that are cool, like a headline, why don't we try to quantify it with things like metrics that show how much we are actually saving? How much money we are saving and how much water we are saving?" Mr Kimura's presence at a green economy summit raised an obvious question, given the volume of criticism directed at AI's water and energy consumption. He argues the technology's footprint depends entirely on how it is designed and deployed. New liquid cooling approaches – immersing processors in nano-material fluids rather than relying on water evaporation – can significantly reduce data centre water use, for example. And AI applied to resource management can drive efficiencies that offset its own demands, he said. "Using AI to actually get to those new technologies will help us to reduce it in the grand scheme of things over time," he said, "and I think that is something that is not necessarily talked about in the common conversation." His company's focus is on sovereign, democratised AI; models small enough to run within a single company or household, keeping data private and computation local. A new family of such models is due imminently. "Giving the power to the consumer – I think that is really what we are trying to do now." Across the morning sessions, it was agreed that the green economy cannot be built by summits alone. Mr Clarke said: "Everybody needs to be involved in this. It is not something that governments or industries can do. A lot of it is the individual person – about your choices when you go into a supermarket." He was particularly pointed about packaging. Around 15 per cent of the waste arriving at WWMC each day consists of single-use items – packaging that consumers did not want, bundled around the product they did want. The solution, he said, requires both consumer pressure and business leadership. "What we need is for more people to be influencing people directly to make the right choices." Mr Mikola is thinking in similarly collective terms. For example, he noted that River Recycle turns electricity into heat in its processing operations, while WWMC turns heat into electricity. "Why don't we just work together?" he asked. “And take the heat once it is there, rather than getting all the losses that it takes to turn it into energy?" That kind of lateral thinking, he suggested, is what a summit like WGES is designed to produce. "I hope [the event] leads to people thinking a bit more outside the box – looking at the bigger picture rather than just your own,” added Mr Mikola. “The solution may not be inside your focus, but there may still be a very good solution out there." This page was produced by The National in partnership with WGES

title: Sheikh Mohammed and Sheikh Hamdan pay tribute after death of 'dedicated' Dubai Police leader
description: Maj Gen Khalifa bin Dhaen Al Mheiri remembered for his loyalty and contributions during five decades of service
content: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai , has paid tribute after the death of Maj Gen Khalifa bin Dhaen Al Mheiri. Sheikh Mohammed described Maj Gen Al Mheiri as “a loyal man” and praised his 50 years of service to the nation. “One of the dedicated leaders of Dubai Police and one of the most faithful who devoted his career to the Al Maktoum family and the citizens over five decades of continuous service,” he wrote on X. Sheikh Mohammed said that Dubai would always remember those who served the emirate with loyalty and dedication. He also offered prayers for Maj Gen Al Mheiri’s family and loved ones. Born in Jumeirah when it was a modest settlement of palm-frond huts and tents, Maj Gen Al Mheiri joined the military at 14. He was among the first to join the Dubai Police. Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, also paid tribute to Maj Gen Al Mheiri. “He was among the first young men to join the Dubai Police after its establishment, and over decades of police service, he held numerous duties and positions. His giving continued after his retirement, supporting a range of charitable, educational and community projects.” Beyond his law enforcement career, Maj Gen Al Mheiri made a significant impact across society. He established Jumeira University to preserve and share his community's cultural heritage. The institution continues to empower future generations with knowledge, skills, and a strong sense of responsibility to the community and nation. On Wednesday, Jumeira University also mourned the passing of its founder. The management extended condolences to Maj Gen Al Mheiri's family, loved ones, and the entire university community, remembering his service and generosity with deep appreciation. He also founded the Bin Dhaen Group. Starting with retail ventures and a trading house established in 1990, the group has grown into a conglomerate spanning trading, industry, contracting, education, real estate and services.

title: 'It feels right': Joe Hart on Enzo Maresca and why he doesn't hold a grudge against Pep Guardiola
description: Former England and Manchester City goalkeeper embracing his new life as a pundit after long and successful playing career
content: Having hung up his gloves and made a smooth transition into punditry, Joe Hart's opinions on the game are increasingly in demand. That was the case this week when the 39-year-old sat down with The National at the Puma Manchester City store in Dubai Mall to discuss everything from Enzo Maresca's start at his former club to his own managerial ambitions – or complete lack of them. Hart's analysis is as measured as his handling once was, and when it comes to Maresca, he likes what he sees. Following Pep Guardiola was always going to be like inheriting a cathedral and being asked to add a new wing, yet Maresca has enjoyed an astonishingly good start to the season, setting a Premier League record by winning his first seven matches in charge. “He’s very, very calm. I think it’s nice that he understands the building. He knows quite a lot of the players,” Hart says of Maresca, who previously spent time as an assistant to Guardiola at the Etihad Stadium. “He’s gone away and done some incredible work [at Leicester and Chelsea]. It feels right. I think that’s the biggest compliment you can pay him. “I think it’s very tough, obviously, to follow someone like Pep Guardiola. Ten years of dominance. He has started really well, [but] he’s the kind of manager who’s not going to want a good start - he’s going to want a whole good career at Manchester City.” Maresca's strong first impression has come at what Hart concedes is a challenging time away from pitch. City have launched an appeal after being found guilty of 114 of 115 financial charges in their long-running case with the Premier League. City have always denied any wrongdoing . Their former goalkeeper believes that the team's performances reflect a strong spirit at the club. “As far as I can see, they seem together. They seem united in how they feel, in how they back the club. The club's been incredible. The fans have [had] a really strong response,” says Hart, who spent 12 years at the club, making 348 appearances, keeping 137 clean sheets and winning two Premier League titles, an FA cup and two League Cups. “There's no getting away from it – it's a difficult moment. But I mean, as I say, inside that training ground, inside that stadium, there's a real team belief. They can only take care of business on the pitch. And that's what they're doing. They're doing a brilliant job." For all of Hart's years of service, the end of his City career was abrupt, as Guardiola decided to make a change in goal shortly after his appointment in 2016. Hart, England's number one at the time, joined Torino on loan before going on to play for Burnley, Tottenham and Celtic, where he added seven more major honours to his resume. Guardiola, who argued that Hart lacked ability with his feet, has since admitted he was wrong not to have given him an opportunity to adapt. “It made me emotional because it was almost validation for how I felt at the time,” says Hart when asked about Guardiola's admission. “But in terms of how we get on as friends and as ex-colleagues, nothing changed for me. I had those conversations with him 10 years ago. He was honest. I wanted him to be as honest as he possibly could be. “It was a unique situation. As a goalkeeper, you either play or you don't. And he didn't feel like he had enough time to get me ready for the team that he needed. And if he didn't have enough time, then I couldn't be there. “We had some really difficult conversations at the time. Shook hands, hugged, and that was it. It was parked and buried and I was happy 10 years ago but I think what he said is more for him rather than me.” With the past behind him, Hart is easing into his new life as a pundit. In February this year, he returned to Shrewsbury Town, the club where he started, as a goalkeeping coach for a few weeks as a favour to manager and friend Gavin Cowan. “Ever since I left them when I was 19, I've not really been able to give anything back,” Hart said. However, that brief stint is no indication of an interest in becoming a full-time coach. “No, I’ll be nowhere near management or coaching - that’s not for me,” he adds. For now, he’s open-minded about future projects and keen to explore new possibilities. He recently joined The Overlap’s new daily programme and has been visiting and joining coaching sessions at City Football Schools (CFS) at Masdar City in Abu Dhabi. Hart grew up in simpler times where “it was more turning up and just playing football”. So, he was struck by the sophistication on show. “The coaching standards are unbelievable,” he said. “The energy, the coaching, the facilities, it was fantastic. And it was great to be around the kids as well.” A position once reserved for whichever child drew the short straw now appears to have a waiting list. Hart was thrilled by how many children were choosing to play between the posts in the UAE capital. “I couldn't believe how many goalkeepers there were,” he said “It's becoming a popular position. The standard was really high.” Hart may have put the gloves down, but judging by the queue in Masdar City, plenty are eager to pick them up.

title: Saudi Arabia's Humain expands Nvidia deal with 84MW AI computing plan
description: New capacity includes 50MW for unnamed US customer
content: Saudi Arabia's Humain has expanded its partnership with US chip maker Nvidia to develop up to 84 megawatts of artificial intelligence computing capacity, including infrastructure for an unnamed American customer, as the kingdom accelerates its push to become a global AI hub. The agreement, announced at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, covers about 27,000 advanced graphics processing units (GPUs), with deployments beginning later this year and further capacity planned for 2027. The expansion builds on a partnership announced in May 2025 during US President Donald Trump 's visit to Riyadh, when Nvidia unveiled plans to supply Humain with hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips over five years. The initial phase involved 18,000 Blackwell processors, part of a broader plan to develop up to 500MW of AI computing capacity over five years. The first phase of the latest agreement will comprise 14MW of Nvidia's Blackwell HGX B300 systems, equivalent to about 6,000 GPUs, with deployment starting in the fourth quarter. The infrastructure will support Humain Cloud customers, including AI companies, government entities and businesses. A further 70MW of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin infrastructure, representing about 21,000 GPUs, is planned from mid-2027. Of that, 50MW will be dedicated to advanced AI workloads for an unidentified US client, with deployment targeted to begin in June. The remaining 20MW will support Humain Cloud, with deployment expected to begin in July or August. The companies said the Vera Rubin projects remain subject to final agreements and deployment plans. GPUs are powerful processors used to train and run AI systems. Blackwell is Nvidia's current generation of AI chips, while Vera Rubin is its successor, designed to handle more complex workloads faster and more efficiently. “We are moving quickly to bring the next generations of Nvidia-accelerated computing into Saudi Arabia at meaningful scale,” Humain chief executive Tareq Amin said. Launched in May 2025 and chaired by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Humain is owned by the kingdom's Public Investment Fund and plans to develop about 3GW of data centre capacity by 2030 and more than 6GW by 2034. Saudi Arabia is competing with the UAE to attract AI investment. In Abu Dhabi, G42, OpenAI and Oracle are developing Stargate UAE , a 1GW computing cluster that forms the first phase of a planned 5GW UAE-US AI campus, with Nvidia also a technology partner. Both Gulf countries depend on US export approvals to obtain advanced AI chips, making Washington's technology restrictions an important factor in their expansion plans. The latest announcement comes days after Saudi Arabia postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference from October 26-29 to next year. This followed a Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300. Mr Amin was among the speakers scheduled to attend gathering, which has become a major platform for announcing investment agreements involving Saudi Arabia's technology and infrastructure sectors. The FII Institute says the annual conference has helped to secure $250 billion in signed agreements and investment pledges since its inception.

title: Sultan Haitham renews centuries-old trade links with London on state visit
description: UK and Oman sign deal to build AI data centre in Salalah, with £1bn of investment pledged
content: Oman has renewed its historic links to the City of London with pledges by Sultan Haitham to grow joint investment and keep trade flowing under the shadow of the Iran war. Sultan Haitham, who is on the first Omani state visit to the UK in 44 years, used a banquet address in the finance, shipping and insurance centre to pledge that ties dating back to 1647 would blossom. Referring to how the London merchants signed a deal in that year to access Oman's ports, Sultan Haitham said: “Not for the last time the private sector got there first.” “We can see that bilateral investments and trade are moving in a positive direction, with concrete efforts being made to encourage investment and building stronger partnership in sectors such as sustainability, financial services and technology.” Speaking at the City's Guildhall, Lady Mayor Susan Langley said Oman's role in maintaining free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz was globally important. “We understand that the freedom of the seas, the security of trade routes, and global stability are the foundations upon which prosperity and peace are built,” she said. “Our partnership has helped protect those foundations for generations, allowing trade to flourish.” More treaties followed in 1798 and 1800, while the UK was involved in a counter-insurgency in Oman as recently as the 1980s. Oman and the UK have signed a series of deals during Sultan Haitham's four-day visit with more than more than £1 billion ($1.34 billion) of investment pledged. One pact was to “secure maritime co-operation through strengthened information-sharing and knowledge exchange with the Omani Maritime Security Centre”. Sultan Haitham met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street before the banquet. The UK leader “gave his thanks for the Oman’s work to reopen the Strait of Hormuz”. “Both leaders agreed on the need to keep the Strait open to reduce the pressure on global supply chains and ease the impact on people at home,” the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement. Sultan Haitham acknowledged that the situation facing his country had “not been great” for more than 40 years but that his country was committed to doing whatever it could to normalise tensions. “We have great relations with Britain and we are all the time co-ordinating our moves and also getting help sometimes,” he said. On Thursday, Sultan Haitham visited the former Olympic Park in East London, which has been one of the capital’s flagship projects for growth and regeneration. The visit was led by the UK's Minister of State for Trade, Anas Sarwar. At Here East, a cluster of buildings that consists of data labs, museums and businesses, Sultan Haitham met chief executives and founders of British and Omani start-ups working at the frontiers of space, health care and artificial intelligence. “What we're showcasing is the best of British technology in those areas, with a view to catalyse on that deepening of that partnership,” said Saj Huq, chief executive of Plexal, which presented the start-up display to Sultan Haitham. Among them is Bio Orbit, founded in 2023 by Katie King and Leonor Teles, which hopes to manufacture drugs in space. The company raised £9.8 million as part of their seed-funding round. Mr Huq told The National that BioOrbit is “reformulating medicines by using crystallisation science in space to develop drug forms that can improve how medicines are delivered and used”. “There are really clear benefits to society and they're a real sector leader,” he said. Another Here East business is SAIF Autonomy, a start-up that builds safety layers for autonomous technology and embodied AI. “They are operating across industry and defence and government” and “helping drive autonomy into complex systems in a responsible way”, Mr Huq added. The Omani climate tech company 44.01, which has also laid foundations in the UK, played a part in the presentation. The company captures carbon emissions and buries them underground, using a natural process that occurs when the gas comes into contact with peridotite, a rock commonly found in Oman. The company won the Prince of Wales’ Earthshot Prize in 2022. “Part of the showcase is showing that we've already got these ties,” Mr Huq said. “The innovation ecosystems are already collaborating and they're growing in region.” The innovation corridor at the former international broadcast centre for the 2012 Olympic Games is also home to Stealth Labs, a venture that specialises in sovereign capabilities in the technology. Sammy Harris, a co-founder, said the visit was a "strong first step" for growing partnerships that secure nationally controlled data capabilities in defence and other spheres between the business and the region. Iran has claimed a handful of attacks on vessels using a so-called Oman route through the Strait of Hormuz this week alone. Figures from data provider Kpler show that oil shipments out of the Gulf hit a high of 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to October 18. The volumes jump and slump depending on the hostility from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and average figures for October to date remain below levels before the war broke out in February. Ships in the Gulf and Red Sea sail hostile narrow straits with their automatic information systems switched off and there is a further lack of clarity about these journeys due to the military-related withholding of satellite imagery over the region. The UK and Oman signed an agreement to build an artificial intelligence data centre in Salalah involving partners from both nations. Officials said the first phase was expected to exceed £1 billion and would create more than 100 highly skilled jobs across the UK by exporting British expertise and attracting returns for UK-backed investors. The UK first signed a Sovereign Investment Partnership with Oman in 2022, with Oman investing £1.7 billion in the UK since its creation, a Foreign Office statement said.

title: Sharjah Animation and Comics Conference: Pixar veterans, comic book artists and a new focus on Arab talent
description: Four-day event returns to Aljada with more than 150 activities, international guests, workshops, film screenings and live concerts
content: A character that begins in a comic book can eventually become the star of an animated film, a video game or an entire fictional universe. This increasingly interconnected approach to storytelling is at the heart of this year's Sharjah Animation and Comics Conference (SACC). The event, being held until Sunday at Aljada , is expanding beyond animation to embrace comics, bringing illustrators, writers and publishers into a programme that previously concentrated on filmmakers and animators. Organised by the Sharjah Book Authority, this year's event features more than 150 activities. These include 55 workshops and masterclasses, more than 40 talks and discussions, 10 film screenings and three live orchestral concerts. More than 75 speakers from over 30 countries are expected to participate. Khoula Al Mujaini, executive director of the SACC, says the expansion reflects changes already taking place across creative industries. "Comics felt like a natural next step because the way people tell and experience stories is already changing," she tells The National . "A character may begin in a comic, move into animation, become a game or develop into an entirely different kind of world. After three editions focused on animation, we felt SACC should reflect that wider creative reality." The expanded programme will explore everything from adapting animation into webtoons to transforming books into interactive experiences. Al Mujaini says that bringing these disciplines together will encourage collaboration between creative communities that increasingly share similar skills and audiences. Among the headline guests is Andrew Gordon, a former Pixar animator whose credits include Monsters, Inc. , Finding Nemo and The Incredibles . He will discuss the studio's approach to storytelling and lead a workshop examining artificial intelligence in animation. Another Pixar veteran, Doug Sweetland, whose credits include Toy Story and Monsters, Inc. , will share insights into directing animated shorts and developing memorable characters. They will be joined by Shuzo Shiota, chief executive of Japanese animation studio Polygon Pictures, and Terry Notary, a movement coach and performance-capture specialist known for his work on Avatar and Planet of the Apes. Notary will lead a workshop demonstrating how posture, breathing and physical movement can help performers create believable digital creatures. Comic book enthusiasts can meet artists Bernard Chang and Ken Lashley, alongside cartoonist Guy Gilchrist and writer and producer Shannon Eric Denton. Sessions will explore character design, drawing techniques and the development of original comics. Other workshops include traditional animation with Disney veteran Robb Pratt, stop-motion filmmaking with Egyptian artist Dina Amin and lightsaber choreography with stunt performer Lauren Mary Kim, who worked on Star Wars: The Clone Wars. Beyond the talks and workshops, the conference is introducing several attractions for fans and collectors. Artist Alley will show original works by regional artists, while the Comic Wall will feature rare and vintage comic books and collectables. At the Dubbing Corner, visitors can try voice acting by recording dialogue for animated scenes. The Meet the Artist programme offers opportunities to interact with international creators and purchase commissioned artwork. Gaming is another major attraction. A dedicated area will feature arcade machines, board games, racing simulators and trading card games, alongside tournaments in EA Sports FC 27 , Tekken 8 and Super Smash Bros Ultimate. A cosplay competition will take place on Saturday, with a Dh25,000 prize pool. Film screenings include Toy Story and Monsters, Inc. , introduced by Pixar animators, as well as The Glassworker , the Pakistani hand-drawn animated feature directed by Usman Riaz. The programme also includes the regional premiere of Walking with Animators and a selection of animated short films. Three orchestral concerts, scheduled for Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, will celebrate film scores, anime and K-pop music, and Disney favourites respectively. While entertainment remains a significant part of the event, Al Mujaini believes the conference can help address some of the structural challenges facing the region's creative industries. She says the Arab world already has the artists, audiences and stories needed to establish a stronger international presence in animation and comics. The challenge is developing sustainable careers and businesses around that talent. "A talented artist still needs access to producers, financing, publishers, broadcasters and distribution," she says. This year's expanded business-to-business programme aims to connect creators and publishers with producers, studio executives and other industry decision makers. Dedicated meetings will explore financing, international co-production, rights management and commercial development, while the Book2Screen Challenge will connect publishers and rights holders with producers interested in adapting written works for the screen. Al Mujaini says such initiatives can help regional creators move beyond individual projects towards developing original intellectual property with commercial potential. "We also need more original projects that reflect our own humour, cultures and visual identities," she says. "The opportunity is not to imitate what already exists elsewhere, but to build stronger pathways for Arab creators to make excellent work and give those stories the chance to travel." The conference will also examine how AI is changing animation production, from generating early concepts to streamlining technical processes. Gordon's workshop on Sunday will explore how AI can support visual development and production while allowing artists to retain control of their work. Al Mujaini believes emerging artists should remain open to new technology while continuing to develop their fundamental skills. "AI can be a useful tool for experimenting with ideas and making certain processes more efficient, but creativity, storytelling and artistic judgement remain essential," she says. "Ultimately, technology should support the artist's vision, not define it." SACC will runs until Sunday at Aljada, Sharjah. Doors open at 1.30pm on Thursday, 12.15pm on Friday and 10.30am at the weekend. Tickets cost Dh85 for students, Dh135 for regular passes and Dh280 for business passes. Premium passes are priced at Dh3,000. Saturday passes are sold out.

title: Dubai pledges Dh150m to support humanitarian campaigns across UAE
description: Vital funds will help several initiatives, including Emirati aid operations in Gaza
content: Dubai on Thursday pledged Dh150 million ($40.8 million) to support humanitarian campaigns across the country, including efforts to deliver life-saving health care and offer a lifeline to war-hit civilians in the Gaza Strip . The Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives will provide the funds to 11 UAE-based charitable groups to strengthen their crucial work both at home and abroad. They include the UAE's Operation Gallant Knight, which was set up in response to the outbreak of the war in Gaza in October 2023 to assist civilians caught up in conflict. Al Jalila Foundation, the charitable arm of Dubai Health and a non-profit organisation dedicated to advancing medical research, education and treatment, will also benefit. The other recipients are: Tarahum Charity Foundation; the Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum Charitable Establishment; Emirates Health Services; the UAE Food Bank; Beit Al Khair Society; Dar Al Ber Society; Fujairah Charity Association; Noor Dubai; and the Digital School. The major investment was announced in the presence of Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. Sheikh Hamdan praised the philanthropic vision of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, who established MBRGI in 2015. He said MBRGI “continues to provide all the necessary means to advance charitable and humanitarian work in the UAE” and noted that the latest allocation highlights its commitment to serving the needs of the community. The signing of the funding agreements was witnessed by Mohammad Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and secretary general of MBRGI. The organisation distributed Dh2.3 billion in funding for 165 million people in 122 countries last year. It was established in 2015 to oversee aid and relief operations, and launch projects to tackle issues such as poverty, hunger, health and education inequality. The latest funding for the UAE's humanitarian campaign for Gaza will boost continuing aid efforts in the enclave, as communities grapple with the effects of the Israel-Hamas war. The MBRGI launched the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative in September, aiming to supply more than 10 million meals to Palestinians. It began flying food parcels to Gaza in partnership with Operation Gallant Knight 3 this month. The initiative was named in honour of Sheikh Ahmed , brother of the Sheikh Mohammed, who died on September 21. It brought together volunteers, community members and admirers of Sheikh Ahmed at Dubai World Trade Centre to prepare food and aid packages for Gaza. The humanitarian bridge will operate through air and sea transport in seven consignments. Six flights will carry 450 tonnes of food parcels and one vessel will transport 4,000 tonnes of supplies to meet the basic nutrition needs of people in Gaza.

title: Postcards from Sant’Agata: A visit to the birthplace of Lamborghini
description: More than 60 years after its founding in a small town in northern Italy, car maker's most extraordinary machines are still built there
content: Sant’Agata Bolognese is a relatively small town between Bologna and Modena in Italy’s “Motor Valley”. Yet it is responsible for some of the world’s most ostentatious and recognisable cars ever made. This, after all, is where Ferruccio Lamborghini established his car company in 1963 and where, more than six decades later, Lamborghini continues to build its vehicles. There is something slightly incongruous about the setting. Sant’Agata still feels modest and agricultural, surrounded by the flat landscape of Emilia-Romagna. And then, amid it all, you encounter the unmistakable Lamborghini shield and a factory producing cars destined for Dubai, Miami or Tokyo. I am touring both the Museo Automobili Lamborghini and the neighbouring factory. The museum is not particularly large, something that works in its favour. Rather than trying to display everything, it tells the company’s story through a carefully curated collection before allowing visitors to see where its latest chapter is being built. The story begins, somewhat improbably, with tractors. By the 1950s, Ferruccio Lamborghini had found success manufacturing agricultural machinery, notably affordable tractors using material salvaged from the Second World War, before deciding to build grand touring cars. The 350 GTV concept appeared in 1963, followed by the production 350 GT the next year and the Jarama in 1970. Viewed today, the 350 GT seems almost conservative. Its long bonnet and curved body resemble many Italian grand tourers of the era, with little of the visual aggression that would become a Lamborghini trademark. But it marks the beginning of an ambition to challenge Italy’s established sports car manufacturers. A few steps away is the car that changed everything. I still don’t think Lamborghini has built anything more beautiful than the Miura. Sixty years after its debut, its proportions remain almost perfect. It sits incredibly low, with distinctive eyelashes surrounding the headlights and a shape that feels elegant rather than aggressive. The museum is marking the Miura’s 60th anniversary, and one highlight is the Miura Roadster, a one-off created by the automotive company Bertone in 1968. Knowing there is no copy makes standing beside it feel particularly special. Nearby is a Miura P400 S. It is less extraordinary, but perhaps better at demonstrating why the car brand has endured. You are left simply appreciating how well the aircraft-wing-inspired shape has aged. At the other extreme is the LM002 . The enormous off-roader looks almost comically out of place among Lamborghini’s sleek supercars. Developed from earlier attempts at creating a military-style vehicle, the production LM002 arrived in 1986 using the 5.2-litre V12 from the Countach Quattrovalvole. Only about 300 were built. It is not the Lamborghini most people picture when they hear the name, which makes it one of the museum’s most interesting cars. Decades before the Urus , Lamborghini was already willing to put its badge on something completely unexpected. The museum tells you what Lamborghini has built. The factory tour shows you how it happens. As I walk on to the production floor, one of the things I notice first is how human hands still play a prominent role. Partially assembled cars move between stations where small teams add components – wiring, piping and interior pieces. Timers count down roughly 24 minutes, the time each station has before the car is meant to move forward. Despite deadlines, nothing feels rushed. The operation is methodical and surprisingly calm. Watching a collection of components gradually become something recognisable is strangely satisfying. The most memorable moment comes when the powertrain and chassis finally meet, a process described during the tour as “a marriage”. It sounds overly romantic until you see it. Before that point, you have an engine and a chassis. Afterwards, you begin to have a car. There is also a special connection between the factory floor and the museum next door. Lamborghini still produces its V12 flagship in the area where the Countach assembly line was established in the 1970s. Today, that car is the Revuelto . What also becomes apparent is how much freedom customers have. Paint colours are only the beginning. Buyers can choose different leathers, stitching, trims and colour combinations. Lamborghini merges physical material selection with cutting-edge digital visualisation tools through its 'phygital' Ad Personam personalisation programme, extending those choices even further. It is one reason why seeing two Lamborghinis that have been configured exactly alike will still feel distinct. After walking through the factory, I also find that it becomes harder to view the finished cars simply as collections of performance figures. Someone fitted the pipes. Someone installed the trim. Someone checked the electronics. For all the technology involved, these still feel like machines constructed by people rather than cookie-cutter builds. Back in the museum, the upper floor feels much more familiar. This is where the Countach, Murcielago, Gallardo, Aventador and Huracan sit alongside some of Lamborghini’s rarer creations. These are the cars that appeared on bedroom walls and in video games, and were cherished as scale models. Seeing them together – all low, wide and rarely subtle – demonstrates how consistently Lamborghini has stuck to its philosophy. The design language changes from generation to generation, but the intention remains remarkably similar: a Lamborghini should elicit excitement even before anyone turns the engine on. The special-edition cars take that idea further. In 2016, the Centenario marked 100 years since Ferruccio Lamborghini’s birth, with only 20 coupes and 20 roadsters made. The Sian combined a naturally aspirated V12 with Lamborghini’s first electrified production powertrain, with 63 coupes produced in reference to the company’s founding year. These are cars most people will only ever see in photographs, in video games or in miniatures. Finding several of them metres apart is one of the pleasures of the museum. But after moving between the historic models, the production line and the modern supercars, it is not the sense of rarity that stays with me. It is the consistency. Lamborghini has changed considerably since 1963. Ferruccio is long gone; the company passed through several owners, while Audi’s acquisition in 1998 brought greater stability, technology and production capacity. Yet the instinct behind the cars remains recognisable. The Miura was radical. The Countach looked like nothing else on the road. The LM002 was an absurd idea that somehow made it into production. Today’s cars continue to chase that sense of theatre. For all the international attention surrounding Lamborghini, it is still fascinating that these machines, some of the loudest and proudest on the road, emerge from one factory in a quiet community in northern Italy.

title: Robinhood picks DIFC for Middle East debut and targets 2027 launch
description: Company to offer trading and custody services across all 10 asset classes approved by DFSA
content: US financial services platform Robinhood is expanding to the Middle East, with the Dubai International Financial Centre becoming its regional headquarters. The company said on Thursday it had been approved by the Dubai Financial Services Authority to offer trading and custody services across all 10 asset classes approved by the regulator, including equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds and investment tokens. “The DIFC is one of the world’s most important financial hubs, and our expansion there brings us closer to building a global platform that enables anyone, anywhere to own the highest quality financial assets,” said Vlad Tenev, chairman and chief executive of Robinhood. Robinhood plans to start offering its products in the region in 2027, giving investors access to a wider range of global financial assets. The company said its Dubai operations will be led by Salah Kaddoura as senior executive officer and president of Robinhood Mena . He will oversee the expansion of the regional team. "Our belief is that Robinhood’s arrival will open up increased access to the market for retail investors," he told The National . "Our expansion is driven by three key factors: demographics, innovation, and strategic regulation." “From our new home in Dubai’s premier financial hub, we’re looking forward to building Robinhood’s regional presence and expanding access to the global financial ecosystem for a new generation of investors,” Mr Kaddoura added. The move comes as Dubai strengthens its position as a financial centre , attracting international companies seeking access to the region’s growing investor base. The number of companies at DIFC grew at a record pace in the first half of this year, despite uncertainty over the Iran war, as the emirate’s financial hub continued to attract banks, wealth and asset managers, and hedge funds from around the globe. DIFC, one of the fastest-growing onshore financial hubs of the broader Middle East, North Africa and South Asia region, registered 2,318 new companies in the 12 months until the end of June, marking a 30 per cent annual increase, the regulator said in July. Global companies that set up their regional offices at DIFC during the first six months of the year include Allianz Trade Middle East, Arrowpoint Investment Partners, Bank of Canada, Blue Mountain Capital, Citadel, Gordian Capital, ICICI Prudential Asset Management, JP Morgan International Advisors, and Varenne Capital Partners. Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority, said Robinhood’s decision to establish its regional headquarters in Dubai reflected growing demand for technology-driven investment services across the Middle East. “With its proven ability to broaden participation in financial markets, Robinhood is well positioned to contribute to the continued development of the region's investment landscape and to connect a new generation of investors with opportunities across global markets,” he said. DIFC is among the key planks of Dubai's growth ambitions and is aligned with the Dubai Economic Agenda, the initiative known as D33, which aims to double the size of the emirate's economy to Dh32 trillion ($8.71 trillion) over the next decade and establish Dubai among the top three global cities. Dubai is also pursuing a Dh100 billion expansion plan for the second phase of the the financial centre, called DIFC Za'abeel District, which on completion will boost overall capacity to 42,000 companies housing 125,000 professionals across more than 1.5 square kilometres of floor space. Demand for office space continued during the first six months of this year with DIFC Square, which has 600,000 square feet of space, becoming 100 per cent pre-leased before completion. With inputs from Salma Arafa

title: Gulf economies to contract 4.8% this year with sharp recovery in 2027, IMF says
description: Fund slashes growth outlook by 6.8 percentage points but expects strong rebound next year if hostilities end
content: Gulf economies are set to shrink 4.8 per cent this year as the Iran war disrupts energy exports and weighs on non-oil activity, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027 , the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. The forecast marks a sharp reversal for the six-member Gulf bloc, with the IMF cutting its 2026 growth projection by 6.8 percentage points from the 2 per cent expansion it expected in April, according to its Regional Economic Outlook released in Dubai on Thursday. The Gulf region posted growth of 4.5 per cent last year. “While some economies have remained relatively resilient, others have experienced severe disruptions, leading to a substantially weaker regional economic outlook since our April forecast,” Jihad Azour , director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia department, said at the report's launch at the Dubai International Financial Centre. “This conflict has disrupted energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence. And the burden of this disruption has fallen most heavily on oil-exporting economies, directly affected by the interruption of energy production and transport,” he said, calling the war a “severe shock” for oil importers. There is divergence between the Gulf countries, with Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar the most affected because of the drop in hydrocarbon production and exports. Their economies are projected to decline by 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, this year. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are “less affected”, with contractions of 3.9 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively, while Oman's economy is projected to grow by 4.1 per cent this year. The sultanate's geographical location, as well as focus on non-oil reforms in recent years is backing its economy, Mr Azour said. The wider Gulf's contraction for this year is similar to the level experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the bloc's GDP shrunk by 4.9 per cent. While the primarily reason for the drop in growth has been due to the oil sector, the bloc's non-oil economy is also forecast to contract by 0.8 per cent this year before returning to 4.5 per cent growth in 2027, underscoring the wider economic fallout from the conflict. Oil and gas production among Gulf exporters directly affected by the conflict plunged from 33 million barrels a day in February to about 19 million in May, with Qatar's output falling as much as 86 per cent, the fund said. Exports have since staged a partial recovery. Gulf crude shipments rose to more than 75 per cent of prewar levels in September, the International Energy Agency said. Oil prices are now projected to average close to $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 per barrel in 2027, compared with $82.20 and $76, respectively, in April, with the forecast peaking at about $110 per barrel in late 2026 before declining steadily, the IMF said. The conflict is also eroding the Gulf's financial buffers. The IMF expects the bloc's current-account surplus to narrow to 1.3 per cent of gross domestic product this year, from 5 per cent in 2025, while its combined fiscal deficit widens to 2.3 per cent of GDP from 0.8 per cent. Inflation is projected to rise to 2.7 per cent. The diversification of trade routes and investment in resilience have significantly helped Gulf countries weather the shock from the war. While the fund anticipates a sharp rebound in Gulf economies next year, the forecast hinges on an end to hostilities and the gradual resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in early 2027. Saudi Arabia, which has been facing an increasing number of attacks by the Yemen's Houthis, has the capacity to handle the impact of conflict, Mr Azour said. “The Saudi economy has during this war has been able to redirect flow of oil, use infrastructure that is on the Red Sea, and therefore the impact of the shock on Saudi comes … second after Oman [which has seen the least impact from the war]. This is a country that is less affected,” he said. “Of course, the recent tension we saw it's having impact on their economic activity. But overall, for a country that is still exporting five to six million barrels a day, with the depths of the market that they have and the strong internal demand, their capacity to withstand the shock is high,” he added. Looking ahead, the biggest downside risk is the “obvious one on the horizon … the risk of another escalation in fighting”, said Hasan AlHasan, senior fellow for Middle East Policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Speaking at a panel discussion on the IMF report, he stressed that geopolitics now “occupies centre-stage in present economic performance but also in future economic planning”. Touching on the Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, he stressed that the region has the resilience to deal with the escalation, but urged for regional integration. “I think what this will depend on is the extent to which countries in the region are able to resolve their differences, and we're seeing very positive signs and encouraging signs in that direction,” he added. Also speaking at the panel, Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, said the Gulf economies have withstood the pressure well, and a big part of that is for energy exports to reach the market. “What is very important is that the region has entered this shock in a very strong position,” she said. “If we look at growth, really since the pandemic, you've seen multiple sectors performing well, multiple economies performing well. The resilience has not only come from looking to diversify the economy, but also from the fiscal side.” While there are uncertainties over how things get resolved and how quickly things normalise, “but given the reforms we've seen, given the balance sheets, given the focus of governments, I'm optimistic on the longer term and medium term outlook”, Ms Malik added.

title: Future travel starts now: 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day kicks off
description: On October 21, international guests will head into the rugged mountain terrain of Moganshan to test JETOUR models
content: The 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day officially opened on Tuesday, October 20 in Wuhu, Anhui Province. The group’s Global Innovation Conference, the flagship launch event, was held in the morning at the R&D Center, bringing together more than 2,000 international guests, media representatives, and users to explore key technological achievements, the product lineup, and future plans for intelligent mobility. At the conference, Yin Tongyue, Chairman of Chery Automobile Co., Ltd. reflected on more than 30 years of innovation at the company and shared his outlook on future industry trends. “With AI, we are redefining not only the automobile, but also the enterprise and the entire industrial ecosystem. In the future, cars will become smarter companions that understand you better, providing a space for greater possibilities in intelligent mobility,” he said. Gao Xinhua, chief technology oficer, delivered a keynote speech on the group’s technological foundations for the intelligent era. “Chery’s vision for technology can be summed up in one sentence: creating greater value for human freedom,” Yin stated. The conference showcased the group’s cutting-edge technology portfolio, from the Sky Dome supercomputing center and Star Sea big data platform to V2G vehicle-to-grid technology and integrated solar-storage-charging solutions. It also highlighted advances in AI foundation models and world models, alongside the real-world application of physical AI in areas such as Robotaxi and AiMOGA Robotics. Together, these innovations contribute to an intelligent technology ecosystem spanning mobility, energy, and everyday life – powered by AI, enabled by data and coordinated across multiple domains. Meanwhile, the R&D Center hosted technology exhibitions and hands-on experience zones, with access arranged in phases for different groups, giving participants the opportunity to engage directly with cutting-edge technologies. Within this landscape of innovation, JETOUR focuses on user needs, translating its technological foundations into tangible travel experiences. JETOUR’s two product series address diverse travel needs, balancing urban commuting and outdoor exploration. The T Series combines intelligent urban comfort with serious off-road capabilities, while the entire lineup features C-DM Super Hybrid technology, easing range anxiety on long journeys. The XWD fully automatic intelligent 4WD, with its ‘7+X’ one-touch intelligent off-road mode, makes challenging conditions such as water crossings, gravel, and steep slopes easier to tackle. Smart cockpit and intelligent driving technologies make journeys more comfortable and reassuring. The G Series is built on GAIA, a new-generation all-terrain intelligent architecture designed for premium models. It integrates a high-efficiency hybrid system with a dedicated off-road chassis. Combined with intelligent interaction and a premium cabin, it unites exceptional off-road capabilities with luxury comfort. That evening, JETOUR hosted an immersive beach camping welcome dinner along the Yangtze River. The built-in high-output V2L technology in JETOUR vehicles supplied power throughout the entire market to enable outdoor cooking and entertainment, weaving technology into everyday travel experiences. JETOUR executives joined international guests to officially kick off the Experience Day’s test-drive program. Technology is meant not only for the showroom, but for the road. From technology showcases and product experiences to the camping fair and real-world test drives, the 2026 JETOUR Global Technology Experience Day connects innovation with real travel scenarios. On October 21, international guests will head deep into the rugged mountain terrain of Moganshan to test JETOUR models across varied road conditions and experience firsthand how technology unlocks new possibilities for travel of travel.

title: F1 title permutations: What Kimi Antonelli needs to be crowned champion this weekend
description: Italian teenager can clinch first place in Austin if results go his way
content: A little over two years ago, just after his 18 th birthday, Kimi Antonelli crashed at Monza in his first-ever Formula One practice session. Today, he stands on the brink of the world championship and could become the sport’s youngest title winner in Austin, Texas, this weekend. Five drivers can still beat him on paper, even if most of them are clinging to the faintest of hopes. Six races remain, and all of them are traditional grand prix weekends as Singapore was the last Sprint weekend. Each GP win is worth 25 points, second place is 18, third is 15 and so on down to a single point for finishing 10th. That leaves a maximum of 150 points on the table. If two drivers finish the season level on points, the title goes to the one with more race wins. Teammate George Russell remains Antonelli’s closest challenger, while seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, four-time champion Max Verstappen, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and defending champion Lando Norris are still technically in contention. Here is what each of the six contenders needs to finish the season as world champion. Where he stands: First on 340 points with eight GP wins. What he needs: Antonelli can win the title in Austin this Sunday if he wins the race and Russell finishes ninth or lower, and Hamilton finishes fifth or lower. Victory would take Antonelli to 365 points and nine GP wins this season. Even if Russell subsequently won all five remaining races to draw level on points, Antonelli would still prevail, as he has secured more race wins. If the Italian finishes second or lower in Austin, his next opportunity comes a week later in Mexico City, on November 1. Where he stands: Second on 238 points, 102 points behind. What he needs: Russell’s best-case scenario involves him winning all six remaining races, which would take him to 388 points. Even then, Antonelli would have to score 48 points or fewer across those six races, which is essentially finishing sixth every weekend. Russell began the year as favourite, considering his experience and the brilliance of the car, and things started brightly for the Briton, who won the opening race in Australia. Since then, reliability issues and his own style of driving have seen him usurped by his younger, more daring teammate. Where he stands: Third on 229 points, 111 behind Antonelli. What he needs: If Hamilton wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 379 points. Antonelli would then have to score 38 points or fewer. In Austin, Hamilton would be eliminated from title contention if Antonelli wins and the Brit finishes fifth or lower. He is also out if Antonelli outscores him by 14 points or more. Hamilton’s second year at Ferrari has seen him be more competitive but he has still only won once this season. He would need six wins in a row and a total collapse from the young driver who replaced him at Mercedes for him to take the crown. Realistically, the chase for a record eighth title will have to wait another year. Where he stands: Fourth on 221 points, 119 behind. What he needs: If Verstappen wins all the remaining races, he will finish on 371 points. Antonelli would then have to score 30 points or fewer, which is worse than seventh place every weekend. If Antonelli scored exactly 31 points, they would tie on 371 points with eight wins each and second places would settle it. In Austin, if Antonelli wins the race, Verstappen is eliminated from title contention wherever he finishes. There may be little hope for Verstappen. He spent most of the year struggling to get the car to compete and did not win a grand prix until October, in Sepang. Red Bull’s progress over the last few weekends has been exceptional, and the burst of form has dragged him back into the title conversation. Antonelli has admitted it unsettles him. It is a warning for next season, but it has probably come too late for this year. Where he stands: Fifth, on 215 points, 125 behind. What he needs: If Leclerc wins all six remaining races, he will finish on 365 points. Antonelli would then have to score 24 points or fewer, which is essentially finishing P8 in every remaining race. Leclerc has virtually no hope of winning the championship and his teammate Hamilton has produced better performances this season. His early exit at Monza, Ferrari’s home race, perfectly demonstrated how the season has drifted away from him. Where he stands: Sixth on 201 points, 139 behind What he needs: If Norris wins all six races, he finishes on 351 points. Antonelli would then have to score 10 points or fewer across six weekends. In Austin, Norris would need to outscore the Italian by at least 15 points just to remain in contention.

title: Israel cannot secure lasting peace while Gaza remains in crisis
description: Allowing hunger and despair to deepen is a political failure as much as a moral one
content: News this week that a lack of funding could result in the UN's World Food Programme cutting aid to roughly half a million people in Gaza is a sobering reminder that a ceasefire is not the same as peace. Although Israel ’s assault on the territory may have slowed somewhat since last year’s truce, the dire conditions that have made life unbearable for so many civilians remain largely intact. The WFP has made clear that the cuts do not reflect declining need. About 1.4 million people in Gaza face acute food insecurity, and hundreds of thousands depend on assistance for even the most basic needs. For families who have lost their homes and any realistic prospect of earning an income, a food parcel or cash payment is an essential lifeline. Beyond the sheer moral urgency of rectifying the situation, however, lie broader consequences. The international community should be under no illusion about what allowing this aid lifeline to fray could mean. As Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative of Gaza's Board of Peace, n in The National earlier this month, leaving the territory in a state of permanent uncertainty is no alternative to a political settlement. His warning that despair is an excellent recruiting tool for extremism should be taken seriously by all those who claim to seek lasting regional security. This is a warning that some Israeli voters will be considering ahead of next week’s general election. Polls suggest a closely contested race, with no clear path to a parliamentary majority. For Palestinians in Gaza, the result carries enormous significance, even though they have no say in determining it. Some have postponed marriages, rebuilding homes or restarting businesses while waiting to see whether a change of Israeli government might offer a different future. Their hopes may prove misplaced. A new Israeli leadership would not automatically bring a significant change in policy, and the security concerns that shape Israeli politics will not disappear overnight. On the other hand, Israeli security cannot be achieved through indefinite military pressure while Gaza’s population remains trapped in poverty . To make matters worse, most Palestinian officials have largely failed their people. The elections that were due to take place next November have been postponed by at least a year, eliminating any hope for renewal at the leadership level. In the short term, donors must urgently close the funding gap, while those controlling access to Gaza must ensure that essential supplies can get in. Humanitarian aid is not the same as political progress, but without it, the prospects for progress will deteriorate further. Those responsible should be aware that allowing hunger and despair to deepen may defer the next crisis, but it will not prevent it.
