Israel’s next government, Palestinian political leaders, international donors and regional partners should recognise that the price of neglecting a two-state solution that is fair to both Palestinians and Israelis will be paid long after the immediate headlines have faded.

title: Code word Gospel: How UK secret service caught soldier selling plans to ‘save Lebanon’
description: Documents released by the UK’s National Archives reveal how Britain caught a desk clerk selling top secret information to Egypt and Iraq
content: At lunchtime on March 16, 1965, Chief Inspector Jock Wilson of London’s Special Branch followed his suspect through the streets surrounding London’s Charing Cross Underground station. Under the railway arches nearby, he witnessed Peter Sydney Allen exchange envelopes with another man. It was time to move in. He arrested Allen, a soldier and desk sergeant working at the Ministry of Defence who had been under surveillance for a month. His companion, Maj Abdul Hafidh Khazal Al Abbassi, an assistant military attaché of the Iraqi embassy, was also detained. Maj Al Abbassi was taken to Canon Row Police Station, where he claimed diplomatic immunity. When his official car arrived a little over an hour later, he was allowed to leave. Allen, however, was taken to New Scotland Yard and charged with selling state secrets to agents from Egypt and Iraq. Among the documents he handed over during a dozen meetings over the course of a month were Top Secret UK and US plans to help Lebanon in the event of an attack on the government. There were also files marked “Assistance for Kuwait”, “Family of Weapons” and an alphabetical list of file names Allen would be able to get his hands on from the cabinets he could access at the War Office. He was later sentenced to 10 years in prison. The operation to arrest Allen, which was given the code word Gospel, has been revealed through the release of a trove of documents from the UK’s National Archives relating to the 1960s. Many cover the Cold War, including a succession of officers working for Russia, plus members of society with Communist affiliations. Labour politician and founder of the National Health Service, Aneurin Bevan, came to the notice of MI5 due to his association with the Communist Party in Russia and the UK and his unspoken criticism of the War Cabinet. Mark Dunton, principal records specialist at the National Archives, told The National the Allen file revealed a remarkably casual attitude to security at the MoD, particularly given the fall-out from spy scandals within its ranks during that era. They appeared to rely on trust and vetting to ensure staff did not betray secrets, but were clearly not always successful. The Allen file appears to suggest that the security services were monitoring the Egyptian embassy in South Street, Mayfair, when they became aware its diplomats were clandestinely meeting a British official – described as 5ft 10in with brown hair and blue eyes, often wearing a brown suit and sheepskin coat – and set about trailing him. Allen had only just begun selling secrets. Astonishingly, his trail of deception had begun when he used a payphone in a corridor of the War Office to ring the Iraqi embassy to ask if they would be interested in meeting him. His reason for selling secrets was simple: he needed money. His wife had been in hospital for a cancer operation, his four children had returned from his mother-in-law’s in Wales, and his bills had mounted up. In his statement he gave when he was questioned, he said: “I was desperate for money and the only way I could see of obtaining any was by use of the top secret documents. “I thought about it for about a fortnight and then telephoned the Iraqi embassy. I used the public call box in the corridor at the War Office and got the military adviser's phone number from the directory. I didn't at that time know who I spoke to but I have since found out that he is Maj Abassi, the assistant military attaché. I told him I was in possession of something which I thought he would be interested in seeing.” His first drop-off, for which he received £20, was made at the embassy in Queen’s Gate, South Kensington, and involved papers regarding Kuwait. A scrap of paper from that first meeting, on which he had scribbled the name and phone number of a colonel who would decide how much he should be paid depending on the usefulness of the secret papers, was found on him when he was arrested. He told police that the colonel asked him if he could get more papers regarding Middle Eastern countries. “A few days later I found a top secret paper, in one of the combination lockers, on the Lebanon, which I thought might be of interest to him,” he said. His agreed drop-off was not at the embassy, but near Charing Cross. This time he was not paid, as he was told they were “of no value to them”. He was also told he should instead try agents at the embassy of Egypt, then known as the United Arab Republic. “I kicked up a bit of a fuss about this so he said if I could bring them something of value, especially on Israel, then they would pay me,” he said. The top secret Lebanon papers are contained in the file, and cover the US and UK’s “joint theatre” plan for action if the Lebanese government requested military assistance to “meet aggression” and “maintain order”. The plan says that Syria and Israel would constitute “a potential external threat” but that it was considered “most unlikely” that either neighbour would carry out any “aggressive acts”. Instead, Syria and Egypt were thought likely to aggravate any internal disorder with the use of propaganda and agents with the aim of aligning the Muslim population with Syria. “The greatest and most likely threat to Lebanese stability lies in the recurrence of internal religious strife,” it said. The action plan involves air and naval surveillance before committing forces “by amphibious assault if necessary”. The 29-page plan says ships of the Mediterranean Fleet and RAF planes should be at seven days' notice, and an army company on 24 hours' notice. Forces would move from a base in Cyprus directly into Lebanon. “Although it is visualised as a limited operation in support of a friendly government, organised military opposition may be encountered and forces should be constituted and prepared for entry against a measure of organised resistance,” it states. Securing the airfield, port and city of Beirut would be the priority. Allen, who had served in Egypt in the 1950s, admitted he had a dozen meetings in total, several of them witnessed by MI5, at which he often received £15. He would meet his contact near Park Lane and they would walk around Curzon St in the heart of Mayfair, or near Charing Cross. He said he did not believe he was offering “anything of consequence”. He was in charge of 11 clerks, but was the person responsible for custody and processing of all top secret documents which came into the office. The papers were kept in two cabinets, and he was the only person who knew the combination. “I would never have handed any information to any Soviet bloc countries and I only did what I did because I was in serious financial trouble,” he said. “Any money I got I passed over to my wife for housekeeping. I have kept nothing for myself. At no stage have I told any of these people who I really am, where I worked or how they could contact me.” The files also contain accounts of discussions by British authorities about what should be done with the agents Allen was meeting. It was decided it was not necessary to demand their removal, but in any case, they were spotted flying out of the UK from London after they had “become compromised”. The Home Secretary, Frank Soskice, was said to be “impressed” when given an account of the case. Chief Inspector Wilson was sent a letter thanking him for his work by Courtenay Young, a senior MI5 officer who was head of the security service’s Soviet counter-espionage section during the Cold War. “Thanks to efficient co-operation and mutual goodwill we managed to clobber Gospel from the start to finish within a month and a day,” he wrote. Mr Dunton has written a book, The MI5 Archive: Official Secrets, with his colleague Stephen Twigge, studying thousands of secret papers released decades after they were filed away. There remains a “massive interest in espionage and spycraft”, he said, with the files rich in detail about surveillance reports, transcripts of telephone calls, listening devices and intercepted letters. Although MI5 does not fall under the usual rules for government records to be released after 30 years, it had chosen to release a plethora of files 50 years or more after the fact. He said the Allen case had echoes of the Portland Spy Ring in its simplicity. Unlikely spies Harry Houghton and Ethel Gee, who worked at the Admiralty Underwater Weapons Establishment, stole classified documents and passed them to a KGB handler before returning them. Mr Dunton said that despite posters with the message “Keep Secrets Secret” being displayed around its offices, the MoD had relied on staff's civil service values to keep them honest. Only when they slipped up, and colleagues became suspicious, would they be caught.

title: War and peace: Trump team now says Putin is a 'humanitarian'
description: Peace envoy Steve Witkoff praises Russian leader during visit to St Petersburg
content: Washington has called Russian President Vladimir Putin many things since his 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Joe Biden branded him “a butcher”, a “murderous dictator” and a “pure thug”. Four years later, the White House has a new adjective for the man wanted by the International Criminal Court: humanitarian. President Donald Trump ’s peace envoy Steve Witkoff used the descriptor yesterday as he met Mr Putin in the grand Constantine Palace ​in St Petersburg, after the Russian leader freed Stephen Hubbard, ⁠a 74-year-old American citizen who had been held in custody since 2022. “You talk so much about my President, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Mr Witkoff said. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.” Mr Witkoff’s comment stunned US politicians from both sides of the aisle. “No. Putin is a stone-cold killer,” Republican Senator John Cornyn wrote on X as he shared footage of the envoy's remarks. “What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” said another Republican senator, Thom Tillis. Mr Witkoff’s praise was jarring, but it was hardly surprising given recent events. On October 9, Mr Trump announced a deal to bring Russian diesel into US and global markets as he tries to ease energy costs before the November 3 midterm elections. On October 16, he went further, waiving parts of a Russia sanctions bill he’d signed less than a month earlier. It's a significant reversal from years of US-Russia policy, and makes a mockery of Washington's sanctions, which were designed to punish Moscow for invading its smaller neighbour. Estimates vary, but Moscow is expected to garner an additional $300 million to $700 million in revenue from the waivers, much of which will be funnelled into Russia’s war machine against Ukraine. Mr Trump has been dogged by accusations that he has a soft spot for Russia ever since he emerged as a presidential candidate in 2016. Hillary Clinton famously called him a “puppet” for Moscow, a claim he angrily rejected. On Monday, he offered a fresh illustration of his appreciation for Moscow. "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," he said, on the same day a Russian drone strike killed six people, including two children, according to Ukrainian authorities. Mr Trump's now open embrace of Mr Putin comes even as Russia has been accused of helping Iran to pinpoint US forces in the Middle East. But Mr Trump is prepared to give Moscow the benefit of the doubt on that. If Russia and China are helping Iran, "it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all", he said on October 12. Underscoring the deepening ties between the Trump White House and the Kremlin, Mr Trump has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying it is time for him to step down and reacting furiously at his unwillingness to capitulate. Ukraine’s struggle for survival appears to be secondary to the President’s desire for a deal to end the war, which is killing tens of thousands of Russian and Ukrainian troops each month. “It's time to make a deal,” Mr Trump said on Tuesday. “Remember this: Though we've given a lot to Ukraine, we've gotten absolutely nothing back.” The cost of the Ukraine war to American taxpayers is a legitimate concern. But the claim that the US has got nothing back from Kyiv reminds me of Monty Python’s “What have the Romans ever done for us?” scene in the Life of Brian. Nothing really, except aqueducts, sanitation, roads and so on. Ukraine has inflicted enormous losses on what until recently was a major US adversary without American troops getting involved. Its battlefield experience has provided the Pentagon with an up-close view of Russian military capabilities and the realities of modern warfare, exposing weaknesses in equipment and assumptions about how a future conflict might play out. The conflict has also given the US lessons in drone warfare, electronic jamming, missile defence and the performance of US weapons against a "near-peer" competitor. Meanwhile, much of the money Mr Trump says went to Ukraine actually supported domestic defence manufacturers, propped up US jobs and expanded America's missile and ammunition production capacities. Perhaps the Trump-Putin bromance will result in a peace deal that Ukraine can stomach, thereby saving countless lives. But given Mr Putin's track record, this seems more like wishful thinking by Mr Trump, who nonetheless appears eager to take Russia at its word. None of it helps the US President or his Republican Party make a coherent closing argument to voters in the final stretch before the midterms.

title: Two killed after drone interception in Saudi Arabia
description: Nepali and Filipino killed, and Indian and Pakistani citizens wounded
content: Two people were killed and two injured in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after falling debris from a drone intercepted by Saudi air defences struck near a processing plant at Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield in the Eastern Province. The two killed were Filipino and Nepali citizens, while the injured were Pakistani and Indian. In a statement on X, the Ministry of Energy said the drone had been aimed at the plant and that falling debris caused a fire in a contractor’s vehicle outside its perimeter. The ministry said the incident had no impact on operations at the oilfield. Meanwhile, the US State Department has ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia, due to increased Houthi attacks on the kingdom, spokesman Tommy Pigott said. The order applies only to non-emergency US government personnel and their families. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have increased hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure, resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions, Mr Pigott said.

title: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh enters race to be next UN secretary general
description: Minister of State previously served as Emirates' representative to world body
content: UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh has entered the race to become the next UN secretary general. State media agency Wam reported on Wednesday that Ms Nusseibeh would be joining the list of candidates for the role leading the world body. Ms Nusseibeh previously served as the country's representative to the UN, and led its delegation during its recent two-year membership on the Security Council. Wam said that in a letter submitted to the UN Security Council from President Sheikh Mohamed, Ms Nusseibeh’s “deep experience of the United Nations, her judgment in addressing the ongoing international challenges, and her record of constructive work” were highlighted. “I have spent much of my professional life working in and around the United Nations, and I have seen first-hand what determined diplomacy can achieve – countries with profound differences finding common ground, and agreement where people said agreement was impossible," Ms Nusseibeh said after her candidacy was announced. "But I have also seen the cost when diplomacy falls short. When the distance between what we promise and what we deliver grows, trust erodes, and so does our ability to act. "I am standing to be Secretary General because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results. That is how we rebuild trust in the United Nations and ensure it delivers meaningful change for the people it exists to serve.” Secretary General Antonio Guterres's second and final term will finish at the end of the year. Ms Nusseibeh joins a crowded list of candidates to become UN secretary general. Eight people have been put forward for the role: Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Argentina’s Rafael Grossi ; Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan; Senegal's Macky Sall; Ecuador's Ivonne Baki ; Chile's Michelle Bachelet; Ecuador's Maria Fernanda Espinosa; and Uganda's Olara Otunnu. But none of the candidates has been able to get enough support among the members of the UN Security Council's members. Deliberations continue at the Security Council, with straw polls indicating that Ms Grynspan is the front-runner. With the current deadlock, it was expected that new candidates would enter the race. If selected, Ms Nusseibeh would be the first woman to hold the position of Secretary General of the UN and only the second Arab, after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali. She would also be the first Gulf Arab to assume the role. Ms Nusseibeh was appointed the UAE's ambassador to the UN in 2013. Before that, she served in a number of positions in the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, launching its Policy Planning Department and serving as its first director for three years. She also served as the head of the International Renewable Energy Agency (Irena) campaign task force at the ministry, and as director of research and communications for the Ministry of State for Federal National Council Affairs. She stepped down from her role as UN ambassador in mid-2024 to take up her role as UAE Minister of State. Former US official Brett McGurk described Ms Nusseibeh as a diplomat “who knows everyone and works with them” to get things done. “She would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said in a post on X. Ms Nusseibeh spoke to The National last month at the General Assembly in New York about the UAE's key messages at the UN and its commitment to multilateralism. “Although it seems that this is a really uncertain time ... a challenging time, it is not a time to give up hope. It is not a time to give up optimism about the future. It is not a time to give up diplomacy and a recommitment to multilateralism,” she said. In announcing her candidacy, Ms Nusseibeh said she wished to "offer myself to this office as I would serve it: speaking frankly with every government and answering to none". According to Wam, if elected, Ms Nusseibeh would prioritise ensuring peace and security worldwide. She called for clearer priorities, leadership and resources closer to the problems the UN exists to solve, stronger accountability for results, less duplication and empowering people to deliver on the field. The UN development system must also respond to a changing world in which progress on the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals remains deeply uneven. As secretary general, she said she would help to forge trustworthy commitments that governments can explain to their citizens. In addition, Ms Nusseibeh would focus on ensuring the equal application of international law, without double standards, which was necessary for the UN to maintain credibility.

title: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security, report says
description: Experts say maritime surveillance gaps could be closed with co-operation on offshore wind farms
content: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security through greater co-operation and surveillance technology, a new analysis says. The report from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington said that although offshore wind infrastructure has become more prevalent in recent decades, too little progress has been made in looking at how it could benefit national security. “By planning for dual-use capability from the outset, the United States can turn energy infrastructure into a force multiplier for national security, one that strengthens surveillance and warning in an increasingly contested maritime environment,” the CSIS report said. The analysis pointed out that in recent years, maritime and subsea infrastructure have become increasingly important – and also vulnerable to attack. “Subsea cables, which carry roughly 95 per cent of the world’s internet traffic, are particularly vulnerable to disruption,” the report said. In May, undersea internet and data cables were damaged in the Red Sea, causing connectivity problems for users in the Middle East, India and Pakistan. The cables were eventually repaired and most experts said that they had probably been severed by accident, but the incident still put subsea cable vulnerability in the spotlight. CSIS's report indicated that the proliferation of aerial drones, autonomous naval tools and unmanned underwater vehicles were also putting maritime security and subsea infrastructure in a more vulnerable position. It added that, concerningly, drone threats no longer come from state actors, but also from gangs and drug traffickers. The report concluded that if private offshore wind farm developers and governments could reach a consensus on how to best equip turbines with surveillance, sensors and data tracking tools, the end result could be “enhanced maritime domain awareness”. It highlighted the addition of surveillance systems to wind farms in and around Norway, Belgium, Poland and the UK. During a round-table discussion on Wednesday, Allegra Dawes, an energy security fellow at CSIS, said greater co-operation in enhancing offshore wind farms for maritime security could create a “force multiplier” effect, particularly for the US. “I think it gives guidance on the technologies that can actually create a stronger national security environment and also a stronger infrastructure backbone for energy,” she explained. Doug Wolfe, chief technology officer for Mighty Waves Energy, added that artificial intelligence could also be used along with the surveillance-enhanced wind turbines to bolster security on several levels. AI, he said, could help automate a lot of different maritime security workflows, while also helping to better understand what's happening under the sea. “It could very quickly characterise and detect whales, different types of whales and frequencies and all of those kinds of things,” he said.

title: Dubai sets new speed limits on five roads under traffic safety drive
description: Changes to routes will come into effect on November 1
content: Dubai's traffic authorities are reducing the speed limits on three roads and increasing them on two others, as part of the Dubai Traffic Safety Strategy. The changes have been authorised by the emirate's Roads and Transport Authority and Dubai Police. The speed limit has been raised from 60kph to 70kph on Al Mustaqbal Street, between Sheikh Rashid Street and Al Meydan Street, and on Latifa bint Hamdan Street, between Sheikh Zayed Road and Al Khail Road. On Al Asayel Street, between Oud Metha Street and Al Meydan Street, the limit will be increased from 60kph to 80kph. The limit on Al Rebat Street, between Marrakech Street and Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Road, will be reduced from 100kph to 90kph, and from 80kph to 70kph on Sheikh Sabah Al Ahmad Al Jaber Al Sabah Street, between 2nd December Street and Khalid bin Al Waleed Street. The changes will come into effect from November 1 and are in line with a major drive by Dubai transport authorities to boost road safety and improve traffic flow to keep pace with the needs of a growing population.

title: 'A sign of the tensions': Why a small tunnel sparked hysteria in Lebanon
description: Alarm over narrow shaft discovered north-east of Beirut reflects internal tensions and fears of renewed conflict
content: When a passer-by stumbled upon a tunnel north-east of Beirut earlier this week, almost immediately alarm bells began ringing over fears it could be connected to Hezbollah. It was the latest in a series of recent incidents that have raised tensions in an uneasy and deeply divided Lebanon, where Hezbollah has resisted government pressure to disarm as part of a stalled plan to halt Israeli bombings and occupation in the southern border region. The discovery of the tunnel in Fanar sparked a deluge of theories online. Some suggested that Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Shiite militia and political party, was building military infrastructure right in the Christian heartland of northern Matn. Others claimed gold prospectors had dug the tunnel. “You can't blame the people. It's because of the whole situation," said a Lebanese security source. "It's a sign of the tensions.” One of Israel's surveillance drones buzzed overhead as they spoke, making a return to the capital after an absence of a few weeks. Ultimately, the alarm over the tunnel appears to have been a storm in a teacup. The Lebanese army was sent to investigate and reported that it descended five metres before extending eight metres horizontally and contained neither weapons nor gold, only digging tools. The current theory is that it was probably a drop site for drug dealers, although no narcotics were found. “It's not for weapons. Maybe for drugs, but for sure not related to ammunition or weapons. It's very primitive, no way it would be for weapons,” said the Lebanese security official. They said the tunnel was very narrow and difficult to manoeuvre inside. “If it was gold I would be there, not here in the office,” they quipped. Another round of unfounded alarm followed the recent revelation that a Shiite businessman had bought dozens of plots of land in northern Matn between 2008 and 2014, allegedly to create a “Shiite crescent” there, according to MTV, a strongly anti-Hezbollah TV station. The businessman, Rida Jaffal, turned out to have no connection to Hezbollah and denied any “political or security project” or links to sanctioned people or groups. Other events that sparked alarm have been very real, and reflect fears that another round of war or internal violence could break out. They include the seizure of half a tonne of explosives from a vehicle travelling towards Beirut that Hezbollah has claimed, and confrontations between youths and security forces in the southern areas of Beirut, a stronghold of the group. “A tunnel in Matn, explosives in Dahr Al Baidar, and clashes with security forces in the southern suburbs … these are dangerous indicators that necessitate putting a definitive end … to Hezbollah's military organisation across all Lebanese territories,” Samy Gemayel, a prominent anti-Hezbollah MP, said after news of the tunnel broke. The clashes he referred to took place last week in the Gallerie Semaan neighbourhood on the edge of Beirut's southern suburbs, where police were sent to raid a warehouse that contained expired medicines, following an order from prosecutors. Upon arrival, they were surrounded by “a number of young men” – widely understood to be Hezbollah members or supporters – before the army was deployed to calm the situation. The two men were detained over the explosives seizure in Dahr Al Baidar, and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has ordered the security forces to expand their investigation. Hezbollah's insistence that the explosives were only for use against Israel has failed to assuage fears, given its connection to bombings of political opponents in the past. The Lebanese army itself has come under pressure both domestically and from abroad – mainly from the US and Israel – for not being proactive enough in containing Hezbollah's arsenal. Senior Lebanese officials are fearful that if the army were to directly confront the group, it could spark a civil war. A Hezbollah official conceded that “no doubt tensions are increasing”, but blamed a US interest in “creating an internal rift” and “internal authorities that seemingly follow every American interest”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called President Joseph Aoun last week and urged him to ensure the explosives seized from Hezbollah were not returned despite its demands. For political opponents of Hezbollah, the cause of the current tensions is clear. “Look, [the situation is] delicate because Hezbollah is refusing to update its system. Remove Hezbollah from the equation and there's nothing delicate any more,” said a senior official of the Lebanese Forces, parliament's largest party, which has long called for Hezbollah's disarmament. “Everybody knows that as long as Hezbollah still has one arm left, we are at risk of another war at any time.”

title: Sheikh Abdullah discusses Middle East security with Italian Foreign Minister
description: UAE and Italy strengthen bilateral relations amid regional security concerns
content: Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, has held talks with Italian deputy leader Antonio Tajani, focusing on Middle East security and bilateral ties. Sheikh Abdullah spoke with Mr Tajani, Italy's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Co-operation, during a phone call on Wednesday, state news agency Wam reported. The two reviewed the state of bilateral relations between the UAE and Italy, discussing ways to deepen their strategic partnership in line with both nations' development priorities and ambitions for sustainable economic growth. Discussions also touched on a broad range of regional and international developments, with particular attention paid to the current situation in the Middle East. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening efforts aimed at promoting security and stability across the region and at the international level.

title: US election candidate detained by Israel at West Bank olive harvest
description: Brad Lander says dozens of rabbis and other participants were also held
content: A candidate in the US midterm elections was briefly detained by Israeli troops during an olive harvest in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday. Brad Lander, a Democrat seeking election to Congress in New York, said he was one of dozens of detainees, who also included a group of rabbis. Mr Lander and others had been taking part in the harvest in a show of support for Palestinians, whose olive farming has become a symbol of tensions with Israel in the West Bank. The Israeli military said it had intervened due to a "security risk posed by conducting an unco-ordinated harvest near an Israeli community". It did not explain what the danger might have been. The army confirmed it had "detained those present". Mr Lander said the group was "simply harvesting olives" in a grove near Nehalim. "The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know," he said. He later said the Israeli military had released him with a warning while others remained in custody. "To be clear: Palestinians face far worse consequences every day," he added. Israel's Foreign Ministry later called Mr Lander's visit a stunt and a "calculated political provocation". Mr Lander is the Democratic nominee in New York's 10th congressional district. Forecasters say he is likely to win election to the House of Representatives in the midterms on November 3. A former city comptroller and self-described “liberal Zionist”, he defeated Representative Dan Goldman in the Democratic primary in June after turning their contest into a referendum on Israel . Mr Lander had criticised Mr Goldman for opposing legislation to block arms sales to Israel and for refusing to call its military campaign in Gaza a genocide . The incident comes days after a Washington Post journalist was attacked by masked Israeli settlers while accompanying Palestinian villagers harvesting olives. Violence involving Israeli settlers has sharply escalated in the occupied territory. At least two Palestinians have been killed by settlers since farmers started heading to their trees in late September. The olive harvest is not only crucial to the economy but also seen as a symbol of Palestinians' connection to the land.

title: Revealed: Full text of Makkah defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan
description: Mutual defence agreement accelerated after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
content: The National has obtained the full text of the Makkah Defence Pact between Saudi Arabia , Turkey and Pakistan after it was submitted to the Turkish parliament for approval. The text, which had not been made public when the agreement was signed in August, was confirmed as authentic by a Turkish parliamenary source and a Pakistani government official. Turkey's parliament must approve the pact before it becomes legally binding. But some articles have already been enacted. They include the appointment of a secretary general and the establishment of a central Strategic Political and Defence Committee. The three countries held an emergency meeting this month to arrange for the rapid deployment of military forces to Saudi Arabia as it comes under attack by Houthi rebels. The text of the pact, which has a Nato-style mutual defence clause, is published in full below. MAKKAH AGREEMENT FOR JOINT DEFENCE BETWEEN THE REPUBLIC OF TÜRKİYE, THE ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF PAKISTAN AND THE KINGDOM OF SAUDI ARABIA The Republic of Türkiye, the Islamic Republic of Pakistan and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (herein after referred to as "Party", "Parties" or "the core Parties"). Keeping in view the principles of mutual respect for sovereignty, principles of the UN charter, international laws and respective domestic laws; the "Parties" agree to further elevate existing cooperation mechanisms, coordination and integration to a joint defence agreement, Confirming their will to advance the relations amongst the "Parties" on the basis of enhanced cooperation, coordination and integration, including interoperability, readiness and effectiveness of armed forces in pursuit of common interests, thereby, cementing the existing bonds of friendship and brotherhood amongst the "Parties" and their peoples, Reaffirming the importance of principles of non-interference in domestic affairs, sovereign equality, territorial integrity and inviolability of internationally recognized borders of the "Parties", expressing that implementation of required mutual assistance measures is fundamental in case of armed aggression against their independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. Noting the importance of joint efforts and coordination in accordance with international law and the Charter of the United Nations for ensuring global and regional peace, stability and security, Noting the desire to deepen the existing cooperation between the authorities of the "Parties", in the fight against terrorism, Emphasizing the importance of strengthening the existing cooperation amongst the "Parties" in regional and international organizations in order to pursue a common stance on international issues, Noting, that the defence and defence industrial cooperation need tu be further strengthened amongst the "Parties", Have agreed on the following: Article 1 The "Parties" will cooperate in ensuring and protecting each other's independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and inviolability of their internationally recognized borders. In case the territorial integrity, sovereignty and internationally recognized borders of any of the "Parties" are threatened or endangered, the "Parties" will utilize all means necessary to eliminate the threats) and dangers). Article 2 Any external armed attack on any of the "Parties" will be considered an attack against all the "Parties". In case of an armed attack or military aggression against one of the "Parties" by another country or a group of countries, the "Parties" will immediately assist the "Party" so attacked, with all possibilities of mutual assistance to each other. Towards this end, the "Parties" will decide on the extent and nature of support to be provided after objective assessment of assistance required and will cooperate with each other, within the scope of available means. including military means and capabilities, with a view to exercise the right of self-defence granted by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations. Article 3 The "Parties", in the light of Article 2 of this Agreement, will closely cooperate in defence, defence industry, and security, promote relations amongst the armed forces of the "Parties", and implement agreed actions to enhance defence cooperation. Article 4 The "Parties" will hold regular consultations on international security issues. The "Parties" will assist and cooperate with each other continuously and efficiently to develop and strengthen individual and joint measures on the-basis of joint assessment to secure their vital interests and eliminate threats or dangers to their national security. Article 5 The "Parties" will strengthen their existing cooperation and joint efforts, including coordination at the operational level, in the fight against terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, that negatively affect regional and international stability and security. Article 6 In order to strengthen defence capabilities, the "Parties" will encourage personnel exchanges between defence institutions, joint, training programs, exercises, deployments and activities to increase the interoperability of the armed forces of the "Parties", both during peace and war. Article 7 In order to strengthen defence capabilities, the "Parties" will support collaboration amongst defence industry as mutually agreed in the following manner: a) Promoting defence co-production. b) Establishing joint research and development projects and defence innovation in specialized technologies. c) Training human capital and supporting military industries within the "Parties" territories, by experts from any "Party". d) Exchanging expertise and lessons learned in the areas of defence industries and defence research, development, and innovation. e) Any other areas as mutually agreed among the "Parties". Article 8 1. The "core Parties" shall establish a "Strategic Political and Defence Committee" comprising the Foreign Minister, Defence Minister and the Chief of Defence (CHoD)/ Chief of General Staff of the "Parties", to provide strategic direction for the joint defence, pursue and develop requirements of the defence and security cooperation between the "Parties" and overcome any hinderance in the execution of this Agreement. The Committee will hold meetings, alternating amongst the "Parties", twice a year. Where necessary, the leaders of the "Parties" may meet once a year. 2. The "Strategic Political and Defence Committee" shall be empowered to set up such subsidiary committees as may be necessary. 3. Separate special agreements/ protocois will be negotiated between the "Parties" for implementation of the areas of cooperation referenced in this Agreement, where required. 4. The "Strategic Political and Defence Committee" shall approve and exercise power over the mechanism and criteria for any other parties to join this agreement, with consensus amongst the "core Parties". 5. The "Strategic Political and Defence Committee" shall have a secretariat based in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The Secretariat shall conclude a headquarters agreement with the Kingdom. Detailed functioning of the Secretariat, its organization and Constitution will be decided by the 'core Parties" with consensus, at a later stage. 6. The Secretariat shall be headed by a Secretary General, who shall be appointed on rotation amongst the "core Parties", for a period of three years. The first Secretary General shall be from the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. 7. The provisions of this article do not prejudice the work of existing military cooperation committees among the "Parties", Article 9 To deepen cooperation in intelligence and appropriate coordination to that end, the "Parties" will share intelligence through secure channels, mutually agreed between the "Parties", with a commitment to information security, data protection and confidentiality. Article 10 The "Parties" shall provide logistic support including arms, ammunition, fuel, spare parts and other equipment support during peace, war, and other. contingencies depending on the availability and compatibility of logistic support services. Article 11 Without prejudice to international laws and respective domestic laws, the "Parties" have agreed to take this agreement as the legal basis in implementing its provisions and to suggest additional legal arrangements, if necessary. Article 12 This Agreement does not prejudice the rights and obligations of the "Parties" arising from the international agreements they have already concluded. Article 13 1. The "Parties" will respect the privacy of confidential information and documents they will obtain within the scope of this Agreement, and will respect national! legislation. 2. Confidential information and documents will not be shared with any government, company, or person of a country other than the "Parties". 3. It will be ensured that the principle of need-to-know-basis will be applied for the access to confidential information and documents, and for those who have appropriate-level security clearance. Article 14 Any dispute arising from the interpretation or application of this Agreementshall be resolved amicably through consultations and negotiations amongst the "Parties". Article 15 This Agreement may be amended by consultations and consensus amongst the "core Parties". Article 16 1. This Agreement shall be ratified in accordance with each Party's applicable procedures and shall come into force from the date of the last deposit of ratification into the headquarters of the secretariat of the "Strategic Political and Defence Committee" 2. This agreement shall remain in force indefinitely. 3. Any "Party" may withdraw from this Agreement after ten years from its coming into force by giving written notification to the other "Parties" through diplomatic channels at least three months prior to its intended withdrawal. 4. The termination of this Agreement or withdrawal from it shall not affect any ongoing activities or projects that have been agreed upon by the "Parties" prior to the termination or withdrawal date. 5. The responsibilities of the Parties regarding the protection of confidential information and documents and preventing its disclosure in accordance with this agreement will continue after the termination of this agreement or withdrawal from it. This Agreement is in triplicate in the Arabic, English and Turkish languages, the three texts being equally authentic. In case of any difference of understanding in the provisions of the texts, English text shall prevail. This Agreement has been signed at Makkah on Friday, 24/2/1448H corresponding 07 August 2026. For the Republic of Turkiye - Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, President For the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia - Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crowm Prince For the Islamic Republic of Pakistan - Muhammed Shehbaz Sharif, Prime Minister

title: UAE's new AI platform to slash VAT refund time for tourists to one day
description: Visitors leaving the country previously had to wait up to nine days for disbursement
content: The UAE has unveiled an artificial intelligence-powered platform that will reduce the waiting time for VAT refunds for tourists, from nine days to one. VAT refunds lower the cost of shopping for visitors by enabling them to recover a large share of the consumption tax. Abdulaziz Al Mulla, director general of the Federal Tax Authority, said the new platform "marks a significant advancement in the tourist tax refund journey, enhancing the tourist experience at their final point of contact with the country". The FTA, part of the Ministry of Finance, teamed up with Planet, the authorised operator of the VAT refund system for tourists in the UAE , to introduce the platform. “It embodies a proactive government model that places customers at the heart of service design, supported by integration and data-sharing between government entities and partners to deliver outstanding services in accordance with best practices," Mr Al Mulla said. “These efforts also reinforce the UAE’s distinguished international standing as a leading global destination for tourism and shopping, supported by its safe environment, attractive landmarks, diverse events and tourism facilities.” The platform comes after authorities introduced a system in 2024, enabling tourists to request VAT refunds directly through registered e-commerce platforms by submitting their travel document details at the time of purchase, before their orders are shipped. "The UAE has become one of the fastest countries in the world for tourist tax refunds, with the total time required for tourists to receive VAT refunds on their purchases reduced to one business day, compared to approximately nine days previously," said Mr Al Mulla. "This achievement reflects the continuous improvements introduced by the Authority to enhance this smart service."

title: PHP security flaw: Websites taken down as OpenAI spots issue with backbone of internet
description: OpenAI says it helped researchers discover the PHP vulnerability that could be exploited by hackers
content: Developers of PHP, a backbone language for the internet , have warned that a security update might take millions of websites offline temporarily, sparking panic in the tech world. The PHP Foundation, which describes itself as a "structured governance model designed to ensure transparency, accountability, and effective stewardship" of the language, announced a security update in a social media post to address "two critical vulnerabilities " that could be exploited by hackers . "PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update," the post said. According to the PHP Foundation, "PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, which confuses many people because the first word of the acronym is the acronym". PHP is an HTML-embedded scripting language designed during the earliest days of the internet that sought to simplify how web developers write and maintain websites quickly. Government websites around the world have gone dark to prepare for the PHP patch and to lessen the likelihood that the vulnerabilities are exploited. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was one of several world leaders to address the issue. "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," she posted on X. "Regarding PHP, which is used on many websites, the PHP security team has issued a warning about two critical vulnerabilities. Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix." The Netherlands, Finland, France and Australia have taken several government services offline temporarily to implement the patch and prevent any problems. In the US, the National Security Agency's cybersecurity division also composed a strongly worded warning. "Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update," the NSA's post on X read. "If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated. NSA will follow up shortly with more specific guidance." According to technology giant OpenAI, one of the company's models found the PHP vulnerability. "Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory," a statement from the maker of ChatGPT read. "It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact." OpenAI said that the discovery of the vulnerability is proof of concept that its Patch the Planet security initiative is creating a safer web infrastructure. "To our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare," the company said. Moshe Siman Tov Bustan, a lead researcher for Ox Security, a New York-based network security firm said that the PHP vulnerability is not just fear without substance. "If you have a publicly accessible PHP instance and haven't patched it, start from the assumption that you're exposed," he said. adding that if evidence of exploitation is found, people should also assume compromise and not just exposure. "This is about as broad as a critical vulnerability gets,” he added. On Wednesday afternoon, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), a division of the Department of Homeland Security also urged organisations, businesses and others to quickly install the patch to update PHP. "These vulnerabilities, known as 'php2shell,' allow for unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP and affect all PHP installations serving web requests," a news release from CISA read in part.

title: Dubai Police issue more than 7,730 traffic fines over noisy vehicles and illegal modifications
description: In first nine months of this year 1,630 vehicles were impounded
content: Dubai Police issued 7,735 traffic fines and impounded 1,630 vehicles for excessive noise and unauthorised modifications during the first nine months of this year, as authorities stepped up efforts to protect residents and improve road safety. The force recorded 2,045 breaches for excessive vehicle noise, resulting in 333 vehicles being impounded. A further 5,690 breaches involved illegal modifications to vehicle engines or chassis, leading to the impounding of 1,297 vehicles. Brigadier Juma Salem bin Suwaidan, director of the traffic department at Dubai Police, said loud vehicles, particularly cars and motorcycles fitted with modified engines or exhaust systems, pose a concern for residents. “Excessive noise can disturb residential neighbourhoods, especially at night. It affects public well-being,” Brig bin Suwaidan said on Wednesday. “Sudden or unusually loud sounds can also distract drivers and other road users, increasing the risk of accidents.” Dubai Police are intensifying inspections and traffic monitoring to identify offenders and take legal action, Brig bin Suwaidan added. Under UAE traffic regulations, driving a vehicle that causes excessive noise carries a Dh2,000 fine and 12 black points. Illegal modifications to a vehicle engine or chassis carry a Dh1,000 fine, 12 black points and 30 days of impoundment. Dubai Police are also preparing to expand the use of devices that detect and measure vehicle noise, with plans to use the technology more on roads and in areas where breaches are reported. “The devices will help authorities identify sources of excessive noise and offending vehicles, strengthening monitoring and enforcement,” Brig bin Suwaidan said. “The expansion reflected the force’s commitment to using smart technologies to improve road safety and protect residents’ quality of life.” He urged motorists, especially young drivers, to comply with traffic laws and avoid illegal engine and exhaust modifications. “Stronger enforcement and public awareness have contributed to a recent decline in excessive vehicle noise,” he said. Dubai Police said last November that they would expand their radar capacity to catch noisy vehicles and bring more calm to the emirate’s roads. The force is using AI-enhanced cameras that can detect noises and document offences whenever the noise limit is crossed. Dubai Police issued 12,019 fines for unauthorised vehicle modifications causing excessive noise and significant changes to engines or chassis in 2024. The force encouraged motorists and community members to visit Aman roads platforms for traffic safety guidance and educational resources aimed at preventing accidents and protecting lives and property.

title: France’s diesel deal with Gulf states will not make fuel 'cheap overnight’ for European country
description: But additional supply gives refiners, distributors and traders confidence that barrels are coming, say experts
content: France's deal to buy diesel from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain will not make the fuel “cheap overnight” for the European country although it will also not make it more expensive, according to experts. The three Gulf states are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said on Tuesday during President Emmanuel Macron's regional tour . The aim is to reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. The deal “will not make French diesel cheap overnight, but it can stop it [from] becoming scarcer and even more expensive”, said Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets. “The bigger value is psychological: France is no longer buying in a panic,” Mr Aslam added. “Gulf supply gives refiners, distributors and traders confidence that physical barrels are coming, which can compress the scarcity premium before it fully reaches the pump.” European diesel has reached about $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. While the deal can temporarily ease France’s diesel supply shortage, it is unlikely to drive a sustained decline in fuel prices, according to Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “The additional diesel arriving in France would ease competition among importers for limited supplies. This could reduce the scarcity premium that buyers pay for immediately available fuel, particularly if inventories are low,” he added. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in both October and November, totalling 190,000 tonnes. The UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. The duration of the supply agreements matter – if UAE and Bahrain shipments continue for several months, they could have a longer-lasting effect on supply security and prices, Mr Valecha said. “If they are temporary or cargoes are delayed, the relief could be short-lived. The wider diesel shortage is a significant driver. The diesel supply squeeze remains severe. The International Energy Agency has warned that shortages could persist well into 2027.” On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. European commercial gasoil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July, while US diesel stocks reached a 14-year seasonal low by September. Combined gasoil exports from Russia and the Middle East dropped by more than 60 per cent, equivalent to 1.3 million barrels per day. With Mr Macron’s current Gulf visit, the focus would remain on making fuel more affordable at the petrol station rather than just securing France’s fuel supply security, Mr Valecha said. “Analysts estimate that a large release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by $20 to $30 per barrel, or about €0.10 to €0.15 per litre, at the pump, with prices possibly dropping within a few days,” he added. The latest deal’s importance “lies in the signal it gives to market”, Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer, said. “Despite the recent escalations, oil products find their way out of the Middle East. One should look beyond this specific deal. More supplies from the Middle East ease oil products tightness globally, irrespective if the buyers of single cargoes are in Europe or elsewhere, as this is a global market,” he said. There is indication that oil product exports from the Middle East are picking up and that refineries in Asia are putting more oil products on the market, he added. However, according to Mr Valecha, diesel exports are not expected to pick up any time soon from the Middle East in a way that could bring down costs significantly. “This is because oil product markets are expected to remain tight through mid-2027, even if current war-related disruptions ease. The reason for this being [that] global supply is constrained by an unusually large upswing in refinery maintenance,” he said. Even when Middle East diesel exports rise again, the price effect will lag the headline, agreed Mr Aslam. “The constraint is not only production – it is secure shipping, insurance, tanker availability and the ability to move refined products reliably into Europe,” he said. “The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are showing why dependable Gulf suppliers matter: sustained cargoes, rather than one-off emergency shipments, are what would truly pull diesel prices down.” Europe could diversify imports to reduce reliance on a single source, with potential deals with the US or Asian suppliers helping to ease the current crunch, according to Mr Valecha. “Fuel tax cuts and price subsidies may also offer immediate relief, but they are costly and risk sustaining demand when supplies are tight,” he said. While there have been suggestions that consumers curb demand by shifting to electric vehicles or car pooling, Europe cannot solve a diesel shortage by simply asking consumers to drive less, said Mr Aslam. “Diesel is the bloodstream of its freight, construction, farming and industry. France and its neighbours need a three-part response: co-ordinated reserve releases, guaranteed supply contracts with reliable producers, and a faster shift of freight toward rail and electrified alternatives,” he said. “The mistake would be treating this as a temporary oil price spike. It is a refining and logistics security problem.”

title: Macron visits Saudi Arabia in show of solidarity amid Houthi attacks
description: He met the Saudi Crown Prince and exchanged views on regional and international developments
content: French President Emmanuel Macron arrived in Riyadh on Wednesday on a surprise visit, in a show of solidarity with Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks. Mr Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during the unannounced stop on ⁠his three-day tour ​of the ⁠Gulf. He had already visited Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait. The two leaders exchanged views on regional and international developments and discussed co-ordinating efforts to enhance regional and international security and stability, the Saudi Press Agency reported. They also reviewed the historical and strategic relations between Saudi Arabia and France, existing co-operation and ways to strengthen ties across various fields, Spa said. Mr Macron is the first western leader to visit the kingdom since Yemen 's Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month. The visit is “to ​demonstrate France's solidarity with the kingdom in the face of attacks launched by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts aimed at securing and diversifying ​hydrocarbon ‌supplies”, the ⁠French ​presidency said. Riyadh has come under heavy fire as Yemen's heaviest fighting in years spilt over into Saudi Arabia. Attacks on the capital's airport killed 17 people and injured 333 this month. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war at the request of the government in 2015, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring ⁠sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace in place until this year. Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept along the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab Al Mandeb strait.

title: What’s the real technology behind the UAE’s world-class public services?
description: The Emirates may not have America’s Silicon Valley, but it has a different advantage
content: The UAE’s e-government services are among the world’s best and frequently involve using cutting-edge digital technologies more effectively than the countries that developed them. The culture of public administration plays a central role in helping us understand the country’s proficiency. It also reminds us how acquiring the best technologies is often the easiest rather than the hardest part of ensuring high-quality government services. In September, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on X that American citizens would be allowed to complete first-time passport applications online starting next year, following the previous launch of online renewal in late 2024. While many Americans rejoiced at the impending jump in convenience, Emiratis’ immediate reaction was most likely surprise that it has taken this long. The Emirates has been allowing online renewal since 2014 – using hardware and software created by Silicon Valley. More generally, despite ranking a respectable 19th in the 2024 UN E-Government Development Index, the US was still eight positions below the UAE. Moreover, the actual quality of its e-services on the ground can be uneven. New York City’s municipal services are among the world’s very best, yet the disbursal of unemployment benefits during the Covid-19 pandemic was disrupted by antiquated systems dating back to the 1970s. An analysis of the US-UAE difference in a transaction as seemingly straightforward as renewing a passport reveals a series of proximate causes. On the technical side, the fragmentation of identification systems under America’s federal structure obstructs the process of generating a centralised workflow. On the administrative side, tightening security restrictions on employment within the federal government makes it harder for agencies to hire the top talent that America’s world-leading technology sector produces. At a broader social level, the partisanship that has developed in the political landscape reduces the incentive that politicians have to prioritise government service delivery. However, these surface-level factors are manifestations of a much deeper difference between the US and the UAE in the culture of public administration. More specifically, the US philosophy towards public administration developed in the 17th and 18th centuries when one of the most salient concerns held by elites and ordinary people alike was the need to erect safeguards that ensure that government officials act in the public interest. This mindset has been codified in the US Constitution and is the cornerstone of its social traditions. In contrast, the UAE emerged in an era when people’s perception of government was that it is the primary vehicle for organising development and delivering prosperity to society. This is reflected in its own societal pillars including the UAE Vision 2021 . America’s history is intertwined with that of the UK, both because many of its population in the 17th and 18th centuries came directly from Britain and because the American intellectuals who drafted its Constitution drew heavy inspiration from the UK. This transmitted core cultural values that Americans take for granted today, with the repeated lesson being that unchecked power breeds abuse. This started with Charles I’s conflict with parliament over taxation, culminating in the bloody English Civil War. The harsh, quasi-military rule of the Interregnum reinforced these fears, while the crisis precipitated by James II’s attempts at turning England back into a Catholic country brought about the 1688 Glorious Revolution and the institutionalisation of checks on the sovereign’s power, with the philosophical underpinning being provided by the work of thinkers such as John Locke. These imported values were augmented by King George III ’s transgressions in dealing with his American colonies, which ultimately caused the 1776 Revolution – a pivotal episode in shaping how ordinary Americans today think about the role of government. The UAE’s history has forged a much more paternalistic and benign view of government. Traditional tribal institutions associated leadership with protection and responsibility for the community’s welfare. Following the formation of the federation in 1971, this relationship was reinforced by the transformation of living standards under leaders such as the UAE’s Founding Father , the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. Within living memory, government directed the development of modern infrastructure, expanded access to education and health care and helped create opportunities that earlier generations could scarcely have imagined. This experience supports an expectation that leaders should actively guide development and mobilise public institutions to solve problems. One result of these diverging US-UAE traditions is different reactions to an inadequate government service such as a malfunctioning passport renewal portal. In the US, the culture prompts the view that “this confirms that civil servants cannot do anything properly”, demotivating politicians who are looking to address the technical and administrative barriers to success and reinforcing the cycle of distrust. In the UAE, in contrast, the culture brings about the response “give this institution the capability to fulfil its responsibilities”, with government agencies rising to the challenge of solving the problem. A key lesson to draw from the example of passport renewal is that possessing the technology to digitise a government transaction is frequently the most straightforward issue that needs to be addressed. What plays a much more important role – and what is much harder to forge – is a culture where government officials do not tolerate failure, and where ensuring the comfort of citizens is considered by citizens and officials alike to be the state’s North Star.

title: UFC 333: Volkanovski targets quick finish as he bids to make history against Evloev in Abu Dhabi
description: Australian puts his featherweight title on the line against undefeated Russian at Etihad Arena
content: Alexander Volkanovski has promised the best version of himself for Saturday's headline bout at UFC 333 – and to deliver a belated wedding-anniversary present to his wife. The Australian puts his UFC featherweight title on the line against top-ranked Russian challenger Movsar Evloev in Abu Dhabi. Plenty wondered if Volkanovski, who many believe is the greatest 145-pounder of all time, was on the decline following back-to-back losses to Islam Makhachev and then Ilia Topuria. He answered those critics in the best way with two polished performances against Diego Lopes. The first saw him reclaim the featherweight belt; the second saw him defend it. At 38, Volkanovski knows he isn't getting any younger. But with greater experience comes greater wisdom. A change in approach to training and preparation means that his best years may still be ahead of him. "Performance-wise, yes," Volkanovski said when asked by The National if he believes he will be the best version of himself against Evloev. "I'm not trying to lie to everyone and say like I'm the exact person I was when I was 22 years old. I'm not saying that, but that don't matter. I'm still in incredible shape. I'm still so explosive. We obviously know I've got that fight IQ. I truly do believe like I can go out there and look the best I've ever looked." They say styles make fights . If Volkanovski has the advantage in striking, Evloev definitely has the upper hand in wrestling. The Russian is undefeated in 20 pro MMA fights, and Volkanovski says his opponent is overdue a shot at UFC gold. He welcomes the challenge. "I just think stylistically, it's a great matchup for me. He does bring a lot of challenges," said Volkanovski. "These are definitely challenges that a lot of other fighters will struggle with, not just me. So these problems, I'll be smiling through the challenges he's going to give me. "What I put myself through in training camp and throughout my career, I'm not going to crumble. I'm never going to panic. That's not going to happen. Like, bring it on. You can try and take me down all day, even if you get me down. I'm going to be smarter and I'll get back up." Few can match Volkanovski's minutes in the octagon, especially in championship bouts. All three of his fights with Max Holloway went the five-round distance, as did his recent double-header with Lopes. Of his 28 victories, 12 have come via the judges' scorecards, with 13 by way of knockout. He has spoken in the build-up about ending the fight in "wild fashion" but is equally prepared to drag Evloev, who is fighting for a UFC title for the first time, into deep waters. He hopes it's the former. Volkanovski has travelled to Abu Dhabi with family in tow, including his wife, Emma. They celebrated their wedding anniversary on Tuesday, and Volkanovski said he hopes to make it a quick night's work for Mrs Volkanovski's sake. "My present will be not making her stress too long on the sidelines," Volkanovski said with a smile. "So I'm going to go out there and try and make it a quick one. "I'm prepared for an absolute war. That's just how it is. But I think I can go out there and take him out, and that's not a knock on him, it's just stylistically where I think we're matched and how I'm going to approach this fight." Saturday's bout will be Volkanovski's 12th consecutive title fight and the sixth defence of the featherweight belt across two reigns. Beat Evloev, and he will surpass the great Jose Aldo for most title fight wins in the division, with nine. Volkanovski said that, at this stage of his career, the numbers mean nothing to him. His motivation comes from testing himself against the best. "I don't care about it," he insisted. "It is cool, but that's not what drives me. The most important thing is the challenges that are in front of me and getting through them challenges. That's what puts a smile on my face." The man hoping to wipe that smile off Volkanovski's face has had to bide his time waiting for a title shot. "I have been waiting seven years since I signed with the UFC for this moment," Evloev said. "Now, it's just three days until the historical moment for me, for my family. I'm grateful for this moment, for this opportunity." Evloev has a body of work that includes victories over Dan Ige, Lopes, Arnold Allen, Aljamain Sterling and most recently Lerone Murphy. The undefeated Russian, 32, is another fighter well drilled in going the distance. Of those 20 wins, 13 have come via decision. Evloev has been down to the coalface so many times it's no wonder his teeth aren't charred black. He agrees with those who see Volkanovski as the GOAT of the featherweight division, but he is determined to seize his moment at Etihad Arena. "I had a couple of five-round fights too. I do a lot of sparring every week, like twice a week, since I was 20, and I got enough experience to fight for five rounds." Evloev said. "In my mind, I was making myself ready to fight against Volkanovski for the last couple of years. To become the best, you need to be champion of your division. In my mind, I won this fight 1,000 times. Mentally, I'm ready, and on Saturday, I'm gonna show you." When asked what it would mean to him to walk out of Abu Dhabi as champion, Evloev said: "I have some feelings inside, but it's hard to explain, and I prefer explaining when I win the belt, not before."

title: 'A matter of time' warning on mass deaths in UK migrant boat crossing
description: Smugglers using mega dinghies to keep up profits as law enforcement cuts of supply of boats
content: A multiple casualty event involving migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats is “only a matter of time”, the UK’s border security chief has warned. Duncan Capps, the Border Security Commander, said he was worried by the increase in the size of boats and the number of migrants getting on to each vessel. Mr Capps told the UK Parliament’s Home Affairs Committee that this was a result of smugglers adapting their tactics in the face of action by the British and French authorities to cut off the supply of boats. But while this has reduced the number of arrivals to the lowest point since 2020 and could even push them to 2019 levels, the risks for the asylum seekers themselves are increasing. A record 230 migrants were spotted this year on a vessel described as a “mega dinghy”. “I think the things that worry me about it most this year have been the increase in size of the boats and the increase in occupancy,” he told MPs. “You've seen this year we had a boat with 230 migrants. It is only a matter of time until we have a mass casualty event in the Channel. It's extraordinary that that has not happened so far.” Mr Capps, a former army general who was commandant of the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, heads the Border Security Command , which was set up by the Labour government after it won the 2024 general election to tackle people smuggling gangs. He told MPs that smugglers were now moving further south from around the Dunkirk and Calais area to Normandy, in a bid to avoid being intercepted while moving their boats to launch sites on beaches. “My absolute aim over this next two or three months working with our French partners is to shut that route down for lots of very good reasons," said Mr Capps. “Not least of which, it's nearly 60 nautical miles. If people try that in the winter, we are going to have loss of life, and it really, really concerns me.” Mr Capps said there are currently around 3,800 migrants in northern France, mostly living in a squalid camp near Dunkirk, which is double the figure of around two years ago. He said that was down to the French making it very difficult to get across the Channel. The UK and France signed a £660 million ($891 million) three-year agreement to prevent migrant Channel crossings, which has been credited with reducing numbers .

title: Mindful Movements: October wellness and fitness news and things to do
description: Fill your calendar with competitive events, visualisation sessions and visits to new athleisure stores this month
content: Cooler weather is almost upon us, meaning it's time to get outside once again. Hiking season may have to wait a few more weeks, but outdoor runs are back on the table, along with meditation sessions under the moonlight. This October also brings a host of studio openings and competitive fitness events. Here's a pick of events and updates to know about this month. Wellfit is opening its first Abu Dhabi outpost on October16. The Hyrox-affiliated fitness centre will have a dedicated training area for the discipline with certified coaches and equipment including sleds, air runners and BikeErgs. The mega-club will also feature 72 cardio machines, 50 pin and plate-loaded strength machines, free-weight and cable training areas, and equipment specifically targeting glutes and hips. A recovery zone will be fitted with Hyperice equipment. Group fitness will be offered in a dedicated studio, alongside a 22-bike spin studio and separate grappling and striking zones. Wellness facilities will include men's and women's saunas and cold plunge pools, experiential showers and changing areas. Families will also be catered for, with children's classes and a dedicated studio offering programmes including Junior Martial Arts. Jumeirah Saadiyat Island is launching The Harmony Programme, a four-week fitness offering that combines Reformer Pilates with strength training to build muscle, improve mobility and boost flexibility. Participants complete four Reformer Pilates sessions and three upper and lower-body strength-training sessions each week, with the programme focusing on areas including core, posture, balance, co-ordination and muscle development. The four-week programme costs Dh3,500 and includes two recovery sessions, complimentary access to spa facilities, one day of pool and beach access, and a 20 per cent discount on spa treatments. A one-week trial is also available for Dh1,000, including a personalised training programme, one recovery session and spa access. Hyrox returns to Abu Dhabi at Adnec Centre for three days of running and functional fitness. The fitness race combines eight 1km runs with eight workout stations, including sled pushes and pulls, rowing, sandbag lunges and wall balls, with competitors racing individually, in pairs or as part of a relay team. For the first time, the opening day on Friday, October 23, will be exclusively for women, with female athletes and spectators taking over the event. The competition will then open up for a full weekend of racing. October 23-25; all-day event; participation tickets start at Dh510; spectator tickets from Dh65 Abu Dhabi wellness studio Bodytree is expanding with a Pilates studio at The Galleria Al Maryah Island, set to open in October. The home-grown brand began with a studio in Al Bateen 19 years ago, and its latest space will focus on Reformer Pilates group classes. Ahead of the opening, Bodytree is offering 50 founding memberships for Dh13,200 per year, with the rate remaining the same for as long as the membership is active. Explore the connection between movement and creativity at Movement Practice Abu Dhabi, a series of workshops led by Lillian Castillo Muller at the Cultural Foundation. October's session, titled Between Tides, explores the space between bodies through touch, weight and listening. Held in collaboration with Yaxen Dance Academy, the three-hour workshop invites participants to experiment with movement and contemporary art forms, including poetry, music and visual imagery, without following a fixed choreography. October 24; 5pm-8pm; free on registration Runners can support wildlife conservation while getting their kilometres in at Run for Impact: Saving the Arabian Sand Cat, taking place on October 25 at Yas Bay Waterfront. Open to all ages and fitness levels, the event offers 3km, 5km and 10km distances, with races beginning from 6.45am. The Dh50 registration fee will go towards research and conservation efforts to protect the Arabian sand cat, which is listed as endangered on the Abu Dhabi Red List of Species. Al Ain Zoo will also host family-friendly activities from 6am to 10am, including themed face painting, photo opportunities and wildlife trivia before an awards ceremony at 9am. October 25; from 6am; Dh50 Banyan Tree Dubai is teaming up with Al Jalila Foundation to support its Pinktober campaign with a retreat exclusively for women on October 24. Attendees will start the morning with a Kundalini yoga session before an interactive breast cancer awareness talk led by experts at holistic health clinic Maison Sante.
