Federal and state authorities say that they are still trying to determine the motive for the attack. The investigation is being supported by the joint counterterrorism task force, including the Australian spy agency ASIO. “We do believe this was a deliberate but isolated incident,” said Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush at a press conference on Wednesday. He said state authorities had “no intelligence holdings” against Mr Nugent. “There was nothing known to us that would’ve arisen or piqued our interest or given any indication that he was an immediate threat,” Mr Bush said. It was unclear whether Mr Nugent has legal representation. In a statement obtained by The Guardian , Mr Nugent’s father and his wife said that Mrs Haines had been a friend for decades and called the attack “unfathomable”. The attack has caused shock in Australia, where physical violence against politicians is very rare, and sparked calls for a cooling of recent escalating rhetoric in the public sphere.

title: Drone attack by SAF kills at least 153 in disputed border region
description: Government of South Sudan summons SAF-backed Sudanese ambassador to protest over attack
content: A drone strike by the Sudanese Armed Forces on a fuel depot in the disputed Abyei region, on the border between Sudan and South Sudan, has killed at least 153 people, official sources said on Wednesday. Three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and a conflict expert, told Reuters that the strike hit a fuel depot that had previously been used by the Rapid Support Forces. Yohana Ngor, caretaker Information Minister in Abyei, said the death toll from the attack on Amiet Market on Monday had risen to 153 from 73 and was likely to climb further. “The fire is still burning, so the recovery process of the dead is still continuing. The situation is terrible,” he added. Some bodies had been burnt to ashes, he said. Video from the scene on Tuesday showed charred, twisted remains of vehicles and buildings. Flames billowed from one building as residents looked at the damage. Mr Ngor blamed the SAF, led by Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, for the strike. Officials in Sudan's SAF-backed government said that the RSF was active in parts of Abyei, a claim Mr Ngor denied. The Government of South Sudan said in a statement that it has “learnt with grave concern of the drone attack carried out by the Sudanese Armed Forces against Amiet Market, situated north of Abyei Town”. It added that the attack struck multiple locations within the market, resulting in civilian casualties, injuries and significant destruction of property. “Following this incident, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Co-operation summoned the ambassador of the Republic of the Sudan to convey the government's strong protest and deep concern regarding the attack and its implications for the security of civilians and the stability of the Abyei area,” it added. “The government calls upon the Republic of the Sudan to refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property. The government further urges that issues relating to the Abyei area be addressed through established diplomatic channels and existing mechanisms for dialogue and engagement,” it warned. The UN Interim Security Force for Abyei had warned in May that the RSF's presence in the region had increased insecurity. It said delays in determining Abyei's fate as a disputed region had put civilians and UN personnel at risk. On Tuesday, the UN strongly condemned a series of drone attacks in Abyei and other areas. “We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure – these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict,” spokesman Stephane Dujarric said in New York. The attack in Abyei pushed the death toll from a series of strikes in recent days past 250, in one of the bloodiest weeks of a civil war that has spilt across Sudan's borders. The war erupted in April 2023 between the SAF and the paramilitary RSF, causing a major humanitarian crisis and drawing in local militias and foreign powers. South Sudan gained independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have laid claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. The region borders Sudan's Kordofan region, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war. Last week, the UN called for an immediate halt to drone attacks in the civil war, warning that the weapons had become the leading cause of civilian casualties this year. Rosemary DiCarlo, undersecretary general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the Security Council that a mutual ban on drones had the “potential to dramatically improve protection for civilians”. UN data shows that more than 1,100 people were killed by drone strikes across Sudan during the first half of this year. Ms DiCarlo's comments on Friday came after an air strike killed five children in a town controlled by the RSF in North Kordofan, according to the Emergency Lawyers, a rights group monitoring abuses in Sudan’s conflict, who blamed the SAF for the attack. Last month, a UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan found that the SAF used foreign-supplied drones in operations that harmed civilians . While it repeated accusations that external players have supported the RSF by facilitating weapons transfers, the report cast a harsher light on the actions of the SAF, which has rejected ceasefire attempts and has vowed to continue the war until it achieves victory. The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan, established by the UN Human Rights Council, said that “available evidence indicates that, since late 2023, the Sudanese Armed Forces has significantly expanded its drone capabilities through foreign-supplied systems”. The findings documented attacks attributed to the SAF on locations where “civilian presence was substantial or readily foreseeable”, citing at least four waves of drone strikes on hospitals, markets and other civilian locations in different areas.

title: Arafat Minhas's record ODI performance powers Pakistan to latest victory
description: Hosts cruise to 87-run win in tri-series against England after all-rounder scores fifty and picks up six wickets
content: Pakistan continued their upward journey in white-ball cricket as they thrashed England by 87 runs in the second match of the ODI tri-series in Rawalpindi on Tuesday. Arafat Minhas put in a record all-round performance to hand Pakistan their second win of the tournament. The hosts batted first and posted 302-9, with contributions from almost their entire line-up. Pakistan's Asian Games final star Hasan Nawaz (79) and Minhas (59) led the way as the team in green crossed the 300-run mark. In reply, England made a strong start as openers Ben Duckett and Tom Banton added 91 for the first wicket. At 165-3 in the 29th over, England seemed on track. But left-arm spinner Minhas turned the game on its head. Minhas ran through the middle and lower order on a responsive pitch, finishing with figures of 6-40 as England were bundled out for 215. It turned out to be one of the finest all-round performances in ODI cricket history. Minhas became only the seventh player to score fifty or more runs and pick up six or more wickets in the same match. Minhas had shown glimpses of his potential earlier in the year during the Pakistan Super League while playing for Multan Sultans, taking nine wickets at an economy of under nine in 10 matches. His younger brother and flamboyant opener Sameer has been talked about more often but the older Minhas, still only 21, has the more well-rounded game, which makes him versatile and a ready-made replacement for the likes of Mohammad Nawaz and Shadab Khan. Pakistan ODI captain Shaheen Afridi said Minhas is a complete cricketer in both aspects of the game. “[Minhas] is a very good talent. He is not just a bowling all-rounder or a batting all-rounder; he is a proper all-rounder. I think the way he started his innings in batting and then delivered in bowling, it's good for us. Hopefully he will deliver in many more games,” the left-arm seamer said. Pakistan have now won five out of eight ODIs this year and 11 out of 17 T20 Internationals. While they haven't won any major ICC tournaments in nearly a decade, the new crop of players are putting in performances that make the team a serious challenger for upcoming world events like the 2027 ODI World Cup and the 2028 T20 World Cup and LA Olympics. “As a team, we did some good things, but we need to improve. Our preparation for the World Cup, how we built this team, the way our fast bowlers bowled, and then Arafat as well … I think it was a good sign for us,” Afridi added. Pakistan had won the preceding T20 series against Sri Lanka following their commendable run at the Asian Games where they lost a close final to India.

title: Iraq closes major border crossing with Iran over 'security arrangements', says official
description: Al Sheeb crossing is gateway for food products, construction materials and pilgrims
content: Iraq has closed the Al Sheeb border crossing with Iran to travellers and goods, according to a government official. The closure, which took effect at 6am local time on Wednesday, will remain in place until further notice, the official told The National . The move followed direct orders from Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi ⁠and the decision was taken to “reconsider ​the ​security ‌arrangements ⁠inside the crossing”, the official said. A border official told Reuters that the closure was due to a review in security and the installation of detection equipment to stop the smuggling of prohibited items. The crossing, in the south-eastern province of Maysan, is one of the main commercial gateways between the two countries, used for transporting food and construction materials, as well as by Iranian pilgrims heading to holy sites in Najaf and Karbala. Other border crossings with Iran are expected to be closed gradually, the government official said. If crossings such as Shalamcheh, Zurbatiyah and Mandali are also closed, it would significantly disrupt Iraq-Iran trade, which exceeded $10 billion last year. Iranian state media reported that Tehran was not given advance notice that the Al Sheeb border crossing would be closed. The matter is under review, Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand was quoted as saying. Temporary closure of border crossings for several hours for security reasons “is considered routine, and in such cases does not require prior notification to the other party”, Mr Zeinivand said. According to an agreement between Iran and Iraq, any closure for more than one day requires advance notice, he said. “Border closures create more problems for Iraqi traders and economic activists, and their negative effects are greater for the other side,” Mr Zeinivand said. “Therefore, this is a common issue, and we hope that the problem will be resolved with investigations carried out.” Iraq had temporarily closed the Shalamcheh crossing in September as a precautionary security measure after drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. The closure of Al Sheeb is likely to push up prices of basic goods, especially fresh produce and Iranian building materials that dominate southern markets. The decision is likely to spark outrage among pro-Iran political blocs, who have already accused the government of leaning too far towards Washington at a time when the US maintains sweeping sanctions on Tehran. Critics within the Co-ordination Framework, the largest Shiite parliamentary bloc for mainly Iran-backed factions, argue that closing commercial crossings effectively enforces US sanctions and harms border provinces that are economically dependent on Iranian trade, while supporters say Baghdad needs to tighten border control and diversify imports. The Prime Minister’s office has not yet issued a formal statement explaining the scope or duration of the closures.

title: Jennifer Lopez completes Abu Dhabi F1 concert line-up for 2026
description: US pop star will join Alex Warren to perform in the capital on December 4, the last act to be named in this year's after race concerts at Etihad Live
content: Jennifer Lopez will perform at this year's Abu Dhabi Formula One Grand Prix after-race concerts , joining US singer-songwriter Alex Warren at Etihad Live on Friday, December 4. The American singer completes the double bill for the second night of the four-day concert series, held alongside the season-ending race at Yas Marina Circuit . Access to the after-race concerts is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders. It will be Lopez's third concert in the capital in less than two years, following a sold-out performance at Saadiyat Nights in February 2025 and a show at Etihad Arena five months later that attracted more than 14,000 fans. The latter was part of her Up All Night international tour, featuring a 90-minute set with elaborate choreography, costume changes and new arrangements of songs spanning her career. Ranked among The National's best UAE concerts of 2025 , the performance included a mash-up of Jenny from the Block and Queen's We Will Rock You , as well as a flamenco-inspired rendition of her debut single If You Had My Love . Her Saadiyat Nights appearance came after a difficult 2024, when her album This Is Me... Now struggled commercially, while its accompanying musical film, This Is Me... Now: A Love Story , drew mixed reviews. A planned North American tour was also cancelled. Lopez has since completed a Las Vegas residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, featuring more than two dozen musical numbers across four acts, with orchestral arrangements accompanying some of her best-known songs. The final performance was filmed for The JLO Show , a concert special scheduled to premiere in the US on November 26. She also teamed up with Brazilian DJ Alok for the single Everything's Fine , released in June in two versions. Lopez launched her recording career with the 1999 album On the 6 , which included If You Had My Love and Waiting for Tonight . Her subsequent hits include Jenny from the Block , On the Floor and Let's Get Loud , while her film credits range from Selena and Maid in Manhattan to Hustlers . Sharing the Friday bill is Warren, who makes his UAE debut after scoring an international hit with Ordinary . His latest album, Wildchild , was released in August, following his 2025 debut You'll Be Alright, Kid . The F1 concert series opens on December 3 with Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson, followed by Lopez and Warren on December 4, Imagine Dragons on December 5, and The Chainsmokers and The Script on race day, December 6.

title: UK approves long-awaited Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
description: Andy Burnham's government, under pressure to cut energy costs, gives go-ahead for project criticised by green groups
content: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea ​gasfield , ending years ​of legal and political wrangling that had ⁠pitted the Labour government's climate commitments against its push ⁠to bolster energy security. Energy Minister Miatta ​Fahnbulleh said the project will start to supply gas to British homes and businesses from as ⁠early as the end of this month. At the same time, she said a new Energy Wealth Fund would be established by the government with a £2 billion downpayment to reinvest oil and ⁠gas revenue into the climate transition. Ms Fahnbulleh said Jackdaw was expected to increase ​domestic gas ⁠production by about 6 per cent at ‌its peak and support the country's gas supply over its lifespan of up to ​11 years, boosting energy security and protecting hundreds of jobs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Adura, the joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor that operates the project, has said Jackdaw will produce gas equivalent to up to 40,000 barrels of oil a day at peak output. Environmental groups could mount a fresh legal challenge to the approval. The issue ​has become a rallying point for climate activists, who say approving new fossil fuel projects undermines Labour's green pledges and ignores warnings from a summer of record-breaking heat across Europe. The fate of Jackdaw had been in ​limbo for years and has forced Mr Burnham to take sides in a battle over the future of the North Sea while risking alienating voters. The relatively small gas project has become a symbol of a bitter political fight over Britain’s energy transition. Approving Jackdaw risked a backlash from some on the left of the Labour Party and the Greens. Rejecting drilling in the field would have fuelled criticism from Reform UK, the Conservatives and the oil industry that climate policies are costing Britain jobs and investment. The previous Conservative government approved the project ‌in 2022, but climate activists challenged ⁠the decision in court alongside approval for ​the Rosebank oil and gasfield. A 2025 ruling barred operators from ​extracting oil ‌or gas until they received fresh government consent that takes into account emissions from the burning ⁠of the fields' hydrocarbons. The decision has taken on added significance for Mr Burnham since ⁠he took office in July. In its 2024 general election manifesto, the Labour Party pledged to block new drilling in the North Sea, but officials say decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank – the largest undeveloped oil and gas reservoir in British waters – fall outside that commitment because they involve licences approved years ago under the previous government. “Jackdaw has been made into this big issue because it’s become a symbol of the wider North Sea debate,” said Jess Ralston, head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, an independent non-profit. “But even if the government approves it and Rosebank, the North Sea debate isn’t going to get any less flammable.” Even once drilling gets under way, few believe the UK could ever compete again with major oil and gas regions. Its stretch of the North Sea is 90 per cent depleted for commercial resources, according to consultant Wood Mackenzie. The international companies that pioneered drilling there 60 years ago have retreated.

title: Iran clings to demands even as threat of renewed US-Israel attacks grows
description: Washington has reportedly sent a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as possibility of resumption in fighting increases
content: Iran will not allow the Strait of Hormuz to fully reopen until the US accepts its terms, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said, warning that Tehran is ready to resume fighting if the stand-off escalates, even as he insists diplomacy remains possible. Indirect negotiations between Iran and the US were continuing through mediators Pakistan and Qatar, Mr Araghchi told Iraqi state television in an interview aired on Wednesday. “Until an agreement or understanding is reached regarding this strait, it will not be open to everyone,” he said. In an opinion article published later in The Financial Times , Mr Araghchi accused Washington of threatening more violence while showing little willingness to work on diplomacy. “Any further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the region will put civilian lives and the well-being of all regional states and the global economy at great risk,” Mr Araghchi wrote. “Given that the White House has shown no willingness to reach an understanding on the way forward, while also threatening more violence, there is little reason to expect progress now." His remarks came after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed an oil supertanker carrying more than two million barrels exploded after hitting a naval mine near the Strait of Hormuz late on Tuesday. It was the latest in a series of such IRGC claims that remain unverified. On Tuesday, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir travelled to Tehran with an official delegation to meditate between the two sides. Qatar, for its part, said communication between Washington and Tehran had “not stopped” and that the aim was to reach a solution as soon as possible. The US and Israel appeared to be considering military options, however. Last week, CNN reported that the US had developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the Mother of All Bombs , or Moab, against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if US President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations. The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its inclusion would extend the threat of renewed military action to Iran's Pickaxe Mountain , a deeply buried site near the Natanz nuclear complex. Separately, The FT reported on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing for large-scale strikes against Iran, having ordered the military to prepare for a major new offensive earlier this month. The Israeli military had prepared a multi-day bombing campaign for the weekend of October 10 that would have struck civilian infrastructure, including power plants as well as nuclear facilities and sites associated with Iran’s leadership, The FT said, quoting three people familiar with the matter. The operation was ultimately shelved amid opposition from Mr Trump, who did not want to restart the conflict before the US midterm elections on November 3, the sources said. The proposed campaign was intended to be more intense than the joint US-Israeli offensive launched against Iran in February, The FT reported. Mr Netanyahu and Mr Trump have nevertheless continued to threaten renewed military action, saying the US and Israel must “finish” the job against Iran. Meanwhile, Fox News, quoting two US officials, reported that the US was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines by the end of November. It would be the third US aircraft carrier in the region. The reports came after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met Mr Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, as the two sides were discussing the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran before the US vote. The visit came a day after Mr Trump publicly endorsed Mr Netanyahu's candidature in Israel's elections. Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was preparing for possible renewed attacks and saw little prospect of a diplomatic breakthrough before the US elections. Mr Trump previously said Washington would not strike Iran again before the vote. In the interview, Mr Araghchi repeated that Iran was preparing for possible renewed US and Israeli military action, despite its stated preference for diplomacy. “Every possibility exists in the future, including the possibility that the Americans and the Zionist regime will launch another war against Iran,” he said. He added that the dispute went beyond Iran’s nuclear programme. “The nuclear issue is nothing more than a pretext," Mr Araghchi said. Meanwhile, Iranian officials threatened to attack undersea cables, data and artificial intelligence centres if fighting resumed. Qatar has warned that threats to cables, sea mines and oil spills in the Strait of Hormuz would harm countries across the region. Shipping through the strait remains severely disrupted, putting pressure on energy markets and regional economies. Oil prices have edged higher on Middle East supply concerns. Brent crude touched $111.99 a barrel on Tuesday, the ⁠highest since May 20.

title: What a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would mean
description: Lines between companies have blurred as ⁠founder Musk expands into AI, robotics and advanced manufacturing
content: Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create ​one ​of the most valuable companies in the ​world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company ⁠SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as ⁠Mr Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing , satellite communications and computing infrastructure, ​including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: A merger would create a ⁠single company at the centre of Mr Musk's long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. “I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained ⁠from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centres), connectivity,” Mr Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing ​the companies ⁠together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Mr Musk's projects ‌already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering ​talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Mr Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence. Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in cars, robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future ​data-centre projects. Mr Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing ‌the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and ⁠Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Mr Musk ​hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production, ​while SpaceX technologies ‌have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could also co-ordinate efforts to secure strategic ⁠supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite ⁠hardware. The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and Nasa. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors ​would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

title: How does a 235-year-old watchmaker thrive in the age of artificial intelligence?
description: As the world around us is reshaped, Girard-Perregaux’s managing director Marc Michel-Amadry is betting on something altogether more human
content: The more artificial intelligence takes over our lives, the more valuable the human hand becomes. That is Marc Michel-Amadry’s theory, and a fitting one to apply at Girard-Perregaux, a 235-year-old watchmaker trying to keep itself relevant. As managing director of the Swiss watch maison, Michel-Amadry believes the future of watchmaking lies, paradoxically, in looking back, towards the human skills and mechanical ingenuity that are becoming increasingly rare in a world of mass production and artificial intelligence. “The more crazy we go with technology and AI running our lives, the more important this connection to heritage, to human craftsmanship becomes,” he says. Michel-Amadry joined Girard-Perregaux in February 2025, following senior roles in the watch industry and at Sotheby’s. His brief is not to reinvent the manufacture, but to restore it to the level of recognition he believes its history deserves. “I have only one ambition: to reveal Girard-Perregaux for what it is and for the values that have always nourished it,” he says. Those values stretch back to Jean-François Bautte, who brought watchmakers, engravers, goldsmiths, jewellers and enamellers under one roof in Geneva in the late 1700s. Rather than relying on a network of specialist workshops, Bautte understood that excellence could be better served by having his artisans work together. That spirit remains central to Michel-Amadry’s vision. “We have been a manufacturer since 1791, and are deeply rooted yet free.” The distinction matters. Girard-Perregaux is an independent house, able to develop movements, cases and designs completely in-house without being trapped by its history – or being beholden to a parent company. With only Ulysse Nardin as a stablemate, Michel-Amadry sees that independence as increasingly important to collectors looking beyond the obvious names. “The beauty of our maison is that it has 235 years of history,” he says. “We are at the same level of legacy as Vacheron Constantin and Patek Philippe, but we have this freedom and this independent position.” The Middle East, with its sophisticated community of collectors, is naturally important to this strategy. But Michel-Amadry believes the region should not be viewed in isolation. “Today, the impact of watchmaking, and horology in particular, is everywhere,” he says. “Wherever you are, in China, Dubai or New York, the level of knowledge, the level of sophistication collectors share and know about our industry is fascinating. Sometimes they know more than me,” he adds with a laugh. What particularly interests him is the changing relationship between technology and craftsmanship. As artificial intelligence and algorithms become embedded in everyday life, he believes the appeal of something made by hand will only grow. “Girard-Perregaux believes very much in AI, but as artisanal intelligence,” he says. That means maintaining skills many contemporary manufacturers might outsource. Enamelling is still carried out in-house, for example, while the maison supports an engraving school in La Chaux-de-Fonds, helping preserve an exacting discipline practised by an increasingly small pool of craftspeople. “Hand-engraving is a magnificent skill, but there are very few people who do it,” he says. “We cannot afford to let this knowledge disappear.” The result is craftsmanship that is deliberately human rather than mechanically immaculate. “People are craving artistry,” he adds. “It is perfect, but it’s not machine-perfect. And that is what makes it beautiful.” Few objects demonstrate this philosophy better than Girard-Perregaux’s La Esmeralda tourbillon, a contemporary timepiece inspired by the pocket watch of the same name that won a gold medal back at the 1889 Paris Universal Exhibition. Its elaborate enamelling and finishing demanded patience and precision, and its modern iteration is no less painstakingly assembled. The same philosophy applies to the maison’s movements. Its grand complications are individually signed by the master watchmaker who creates them, something Michel-Amadry sees as a declaration of authorship as much as of craftsmanship. “We want that level of hand-finishing in our movements, in our cases, everything. We don’t compromise on this,” he says. This fixation on quality runs through Michel-Amadry’s ambitions for the maison. He has previously said Girard-Perregaux deserves to be “not bigger, but better known”. Its clients, he believes, are drawn by a deep appreciation of “all the work that has been done, from the design to the development to the finishing. “We want to bring a different status to the people who embark into Girard-Perregaux. “It is not about saying: ‘I’m rich. I’m powerful.’ It’s more about: ‘I know how this watch has been made and it has been made uncompromisingly.’” That philosophy also informs how Girard-Perregaux wants collectors to encounter the brand. At its headquarters, visitors can meet watchmakers directly rather than simply observing the manufacturing process through glass. Its villa is part museum, part private house and part destination. Visitors eat meals prepared by an in-house chef, wander through the workshops and encounter beehives in the gardens, with jars of honey given to departing guests. It is an unusually personal approach for a luxury house. “It is a place where you will not only meet a brand, an idea and a field of horology, but you will also meet people,” Michel-Amadry says. Even its new Geneva boutique was designed internally by the brand’s chief marketing officer, who has an architectural background. “Who else can best incarnate what we want to stand for than us?” Michel-Amadry notes. That instinct is embedded in Girard-Perregaux’s history. One obvious example is the Laureato, which recently celebrated its 50th anniversary. Introduced in 1975, the sports watch is defined by its eight-sided bezel designed in-house. Michel-Amadry believes its longevity comes from its ability to evolve without losing its distinctive identity: a Laureato from the 1980s can sit comfortably beside one made today. “It’s not about having the latest Laureato versus a beautiful Laureato from 1985 or 1992,” he says. “They are all relevant, and we are seriously proud of that.” The watch’s importance extends beyond design. The Laureato was created during an era when the industry grappled with the arrival of quartz, and Girard-Perregaux embraced the technology, creating the Calibre 350 in 1971, which set the standard for the now familiar frequency of 32,768Hz. When the Laureato launched four years later, it was powered by its descendant, the Calibre 705. For Michel-Amadry, it is a reminder that heritage and innovation are inseparable at Girard-Perregaux. Its history is not simply a catalogue of old watches to revisit, but also a record of horological experimentation. Perhaps the clearest expression of this is the Three Bridges. First conceived by Constant Girard in 1867, it transformed a conventional movement by placing its components beneath three distinctive bridges. Rather than hiding the mechanics beneath the dial, Girard revealed them. “It was more than skeletonisation,” Michel-Amadry says. “It was to change the whole view on how you create a movement: to show, to make the invisible visible, and to reveal the beauty within.” Patented in 1884, the design remains a signature and was reinterpreted for the Laureato 50th Anniversary Three Gold Bridges. Limited to 50 pieces, it unites two strands of Girard-Perregaux’s visual language in one watch. Michel-Amadry’s ambition for the house may also be more personal. Born in La Chaux-de-Fonds himself, he was drawn to Girard-Perregaux long before joining the company. For his 40th birthday, he bought himself a Girard-Perregaux WW.TC chronograph. “This was my celebration,” he says of the milestone. “I felt the watch was absolutely exceptional.” It’s hard to imagine someone more invested in the watchmaker’s next chapter.

title: Abu Dhabi to trial wearable tech in pregnancy to tackle premature birth risks
description: Women considered high risk to be provided with Oura Ring devices under Project Cradle
content: Women in Abu Dhabi facing high-risk pregnancies are to be provided with wearable devices under a project exploring how technology can monitor the warning signs over premature births. The emirate's Department of Health has launched Project Cradle, a two-year study in collaboration with smart ring maker Oura, to identify risks in pregnancy and enable medics to intervene sooner to offer potentially life-saving support to mothers and babies. The initiative was unveiled by Noura Al Ghaithi, undersecretary of the Department of Health, and Oura chief executive Tom Hale at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, being held at Adnec until Thursday. Project Cradle will combine continuous wearable data from the use of the Oura Ring – a titanium smart ring that tracks key metrics such as sleep patterns, heart rate, temperature and stress – with Abu Dhabi’s clinical and genomic data to better understand risk factors around preterm birth. Research suggests that biometrics such as heart rate for pregnant women shift in the weeks before delivery. The project will test whether such changes can be detected in individual women, allowing health professionals to take proactive action. The study will get under way in the coming weeks and will follow an Abu Dhabi-based sample of women considered high risk who will wear the Oura Ring from early pregnancy until delivery. The latest Oura Ring 5 is on sale in the UAE for Dh1,599 and is one of several wearable tech products rolled out by the Finnish company. During the trial, the Oura Ring will monitor biometrics such as heart rate, sleep and activity, which researchers will pair with clinical outcomes to build a comprehensive data set. The study will investigate whether a reliable physiological signal appears before spontaneous preterm labour. It will also assess whether that signal could define a clinically actionable threshold – early enough for care teams to give treatments help the baby, such as for the lungs and brains, or to arrange transfer to specialist neonatal care. Corniche Hospital and Mediclinic Airport Road, two of the capital's leading maternal care centres, will take part in the pilot phase. “In Abu Dhabi , we are building an intelligent health system of the future,” said Dr Al Ghaithi. “Continuous sensing enables a shift from reactive care to healthcare that anticipates risk, detects warning signs sooner, and enables faster, more precise and personalised intervention. “Project Cradle brings this approach to pregnancy and birth, one of the most pivotal moments in life, building the evidence to guide more timely care. “Women's health and fertility are at the heart of Abu Dhabi’s health priorities. Our ambition is to become a leading centre for reproductive health that is grounded in research that advances care.” Mr Hale said the partnership highlighted the potential for health care and technology to combine to improve lives. “Project Cradle shows what could be possible when a forward-thinking health system combines clinical excellence with accurate, continuous monitoring,” he said. “We're proud to work alongside a health authority setting that standard, improving outcomes for families in the Emirate, and creating pathways that can be used across the world to improve health.” Premature, or preterm, birth is when a baby is born before 37 weeks of pregnancy and can occur spontaneously or following medical intervention. It affects one in 10 births worldwide and remains one of the most unpredictable complications in pregnancy and can lead to a wide variety of long-term health challenges for mother and child. Common conditions that affect premature babies include anaemia, respiratory issues, jaundice, bleeding to the brain and heart problems. They can also be at heightened risk of developmental challenges such as learning disabilities, hearing and vision problems and cerebral palsy. Mothers who go through premature labours are more likely to face anxiety, pospartum depression, post traumatic stress disorders and problems bonding with their babies, according to health experts. “We know today that we can identify about two weeks before labour what the signs of the onset of labour are,” said Mr Hale. “What we want to do is take those signals and see if we can identify them in preterm births.” Oura says a study of 10,000 pregnancies found physiological changes across the trimesters, including changes about two weeks before labour. Shyamal Patel, Oura’s global senior vice president of Science, said the new study will test whether such patterns can be detected in an individual woman. “Physiological changes like changes in heart rate, heart-rate variability, body temperature, even things like sleep patterns change,” Patel said. “We saw clear changes that occur through the different trimesters of pregnancy, including changes about two weeks prior to labour.” Wearable technology is playing a more significant role in preventive health care. A five-pillar framework has been set out for Abu Dhabi to manage the integration of tech into everyday care. It has been developed by health authorities in partnership with Knowledge Contributor Deloitte, and includes guidance on consumer adoption, as well as privacy and clinical regulation. According to Deloitte, the global wearable technology market was valued at $92.9 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $229.9 billion by 2033. Disease prevention guidance is already operating under Department of Health protocols. Under the authority’s Sahatna platform, data gleaned from wearable devices is paired with longitudinal health records from Malaffi to generate a personalised health age score. It gives users insights into the clinical and lifestyle factors influencing their health, and suggest what amendments can be made to improve their quality of life.

title: Uddish Suri on dismissing Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, selection for ADT10 and eyeing a UAE future with his brother
description: Teen all-rounder is following in footsteps of older sibling Tanish as one of the brightest young prospects in the Emirates
content: When Uddish Suri takes leave from his mechanical engineering lectures and plays against some of the world’s biggest hitters in cricket’s fastest format, he might be forgiven for being nervous. The 18-year-old all-rounder will be making his franchise cricket bow when he plays in the Abu Dhabi T10 next month. The Dubai-born left-arm wrist-spinner acknowledged he hasn’t had the chance to worry about feeling daunted by the challenge ahead. Instead, he said, he physically jumped for joy after making the cut at the draft for the reconfigured 10-over league . Plus, he has already pitted himself against the most destructive young batter in the world – and with no small measure of success, too. So why worry? “Manifestation is probably the biggest key in life,” Uddish said of bowling to Vaibhav Sooryavanshi in the Under-19 Asia Cup last December, between the two IPLs which launched the teen batter as a global star of cricket. “One and a half months before the tournament, I would watch his videos online. And I was always manifesting that I would be the one getting him out.” It nearly happened immediately. With just the second ball he bowled in the fixture at ICC Academy in Dubai, Uddish had Sooryavanshi dropped. Sooryavanshi proceeded to plunder 171 from 95 balls. But Uddish escaped serious punishment in the wunderkind’s latest act of savagery on the bowling attacks of the world. Of the 14 sixes Sooryavanshi hit, just one was off Uddish, as well as one boundary besides. Then, in his penultimate over, he bowled him out. “For a month I had been preparing to get him out,” Uddish said. “What areas am I going to bowl to him? What lengths am I going to bowl to him? I bowled eight overs to him on the trot. “The length that I was bowling to him, he was getting frustrated at times. He was playing the wrong shot, and finally, towards the end, when it was my second last over of the spell, I bowled him. “It was a great feeling to get him out.” He will be pitting his wits against the young stars of India and Pakistan again next month, when the U19 Asia Cup returns in Oman. After that, he will be straight into action in the Abu Dhabi T10 . “I was watching the auction, and I just jumped with joy,” Uddish said of being drafted to play for UAE Bulls, where his teammates will be IPL stars like Kieron Pollard and Sunil Narine. “I started running all over my house, upstairs, down. I gave a hug to parents, who were really happy for me. “Then I went into my temple because I believe in my God so much and I think whatever has happened to me is only because of him. “I was there for five minutes talking to my God and it was a really happy moment for me.” While he was in his temple, he missed a phone call from the person he is closest to. Brother Tanish was on tour in the United States with the UAE senior team. The 21-year-old wicketkeeper batter is one of the brightest young talents in UAE cricket. A day after his younger sibling was drafted for the T10, Tanish landed a $10,000 deal to play in the DP World ILT20, even though he might be unavailable because of a clash with national team duty . “Unluckily, I did go unsold, but my brother got picked,” Uddish said of ILT20 auction day, when over $1 million was spent recruiting UAE players . “I was in my university class and I had my phone open to see YouTube. Tanish’s name came up and I saw Sharjah Warriorz had put a bid in and he got picked for $10,000. “Obviously in class I can't just be like, 'I'm leaving'. But after five minutes, when my class ended, the first thing I did was ring my brother.” Another thing he has manifested is playing for the UAE senior team alongside Tanish. “That is both of our dreams together,” Uddish said. “Playing in the same team as your brother is a very great feeling. “I think our parents would want that to happen; seeing both their sons on the TV one day playing in the same team with each other. “It would also help because we can communicate with each other. There have been quite a few times where I have been struggling to find my length or whatever. “I would rather talk to my brother rather than talking to someone else because my comfort zone is with him. He knows where my strengths lie and my weaknesses lie.”

title: Ballon d’Or 2026: Nominees, favourites, ceremony date and how to watch
description: Football's biggest individual award set to be handed out in London
content: The 2026 Ballon d'Or winner will be announced on Monday night at a glittering ceremony in London. The 70th staging of the event will be the first to be held outside of France, with it moving to England as a tribute to Stanley Matthews, who won the first ever Ballon d'Or in 1956. With Harry Kane among the favourites for the men's award, that choice of location could yet prove to be particularly apt. Kane will face stiff opposition from Spanish wonderkid Lamine Yamal, his Bayern Munich teammate Michael Olise, Kylian Mbappe , or any number of Paris Saint-Germain players. The French and European champions have no fewer than 10 nominees on the 30-man shortlist. Argentine great Lionel Messi is also in the running after a spectacular World Cup, but is considered an outsider now that he plays his club football in the US for Inter Miami. There is no place on the list for his great rival Cristiano Ronaldo. Here's everything you need to know about the 2026 Ballon d'Or . The accolade is regarded as a way to crown the best player in the world, and is therefore the highest individual honour a footballer can achieve. In what is now a joint partnership between Uefa, France Football and L'Equipe , the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards will honour last season's best players, coaches and clubs, in addition to the top scorer, goalkeeper, young player and humanitarian. Presented annually by France Football since 1956, the Ballon d'Or started as a way to reward the world's best male player. It has expanded over the years and has become more like football's answer to the Oscars, with female players, coaches and teams all now invited to the party. It was first won in 1956 by the Englishman Matthews, who edged out the Real Madrid legend Alfredo Di Stefano, who would claim it the following year. Messi has won it the most times, with eight in his trophy cabinet, ahead of Ronaldo , who has five. The award is now based on the results of last season instead of the calendar year. This is the period from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026, with the window concluding after the summer's World Cup final. Although the event is now a joint effort, France Football, the originators of the Ballon d'Or, retain their voting system and it is decided as follows: The award is based on three main criteria: The decision is made by an international jury of journalists, with one representative per country – from the top 100 in the latest Fifa rankings for men and the top 50 for women. Each juror selects 10 players in descending order of merit from a list of 30 established by the editorial staff of France Football and L'Equipe . The Ballon d'Or is awarded to the player with the highest number of points. In the case of a tie, the players are separated by the number of first-place votes. If the tie remains, they are separated by the number of second-place votes, then by the number of third-place votes, and so on. The 70th edition of the awards will take place on Monday, October 26, at the London Palladium Theatre. The ceremony will begin at 8pm local time (11pm UAE). It will be hosted by Kate Scott and Thierry Henry.
