title: Lebanon’s battle for sovereignty must extend to its banks
description: Depositors are still paying for a crisis they did not create
content: The International Monetary Fund and World Bank Annual Meetings took place in Bangkok last week. One participant from the Middle East – Lebanon – is confronting a question larger than any bailout: can the state recover authority over both force and finance? Although Hezbollah ’s independent arsenal has long denied the state full control over war and peace, sovereignty today also depends on the state’s ability to regulate finance, protect savings, collect revenue, extend credit and enforce the law. That is why economic reform belongs inside Lebanon’s sovereignty debate, not beside it. That issue is now squarely with the IMF. Nearly seven years after Lebanon’s financial collapse, depositors are still paying for a crisis they did not create. More than $70 billion (Dh257.07 billion) in losses have accumulated across the state, the central bank and commercial banks, while the political question of who will bear them remains unresolved. As a member of Parliament, I have watched that question move through our institutions for years. Parliament took an important step in August by approving the amended Bank Resolution Law. But this progress should not be mistaken for domestic consensus, as reform-minded officials remain a minority within Lebanon’s power structure, and recent gains have depended heavily on IMF and other external pressure. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has been among the few senior officials arguing that Lebanon is serious about reform and ready for an IMF programme. Even as he made that case, President Joseph Aoun referred article 3 of the law to the Constitutional Council, reopening a dispute over the central bank’s powers. Whatever the legal merits, the move cast fresh doubt on the reform message. The next battle is the Financial Stabilisation and Depositor Recovery Law (or Gap Law) which will decide how losses are allocated and depositors treated. The challenge then is political as much as technical. Lebanon’s banking lobby, led by the Association of Banks in Lebanon, remains a powerful organised interest, which has sought to shape restructuring, loss allocation and shareholder accountability, drawing on political allies in Parliament, including within the Finance and Budget Committee. Having sat through these debates, I know this firsthand – and the pressure is not confined to Parliament. The banking lobby has repeatedly mobilised political and media influence to shape reform. Delay also carries a security cost. Lebanon’s dollarised cash economy was estimated at about $9.9 billion in 2022, nearly half of gross domestic product. Not all cash activity is illicit, but at that scale the state loses visibility over financial flows, tax collection becomes harder and money-laundering risk rises. Hezbollah has long relied on cash, exchange houses, transfer networks and institutions outside conventional banking channels. Reuters recently reported that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to assist displaced families, though the US State Department disputed the account. Whatever the exact figure, Lebanon cannot fully confront Hezbollah’s financing while opaque cash channels dominate and financial reform is delayed. Hezbollah and the banking lobby are neither allies nor equivalent. However, each exploits different forms of state weakness, leaving Lebanon less able to regulate money, enforce the law and command public trust. Treating Hezbollah’s weapons and financial reform as separate files, as has tended to be the case even in Washington, makes little sense: a state that cannot trace money, protect deposits, restore credit or finance businesses has fewer tools to compete with a parallel armed, financial and social system. Lebanon therefore needs both exclusive state control over arms and a financial system strong enough to sustain state authority. The coming debate over the Gap Law will test whether Lebanon can put the public interest ahead of organised privilege. As an elected member of Parliament, my position is clear: ordinary depositors and taxpayers cannot again be asked to absorb losses while shareholders, insiders or those who benefited from the old system are insulated. Losses must be allocated transparently according to a credible hierarchy of claims, with accountability and a viable banking sector capable of extending credit again. That is why Bangkok matters. The IMF has made clear that an appropriate Gap Law is central to any new programme. The challenge is whether Lebanon arrives with a credible path to implementation or another reform package that is diluted at home. Lebanon’s international partners, especially the US and the IMF, can bolster a serious reform programme, but the case for reform is Lebanese before it is international. Businesses need credit, citizens need access to their savings, and the state needs revenue and financial visibility. This is why Parliament and the government must deliver financial reform alongside exclusive state control over arms. Lebanon cannot rebuild sovereignty while leaving either source of state weakness intact.

title: How Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial is reimagining the meaning of home
description: Artistic director Elvira Dyangani Ose on bringing art into everyday life and reflecting the capital's evolving identity
content: In a city where residents from around the world share the same streets, public spaces and daily routines, art can offer an unexpected way of bringing people together. That idea is central to the second Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial , which begins in Al Ain on October 23 before expanding to the capital on November 15. The exhibition, called Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place, brings together 21 Emirati and international artists whose installations will occupy public spaces until February 15. “The question that I have always pursued is the idea of what makes us come together,” artistic director Elvira Dyangani Ose tells The National . “What does it mean to be together?” Ose, who also serves as artistic director of Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa, has spent much of her career examining the histories represented in cultural institutions and how audiences engage with them. Her previous roles include director of Barcelona's Museu d'Art Contemporani and curator of international art at Tate Modern. Working across Abu Dhabi's public spaces, however, presents a different challenge. In a museum, visitors generally arrive intending to encounter art. Outside, people might come across an installation while shopping, walking or going about their daily routines. “You have to bring together a proposition that takes the public into account, a public that doesn't necessarily think of themselves as an audience,” Ose says. She believes this gives artists and curators greater responsibility. Their works enter spaces that communities already use, often without considering them places for artistic encounters. Abu Dhabi's diverse population makes the question of to whom public art should speak particularly interesting. The exhibition's theme emerged from Ose's longstanding interest in the relationships that bring people together, whether within families, communities or societies. “A place is a physical structure we share, but the sense of our own place, the sense of home, the condition of home, is something that goes beyond the structure,” she says. “It's something more personal.” Rather than offering a fixed definition of home, the biennial explores how people develop attachments to places through experiences, memories and shared histories. Ose's earlier visits to the UAE helped shape her approach. Having attended Art Dubai and the Sharjah Biennial, she was struck by the distinct identities of the emirates and the ways their material cultures influence their development. Abu Dhabi's cultural ambitions were another attraction. With Louvre Abu Dhabi established, Zayed National Museum open and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi approaching completion, Ose encountered a city increasingly expressing its ambitions through cultural institutions. “There is an incredible imaginary to be built,” she says. She thinks Abu Dhabi's changing urban landscape offers possibilities that older cities do not necessarily have. In many European and American cities, monuments and statues preserve particular historical narratives, influencing how public spaces are understood and what changes can be imagined. Abu Dhabi, by comparison, offers opportunities to consider how those spaces might develop and what meanings future generations will attach to them. Few areas illustrate this more clearly than Mina Zayed, where several biennial installations will be placed. The district has continued to change throughout the exhibition's development, a trend Ose sees as an opportunity to engage with the city's evolving identity. The area's maritime history also provides material for artists to explore. Emirati artist Khalid Al Banna is developing a tribute to fishing nets and the practices of the communities that have used them. American artist Nari Ward also works with fishing nets, although his approach considers memory, movement and the trajectories connecting different lives. Ward's work will be presented in a boatyard in Mina Zayed , where the remnants of fishing vessels connect the installation to the area's history. These relationships between artworks and locations are central to Ose's approach. “We didn't want anything that felt artificial,” she says. “That engagement with the material culture has to be real and vivid.” The aim is to engage with histories and practices already embedded in the landscape while allowing artists to interpret them through their own perspectives. In Al Ain, Asuncion Molinos Gordo draws on her research into the UAE's traditional aflaj irrigation systems and the ways they have influenced the landscape. Other works explore aspects of the emirate that residents may rarely encounter. French artist Laure Prouvost is presenting an octopus-themed installation, while Argentinian artist Mercedes Azpilicueta is drawing inspiration from the coral life beneath Abu Dhabi's waters. Together, these projects consider the relationship between the places people inhabit and the natural environments, traditions and histories that contribute to their character. The exhibition also features artists including Ibrahim Mahama, Yinka Shonibare, Akram Zaatari, Kapwani Kiwanga, Marinella Senatore and Reena Saini Kallat. Although smaller than the inaugural edition, which ran from November 2024 to April 2025 and featured more than 50 projects, the second biennial, Ose says, will place greater emphasis on monumental works, interaction with communities and varied experiences. Sites include MiZa and Souq Al Mina in Mina Zayed, Saadiyat Cultural District, Hidd Al Saadiyat and locations across Al Ain. A public programme will provide opportunities for visitors to engage with the artworks through conversations and other activities. The biennial also builds on the first edition's legacy, which saw several installations acquired or retained as permanent public artworks. Ose says some works in the new exhibition are intended to remain in the city, while others have been conceived as temporary experiences. The distinction matters because an artwork can serve different purposes depending on its location and intended lifespan. Some might preserve a particular history, while others invite people to experience familiar surroundings in an unfamiliar way. Ose is especially interested in the emotional connections that art can create, sometimes through experiences seemingly removed from their immediate surroundings. She describes the possibility of an artwork allowing people to listen to birds from different parts of the world, including species that may no longer exist. Such encounters, she thinks, can take visitors somewhere unexpected while remaining grounded in the physical environment where they occur. “I like the idea that yes, there are things that have to be related to the place, but you also want art to take you far away from your everyday,” she says. Ultimately, Ose hopes the biennial can interrupt familiar routines and offer moments of discovery, taking people towards “something magical, something new, something that made them think differently”. Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial opens in Al Ain on October 23 and in Abu Dhabi on November 15. It runs until February 15, 2027.

title: Gulf unity is about more than shared history
description: In uncertain times, some challenges are better addressed collectively
content: Many of the Gulf countries’ greatest achievements have been built on ambition and an ability to look beyond the limits of geography. During the past half-century, the region and its people have undergone a profound transformation. Small trading ports and pearl-diving communities have become cutting-edge, cosmopolitan cities that serve as global centres for commerce and connection, investment and diplomacy. Those achievements are real, but, of course, they were also in the shadow of challenges over the years – be they regional or global. Today, ongoing regional conflicts are questioning old assumptions. As trade and shipping routes are disrupted and economies buffeted, several leaders are calling on Gulf countries to build on their considerable common ties to better weather this geopolitical storm. This was the thinking displayed on Monday when Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai , emphasised how the bonds between the Gulf nations are too important to be undermined by those who seek to sow division. “The Gulf is a great tree whose branches have multiplied, whose fruits have adorned it, and whose shades have bloomed,” Sheikh Mohamed posted , “but its root is one, and its trunk is one, and its water is one, and its destiny is one, God willing.” Far from basking in nostalgia or sentiment, however, his message on X was a timely reminder that unity is a source of strength for the Gulf. An aligned approach to critical issues is important at a time when geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty are testing countries everywhere. Similarly, Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, earlier this week also called for renewed regional co-ordination . “There is a need to revitalise joint Gulf action, particularly in its security and defence dimensions, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he posted on X. Often, each member of the GCC has pursued its own development model, shaped by its particular circumstances and ambitions. That is natural, and no-one is arguing that better, targeted regional co-operation has to mean a loss of any autonomy. Each Gulf country has its own institutions and identity, and there is much value in preserving the diversity of approaches that has helped the region soar. Instead of uniformity, co-operation means recognising that some challenges are better addressed collectively, and that one country’s success can create opportunities for its neighbours. That was a central reason why the GCC was set up in 1981, here in Abu Dhabi. Furthermore, while individual economies carry considerable weight, when co-ordinated, they have the potential to exert an influence that reaches well beyond the sum of their national achievements. Many of the foundations for such collaboration are already in place. GCC members share maritime routes, have common security concerns and all seek to diversify their economies and develop new industries. Gulf societies are anchored by family ties and a common heritage that predates modern borders. Such connections offer a strong basis for practical partnerships. National identity and regional solidarity need not compete. The Gulf’s countries remain distinct while recognising the advantages of shared purpose. In a world where influence increasingly depends on partnerships as well as economic strength, this is a strategic imperative. The Gulf’s history demonstrates what determined leadership and a willingness to embrace change can accomplish – its future will do the same.

title: An AI slowdown could be exactly what businesses need
description: Most companies are nowhere close to exhausting today’s technological capabilities
content: The artificial intelligence industry has spent years feathering the accelerator of frontier model development in a fierce contest to dominate the technology . Now, it is considering something that until recently seemed almost unthinkable: slamming on the brakes. The prospects of the frontier labs are closely linked to the fortunes of the US stock market, and they buttress vast spending on infrastructure. But for businesses still working out how to harness AI’s illusive productivity gains, a slowdown is not a bad thing. It will give them time to close the yawning gap between AI’s accelerating capabilities and their productive use of them. Still, calls to pace the frontier grow louder. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei made the case in an essay in which he said capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand, align and control them. His proposal was to deliberately slow the improvement enough to give safety research and independent evaluation time to catch up. There remains considerable disagreement over whether this is practical, desirable or possible. But that’s beside the point for businesses, since most of them are nowhere close to exhausting the AI capabilities they already possess. According to the Stanford 2026 AI Index, 88 per cent of organisations surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function last year. But breadth of adoption is not the same thing as depth. The research shows that the use of AI agents remained in the single digits across almost every business function. Relatively few have fundamentally redesigned how work gets done around it. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis found that generative AI accounted for only 5.7 per cent of total working hours by August last year. This tells us that companies already have powerful AI, and are simply failing to make the most of it. They don’t need another massive leap in model capability to claim the productivity gains that are already on the table. A METR randomised study found that experienced open-source developers working on highly familiar repositories actually took 19 per cent longer when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools. The reason is that the bottleneck is increasingly organisational. Companies have to connect models to proprietary data. They have to integrate AI into existing systems. And they need to redesign workflows rather than simply insert a chatbot into them. They also need appropriate governance, security and human oversight, while employees have to learn how to delegate effectively to AI. Managers, meanwhile, need to rethink roles, performance measures and decision rights. Those changes happen at a comparatively glacial pace when compared with the speed at which AI labs have been pushing the frontier. OpenAI's enterprise research finds that the heaviest AI adopters use substantially more capabilities across more tasks than the median employee. These intensive users report much larger productivity benefits. Seventy-five per cent of surveyed workers also reported being able to perform tasks using AI that they previously could not do. So the AI productivity frontier inside most companies sits far behind the technological one. This is not unusual. General-purpose technologies typically arrive before organisations learn how to exploit them. Electricity existed before factories were redesigned around distributed electric motors, and computers came along long before companies reorganised processes around digital information. AI is likely to follow the same pattern, which only strengthens the case for hitting the brakes. That will not stall the AI economy , which is so crucial to public equity markets, because it will give companies the badly needed time to extract value from the marvellous capabilities already at their fingertips. That means moving beyond experimentation towards workflow redesign. Moving from individual productivity tools towards end-to-end processes. Connecting AI to enterprise data and systems. Using agents where they genuinely add value. Building governance that allows experimentation without unacceptable risk. And, perhaps most importantly, developing the organisational capabilities required to use AI well. Executives should continue watching the frontier, of course. Better models will create new opportunities, and a substantial slowdown is far from guaranteed. But they should not confuse a slower technological frontier with a slower business opportunity. Even if frontier development paused dramatically tomorrow, companies would still have an enormous backlog of economically valuable opportunities across customer service, software development, finance , procurement, marketing and many other functions. So just because the frontier slows, it doesn’t mean the business opportunity does. The AI race, at least for enterprise users, needs to shift from simply building better AI to building better businesses around it.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo misses penalty and open goal on return to action with Al Nassr
description: Tijjani Reijnders fires late winner as Al Qadsiah go top of Saudi Pro League table
content: Cristiano Ronaldo had a difficult night as Al Nassr scraped a 1-0 victory over Neom at Awwal Park in the Saudi Pro League on Tuesday. The Portugal striker looked set to claim his 982nd career goal but surprisingly failed to convert a penalty just before half-time. The 41-year-old fired his effort wide of the mark after his international teammate Joao Felix had been fouled inside the box. It was the fourth time he had missed in 31 penalties taken for Al Nassr . His poor night continued after the break as he wasted another great chance, firing over the crossbar from close range after being set up by Sadio Mane. Another missed chance - this time a header – wrapped up miserable night for the veteran as he chases the 1,000 career goals milestone. Luckily for Ronaldo , his wastefulness did not cost Al Nassr vital points in the title race as Felix scored the game's only goal. He found the target with a long-range shot in the 61st minute after being teed up by Angelo. The win keeps Al Nassr third, two points behind Al Hilal and three adrift of leaders Al Qadsiah. Manager Ange Postecoglou defended Ronaldo after his tricky night in front of goal. “This is the nature of football, and it is good that we create this number of chances, and we will work on making up for the mistakes,” he said. “We work as a family, so a win will be good for everyone and a loss will fall upon the whole team, so we must support one another and move forward.” Tijjani Reijnders is fast becoming clutch for Al Qadsiah following his summer move from Manchester City. The Dutch international showed his worth again with a 96th-minute winner after a tough battle with Al Taawoun on Tuesday night. The win took Brendan Rodgers' side back to the summit on 25 points. Al Qadsiah host Al Hilal next in a top-of-the-table clash on Friday. Elsewhere, two goals each from George Ilenikhena and Youssef En-Nesyri fired Al Ittihad to a 4-1 win over Al Ettifaq.

title: Como vs Manchester United: Cesc Fabregas thrives as old rival Michael Carrick faces growing pressure
description: Former midfield foes on the pitch in England go head-to-head as managers in Champions League on Wednesday
content: At the picturesque Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, located on the south-west tip of Lake Como in Northern Italy, two old English Premier League midfield rivals will go head-to-head for the first time as managers on Wednesday evening. In the dugout for Serie A side Como for their Uefa Champions League clash with Manchester United will be Cesc Fabregas, the Spanish World Cup winner who made more than 500 appearances during spells with Arsenal and Chelsea separated by three seasons at Barcelona. On the away bench will be Michael Carrick, the English schemer who pulled the strings for West Ham United, Tottenham Hotspur and, predominantly, the Red Devils, across close to 700 matches that overlapped Fabregas's two stints in England. Both Fabregas, 39, and Carrick, 45, enjoyed hugely successful, trophy-laden playing careers, with both also deciding to make the jump into coaching immediately after hanging up their boots. In the summer of 2022, Fabregas left Monaco as a free agent to join then second-tier Como, an arrival that then chief executive Denis Wise – the former England and Chelsea midfielder – described as being “fundamental to our three-year plan to reach Serie A”. The Lombardy outfit had endured a catastrophic free fall after being relegated from Serie A in 2003, dropping down the divisions while also twice going bankrupt. As recently as 2019, they had been in the non-professional fourth tier, but that was also the year Indonesian tobacco manufacturer Djarum took over and the club's fortunes quickly changed. After one season as a player, when Como finished 13th, Fabregas joined the club's coaching staff and was soon appointed first-team caretaker manager after Moreno Longo was sacked. The team duly rose from seventh to third in Serie B before Welshman Osian Roberts took over as interim manager with Fabregas dropping to assistant, as he did not yet have the required Uefa coaching badges. Then, in a dramatic end to the 2023-24 campaign, Como secured a place back in the top-flight for the first time in 21 years after Simone Verdi's 75th-minute penalty earned them a 1-1 draw with Cosenza – clinching the second and final automatic promotion spot behind Parma. During that summer, Fabregas was formally appointed as manager, while Roberts took over as head of development. In his first full season in charge, which included a club-record six consecutive Serie A wins, Fabregas led Como to a comfortable 10th-place finish. Just 12 months later, the club finished fourth – ahead of Italian giants AC Milan and Juventus – thanks to a 4-1 thrashing of Cremonese on the final day of the season, securing Champions League football for the first time in their history. Como ended the campaign as Serie A's second-highest scorers with 65 goals, and with the meanest defence conceding just 29 times. “It's up there with all my achievements for how it was done and with whom we did it, because we did it with very young players, almost all of them are under 23 years old. That's amazing,” said Fabregas, who – along with France legend Thierry Henry – is a minority shareholder in the club. Ambitions stepped up a gear during the summer as around €130 million was spent on the likes of defender Trevoh Chalobah (€40 million from Chelsea), winger Jesus Rodriguez (€30m from Real Betis) and Argentine playmaker Nico Paz (€60m from Real Madrid). The latter joined Como for just €6m two years ago, in a deal that included a sell-on clause and buy-back options for Madrid and has been a revelation – scoring 21 and assisting as many in 84 appearances. During the summer, Como forked out a further club-record €60m in a deal with Madrid for the 21-year-old, who has blossomed during his time in Italy. The deal includes another buy-back option of €80m that is only active next summer. “Nico Paz has everything, physique and quality,” Fabregas told La Gazzetta dello Sport in August. “Nico has extraordinary courage, vision and ambition. He is 21 years old, but it feels like he's been playing for a decade.” Como's Champions League campaign opened with a memorable 4-1 home demolition of RB Leipzig, but they then lost 3-2 at Feyenoord last week. Next up will be three-time European champions United. “It's a great match against one of the best and biggest teams in history,” Fabregas told Uefa.com. “It will be a beautiful occasion for the whole city, for the whole club, for all the fans, for the players, for the staff. It's a match to dream about.” Over in Manchester, Carrick – like Fabregas – also went through a successful caretaker period before being given the United job full-time. Taking over from the sacked Ruben Amorim in January, with United in sixth place and out of both domestic cup competitions, Carrick was back for his second temporary stint, having been in charge for three games in 2021 following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's exit. It was a risky choice for United as Carrick's managerial CV consisted of two-and-a-half years in the second tier with Middlesbrough before he was sacked in June 2025. But his impact at Old Trafford was impressive as he guided United to third place and a return to the Champions League, with his reward being a two-year permanent contract . Carrick talked of “the magic of Manchester United” and “challenging for the biggest honours again” after his new deal was announced. But having played 464 games for the club over 12 years, as well as being on the coaching and managerial staff for nearly four more, he would have been acutely aware of the pressures involved in occupying the United hot seat. And that pressure intensifies if your team goes on a six-game winless streak like the one Carrick's is currently going through – their worst since 2019. Sunday's Premier League draw at Leeds United leaves the Red Devils down in 13th place on seven points – 14 shy of leaders Manchester City. And Carrick's cause has not been helped by defender Lisandro Martinez's incendiary interview after last week's Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid, or by the poor form of key midfielder and captain Bruno Fernandes. Next up will be Como and his old midfield foe Fabregas, but the Spaniard dismissed any idea that they were facing a club in chaos. “Crisis? You make them up. We don’t feel them. We’re footballers. We’re professionals,” insisted Fabregas on Tuesday. “All we want to do is play and compete. I don’t believe in crises. Man United have great players. Tomorrow we’re going to go out there and try to win.”

title: Iraqi father’s heartfelt plea to save five-year-old son with rare muscle disease
description: Family need to raise $2.9m to pay for Duchenne muscle dystrophy treatment
content: An Iraqi father watched on helplessly as his five-year-old son collapsed after walking for a few metres, only for the boy to look up, smiling, before talking of his dream of becoming a Formula One driver. Such moments are heartbreaking for Saban Hassan, 42, as his son, Ali, was recently diagnosed in the UAE with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a rare and aggressive genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The family, who live in Iraq, have been told gene therapy could be an option but the quoted a price of Dh10.6 million ($2.9 million) is far beyond their means. They have also been told Ali may have only a year left to live if treatment does not start soon. This has led Mr Hassan to launch a fund-raising drive to save the life of his little boy and he is pleading for help to reach the target. The initial appeal in his homeland raised some money but fell significantly short of the amount needed. “All doors are closed in front of me, I don’t know what to do,” the worried father told The National . “I made a donation drive in Iraq but I only managed to raise 2 per cent of the money.” Ali’s difficulties first became apparent when his parents noticed problems with communication and behaviour, including marked hyperactivity. He underwent neurological evaluations for about two years before more symptoms emerged. He began struggling to climb stairs and had difficulty standing up after sitting on the floor. Walking then became increasingly difficult. A genetic test from a sample sent to Al Jalila Children’s Hospital in Dubai in August confirmed that Ali had DMD. Mr Hassan said the family were devastated when they learnt of the diagnosis, which was compounded at the start of August this year when they found out how much the treatment would cost. The news left the family struggling to comprehend how they would find such an enormous sum. Mr Hassan said they sat in silence, looking at their son and wondering how they could afford to provide the gene therapy treatment. “He is my eldest son and I have a one-year-old daughter,” he said. “Watching Ali dying in front of me – knowing there is treatment but it's impossible to get – is shattering my heart and his mother's every day.” Selling the family home would make little difference to the amount required, the father said. “Even if I sold my house in Iraq to pay the treatment, I will cover only 10 per cent of the cost,” he said. Determined not to give up, however, he began approaching charities, officials in Iraq and prominent individuals, hoping someone would be able to help. But his appeals were met with rejection, with some telling him the amount was simply too large for anyone to provide. He then turned his attention to the UAE, where the treatment is available, and to places further afield. “I hope my voice reaches the people around the world to help me raise the funds for the treatment,” he said. “I hope the UAE’s generosity will reach my son, Ali, and save his life.” In August, The National reported how a Jordanian mother's plea to save her toddler was answered by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, who covered the cost of medical treatment for her daughter. It was confirmed Katia Abu Al Saud, who was 16 months old at the time, would have treatment for spinal muscular atrophy, another rare genetic disorder, at Al Jalila Children's Hospital. Katia's mother, Nour Roudnahal, appealed for assistance with the $2.4 million treatment, which the family could not afford, and her request gained attention on social media, before Sheikh Mohammed duly obliged. In March 2021, Sheikh Mohammed covered the Dh8 million ($762,300) treatment for Iraqi toddler Laveen Jabbar Al Kutyashi, who received the drug Zolgensma, a one-time prescription gene-replacement therapy, at Al Jalila. In July 2025, the Dubai Ruler pledged to pay the Dh7 million treatment costs for a Syrian girl with SMA after hearing her father's public appeal. He also paid for treatment for 15-year-old Fatima Ahmed Hassan, who was diagnosed with sarcoma. After several months of care, she was declared free of cancer.

title: Lamine Yamal magic cannot save Barcelona: 'PSG were better than us'
description: Foden hits hat-trick for Man City as goals flow once again on matchday three of Champions League
content: Paris Saint-Germain underlined their status ​as Europe's best side by beating Barcelona 4-2 in a blockbuster Champions ⁠League clash on Tuesday, while Liverpool and Manchester City also claimed victories. Desire Doue, Lucas Hernandez, ⁠Vitinha and Fabian Ruiz scored for PSG, with Xavi Espart and Lamine ​Yamal twice pulling Barcelona level in the second half. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice as Liverpool fought back from two goals down to beat Villarreal 4-3 ⁠in a thrilling encounter at Anfield. Phil Foden scored a hat-trick to lead Manchester City to a 5-1 win over AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium, with Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki also on the scoresheet as Erling Haaland was rested. Barcelona arrived at the Parc des Princes with a perfect record across all ⁠competitions this season, but PSG proved more clinical in a breathless contest to hand the Catalans their first defeat of the campaign. The relentless tempo ​took its ⁠toll, with PSG's Ousmane Dembele, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and ‌Marquinhos, along with Barcelona's Dani Olmo, all forced off through injury. PSG peppered the Barcelona goal in the opening five minutes, with Kvaratskhelia hitting the ​post, before the game settled into a rhythm. The hosts gradually took control of midfield and went ahead after Yamal surrendered possession in his own half, allowing Doue to drive a fierce low shot into the corner. Goalkeeper Joan Garcia produced several saves to keep Barcelona in the contest before Espart, making his first Champions League start, created and finished a superb move to equalise in the 55th minute. Ferran Torres hit the post against his former club before Hernandez headed PSG in front from a corner in the 72nd minute, starting a burst of four goals in 14 minutes. Lamine equalised again for Barcelona with a brilliant individual effort in the 79th minute, before Vitinha responded for PSG with a fine strike 109 seconds later. As Hansi Flick's side searched for an equaliser, Fabian Ruiz converted an Achraf Hakimi cross at the back post to seal the victory. The result lifted PSG on to nine points and top of the Champions League standings, ahead of Liverpool on goal difference. “It was a fantastic game from both teams. PSG showed they are better than us,” admitted Flick afterwards. “They have a lot of quality in transition. Also, in the final 10 minutes we weren’t fresh, although that’s not an excuse. We didn’t have the best preparation for this game. We have to analyse it and do things better.” Foden netted a hat-trick as Man City comfortably dispatched AEK Athens at the Etihad Stadium. Anderson opened the scoring for the hosts in the 12th minute before Foden doubled the advantage in the 34th. AEK Athens pulled a goal back ​through Stavros Pilios in the 52nd minute, but Cherki restored City's two-goal cushion five minutes later. Foden added his ‌second of the night in the 65th minute and ⁠completed his treble 11 minutes later to wrap up a dominant performance. Haaland ​was an unused substitute, as City gave their leading striker a rest amid a demanding fixture schedule. The ‌visitors stunned the Anfield crowd when Georges Mikautadze struck in the fourth minute before Sergi Cardona doubled Villarreal's lead in the 29th. Liverpool's fightback started with two ⁠headers as Mac Allister pulled a goal back in the 36th minute before Ronald Araujo equalised in first-half stoppage time. Mac Allister completed ⁠the turnaround with his second goal in the 65th minute, and Florian Wirtz hammered home a fourth in the 69th to cap a rampant spell for the hosts. Tani Oluwaseyi pulled one back for Villarreal in the 87th minute, but Liverpool survived the late pressure to secure the points. Elsewhere, Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez levelled in the second half to earn them a 1-1 draw with VfB Stuttgart, who took the lead through Jamie Leweling ​before the break. Morten Hjulmand was sent off in the 64th minute, leaving Atletico with 10 men for the closing stages. Napoli edged Bodo/Glimt 4-3 and PSV Eindhoven held off Porto for a 1-0 win, while AS Roma cruised to a 4-0 victory over Slovan Bratislava. Earlier, Borussia Dortmund won 2-1 against Champions League debutants Sabah, while a 90th-minute equaliser from Pavel Kacor earned Slavia Prague a point in a 2-2 draw at Fenerbahce.

title: Trump says Ilhan Omar could face jail as he attacks her Somali roots
description: US President calls the Minnesota Democrat 'a disgrace' and disparages Somalia in personal remarks
content: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Democratic representative Ilhan Omar could go to jail, and criticised her Somali heritage. Speaking during an event in the Oval Office during which he unveiled a federal fraud whistleblower incentive programme, Mr Trump said Ms Omar was “a sick and very dishonest person” who “hates our country”. "She could also go to jail. You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail. This is just my opinion. I think she's a sick, a very dishonest person who hates our country," he said. Mr Trump has repeatedly attacked Ms Omar, a Somali-born American citizen and one of the first Muslim women elected to Congress. This month, US federal agents raided her home in Washington amid a criminal fraud investigation into her immigration paperwork. Ms Omar has repeatedly denied allegations of wrongdoing, describing them as false and politically motivated. She arrived in the US as a child, fleeing the civil war in Somalia. In 2019, she was elected to Congress to represent Minnesota's 5th District. A critic of Mr Trump, she is seeking another term for the seat in the November 3 midterms . Minnesota is home to a large Somali community. "It's a real [expletive]," Mr Trump said of Somalia. "It's got no government ... all they do is have people running around shooting each other." "She's a disgrace to our country, and it's amazing that she can get elected, but Somalians vote for her." Mr Trump's comments come amid a rise in Islamophobic speech , much of it directed at Muslim candidates and elected officials. He also frequently attacks Abdul El-Sayed , who is running for a Senate seat in Michigan. If he wins, he would be the first Muslim senator in US history. Much of Mr Trump's attacks have been taking place during his campaign rallies and online.

title: UAE is powering along with US technology co-operation, Yousef Al Otaiba says
description: Amid conflict in region, UAE's ambassador to US tells of perseverance, continued investments and security agreements
content: Despite the US war with Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the UAE is moving ahead with investment and technology plans in America, according to the UAE's ambassador to Washington . In a letter written on Monday to the US-UAE Business Council, Yousef Al Otaiba, who is also a Minister of State, said neither the UAE nor members of the council flinched during the challenges presented by the conflict. "We adapt, we persevere – and more than ever, we do it in close partnership with the US," he wrote. "Our commitments to the United States remain firm, our major investments are moving forward, and expanded access to advanced technology is opening further opportunities." Mr Al Otaiba also told council members that his country had "earned its place among America's most trusted partners", and said the UAE would never put that trust at risk. The US has over the years entrusted the UAE to use and operate US defence systems, F-16s and Apache helicopters, which have assisted the country in dealing with aggression from Iran this year, he wrote. "This not only shielded the UAE homeland, it was also a key link in the integrated network that defended American personnel, assets and allies across the region," Mr Al Otaiba said. In July, the US Department of Commerce significantly upgraded the UAE's export status, giving it “enhanced favourable treatment” and making it easier to export and transfer US military equipment, satellites, spacecraft, and artificial intelligence and energy technology. Mr Al Otaiba said that upgrade will help to strengthen the UAE and US in years to come. "More speed, more scale and more opportunity on both sides," he wrote to business council members. He said the upgrade was a tremendous vote of confidence in the UAE's technological commitment to making sure sophisticated tools stay out of the wrong hands. "We have implemented extensive legal, institutional and structural protections," Mr Al Otaiba wrote. "These include ring-fenced security environments, approved end users, verifiable non-diversion, vetted personnel and continuous monitoring." He spoke of the recent announcement of UAE-based Space42 signing a $1 billion communications deal with US-based Viasat, and of Emirates, Etihad and flydubai placing more than $65 billion worth of orders for Boeing aircraft with General Electric engines as proof of how both the US and UAE were benefitting. "Together, these investments expand American manufacturing, energy and computing capacity while creating opportunities for US companies to innovate and grow," he said. The letter also highlighted the UAE's 10-year, $1.4 trillion tech investment framework in the US, which Mr Al Otaiba said was ahead of schedule. "The UAE has purchased and invested hundreds of billions of dollars in US technologies, companies and energy projects," he said, adding "that capital is already at work". For several years, the US and UAE have worked closely amid the AI development boom. The UAE has been regarded by many technology executives as being ahead of the curve on AI. In May, after several months of working out security details, the first shipments of US-based Nvidia's highly sought-after CPUs and GPUs, critical for AI infrastructure, arrived in the UAE. "The five-gigawatt UAE-US AI Campus, built with American partners and powered by American chips, is more than infrastructure, it is a statement of UAE resolve and clearly exemplifies the depth of the bilateral relationship," Mr Al Otaiba said. He said the geopolitical obstacles over the past year, although challenging at times, have strengthened the UAE-US connection, and that the Emirates would fulfil its promises to protect US technology and find ways to create more opportunities for both countries. "These are the messages I ask you to carry to all your colleagues, boards and networks," Mr Al Otaiba said. In a statement to The National upon reflection of his letter to the US-UAE Business Council, the UAE ambassador highlighted the UAE's reliability in diplomacy. "From civil nuclear cooperation to Major Defense Partner to A:5, the UAE has proven time and again it is one of America's most trusted partners," he said. "Our commitments are firm, our safeguards verifiable and our resolve unchanged ... we will continue to deliver."

title: 'Dark fleet' under spotlight in latest US move to ease rising energy costs
description: Trump administration wants to move ships from 'bad-guy fleet' to 'good-guy fleet'
content: The US is turning to an unlikely saviour in its latest efforts to ease rising energy prices: the “ dark fleet ” that it has spent years sanctioning. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright revealed the administration's latest endeavour on Monday, telling those at a New York event that Washington wants to “move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet'". The dark fleet, sometimes referred to as the shadow fleet, refers to a group of ships that sail outside conventional shipping regulations. These vessels use deceptive shipping practices to transport cargo that is under sanctions or high risk, deliberately concealing it to avoid detection. Estimates on the size of the fleet vary. Mr Wright said he believes there are about 1,600 vessels. Data from TankerTrackers set the number at 1,480 active ships, while maritime company Windward said it has identified 1,100 dark fleet vessels. The dark fleet has grown in recent years after sanctions were imposed on Russian oil in response to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. Many of these vessels are past the 15-year threshold that marks the point at which technical failures begin to mount, adding to environmental safety risks. Mr Wright said the administration's plan would involve investors buying and refurbishing these idle sanctioned vessels before using them to transport legitimate oil. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more,” he said. The US has delisted sanctioned vessels before. In March, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control removed sanctions on the Panama-flagged crude oil supertanker Kiara M, which had been placed as part of the Trump administration's pressure campaign on Venezuela . Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's Centre on Global Energy Policy, said the move does little to address the security issue facing seafarers today in the Strait of Hormuz. At least 15 container ships have been struck in the waterway in the past 10 days. “You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets,” Mr Nephew said. War risk insurance premiums have surged since the start of the conflict. Rates have climbed to as high as 10 per cent of hull value, compared to 0.25 per cent before the conflict, adding millions to the premiums ship and cargo owners pay. Mr Wright's comments also come less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russian diesel in an agreement with President Vladimir Putin. Mr Trump said the agreement would include Moscow supplying millions of barrels of diesel to US and global markets. With only two weeks until the US midterm elections on November 3, diesel prices at the pump have risen to more than $6 a gallon [$1.59 a litre] on average, compared to about $3 the same time last year. Wholesale diesel prices passed $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and hit all-time highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US, the International Energy Agency said in an October 14 report. The seven-day moving average for tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was seven vessels for the week ending September 18, a small fraction of its pre-war levels, according to the International Monetary Fund's PortWatch monitor. Analysts at Kpler estimate only 24 of the about 160 vessels under sanctions from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. “If this is about getting ships out of sanctions, fine, no problem, proceed as you wish. If this is about solving the problem with whether we can get enough diesel and other products to market, this is not it," Mr Nephew said.

title: RAF Fairford suspects face new charges of working for Iranian intelligence
description: PM Andy Burnham said incident at Fairford was likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran
content: British authorities arrested two men on suspicion of ⁠assisting Iranian intelligence in a second set of charges for suspects after an alleged plot at RAF Fairford airbase last month. Counter-Terrorism Policing said on Tuesday that the men would face a new charge under the National Security Act. The US withdrew its B-1 bombers from Fairford after five British men were arrested ​outside ⁠the military base in ‌south-west England in the early hours of September ​27. Two other men were later arrested by police, although all seven were released on bail. A statement on Tuesday said authorities had re-arrested a British national, 24, who was initially arrested outside RAF Fairford, and British-Iranian dual national, 25, who had previously been arrested in London. "This is ‌very much a live ⁠investigation and our evidence ​gathering continues, but at this time our position ​remains ‌the same: we consider it highly likely that there is ⁠Iranian state involvement," assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the ​UK, said in a statement. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said ⁠that the activity at Fairford was likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, while Iran's ambassador to Britain was called in for a diplomatic rebuke. Iran rejects the allegations. "We know the public have unanswered questions," ​Mr Taylor said. "I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will." US officials said they remain confident that no operational problems had been caused by returning the bombers from the UK, which is the only European country that allows in aircraft involved in the Washington's Iran operations. "While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," a Defence Department official said in a statement at the time. Jonathan Hackett, a former US Marines interrogator, told a panel hosted by the Royal United Services Institute think tank this week that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps regarded the UK as a soft target for sabotage operations. "Because the UK is one of the only allies and partners that's allowing the United States to land strategic bombers like the B-1B Lancer," Mr Hackett said. "British international overseas territories like Diego Garcia, are the fallback location for those bombers. Other partners, Nato partners, are not allowing those assets to land. So the IRGC is looking at the UK as kind of an accomplice in this, and is targeting it as much as it can. "It's a low capability but it's still a threat."

title: Iran not an 'evil regime', US ambassador Tom Barrack says
description: Remarks go against Trump administration stance and come as US-Iran talks remain stalled
content: Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey, sparked controversy on Tuesday when he said Iran's government was "not an evil regime", an assessment that goes against years of messages from the administration of President Donald Trump . The remarks by Mr Barrack, who is also Mr Trump's special envoy for Syria and Iraq, come as talks between the US and Iran remain stalled despite signs of increased diplomatic activity in Tehran. At the Global Security Forum in Doha, Mr Barrack differentiated between Iran's ruling religious class and the actions of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which he said “has become an adversary” and whose role with Israel “has been a problem”. “It’s a theocracy," he said of Tehran's government. "It’s not an evil regime, that has nothing to do with it. That’s a religious content and practice that we all respect.” The Trump administration has repeatedly used the word “evil” to describe Iran's regime, including in official White House statements and remarks by senior officials such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The State Department did not comment. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Breitbart News in a report broadcast on Sunday that Iran is "the number one driver of instability and war and conflict, and the number one obstacle to peace in the Middle East is the Islamic regime in Tehran". On a visit to India on Tuesday, Mr Rubio compared Iran's tactics against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to those used by Nazi Germany's submarines during the Second World War. Mr Barrack has a long record of provocative comments about governance in the Middle East and on other issues, including calling Hezbollah and Israel "equally untrustworthy", suggesting Israel " still " occupies the Golan Heights, and saying that Lebanon was at risk of becoming Bilad Al Sham again, the historical name for the Syria region. Washington and Tehran remain locked in a conflict that started nearly eight months ago, with negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme at an apparent impasse. Mr Barrack said the US should pursue a negotiated settlement rather than seek to impose regime change, saying Washington's previous attempts to change governments in the region had repeatedly failed. “We’ve had 23 regime changes and none of them have worked,” he said. “Every time we try and intervene and change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake.” The remarks prompted a swift backlash from US conservative commentators, who accused Mr Barrack of playing down the Iranian government's repression and hostility towards Israel. "Tom Barrack has gone rogue again, pushing his own insane agenda and giving aid and comfort to genocidal maniacs," said Mark Levin, a conservative broadcaster. "This has to be one of the most outrageous statements yet, about the mass killing, nuclear-obsessed Islamist terrorist Iranian regime." Russia 's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Monday, a day after the Russian minister held talks in Bahrain , where Gulf countries urged him to lobby Tehran to stop its drone and missile attacks on its neighbours. In Iran, Mr Lavrov, who also met President Masoud Pezeshkian, said Russia was prepared to "assist in finding acceptable negotiated solutions" to resolve the crisis. During Mr Rubio's visit to India, he also raised the prospect of Reliance Industries refining more Venezuelan crude and possibly increasing its involvement in oil production in the country. The US is looking to boost global oil supplies to ease shortages caused by the war with Iran and Russia's war against Ukraine.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed and France's Macron tour Abu Dhabi defence companies
description: Leaders witness signing of defence partnership as nations bolster ties
content: President Sheikh Mohamed and Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday toured companies operated by the UAE's largest defence group as part of the French President's official visit to the Gulf . Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Macron inspected advanced manufacturing sites at Tawazun Industrial Park in Abu Dhabi. The companies included Abu Dhabi Autonomous Systems Investments, EPI, Halcon and Powertech, all high-tech entities which form part of the Edge Group. The two leaders were briefed on the industrial park's key role in supporting domestic, regional and international companies. Sheikh Mohamed was joined by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohamed, Deputy Chairman of the Presidential Court for Special Affairs, Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad, Adviser to the UAE President, and a number of ministers and senior officials. Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Macron also witnessed the exchange of a strategic defence partnership framework between the UAE and France. The framework was exchanged between Mohammed Al Mazrouei, Minister of State for Defence Affairs, and Catherine Vautrin, France's Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs. Sheikh Mohamed later bade farewell to Mr Macron as he concluded the UAE leg of his Gulf visit, which began in Kuwait on Monday. The French leader arrived in Bahrain after concluding the UAE leg of his tour and is to also travel to Qatar. The UAE and France signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as part of Mr Macron's official visit. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three deals focusing on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation, and explore new applications across several fields, the Abu Dhabi Media Office reported.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed meets global health leaders at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit
description: Delegation of experts gathered from three-day summit focused on predictive health care
content: President Sheikh Mohamed received global health leaders gathering in Abu Dhabi for a three-day summit focused on predictive healthcare innovation. Sheikh Mohamed met a delegation of international health experts attending the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, which runs until Thursday under the theme: "To Sense is to Predict". He welcomed the group and expressed his hopes that their discussions would produce meaningful results for people worldwide. Sheikh Mohamed reaffirmed that health remains a central priority for the UAE , describing the nation's people as its greatest asset, state news agency Wam reported. He stressed the country's commitment to expanding investment in the sector as part of a broader effort to build a sustainable healthcare system capable of improving quality of life across society. The Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit is a key gathering for health leaders seeking to shape the future of global care. The UAE has in recent years placed itself as a regional centre for medical innovation, with significant public and private investment directed towards modernising health care and increasing access to advanced medical services for residents and citizens.

title: Rubio rejects claims of slow US weapons delivery to Ukraine
description: Trump administration has not approved transfer of interceptor missiles to Kyiv, reports say
content: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected accusations that the US has been slow to deliver weapons bought by Ukraine, which remains locked in brutal war with Russia. The Washington Post first reported a day earlier that the Pentagon has been slowing delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv. "I know one of the things that [Ukrainian] President [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy has been talking about is that he’s been trying to buy interceptors, and I understand. So does every other country in the world," Mr Rubio told media in India . "We have our own needs, too." But he stressed that everything "remains the same" on US commitments to Kyiv, including sharing intelligence, and said he had spoken with Mr Zelenskyy to clarify Washington's position. "We have a global defence footprint, and many of our installations around the world require defence," Mr Rubio said. "So there’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine." In a statement, the Pentagon also said the policy towards Ukraine was unchanged. The comments come amid increased concern in Ukraine over the delivery of the defence equipment, acquired through Purl, the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List – a Nato programme that allies use to finance the purchase of US weaponry for Kyiv. “The missiles are ready and they could already be in Ukraine,” Mr Zelenskyy said on a call with a bipartisan group of senators on Monday. “But unfortunately, there is still no approval.” Ukraine has almost no US-supplied Patriot interceptors left, Mr Zelenskyy said. He said the US is supplying only 12 Patriot interceptor missiles a month – a quarter of the number provided under former president Joe Biden. The Kyiv Independent quoted a Ukrainian official as saying Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth "has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them". Relations are fraying between Ukraine and the US. President Donald Trump has called on Mr Zelenksyy to end strikes on Russian oil sites amid a global energy crunch caused in part by the war in Iran. Last week, Mr Trump claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire", a day after Washington temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were intended to limit Moscow’s revenue for its war against Kyiv. Mr Trump said the move was made to try to keep Russia at the negotiating table. Mr Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen its war effort. Mr Trump accused Mr Zelenskyy in a Truth Social post of wanting the war to continue. Meanwhile, Elon Musk reportedly ordered a slowdown for his military-grade version of Starlink, which provides internet services by satellite to hard-to-reach places. The Wall Street Journal , quoting US officials and sources, said Mr Musk had capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to Starlink , making some offensive and interceptor drones ineffective. In response to complaints of slowed speeds, Mr Musk posted on his social media platform X that Starshield systems "are owned and controlled by the US government". "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [Mr Trump]," Mr Musk wrote. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." The WSJ said Mr Musk had approached Mr Trump and other officials about the slowdown. Commenting on a post on X in which Mr Trump speaks of Ukraine attacking Russian oil refineries, Mr Musk wrote that Mr Zelenskyy "has gone too far".

title: Yemenis struggle as prices double in besieged Taiz
description: Government forces say they carried out almost 750 operations using aircraft, artillery and snipers in fight with Houthis
content: The prices of food and fuel have doubled in the city of Taiz as it struggles under a Houthi siege, the UN warned on Tuesday, as it urged the Yemeni rebels to let supplies enter. The fuel crunch is affecting hospitals and putting patients' lives in danger, while many families in Taiz are struggling to obtain water, said Laurent Bukera, a UN humanitarian official in Yemen. The Yemeni government on Tuesday accused the Houthis of firing a mortar shell at an ambulance in Taiz, killing two people including an 18-year-old girl. It said the rebels were carrying out “indiscriminate shelling of residential areas”. The government announced a series of counter-attacks as it tries to regain territory from the Houthis. An offensive by the Iran-backed group in recent weeks has reignited Yemen 's civil war and opened a new front in the wider Middle East conflict. Yemeni forces carried out almost 750 operations involving warplanes, drones, artillery, rocket launchers and snipers, official media said. Army spokesman Col Majid Al Nuzaili said targets included Houthi firing positions and command centres. The Houthis, whose repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia have caused hundreds of casualties and blocked flights to the kingdom, claimed attacks on Tuesday on the border areas of Jizan and Asir. A Saudi-led coalition backing the government in Yemen said a drone had been destroyed over Riyadh. Col Al Nuzaili said Yemeni government forces were “intensifying their combat pressure” in Taiz, a city that has become critical to the struggle for western Yemen. Houthi gains on the west coast have raised fears of ships being attacked in the Red Sea , with potential implications far beyond Yemen. Mr Bukera, the UN official, said the health system in Taiz was on the brink of collapse, as road closures and a lack of security lead to supplies not reaching inhabitants. “The shortage of energy supplies needed to run hospitals and the availability of medical oxygen is endangering the lives of hundreds of patients. Prices of the remaining food and fuel supplies have more than doubled, exacerbating the pressure on families who are already struggling to meet their basic needs,” he said. “Of particular concern is the difficulty faced by hundreds of thousands of families in accessing water, as water production in the city has dropped to half its capacity and available alternatives have run out.” Mr Bukera urged Houthi authorities to open “safe passages” to allow basic goods to enter. The warning came a day after a Houthi attack on a military training camp killed at least 73 people in Shabwa province, raising fears of further escalation. The attack injured more than 200 people, while 14 remained missing on Tuesday, Shabwa Governor Awad Al Wazir said. Injured recruit Nasser Sheikh Bahaj said three missiles struck as security personnel were training. He told Yemeni media that reconnaissance aircraft had flown over the camp during the previous three nights, filming the site. Reports from Shabwa General Hospital and other medical sites in the city of Ataq, the capital of Shabwa governorate, described chaotic scenes as ambulances and private vehicles carried casualties. Fighting has spread across Yemen since the initial Houthi push to the sea last month. Last Thursday, Houthi missiles were fired at the Presidential Palace in Aden, killing five people.

title: Sheikh Khaled meets Prime Minister of Singapore in Zayed National Museum
description: Lawrence Wong is on official visit to the UAE
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of Abu Dhabi Executive Council, met with Lawrence Wong, Prime Minister of Singapore on Tuesday. During the meeting, the two sides exchanged cordial discussions on the deep-rooted relations between the UAE and Singapore and their close partnership, reported Abu Dhabi Media Office. Sheikh Khaled accompanied Mr Wong on a tour of Zayed National Museum. Mr Wong is on an official visit to the USAE, the media office added.

title: Abu Dhabi gene therapy frees thalassaemia patient from more blood transfusions
description: Yas Clinic and ADSCC achieve medical milestone for patient in UAE
content: A thalassaemia patient in Abu Dhabi has become transfusion-independent following gene-therapy treatment, marking a medical milestone in the UAE. The 43-year-old patient, known only as Fahad, spent years managing transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, requiring treatment every three to four weeks to maintain stable haemoglobin levels. The condition also led to an overload or iron and a constant need for iron chelation therapy, affecting his quality of life, state news agency Wam reported on Tuesday. Thalassaemia is a group of blood disorders, sufferers of which lack haemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that carries oxygen in the blood. Low levels can make patients anaemic, and cause fatigue and shortness of breath. About 18 months ago, Fahad was referred to Yas Clinic and the Abu Dhabi Stem Cells Centre (ADSCC), where scientists were working to introduce advanced gene therapy treatment to the country. Gene therapy has emerged as one of the most important developments in treating inherited blood disorders, offering a long-term solution for patients without access to a suitable bone marrow donor. Fahad was identified as a suitable candidate. His treatment involved the collection of his own stem cells, which were genetically modified before being reinfused following preparatory therapy. He has since remained under medical supervision and is no longer reliant on regular transfusion. Dr Maysoon Al Karam, chief medical officer at Yas Clinic, said the case reflected the UAE's commitment to making advanced therapies accessible to patients domestically. “This marks an important milestone in expanding access to innovative treatment options and reinforces Abu Dhabi's position as a regional centre for advanced health care and medical innovation,” she said. Dr Mohammed Abu Haleeqa, haematologist at Yas Clinic, described the outcome as life-changing for patients who have spent most of their lives dependent on regular transfusion. “Gene therapy offers the opportunity to address the underlying cause of the disease using the patient's own genetically modified cells, providing an advanced treatment option for patients who may not have suitable donors for transplantation,” Dr Abu Haleeqa said.

title: Gaza families fear losing their last lifeline after WFP aid cuts
description: UN agency to reduce cash and food handouts in the Palestinian territory because of a lack of funding
content: Palestinian families who lost their homes and livelihoods in the Gaza war say the World Food Programme’s decision to cut food and cash assistance to about 500,000 people could deprive them of their only means of survival. The WFP announced the decision on Monday, saying it was because of a lack of funding. "This is not because the needs are going down, and it's not because we aren't able to bring in the food. This is only because we have less funding,” said Carl Skau , acting head of the UN agency. For nearly two years, Ahmed Al Haj, 53, has relied on financial assistance from the WFP to feed his family after losing his home and livelihood during the war in Gaza. Every two or three months, Mr Al Haj receives a payment of 1,250 Israeli shekels (about $380), which has become his family’s main source of support as they struggle to survive in a displacement camp in Al Mawasi, in southern Gaza . “WFP assistance is extremely important to me, and my family depends on it to survive,” he told The National . “After hearing the news that assistance would be reduced for half a million people in Gaza. I became afraid that my financial support might be cut off.” Originally from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, Mr Al Haj has been living in a tent with his family since their home was destroyed during the war. He and his eldest son, Ahmed, were injured and continue to receive medical treatment, leaving them unable to work even if jobs were available. “We should be the ones providing for our family but unfortunately, there are no jobs available. Even if there were, our injuries would prevent us from working,” he said. Mr Al Haj said he contacted the WFP's offices in Gaza to ask whether his assistance would continue, but was told the new list of beneficiaries had not yet been approved. “I hope the assistance continues because if it stops, my family and I will have nothing left to depend on,” he said. “We will be left completely without any source of income.” Mr Al Haj's fears are shared by other displaced Palestinians, who depend on humanitarian assistance to meet their most basic needs amid widespread unemployment, the destruction of businesses and growing uncertainty over the sustainability of international aid programmes. The cuts announced on Monday will reduce the number of Palestinians receiving monthly WFP assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, the agency said. The reductions go beyond the number of beneficiaries. Families who previously received two food parcels will receive one, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour. The number of hot meals distributed daily will be cut from 250,000 thousand to 150,000, while cash assistance to 75,000 families has also been reduced. The WFP said it received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years and urgently needs $400 million to maintain essential programmes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank over the next six months. The announcement comes as an estimated 1.4 million people in Gaza, or 67 per cent of the population, face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. About 200,000 are experiencing emergency levels of hunger, the WFP says. Although food security has improved modestly since the October 2025 ceasefire, the agency warned that those gains are fragile and could be reversed if humanitarian assistance continues to decline. A WFP employee in Gaza told The National that reductions in humanitarian assistance had already become evident over the past month to six weeks, with the number of aid lorries arriving falling sharply. “On days when the [border] crossing was operating, we used to receive more than 25 trucks a day carrying aid for distribution to residents. But for approximately the past month and a half, the number of trucks has not exceeded eight or 10, even on the best days," they said. “On some days, only five trucks enter. We have been informed internally more than once that these reductions are due to a shortage of funding and donations for Gaza. “There have also been reductions in the cash assistance programme. More than 100,000 families previously received 1,250 shekels during each payment cycle, but they will now receive only 750 shekels, according to specific criteria.” For Mohammed Abu Ailwa, 46, the reductions threaten one of the few remaining sources of food for his family of nine, including two people with disabilities, who live in a displacement camp near Gaza city’s port. Mr Abu Ailwa owned a small grocery shop in Al Shati refugee camp that was destroyed in the war. He now depends on monthly WFP parcels containing lentils, rice, cooking oil, flour and canned goods. “World Food Programme assistance is a lifeline for us in Gaza,” he said. “It is true that the food items are repetitive and available in local markets, but people like me who have no money depend on the monthly WFP food parcel.” Mr Abu Ailwa said he was deeply worried about how he would provide for his family, especially as many community kitchens that offered free meals had stopped operating. “The food parcels and assistance should be increased, not reduced,” he said. Even before the latest reductions, he said, the assistance was not enough to meet his family’s needs but “having a little is better than having nothing at all”. The loss of humanitarian assistance could have consequences beyond hunger, according to economic analyst Ahmed Abu Qamar, who said it could further weaken the territory’s already devastated economy. Mr Abu Qamar said the food and cash assistance not only helped families survive but also supported the local economy by enabling households to buy essential goods. Reducing that support would lower buying power, weaken demand in local markets and place more pressure on traders and the few businesses still operating. “As a result, local markets risk becoming trapped in a vicious cycle of rising poverty, declining consumption and weakening economic activity,” Mr Abu Qamar said. He questioned the sustainability of humanitarian programmes in a territory where much of the population has lost their means to earn a living. Repeated reductions attributed to funding shortages, Mr Abu Qamar said, raise concerns about whether the humanitarian response can continue to meet Gaza’s growing needs. The crisis is not only about the quantity of food entering Gaza, but also its quality and diversity. Limited varieties of food, including flour and canned goods, cannot compensate for fresh and nutritionally balanced products, he said. The WFP said only one in five children in Gaza has a sufficiently diverse diet. With more than 80 per cent of the population unemployed, many families cannot afford fresh vegetables and protein-rich foods even when they are available. Mr Abu Qamar called for sustained humanitarian funding, better management and diversification of food supplies, and the restoration of UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, to its full operational role. With winter approaching and hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians still living in temporary shelters, the aid reduction threatens to place more hardship on families struggling to meet their daily needs.

title: Oversight board blasts Meta for removing content linked to 'No Kings' movement and Brazilian election
description: Tech firm blames removal on technological glitches but critics complain of suppression
content: Meta’s Oversight Board said the company 's content moderation failures led to the removal of “No Kings” political activist accounts in the US and others focused on the Brazilian elections from several of its platforms. The so-called No Kings protests oppose some of President Donald Trump 's policies and executive actions. Brazil's contentious election process has pitted current President Luiz Inacio 'Lula' da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro, one of former leader Jair Bolsonaro's sons. “We have repeatedly warned that during elections and periods of heightened political tension, Meta's content moderation failures often manifest themselves in two ways: overenforcement that suppresses political speech and underenforcement that undermines electoral integrity,” said the Oversight Board , which provides independent guidance and critiques of the company's actions. The board said No Kings accounts should have featured in the company's cross-check programme, which would then have probably prevented the technical error from occurring. “It remains unclear why Meta’s election integrity efforts did not lead to a much quicker resolution,” the board wrote. Last weekend, with nationwide No Kings protests scheduled to take place, the activists' social media accounts on Meta were removed. Meta blamed the removal on a series of technological glitches but critics say No Kings content was suppressed. Mr da Silva's team has said his profile was intentionally hidden from searches on purpose. Brazil’s top electoral court this week doubled a daily fine for Meta, saying it had failed to comply with an order about how political content is shown on its platforms. “It’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled,” the board statement read. Created in 2018, the board is designed to provide independent supervision of Meta's content moderation on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, particularly once users feel they have exhausted the company’s appeals processes.
