The board was created largely as a response to the deluge of inauthentic content originating from Russia that appeared in users' news feeds in the lead-up to the 2016 US presidential election. Such content led to a number of congressional investigations and Mark Zuckerberg , Meta’s chief executive, giving evidence at a hearing in Washington. Meta announced last year it would be automating its content moderation approach . “Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s 'reading' behaviour,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone posted on Threads of the current incident. “Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error. Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologise.” But Meta's response has done little to calm critics. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy suggested that if the Democrats win back the House and Senate in the midterm elections, Big Tech companies such as Meta would come under increased scrutiny. “Outrageous,” he posted on X, referring to the deactivation of the No Kings accounts. “Put this on the January investigation list.”

title: Sheikh Abdullah joins US and India counterparts for talks in Mumbai
description: Economic ties, technology and regional stability on agenda at trilateral meeting
content: Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, met his Indian and American counterparts in Mumbai on Tuesday for trilateral talks aimed at deepening co-operation across key sectors. Sheikh Abdullah met India's External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the Indian financial capital, where talks centred on expanding ties across the economy, trade, investment, technology and artificial intelligence. The three ministers explored ways to advance shared interests, deepen economic integration, and enhance regional and international co-operation, with sustainable development featuring high on the agenda. Sheikh Abdullah underscored the depth of the UAE's strategic relationships with India and the US, noting that the two partnerships continue to grow. He highlighted a shared commitment to capitalising on opportunities across various sectors in support of common development goals. Also addressed were regional and international developments, with the three ministers exchanging views on issues of mutual concern. Discussions touched on continuing efforts to strengthen security and stability, as well as to promote development and prosperity across the region and beyond. Reem Al Hashimy, Minister of State for International Co-operation, attended the meeting alongside Sheikh Abdullah. In Washington, President Donald Trump said the US and India were "pretty close" to finalising a trade deal. "They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal," he said. Mr Trump also said it "could be a much different kind of deal", without providing further details.

title: Weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Foundayo to be packaged in UAE
description: Agreement between Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Bio and Eli Lilly means weight-loss drugs will be packaged in UAE and distributed across region and further afield
content: A deal has been signed enabling US company Eli Lilly to package weight-loss drugs in the UAE . Under the agreement with Mubadala Bio, Mounjaro, as well as Foundayo, Lilly’s oral medicine – will be packaged in the UAE before being distributed across the region and further afield, said Hamad Almarzooqi, Mubadala Bio's deputy chief executive, who was speaking on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit on Tuesday. “They will be contract-manufactured here in the UAE and distributed around the world,” he said. The agreement will “support reliable access to innovative medicines while strengthening the UAE's role in the global life-sciences supply chain”. Earlier this year, The National revealed the UAE's efforts to drive down obesity rates could deliver a $51 billion boost to productivity, keep the military fighting fit and raise educational standards, according to a report. About 32 per cent of the UAE population is on course to be obese by 2031. The condition heightens the risk of diabetes, heart disease and hypertension. A joint study by Eli Lilly and market analysts Whiteshield, in collaboration with the Ministry of Economy and Tourism, suggests that figure could be reduced to 18 per cent within the same time frame, with accelerated intervention. The National has also reported how UAE residents have been urged to take weight-loss pills responsibly and on medical advice only. In June, it was announced the Wegovy weight-loss pill had been approved for use in the UAE. The oral medicine was already being prescribed for weight loss in the UAE, using an injection pen. Misuse of prescription drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro has surged in recent years, with people turning to the injectable medications for their rapid weight-loss effects. Health authorities around the world have struggled to contain the use of unregulated off-brand injectables without a prescription for cosmetic purposes, often driven by social-media trends and peer pressure. Mubadala Bio was established in May last year to strengthen medicine security, address prevalent diseases and build domestic expertise. Most pharmaceutical products used in the UAE are imported, Mr Almarzooqi said. The company has a five-year plan to bring that figure down but has yet to set a target publicly. “Mubadala Bio was created for three reasons: to ensure drug security in the UAE, to address the most prevalent diseases in the UAE, and to build that local ecosystem and talent within the company,” he said. The company said it had maintained supplies of essential medicines during spells of disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz throughout this year. Before the strait was closed, Mubadala Bio increased stocks of raw materials, arranged alternative shipping routes by air and land, and used other ports in the UAE. Some raw materials were sourced locally. “Many of our raw materials for essential drugs are manufactured here in the UAE,” Mr Almarzooqi said. “That helped us supply the country … when disruptions were happening.” The company’s aim, he said, was to make essential medicine available when patients need them, “not delayed, not out of stock, not in a ship somewhere”. “A patient on dialysis cannot postpone this treatment,” he said. “A patient with diabetes needs continuous assurance of continuity of insulin. A lady who’s getting cancer treatment in a hospital needs assurance that her treatment is available at all times. “We’re dealing with people’s lives.” Mubadala Bio runs four manufacturing plants in the UAE. Bioventure Healthcare, in Jebel Ali, makes soft-gelatin capsules and has a high-potency oncology site that also produces hormones. It has launched more than four oncology products and female fertility hormones, with more in the pipeline, Mr Almarzooqi said. He added the agreements with international drug manufacturers were not all about importing medicine. Companies had chosen the UAE, he said, “because of the talent that we have, because of the connectivity and the outreach that we have and because of the quality of the finished goods that we produce”. Building trust in locally made generic medicine would depend on how well the products worked, he said. “We are very comfortable that our products meet the highest global standards,” he added.

title: Dh1m gets you in the queue for Tesla's new Roadster in the UAE
description: The 'flying' Rocket model will be available by invitation only
content: Tesla has opened the ordering process for its next-generation Roadster in the UAE – but the “flying” version is not yet available. The Roadster, unveiled by Tesla chief executive Elon Musk at a demonstration in Texas last week, comes in three models: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. UAE customers can reserve the Performance with an initial refundable payment of Dh20,000 ($4,847), followed by another Dh190,000 within 10 days. The more powerful Thrust requires the same initial payment, followed by Dh1 million within 10 days. The car's built-in thrusters are purely for acceleration, not flight. The Rocket model – which is fitted with SpaceX -made thrusters – demonstrated its ability to “fly” last week. It can be bought through invitation only and remains unavailable in the UAE. It has yet to be revealed how Tesla will determine who can get hold of this top-end version. Tesla has made clear payments are deposits, as the final prices have yet to be decided. The Texas-based company plans to start production of the next-generation vehicles in 2028. Tesla has said availability of the Rocket is subject to domestic laws and regulations, and that configuration will not be offered in all regions. The “flying” capabilities of the Rocket Roadster have raised questions about the legality of such vehicles on roads, whether it would be classified as an aircraft and what approvals would be required. Flying raises a separate set of legal questions. UAE law states that aircraft operating in the Emirates must meet registration, licensing and airworthiness requirements. Hefty fines await those who breach these laws. However, the UAE is already developing regulations and infrastructure for flying taxis. In July, the General Civil Aviation Authority certified Dubai 's first purpose-built commercial vertiport for electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The UAE has separate laws governing road vehicles and aircraft but there is no publicly established approval framework specifically addressing a vehicle such as the Rocket Roadster. Federal regulations in the Emirates stipulate all vehicles must be registered and licensed, meet approved technical and safety standards and undergo inspection as part of the registration process. They require approval for substantial changes to the body, chassis or engine power, although this concerns modifications and does not necessarily apply to factory-built vehicles. The authority has also published operating procedures for such aircraft at Abu Dhabi's Al Bateen Executive Airport. But these frameworks do not automatically establish whether a vehicle designed for both roads and flight, such as the Rocket, would be permitted to operate. The Roadster would still need to meet UAE road regulations – and the Rocket version is expected to require particular aviation approval.

title: Sheikh Khaled to visit Greece for talks with Prime Minister Mitsotakis
description: Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi heads to Athens to strengthen UAE-Greece strategic partnership
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of Abu Dhabi Executive Council, is set to begin an official visit to Greece on Wednesday, aimed at strengthening ties between the two nations. The visit comes at the invitation of Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and marks a milestone in the relationship between the UAE and Greece, which have maintained diplomatic relations for five decades, state news agency Wam reported. Sheikh Khaled and Mr Mitsotakis are expected to hold talks focused on expanding bilateral co-operation across areas of shared priorities.

title: Nuclear watchdog praises UAE response to drone strike on Barakah plant
description: International Atomic Energy Agency carried out fact-finding mission to assess response
content: The UAE's response to an attack on the Barakah nuclear plant in May was swift and effective, the International Atomic Energy Agency has concluded. A drone launched from Iraq struck a generator outside the inner perimeter of the Barakah plant, causing a fire that was brought under control. Dozens of countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, the UK, the US, France and Pakistan, as well as the EU, signed a statement condemning the attack. The IAEA concluded on Tuesday that national authorities and Barakah Nuclear Power Plant had appropriately responded to the loss of off-site power due to the drone strike on May 17. The finding was reached by a six-person mission team from the nuclear agency who were in the UAE from October 12 to October 20 at the request of the government. Effective action was taken to maintain safety during the event, including prompt national and international notification, implementation of the established emergency response procedures, and public communication, the IAEA said in a statement. Its team visited the affected areas of the plant and key emergency response facilities, reviewed operating and emergency procedures, and met the senior management and technical staff of BNPP and the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation (FANR), the UAE’s independent nuclear regulator. The team focused on plant response actions, national arrangements for emergency preparedness and response, lessons learnt from the incident, and the reactor operator’s arrangements to ensure safety, the statement added. “By requesting this mission, FANR and BNPP have demonstrated their strong commitment to safety and continuous improvement,” said Amgad Shokr, director of the IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre and leader of the mission team. Barakah Nuclear Power Plant was “encouraged to continue implementing the organisational and technical measures identified through the assessment of lessons learnt from the event”. “The UAE has established a robust and comprehensive nuclear emergency preparedness and response system in line with the highest international standards, developed in close co-operation with the IAEA,” said Hamad Al Kaabi, director general of FANR. “The UAE shares the position of the international community and the IAEA on the importance of protecting nuclear facilities at all times. We will continue working closely with the IAEA and our national partners to enhance the safety and security of nuclear facilities and ensure the protection of the community and the environment.”

title: What’s happened to our understanding of competence?
description: How we recognise competence has changed, and AI may be exposing just how far that shift has gone
content: Every age believes it understands the meaning of its most important words, even as the realities they describe quietly change beneath them. “Freedom”, “responsibility”, “authority” and “trust” have survived centuries of transformation, yet none means precisely what it meant to previous generations. “Competence” may have undergone a similar transformation, although one particularly difficult to recognise because we continue to use the word with such confidence. We describe physicians, judges, teachers, engineers and leaders as “competent” as though the quality were self-evident and essentially unchanged. Yet the characteristics through which competence is recognised have shifted considerably. Now, AI may be exposing just how far that shift has gone. For much of professional history , competence revealed itself most clearly when certainty became impossible. The competent physician possessed medical knowledge, but the difficult patient was precisely the one for whom evidence and established practice did not produce an obvious answer. The competent judge knew the law , but judgment became necessary where applying a general principle to a particular human situation required interpretation. The competent leader understood the organisation, but leadership mattered most when precedent could no longer determine what should happen next. Competence therefore contained a common element: the ability to act responsibly when rules, knowledge and experience had carried the professional as far as they could. Knowledge remained the foundation upon which judgment rested. Yet professional competence included an acceptance that reality would occasionally exceed whatever systems had been designed to describe it. Expertise was valuable not because the expert always possessed an answer, but because the expert could recognise when an answer remained uncertain and still assume responsibility for deciding what should happen next. Modern institutions had good reasons to become uncomfortable with such an elusive definition. As organisations grew larger, professions more specialised and decisions more consequential, institutions needed to identify competence, certify it, reproduce it and evaluate it at scale. Medical education developed standardised examinations and professional guidelines; corporations created performance metrics and competency frameworks; universities formalised assessment; regulators demanded demonstrable standards. These developments represented genuine progress because they reduced arbitrary authority, made professional standards more transparent and allowed expertise to travel beyond the individuals and institutions in which it had originally developed. Yet something subtle happened in the process. The indicators through which competence could be recognised gradually became entangled with competence itself. Consistency came to signal reliability, procedural correctness to signal professionalism, measurable performance to signal effectiveness and confident communication to signal understanding. The difficulty begins when characteristics designed to make competence visible become the definition by which competence is understood. The distinction matters because what can be measured and standardised tends to be what institutions become best at recognising. A professional who produces clear answers, follows established processes, communicates fluently, and performs consistently leaves behind abundant evidence of competence. Someone whose greatest contribution lies in recognising that the framework itself no longer fits the situation may leave considerably less. The more organisations depend upon observable signals to identify expertise, the greater the danger that they privilege what competence looks like over what competence actually does. This transformation began long before AI, which is interesting precisely because it exposes a problem that technology did not create. Generative systems can now produce many of the signals that modern institutions have learned to associate with competence: articulate language, structured reasoning, rapid synthesis, polished presentations, confident recommendations and plausible explanations. What once required considerable professional effort can increasingly be produced within seconds. The obvious conclusion is that AI threatens traditional forms of expertise. A more interesting possibility is that AI is revealing how impoverished our definition of expertise had already become. If eloquence can be generated, consistency automated, information retrieved instantly and plausible answers produced at negligible cost, then perhaps these qualities were never competence itself. We may be entering an era in which the visible performance of competence becomes increasingly abundant while competence itself remains as difficult to cultivate as before. A beautifully structured analysis may reveal considerable judgment or merely competent use of a machine. The output alone increasingly tells us less about the intellectual process that produced it. The useful response is not to retreat into some mysterious realm of human intuition that machines can never reach, but to ask which dimensions of competence become more important as its traditional signals become less informative. Here the older understanding becomes unexpectedly relevant, because it reminds us that competence was never merely the production of correct answers. Competence also involves recognising which question deserves to be asked, distinguishing the relevant from the merely available, understanding when a general rule fits a particular situation and when it does not, identifying uncertainty rather than disguising it, and accepting responsibility for consequences that cannot be transferred to the system that informed the decision. None of these qualities requires rejecting AI. Intelligent systems may improve each of them by expanding the information available to professionals, challenging assumptions, and revealing patterns human beings would otherwise miss. But better information does not eliminate the need to decide what that information means in a particular context. This matters for the way institutions educate, recruit and evaluate people. Universities may need to care less about whether students can reproduce convincing answers and more about whether they can interrogate them. Organisations may need to look beyond fluency and responsiveness when identifying talent. Professional education may need to make uncertainty, interpretation and responsibility more explicit. Leadership development may need to place greater value on recognising when an established framework no longer describes the reality it was designed to manage. None of this requires abandoning standards, metrics or procedures. Modern institutions could not function without them, and a return to purely subjective assessments of expertise would recreate precisely the problems that standardisation was designed to solve. The challenge is to preserve the benefits of making competence visible without mistaking visibility for competence itself. Perhaps, then, AI is not changing the meaning of competence so much as forcing us to notice that we had already changed it. Over decades, we moved from an understanding centred on judgment under uncertainty toward one increasingly associated with consistency, demonstrable performance and the reliable production of answers. That transition brought enormous benefits, but it also narrowed our field of vision. Now that machines can reproduce many of those visible characteristics with extraordinary ease, the distinction we allowed to fade has become difficult to ignore. The question is therefore no longer whether AI will make human beings less competent. It is whether institutions will continue recognising competence through signals that technology has made increasingly unreliable, or whether we will recover a richer understanding of what competence was always supposed to describe: not simply knowing the answer, but knowing what to do when the answer is no longer enough.

title: Halloween costumes 2026: From Pitbull to Bad Bunny's bushes, seven pop culture-inspired looks to try
description: These DIY dress-up ideas will make you stand out from the crowd on the spookiest night of the year
content: With Halloween fast approaching, the race is on to get your costume organised. While classic costumes such as witches and wizards are always an option, tapping into the zeitgeist with a pop culture-appropriate costume is much more fun. Whether you want to look super-niche or instantly recognisable, these costume ideas are fun, occasionally spooky and will ship in time for October 31. Apple TV’s horror-comedy series Widow’s Bay has been winning fans and awards, thanks to its spooky Scooby Doo -esque premise. Cursed island? Check. Unexplained goings-on? Check. Eccentric inhabitants? Double check. Speaking of which, as the quirky assistant to Mayor Tom Loftis, Patricia Moyer (Kate O’Flynn) has emerged as a fan favourite. For Halloween, channel Patricia in episode four, Beach Reads , in which she (spoiler alert) finds a malevolent spell book disguised as a self-help guide and inadvertently entrances the islanders at a party. To achieve the look, you’ll need a red floral dress, a sturdy headband, antlers, some branches, a toy fox and some arts and crafts skills. Matt Damon’s Odysseus, Zendaya’s Athena, Anne Hathaway’s Penelope and Tom Holland’s Telemachus … there’s a wealth of Halloween inspiration to be found in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster epic The Odyssey . For Damon’s Odysseus, you can save or splurge as you wish. If you already have a beard, wrapping a dark-coloured sheet around yourself like a cloak will do as a last-minute dress-up idea. The same goes for Zendaya, whose looks as the goddess Athena are close to outfits you'd have dressed up in as a child, requiring you to wrap a white sheet around yourself, and voila. But those keen to put in a bit more effort can snap up a Greek goddess costume. For men, online options tend not to differentiate between Greek and Roman soldiers, so the scariest thing that might happen on Halloween is that an ancient history expert gets annoyed at you. Don a blonde wig and rhinestones to pay tribute to the late, great Dolly Parton. The country music legend, who died on August 25, is likely to be a popular choice this year. If you’re looking for a costume that is instantly recognisable and won’t have people asking, “Who did you come as?” then channel one of Parton’s many eras. From the rhinestone-studded dresses of her early years to the tight onstage jumpsuits that were her signature, make sure the hair is high and the smile is wide to make her proud. Pop star Mariah Carey went viral in October after posting a picture of herself on Instagram in front of Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper , at the Refectory of the Church of Santa Maria delle Grazie, in Milan. It wasn’t the famous painting that became an instant meme, but rather the singer’s facial expression. Mariah could not have looked less impressed with the celebrated artwork. With an expression as sparse as her Instagram caption – “The Last Supper” – people online were wild with comments such as: “One of the most important creations in all of human history, and also some mural” and “the last diva at the last supper”. To recreate the moment, head to your local Desco to print out a large copy of The Last Supper and affix it to your back, then don a black hooded jacket and a long blonde wig, with an “over it” look on your face. It’s been a huge year for Mr Worldwide. In July, at the BST Hyde Park show in London, Pitbull and his fans set an official world record for the largest gathering of people wearing bald caps, with 22,141 participants dressing up like the global pop star. His I’m Back tour sold out across North America and Europe and he released his 14th studio album, Pitcoin , in October. This Halloween, make like his many fans and pay homage by putting his most recognisable feature – his bald head – front and centre. To complete the look, you'll need a black suit, white shirt and sunglasses. Bonus points for drawn-on facial hair. This one is niche but, if you know, you know. Headlining the Super Bowl LX halftime show, Bad Bunny used people dressed as bushes to honour Puerto Rico's agricultural history. Aiming to represent the US territory's sugarcane fields and the farmers who work in them, but with NFL rules restricting the number of heavy prop carts allowed on the field to protect the turf, the rapper had 380 performers dress as sugarcane grass to create the backdrop. For your own version, you'll need bundles of artificial grass, which you can attach to a dark green hoodie around the arms and shoulders with zip ties. The Stephen King novel and 1976 film have been given another lease of life thanks to the series on Amazon Prime Video. Eagle-eyed horror fans will note that Carrie’s prom dress during that famous scene is no longer the baby pink of the original but is now silvery grey. The ill-fated tiara remains, though. To become the best-dressed pyro at the prom this year, be sure to douse yourself in fake blood either before or, for more effect, halfway through the night.

title: UAE and France deepen defence ties with Rafale F5 fighter-jet deal
description: Energy, AI and advanced technology will also be focus areas for the two countries
content: Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war. They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi. The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties. Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations. The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group , a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war. Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit. Edge , set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare. The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency. Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement. The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space. The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons. Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said. France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year. France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi. In AI and advanced technology, three agreements were signed with France's AI start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several key sectors, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office. The deals involve Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi's G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI will focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog's deal with AMI Labs focuses on exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications, creating new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technologies and identify opportunities to enhance operational efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts covering a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy. The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website. UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

title: Opinion polls suggest stalemate one week before Israeli election
description: No clear majority in divided state is stoking fears of escalation at home and abroad
content: In a week’s time, Israelis will head to the polls in what many are calling the most important election in its history. Despite the usual ups and downs of the Israeli news cycle, polls have remained largely stable for months: neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor that of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, is near a majority. Israeli voters are bracing themselves. There is a widespread feeling that this polling stalemate in such a divided country, combined with regional tension and hostility, could make for a busy week. The average of the past three surveys conducted by Israel’s mainstream pollsters puts Mr Eisenkot on 52 seats, one ahead of Mr Netanyahu. That means 17 unaligned seats are up for grabs, fuelling speculation that the next government will be formed after coalition negotiations, which could take months. If there is no agreement on a coalition, another election will be held. This has happened many times in Israel’s recent history. However, the election results could be decisive. Opinion polls are far from foolproof, and in any case not all indicate a stalemate. A smaller group of less mainstream surveys published by right-wing news channels place Mr Netanyahu’s bloc in a better position, with Channel 14 forecasting a one-seat majority in a poll on Sunday. It still charts a gradual decline in support for the coalition over recent weeks. Many voters are highlighting Mr Netanyahu's formidable ability as a politician. His talent for creating unlikely coalitions and undermining opponents is clear. Israel’s military is on high alert, and there are fears of another round of fighting with Iran, possibly even before polls open, creating more uncertainty that could well favour Mr Netanyahu. US President Donald Trump’s endorsement of him on Sunday was a surprise, which could reinforce the incumbent's credentials as a statesman for some voters. There is one clear path to victory for the mainstream opposition bloc – joining forces with Israel’s Arab parties. Many opposition parties, including Mr Eisenkot’s, have said they will not form a government with parties that typically represent the country's Palestinians, who make up about 20 per cent of the population. With polls suggesting a significant increase in turnout among Palestinian citizens, the group could become too significant to ignore. If Mr Eisenkot does find a way to make them part of his coalition, or the more likely option of a support-from-outside arrangement, the far-right would erupt. In that event, he may be described as a traitor and some of his current bloc partners might walk out.

title: Which airlines are flying to Riyadh? Latest schedules and cancellations
description: Saudi carriers and selected international airlines list services, but cancellations, diversions and restrictions continue
content: Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has reopened, but travel to the Saudi capital remains disrupted, with selected flights on the schedule alongside cancellations and diversions. Flightradar24’s arrivals and departures boards for Tuesday show services scheduled by Saudi carriers Saudia, Riyadh Air , flynas and flyadeal alongside some international airlines such as Air Cairo and ITA Airways. Domestic flights continue, with services listed to destinations including Jeddah, Dammam and Abha. However, cancellations have affected some Saudi-operated flights as well as international connections. For passengers planning to travel to Riyadh, here’s what to know. Saudi carriers have several services to Dubai listed on the departures board, including Riyadh Air flight RX243, flynas flights XY207 and XY211, and Saudia flight SV560. Air Arabia’s flights between Sharjah and Riyadh remain cancelled, with the airline yet to announce a date for their resumption. Other UAE connections are also marked as cancelled, including Emirates flight EK820 and flydubai flight FZ848 from Riyadh to Dubai, alongside Etihad Airways flight EY556 to Abu Dhabi. On the arrivals board, Etihad flight EY555 from Abu Dhabi was cancelled, as were Emirates flight EK819 and flydubai flight FZ847 from Dubai. Selected international services are also listed on flight schedules, connecting Riyadh with Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Italy and the UK. Scheduled arrivals included Air Cairo flight SM469 from Cairo, Riyadh Air flight RX418 from Manchester and ITA Airways flight AZ838 from Rome Fiumicino. Outbound services included Riyadh Air flight RX331 to Cairo, flynas flight XY223 to Doha and flyadeal flight F3573 to Istanbul. The disruption has included flights being sent to alternative airports. Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked on the arrivals board as being diverted to Dammam, rather than arriving in Riyadh. Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked as diverted to Dammam, while Saudia flight SV885 from Guangzhou was listed as diverted to Jeddah. Arriving and departing flights remain subject to permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation, Reuters reported. Several international airlines have retained suspensions lasting weeks or months. Travellers should check their flight directly with the operating airline before leaving for the airport and monitor messages about changes to their booking. Those with onward connections should confirm the status of both flights and ask their airline about arrangements if disruption affects their journey. Passengers whose services have been cancelled should contact their airline or booking agent to discuss the rebooking or refund options available under their ticket conditions.

title: No cancellation of planned FDI in UAE this year despite Iran war, Ministry of Investment says
description: The Emirates remains on course to achieve its 2031 FDI target of $65bn annual inflow, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi tells The National
content: No planned foreign direct investment in the UAE has been cancelled this year, despite the uncertainties created by the US-Iran war, a senior government official has said. The overall stock of FDI in the UAE this year might be fractionally lower than the record levels achieved in 2025, as global investors assess the impact of conflict in the region. However, the Emirates remains firmly on course to achieve its 2031 FDI targets, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment, told The National in an interview on Tuesday. “Everyone we've spoken to has said: 'We haven't cancelled our plans. We are just either waiting, or we're delaying a little bit, or we're decreasing the quantum a little bit but the country is capable of making up,'” Mr Alhawi said on the sidelines of the 10th HSBC Future Forum in Dubai. “Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.” The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis. “I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said. FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development ( Unctad ) data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the past few years and was expected to continue on the growth trajectory this year before the war-driven disruption to economy and trade. Like its peers in the six-member economic bloc of the Gulf Co-operation Council and its Arab neighbours, the UAE has faced waves of missile and drone attacks, but Mr Alhawi said it remains “100 per cent” on target to achieve the $65 billion annual FDI targets by 2031. “You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.” While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, the UAE federal government is focused on investing in its own economy. Special attention is being paid to developing ports and related infrastructure on the East Coast, as well as improving and expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure. “Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said. “We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.” The UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story. Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said. “We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.” Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding requirements to build the planned infrastructure projects. The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Menat Infrastructure report indicates. “Ultimately, these large-scale projects, such as Al Maktoum [International] Airport, the Dubai sewage system and developments in Fujairah, have strong government backing,” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE, told The National . “So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.” The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”. HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors. The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday. Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said. The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline. The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows “Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

title: Fadi El Khatib on opening new wellness hub Club 15: 'This is my thank you to Dubai'
description: Lebanese basketball player-turned-entrepreneur has opened a 15,000 sqm sports and lifestyle destination in Al Quoz where people can train, work, play and connect
content: When the unexpected strikes, it’s hard to predict how one will react. Some freeze, others make impulsive decisions, and a few choose optimism. Fewer still decide that it’s the perfect time to launch an ambitious wellness venture as a bid for community and connection. But that is exactly what ran through Fadi El Khatib’s mind earlier this year, just weeks after the Iran war began on February 28. “The belief in the city and the country,” says El Khatib when asked why he decided to open Club 15. The former professional basketball player-turned-entrepreneur, whose career spanned more than 25 years as he played for clubs across Lebanon, as well as Syria, Ukraine and China, had the idea to create a “sports city within a city” in March this year. Just a month later, the ball started rolling on the project. The doors to Club 15, a 15,000-square-metre sports and lifestyle destination in Dubai's Al Quoz area, opened for its soft launch on Monday. For those seeking movement, they can look to the hub's seven professional padel courts, three full-sized basketball courts, a two-storey, 5,700 sqm gym, Reformer Pilates and studio spaces and a 25-metre semi-Olympic swimming pool. Recovery is added with ice baths and infrared sauna facilities. There is also a rooftop training space and an on-site physiotherapy clinic. At the time of writing, membership models and prices were still being finalised. However, El Khatib says attainability is important to him in more ways than one. Namely, making sure the set-up he has created is convenient for families. His vision is for Club 15 to be the kind of destination where families can move seamlessly through the day together. “I want to encourage parents to go and work out. Because I know the hassle of any parent is: where do I put my kid?” says El Khatib. Club 15 also includes social and workspaces, a gaming lounge, a podcast studio, kids' facilities, gymnastics and parkour, with youth academies also forming part of the project. The idea itself was born within his family, as 15 was El Khatib's jersey number throughout his professional career. Today, the number has also taken on significance within his four children – sons Jihad, Hadi and Joud, and daughter Joury. “My eldest boy is an NBA prospect carrying the national team with number 15,” he says. Jihad El Khatib plays as a forward for Club Centrale Al Markaziyyah (also known as Central Club) in the Lebanese Basketball League and represents the Lebanese national team. “My other son is playing pro wearing number 15,” he says. “Joud, who plays with Champs, is wearing number 15. My daughter is also wearing number 15.” When his family moved to the UAE earlier in the year, following unrest in Lebanon, they sat together discussing how much the number meant to each of them personally. “It's very emotional … so it's a continuation of the number, and it brought my family together.” When The National visits on the soft launch opening day, it's still very much a work in progress. Although many of the workout spaces are functional – El Khatib joins us fresh from a competitive game of padel – the on-site Joe and the Juice cafe isn't ready to open yet, there is still some red tape around certain areas, and the softer furnishings are lacking. Future additions will include a cycling and running track, he tells us, alongside installing red-light panels in the Pilates studio and equipment that would allow the yoga studio to host heated classes. “My career was based on gym, swimming and hot power yoga,” he says. “Yoga with heat is a real workout. It gives more mobility and flexibility so you stretch more, which causes soreness the next day. It's one of the best things I've ever done.” While padel is his latest love, his career – which earned him the nickname the "Lebanese Tiger" – was built on the basketball court before he moved into the business realm of fitness, founding Champs Sports Club and expanding the brand across the UAE. Members can expect to see El Khatib in just about every corner of the site. He even jokes about building an apartment on the rooftop. Although he's happy to try everything, doing too much is where people go wrong. “People are overdoing things,” he says. “Anyone not experienced enough in wellness gets messed up trying everything because of trends on Instagram or social media. Keep it simple, study your body, don't overdo things just to follow trends.” In a world always searching for AI cheats and biohacking solutions, El Khatib says nothing can replace the “old school” method of hitting the gym, using the machines, and picking up the dumbbells. “You will never be able to replace this.” They're lessons learnt from a long career in the fitness industry. But his biggest lesson has been the value of grit. “Basketball gave me the mental toughness and the will. You'll face hurdles, obstacles, challenges. Keep going, keep chasing your goals. Never stop.” That perhaps explains why Club 15 was born in what has undoubtedly been a challenging year for businesses in Dubai. For El Khatib, it is his thank you to the city – and all he wants to hear from members walking out the door is a thank you in return. “I don't call Dubai a hotel,” says El Khatib. “When things happen, you don't pack your things and move out. You keep on developing, sending messages to people all around the world.”

title: UAE climate ministry says 'unusual odour' reported in Dubai and Sharjah no cause for concern
description: Authorities investigating as residents in parts of emirates report unusual odour
content: The UAE government on Wednesday said it was investigating “unusual odours” reported across a number of emirates and has moved to assure the public there is no cause for concern. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said it is working with local authorities to verify the nature and source of the smell. Residents in parts of Sharjah and Dubai said on social media and other platforms that there was a strong smell similar to fuel or gas. “Response efforts and field monitoring remain ongoing to reduce the odours and accelerate their dissipation,” the ministry said in a statement on social media. The ministry stressed that assessments conducted had found “no indications of concern” and said the public would be informed should any developments arise that require precautionary measures. The cause of the smell is still to be determined. The National has previously reported on the environmental effects of tanker strikes in the Arabian Gulf, resulting from the Iran war. Experts have cautioned that oil spills and toxic debris from such attacks could be harmful to the environment and wildlife for years . Sharjah's police chief on Tuesday offered reassurances after complaints about an unusual smell spreading in some emirates. Lt Gen Abdullah bin Amer told Sharjah's Direct Line radio programme on Tuesday afternoon that the situation was stable and posed no threat. Sharjah Police did not say what was causing the smell when asked by The National . “We have noted complaints from some members of the public about odours spreading across Sharjah and neighbouring emirates,” said Lt Gen bin Amer. “We would like to reassure the public that the situation is safe and stable and that there is nothing posing a threat. The relevant federal authorities are investigating the matter, and we will provide updates as they become available.” Dubai Police and the emirate's municipality have also been contacted for comment. Prashant Kumar, professor of air quality and health at the University of Surrey in the UK, said that air pollution – and the smells that it brings with it – can travel over long distances. “The smell can travel tens of kilometres,” he said. “It depends on the meteorological conditions, it depends on the wind speed and the wind direction. You can easily have the longer-range transport of pollutants from one place to another.” He indicated that it was even possible that smells could travel across the Arabian Gulf, so the source of any smell experienced by UAE residents may not be nearby. “There was an incident of that kind in the UK that was transported from France,” he said. In 2013, a chemical leak from an industrial plant in Rouen in northern France caused large parts of southern England to be blanketed by a bad smell, with police reportedly receiving calls from concerned residents. Prof Kumar said there is scientific technology that can be used to trace air pollution back to its source. While the source of the smell remains unclear, Dr Diana Francis, an associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences (Engeos) Lab at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said oil spills in the Gulf from the recent conflict could create odours. “When an oil spill happens it continues to move with the currents unless it is removed and cleaned completely,” she said. “Several spills can also move with the currents and accumulate in favourable gyre [rotating ocean current] areas. Then with time, heat and winds they evaporate into the air and give fuel like odours. “Oil doesn't mix with water, it continues to float until it is removed or evaporate with time.”

title: Iran says Iraq has agreed to expel opposition groups from Kurdistan region
description: Tehran ambassador's claim not mentioned in Iraqi statement issued after joint security meeting in Baghdad
content: Iran's ambassador to Baghdad on Tuesday said Iraq had agreed to either expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in the Kurdistan region or hand them over to Tehran. The claim by Mohammad Al Sadegh came after he attended a meeting of the Iraq-Iran joint security committee in Baghdad on Monday. Qasim Al Aboudi, the National Security Adviser, led the Iraqi delegation, which also featured representatives of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region. In a statement on X, Mr Al Sadegh said both sides had agreed “to remove elements of Iranian separatist terrorist groups from the Kurdistan region of Iraq or hand them over to Iran”. There was no immediate comment from the Iraqi government or the Kurdistan region, nor from Mr Al Aboudi. An official Iraqi readout of the meeting said both sides had discussed implementing the joint security agreement and the “outstanding files and problems”, and identified the “appropriate solutions”. The apparent deal came only days after Iraq's parliament endorsed Yassir Al Maliki, the son-in-law of the pro-Iran State of Law Coalition leader and former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki , as Interior Minister. Officials from Iranian Kurdish groups said they had not received any notice of a decision to expel them. "To date, we have not received any official communication from either the Iraqi federal government or the Kurdistan Regional Government," Hejar Berenji, the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan's (PDKI) representative to the US, told The National . "We have to wait, because the KRG is the mediator on this issue," said an official with one of the Iranian Kurdish parties, who asked not to be named. Tehran has long placed pressure on both the Kurdistan Regional Government and Baghdad to eject the groups, so far to little avail. Such a move is considered unlikely, not least because some of them have been present in Iraq's Kurdistan region long before its regional government took on its current form. “We are not going to do that [tell them to leave] because they are our people,” Darbaz Rasool, a senior official in the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, one of two main political parties in the Kurdistan Region’s coalition government, told The National earlier this year. Iraq and Iran signed a bilateral security agreement in March 2023, under which Baghdad committed to disarming Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and relocating them from the border area, and preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on Iran. Groups such as the PDKI, Komala, the Free Life Party of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Freedom Party were to hand over their heavy weapons and move to camps farther from the border. Iraqi officials said at the time families would be relocated to five designated camps in the Kurdistan region while the UN refugee agency would process asylum claims. The groups, some of which have been based in northern Iraq since the 1980s – after the Islamic Revolution and during the Iran-Iraq war – are seeking greater rights for Iran's Kurdish minority. Tehran accuses them of terrorism and of fuelling unrest, such as the 2022 protests that followed the death of Mahsa Amini. In a sign of growing pressure on Baghdad and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region, over the presence of these groups, Nechirvan Barzani, President of Kurdistan Region, said last week: “Unfortunately, the [Iranian] Kurdish opposition forces acted in a highly irresponsible manner and placed the Kurdistan region in an extremely difficult position. “An armed force cannot view the Kurdistan region as a safe haven and then operate from its territory to threaten a neighbouring country,” he said, in reference to reports that the groups were planning to move into Iran, with US backing. Implementation of the security agreement has been uneven. Baghdad says it has moved fighters from border areas and closed some headquarters, while Tehran has repeatedly called the measures insufficient and continued to carry out drone and missile strikes on opposition camps in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah provinces. Expelling these groups or handing them over to Iran would mark a significant hardening of Iraq's position if confirmed, raising legal and humanitarian questions given that thousands of Iranian Kurdish refugees live in Iraq, most in the Kurdistan region. The Kurdistan Regional Government has previously opposed forced return, calling for a peaceful resolution that respects Iraq's constitution, which bars armed groups from threatening neighbours, while also protecting refugee rights.

title: US peace talks off without sanctions removal, Iran tells Pakistan
description: Qatar says communication between Tehran and Washington 'has not stopped' amid push for resolution
content: Iran 's President Masoud Pezeshkian said the US must remove sanctions for negotiations to resume as he met the army chief of mediator Pakistan on Tuesday. Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir was in Tehran with an official delegation to meet senior Iranian officials, amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war. Qatar, another mediator in the conflict, said on Tuesday that communication between Iran and the US has "not stopped" and the aim was to reach a solution "as soon as possible”. Mr Pezeshkian told the Pakistani defence chief that the US "must lift threats and sanctions before any talks", Iranian state media said. "It is not possible to increase the severity of sanctions and pressure day by day and close the paths and roads to our country, and then claim to have dialogue and negotiation," he said. The Iranian leadership has often sent contradictory signs about the prospects for peace. A day earlier, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that Iran saw "no military solution" to the Middle East crisis. Field Marshal Munir’s visit came as Reuters quoted Iranian officials as saying Tehran had been deliberately prolonging negotiations with Washington to weaken US President Donald Trump politically before November’s midterm elections , while preparing for possible renewed military action. “Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” one Iranian official was quoted as saying. “The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory.” The same report quoted Iranian officials as saying there was little prospect of a breakthrough before the November 3 vote. Ibrahim Al Hashmi, media director at Qatar’s Foreign Ministry, warned that threats to cut internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz , along with dangers caused by sea mines and oil spills, would harm regional countries, including Iran, and urged Tehran to respect freedom of navigation and environmental protection. His statement comes after Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said regional undersea cables , data centres and AI sites could be attacked if hostilities with the US resume. Tehran wants its conditions for ending hostilities and reopening the strait to be met before nuclear negotiations begin. Iran has proposed reopening the waterway within seven days under its control, in exchange for lifting the US maritime blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, the release of frozen assets and an end to hostilities on all fronts. The deadlock comes as Iran’s economy faces mounting pressure from sanctions and the blockade. Shipping through the strait remains severely disrupted. Iranian hardline news agency Fars suggested Field Marshal Munir’s visit was linked to rising oil prices, reporting that the trip had appeared unlikely to happen as late as Sunday, but his trip was finalised on Monday afternoon as the price of crude approached $110 a barrel. A source told Fars that previous visits by mediators had helped to lower oil prices, but had produced no significant progress in negotiations. Mr Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran’s proposal remained on the table and that messages continued to be exchanged through mediators. Tehran believed US and Israeli attacks could resume, despite Mr Trump saying Washington would not strike Iran again before November 3, Reuters reported. The officials said Tehran’s distrust of Washington had deepened after attacks that derailed diplomatic efforts, including strikes in June 2025 and the launch of the war in February, shortly after another round of talks ended. The threat of renewed military action extends to Pickaxe Mountain , a deeply buried site near Natanz nuclear complex. Tehran has warned that any US attack on the site would lead to retaliation. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei dismissed claims Washington could strike the site without facing a response, describing the idea as “nothing more than a claim”. “Do you believe Iran would say ‘strike’ and we would remain silent?” Mr Baghaei said. He added that “the era of hitting and running is over”. He said Iran would not leave any attack unanswered and warned the US would suffer a blow at least equal in magnitude to any strike it carried out. Mr Trump has threatened a possible strike on Pickaxe Mountain, where Iran is building a heavily fortified underground facility, the precise purpose of which remains unclear.

title: Sultan of Oman welcomed by King Charles for UK state visit
description: Royal salute fired at Home Park in Windsor before carriage procession
content: King Charles III has welcomed Sultan Haitham of Oman to Windsor, on the outskirts of London, at the start of a three-day state visit , the first by an Omani head of state in 44 years. Sultan Haitham was escorted from his London residence to Windsor by Prince William, the Prince of Wales, where the Omani ruler was given a ceremonial welcome, including a royal salute fired by the King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery. The Omani and British national anthems were also played. A royal salute was also fired at the Tower of London. He then joined the king in the Irish State Coach for a horse-drawn carriage procession in the rain through the town to Windsor Castle, with the route lined by the armed forces. Queen Camilla was joined in the Scottish State Coach by Oman’s Deputy Prime Minister for Defence Affairs, Shihab bin Tariq. Prince William and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales, were joined in the Australian State Coach by Theyazin bin Haitham, Crown Prince and Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs, and Loay bin Ghalib, Secretary General of the Diwan of the Royal Court. Other ministers made up the rest of the procession. On arrival at the castle, the sultan, accompanied by the king, inspected the guard of honour, declining to use umbrellas. The last time an Omani ruler paid a state visit to the UK was in 1982, when Sultan Qaboos visited Queen Elizabeth II. Sultan Haitham then spent the day with the king and queen. The Omani ruler viewed a special exhibition of items relating to Oman from the Royal Collection, including the Order of Al Said presented to Queen Elizabeth II by Sultan Qaboos during his 1982 visit and photographs from Queen Elizabeth II's 1979 state visit to Oman. He was then attending a banquet at Windsor Castle on Tuesday evening. He will hold talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street on Wednesday. The pair spoke in July, shortly after Mr Burnham became Prime Minister, when they discussed efforts to free up navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier that month, Sultan Haitham also met Keir Starmer, Britain's leader at the time, in Downing Street. Sultan Haitham is to attend a banquet in the City of London on Wednesday evening and will visit the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in East London on Thursday to see how the former Olympic site has become an economic centre. Omani business leaders promoting the country’s free zones gathered alongside business leaders, investors and policy makers at Guildhall on Tuesday to discuss opportunities following the UK-GCC trade agreement signed earlier this year. A “major mandate” of Sultan Haitham’s visit was to facilitate investment between the UK and Oman, Haitham Al Salmi, CEO of Muscat Stock Exchange told The National. “ There are a lot of businesses to be discussed at this time,” he said. The exchange was building relationships with the London Stock Exchange, as it seeks an upgrade from a frontier market to a secondary emerging one, he said. FTSE Russell put the exchange on the watch list for an upgrade in September. “Different investors with different appetites can hit both developed markets and emerging markets at the same time,” he said. The meeting heard optimism about collaborations in healthcare, with the UK’s expertise in life sciences and genomics able to develop public health institutions in the Gulf, while Gulf countries were ahead in digitalising their public health systems. “The UK is an example of a system that is plainly under the weight of ageing and chronic disease. Whereas the GCC countries are much younger,” said Jonathan Symonds, chairman of British pharmaceuticals company GSK. “The GCC countries really offer a window into what the health system of the future will look like. Because you are not overburdened by huge demand. You can build it up from the ground up,” he said. Richard Stanford, a retired military officer and now chairman of the British Omani Society, who served extensively in the sultanate, said the relationship between the two countries goes back hundreds of years. He described the relationship as “unique, special and founded on mutual respect”. He said the state visit was an “embodiment” of how important the relationship is between the countries and the two royal families. He said that as maritime nations both bring a “certain attitude to Gulf and global politics” based on centuries of connection, trade and diplomacy.

title: UK mission to defend Saudi Arabia adds Typhoon jets
description: Additional defensive military ​assistance follows ⁠renewed Houthi attacks
content: RAF Typhoon fighter jets will be deployed to defend Saudi cities and infrastructure against aerial attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia . “The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets,” an official statement said on Tuesday. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.” The UK will also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft with heavy-lift capability to move kit around Saudi Arabia, and British military advisers will support Saudi counterparts on the ground. In September, Britain said it would provide additional defensive military ​assistance to ‌Saudi Arabia following ⁠renewed Houthi attacks, including ​an RAF Voyager air-to-air ​refuelling aircraft. ‌That announcement did not include ⁠fighter jet support. In March, Downing Street announced that four fighters would head to the region to provide defensive cover from Iranian missiles. That was an expansion of the UK presence, with the aircraft joining four Typhoons already deployed in Qatar to “provide further defensive support to regional allies under attack from Iran”. Houthi attacks have ⁠intensified in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, with Yemen authorities saying on Monday that a strike on a ​government security forces training camp had killed 58 people. "The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," said UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting. "The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region." Strikes on Riyadh’s airport have killed more than a dozen people and disrupted flights in October, while oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran and a cross-country pipeline have also been hit during the conflict. Air-raid alerts sounded in the Saudi capital on Monday night in a sign of the continuing security risks. “The Houthis’ attempts to destabilise the region and undermine the security and stability of the Middle East are unacceptable,” added the Ministry of Defence statement. “This reckless behaviour deepens Yemen’s already devastating humanitarian crisis, and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed. “Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK – driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen.” The Houthi arsenal has been boosted by the development of the 1,800km range the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre as it closes on its target at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It also introduced an airburst version of a Badr rocket that it claims exploded next to a Typhoon inside Yemen earlier this month. The IISS Military Balance says that Saudi Arabia's airforce boasts three squadrons of Typhoon and a further three squadrons of the older Tornado British fighter jet. The Typhoon boasts a 27mm Mauser gun with 150 rounds that could be used to shoot done slow moving drones. But cruise and ballistic too fast for cannon. The UK has also shipped Sky Sabre air defence to protect the Saudi Typhoons in battle.

title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
description: Iran-aligned rebels claim responsibility for series of attacks on Saudi Arabia over the past days
content: Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month. The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf. The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar. With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation. "Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said. "Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation." Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday that Washington was willing to allow oil tankers placed under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude. Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that, as of Monday, only 24 of the nearly 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. Wholesale diesel, meanwhile, already surpassed $200 per gallon in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US, the Paris-based IEA said last week.

title: Are Israel’s Lebanon talks a path to peace, or a pretext for continued occupation?
description: Israel seeks to fragment and destabilise its neighbours, retain buffer zones inside their territory and pursue perpetual war
content: This week, Lebanese and Israeli military representatives are meeting in Tampa , Florida, to discuss implementation of the so-called “pilot zones” plan to advance the Lebanese army’s disarmament of Hezbollah. It’s improbable that there will be any breakthroughs, but more significantly, it’s unlikely Israel actually seeks one. Reportedly, the meeting is being held to discuss, among other things, the technical dimensions of the pilot zones, including a verification mechanism to report on the disarmament process. Also on the table may be discussions of the Lebanese refusal to conduct searches in private homes, where Hezbollah has allegedly stored large quantities of weapons, because this would represent a violation of the law. Article 14 of the Constitution, for instance, affirms “the citizen’s place of residence is inviolable”. These technical matters notwithstanding, the reason the pilot zones scheme has not advanced significantly since the signing of June 26 Tripartite Framework Agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US has to be sought elsewhere. It is mainly a consequence of Israel’s refusal to cede any territory to allow the Lebanese army to advance in the plan. This is largely tied to an Israeli desire to pursue a security doctrine in Lebanon that is independent of any of the constraints that an agreement would impose. Israel appears to have accepted negotiations with Lebanon for two primary reasons: to placate the administration of US President Donald Trump, which pushed for such a process; and to have on paper an agreement with Lebanon that would justify Israel’s continued presence in Lebanon if Beirut failed to fulfil the central condition of disarming Hezbollah. The Israelis have succeeded on both counts. The US administration is on board with Israel, putting no pressure on it to withdraw its forces from Lebanese land. At the same time, the June agreement imposed all conditions on the Lebanese side, above all Hezbollah’s disarmament , without requiring Israel to fulfil any of its own. Indeed, the term “withdrawal” is not even in the document, and there is no timetable for what the text describes as a progressive [Israeli] redeployment out of Lebanese territory. The agreement makes vague promises on Israeli actions that can only be implemented in the case of prior Lebanese actions, without recognising Lebanon’s sovereign rights over its own territory. Its sovereignty over Israeli-occupied parts of the south is qualified. Israel doesn’t expect Lebanon’s government to disarm Hezbollah by force, so it now has a formal excuse to remain in the south indefinitely. What we have, therefore, is a structurally flawed agreement that, by failing to gain traction, will give the Israelis wide latitude to pursue their own security agenda in southern Lebanon. Already, the Israelis have razed dozens of mainly Shiite villages, burned large swathes of agricultural fields and olive groves and bombed land using white phosphorous , thereby making it impossible to grow fruits and vegetables. The objective here is similar to the one employed in Gaza , namely to make the southern border region uninhabitable, in what could very well be an open-ended occupation. This comes at a time when Israel’s security doctrine has changed radically, and differs significantly from what it was in the past. In a much-discussed article for Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, for which he serves as executive director, Tamir Hayman, a former chief of the Israeli military’s Intelligence Directorate, outlined what he saw as a new Israeli approach to security. This will have a fundamental impact on how Israel deals with Lebanon. Five of Mr Hayman’s conclusions stand out. The first is that Israel views peace as a means rather than an end, and that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”. The second is that Arab states are not genuine nation states, but “collections of ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision”. In light of this, “undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process”. A third conclusion of Mr Hayman is that, for Israel, “war is essential to national security, and cannot be replaced by a state of peace”.
