A fourth conclusion is that Israel must no longer be dependent on the US, which is a “declining power”, whose shifts will ultimately lead to the abandonment of Israel. And a fifth conclusion is that the Israelis must adopt a forward defence strategy through “defence zones” that “enable Israel to move the war into enemy territory as quickly as possible”. Mr Hayman’s bleak analysis is based on his deep knowledge of Israeli strategic thinking, but others too have reached similar conclusions. In light of this, those who believe that a Lebanese-Israeli peace is a priority for Israel are naive. Instead, Israel seeks to fragment and destabilise its neighbours, such as Lebanon and Syria, retain buffer zones inside their territory, pursue perpetual war, and will not hesitate to turn against Washington’s preferences if these run against Israeli priorities. That is principally why we should not expect much from the Lebanese-Israeli talks, and why Lebanon is right in avoiding domestic conflict with Hezbollah just to placate the Israelis . Hezbollah is a major problem for Lebanon, undoubtedly, but it makes little sense today to risk internal Lebanese strife just to satisfy an Israel that appears to be committed to destabilising Lebanon and consolidating its occupation.

title: Europe to see 'biggest-ever' increase in air fares next year, Ryanair chief says
description: Tickets to increase by up to 20 per cent as Iran war drives up oil prices, O’Leary warns
content: Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices , forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability. Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

title: Jiri Prochazka on learning from mistakes and why he is picking Evloev and Yan at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi
description: Czech Republic fighter will make his comeback next month during UFC Fight Night in Doha after chastening loss in April
content: Former UFC light heavyweight champion Jiri Prochazka is leaving no stone unturned as he sweats it out in Thailand, training for his UFC return in Doha next month. Prochazka takes on up-and-coming contender Navajo Stirling in UFC Fight Night on November 21 in Doha, in what will be the promotion's second visit to Qatar. Czech Republic’s Prochazka has a point to prove. He is making a comeback after a chastening defeat to Carlos Ulberg in their title fight for the vacant light heavyweight championship in April at UFC 327. There, he suffered a first-round knockout despite Ulberg injuring his knee badly early in the bout. Lessons have been learnt from the defeat. The main one is to finish the contest at the first available opportunity. “Everything was settled,” Prochazka told The National about the fight against Ulberg. “Everything was successful … kicks, good distance, the pressure, all these things. But once I saw my opponent was hurt … I was too much emotional. I felt like I need to work more to win the fight. Not just like that, not just one kick, and I see the crashing leg. I just didn't accept the easy win. So I started to play this game ‘OK, let's go, let's go for a brawl. I'm giving you the same chances’. And that was a big mistake. I learnt from that a lot. We are still learning. “Then he just punched me, and that was it, that was the fight.” That result forced Prochazka, 34, to go back to the drawing board. “I made a lot of changes after my last fight. It's really deep preparation, because I made a lot of changes. I don't want to just go from fight to fight and take whatever results. I really want to win. Really want to go to Qatar and show everyone that I am one of the best fighters in the world,” Prochazka said. There will be remnants from the last fight in Doha. His opponent Stirling enters the contest unbeaten and has a 6-0 record in the UFC. Plus, the Kiwi is sparring with Ulberg. Prochazka says he is prepared. “My main weapon is to adjust. To change whatever I need to change to win the next fight. So, I really don't care if he's preparing with Ulberg or with whoever. He's a good opponent. But I believe I see a lot of space to catch him. And this is what I'm going to do.” Next month will mark Prochazka’s second visit to the Gulf. His first one was the path-breaking UFC 251 in Abu Dhabi in 2020 at the height of the coronavirus pandemic, where UFC was the only major sporting event taking place across the globe. Abu Dhabi will be in focus this week as well. The Etihad Arena hosts UFC 333 , where Alexander Volkanovski will defend his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev in the headline bout, while Petr Yan and Merab Dvalishvili play out their epic trilogy in the co-main event. Prochazka has picked out his favourites for Saturday. “I'm a fan of Volkanovski's style. And Volkanovski’s smart mindset. Yeah, but I see Evloev is really, like, a hard worker. So there is a lot of chances for Evloev to win the fight. Let the better man win,” Prochazka said. “In the second match … I know, personally, Merab. I like him, like his style. But I believe Petr Yan is a smarter fighter. He is a much smarter fighter because he has more techniques. His style is something that inspires me. It's a great inspiration, especially some throws and high intensity of work.” The Gulf region will forever be special to Prochazka. He made his promotional debut in UFC at Fight Island in 2020 and won. “Abu Dhabi was an amazing experience because it was a totally new thing in the world,” Prochazka recalled. “It was like a miracle for fighting sports, because all the world stopped because of coronavirus. Only one thing was going on, and that was UFC. For me, it was, like, I stepped into the league of the best. ‘I'm here, and I'm going for the title. And let me show my best’.”

title: AI has developed a memory problem
description: Data centre boom is constraining the world’s supply of memory chips, leading to 'chipflation' and making your everyday electronics more expensive
content: Building a PC or buying electronic components for your devices is becoming more expensive. A 32-gigabyte Corsair computer memory kit cost $52 on Amazon's US page in June 2025. By September 2026, the same kit was selling for $250, an increase of about 380 per cent. And it is not only RAM that is affected. An analysis by The National of Amazon US prices for 18 popular memory and storage products found that every one had risen by between 85 per cent and 553 per cent. A Crucial 1TB SSD (Solid State Drive) went from $100 to $392, while a Corsair DDR5 memory kit, used in many newer gaming PCs, jumped from $125 to $550. For years, building your own PC from scratch gave some users much-needed control over performance and price. One could spend more on the parts that mattered, keeping those that still worked and upgrading over time. However, rising component prices are making that harder, as much of the process is enabled by memory and storage chips. The reason behind this? The AI industry is becoming insatiably reliant on memory chips. Many are calling the surging cost phenomeonon 'chipflation'. Manufacturers that supply everyday consumer electronics are increasingly serving the AI industry, whose biggest customers are committing billions of dollars to new computing capacity. Two types of chips are causing prices to soar; both are sought after by consumers and the artificial intelligence industry. DRAM provides the working memory that computers and phones use to run applications. NAND flash stores files in SSDs, memory cards and other devices. AI infrastructure needs both. One particularly valuable product is high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, which supplies data to the powerful processors running AI models. HBM chips are a specialised form of DRAM. And now manufacturers must decide how to divide production capacity and investment between products. Larger AI contracts and long-term pay cheques are giving memory makers a strong incentive to prioritise AI needs over consumer products. The consultancy group Bain says the shift is already “worsening shortages and raising the prices of smartphones and PCs”. The five largest cloud companies could spend $780 billion on infrastructure this year, nearly five times the amount they did three years ago. HBM chip sales have risen from about $4 billion in 2023 to an estimated $77 billion this year. This, in turn, has reversed years of falling prices in the industry. Even hard drives, which store data on spinning disks rather than on memory chips, have become more expensive since 2023. In October 2025, OpenAI announced partnerships with Samsung and SK Hynix for its Stargate data centre initiative, outlining plans targeting up to 900,000 DRAM wafer starts per month. This represented future demand and capacity expansion, rather than memory immediately removed from the consumer market. A month later, Samsung raised prices for some memory chips by as much as 60 per cent compared with September. The pressure became apparent at the retail level almost immediately. We analysed Keepa data, which tracks historical prices across most Amazon.com products. What we found was that Amazon.com had Corsair’s DDR5 kit available for only 11 to 21 per cent of the time between November 2025 and February 2026, compared with availability throughout the previous summer. In the UAE, 11 of 14 storage products tracked on Sharaf DG’s website were listed as out of stock on October 1, including every internal SSD in the sample. "Memory manufacturers are allocating more production capacity towards high-margin server products, including the memory required for AI infrastructure. The capacity continues to move towards server applications, leaving less available for conventional PC DRAM," Kevin Sebastian, a creative director and technology commentator in the UAE, tells The National . "Storage is being squeezed too NAND flash is the technology behind SSDs, USB storage and many memory cards, and it has experienced its own sharp price increases." For decades, gamers, video editors, and other demanding users have often chosen each computer component separately to tailor their computers to their needs. Replacing individual parts can also extend their computers' lives. But the savings depend on what those parts cost. Large PC manufacturers may have some protection through existing contracts, while individual builders pay current retail prices. That raises the possibility that a pre-built computer could offer better value than an equivalent machine assembled from parts purchased separately. This, of course, will still depend on the specifications, the retailer and when the components were bought. Higher RAM and SSD prices alone do not establish that building a PC is now more expensive in every case. The same calculation applies to people trying to extend the life of an older machine. An upgrade may still cost less than a replacement computer, but rising component prices can narrow the savings. Consumers may consequently spend more, accept lower specifications or hold on to devices longer. Which is what PC builders in the UAE are going through now - and the figures are eye-watering and budget-busting. During the first half of 2025, a decent 32GB DDR5-6000 kit could be bought anywhere from Dh400 and Dh500 in the UAE, while archived search results on Amazon UAE show several 32GB DDR5 kits at Dh400 to Dh520, according to data compiled by Kevin Sebastian, a creative director and technology commentator in the UAE. A Dubai gaming community PC build from April 2025 listed a Corsair Vengeance 32GB DDR5 kit at Dh449. Today, prices are unrecognisable: current listings show 32GB DDR5 modules and kits exceeding Dh2,000, including a Kingston Fury Beast 32GB DDR5-6000 module at around Dh2,250. And while some higher-end Kingston kits have been listed above Dh3,000 on sites such as Microless and Amazon, it is still possible to get them at a lower price, but they are few and far between, and are still well about Dh2,000. Even prices for made-for-the-masses SD cards have jumped: a SanDisk Extreme 256GB microSD card currently sits around Dh190 to Dh280, compared to Dh120 to Dh150 a year earlier. "That’s just how distorted the market has become ... a component that could comfortably occupy less than 10 per cent of a mid-range gaming PC budget last year can now consume a much larger share of it," Mr Sebastian tells The National . Graphic cards have also been hit, primarily because each one carries several gigabytes of fast memory. Prices of GDDR6 and GDDR7 chips used in graphics cards rose by several hundred per cent within months of AI data centres absorbing supply. The effect is starkest at the top end. Nvidia’s flagship RTX 5090 was launched in January 2025 at $1,999. By July 2026 it was listed at about $4,329 on Amazon US, more than double. In the UAE, some RTX 5090 listings now range from Dh25,000 to Dh30,000, "Imagine a retailer bought a shipment of RAM at Dh400 per kit; normally it could add its margin and sell those kits relatively cheaply. If replacing that inventory now costs Dh1,200 or Dh1,500, selling the remaining stock at the old price makes much less financial sense," Mr Sebastian says. "Retailers therefore have to decide whether to increase prices immediately, reduce margins or risk being unable to restock the product. That is one reason consumers can see enormous differences between shops and even between two models with very similar specifications." Meanwhile, some chipmakers are reporting record earnings. Micron reported quarterly revenue of $54.2 billion, about 4.8 times the level a year earlier. Its operating margin climbed from 32 per cent to almost 81 per cent. Samsung’s memory business also reported strong profits, even as its mobile phone division recorded its first operating loss, partly linked to rising component costs. Investors have rewarded the chipmakers even more. Shares in SanDisk, spun off from Western Digital in February 2025, have risen almost 38 times since the end of June 2025. Kioxia's shares are up about 20 times. Both specialise in the NAND chips used for storage. Meanwhile, IDC expects global PC shipments to fall 11.3 per cent this year and average prices to rise 18.3 per cent. That average reflects both prices and the mix of computers sold. Some SSD prices have eased from their highs, but expanding supply takes time. Deloitte estimates new factories may not add meaningful capacity until 2029 or 2030. Bain's report goes on to describe the market shift as “structural, not cyclical”. That does not mean prices cannot fall, but it raises a longer-term question about whom manufacturers build their capacity for. For now, an industry racing to build the next generation of AI is making some everyday technology more expensive to maintain.

title: 'Gulf security is our security', says former UK defence secretary
description: As Washington's priorities turn to homeland defence and the Indo-Pacific, UK must support their allies, says Michael Fallon
content: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis , because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Sir Michael Fallon has told The National . The US , he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”. That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”. With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.” For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis . “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024. Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion. Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.” It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given. However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.” “Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.” The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”. “So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said. The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia , declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran. Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”. “Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.” The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”. Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.” Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course. Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”. Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism ”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS. The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow. He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress. “I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said. The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness. “He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine 's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”. Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.” Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.” Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.” The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September. The stakes are highest in Ukraine . “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.” A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato ”. Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”. “China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.” The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”. Asked whether the world is at a tipping point, Sir Michael did not hesitate. “Yes, I think we are. We're certainly in a new age, I think, of instability and uncertainty.” He does not expect a return to the old order. “I don't think it's gonna snap back to the kind of rules-based international co-operation and international institutions that we used to respect, the United Nations , the World Trade Organisation.” The danger, he said, is a mistake. “We're standing up to each other now,” he said, with missiles, air-defence systems and drones facing off from the edge of Romania to the islands of the Gulf. He gives the potential example of a local battery commander who “sees something coming in on the radar, and his job is to defend”. “It turns out to be a civilian airliner,” he adds. “You have a capacity now for miscalculation, that with so much conflict going on in both regions of the world, that somebody makes a mistake, and then there's a response, and people's lives are lost.” For Britain and its allies in the Gulf and Europe, that is the world they must now plan for. “We are in a new age of instability, and I think this is now the new norm that we have to live with,” Sir Michael said.

title: Study of thousands of ancient tombs in UAE, Oman and Saudi Arabia unearths secrets buried in the past
description: Four-year project offers glimpse into early trade routes and shared customs dating back centuries
content: Tens of thousands of burial tombs have been mapped in the UAE , Oman and Saudi Arabia as part of a project that has shed fresh light on life in previous millennia. The Arabiancairns initiative, which began in 2022, has documented tombs on hilltops, terraces and plains over thousands of square kilometres. The work, funded by the French National Research Agency (ANR), has highlighted evidence of agriculture and pinpointed trading links, offering new insights. Initially supported for four years, the initiative has had its funding renewed into 2027 and more fieldwork is already planned. Arabiancairns focuses on protohistoric Arabia, covering about 5500 BCE to 300 CE. This includes the Bronze Age, which ran from around 3200 BCE to 1300 BCE and the subsequent Iron Age, which lasted until about 300 BCE. Researchers are analysing the distribution of tombs and how they relate to the surrounding landscape, and the architecture of particular sites and how they were altered over time. Chemical analysis helps the scientists understand how old sites are, what people ate and how they moved around. Once the project is completed, a database of funerary monuments, giving their precise locations, will be made publicly available. A key area analysed is around Bisya in central Oman, where, across about 4,700 square kilometres, around 5,500 tombs have been mapped and confirmed by foot surveys and satellite data. “These monuments were built at different times, many contained several burials, and some were reused long after their original construction,” said Dr Olivia Munoz, from the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) Trajectories Lab and the Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University. At Dhabtiyah in eastern Saudi Arabia, similar patterns have been seen, with burial episodes within the same tomb separated by roughly a millennium. “Our research also highlights similarities in funerary architecture and practices across large parts of Arabia, alongside regional differences,” Dr Munoz said. “However, we cannot be certain what particular architectural features meant to their builders, or whether the same features carried the same meaning for different communities.” Around Bisya, Dr Munoz said it seemed that much of the population – not just elites – could have been buried in the tombs, as there was no known alternative form of burial from the same period. “Excavated tombs have yielded the remains of people of different ages, including children,” Dr Munoz added. “Some contain a single person, while others were used for collective burial, with further individuals placed in the chamber as deaths occurred. “The presence of children alongside adults suggests that some of these groups may have shared family ties, although this alone cannot establish kinship.” Adding to the suggestion that there was not heavy social stratification is the fact that substantially larger homes that could have housed an elite have not been found. However, it is possible, Dr Munoz said, that there were differences in social status that had not left any archaeological traces. Rather than indicating the size of the population at any time, the abundance of tombs suggests that people lived in or regularly visited the region over a long period, Dr Munoz said. The French Archaeological Mission to Central Oman, working at Bisya, is directed by Mathilde Jean of the Universite Paris Nanterre and Martin Sauvage of the CNRS Arscan Lab. Dr Munoz said there were similarities between the finds at Bisya and discoveries elsewhere, including at sites in the UAE. “The beads discovered at Bisya, for example, have parallels at Hili, Jebel Hafit and Umm an-Nar, in what is now the UAE,” she said. “The tomb architecture, likewise, belongs to traditions found across the Oman peninsula and, more broadly, elsewhere in the Arabian Peninsula. “These similarities point to a shared culture, reflected in common knowledge, practices and tastes, as well as exchanges of goods between communities.” However, such links do not indicate, Dr Munoz said, that there were direct connections between Bisya and other sites or that the communities were part of a single political identity. “Rather, they point to communities with much in common, but also with local ways of life and probably their own networks of contacts and exchange,” she added. Dr Munoz said that objects deposited with the dead offered clues about craftsmanship, personal adornment and exchange. “For example, a shark tooth and hundreds of marine-shell beads found in one of the tombs point to contact with the coast,” she said. Also, imported pottery shows there were trading links that extended much further afield, to Mesopotamia, Iran and Balochistan, an historical region that covers parts of present-day Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan. “These finds show that inland communities participated in wider networks through which objects, materials and potentially ideas circulated, alongside foodstuffs or other products that may have been transported in pottery vessels,” Dr Munoz said. Copper was a likely export, as during the Bronze Age the Oman peninsula was an important copper producer. Dried or salted fish, animal hides, dates and other palm products, worked shell ornaments and stone used for vessels or sculpture may also have been exported. Imports were probably equally varied, Dr Munoz said, with communities possibly obtaining textiles, grain, oils and other foodstuffs from Mesopotamia, and timber, textiles and ornaments from the Indus region, which straddles present-day Pakistan and India. “Some of these products leave little archaeological trace,” she said. “Pottery survives much better, but a vessel may have travelled because of what it contained, rather than because someone wanted the pot itself.” The presence of imported vessels at Bisya does not necessarily indicate that someone from there travelled to the place of manufacture, as the object could, Dr Munoz said, have reached a coastal settlement by boat and passed through several hands before arriving inland. “Merchants and markets may have played a part, with goods moving between major settlements and then being distributed more locally,” she said. At this time dromedary camels had not been domesticated, so goods may have been carried by people, donkeys or cattle. While the tombs have yielded a wealth of fascinating information, some aspects of life remain tantalisingly out of reach in the absence of written records. For example, Dr Munoz said it was difficult to reconstruct symbolic beliefs and political organisation from thousands of years ago.

title: Love is Blind Habibi season two: Release date, cast and all we know so far
description: Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi to guide 27 singles through Arabic dating show’s next instalment
content: Love is Blind Habibi will return to Netflix on November 12, bringing 27 single people from across the Arab world into the pods to find a partner without seeing one another. The Arabic-language adaptation returns following an International Emmy nomination, continuing an experiment in which couples become engaged before discovering whether their connection can survive beyond the pods. Here is what we know about the new season. The second season will launch globally on Netflix on November 12. It will comprise 10 episodes, although the announcement does not specify whether they will be released together or in batches. Netflix has released the first images of the new group, which comprises 13 men and 14 women from across the Arab world. That is an increase from the 20 participants introduced in season one, which featured an equal number of men and women. Netflix has now revealed all 27 contestants, whose names, ages and nationalities are included in The National 's guide to the season two cast . Breidy and Saidi will host season two, replacing Khaled Saqer and Elham Ali, the celebrity couple who presented the first season. The new hosts will accompany the participants through the experiment, from their initial search for a partner to the decisions that follow once they meet face to face. The series follows single people who get to know prospective partners through conversations in separate pods, where they can hear each other but cannot see one another. Those who form a connection can choose to get engaged before meeting in person. Their relationships are then tested outside the pods, where physical attraction, family expectations and the practicalities of building a life together influence whether they go ahead with a wedding. Netflix says the new season will again explore the role of family and tradition in the participants’ decisions, alongside the challenges of modern dating. Season one featured 20 singles from across the Arab world. The cast represented a variety of professions and backgrounds, with many saying family, honesty and long-term commitment were their central values. Participants were from countries including Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Syria, Morocco, Tunisia, Jordan and Iraq, reflecting the show’s pan-Arab scope. The latest announcement does not identify filming locations for season two. The first season was filmed in the UAE and Lebanon, with scenes shot in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Its Lebanese locations included EddeSands Hotel & Wellness Resort in Byblos, north of Beirut, where couples spent time together after leaving the pods. Netflix has not confirmed whether any structural changes have been made for season two. More details are expected closer to its release. Netflix has not yet released a stand-alone trailer or teaser for season two, but parts of the new season can be seen in its teaser for all of its 2026 Arabic content. At the reunion special for season one, more than a year after filming wrapped, only one couple from Love Is Blind: Habibi had gone the distance to marriage: Safa and Mohammed. Other couples from the season had mixed outcomes. Asma and Khatab did not marry and eventually split after a brief period together. Hajar and Simo ended their relationship before the wedding. Dounia and Chafic were dating again at reunion time, but confirmed they had parted ways in 2025. Karma and Ammar, as well as Nour and Mido, also ended their engagements.

title: UK national security adviser’s wife Sarah Helm calls for Palestine Action ban to be lifted
description: Police say writer's social media post appearing to support banned group does not meet criminal threshold
content: Sarah Helm, the writer and wife of Britain’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell , has called for the UK's ban on the Palestine Action group to be lifted, after a police investigation into her social media posts. The UK has proscribed the pro-Palestine group as a terrorist organisation, and expressing support for the group is a criminal offence. Police said at the weekend they closed their investigation of an earlier post by Ms Helm, and decided they would take no action as it did not meet the criminal threshold. On Monday, Ms Helm asked: “Where do I sign?” in response to a letter calling for the ban to be lifted and backing Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher Faber after they decided her books would no longer be sold in the UK. Ms Rooney had been warned her plan to donate earnings from sales could be considered a criminal offence. Ms Helm, a former Middle East correspondent for The Independent newspaper, had written “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” in response to a clip criticising Ms Rooney. Her stance on Palestine Action, which was banned in the UK in 2025 after an attack on a UK airbase, has led to questions whether it will affect Mr Powell’s role within government. More than 3,500 people have been arrested for supporting Palestine Action in the UK, mostly for holding up placards at demonstrations. The issue was raised by parliamentarians on Tuesday, who questioned whether Ms Helm had been included when Mr Powell was vetted for his post. "Were Sarah Helm’s posts ignored or were they accepted as OK?" asked Baroness Ludford in the House of Lords. Lord Callanan, a Tory peer, raised further posts by Ms Helm in which she suggested her husband had played no part in the decision to proscribe Palestine Action. He asked how Ms Helm could know if Mr Powell was involved or not, when "none of us know who in government was involved in that decision". Baroness Fiona Twycross said Ms Helm did not represent the government and stressed it was important to maintain the distinction between government employees and their families. Last month, the UK imposed sanctions aimed at illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Israeli government was turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. Mr Powell visited Israel earlier this month in a bid to persuade the Israeli government not to close the UK’s consulate general in Jerusalem, in response to the sanctions. The Consulate opened in 1838 and handles the country's relations with Palestinians in ​the city as ⁠well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians. Mr Powell held talks with Israeli officials but ultimately failed to reach an agreement to keep it open. Instead it was downgraded to a mission and the number of staff reduced from 30 to a handful. However, the compromise meant the UK did not enact a tit-for-tat removal of Israeli diplomatic staff from Britain. In her latest social media post, Ms Helm wrote of Ms Rooney: “She’s free yes and found not guilty of posting a terrorist tweet, whereas others guilty of holding terrorist banners? So where do I sign the letter calling for such absurdity to halt and for Palestine Action to be unbanned under the Terrorism act?” Ms Helm’s support of Ms Rooney has led to scrutiny of her social media posts, which have been frequent and vociferous in backing pro-Palestinian causes. Former Foreign Office official Ben Judah has highlighted posts made by Ms Helm after the October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas, saying they were “genuinely shocking”. In response to comments from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s saying Israel had a right to defend itself after “terrorists struck at the heart of Israel capturing and killing innocent women and children”, Ms Helm wrote “Not for the first time Von der Leyen is spouting empty dangerous glib tropes on a subject she apparently doesn’t understand”.

title: UAE bans veterinary use of antibiotic in bid to tackle drug resistance
description: Ciprofloxacin outlawed from November 1 in drive to protect efficacy of treatments for humans
content: The UAE is banning the veterinary use of ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic, from November 1 under a drive to curb drug resistance and boost patient safety. Ciprofloxacin is commonly used to treat bacterial infections. It belongs to a class of bacteria-killing antibiotics called fluoroquinolones. These have been classified as critically important antimicrobials (CIAs) for human medicine because of their role in treating conditions such as urinary tract infections, sepsis pneumonia and joint infections. The drug is also prescribed for animals, including dogs and cats, suffering infections such as those affecting skin and the bladder. National pharmaceutical regulator the Emirates Drug Establishment said ciprofloxacin would be prohibited in an effort to “preserve the effectiveness of treatments used in human medicine”. The EDE said inappropriate use of the drug for animals could contribute to the development of bacterial resistance, hampering the efficacy of medicines and “posing a public health challenge”. The move followed a scientific assessment of data related to antimicrobial resistance, including studies submitted by United Arab Emirates University. Dr Ruqaya Aqeel Al Bastaki, acting executive director of the Medical Products Regulation Sector at the EDE, said such decisions take into account risks associated with individual products and their impact on treatment priorities. She said the regulator would respond to concerns over antimicrobial resistance to safeguard public health. The ban covers veterinary medicinal products and raw materials containing ciprofloxacin. It affects nine products: eight that are imported and one that is locally registered. The EDE has told relevant establishments to stop manufacturing, importing and supplying the products, and to withdraw existing stocks from the local market before the ban takes effect. Remaining stocks should be re-exported or disposed of in accordance with approved procedures. Establishments must submit documents confirming that the required measures have been completed. The EDE said it was preparing a plan to monitor compliance within the specified time frame. Antimicrobial resistance is when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites do not respond to medicines, making infections more difficult or impossible to treat and increasing the risk of the spread of disease. It is estimated to have contributed to more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021, according to the most recent figures published by the World Health Organisation. The WHO said the misuse and overuse of antimicrobial drugs was accelerating the development and spread of drug-resistant pathogens. About one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections were resistant to antibiotics as of 2023, prompting the WHO to declare that the world was facing a “antimicrobial research and development crisis”, with few medicines in the pipeline to address the issue.

title: Unusual case of Oman's Sultan Haitham beginning UK state visit from his front door
description: Sultan Haitham travels from his private home in London to Windsor during first state visit since 1982
content: The heir to the British throne will meet the Sultan of Oman at his London home today, highlighting the long presence of Muscat's rulers in the British capital. The Prince of Wales and Sultan Haitham will travel to Windsor Castle to be met by King Charles III at the start of the Sultan's state visit to the UK. The last time a Sultan of Oman paid a state visit to the UK was in 1982, when Sultan Al Qaboos visited Queen Elizabeth II. Then the Sultan joined the royal convoy from Victoria Station. In 1967 when Saudi Arabia's King Faisal was on a visit he arrived by car outside the Tate Gallery (now Tate Britain) on Millbank in London. More recently state visits have begun at embassies or hotels. King Charles and Sultan Haitham will spend Tuesday at Windsor Castle, with a state banquet and engagements involving the Queen and members of the royal family planned. The King last hosted Sultan Haitham in 2025 for tea at Windsor Castle during a private visit. It is the collection from the Sultan's London residence – which is listed in UK planning documents as Grove House in Regent's Park – that is being seen as a sign of respect. The villa was built between 1822 and 1824 for the geologist Bellas Greenough, and designed by the architect Decimus Burton, according to the National Archives. The Grade I-listed building, which also sits along the Grand Union Canal, is believed to be the least altered of the historic villas surrounding Regent's Park, according to Neil Tomlinson Architects, which replaced the roof in 2014. The four-acre site is among one of the largest private gardens in the city, “made up of an ornamental garden with outbuildings including stables, an annex and small garden follies”, according to the architecture practice. It is not known when the Sultan of Oman bought Grove House. But the architectural history website London Canals says the house was sold in 1993 for £25 million – making it the most expensive property in London at the time. Council planning documents from the time describe the home as “the official London residence of His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said, the Ruler of Oman , on his visits to the capital”. Guests at the home have included former prime minister David Cameron when he was leader of the opposition. Planning documents revealed more than a decade ago that the house was used by the visiting Omanis. “His Majesty routinely receives guests at Grove House who, by their nature, are also heads of state, foreign dignitaries and senior representatives of the House of Windsor and the government of the United Kingdom,” a statement objecting to the installation of a public cycle stand said. The Sultan owns two homes in the capital. King Charles and Queen Camilla will welcome the Sultan at the Royal Dais in Windsor, as a Royal Salute is fired at the Home Park in Windsor, and at the Tower of London. The royals, including Prince William and Princess Catherine, and the Sultan will travel through Windsor town to the castle in a carriage procession. As Prince of Wales, the King visited Oman on four occasions. He travelled to Muscat to offer condolences following the death of Sultan Qaboos in January 2020. As Duchess of Cornwall, Queen Camilla accompanied the King on a two-day visit to Oman in November 2016. In the quadrangle of Windsor Castle, a guard of honour will give a royal salute and the regimental band will play the Omani and British national anthems as the carriage procession arrives. The Sultan, accompanied by the King, will inspect the guard of honour before rejoining the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales to watch the military march-past. The last 1982 visit took place not long after the two countries had worked as partners in a counter-insurgency that raged since 1965. The initial disturbances started in Dhofar by Marxist groups and spread across the territory. Following lunch in the state dining room, the King and Queen will invite the Sultan to view an exhibition of items relating to Oman from the Royal Collection, in the Green Drawing Room. There will be “enhanced security measures” around Windsor Castle during the visit, according to a Thames Valley Police spokesman. “As a force, we have a vast amount of experience in policing royal events in Windsor and significant planning and preparation has gone into this event,” he added. “We will ensure everyone attending the state visit, including dignitaries and spectators, as well as the public, are kept safe to enjoy the occasion.” The Sultan of Oman will meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday. It is believed that diplomatic meetings between the country's two foreign ministers will also take place on that day close to the King's residence in London. Sultan Haitham was the first leader hosted at Downing Street by former prime minister Keir Starmer in August 2024, after he was elected. They met again in July of this year, just days before Mr Starmer stepped down. Sultan Haitham will attend a banquet at Guildhall hosted by the Lady Mayor and the City of London Corporation and joined by the Duke of Gloucester. The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford will also be part of the visit, with the Sultan visiting the Here East business and culture campus to view “one of the world's most successful post-Olympic regeneration projects”. He will also view small to medium-sized businesses focused on energy, renewables, technology, space and defence inside the workspace Plexal. The visit comes at a crucial time for UK-Oman relations given the crisis in the Gulf and Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has emerged as a vital mediator, agreeing an alternative traffic system for the Strait of Hormuz with Iran. It has also served as a mediator for discussions with the Iran-backed Houthis at several stages of the war in Yemen. The late Sultan Qaboos is said to have had a good relationship with Queen Elizabeth II. The late Queen first met him in Muscat in 1979, where she sailed along the Gulf on the royal yacht Britannia. In 2010, Queen Elizabeth made a state visit to Oman, where the Sultan gave her an engraved gold vase. “My state visit to Oman in 2010 remains a cherished memory,” Queen Elizabeth said when Sultan Qaboos died in 2020. “May the long history of loyal friendship between our two countries continue.”

title: Sharjah Film Platform to screen 26 films and host Oscar-nominated director Abderrahmane Sissako
description: The 10-day festival will feature international and Emirati cinema, alongside screenings, workshops and a masterclass with the Mauritanian filmmaker
content: The ninth Sharjah Film Platform is to return on October 30, presenting 26 films from around the world and a retrospective celebrating Oscar-nominated director Abderrahmane Sissako. Organised by Sharjah Art Foundation, the 10-day festival will run until November 8 and bring together emerging and established filmmakers from countries including Palestine, Lebanon, Kazakhstan, Mexico, India and Haiti. The festival will open with Letters (2025), an anthology of 17 short films by Lebanese director Josef Khallouf that reflects on his country's recent history. An Incomplete Drowning (2026), directed by Palestinian artist Larissa Sansour and Denmark's Soren Lind, will close the event. Set aboard a ghostly ship drifting in the Mediterranean, the experimental film brings together figures from different periods of Palestinian history to examine colonialism, memory and the ability of objects to preserve the past. This year's Director in Focus programme will celebrate Mauritanian filmmaker Sissako, who will travel to Sharjah to lead a masterclass exploring his filmmaking practice. The retrospective will feature three of his films: Bamako (2006), Timbuktu (2014) and Black Tea (2024). Known for exploring identity, displacement and political realities across Africa, Sissako received an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film for Timbuktu , which depicts life under extremist rule in Mali. His earlier film, Bamako , examines international financial institutions through a fictional trial staged in a Malian courtyard. Emirati cinema will also be represented through Hind Saeed Al Basti's Alia and Meera , which follows two best friends whose small lie uncovers a family secret. The festival will also continue its First Takes initiative for a second year, bringing together aspiring filmmakers from NYU Abu Dhabi, Zayed University, the American University of Sharjah and the University of the Arts Sharjah. Developed in collaboration with Germany's Kurzfilm Festival Hamburg, the programme includes pitching workshops, feedback sessions and networking opportunities for film students. Screenings will take place at Mirage City Cinema, Sharjah Art Foundation's open-air cinema in Al Mureijah Square, as well as other venues across the emirate. Sharjah Film Platform 9 runs from October 30 to November 8

title: Gulf states to boost diesel shipments to struggling France
description: UAE, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia to increase deliveries in coming weeks, Paris sources say
content: The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said, as President Emmanuel Macron continued his tour of the Gulf. The aim is reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. “The greater the quantity, the lower the price. It’s quite simple,” an adviser to French President Emmanuel Macron said. A large part of the deal was negotiated by Mr Macron during a tour of the Gulf that started with visits to Kuwait and the UAE on Monday. He visited Bahrain on Tuesday, before travelling on to Qatar. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in October and November, bringing the total to 190,000 tonnes over the two months. In addition, the UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. “These are political commitments obtained from countries in the region because they know us and they know we are reliable – because we have been there during every critical moment, notably by deploying air defence capabilities,” the adviser said. Sales are to go through French energy company TotalEnergies, whose chief executive, Patrick Pouyanne, has accompanied Mr Macron on his Gulf tour. “Our mission is primarily to secure supplies because there is a risk. We have a diesel deficit, as we are a major importer,” Mr Pouyanne said. “We are in contact with [...] national companies and we are going to sign a contract specifically for France. The commitment in Saudi Arabia is to ensure that supplies continue beyond November.” The announcement is a political win for Mr Macron, who is under pressure in France, which is in the grip of large-scale protests over a cost-of-living crisis. Some demonstrations have turned violent. Authorities have imposed a curfew in central Paris and other parts of the country. European diesel is currently trading at almost $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. During Mr Macron's stop in the UAE on Monday, France and the UAE signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as the countries strengthen investment and economic ties. The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three agreements focused on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several fields, Abu Dhabi Media office reported. The deals cover Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi’s G42 and computing company Analog. MBZUAI is to focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models. Analog’s deal with AMI Labs is related to exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications and opening new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors. AI is a cornerstone of French-Emirati relations. During a visit by Sheikh Mohamed to France in February 2025, the UAE announced that billions of euros was to be investment in an AI campus and date centre project near Paris. The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technology and opportunities for operational improvements to help enhance efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems. Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts relating to a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project. “These agreements demonstrate both countries’ commitment to broadening economic and investment co-operation, strengthening integration between their industrial, technological and research capabilities, and opening new avenues for public-private partnerships to support the development of innovative and sustainable solutions in shared priority sectors,” Abu Dhabi Media office said.

title: UFC in Abu Dhabi: Kamaru Usman and Song Yadong added to Showdown Week
description: In the run-up to UFC 333, the world's leading MMA promotion is putting on two UFC Fan Experiences, including public workouts, meet-and-greets and live events
content: Fight fans will get the chance to meet some of the UFC's biggest names during Abu Dhabi Showdown Week . In the run-up to UFC 333 at Etihad Arena on Saturday, the world's leading MMA promotion is putting on two UFC Fan Experiences, including public workouts, meet-and-greets and live events. Fans will get the chance to meet former UFC welterweight champion Kamaru Usman, featherweight contender Jean Silva and Moroccan featherweight Marwan Rahiki at Yas Mall on Wednesday. This will follow the public workouts of the main-event fighters, Alexander Volkanovski and Movsar Evloev, and the co-main eventers, Petr Yan and Merab Dvalishvili . Volkanovski defends his featherweight title against Evloev at UFC 333, while Dvalishvili will attempt to reclaim the bantamweight strap he lost to Yan in December. Usman has fond memories of Abu Dhabi. "The Nigerian Nightmare" successfully defended his UFC welterweight title against Jorge Masvidal on Fight Island in July 2020. “Abu Dhabi has always been a special place for me and for UFC. I have some great memories of competing here, and the fans always bring incredible energy," said Usman. "Abu Dhabi Showdown Week is a great opportunity for us to connect with the fans outside the octagon, and I’m excited to be back, meet them and be part of another huge week for UFC in Abu Dhabi.” On Friday, fans can meet with bantamweight contender Song Yadong, lightweight Mauricio Ruffy and Palestinian-American heavyweight Sean Sharaf at Yas Bay Waterfront from 7pm. Yadong will have a keen eye on the Yan-Dvalishvili fight , with the Chinese hoping he will be next in line to face the winner. “I’ve heard so many great things about UFC in Abu Dhabi and the atmosphere during Abu Dhabi Showdown Week, so I’m really excited to finally experience it and be part of the week," he said. "UFC 333 is a huge card with some incredible fights. Of course, Petr Yan against Merab Dvalishvili is one I’m really looking forward to, and I can’t wait to meet the fans and experience the energy in Abu Dhabi.” The press conferences for UFC 333 will be held on Thursday at Etihad Arena (4-5.30pm). Fans are invited to attend for free. The weigh-ins will then take place on Friday, with the closed official weigh-ins scheduled for 8am, before ceremonial weigh-ins in the evening at Etihad Arena (4-6.30pm), which are open to the public. Former UFC bantamweight champion Aljamain Sterling and Moroccan featherweight Marwan Rahiki will take part in a special live Q&A at Etihad Arena before the ceremonial weigh-ins. Also on Friday, Power Slap 25 takes place at Space42 Arena, headlined by a super heavyweight title rematch between Dayne “Da Hawaiian Hitman” Viernes and Vasilii “Dumpling” Kamotskii. UFC 333 takes place on Saturday, October 24. The preliminary card is scheduled to begin around 6pm UAE time, with the main card expected to start around 10pm.

title: French riots hold a warning for British reformers
description: Efforts to create opportunities for those in their 20s must not fall flat in Europe
content: For someone in the UK, the riots in France are all too familiar. The sight of mostly young, masked, hooded people kicking in shopfronts, rampaging and looting shelves, and attacks on the police and emergency services – they occur with regular frequency across the Channel. French authorities admitted they lost control in certain major flashpoints in cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon. The following day they were locked in crisis talks with online reseller sites, including Vinted, over tools to crackdown on a sudden flood of items from looted premises. On Tuesday, prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said localised curfews had stemmed the tide of protest overnight. No one, though, is under any illusion that what we witnessed in Paris could not spread to other major cities in Europe. In 2011 the UK experienced similar scenes and there have been repeated, sporadic flare-ups since then. This summer in London, gangs of youths trashed supermarkets and stores. At weekends, mobs descend periodically on a selected target, drawn by social media, then proceed to force their entry, threaten staff and customers and ransack the contents. It would not take much to spark something bigger and broader, as France is experiencing. The powder keg is waiting to be lit. The French rioting arose from a student campaign against poor state schooling. Others joined in, venting their anger at the rising cost of living. In Spain, Portugal and Italy, there have been mass demonstrations at increased rents and foreign investment funds buying up property. In Albania, there were marches against the government, focusing on corruption, absence of jobs and declining education standards. In all these places, the pattern is familiar, of peaceful opposition soon giving way to violent uprising and thuggishness. Always, the young are to the fore. It cannot be coincidence that in France, between 1.4 million and 1.5 million people aged 18-29 are classified as "Neets" – not in education, employment or training. In the UK, the term is officially used for 18-24s, where the total is one million and climbing. The percentages of Neets in both countries and in the EU are similar: 13 per cent in France and the UK, 11 per cent in the EU. That is an awful lot of young folks with nothing to do, little to deter them, no money, few prospects and a disregard for officialdom that has ignored them. Those are nationwide figures. In some locations, in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the proportion of Neets is far higher. It should not be a surprise, then, that the outlets they hit are typically designer and clothing outlets. They want what the rest are having. Alan Milburn, the former Labour Health Secretary who has written a landmark report in the UK highlighting the depth of the growing crisis, calls it a "youth detachment" problem. Mr Milburn says that 60 per cent of the UK Neets have never had any form of job. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned of the "economic catastrophe and moral failure" facing society. He said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system that prioritises the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and policies of previous governments have all contributed to the bulging Neets bubble. Mr Burnham is pushing for his administration, as he puts it, to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system". Writing in The Times , he said: "Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point." He is following up with plans aimed at giving thousands of young people job opportunities. Mr Burnham quotes the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, showing that of the one million Neets, about 39 per cent are unemployed while the remaining 61 per cent are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work. There are 331,000 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits, almost double the level in 2016. The UK government will spend £353 billion ($469.59 billion) on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is absorbed by benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments. Mr Burnham wrote that this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

title: Hiring in the UAE rebounds in third quarter despite uncertainty fuelled by Middle East conflict
description: Energy, strategy and finance among key sectors across Gulf to boost recruitment, report finds
content: Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to growth of 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf , as business demand recovers, a report has found. After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index. Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added. Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar , 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries. The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens. The fund also expects Saudi Arabia 's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. Oman is the only Gulf member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. However, all the six states are anticipated to post growth in 2027, the IMF said. The contraction in Gulf hiring "lasted a single quarter and the market is now back within the modest growth range seen through 2025", Cooper Fitch said. "Growth extended across a wider range of functions than in the previous quarter, with paused mandates resuming in sectors such as energy." Hiring in energy recorded the sharpest increase at 7 per cent across the Gulf in the July-September period. Mandates stalled during the regional tensions returned steadily as conditions eased, the report said. "Clients resumed searches where they left off. In the UAE, growth came from across the energy market, including nuclear and renewables," it added. The delivery of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 pipeline also supported the sector's growth. "Project directors, commissioning specialists and contracts leaders remained difficult to secure. Candidates with scarce technical skills continued to receive multiple offers, keeping the market firmly in their favour," the report added. Hiring in finance grew 5 per cent, strategy rose 6 per cent – its first increase of 2026, while real estate and software employment was up 4 per cent. Recruitment in sales and marketing rose 3 per cent in the third quarter, "reflecting cautious confidence rather than a broad hiring rebound", while human resources grew 2 per cent, the report said. However, hiring in banking declined 4 per cent, while investment management fell by 5 per cent "after a strong run of hiring earlier in the year, driven by regional platform expansion and fund activity". While hiring picked up in the third quarter, it remained selective, Cooper Fitch said. "Clients focused on advancing active searches and securing specialist capability rather than broad expansion, and several markets and parts of financial services saw lower activity," it said. Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, it remains to be seen whether the improvement can be sustained. "Business demand has provided a firmer base, but costs remain elevated and visibility on trade and shipping is still limited," the report said. "Competition for scarce specialist talent has also intensified, adding pressure on employers seeking to secure critical capability."

title: 'I'm postponing my marriage': Gazans put lives on hold as they await Israeli election
description: Many Palestinians hoping Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu will lose power in October 27 vote
content: In Gaza , the fate of a destroyed supermarket, a family home and even a marriage now rest on an election in Israel in which the Palestinians affected have no vote. Munir Abu Wadi, the owner of the supermarket in Jabalia refugee camp, is waiting to see whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netaynahu is removed from power on October 27 before he sets about rebuilding his business. “Many people have put their lives on hold until after the Israeli election,” Mr Abu Wadi told The National . “I am one of them.” Across Gaza, residents say decisions about family life and business have been postponed in anticipation of the vote. After years of war and displacement, some see the Israeli election as a possible turning point, while acknowledging a change of government may bring no immediate improvement. “We always believe tomorrow might be better than today,” Mr Abu Wadi said. “That is why many people in Gaza are pinning their hopes on the Israeli election and hoping Netanyahu government will fall.” The next Israeli government will address issues such as Gaza's reconstruction, the disarmament of Hamas and an international backlash against settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israelis is electing the 120 members of the Knesset rather than voting directly for a prime minister, meaning the final outcome will depend on coalition negotiations. Mr Netanyahu is vying for power with an opposition from which former general Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as a leading challenger. Recent opinion polls have placed Mr Eisenkot’s Yashar party ahead of or close to Mr Netanyahu’s Likud. The Israeli opposition generally supports a tough approach to Palestine and Iran , finding fault with Mr Netanyahu for his handling of the conflicts rather than calling for concessions. Still, for people in Gaza, the election has become a date around which to plan deeply personal decisions. Mustafa Mousa, 30, has resisted months of pressure from his family to become engaged. His house is still stand-in but he says marriage requires more than money and accommodation. “It also requires stability and peace of mind,” he told The National. Mr Mousa said he would wait until the election results offered a clear picture of Gaza’s future before deciding whether to proceed with an engagement. “The election may not affect us immediately but its outcome will certainly influence the detail of daily life,” he said. “I told my family that I would postpone my engagement and marriage until after the Israeli election.” The calculation is different but equally consequential for Mahdi Abu Al Qumsan, 52, whose home was demolished during an Israeli military incursion into Gaza city. Mr Abu Al Qumsan and his family of 11 are now living as displaced people in Deir Al Balah. He hopes to clear the rubble from his home in Gaza city, and construct a basic shelter using plastic sheets, tarpaulin, wood and stones. He has started gathering materials but has yet to start the work. “To be honest, I’m not placing much hope in the Israel election,” he said. “But if Netanyahu loses, the outcome could be slightly better for us. It might encourage me to carry out what I have been planning.” Mr Abu Al Qumsan wants his family to live again in the neighbourhood where his children were born and where he himself grow up. But with materials scarce and Gaza’s political future unclear, even the construction of a makeshift shelter feels like a gamble. Political analyst Emad Omar said many Palestinians had come to view the election as exceptional because of the influence Israeli policy has over almost every part of their social and economic lives. A Netanyahu victory would deepen fears that the policies and military approach of his right-wing coalition would continue, Mr Omar said. If he fails to form another government, Palestinians might hope for greater engagement with the Palestinian Authority and progress on Gaza‘s recovery and reconstruction. But a change in leadership would not necessarily mean a fundamental shift in Israel policy towards Gaza. Mr Eisenkot, who served in Mr Netanyahu‘s war cabinet before resigning in 2024 over what he said was a lack of strategy, has broadly supported Israeli military operations while criticising the government’s management of the war. Mr Abu Wadi also acknowledged that Netanyahu’s successor might not offer Palestinians a substantiality different future. “It’s true that whoever comes next may not be any better,” he said. “But people are eager, at the very least, to see the departure of those whose names have become associated with the war.” Polling suggests Mr Netanyahu faces a serious challenge but uncertainty over possible coalitions mean the outcome remains difficult to predict. Few analysts would count out Mr Netanyahu, who has led Israel for all but an 18-month period since 2009. There are also fears in Gaza about what could happen before polling day. Mr Omar said Palestinians were concerned that a new military escalation might alter the course of the campaign. “No one can predict what Netanyahu is thinking,” he said. “There is concern that he may initiate a major event before the vote in an attempt to change the political landscape or shift opinion polls in his favour.”

title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced Israel visit amid Iran war concerns
description: Pentagon chief's trip comes day after Trump publicly endorsed Israeli Prime Minister for re-election
content: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel, as the two sides discuss the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran, American media reported. The meeting, which was also attended by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, took place on Monday evening at Ovda Airbase in southern Israel, Axios said in a report quoting two sources. The visit was also reported by CNN, which quoted two sources and a US official. The Pentagon has declined to comment on Mr Hegseth’s movements. He was also reported to have met US troops at the base and later posted an image of himself visiting personnel from US Central Command, which oversees American military operations across the Middle East. The visit came days before Israel’s October 27 election and a day after US President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Mr Netanyahu , calling him a “great warrior prime minister”. In footage shared by Mr Netanyahu on Tuesday, the Israeli leader thanked Mr Trump for his support and described him as “by far, the greatest friend Israel has ever had and will have in the White House”. “Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it, and we’ll finish it together,” Mr Netanyahu said. Mr Netanyahu said the alliance between the two countries had demonstrated that they could achieve significant results together. He added there was scope to expand the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and several Arab states during Mr Trump’s first term in office. Mr Netanyahu also praised the US President for confronting what he described as the greatest danger facing Americans – an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. “We won’t let it happen,” he said. Mr Trump’s endorsement appeared to reflect shared strategic interests over Iran, as well as the political importance of maintaining a close relationship with Mr Netanyahu during a volatile period for the region. The backing also gives Mr Netanyahu a boost before the election as he seeks to present his relationship with Washington as an asset for Israeli security. Mr Trump, meanwhile, has an interest in maintaining a reliable Israeli partner as his administration pursues its regional objectives. But the two leaders have reportedly differed over the direction of the Iran war and the prospects for diplomatic initiatives in Gaza and elsewhere. There has been no public confirmation of a specific agreement linking the endorsement to Israeli policy concessions or renewed military action.

title: Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed hails growing momentum of UAE-India ties in Mumbai meeting with foreign minister
description: Sheikh Abdullah emphasises significance of historic ties in talks with Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar
content: Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed , Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, on Monday met Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar , India's Minister of External Affairs, in Mumbai for high-level talks as part of a working visit to the country. The discussions centred on efforts to bolster long-standing ties between the nations, with a focus on further collaboration across the economy, trade, investment, culture and energy. Sheikh Abdullah emphasised the significance of the UAE's relations with India and set out plans to build on the foundations for growth laid down by their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa), which has been in place since 2022. The deal – the first signed by the Emirates – pushed bilateral trade beyond $85 billion. The agreement means India is the UAE's largest trading partner, with the UAE becoming India's third-largest trading partner. India and the UAE enjoy a robust alliance that dates back to the formation of the Emirates. The UAE is now home to about four million Indian citizens, the largest expatriate community in the country. Sheikh Abdullah said the UAE-India partnership was continuing to gain momentum, helping to reinforce the countries as key drivers of global economic growth. The two ministers also discussed regional and international developments and spoke of ways of protect peace and security, state news agency Wam reported. Sheikh Abdullah was welcomed at the start of his visit by Mangal Prabhat Lodha, India's Minister of Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, and senior officials. Sheikh Abdullah's trip serves to demonstrate the strength of relations between the two countries, which have flourished in recent years. In May, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made an official visit to the Emirates, during which he met President Sheikh Mohamed. Sheikh Mohamed made a working visit to New Delhi in January, where he and Mr Modi pledged to deepen co-operation in sectors including artificial intelligence, the economy and food security, during discussions at the Prime Minister's residence. Mr Modi made a two-day visit to the UAE in 2024, where he addressed a crowd of 40,000 Indians at Zayed Sports City Stadium . He also spoke at the World Governments Summit in Dubai, before inaugurating the first Hindu temple in Abu Dhabi .

title: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project
description: UAE developer plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over next three to five years
content: UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said.
