The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment. “We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.” Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far. Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January. It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity. Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres. Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah. Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said. Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA. Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement. Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said. “The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.” “The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.” Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund. By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail. Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report. The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter. The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom. “We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said. The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years. The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added. “The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

title: Morocco's new Prime Minister puts two-state solution at heart of foreign policy agenda
description: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri pledges major economic reforms as she presents programme to parliament
content: Morocco's Prime Minister Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri vowed to support the Palestinian cause by pushing for a two-state solution as she presented her government's programme to the parliament. The country last week swore in its new government, led by its first female prime minister, in a ceremony presided over by King Mohammed VI. Ms El Mansouri kept several former government ministers in their posts, including Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit. The government formation followed a deal between Ms El Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, which won the September 23 election, and three other parties. The coalition holds 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority. On Monday, she presented her government's programme to members of both houses of parliament, outlining a five-year agenda focused on tackling corruption, strengthening the social welfare state, integrating young people into the economy, protecting sovereignty and building a productive economy. Ms El Mansouri stressed "Morocco’s long-standing position on the Palestinian cause and Jerusalem", as well as her "support for a peaceful settlement based on a two-state solution that would ensure a just and lasting peace". In September, Israel and Morocco agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties by elevating missions to full embassies. Ms El Mansouri also promised to "mobilise international support for Morocco's autonomy proposal" for the Sahara region and to "accelerate economic development in the southern provinces" to strengthen the region's role as "Morocco's gateway to Africa". On the economy, she said her government aimed for ​average ​annual economic ​growth of 5 per cent from ⁠2027 to 2031, up from an ⁠expected 4.7 per cent this year. She aims to keep the fiscal deficit under 3 per cent of GDP and maintain inflation at 2 per cent "to protect purchasing power and stability". The government also plans to expand the tax base and reform the income tax, raise direct social aid to needy households, reduce food prices and push private investment to two thirds of total national investment. Public debt is to drop to about 62 per cent of GDP by 2031, she said. There are plans to improve the efficiency of public enterprises and ​criminalise illicit enrichment and conflicts ‌of interest, Ms El Mansouri said. "We ⁠believe that institutions will ​not regain public trust without an effective ​fight ‌against corruption and conflicts of interest," she added. The government faces pressure to address unemployment and demands for better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo handed 30-day suspension and €255 fine by Portuguese FA
description: Al Nassr forward will miss no Portugal games and is free to play in November's Nations League matches
content: Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and ordered to pay a fine of €255 as punishment for walking out on the national team earlier this month. The Portuguese Football Federation's (FPF) disciplinary council said it had upheld the charge against the 41-year-old forward in full. Ronaldo left Portugal's base in ​Copenhagen ⁠before their Uefa Nations ‌League match against Denmark earlier this month, having ​accused head coach Jorge Jesus of twice breaking his word about his role after he was an unused substitute against Norway. Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal's 2-1 win. The disciplinary council found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) of the federation's disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on October 9. In a lengthy statement, Ronaldo, 41, later apologised for ⁠failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match ⁠and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any punishment arising from the incident. Ronaldo earns a reported €4 million a week at Saudi Pro League side Al Nassr. The fine imposed on him represents 0.0064% of his weekly salary. His suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will not miss any Portugal matches with the next international window November 12-17. Portugal face Denmark in the Nations League again on 14 November before travelling to Wales three days later. FPF president Pedro Proenca has said ​everyone within the federation wanted Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved. The five-time Ballon d'Or winner has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances – both men's world records – helping them win Euro 2016 and the two Nations League titles.

title: PSG vs Barcelona: Flick’s flying side take on European champions before El Clasico date with Real Madrid
description: Catalan giants have made red hot start to season but head into defining week and two heavyweight clashes
content: Barcelona have scored 48 goals so far this season at an average of more than four per game, with 39 of them in La Liga – that’s 16 more than Real Madrid, the next highest scorers. The Catalans have won all nine of their league games, a club and a league record achieved only once before – by a great Real Madrid side in 1968/69. Barcelona can go clear with a win in their next game – against Madrid in Sunday’s El Clasico. Even by their own high standards, it has been an astonishing start to the season. But Hansi Flick’s side now face their toughest week. As well as playing Madrid, they face back-to-back European champions Paris Saint-Germain away on Tuesday. PSG are managed by Luis Enrique , the last man to lead Barcelona to the Champions League title, back in 2015. Barca’s latest superb performance came in Saturday’s 5-2 win against a Real Betis team that was previously unbeaten at home and had hosted a first Champions League game in midweek. It was a superb contest with superb goals, the best being the opener from Lamine Yamal after 10 minutes. Among the favourites to win the Ballon d’Or, the forward is arguably the best player in the world right now. The 19-year-old has scored nine goals and boasts nine assists in his first 11 games. Is there a danger that he’s playing too much - he also played in all four of Spain’s Nations League matches during the international break - or is he a machine who cannot play too much? Last week, statistics showed that he spent 45 per cent of the match walking and 32 per cent jogging. The view from the club is that he knows how to pace himself and manage himself during matches and that he’s running significantly less than other players. A certain Lionel Messi had similar traits. It helps that Yamal is surrounded by brilliance – and that’s not only his four-year-old half-brother Kenye, who brings smiles to the other players with his enthusiasm and mispronunciation of their names, including Ani Olmo (Dani Olmo), Pedli (Pedri) or Elemanovski (Lewandowski), the Polish striker he still thinks plays with his brother. Lewandowski was the main striker during his four seasons at the club, but he’s barely been missed having moved to Chicago in the summer just before his 38th birthday. Barca had five different goalscorers at Betis. Rodri has slotted in from Manchester City, looking just as imperious as a man who is captain of world champions Spain should. He’s brought experience, and similar can be said of the versatile Gabriel Jesus, 29, who only cost €10 million and has already scored four goals. The club benefits from being a destination where players want to move. Little wonder Marcus Rashford wanted to stay after his loan spell last season, yet Barcelona surprised football by going for Anthony Gordon from Newcastle United instead. Gordon has been a success so far. The Liverpudlian, 25, has endeared himself to fans with good performances and speaking well in Spanish and even some Catalan. His enthusiasm, joy and an assist every two games have done Gordon no harm either. He’s an intelligent footballer and being in a better team has made him a better player. Gordon plays on the left wing and is being utilised well as part of a strong squad – he scored last week as his side came from a goal down to beat Galatasaray 4-1 away, then came off the bench in Saturday’s win over Betis. Karim Adeyemi, another new signing, feels like a wild card that is paying off. Like Jesus, the 24-year-old, signed from Dortmund, can play across the front. He’s featured in every Barca game so far, starting four from 11, scoring four and making three assists. His link-up down the left with Barcelona-born Xavi Espart, a 19-year-old left back, is effective. Barcelona have at least two outstanding players for every position and no attack in world football comes close – but they’re supported by so many of Spain’s World Cup winners: Dani Olmo, Pau Cubarsi, Pedri, Gavi, Eric Garcia and goalkeeper Joan Garcia. Defender Eric, 25, will be out for a month with a thigh injury picked up on Saturday. The right back, who captained the side in the previous league game, a 3-0 win against Getafe, will be missed and that area could be a problem as Jules Kounde (ankle) will also miss the game in Paris and perhaps also the Clasico. In brighter injury news, Frenkie de Jong is back after a ligament tear at the World Cup, which kept him out for over 100 days. At least they had Pedri and Rodri in his position. There’s Gavi, too, but the 22-year-old is yet to reestablish himself after serious injuries. Barcelona have been brilliant so far this season. It’s a shame that more fans can’t see them in person since Camp Nou’s long redevelopment still restricts the capacity to 62,600 against an eventual total of 105,000 in 2028. A shame too that tickets to see matches are so prohibitively expensive for non-season ticket holders, but there’s no denying the quality of their football.

title: Saudi Pro League: Al Hilal back on top thanks to Gabriel Martinelli's late winner against Al Hazem
description: Victory sets up a top-of-the-table clash against Al Qadsiah on Friday
content: Gabriel Martinelli's late winner against Al Hazem took Al Hilal back to the top of the Saudi Pro League, while Al Ahli held on for a 3-2 victory away to Al Fayha. Hilal dominated Hazem, creating 19 chances but was left frustrated by a glut of missed opportunities and the inspired presence of Jindrich Stanek in the Hazem goal. Simone Inzaghi's side looked to be heading for their first stalemate of the campaign until Brazilian forward Martinelli , a summer recruit from Arsenal, rose unmarked in the area to head home in the 89th minute. "I am happy with the victory and with the outstanding performance and high focus shown by everyone. We created many opportunities during the course of the match," Inzaghi told reporters. The win moved Hilal back to the top of the standings on 24 points, two ahead of Al Qadsiah. It sets up a mouthwatering clash between the top two on Friday. "We have an important match ahead of us against Al Qadsiah, a team with high-level players and a capable coaching staff, and they have been performing well recently. We will work on preparing in the best possible way to achieve victory," Inzaghi added. Al Ahli's hard-fought win came courtesy of an Artem Bondarenko double and a Firas Al Buraikan penalty. A thunderbolt from Hugo Moura had given Fayha the lead in the 45th minute before Bondarenko equalised in injury time, the big Ukrainian powering in a header after excellent wing play from Saad Balobaid. Al Buraikan banged home from the penalty spot to give Ahli the lead after Matheus Goncalves was brought down, but the lead lasted only six minutes as Jason pulled Fayha level in the 65th minute with a clever free kick. Bondarenko grabbed his second of the game on 70 minutes, getting the final touch following a goalmouth scramble to secure Ahli the three points. “The spirit was present today to come back in the result. Despite making some mistakes, I praise the players for their fighting spirit and for achieving the victory,” said Ahli coach Marino Pusic. On Bondarenko, a player he worked with during his time at Shakhtar Donetsk, Pusic said: "Today Artem helped us to win and score the goals. The player only needs to feel the support of his teammates, and that is what happened today.” The win moved Al Ahli to 18 points and third place after 10 rounds. Elsewhere, three goals in the last 25 minutes saw Al Khaleej take a 3-2 victory at Al Fateh while Al Shabab played out a 2-2 draw at home to Al Faisaly.

title: NBA salaries 2026/27: Who are the highest-paid players as new season gets under way?
description: New York Knicks will be looking to defend the championship when play begins on Tuesday
content: The 2026/27 NBA season tips-off on Tuesday and the New York Knicks will be hoping to retain the title they famously won last season. The Knicks defeated San Antonio Spurs in the NBA finals, ending a remarkable 53-year wait for the title. The legendary LeBron James , meanwhile, will enter a record-setting 24th NBA season following his decision to take a pay cut and join the Philadelphia 76ers after eight seasons with the LA Lakers. According to reports, LeBron accepted a contract worth around $8 million over two seasons, which is substantially lower than the deal worth $53m during his final season with the Lakers. title: Universities in UAE enjoy enrolment surge amid decline in Gulf students heading to UK
description: Institutions expanding academic offerings to support growing demand
content: Leading UAE universities are investing in the future as they seek to capitalise on growing demand for higher education in the country - amid a sharp decline in students heading to the UK. Institutes unveiled expansion drives, new programmes and plans to attract more learners from across the Emirates and beyond at a flagship education fair in Abu Dhabi on Monday. The number of students enrolled at universities in the UAE reached 218,000 in the 2025/26 academic year, a 15 per cent rise on an annual basis. Hundreds of high-school pupils gathered at Adnec at the 20th annual Najah event on Monday, as they prepare to take the next step on their academic journeys. The continued growth in the UAE higher education landscape comes as the number of people in the Gulf choosing to study in the UK continues to decline. Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said. The number of student visa applications from the UAE has fallen from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. Abu Dhabi University is to launch eight new undergraduate programmes at its Dubai campus – starting next year – to bolster its national presence. “Dubai has become a hub for international education and we would like to be part of that market,” Bassam Murra, executive director of marketing, enrolment and registration at the university, told The National at the event. “There is a plan to expand and to offer more programmes and to grow our population in Dubai,” he said. “Even in our planning, if it's required that we expand our facility itself, this is something we want to consider.” The Dubai campus will offer new programmes in subjects such as artificial intelligence, engineering, international relations, law and psychology. It offers an opportunity for UAE universities aiming to entice more students as they build their academic reputations internationally. The University of Sharjah was ranked best in the UAE for medicine in the US News Best Global Universities Rankings and has also been climbing the ranks of the QS World University Rankings. “Our goal is to be always in the top and to bring students from both outside the country and inside the country,” May Bin Hadda, admissions officer at the University of Sharjah, told The National . The university welcomed more than 5,000 new students at the start of this academic year. Emirates Aviation University reported a similar result, with a high intake this year especially from abroad. A representative said admissions had been busier than ever, with strong interest from around the world. “Dubai’s position as a global aviation hub continues to be a major attraction for international applicants,” they added. Liwa University has also recorded “significant” growth. “Both the Abu Dhabi and Al Ain campuses are packed in all specialisations,” said Adam Al Bahti, integrated marketing manager at Liwa University. “We feel there's a big demand in the market, especially for programmes in AI and in medical and health sciences.” While primarily focused on domestic pupils, Liwa University is hoping to attract more international students in the coming years. In July, the UAE launched a new higher education award aimed at shining a light on the achievements of the country's best universities and helping to “foster a culture of excellence”. Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, said the UAE Higher Award for Education would support initiatives that “create a sustainable impact” and advance the nation's “readiness for the future”. The UAE has taken significant steps in recent years to raise standards in the higher education sector, which has been reflected by impressive performances in global education league tables. In June, Abu Dhabi's Khalifa University of Science and Technology broke new ground by being the first in the UAE to feature in the top 150 of the QS World University Rankings 2027. The university rose 30 places to 147th, cementing its place as the country's leading institution for the ninth consecutive year. The QS rankings evaluated 8,808 universities across 106 places, with 1,504 seats of learning named in the final list. The university was ranked 12th worldwide for the international make-up of its faculty, reflecting its work in moulding young minds drawn from around the globe. In January, Abu Dhabi University was named among the top 100 for business and economic studies in another global league table, outranking renowned institutions from the US, UK and China. It was placed 81st out of more than 1,000 institutions assessed in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026. The list comprised universities from 91 countries.

title: UAE tax rules: What businesses can claim for employee expenses
description: New guidance covers staff transport, meals, accommodation, mobile phones and parking
content: Giving employees the tools they need to do their jobs effectively is a timeless business requirement. Whether a company has standard lists of equipment and resources for different grades and functions, which it should to make onboarding easier, most businesses could produce such lists without much difficulty. There are, however, tax considerations, particularly corporation tax and VAT . Thankfully, Federal Tax Authority Decision No 17 of 2026 has helpfully brought together answers to many of the questions businesses might have. There are five main sections, starting with transport provided for staff. It's critical that employees are not charged for the service and that transport is provided only between their homes and workplaces. Could there be a collection point for several employees, provided it is a reasonable distance from their homes? I would imagine so. Cash payments instead of transport cannot be offered, and there should be no identifiable non-business benefit. Could one employee who fails either test affect the entire arrangement? The decision says nothing about separating qualifying and non-qualifying cases. Best not be the person who tests the rules. What about pooling transport between two neighbouring companies? If the company providing the service changes according to a weekly schedule, would that complicate matters? A strict interpretation would require whichever company provides the service to invoice its commercial neighbour. I don't see how this can be avoided. Anything more complicated might best be outsourced for simplicity. Next is the provision of food and beverages. This is permissible where employees live so remotely that returning home is impractical. What constitutes remote is not defined, although I would interpret it as being unable to reach home within a reasonable time, given an individual's circumstances. This raises the possibility that only a small proportion of the workforce might qualify. No guidance has been provided on whether a minimum number of employees must meet the conditions. The provision must be linked to an employee's role and circumstances, including their workplace or residence. Suitable facilities should not be available at their accommodation or workplace, nor should local food outlets be reasonably accessible. Again, cash payments instead of food and beverages should not be an option. Moving on to company-provided accommodation, this must be an operational necessity. Perhaps the work site is in the Empty Quarter, 100 miles (160km) from the nearest town. Difficult access could make it reasonable to accommodate employees on or near the site. Accommodation should be suitable but not luxurious. No swimming pools, expansive manicured gardens, extensive household staff or additional reception rooms. The rules for onboarding new employees are a little more relaxed. Accommodation can be provided for up to 30 days, and the expense claimed, provided it is not ostentatious. Notably, the decision does not exclude employees who have already been living in the country, regardless of how long they have been here. I recall benefiting from such an arrangement when starting a role in the late 2000s. I believe there were two reasons for it. First, treating new starters differently would have been inconvenient. Second, with international personnel flying in and out of the region, putting everyone in the same hotel helped employees become familiar with the business and encouraged social interaction. Mobile phones are another area where guidance already existed, and the new decision restates and expands on it. Devices must be required for work and used only for business purposes. Each invoice should be reviewed, with personal calls identified and excluded from VAT or corporation tax claims. A company may decide to absorb the non-deductible cost rather than introduce an internal system for recovering personal expenses. Sometimes the administrative cost can outweigh the value of recovering small amounts spent on company assets. The new requirement is for a formal standard operating policy. This must be communicated to everyone affected, reviewed periodically, updated when necessary and demonstrably enforced. For businesses without standard operating procedures, this would be a good place to start. If I could, as an accountant, give human resources departments one task, it would be to map every business process and identify the roles and individuals responsible for each. This would strengthen both control and continuity. I can think of few projects more valuable when reassessing internal efficiency, particularly in an AI-driven world where automation is the mot du jour . Lastly comes parking, which is subject to the same requirements as mobile phones.

title: How to make the most of Abu Dhabi 2029
description: By hosting IMF and World Bank meetings, the UAE will help shape the global agenda
content: Twenty-three years ago, Dubai hosted the Annual Meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund . These important conversations took place during a pivotal year for the UAE and the wider Middle East. The country’s economic ambitions were being realised and expanded – the launch of Emirates airline being a prime example. A few months earlier, the US-led invasion of Iraq toppled Saddam Hussein, unleashing consequences that were felt across the whole region. Fast forward to today, and although much has changed, some things remain the same. The UAE is still setting itself challenging goals for the future and as the second-largest Arab economy it continues to set an ambitious pace. However, the region is again marked by turmoil as the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel continues, and Yemen re-emerges as a deadly flashpoint. Another echo of 2003 is the news that the World Bank and IMF will hold their meetings in Abu Dhabi in three years’ time. For the UAE, this will be an opportunity to welcome the world’s financial elite to the capital and to help set the agenda over the coming years. It could help change the conversation about how the global economy works and whose interests it serves. Although three years away, the meetings will take place against a backdrop of persistent global economic pressures. Many developing countries face expensive borrowing, unsustainable debt and falling development aid. Climate change and technological disruption also mean that it cannot be "business as usual". Meeting such challenges requires a wide range of perspectives, including those of emerging economies. Abu Dhabi is well placed to encourage that exchange. This is because the UAE’s established position as a trading hub with relationships across emerging markets – plus its engagement with multilateral and minilateral groupings such as Brics – give it connections that span different economic and political systems. At a time when international co-operation is fragmenting, the Emirates can provide a venue where competing interests meet and solutions are explored. There has also been a recent welcome sign of the UAE’s growing contribution to global governance. The election of Ali Alhosani as the first Emirati executive director at the IMF reflects the increasing presence of UAE expertise in key roles. The preparations for 2029 should build on this progress. Such work will require Emirati economists, financiers, researchers and policymakers to tackle questions ranging from sovereign debt and development finance to monetary stability and digital innovation. That expertise will be valuable long after the delegates depart, strengthening the country’s capacity to contribute to international economic policy. Crucially, the meetings' success will be determined by how the voices of smaller economies and indebted nations find a meaningful place alongside those of leading finance ministers and central bank governors. Different political cultures can find a platform in the UAE to be represented in a spirit of constructive debate, without the expectation that everyone must agree. Abu Dhabi should welcome the world, but it should also challenge it. The ultimate measure of success will be whether the conversations held in 2029 produce better co-operation, fairer access to finance and real opportunities for nations seeking a more prosperous future.

title: US midterms: Iran war and cost of living put Trump’s foreign policy under pressure
description: November 3 elections could reshape Trump’s approach to Iran and the wider Middle East
content: US foreign policy is playing an outsized role in this year's midterm elections, thanks largely to President Donald Trump 's war against Iran and its effect on the cost of living for Americans. Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are trying to win back some power on November 3, having spent two years in the political wilderness after a disastrous performance during the 2024 presidential election. A Democratic victory in either chamber would give the opposition greater powers to oppose Mr Trump's agenda, and the ability to launch investigations and call witnesses to testify about action the administration has taken. Recent polling gives the Democrats a more-than 85 per cent chance of winning the House, where they only need to flip a handful of seats. The Senate is a trickier task for Democrats, who need to gain four seats to secure a majority, including at least two in states Mr Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Front and centre of many political debates in the US is the cost of living, particularly petrol prices, which have risen by nearly 50 per cent since Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched their war against Iran on February 28. Diesel, the lifeblood of the trucking industry, has been even harder hit, having risen by about two thirds. Costs for farmers, truckers and businesses have soared, with high prices being passed on to consumers in many instances. "The Republican Party and candidates are being killed by the higher prices," Kristin Diwan a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told The National. "To the extent that people blame them on the Iran war, that is also a liability. The war is extremely unpopular and that crosses party lines." Mr Trump has sought to lower prices by allowing Russia to export diesel, something many Americans are queasy about. A survey published this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 86 per cent of Americans believed the Iran war had harmed the cost of living, while 68 per cent said it had not been worth fighting. Dina Smeltz, managing director and chairwoman of public opinion and foreign policy at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, said the administration's policies had made the connection between international affairs and household finances more apparent. “By disrupting some of the stability in traditional US foreign policy stances, the Trump administration’s policies seem to have sharpened how Americans link US actions abroad and their daily lives,” she said. The survey also found that 72 per cent believed the conflict had damaged America's relations with its allies. Andrew Payne, research director for Europe, Russia and the Americas at Chatham House, said the elections are an unusual moment when international affairs could influence domestic political outcomes. "Foreign policy rarely decides US elections," he wrote in an analysis published on October 15. "But this year, the economy is foreign policy." Polls this month show Mr Trump's approval ratings hitting new lows , with Americans particularly unhappy about the economy and cost of living. An AP-Norc survey shows that 65 per cent of US adults say higher-than-usual prices are the result of Mr Trump’s policies. This is compared to October 2022, under predecessor Joe Biden, when 44 per cent of the public said higher prices were due to presidential policies. And a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Monday found Mr Trump's approval rating at a record low of 31 per cent. "Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference," Mr Payne said. Many Republican candidates are facing uphill battles as they try to distance themselves from some of Mr Trump's policies. He campaigned on a pledge to avoid foreign military entanglements and to lower the cost of living. Instead, he started a new war and inflation has risen more than expected since he took office. When Mr Trump announced military operations against Iran, he did so without first securing congressional authorisation, leading to a debate about the limits of presidential war powers. Thanks to four Republican representatives voting alongside the Democrats, the House has already voted to constrain Mr Trump's war powers, although the Senate did not follow suit. A Democratic majority in either or both chambers would probably increase friction with the White House over the Iran conflict, which Mr Trump has said will end one way or another immediately after the midterms. If they win, the Democrats are expected to hold a host of hearings, including on the true financial cost of the war and whether the US military was prepared for a new war in the Middle East. Democrats will use those hearings to try to seize an early narrative as voters start looking towards the 2028 presidential election. A Democratic majority in Congress could have broader foreign implications, too. US military assistance to Israel, sanctions and Washington's relationships with governments across the Gulf could all become subjects of deeper congressional scrutiny. The war in Ukraine could also become an issue for Republicans in the midterms, particularly since Mr Trump has waived sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports. The move has been condemned by Republicans and Democrats and a recent YouGov poll of more than 5,500 US adults opposed the agreement. Governments across the Middle East will be wondering about the extent to which Democrats will constrain Mr Trump, and whether the election will fundamentally shift US foreign policy, or just make it harder for the President to get things done. "The Democratic Party has shown more scepticism about favourable deals with Saudi Arabia. This will make legislation such as the nuclear agreement [with Riyadh] more difficult to pass through Congress, although probably not beyond Trump's veto power," Ms Diwan said. Still, she noted that Mr Trump is not inclined to defer to Congress, even when he is legally obliged to do so. "I don’t think the defeat in the election will constrain him," she said.

title: Doctors and teachers to benefit from AI but safeguards needed to protect sensitive information
description: Patient records, personal data and financial details could be at risk without protection
content: Experts have warned that strong cybersecurity safeguards are needed to protect sensitive information as artificial intelligence plays a growing role in health care and education. The UAE is expanding AI use across essential services as part of a wider drive to develop the technology. Abu Dhabi’s government digital strategy for 2025 to 2027 is backed by Dh13 billion ($3.54 billion), while the Ministry of Education has developed an AI literacy framework covering kindergarten to Grade 12. In May, the UAE Cabinet also approved a national policy to advance digital health care and AI, including developing medical systems and preparing healthcare workers to use the technology. But information such as patient records, personal data and financial details could be at risk when shared with AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude. Nisha Sanghani, partner and head of Middle East at Ashurst Perkins Coie Risk Advisory, said the acceleration in the use of AI must be met with significant cybersecurity investments to keep sensitive information safe, and to train people using these tools to avoid breach risks. “As adoption accelerates, safety, governance and accountability need to advance at the same pace as innovation – particularly where AI may influence decisions about a person’s health, development or future,” said Ms Sanghani. “In health care and education, the measure of AI success cannot simply be how quickly we adopt it, but whether it delivers better outcomes that people can trust.” Ms Sanghani said the shift from experiments to everyday services increased the importance of oversight, but that the UAE had an opportunity to demonstrate how AI could be used responsibly on a large scale. “For organisations operating here in the UAE, the question is moving beyond ‘where can we use AI?’ to ‘where can AI genuinely create better outcomes, and what needs to be true for us to trust it?” Nalla Karunanithy, chief executive of digital health and e-commerce at Aster DM Healthcare told The National the organisation was using AI to read X-rays alongside radiologists, measure cardiac MRI scans and supports early detection of coronary artery disease. This helps save time for doctors so “the clinician's time goes towards judgment,” said Mr Karunanithy. “The AI detects, measures or flags; the clinician interprets, decides and signs.” But as AI becomes more widely used, healthcare providers must control which systems can access medical information and what happens to it afterwards. Aster stores patient information in the UAE and assesses each AI system before allowing it access, Mr Karunanithy said. Testing is not done with real patient data and only approved systems receive necessary information. “Our group AI governance policy prohibits external providers from using patient information to train their models or for any purpose beyond the approved scope,” he said. UAE healthcare provider NMC Healthcare is centralising information across its 70 centres, said Ahmed Hafez, director of solution engineering for the Middle East, Turkey and Africa at data company Snowflake. He added that the work was intended to improve understanding of hospital operations and support decisions at the point of care. Vladislav Tushkanov, research and development group manager at cybersecurity company Kaspersky, told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi that personal data had to be kept safe. “We need to understand how we educate our workforce, how we make them understand that it's OK to use the internal AI systems to process information, but you cannot send personally identifiable information in the cloud,” he said. Aster said it had rejected solutions that could not meet its data residency requirements. Staff must use approved enterprise tools, with its AI Centre of Excellence overseeing their assessment and adoption. Last year, hackers claimed responsibility for a large-scale data breach at American Hospital in Dubai, reportedly seizing 450 million patient records. The hospital was contacted for comment but had not responded at the time of publication. However, despite the possible consequences of mistakes, Costi Perricos, Deloitte’s global generative AI leader, said that this should not prevent organisations from using AI. “You shouldn't turn away just because we need to be more careful about this,” he said. He added that the Middle East’s access to capital and technology, combined with its willingness to pursue new ideas, raised opportunities to develop the AI sector. Introducing tools is only one part of the work, Mr Perricos said. Organisations also need to prepare employees for changes to how they did their jobs. Bikram Mukhi, chief strategy officer at Soika Labs, said human oversight remained critical, particularly in education. “We live in very interesting times where technology is moving faster than the rate of adoption.” Users need to understand that the technology is still developing and that new capabilities could bring new risks, he said, adding that governments and regulated businesses are also seeking greater control over the information and infrastructure used by their AI systems. “AI just can't be just deployed across the board,” said Shadi Hatoum, regional manager for the Middle East and Africa at data platform company Tealium. Different uses require different standards and measures of success, he said.
