title: US allowing 'dark fleet' oil tankers to ship crude, Energy Secretary says
description: Chris Wright rejects suggestions that the approval process is lifting sanctions
content: US President Donald Trump's administration is allowing oil tankers under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday. Mr Wright told a Citadel Securities event in New York that this would involve investors buying and refurbishing idled sanctioned tankers, then using them to transport legal oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” Mr Wright said. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more.” He said there are about 1,600 tankers in the "dark fleet", and that dozens or hundreds could be added to the legitimate ships. It is the latest attempt by the Trump administration to reduce energy prices , which have soared amid the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz . Brent crude, the global benchmark for much of the world's oil, settled 0.48 per cent lower on Monday at $109.3 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, was 0.61 per cent lower at $98.42. Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that only 24 of the about 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. “With war risk, rather than vessel availability alone, driving freight costs in the Middle East Gulf, sanctions relief risks delivering limited commercial benefits while weakening geopolitical leverage,” analysts wrote. Mr Wright rejected the idea that the process would be dropping penalties from ships that would carry crude from Russia, Iran or other countries on which the US imposed sanctions. “We are converting dark tankers to legitimate tankers,” he said.

title: Lebanon to reject direct military co-ordination with Israel at Florida talks
description: Lebanese officials expect little progress on Israeli withdrawal before general election next week
content: Lebanon is rejecting US-backed proposals for its troops to co-ordinate directly with the Israeli army, officials said before talks resume in Florida on Tuesday. They said they expected limited progress before Israel's legislative elections next week. The latest round of direct talks, bringing together Lebanese and Israeli military delegations in Tampa, follows a decision last month to formally separate the political and military aspects of the negotiations. The aim is to negotiate an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon. The price demanded by Israel is for Hezbollah to be disarmed. However, Lebanon is pushing back against the idea of direct military co-ordination. “The issue keeps coming up but we always tell them 'no, we will not do that,'” one Lebanese political official close to the discussions said. They added that any future talks must continue to involve American mediation. “There are Israelis and Lebanese, with the Americans in the middle. That's it and that's how it will remain. Our position has always been that there should be a third party for verification.” The proposed verification mechanism would oversee the agreements in so-called “pilot zones” – areas of southern Lebanon where Hezbollah would disarm, Israeli forces would withdraw and the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) would assume control. Progress has stalled for months since the first pilot zones were established in July . The process remains untested, with no agreed mechanism to verify compliance by all sides, while critics point out that the initial zones had no Israeli military presence to begin with. Israel continues to demand Hezbollah's disarmament as a condition for its withdrawal and has cast doubt on the LAF's ability to carry out the process. Political uncertainty in Israel has further hampered talks, with legislative elections scheduled for the end of the month leaving Lebanese officials expecting little movement on the more contentious issues until the poll is over. “There's no real political track between [Lebanon and Israel] because there's a dead end until it's clear what the new government in Israel will be,” a political source told The National . The election of a hard-line Israeli government could lead to more delays. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told media on Sunday that he does not trust the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah. “That's why we said that as long as it is not disarmed, we will remain in this zone that changed the situation in the north,” he said. One source acknowledged mounting pressure on Lebanon to “do more to show movement on expanding the authority of the state [by] moving against Hezbollah at least in small steps”. But all Lebanese officials who spoke to The National expressed low expectations for the talks, describing them as largely technical and an opportunity for Lebanon to repeat its demands for a full Israeli withdrawal from the occupied south. “We don’t expect any major decisions or an expansion of the pilot zones tomorrow and the verification mechanism won't be established,” a military source said. “We will as usual shine a light on the [Israeli] aggression and the ceasefire violations, and demand a full withdrawal from the south – the same demands as always.” Still, Lebanon sees little alternative to continuing with the negotiations, even as officials increasingly question whether they can produce Israeli concessions. Lebanon entered direct talks hoping the US would use its leverage over Israel to secure an end to attacks in the south and begin a phased Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory. Instead, Israeli military operations and demolitions have continued alongside the discussions, including beyond the boundaries of Israel's own declared “security” zone – leaving Lebanese officials in doubt as to what the diplomatic process has achieved so far.

title: Anthropic commits 5% stake to 'public benefit fund' amid growing AI backlash
description: Elon Musk also promises to give one share of SpaceX 'to every kid in America' next year
content: Claude developer Anthropic has announced it is committing 5 per cent of its shares to a “public benefit fund” amid growing backlash over artificial intelligence. And Tesla boss Elon Musk has promised to give a share in his SpaceX company to “every kid in America” next year. AI start-up Anthropic said in a blog post the fund would be a wholly owned liability company and that it would receive an additional 2 per cent of Anthropic shares at the board's discretion for every 50 per cent increase in the company's value above a to-be-announced baseline. It said establishing the fund, which would be subject to shareholder approval, will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations “to traditional non-profit or direct distributions to specific populations”. “Because of the way the fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” it said on Sunday. The company is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, possibly as soon as November. The company said in June it had submitted a confidential filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO. Abu Dhabi technology investment firm MGX took part in Anthropic's recent $65 billion funding round. Anthropic gave the labour market as one area of focus for the fund, with a $200 million commitment to study the issue. Research from the International Monetary Fund estimates about 60 per cent of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI. Separate research from Goldman Sachs said recent anecdotes and data suggest AI displacement in the US could be strong among entry-level workers. Mr Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement on X saying, “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public." He pledged one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year in a separate post on Monday, without providing further details. “This will be the first of many,” Mr Musk wrote. Later on Monday, President Donald Trump hailed Mr Musk's suggestion, which he implied would be applied to the Trump Accounts programme. "This is exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS — Bringing together the GREAT PRIVATE SECTOR, Elon and so many more, to invest in our children, by far our greatest and most important asset, and give every American Child a piece of the American Dream," Mr Trump wrote on social media. The programme allows donors to make contributions without paying a capital gains tax, in some circumstances. The Treasury Department said in a September notice that it was seeking to automatically enrol up to 60 million children in the programme. With about 73 million people under 18 years of age in the US, the pledge would be valued at about $10.7 billion at the company's Friday close at $146.03 a share. SpaceX was trading 0.78 per cent higher at $147.33 a share as of 2:30pm ET (8pm GST) on Monday. The pledges from Anthropic and Mr Musk come as Americans grow more concerned about AI. A recent AP-Norc poll found 64 per cent of US adults believe the technology is developing “too fast”, compared to 27 per cent saying development has been “about right” and 8 per cent saying it is moving “too slow”. Building the massive data centres housing the technology is also leading to rising energy costs. A recent poll from Quinnipiac University said about 73 per cent of US voters oppose the building of data centres in their communities. AI executives and President Donald Trump have recently adopted a defensive stance amid this growing backlash, with the US leader calling AI anxieties a "hoax". In September, he hosted chief executives from Nvidia, Meta and other Big Tech firms at the White House, where they signed what was billed as a morally binding agreement to help police AI. The document encourages companies to "implement robust internal controls" to monitor models during training, empower an internal team to ensure controls are operating as intended, link up with an independent external auditor, and designate an independent committee to oversee and receive reports from the team operating the controls. Mr Trump has also opposed AI regulations, saying such orders would put the US at a disadvantage against China in the AI race.

title: Prosecutors call Saudi suspect and ex-OpenAI worker Abdulrahman Alfozan 'an ongoing danger'
description: US Justice Department describes Saudi citizen as 'flight risk' and recommends he remain in custody
content: US prosecutors said on Monday that Abdulrahman Alfozan , a Saudi citizen accused of hiding a recording device at OpenAI's headquarters, “presents an ongoing danger” and should not be released from custody. In a court filing, the US Justice Department responded to a request from Mr Alfozan's lawyer in California that sought to grant his release amid the continuing investigation, which is expected to culminate in a criminal trial. “The defendant presents an ongoing danger to the community and a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate,” Craig Missakian, a lawyer for the US Justice Department wrote. According to the department's memo in support of continuing the suspect's detention, “a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for” a flight for Mr Alfozan's wife and son several days after he was arrested. “The day before she left the US, the defendant’s wife told the FBI agents who interviewed her that her US visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia – and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same,” US prosecutors wrote. Mr Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and former OpenAI employee, was arrested on October 8 over accusations he had hidden a recording device at the company's offices in San Francisco. Investigators said last week that Mr Alfozan planted the device – a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3, manufactured by a company in China – behind a television in a conference room. The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said. Mr Alfozan started working for the OpenAI product team in July last year. He was fired on the same day of his arrest, the company said. According to the original criminal complaint previous filed by prosecutors, actions taken by Mr Alfozan indicated he planned to depart the US swiftly. “Indeed, the defendant, his wife and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) … and defendant has the means and the incentive to flee the US sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested,” the initial filing reads. Last week, California lawyer William Pernik told The National he was still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court. “Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik said in an email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why.” On Friday, Mr Pernik filed a court request to get Mr Alfozan out of custody on the condition he wears a GPS ankle tag, remains at his home in Millbrae, California and surrenders his passport. The filing also proposed a “an appearance bond co-signed by sureties from his Bay Area community and supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”. According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP. Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2016 and then earned a master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley. According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He was scheduled to appear in court for a detention hearing on October 19. “If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department read. OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.

title: World Food Programme to cut aid to half a million people in Gaza amid funding shortfall
description: Cuts come as winter approaches and recent improvements in food security remain fragile
content: The UN's World Food Programme announced on Monday that it would need to cut aid to roughly half a million people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall. The cuts come as winter approaches and recent improvements in food security remain fragile. “I want to be clear: this is not because the needs are going down, and it's not because we aren't able to bring in the food,” Carl Skau , acting executive director of WFP, said. “This is only because we have less funding.” Mr Skau described the situation in Gaza as “absolutely brutal” and said that WFP was seeking $450 million in funding to help those in need over the next six months. “People are living in flimsy makeshift shelters, or their destroyed homes among sewage and piles of garbage,” he told reporters during a briefing. “They line up with buckets at water trucks to get the clean water they need for the day. There are no jobs, no way of making an income.” Over the past three years, WFP has provided aid services for up to 90 per cent of families in Gaza, and since the October 2025 ceasefire has been reaching about 1.6 million people every month with parcels and other food aid. Mr Skau said WFP is also supporting about 80 per cent of bakeries in the enclave. But funding cuts mean hundreds of thousands will lose access to the programme. “We will do our best to prioritise those in most need – this is not an easy exercise,” Mr Skau said, adding that services are likely to be focused on the sick, children at risk of malnutrition and those “whose safety is at risk and who are often pushed to move”. He added that a sense of hopelessness has begun to take root in the enclave, where UN teams have recorded up to 50 air strikes and other attacks per day over the past week. “People are beginning to lose hope. There was hope at the start of the ceasefire, still also in January, February, that things would change for the better ... and I think now there is this sense of a standstill,” Mr Skau said. “Many I spoke to feel forgotten by everyone.” In the West Bank , where Israeli settler violence has skyrocketed in recent months, the WFP chief said the situation was turning dire. The annual olive harvest has become a flashpoint for confrontations between settlers and Palestinian farmers. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled) recorded an average of 39 incidents a day from October 1 to October 9, compared with around 20 per day in September. The latest violence comes amid planned settlement expansion in the West Bank, with the government approving dozens of new settlements and legalising numerous outposts. Mr Skau said that settler attacks in the past two weeks surpassed the whole of last year in terms of number of attacks. “This used to be a human rights and protection crisis – and primarily it's still a human rights and protection crisis – but it's now also becoming a hunger crisis because food insecurity has more than doubled in the last three years,” he explained. “Almost a million Palestinians now need food assistance, and yet also in the West Bank, we are now forced to cut back.”

title: Ras Al Khaimah targets Chinese investment at Shenzhen business summit
description: Sheikh Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah, addresses Chinese business leaders
content: Sheikh Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah , told nearly 300 business leaders in south-east China that the emirate is built for long-term partnerships. The Ras Al Khaimah-China Business Summit, held in Shenzhen on Monday, brought together government representatives, investors and business leaders under the theme “Together Towards Shared Value”. The event showcased investment opportunities across advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, digital technology, renewable energy and logistics, state news agency reported. Sheikh Saud told attendees more than 400 Chinese companies are already operating in Ras Al Khaimah, part of a broader community of thousands of Chinese businesses established in the UAE. He described Ras Al Khaimah as the UAE's northern gateway, positioning it as a conduit connecting Chinese firms to markets across the Middle East, Africa and Europe, complementary to China's Belt and Road Initiative. “Our progress is measured not by short-term success but by the legacy we leave for future generations,” Sheikh Saud said. “We are building an economy that is resilient, diversified and integrated into global supply chains, while preserving the quality of life and opportunity that make Ras Al Khaimah a distinctive place to live, work and do business.”

title: Global financial firms with over $5tn in assets announce plans to establish ADGM presence
description: Fourteen companies aim to set up new base at Abu Dhabi's financial centre
content: Global financial institutions managing more than $5 trillion in assets have announced plans to establish a presence in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM amid rapid expansion of the emirate’s economy. Overall, 14 financial firms have plans to set up base at the international financial centre, state news agency Wam reported on Monday, quoting ADGM chairman Ahmed Al Zaabi. “In 2025, Abu Dhabi's economy grew by 7 per cent and our non-oil economy grew by 8 per cent, contributing more than half of total gross domestic product,” Mr Al Zaabi told the third Abu Dhabi Investment Forum in London. Established in 2015, the ADGM operates under the direct application of English Common Law, with independent courts and a regulatory framework supporting it. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. ADGM has been attracting a number of high-profile companies in recent months, including global private markets firm Pantheon , private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, as well as global private markets firm Pantheon, have also recently opened offices in the ADGM. Last month, Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of the ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager. Collectively, asset managers which had already established operations in the ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management, the ADGM said last month. Abu Dhabi is developing industries across artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, energy and life sciences that will shape future markets, Mr Al Zaabi said, as reported by Wam on Monday. “Our businesses are extending their international reach, establishing partnerships and entering new markets. Abu Dhabi has long-term capital competitive energy, world-class infrastructure and access to some of the world's fastest-growing markets,” he said.

title: Saudi Arabia postpones FII conference in Riyadh after Houthi attacks
description: Annual gathering was scheduled for this month but will take place in 2027
author_name: Shweta Jain, Salim A. Essaid, Kyle Fitzgerald
content: Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference after a surge in Houthi attacks on the kingdom. The annual gathering was scheduled to take place from October 26 to 29 in Riyadh. FII chief executive Princess Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said in a statement the 10th edition of the conference "will now take place in 2027", and that the new dates would be announced "very soon". Ms Al Saud said the decision to postpone the gathering "comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates". "Because this is our landmark 10th edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves," she said in a statement. "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best." The decision to postpone the event follows a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group, including strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. The attacks have disrupted air travel and raised security concerns among international executives and investors. One source told The National their company had remained committed to attending the event despite the attacks on the airport and characterised their mood as "calm and level-headed". They also said they appreciate that safety is a higher priority. The 10th edition of FII was expected to bring together senior government officials, global financiers and corporate leaders, including BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink and JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, to discuss investment opportunities and economic growth. Launched in 2017, FII has become a vital platform for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to promote Vision 2030, the kingdom’s economic diversification programme aimed at reducing reliance on oil and attracting foreign capital. The postponement adds to a growing list of international events affected by the conflict. Saudi Arabia and the EU have postponed a planned summit, while several sporting and cultural events have also been delayed or cancelled amid security concerns, according to a Reuters report. On Monday, Saudi Arabia also announced the cancellation of two more events – Intersec Saudi Arabia and Saudi Retail Forum, according to organisers of both events. Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, which was due to take place from November 16-18 will now be held in October 2027, organiser Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said on Monday. The Saudi Retail Forum, which was originally scheduled to take place on November 19, has officially been postponed to March 2027. “The decision follows close monitoring of recent developments in Saudi Arabia and was taken in co-ordination with the venue, the local government partners, and the event’s local and international stakeholders,” Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said. It added that the postponement prioritises the safety and security of exhibitors, visitors, partners, suppliers and staff, while “aiming to preserve the international scale and high-calibre attendance”.

title: Zelenskyy claims delivery of vital war supplies for Ukraine delayed by US
description: President says 'political agreements' yet to be implemented
content: Ukrainian ​President ​ Volodymyr ​Zelenskyy ⁠on Monday accused the US ⁠of holding up the delivery of vital supplies, but the Pentagon said there had been no changes to how it sends provisions to Kyiv. In ‌a post ​on X, which came as Russian attacks damaged more than 10 energy sites, Mr Zelenskyy said the delays were at the level of the US Defence Department. He ​added ⁠some ​ political agreements ​on the delivery of ⁠air defence supplies ⁠had not been put into practice. Mr Zelenskyy ordered his senior team to contact “partners who can swiftly strengthen our defence”. The Pentagon said in a statement that there had been no change in policy regarding the sharing of intelligence or any capabilities that enables Europe to provide supplies to Ukraine. "The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List initiative, through which Nato allies and partners provide commensurate contributions for US-provided defence articles and services, continues unaltered," the department said. Ukraine ​has been relying heavily on US intelligence ​to detect incoming missiles. Overnight, Russia launched one of its broadest air assaults in months, cutting power to more than half a million households. It fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, and more than 200 drones across Ukraine in ⁠attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odessa in the south and Volyn ​and Rivne ⁠in the west. More than 10 energy sites were damaged, Mr Zelenskyy said, complaining that Ukraine had received no advance warning of the Russian ballistic missile strike from its partners. The strikes killed one woman in Kyiv and two more people in the ​industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said. “Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight and, once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” Mr Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app. “When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.” In a later statement on X, Ukraine's President said he had held a meeting about how to prepare the country’s infrastructure for winter, throughout which increased energy will be required for heating. He said he would hold a follow-up meeting to review the results of all the discussions that had taken place on Monday and expected “concrete results”. Mr Zelenskyy said he was increasing orders for interceptors that have proven effective against Iranian-made Shahed drones, and was engaging with Baltic countries for support on logistics. He also said Ukraine was still unable to fully access the Starlink/Starshield services provided by Elon Musk’s company. He said the equipment stops working at speeds of 130kph-161kph. This was limiting the type of drones that could be used to intercept attacks. “Speed matters when it comes to protecting lives,” he said. Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian air force, said Kyiv had received no warning ahead of the first ballistic missile strike overnight but did receive information before a second attack. “For some reason, no information was ​received the first time, a matter our experts are investigating together with ‌our partners, as this is not the first ⁠time such a situation has occurred,” Mr Ihnat said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied Washington had paused some intelligence ​sharing with Ukraine, ‌contradicting Mr Zelenskyy's claim. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces carried out a “massive ⁠strike” using precision weapons and attack drones against Ukrainian defence industry facilities, drone and cruise missile storage sites and a data centre. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the energy sector was the main target of the attacks, with damage reported across the country. Railway stations, pharmaceutical warehouses, commercial properties and residential buildings were also damaged, he said.

title: Alain Ducasse on Rabat restaurant opening: 'We don't have the capacity to compete with Moroccan cuisine'
description: French chef has opened his first restaurant in Morocco and his next stop is expanding his culinary feats across the UAE
content: Chef Alain Ducasse views the pursuit of new flavours and ingredients as an ongoing quest. After a career spanning more than 50 years, during which restaurants under his leadership were awarded a total of 21 Michelin stars , he continues his journey of culinary inspiration while travelling across continents. And most recently, that exploration has led to new feats for the chef. Ahead of Chef Ducasse's Abu Dhabi opening in the coming months, Aldabaran by Alain Ducasse opened its doors in Rabat, Morocco – his first property on the African continent – in late September. “I liked the idea of creating an extraordinary restaurant in this building in Rabat,” Ducasse tells The National as we sit on the 33rd floor of the King Mohammed VI Tower. It's the tallest building in Morocco, and floors 29 through 46 are home to Waldorf Astoria Rabat Sale. “But not [the idea] to confront Moroccan gastronomy. We do not have the capacity to compete,” he quickly adds. The realisation came after sitting down for what he describes as a “very delicious meal” several months ago. “I had a Moroccan dinner cooked by an extraordinary woman. That's why I know that today we aren't capable of producing true Moroccan taste.” That will come in time, he says, once his team is embedded in the local culinary scene. For now, Ducasse's menu is Mediterranean – which in itself ties in foods and flavours from as many as 20 distinct countries. But Morocco's influence can still be found. The team incorporates the best fresh regional produce that the country has to offer and 85 per cent of the restaurant's products are locally sourced, Ducasse says. “We are close to the ocean and the land is generous. So that's enough for me to cook. Plus, there is a population interested in food and I think they will be won over by what we have to offer.” On the menu, guests can expect dishes such as street food-style chickpea panisse, rich lamb caponata and blue lobster with a spicy kick. Although he won't describe the menu as Moroccan, there are familiar flavours and ingredients throughout. And every new location Ducasse visits is a source of inspiration to him, he says, recalling a recent trip around Asia. “Last week I discovered something extraordinary and next week I will discover something else,” he says. His next stop is the UAE capital. The chef will open two properties by the end of 2027 in the UAE after Ecole Ducasse, his culinary school, opened in 2023 in Abu Dhabi. Alain Ducasse Cafe, a chocolate shop concept, will open in Saadiyat Grove before the end of the year. “It’s going to be a bit like [the cafe in] Osaka, with a chocolate shop, a tea room with small bites and finger food,” he says of the new venture. But he is no stranger to the region. Idam by Alain Ducasse is one of Qatar's three Michelin-starred restaurants, bringing French cuisine with Middle Eastern touches. Jiwan, his other Doha property, puts a modern take on Qatari dishes. He says it is no coincidence that the chef from Jiwan, Morgan Perrigaud, took over the kitchen at Aldabaran. “We've well understood the taste of the Middle East,” Ducasse says. “From our experience and crafting the menu to appeal to Qataris, we drew from Lebanese and North African influences. And certainly, step by step, we might integrate this North African and Middle Eastern sphere of influence here.” Ducasse is also set to open a flagship French-American steakhouse in the upcoming Wynn Al Marjan Island gaming resort next year . For now, the chef continues his quest. “Everything inspires me,” Ducasse says. “Looking at the world. The markets, the competition, going to eat at fellow chefs' places. The most important thing is to digest it and share it.”

title: The UK’s power grid failures have come home to roost
description: The data boom and rising digital economy should make electricity a top priority, but Britain is running hard just to stand still
content: For a demonstration of just how badly Britain is blighted by bottlenecks, the loss of a flagship Microsoft data centre deal is Exhibit A. Just north of London is a piece of waste ground covered with broken concrete. The site, at Loughton in Essex, had been designated as the UK’s flagship entry point into the global data-centre race. Instead, last week it was at the forefront of the markets’ collapsing confidence that the worldwide data-centre boom can ever be delivered. That market reticence should not let the UK off the hook. There is a particular regulatory and leadership failure in the country that serves as a warning for other nations overly dedicated to a regulatory economy. When US President Donald Trump made his state visit to the UK just over a year ago, Microsoft announced a $30 billion (Dh110 billion) commitment to the country. Of that, $2 billion was allotted to this patch of London’s suburban fringe for a data centre. A Microsoft blog post read: “This investment will enable us to build the country’s largest supercomputer – with more than 23,000 Nvidia GPUs – in partnership with Nscale.” The good vibes kept on coming with Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, saying the UK would be an “AI superpower” with all this investment in the pipeline. What went wrong was that the failures in the UK’s national electricity grid have come home to roost. Instead of connecting to the electric network next year as had been expected after Nscale’s announcement, now the facility will not have a connection date until the 2030s. Nscale has quietly accepted the blow with a sigh of futility. "This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," it said. The British technology company’s other projects are in alternative locations outside the UK, such as Norway, Portugal and the US. The growth blight for the UK as a result of the decline in its electric architecture is only just beginning. The country has the most expensive electricity of any major nation. Large-scale industrial operations based around petrochemicals or refining of oil into products such as diesel have steadily shut down across the country. In the 1980s when the coal mines were shutting down, their names would be tagged in labels across large banners that followed the colliery bands. Now the loss of names such as Grangemouth, which made two thirds of all the refined oil products used by Scotland, are briefly noted inside newspapers. The idea of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government is that the UK can re-industrialise. Contrary to expectations, the country had until recent years done a decent job of maintaining a network of facilities that were supplying its own and export markets. This is now stuck in a vortex of decline that largely centres around the National Grid and its projected shortages. The data centre boom is catching it out in new ways. The UK has been a trailblazer in harnessing wind from offshore turbines that have been constructed in massive arrays. Yet even this generation is not being exploited in the ways that it could. The National Grid has failed to match its capacity to transmit the energy into its systems. In fact, Britain spends more than £1.5 billion (Dh7.34 billion) a year on “constraint payments” to turn off wind farms and use gas plant generation instead because the electricity grid could become unbalanced. That is not all. Note the Nscale statement said there was a London-wide problem with the grid. The gas plants have clustered in the middle of the country and so getting their output to the country’s largest economy – London – is problematic. The country is also being forced to make payments to obtain emergency supplies through interconnectors from foreign nations at an increasing rate. Last week an emergency drawn down from France is believed to have cost almost £40 million alone. The figure for all of September for “balancing payments” ran to £500 million. This time of year, European countries that use a lot of wind power are often confronted by a lack of wind. Worryingly for the UK, this year there has been good wind availability, yet the country is still facing increasing and steep payments to keep its electric network functioning. That is while charging vast sums for its output to customers. It is also unable to deliver an architecture of future capacity growth that meets the needs of flagship investors. All the while planners in other parts of the system worry that the UK has failed, like Germany, to upgrade its storage of imported natural gas, a commodity undergoing a supply crunch because of the Iran war and the arrival of El Nino. The figures show that the underground gas storage available to the UK energy suppliers was only 48 per cent full at the start of October, the lowest among its neighbours. With the rise of the digital economy and the data boom, one would expect electricity to be the greatest priority in the UK’s economic management. Allow me to let you down with some figures. The National Energy System Operator, which draws that interconnector power to balance the system, says that electricity should represent 70 per cent of the UK’s power mix by 2050. Last year it was just a shade under 20 per cent, with 25 years to go to the deadline.. Last year it was just a shade under 20 per cent, with 25 years ago. Go back 25 years to the year 2000 and the electric part of the power mix was also hovering at 20 per cent. In a world of rapid advances, the UK is effectively running too hard just to stand still.

title: Dubai airport tries self-driving wheelchair for quicker trip from check-in to plane
description: Dubai AccessAbilities Expo shows how cutting-edge tech is helping ease of access for travel and health care
content: Air travel and health care for people with disabilities are set for dramatic improvements as new global assistive technology raises standards. From special airport services to fast-track options in healthcare settings, the latest assisted living options were on show at the Dubai AccessAbilities Expo on Monday. The latest technology was on display to support people with impaired mobility, sight and hearing, and those with intellectual disabilities, while disabled people were invited to try out the latest solutions at Dubai World Trade Centre. These included an autonomous wheelchair being tested at Dubai International Airport, to carry passengers from check-in to their gate. The chair is fitted with four light detection and ranging cameras and can be programmed to collect passengers from the lounge and take them on to the plane during boarding. A manual override allows passengers travelling alone to stop at any point in the airport en route to the departure gates. The equipment is being tested by Dnata at concourse D in Terminal 1, with airport operators looking to expand the trial to Terminal 3. Suhail Amshan, senior manager in the office of accessibility and inclusion at Emirates, said the airline was improving access for passengers with disabilities. “Over the last few years, we've seen a lot more people get comfortable with the idea that they can actually speak about their accommodation requirements and that in itself is huge for us,” Mr Amshan said. “Coming into the airports can feel a little overwhelming. In the past, people might not have felt comfortable enough to approach anyone from Emirates to make certain accommodations to make their travel slightly more comfortable.” Emirates has been certified as the world’s first autism-certified airline by the International Board of Credentialling and Continuing Education Standards. Certification involved the training of more than 30,000 front line staff and cabin crew to understand autism and certain special requirements for air travel. Support included digital sensory guides, sensory products for neurodivergent passengers, such as fidget toys, and tailored assistance. The airline’s travel rehearsal programmes that allow families to acclimatise to airport procedures before flying have been introduced in about 80 airports since they were launched in 2023. Emirates has also incorporated business-class lounges, biometric passport scanners and check-in desks designed for wheelchair access. “The first time that crew interact with a person with a disability, the scenario might not have been something they've been trained for,” said Mr Amshan. “Everyone has a different requirement and deals with travel in different ways. Our staff are trained to answer all questions and have tools on their hands and resources for them to constantly be able to customise solutions for that person. There are lots of things that we are still not familiar with or are aware of. It is an ever-evolving space from our perspective.” At Dubai International Airport, there are now eight dedicated services for people of determination, while 55,524 learners across 14 entities have completed accessibility training to help deliver more inclusive support throughout the journey. Dubai Airports has also distributed over 40,000 Sunflower Lanyards, helping guests with hidden disabilities discreetly indicate that they may need additional support. “Accessibility is about giving every guest the confidence to travel with dignity and as independently and seamlessly as possible,” said Fatma Taher, head of strategic projects and government agenda at Dubai Airports. “Through our DXB for All strategy, we are advancing accessibility across our infrastructure, service design and training, bringing our airport community together to better support people of determination and guests with diverse needs." According to the US digital accessibility services company Onward Accessibility, the Middle East is home to more than 50 million people with disabilities, representing a significant demographic. The mobility aids market alone is expected to reach $1.1 billion by 2031 and the global assistive technology market for people with disabilities and older people is projected to reach $98.7 billion by 2033. Dubai Health Authority presented its Sanadhum initiative during the exhibition. The regulatory and awareness project aims to strengthen health centres' compliance with special requirements for people of determination, including provisions of the Dubai Universal Design Code and health policies. It includes field inspection campaigns across all health services to verify their readiness and ensure ease of access and priority. The DHA hopes it will contribute to a safer and more accessible healthcare environment for all. “Providing comprehensive health care goes beyond developing infrastructure and services,” said Asma Al Sharif, chief executive of DHA’s Health Regulatory Sector. “It extends to building an integrated health system that considers the needs of people of determination and ensures they can access services efficiently, with dignity and independence.” People with disabilities represent about 10 to 16 per cent of the population of any society. About 1.3 billion people worldwide live with some form of disability, including more than 50 million people in the Middle East, the World Health Organisation estimates. Global studies indicate 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2030, while only 10 per cent have access to the products they need. Other technology on show at the exhibition included AI-powered smart glasses offering real-time translation and assistance for people with visual disabilities. Elsewhere, advanced electronic prosthetic limbs designed to replicate natural movement and provide users with greater independence were demonstrated. Ghassan Suleiman, chief executive of the AccessAbilities Expo, said the event had evolved into a global platform for exchanging expertise and helping to shape the future of accessibility and inclusion as it enters its eighth year. “Technological developments such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality and the Internet of Things have accelerated innovation across the sector,” he said. “This has helped improve the quality of life of millions of people around the world.”

title: Parts of UAE hit by heavy rain and hail as alert issued over 50kph winds
description: Emirates has faced unstable weather this month, even as temperatures remain high
content: Parts of the UAE were lashed by heavy rain, high winds and hail on Monday afternoon, with more adverse weather in prospect in the days to come. The National Centre of Meteorology issued an alert over strong winds expected to reach speeds of up to 50kph in some coastal and inland areas, lifting dust up into the skies and hampering visibility . Storm Centre – a popular online weather-tracking platform – shared video footage of downpours across areas of Sharjah and Fujairah. The Northern Emirates in particular have faced a sustained spell of rain in recent days, even as temperatures remain unseasonably high in the Emirates. In its latest five-day weather bulletin, the NCM forecasts more rain, powerful winds and cloudy conditions until Friday. The weather bureau forecasts fog could drift in over western areas of the country by Friday, causing challenging conditions on the roads. The NCM's online weather map shows that Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah and Al Ain are set to be hit by heavy rain until Wednesday. Abu Dhabi and Dubai, however, are expected to avoid the wet weather, but high humidity will bring more muggy conditions during the week. Despite the unsettled weather persisting, temperatures will remain high over the coming days, topping 40°C in Al Ain and remaining in the high 30s in much of the country. October has been warmer than usual this year, with the UAE National Centre of Meteorology issuing a climate update on the El Nino weather phenomenon, forecast to be the strongest on record. Instead of the typical October drop into comfortable autumn weather, El Nino is trapping a blanket of high pressure over the Arabian Peninsula, driving temperatures well above the seasonal average. The UAE's average daily temperature in October stands at 29.7°C, according to the NCM's latest monthly weather summary. On Saturday, the General Civil Aviation Authority warned that changing weather may affect operations at airports across the country, potentially causing delays. Such conditions are a recurring feature of autumn in the UAE.

title: Egypt's pledge to support Saudi Arabia against Houthis: What's on the table?
description: State and its allies have closed ranks behind the Defence Council's decision
content: Egypt's pledge to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks from Yemen has rallied the state and its allies, but it has also drawn calls for caution amid an escalating situation in the Middle East due to the impact of the Iran war. From the steps required in parliament to the arguments put forward by different camps in Egypt, the nature of any military support remains uncertain. Here is a breakdown of the practical steps involved and the debate unfolding in the country with the Arab world's largest population and largest army . Parliament is expected to approve the request. The constitution requires approval by two-thirds of the 596-member House, or 398 votes, before troops can be sent on a combat mission abroad. The four main pro-government parties alone won 403 of the 568 elected seats in last year's election. Approval would give President Abdel Fattah El Sisi , as supreme commander of the armed forces, the legal authority to deploy troops, but it would not send them automatically. Egypt will act only if Riyadh asks, and no formal Saudi request has been announced. The National Defence Council, chaired by Mr El Sisi, met at Al Ittihadiya Palace on Sunday. It declared Egypt's "full solidarity" with the kingdom and pledged "all necessary and possible forms of support" to defend its security, its territory and the Islamic holy sites. The council met a day after Mr El Sisi told a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy that it was "inconceivable" Egypt would allow Saudi Arabia's security to be harmed. He asked parliament to authorise action "if we are asked". Neither statement said what form the support would take, how many troops might be sent or for how long. That silence has shaped much of the reaction since. The pledge follows near-daily Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia since early October. The deadliest attack was at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which killed and injured hundreds. Among them was Azza Ramzy, a 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant from Beheira province. The vote, which was initially pushed from Sunday to Tuesday amid reports of heated debate in the house, was postponed again on Monday afternoon for a whole week, a parliamentary source confirmed to The National . However, the source said that a decision could still be made on the matter before the deadline passed. About 300 MPs asked to speak in the closed sessions, according to local media. Some MPs have also pressed for details on the mission's nature and scope before they cast their vote. Three MPs said they would abstain in the vote. However, Mostafa Bakry, an MP and TV host close to the state, played down any rift. "There was an overwhelming majority," he said. "No MP has rejected the authorisation. Within ruling circles, support has been swift and near unanimous. Pro-government Mostaqbal Watan, the largest party in parliament, declared its backing as MPs convened on Sunday, followed by Homat Al Watan, the National Front and the People's Republican Party. The Salafist Nour Party also backed the request. El Sayed El Badawi, leader of the Wafd, Egypt's oldest liberal party, said Saudi Arabia's security was "an inseparable part" of Egypt's own. Supporters point to the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks on shipping have already cost the Suez Canal heavily in lost revenue. They also point to gratitude for Saudi's continued financial support of Egypt. Central bank data show a $5.3 billion Saudi deposit, part of $10.3 billion Riyadh holds at Egypt's central bank, maturing this month, with Cairo facing a potentially costly repayment unless Riyadh agrees to roll it over. Pro-government figures have cast the move as purely defensive. TV hosts told viewers it concerned protecting Saudi Arabia, not declaring war or going into another country. Between the loyalists and others who question the move, sits a camp that backs Saudi Arabia but wants clarifications on any mission. The Egyptian Social Democratic Party told its MPs to abstain. It said its solidarity with Riyadh was "steadfast", but Egypt's national security "requires clarity of objectives", and military participation must not become "an open-ended commitment". The party also cited lost canal revenue and the strain on the state budget. Ayman Nour, the exiled leader of the liberal Ghad Party, wrote to Speaker Hisham Badawi before Sunday's session. Defending Saudi Arabia was "an Arab duty", he said, but "authorisation is not a blank cheque". He listed 10 safeguards, including a fixed duration, a defined geographical scope, and regular reports to parliament. He cited Egypt's intervention in Yemen in the 1960s, a war many Egyptians still call "Egypt's Vietnam", as a lesson. Hamdeen Sabahi, a former presidential candidate, went further. Egypt should be "a sponsor of reconciliation", he wrote on Facebook, and should "not send its army to defend one brother, but to establish peace between the two brothers". Al Azhar , the country's highest seat of Sunni learning, called for "an immediate and comprehensive halt" to fighting in the region and proposed an urgent Arab and Islamic mediation committee. Others reject a combat role altogether. On the far left, the Revolutionary Socialist Current issued a statement headlined "No to war". Business leaders have largely stayed out of the debate.

title: Lebanese army bolsters Beirut patrols after tensions surge
description: PM Salam orders expanded investigation into explosives seized from Hezbollah
content: Lebanese Armed Forces personnel have stepped up patrols in Beirut and its sensitive southern suburbs after a surge in tensions with Hezbollah supporters. The army published images of heavily armed convoys patrolling the capital and temporary checkpoints being set up “to pursue wanted individuals and those disrupting security”. The tension has partly been fuelled by the recent seizure of half a tonne of explosives by Lebanese authorities before Hezbollah could transfer them to the capital's suburbs, where the group has a strong presence. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has ordered that authorities “expand the investigation” into the explosives interception at the Dahr Al Baidar checkpoint in the Bekaa Valley. The US weighed in last week, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to ensure explosives seized from Hezbollah are not returned to the group. Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese political party and armed group, has claimed ownership of the 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4, saying they were to be used against the Israeli military forces that currently occupy swathes of south Lebanon. Hezbollah had demanded the release of the two drivers and the explosives. The seizure of the explosives, which heightens tension over a push by the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah, led to supporters of the group gathering to show their backing. Further exacerbating the situation was an incident in the Gallerie Semaan neighbourhood on the edge of Beirut's southern suburbs. Police were sent to raid a warehouse there that contained spoiled medicines, following an order from prosecutors. According to the Internal Security Forces, they were quickly surrounded by “a number of young men gathered on their motorcycles [who] attempted to prevent the force from raiding the warehouse”. The army was eventually deployed to calm the situation. Mohammed Qassem, the son of Hezbollah Secretary General Naim Qassem , on Sunday published a statement denying any link to the warehouse in response to social media rumours he was connected to it. Hezbollah said the incident took place after the ISF entered “without following the agreed procedures between the group and security authorities”.

title: UAE Team Emirates-XRG end season on a high as Tadej Pogacar outlines plan for 2027
description: Newly crowned world champion Brandon McNulty claims Veneto Classic title while Slovenian superstar reveals Grand Tour aims for next year
content: UAE Team Emirates-XRG completed their latest season of cycling domination in appropriate fashion as Brandon McNulty sealed an impressive victory at the one-day Veneto Classic. The American rider crossed the finishing line more than a minute ahead of Anthon Charmig (Uno-X Mobility) on Sunday, with McNulty's teammate Pavel Sivakov – on his final outing for the team – claiming the third and final podium spot in Italy. McNulty took the win wearing the rainbow jersey, earned when he replaced another one of his teammates – the injured Tadej Pogacar – as world road race champion after the 28-year-old triumphed in last month's race in Montreal. “It’s a really nice way to finish the season,” said McNulty, following his first win since taking gold in Canada. “We had a really strong team today and everyone played their part. We had good numbers in the front group, which gave us options, and when I got away with Charmig I knew I had to try to make the difference on the final climbs. I managed to get a gap on Diesel Farm and from there it was just full gas to the finish. “I’ve raced a lot these last few weeks since Montreal and I’ve been pushing to get that first win in the rainbow jersey, so to do it here on the last day of the season, with my wife on the finish line is pretty perfect.” Over in France, meanwhile, UAE Team Emirates -XRG's Jay Vine took second place at the Chrono des Nations, a 45.4km individual time trial around Les Herbiers. The Australian rider made it three consecutive runner-up finishes at the event when he came home 2 mins 11 secs behind runaway winner Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe), with Stefan Kung (Tudor Pro Cycling) third. It was a fitting finale for the Emirati team, who ended the campaign with 78 victories, maintaining their grip on the UCI World Tour, whose rankings they have topped since 2023. Slovenian superstar Pogacar again leads the individual rankings, with his Mexican teammate Isaac del Toro third, behind second-placed Belgian rider Evenepoel. Despite the horror crash at the Vuelta a Espana that ended his campaign prematurely, it was another remarkable season for 28-year-old Pogacar, who topped the podium at Strade Bianche, Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Liege-Bastogne-Liege and Tour de Suisse, as well as winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title . Pogacar was also on course to complete the Grand Tour Slam by winning in Spain until the smash on Stage 8 that left him needing surgery on a broken collarbone, preventing him the opportunity of defending his world and European titles. His recovery appears to be on track though as Pogacar has posted videos on social media of him back on his bike alongside partner Urska Zigart. “The injury was pretty serious,” Pogacar said at a charity golf tournament back home in Slovenia at the weekend. “Not only my collarbone and vertebrae, but also a concussion, so it took me a while – I’d say about five weeks – to get back on the bike.” The fact the European Championships were taking place in Slovenia provided an added temptation to speed up his rehabilitation. “But less than two weeks before the European Championships, I realised there was no point in racing. If I were to crash again, the consequences could be very serious. And that wouldn’t end well,” he admitted to Slovenian media outlet Siol. Pogacar also revealed that he is returning to Abu Dhabi next week where he will be having talks with team management about plans for 2027. “Given that I finished the season quite some time ago, we will have a concrete discussion about what we will do next season,” he said. “My wish is the World Championship in combination with the Tour and Vuelta, which didn't work out this year. Although I would rather go to the Giro, I will have to tick off the Vuelta at some point … But as far as my participation in the next Giro is concerned, that’s highly unlikely.”

title: French Foreign Minister warns post-Unifil security vacuum in south Lebanon must be avoided
description: Failure to replace UN mission would be 'extremely dangerous', Jean-Noel Barrot says during Beirut visit
content: France's Foreign Minister has underlined the need for a “new international framework” to support Lebanese security forces after the mandate of the UN peacekeeping mission in south Lebanon (Unifil) expires at the end of the year. Jean-Noel Barrot, who was accompanied on a weekend visit to Beirut by Alice Rufo, the French Armed Forces Minister, said a “security vacuum” must not develop when Unifil ends its mission after nearly five decades. Post- Unifil international presence and support is still to be defined but French diplomatic sources said ahead of the visit that any security vacuum in south Lebanon would be “extremely dangerous”. Mr Barrot and Ms Rufo held meetings with senior Lebanese officials during their visit, including President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri and army commander Gen Rodolphe Haykal. While Mr Aoun would prefer to extend Unifil's mandate, he said if that were not possible, Beirut would welcome “any formula that ensures an international presence in the south”. The US and Israel pressured the UN to end Unifil's mandate, saying the force was partly to blame for the failure to prevent repeated conflicts across the Blue Line, the UN-demarcated border that separates southern Lebanon and Israel. The French ministers stressed the need to support the underfunded and under-equipped Lebanese Armed Forces as it continues with the uphill task of bringing all weapons under state control. This would mean disarming Hezbollah , which the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group and political party has so far resisted. Israel's military currently occupies about 65 towns and villages in southern Lebanon, where it has declared a security zone along the border after the latest round of fighting with Hezbollah broke out in early March. Last week, the European Union announced the establishment of a support mission for the Lebanese Armed Forces , with an initial mandate of three years. The mission will work to strengthen the capacity of the Lebanese Armed Forces and the Internal Security Forces, as well as supporting maritime security, although EU leaders have stressed it is not intended as a replacement for Unifil.

title: Qatar to seek regional and international partners in defence production push
description: Gas-rich Gulf nation to tie up with regional partner and US to boost domestic manufacturing
content: Qatar will soon announce a defence production plant as the gas-rich Gulf nation looks to boost domestic defence capabilities. Defence Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman said Qatar would team up with a regional partner and other countries such as the US, UK and France “to make sure either we ⁠do local protection or we are investing in some of these companies”, Reuters reported on Monday. Sheikh Saoud was speaking at the Global Security Forum in ⁠Doha. The announcement comes after Qatar and other Gulf countries have come under heavy attack during the Iran war, with energy sites and civilian infrastructure suffering damage. Parts of Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City – which supplies one fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas – was destroyed, with the Gulf nation declaring long-term force majeure on contracts with some buyers across the globe. "It is possible that the plant will continue to build on regional efforts by some states of increasingly localised defence production, including arms and components," Zain Hussain, a researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute told The National. He added Qatar was the world's fourth-largest importer of arms between 2021 and 2025 and is relying heavily on its imports for its arms capabilities. The UAE and Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s two largest economies, are already investing in domestic defence capabilities, with Edge Group and the kingdom’s Saudi Arabian Military Industries (Sami) playing a key role. Edge systems, including jammers, were successful in eliminating 85 per cent of Iranian drones that have been launched at the UAE during the Iran war, Hamad Al Marar , the group's managing director and chief executive, told The National in an interview at the Make it in the Emirates event in Abu Dhabi in May. Edge , set up in 2019, specialises in building advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare, with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. Military spending in the Middle East has continued to rise as regional conflicts rage, a report from Sipri has found, increasing to an estimated $218 billion in 2025, up 0.1 per cent compared to previous year. However, it had increased by 36 per cent over the decade from 2016 to 2025, the Sipri report said. The region’s largest spender in 2025 was Saudi Arabia, with estimated expenditure of $83.2 billion. Its spending was 1.4 per cent higher than in 2024 and 12 per cent higher than in 2016. Qatar’s lack of industrial and supply chain depth is a key structural constraint to set up any major defence production venture, Albert Vidal Ribe, a research associate for Middle East defence industry and procurement at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said. “If anything, I could see Qatar announcing the local production of UAV interceptors, relatively simple systems that could be realistically produced locally and would bolster Qatar’s counter-drone defences.” Qatar set up Barzan Holdings a decade ago but “has little to show in terms of meaningful localised defence manufacturing”, with its subsidiaries producing rifles and small calibre ammunition, he added.

title: Bottling the soul: Why Loewe’s perfumer believes you should never have only one signature scent
description: Nuria Cruelles explains why scent should change with your mood, memories and the moment
content: “I think perfume is like synaesthesia,” says Loewe perfumer Nuria Cruelles. “You can close your eyes and feel textures, temperatures, colours, moments.” For Cruelles, scent is less a finishing touch than a way of viewing the world, and she describes it with the sort of language usually reserved for art, architecture, music and gastronomy. This approach informs Loewe Perfumes’ Crafted Collection, where individual ingredients take centre stage. Launched in October last year with three scents – Iris Root, Bittersweet Oud and Roasted Vanilla – the collection has now expanded to five new perfumes. Rather than treating iris, oud or vanilla simply as components in a formula, Cruelles explores their personalities, building compositions around the relationships between them. “Oud is very rustic, animalic,” she says. “It has a lot of buttery facets also.” To reveal a brighter side, she pairs it with orange, creating what she calls a “contrast marriage”, setting the dark, earthy character of oud against zesty citrus. The new scents also draw on nature. Field Diary blends citrus, lychee and sandalwood; Sweet Woodland pairs florals with ginger and cognac; Rosetopia deepens rose with amber; Smoky Rain evokes a summer storm; and Verdant Grove layers pistachio and iris with caramel, vanilla and cedarwood. For Cruelles, however, the interest lies less in individual ingredients than in what happens when they meet. Take timut pepper, used in Iris Root. Despite its name, the Himalayan spice smells far removed from conventional black pepper, and instead has grapefruit and moss-like facets. Against creamy, sensual iris, it creates what Cruelles calls an “explosion”. Verdant Grove is more harmonious, pairing carrot seed with iris in what she describes as an “affinity marriage”. There are, she explains, three ways ingredients can interact: contrast, affinity or hedonism. “Hedonism for me is when it’s something unexpected, surprising, elegant and sophisticated,” she says. That spirit of experimentation has particular resonance in the Middle East, where fragrance has long been woven into daily life. Layering and combining scents are part of an established perfume culture – one Cruelles believes is increasingly influencing the rest of the world. “For me, the Middle East is where perfume was born,” says Cruelles, who has visited the region several times. “Everything centres around perfume. Every day, people mix, layer and play.” She sees a natural affinity between that tradition and the growing appetite in the West for fragrance as something to experiment with rather than a permanent signature. “I am happy that nowadays we have this whole range of perfumes to play with, to combine, to choose for each moment.” The notion of a signature scent worn for years, she believes, can be limiting. The nose eventually becomes accustomed to a familiar fragrance, making it increasingly invisible to its wearer. “Our nose identifies new essences because we read the air all the time,” she explains. “So we have to re-educate our nose to feel the sensation of new moments, new sensations.” Choosing perfume is therefore closer to choosing clothes or jewellery than to adopting a permanent identity. “That’s why I always say there are different perfumes for different moments. It’s like clothes. You choose your clothes depending on your day, like your jewellery.” Cruelles’s method may sound scientific, but at its core it is experimental. “Sometimes I think: ‘I’m going to use this ingredient to make this effect.’ And then, it turns out to be completely different and it surprises me,” she says. Timut pepper was one such lesson. “It ruined my formulas,” Cruelles says with a laugh. “I thought: ‘Why is this amazing ingredient ruining everything?’” The answer was ultimately one of proportion. “The right amount and the right ingredients. That is the key.” She compares crafting a scent to baking: too much or too little flour can alter the structure of a cake, while in perfumery a subtle adjustment can transform a composition. But there is no recipe book for an entirely new perfume. “You have to play and try. We make a lot of trials.” Cruelles’s Spanish heritage also informs her work for Loewe, whose roots stretch back to 19th-century Madrid. Native ingredients form part of her olfactory vocabulary, including rockrose, also known as labdanum. Resinous, leathery and woody, labdanum has a forceful presence. Rather than suppressing it, Cruelles uses co-distillation to soften its rougher edges and reveal a more rounded character.“ When I chose this ingredient, I was afraid,” she admits. “It has a lot of personality. It’s very rustic, strong and balsamic.” The experiment succeeded. “It made the fragrance whole,” she says. “Everything is integrated. There are no facets, angles or sharp edges. Everything has to be round.” For Cruelles, scent is also a sensory language. Sandalwood feels soft and transparent, almost white, while citrus is sharper and more effervescent, appearing in shades of orange, yellow or even metallic. Aldehydes can feel almost hot. “I have a good nose,” she says, comparing her relationship with scent to someone with an exceptional ear for music. “My nose reads the air for me, and it’s like every scent molecule makes music in my brain.” That philosophy informed one of Loewe’s most recognisable olfactory creations, Tomato Leaves, which was developed as a scented candle from Cruelles’s childhood memories of summers spent peeling tomatoes with her grandmother. Its pungent green scent offered an unexpected interpretation of a familiar ingredient. The candle subsequently became a social media phenomenon during the so-called Tomato Girl Summer trend of 2023. Perhaps Cruelles’s most poetic description is reserved for oud. If vanilla feels like a comforting embrace, oud is grounding. “For me, it is roots, because it anchors you to the earth,” she says. The perfumer imagines the human body as a plant: the legs are roots, the body becomes wood and spices, and the face represents flowers. Oud and vetiver belong to that root system. “It’s where you’re stuck on the earth. Because as a creative, we always fly.” That tension between grounding and imagination neatly describes her creative process. It may begin instinctively, but there is discipline behind it. Every ingredient must have a reason for being there.“It’s like an architect in my brain,” she says. “I am building things, and everything has to connect.” There may be a commercial brief behind a new Loewe fragrance, but Cruelles insists the creative interpretation remains hers. Ultimately, she sees the bottle and the liquid inside it as two entirely different things. “The bottle is the dress,” she says. “But the perfume is the soul.”For a perfumer who translates landscapes, ingredients, memories and emotions into invisible form, it is an apt distinction. The dress may catch the eye, but the soul is what lingers.

title: 'I am proud to be a Gulf citizen': Sheikh Mohammed urges unity and rejects attempts to sow division
description: Vice President and Ruler of Dubai highlights need for region to stand together
content: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, on Monday hailed the deep-rooted ties uniting the countries of the Gulf – and rejected all efforts to sow division between them. Sheikh Mohammed, in an uplifting message shared on social media, reflected on the region's remarkable transformation from “simple towns to global metropolises”, evolving from “modest fishing ports to navigating international routes”. He spoke warmly of how the “sons of the Gulf” had cemented their status as key players on the global stage, holding major events and driving economic growth, while staying true to their deep-rooted heritage and proud identity. In a year in which the Gulf has faced significant adversity – with the UAE among the states to face a barrage of missile and drone strikes from Iran, and Saudi Arabia coming under attack from the Houthi rebels in Yemen – Sheikh Mohammed emphasised the importance of standing together to build for a better future. He pledged that the unity forged out of history, borders and economic progress should not be disrupted by social media misinformation and “narrow-minded agendas”. He said such campaigns could not “erase centuries of neighbourliness, or alter the facts of geography, or change the reality of lineages”. The heartfelt address to the Gulf people is an excerpt from his new book, The Letters . “For what united the Gulf was not political agreements, but generations who lived along its shores,” Sheikh Mohammed wrote. “In the Gulf, hearts met before borders, and lineages embraced before homelands, and love flourished before development. “The Gulf is a great tree whose branches have multiplied, whose fruits have adorned it, and whose shades have bloomed, but its root is one, and its trunk is one, and its water is one, and its destiny is one, God willing.” Striking an optimistic tone, Sheikh Mohammed said when the aspirations of the Gulf align, they are able to turn projects that may initially seem impossible into reality. He said history offers lessons that the “whole is stronger than the sum of its parts” and that strength is not in erasing differences but in working together to create new opportunities. “I am optimistic about the Gulf and I shall remain so,” Sheikh Mohammed wrote. “The Gulf endures, God willing, with its desert, with its sons, with its sea and its ports, with its projects and the resolve of its generations, with its spaces in which our dreams will soar to keep our Gulf one and our people one, proclaiming with an unbroken voice: I am a Gulf citizen and I am proud to be a Gulf citizen.” The Dubai Ruler's remarks came after Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, had stressed the need to “transcend the folly and pettiness we witness in Gulf squabbles across social media”. “We are passing through a pivotal stage that demands awareness and responsibility from us all,” Dr Gargash wrote on X on Saturday. “We may differ in our assessments of situations, but there is no substitute for solidarity, prioritising wisdom, and rejecting bickering.” Dr Gargash welcomed a meeting on Sunday between President Sheikh Mohamed and Prince Khalid bin Salman, the Saudi Minister of Defence. Sheikh Mohamed and Prince Khalid exchanged views on regional developments with the aim of contributing to strengthening security and stability, and achieving lasting peace in the region, state news agency Wam reported. Sheikh Mans our bin Zayed , Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, also attended the meeting on Sunday, as did Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, Deputy Ruler of Abu Dhabi and National Security Adviser. The meetings affirmed the depth and solidity of Emirati-Saudi relations, Dr Gargash said. “For our security and destiny are shared, and our partnership is one of the pillars of Gulf stability and prosperity, while the wisdom of the two leaderships and the sincerity of positions in times of adversity provide the most eloquent response to every bet against that,” Dr Gargash said. Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, held phone calls with foreign ministers on Sunday and Monday regarding security and stability in the region. On Monday, Sheikh Abdullah held phone calls with Johann Wadephul, German Foreign Minister; Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, Minister of Foreign Affairs for Bahrain; and Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah, Minister of Foreign Affairs for Saudi Arabia. Sheikh Abdullah shared calls on Sunday with Nasser Bourita, Morocco's Minister of Foreign Affairs; Badr Abdelatty, Egyptian Foreign Minister; Ayman Safadi, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs for Jordan; Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Qatar; and Badr Al Busaidi, Foreign Minister of Oman, state news agency Wam reported.

title: Threats and invitations: Houthis send mixed signals on Yemen peace
description: Houthi official welcomes mediation but threatens countries offering support to Saudi Arabia
content: Yemen 's Houthis are talking peace while warning of a wider war. The Iran-backed rebels are blaming Saudi Arabia for stalling negotiations even as they threaten countries that may join the kingdom's military campaign. On Sunday, Houthi spokesman Mohammad Abdulsalam accused Saudi Arabia of failing to honour previous agreements and delaying its response to proposals aimed at bringing peace to the Yemen. In a post on X, he said the Houthis had communicated with Saudi Arabia “directly and indirectly” in June, demanding it “respond to what we had agreed upon in the road map before the Al Aqsa Flood and we presented more than one proposal, but unfortunately, it did not advance a single step”. Al Aqsa Flood was the name of the Hamas-led incursion into southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 250 hostages were taken to Gaza, before Israel launched a two-year war in the strip in which more than 74,300 Palestinians have been killed and hundreds of thousands injured.
