Meanwhile, Houthi politburo member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told Qatar-based Al Arabi Television in an interview that the militia was open to ending the war. “We welcome any mediation, Arab or Islamic, to reach peace, which entails ending the war and the blockade from both sides – whether from Iran , Pakistan or Turkey,” he said. In the same breath, he continued to threaten any country that enters the war alongside Saudi Arabia. Egypt was the latest to suggest it is ready to provide the kingdom with assistance after the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi airports and oil sites last week, killing dozens of civilians and injuring hundreds of others. President ​Abdel Fattah Al Sisi has requested an emergency session of Egypt's parliament to authorise the military to provide support to the kingdom. The vote has not yet taken place but approval of the plan would significantly widen the scope of the war. There is scepticism about the Houthis' apparent change of heart, especially after the rebels seemingly started the escalation in August and subsequently advocated a continuation of the conflict. “The Houthis tend to welcome mediation when they come under military pressure and suffer heavy losses,” wrote Nadwa Al Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute. “But once a ceasefire is reached, they exploit it to regroup, replenish their ranks and prepare for the next offensive. For them, ceasefires are tactical pauses, not steps towards peace.”

title: Yemen fighting threatens to widen after 73 killed in Houthi attack on training camp
description: Strike comes as government forces advance towards Bab Al Mandeb strait and rebels claim attacks on Saudi targets
content: At least 73 people were killed in a Houthi missile attack on a military training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province, raising fears of further escalation as government forces push to recapture rebel-held territory near the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Monday's attack on Al Alam camp also wounded more than 200 people, while 14 remained missing, Shabwa Governor Awad Al Wazir said. Injured recruit Nasser Sheikh Bahaj said three missiles struck as security personnel were training. He described a scene of explosions, flying shrapnel and injured colleagues calling desperately for help. “We woke up for dawn prayers, then had breakfast and entered the training ground … suddenly we heard a loud explosion and shrapnel flew everywhere. Three missiles fell on the camp,” Mr Bahaj was quoted as saying in Yemeni media. He said reconnaissance aircraft had flown over the camp during the previous three nights, filming the site. He added that he was wounded by shrapnel and remained at the scene, where other recruits suffered serious injuries. “I sat holding my wound and heard my colleagues shouting, ‘Ambulance. Vehicles. Save us.’ Some had lost their hands, while others were injured in their legs,” he said. A driver helped him board a military vehicle carrying about 10 seriously wounded people, who were taken to the Authority Hospital in provincial capital Ataq. Video showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground at the Martyr Ahmed Al Sulaymani training centre, where new recruits were attending a training course. The Houthis acknowledged attacking the facility, describing it as a concentration of “Saudi enemy” forces managed by officers from the kingdom. The Iran-backed group claimed Saudi personnel were among dozens of people killed or wounded. Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reports from Shabwa General Hospital and other medical sites in Ataq described chaotic scenes as ambulances and private vehicles carried casualties. Medical sources said some of the wounded were in critical condition, while residents responded to urgent appeals for blood donations. Shabwa authorities called for urgent military and security measures to prevent further attacks, urging Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition to provide air defence systems, early-warning capabilities and other equipment. Rashad Al Alimi, head of the council, condemned the attack and accused the Houthis of “resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they faced pressure or their plans were thwarted”. He instructed authorities to respond firmly, the official Saba news agency reported. The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis said it tracked and attacked traditional fishing boats suspected of smuggling weapons to the Houthis. Footage released by the coalition's joint forces command showed a vessel at sea under surveillance, highlighted by a red circle before apparent explosions. In a statement, the coalition said the use of traditional maritime vessels to smuggle weapons and military equipment threatened Yemen's security, as well as regional and international stability. The Houthis have recently attacked government-held sites, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital. A missile and drone attack on the presidential palace killed five security personnel, Yemeni authorities said. The Houthis also claimed on Monday to have attacked Saudi energy, airport and military targets, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha airport. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the claims. Yemeni government forces this month launched a campaign to recapture Houthi-held areas, making advances near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, while the rebels continue to besiege Taiz , a major stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highlands. Shabwa, an energy-rich province on Yemen’s southern coast, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas site, the country’s largest industrial investment. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. A Saudi-led military intervention followed in 2015, at the request of the government. A truce brokered in 2022 held until this year, when fighting intensified again. The conflict has become another front in the wider US-Israeli war against Iran, with the Houthis escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia , the world’s largest crude exporter. Yemen is gripped by one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with renewed fighting threatening to worsen conditions for civilians.

title: Riyadh airport reopens: Which airlines are still cancelling flights to Saudi Arabia?
description: UAE and other international services remain suspended despite airport reopening
content: Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reopened on Sunday, after it was closed because of attacks by the Houthi rebels in Yemen. However, many airlines have not yet lifted their suspension of flights to the Saudi capital and other destinations in the kingdom. Some carriers have extended cancellations into November and beyond, while others are preparing to resume services. The disruption comes amid wider regional uncertainty, which has already affected airlines’ Middle East operations . Here’s how major airlines have adjusted operations and when flights are expected to resume. Etihad Airways has extended flight cancellations between Abu Dhabi and three Saudi cities until October 24, due to regional disruption. All services to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have been cancelled until that date. The following flights have also been cancelled: EY601 and EY603 from Abu Dhabi to Jeddah; EY602 and EY604 from Jeddah to Abu Dhabi. Emirates services from Dubai to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have been affected by cancellations and schedule changes. According to Flightradar24, Jeddah-bound flights EK801, EK805 and EK803 have been cancelled on October 19 and 20, with services scheduled to resume on October 21. Dubai to Riyadh flights EK815, EK819 and EK817 have also been cancelled. EK817 is scheduled to resume on October 20, followed by EK815 and EK819 on October 21. The airline has cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha up to and including October 24. Air Arabia has cancelled services between Sharjah and several Saudi destinations including Riyadh, Abha, Dammam and Taif. No resumption date has been announced. The airline has temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam up to and including October 24. Meanwhile, its services to Jeddah have been reduced from seven daily flights to four. Gulf Air has said flights after Sunday, October 18 are currently proceeding as scheduled, following its previously announced Riyadh cancellations. Oman Air has announced that all flights to and from Riyadh are suspended until October 22. The Omani low-cost airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until October 31, citing regional security developments. The French airline has extended its suspension of flights to and from Riyadh up to October 24. British Airways is scheduled to return with a limited service to Riyadh on November 3, operating one flight daily, according to previously announced plans. The airline discontinued flights to Jeddah in April as part of wider changes to its Middle East operations. Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until October 24. The Indian low-cost airline has suspended flights to and from Riyadh until October 24 and Jeddah until October 21. The Hong Kong airline has extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh up to January 31, 2027. The airline announced a temporary suspension of flights to Riyadh on October 9, without setting out a resumption date. The Pakistan Airports Authority said at the time that its other Saudi services were continuing as usual. The US airline has postponed the launch of flights between Atlanta and Riyadh until March 2027. Services had been scheduled to begin on October 23. The Indian airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah up to October 24. The German airline has suspended flights to Riyadh until November 18, extending its previously announced October 16 deadline. The Lufthansa Group’s advisory also lists Dammam services as suspended through November 30. Eurowings, part of the group, is scheduled to resume flights to Jeddah on November 12. Malaysia Airlines has announced that flights to and from Jeddah and Madinah will resume on October 18 after a safety review. The Dutch airline has extended cancellations of all flights to Riyadh and Dammam up to October 31. The Philippine flag carrier has suspended Riyadh flights PR654 and PR655 until November 29, citing the security situation at King Khalid International Airport. The Singapore Airlines-owned low-cost carrier has cancelled flights between Singapore and Jeddah until December 2.

title: Sheikha Latifah on her 20 years of Asian Games success and new Olympic dream
description: Emirati rider has enjoyed success at highest level for two decades and tells The National she hopes to compete at LA 2028
content: Sheikha Latifah Bint Ahmed Bin Maktoum Al Maktoum does not remember the first time she got on a horse. Riding to her is like speaking, or walking – a skill a child picks up without even realising, and just keeps on doing it forever, or for as long as they possibly can. Earlier this month, Sheikha Latifah, riding her bay coat stallion Cornet XL, helped the UAE secure a silver medal in team jumping at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. It was her fourth career medal won at the Games, and it came 20 years after she clinched her first at Doha 2006. Making the podium on the continental stage two decades apart is a remarkable feat. Did Sheikha Latifah ever consider that to be a possibility when she claimed her first Asian Games medal 20 years ago? “I think so. I think it's in our DNA,” the 41-year-old Emirati told The National from her base in Germany following her successful trip to Japan . “I think for us riders, I don't ever think we'd want to stop. We'd always have something to do with it.” It takes a special kind of passion, discipline, and skill to be able to compete at the highest level in any sport for so long and Sheikha Latifah does not take that longevity for granted. “It means a lot,” she says. “The first Asian Games, I did it with an eight-year-old [horse]. An eight-year-old is very young to do a championship like that. I got him as a seven-year-old, the same as Cornet XL, I got him as a seven-year-old, and we built up together. “So I think now three horses that I've done the Asian Games with, I've had from young horses and built up. “I don't know how to explain it, but it's just a different feeling when you bring up a horse instead of getting something ready to do it because it takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of effort and you go through a lot of ups and downs building up horses. So that for me is something special.” The past few weeks have been particularly special for Sheikha Latifah, not just because she made her first Asian Games podium since Guangzhou 2010, where she took individual and team silver medals atop Kalaska de Semilly. In August, she made her long-awaited return to the World Equestrian Games (WEG), competing at the global stage for the first time since her debut appearance back in 2010. She got the call just two weeks before the WEG when her compatriot Abdullah Al Marri suffered an injury that ruled him out of the competition, freeing up a spot on the UAE team. “I was actually preparing for that [a call-up] my whole summer tour because I was on the long list so I was preparing for it,” she said. “I chose my shows, built up the horse. So when I got the call, I was ready. I think the team wasn't sure just because my horse didn't do as many big classes as they would like, but I have a lot of confidence in him and I really believed that he was made for this from the day I bought him.” The past few months have given Sheikha Latifah the confidence she needed to tackle her next big goal with Cornet XL, which is to qualify for the Olympics. She is no stranger to that stage either as she happens to be the first Emirati woman – alongside Sheikha Maitha bint Mohammed bin Rashid – to compete at an Olympic Games, having represented the UAE in showjumping in Beijing 2008. “I think it's every rider's dream. I think the first Olympics I did it was just very foreign to me,” she reflected. “Everything was new and I was very nervous. I had a 10-year-old horse that I brought up, 10-year-olds are considered young at that level. Me being very young at the time it was very new and I think now I know what it takes to be there. “I know what the horse needs. I have a plan and if I don't believe I could represent the country in the best possible light, I wouldn't even attempt it. But I think I really have a fantastic horse and we're a great combination me and him. We're going to try, Inshallah.” Sheikha Latifah believes “trusting the process” is the biggest lesson she is taking with her along this upcoming journey towards a possible second Olympics appearance. “Sometimes like with Cornet XL we went through a lot of ups and downs. He's such a big horse and I'm very little and he's very strong but very sensitive and I really had to find a way that he was happy but I could also still control him because he doesn't like to have me control him completely and he likes to be how he wants to be,” she said. “But at the level we're jumping, I have to also have a say in what I want in the ring. I have to be able to make a decision and when I make a decision he has to respond, and in the beginning that was very difficult just because he's so big but also so sensitive so I really had to find a way with him and that we both came to an understanding.” She gives a lot of credit to experienced Saudi rider Ramzy Al Duhami, who won team bronze at the London 2012 Olympics and has been Sheikha Latifah’s coach and mentor for many years. “He really inspires me in the way he thinks,” she said of Al Duhami. “What I really like is he's always horse first, so like we never think, oh we want the horse to go this way? No, it’s how do we do best to get the best out of the horse? If I need to change the way I'm riding, if I need to sit more, if I need to be out of the saddle, if I need to have the nose out, if I need to have the nose in, it's all how to get the best out of the horse. “And for me that's why it never gets boring because every horse is different and every horse likes to go a certain way and that's how I get inspired because it's just never boring.” Sheikha Latifah was one of five Emirati women to win medals at the recently-concluded Asian Games and she has proudly witnessed the growth of women’s sport in the UAE over the past two decades. As a pioneer herself, she knows she has played a part in pushing women’s sport forward in the country and it’s a role she takes very seriously. “It means a lot and I really am also inspired by the other athletes, whether it's male or female, I'm really inspired by them,” she added. “It's just you always feel when someone is able to raise your flag in a big occasion you feel like you're part of it, so it doesn't matter what sport but anything that raises the UAE flag I always feel like I'm a part of it and I think it goes the same way for all of us, whether it's in athletics, whether it's in judo. I think for us it's just we're all proud of each other.”

title: Iranian 'terror mastermind' feared to be plotting attacks from behind bars
description: US authorities believe Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al Saadi is using coded messages to enlist others
content: An Iranian operative accused of planning dozens of anti-Semitic attacks in Europe and the US has been reportedly plotting further assaults from behind bars. US authorities believe Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al Saadi has been using coded messages in telephone calls from prison to push others into carrying out new plots, directing $1million in money transfers and overseeing the release of propaganda videos. The accusations are contained in US Department of Justice documents reported by The Times . Jonathan Hackett, a US intelligence expert, said Iranian operations in the UK had recovered from a dip in mid-year around the time of Al Saadi's transfer to US custody. He surmised an associate of Al Saadi on the outside had been mobilised. "Another person like Al Saadi, working within the same circle, has been remotely contacting and recruiting and tasking assets inside the UK," he told the UK think tank Rusi. "Most likely, this seems to be a resumption of the exact same operations the IRGC had [undertaken]. So that means Iran is operating at the maximum of its capability in the UK." Mr Al Saadi, a 32-year-old dual citizen of Iran and Iraq, was charged in New York in May with six counts of terrorism-related offences for his alleged activities as an operative of the Iraqi militia group Kataib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Both organisations have been placed under sanctions and designated as terrorist groups by the US. He is also alleged to be behind Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia , also known as Ashab Al Yamin, which translates as the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right Hand and has been blamed for a series of fire-bombings at Jewish locations in London and synagogues in Europe. The US targets were a New York City synagogue and two Jewish institutions in Los Angeles, California, and Scottsdale, Arizona, according to prosecutors. UK security services have said that more than 50 Iran-linked arrests have been made in the past year as Tehran’s plots against targets in the UK intensify . Mr Al Saadi was extradited to the US from Turkey and is being held without bail in a federal centre in New York. He is expected to face trial next summer and faces life in prison if convicted of the most serious charges against him. His legal team has said he faces “political prosecution” and complained about the measures he is subject to in detention, including near-solitary confinement and strict limits on contact with family. “By keeping Mr Al Saadi in extreme solitary confinement and aggressively curtailing his access to information, the government is violating his rights under the constitution and the third Geneva Convention. We will continue to vigorously challenge these inhumane conditions,” The Times quoted his lawyers, Federal Defenders of New York, as saying. They said the reasons for the restrictions did not hold up to scrutiny and relied on speculation and misinterpretation. The documents filed by the Justice Department highlight suspicion that Mr Al Saadi used a FaceTime call with a woman thought to be his mother to urge further attacks. A video of the call in which he said “we shall not care whether we fall upon death or death falls upon us as long as we are on the path of truth” was shared on social media and viewed almost 100,000 times. In a phone call, he asked about a member of Kataib Hezbollah and “work” for what the FBI believe is an IRGC operative. The FBI cut short one call in which there was reference to a gun and money. The Justice Department documents said there were concerns he was “enlisting third parties to engage in certain conduct, including planning or even carrying out more attacks such as the European terrorist attacks”. Mr Al Saadi is accused of being a commander in Kataib Hezbollah which was placed under sanctions after years of attacks on US forces stationed in the Middle East, particularly in Iraq. Mr Al Saadi is alleged to have worked closely with Maj Gen Qassem Suleimani, the commander of the IRGC's Quds Force, who was killed during a US air strike in early 2020, and Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Mahdi Al Muhandis, who died in the same strike. Mr Al Saadi’s social media accounts showed photographs of him with Maj Gen Suleimani at a military-related facility. Mr Al Saadi is alleged to have called on others to attack and kill Americans, including in retribution for the deaths of Maj Gen Suleimani and Al Muhandis. He posted about the attacks on social media platforms such as Snapchat and Telegram and spoke about them in phone calls recorded by an FBI informant whose help he solicited in planning attacks in the US, the complaint said. Al Saadi told the informant he was willing to kill people in any such attacks, prosecutors allege.

title: Reportage Group and Sabah Investment Group showcase Sea Breeze Projects in Azerbaijan
description: Sea Breeze is an integrated residential and resort destination on the Caspian coast near Baku
content: Reportage Group continues to expand its international presence through its strategic partnership with Sabah Investment Group, as the two companies hosted an event in Abu Dhabi to showcase four real estate projects within Sea Breeze, an integrated residential and resort destination on the Caspian coast near Baku, Azerbaijan. Bringing together sales teams, media representatives and guests, the event highlighted Azerbaijan’s role in Reportage Group’s international growth strategy and how the projects contribute to the wider vision for Sea Breeze. The event featured Reportage Heights, Panorama by Elie Saab, Arabian Ranches Baku and Brabus Island, highlighting their master plans, key features and positioning within the wider destination. It also provided attendees and media representatives with a deeper understanding of Azerbaijan’s real estate market and the investment opportunities within Sea Breeze, alongside the destination’s residential, tourism and leisure offerings. Each of the four projects offers a distinct residential concept within Sea Breeze, catering to different lifestyles and buyer preferences. Reportage Heights features modern waterfront apartments with panoramic sea views, spacious terraces and leisure facilities, while Panorama by ELIE SAAB introduces branded residences with interiors designed by ELIE SAAB Maison, reflecting the fashion house’s signature design aesthetic. Inspired by Eastern architecture, Arabian Ranches Baku offers apartments and townhouses designed around family living and resort-style amenities. Meanwhile, BRABUS Island Baku brings the German luxury brand’s distinctive design approach to the Caspian coast through a collection of waterfront residences and villas. Andrea Nucera, Group Managing Director at Reportage Group, said, “Our approach to international growth is to identify markets where we can deliver projects that respond to local demand and create long-term value. Sea Breeze brings together residential living, tourism and leisure within one destination, offering scope for a diverse portfolio that serves different buyer needs. Through our collaboration with Sabah Investment Group, we are bringing this approach to Azerbaijan, combining our development expertise with local market insight to deliver distinctive projects within Sea Breeze." Orkhan Mustafayev, Founder and Chairman of Sabah Investment Group, said, “Our collaboration with Reportage Group reflects a shared ambition to contribute to Azerbaijan's real estate sector and strengthen Sea Breeze's appeal as a destination to live, visit and invest. By bringing together projects with different property types, features and lifestyle offerings, we aim to provide buyers with a range of options within a single integrated destination.” Sea Breeze is located on the Caspian Sea coast, approximately 30 minutes from central Baku, and spans around 500 hectares. The development includes more than three million square metres of completed residential and commercial space and is home to more than 20,000 residents. Founded by businessman Emin Agalarov, Sea Breeze is being developed as an integrated community combining residential and tourism accommodation with commercial and leisure facilities. Its master plan, designed by British firm Scott Brownrigg, covers an 18-kilometre coastal strip, with all phases targeted for completion by 2035.

title: Canada increases Gulf diplomacy to push for peace and reopening of Strait of Hormuz
description: Foreign Minister Anita Anand says Ottawa is engaging with countries around world to uphold international law and support regional stability
content: “Diplomacy is the art of the possible,” Canada's Foreign Minister Anita Anand said. That has been at the heart of talks with regional partners aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East, opposing Iranian aggression and restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. She spoke to The National in Dubai, with her visit to the UAE intended to reinforce Canada's opposition to Iranian attacks and Ottawa's support for the complete reopening of the strait, which is vital for global energy supplies and trade. “We are in a phase of our foreign policy where we are deeply engaged with countries around the world to ensure that we are standing for peace, standing for state sovereignty and that we show our promise that we are here for them,” she said. “That's one of the reasons why I'm here today." Ms Anand met Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed , Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, during her visit, with the ministers discussing bilateral ties and regional stability. She added that relations between two countries have been “consistently elevated". Canada and the UAE have increased diplomatic engagement as regional tensions heightened, with both governments discussing the implications for security and stability across the Middle East. There had also been a push to strengthen ties last year, with Prime Minister Mark Carney travelling to the UAE in November 2025. He was the first Canadian leader to visit in the country in more than four decades. Mr Carney’s government has also sought to strengthen investment ties with the Gulf , while reducing its reliance on the US market. “But over and above trade , there is the question of regional stability and the importance of speaking out against the retaliatory attacks from Iran and making sure that we also support freedom of navigation in your [the UAE’s] backyard, in the Strait of Hormuz,” Ms Anand said. She praised the UAE and other Gulf states for maintaining normal life while responding firmly to Iranian aggression. “I greatly respect the ability of each of the countries who are being hit by these attacks, including the UAE, to continue to live lives as normally as possible on the one hand, but to take a strong stand against these attacks on the other,” she said. Iran launched ballistic missiles and drones at its Gulf neighbours, aiming at civilian infrastructure including energy sites and airports. The US and Iran signed an agreement in June intended to pave the way for a final peace settlement. But attacks have continued, particularly on shipping, and Washington and Tehran have traded threats. The war has spilt over into escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with the kingdom attacked repeatedly in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group. Ms Anand expressed concern about the attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly strikes on Riyadh airport, and said she had been in contact with the kingdom's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, to convey Canada's support. “Well, of course, the attacks that Saudi Arabia specifically is enduring are very, very concerning,” she added. Canada's concerns extend to Tehran's wider regional conduct, with Ms Anand stressing Ottawa's long-standing opposition to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its record on human rights. She said Canada had taken action against people and entities linked to repression and rights abuses. The IRGC has been listed as a terrorist entity under Canadian law for more than two years, she added. “We are particularly concerned with Iranian women and girls. And we will continue to voice that concern,” she said. Canada has imposed sanctions on Iran over alleged rights abuses, repression and activities that Ottawa says threaten regional security. The latest measures were announced in September and applied to five people and five entities accused of involvement in digital surveillance and other rights breaches. “I'd like to present Canada as a country that cares deeply about the region and the respect for international law and international human rights,” Ms Anand said. Humanitarian assistance also remains a priority for Canada across the Middle East, with the situation in Gaza among the issues discussed during her visit. Since the launch of Operation Gallant Knight 3 , the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid given to the enclave since 2023. She also raised concerns about Lebanon , particularly the actions of Iran-backed Hezbollah, and said Canada had provided about $40 million in humanitarian aid to the country. On Syria, Ms Anand said Canada was continuing to relax some sanctions imposed during the rule of former president Bashar Al Assad, as Ottawa pursues rapprochement with Damascus. “I have invited the Foreign Minister of Syria [Asaad Al Shibani] to come to Canada, and we are working on establishing a date for that meeting,” she added. Ms Anand said Canada wanted to continue working with regional partners to support stability, respect for sovereignty and international law.

title: ‘He is golf’s living legend’: Fans urged not to take Rory McIlroy’s return to Dubai Desert Classic for granted
description: World No 2 will be looking for a fifth Dallah Trophy when he plays at Emirates Golf Club in January
content: Rory McIlroy and the Hero Dubai Desert Classic might feel inextricably linked. But spectators are being urged not to take his presence at the Emirates Golf Club for granted. McIlroy has been playing at the region’s oldest European Tour event for over 20 years now. On Monday it was confirmed he will be heading back to the Majlis Course for a tilt at a fifth Dallah Trophy in January. He has been a visible part of the growth of the city. It is debatable which method is better for dating pictures of past Desert Classics: counting the number of skyscrapers in Dubai Marina, or the volume – and, lately, greyness – of McIlroy’s hair. Now aged 37, McIlroy is not going to be pensioned off any time soon. But the Northern Irishman has said he plans to reduce his schedule in the future. He wants to focus on adding to his haul of six majors, streamline his bid to return to World No 1, and spend more time with his family. Given his CV, McIlroy is in a position to be picky. His sweet spot, he has suggested, could be around 18 to 20 events per season. If four of those are majors, plus play-off series tournaments on both the US and European tours, and some obvious signature events Stateside, that does not leave a huge amount of wiggle room for those wanting to host him. He could be more in demand than ever. Even without the No 1 rankings tag which Scottie Scheffler has been hogging so voraciously for so long, McIlroy is the most recognisable figure playing the game. Or, as Simon Corkill , the Desert Classic’s tournament director, puts it: “He’s golf’s living legend.” “You use the word legend; he's certainly there and there are some others still playing,” Corkill said. “But he's the one who is front and centre at the moment. Tiger [Woods’] career is not where it should be at the moment and I think he's going to struggle to come back with what's going on in his world. “But Rory is there, exhibiting it week in, week out, and we can't take it for granted.” McIlroy is also booked for two UAE events next month – the DP World Tour finale on consecutive weeks in Abu Dhabi and at Jumeirah Golf Estates in Dubai. Corkill said it is lucky he has such an affinity with the Classic, which is where he won his first Tour title, that it means he is happy to keep returning. “He's not going to come to Dubai every year going forward,” Corkill said. “He's openly said he wants to reduce his schedule, and he's going to pick and choose the events he likes. He really likes the Hero Dubai Classic, which is great for us.” Although his participation in next year’s Classic has just been announced, the decision was made in the summer, around the time of the Open Championship. At the time, the Iran war was central to the news cycle. A number of leading players said they were wary of heading to the Gulf when the Tour was due to return there later in the year. Corkill said McIlroy’s knowledge of the region – as a former resident, with many friends still based here – meant he was quickly convinced of its security. “He was fully reassured,” Corkill said. “He had spoken to a lot of his friends here prior to the conversations we were having, and got the assurances of what was actually happening on the ground in Dubai. “He can hear it from me. He can hear it from the DP World Tour, which he did. But it obviously gives him some comfort when he's got some close friends here also saying the same thing.” Corkill said McIlroy’s presence at the Classic is an ideal way to launch the first big tournament of the DP World Tour season. “We really want to make sure that beginning of January is that real opening party,” Corkill said. “It's not technically the start of the DP World Tour season. But it's very much that back-to-school event. “Everyone's excited to see each other. Everyone's been away over the festive period, or been travelling and it's important to us to keep that vibe. “We’re certainly not writing Rory off yet. He's got plenty more years in him and I think he will pick and choose the events he really enjoys. I think hopefully we're still one of those.”

title: Arab vote could prove decisive in Israel’s election as fears grow over far right
description: As polls continue to predict a deadlock,  community has become one of the most closely watched in the lead-up to voting
content: Unlike many in her community, Umaima Luwabneh is determined to vote in Israel’s elections . She will be doing so with her son, Iyad, foremost in her thoughts. He was killed by police last year, in a wave of violent crime that has devastated Israel’s Arab community since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power. One of his most controversial appointments was ultranationalist Itamar Ben-Gvir as minister in charge of the police. He has eight convictions, including for racism and for support of an anti-Palestinian terrorist organisation. “There’s a very severe negligence on the part of the Israeli state at the moment,” Ms Luwabneh told The National , as she stood outside a modest gathering hosted by activists trying to increase Arab turnout in the elections in the northern city of Nazareth. “I have come to help people understand that they have to go to vote. I would say it’s even mandatory,” she said during a coffee break between impassioned speeches and musical recitals, in both Hebrew and Arabic. “If we change the government hopefully there will be security and peace. If we don’t, it will be a big problem.” Ms Luwabneh's story compelled her to join this small group of Arab and Jewish-Israeli campaigners. They were a somewhat incongruous sight in today’s divided country. Mr Ben-Gvir was mentioned dozens of times. The activists have their work cut out for them this year. Palestinians with Israeli passports make up about 20 per cent of Israel’s population but, during the last elections, only about 50 per cent of eligible voters cast their ballots. Pollster Dahlia Scheindlin told The National that the drive to encourage more people to vote could be working. “There’s high expectation of high turnout relative to last time. We’re looking at 60 per cent, possibly more than that. I can’t predict it, but that’s what polls have been showing and it's very much backed by anecdotes. All my Arab friends, colleagues and people on the street are saying the same thing: we all want to go vote and that there’s a huge fear factor about Itamar Ben-Gvir being in the next government.” If they head to the polls en masse in 2026, they will form a significant bloc in Israel’s complicated electoral mathematics, where one seat in the 120-seat Knesset can make or break a coalition. As polls continue to predict a deadlock, their vote has become one of the most closely watched trends in the lead-up to election day. Palestinian citizens of Israel are descendants of Palestinians who stayed inside the territory after Israel was created in 1948. They have long complained of discrimination and are often attacked, particularly during election cycles, by Israel’s growing right wing. Mr Netanyahu’s coalition has brought about troubles of a different magnitude. A crackdown on freedom of expression, a rise in attacks and intimidation from the far-right, underinvestment, settler and military violence in the occupied West Bank and the devastation of the war in Gaza are some of the issues the community has had to confront during the government’s term. Despite the historically tough odds and today’s grim reality, the conference in Nazareth tried to inspire optimism. It was held under the banner “This Time We Can” and organised by the Israeli-Palestinian activist group Standing Together. The movement briefly fielded a political party in the election campaign, although the party was disbanded amid fears it could further split the vote on Israel’s beleaguered left. Now the group is focusing its efforts on getting Arab Israelis to vote. The room was nearly full, mostly with older citizens. Clatters and shouts from a nearby boxing gym could be heard outside. The vast Church of the Annunciation loomed in the distance near the once-bustling old city. Tourist numbers have crashed since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks. Those present listened patiently and asked questions. Nonetheless, the meeting had less energy than the packed election events organised by Israel’s surging far-right, which heads to the polls propelled by the momentum of four years of ideological gains, often at the expense of Palestinians, whether or not they are Israeli citizens. Even in this heavily Palestinian area, the reach of the far-right was clear. On the main roads leading to Nazareth, most election posters were for the Arab parties. The exception was for Mr Netanyahu’s Likud Party, for whom there are posters even inside the city that condemn Arab parties and left-wing Jewish candidates. Next to a group of them outside Nazareth, young religious Jewish activists, probably too young to vote in the coming elections, were carrying flags and signs in support of the government, as Arab commuters made their way back home. The same posters are found throughout the settlements in the occupied West Bank. Part of Israel’s far-right agenda over the past four years has been an intense campaign of delegitimisation of Arab parties, spearheaded by figures in the government. Many Arab politicians and parties were barred from running by the Central Elections Committee earlier in the year. One representative, Sami Abu Shehadeh, withdrew from the race, after Supreme Court judges on appeal told him a majority of the panel would disqualify him. The court also considered the CEC’s decision to disqualify a far-left Jewish member of the Knesset and two Arab political parties, Ra’am and the Joint List. It eventually overturned the CEC’s bans. It is an astonishing state of affairs, just four years after Arab parties formed a crucial part of the broad “government of change” coalition led by current candidates Naftali Bennet and Yair Lapid, and as supporters of Israel continue to trumpet their country as the only democracy in the Middle East. And now, many of the leaders of the opposition, including some of the very same Jewish politicians who sat with Arabs last time round, have promised they will never do so again, even though the community’s votes might well be crucial to forming an opposition government. Faced with these hurdles, participants at the conference tried to keep attendees focused on the point of voting. Political scientist Dr Thair Abu Rass, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, told the crowd that these were “the most important elections of our lives”. He mentioned the massive surge in murders under Mr Ben-Gvir, as well as the government’s attack on Israel’s judiciary, which drew massive street protests before the Gaza War. It was not an issue that animated many, but Mr Abu Rass argued that weakened courts in an increasingly right-wing Israel would be a disaster for Palestinian citizens. “It will be the law of the majority, the law of the strongest. We live in a state where the right is a majority, even if Netanyahu leaves,” he said. "If they succeed in Gaza, they will succeed in the West Bank, then in Jerusalem. After that it will be us.”

title: UAE amends e-invoicing regulations as implementation deadline draws closer
description: Ministry to offer temporary exclusion for business transactions between entities that are part of the same tax group for two years
content: The UAE's Ministry of Finance has made amendments to its e-invoicing system that will apply to value-added tax filing in the country from next year. Authorities are introducing a temporary exclusion for business transactions between entities that are members of the same tax group for two years, starting from January 1, 2027, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday. Such transactions will be treated as "excluded transactions" throughout the 24-month period, "giving businesses greater flexibility and more time to adapt to the system", the ministry said. David Daly, a partner at Gulf Tax Accounting Group, said the move was "welcome", but more clarity would be needed to understand specific details. For instance, in a scenario where each entity also issues invoices to non-tax group members, it still needs to be known whether these must be managed through the e-invoicing system, he said. The ministry's latest decision also amends article 11 on the storage of electronic invoice and electronic credit note data. Under the amended provision, entities must retain all electronic invoices, electronic credit notes and any associated data for the period prescribed under the Tax Procedures Law, and ensure that such records can be provided to the Federal Tax Authority on request, the ministry said. The decision "removes the previous requirement that such data be stored within the UAE, thereby shifting the focus from the location of storage to the retention and accessibility of records for tax compliance purposes", it added. The amendments also remove the requirement for companies to notify the FTA of a system failure within two business days of it happening. The ministry said the amendments are aimed at improving the ease of doing business in the UAE "by reducing operational burdens on businesses, providing greater flexibility during the implementation of the electronic invoicing system, and ensuring that regulatory requirements support an efficient and business-friendly environment". The latest decision comes as the first major compliance requirement in the phased transition to e-invoicing approaches on October 30. The ministry extended the deadline for appointing an accredited service provider (ASP) for businesses in the UAE with annual revenue of Dh50 million ($13.6 million) or more to October 30, from July 1, under the first phase of the programme. Under the UAE's unified e-invoicing model, all qualifying transactions must be validated and sent through an ASP.

title: Shah Rukh Khan to launch Indian music festival UNIFYD in Abu Dhabi
description: Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam lead line-up for inaugural event at Yas Island
content: Bollywood superstar Shah Rukh Khan is launching a new music festival, UNIFYD, to be held in Abu Dhabi next year. Top Indian singers Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam are among the first names announced on the line-up. The inaugural event is to take place on March 20 at Etihad Live on Yas Island. It is to bring together more than 15 artists across several stages for a one-day programme focused on Indian music and culture. The festival will be produced by D'YAVOL Live and District, in collaboration with the Department of Culture and Tourism in Abu Dhabi and Miral . Khan will oversee its artistic direction and creative vision. “I’ve spent a lifetime telling stories on screen and watching them bring people together. Music has that same extraordinary power," he said. "The festival promises to be a true spectacle in terms of its scale, energy and grandeur." Khan is no stranger to major events in Abu Dhabi, having hosted the IIFA Awards on Yas Island in 2024. Singh and Aujla are among the first acts announced, while Nigam will perform a special set marking his first appearance at a music festival, organisers said. They will be joined by Jonita, Shalmali Kholgade, Patiala Mehfil, Simran Choudhary, Nooriyah, Curtain Blue, Tech Panda x Kenzani, Rusha & Blizza, Stick No Bills, BOH!B, Priyanka and Unnayanaa. The line-up spans Hindi film music, Punjabi music and other genres, with more performers still to be announced. Performances will take place across several stages over a single day. “Indian music is already global," said Bunty Singh, co-founder of D’YAVOL Live. "UNIFYD gives that cultural force a festival platform that matches its scale, ambition and influence. Bringing together artists of this stature on the same day, in a line-up that has never existed before, is what makes the first edition so special.” Organisers also plan to expand UNIFYD to other cities and international markets after its debut in Abu Dhabi . “Indian music is already global," said Bunty Singh, co-founder of D’YAVOL Live. "UNIFYD gives that cultural force a festival platform that matches its scale, ambition and influence. Bringing together artists of this stature on the same day, in a line-up that has never existed before, is what makes the first edition so special.” Tickets will be available exclusively through the District app. The general sale opens at 10.30am on October 20. Ticket prices have not yet been revealed.

title: Still sweating in October? UAE temperatures remain high as El Nino intensifies
description: Scientists predict strongest El Nino on record will last until March 2027
content: If autumn feels like it’s taking an age to arrive, you’re not imagining it. October has been warmer than usual this year, with the UAE National Centre of Meteorology issuing a major climate update on the El Nino weather phenomenon , which has been forecast to be the strongest on record. Sea surface temperatures in the Pacific have reached between 2.3°C and 3°C above the long-term average, cementing this year’s event as a global weather disruptor. Instead of the predictable October drop into comfortable autumn weather, the phenomenon is trapping a blanket of high pressure over the Arabian Peninsula, driving temperatures well above seasonal averages. Recent maximum temperatures across the country have ranged between 37°C and 43°C, with some areas experiencing temperatures 4°C higher than usual. The UAE's average daily temperature in October stands at 29.7°C, according to the NCM's latest monthly weather summary. October and November are expected to feel the peak of the El Nino cycle, with higher rainfall than usual also expected, including severe bouts that could raise the risk of flooding, although this is not guaranteed. The NCM projects a 96 per cent probability that these potentially volatile conditions will persist through to March 2027, with secondary environmental impacts such as lingering into April. Speaking to The National in September, Dr Diana Francis, associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences (Engeos) Laboratory at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said the region should prepare for more rainfall. “El Nino generally tilts the Gulf and parts of the Arabian Peninsula towards wetter conditions, enhanced moisture transport and a greater chance of heavy rain episodes,” she said. If rainfall levels increase, “very intense downpours may become more likely, according to Dr Andries-Jan de Vries, of the Institute of Earth Surface Dynamics at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland. “In combination with dry soils, with mountains and valleys, they can easily accumulate rainwater that can fall in a very short period of time, and that can then lead to flooding ,” he said. Parts of the UAE were hit by severe flooding in late March this year, almost two years after the country experienced its most extreme rain on record, late into what was described as the fifth-strongest El Nino on record. A study in Nature Scientific Reports in June with the title “ An extreme rainfall event over the United Arab Emirates in April 2024: Role of dynamic and thermodynamic drivers”, said that El Nino “may have contributed to a large-scale background environment favourable for above-normal April rainfall over the region”. After the 2024 floods , the authorities began investing heavily to improve drainage and make the country better able to cope with severe rains. The El Nino-Southern Oscillation, to use its full name, is a natural phenomenon in which the upwelling of water causes warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, with knock-on effects on the global climate. An opposite phenomenon, La Nina, is linked to cooler temperatures in that part of the Pacific Ocean. According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, El Nino and La Nina each last between nine months and a year and happen irregularly, typically every two to seven years. El Nino is seen slightly more often, and the one occurring this year and into next year has been forecast to be exceptionally strong. The World Meteorological Organisation recently said there were “exceptionally warm tropical Pacific Ocean conditions” and warned that a very strong El Nino could “significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather”. A recent study in Weather and Climate Dynamics called “The influence of El Nino-Southern Oscillation on cool-season precipitation variability in the arid Middle East ”, highlighted three mechanisms that cause El Nino to influence weather in the Gulf region. Firstly, El Nino’s warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific are typically associated with colder sea-surface temperatures and reduced tropical convection around Indonesia and the West Pacific. “That influences the regional circulation over South Asia and the Indian Ocean, and we have a change in the transport of moisture in the atmosphere,” said Dr De Vries, the first author of the paper. This results in an increase in moisture coming into the region. A second pathway is an alternating pattern of high and low-pressure systems running eastward from the warmer region in the Pacific, stretching over North America, the North Atlantic and Europe to the Middle East. This goes along with a low-pressure system over the Middle East, which is more favourable for precipitation. A third cause is that during El Nino conditions, the subtropical jet stream over North Africa and the Middle East – a band of fast-flowing air blowing from west to east about 12km to 14km above the Earth’s surface – is shifted slightly south, towards the equator. This allows mid-latitude storms to more easily enter the Middle East region. While El Nino makes wetter conditions in the Gulf region more likely, it does not make them certain. “El Niño increases the likelihood of wetter conditions but does not guarantee them. Rainfall in the region varies greatly from one year to another,” said Dr Zouhair Lachkar, a senior research scientist in New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said El Nino was not always linked to higher rainfall. So while a stronger-than-normal El Nino is statistically more likely to have a greater effect on rainfall than an average one, it may not have a major impact. Effects on rainfall are most likely this October and November, and in March, April and May next year. Even though El Nino warms the climate globally, Dr Francis said its impacts on UAE and Gulf temperatures were “relatively weak”. “Background climate warming, Gulf/Arabian Sea temperatures and regional circulation will be at least as important,” she said. “The impact of El Nino in the Gulf happens a few months after it is established in the Pacific. Most probably its impacts will be felt here from mid-autumn onward, and in those seasons it is mainly the rainfall patterns that will be influenced, less the temperature.” Dr Lachkar said that research at NYU Abu Dhabi showed that El Nino does not necessarily produce higher sea-surface temperatures in the Arabian Gulf. “In fact, we found that La Nina has historically been more favourable to exceptionally high summer sea-surface temperatures in the Gulf,” he said. Should there be increased rainfall in the UAE, the impact on the natural environment could be positive. Prof John Burt, director of NYU Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said if El Nino brought more winter rain, it could lead to “a marked increase in plant growth across our deserts and mountains”. “Sufficient rain during the cooler months can trigger widespread germination of seeds, plus flowering and renewed growth in established shrubs,” he said. "These responses extend through the food web: vegetation provides food for herbivores, flowers support pollinating insects, and greater insect abundance benefits birds, reptiles and small mammals. A productive winter can also replenish seed reserves, supporting future plant generations after the visible greenery disappears.” He said that while a wetter winter could promote natural regeneration, lasting benefits would depend on the intensity of the initial rainfall events and the subsequent weather. “Rain that initiates germination must be followed by conditions that allow seedlings to survive, such as continued soil moisture in the weeks and months that follow,” he said. “In contrast, brief but intense downpours can erode soils and uproot vegetation, particularly in mountain wadis and the gravel plains at the foothills.” He said it is not known if summer temperatures next year will be higher than normal, but that the centre will monitor this closely. “Marine organisms already live very close to their upper heat limits in summer, and are vulnerable to being pushed over the edge,” he said. A previous version of this article was published on September 14.

title: Smit Machchhar interview: What happened inside the cockpit of flydubai Flight 1073
description: From his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, hero captain tells The National of the moment his co-pilot turned on him at 34,000ft
content: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board. In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft. Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane. Capt Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for getting the cockpit door, locked from the inside, open and allowing the attack to be foiled. All of the 172 passengers and crew on board the September 30 flight survived. The first officer has been detained in the UAE and faces terrorism charges . The statements made in this interview reflect the interviewee’s recollection of events, based on his personal experience and his perception of them at the time they occurred. In his interview with The National at Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar revealed: Narrating the hijacking to a media outlet for the first time, Capt Machchhar said he thought the blow to his head was from a cockpit panel that had collapsed. “The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head,” he said. “It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.” He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.” Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking [at] outlines.” Capt Machchhar is not entirely clear how events unfolded nor the timeline. But he managed to open the cockpit after several attempts. He explained that every time he had to exert himself physically, he would lose blood and consciousness. “Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door," he said. "And [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit.” He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door. “The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.” Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive. “At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. "And I was constantly looking for the door. I did go for it. I did push it … the next thing I remember was I was facedown, lying with, thank God, the cockpit door open. I was between the cockpit and the galley.” Capt Machchhar said there was “so much chaos and commotion” as he was hauled out of the cockpit. It was at that moment that passengers and crew seized the first officer. A pair of flydubai pilots who were travelling as passengers took control of the plane. “If I have to say how many people were trying to control the situation, I would say a million. I know it doesn't make sense, but, yeah, I would say a million people were trying to take over control,” he said. He described the moment others came to his rescue as “magic”, saying: “The next thing I remember was [being] pulled out by one of the passengers. And then, soon after that, the senior cabin crew thankfully reached where I was and did his magic. And yeah, that's how I'm speaking to you today.” Recovering in his bed in Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar has been trying to piece together events in the two weeks since the failed terror plot. He remembers praying as the cabin crew chief and others, including dentist Shota Musaev, tried to stem the bleeding from his wounds. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National last week . “He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.” Capt Machchhar was clearly emotional as he spoke. He said: “I prayed a lot. I thought about my son, my daughter, and prayed. That was the point where I would say I didn't give up.” He spoke frankly: “Did I give up? No. I can 100 per cent tell you I did not give up. But was I sure I was going to make it? No.” Asked whether he suspected anything from his co-pilot's behaviour, he said he did not notice anything. “If there was something that could have hinted earlier on the ground or something, yes, of course, I would have acted. I would have spoken up. I would have questioned some things like that,” he explained. He described that morning as ordinary, saying it was the first time he had met the first officer. “It was a morning flight. So, yeah, there was some small talk, but there was not really like a deep conversation,” he said. Capt Machchhar added: “We avoid getting into deep conversations, especially during high-intensity or high-density airspace, especially nowadays with all the restrictions. Saudi is very high density.” "Nothing until that point would have caused me to think that: 'Hey, hold on, there's something off.'” There has been speculation about why the first officer attacked his colleague when the plane was an hour away from Tel Aviv airport, which prosecutors said he intended to crash into. “I won't say I've been thinking a lot about it, but yes, I did give it a thought. It makes no sense to me,” Capt Machchhar said. There was also much scrutiny over the presence of a cockpit axe, and how the co-pilot was radicalised. Asked whether aviation security will change as a result of the close call, Capt Machchhar said: “I think so. And for good." He added: “I won't blame it on anyone. You've got to learn from the event … I would just say: learn from whatever's happened and then make sure that this doesn't happen again, ever.” Capt Machchhar, who lives with his wife and children in the UAE, faces a long recovery but wants to return to the cockpit. “Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all,” he said with a smile. “I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”

title: Araghchi says Iran sees 'no military solution' to Middle East crisis
description: Foreign Minister calls for new regional security arrangement in meeting with Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov
content: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Monday his country saw "no military solution" to the crisis in the Middle East, as he met Russia 's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran. Mr Araghchi met Mr Lavrov a day after the Russian minister held talks in Bahrain , where Gulf countries urged him to lobby Tehran to stop its drone and missile attacks on its neighbours. In Iran, Mr Lavrov - who also met President Masoud Pezeshkian - said Russia was prepared to "assist in finding acceptable negotiated solutions" to resolve the crisis. His talks come with Russia launching fierce strikes in its own war in Ukraine . Mr Araghchi said Iran's "common view with Russia is that regional issues have no military solution", his ministry said. "They must be pursued through diplomacy and political solutions." He called countries in the region to work towards ​a joint ‌security arrangement, echoing a plea by Iraq on Monday for the Gulf to resolve its own issues without the influence of foreign powers. "We ⁠welcome ​any initiative ​that ‌leads to security ⁠from within without the ⁠presence of foreign forces, and consider it the right move," Mr Araghchi ​said. Mr Lavrov was in Tehran “to discuss de-escalation steps”, Russia's Tass news agency reported. The talks were also to focus on “strengthening the comprehensive partnership” between the two countries, Tass said. The visit comes as tension escalates over shipping security and the prospect of renewed war between Iran and the US, after President Donald Trump warned overnight that Washington could “soon finish the job” unless Tehran rapidly changes its behaviour. Tehran condemned Mr Trump's threat. “Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. “Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too.” Speeches hardened over the weekend. Iran’s new Defence Minister Mehrdad Ketabchi warned on Sunday that the country was ready to respond to any US attack involving the “ Mother of All Bombs ”. On Monday, Brig Gen Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander-in-chief, went further, saying Iran had the “father of missiles” ready to strike its enemy’s energy infrastructure and investments across the region if attacked. In a meeting between Mr Lavrov and Gulf Co-operation Council foreign ministers in Manama on Sunday, the bloc called on Russia to play an active role in securing Iranian compliance with UN resolutions, ending attacks on Gulf states and pursuing serious dialogue. Mr Lavrov has called for a diplomatic solution to the regional crisis, presenting an updated Russian plan for collective security in the Gulf that envisages direct dialogue among coastal states and neighbouring countries, including Iraq and Jordan. “We all believe that it is important for all the Gulf states to have their own word in how to resolve this strategic crisis,” Mr Lavrov said. He said Moscow supported direct dialogue between Gulf states and their neighbours, adding that Russia respected agreements reached so far. “We focus on removing core reasons for conflict,” Mr Lavrov said. “We stand for absolute respect for agreements reached so far. Unfortunately, our western counterparts do not follow the same value.” At Sunday's meeting in the Bahraini capital, GCC Secretary General Jasem Al Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 ballistic missile and drone attacks since February 28, when the US and Israel began their war against Iran. He said strikes had hit airports, ports, power stations, water desalination plants and oil and gas terminals. The bloc also warned that disruption to maritime navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, alongside threats to shipping in the Red Sea and Bab Al Mandeb strait, endangered global energy and food security and international supply chains. It called for maritime traffic through Hormuz to return to its prewar status. Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers using a US-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the conflict. On Monday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said an oil tanker struck a naval mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. The claim could not be independently verified. The IRGC said the vessel’s crew had switched off its positioning and navigation systems and were attempting to leave the waterway through an “unauthorised” southern route. It offered no evidence of a mine, and it is unclear whether the incident is linked to a US-backed shipping route along Oman’s coast, which Tehran may want to discourage companies from using. Iran’s hardline Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, meanwhile warned governments and businesses against funding AI and data companies he accuses of supporting US and Israeli military operations. In a post on X, Mr Ghalibaf announced plans for a “Gulf Data Authority” and warned that companies providing finance, land or energy to such firms would face Iranian enforcement measures. The post did not explain how the proposed authority would operate or explicitly threaten undersea cables. However, it follows a separate warning by Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, that regional undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities could be targeted if hostilities with the US resume.

title: Pep Guardiola urges world not to forget Gaza in UNRWA appeal
description: Solidarity with Palestine cannot take a break, former Manchester City manager says in video highlighting decades of displacement
content: Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has urged the world not to forget Palestinians in the war-ravaged Gaza strip. He spoke in a video appeal for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. The video published late on Sunday calls for continued solidarity and asks people to donate to the agency. “They are not statistics,” Guardiola says of those killed, describing them as people with “names and faces, families, dreams and memories”. “They are not collateral damage. They are girls and boys.” He warns that accepting language that conceals suffering erodes humanity. The appeal describes children in Gaza searching for parents in the rubble, going hungry and being left alone. “We see them lose everything before they have even had the chance to grow up,” he says. He rejects the idea that Palestinian suffering is remote from the rest of the world. “Their lives matter just as much as ours,” he says. “Solidarity with Palestine cannot take a break. Neither can our responsibility.” The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, health authorities in the territory say, since Hamas -led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023. The video also highlights decades of displacement and violence endured by Palestinian refugees. “We deeply admire the resilience of the Palestinian people. But they should not have to be resilient,” Guardiola says. “No child should grow up learning how to survive before learning how to live.” Israel launched a military offensive on Gaza after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks, which Israeli authorities say killed about 1,200 people and resulted in about 250 being taken hostage. Gaza’s Health Ministry says more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire took effect in October 2025. UNRWA, established in 1949, provides health care, protection and aid to refugees and helps to preserve their history and identity. It has operated in Gaza, the occupied West Bank , Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. Israel has barred the agency from operating in territory that it controls, accusing UNRWA of links to Hamas. The agency denies the allegation. “Silence today is a way of taking sides, but we cannot look the other way,” Guardiola says. “Palestine matters, and Palestine needs justice and peace.” Guardiola left his role as Manchester City manager at the end of last season following a 10-year reign that saw the club win 17 major trophies, including six Premier League titles and a Uefa Champions League crown.

title: Who is Tiger Shroff and what do we know about the shooting of the Bollywood star?
description: Indian actor escaped unharmed after gunmen opened fire on his car in Mumbai, injuring two people
content: Bollywood star Tiger Shroff, 36, escaped a shooting in Mumbai on the evening of Sunday, October 18, after gunmen opened fire on his car in the city's Juhu district. The attack left two people wounded and authorities are investigating claims that the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, a criminal network previously linked to threats against Bollywood figures, was responsible. Born Jai Hemant Shroff in 1990, the actor is the son of Bollywood star Jackie Shroff and film producer Ayesha Shroff. He made his film debut in the 2014 romantic-action film Heropanti and became known for his martial arts skills, elaborate stunts and dance performances. His best-known films include the Baaghi franchise, War alongside Hrithik Roshan, and Bade Miyan Chote Miyan with Akshay Kumar. His most recent theatrical release was Baaghi 4 in 2025. Shroff has also filmed in the UAE. His 2022 action film Heropanti 2 , co-starring Tara Sutaria and Nawazuddin Siddiqui, was partly shot in Dubai and Al Ain. The production included filming at Telal Resort Al Ain, on the outskirts of the city, with Shroff and Sutaria visiting the location in February 2022. The attack took place at about 7pm, near Pushpa Narsee Park in Juhu, as Shroff was returning home after playing football. Police said three men approached on a motorcycle, with two opening fire on the actor's vehicle before fleeing. Shroff escaped without serious injury, although some reports said he sustained minor abrasions. His driver suffered a gunshot wound to the hand, while another driver nearby was also injured. Both received hospital treatment. Videos circulating online appear to show the attackers firing at Shroff's car. Two men identifying themselves as Anil Pandit and Harman Sandhu have claimed responsibility for the shooting, alleging links to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. The criminal network, named after imprisoned gangster Lawrence Bishnoi, has previously been associated with threats against Bollywood figures, particularly Salman Khan. A message circulated online after the shooting reportedly warned film industry figures against working with Khan, suggesting a possible motive for the attack. However, police have not conclusively established who was responsible, nor have they verified the claims made on behalf of the gang. Mumbai police have formed 15 teams to investigate the shooting, examining CCTV footage and tracing the attackers' movements. Investigators have reportedly recovered a motorcycle, believed to have been used in the escape, near Andheri railway station. One person has reportedly been detained for questioning, although police have yet to establish the identities of those responsible. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has ordered a thorough investigation.

title: Dubai Investments to list DIP Holding shares in first DFM IPO this year
description: Company plans to sell 20% stake in Dubai Investments Park operator
content: Dubai Investments , a Dubai-listed conglomerate, is selling a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year. The deal will comprise the sale of 1.74 billion shares by existing shareholders in DIP Holding, which owns the mixed-use development Dubai Investments Park, the company said on Monday. Parent Dubai Investments will continue to control the remaining 80 per cent shareholding in DIP Holding, contingent on the offering size remaining unchanged and all shares on sale being allocated to investors, it said. Subscriptions for the sale are set to open on October 27 and will run until November 3. Final pricing for the deal will be announced on November 4. DIP Holding shares are expected to start trading on the Dubai Financial Market on November 11, according to the offer document. "Our IPO marks an important milestone in DIP Holding’s journey and reflects the strength and resilience of our differentiated, infrastructure-like business model, said Omar Al Mesmar, chief executive of DIP Holding. "Looking ahead, we see clear opportunities to build on this foundation." The deal breaks the lull in the IPO market in the UAE. The Arab world’s second-largest economy was a hotbed for public floats, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of IPOs over the past few years. The Middle East IPO market last year slowed after it was hit by lower oil prices , geopolitical unrest and weaker post-listing performances. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, has further disrupted the already slowing momentum as companies put their plans of tapping equities markets to raise capital on hold. Dubai Investments , in which the sovereign investment fund Investment Corporation of Dubai holds a stake, was among the UAE companies that expressed intentions to list shares in its units before war-driven volatility sapped deal volumes. The company in September last year said that it was in talks with banks and planned to list up to 25 per cent of Dubai Investments Park. Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate. DIP Holding intends to adopt a semi-annual cash dividend distribution policy. The company expects to pay annualised dividends of Dh700 million, Dh725 million and Dh750 million for 2026, 2027 and 2028 financial years, respectively. In 2029, the company expects to pay dividends in line with, or above the 2028 payout, it said in the offer document. "Our intention to list DIP Holding on the Dubai Financial Market represents a natural next step in a journey that began more than 25 years ago," said DIP Holding chairman Khalid bin Kalban. "What began as an ambitious vision for an integrated mixed-use destination has developed into a fully established and highly sought-after platform supporting businesses and communities across the logistics, industrial, commercial and residential sectors."

title: T20 cricket at LA 2028 Olympics: India, Pakistan and the qualification race explained
description: Men's teams at Games to be decided by ICC rankings at end of the year
content: Despite India's successful title defence at the T20 World Cup earlier in the year and their win at the Asian Games, it has been a pretty grim in bilateral series. India were blanked by Ireland and England in T20s in their backyard across six completed matches , while the West Indies further exposed the weaknesses in India's T20 armour, levelling the T20 series 2-2 on Saturday. New captain Shreyas Iyer has had a rough start to his reign, although he has an Asian Games gold medal to show for his efforts. Generally, bilateral matches do not count for much outside a World Cup cycle. But there is an incentive this year for teams to maintain their standards - qualification spots for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics . Cricket is returning to the Olympics after well over a century. As expected, T20 is the chosen format. However, just like at the Asian Games, there are limited spots available, even though there are many competitive teams in world cricket. Japan recently came within two runs of defeating double world champions India. A total of six nations will compete in the men’s and women’s T20 competitions, with at least one team each from Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa. Hosts USA are also set to get one of the spots.
