The women's section has largely been locked in, with Australia, Great Britain (England), India and South Africa qualifying by virtue of being the highest-placed eligible finishers at the end of the women's T20 World Cup earlier in the year. However, the criteria is different for the men's side. The highest-ranked teams from Africa, Asia, Europe and Oceania on December 31, 2026, will qualify for LA 2028. England are the top-ranked T20 team and would have qualified even if they weren't as there are no other European teams in the top 10. South Africa (ranked fifth) too are certain to be through as their next closest challengers Zimbabwe (12th) are well behind in T20 rankings. Oceania sees a tougher battle between Australia and New Zealand, ranked third and fourth respectively but separated by a substantial 13 ranking points. In Asia, India look most likely to qualify automatically for the LA Olympics despite their recent struggles. India are ranked second in the world while their closest continental challengers Pakistan are sixth. However, there is a massive gap of 27 points between the two. India have five T20s against New Zealand and three against Sri Lanka remaining in the 2026 calendar. Even if they lose every single match, India will still only go down to third - according to the ICC's rankings predictor - and remain out of reach for their neighbours. India, therefore, are almost certain to qualify for the 2028 LA Olympics T20s directly, especially since Pakistan have no T20 match scheduled for the rest of the year. However, the team in green can still make it to the Olympics. One final spot at the LA Olympics will be decided via a qualifier, where Pakistan might have to fight teams like New Zealand, Zimbabwe, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan. The West Indies will have a separate Games pathway. If the Windies gain automatic qualification spot via rankings by the end of the year, there will be a dedicated qualifier event to determine the Caribbean nation which will then feature in the Olympics qualifier.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed holds talks with Macron on energy and AI
description: French President on tour of the Gulf to strengthen energy and defence ties
content: President Sheikh Mohamed received France's President Emmanuel Macron in Abu Dhabi on Monday. An official reception ceremony was held for Mr Macron, who is in the UAE on an official visit as part of his tour of the Gulf. Mr Macron is seeking to deepen energy and defence ties with Gulf states during a three-day visit that started on Monday with Kuwait and the UAE, as his government struggles with a cost-of-living crisis fuelled by high energy prices. Talks in Abu Dhabi focused on energy, artificial intelligence and the energy crisis caused by the Iran war. As the conflict unfolds, France and other European nations have sought to portray themselves as key allies of Gulf states, including the UAE, despite being able to do little to contain a war to which they are not party. “Key topics included developments in the Middle East and efforts to contain their repercussions on maritime security and global energy supplies,” state news agency Wam reported. Earlier, Mr Macron had a one-on-one meeting with the Emir of Kuwait, Sheikh Meshal, for an hour and a half on Monday. He flew to Kuwait City only hours after a giving solemn televised address to the French nation in which he promised his Gulf tour would help secure energy supplies. In the UAE, the reception was attended by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohamed, Deputy Chairman of the Presidential Court for Special Affairs, and Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad, adviser to the UAE President. This is likely to be one of Mr Macron’s last major Gulf trips before the presidential election in France in six months, at which he is ineligible to run again. The President's joint offer with the UK in April to launch an international maritime coalition to defend ships in the Strait of Hormuz awaits a political agreement between the US and Iran. There were no statements in Kuwait City but a series of agreements focused on defence and AI. The executive vice-president for Airbus sales, Benoit de Saint Exupery, and the executive director of the Kuwait Investment Authority, Sheikh Saud Salem Abdulaziz Al Sabah, signed a partnership that includes the renewal of the Kuwait Airways fleet. The chief executives of industry giants TotalEnergies and Engie will be travelling with Mr Macron, as well as the president of Campus AI, a major technological complex under construction near Paris that benefits from billions in UAE funding. Also present were French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure. The visit, which will end in Qatar on Wednesday after a stop in Bahrain, comes despite France's worst civil unrest in years , with more than 2,000 people arrested for torching and ransacking property. In a statement on Sunday night, Mr Macron said he felt “anger” and “shame”. He has vowed that those responsible for looting and destruction will “have to pay”. The government is expected to put forward concrete proposals for young people this week. The UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar have all had energy sites attacked during the US-Iran war , which has also curtailed oil exports through the strait. With Yemen's Houthi rebels now pushing for control of a second strait, the Bab Al Mandeb strait, there are fears the global energy crunch could worsen. “In light of the crisis gripping the Middle East, the President will continue his efforts with regional leaders to promote a return to stability and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” an Elysee Palace source said. “Discussions will also focus on securing and diversifying our energy supplies and their transport routes, with the aim of limiting the impact of the energy crisis on the daily lives of French people.” Mr Macron has made several trips to the UAE as French President. Last December he met Sheikh Mohamed at the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi and spoke to French troops based in the country. Earlier visits included his attendance at the Cop28 climate summit , which took place in Dubai in 2023, and a trip in 2017 to the opening ceremony of Louvre Abu Dhabi . Mr Macron's most recent Middle East trip was a visit to Damascus in July – the first appearance in post-civil-war Syria by a major western leader. For Mr Macron, diplomacy abroad offers an opportunity to project leadership on the international stage. But with unrest escalating at home, keeping the focus on France’s role in the world is becoming more difficult. The question is whether those diplomatic efforts will cut through the growing anger at home.

title: Adesanya wizardry and Khabib choking out Poirier: Five memorable UFC title fights in Abu Dhabi
description: We take a trip down memory lane as part of the build-up to UFC 333 at Etihad Arena
content: Abu Dhabi fight fans will witness two title fights when the world's leading MMA promotion returns to the UAE this Saturday, October 24. Topping the bill is featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski , who puts his belt on the line against top-ranked Movsar Evloev. The co-main event sees Petr Yan defend his bantamweight belt against the man he dethroned last December, Merab Dvalishvili. Abu Dhabi has a long history of memorable title bouts. We take a look back at five of the best. When the Covid-19 pandemic caused most of the world to shut down, the UFC needed a new home to keep events going. Abu Dhabi stepped in and Yas Island became Fight Island. Strict protocols included journalists holed up in nearby hotels for weeks at a time, having meals delivered to their rooms daily. Abu Dhabi helped keep the sport of MMA alive. Crowds at Fight Island were restricted, which made the sound of every taunt audible, every punch and kick echo around the specially constructed venue. Those lucky enough to attend UFC 253 got to see a wizard at work. Israel Adesanya was at the peak of his powers, putting his undefeated 19-0 record and his UFC middleweight title on the line against Paulo Costa, who probably weighed the 185lb limit for the few seconds he had to stand on the scales at weigh-in. Adesanya delivered a striking masterclass, picking off the Brazilian at will. Adesanya chewed up Costa's lead leg before a second-round TKO cemented his place as the best middleweight since the great Anderson Silva. If Fight Island was notable for the eerie silence, UFC 242 will be remembered for its deafening roars. The reason for the decibels amping up was down to one man: Khabib Nurmagomedov. Khabib drew energetic crowds throughout fight week. Abu Dhabi had erected a venue specifically for the event on Yas Island called The Arena . Over 13,000 were in attendance, many sporting Khabib's famous “papakha” headpiece. In 2019, he was at his brilliant best . The Dagestani destroyer put his UFC lightweight title on the line against interim champ Dustin Poirier. From the first round, Nurmagomedov established control, wrestling the American to the ground, softening him up with crunching ground-and-pound and attempting several submissions. He finally landed one in Round 3, with Poirier forced to tap out as Nurmagomedov cinched in a rear-naked choke. He jumped the octagon fence to hug UFC president Dana White, a stark contrast to his post-fight antics following his win over Conor McGregor the previous year, an incident that lives on in infamy. Nurmagomedov was magnanimous in victory; Poirier humble in defeat. A love affair between Abu Dhabi and the undefeated Russian was established and endures to this day. Even in retirement, he still gets the biggest pop from the crowd at UFC Abu Dhabi events. Alexander 'The Great' is no stranger to these shores. His headline bout at UFC 333 will be the fourth time the Australian has fought in Abu Dhabi. Volkanovski had ended Holloway’s reign at the top of the featherweight division in December 2019, earning a unanimous decision few had predicted. He was quick to grant the Hawaii native a rematch, knowing another victory over a fighter as talented as Holloway would offer legitimacy to his claim as the new ruler of the 145lb division. That fight took place at UFC 251 and was an absolute tear-up. Holloway came out of the gates firing, using creative kicks and punch combinations behind a masterful jab. Volkanovski showed true grit to hang tough, grab a foothold in the contest, and slowly assert his own dominance. The scorecards would later reveal all three judges had scored the first two rounds to Holloway, with rounds 3 and 4 for Volkanovski. Fighters have a sense of the way the fight is going, and so both probably knew it would all come down to the final round to determine who walked off with the strap. Volkanovski was judged to have edged it – a decision that still rankles with Holloway to this day . Either way, Abu Dhabi got to witness two of the best featherweights of all time go toe-to-toe for championship gold. Charles Oliveira arrived in Abu Dhabi ahead of UFC 280 still recognised by many as the unofficial champion of the lightweight division. The Brazilian had been controversially stripped of the belt before his fight with Justin Gaethje at UFC 274 for missing the 155lb weight limit – by half a pound. Many thought the punishment was excessive, since non-title fights are allowed a half-pound exemption. It is the only time in UFC history a title has been vacated due to missing weight. Officially, his bout with Islam Makhachev was for the vacant belt. Oliveira had been on a tear, the division's bogeyman, owner of a host of UFC records, including most submission wins, most finishes and most Performance of the Night bonuses. Makhachev, the protege of Khabib Nurmagomedov, boasted a record of 23 wins against one defeat, and his ascent had many wondering if he would one day surpass the accomplishments of his mentor. The UFC had pitted the two best in its deepest division against each other. Oliveira was on his back early, a position he is infinitely comfortable with, but the Dagestani's grappling and ground control proved the superior weapons. A straight left in Round 2 floored Oliveira, and Makhachev did not need a second invite. More used to making his opponents tap, the sight of Oliveira frantically signalling that Makhachev's squeeze on a perfectly executed arm bar was too hot to handle is a sight few will forget. Glover Teixeira was finally given another shot at UFC gold at UFC 267 when he faced light heavyweight belt holder Jan Blachowicz. Teixeira thought his chance had passed him by. For four years, he was unable to fight in the US due to prolonged visa and immigration issues. Bureaucracy and legal red tape had robbed him of his best years in the UFC. But at age 42, he was given a second title shot, seven years after his first, a defeat to the indomitable Jon Jones. Blachowicz, four years Teixeira's junior, entered as a heavy favourite and was expected to dominate with his legendary “Polish power”. Teixeira had other ideas. The Brazilian immediately implemented his grappling, grounding Błachowicz in the first round. In the second, after staggering the champion with a left hook, Teixeira executed another takedown, quickly transitioned to the back, and forced Błachowicz to tap to a rear-naked choke . No one who has met or spent any sort of time with Teixeira begrudged him his moment. His victory over Błachowicz made him the oldest first-time UFC champion, the second oldest overall after Randy Couture and only the third fighter to win a world title in his forties (Couture and Daniel Cormier are the other two).

title: France in flames: Emmanuel Macron urges calm after worst unrest in years
description: Historic town hall torched, shops ransacked and 2,000 arrested in nationwide protests
content: President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday as France reeled from one of its most violent ​days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested and hundreds of police injured. "Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people ⁠do this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation. "Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and ​shame." Nationwide demonstrations ⁠erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police across the country. One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made more than 2,000 arrests across France, while more than 600 officers were ⁠injured, the Interior Minister said. “It's like a war zone here,” said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who was in Paris with his ​children and said the protests forced him ‌to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, a trouble hotspot on Saturday. More than half a million people joined marches in ​scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent about rising living costs and declining public services. The unrest laid bare the deep anger at Mr Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power. Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate grievances and ​their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc. The government has blamed the violence on hard-left and ultra-left groups, as well as criminals who it said instigated the looting. While many protested peacefully, violent groups attacked public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers. A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday. In Paris, smashed shop windows, burnt-out bicycles and spray-painted slogans bore witness to a day that began largely with peaceful demonstrations but descended into violence. In Limoges, in the south-west of the country, mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos ​after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set on fire and largely destroyed in an arson attack on ‌Saturday. The violence drew comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated ⁠Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral. “There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town ​hall, and the people inside feared for their lives,” Mr Guerin told Reuters. He threatened to resign if the city ​did not receive the funds ‌needed to repair the building. The unrest has increased pressure on Mr Macron and his government before a ⁠presidential election due next year. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged ⁠support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. “Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” Mr Lescure said in a statement. Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave said up to 100 stores had been looted in his city, while Marseille mayor Benoit Payan announced emergency financial aid to support those businesses affected by the violence. French retailer Carrefour's chief executive Alexandre Bompard told the broadcaster BFMTV ​that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into tens of millions of euros. The youth protests began last month over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living.

title: Who is Hasan Piker, the Twitch streamer who praised the Houthis?
description: Support for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed puts Piker in Republican crosshairs before midterms
content: The US Republican Party has an unlikely new political target before the midterm elections: Hasan Piker, a Turkish-American socialist who has fiercely criticised Israel, praised the Houthi rebels in Yemen and is backing the Democratic candidate in a key Senate race. Although most American voters remain unfamiliar with him, Piker's views on US foreign policy are attracting growing attention as President Donald Trump and the Republican Party amplify his commentary. In interviews and during thousands of hours of live opining on the Twitch streaming platform, Piker has condemned Israel as a “fascist” state, described ultra-Orthodox Jews as “inbred” and spoken in support of the Houthis, Hezbollah and Hamas. He also said “America deserved 9/11" and has called the US the world's “top terrorist organisation”. Piker later said he would be more careful about using the word “inbred” and has apologised for his comments about the September 11, 2001, attacks, saying the wording was inappropriate. Broadcasting under the online moniker HasanAbi, Piker has amassed more than three million followers on Twitch and about two million subscribers on his YouTube channel. Much of the 35-year-old broadcaster's audience is men under 30, and he has been described as a Joe Rogan or a Charlie Kirk for the left. “The way that I'm portrayed in the media is an America-hating communist Islamist fundamentalist who wants to secretly do jihad, and then also at the same time, very woke and gay,” he told NPR in an interview this week. “So there's this weird inconsistency in their messaging. I don't fully understand it, but who I am is very simple: I'm a socialist. I'm an anti-imperialist. I want what's best for Americans and I want what's best for everyone all around the world.” Piker's comments have drawn condemnation from some quarters for years, but criticism has recently reached a fever pitch, thanks partly to his enthusiastic support of Abdul El-Sayed , the Democrat running for the US Senate in a key race in Michigan. If elected, Mr El-Sayed, who has faced overt Islamophobia from Mr Trump, would become the first Muslim senator. Piker has praised Mr El-Sayed's long-standing support for universal health care, an idea known in the US as Medicare For All, and called him a “wonderful candidate”. The two have made appearances together at campaign events, and Mr El-Sayed has appeared on Piker's Twitch stream. Mr El-Sayed has faced repeated questions about Piker's controversial statements. He condemned Piker’s “America deserved 9/11” remark, calling it “a dumb statement”, but he has resisted calls to disavow the polemicist altogether. Facing a very tight Senate race in Michigan that will help decide whether the Democrats can reclaim the upper chamber, Republicans have sought to capitalise on Mr El-Sayed's relationship with Piker and tie him to his most controversial statements. Mr Trump last month called Piker a “terrible liability” and a “communist”, while Republican-aligned advertising in Michigan has used clips of his most provocative remarks to attack Mr El-Sayed. One advertisement accuses Mr El-Sayed of giving “comfort” to the hatred behind the September 11 attacks, splicing Piker’s claim that America “deserved 9/11” with footage of the two men campaigning together. “Of course, I say incendiary things, but it's not reflected on in the same way when someone who's white, Christian, born and raised in America is saying incendiary things,” Piker told NPR. He said he had never been formally involved in Mr El-Sayed's campaign and said the Republican effort to associate candidates with his most controversial remarks was an attempt to distract from the administration's economic record. But Piker's foreign policy positions are only part of the reason he has become a target for Republicans. His growing influence among younger Americans has given him a prominent platform as the Democratic Party struggles to define its identity. Since losing to Mr Trump in 2024, the Democrats have been unable to agree on whether they should skew further to the left or stick with the more cautious, centrist politics favoured by party elders. Piker began his career in political commentary with The Young Turks , the progressive online news network founded by his uncle Cenk Uygur, before starting on Twitch. He also supported New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani , a democratic socialist that Democrat doyens were initially nervous to endorse. His support provided more fodder for Republicans as they seek to portray Democrats as too radical for mainstream voters. When it comes to the Middle East, Piker has drawn intense scrutiny over his criticism of Israel. In January 2026, he described Hamas as “a thousand times better than a fascist settler colonial apartheid state”, referring to Israel. In an appearance on the Pod Save America podcast in April, he was challenged about the comparison and whether he genuinely believed it. “I stand by that,” he replied. He went on to say he would choose Hamas over Israel in such a comparison, describing himself as a “lesser evil voter”. He also acknowledged that the remark was intended to provoke. Still, he told NPR that he did not necessarily regard all of his commentary as “perfect”. “Think about what it means to speak for 21,000 [cumulative] hours about politics every single day, for eight hours a day,” he said. “I think it's shocking that there's only a handful of clips that people deploy.” Recent commentary on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis has also drawn scrutiny. In a lengthy Twitch broadcast, Piker argued that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, were not simply an Iranian proxy but a movement pursuing its own political interests and a degree of sovereignty within Yemen. Piker has also defended Houthi missile and drone attacks as legitimate anti-imperialist resistance, despite the threat they pose to Gulf civilian infrastructure and international shipping. He has praised the Houthis' ability to withstand US military pressure. In a stream last year, he said: “What the Houthis are doing, on the other hand, is resistance. And it’s not only moral, but it’s just.” The US designated the Houthis a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in March 2025, but Washington has also sought to limit its military entanglements with the group. Under a ceasefire brokered by Oman in May that year, the Trump administration agreed to halt its bombing campaign in return for a commitment by the Houthis not to attack US vessels. But Mr Trump has suggested the relatively hands-off approach may change after the midterms. “I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!” he said this week.

title: Rana Begum comes full circle with Taking Form, a colourful new exhibition in Dubai
description: Nearly two decades after her first solo exhibition at The Third Line, the British-Bangladeshi artist returns with new work that reflects her evolving relationship with colour
content: Two swabs of colour meet at the corners. An orange, bold and of a sunset hue, is overtaken by a smear of forest green. The two colours don’t mix, making how they interact all the more remarkable. The original vivacity of the orange is subdued underneath the green, with only a dark trace of its outline remaining. Like the rest of the watercolour works in Rana Begum ’s exhibition at The Third Line, the piece shows us that not all colours are equal. The shade of green that overpowers the orange finds its match in another work against a deep, royal purple. In yet another piece, that same purple runs across a luminescent yellow, affecting and being affected by the colour just the same. Elsewhere, trio of pinks are chained together, revealing deeper hues that veer towards orange. Much like the law of the jungle favours the strong, there is a law of colours that is often only revealed upon application. The nature of the pigment, as well as the material on which it is applied all play a part, as does, of course, the bias of the eye. Begum tests these interactions across various mediums in Taking Form. The watercolours are the smallest pieces in the exhibition. Yet, they offer a key into how to view the other, more monumental pieces within the show. “I felt the show needed these works on paper,” Begum tells The National . “I’ve been thinking about the tapestries, about the paintings for a while. But it’s all kind of in my head, and I wanted to express that fluidity and the way I have been thinking about colour.” The centrepiece of the exhibition is a trio of tapestry pieces, suspended from the high ceiling of the gallery. Much like the watercolours, they express an interplay of colours. The technical aspects of the weaving is stunning. Dark indigo threads run long against pyramids of colour of varying shades of blue and burgundy. The common threads are inconspicuous when viewed from a short distance. Up close, the commonality blooms. It is a different interplay of colour than the ones on the watercolours, alluding less to jungle laws than to a more cohesive interaction between the hues. “It took me a whole to figure out how the colours would interact,” Begum says. “The piece, in the front, you see ridges. You stand on the left side, you see one colour that stands out more, and as you walk around to the right, you see another.” The reverse side of the tapestries, rather than showing the needlework of the piece, exhibits a pattern of its own. This required some experimentation, Begum says. “The weaving technique is really interesting and fascinating how that works,” she says. “I worked with a UK-based company Dash & Miller that designed the weave. They were able to come up with the ridges. “We had to identify a different set of rules for the back. You could have just two colours or more, but it just can't be the same as what's at the front. The two sides are woven as one. There is a front, middle and back – but even on the back, you see some of the front seeping through. The process is really interesting.” The paintings within taking form continue these explorations of colour on linen canvases as well as medium-density fibreboard. Here, Begum lets the colour accentuate the properties of the materials they are applied on. The chips and straws of the fibreboard are highlighted in shades of pink. The linen’s tufts, meanwhile, are all the more heightened in colourful square triangle compositions. Given her fluidity in testing colour interactions, it is surprising to hear Begum say that she “struggled with colour” when she first began delving into abstraction as an artist, veering away from her early, figurative works. “I really struggled with colour. I felt like I was kind of living and breathing colour, from the culture that I come from growing up, partly in Bangladesh , wearing saris and salwar kameez, constantly surrounded by colour. You’d think I’d be very confident, but actually, I really struggled when I went into abstraction. I had a long list of things that I needed to explore, and one of those things was colour.” Her first solo exhibition, Colour Codes, which was held at The Third Line in 2007, was informed by these interactions. “I used that opportunity to kind of really focus on colour and relationship with one another,” she says. Begum used various kinds of adhesive tape that she had collected from around the world, applying them in lines and coating them with resin to test colour interactions. “That material gave me the opportunity to be more instinctive. I could peel the tape off and apply another colour. You could see things happening quite fast.” Almost two decades later, and Begum is now marking her fifth exhibition at The Third Line with Taking Form. She returns as a globally-established artist – Begum is the winner of the 2017 Abraaj Group Art Prize , as well as a member of the Royal Academy of Arts . Taking Form, as such, represents the continuing experiments of Begum’s long-standing fascination with colour. The artist calls her fifth exhibition at The Third Line a “full circle” moment, but much like the circle of the archetypal hero’s journey, Begum returns as an artist changed, more confident and certain with how she conducts her experiments, displaying a mastery over the colours that once unnerved her. Rana Begum's exhibition Taking Form is on at The Third Line until November 10

title: Oman could become a cornerstone of Gulf energy security, but risks remain
description: Iran war has strengthened sultanate's strategic role, but new energy projects bring financial and security risks.
content: In its heyday, Oman’s maritime empire stretched from Mozambique and Zanzibar to Gwadar in Pakistan. The modern sultanate does not extend so far, but it still holds an important position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has gained economically from the conflict, while seeking to mediate peace. Now it could make itself a foundation stone of Gulf security. The war has forced the IMF to downgrade economic growth forecasts across the region. But Oman is expected to expand by 4.1 per cent. It has managed to bring down its debt burden from a worrying 68 per cent of GDP in 2020 to a much more comfortable 35 to 36 per cent of GDP. The sultanate benefits from record oil and gas exports at a time of high prices, as well as from the rest of its heavy industrial base in refined petroleum, fertilisers and aluminium. The endless queues of lorries to and from the UAE border tell eloquently of Oman’s essential role as a transit route for goods . In May 2024, in a fortunate piece of advance planning, construction began on Hafeet Rail, which will link the industrial city of Sohar with Al Ain and Abu Dhabi . This is intended to be finished by the final quarter of 2027 and will be an invaluable route for industrial inputs to the UAE and for the export of finished products such as steel and aluminium. By late next year, Oman should also finish a direct connection to the GCC electricity grid, allowing it to exchange more power. This will benefit its fast-growing renewable sector. Oman has not stayed entirely out of the front line during the war. The oil terminals of Mina Al Fahal, Duqm and Salalah, and Sohar were attacked by drones, and several ships have been struck in its mainland waters, not to mention all those hit while crossing the Omani lane of the Strait of Hormuz. But the sultanate has suffered much less physical damage and disruption than its Gulf neighbours. In 2016, the oil minister at the time, Mohammed Al Rumhi announced plans for an enormous 200-million barrel petroleum storage terminal at Duqm on its south-east coast. By comparison, Fujairah, which has also emerged as a strategic node during the war and is a central global refuelling point, has about 120 million barrels of capacity. Muscat’s intention was to reorient its crude oil exports from the crowded northern coast to a new terminal, which would also have the happy effect of shifting them further from Iran. It also had in mind that other GCC nations might connect to Duqm, to give themselves an option in case of a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait, which has no alternative outlet, was said to be interested. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation eventually invested in the major new refinery there. But it seemed far-fetched that a new pipeline route would be needed. Eventually only 5.2 million barrels of crude storage were built, mostly to serve the refinery. Drones, missiles, and Washington’s decision to confront Tehran on the battlefield changed that. Now Saudi Aramco is studying a pipeline to Duqm, estimated to span 1,000 to 1,200 kilometres through the dunes of the Empty Quarter, and expected to cost $7 billion. This new node has the advantage of bypassing not just Hormuz, but also the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi exports through the kingdom's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu have been hampered by attacks from the Houthis in Yemen and Iranian allies in Iraq. A Kuwait Oil Company representative told the World Energy Congress in Riyadh last week that his country was evaluating a possible route to Duqm, as well as through the UAE or Saudi Arabia. This would most probably involve delivering oil by tanker to a Saudi or UAE port for onward transport, rather than transporting it all the way overland. State energy investor OQ has announced plans to expand Duqm’s storage to 10 million barrels within three years, and eventually 40 million barrels. It is also considering buying two tankers to hold 4 million barrels in floating storage. In September, it signed an agreement with a German company to design a new marine bunkering site at the port of Shinas, just south of the UAE border. This would be about a third the size of Fujairah, which ranks as the world’s second or third-largest ship refuelling hub. Nevertheless, Oman’s centrality to the Gulf’s new infrastructure carries three risks. First, its sites are not much further from Iran than the rest of the Gulf is, and can still be attacked if hostilities escalate. Indeed, Muscat might even put itself in the line of fire if Tehran decides it cannot tolerate too much by-passing of the totemic Strait of Hormuz. The second is almost the opposite: if peace breaks out, much of this infrastructure might seem unnecessary. New pipelines will take from three to five years to build. By then, regional politics and security may look very different. Projects may be terminated halfway through, or left little-used. Oman does not have the deep pockets of its neighbours, who are able to invest heavily in strategic security. Third is that many of these projects are clearly competing with existing Gulf terminals. There is already some disquiet over Muscat’s apparent closeness to Tehran at times during its mediation. Most notably, this surfaced in the debate over tolls for use of the Strait, or essentially Iranian extortion. The other Gulf nations have suffered and spent heavily in the conflict. Of course, they want to leverage Oman’s strategic depth. But they do not want to make obsolete their own decades of massive investment in centres such as Fujairah, Jebel Ali and Yanbu, and new projects at sites such as Khor Fakkan, Al Rugaylat and Dibba. Past such ventures across Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have suffered from sabotage, nationalisation, or commercial breakdowns. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman wisely pointed out that successful multinational pipelines require stakeholders from all sides. Tying Gulf security to Oman needs not only sinews of steel, but political harmony.

title: Flydubai captain’s heroism reminds us of the best of humanity
description: Smit Machchhar has shown that our shared fate is not an abstract idea
content: In a world too often marked by division and self-interest, Capt Smit Machchhar has reminded millions that humanity’s greatest strength lies in its capacity for solidarity and selflessness even in the face of adversity . The flydubai captain’s actions aboard Flight 1073 on September 30, when he fought to protect his aircraft, passengers and crew, were nothing short of extraordinary. His interview to The National , in which he recounted the ordeal on what was meant to be a routine flight, offers a glimpse of the courage required to act when so many lives hang in the balance. At about 34,000 feet, and with an hour still go for touchdown, he was struck from behind by a co-pilot he had only met that morning, and who had shown no hint of what prosecutors later called a premeditated terrorist plot. Bleeding heavily and repeatedly losing consciousness, he heard the engines spool down as the Boeing 737 plunged. He somehow found the strength to reach the cabin door and pushed it open. All 172 people on board eventually survived . What was particularly striking about the interview was Capt Machchhar’s reluctance to take credit for his actions . He was quick to point to everyone else who helped – the cabin crew who treated him, the dentist who held pressure on his wounds for close to an hour, the passengers who subdued the attacker and those who took the controls to ensure a safe landing. “If I have to say how many people were trying to control the situation, I would say a million,” he said. “I know it doesn’t make sense, but, yeah, I would say a million people were trying to take over control.” These remarks, as well as accounts from others on the flight, make one thing clear: while Capt Machchhar’s courage was the spark, the rescue was a collective effort. That is a lesson worth absorbing. In the age of atomisation – in which people are increasingly driven by personal goals to the point of being insular and detached – the actions taken by all those on board should give the rest of us a sense that we are all in this together . Such instances also offer hope and optimism in our capacity to do good, to fight the good fight and to act in the larger interest of humanity. Outstanding as the pilot was on that fateful day, we witness the quieter versions of the same instinct whenever a crisis, such as a natural disaster , strikes. Think of the many times we have seen or heard of neighbours pulling neighbours from rubble, volunteers wading through floodwater, strangers opening their homes, and countries helping countries regardless of their bilateral relations. During the interview, Capt Machchhar thanked the UAE for his care and the chance to return to his family. He spoke of praying for his children in the darkest moments. Most telling, however, was his insistence that he did not give up during those moments. That refusal to let others die is an important reminder that humanity’s shared fate is not an abstract idea . There are, of course, practical lessons to be learnt from the September 30 attempted terror attack on Flight 1073 – the captain himself expects a review of aviation security. But it is the human lessons that will – and should – endure for years to come.

title: Your lung health should not have to wait
description: Early intervention changes outcomes for those living with pulmonary fibrosis, writes Ousama Al Haj, General Manager and Head of Human Pharma, Near East and UAE, Boehringer Ingelheim
content: Estimates suggest that as many as 9.2 million people worldwide may be living with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or progressive pulmonary fibrosis. But there are no statistics that tell how many people put off going to the doctor to get that nagging cough checked. Pulmonary fibrosis is progressive and irreversible. It scars the lungs, making them stiff and rigid where they should be soft and elastic. Over time, the impact compounds. Daily activities become exhausting. The disease carries a heavy burden, not just physical but emotional and social. Patients lose independence. Families lose time. Yet studies indicate that diagnosis may be delayed by approximately one to two years, as early symptoms can be mistaken for ageing, reduced fitness or more common respiratory conditions. During that time, patients are confused. They attribute symptoms to ageing. They assume it will pass. They hesitate to see their doctor, perhaps afraid of what they might hear, or simply not recognising the signs for what they are. The Elevator Campaign speaks to this hesitation directly. That moment in the elevator. That conversation you know you need to have but keep postponing. That appointment you push to next month, then the month after. The field of pulmonary fibrosis has evolved considerably. We have moved from accepting minimal options to understanding the critical role of early intervention. Yet we have also learned that simply having a treatment is not enough. Treatment adherence, tolerability, and patient quality of life remain central challenges. If patients cannot tolerate a therapy, or if the burden of side effects eclipses the benefits of treatment, then we have not truly solved the problem. This is where the conversation must shift. The question is no longer just whether a treatment slows disease progression. It is whether that treatment enables patients to remain on their treatment journey prescribed to them to manage their condition. The approval of a new treatment option in the UAE signals something important: the field is advancing. Not as a disease patients must manage alone with limited options and difficult trade-offs, but as a condition where early detection and sustained, tolerable treatment can materially impact the patient journey. This is not about replacing one drug with another. It is about what becomes possible when treatment is accessible, sustainable, and truly patient-centered. When patients can commit to therapy without sacrificing what they do in their daily life, then we have truly started to make impact. But one new therapy is not enough. The gaps remain enormous. Up to half of those diagnosed remain untreated entirely. The disease remains underdiagnosed and often misunderstood. Your lungs deserve the same vigilance you give to every other part of your health. A persistent cough is not normal. Breathlessness with minimal exertion is not aging. Fatigue that worsens is not something to wait out. Speak to your healthcare professional. That is what we are pitching for. For your lungs. For your ability to breathe without struggle. For the future you deserve.
