Financial and insurance activities were among the strongest performers in the first half, expanding 8.8 per cent in real terms to Dh65.9 billion, compared with Dh60.6 billion a year earlier. The sector's contribution to GDP increased to 14 per cent from 12.5 per cent, highlighting its growing importance to the emirate's economy. The expansion comes as the Dubai International Financial Centre continues to attract international financial institutions , with the number of companies operating at the financial hub exceeding 10,000 in the first half of the year. Healthcare and social work activities recorded the fastest growth, expanding 14.3 per cent, while information and communication activities increased 2.7 per cent. Construction grew 2.4 per cent in real terms, generating Dh33.2 billion in value added, while government services expanded 2.9 per cent. However, several major sectors contracted during the period. Wholesale and retail trade, Dubai's largest economic activity, declined 6 per cent in real terms, although it continued to account for 20.5 per cent of GDP. Transport and storage fell 7.4 per cent, while real estate activity contracted 2.5 per cent in constant prices, despite growing 5.4 per cent at current prices. Manufacturing also declined 0.9 per cent in real terms. The slowdown reflects wider economic challenges across the region, with the UAE's economy expanding just 0.4 per cent in the first half amid disruption caused by the Iran war. However, despite the geopolitical headwinds, trade in the first six months of this year through Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez) free zones achieved another record. The total value of trade across its three economic zones climbed 17 per cent annually to Dh246 billion, Dubai Media Office said on Sunday. The results marked Diez's sixth consecutive year of record first-half trade performance, reflecting the confidence of investors and international trade stakeholders in Dubai's and the UAE's position at the heart of global trade. The value of imports during the first half rose to Dh134.8 billion, a 14 per cent increase compared to the same period last year. Re-exports grew by 22 per cent to about Dh109 billion. Trade volumes reached approximately 270,000 tonnes during the first half of the year, compared to approximately 298,000 tonnes during the same period in 2025, the media office said. Dubai is moving ahead with Dh2.1 trillion in projects covering housing, aviation and transport, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, as part of efforts to support long-term economic growth. Meanwhile, Dubai CommerCity announced a Dh1.8 billion expansion this month to boost its digital commerce sector and attract more technology investment. Mr Almarri said that continued growth across strategic sectors highlighted the strength of Dubai's economic fundamentals and its focus on long-term development. Dubai is pressing ahead with its D33 economic agenda, which aims to strengthen its position as a global business and investment centre. The emirate has also introduced measures to support businesses, including a Dh1.5 billion economic relief package announced in May to help sectors affected by regional uncertainty.

title: IPL 2027: Yuvraj Singh, Sourav Ganguly and Zaheer Khan lead coaching shake-up
description: Franchises ring changes ahead of 20th edition of T20 league
content: IPL 2027 will be the 20th edition of the T20 league, with the Indian cricket board planning to celebrate the milestone moment on a big scale. The teams are also busy. A number of sides have already made changes ahead of the new season, with most developments taking place at the management level. Here is the story so far ahead of IPL 2027. One of the bigger developments ahead of IPL 2027 is the recruitment of India’s multiple World Cup winner Yuvraj Singh as coach. Former India all-rounder Yuvraj was unveiled as Delhi Capitals' assistant and batting coach. It will be Yuvraj’s first official stint as coach, having earlier mentored young batters like Abhishek Sharma in his personal capacity. “I am excited to begin a new chapter in my life with the Delhi Capitals,” Yuvraj said in a statement. “I have an old association with the franchise and know the owners well, which makes this a special opportunity for me.” Delhi Capitals have once again undergone a major personnel change, coinciding with change of management control; the franchise’s co-owners exchange management control every two years. Former India captain Sourav Ganguly will be in charge of Delhi Capitals franchise after being appointed ⁠as head coach for the 2027 season. Ganguly will have his protege Yuvraj in the dugout as he embarks upon another stint with the franchise that is yet to the win the league title. Ganguly joined the Delhi franchise as an adviser in 2019 and also was the ⁠team's director of cricket in 2023/24. The former opener took over from Hemang Badani. The biggest move in the IPL happened at Chennai as Stephen Fleming stepped down as head coach of the highly successful Super Kings after 18 years in charge. Fleming had formed a wildly successful partnership with Chennai icon MS Dhoni, which brought in five IPL and two (defunct) Champions League T20 titles. However, with Dhoni largely out of the picture and the Super Kings struggling over the last three seasons, Fleming’s tenure came to an end. The former New Zealand captain quickly moved to a set-up that should suit his cricket philosophy – the England Test squad. Fleming took over from Brendon McCullum , who remains England’s white-ball coach, after a tumultuous year which was riddled with questionable player and team behaviour. Fleming’s former Chennai associate Eric Simons has joined him as Test bowling coach. The wicketkeeper batter returned to Delhi Capitals for the 2027 season after completing his trade from Lucknow Super Giants. Pant had become the most expensive Indian player in IPL history when he was acquired by Lucknow for a record $3.2 million in 2025 . But that price tag weighed him down as he failed to turn things around at the Super Giants, resulting in a trade that has seen Pant take a substantial pay cut. In return, Lucknow got the services of left-arm spinner Kuldeep Yadav. Both players returned to the cities where they played at the domestic level. For Pant, it will be a critical season as he seems to be slipping down the pecking order in Indian cricket, being frozen out of the T20 side and not considered in ODIs as well. A good IPL 2027 could see him force his way into the team for the ODI World Cup in southern Africa next year. The 2011 World Cup winner has been appointed as the new Chennai coach, taking over from Fleming, and reuniting with his former captain Dhoni who remains an active player on paper. Zaheer was with Mumbai Indians management from 2018 until 2022, before being named as mentor of Lucknow. Now, he takes over as head coach of the most successful franchise in IPL history, with the aim of forming a clear path ahead with the talismanic Dhoni expected to move further away from the playing side of the team. This seems like a never ending saga. India all-rounder Hardik Pandya left the Mumbai Indians franchise, enjoyed a wildly successful two seasons at Gujarat Titans, was brought back to Mumbai in a hugely controversial move and has been struggling there since, with Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav and Jasprit Bumrah also in leadership positions. Now, there is a strong possibility that Rohit is handed the captaincy once again, with the India opener having hit form at the international level in ODIs. Pandya, meanwhile, is struggling with fitness with multiple injuries this season and doubts over his long-term availability. Pandya, however, remains an attractive option for many franchises as he is one of the few quality all-rounders in the country with a proven record with title winning sides. The seam-bowling all-rounder could be traded ahead of IPL 2027. Elsewhere, Sunrisers Hyderabad brought left-arm seamer T. Natarajan back into the team, trading him from Delhi Capitals who got leg-spinner Zeeshan Ansari in return. Big changes are taking place at Mumbai Indians. The franchise parted ways with head coach Mahela Jayawardene . The Sri Lankan great was Mumbai's head coach for the last two seasons - his second stint with the franchise - and coincided with a leadership crisis where Pandya was brought in as captain despite the presence of MI veterans Rohit, Suryakumar and Bumrah. "Mumbai Indians has been a very special part of my journey for over a decade now," Jayawardene said in an statement. "The players, coaching team, and above all the fans have made this an experience I will always treasure."

title: UAE Property: 'Can I stay in my company-rented apartment after resigning?'
description: Person living in the property and legal tenant may not be the same person
content: Question: I recently relocated to Dubai for work and my employer has rented an apartment for me as part of my package. The tenancy contract is in the company's name and the company pays the rent directly to the landlord, although I'm the person living there with my family. I'm considering leaving the company for another job. The HR department has told me that if I resign, I may have to leave the apartment almost immediately because the company is technically the tenant. I assumed that because this is our family home and there is still plenty of time remaining on the tenancy contract, we'd be entitled to stay until it expires. Who actually has the rights in this situation – me or my employer? Michael, Dubai Answer: This is one of those situations where the person living in a property and the legal tenant aren't necessarily the same person. If your employer is named as the tenant on both the tenancy agreement and Ejari, then the contractual relationship with the landlord is primarily with the company, not you personally. Your right to occupy the apartment may therefore come from your employment package rather than from having an independent tenancy relationship with the landlord. I'd check three things before making any assumptions: the tenancy agreement, the Ejari registration and your employment contract or company housing policy. There may be specific provisions explaining what happens to company-provided accommodation when employment ends. I wouldn't assume that the remaining term of the tenancy automatically gives your family the right to remain. Equally, however, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to move. If you like the apartment, approach the landlord early. They may be happy to replace the corporate tenancy with a new agreement in your name once the company's obligations have been dealt with. You're already living in the property and presumably you've looked after it. From the landlord's perspective, retaining a known occupant may be preferable to remarketing the apartment and accepting the risk of a vacancy period. Just make sure any new arrangement is formally documented. Don't rely on an informal understanding that you can simply “take over” the company's tenancy. Q: I'm considering buying an off-plan apartment in Dubai and the developer is advertising a “guaranteed 10 per cent return for three years after handover”. On paper, it looks fantastic. The projected return is considerably higher than I could achieve from a normal long-term rental, and the broker says I don't need to worry about finding tenants because everything will be managed for me. What I'm struggling to understand is where the 10 per cent actually comes from. If the apartment doesn't generate enough rental income, is the developer legally required to make up the difference? And should I be suspicious when a guaranteed return looks much higher than normal market rent? Daniel, Manchester A: Whenever somebody uses the word “guaranteed” in an investment proposition, my next question is always: guaranteed by whom, and where exactly is that guarantee written down? Don't assess the investment on the headline percentage alone. Ask for the actual rental guarantee agreement and establish which legal entity is responsible for paying you. Is it the developer, management company or another company entirely? A guarantee is ultimately only as strong as the entity standing behind it. Then establish exactly how the 10 per cent is calculated. Is it based on the original purchase price, the amount you've paid, or another figure? Are service charges, furnishing costs, management fees and maintenance deducted before or after your guaranteed payment? I'd also want to know whether you're free to occupy or sell the apartment during the guarantee period and what happens to the arrangement if you do. There may be restrictions that aren't obvious from the headline advertisement. Most importantly, compare the promised income with the property's realistic open-market rental value. If a Dh2 million apartment would ordinarily rent for Dh120,000 a year, that's a 6 per cent gross yield. Someone promising Dh200,000 every year isn't creating the additional Dh80,000 through magic. There is an economic reason for it somewhere, and you need to understand where the money is coming from. Sometimes, these schemes are perfectly legitimate and genuinely useful to an investor. In other cases, part of the promised return may effectively have been incorporated into a higher purchase price. So I'd judge the property first and the guarantee second. Look at comparable prices, realistic rent, location, developer track record and likely resale demand without including the incentive. Then, ask yourself one simple question: if the guarantee disappeared tomorrow, would I still be happy owning this apartment at the price I'm paying? If the answer is no, I'd think very carefully before signing anything. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

title: Rarely seen on screen, Nagaland is now in the Oscars race thanks to Angh
description: Director Theja Rio reflects on what international recognition means for one of India's least-represented regions
content: When Angh , a film set in a remote corner of north-east India rarely depicted on screen, won the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, it made history in more ways than one. The debut feature by 31-year-old Naga filmmaker Theja Rio became the first Indian film to win the prestigious award, earning a place in the race for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards. Thanks to a change in Oscar eligibility rules, the victory means Angh can compete for consideration independently of India's official submission, the Marathi-language film Gondhal . Told primarily in Konyak , the language of one of Nagaland 's many indigenous Naga tribes, the film explores the tension between ancestral traditions and the arrival of Christianity in the region in the 1960s. For Rio, the international recognition is particularly meaningful. “Growing up, I've never seen Nagaland in a film before or in a series before,” he tells The National . “And very often, every time you introduce yourself, you're getting into the backdrops of where you come from and then you're having to describe geographically where exactly it is.” Rio first explored the story in a short film in 2019, inspired by a visit to Nagaland's Mon district three years earlier. But he soon realised that the characters and the cultural transformations he wanted to explore needed more room to develop, prompting him to expand the story into his first feature. The response since the Toronto victory has exceeded his expectations, he says. Rio returned to Nagaland last month to celebrations and messages of pride, while the film has attracted attention from across India and beyond. “It's been a fever dream,” he says. “It's just my debut feature and it's yet to release, but to receive the reactions we have received and the fact that anyone is interested in having to hear what I have to say is completely baffling, but something that I'm very grateful about. “And just being able to make our people feel represented is by far the most heartwarming thing.” It is a fitting response to a film concerned with identity and belonging, and with what happens when the world around a community changes faster than its people can adapt. Set in Nagaland in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba (played by Anghlong Konyak), an ageing Konyak village chief, and his son as they confront the arrival of a Christian missionary and the changes it brings to their traditional way of life. The story is not simply about the clash between two belief systems. It explores the uncertainty of people caught between generations, as familiar customs begin to disappear and new ideas reshape their understanding of the world. During his journey to Mon, a district in eastern Nagaland bordering Myanmar, Rio encountered elderly Konyak men with traditional facial tattoos whose appearances reflected a way of life that had largely disappeared. “Mon is a very interesting place in the sense that they still have a lot of the practices and a lot of the structures from their older traditions that is still exist, while at the same time, like the rest of Nagaland, it has also become very modern in a sense,” he explains. “There were a lot of the tattooed faces but they were all dressed in modern clothes.” The contrast fascinated him. Here were people whose faces carried the visible history of an earlier generation, yet who were living in a world transformed by religion, education and modernity. The encounter also connected with Rio's long-standing fascination with characters whose lives have been overtaken by history. “I wanted to make a film about those people who have gone through that phase of rapid transition in the 60s and the 70s,” he says. “I'm very interested and very passionate about characters that have been sort of left behind by time. There's something very tragic and melancholic about characters like that.” It was the combination of these two ideas – a community experiencing profound change and a character struggling to hold on to an older world – that eventually became Angh . The relationship between Christianity and indigenous Naga traditions is not merely a subject from the past, it's a question that touches Rio's own identity. Christianity is now deeply embedded in much of Nagaland's society, but its spread also coincided with the decline of ancestral beliefs and practices. Exploring that history can be sensitive, particularly when it involves examining the consequences of missionary activity. Rio, who is Christian, was determined not to portray either side as entirely right or wrong. “It was very important to not antagonise any side,” he says. “I see both sides of it, and that's why I feel all my characters have a lot of depth. They're not one-dimensional characters who are almost caricature like. They're not there to play a villain or there just to be the opposition of the other.” That approach shapes the relationship between the village chief and the missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall. “When you watch the film, you'll realise that the white priest comes with the best intention, but from Anghba's perspective, he poses a threat to the community and to the culture that he is trying to hold on to. “That's one of the reasons why I like to make films about things that I'm conflicted about rather than make films about things that I'm sure about, which is dangerously treading the propaganda line.” But how did a story so deeply rooted in Nagaland's history and culture strike a chord with an international jury at one of the world's biggest film festivals? At the Toronto International Film Festival, jury members praised Angh “for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking and deeply resonant portrait of a world”. “We praise the filmmaker’s vision, audacity and courage,” they said. For Rio, the film's universal appeal lies in its themes of rapid change and cultural preservation. “The film is something that is obviously very culturally specific, but thematically something that is very universal,” he says. “We're living in a time where we're dealing with great change happening at a rapid speed than it's ever been. So in that sense, it's quite topical as well. “There's also so much conversation about conservation of, not just the environment, but of culture. So I think the film is very topical in that sense.” When Rio was developing Angh as a short film in 2019, he had already realised the characters and their conflicts required a larger canvas. “I was struggling to compress the entire thing into a short film, and I knew it was always meant to be a feature. The characters, the conflict, it's just too big to be restricted into a short film format,” he says. At the time, however, he lacked the experience and resources to make a full-length production. The short film's positive reception on the festival circuit encouraged him to expand the screenplay. He subsequently studied at the National Film and Television School in the UK, where working on other projects gave him time away from the story. When he returned to it, he had gained experience and a new perspective on the material. Supporting him through much of that journey has been Nancy Nisa Beso, a long-time film producer whose career spans more than two decades across documentary, commercial and independent filmmaking. Beso has known Rio since childhood and has worked with him on several projects, including the original short film. The success of Angh is the culmination of years of dedication rather than an overnight breakthrough, she says. “Technically, while this is his first feature film, he has been working on films for the last 11 years of his life,” she says. “This is a product of 11 years of just working towards your skill and expanding what you built.” The feature presented numerous challenges, particularly when it came to casting. With few professional actors available locally, Rio and his team travelled through villages in the Mon region searching for people who could convincingly portray the characters. “We had no option but to cast non-actors because we don't have professional actors where we come from, so it wasn't necessarily a choice,” Rio says. The lead role eventually went to Konyak, a stand-up comedian Rio discovered on YouTube after struggling to find someone with the necessary screen presence. Rio's decision to shoot on 16mm film, despite its many logistical challenges, was equally deliberate. He had been influenced by archival photographs and footage of the region taken during the early years of missionary activity. “There's something about film that is so filled with nostalgia. Obviously, I wasn't around in the 60s. But it's something that has a texture that's so atmospheric and so mystique,” he says. The project also received backing from the Red Sea Fund, an initiative of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea International Film Festival supporting filmmakers from the Arab world, Africa and Asia. But making history at Toronto was one thing. Now comes the challenge of turning that victory into an Oscar nomination. For Rio and his team, the coming months will be a whirlwind of screenings, meetings with Academy voters, networking and fund-raising. The film's Platform Prize win has opened the door to consideration for Best International Feature Film, but securing a place on the shortlist, let alone among the final five nominees, will require an entirely different kind of effort. Preliminary voting for the Oscars' Best International Feature Film will take place from December 7 to 11, with the shortlist announced on December 15. Nominations voting will run from January 11 to 15, with the final five nominees for the category announced alongside the other Oscar nominations on January 21. Producer Beso is preparing for a campaign that will take the filmmakers from India to Britain and the US, with Los Angeles and New York becoming key stops. “The plan is to move to LA very soon, but we are also in the meantime trying to get all the Academy members to watch the film, whether it's in India or in the UK and in the US,” she says. “The next few months are very exciting, but it's also like a marathon. “Every day there is lobbying and interviews. I usually say a producer's job is to beg, borrow and steal. So right now I'm in the begging stage. “It's expensive to make a film, but it's even more expensive to do that entire campaign.” For Rio, who has already experienced a remarkable few weeks since Toronto, the prospect of navigating Hollywood's awards circuit is another unfamiliar chapter. “I don't know what I'm getting into, but I'm looking forward to it,” he says.

title: Iraq’s dinar devaluation tests efforts to protect consumers from rising prices
description: Weaker currency has prompted concern among residents warning of rising living costs, while others stand to benefit from earning in dollars
content: Iraq’s decision to devalue its currency has exposed the competing interests of households and the state, as residents warn of rising living costs while economists argue the move could help protect public finances amid a sharp fall in oil revenue. The Central Bank of Iraq raised the official dollar selling rate from 1,320 to 1,520 dinars on October 7, a devaluation of about 15 per cent. The move came as disruption to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz exerted additional pressure on government revenue and its capacity to finance public spending. “The situation is very bad,” one market owner in Erbil lamented. He said the price of goods has been rising since the Iran war broke out in February, particularly due to higher transport costs as most items come from Turkey and Iran. Iraq imports a substantial share of the products it uses, including food, medicine and consumer goods. For Iraqis paid in dinars, the weaker currency threatens to erode purchasing power. But the effects are not uniform, as those earning in dollars may receive more dinars when converting their salaries, while people with dollar-denominated expenses face a different calculation. In Erbil, where rent is often set in dollars, the exchange-rate change can have a direct effect on tenants paid in dinars. The measure places economic pressure on tenants who need to buy dollars with their dinar salaries, although the actual cost depends on the exchange rate available to them and how rent is paid. The gap between the official and parallel-market rates adds another layer to the pressure on households. While the official public rate is 1,520 dinars to the dollar, people and businesses seeking cash dollars often turn to exchange shops, where the price fluctuates according to supply and demand. In Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Iraqi Kurdistan region, the dollar was selling for about 166,350 dinars per $100 this week, around nine per cent above the official rate. The parallel-market rate rose sharply after the devaluation was announced on October 7, when exchange shops in the city quoted selling prices as high as 180,000 dinars per $100. The rate subsequently eased, although it remained above the official figure. The National visited several exchange shops in the Eskan neighbourhood of Erbil, where many dollar shops can be found, but employees declined to comment on the fluctuations. Dollar-denominated rents are part of a wider pattern in Iraq, where the dollar plays a prominent role in parts of the property market and some business dealings, even though most salaries and everyday purchases are made in dinars . The result is that households can be exposed on several fronts – rent may become more expensive in the national currency, while imported food, household goods and other products may also rise in price as businesses face higher costs for dollars. The use of the US dollar for some expenses while the majority of salaries are in Iraqi dinar “is what is fundamentally wrong with us”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The National . Those paid in dollars may benefit from converting their income into more dinars to cover expenses. But the advantage is less straightforward for people who also pay rent or other bills in dollars, since those costs do not become cheaper simply because the exchange rate changes. Ahmad Abbas, who receives his income in dollars, said: “It’s safer to be paid in dollars because it’s unstable when it comes to the currency here. My rent is in dollars and my bills are in Iraqi dinars but I expect prices to go higher, so at the end of the day it will kind of be the same.” He had observed prices rising during the war earlier this year but said they were “even higher now”. “I went to the market the other day and bought the same detergent for 20,000 Iraqi dinar and before it used to cost 9,000,” he said. The decision has prompted criticism from residents and political factions, with legislators demanding explanations from the government and proposing measures to contain price increases. Others argue the adjustment was necessary to help Baghdad meet its financial obligations. “There is no denying the affect is there but it’s not as dramatic as people make it out to be,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “The country had to do something,” he said, before adding he was “surprised it was proactive”. “In the past we didn’t act but we acted while the reserves are still healthy,” he added. At the Meri Forum in Erbil on Tuesday, Samir Fakhri, director general of the Statistics and Research Directorate at the Central Bank, defended the devaluation, arguing it was necessary to protect the country's foreign currency reserves following the decline in oil revenue. He highlighted Iraq's dependence on oil , which accounts for more than 90 per cent of government revenue, leaving public finances particularly vulnerable to disruptions in exports. He explained the scale of government spending and the pressure it places on the Central Bank of Iraq to supply dollars, arguing the exchange-rate adjustment must be considered alongside the country's wider financial difficulties. The argument in favour of devaluation is that Baghdad receives more dinars for every dollar earned from oil exports, helping it finance salaries and other domestic spending even as oil income comes under pressure. But that fiscal benefit does not necessarily translate into greater purchasing power for households. The government led by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has said it needs to maintain public spending and ensure salaries can be paid despite the loss of oil income. But opposition has grown within parliament, with politicians questioning why the measure was adopted and whether alternative options were adequately considered. The Co-ordination Framework , the main alliance of Shiite political parties that backs the government in Baghdad, has called for measures to limit the burden on citizens. “We can’t catch a break from them,” said Rizgar Ali, a taxi driver in Erbil, referring to the Iraqi government. “I have relatives who are public servants and their salaries are always delayed because Baghdad doesn’t send us our budget and now they’re weakening the money.” The recurring delays, amid disputes between Baghdad and Erbil over oil revenue and budget allocations, leave many households with limited financial flexibility to absorb higher prices and currency costs. Mr Ali complained about the rise in petrol prices and said he has to refuel his car frequently, making driving passengers around the city a much more difficult source of income – he turns the engine off at most traffic lights. Mr Tabaqchali said the current situation reminds him of the devaluation in 2020 when Iraq faced a similar dilemma during the Covid-19 pandemic, when a collapse in oil prices and a decline in revenue left the government struggling to finance its budget. The adjustment was intended to generate more dinar revenue from oil sales, ease the budget deficit and help the government meet its spending obligations. In January 2023, the government of prime minister at the time, Mohammed Shia Al Sudani, moved in the opposite direction, strengthening the dinar and setting the public exchange rate at 1,320 per dollar after the currency weakened on the parallel market amid tighter US restrictions on dollar transfers and increased scrutiny of Iraqi banks. That decision, too, was met with concern by residents because the dollar continued to trade at a higher value on the parallel market. The latest devaluation reverses that strengthening. Whether the devaluation achieves its intended financial objectives will depend not only on oil revenue and foreign currency reserves, but also on the government's ability to prevent unjustified price increases, protect lower-income families and pursue reforms that reduce Iraq's reliance on oil. Mr Tabaqchali also highlighted government subsidies as a means of cushioning the impact on lower-income Iraqis. Subsidies on fuel and some basic services, alongside the public distribution system that provides subsidised staple foods, can help shield poorer households from some of the immediate effects of a weaker currency. The government has also pledged to maintain fuel and basic-service subsidies following the latest devaluation, while considering customs relief for food and essential goods. However, subsidies do not cover all household expenses, such as rent, and imported goods can still become more expensive. “The worst is over for us as long as we continue shipping through the [Strait of] Hormuz,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “This doesn’t mean we have passed the crisis because the damage has been done and we have to adjust. The devaluation is part of a bigger thing, like structural changes to our budget services.”

title: Egypt's North Coast: Where to go on the Mediterranean and what's coming next
description: Tourism Minister says coast west of Alexandria to be region's hot destination for decades
content: Ask Sherif Fathy where Egypt's next big holiday destination lies and he points north to the Mediterranean. “It’s what we call ‘sun and fun’,” the Egyptian Minister of Tourism and Antiquities says with a smile. "That coast has huge investments going on now, and it will be the summer destination of the Mediterranean for the coming decades," Fathy tells The National on the sidelines of World Travel and Tourism Council’s Global Summit in Malta last week. "The growth is big.” That extends to national figures, as Fathy says Egypt had welcomed about 14.4 million international tourists in 2026 by the end of September, despite regional tension slowing growth. "We expect to end the year with 20 million." Much of that runs through Cairo. The Grand Egyptian Museum , which opened in November 2025, is now "the jewel of the crown", Fathy says. "Everybody is trying to reroute his trip, start or end his trip in Cairo." It welcomed about four million visitors between its opening and the end of August, and Fathy expects that figure to reach five million a year. Yet the coastline running west from Alexandria towards Libya, known to Egyptians as the Sahel, has long been where Cairo families escape the summer heat. Now it is being sold to the wider world, and Fathy says the numbers prove demand is there. For example, charter flights into El Alamein, he says, grew by 540 per cent last year and by a further 50 per cent this summer. The growth "could have been more, but we didn't have enough rooms," he adds. That shortage is being tackled, however. "The properties being built there are extremely luxurious," Fathy says, and he expects the beach clubs and nightlife to be a big part of the draw. Is it a good fit for UAE travellers? "Definitely," he says, describing UAE families who book the same hotels year after year and "come and enjoy it every summer". Here is where to go along the coast, heading west. Most visitors fly in. El Alamein's airport is one of three serving the coast, and Fathy says it will soon be enlarged, along with the airport at Marsa Matrouh further west. This summer, Alamein International was served by 15 airlines, including Etihad and flydubai alongside Saudia, Flynas and Air Cairo, although many routes are seasonal. Alexandria's Borg El Arab airport is the other main gateway, and the city makes an easy first or last night. By road, New Alamein is about 250km from Cairo, which is under a three-hour drive. It’s worth noting that locals place everything by its kilometre marker along the coastal road, so you will hear a resort described as being at "Km 126". Best for: summer festivals and Second World War history The coast's main hub begins around Marina El Alamein at Km 100. Officials expect about 300,000 visitors to Alamein in 2026, up from about 170,000 last year. New Alamein was planned as a year-round city, with an opera house, universities and residential districts alongside its beaches. In summer, it fills with concerts and festivals. This year's Yalla Sahel drew Gulf visitors to shows by Egyptian and Arab stars such as Amr Diab and Elissa. The town is better known for the Second World War battles fought here in 1942. El Alamein Military Museum displays weapons and uniforms from the campaign. Nearby, the El Alamein War Cemetery holds the graves of thousands of Commonwealth soldiers and a German cemetery commemorates those who died in the battle. Best for: luxury resorts and beach clubs Between Km 124 and Km 144, on the International Coastal Road, Sidi Abdel Rahman is the coast's upscale heart, with high-end resorts, beaches and a busy entertainment scene. Marassi, at Km 126, is one of the best-known names on the coast, with several beaches, world-class hotels, residential villages, an 18-hole golf course and the first water park in Egypt’s North Coast. A little further west, Ghazala Bay is quieter, private and exclusive, while El Dabaa offers calmer beaches with soft white sand and turquoise water. Much of this stretch is gated resort communities, so check day access beforehand. Best for: what's coming next, with a UAE connection The biggest change on the coast is being built with Emirati investment. Abu Dhabi's ADQ appointed Modon Holding as master developer of Ras El Hekma in 2024, on a site of more than 170 million square metres. The first district, Wadi Yemm, will be anchored by a lighthouse and a 10,000-seat amphitheatre. It includes a Montage hotel with about 200 rooms and suites, plus 96 branded villas. Beach club brand Nammos has also unveiled plans for a Cycladic-inspired resort, beach club and 72 one- to four-bedroom branded residences, plus a penthouse and retail village. None of it is open yet. As of July, the project was in full construction with completion dates scheduled for 2028, so for now Ras El Hekma is one to watch rather than book. Beyond it, Sidi Heneish has wide, largely untouched beaches and is starting to attract luxury developers. Best for: hidden coves and Bedouin culture Further west, Marsa Matrouh is a city rather than a resort strip. Fathy points to the Bedouin experience as one of the coast's draws. The real attraction is the water. Ageeba Beach is a cove tucked between two hills and reached by a flight of steps. Cleopatra's Bath is a pool inside a rock cave where the waves break. Legend says the queen bathed there. Lagoon Beach, with its pearl-white sand and clear water, suits families. For a break from the sea, the Rommel Museum, opened in 1977 in memory of German field marshal Erwin Rommel, holds Second World War artefacts. Best for: desert landscapes and ecotourism The coast itself is about “sun and fun”, Fathy says, but "it can be combined with ecotourism in Siwa". The oasis lies well inland – close to the Libyan border – and is a long drive from the coast. It’s worth the effort, however, as it’s a leading ecotourism destination for the country, famed for its mud-brick architecture, natural landscapes and distinctive Berber culture . Visit the old Shali fortress, a medieval citadel uniquely built from a salt-and-mud material called kershef. Or see the salt lakes, a network of saline pools and natural springs, which are said to be healing and glow in vivid colours. Elsewhere, the Temple of the Oracle, built in the 6 th century BC, is linked in legend to Alexander the Great.

title: Erling Haaland scores twice as Manchester City set Premier League record
description: City beat Ipswich Town 3-2 to make it seven wins in a row in league
content: Manchester City secured their seventh straight win in the Premier League as Erling Haaland scored twice in a 3-2 win over Ipswich Town on Saturday. Haaland scored a brace after Phil Foden scored the opener, which was cancelled out by Daizen Maeda, as Enzo Maresca 's side moved six points clear at the top of the table. City thus made it seven straight wins at the start of the Premier League – the first time they had managed such a feat in the club's history. City also became the third team in Premier League history to win their first seven games of the season. City were playing in front of home fans at the Etihad Stadium. City fans showed their support with inflatable bananas, a symbol of their rise from lower division football. There is uncertainty in the Premier League following an independent commission's findings over City's financial dealings and the club's subsequent appeal over the decision. City have denied any wrongdoing. On the pitch, it was business as usual with Norwegian ​goal machine Haaland leading the way. Foden gave City a short-lived lead cancelled out by Maeda, but Haaland restored the home side's advantage before halftime with a header from Mateo Kovacic's cross. Haaland then gave his side some breathing space with his second in the 69th minute, powering past Ipswich's Abdoul Ouattara before a low finish into the corner. He was denied a hat-trick by an offside decision and Ipswich got a lifeline when Zian Flemming tucked away a penalty in stoppage time but City bagged the points. City thus bounced back from the defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League. City's goalscorer Foden lauded the work put in by manager Maresca early into his tenure. “He (Maresca) has settled in really well, the lads are buying into what he wants to do,” Foden told BBC Match of the Day . “There's a lot of things to improve still and today is a good example of that, we can do a lot better. “We have to give Ipswich a lot of respect. They played a brilliant game. Good on the ball, aggressive and made it difficult. It's not always going to be pretty it's just about getting the result. and we did that today so I'm really happy.” Liverpool came ⁠from a goal down to beat Brentford 2-1 away although they were helped by the previously unbeaten hosts being reduced to 10 men shortly before halftime when Yehor Yarmolyuk was shown a straight red card for a head butt. Liverpool fell behind at Brentford with Keane Lewis-Potter putting the hosts in front. Brentford were in control but Yarmolyuk's rush of blood when he clashed with Jeremy Jacquet at a Liverpool corner changed the game. After referee John Brooks was invited to check a VAR monitor, he showed the red card. Liverpool huffed and puffed after the break before Victor Munoz finally levelled in the 62nd minute when he cut in to beat keeper Caoimhin Kelleher with a left-foot ​finish. Alexander Isak won it for Andoni Iraola's side eight minutes later with a clinical strike from Bradley Barcola's assist. Brentford ended with nine men after Vitaly Janelt got a second yellow card for a foul on substitute Rio Ngumoha.

title: 'My soul is Iraqi, my heart is Emirati': Iraqi community comes together in celebration in Dubai
description: Traditional music, food and displays help strengthen cultural ties between two nations
content: Thousands of Iraqis living in the UAE came together at Expo City Dubai on Saturday to celebrate their heritage and the close ties between their homeland and the Emirates. The second Emirates Loves Iraq community event brought Iraqi and Emirati guests together for a celebration of Iraqi culture, featuring traditional music, food and displays inspired by some of the country's most recognisable landmarks. Held at the conference centre at Expo City Dubai, the gathering was designed to strengthen cultural ties between the two countries while giving Iraqi residents an opportunity to reconnect with their roots and celebrate their shared identity. Families dressed in traditional Iraqi clothing enjoyed folk performances and cuisine, while others used the occasion to reunite with friends and members of the community. Sheikh Nahyan bin Mubarak, Minister of Tolerance and Coexistence, attended the event and praised the contribution of Iraqis to life in the Emirates. "This celebration for the Iraqi community in the UAE expresses their love for the UAE and the love of the UAE for Iraq," he said. "In the UAE, we are proud of the Iraqis living among us. We work to strengthen the bridges of love between the two nations." Sheikh Nahyan highlighted Iraq's rich cultural heritage and its historic contribution to human civilisation, describing the country as the birthplace of some of humanity's most important innovations. "The first wheel and the first letters were invented in Iraq. It is the place that witnessed the birth of civilisation. Iraq will always be a beacon of glory," he said. "Iraq is working towards peace and prosperity, and the UAE is committed to supporting Iraq's progress. The UAE loves Iraq." For many Iraqis, the celebration was an opportunity to reflect on the lives they have built in the Emirates while maintaining a strong connection to their homeland. Mohammed Al Tawaiji, 48, who has lived in the UAE for 20 years, said he felt welcome from the moment he arrived. "I never felt that I was a stranger here. My soul is Iraqi and my heart is Emirati," he told The National . "I'm proud to be part of this country and to have witnessed its major development." He said the similarities between Iraqi and Emirati cultures had helped him settle into life in the UAE. "Iraqis and Emiratis both care about educating their younger generations and know how to live alongside people of other nationalities. There are a lot of similarities between the two nations, and that's why I never felt like a stranger here." Afnan Al Rawi, an Iraqi doctor who has lived in Dubai for 17 years, said the two communities shared traditions and values. "We have similar traditions, and the most important thing is that we love each other," she said. "Emiratis understand our accent well, and gatherings like this bring nations closer together and spread positivity." For younger members of the community who have grown up in the Emirates, the celebration offered a chance to explore their Iraqi identity. Ali Mohammed, 22, a student at Emirates Aviation University, was born in the UAE and considers it his home. "The UAE is definitely home for me. It is a great place to live, study and work," he said. "I never felt like a stranger here, and this event is great because I can reunite with my fellow Iraqis." For some people, the event provided a rare opportunity to meet other Iraqis and enjoy familiar traditions. Afraa Al Rubaie, who has lived in Dubai for 25 years, said such gatherings were particularly important for people who had spent much of their lives away from their homeland. "It's hard to meet other Iraqis at work or in our residential areas, so this event is a chance to come together and enjoy our food, music and rich culture," she said. "Thanks to the UAE for giving us the opportunity to feel like we are in Iraq." She said the hospitality she had experienced in the Emirates reminded her of home. "Iraqis and Emiratis share the same hospitality and generosity. Here, we don't feel far away from our homeland because Emiratis always welcome us with a smile." The celebration also attracted Emiratis with personal connections to Iraq. Ibrahim Ali Binhatem, an Emirati writer, said his fascination with Iraqi history and culture began when he was young. His affection for the country grew over the years, and he eventually married an Iraqi woman and named their daughter Baghdad, after the Iraqi capital. "I have many Iraqi friends here in the UAE, and I've always loved the history and culture of Iraq," he said. "I used to read about Iraq and became fascinated by the traditions of Baghdad. I even named my daughter Baghdad." He said he attended the celebration to share in the community's pride in its heritage. "I came here to take part in this beautiful gathering with Iraqis. They are wonderful people with an incredibly rich history."

title: Emi Martinez's horror injury mars Chelsea's win over Everton
description: Argentine goalkeeper suffers head injury after collision with Jarrad Branthwaite during 2-0 win
content: ​Pedro Neto scored twice as Chelsea beat Everton ​2-0 ​in ​the Premier League ⁠on Saturday but the match was overshadowed by an injury to ⁠goalkeeper Emi Martinez. After a goalless ​but ⁠first-half that produced five yellow ​cards and several heated exchanges, Chelsea went ahead less than a minute after the restart when an unmarked Neto swept home. The game was paused for over 10 minutes when Chelsea goalkeeper Martinez was taken off on a stretcher following a clash of heads with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite. Chelsea's ​21-year-old keeper Mike ‌Penders came on ⁠for his Premier ​League debut. Chelsea doubled their ​lead ‌in the 90th minute when Neto ⁠pounced on a loose ball after ⁠Jordan Henderson's free kick was blocked by the wall, finding the bottom corner with a composed finish ​as Everton suffered their first defeat of the season. The 33-year-old Argentina goalkeeper, who won the World Cup in 2022, had signed a three-year deal with the Blues after competing his move from Aston Villa in August. Chelsea goalscorer Neto dedicated the victory to Martinez. “We are really pleased. Shame for Emi [Martinez] but we wish you all the best. This win is for him,” Neto told TNT Sports “We need a clean sheet to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike [Penders] did as well. “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.” Martinez was taken to hospital given the seriousness of the collision. Martinez's injury gave 21-year-old keeper Penders ⁠the opportunity to make his league debut and he managed to help ​Chelsea ⁠keep a clean sheet in ‌the league for the first time since January, ending a run of 22 ​games without one. Manager Xabi Alonso revealed Martinez had suffered a concussion. “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait,” Alonso said. “What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.”

title: El Sisi insists he will leave office in 2030 as he outlines succession plan
description: Egyptian President says military academy to launch training programme to produce next head of state and government leaders
content: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi insisted on Saturday that he would not seek another term when his current mandate ends in 2030, as he outlined a plan to prepare a new generation of leaders to succeed him. "My term in office ends in 2030 and this is a total given and will not be debated," Mr El Sisi said at a military ceremony marking the graduation of new cadets. "But I will not abandon the state of Egypt before it's rich with its sons who can shoulder the responsibility after me." He said the military academy would invite up to 1,000 candidates with doctorates from Egyptian or foreign universities to attend a 30-month course to teach them "what is a nation and how to protect it". The armed forces are to sponsor the course. Those who finish it will be the next generation of the country's leaders, he said. "The academy will prepare people to know what a nation is and how to protect it ... Egypt is not sterile. It's capable of producing a leader a 100 times better than me who can come along and take over. I need the Egyptian people to support this idea," he added. He said applicants must be between the ages of 40 and 50 and will be interviewed and vetted before they are enrolled. He did not specify whether both civilian and military candidates can apply, leaving the door open for another army officer like him to seek election in 2030. If implemented, the president's proposal would mean a new set of conditions that anyone who wishes to run for the post in 2030 must meet. Though it is unclear now, critics reacting on social media to Mr El Sisi's comments suggested that such conditions would require a constitutional amendment. The military academy has rapidly assumed a central role in Egypt's government in the last few years, with Mr El Sisi insisting that government employees, from school teachers to mosque imams and diplomats, must train there before they can be hired or promoted. The process is seen by some as part of the Egyptian leader's drive to place the armed forces as the nation's final authority, with control over vital sectors of the economy, foreign policy and security. Mr El Sisi also called on parliament to pass legislation enshrining a constitutional provision that designates the armed forces as the protector of the state, democracy and the country’s territorial integrity. The proposal points to his desire for the military, from which he emerged, to retain its powerful position at the heart of Egypt’s political system. He dismissed as malicious rumours that he was grooming a member of his family to succeed him. "There is no such thing. The state of Egypt is a very big state and that talk is not feasible or appropriate." Mr El Sisi surprised Egyptians this week when he announced that there would be no changes to the constitution to allow him to stay at the helm beyond 2030. His announcement sparked a wave of social media posts, some in accounts known to be linked to the government or security agencies, urging him to stay in power. Mr El Sisi, 71, has repeatedly warned in recent days against attempts to undermine the state, arguing that Egypt would be unable to recover if it collapsed. By the time Mr El Sisi's current term ends in 2030, he will have served as president for 16 years. He owes his current term in office to constitutional amendments in 2019, which were adopted in a national referendum. Before the changes were adopted, the constitution stipulated that no president could serve more than two four-year terms. The amendments kept the two-term cap, but extended the term to six years. In a clause added for Mr El Sisi's benefit, the amendments considered the first of his two terms in office to have begun in 2018, not 2014, when he was first elected. Egypt's constitution is a relatively progressive document adopted in a nationwide referendum in 2014, three years after Hosni Mubarak was removed from power in an uprising. Many Egyptians regard Mr El Sisi as a safe pair of hands at a time when the Middle East is embroiled in conflict, with wars in Gaza, Egypt's neighbour to the east, Sudan, to the south, and political instability in Libya , on the western border. The fallout from the Iran war , including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, has affected Egypt's economy, increasing its already high energy import bills and hitting Suez Canal revenue. Supporters of Mr El Sisi credit his government with maintaining stability amid these challenges. Critics, however, argue that government policies have contributed to the country’s economic difficulties. They point to heavy domestic and foreign borrowing and spending on large-scale infrastructure projects that may take years to generate meaningful returns. They also fault the government for failing to resolve a decade-old dispute with Ethiopia over the Nile, warning that the country’s vital water supply could be threatened by the dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Mr El Sisi rejects such criticism, arguing that billions of dollars spent on infrastructure and modern transport – including a Cairo monorail, an advanced electric train network and a new administrative capital – will help position Egypt to attract substantial foreign investment. He has also accused Ethiopia of exploiting the turmoil that followed Mubarak’s removal in 2011 to begin construction of the massive dam on the Blue Nile, the river's main tributary and the source of more than 80 per cent of the water flowing downstream.

title: OIC foreign ministers meet in Baghdad as regional crises top agenda
description: Two-day talks to focus on Iran war, Palestine and economic co-operation
content: Regional conflicts and Palestine topped the agenda as the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation (OIC) began in Baghdad on Saturday. Foreign ministers of member states attended the first day of the two-day meeting, which is being held in the Iraq capital for the first time in 45 years. The meeting is being held under the theme of “Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development”. It is to address Israel ’s attacks on Gaza and the recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, as well as crisis zones across the Islamic world. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi opened the meeting, calling for greater co-operation among Islamic countries to address mounting challenges. “The crises we are witnessing at the regional and international levels call for greater joint action to protect the interests of our peoples,” he said. "Iraq continues to suffer from the consequences of regional conflicts and their economic repercussions." The meeting is being held in Baghdad because it is "the cradle of civilisation, science, thought and history", he added. Mr Al Zaidi announced the formation of an Iraqi initiative aimed at integrating energy grids, railway networks, transport and digital communications among OIC countries. The development of a digital payment system and trade platforms will also form part of the initiative. The move aims to promote security, stability and prosperity and strengthen the ability of member states to confront challenges, Mr Al Zaidi said. Referring to the regional conflicts , he thanked Pakistan for its efforts to defuse tension and urged OIC member states to follow suit. OIC Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed described the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as a "flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty and of the sanctity of the Islamic holy sites". He said he would work to "strengthen preventive diplomacy and to activate the OIC's mediation unit" to put an end to the crisis. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is among those to attend the meeting, having arrived in Baghdad early on Saturday. He held meetings with the foreign ministers of Turkey and Egypt, Hakan Fidan and Badr Abdelatty, on the sidelines of the meeting. Mr Araghchi said Iran was ready to help stop the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, one of Tehran’s main proxy militant groups. He had previously offered to help enable dialogue between the two sides during a phone call with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan last week. Mr Araghchi said that a military solution was not an option to end the years-long civil war in Yemen.

title: Abu Dhabi launches rescue network for injured or stranded wildlife
description: Initiative brings together government entities, NGOs and community to help rehabilitate animals
content: Abu Dhabi has launched a co-ordinated wildlife rescue network to help protect the emirate's biodiversity. The Abu Dhabi Wildlife Response Network, announced on Saturday by the emirate's Environment Agency, is a collaborative framework comprising government entities, non-governmental organisations, academic institutions, private stakeholders and community members. The network is designed to improve the speed and quality of responses to wildlife in distress across the emirate. The launch was announced at an event on Saadiyat Island, which concluded with the release of rehabilitated sea turtles. Authorities also recognised people and organisations that have contributed to wildlife rescue and rehabilitation efforts. The network builds on the agency's decade of experience in wildlife rescue and rehabilitation, which began with sea turtles in 2016 before expanding to include sea snakes, dugongs, dolphins and birds. The initiative provides a digital framework for logging and managing rescues, dispatching field teams, overseeing rehabilitation and co-ordinating the release of animals back into their natural habitats. Maitha Al Hameli, acting executive director of terrestrial and marine biodiversity at the agency, said the network reflected the belief that protecting wildlife required quick action, deep knowledge and close collaboration. "Through this network, we are providing the care that injured or stranded animals need, giving them the best possible chance to recover and return to their natural habitats," Ms Al Hameli said. Data gathered through rescue cases, the monitoring of species' health and mortality investigations will be used to strengthen conservation strategies and inform long-term recovery measures. The agency plans to expand the network through real-time tracking technology, training for rescue teams and international collaboration to manage complex wildlife emergencies. Public education and engagement will also be remain central to the initiative.

title: Dubai company wins top economy award after making nearly half the world's kiteboards
description: Sheikh Hamdan praises SWS Board Technology for Dubai-it prize
content: A Dubai-based manufacturer that has grown to produce nearly half the world's kiteboards and wakeboards has won a prestigious award for economic achievement. SWS Board Technology was named the winner of the Dubai-it Award in the economy field by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. Founded by Rainier Nouhra, the company manufactures about a third of the world's snowboards and nearly half of its kiteboards and wakeboards. Its annual production capacity exceeds 450,000 boards. More than six million boards have been sold across international markets, with Dubai-made products reaching competitions including the Winter Olympic Games. Mr Nouhra combined engineering expertise and a background in composite manufacturing to build the business in Dubai, investing in research and development to improve product quality and manufacturing efficiency. SWS Board Technology has developed an integrated industrial chain spanning research, engineering, production, quality control and global distribution. It has established itself as a primary partner for leading snow and water sports brands. Sheikh Hamdan said the achievement reflected Dubai's capacity to identify opportunity where others least expected it. "Who would have imagined that one of the world's largest snowboard manufacturing operations would emerge from a city that was once desert? This is Dubai-it, seeing opportunity where others least expect it, and turning it into extraordinary achievement, with excellence in record time," he said. SWS Board Technology has also developed programmes to reuse about 95 per cent of a board's materials to manufacture new ones, boosting the circular economy push. Mohammed Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and Chairman of the Executive Office of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, said the award recognised a project that had grown from Dubai to dominate the global market in a field where the region previously had little presence.

title: Apple to 'work hard' to fulfil iPhone Duo deliveries as orders overwhelm stock
description: Earliest shipping date in the UAE pushed back to January 22, online platform shows
content: Apple has said it will "work hard" to fulfil demand for its much-anticipated foldable iPhone Duo , as orders overwhelm supply and cause delivery dates to be pushed back. The device, the California-based company's long-awaited entry into the foldable market, was introduced alongside Apple's iPhone 18 Pro last month and is the first new major hardware release under chief executive John Ternus. Apple began accepting online orders for the Duo on Friday, but customers were reported to have quickly seen delivery estimates being pushed back from November to December and, as of Saturday, towards the end of January. In the UAE, Apple's online platform shows a delivery estimate of January 22, similar to its US and UK sites, applying to all four storage capacities and two colour options. It is unclear whether there are earlier or later dates in other areas. By contrast, delivery estimates for the iPhone 18 Pro are about two to three weeks. The period after a new iPhone is launched usually presents longer lead times, but those are eventually whittled down – in later periods to as little as a week – after the launch hype has eased. “The preorder demand for iPhone Duo ... has been nothing short of extraordinary," an Apple representative said in a statement to The National on Saturday. They added that the company aimed to get the devices to users "as quickly as possible". Online orders will continue while the company "looks forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores worldwide", the representative said. Considering the appetite shown by consumers, the delays could also be a positive signal for Apple's foldable – its debut device after the market went mainstream nearly a decade ago. It could also be a sign of further growth in the category, especially after Samsung Electronics reported record orders for its latest Galaxy Z foldables , which were introduced in July. Apple does not break down order and sales numbers. Counterpoint Research last month said the company was expected to sell about six million Duos this year owing to the strong demand potential driven by its “bold” pricing, which is just $100 above its main competitor, the refreshed Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8. Observers had expected a higher price point for the iPhone Duo. Sales could now hit about 14 million, adding about $28 billion to the company's revenue for the 2027 fiscal year, Bloomberg Intelligence estimates. The iPhone Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599.

title: Noura Al Kaabi joins Hillary Clinton at Forbes 30/50 Summit to champion women leaders
description: UAE minister discusses growing influence of women, digital trust and cross-cultural dialogue in New York
content: UAE Minister of State Noura Al Kaabi joined former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton in New York on Saturday to discuss the expanding role of women in global leadership. Ms Al Kaabi appeared alongside Ms Clinton at the Forbes 30/50 Summit's fifth anniversary, participating in a session called "Across Borders and Generations: Women Defining Global Leadership". The discussion centred on the growing influence of women in positions of global authority and the importance of fostering dialogue across cultures and generations. Ms Al Kaabi used the platform to highlight the UAE's commitment to promoting mutual understanding and international co-operation. She emphasised that sustained engagement remains essential to addressing rapidly shifting geopolitical and technological landscapes. She also addressed the importance of credible information and responsible communication in an interconnected world. Ms Al Kaabi called for greater efforts to strengthen public trust and improve awareness of how to navigate the digital landscape. She referred to the growing influence of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. On the subject of female leadership, Ms Al Kaabi outlined the UAE's efforts to empower women and ensure their meaningful participation in decision-making across various sectors. She highlighted education, access to opportunities and institutional support as critical pillars in preparing the next generation of women leaders. Ms Al Kaabi also emphasised the broader contribution of women to international co-operation, describing their role as pivotal in addressing differences across cultures and generations, and shaping a more inclusive and collaborative future. The Forbes 30/50 Summit brings together women with 30 years of experience and those under 50 years of age to exchange knowledge and drive progress on issues of global significance.

title: El Sisi seeks parliamentary approval to defend Saudi Arabia if asked
description: Egyptian President calls for emergency session to authorise intervention as kingdom faces Houthi attacks
content: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi on Saturday called on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise him to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia if asked by the kingdom. Saudi Arabia is facing attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis . Fighting erupted in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime blockade" of Saudi ports and seized additional territory in Yemen . Saudi-led forces launched a full-scale military campaign against the group this month. Speaking at a graduation ceremony for military academy and college cadets, Mr El Sisi said the move would require parliamentary approval. “I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise us to take action to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia, if we are asked to do so,” he said. Egypt's House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, announced it is to meet on Sunday. “This move and this defence require approval from the Egyptian parliament. I hope parliament will convene an emergency session to grant this authorisation. "I am not speaking about attacking or waging war. We are seeking only to defend.” Mr El Sisi said Egypt stood firmly behind efforts to protect the territory of its Gulf allies. Egypt "will take any measures necessary to protect and defend” Saudi Arabia, he said. "I want to tell the whole world that we are not looking for a role to play, but it is absolutely unacceptable for us to allow the kingdom of Saudi Arabia to be targeted or for its security and stability to be undermined," he added. Egypt has traditionally been a close ally of Gulf states , some of which have repeatedly offered financial support during its economic crises. Mr El Sisi has insisted that the security of Cairo's Gulf Arab allies is integral to his country's national security. On Saturday, he praised their economic assistance in the aftermath of Egypt's 2011 uprising. He asked the military academy's graduates and members of the audience to give a salute to Gulf states in recognition for their help. The Houthis are fighting against Yemen’s internationally recognised government and its Saudi allies. The Yemeni rebels launched this week a missile and drone attack on the presidential palace in Aden , which has been the seat of the Yemeni government since 2015. The strikes killed and injured security personnel. The Houthis, one of Tehran ’s main proxy militant groups, claimed they were attacking a Saudi military command centre in the city. Attacks on Aden's airport also risk isolating Yemen’s government from its main backer and supplier. The fighting has not been confined to Yemen. The Houthis last week carried out attacks on Riyadh’s main airport, killing 17 people, injuring more than 300 and forcing a complete shutdown of operations. There have been 20 strikes on the airport since the start of October.

title: Egypt boosted by Moody's upgrade as inflation eases and investor confidence grows
description: Reforms have helped reduce government debt and interest burdens
content: Moody's Ratings has raised Egypt's sovereign credit score due to easing inflation and growing business confidence as the country introduces economic reforms . The upgrade to B3 was underpinned by efforts focused on fiscal consolidation and structural reforms, which have helped reduce government debt and interest burdens, the New York-based ratings agency said on Friday. A B3 rating is still six notches below investment grade, which makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funds when the need to borrow arises. But the upgrade pulled Egypt out of the "substantial risk" level. "Stronger revenue collection and expenditure restraint have supported [Egypt's] progress," analysts at Moody's said. Cairo's shift to a flexible exchange rate and tighter monetary policy has strengthened external buffers and the economy's capacity to absorb shocks, they added. "The government's ability to sustain this credit-positive trend despite a challenging external environment and higher oil prices highlights the durability of the improvement, rooted in increased policy effectiveness," Moody's said. The agency also gave Egypt a positive outlook, noting sustained fiscal discipline and continued reforms that have performed better than expected. That could be further driven by "stronger growth, more effective revenue collection and a faster decline in domestic borrowing costs as inflation eases and investor confidence strengthens", it added. Fitch and S&P Global affirmed their ratings on Egypt last week, with both referring to the country's progress. Egypt has been battling economic challenges and elevated inflation, but the government has taken steps to counter their effects. "The reform of Egypt's monetary policy framework since March 2024 has strengthened the sovereign's ability to absorb external shocks," the Moody's analysts said. "The unification of the foreign exchange market and adoption of a flexible exchange rate reduced foreign currency distortions, eliminated chronic foreign currency shortages, and allowed the currency to adjust to changes in capital flows without depleting official foreign-currency buffers, unlike in 2022." As a net energy importer, Egypt was forced to introduce fuel-saving measures as the war in Iran drove up oil and gas prices, adding to inflationary pressures and the cost of living. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, Capmas data show. Higher inflation might prompt a policy reversal at the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates. But the Arab world's most populous nation has been able to weather the economic fallout from the regional conflict relatively well, helped by policies centred on exchange-rate flexibility, energy price adjustments and spending controls. "The resilience of the updated macroeconomic policy framework has been tested by the sharp rise in oil prices and a confidence shock," Moody's said, referring to the decision by authorities to adjust domestic fuel and electricity prices, use expenditure contingencies and energy-conservation measures, and expand targeted social support rather than reversing energy price reforms. "These measures limited the fiscal consequences of higher commodity prices and helped preserve macroeconomic stability," the agency added. In July, Egypt was able to unlock about $1.8 billion in funding after clearing the latest review from its expanded economic programme with the International Monetary Fund .

title: UFC 333: Fight card, Abu Dhabi Showdown Week and all you need to know
description: An action-packed week in store ahead of Saturday's fight night at Etihad Arena
content: The UFC will host its 24th Abu Dhabi show next week when Alexander Volkanovski defends his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev in the headline bout. With a stacked card and much more happening throughout fight week, UFC 333 has a lot going on. Here is everything you need to know. UFC 333 is a mixed martial arts event from the UFC. The event will be headlined by the UFC featherweight champion Volkanovski putting his belt on the line against Evloev. There will be a total of 10 fights. Fight night will be held at Etihad Arena on Yas Island in Abu Dhabi . It will be the 12th UFC event staged at the venue. UFC 333 takes place on Saturday, October 24. The preliminary card is scheduled to begin around 6pm UAE time, with the main card expected to start around 10pm. Volkanovski is widely regarded as one of the best featherweights in history. The Australian won the vacant title with a dominant performance over Diego Lopes in April 2025 and backed that up with a similar display in their rematch in February, winning both by unanimous decision. This is Volkanovski's second run as UFC featherweight champion . In total, this will be his sixth title defence and his 11th straight title fight. Top-ranked Evloev earned his shot at gold after taking a contentious decision over Lerone Murphy in March. The Russian is undefeated in 20 pro- MMA bouts, while Volkanovski's record stands at 28 wins against four losses – twice to Islam Makhachev, once to Ilia Topuria and a defeat earlier in his career to Corey Nelson. The co-main event will see Petr Yan and Merab Dvalishvili play out their trilogy in Abu Dhabi. Yan (20-5) arrives in the UAE as UFC bantamweight champion, having dethroned Dvalishvili when they last met in December 2025. The Russian's consummate boxing and takedown defence won out against Dvalishvili, who was defending his title for a fourth time in the calendar year. Dvalishvili (21-5) won their first meeting and has vowed to exact revenge on the Russian and settle their rivalry once and for all . Following Losene Keita's viral first-round knockout of Muhammas Naimov, the Belgian is a short-notice replacement for Arnold Allen and will face American featherweight Aaron Pico. English flyweight Lone'er Kavanagh will test his skills against Ramazan Temirov of Uzbekistan, and Alexander Volkov meets fellow Russian Rizvan Kuniev in a heavyweight clash to round out the main card. At the top of the prelims, Azamat Murzakanov will look to get back in the win column after his 12-fight win streak was halted by Paulo Costa in his last bout. The heavy-handed Russian takes on former light heavyweight title contender Dominick Reyes. There are two UFC Fan Experiences to attend throughout the week, one at Yas Mall (Monday-Saturday) and the other at Yas Bay Plaza (Wednesday-Sunday). The events are free and open to the public. Fans can get involved in immersive experiences and buy UFC merchandise at the stores. Timings: Yas Mall: Monday to Thursday, 10am to 10pm; Friday and Saturday from 10am to midnight. Yas Bay Plaza: Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday, 4-10pm; Friday, 4pm to midnight; Saturday, 4pm to 2am. Fans can attend the public workout on Wednesday at Yas Mall's Town Centre (5-7pm), where the headline and co-main event fighters will go through their paces. The press conferences will be held on Thursday at Etihad Arena (4-5.30pm). Fans are also invited to attend for free. The weigh-ins will then take place on Friday, with the closed official weigh-ins scheduled for 8am before ceremonial weigh-ins in the evening at Etihad Arena (4-6.30pm), which are open to the public. Tickets can be purchased at www.ticketmaster.ae. The event can be watched live in the UAE on Starzplay.

title: IMF to accelerate talks with Iraq and Lebanon as Mena support grows
description: Fund looking at opportunities in region, managing director Kristalina Georgieva says
content: The International Monetary Fund is to advance discussions with Iraq and Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa, its managing director has said.
