Baghdad had approached the Washington-based fund for a potential programme, as the IMF continues to look at opportunities in the region, signalling it will be ready for any nation that may seek its assistance, Kristalina Georgieva said. "We will support Iraq very firmly. We would get Iraq both money and policy support," she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand on Saturday. She also noted IMF support in Egypt and Jordan. "We are in very intense discussions with the Lebanese authorities," she added. "We have made significant progress towards a programme. [There is] still a bit more work to do together and I'm confident we will be successful." Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. But Baghdad has been driving efforts to boost its standing. Last month at the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans. Lebanon, meanwhile, is heavily reliant on imports, making it more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies caused by the regional war. Beirut is also still dealing with the effects of the economic crisis that began in 2019. That was one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank, which also projected Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026. The IMF said this month that it would assess any potential changes to Lebanon's bank resolution law to ensure they were consistent with international standards. On Wednesday, the governor of Lebanon's central bank, Karim Souaid, told Bloomberg that he was expecting a "breakthrough" by the end of 2026 in IMF talks on the law, which stipulates it would repay depositors whose savings were entangled in the country’s financial collapse. "Programmes for Iraq and Lebanon would go a long way," Ms Georgieva said. She also acknowledged efforts by governments in the Gulf, whose pursuit of reforms have allowed them to "cushion the impact of the shock that has impacted them". "It would've been much worse if ... many of them have not done reforms and been building buffers," she added.

title: UAE spin star Suraksha Kotte on World Cup dream and playing on to honour her late father
description: Slow bowler was outstanding as national team caught the eye at Women’s Asia Cup in Dubai
content: When the UAE women’s team were on the brink of their finest win to date, at the start of last month, their outstanding player might have been thinking to herself: “I’m glad I stuck with this.” And, perhaps, how proud her dad might have been. The national team had Bangladesh pinned down in the Women’s Asia Cup at Dubai International Stadium. They needed to win to advance to the knockout stage of the competition, and Suraksha Kotte had given them a shot at doing so. The UAE were giving away lots of places in the world rankings to their opposition, and years’ worth of experience. Looking at Suraksha, you would not have known it. Bowling spin with the new ball, she tied the Bangladesh top order in knots, on her way to figures of 3-11 in four overs. As it turned out, the UAE fell short in the run chase. But it was another sign the national team are finding their place among the leading sides of the women’s game. The identity of the opposition was significant, too. Bangladesh were the opponents when the UAE played their first women’s international match in 2007. It was rather a mismatch , with the UAE being bowled out for just nine runs. Suraksha was just four years old back then, and 12 months away from moving with her family to live in Dubai. Now she is one of a cohort of players who have turned the UAE side from easy-beats into serious Asian cricket contenders. But, now aged 23, Suraksha might have been lost to the sport, and not just because she has an exacting day job. Her father, Sudheer, died in March 2021. She and her brother were students at the time. But their suddenly altered circumstances meant they had to consider leaving Dubai and returning to the family’s hometown in Andhra Pradesh in India. Somehow, they managed to make it work. Mother Shrisha found work at GE – her late husband’s old workplace. Suraksha has since graduated to become an associate project manager for software giants Oracle, and brother Suraj works for Nissan. And, away from her day job, Suraksha has managed to maintain a highly impressive cricket career, too. All inspired by someone in particular. “He's one of the reasons why I'm still playing cricket; it's for him,” Suraksha said of father Sudheer. “He was there at the time of my debut, but he didn’t see when I was properly performing, and playing for the team regularly. “He had been there throughout my development phase. We used to get up in the morning, and he’d say, ‘Let's go practice’. It was like a typical dad-daughter story. “For most female cricketers, the dream starts with their dad and then their brother. My dad was a huge cricket fanatic. He enrolled my brother into an academy and I just went along with my dad.” Suraksha remembers how proud her father had been when she made her senior debut, against Malaysia in Bangkok. “You couldn't imagine the happiness he had,” she said. “He went to the office and he was telling all of his colleagues with excitement, ‘Oh my daughter's playing with UAE, she's playing cricket internationally. And that’s a pretty big deal.’” Given the challenges her family have faced, she is glad to have had such a reliable support network to call on. The UAE women’s team have grown up together, and Suraksha regards them as family. “We're a small circle,” she said. “We've grown up with each other. Our families meet so often, we've actually become like one huge family. “That strengthens our bond even more. It really feels like we're on this journey together and we have a dream of qualifying for the World Cup. “It feels amazing that we're able to be on this path together at this moment. We're just really grateful for this.” The women’s side have yet to play at a leading global event, but they have been closing the gap on the game’s elite. They pushed Sri Lanka close in T20 World Cup qualifying, just as they did against Bangladesh in the Asia Cup. They have taken scalps of full member nations, including against Zimbabwe in one-day international cricket. Suraksha echoed the sentiments of her captain, Esha Oza, who said they need more matches against sides from Test nations if they were to take the next step. “We play these teams once in two years, so imagine what we can do with more exposure, and playing them every few months,” she said. “As a team we can grow to that level with the exposure, with the right skills, with the right mindset. We can cross many scores that we haven't even thought of right now. We can achieve that for sure.”

title: Lebanon airport fails to meet UN certification requirements, report finds
description: Lack of certification casts doubt over return of direct US-Beirut flights
content: Lebanon’s main airport lacks valid certification and has regulatory shortcomings that could delay the resumption of direct flights between Beirut and the US , Reuters has reported the UN aviation agency as saying. US President Donald Trump signed an order last month to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight ⁠847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985. While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Mr Trump's order a "significant first step towards restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States". But the UN's International ⁠Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system. The findings could complicate Mr Trump’s efforts to restore direct flights. The agency sent an internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September. Three US airline officials told Reuters that they did not expect American carriers to resume services to Lebanon in the near term, owing to security concerns. The ICAO report summary said Beirut airport’s firefighting resources were equipped to handle single-aisle aircraft but not the twin-aisle jets typically used on long-haul routes. The airport also lacks an emergency plan and its conditional certification has expired. “This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status,” the agency said in the summary. The report also identified shortcomings at the LCAA, including a lack of qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing and the absence of a fully established, independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined responsibilities. The findings were discussed at a two-day workshop last month involving officials from ICAO, the Lebanese government and the FAA, according to Reuters, which reviewed the meeting’s agenda. Lebanon’s Minister of Public Works and Transport, Fayez Rasamny , said the country was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport beginning on Saturday. The Civil Aviation Authority expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days. “Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA and corrective action had already been initiated,” said Mr Rasamny, adding that progress had been delayed by war. Israeli troops remain in southern Lebanon and have continued to carry out strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June. Hezbollah , which was not party to the agreement, has rejected it. The FAA declined to comment on the report, while the ICAO said it could not comment on matters concerning specific countries but conducts targeted analyses for member states, Reuters reported. The certification concerns come amid wider security risks affecting air travel in the Middle East . Foreign airlines have avoided large areas of regional airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February led to wider hostilities. The US State Department advises American citizens against travelling to Lebanon because of security concerns. The FAA has also called for caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace because of heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risk of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory. Lebanon’s aviation authorities and its national carrier have continued to maintain air navigation services and flights despite the challenges, helping to support an economy heavily reliant on tourism and remittances. Although there are currently no direct flights between Beirut and the US, Lebanon remains connected to several major European cities. The EU's Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and noted that European airlines must conduct their own assessments of an airport’s safety and operational readiness before beginning services.

title: UAE flight delays possible as autumn weather causes reduced visibility
description: Authorities urge travellers to check for updates from airports and airlines
content: Travellers across the UAE should prepare for possible flight delays as seasonal weather causes reduced visibility in parts of the country. The General Civil Aviation Authority has warned that changing weather may affect operations at airports across the country, potentially causing some delays. Such conditions are a recurring feature of the autumn season in the UAE. Airlines and airport operators have introduced measures to deal with the issue in line with established operational procedures and aviation safety requirements, the authority said. It emphasised that any disruptions would be managed in accordance with strict safety protocols. Passengers have been advised to check for updates through official airline and airport channels. The cooler winter months bring frequent fog, which envelopes skyscrapers on the coast, as well as dunes deep in the desert. About 95 per cent of the fog in the UAE is radiation fog, which forms in the early hours as heat absorbed by the Earth's surface during the day radiates into the air, causing water droplets to form. It dissipates in the heat of the sun. Advection fog is another type seen in the UAE. It forms when warm, moist air passes over a cool surface, creating water vapour. Heavy fog led authorities to reduce speed limits in Abu Dhabi this week, with a safety warning issued in Dubai . Alerts were sent to motorists in parts of Abu Dhabi, warning them that speed limits had been reduced to 80kph, while drivers were urged to exercise caution on the roads in Dubai owing to poor visibility. The country has averaged 132 days of fog formation a year since records began in 2006. The longest stretch was recorded in 2010, when there were 17 days of fog and five days of mist in January.

title: Yemen's Houthis launch missile attacks on Aden airport
description: Government forces say they have advanced in Marib and 'neutralised' 430 fighters
content: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched missiles at Aden International Airport late on Friday, a day after carrying out a deadly attack on the presidential palace in the port city. Aden has been the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government since 2015, when the Houthis seized the capital city, Sanaa, igniting a civil war. The Houthis are now fighting against the government and Saudi Arabia. Yemeni Information Minister Moammar Eryani said two missiles landed near the airport's runway, 500 metres from an aircraft that was preparing to take off. He said civilians on the plane are all safe and described the attack as a "grave violation of international laws and norms”. The Aden Security Department said the incident was ‌the second attack on the airport in less than a week. The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said an attack was launched against “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province”, as well as a weapons depot. The security department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for take off when the missiles landed. The attack comes after five people were killed in a Houthi attack on Al Maashiq presidential palace. It was the first time the group attacked the palace since fighting in Yemen resumed last month after a four-year lull. Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba, told The National that the Houthis will not succeed in disrupting public life or undermining state authority as the government pushes ahead with a military and political campaign against them. "Aden will remain the centre of government operations despite the deadly Houthi attack on the city's presidential palace ," he said. Heavy fighting continues between government forces and the Houthis. The renewed conflict has raised fears of a further deterioration ​in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions ‌are worsening rapidly. Yemen has ⁠become another front in the wider regional war ​that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemeni government forces said on Friday that troops had advanced in Marib province, north-east of Sanaa. Military spokesman Majed Al Nazili said government forces, with air support, had made significant “territorial gains” in the eastern part of the province, securing “key positions”. More than 430 Houthi fighters have been “neutralised” in the past 24 hours, he said, while destroying or disabling more than 100 of their vehicles and military assets. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis released aerial footage, dated October 16, that showed what it described as strikes on a Houthi weapons-smuggling operation in the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah. The nearly six-minute black-and-white video, which identifies the date and location at the start, shows apparent air strikes on lorries, small boats and what appear to be storage sites.

title: Battle for Taiz is for whole of western Yemen, warns ex-PM Maeen Abdelmalik Saeed
description: Houthis attempting to consolidate control on outskirts of city before imposing full siege
content: The Houthis' siege of Taiz is a slow-burning campaign that could signal the eventual fall of western Yemen, a former prime minister of the country has warned. Maeen Abdelmalik Saeed, who held office from 2018 to 2024, said the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen is an important stronghold for the government that needs to be defended at all costs. “It’s a battle which concerns all of the west [of Yemen],” he told The National . “There is no opportunity after that if we can’t reclaim Taiz again, to build a new momentum against the Houthis and Sanaa. This is the importance of Taiz.” There is still time, said Mr Saeed, because the Houthis currently control “significant, important heights” in the Yemeni Highlands around Taiz but are now in a consolidation phase. They had closed off most of the roads into the city of slightly less than one million people but had stopped short of a complete blockade. This was to buy time to consolidate control in the rural outskirts of the city, said Mr Saeed. “They are trying to control all the roads to the city and it seems that they want to seize control of these rural areas and absorb them before they expand into the city. The Houthis will close the siege when they control all these areas.” The attack on Taiz is “intense and ongoing”, said Mr Saeed. “There is a severe shortage of medicine and fuel in the city's hospitals,” he added. The rebel group invaded the south-west coast of Yemen last month to enforce its blockade on oil being shipped from Saudi Arabia. Its capture of the port city of Mokha gave it control of the Bab Al Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia relied on to export oil. A government-led offensive has seized the centre of Mokha but heavy bombardment from the surrounding hills still held by Houthi forces is taking place. The pattern of fighting demonstrates Houthi ambitions to capture other key cities in western Yemen, Mr Saeed warned. On Thursday, Houthi missiles were fired at the Presidential Palace in Aden, killing five people. There are also signs the Houthis are planning to attack Lahj, a city less than 40km from Aden that houses one of Yemen’s largest military camps, Mr Saeed, who now serves as presidential adviser, said Lahj is well positioned for the Houthis to launch assaults on their “three main targets” of Taiz, Aden and Mareb. Though food and fuel could still enter Taiz from Aden, this relief would be only temporary. “In a matter of days or weeks, we will see a siege and attempts to enter the city,” he said. Yet the group knows it will face considerable resistance within Taiz and on its outskirts. “The Houthis always rely on their radical religious teachings – the only obstacle to this was Taiz, because it carried the idea of democracy and the modern state,” said Mr Saeed, who comes from the city. Some tribal families from the Hashemite dynasties may be more sympathetic to an agreement with the Houthis. But local resistance to the group would form quickly, drawing on Taiz’s history of being ruled by Zaydi Imams of northern Yemen, he said. The Houthis would struggle to finance the administration of Taiz. “They cannot provide salaries, they don’t have the financial resources to run the city. Militarily they might succeed for a while, but it will be a burden and a threat,” said Mr Saeed. The Houthis have hit Saudi Aramco facilities and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh recent days, in addition to attacking Saudi ships passing through the Bab Al Mandeb strait. A Saudi official on Thursday conceded that the Houthi advances in Yemen were being “encouraged by Iran ”, which continues to arm and train the militia. Mr Saeed agreed, saying he believes Iran is playing “one of its last cards” in the Gulf, since Arab states have adapted to attacks on supply lines. “Iranians may be upset that the way of raising the costs and threatening the Gulf countries is not doing the job.” Houthi capabilities have grown in the past five years. They now have advanced weaponry, for which the Yemeni government and its Gulf allies were unprepared. The group is allegedly using Chinese technology to manufacture weapons in the city of Hodeidah, according to the Conflict Armament Research Group. The internationally recognised Yemeni government has spoken to Chinese counterparts on the matter but Beijing denied involvement. “They denied it, they said 'maybe it’s a third party,'” said Mr Saeed. Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba said China had promised to investigate the matter. The situation could encourage other groups such as Al Shabab in Somalia to follow suit in developing new missiles. “The problem is that this will encourage different radical groups to adopt this cheap technology,” said Mr Saeed.

title: Saudi air defence demands vie with Europe's needs to counter Russian threat
description: Britain and France risk weakening Moscow deterrent if they divert air defence systems from the Baltics, military experts warn
content: European allies are struggling to supply Saudi Arabia with more air defence weapons as they are needed for protection against the Russian threat , military analysts have told The National . Saudi Arabia is pressing for more air defence systems to counter rebel Houthi attacks, but defence sources have disclosed that Britain and France cannot “strip out” systems without weakening the deterrent against Russia in the Baltics. Britain is among the European allies who are sending significant arms supplies to Ukraine including a reported consignment this week of Stormshadow cruise missiles to strike Russian military infrastructure. But Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer, said Saudi Arabia remains in urgent need of more air defence capabilities from Britain, France, Italy and the US. “They need it because they are a big country,” she said. “They've got a lot of big targets that are easily spottable on Google Earth and they're up against people who have got sufficient ballistic missiles.” The kingdom’s vulnerability has been demonstrated by the Houthi missile attack on King Khalid International Airport last Saturday that killed 12 people and injured 309. This suggests that Yemeni rebels are more willing to attack civilian targets and given Saudi Arabia is five times the size of Ukraine it needs more defences. But with commitments to Eastern Europe and the desperate need in Ukraine for missile and drone interceptors, the cupboard is bare in many western countries. France has announced it will send defensive military systems to cover the key Red Sea port of Yanbu but has not given details of the equipment in question. “We have very little left in the locker to give,” a UK defence source said. “We really have nothing to send over to them.” Britain already has a battery of Sky Sabre air defence systems at King Fahd Air Base, operated by 16th Regiment Royal Artillery but sending more would mean taking them from Eastern Europe, where British and French armoured deployments are intended to deter Moscow from invading. “If they ask the UK to send them more Sky Sabre, where will they get it?” Dr Nusbacher said. “Well, the answer is we've got to strip it out of the Baltics.” The analyst, who has warned of the dangers of a spreading global conflict, said withdrawing defences from Eastern Europe would weaken a key deterrent at a time when Russia was testing western resolve. “What we see here is that we are being asked to dislocate combat power,” she said. “The French are being asked to dislocate combat power from Eastern Europe, from one theatre of this wider war to another theatre of this war.” A reduction in air defence deployments, she argued, could encourage Russia to become “even more kinetic”. American Patriot systems in the Middle East have been prioritised to protect US bases, with spare interceptors already drawn down from western Pacific stocks. But a western diplomatic source said Saudi Arabia is keen for Britain to take a greater role in its defence. “The Saudis are desperate for more UK involvement,” the source said. “It is seen still as a reliable, trustworthy partner with military capabilities and they would hugely welcome greater UK involvement. They need hardware in terms of air defence systems and are desperate for more of that.” It is understood that until recently the kingdom had been firing five to seven interceptors at each incoming missile, but to conserve stocks was now using only a couple at a time. Francis Tusa, editor of Defence Eye , said Britain could offer a small number of Rapid Ranger systems, which can mount Starstreak and Martlet missiles for short-range air defence. “We've only got a couple of dozen of those and we've already deployed some in Saudi Arabia,” he said. Britain could send a Type-45 destroyer into the southern Red Sea to provide ballistic missile defence and deploy RAF Typhoon fighters to Saudi Arabia, as it did to cover the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain earlier in the year. France and Italy could potentially provide their SAMP/T systems that are armed with the highly effective Aster interceptors but again they already have commitments. Britain is expected to provide intelligence gathered through surveillance satellites and, potentially, listening stations in Cyprus, including facilities in the Troodos Mountains, to monitor Houthi activity. Joe Walker-Cousins, a former UK diplomatic official who has spent 25 years working in the Middle East and is now based in Saudi Arabia, said Britain should discretely offer more diplomatic and intelligence support. The UK had major commitments in Ukraine and the Baltic states, but meanwhile the Middle East was “becoming increasingly uncertain”. “Investment in air defence must become a much greater priority, not just so we can stand shoulder to shoulder with our friends in the Gulf but also back home,” he said, speaking from Riyadh. “Britain is a global player and must be prepared to meet its global commitments,” he added. “That requires a major and sustained increase in defence spending. Anything less leaves Britain and its allies perilously exposed and projects a weakness that only encourages malign actors to push further.”

title: Heritage is not fixed in the past but reinvented in real time
description: Unesco's International Day of the Intangible Cultural Heritage invites us to consider the practices and knowledge communities pass forward
content: When I moved to Abu Dhabi 12 years ago, much of what drew me here was still a promise. Looking at the undeveloped desert around NYU Abu Dhabi ’s campus, where I then lived, what I saw was not absence, but potential. The museums taking shape on Saadiyat Island and the country’s commitment to arts and culture offered an opportunity to help build something for which the possibilities were still unfolding. Today, I work within an ever-widening cultural community. Audiences move between museums, festivals , concerts and performances, and some who first came to watch are now creating work themselves. New institutions are opening, and new colleagues are becoming friends and collaborators. The International Day of the Intangible Cultural Heritage prompts me to consider how these encounters help people draw from the past, learn from one another and build the culture future generations will inherit. Heritage is not fixed in the past. Intangible cultural heritage is constantly renewed through music, storytelling, crafts, performance, celebrations and knowledge passed across generations and reinvented in real time. Communities sustain these practices through teaching and participation, adapting them as their lives change. Our role is to support the people who carry them forward. For me, the arts are social infrastructure. They give people with different lived experiences reasons to gather and become part of a community. A performance can begin a conversation, introduce future collaborators or persuade someone that they, too, have a story worth telling. Sustained opportunities to participate, make work and learn from others help transform cultural investment into a lasting contribution to the life of a country. Earlier this month, I participated in a LiveX panel where the Royal College of Art’s Prof Adrian Lahoud compared the opportunity New York represented for earlier generations of newcomers with what Abu Dhabi and Dubai represent today. As a lifelong New Yorker, I recognise a similar energy of ambitious people arriving with different experiences and a belief that they could build a life together. Abu Dhabi’s cultural character will continue to develop from its own history, rooted in Emirati heritage and shaped by the lives and encounters of people here. Its neighbourhoods and artistic communities will look different from New York’s, and the significance of today’s beginnings may only become clear a generation from now. I think of the words of Zaki Nusseibeh, cultural adviser to the UAE President, in The New York Times , which I read the week I moved here in 2014. “We know we cannot create culture overnight,” he said, describing the forthcoming museums, “so we can find our own voice. Hopefully, in 20 or 30 years’ time, we will have our own cultural elite, so our young people won’t have to go to London or Paris to learn about art.” We are already starting to meet that aspiration. I have met people who first visited us on high school trips, became NYUAD students, encountered unfamiliar performances, took workshops and became artists whose work we present and commission. A children’s matinee can open a possibility that stays with someone for years. Artists need opportunities to develop their practice and sustain a career. The Arts Centre’s Numoo professional development accelerator provides practical knowledge and builds networks across artforms and backgrounds. People find collaborators and develop work we could not have anticipated when we brought them together, sharing stories that help others understand life here. Hekayah | The Story , our annual gathering celebrating the UAE’s National Day, Eid Al Etihad, asks: how do you create a national narrative? Poets and musicians from different backgrounds are selected collaboratively by curators from the UAE’s literary and performing arts communities. Sharing stories shaped by their histories, heritages and experiences of home, they give the country’s many voices and languages a stage. This year’s first collaboration with Public Art Abu Dhabi extends that opportunity for shared storytelling. In the same LiveX conversation, architect Bjarke Ingels recalled Leonard Cohen’s lyric, “There is a crack in everything / That’s how the light gets in.” He was discussing openings for the unanticipated in a city’s development, spaces where magic can happen. Putting that intention into practice means creating conditions for serendipity: affordable communities where artists can live near one another, meet regularly, exchange ideas and stumble upon collaborators. Urban planning can enable encounters even when we cannot predict what will follow. Some ideas will falter or change direction; others become more interesting through an unexpected contribution. A cultural scene needs room for that imperfect process, recognising that failure can be as important as inspiration. Audiences bring their own perspectives, too. At The Arts Centre’s opening concert this season, Fanfarai, a French North African brass and percussion ensemble, shared the evening with New Orleans’s Dirty Dozen Brass Band. I noticed people clapping on different beats, bringing their own musical instincts to the performance. Yet they shared the joy of being there together, creating a new common history. After shows, people tell me about friendships and experiences that have helped them make Abu Dhabi their home. The International Day of the Intangible Cultural Heritage invites us to consider our responsibility to the practices and knowledge communities value and pass forward. Preserving and extending them means supporting people to practice, teach, perform and contribute, recognising that what they pass on will change. The promise that brought me here has become visible in the work people make and the connections they form. We can honour what they bring while leaving room for discoveries none of us could have planned. As Octavia E Butler wrote in Parable of the Sower, the subject of the first show of The Arts Centre’s inaugural season: “The only lasting truth is change.”

title: Azerbaijan ban on headscarves in schools opens rift with ally Turkey
description: Dispute after girls wearing hijab barred from classrooms
content: The famous saying goes that Turkey and Azerbaijan are “one nation, two states”. Such are the countries’ ties that Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, founding father of the modern Turkish Republic, said: “ Azerbaijan 's joy is our joy, its sorrow is our sorrow.” But a row over school uniform rules threatens to sour decades of close ties between Azerbaijan and Turkey , countries that share a defence pact, billions of dollars in annual trade, and whose languages are so similar that they are mutually intelligible. Azerbaijan’s cabinet last month approved a ban on items of clothing that are “inconsistent with the principle of secularism”. It made no explicit mention of headscarves, but in recent days videos have circulated on social media showing schoolgirls wearing hijabs in floods of tears, saying they had been barred from their classrooms. “My mother thinks I’m in there getting an education, but they put me in a room, like a tiny shack, and hid me from the other children,” one girl was filmed saying. State television in the majority-Muslim former Soviet state said this week that new rules effectively banning girls from wearing headscarves to school were an effort by the government “block every move that seeks to add Arab-Persian values” to Azerbaijani national identity. While headscarves are permissible elsewhere, “School has a school uniform, and so on, and everyone must respect and abide by this rule,” a presenter on AZ TV said. Analysts said the move stemmed from fears in Baku of Iranian influence and a desire to maintain the country’s strong tradition of secularism, but it also prompted sharp criticism from Turkey. Tensions boiled over on Monday, when Oktay Saral, a senior adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said Azerbaijan’s decisions denied headscarf-wearing girls the right to education, and that Azerbaijan should “correct this mistake as soon as possible”. Members of parliament from Mr Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) joined in the unusually sharp criticism. Zehranur Aydemir, an MP for the capital, Ankara, said that the “wrongdoing” was a “violation of freedom of religion and the right to education”. Sabir Askeroglu, an Ankara-based international relations analyst, said the disagreements could have a “negative impact” on Turkish-Azerbaijani relations, but added that it was more likely to be at a societal level than a serious deterioration in bilateral ties. “The main risk is not the disagreement itself, but the possibility that reciprocal accusations could gradually erode public trust between the two countries,” he told The National. A Shiite Muslim majority nation of 10.4 million in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan’s Soviet history means religious observance is far less a feature of daily life than in neighbouring Turkey and Iran. In the latter, women have long fought against mandatory hijab rules imposed since the 1979 revolution that brought the current clerical leadership to power. In 2020, Turkish military support helped Baku regain from Armenia territory internationally recognised as Azerbaijani in the Nagorno-Karabakh region, while Azerbaijan’s close military, defence and intelligence ties with Israel have been a source of tension with neighbouring Iran. Turkey used to have expanding ties with Israel too, but relations nosedived after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza. The headscarf issue is such a sore point in Turkey because of its own fraught history with Muslim women’s dress. In the 1990s, Turkey’s then-strictly secular authorities, fearful of the rise of political Islam, banned women and girls from wearing headscarves in schools, universities and government jobs. That forced many women to choose between their faith and an education or career. Many political observers partly credit Mr Erdogan's rise to his dismantling of such policies. Emine Ilyas heads the 28th February Students’ Association, a group representing Turkish women whose education was interrupted in the 1990s because they wore headscarves. Commenting on the Azerbaijani ban on social media, she said no “bureaucratic tutelage” could be a “cover for restricting fundamental rights and freedoms”. Members of the Turkish opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), widely seen as less religiously conservative and more secular than Mr Erdogan’s AKP, also said Azerbaijan should reconsider its decision. “Let them [women] choose the clothing they wish to wear,” CHP leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu said. In Azerbaijan, President Ilham Aliyev’s party hit back with unusually strong criticism of Turkey and Mr Erdogan’s AKP. The New Azerbaijan Party said in a statement on Tuesday that the comments from Mr Saral and AKP legislators were “populist and irresponsible”. “No state in the Islamic world has the right to dictate its will to other Muslim peoples, to interfere in their internal affairs, or to see itself as superior to others,” it said. The headscarf ban prompted protests outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul, and in Azerbaijan, the Interior Ministry said on Monday that 37 people had been detained for disrupting public order while opposing enforcement of the rules, Reuters reported. Internet monitor NetBlocks said restrictions to TikTok, Instagram and X web platforms were in place on multiple internet providers in the country. Footage shared on social media showed Azerbaijani women angrily addressing messages to authorities, including MPs and the security forces. “Four cars of state officials came to my door early in the morning, saying it is forbidden for your child to come to school wearing a hijab,” one mother shouted in a scene caught on video and shared widely on social media. The scenes are unusual in Azerbaijan, where human rights groups have long criticised severe restrictions on freedom of speech, as well as authoritarian political rule by Mr Aliyev. Vasif Huseynov, a department head at the Azerbaijani state-run Centre of Analysis of International Relations, said the school uniform rules were a move against Iranian attempts to expand adherence to Tehran’s religious ideologies into the country. “It is precisely for this reason that the steps taken by the Azerbaijani government are aimed at protecting our national interests, our national values, our tradition of secularism spanning over a century, and the stability of our country,” he said in a post on X. Turkey’s fraught experience with the headscarf ban in the 1990s did not apply to Azerbaijan, he added. “Certain issues cannot be properly understood by viewing them solely through the lens of Turkey’s realities.” Over the past week, Turkish officials have attempted to calm tensions by promoting the long history of watertight strategic and economic ties with Azerbaijan. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan was welcomed by President Aliyev when he travelled to Baku for a summit on Thursday and told journalists that any issues would be addressed “by sitting down and talking them over”. “There is absolutely no need for these matters to be turned into tools for propaganda on social media,” he said. The primary responsibility for managing the disagreement lies with the political decision-makers in both countries, analyst Mr Askeroglu said. “Turkish officials should use a balanced tone that respects Azerbaijan's sovereignty and domestic legal framework while also taking sensitivities within Turkish public opinion into account,” he told The National . “Similarly, Azerbaijani officials should avoid interpreting all criticism expressed in Turkey as an attempt to interfere in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.”

title: Up in the air: Tesla's 'flying' Roadster raises more questions than answers
description: Issues include whether you need a pilot's licence to operate it and who would insure it
content: Elon Musk 's Tesla Motors has flaunted a new flying car – well, sort of. Mr Musk described it as “something that you haven’t seen in any movie” but it's not exactly Back to the Future stuff. However, the stunt seems to offer a glimpse of the future of transport. It's a great idea, but several points need clarity before road-and-air-legal cars become a reality. Late on Thursday, Texas-based Tesla introduced the redesigned Roadster, the electric vehicle maker's original model. It was a long-awaited unveiling for the new version of the car after production ceased in 2012. The Roadster was “launched” off a curved ramp, flipped over in mid-air and landed with the help of built-in thrusters designed by Mr Musk's other major venture, SpaceX. The car was also made to fly and barrel-roll over a line of Tesla vehicles, including its electric cars, Semi Truck and Cybertruck, although it seemed to take off vertically as it neared the first vehicle rather than launching well before. The latest Roadster, which is set to go into production in 2028, is billed as going from zero to 100kph in a second – significantly faster than the first-generation model, which achieved that speed in under four seconds. At the event at SpaceX's hub in McGregor, Texas, Mr Musk said the new Roadster used an “advanced ultra-high pressure air tank”, with 10 nozzles that carry about 250kg of air, which can recharge by itself without the use of any propellant. Air tanks are critical in vehicle systems, as they are key components for brakes, suspension, tyres and thrusters. In the space race – one of Mr Musk's closely-watched endeavours – they are very high pressure to support propulsion. The Roadster's air tank will “literally puff itself up and be able to do these manoeuvres whenever you'd like”, Mr Musk said. However, the thruster-powered Roadsters will only come in limited-edition models and there will not be any street-legal versions. That means not everyone can, at least not yet, “fly a car”, let alone perform barrel-rolls and kick-flips with the upcoming Roadster – especially as laws on the vehicle are both very tight and vague. In the mid-2010s, US regulations had stated that flying cars would need two licences – one for the road and one for the air. The very niche nature of flying cars – whose technologies are still very much in their infancy – makes it difficult to assess rules by region. Whoever drives the flying car is another issue. A notable example of this was the AirCar, which was granted an airworthiness certification by Slovakian authorities in 2022. Its maker, Klein Vision, subsequently said its operator would need a pilot's licence – not just a driver's licence – to operate it. Mr Musk acknowledged this, saying, “I'm not sure if it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.” However, he emphasises that with the new Roadster, “we can go further … this will be an actual car on the roads”. Then there's the thought of having to load a car with compressed gas, which can cause explosions and raise alarm bells for owners and insurers. “[It's] a tremendous feat of engineering. It’s hard to argue otherwise,” said David Thomas, director of content marketing at US software developer CDK Global. “I’m not sure where you fill up a car with that. And it’s unlikely anyone will insure it either.” And after ensuring any flying car is safe and legal, commercialisation is also a big question, said George Agathangelou, general manager and executive director of Cyprus-based financial services firm Teroxx. “Would drivers need aviation certification or a pilot’s licence? What happens to liability, insurance and airspace restrictions,” he said. “Imagine explaining to your insurer that you didn’t rear-end another vehicle, you attempted to fly over it.” Tesla isn't the first to unveil such a vehicle: in 2021, Britain's McMurtry introduced the Speirling, an electric hypercar using powerful fans to generate downforce. Tesla's approach is different as it combines suction with thrusters. Mr Musk made sure that there was an audience to witness the Roadster stunts in Texas and ensure people would not claim it was AI. Analysts at Chinese logistics company Raman Technology noted that it was “not antigravity magic, [as] it integrates aerospace technology inside an electric vehicle”.

title: 'Noticeable' rise in UAE children suffering issues linked to excessive screen time
description: Parents urged to limit children’s screen use as doctors and teachers highlight problems with sleep and concentration
content: Doctors in the UAE are reporting a growing number of children suffering from issues such as difficulty sleeping and concentrating that are linked to excessive screen time, prompting warnings that restrictions on phone use in schools are not enough to protect young people. Dr Sudha Rao, a specialist in paediatrics at Aster Clinic in Al Jaddaf, told The National she had seen a noticeable increase in children experiencing problems associated with prolonged use of screens, particularly use late at night. "There has been a substantial rise in children presenting with sleep disruptions leading to disorganized body clock or “circadian rhythms”, leading to fatigue, eye health issues such as myopia or near-sightedness," she said. "There are also behavioural concerns that are directly tied to excessive screen use, like 'digital tantrums'." Health and education experts are urging parents to take greater responsibility for children’s screen habits, including keeping phones and other devices out of bedrooms. Their concerns are supported by research from Saudi Arabia involving 500 children aged six to 12. It found that 66.7 per cent of those using screens for more than four hours a day had difficulty falling asleep, compared with 9.5 per cent of those using them for less than an hour. Dr Rao also cited an Omani study that reported a 33.7 per cent figure for poor sleep among students with screen-induced visual impairment. She said paediatric behavioural reports and UAE school studies authorised by the Dubai Health Authority found that children with less than two hours of recreational screen time a day scored 20 to 25 per cent higher in attention and memory tasks than children whose screen time exceeded four hours. School leaders said that while technology was necessary for some learning and entertainment, the challenge recognising when devices were crowding out activities children needed for healthy development. “The question is no longer simply how much time children spend on screens, but what they are exposed to, how they engage and what essential developmental experiences may be displaced,” said Nevita Pandya, chief executive and principal of Gems International School, Dubai Hills. Teachers are increasingly noticing pupils displaying signs of tiredness, difficulties concentrating and problems with managing frustration. These are complex issues with several possible causes alongside excessive screen use, but boundaries during the day need to be supported at home, said Helen Pereira-Raso, superintendent and chief executive of Gems Dubai American Academy. “For example, a school can intentionally protect attention and engagement throughout the day, but a child who is regularly losing sleep because of recreational device use may still struggle to participate fully in learning.” Dr Rao said parents should look at how screen habits affect children's daily lives, including homework, physical play, family meals and friendships. “It is also deeply concerning if the screen viewing becomes the only way a child manages boredom, stress, sadness or difficult emotions,” she said. The concerns become greater as children grow older. Ms Pandya said younger children could miss opportunities for conversation, imaginative play and social interaction, while adolescents faced challenges with sleep, social comparison and peer relationships. Experts recommend consistent routines that include keeping devices out of bedrooms overnight and protecting family time. Phones, tablets and gaming devices could be left to charge in a shared space for one or two hours before bedtime, Dr Rao recommended. She also suggested screen-free mealtimes. For families facing distress or arguments when a device is taken away, she advised giving children advance warning and establishing predictable stop times. Timers could help in such cases and make the boundary clear. Planning activities to follow, such as going outside or playing with a pet, can also help ease the transition. She recommended that parents remain calm and acknowledge the frustration without abandoning the agreed limit. Ms Pereira-Raso said parents also need to understand what children are doing online and how it makes them feel. “We must also recognise that children need more than restrictions. They need adults who are curious about their digital experiences, who engage in conversations about what they encounter online, and who help them develop the capacity to make thoughtful choices.” At Gems International School, Dubai Hills, personal phones must remain “on site, out of sight”. Ms Pandya said the policy aimed to protect pupils' attention and reduce distraction. “Clear boundaries are an important part of a purposeful learning environment,” she said. Managing screen use should allow room for purposeful digital learning alongside reading, practical activities and face-to-face discussion. “We cannot treat all screen time as equal,” said Ms Pereira-Raso. “A child passively consuming content for hours is having a fundamentally different experience from one using technology to investigate a complex problem, collaborate with peers, develop an idea or create something meaningful.” Preparing children for a technologically advanced world also needs effort to develop children's ability to concentrate, make decisions and manage distractions independently. “However, being future-ready does not mean spending more time on devices.” These expectations also apply to adults, Ms Pandya said. She encouraged parents to examine their own relationship with technology. Ms Pereira-Raso suggested setting an example by putting phones away during conversations to demonstrate the habits families want their children to learn. “Children are observing how we manage our own attention, whether we put our phones away during conversations, and how present we are in our relationships with them,” she said.

title: Street Fighter's Rayna Vallandingham kicks down stereotypes for Indian women on screen
description: Actress of Indian-Dutch descent hopes to be role model she struggled to find growing up
content: By the time Rayna Vallandingham was eight, she had become a taekwondo world champion. Yet when she looked to film and television, she struggled to find an Indian woman whose story reflected her own. The years she spent training and competing had given her a different idea of what she could become. Now, with her roles in Cobra Kai and Street Fighter , she wants young girls watching her to have what she missed growing up: someone who makes their ambitions feel possible. “Growing up, when I watched Indian women on screen, they were always portrayed the same way, and it was in a very nerdy way,” she says. “It was always the schoolgirl with the protective parents, and I was like: ‘That’s just not my experience at all.’ And I wanted to rewrite the slate on that and break those stereotypes.” The American actress, whose mother is of Indian origin and father is of Dutch descent, plays Juli in director Kitao Sakurai’s new Street Fighter film . It follows her appearance as Zara Malik in the final seasooon of Netflix’s Cobra Kai , another role that drew on the martial arts skills she has been developing since childhood. Vallandingham's parents initially enrolled her in martial arts classes to help the shy child become more confident. As her training progressed, her grandfather drove her to the dojo and she fitted sessions around the school day, sometimes returning at lunchtime and again in the evening. She went on to become a 13-time world champion. Playing Zara brought together her sporting experience and Indian heritage. She drew on her grandparents' speech patterns to develop the character’s accent, as she told Vogue India . Her move into Street Fighter places her in an ensemble of women with their own motivations and personalities alongside their fighting skills. Sakurai describes them as strong and complicated, an approach Vallandingham welcomed. “The first time I read the script, I was like: 'Yes, they hit the nail on the head,'” she says. “So I was levitating. I was just so happy with it.” The film also brought together actresses at very different stages of their martial arts training. Vallandingham arrived with years of competition behind her, while Callina Liang, who plays Chun-Li, was making her first action film. “Playing the character and prepping for Chun-Li, it changed my life completely,” Liang says. “I went into weightlifting, I was training [in] stunts, martial arts … both things now are a huge part of my life, so I've got to thank the role for that. “It taught me that it’s amazing to be strong and feel capable, and now I feel safer when I’m on the street alone at night, which is just great.” Vallandingham hopes that seeing women in these roles will encourage girls to consider what they might be capable of. She has had young fans approach her to explain what her work means to them, encounters she says leave her crying on the spot. “Representation is so important because if I can have a daughter one day and have her look up to me and realise almost inherently that she can do anything she wants and there’s no box she has to fit in, that would mean the world to me,” Vallandingham says. “So that’s my mission statement.” That life-changing moment of recognition may have already come for some girls, according to David Dastmalchian , who plays M Bison. “I love that my nine-year-old daughter got to see the screening of the film sitting next to Rayna and Callina, and was just like: ‘Wow! That’s so awesome,’” he says. “It’s such a cool feeling.” Street Fighter is now in cinemas across the Middle East

title: Grynspan stays ahead in sixth UN secretary general vote, but two veto nations say no
description: Latest poll offers clearer picture of which candidates have realistic chance of becoming next UN chief
content: The UN Security Council on Friday held a sixth vote to choose the next Secretary General , with Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan narrowly retaining her lead in the race. She has remained the front-runner, securing the minimum nine encouraging votes in the latest round and five discouraging votes, including two from permanent council members. Argentina's Rafael Grossi secured eight encouraging votes and six discouraging votes, while Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett also received eight encouraging votes and six discouraging votes. Both faced opposition from two permanent members. Panamanian President Jose Mulino, whose country is one of the non-permanent members of the council, declared before the vote that his country would vote for Mr Grossi. Unlike the five previous rounds of voting, Friday’s poll offered a clearer picture of which candidates had a realistic chance of becoming the next UN secretary general and which faced opposition from the world's most powerful nations. For the first time in this selection process, council members cast colour-coded ballots, distinguishing the votes of the five permanent members – Britain, China, France, Russia and the US – from those of the 10 elected members. When Secretary General Antonio Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement. Minh-Thu Pham, co-founder of the Starling Institute and a former adviser to UN secretary general Kofi Annan, said the narrowing gap between the three leading candidates emphasised the growing uncertainty surrounding the race. “Compared to previous rounds, differences between the top three are very, very slim now,” Ms Pham told The National . “It seems to be a split decision with no P5 convergence. It means there is a path open for new entrants,” she added, referring to the five permanent members of the council. But Ms Pham warned that a new contender would not necessarily break the deadlock. "It could get messy," she said. None of the seven candidates who participated in the October 16 poll has withdrawn, and no new candidates have entered the race yet. US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz , said after the vote that Washington wanted a secretary general who would refocus the organisation on its core mandate of maintaining international peace and security. “We think that this institution needs strong, energetic leadership that is going to take the United Nations back to basics,” Mr Waltz told reporters, calling for greater efficiency and a renewed emphasis on peace and security. He also played down the importance of regional rotation and gender in selecting the next UN chief, saying Washington's priority was finding the most qualified candidate. “We understand there is a desire for regional rotation. Of course, if the best candidate's a woman, we would welcome that, but we really just need the best candidate,” Mr Waltz said. “This institution, after 80 years, has tried to become everything to everyone, and we need it. We put it on a diet, so to speak.” Ms Pham said it was encouraging to hear Mr Waltz say that he thinks the council can finish before the end of the year. “Otherwise it could deepen doubts about the council and the UN,” she said. But she warned that time was running out for new candidates to enter the race and secure sufficient support for the post. “Even if the US, China, and Russia agreed behind the scenes on a candidate, we’re in an environment where the other council members may not go along,” she said. Unlike in 2006, when Washington and Beijing were able to rally support for Ban Ki-moon, Ms Pham suggested the US could now favour a candidate who would struggle to win broader backing. Any attempt to accelerate the process could also provoke resistance from the General Assembly, she said, particularly if the council moved to vote on new candidates without giving them an opportunity to participate in the usual informal hearings. “A lot of pieces have to fall into place, and we’re running out of time,” she said.

title: Oil tanker struck in Strait of Hormuz, says Indian ports minister
description: Attack highlights how Iran war has increased risks to commercial shipping in crucial waterway
content: A crude oil tanker carrying 15 Indian crew members was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the country's Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways said. Sarbananda Sonowal said all Indian citizens on the vessel, the MT ST 3, were safe and had not been injured. He said on X that India remains "in close contact with the ship management companies to ensure the ongoing security and well-being of our crew members". The Indian government this month condemned an attack on a vessel owned by Dubai shipping company Onex that was struck by a projectile in the strait. Twelve crew members on the MT On Peace were injured in the attack, including 11 Indians, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement. On Thursday, a Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the strait after being struck by a projectile. All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were moved to safety and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority said. The incidents highlight how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the vital global energy supply route. Attacks on vessels transiting the waterway have surged to a record high, with at least two ships sunk. The strikes, attributed to Iran, have caused crude oil prices to rocket, with prices above $100 a barrel in the US. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has used drones, missiles and sea mines in the strait to choke off exports and drive up oil prices in a bid to increase economic pressure on the US.

title: Morocco government sworn in under first female Prime Minister Fatima El Mansouri
description: Two women named in cabinet as several ministers retain posts
content: Morocco has sworn in its new government under its first female prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri , in a ceremony presided over by King Mohammed VI. Ms El Mansouri kept several members of the former government in their posts, including Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit. The 20 members of her cabinet also includes 11 ministers delegate. The government formation came after Ms El Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the election on September 23, reached a deal with three other parties this week. The coalition, which includes moderate socialist parties ⁠and the nationalist Istiqlal, together hold 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority. Other cabinet members who kept their posts were Justice Minister Abdel Latif Wahbi, Nizar Baraka as Minister of Equipment, Water and Forests, Riadh Mezzour as Minister of Industry, Trade, Investment and Economic Integration, and Abdellatif Loudiyi as Minister Delegate in charge of Defence. Morocco 's ​football ⁠federation chief and former budget ​minister Fouzi ⁠Lekjaa was appointed as the Economy ⁠and Finance ​Minister, state news agency MAP reported. PAM member Khalid Hatimi was appointed Minister of Agriculture, Maritime Fisheries and Food Sovereignty. Leader of the Party of Progress and Socialism, Nabil Benabdallah, a former housing minister, returned to government as Education Minister, while fellow PPS member Charafat Afailal was named Energy Minister. Ms Afailal is one of two women appointed as ministers by Ms El Mansouri, along with Najwa Kokos, who was given the portfolio of Family, Social Development and Equality. Four of the 11 ministers delegate are also women. The new government is under pressure to address unemployment and ​demands for ⁠better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.

title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia praises Trump as she leaves job - after five days
description: Criticism and questions over her credentials arose after disastrous first press conference this week
content: Katie Zacharia has left her role as the White House press secretary after only five days in the job. In a post on X, she said it was an honour to work for US President Donald Trump and hailed him as a "thoughtful, enthusiastic and hardworking man". Earlier on Friday, Mr Trump said he had told Ms Zacharia to “reconsider” her role after a disastrous first week. Speaking to reporters as he travelled to Georgia for a campaign event, Mr Trump said she had been treated “very badly by the media”. “I told her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I would reconsider.' Maybe it's not for her,” he said. Following the comments, Fox News, quoting a White House official, reported that Ms Zacharia was “transitioning” out of the role. The New York Times , quoting sources, reported that she had been fired. The shock departure follows an eventful few days for Ms Zacharia, who held her first White House briefing on Tuesday. The briefing lasted 14 minutes and she took only three questions from journalists. She also appeared to struggle to read a prepared statement. Her performance drew criticism and mockery on social media, and questions were also raised over her credentials. When Mr Trump announced her appointment, he described her as an attorney. A graduate of Pepperdine University's law school in California , Ms Zacharia later acknowledged that she had taken the bar exam once but had not passed. In previous media appearances, she has described herself as a lawyer and said that she had practised law at a firm in China . On Friday, Mr Trump said he had not hired her as a lawyer and that her credentials were not an issue. Ms Zacharia did not accompany Mr Trump to Georgia, according to a list circulated by the White House. Typically, the press secretary travels with the President. Her departure evokes that of Anthony Scaramucci , who served as White House communications director for just 11 days during Mr Trump's first administration. Ms Zacharia was appointed after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary.

title: My Dubai Salary: 'I earn up to Dh45,000 a month coaching wellness to women in midlife’
description: Monika Singh, founder of Monika Sphere, built a fitness business from scratch in Dubai after leaving dentistry behind
content: Monika Singh arrived in Dubai 12 years ago with a dentistry degree from India and a plan to sit her Dubai Health Authority licensing exams to practise in the UAE. Then she started attending group workout classes while she studied, discovered a love for dance fitness and never looked back. Today, she runs Monika Sphere, a women's wellness coaching business specialising in women in midlife, a niche she arrived at through her own experience with perimenopause after having her son, now seven. She now works exclusively within Arabian Ranches 1 and 2, coaches 23 clients, and earns between Dh42,000 and Dh45,000 a month. Before I started my own thing, I was doing group exercise classes in Fitness First and some other studios across Dubai. That was my starting point in the industry. I was never into fitness , honestly. I started attending dance fitness classes, and it just kind of stayed with me, and I was like, “Oh wow, I really want to do this.” I told my husband; I expressed my feelings to him, and he was very supportive. From there, I started my journey into fitness. I took my Zumba training, then I went into a group exercise leadership programme. Then I did my yoga training, Les Mills Body Balance training, then personal training and sound healing. A lot of things happened, and here I am today. I’ve set up my own company. I have been training 23 ladies, and I'm just around Ranches 1 and 2 – I don't go outside because of commute time, and I also don't have time to go out and train people. My average earnings are Dh42,000 to Dh45,000 a month. My training is not just about typical strength training. Of course, strength training is important for women, but other factors come into play, like mobility, recovery, your sleep, your meditation, and your breathwork. Everything comes together to give you a balanced and sustainable fitness regime. I also specialise in women in midlife. This came to me through my own experience. After I delivered a baby, and as I entered my midlife phase – that is, perimenopause – I realised that my energy was not the same, my sleep was getting affected, and my responsibilities were different. And I realised the same complaint was coming from the women that I coach. Coming from a medical background, I have more understanding of human anatomy and physiology. I decided to dive more into this and study women's wellness, especially in midlife. I took my training, and now I am helping women achieve their goals without punishing themselves. Yes, I do save. I'm not investing yet, but I do take care of my daily routine. I have a boy – seven years old – so I manage his school fees, then take care of my car loan, and some house chores. I keep around Dh3,000 to Dh4,000 aside for household expenses, and the rest I save. My husband takes care of the rest of the house. When I was in university studying dentistry , we were given a very small amount of pocket money, and you had to manage that throughout the week. You wouldn't get more than that – that was the rule set by our parents, because in India it's like that. That's how I learnt how to manage my expenses. Honestly, I didn't learn anything about investing because we were not given the right to make any decisions on that. It was all my father who used to do that, not us. Currently, my goal is to launch my online portal. I have been saving for that because launching an online portal, an app, and everything else is expensive. Long-term, we have a plan to get a new, bigger house after I launch my online portal, once it becomes successful and once we start getting more and more income. That is our first plan. I want to be a known personality, a successful businesswoman – among people in the UAE who are known for their work.

title: Arabic word of the week: 'Finjan', the humble cup that symbolises hospitality
description: From Persian origins to a place in Arab coffee traditions, it bears a meaning far greater than its size
content: Some of the most meaningful gestures in Arab culture come in small packages. A finjan, the little cup traditionally used to serve Arabic coffee, is one such example. Though modest in size, it represents hospitality, generosity and the bonds formed through shared experiences. Our Arabic word of the week , finjan, translates to cup, particularly a small vessel used for coffee or tea. Its plural is fanajeen, while in Gulf dialects, including Emirati Arabic, it is commonly pronounced finyan or finyal. The word is generally traced to the Persian pingan, meaning a bowl or drinking vessel, which was adapted into Arabic through centuries of cultural exchange. The word has also travelled beyond Arabic. Turkish uses fincan for a cup, reflecting the shared vocabulary that developed across neighbouring regions. While finjan can refer to an ordinary drinking cup, its strongest cultural associations are with gahwa, the traditional Arabic coffee served throughout the Arabian Gulf. The finjan is usually small, handleless and made from porcelain or ceramic. Some are plain white, while others feature intricate geometric patterns, floral motifs, Arabic calligraphy or gold detailing. These decorations can draw on regional artistic traditions, transforming an everyday drinking vessel into a miniature canvas. Its size is deliberate, allowing coffee to be served in modest quantities and refilled throughout a gathering. In the UAE and much of the Arabian Peninsula, offering a finjan is an established expression of welcome. Coffee is poured from a dallah , the distinctive long-spouted pot, and traditionally presented first to the eldest or most honoured guest. The cup is received with the right hand, and the coffee is generally poured only a quarter or a third of the way up. A gentle shake of the empty finjan signals that the guest has had enough. These gestures form a language of their own, allowing hosts and guests to communicate respect and appreciation without exchanging a word. The tradition also extends into Bedouin customs, in which successive cups have acquired symbolic meanings. Finjan al dhaif represents hospitality, finjan al kaif is associated with enjoyment, while finjan al saif evokes loyalty and a willingness to defend one's companions. In 2015, Arabic coffee was inscribed on Unesco 's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising its cultural importance. The finjan also occupies a place in Arabic poetry. Syrian poet Nizar Qabbani famously used the cup as a symbol of fate and romantic longing in Qari'at Al Finjan , a poem later immortalised in song by Egyptian singer Abdel Halim Hafez. The poem centres on a fortune-teller who examines an overturned coffee cup and predicts a man's troubled romantic future. Through the familiar practice of reading coffee grounds, Qabbani transforms the finjan into a vessel of destiny, longing and heartbreak. Whether used for conversation, ceremony or fortune-telling, the finjan is rarely just a drinking vessel. Its significance comes from what happens around it: an invitation to sit, an opportunity to talk and an expression of welcome repeated with every refill.

title: I can't imagine life without my phone. But sometimes I wish I could
description: With so many ways to communicate, it often feels as if we are paying less attention to the people right in front of us
content: More than a decade ago, I went on a personal retreat. For seven days, I wasn’t allowed to use a mobile phone. The first few days were difficult. It took discipline not to reach for a phone, check a message, or wonder what was happening outside. But as the days passed, I got used to the silence. Looking back, those seven days were some of the most peaceful and calm moments of my life. If I were given the chance to experience that again, I wouldn’t hesitate. Lately, I’ve found myself missing something I never thought I would: life without a mobile phone . Not because life was necessarily better then, but because it felt less demanding. I grew up at a time when having a phone in your pocket wasn’t normal. My first personal communication device was a pager. Then came mobile phones that could only make calls and send text messages. Mobile internet followed and then social media . Slowly, the mobile phone went from being something we used when we needed it to something that seems to be with us every waking hour. I know many people today can’t imagine leaving home without their phones. I’m one of them. If I realise I’ve left mine behind, I will probably go back and get it. But sometimes I wonder whether being connected all the time has actually made us feel more connected. Life feels more chaotic now. There is less privacy, more distraction and an expectation that we should always be reachable. Despite having so many ways to communicate, sometimes it feels as if we are paying less attention to the people right in front of us. I often see families or groups of friends eating together in restaurants while everyone is looking at their own phone. Couples sit across from each other scrolling through separate screens. Sometimes you’re talking to someone and realise they’re only half-listening because they’re also checking their phone. And I’m guilty of it, too. I know I spend more time on my phone than I should. Lately, I’ve been undergoing physiotherapy because of poor posture, and back and neck pain. My doctor mentioned that constantly using a mobile phone can contribute to these problems. It made me realise just how much time I spend looking down at a screen without even noticing it. But apart from the physical effects, there are smaller things about life before mobile phones became such a big part of our day that I miss. One is the simplicity of being unreachable. If someone called your house on the old landline and you weren’t home, they simply called again later. There was no anxiety about blue ticks, missed messages or being left on read. Nobody wondered why you hadn’t replied after 20 minutes. You didn’t need to explain where you were or why you hadn’t answered. Being unreachable was normal. We made plans and trusted people to show up. If someone said, “I’ll meet you there at 3pm”, you had to make an effort to be there because you couldn’t easily send a last-minute message saying you were running late. We memorised phone numbers and asked people for directions. If we were waiting for a bus, sitting alone in a cafe or standing in a queue, we simply waited. We watched people, looked around or let our minds wander. Sometimes we were bored and that was fine. Today, the moment there is nothing to do, it’s almost automatic to reach for a phone. A few minutes waiting for an appointment or standing in a queue is enough to start scrolling. I also miss how private life used to feel. Not every meal, holiday, birthday or ordinary moment needed to be photographed and shared. We took pictures because we wanted to remember something, not because we felt other people needed to see what we were doing. We went to concerts and watched the stage instead of watching the performance through a phone screen. A holiday could simply be a holiday and a meal could just be a meal. Some memories belonged only to the people who were there. Of course, I’m not pretending everything was better before mobile phones. Far from it. I certainly don’t miss getting lost because I didn’t have Google Maps . I don’t miss searching for a payphone when I needed to call someone or physically going to a bank just to transfer money or pay a bill. Today, we can do all those things in seconds. Maps, banking, cameras, news, music, messaging and video calls are all available through one device in our pocket. For me, being able to communicate easily with people far away is particularly important. I am the daughter of a retired Overseas Filipino Worker , and I later became an OFW myself. For families like ours, mobile phones and the internet have completely changed what it means to live far away from the people we love. When my father was working overseas, communicating with him was nothing like it is today. We wrote letters that could take what felt like ages to arrive. Sometimes we recorded our voices on cassette tapes. We would put the tape in a package and send it to him, and he would do the same for us. Then we waited. There was always something exciting about receiving those packages. You had waited so long to hear that familiar voice. Communication required patience because there was no way to simply pick up a phone and make a video call. For OFWs today, that distance can feel very different. Someone can finish work, open an app, and immediately see their family back home. Parents working abroad can watch their children grow through video calls. Families can be part of birthdays, celebrations, and even ordinary days despite living thousands of kilometres apart. That is something I would never want to lose. But I think convenience has also changed us. We are connected for almost every waking hour. Messages arrive throughout the day. Social media gives us an endless view of other people’s lives. Even when we have nothing to do, we rarely allow ourselves to do nothing. Somewhere along the way, being constantly available became normal. I don’t really want to go back to the days of payphones, paper maps or waiting weeks for a letter. What I miss is much simpler. There was a time when I could sit with someone and have a conversation without a phone sitting on the table between us. If I was waiting for a friend, I waited. Maybe I watched people passing by or just looked around. I didn’t feel that every empty minute had to be filled with something. I suppose that is one reason I still remember my seven-day retreat so clearly. In the beginning, not having my phone was uncomfortable. I kept thinking about what I might be missing. But after a few days, I got used to it and eventually stopped looking for it. I’m not saying I want to get rid of my mobile phone. I don’t. I just want to become better at knowing when to put it down. Because I miss the way we lived when they didn’t take up so much of our attention.
