I miss being unreachable for a few hours and nobody finding that unusual. I miss going home at the end of the day and feeling that the day was actually over. There was no endless scrolling before bed, no last check of messages and no need to see what everyone else was doing. Whatever was happening could wait until the next day. And we were perfectly fine with that.

title: Aman Nai Lert Bangkok review: What it's like to stay at the city's most expensive hotel
description: Spacious suites, exceptional service and a secluded setting offer guests a luxury retreat in the heart of the Thai capital
content: There's luxury and then there's Aman . The hotel brand has built its reputation on properties where privacy, personalised service and meticulous attention to detail matter as much as five-star facilities. Often found in remote or secluded settings , its hotels are designed to make guests feel removed from the outside world, even in the middle of bustling Bangkok . That sense of exclusivity begins before my partner and I even reach the hotel. As soon as we step off the plane at Suvarnabhumi Airport, our host, Trin, greets us and guides us through the terminal. While other passengers from our flight head towards the main immigration queues, we're led in a different direction, through the diplomatic and cabin crew lane. This makes what can be a tiring part of arriving in Bangkok remarkably smooth. It feels like an excellent start to my partner's first time in Thailand as we move through immigration quickly. Trin waits with us for our luggage, even offering to collect it from the belt. While it's a kind gesture, we assure him we can manage. From there, we're led to our waiting BMW i7, stocked with bottles of water, artisanal chocolates and ginger chews. Our driver, Mod, hands us cold towels to freshen up. These are particularly welcome after our almost seven-hour overnight flight. Our seats have massage functions and window coverings offer privacy from the traffic outside, allowing us to settle in as we are driven into the city. Much like other Aman properties, the hotel is deliberately intimate, with only 52 suites. The smallest cover an impressive 94 square metres, making them particularly spacious for a city hotel. Despite being in the middle of Bangkok, the whole space feels remarkably private and secluded, and we rarely see other guests in the hallways or lifts. We are staying in a premier suite on the 12th floor. Floor-to-ceiling windows provide plenty of natural light and views across the city skyline. An oversized king bed and window seat sit alongside a separate living area with a large daybed, dining table and desk, making the suite feel more like a small apartment than a conventional hotel room. The generous amount of space continues in the bathroom, with a free-standing soaking tub, double vanities and a large marble rain shower. Pivoting panels between the bathroom and bedroom can also be opened, making the already sizeable suite feel even larger. The hotel has seven restaurants and bars, although most of our dining takes place on the ninth floor. This is where Arva, Aman's Italian restaurant, serves breakfast as well as lunch and dinner, while 1872 offers Thai and western dishes, afternoon tea and drinks. Other options are found within the Aman Club on the 19th floor, including the Japanese teppanyaki restaurant Hiori, omakase concept Sesui and the Aman Lounge. On our first night, we have dinner at Arva. We start with the Napoli pizzette (750 Thai baht), followed by minestrone soup (500 baht), linguine all'astice (2,500 baht) and risotto allo zafferano (1,050 baht). We're impressed by how well the restaurant does Italian food, especially in a city where excellent Thai cuisine is everywhere. Dessert is a highlight. The tiramisu (650 baht) isn't overly sweet and has a pronounced coffee flavour, while the fetta fiorentina (550 baht) pairs dark chocolate with a sharp sherbet that work surprisingly well together. However, what stands out perhaps more than the food is the hospitality. When I mention I'm feeling cold because of the air conditioning, a member of staff brings me a scarf to wear. I'm also feeling congested and, without even asking, they prepare a warm lemon and honey tea . During our stay, we also visit 1872, the hotel's all-day dining restaurant. I order an iced Thai milk tea, while my partner opts for the Garden Keeper, a mocktail combining pineapple, banana, mint and honey with grapefruit and rosemary tonic. We share a rocket and fig salad, falafel sandwich with spicy sauce and French fries, vegetable toast and pad see ew. The latter proves a particularly good introduction to quality Thai food for my partner. We finish with the classic Thai dessert of mango sticky rice. Despite being in the centre of Bangkok, we barely hear any of the city's traffic or other noise while inside the hotel. Set within the seven-acre Nai Lert Park , it is surrounded by greenery and feels incredibly private. The hotel is within walking distance of shopping centres including Central Embassy, but most of Bangkok's major sights require a car or public transport. This isn't much of an inconvenience, though, as rides through apps such as Grab are easy to arrange and the hotel is well placed for exploring other parts of central Bangkok. The wellness facilities are extensive, with a 265 square-metre fitness centre equipped with Technogym machines, dedicated movement and Pilates studios, and a 25-metre outdoor swimming pool. The Aman Spa, on the 10th floor, has seven treatment rooms, including one dedicated to Thai massage, as well as hydrotherapy facilities with dry and steam saunas, hot tubs, cold plunge pools and experiential showers. Traditional Thai massage and herbal treatments are on offer, and I opt for the 90-minute Rice Compress oil massage, a treatment exclusive to Aman Nai Lert Bangkok. Gently heated rice compresses are used alongside a choice of signature oil, with the treatment designed to relax tense muscles and promote smoother skin. I'm given ginger and lemon balm tea before my therapist, Jan, begins the treatment. It's so relaxing that I fall asleep several times. There's also a thoughtful touch at the end: I'm given rice compresses to take home, along with instructions on how to heat and use them. From the moment we step off our flight, Aman Nai Lert Bangkok makes it clear that we are being looked after. The service is attentive without feeling intrusive, and despite the number of staff quietly working, we are rarely disturbed when we're in our room. Butler services and requests can be handled easily over WhatsApp, meaning there's little need to call reception or seek someone out. For example, when I ask for a clothes steamer after unpacking crumpled clothes from our suitcases, I return later to find a full-sized standing steamer in our room. Aman Nai Lert Bangkok is the city's most expensive hotel, but much of what is being paid for isn't immediately obvious. The luxury here is in the sizeable suites, exceptional privacy and attentive service. Perhaps its greatest strength is how removed it feels from the city despite being right in the middle of it. For those willing to pay for it, the real luxury here is having the energy of one of Asia's busiest cities on your doorstep while feeling almost entirely removed from it. Room rates vary depending on the season. My room starts at $1,748 (Dh6,420) per night, excluding taxes. Check-in is from 3pm and checkout is by noon, with both flexible subject to availability. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: How a chance encounter with a sheep inspired a film about Palestinian displacement
description: In Concrete Land, director Asmahan Bkerat chronicles eight years in the lives of an Afro-Palestinian Bedouin family in Jordan, capturing their struggle to hold on to their home as eviction threatens their way of life
content: Sometimes the best documentaries start out on a whim. When Asmahan Bkerat met the Palestinian Bedouin family at the heart of her debut Concrete Land , she had no idea that eight years later she’d be presenting their story to the world. We’re sitting in Sea Containers hotel, right by the Thames, the day after the UK premiere at the London Film Festival . Just a few seats away are two of her subjects, Awad and his daughter Eman, and it’s the first time they’ve left Jordan. “It’s a complete culture shock for them,” says Bkerat. “First train ride, first plane … everything!” Bkerat gives me a promotional pin badge for the film, bearing a picture of Badrya, a woolly black sheep and one of the characters in this striking familial portrait. It all started when, quite by coincidence, Bkerat and her friend Ban Marqua (the film’s eventual editor and producer) met Badrya and her owner, Hakima, one of the family’s elders, on the outskirts of Amman. “The sheep is walking beside her like a dog,” she smiles. “That was a conversation starter.” Hakima invited them to her home. “We were very surprised to find a small tent settlement embedded in the city. I’d never seen that before.” Bkerat began shooting – initially resulting in a 2017 sheep-focused short, called Badrya . Encouraged to keep going, she kept the cameras rolling – capturing an overwhelming 400 hours of footage. “I did question myself a couple of times on what I was doing because in the middle you don’t know if it’s going anywhere,” she says. “You anticipate for something to happen, but it might not. There might be a story. There might not be a story. It took a lot of patience. But they were very patient with me, honestly. I was filming them sleeping. I was filming them crying. I was there all the time.” What ultimately emerged is a powerful tale of displacement , as this Afro-Palestinian family is facing the loss of the land they live on, thanks to proposed construction. It hardly helps that one of their neighbours, living in a luxurious-looking walled villa, has filed an eviction order. His callous argument is that the families living in this nearby tented settlement cause pollution – noise, smell, refuse. “I think his mentality speaks to a much wider perspective of thinking about yourself and not thinking about others,” says Bkerat. “And the way he looked down on people … he’s just treating them like they’re nothing.” The film took on far greater resonance after the events of October 7, 2023 , and the subsequent destruction of Gaza by Israeli forces. “I think we all became aware that inherently all stories are political,” says Bkerat. “And now more than ever because the reality of the region shapes all of our experiences. I think one of the things that the film speaks to is that displacement and colonisation does not only happen on the ground in the same country. In fact, it has a much wider ripple effect that affects everybody, and it continues for generations.” One of the most heartbreaking scenes comes as Hakima is mourning the loss of her extended family in Gaza, many of whom have been killed. “Today my heart is with Gaza ,” she cries, as she sings a traditional Bedouin song, one that expresses her utter helplessness, being stranded from her folk. “She’s describing her pain and she just wants to go back to her homeland,” says Bkerat, who admits she was “very surprised” by this sudden outburst. “I had to contain myself and not respond because I wanted to capture it.” Aside from the slightly bizarre quirk that two other films ( The History of Concrete ; Concrete Turned To Sand ) are also on the festival circuit right now, the English title of Bkerat’s film also lodges in the mind. It’s about the “juxtaposition between the concrete and the land”, she explains, “and how sterile and inorganic concrete is in comparison to the land, and how it devours everything … I think it’s fitting in a way. It describes the state of the world. Everything is turning into concrete.” No pun intended, but Bkerat’s next task is to shepherd the film into the world. While it’s set to be screened at the famous documentary festival IDFA and the London Palestinian Film Festival in November, her biggest concern is making sure those in the Bedouin community see it. Easier said than done. “In Jordan, we have only a couple of cinemas, maybe five in the whole country.” A mobile screens-on-wheels is one possible solution, to “put the film out there as much as possible”. For a filmmaker who hadn’t even seen an observational documentary until she 2018’s Afghan activist story Laila at the Bridge , she’s now fully committed to the art form. Alongside various projects she’s developing, Bkerat is working with colleagues to establish the first documentary association in the West Asia and North Africa region. “We have a few organisations that support documentary, but not an association that supports documentary filmmakers,” she explains. As they say, from little acorns do mighty oaks grow.

title: Israeli expansion across Golan Heights frontier takes toll on Syrian farmers
description: Many have lost their livelihood after their land was destroyed or cut off by a new military line known as Sufa 53
content: In the 19th century, Hasan Saadeddin’s clan left what is now Jordan after a tribal feud and settled in the Golan Heights. The clan became owners of land close to Jabata Al Khashab in Syria 's Quneitra province, near the high ground that Israel occupied in 1967. For nearly three decades, Mr Saadeddin farmed the quarter-hectare he owns in peace. With plentiful rain and rich soil on the strategic plateau, his trees produced prized olives, cherries and plums. A 1974 armistice ensured calm in the area – until the 2011 to 2024 Syrian civil war. His life came crashing down in April 2024, when Israeli forces arrested his son Saddam, then 16, during an incursion across the armistice line. “Saddam was not a threat to anyone. I haven’t heard from him. He is now almost 19,” Mr Saadeddin said. By the end of 2024, his land had disappeared behind a new Israeli military line, a result of the upheavals in Syria and the wider Middle East. The area is a focal point of US-sponsored talks between Israel and Syria on security arrangements and eventual peace. The last known discussion was held in Jordan's capital, Amman, in August, but the talks have been inconclusive, with Syria demanding that Israeli forces return to the armistice line. Instead, Israel has begun creating a new military line beyond the Golan highlands that it occupied in the 1967 war and annexed in 1981. “They bulldozed and torched my land,” Mr Saadeddin said, pointing to a row of trees behind an earth barrier that forms part of the new line, known as Sufa 53 , named after an Israeli brigade. Syrian authorities said last week that Israel was extending the line south towards the Yarmouk River basin, near the border with Jordan. Israel has not officially acknowledged the existence of Sufa 53. “It is not a continuous line yet,” an official in Quneitra said. He said Israel had built seven military outposts in newly occupied Syrian territory as a precursor to the line – six in Quneitra and one in Deraa. One outpost is clearly visible across a wooded area near Jabata Al Khashab. Israeli patrols enter the village almost daily, according to residents, looking for weapons and questioning passers-by. Mr Saadeddin is not the only farmer along the frontier to be affected by Israel's new military line. Agricultural engineer Asia Al Ali, who works with the Quneitra governorate, said Israel had taken over 1,160 hectares of farmland and wooded areas near Jabata Al Khashab and other parts of the frontier. Israel destroyed 40 per cent of those areas in its drive to build the Sufa 53 line, she said. Around 250 farmers can no longer access their land, or it was made unusable. “There has been a lot of [Israeli] escalation lately, and sometimes direct shooting,” said Ms Al Ali, adding that Israeli troops began spraying “poisonous material” this year to kill crops. Israel began building the line in 2022, near the Syrian town of Hader in northern Quneitra, after the Syrian side of the frontier fell under Iranian influence. Members of the Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, defending the Assad regime in Syria, operated in the region and formed loyalist militias. Israeli positions came under rocket fire. Israel responded with air strikes and incursions. The dynamics changed sharply after militant forces led by current Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara ousted Bashar Al Assad's government in December 2024. In the following weeks, Israel sent troops across the frontier and mounted an air campaign that destroyed large amounts of Syrian military hardware, without targeting members of the new order. The US, which emerged as the most powerful backer of the new government, initiated talks between Syria and Israel to reach security arrangements and an eventual peace deal. On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had phoned Mr Al Shara in July last year, after Israeli planes bombed government and military targets in central Damascus and near the presidential palace. Mr Netanyahu apparently warned Mr Al Shara against pursuing a deadly campaign to subdue the mostly Druze southern governorate of Sweida. It was the first known instance of the Syrian and Israeli leaders speaking to each other. However, the Israeli incursions have increased, with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights saying that 280 were recorded in September alone. Forty-nine Syrians remain in Israeli detention after Israel released 14 last month. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in August that the military performed what he described as daily activity to “eliminate threats and remnants of the Assad regime” and to prevent “dangerous consolidation of the new regime”. Carmit Valensi, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said Mr Al Shara “may have become substantially more pragmatic, but the system around him has not necessarily undergone the same transformation”. Ms Valensi said the Syrian President was surrounded by former members of Hayat Tahrir Al Sham, the former Al Qaeda affiliate he founded during the civil war, and hardline security commanders. “The test is no longer simply whether Al Shara has changed. It is whether he can discipline, transform and ultimately institutionalise the system around him.” However, a prolonged Israeli military presence and repeated incursions could weaken Mr Al Shara to the advantage of “ISIS, Iranian networks, Hezbollah, Palestinian factions, arms trafficking and local militias”, she said. “In that sense, fragmentation can create tactical advantages but strategic instability.” In Quneitra, Syrian security forces have set up roadblocks to guard against infiltrators who could try to attack Israeli positions. Syrians who are not from the province need permission to enter parts of a buffer zone created in 1974, which has been shrinking because of the territorial grabs by Israel. Unlike during the Assad regime, Syrian authorities have avoided using threatening rhetoric against Israel and focused on garnering condemnation of its actions from allies, and promoting cases, such as that of Mr Saadeddin, to show the human impact. An Arab-Israeli lawyer heard about the case and recently contacted Mr Saadeddin, offering to try to help his son. Since losing his land, Mr Saadeddin has been working for other land owners. This week, he was supervising two dozen workers brought from eastern Syria to harvest olives around Jabata Al Khashab. Additional reporting by Thomas Helm in Jerusalem

title: Former soldier braves blisters and bears to complete epic 1,700km run across three countries
description: Nick Coats reached Turkey after running unsupported through the wilderness of northern Greece and Albania
content: Dodging bears, wolves and wild dogs and enduring days of isolation, one man has been tested mentally as much as physically while attempting to run 1,700km across three nations in just 40 days. Former British soldier Nick Coats , 39, arrived in Cappadocia in Turkey late on Wednesday evening after running through Greece and Albania to support a UK men’s mental health charity. The fitness coach, who lives in Dubai , set his sights on the ultra-endurance challenge after seeing friends and colleagues struggle with their mental health. Running through the Albanian mountains while carrying a 12kg rucksack at 35C was a particular challenge, as was managing feet ravaged by blisters and the daily wear and tear of long-distance running. “The last day was a 54km day to get to the hotel at around 7pm, which was hugely satisfying,” Mr Coats told The National from the comfort of his hotel room. “Arriving in Cappadocia town, I was met by the mayor, the mayor's wife and the assistant mayor, so it couldn’t have been more welcoming. “The distances between the towns, the availability of resources, and not being able to find a place to stay every night was ridiculously challenging. The main message here is that endurance is such a good teacher when it comes to how to deal with our struggles in daily life.” He began running on September 5 in Albania and travelled through Greece before reaching the finishing line in Cappadocia. The route included two organised ultramarathons, starting with the two-day 100km Ultra 4 Veterans Albania mountain race. During his daily marathons, he would contend with weather extremes, steep climbs and hidden wildlife along the way. “I was contending with these guardian dogs, which are the most incredible beasts,” he said. “Coming across those when you're running is quite intimidating, which added to the rawness. In northern Greece, I constantly had warnings of bears and wolves out in the forests, but I never saw any. Even running on the motorways was quite exciting because the lorries were honking in support and policemen on the hard shoulder were also extremely supportive.” His girlfriend, friends and family flew out to join him for the latter stages, which brought huge relief from the long days of loneliness, he said. Mr Coats served for seven years in the British Army as a member of the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, after which he found it difficult to adjust to civilian life. He took up ultramarathon running shortly after moving to Singapore and his marriage breaking down. He is now a personal fitness coach in Dubai and supports others looking to maximise their chances of completing similar endurance events. Although he has reached his final destination, his efforts are not quite over, as he plans to join hundreds of other runners on the 119km Cappadocia Ultra Trail on Saturday. He aims to raise funds for the UK’s Check in on a Mate initiative, which seeks to improve men's mental health and promote regular conversations about challenging issues. He also hopes to introduce education programmes in schools and train teachers to speak to young people who may be facing mental health challenges. He said he hopes the scheme can be replicated in the UAE. “This has been about reaching people with the message that you're not alone, and to break the silence around men's mental health. To decriminalise attempted suicide in the UAE is a massive step in the right direction. “We want to catch the warning signs of mental health that could be leading people down a difficult path of isolating themselves, or changes in behaviour that could be a red flag. I'm really hoping that in due course we can look to create something like that in the UAE as well and get into these schools and communities to create more mental health first aiders. Now we can start to talk about it a lot more openly. “This has made me realise how much the human body is capable of, and it's actually the mind that will be your downfall. If you can control those moments, then the body will follow, there is no doubt about it.”

title: Judge by day, novelist by night: How Ashraf Elashmawy found compassion through fiction
description: The Egyptian author and Sheikh Zayed Book Award winner discusses how 36 years in his country's judiciary have shaped his fiction
content: One of the stranger cases Ashraf Elashmawy investigated during his legal career involved a missing bird. It was 1990, and the young Egyptian prosecutor was assigned a case involving a peacock stolen from Cairo Zoo. “The bird was actually taken home by the zoo guard, slaughtered by his wife and served with molokhia, a traditional Egyptian dish,” Elashmawy recalls. The incident later found its way into his 2019 novel The House of the Coptic Woman , which follows a young prosecutor investigating mysterious deaths in rural Egypt amid rising religious tension. Now an established criminal court judge and acclaimed novelist , whose latest book Births in the Zoo won this year's Sheikh Zayed Book Award , Elashmawy says his legal career has given him a more intimate view of Egyptian society, where everyday events can be stranger than anything a novelist can conjure. “I don't think I write fantasy as much as I write absurd realism. Because reality itself is actually very absurd. “I think reality has surpassed the imagination of writers everywhere in the world,” he tells The National at Frankfurt Book Fair , where he confirmed that an English translation of Births in the Zoo is under way. Originally published in Arabic in 2024, the book consists of three interconnected novellas about Egyptians whose attempts to improve their lives lead them into increasingly difficult circumstances. One follows a young man who agrees to serve a prison sentence on behalf of someone from a wealthy family in exchange for financial security. Another tells the story of Fayez Hanna, a Christian pig farmer who adopts a Muslim identity to conceal his past after religious extremists burn down his farm. In the title novella, a veterinary graduate becomes entangled in the zoo's internal politics. While satire and dark humour run through the collection, Elashmawy says the three stories are driven by frustration with social restrictions and the human tendency towards deception and self-interest. “I think this preoccupation leads me to satirise the reality in which these people live. The satire comes naturally, without being deliberate,” he adds. “You can't force satire. That's the difficult thing with using it, as readers know when you are being forceful with it, and I won't be able to defend what I've written. You have to write what you believe in.” That combination of conviction and observation has been shaped partly by Elashmawy's 36 years in Egypt's judiciary, during which he rose from public prosecutor to president of the Cairo Criminal Court. The experience, he says, has influenced both his writing and how he approaches people appearing before him. “The judiciary has made me a better writer, and I do feel I have an advantage that other writers don't necessarily have because every day I see thousands of stories, hundreds of stories, about people, criminals and victims,” he says. “At the same time, publishing, literature, writing and meeting readers have made me a more merciful and more humane judge.” For Elashmawy, being a judge and developing fictional characters require a similar understanding of human behaviour, looking beyond an offence to consider a person's upbringing, motivations and circumstances. “A judge is not a machine that applies the law, opens a book, sees the punishment and applies it to the criminal. He takes into consideration the circumstances of a person's social upbringing. Was this criminal a victim of society? Was this criminal greedy? Was this criminal authoritarian? Was this criminal a victim of other people?” he says. He brings a similar approach to his literary work, drawing on experiences accumulated over the years to develop stories and settings for his novels. “As a novelist and a judge, they are interconnected. But when I write, I completely free myself from the judge. Completely. I take off the judge's robe. “When I go to court, I put on the judge's robe, but my novelist's mind does not stop working. It remains occupied with what is around me. Sometimes I see images and scenes that could become novels, and I write them down on a piece of paper,” he says. The title of Births in the Zoo also emerged from real-life research. Elashmawy discovered that children born to employees living inside Cairo Zoo could have the zoo officially recorded as their birthplace. “There is a person who was born in the zoo. An Egyptian man born in 1951 in the zoo. He is still living in Cairo today, and his birth certificate and identity card say that he was born in the zoo. “When I won the Sheikh Zayed Book Award, he called me and said, ‘I deserve half the prize.’ In a way, he is right.” For Elashmawy, the award's value lies beyond its financial prize and recognition, particularly in the opportunities it provides to meet foreign publishers, attend international book fairs and reach readers through translation . “I do feel a great sense of pride after winning the Sheikh Zayed Book Award, not simply because it is one of the biggest prizes in the Arab world,” he says. “There are other prizes that offer substantial financial rewards or lead to increased book sales. But this particular award offers you more after winning it than before. It provides a bridge to western culture, so this is extremely important.” Yet despite the awards and growing international readership, Elashmawy says he continues to regard writing as a welcome break from his judicial work rather than a professional obligation. “I love this hobby of mine. I still don't consider myself a professional. I'm still an amateur,” he says. “That is important to me because I love writing. I feel that it's a game, and that I'm a child at play.”

title: The challenge of raising a generation of readers in the age of screens
description: With children growing up surrounded by digital distractions, experts in the UAE say parents must rethink how they encourage them to pick up a book
content: When Deema Al Alami’s son asks for a new book , the answer is always "yes". There are no spending limits and no questions about whether he really needs another one. A game for the iPad , on the other hand, is an entirely different proposition. “If my son ever says he wants to go buy a book, there’s no budget,” she says. “He can ask me to buy a book any time, anywhere, whenever he wants. If he asks for an iPad game, I make him suffer until he gets one.” There are other incentives, too. Bedtime might officially be 8.30pm, but reading earns an extra 30 minutes. Books can be accompanied by hot chocolate, while family conversations often revolve around the novels Deema, a Palestinian children's author and co-founder of Arab Child Summit, is enjoying. “I do these small things just to put it in my kids’ head that the act of reading itself is rewarding,” she says. It is a philosophy that reflects a growing challenge facing parents and educators across the UAE: how to encourage children to pick up a book when screens offer an endless supply of instant entertainment. For many families, that challenge is complicated by another consideration. In a country where children frequently move between Arabic, English and sometimes other languages, developing a love of reading can also mean navigating questions of identity, culture and belonging. Yet experts believe the solution is not necessarily to wage war on technology, but to make books a natural and rewarding part of children’s lives. For Ahlam Bolooki, chief executive of the Emirates Literature Foundation, the groundwork for a lifelong reading habit is laid long before children enter a classroom. “Our research has found that if you read to your child daily in the early years of their development, there’s a 63 per cent chance that they will read independently,” she says. “If you read to them once a week, that drops to around 19 per cent.” The figures suggest that what happens at home can have a profound influence on children’s future relationship with books. But establishing that habit may require a cultural shift for some families. “When we grew up, it wasn’t something our parents did,” Ahlam says. “We are very much an oral storytelling culture, so I remember great aunts and my parents telling us stories of Arabian and folk tales from the region, but it was always oral, there wasn’t a book in your hand.” Crucially, however, reading should not always be treated as an educational exercise. The Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, encourages children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested. “There needs to be time where children can interact with books freely, not as something they have to do or be questioned about, just going and taking what they feel drawn to and spending time with it.” It is a distinction echoed by Deema, a former primary schoolteacher, who believes schools can sometimes become so focused on measuring literacy that they neglect the pleasure of reading. “Literacy rates are improving globally, but are children learning how to read for joy, for pleasure? That is the gap,” she says. She remembers reading aloud to her pupils every day, an experience they eagerly anticipated, and believes older children should also be given greater freedom over their choices rather than being stuck with set reading lists. “We have reading lists, but why can’t we give space for students to actually choose their own reading within a certain genre?” Such an approach, she argues, would not prevent teachers from analysing language, characters or plot while it would give pupils more ownership of the experience and a chance to read stories they can relate to, while showing there are many different ways to write a story. For parents trying to establish those habits, however, books face formidable competition. Digital devices are embedded in children’s education, entertainment and social lives, while artificial intelligence is creating new ways to access information without necessarily having to read deeply or investigate a subject. Ahlam believes attempts to eliminate technology entirely are unrealistic. “There is no point fighting technology at this point. It is a part of their lives and it is a part of their future. It is here to stay.” Children, she argues, must learn to navigate technology and AI effectively. But she worries about what might be lost if they become accustomed to receiving immediate answers. “The danger in children being exposed to AI so early on might mean that they are satisfied with the early answer and they don’t dig deeper.” For adults who developed their thinking skills before AI became widely available, questioning information and seeking alternative perspectives may feel more natural. The challenge is ensuring children develop those same instincts rather than simply accepting the first response a machine provides. Ahlam welcomes recent moves in the UAE to limit laptop use in some year groups, believing children need opportunities to develop their imagination and concentration without constant digital intervention. “When we talk about reading deeply and developing that love of reading, it’s not only about the act of reading, it’s about building that ability to let your mind wander and ponder on a thought.” Reading, in other words, is about more than absorbing information. It creates space for reflection, curiosity and independent thought. For Deema, parents also need to examine their own relationship with technology. “There’s also the element of leading by example. If the kids see that their parents are sitting on the sofa scrolling all night, you’re embedding a behaviour there.” The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing reading. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. But in the UAE, encouraging children to read brings particular linguistic challenges. For many Arab families, English dominates entertainment, online content and much of children’s social environment, even when Arabic remains the language of home and cultural identity. Deema knows the imbalance from personal experience. “I’m bilingual. I grew up reading primarily English and Arabic books, but most of the English books did not reflect my identity in any way,” she says. Now a mother herself, she makes a conscious effort to introduce her sons to books that reflect their culture and experiences, “I believe that reading is not about deciphering the words and understanding, but seeing yourself and others in different experiences.” She believes the availability of Arabic children’s literature has improved considerably, helped by smaller publishers and parents determined to produce the stories they could not find for their own families. Through her From Mother to Author programme, she supports Arab mothers who want to become published writers. “When I was young, for every one Arabic book about friendship, you would find 30 incredible titles in English. Now, I think Arab children are seeing themselves more and more.” But greater availability does not automatically mean children will encounter those books. “Entertainment is primarily in English, especially here in the UAE,” she says. “Unfortunately, teachers, Arabic teachers, Arab parents, they are fighting a tsunami of English content.” She believes too much responsibility is placed on schools to produce confident Arabic readers when children have relatively limited opportunities to engage with the language outside lessons. “We give them 200 minutes a week and we tell them we want bilingual kids. We’re expecting way too much from children who are not exposed to the language.” The answer, she believes, is to make Arabic a language of enjoyment rather than something associated primarily with schoolwork. “Should it just be in the classroom? Are parents trying to make it accessible in terms of an enjoyment language at home?” Dr Fajer Bin Rashed, assistant professor and literacy researcher at the Australian University in Kuwait, argues that even describing many Arab children as bilingual fails to capture the complexity of their linguistic lives. A child might speak a regional variety of Arabic at home, study Modern Standard Arabic at school and use English in other lessons or social situations. “When I refer to Arab children that speak an additional language like English, French, Spanish, I never refer to them as bilingual children,” she says. “I always refer to them as multilingual children.” That distinction matters when assessing literacy. Unlike children who learn to read in essentially the same language variety they speak at home, Arabic-speaking pupils must often bridge a gap between everyday speech and the formal written language. Dr Bin Rashed's research focuses on literacy education, bilingualism, multiculturalism and social-emotional learning. She warns against drawing simplistic conclusions from international reading assessments that compare children growing up in very different linguistic environments. “The danger of international assessments is where Arab children are compared to those in the USA, for example, or anywhere where they speak the same variety of English at home and at school. That isn’t equal.” However, she rejects the suggestion that growing up with multiple languages necessarily delays reading development. “I don’t think that raising bilingual or multilingual children actually slows down the reading. It doesn’t.” Children’s progress, she says, depends on their exposure to each language, the opportunities they have to practise and the social environments in which those languages are used. Skills developed in one language can also support learning in another, although the extent of that transfer varies. Dr Bin Rashed believes parents should embrace the natural movement between languages rather than treating it as a problem. “Some people think of code switching as a negative thing. Code switching is a natural part of bilingual communication.” For families, this means reading together need not involve rigidly separating languages. Parents can explain unfamiliar words, translate ideas and move between Arabic and English while maintaining the pleasure of the story. The important thing is to understand what they hope to achieve from the experience. “Are you reading for pure joy? Are you reading to help improve an additional language? Are you reading for bonding? Are you reading for social and emotional development?” Each is a legitimate reason to open a book. All three experts return to a deceptively simple principle: children are more likely to become readers when books are part of the world around them. For Dr Bin Rashed, that starts with parents demonstrating the behaviour they want to encourage. “I always say it to everybody: model, model, model reading. If you’re not going to model reading in front of your children, they’re not going to do it.” Ahlam believes schools can help compensate when reading is not already established at home. She highlights the transformative influence of a good school library and, particularly, a librarian who understands how to connect individual children with the right stories. The Emirates Literature Foundation School Librarian of the Year Award 2026 recently honoured the top UAE school librarians at the Museum of the Future in Dubai. “You see the difference of someone who’s just sort of keeping the lights on and keeping it tidy, and someone who has created a safe space in their library and knows how to find the right stories for the right child,” says Ahlam. For younger children, Deema believes physical books remain especially important. Even before they can understand the words, babies and toddlers are learning through the experience of handling books, turning pages and exploring how they work. “They’re biting, they’re chewing on the book, they’re throwing the book, they’re opening them. For me, this is reading.” She believes that, as children grow older, reading should become something they associate with freedom, pleasure and family connection rather than obligation. Ahlam, meanwhile, is optimistic that a generation raised in the digital age might ultimately rediscover the value of books. “I think if things are cyclical, maybe we were the generation that dropped off and they’re going to bring it back,” she says. “Because they’re growing up in such an incredible era of children’s literature as well.” The challenge for parents and schools is ensuring children have the opportunity to discover it. And that may be as simple as putting down their own phones, picking up a book and showing children what they have been missing.

title: Iran’s shadow war in Britain demands more than tough words
description: Tehran has denied responsibility for a series of incidents and attacks in the UK, but it has a long history of operating beyond its borders
content: On Tuesday, Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the UK’s domestic counterintelligence and security agency, gave his annual speech about the threats faced by his country. Iran loomed large, second only to Russia. According to Mr McCallum, Iran was “keen on subcontracting its UK violence” and has spent this year expanding its hybrid campaign across the country. He said that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests over the previous 12 months, with much of the aggression targeting Britain’s Jewish communities. Iran has long had a history of operating beyond its borders. Its neighbours know only too well how it uses proxies and hires criminals to do its nefarious bidding. But until recently, its activities in Britain were mainly targeted at its own dissidents and Persian-language media. In March 2024, for example, Pouria Zeraati, a presenter on the Iran International television station, was stabbed by Romanian criminals; the court found that the attack had been carried out on behalf of Iran. This escalated after the war began in February. There have been a series of incidents and attacks, mostly on the Jewish community in the UK, which the authorities have attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps . Many of them have been claimed by Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, or Hayi, which Britain regards as a proxy for the IRGC. In March, two men were charged with spying on London’s Jewish community and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Later that month, four ambulances belonging to the Jewish paramedic charity Hatzola were destroyed and a synagogue damaged in an arson attack claimed by Hayi. In April, there was a wave of attacks against synagogues and Jewish community centres in London. Last month, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, a US bomber base used in operations against Iran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament the incident was “almost certainly directed” by the IRGC. This month, two men were charged with preparing acts of terrorism; prosecutors say they scouted a synagogue and the Jewish Museum in Manchester. Iran has furiously – if implausibly – denied responsibility. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Britain about the RAF Fairford arrests “you’re barking up the wrong tree”, despite the fact that the IRGC had publicly declared the base a legitimate target. Britain has not been shy of attributing responsibility for the attacks to Iran, and expressing its outrage. In May this year, then-prime minister Keir Starmer said “our message to Iran … is that it will not be tolerated”. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in July that “Iran and Russia are using proxies and thugs to do their dirty work on our shores”. Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the opposition Conservative party, has called the attacks on the Jewish community a national emergency. But do Britain’s actions match up to the rhetoric? The answer is a qualified “yes”, but with room to do much more. £250 million (about $330 million) over three years has been allocated to protect the Jewish community. The government has taken a series of steps to clamp down on hostile state activity in general, and on the IRGC in particular. The IRGC and Hayi have been designated under the National Security (State Threats) Act, a new law to make it easier to tackle state threats. As a result, someone found guilty of supporting them now faces up to 14 years in prison; Iran’s Foreign Ministry called this a “despicable and provocative act”. The difficulty lies in the way that Iran mounts these operations. A minority of those accused are Iranian nationals, some of whom have come over by small boats from France to claim refugee status. But it would be a mistake to make this about Britain’s immigration policy, because most of the attacks are committed by young criminals hired, directed and paid online. The amounts of money are small. The controllers sit in Iran or Iraq and use Telegram and Snapchat to give instructions to their proxies. The attacks on the Hatzola ambulances, for example, were committed by four young British men then aged 17 to 20. These are not ideological lions, but petty criminals paid by the job. Breaking this model will not be easy, and nor will it be straightforward to go after the controllers rather than the foot soldiers. Doing so will require painstaking effort to target the gangs that sometimes broker the work, to trace the payments and to work with the online platforms to identify the networks. The problem is less an over-tolerant climate, and more the market in criminals for hire and unpoliced messaging apps. That said, the climate still matters. Growing anti-Semitism provides a target set and cover. Extremist preachers still inspire self-directed extremists in the UK, such as the ISIS-inspired man who attacked a synagogue in Manchester in October last year. If Britain wanted to get tougher still, there are steps it could take. It could screen more rigorously asylum-seekers from Iran, though many of them are indeed fleeing the regime, themselves targeted by the IRGC rather than its agents. It could tighten rules on hate preachers and keep the pro-Iran Al Quds Day march banned. It could chill still further the relationship with Iran. It could expel diplomats or downgrade the Iranian embassy, though the Foreign Office remains keen to keep open the British embassy in Tehran . It could close the Islamic Centre of England, described by a Minister to Parliament as “the official religious representative” of Iran’s Supreme Leader in the UK; stop giving visas to clerics trained by the Iranian regime; give the Charity Commission, a regulatory body, powers to deregister “charities” that are a front for hostile state activity. It could even fight fire with fire and use the British state’s own capabilities to cause the regime pain inside Iran. But in the end, for as long as an IRGC controller can sit in Tehran and use Telegram to direct a teenager to firebomb a synagogue, and the British state neither disrupts the operation nor imposes a sufficient cost on Iran for mounting it, we must expect the attacks to continue.

title: Deadly air strike on goldminers lays bare a Sudan deeply mired in economic deprivation caused by war
description: The conflict has forced hundreds of thousands into dangerous work in remote, inhospitable regions so they can feed their families
content: The Sudanese man in the video speaks with obvious elation. “Come on, you guys, quit your jobs selling food in the market and come and join us,” he says as he chips away at a rocky wall rich with glittering gold veins. “We have discovered where the gold is and it's a huge treasure trove,” he adds in the video purportedly shot in a gold mine and shared widely online. “We had been digging for 16 months before we reached these rocks. It has been exhausting,” claims the young man, speaking directly to camera. With every extraction made by the slender, bearded man, another man standing nearby watching chants “Allahu akbar!” in a voice filled with jubilation and gratitude. The video was shot last month in a mountainous area in northern Sudan near the Egyptian border and the Red Sea. It is where scores of Sudanese goldminers were killed in an air strike on October 10. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. In a Sudan already torn by the ravages of a civil war that has claimed tens of thousands of lives, the goldminers' deaths have touched a raw nerve among Sudanese, plunging the vast Afro-Arab country into grief and rage. Many have taken to social media to lament the fate of their impoverished yet resource-rich nation, where the war has forced hundreds of thousands into the dangerous work of mining in remote and inhospitable regions so they can feed their families. They blame the military-aligned government for failing to protect its people and question the sincerity of its public declarations that it intends to launch an inquiry. Neither Egypt nor Sudan has said who might have been behind the attack. Statements by the authorities in the two allied nations spoke of respect for each other's sovereignty and borders. Both said they were investigating the incident, with Sudanese human rights and watchdog groups putting the death toll at 72 and unconfirmed Sudanese media reports saying as many as 200 had been killed. Images ​and video shared online, which The National has been unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn across rubble, others wrapped in sheets and survivors, mostly men in their 20s and 30s, bristling with anger. But regardless of who was responsible, the tragic deaths have laid bare the grim reality of a country blighted by more civil wars in the past 70 years than any other nation. At least 14 million people have been displaced in the current conflict and widespread hunger has plagued the population. Gold prospectors head to the mines equipped with sledgehammers, chisels, jerry cans filled with drinking water, torches and food. They stay on-site for weeks, sometimes months, before returning home for a break or sojourn at shanty towns that have popped up to cater for the miners' needs. Many of the men who chose gold prospecting to make a living are natives of the western Darfur and central Kordofan regions who have been displaced by the fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and its enemy, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Hashem Darar, 27, a native of eastern Sudan, counts himself lucky to escape the air strike. “I was out of the site at the time of the attack. I was buying food and water, and selling gold we extracted at a nearby Al Ansari market in Al Oqaidat,” he said, referring to the region where the attack took place. “I am saddened by the death of the men I got to know the past two months. We joked and laughed as we toiled among the rocks and in the dust, and I just lost them like this,” he said. “When I heard the blast, I rushed back to help the wounded and recover the bodies from under the rubble.” Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign parties seeking quick profit. In several ways, the country's current gold rush is a by-product of most of the Sudan’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011. The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold in Sudan. Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million. Official figures say Sudanese government revenue from gold exports stands at about $2 billion but experts say smuggling and the use of gold outside official channels account for far more. Last year, for example, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated at primitive local refineries. Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda.

title: Palisades nuclear reactor restart continues despite work environment safety findings
description: US nuclear regulator will allow owner Holtec to retrieve tipped fuel assembly
content: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has granted permission to Holtec International, owner of the Palisades nuclear reactor , to retrieve a potentially compromised fuel assembly, although the plant received a warning about its work environment. At some point after August 30, as new fuel was being lowered into the reactor, one of the fuel assemblies tipped, causing the plant's planned restart to be placed on hold. If Holtec successfully retrieves the fuel assembly, efforts to restart the plant are likely to move forward with NRC oversight. The Palisades reactor, bought by Holtec after it was decommissioned in 2022, has become a poster child for the US nuclear energy renaissance driven by artificial intelligence data centres. The NRC said no radiation was released during the incident at the reactor, in Covert , Michigan. Amid the controversy, the NRC sent a letter to Holtec following an inspection that determined that although Palisades maintained a safety-conscious work environment overall, “a chilled work environment” existed in the supply chain and quality assurance departments. The NRC explained: “Employees in these two work departments are hesitant to raise safety concerns using all available avenues without fear of retaliation.” Patrick O’Brien, Holtec director of government affairs and communications, said the company was “taking actions to address these issues and will continue our work to maintain and strengthen a healthy safety-conscious work environment”. But the response to the NRC findings has failed to calm fears among those concerned about the plant's work environment and the restarting of “ zombie reactors ”. “Holtec's unprecedented restart of the Palisades zombie reactor will risk a Chernobyl or Fukushima-scale catastrophe a hundred yards from the shoreline of the Great Lakes, drinking water supply for more than 40 million people in eight US states, two Canadian provinces and a large number of Indigenous Nations,” said Kevin Kamps, executive director for environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan. Arnie Gundersen, a nuclear engineer and expert adviser for the organisation, called the NRC's decision to approve Holtec's strategy for retrieving the tipped fuel assembly “ironic”. “In the last four weeks, Palisades lost control and tipped a nuclear fuel bundle and couldn’t get it out, nine out of 15 licensed reactor operators failed their exam, and more than half of the people in their quality assurance and procurement departments feel they will be fired by management if they bring concerns forward,” he said, and yet “ironically … the NRC just gave them permission to begin loading fuel again!” He added that the subsequent report from the NRC indicated that the “fuel assembly exhibits significant bowing”. In a statement to The National , a spokesperson for the NRC reiterated that the findings related to a chilled work environment were limited to the Palisades “supply chain and quality assurance departments”, adding that the government agency “did not identify any violations or significant plant safety issues but has concerns about the work environment's impact on these departments.” That spokesperson also said that the NRC will “continue to verify that safety requirements are met”. As for approving Holtec’s method of retrieving the tipped fuel assembly, the NRC indicated that its “specialists and resident inspectors will continue monitoring removal activities.” In a statement, however, Holtec said that it appreciated the government agency's decision. “The proposed recovery approach was supported by engineering evaluations addressing structural integrity, fuel handling, thermal conditions, and radiation protection,” Holtec said. A source close to Holtec recently told The National that the company hoped to have Palisades back online by March 2027. Holtec has yet to provide a timeline. “Palisades will return to service when all required work is complete and all federal requirements and industry standards are met,” Mr O'Brien said. “Our team of more than 1,000 nuclear professionals continues this work in parallel with the fuel assembly recovery effort.” Before shutting down 2022, the Palisades reactor was no stranger to controversy. In 2012, an NRC report warned about the work culture at the plant, where it said safety concerns were often dismissed. In 2016, security staff were placed on leave from the plant, which was then owned by Entergy, for failing to properly follow fire prevention protocol. In October 2025, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, but was not seriously injured.

title: UN demands immediate end to drone attacks in Sudan as civilian deaths mount
description: Fighting has intensified across Kordofan region in conflict that has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions
content: The UN on Friday called for an immediate halt to drone attacks in Sudan's civil war, warning that the weapons have become the leading cause of civilian casualties this year. Fighting has intensified in recent weeks across the strategic Kordofan region, which connects eastern and western Sudan, as the Sudanese military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) battle for control of territory. Three and a half years of war has killed tens of thousands of people and forced millions from their homes. Rosemary DiCarlo, UN undersecretary general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the Security Council that a mutual ban on drones had the “potential to dramatically improve protection for civilians”. “At a minimum, they [the warring parties] should agree on concrete commitments and operational arrangements to strictly regulate their drone use,” she said. UN data shows that more than 1,100 people were killed by drone strikes across Sudan during the first half of this year. Ms DiCarlo condemned an October 3 drone strike that hit two lorries contracted by the World Food Programme and killed a driver. The lorries were clearly marked and had the required travel permits, she said. She also warned that Sudan's warring parties showed little willingness to negotiate an end to the conflict. “They are not moving closer to dialogue,” she said. “On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.” Her comments come after an air strike killed five children in a town controlled by the RSF in North Kordofan on Thursday, according to the Emergency Lawyers, a rights group monitoring abuses in Sudan’s conflict, who blamed the army for the attack. Sudan’s army chief and de facto leader, Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan , said he had assured US President Donald Trump of his commitment to peace, despite months of stalled negotiations. Britain’s deputy UN ambassador, Kate Foster, called for tougher sanctions against those supplying weapons to and financing Sudan’s warring parties. “The external support sustaining this conflict needs to end,” Ms Foster told the council. “The advancing drone capabilities we are witnessing are procured, financed, transferred and sustained through networks outside of Sudan.” She also called for changes to the Security Council’s sanctions regime. “The Security Council Sudan sanctions regime needs to evolve to reflect how this war is being fought today,” she said. Ms Foster added that Britain supported strengthening sanctions to increase pressure on those supplying, financing and enabling the war. US deputy ambassador to the UN Jeff Bartos called for an immediate humanitarian truce in Sudan and an expansion of the Security Council’s arms embargo, warning that continued weapon supplies were fuelling the conflict and undermining peace efforts. “We need a humanitarian truce. Let me repeat that: we need a humanitarian truce,” Mr Bartos told the council. He said a ceasefire was essential to enable an inclusive political dialogue and transition to civilian-led government. He said drone attacks and air strikes continued to kill and injure civilians daily, citing a strike on a displacement shelter in Blue Nile state last week, reportedly carried out by the RSF, that killed more than 30 displaced people. “An expanded arms embargo will raise the cost of continued conflict and impede the ability of external actors to provide military support to the warring parties,” Mr Bartos said. “The United States will continue to push to expand the sanctions regime to better reflect the realities of a conflict that now spans the entire country.”

title: Qatar pledges to help modernise Lebanon's energy sector with electricity project
description: Doha to finance and operate project that includes solar power plant
content: Qatar will finance and operate an electricity project to support and modernise the ailing Lebanese energy sector, Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Friday. He made the comments during a visit to Beirut by the Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman. Lebanon's dire electricity situation was a key focus of talks among senior officials. “Qatar will finance, implement and operate the electricity project, without the Lebanese Treasury bearing any prior investment cost,” Mr Salam said alongside Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Foreign Minister of the gas-rich Gulf state. Sheikh Mohammed said QatarEnergy had reached an agreement with French company TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon as an initial project. The aim is to develop a major investment project “that would benefit the Lebanese economy, as well as the Qatari companies and entities participating in it”, he said. While the use of solar panels in Lebanon has increased in recent years, the initial cost is prohibitive for most households. Mr Salam said the project aimed to provide a more stable source of electricity at a lower cost. It would help in “rehabilitating, developing and modernising the electricity production infrastructure” in Lebanon, he said. Lebanon is in a precarious financial situation, with its economy expected to contract by 6 to 7 per cent this year, leaving the government heavily reliant on outside support. A report published by The National this week details how diesel-powered private generators were supplying around half of Lebanon's electricity production at the beginning of this year – a figure likely to have risen since then – but at a high cost to consumers. “There's a serious will to arrange a solution for the electricity [situation] in Lebanon,” a Lebanese official told The National. Another said Qatar and Lebanon were in the “final stages” of finalising an agreement. “Qatar will remain supportive of Lebanon and will seek to provide comprehensive solutions to the energy issue in the country,” Sheikh Mohammed said after meeting President Joseph Aoun and Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi at the presidential palace in Baabda. He added that “the energy sector is at the heart of interests” and that “Qatar seeks to provide integrated solutions in this field”. Sheikh Mohammed also met influential Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri and army commander General Rodolphe Haykal. Lebanon's dependence on expensive diesel imports to run private generators has pushed up already steep energy bills amid rising global oil prices due to the Iran war. This has added further strain on households and businesses still reeling from the 2019 economic crisis. State utility Electricite du Liban is unable to provide more than a few hours of power a day. The situation is so serious that Energy Minister Joe Saddi, who also met Sheikh Mohammed, has begun boycotting cabinet sessions in protest at what he sees as a lack of government support. Lebanon's energy sector has suffered from a lack of investment that successive governments have failed to address. The Gulf was once a major source of assistance to Lebanon, but pulled back in recent years over the perceived increase in influence of Iran-backed Hezbollah over Lebanese affairs. Qatar in particular played a vital role in rebuilding Lebanon following the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war. Such funding has been less forthcoming following the latest chapters of that conflict in 2024 and 2026.

title: UAE's Ali Alhosani becomes first Emirati to be elected executive director at IMF
description: Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed hails national talent who will represent the UAE worldwide
content: The UAE's Ali Alhosani has been elected executive director at the International Monetary Fund, becoming the first Emirati to hold the senior international position. Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, announced the news on Friday and wished Mr Alhosani success in his new role. Sheikh Maktoum said the UAE's representation of the Arab Group countries and the Maldives on the IMF executive board reflects the strength of the country's economic model and its ability to bring successful national experiences in financial development. He said appointing national talent to leadership roles in international financial institutions reflects the UAE leadership's vision for strengthening the country's global economic influence. He added that the appointment highlights the UAE’s continuing efforts to expand its representation and leadership in international financial organisations. In a social media post, he wrote: “I am proud of our national talent who represent the UAE with distinction in addressing international economic and financial matters. I wish Ali Alhosani every success in his new role at the IMF.” Mr Alhosani previously served as deputy executive director of the Arab Group at the IMF. He expressed his deepest gratitude and appreciation to the UAE leadership for the confidence placed in him to represent the UAE and the Arab Group. “The selection of the UAE to lead the Group reflects member countries’ confidence in the country’s sound judgement and its ability to support their development priorities and financial and economic reform programmes,” he said. Alhosani said the next phase would focus on supporting the priorities of the Group’s countries by strengthening the IMF’s role in financing, economic assessment and capacity building. Particular attention would also be given to countries facing crises or exceptional economic circumstances through responsive frameworks designed to support their development aspirations. He added: “We also look forward to building strategic partnerships with representatives of other countries and constituencies and exchanging expertise with them, including by sharing the UAE’s successful experience in building a robust and integrated financial and monetary system." The IMF's executive board oversees its day-to-day business. It consists of 25 executive directors, elected by member countries, and the managing director. The IMF member countries are represented on its executive board, which discusses how their economic policies affect their own economies and the global economy. The board also approves financial assistance for countries facing temporary balance of payment problems and oversees the IMF's training and technical support programmes. Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva currently leads the IMF, heads the organisation's staff and chairs the executive board.

title: JP Morgan deepens critical minerals push
description: Andrew Frame's appointment as head of critical minerals strategy comes amid private and federal capital injection into sector
content: JP Morgan has appointed an executive to lead the company's critical mineral efforts under its $1.5 trillion drive to invest in industries deemed significant to US national economic security. Andrew Frame will oversee the Security and Resilience Initiative's critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, a company representative confirmed to The National . Mr Frame's mandate will centre on addressing bottlenecks across the value chain for an industry considered essential to advanced manufacturing, energy and defence, they said. Mr Frame's appointment was first reported by Mining.com. JP Morgan launched its 10-year, $1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative last year. The drive spans four sectors – supply chain and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier and strategic technology. The bank said those are then divided into 27 subsections ranging from fishing to critical defence components. Critical minerals fall under the supply chain and advanced manufacturing category, while battery storage and grid resilience fall under defence and aerospace. Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and quantum computing make up the initiative's frontier strategies sector. The $1.5 trillion builds on the previously announced $1 trillion the company planned to finance over the next decade. The commitment includes a separate $10 billion allocation for direct equity investments. “It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing – all of which are essential for our national security,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said. Mr Dimon told analysts during the company's third-quarter earnings call this week that the company “probably” deployed more than $200 billion in the first year. Mr Frame's appointment makes him an integral part of the US critical minerals push amid a string of private and federal capital injection into the sector to strengthen the country's supply chain . Since 2025, the US government has announced $10.8 billion in investments , including $5.1 billion in total private capital, in 14 critical minerals companies, using a range of tools from equity stakes to grants, loans and offtake agreements, according to the Council of Foreign Relations. In September, Houston-based start-up Hertha Metals said it had closed a $133.65 million Series A round that includes a $65 million equity investment from the Pentagon. The company is planning on producing high-purity iron for rare-earth magnets needed for F-35 fighter jets and missile-guidance systems. The US government also holds equity stakes in companies across the critical minerals supply chain including MP Materials, USA Rare Earth, and Canada-based Lithium Americas. Also in September, Glencore and Mercuria became the first two companies to participate in VaultCo, a public-private partnership designed to implement the administration's Project Vault initiative. Glencore said its $500 million commitment from Export-Import Bank will allow it to create a critical minerals reserve in the US. Mercuria also announced a $500 million commitment, bringing the total pledge from the companies to $1 billion. “Mineral security is national security. VaultCo is working to ensure the US industrial base has access to the critical minerals needed to build the products everyday Americans rely on and lead the world when they need it most,” ValtCo executive chair Brett Lambert said.

title: China targets AI technology exports with new controls as US trade truce frays
description: Draft rules would expand Beijing's oversight of cross-border technology transfers and licensing arrangements
content: China has proposed new export controls on 40 strategic technology systems, including 23 linked to artificial intelligence, in a move that could test its fragile trade truce with the US and deepen the rivalry between the world's two largest economies . The draft rules, unveiled on Friday, would give Beijing greater oversight of technology transfers spanning AI chips, large language models, solar energy and biotechnology. China said the move was aimed at curbing the misuse of the technology. Most can still be exported without heavy restrictions and licensing would be simplified. Beijing will seek public opinion on the proposal until November 15, after which it will announce a final version of the controls. “The announcement is extremely expansive and it will take time to fully assess its implications,” said Leonhard Xu, a senior consultant at Sinolytics, a Berlin-based consultancy. “AI seems to be the big centrepiece … but the registration requirement starts immediately, even for exports that have already started shipping. Also, always important to note that export control does not equal an export ban in most cases,” he said. China and the US have been locked in a largely bitter trade war, as Washington seeks to control Beijing's global influence. Technology, and AI in particular, has become a major driver of the rivalry. AI has become key for Chinese exports, which jumped more than 36 per cent year-on-year in September, markedly better than a previously anticipated 25.5 per cent, underscored by AI products, according to IndexBox data. Industry observers believe the move will have notable implications on China's economic engine and its trade strategy against the US, with which it is competing for leadership in the AI race. Last month, Washington and Beijing ​agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and start dialogue on AI, after Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House. Erin Browne, the US Treasury's undersecretary for international ‌affairs, told Reuters that Washington was pushing for its partners in the International Monetary Fund to rename AI “super intelligence”, a term championed by the Trump administration. China's move indicates that the “fragility of our trade truce cannot be overstated”, said Wendy Cutler, a senior vice president at the New York-based non-profit Asia Institute, who also warned that it is “only be a matter of time” until the US responds with its own restrictive measures. “Despite the agreement on constructive strategic stability, China has announced it is working on a new export restriction tool on solar, AI and other products, allowing Beijing to have better control over export levels, destinations, etc,” she said. “This once again shows that despite the two-month extension of our trade truce, Beijing is going full steam ahead in efforts to control exports of strategic goods to the US and others.” Ting Peng, a partner at BZW Law Firm in Shenzhen who specialises in trade compliance, said the registration requirements extend beyond conventional technology transfers, as they cover certain cross-border IP transfers and licensing arrangements, as well as changes in ownership or actual control of domestic technology, to overseas entities. These implications may extend to cross-border investment and corporate transactions, she noted. “Companies involved in cross-border acquisitions, IP restructuring or international licensing arrangements should assess whether their transactions involving the relevant technologies trigger the new registration requirements,” Ms Ting said. “This is particularly relevant to the biopharmaceutical sector, which has seen significant M&A [mergers and acquisitions] activity over the past two years.”

title: Settlers beat Washington Post journalist during attack on Palestinian olive harvest
description: Settler attacks have risen sharply in October as harvest season begins
content: A Washington Post photojournalist was among several people attacked by Israeli settlers while accompanying Palestinian villagers harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday. “Dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on the villagers, the Post said. Freelancer Heidi Levine was wearing a protective vest clearly marked “Press” when she was attacked. “She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said. Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah, where she was pictured lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on her left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries. “I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had [on] my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she told reporters from the hospital. Witnesses said they saw about 80 settlers, some carrying gas canisters, descending on the olive grove where Palestinians from Abu Falah village had gathered to pick the fruit, Reuters reported. “The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, a farmer who witnessed the assault. The Israeli military appeared but the attack continued. Rights groups, witnesses and victims have documented and recounted incidents where settlers were protected by the Israeli army. Live gunfire was heard in the area and at least one settler was seen firing a gun, Reuters reported. The US State Department said it was aware of the reports. "We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance," a spokesperson said in a statement. The official said the US was in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the official said. The harvest season officially began on Thursday but Palestinian farmers have been out in their groves for weeks, fearing thefts by Israeli settlers who are posting social media campaigns encouraging people to steal the olives.
