Violence in the West Bank has soared since October 7, 2023, and last year reached the highest level recorded since 2006, the UN said. September was the most violent month this year, but the attacks have risen sharply in October. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled) recorded an average of 39 incidents a day from October 1 to October 9, compared with around 20 per day in September.

title: Dubai Police arrest eight over alleged illegal driving licence scam
description: Suspects accused of selling international licences for Dh10,000 apiece
content: Dubai Police have arrested eight people suspected of running a network that allegedly supplied people with driving licences, the recipients of which could then bypass the usual training and tests involved to get behind the wheel on UAE roads. For Dh10,000 ($2,720), the suspects would procure a driving licence from a neighbouring country for customers who had never travelled there. This allowed buyers to take advantage of the UAE's international driving licence exchange rule, which allows eligible holders to convert the licence directly into a UAE one. Dubai Police's General Department of Criminal Investigation made the arrests in co-ordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Dubai’s Roads and Transport Authority (RTA). Police said the suspects used offices belonging to transaction-processing companies in the UAE to approach potential customers and promote their services. Customers were given licences from a neighbouring country without the need to travel there, take driving lessons or pass mandatory driving tests. These licences could then be presented to Dubai's RTA for exchange under international agreements between the UAE and other countries. Dubai Police warned that driving lessons and tests help ensure motorists have the skills and knowledge needed to drive safely. Bypassing these requirements and allowing unqualified people to drive could put other motorists, passengers and pedestrians in danger. Anyone who pays for a driving licence obtained through illegal means may face penalties and legal action. The force said exchanging a fraudulently obtained international licence for a UAE licence does not make the original licence legitimate or remove responsibility for any wrongdoing. Anyone seeking a driving licence is advised to follow official procedures and deal only with authorised entities. Residents are also urged to report individuals or companies offering licences through unlawful means.

title: Abu Dhabi launches TAMM Global to export AI-powered government services worldwide
description: TAMM app is going global, bringing AI-driven services to governments worldwide
content: Abu Dhabi has established TAMM Global, a new company that will export the emirate's AI-powered unified government services platform to international markets. The Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE) announced the creation of the company under the directive of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council. TAMM Global will develop, manage and deliver an integrated system of digital government services, owning and operating specialised digital platforms while holding the associated intellectual property rights. Ahmed Al Kuttab, chairman of DGE, said TAMM had become an integral part of how people and businesses interact with government since it was launched in 2005. “Through the announcement of TAMM Global's establishment, we are building on that success by making capabilities developed and proven effective and efficient in Abu Dhabi available to governments seeking to deliver better outcomes for their people,” Mr Al Kuttab said. The platform currently brings together more than 1,200 public and private-sector services through a single digital gateway, saving each user about nine visits to government service centres per year – equivalent to an estimated 12 hours annually. Customer satisfaction has risen to 94.5 per cent, up from 78 per cent in 2022, before artificial intelligence was integrated into the platform, while the cost of providing services has fallen by 30 per cent. As an independent private-sector company, TAMM Global will team up directly with governments, organisations and institutions worldwide, licensing the platform's architecture and implementation methodologies. Governments will be able to adapt prebuilt services and digital capabilities to their own legal and regulatory frameworks, enabling faster deployment without replicating every stage of development. TAMM's international standing has grown considerably in recent years. In 2025, it was named the world's best e-government initiative at the UN-backed World Summit on the Information Society Prizes, and this year won the Government category across Europe, the Middle East and Asia in the Gartner Eye on Innovation Awards.

title: Michael Carrick says Man United have already 'moved on' from Lisandro Martinez outburst
description: Defender had criticised club's hierarchy after Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid
content: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said the team has addressed Lisandro Martinez's controversial remarks about the club's management and moved on from the controversy. United defender Martinez had to issue an apology on Thursday for criticising ​the ​club's hierarchy following their ​Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, highlighting the lack of investments and singling out United director of football Jason Wilcox. Martinez then held talks with the manager and ⁠senior officials, before issuing an apology. Carrick said the chapter is now closed. “It's done really,” Carrick said on Friday. “We've moved on from that. It was one of those things. He has come out and acknowledged the situation and as a group we have moved on. “It is really not a drama for us as a group. The boys have trained really well, there was a really good feeling around training this morning. “From the outside [you are] after some big information about big discussions but it was pretty simple. We all understood the situation and what it meant. He made his statement and acknowledges that it was a mistake from him and that was it really.” In his apology, Martinez said he got carried away in his post-match interview. “Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager,” Martinez said in an Instagram post. “It was a very positive conversation where we were able to exchange ​views ⁠and speak openly about what ‌happened after Tuesday's game.” Martinez said that his frustration following the defeat had got the better of him and apologised for choosing the wrong moment to air his feelings. “Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity,” he said. “The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”

title: Abu Dhabi scientists use AI to develop pain killer 'more effective than morphine'
description: Drug has shown 'unprecedented' results in initial tests, Insilico Medicine president says
content: Researchers in the UAE have used artificial intelligence to develop a pain killer that they believe could be more effective than morphine. Insilico Medicine , a clinical-stage biotechnology company with scientists working in Abu Dhabi's Masdar City, created the pill to treat acute and chronic pain. The drug, known as ISM9528, has produced promising during results initial trials and the next step is to test it on humans. Nine out of 10 potential drugs that reach the human testing stage fail to be approved , health experts say. But there has been cause for optimism among the Insilico team. “To see a non-opioid candidate outperform morphine in preclinical models is unprecedented,” Alex Aliper, president and co-founder of the company, told The National . Insilico believe the drug could be used as an alternative to opioid medication, reducing the risk of dependence and addiction. When asked about reported side effects, Mr Aliper said it was "so far, so good". Tests showed a "very clean profile on several species in preclinical studies – we will conduct an extensive safety evaluation in further clinical trials". The company said the global pain medicine market was worth more than $100 billion. There is a significant need for effective non-addictive treatments, it added. “If you have a safe, non-addictive way to treat pain, that’s a game changer,” Mr Aliper said. The Insilico team in Abu Dhabi are also in the early stages of developing a drug that they hope could be used to treat a number of cancers, including glioblastoma, which aggressively attacks the brain. The researchers work at Insilico’s AI and drug discovery centre in Masdar City. Most of the company’s AI team is based in Abu Dhabi, with other offices in Boston, Montreal, Hong Kong and Shanghai. “Developing ISM9528, a potential treatment for pain, right here in Abu Dhabi demonstrates how the UAE's thriving innovation ecosystem has made huge leaps over the past few years," said Ahmed Al Suwaidi, Insilico’s associate director of strategic partnerships and business development for Middle East. The company is using "advanced locally based AI capabilities to develop ground-breaking, real-world medical solutions that address a critical global health care challenge", he added. Insilico’s executives described the development of the two drugs as a significant regional milestone, as the discovery of novel medicine had historically been concentrated in a small number of countries. They said the Abu Dhabi team showed how the UAE could expand drug discovery capabilities and develop medicine for global use. Insilico was founded in 2014 and began developing its AI platform that year. It launched the first end-to-end AI-driven platform Pharma.AI, in 2020. The platform helps researchers identify biological mechanisms linked to disease, select a target and design molecules that could act on it. Researchers then synthesise selected molecules and test them in labs and preclinical models. The company said it normally took about 12 to 18 months after starting a project to nominate a preclinical candidate, compared with about five years in traditional drug discovery processes. A preclinical candidate is the term for a potential new drug chosen to undergo safety testing, before being tested on humans. Insilico said it was on track to nominate about one candidate a month this year, while large pharmaceutical companies typically nominate four or five a year. The National reported this month about how the company was working to develop a drug to tackle blood cancer. The company believes the use of AI helps to reduce the number of research cycles and narrows down which molecules to make and test. “It’s like having a more precise way to model biology and chemistry at your disposal,” Mr Aliper said. “You have an intelligent system designing molecules for you, with your guidance.” Insilico estimates that its approach could bring the cost of early drug discovery down from tens of millions of dollars to millions. Mr Aliper said that could make it more viable to pursue treatments for rare diseases that have attracted less investment. But AI does not shorten the human trial process, the company added. Clinical trials can take about a decade to complete, depending on the disease, and are subject to regulatory review. “The analogy we use is there is a highway,” Mr Aliper said. "You can overtake cars on the highway, move really fast, but when you reach downtown, that is clinical trials. You need to move with the speed of traffic.”

title: Working with Austin Abrams on Whalefall made even Josh Brolin uncomfortable
description: Resident Evil star turns a story about a man trapped inside a whale into a moving father-son drama
content: Austin Abrams has a way of making you care about a character before you quite understand him. There is something familiar in his awkwardness and flaws, even when he is keeping much of himself hidden. It helped him stand out in last year’s Weapons , and has become harder to overlook as he has moved into leading roles in Resident Evil and now Whalefall . The latter gives him an extraordinary situation to make believable. Playing a young diver swallowed by a sperm whale, Abrams spends much of the film alone, trying to escape before his oxygen runs out. It is the young man himself who holds our attention – his fear, his frustrations and the unfinished business with his father that brought him into the water. What sounds like a premise built for a couple of hours of high-concept fun becomes something unexpectedly moving. Directed by Brian Duffield and adapted from Daniel Kraus’s novel, Whalefall follows Jay Gardiner, played by Abrams, who goes diving off California’s coast to recover his father’s remains. He has an hour of oxygen left when he is swallowed, and the lessons his father taught him may be his best chance of getting out. Josh Brolin plays his father Mitt, appearing in flashbacks that gradually explain the relationship. The two actors had already worked together in Weapons , but Whalefall puts their scenes at the centre of how we understand Jay. And to achieve them, both actors thrived on the tension between them, even if it took a toll. “With him, it was fun because he got super into it, and it was super uncomfortable, even for me,” Brolin tells The National . “The discomfort that you see on the screen, I think that was a result of that discomfort on set.” Abrams has kept a similar distance from co-stars before. During Wolfs , he resisted George Clooney and Brad Pitt’s attempts to befriend him, preserving the awe his character felt towards theirs. A September GQ profile described him wincing at the word “method”, though he was more comfortable explaining the thinking behind it. “If everyone’s game for it, we might as well let these real dynamics hang,” he said. It was Abrams who kept the tension going even when cameras stopped rolling on the Whalefall set. He explained that breaking it would have risked losing something he and Brolin had created and were both feeling. He acknowledged that this would not be the right approach to every film, but it suited this one. Their scenes give Abrams a different challenge from the physical demands of the survival story. With Mitt, Jay has years of disappointment and resentment behind him, alongside a desire to connect that neither quite knows how to express. The film needs us to understand why the relationship continues to occupy him, even while he is trying to stay alive. “Josh is always going to new places, and he’s always challenging himself. You don’t always find that,” Abrams says. “You hope you would find that in a partner – that they’ll go full throttle. “If someone’s been doing it for a while, they find their tricks and the things that work for them. But Josh is willing to go there and keep exploring. I’m grateful that he’s still excavating and still going there.” Brolin remembers being fascinated by experimental theatre, particularly the idea of actors rehearsing for six months to see what effect their work might have. “I think young actors are looking back at certain actors and saying, ‘What was that? Instead of just entertainment, what is getting into a role? What is full conviction? What is experimenting?’,” he says. “You try to do movies that slap you awake. You want to have a full experience.” In the film, Jay can shut his father out but still want his approval. Abrams makes both impulses feel true, drawing us close to someone who struggles to let anyone in. How much of his real life goes into that is harder to separate. “It’s everything,” Abrams says. “It’s the things that you don’t want to look at or are painful to look at. Then it’s going to hopefully go in to new territory and new lands you’ve never been to before. That’s definitely the hope.” Whalefall is in cinemas now across the Middle East

title: Foxtrot gang's teenage hitman jailed for 20 years over UK murder plot
description: Norwegian Johannes Natland was hired by Iran-backed criminals to shoot unknown target
content: A Norwegian teenager who flew to the UK to carry out a murder on behalf of Iran-backed criminals has been jailed for 20 years. Johannes Natland, 19, was hired by the Foxtrot crime network to carry out a “hit” on an unknown target in exchange for £21,000 ($28,000). The network, along with its founder, Kurdish-born gangster Rawa Majid , has been placed under sanctions by the US and the UK for carrying out attacks on Jewish and Israeli targets on behalf of Iran , using teenagers recruited through social media apps. It is known for hiring teenagers for attacks that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service". In sentencing Natland, Justice Cheema-Grubb said: "The Foxtrot network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes. You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target." She said Natland, from Stavanger in south-west Norway , must spend a minimum of 13 years in custody. He was arrested in ⁠a hotel room in Huddersfield, northern ​England, ⁠in March ‌2025 with two firearms and ammunition in ​his possession. He imitated holding a firearm and pretended to shoot one of the officers, who recovered £2,000 in cash from the room. Natland admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder and claimed he did not intend to ​carry out the ‌plan. But he was ⁠convicted in July ​after a retrial and ​was sentenced ‌at London's Woolwich Crown Court to ⁠detention for 20 years. The case was the first recorded instance of the network organising an attack in Britain. "Natland was arrested just hours before he was due to carry out an assassination here in the UK," said Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London. “Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot network, an organised criminal group ... orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime. “The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case. However, as recent events have shown, CTP will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK." She said criminal proxies were “one of the tactics increasingly used by foreign states seeking to cause harm" to the UK. "They often recruit people online with promises of significant financial reward," she added. "But the reality is that those carrying out these tasks are viewed as disposable assets by those directing them. They are used when convenient and abandoned when circumstances change.” Natland was the latest ⁠young adult to stand trial in Britain over serious criminal acts allegedly carried out after being recruited ​online for money, often as an unwitting proxy for a foreign state. This week, the head of the UK’s domestic intelligence service, Ken McCallum, said MI5 had made more than 50 arrests in the past year specifically linked to Iran operations. Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division, described Natland’s actions as a “calculated plan to kill for money” and said the case showed how organised crime networks operated “across borders and exploit young people to carry out serious violence”. The court heard Natland had been recruited when an individual referred to as Agent 47 used social media to contact a figure with the username Generalen to ask for someone to carry out an assassination in the UK. In the message, Agent 47 told Generalen that there was €25,000 ($24,306) “in the pot”. Swedish police believe Agent 47 is Ali Shehab Ahmed , a senior figure in the Foxtrot network, who was arrested in Sulaymaniyah in Iraq in December.

title: Indian embassy in UAE issues warning over fake job offers and visa scams
description: Missions receive complaints about agencies advertising employment opportunities overseas
content: Bogus agencies are targeting Indians with fake job advertisements in the UAE and Europe, luring unsuspecting applicants with false promises of employment and residency in exchange for payment. In an advisory, the Indian embassy in Abu Dhabi and the consulate general of India in Dubai have urged Indians to exercise caution when dealing with private visa and migration agencies based outside India, including some operating in the Emirates. The missions said they have received complaints of agencies advertising third-country employment opportunities and residency visa services. The consulate told The National it has “received a large number of complaints, mostly from southern states of India, directly from individuals or through welfare associations”. “The job offers are mostly for European countries,” a representative said. "Social media is the most common source of such advertisements and in most cases the individuals have transferred their money from India." The missions advised would-be job applicants not to rely solely on social media advertisements or promises from private visa-processing agencies. They should verify visa requirements, application procedures and authorised channels directly with the embassy or consulate of the country they want to visit. Applicants were also told to consult official government websites for the latest immigration information before making payments or sharing personal documents, and were urged to be wary of anyone promising overseas jobs or residency permits in exchange for payment. The latest advisory follows a warning issued by the Indian embassy in Abu Dhabi in August about unauthorised people offering consular services. According to previous warnings, scammers have targeted Indian citizens, particularly blue-collar workers, by posing as agents who claim they can arrange emergency certificates, exit permits, Emirates ID, visa regularisation and employment. In some cases, fraudsters obtain victims' facial images and fingerprint scans under false pretences. They may then misuse this information to conduct financial transactions, open bank accounts or get loans and credit cards in victims' names without their knowledge or consent. Victims could then face financial liabilities and potential legal consequences, including fines, travel bans or imprisonment. The missions have urged Indian citizens to verify the credentials of anyone offering consular or immigration-related services before sharing biometric data or other sensitive personal information. India's top crime-investigating agency, the Central Bureau of Investigation, also warned citizens on Friday about passport-related fraud involving people impersonating agents or police officials. The CBI said fraudsters may promise faster processing, guaranteed approval or immediate appointments while demanding money and personal information. Some also create lookalike websites of official passport portals to collect application fees, banking details and identity documents. Other scams involve fake police verification calls in which victims are threatened with delays, passport cancellation or legal action unless they pay a fine or disclose personal information. Scammers may also offer fake passport updates, renewals and delivery services to extract money and sensitive data. The CBI reiterated that no agent can guarantee passport approval or promise special access to urgent processing. It offered tips to avoid falling victim to recruitment, visa and passport scams.

title: Beauty during breast cancer treatment: Products to use and ingredients to avoid
description: Cancer drugs can cause skin to thin, bruise and crack, so here are items, routines and adaptations experts suggest to maintain a supportive self-care routine
content: With so many aspects of life upturned and disrupted by a cancer diagnosis and subsequent treatment, some women find that sticking to usual routines can support emotional stability and a sense of control during an uncertain period. “For me, maintaining my skincare routine was a way of looking after myself and holding on to a sense of normality during a challenging time,” says breast cancer survivor Azza Mohammed. “Throughout my treatment, I continued taking care of my skin and never allowed the illness to take away my sense of self or negatively affect my outlook on life.” Something as simple as investing in a rich cream for weakened skin, oil for sore nails, or a balm for cracked skin requires little physical effort but can have a huge effect on mental health and self-esteem. “I think it's incredibly important, and not just for the skin,” says Dr Parisa Khonsari at Sequoia Clinic, Dubai. “Going through breast cancer treatment can be physically and emotionally exhausting. On top of dealing with the diagnosis and treatment itself, women may experience hair loss, changes in their skin, weight fluctuations, surgical scars and changes in how they recognise themselves in the mirror. “I think we sometimes underestimate how much that can affect someone's confidence and emotional well-being,” she adds. “For many women, skincare, make-up or going to the salon is more than just a beauty routine. It's a little bit of normality. It's something familiar that they enjoy, and something they still have control over when so much else feels outside their control.” Cancer treatments affect skin by disrupting fast-growing cells, altering the skin barrier, and causing inflammation, with different therapies having different dermatological impacts. “Cancer treatments affect the skin in three main ways,” says onco-dermatology specialist Dr Catherine Borysiewicz. “They weaken the skin barrier, causing dryness, itching, roughness and painful cracks. They target the hair and nails, and they alter the immune and cellular pathways in the skin.” The wide range of therapies used to treat breast cancer each come with their own side effects. Chemotherapy causes hair loss, changes to the nails and hand–foot syndrome – a painful tingling, redness, swelling and peeling of the palms and soles. When it comes to radiotherapy, “even with today’s highly targeted techniques, around 95 per cent of patients develop some degree of radiation dermatitis in the treated area, ranging from mild pinkness to moist, weeping skin,” says Borysiewicz. “Targeted therapies can cause acne-like eruptions and nail fold [the skin around the nail] inflammation, immunotherapy can cause intense itching and eczema-like rashes, and hormone therapies can bring on menopausal skin changes, including dryness, thinning and loss of elasticity,” Borysiewicz explains. Patients are advised to avoid certain ingredients found in beauty and cosmetic products, not because they will adversely affect treatment, but because of their potential effects on skin immunity and integrity, wound healing and the risk of bleeding or infection. “Women undergoing breast cancer treatment may need to modify or postpone certain beauty treatments,” says Dr Ankita Tuknayat, dermatology specialist at Aster Clinic. “Treatments like deep tissue sculpting, Botox, dermal fillers, aggressive chemical peels, lasers, high-intensity focused ultrasound and even manicures or pedicures should be avoided during active treatment for breast cancer.” She added: “Patients with neuropathy [nerve damage] should also take extra care with hot water and heated foot spas.” With the skin barrier compromised, ingredients such as fragrances and essential oils found in perfumed moisturisers, body washes and bath oils can irritate skin and cause allergic reactions, while alcohol-based products such as those found in toners, perfumes and scented body sprays can dry out the skin. “This isn’t the time for anything that works the skin hard,” says facialist Rosie Osbourne. “I’d pause retinoids, strong exfoliating acids, benzoyl peroxide and fragrance or essential oils. Some women with hormone-sensitive cancers also prefer to avoid parabens or plant oestrogens. Strip it right back and always check with your oncology team first.” Retinoids are found in most anti-ageing serums, night creams and eye creams, as well as exfoliating acids in toners, peel pads and products that promise a “glow”. Benzoyl peroxide is found in spot treatments. “Packaging also matters more than most people realise,” says Borysiewicz. “Pumps and tubes reduce the risk of bacterial contamination [compared to open-mouth jars], which is important when skin is fragile and immunity may be lowered.” For UAE resident Fadwa Hussein, who was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2017, her self-care routine became about adaptation rather than complete change. “I underwent chemotherapy and surgery – specifically, a bilateral mastectomy,” she says. “Regarding my daily routine and the products I used, I started using an eyebrow pencil because I lost my eyebrows due to chemotherapy, and I used very little make-up. During radiation therapy, the doctor recommended washing with baby shampoo, so I used the brands Johnson’s and Sebamed.” In a word, yes. Self-care and taking time for yourself outside treatment and other commitments are great ways to relax and quiet the mind. “During active treatment, we usually start with facials,” says Salina Handa, founder and creative director of Sensasia spas. “They’re calm, they don’t involve the body, and they give back something cancer treatment often takes away, which is an hour where you’re the one being looked after, not examined. Many women tell us that feeling good about their skin again helps them feel like themselves.” Gentleness is vital, with regular treatments adapted to suit the client rather than using an entirely different treatment. “After a client’s oncology team gives the all-clear or once she’s finished treatment, we would offer body treatments, but adapted,” adds Handa. “This would mean lighter pressure, slower strokes and shorter sessions, supportive positioning with pillows, fragrance-free or very low-fragrance products, no heat and no work on scars, surgery sites, radiotherapy areas, ports, or any limb at risk of lymphoedema [a build-up of lymphatic fluid causing swelling].” There are also treatments designed for people undergoing cancer care. In 2025, Jumeirah's Talise Spa began collaborating with Ground, an Irish-born skincare collection focused on natural products, with a dermatologist-tested spa ritual line designed specifically to support people living with or recovering from cancer. Talise Spa also introduced massages designed specially for those undergoing treatment. Some products are formulated specifically for women undergoing cancer treatment, while others work because their ingredients won’t irritate weakened skin. “Think barrier repair, fragrance-free products and minimal ingredients,” says Osbourne. “La Roche-Posay Cicaplast, Avene Cicalfate+ and Aquaphor are trusted by oncologists. Brands like Jennifer Young are formulated specifically for people going through cancer treatment. My essentials are a creamy cleanser, a ceramide-rich moisturiser, a rich balm for lips and cuticles and a mineral SPF every single day.” “Several dermo-cosmetic brands now have oncology-focused ranges developed with dermatologists, oncologists and patient groups,” adds Borysiewicz. “However, ‘oncology’ products are not regulated differently; what matters is a gentle, well-tested formulation and a consistent routine, ideally started before treatment begins.”

title: Lebanese influencer Dr Food released from prison after amnesty law comes into force
description: Georges Dib had been given life sentence for drug trafficking
content: The Lebanese social media influencer known as Dr Food has been released from prison after the country's general amnesty law came into effect. Dr Food, whose real name is Georges Dib, had been sentenced earlier this year to life in prison for drug trafficking. He was released on Thursday, with footage posted online showing him being greeted in his hometown in the northern governorate of Akkar. The case drew considerable interest in Lebanon, with Dr Food having amassed more than 8.5 million followers on TikTok. He sells a line of branded confectionery and pastries. Prosecutors accused him of hiding hundreds of kilograms of hashish inside products to be exported abroad. His business dealings had been under scrutiny since 2024, when a Lebanese judge issued an arrest warrant relating to “manufacturing, trafficking and smuggling drugs abroad”. Security forces discovered sweets and food items “stuffed with drugs” at Beirut 's Rafic Hariri International Airport that were intended for the Gulf. Dr Food evaded justice for about two years, often changing location, cars and phone number – but continued to post on social media. In March, shortly after the latest round of fighting between Israel and Hezbollah began, he posted a video on his Instagram account, which has 1.8 million followers, handing out food to displaced people on Beirut's Corniche. A life sentence was handed down in his absence in July 2026. He was tracked down and arrested at his home in Akkar a month later. Because his crimes were committed before March 1, 2026, he was eligible to be released under the amnesty law . The measure formally came into law on Thursday after its publication in the Official Gazette . Dr Food had this month been granted bail in a domestic violence case brought by his former wife, but remained in jail because of the drugs case. The amnesty law was aimed mainly at easing severe overcrowding in jails in Lebanon, which has a current prison population of about 8,500 but a capacity of only 4,500. While those convicted of drug charges are able to benefit and be released, among the crimes excluded from the amnesty are terrorism offences, whether committed against civilians or the army, premeditated murder and rape. Lebanon's last amnesty of a similar size came into effect in 1991 after the 1975-1990 civil war, when most fighters were pardoned.

title: 'I was innocent': Former Dubai resident gives first interview after five-year detention in Iraq
description: Robert Pether to undergo surgery for skin cancer and plans legal recourse for arbitrary captivity
content: A former Dubai resident detained for five years in Iraq over a contract dispute will take time to adjust to freedom and is determined to fight for vindication after the “dark times” he endured. Australian engineer Robert Pether was released from prison in Baghdad in June last year but was barred from leaving the country due to financial claims linked to a case over a contract dispute between his employer and authorities in Iraq. “The concept of freedom is still kicking in for me because it's been a long time and I'm still adjusting,” Mr Pether, 50, told The National in his first interview since returning to Dublin on Monday. Spending time with family who now live in Ireland will be his main priority. He will soon have surgery to treat high-risk skin cancer, which deteriorated while he was in prison. “I'm having surgery in the next few days,” he said. “But it will be fixed, there's no doubt about that. We caught it in time.” He will consult lawyers over the next few months to address the “huge injustice ” he suffered. Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, both of whom lived in Dubai, travelled to Baghdad in April 2021 and were locked up four months later. They were fined $12 million over a contract dispute between their employer CME Consulting and the Central Bank of Iraq. “I'm looking for accountability,” he told The National . “I was innocent when I was arrested. We did nothing wrong. “What was done to us was not reasonable, was not justice. So there does need to be accountability. I'm not at a stage where I'm going to identify who we're looking at for that accountability. I will let lawyers keep working on that.” Mr Pether did not share details of the legal case he plans to pursue and is aware of the challenging road ahead. “It will all be made known when the time is right. What we went through, no one, no innocent person should have to be subjected to … that is not something that you can just snap your fingers and say it's finished. “There needs to be some balance and that's where we're seeking accountability among the people who caused this, the people who are truly responsible for it … so that we feel more vindicated.” Mr Pether sought to give strength to others who have been wrongly incarcerated and their families. “Do not give up. That's really all I could tell them. Do not give in. You have to keep fighting,” he told The National . “There is an end. There is a way through … arbitrary detention is completely unjust but unfortunately it still happens. It will continue to happen. You just have to be strong enough to get through it.” The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention in 2021 deemed that Mr Pether’s detention breached international law and said he was being used as leverage in a commercial dispute. Mr Pether said his pursuit of justice also aims to deter those who consider detain innocent people unjustly. “The fact that we did suffer a huge injustice … it's going to be a long path but it's one that needs to be crossed,” he said. “This is not just for me, this is for other people … because it will happen again. I will not be the last … if we do bring in some measures of accountability and a way to achieve accountability, it will help the next person. And perhaps give people thought, to not put people into arbitrary detention.” His first priority is his family and he will then set aside time with lawyers. “In terms of actually making something happen, it will take months or years,” Mr Pether said. “I'm prepared for that, as is my wife. We've already discussed it, this is part of the healing process for us.” Conversations with his wife, Desree, and children, Flynn, Oscar and Nala, gave him courage . Speaking to former hostage Terry Waite, the Archbishop of Canterbury's special envoy kidnapped in Beirut in 1987 and held in captivity for five years – four of those in solitary confinement – helped him make crucial choices to draw on his inner resilience to survive his prison ordeal. “Terry and I started talking soon after my incarceration,” Mr Pether said. “The very first discussion we had, he said that I needed to make some hard decisions, and I had to decide how I was going to survive. There was never any question of if, it was always how.” Building mental fortitude, distancing himself from other prisoners and trying to keep tight control of his emotions proved to be his lifeline. “I personally decided I'd be better off isolating myself, relying on myself and my own internal strength,” Mr Pether told The National . His wife Desree and the embassy sent over books and immersing himself in reading took him away from the prison walls. After his release from jail last year, Mr Pether lived in a secure compound and his reading continued to give clarity of mind. “Reading books was a form of escapism that helped me build up my strength,” he said. “Basically that was how I got through the years in prison and the last 12 months when I was hidden away somewhere quietly and I had a few people I would speak to daily and catch up with … “I’m a fairly voracious reader, so anything I could get my hands on, I was reading. It was a way to fill in time and also a way to keep my brain moving, so that I could think about things more clearly.” The Pether family have spoken about being robbed of sharing personal milestones, from graduations to birthdays. “There were a lot of dark times but we got through them,” he said. “My wife used to prop me up when I was really down. There were times it was a roller coaster … each time it went down, it went further down and that was hard because then you had to drag yourself back up from there.” He initially thought the case would be resolved quickly, then as months and years passed there were times he lost hope. “I'll be honest, there were times when I did question that – 'will I actually go home?’” Mr Pether said. “It was a matter of trying to avoid the really dark patches, keeping the mental strength to know I would go home. It was just a question of when.” Conversations with his wife and children encouraged him to keep going. “My family was always on my mind, my wife especially, and there was never any question of not getting back,” he said. “What she was doing was not just fighting for my freedom. She was also propping up myself, our children, holding our family together. And it was her strength, sharing her strength with me, that helped.”

title: Can memories be trusted? Abu Dhabi exhibition explores how the past changes with every recollection
description: Hyphen Contemporary founder Cecelia Jihu-Sara brings together five emerging UAE-based artists to explore nostalgia, identity and the fragility of memory
content: Every time we recall a memory, we risk changing it. Details shift, emotions take on new meaning and experiences we consider precious may bear increasingly little resemblance to what actually happened. This phenomenon, known as memory reconsolidation, is the starting point for Consolidation is Reconsolidation, an exhibition that brings together five UAE-based artists at Region, in Abu Dhabi's MiZa district. Running until Monday, the exhibition marks the launch of Hyphen Contemporary, a curatorial platform founded by Cecelia Jihu-Sara to champion emerging artists and introduce new collectors to contemporary art. Through photography, painting, sculpture and scent, the artists question how memories are preserved, distorted and reconstructed, whether through family archives, digital records or personal experiences. “The memories we recall most often are often actually the least reliable,” Jihu-Sara tells The National . The exhibition arrives at a time when almost every experience can be documented, yet the resulting records may be no more permanent or trustworthy than our own recollections. Jihu-Sara says the relationship between experiencing moments and recording them has changed. Concerts, gatherings and everyday encounters increasingly take place through smartphone screens, raising questions about what is preserved and what is lost. “Are you truly experiencing it?” she asks. “If you're behind your phone, who are you then experiencing it for?” Digital recordings may capture sights and sounds, but they cannot necessarily reproduce the emotions attached to an event. The vulnerability of online archives, from disappearing files to AI manipulation , further complicates the distinction between documentation and truth. These concerns are reflected in the work of Sara Kamar, born in Abu Dhabi in 2003, whose paintings and sculptures examine memory, identity and digital infrastructure. Her practice considers what happens when technology becomes an extension of human recollection, with smartphones and cloud storage increasingly replacing journals and physical photographs. Jihu-Sara thinks the immediacy of digital photography has also changed how people value their records, pointing to camera rolls filled with screenshots and images that are rarely revisited. A more sensory approach emerges in the work of Layla Doueidi, whose practice draws on her Syrian-Lebanese heritage, family archives and a recent return to Syria. Born in Beirut in 2001, Doueidi uses photography and scent to explore inherited and lived memories. Her wax works incorporate fragrances influenced by her father's career as a perfumer. Jihu-Sara says the appeal lies in how smell can trigger recollections that are difficult to access through images or words. A visit to Doueidi's studio, where the artist introduced her to various fragrances, demonstrated how differently people respond to the same scent. “I really love the kind of activation of the work that happens with the scent works, like the leaning in,” she says. “You really have to engage with the work and everyone has a different reaction to it.” Unlike photographs or paintings, scent demands physical participation. The same fragrance may evoke different memories depending on someone's experiences, while the blurred appearance of the wax reflects the haziness of recollection, particularly from childhood. Photography takes on a more fragmented character in the work of Martin Ong Yambao, a Filipino artist who incorporates found photographic material and the traditional healing ritual of pagtatawas, usually performed by a folk healer using prayers and molten candle wax. His unusual treatment of photographic images first caught Jihu-Sara's attention during Art Dubai earlier this year. Intrigued by the process, she arranged a studio visit and watched him manipulate the images using a candle. “I hadn't seen anything like it,” she says. “I just really fell in love with the works.” The process produces distorted imagery that reflects the way memories can change through repeated recollection. Yambao's connection to the exhibition's location emerged when he revealed that he already had a roll of film from Mina Zayed, which became particularly relevant to a show taking place in the district. Place and nostalgia are central to the work of Emirati artist Rayan Aljneibi, whose background in archival science informs her examination of how locations are documented, remembered and transformed. Her new works, including the Fragmented Recall series and steel pieces, examine the changing character of familiar surroundings. Jihu-Sara says she was struck by the distinctly local character of Aljneibi's photography. She had initially encountered the work through an Instagram post shared by fellow exhibiting artist Husna Samer, without knowing Aljneibi was Emirati. “There's such a feeling of nostalgia around her photos and these everyday kind of imagery and places and feelings that everyone here can relate to and recognise,” she says. Including an Emirati artist was not initially a curatorial requirement, but Jihu-Sara believes Aljneibi's work offers a meaningful examination of a country undergoing rapid transformation. Samer, the exhibition's youngest participant, uses symbolism and surrealism to explore identity, remembrance and the shifting meaning of home. Beyond its subject matter, Consolidation is Reconsolidation also establishes the ambitions of Hyphen Contemporary. Jihu-Sara's route into curating was unconventional. Raised in the UK, she studied mechanical engineering and worked as a project manager specialising in highways and railways before moving to the UAE two years ago. After working at a gallery in Alserkal Avenue, she enrolled in a master's programme in History of Art and Museum Studies at Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi. An assignment to imagine a museum for the capital led to the concept of Hyphen Museum, which eventually inspired her independent curatorial platform. Jihu-Sara says the hyphen represents connections between cultures, identities and experiences in the UAE, where people from different backgrounds constantly interact. It also reflects her ambition to connect emerging artists with people considering buying art for the first time. Drawing on her own experience purchasing her first artwork at an emerging gallery in East London, Jihu-Sara wants to make collecting more accessible while giving younger artists the space to present their practices seriously. “You can walk into a gallery, and no matter how much money you have, you're not going to spend $20,000 on your first artwork,” she says. “It kind of has to start somewhere.” That thinking informs the exhibition's deliberately restrained presentation. Jihu-Sara initially considered displaying twice as many works but reduced the selection to give each piece a distinct purpose within the wider narrative. She thinks smaller tightly curated exhibitions can be more welcoming to audiences unfamiliar with contemporary art, allowing visitors to engage with individual works without becoming overwhelmed. “I didn't want it to be like a bazaar,” she says. “It's not a shop. It's an exhibition.” Consolidation is Reconsolidation runs until October 19 at Region, MiZa, Abu Dhabi. It's open daily from 9am to 9pm

title: Yemen government will remain in Aden despite Houthi attack, says official
description: At least five security personnel were killed and 16 others injured in strikes on presidential palace
content: Yemen 's southern port city of Aden will remain the centre of government operations despite a deadly Houthi attack on the city's presidential palace , an official told The National on Friday. Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba, said the Iran-backed Houthi rebels will not succeed in disrupting public life or undermining state authority as the government pushes ahead with a military and political campaign against them. Mr Al Noman said the government will continue to function from Aden despite security pressures and repeated Houthi attempts to destabilise areas under its control. At least five security personnel were killed and 16 others injured when Houthi missiles struck the presidential palace in Aden on Thursday, Yemen's Health Ministry said. It was the first time the Houthis had targeted Al Maashiq Palace, the seat of the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government, since fighting in Yemen resumed last month after a four-year lull. “The government condemns in the strongest terms possible this terrorist attack, and reaffirms that such acts of violence and intimidation will not deter it from fulfilling its constitutional responsibilities, protecting its citizens and safeguarding state institutions,” Mr Al Noman said. The government instructed military and security authorities to take the necessary measures to “protect state institutions, confront terrorist threats and respond appropriately to the sources of those threats” following the attack. Mr Al Noman said the government remains committed to advancing Operation Dawn of Yemen, a campaign launched this month to regain control of the entire country, including the capital Sanaa that the rebels seized in 2014, and to restore state institutions. Government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition have partially reversed Houthi advances along the Red Sea coast in south-west Yemen. The rebels have imposed a siege on the city of Taiz , creating severe shortages of food, fuel and other essentials. The Houthis have also launched repeated missile and drone attacks on airports and oil sites in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, killing 19 people and injuring hundreds. Most of the casualties were from a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10. On Friday, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government intercepted and destroyed a drone launched towards Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said. On Thursday, Syria's Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani visited Riyadh and held talks with Saudi officials, following a visit by President Ahmad Al Shara earlier in the month. They discussed “bilateral relations and regional developments”, the Saudi state news agency reported. Mr Al Shara's visit led to reports that Riyadh had asked Damascus to send troops to support the kingdom against the Houthis in Yemen, a claim Syria strongly denied.

title: Oil touches $110 on continued uncertainty over Middle East supplies
description: Despite worries, crude flows out of the region have largely recovered, analyst says
content: Oil prices jumped by more than 3 per cent on Friday, with Brent touching $110 for the first time since May, as lingering concerns over the Middle East conflict stoked supply worries . Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, gained 3.72 per cent to settle at 109.86 a barrel, which was its highest close since mid-May. West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 3.55 per cent to hit $101.41, the first time it has topped $100 in nearly a month. For the week, Brent gained nearly 5 per cent, while WTI jumped by more than 10 per cent. Both traded lower earlier in the session. Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies. Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have also added to concerns. Those have prompted moves to ensure ample supplies globally. The International Energy Agency on Thursday said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. The IEA said wholesale diesel surpassed $200 in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US. The average US diesel price at the pump was $6.32 a gallon on Friday, compared to last week's average of $6.27 a gallon. The Paris-based agency also pointed out that exports out of the Middle East have recovered to pre-crisis levels and that oil storage globally is not tight. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . There were 82 ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch last month, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels per day, shipping analytics company Vortexa said. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. Current oil market levels “still seem to be somewhat lofty compared to market realities … [but] we are not running out of oil, as flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered,” said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next-generation research at Swiss lender Julius Baer. “Instead of tilting the oil market into a deficit, the Iran war has mainly erased the surplus that had been built in 2025.” G7 leaders pledged this month to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by releasing 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves to help stabilise markets. And in a surprise move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions to enable Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries continued on Thursday after Moscow was accused of violating President Trump's ceasefire on targeting energy sites last week. Russia's Ryazan oil refinery suspended operations at one of its crude distillation units following a drone attack, Reuters reported. The IEA on Wednesday warned that the global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war was set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories not expected to recover until the second half of 2027. Gold, meanwhile, posted a weekly loss as investors sought clues from the US Federal Reserve on more interest rate increases. The precious metal, which is regarded as a safe haven asset, added 0.40 per cent to 4,165.58 an ounce. Silver was flat at $57 an ounce.

title: Pakistan's Asian Games final star Hasan Nawaz added to Desert Vipers squad for ILT20 2026
description: Middle order batter joins Babar Azam and fellow national teammates for fifth season of league
content: Hasan Nawaz became the fifth Pakistan player to join the Desert Vipers squad ahead of the fifth season of the DP World International League T20 (ILT20). Nawaz returns to the Vipers dugout after his debut season with the franchise in the title-winning campaign last term. The middle order batter replaces England’s Aneurin Donald who has been selected for England’s upcoming T20 series in Australia. The 24-year-old batter will enter the tournament high on confidence, having come close to the Asian Games T20 gold medal in Japan. During the title match against a full-strength Indian team, Nawaz smashed 96 from 51 balls as Pakistan almost chased down the target of 212, losing by 19 runs. Last month, Nawaz scored 47 in the final to help Antigua and Barbuda win the Caribbean Premier League title. Pakistan, meanwhile, completed a T20 series win at home against Sri Lanka this month. Now, as many as five Pakistan international stars will be competing for the Desert Vipers when the ILT20 kicks off on November 21. Nawaz joins Babar Azam , Naseem Shah, Fakhar Zaman and Shadab Khan in the Vipers team. Interestingly, Desert Vipers are the only franchise not under Indian ownership and face no competition while recruiting Pakistan players. “The fact we have been able to secure the services of Hasan as his replacement is fantastic from our perspective,” Desert Vipers CEO Phil Oliver said. “He was a key member of the Vipers squad in our successful Season 4 and so he will slot in very easily to our set-up. And, on top of that, he has been in terrific form this year, scoring runs for the Quetta franchise in the Pakistan Super League (PSL) and then being a vital component of the Antigua and Barbuda franchise’s run to the Caribbean Premier League (CPL) title. “We look forward to welcoming Hasan back to the Vipers for Season 5 and hope he will play his part as we look to go back-to-back in the upcoming tournament.” The Vipers begin their title defence on the opening day of Season 5, playing MI Emirates at the Dubai International Stadium. The ILT20 runs from November 21 to December 20.

title: Abu Dhabi's IMI rejects UK Ofcom report into Telegraph bid
description: Media regulator's 'methodology, reasoning and conclusions' criticised
content: International Media Investments (IMI) has rejected Ofcom’s report into RedBird IMI’s bid for The Telegraph , criticising its “methodology, reasoning and conclusions which were reached before the evidence was examined”. The British media regulator’s report, which has been released by the UK's Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, followed a protracted takeover saga involving the British newspaper group which ended when it was acquired by German media conglomerate Axel Springer in April. The report was part of an initial review by Ofcom but that was halted after Redbird IMI sold the newspaper group at a profit. While the purpose of the report was the actual acquisition, the UK government chose to publish the report without the completion of the full process. IMI, the Abu Dhabi-based media company which was part of a joint venture with RedBird bidding for The Telegraph , responded to the report with a statement criticising the regulator’s investigation and defending the editorial independence of its titles. IMI’s media assets include The National and Sky News Arabia. In a statement released on Friday, IMI said: “Ofcom was tasked with assessing a commercial media company. It failed to do so. In an astonishing admission written into the report itself, Ofcom states that it was ‘not necessary to rely on information about the reported past behaviour of IMI associated businesses’. In plain English: a public regulator tasked with evaluating IMI admitted on the record that it ignored IMI’s actual track record to reach its verdict.” The Culture Secretary Lisa ​Nandy later ⁠said ⁠she would ​not refer Axel Springer's ⁠purchase of the Telegraph to a ⁠more detailed competition investigation and the government's interest in the takeover would lapse ‌as a result ⁠of her ​decision. A respected British business leader and politician added his voice to IMI's criticism of the publication of the Ofcom report. "Britain cannot spend half its time courting investment from the Gulf and the other half putting up barriers when that investment arrives," billionaire property developer Nick Candy and treasurer of the Reform Party told The National . "The Government's handling of the RedBird IMI deal was a total disaster and a missed opportunity for British business, and revisiting a two-year-old report now only serves to undermine international investor confidence further. If we want Britain to be taken seriously as a destination for global capital, we need to start acting like it." For its part, IMI accused Ofcom of using “an arbitrary and biased set of assumptions, conflating the commercial interests of a private company with the conduct of a sovereign state”. “It is not the role of a British media regulator to adjudicate the laws and governance of foreign nations,” IMI added in its statement. IMI pointed out that Ofcom “gave no weight” to the company’s legally binding undertakings – notably never to influence The Telegraph’s editorial decisions. An Independent Editorial Trust would have had veto power over the appointment and removal of the Telegraph’s Editor-in-Chief. Indeed, IMI noted, Ofcom’s report made no findings of editorial interference against the company. Ofcom accepted The National’s strong compliance record with the Editors’ Code of Practice, that there have been no IPSO rulings against it, and that every historical allegation regarding its newsroom predates IMI’s ownership. Furthermore, Ofcom “admits that there appears to be a viable commercial incentive and rationale for RedBird IMI’s acquisition of the Telegraph ”. IMI also criticised the way the Ofcom report was presented. “Regulatory decisions in British media have historically been decided on conduct, binding commitments, and commercial incentives. The RedBird IMI bid was not judged on the facts or on IMI’s track record. It was judged on its origin and not its conduct. IMI encourages investors to read the report thoroughly. “Allegations are not findings. Association is not control. Speculation is not evidence. IMI rejects any suggestion that it has ever interfered, or would ever interfere, in the editorial independence of its media outlets.”
