title: 48 hours in Tashkent: How best to explore the Uzbekistan capital
description: Once a stop on the Silk Road, the city is now a melting pot of Islamic history and brutalist architecture
content: Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan and its largest city, has stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road for centuries. It has also been destroyed and rebuilt several times. Once a caravanserai, a roadside inn that offered lodging for merchants primarily along the Silk Road , much of the city was destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1219. Centuries later, in 1966, an earthquake left large parts of Tashkent in ruins. The 20th-century city that emerged from the reconstruction was very different, with wide avenues, vast public spaces and imposing Soviet-era buildings. Today, Tashkent is a mix of Soviet modernist buildings, Islamic monuments, green spaces and a new generation of creative designers, artists and hoteliers giving the city a contemporary identity. Here is a tried-and-tested itinerary to explore Tashkent in 48 hours. After eating breakfast at Farovon Tashkent hotel, I start my day by walking 10 minutes to the old part of Tashkent past mud houses and mulberry trees. There, the Hazrati Imam Complex, with turquoise domes, sand-coloured brickwork, carved wooden doors and intricate tile work replaces the concrete architecture of the city centre. The complex was built around the grave of Abu Bakr Kaffal, also known as Hazrati Imam, one of the city’s early Islamic scholars and a preacher, who was also a master of making locks and keys. From there, I wander through the 16th-century Barak-Khan Madrasah. The spaces that once housed students have now become shops selling traditional crafts from carved wooden Quran stands and miniature paintings to ceramics and fabrics covered in colourful Suzani embroidery. Entry to the complex is free and it is open daily from 9am to 9pm. Visitors should dress modestly, with women required to cover their heads when entering the religious sites. Close by is the Centre for Islamic Civilisation, which opened in March 2026. Spread across a vast site, the centre explores the history of Islamic civilisation through faith, science, art, literature and craftsmanship. Inside, I journey through centuries of history from early Quranic manuscripts behind glass, some decorated with gold, to ceramics, metalwork, calligraphy and miniature paintings. The centre is open from 9am to 10pm. Entry is $25 for foreign visitors. Plov is an one-pot rice dish that is omnipresent in the country, with each region proud of its own variation. Besh Qozon, near the Tashkent Television Tower on Guards Colonel Khodjaev Street, a 10-minute cab ride from the old city, is famous for the gargantuan quantities of plov cooked at the restaurant every day. I watch cooks prepare plov in enormous kazan cauldrons. Long paddles move through mountains of rice, carrots, onions and chickpeas, with large pieces of meat, tied in bundles, added to the mixture and cooked in sheep fat and vegetable oil. Steam rises from the pots as the cooks work with an ease that comes from years of repetition and waiters serve it on plates deftly, with the dishes topped with garlic bulbs or quail eggs. Tashkent's Soviet legacy is particularly striking in the city’s architecture, with a blend of brutalist forms, grand modernist structures and use of elaborate mosaics and sculptural elements alongside Uzbek Islamic motifs called Tashkent modernism. After lunch, I venture to Hotel Uzbekistan, a 15-minute drive away. The building is a notable example of brutalist and modernist architecture, built about 90 metres from Amir Timur Square. Established in the 1970s, the hotel's honeycomb-like facade is not only decorative but also helps filter the intense sunlight. A detour worth taking, if you're interested in architecture from the era, is to the Tashkent State Circus. It is closer to the old city and is another remarkable Soviet-era building. Its sweeping white dome and clean modernist lines give it the appearance of a futuristic space shuttle. From there I make a stop at the Teplo shop on Nukus Street, a concept store and cultural space, a 10-minute drive from Amir Timur Square. I browse through the work of young Uzbek designers displayed alongside traditional crafts. Fashion, ceramics, textiles and graphic design come together, with familiar Uzbek motifs and Suzani embroidery reinterpreted in a more contemporary way on jackets and dresses. Lali, which opened in 2024, is a 15-minute cab ride from my hotel and is part of a chain across Central Asian countries. The extensive menu takes you across the different regions of Uzbekistan, with old recipes combined with modern culinary traditions. Furnished in azure, blue tones and local ikat fabric-covered sofas, it has an open kitchen. Order iconic Samarkand plov, manty with beef and lamb shashlik. From there, I retire to Farovon Tashkent for the night. A new boutique property, it is decorated in traditional style with rugs, carpets and ceramics, in the historic part of the city. The Art Deco-style Tashkent Metro is an unexpected architectural experience and is spotlessly clean. Each station has its own theme and design, with marble, granite, mosaics, chandeliers and reliefs celebrating everything from Uzbek history and literature, to science and space exploration. Chorsu Station is the closest to my hotel, but I love Kosmonavtlar Station, with shiny green glass columns and ceramic medallions, where the theme is the Soviet space dream, depicted in deep blues and cosmic motifs. Alisher Navoi Station is another marvel, with carved arches and intricate ceramic panels in cobalt and emerald hues. The Tashkent Metro is open daily from 5am until midnight. The price of one ticket is 2,000 Uzbekistani som ($0.14). For a slice of everyday Tashkent, I take the Metro back to Chorsu Bazaar, getting off at Chorsu Station. The bazaar's building is noted for its an enormous blue dome, which dominates the market and is an interesting example of Soviet architecture influenced by traditional Central Asian market halls. Underneath the dome, the atmosphere is energetic and lively. Sellers stand next to huge pyramids of spices, dried apricots, walnuts, raisins and pomegranates. I browse through traditional clothes, pottery and ceramics. Hungry for lunch, I then walk through the food court, where the smell of coriander, cumin and roasting meat fills the air. It is open daily from 7am until 7pm. This compact museum, which can be reached from the Kosmonavtlar Metro station, is housed in a beautiful mansion of former Russian diplomat Alexander Polovtsov. It is decorated with ganch – painted plaster – and wood, with exquisitely painted and carved ceilings with cornices. It showcases the best of Uzbek art and crafts, including knives from Chust, ceramics from Rishtan, silk from Margilan, traditional clothes and gold embroidery from Bukhara, Suzani embroidery and ikat fabrics. I love the section on different kinds of skullcaps from across the country, with specific motifs and symbolism, and the traditional musical instruments. The museum is open from 9am to 6pm and the entrance fee is $2.50. It is worth venturing across town to Tashkent Central Park, a favourite destination for families, with 100-year-old acacias and oak trees, as well as statues, sprawling lawns, amusement rides, a carousel and fountains. I see men playing accordions and walk past food stands and shallow ponds filled with fish. With babies in strollers, young people jogging, and others sitting on benches, this is truly a slice of local life. It is open from 10am to 11pm. Dinner at Afsona on Uqchi Street comes highly recommended. Decorated with carved wood and blue-and-white ceramics, with folk music playing in the background, this upmarket restaurant serves Uzbek cuisine with a contemporary touch, from crisp samsas to pumpkin manti and lagman noodles. If you are feeling adventurous, try their horse meat dish called norin. Finish with chak chak, a fried honey cake with almonds. There are several daily flights to Tashkent. From Dubai, travel with flydubai, Uzbekistan Airways or Centrum Air; from Sharjah fly with Air Arabia; and from Abu Dhabi book a trip with Etihad Airways, which launched the route in August.

title: The fearless ambition of Mohamed Faisal Mostafa
description: From childhood stunts to the set of Dune: Part Three, the Emirati actor has built a career on taking risks. Now his sights are set on Hollywood and helping to build a more robust film industry at home
content: On the set of Dune: Part Three , Mohamed Faisal Mostafa watched closely as Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya and Jason Momoa prepared for their scenes. Each day, he saw how they learnt their lines, how they worked, how they treated the people around them. The Emirati actor wanted to reach that level himself, and here he could see what it took. “I sat back and I saw it all and I said to myself: ‘This is not unattainable.’ I can be there and, inshallah, I will be there so long as I keep consistent,” he says. Mostafa joined the production as a stunt performer. Director Denis Villeneuve knew he also acted and began finding opportunities for him to do more on camera. As the shoot was coming to an end, Mostafa went up to thank him for his support. “He said: ‘Mohamed, there’s no need to thank me. You’re a natural. You’re a very talented actor.’” Even recounting it now gives Mostafa goosebumps. He holds out his arm to show them. It was a moment he’d been ready for nearly his whole life. Long before he worked with Villeneuve, a young Mostafa was jumping off a moving bicycle for his brother, director Ali Mostafa. Ali was making home movies, and Mostafa was already fearless, at the age of six or seven, in front of his brother’s camera. As Ali kept making films, Mostafa kept helping. That bond is still strong decades later – every year on Ali’s birthday, he calls him “my brother, my teacher and my friend”. But for years, film was one of several possible futures. Mostafa played professional football, worked in finance, ran a digital transformation agency and was involved in his family’s business. Acting fitted around those pursuits, even as the parts grew bigger and took him further from home. He could keep building a career in business, with success nearly certain. But something in him knew he had to choose the harder path. “I think you need to find an area of focus if you want to succeed,” he says. Dedicating himself to film full time makes the auditions his UK agent sends him feel more consequential. A major production could give him the credit that leads to another job, then another. Yet a few lines are sometimes enough for him to turn one down. Even now, terrorists and other stereotypical Arab characters keep coming his way from major studios and streaming platforms, offering a route into the industry he has chosen to depend on. “Trust me, it is not easy to say no to these because some of them are massive, life-changing projects,” he says. “I love acting, and it’s the only thing I do right now. It’s also what’s going to generate me income, put food on my table and support my future.” But he has to consider what accepting a part would mean beyond his own career. He is willing to play a villain; the concern is a story that leaves an audience with another reason to distrust Arabs. He wants the roles he earns to expand what people understand about Emiratis and Muslim Arabs. He carries the responsibility for his country’s reputation as personally as he does for his own family’s. “It’s part of who I am,” he says. “It’s every action I do in the morning, when I wake up. I want to prove something to my family, my country, our leaders, myself.” There is a chance to take that work further at home, too. Dune: Part Three reaches cinemas this December and Dubai International Film Festival will return on December 8 after a decade-long hiatus. Mostafa has established MFM Media in Abu Dhabi, working on production services, product placement and Emirati talent management. He wants to help to get films made and give other performers the connections he struggled to find. DIFF’s return gives that ambition a place to develop, bringing filmmakers, actors and investors together in Dubai. Mostafa wants the next Emirati actor pursuing an international career to have more help and more work available here before setting off. His own route into film took years to become clear. As a goalkeeper for Al Ain and Al Wasl, Mostafa turned his childhood love of football into a career before serious injuries ended it. His work with Ali continued as his brother moved into feature films, casting Mostafa in City of Life (2009) and From A to B (2014), then giving him a larger role in the post-apocalyptic thriller The Worthy (2016). Mostafa also appeared in the Emirati military action film Al Kameen (2021), one of the biggest box-office hits the country has produced. An open audition in London for Disney’s live-action Aladdin (2019), which eventually starred Mena Massoud and Will Smith, gave Mostafa a glimpse of how far acting might take him. He did not get the role. At the time, he carried on with other pursuits, but the possibility stayed with him: he had put himself forward for a production watched around the world, in which he could have represented the UAE. “I realised that this can actually happen, and that I love acting and I’m not bad at it. So I had to keep going,” he says. Finding an agent in Britain involved repeated approaches and rejections. When Hijack – the Apple TV thriller also starring Idris Elba – came, Mostafa finally had an international role to prepare for. He would play Abdullah, a Dubai air-traffic controller investigating suspicious events around a flight to London. A driver collected him from a friend’s house on his first day of filming. During the journey, Mostafa questioned whether he was good enough to be there. Once he arrived, the more experienced actors treated him as an equal, and director Jim Field Smith welcomed his contributions. Mostafa helped with details of Emirati behaviour, including the way people hold their hands when greeting one another. He realised the pressure was helping him perform – a feeling he recognised from his years on the football field. “There’s nerves, but they’re nice nerves – the nerves that lock you in,” he said when Hijack was released in 2023. The 2024 television drama Khattaf asked more of him. Ali gave him a lead role to carry through a whole series, playing an Emirati fighter making his way through Asia’s underground combat scene. The boy who had done stunts for his brother now had years of sport and Muay Thai training behind him when stunt co-ordinator Najmeddin Scorpion began teaching him fight choreography. One move, known as the Black Widow, required Mostafa to hook a leg around another performer’s neck, swing around him and land on his own feet as the other man flipped away. He learnt quickly. An injury left his elbow so swollen it had to be bandaged, but his character was supposed to be injured in the next fight scene. The bandage stayed on for the camera – the injury served the scene, and that’s all that mattered to him. Away from the fight choreography, Mostafa was working out the character’s childhood and family relationships, comparing them with his own. He wanted to understand the parents, how they had become the people they were, and how their behaviour had shaped their son. Early in the shoot, he drew on painful memories from his own life when a scene required him to cry. By the time he filmed a sequence in prison, he had spent enough time with the character to find the emotion in his story. “I wasn’t thinking for a second about Mohamed. I was thinking about Khattaf, and I had tears rolling down my face, and I felt and I became,” he says. “That’s what acting is. Acting is becoming.” Talking about that scene brings out the goosebumps again. Mostafa wants another role he can spend that kind of time on, and another production willing to put him at the centre of its story. The ambition to join the main cast of a Hollywood film now comes with a clearer understanding of what he would want to do once he got there. Between Hijack , Khattaf and Dune , he has accumulated experience that has prepared him for the next step. He is grateful for each opportunity, although he has started to question how often he describes himself as lucky. It can leave out the work that earned him a place on those sets. “At some point, you have to realise you’re there for a reason. You were chosen,” Mostafa says. Alongside that confidence, his faith shapes what he wants to do with the opportunities he earns. Mostafa has grown up seeing words he uses in his religious life associated with violence in western news and films. They belong to his everyday experience of gratitude and service, and he wants audiences to understand what they mean to him. “Allahu akbar is the most beautiful term,” he says. “The direct definition of it is God is the greatest. No matter what happens in our life, we constantly remind ourselves that this is God’s plan, and He is greatest.” Holding a door open for someone is among the examples Mostafa gives when explaining his understanding of jihad. “Any act of service, any sacrifice, whether it’s small or big, is jihad.” Those words are part of the steadfast identity he carries into each audition. A role that reinforces their association with violence has consequences for him beyond the time he would spend playing it. He has to trust that there will be another opportunity after the one he declines. “When you walk with your value system intact, you might be saying no to those things. But I have this faith in God that other things will come that are much bigger.” Waiting for the right part leaves much of that future in other people’s hands. With support from Abu Dhabi’s Creative Media Authority, Mostafa established MFM at Yas Creative Hub, putting his business experience to work in film. “I can’t just be an actor with an agent in London waiting for auditions,” he says. “I have to create my movies. I need to collaborate.” The work he had been dividing his time between could now support his ambitions in film. Mostafa had arranged sponsorships for fighters and concerts; he could bring brands into productions and draw on his finance background in discussions with investors. The difficulties he had faced in finding representation gave him a reason to help other Emirati performers approach the industry. Mostafa takes a sip of coffee, holds it up, and suggests it might be one of the best he has had. “Just a little product placement,” he jokes. Behind the brand partnerships, however, is a struggle familiar to the filmmakers who approach MFM. “The biggest problem I’m seeing is funding,” Mostafa says. He is working to explain the film business to investors who are more familiar with property and technology, taking them through production costs, distribution and incentives. He expects it to take years. When City of Life had its premiere at DIFF in 2009, Mostafa watched the industry gather around his brother’s debut feature. When the festival returns, he will have a company to bring into those conversations, as well as his own ambitions as an actor. Finding the money for a film could give several performers their next job, and the time on set they need to improve. He saw how quickly that possibility could take hold on Dune . Fellow Emirati Rashed Dawood, a mixed martial arts fighter, was working on his first film as a stunt performer. Dawood discovered how much he enjoyed being on set and wanted to do it again. For him to develop that interest into a career, there would have to be another production, and another after that. “We’re not going to have a Dune come every year. We need to work on and scale up independent filmmaking,” Mostafa says. Mostafa needs the next production, too. He wants another chance to get as deeply into a character as he did in Khattaf . He is working to help get those films made, while pursuing the roles he believes he can carry. “I’m confident enough to know I can be in a blockbuster film as one of the main cast,” he says. “I just need to keep pushing, but I know I can do it.” The fearlessness that put him in front of Ali’s camera has stayed with him. Now Mostafa wants to take it into a role where audiences around the world will see an Emirati actor leading the story. He is ready for the scrutiny that will come with it, and for the work it will demand of him. “I would never be given that opportunity and not know the responsibility I’ll carry being there,” he says. “And also the responsibility I’d need to have to make sure I perform at the highest level because of what I represent.” Fashion Director: Sarah Maisey Photographer: Chris Whiteoak Shot on location at Jumeirah Beach Hotel and Mohamed's family home in Dubai

title: Alex Eala has 'put the Philippines on world tennis map'
description: Filipina star decided to represent country at Asian Games despite risk of hefty fine from WTA
content: The Philippine tennis body has lauded young sensation Alex Eala for raising the profile of tennis in the country, highlighting her decision to represent her nation at the 2026 Asian Games despite the risk of penalty. Eala had risked a hefty fine for skipping WTA's mandatory China Open as she represented the Philippines at the Japan Asian Games. While she lost her semi-final in Nagoya to Wang Xiyu, her actions did not go unnoticed. Eala has since suffered early exits in Singapore and Wuhan. But for the Philippine Tennis Association (PHILTA), she has already done a lot. “Alex Eala has already achieved what many once thought impossible. She has single-handedly put the Philippines on the world tennis map,” PHILTA secretary general John Rey Tiangco said. “Her rise to world No 18, her WTA title, and her victories over some of the world's best players are milestones that have changed the landscape of Philippine tennis.” Tiangco said Eala's decision to play for her country, even as other athletes decided to feature in China, was praiseworthy. “We are equally grateful for her decision to represent our country at the Asian Games, putting the Philippine flag ahead of other opportunities. “At this level of competition, victories and defeats are part of the journey. What matters is Alex's determination to keep improving, her discipline, and her commitment to the sport. “Alex has already won something bigger than any single tournament. She has inspired a nation and opened doors for the next generation of Filipino tennis players.” Meanwhile, Indonesia's Janice Tjen saw her Wuhan Open campaign come to an end in China on Thursday. American Ann Li, who upset the top seed Aryna Sabalenka in the second round, moved into the quarter-finals with a 6-1, 7-6 (1) victory over Tjen. Li will take on seventh seed Iga Swiatek of Poland in the last eight. Swiatek had on Thursday completed the 150th WTA 1000 win of ⁠her career.

title: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting
description: Teenage attacker entered building by shooting through locked doors, police say
content: Four people, including three children, have been killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon. The attack in the city of Bend was carried out by a 16-year-old boy, police said. An armed bystander pursued the assailant into the school and shot him dead, officials added. The children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A teacher was also killed. Another teacher and a ​seven-year-old pupil were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a media conference. The attacker entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without ​offering ⁠any further details. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek hailed the armed bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life" at Silver Rail Elementary School. "No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," Ms Kotek said. "As we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to cry privately." Bend, in rural central Oregon, is home to about 100,000 people and is about 280km south-east of Portland. Silver Rail Elementary School offers classes from kindergarten through to fifth ⁠grade – about ages five to 11 – and has about 450 pupils and 40 ⁠staff members, officials said. Police said they received a call at about 1pm that indicated a man had shot into a car at Silver Rail Elementary School. Moments later, emergency dispatchers received calls "reporting that a person had entered the school ​and began shooting", police said in a statement. Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead.

title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
description: Lender targets $19bn in critical minerals financing, as it identifies 20 countries to join projects
content: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

title: Israeli company used online ads to run spy operation against 'hundreds of millions of people'
description: Ads only needed to load on website for spying to occur, research groups warn
content: Israeli digital advertising ⁠agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a network of online advertisements that it used to track ⁠targets and hack their devices, research groups said. Reports from Canadian group Citizen Lab and US advertising security company Confiant found that Discover-Tech's services gave Candiru, ​an Israeli spyware company blacklisted by the US government, as well as other Israeli surveillance groups, access to advertising platforms run by companies including Google, Comcast and Russia's Yandex. Discover-Tech's online ads, often ⁠for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds , reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said. People who visited sites or used apps with ​the malicious ⁠ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes try to extract phone numbers from smartphone users, researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur. Some ads would be used ​to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, the research groups said. But Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume. Discover-Tech was issuing at least 10 million ads a day around the world, with data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching allowing it to track people beyond the reach of its ads, Confiant co-founder Jerome Dangu said. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," he added. Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at Qatar's Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025. That was confirmed because the media group shared its network logs with the group, it added. Al Jazeera said in a statement that it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said. Mr Dangu said the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive ​categories", including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, including the Palestinian ‌territories, were saturated by the Israeli company's ads. "You go to almost ⁠any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them ​a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he added. Citizen Lab said it had evidence that the malicious ads were ​shown to people in the ‌UN, Nato, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. The ads also appeared in networks including technology companies such as Nvidia and Sandisk, as well as media organisations ⁠in Mexico, Israel and Europe. Discover-Tech is now to be frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies". IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email ​that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved entities last week after an audit identified policy breaches.

title: Animals (Netflix)
description: Ben Affleck directs and stars in this political thriller as Mark Kimball
content: Ben Affleck plays Mark Kimball, a candidate for Los Angeles mayor whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel when his son is kidnapped. Together with his wife Abigail (Kerry Washington), Mark must scramble to raise the ransom while navigating a web of deception that threatens to tear the family apart. Affleck is joined by an ensemble cast including Gillian Anderson, Steven Yeun, Adriana Paz and Luis Gerardo Méndez. The film marks another directorial outing for Affleck, whose previous work behind the camera includes the Oscar-winning Argo . Air date: October 9

title: Matchbox: The Movie (Apple TV)
description: Sam Hargrave, best known for the Extraction films, directs this action-adventure movie
content: Inspired by Mattel’s Matchbox toy cars, this action-adventure stars John Cena as Sean, an undercover CIA agent who returns to his small hometown after a long absence and reunites with the group of childhood friends he once led. His homecoming quickly takes a turn when he unwittingly drags them into a globe-trotting international pursuit to save the world. Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson and Arturo Castro are among the ensemble cast, while stuntman-turned-filmmaker Sam Hargrave directs. Air date: October 9

title: Who was Tenzing Norgay? The real story behind Apple TV's Everest film
description: As the new movie revisits the ascent of Mount Everest in 1953, we look at the life of the Sherpa mountaineer who reached the summit alongside Edmund Hillary
content: On May 29, 1953, two men stood at the summit of Mount Everest, becoming the first people confirmed to have reached the top of the world's highest mountain. One was Edmund Hillary , a New Zealand mountaineer whose name would become synonymous with the historic achievement. The other was Tenzing Norgay , an experienced Sherpa climber who had spent years attempting to conquer the mountain. Their extraordinary journey is the subject of Tenzing , a new Apple TV film that shifts the spotlight towards the man whose role in one of mountaineering's greatest achievements has not always received equal attention. Directed by Jennifer Peedom, the film stars Genden Phuntsok as Norgay, Tom Hiddleston as Hillary and Willem Dafoe as John Hunt, the British expedition leader. It was released in select cinemas on October 9 and begins streaming globally on Apple TV on Friday. But Tenzing is more than a recreation of the dangerous climb. It also explores the cultural divisions within the expedition, Norgay's determination to be recognised as a mountaineer rather than simply a guide, and his deeply personal relationship with Everest . Born around 1914, Norgay came from a Sherpa family in the Himalayan region, although details of his birthplace remain disputed. Accounts of his early life differ, with some placing his birth in Nepal and others in Tibet . What is clear is that he grew up close to the mountains that would come to define his life. He eventually moved to Darjeeling in India, which had become an important base for mountaineering expeditions attempting to explore the Himalayas . Norgay began working on Everest expeditions in 1935, initially carrying supplies for foreign climbers. Over the following years, he developed into an exceptionally skilled mountaineer, learning to navigate treacherous terrain and work at altitudes where even breathing became difficult. Despite being unable to read or write, he spoke several languages and became an important figure in organising and leading Sherpa climbing teams. By the time he joined the British expedition in 1953, Norgay had already attempted to reach Everest's summit six times. A year earlier, he had come close during a Swiss expedition alongside Raymond Lambert, reaching approximately 8,600 metres before being forced to turn back. His seventh attempt, alongside Hillary, would finally prove successful. Unlike many accounts of the 1953 expedition, which have traditionally focused on Hillary or the wider British effort, Tenzing approaches the historic climb from Norgay's perspective. The film follows his determination to be recognised as a full member of the expedition, rather than simply someone employed to assist the western climbers. His wife Dawa, played by Thinley Lhamo, is portrayed as an important source of encouragement, while Caitríona Balfe plays expedition secretary Jill Henderson, who supports his efforts to secure a place on the climbing team. Australian filmmaker Peedom, whose previous work includes the 2015 documentary Sherpa , has described the film as an opportunity to place Norgay at the centre of a story in which he has often been overshadowed. To prepare for their roles, Phuntsok and Hiddleston travelled to Nepal and trekked towards Everest Base Camp , meeting Sherpa mountaineers and learning more about the region and its climbing history. Norgay's son Norbu Tenzing is an executive producer of the film, bringing a direct family connection to the production. Tenzing is now streaming on Apple TV

title: Below (Netflix)
description: Josh Hartnett leads this six-part thriller set in a small fishing town in Newfoundland, Canada
content: Josh Hartnett plays fisherman Calvin Penney, who is haunted by the mysterious death of his father decades earlier. When an unidentified sea creature begins terrorising the community, Calvin teams up with a visiting marine researcher Fonda Howander, played by Mackenzie Davis ( Speak No Evil ), to uncover what is lurking beneath the water while trying to protect his family and their way of life. Created by The Umbrella Academy writer Jesse McKeown, the series also stars Charlie Heaton ( Stranger Things ), who plays Calvin’s son Wade. Air date: October 8

title: Carrie (Prime Video)
description: The series marks the first time King’s 1974 debut novel has been adapted as a television series
content: Stephen King’s classic horror story is reimagined for a new generation in this eight-part series from Mike Flanagan, the creator behind The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass . Summer H Howell stars as Carrie White, a sheltered teenager who is thrust into a public high school after the death of her father. She becomes the target of a viral bullying scandal while also discovering she possesses telekinetic powers. Samantha Sloyan plays Carrie’s fiercely protective mother, Margaret, with a cast that also includes Amber Midthunder as gym teacher Rita Desjardin, and Matthew Lillard as principal Henry Grayle. The series arrives 50 years after Brian De Palma’s acclaimed 1976 film starring Sissy Spacek. Air date: October 7

title: Investor confidence in Gulf remains strong despite war, says World Economic Forum's regional chief
description: Diversification has helped region withstand crisis despite IMF downgrading growth forecasts
content: Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war , with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said. Kelsey Goodman, head of Middle East and North Africa at the World Economic Forum (WEF), told The National that the region’s economic fundamentals remained solid despite geopolitical uncertainty. Her comments come as the International Monetary Fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies amid the effects of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s still widespread investor confidence in the region,” Ms Goodman said. “The fundamentals are solid even if the surrounding area is uncertain, but it calls for the need for dialogue and co-operation and hopefully a return to peace and resiliency in the region.” Speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai , which concluded on Thursday, Ms Goodman said efforts to diversify Gulf economies had helped them withstand recent shocks and would be crucial to their recovery. “Diversification really is key, and the companies and the economies that have been able to have already built in diversity into their plan are the ones that have been most resilient," she said. "Resiliency is something that you have to prepare for. It's not something that you can build only in times of crisis.” Foresight simulations were carried out at the meeting on Thursday, in which participants rehearsed responses to unfolding geopolitical and technological crises. “This meeting has really emphasised that dialogue and co-operation are not luxuries for easy times. They're essential precisely when the world is at its most complicated,” said Ms Goodman. Even with this in mind, she said the mood at the meeting was positive. “I think it speaks to the resiliency of Dubai, and we hope that the participants are leaving with a message of hope and renewed belief in the power of moving from foresight into action,” she said. In recent years, the UAE has prioritised artificial intelligence investments, with trillions of dollars earmarked for the technology, including building data centres. A newly published WEF report showed the potential of artificial intelligence in unlocking upwards of $1 trillion by 2030 in the region. Ms Goodman believes the investments countries are making in the AI sphere could return, but that regional uncertainty creates more barriers to reaching these goals. “For the economies to realise this value, it's going to take a lot of co-operation across all sectors of society,” she said. “That's going to include long-term planning from governments, but also having the regulation, the energy infrastructure, and the business applications for these new technologies.” While blocked trade routes have affected shipping and petrol prices have risen, Ms Goodman said the war's impact on the travel and tourism sector could also affect labour markets, especially given the high numbers of migrant workers in the country. The UAE workforce is made up of approximately 8.7 million migrant workers. “The Gulf really relies on a very mobile labour market with a lot of connections outside the region,” she said. “These are areas where there could potentially be short a ges.”

title: Preparations for 2027 ​Asian ​Cup ​in Saudi Arabia 'progressing according to schedule'
description: Organising ​committee confident of hosting tournament in kingdom in January
content: The local organising ​committee of the 2027 Asian Cup said preparations for hosting the continental tournament in Saudi Arabia are going ahead as per schedule despite recent attacks in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia saw a number of events called off or postponed as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Multiple attacks on airports in the country forced the Six Kings men's tennis tournament , scheduled for October 21-24, and the Fifa Esports final, set for October 16-25, to be postponed. Three matches in the Saudi Pro League this weekend were rescheduled to later in the season due to “logistical considerations”. Earlier, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said ‌it was open to the idea of ⁠delaying the Asian Cup until ​2028 if needed. The continental tournament is scheduled to ​kick ‌off on January 7 across venues in Riyadh, Jeddah ⁠and Al Khobar. However, ⁠the tournament's local organising committee said preparations are going ahead according to schedule. “Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” ​the organising committee ‌said, adding ⁠that the tournament ​remains on track to ​be ‌held from January 7 to ⁠February 5, 2027. “The LOC ⁠will continue to monitor ​developments relevant to the tournament and ​ensure ‌the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful ⁠delivery.” Earlier this week, AFC president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said the confederation was in “no hurry” to decide ​whether the tournament needed to be postponed. “We ​can wait until the end of November. Things can change very quickly for ‌better or worse in the region and ⁠it is question of seeing what happens,” Al Khalifa told ​reporters in Zurich during the Fifa Council meeting. The Korea Football Association (KFA) said it was in ⁠communication with the AFC. “We are closely monitoring the situation in Saudi Arabia and plan to continue discussions regarding overall developments,” the KFA said in a statement. The previous Asian Cup was ​delayed by a year after China withdrew as hosts because of Covid-19 restrictions, with Qatar stepping in to stage the tournament in early 2024. The Asian Tour postponed its ​season-ending ​Saudi International ​⁠in the aftermath of ⁠attacks in Riyadh. "The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to a standard befitting its international stature," an Asian Tour statement said. The $5 million ​flagship event, which is ‌sponsored by the ⁠Saudi Public Investment ​Fund (PIF), was scheduled to take ​place ‌at Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 ⁠to 21. "The PIF Saudi International is ⁠one of the most important events on the Asian Tour calendar and we look forward to seeing our players ​compete in Riyadh in the future," Asian Tour Commissioner Cho Minn Thant said.

title: Iraqi parliament approves key cabinet posts, including US-sanctioned deputy PM
description: Politicians vote to name son-in-law of former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki as interior minister
content: Iraq’s parliament voted to fill a series of long‑vacant cabinet posts late on Thursday, completing Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi’s government and approving a deputy prime minister who is under US sanctions . The government formation process has been completed five months after Mr Al Zaidi took office, with 11 key positions approved at a full parliamentary session in Baghdad. Those included the country's Defence Minister, Nayef Al Shammari, and Interior Minister Yasir Al Maliki. Mr Al Zaidi said in a statement that the completion of his cabinet marked the start of “accelerated, diligent work” and pledged to push ahead with the government’s policies . He said the regional conflict had posed exceptional economic and security challenges to Iraq. Politicians also endorsed Laith Al Khazali as one of three deputy prime ministers. He is the brother of Qais Al Khazali, leader of the Iran‑backed Asaib Ahl Al Haq militia. The US designated the group as a foreign terrorist organisation in 2020 and has accused it of attacks on US and coalition forces. Both brothers were named “specially designated global terrorists” and Laith was arrested by US forces in 2007 over allegations related to a January attack in Karbala that killed five American soldiers. Parliament approved two other deputy prime ministers – Mohammed Ali Tamim of the Sunni Taqadum Party and Asas Coalition leader Muhsin Al Mandalawi. Votes were postponed for the nominee for migration and displacement minister owing to disagreement among parties, politicians said. The nomination of Mr Al Khazali drew sharp criticism from Washington. Republican Representative Joe Wilson condemned the appointment , describing him as an “Iranian puppet whose militia killed Americans and Iraqis". “He is no better than ISIS, maybe even worse. It is outrageous but sadly not shocking that he has been appointed deputy PM of Iraq,” Mr Wilson wrote on X. Another controversial name is Mr Al Maliki, the son-in-law of former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki. When he was in power, Iraq lost nearly a third of its territory to ISIS in 2014, a collapse that ultimately forced him to resign. He is known to have strong connections with Iran and is often described as an influential power-broker in Iraqi politics. The nomination raises questions about how Iraq will manage its ties with the US. Sajad Jiyad, an Iraq expert with the Century Foundation, told The National that Shiite parties within the ruling coalition appear confident the appointments will not trigger a major rupture with Washington. Mr Jiyad said the move to nominate Mr Al Khazali might be to encourage other Iran‑aligned factions to integrate into state structures and dissolve their armed wings, by signalling that participation in formal politics can lead to senior government posts. Asaib Ahl Al Haq has grown into one of Iraq’s most influential Shia parties, now holding both ministerial positions and a deputy premiership. Mr Al Zaidi's government has pledged to introduce economic ⁠reforms and anti-corruption measures, as well as taking steps to strengthen state institutions. But many challenges lie ahead, including rebuilding an economy hit by regional instability, ​tackling endemic corruption and bringing Iran-backed armed groups under greater state control.

title: Drop in Gulf student visa applications shows dwindling appetite for UK universities
description: UAE records 59 per cent decline in applications in four years
content: The number of students from the Gulf choosing to study in the UK has plunged in recent years, most drastically from the UAE, figures show. Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said. While there was an inevitable drop in numbers caused by the Covid pandemic, these had bounced back by 2022, before the UK began issuing its policies to restrict student visas. The number of student visa applications from the UAE then began to drop, falling 59 per cent in the next four years, from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. These covered students who have been offered a place at an institution to study for a bachelor, graduate, PhD or other higher education courses. There was a 36 per cent drop in 2025 alone compared with the previous year. There were 13 per cent fewer applications from students in Saudi Arabia between 2023 and 2025, dropping from 5,814 to 5,049. In Bahrain, a 26 per cent decline has been recorded, from 545 applications in 2023 to 403 in 2025. Qatar recorded a drop of about 14 per cent between 2023 and 2025, from 1,056 to 910 applications. The outliers are Kuwait, which saw an 11 per cent rise in applications, from 4,499 in 2023 to 5,034 in 2025, and Oman, which grew from 996 to 1,018. Figures for spring and summer visa applications will be released by the Home Office next month and are expected to continue the downward trend. The first quarter of this year showed a decline of almost a third (29.2 per cent) of applications from Saudi students. UAE applications for the same period remained steady, moving from 16 in the first three months of 2025 to 15 in the same period of 2026. Professionals in the higher education sector have warned the numbers could keep declining as UK immigration restrictions make studying in the country less appealing. Many students regard a degree in the UK as an investment towards a career in the country. But from next year, students will have only 18 months to find a job in the UK after their graduation, compared to the previous allowance of two years. This follows increases to the Immigration Health Surcharge and student visa fees, and a higher chance of visa refusal. The general salary threshold for skilled workers' visas is also set to rise, with the discount for graduates removed, according the Labour government's White Paper on Immigration. The UK government was criticised this week for removing incentives for overseas students to pursue a degree course at a British university. “Given politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes, such as the infamous small boats, the factors pulling international students to come and study in the UK have been trimmed back again,” wrote Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institution in an analysis. This is compounded by financial penalties for universities that award spaces to students whose visa applications are later rejected. This has reportedly led to institutions withdrawing their offers to would-be students, mainly from India, China and Nigeria, to avoid paying any penalty should their visa applications be unsuccessful . For Gulf students, other factors such as safety concerns could also be fuelling the decline. A Saudi student was killed last year in a knife attack in Cambridge while studying an English language course, prompting his uncle to say the UK was “rapidly losing its global reputation”. There are also fears of radicalisation on campuses. The UAE – which has urged western governments to ban the Muslim Brotherhood organisation – was reported by the Financial Times this year to have scrapped its state-funded scholarships to some British universities. The UK government introduced new measures to protect students from extremism on campus this year. This includes supporting universities to carry out appropriate risk checks where free speech crosses into unlawful activity or support for terrorism.

title: Serial champions India continue bewildering struggle in bilateral series
description: Team has won every major title in recent seasons but are losing a lot more outside big tournaments
content: Can you be critical of a side that has won every major competition it has entered since 2024? Possibly. Especially when you put in performances like the Indian team has done in between those fine results. Since the 2024 T20 World Cup win , India have won the 50-over ICC Champions Trophy, Asia Cup, and successfully defended their T20 world title and the Asian Games gold medal this year. But right alongside, the team were also been whitewashed at home in Tests by New Zealand and South Africa – having been undefeated in their backyard for over a decade, lost the Border Gavaskar Trophy to Australia, embarrassed by Ireland (in T20s) and England (T20s and ODIs) right after their World Cup win this year and are now being taken apart by a spirited West Indies at home. The double T20 world champions were outplayed in the fourth match of the five-game T20 series against the Windies, falling to a 24-run loss in Hyderabad. The series is now tied 2-2. In the preceding ODI series, the West Indies easily chased down a target of 350 and also smashed 400 in the second game. That series was won 2-1 by India but they were stretched well past their limits. It's the same story in the T20s. In fact, India have been hammered for the third straight bilateral T20 series – defeats to Ireland and England away and now an uphill battle against the Caribbean side. If the Windies secure the T20 series win on Saturday, it wouldn’t be a surprise. Shouldn’t that worry Indian cricket management? It should, but what can they do when the team ends up winning every major tournament? India won a world and a continental title in 2026. The same set of players have also been thrashed by Ireland, England and the Windies in the same year. How do you reconcile both facts? There are two ways to look at it. One is that India have mastered the art of stumbling their way through low priority bilateral series and somehow finding the perfect formula when the big tournaments come around. The other is India were playing major tournaments in Asian conditions for the last two years and would have been found out if any of the events were held in England or Australia. There is only one way to find out – wait for next two years. The next big assignment for all teams is the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, followed by the 2028 T20 World Cup Down Under and the Los Angeles Olympics in the same year. Indian fans and cricket administrators might prefer to wait until all three assignments are completed, before taking stock of the situation. Around 10 or so years back, India were the undisputed champions of bilateral series, home and away. But they did not win a single major tournament, much to the pain of the then captain Virat Kohli. The script has flipped completely, where the players endure bewildering losses home and away in all formats, only to go back to their homes with another winners' medal in the cabinet. This can’t last long though. Conditions in South Africa and Australia are going to be daunting even for the most in-form Indian team, let alone a group that can barely stand still. It could open some deep wounds. One thing is clear – India do not have ready replacements for their veterans. The fitness concerns of all-rounder Hardik Pandya and workload management of Jasprit Bumrah have ruined the balance of the white-ball teams, while they still have not found a reliable substitute for Mohammad Shami or even Mohammad Siraj. No wonder the ageing Kohli and Rohit Sharma are guaranteed to play the ODI World Cup next year. Fast bowler Bhuvneshwar Kumar is back in the T20 team for the forthcoming New Zealand tour; he last played for India in 2022. Fellow veteran quick Shami is highly likely to be back before the ODI World Cup, especially since the Indian team’s selection panel is undergoing a change with older yet in-form players being given a look-in once again. Maybe, India will win a couple of more titles and fans will forget about pain of the bilaterals. If not, then there will be a feeding frenzy.

title: Premier League predictions: Leeds pile pressure on Michael Carrick and Man United
description: We pick out the winners and losers from the latest round of English top-flight fixtures
content: Everton maintained their unbeaten record after a 2-2 stalemate at Hull City last weekend, with the Merseysiders' fourth draw in six matches leaving them in fifth place on 10 points. Chelsea ended a three-game run without a win by trouncing Bournemouth 5-1 at Stamford Bridge – with Jordan Henderson and Joao Pedro both bagging a brace – and are also on 10 points. Prediction: Everton 1 Chelsea 2 Brentford have an identical record to Everton – two wins and four draws – but hold fourth spot thanks to a superior goal difference. The Bees earned a point at Aston Villa on Saturday thanks to Kristoffer Ajer's late leveller. Liverpool fell to a chastening 3-0 home thumping by Manchester City at Anfield last week, a defeat sparked by Ryan Gravenberch's red card, ending their unbeaten record and dropping them down to ninth in the table. Andoni Iraola's side picked themselves up by thrashing LASK 6-3 in the Uefa Champions League on Wednesday when £123 million summer signing Bradley Barcola scored a hat-trick – his first goals for the club. Prediction: Brentford 2 Liverpool 2 The pressure continues to mount on Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa who is still without a win following their 2-1 loss at Ipswich Town, despite his team leading with just two minutes left. The Cottagers are bottom of the table with two points. Hull's draw with Everton means the Tiger remain in the top half of the table, although they have gone four matches without victory now. They are ninth in the standings, but just one point outside the top four. Prediction: Fulham 1 Hull 3 Table-topping City silenced a baying Anfield crowd last weekend, coming away with a convincing victory and maintaining their perfect record of nine wins in nine games. They were brought back down to earth midweek when Champions League title-holders Paris Saint-Germain came away from the Etihad Stadium with a 4-2 victory . Ipswich sealed their third win in six matches by defeating Fulham thanks to late goals from Abdoul Ouattara and Dara O'Shea leaving Gary O'Neil's team in 10th place. Prediction: Man City 3 Ipswich 0 Newcastle fell to second successive Monday night battering on their travels this week having lost 4-1 to both Leeds and Coventry. The Magpies have now conceded 13 goals, the joint worst defensive record in the top-flight, and drop down to 11th spot. Villa's draw with Brentford means they still only have one league win to their name and sit in 16th place. Unai Emery's side hit their stride on Wednesday, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park with Nicolas Jackson and Ross Barkley both scoring twice. Prediction: Newcastle 2 Villa 2 Marco Rose's tough start as Bournemouth manager hit a new low last week with a heavy loss at Chelsea meaning the Cherries are still waiting for their first league win this season. In the Europa League on Thursday, Bournemouth won 3-0 against Sturm Graz at the Vitality Stadium. Sunderland's home defeat against Brighton means the Black Cats have lost three successive league games and took just a single point from a possible 12. They are one point and one place outside the bottom three. Roger le Bris's side travelled to Portuguese outfit Torreense in the Europa League on Thursday and won 2-1. Prediction: Bournemouth 1 Sunderland 0 Third-place Brighton are looking to win their fourth league game on the spin having defeated Sunderland 2-0 with Maxim de Cuyper and Jaouen Hadjam providing the goals. The Seagulls opened their Europa Conference League campaign on Thursday against Lithuanian side Kauno Zalgiris, winning 4-0 on the south coast. Palace earned their second win of the campaign by beating Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park last weekend and have now lost just once in four games. The Eagles were away to Lyon in the Europa League on Thursday and lost 3-2. Prediction: Brighton 2 Palace 0 Leeds fell to their first defeat of the season last time out when they were beaten 2-1 at Arsenal but Daniel Farke's team remain just a point outside the top four and it should be a bouncing atmosphere at Elland Road on Sunday. Lisandro Martinez added fuel to the fire after the midweek Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid with his public criticism of the club . Prediction: Leeds 3 Man United 1 Forest manager Oliver Glasner suffered a miserable return to previous club Palace last week and is looking to avoid a third successive defeat. Champions Arsenal recovered from their loss at Brighton by earning a comeback victory against Leeds with substitute Bruno Guimaraes scoring the winner. A 3-0 Champions League win over Lille followed midweek with Bukayo Saka scoring one and setting up another.
