Spurs have drawn three and lost three so far. Coventry have now won two on the trot after beating Nottingham Forest and Newcastle which ended a run of four defeats. Prediction: Spurs 2 Coventry 1

title: Prevention becomes predictive: How Abu Dhabi is learning to read health risks before symptoms appear
description: Genomics, health data and AI are helping Abu Dhabi develop more personalised prevention, with earlier intervention and healthier lives as the goal
content: For a family welcoming a newborn, prevention can begin before there is any outward sign of illness. For an adult attending a routine check-up, it could mean understanding a developing health risk early enough to change its course. These are the possibilities behind Abu Dhabi’s move towards predictive health care. Advice on exercise, nutrition and regular screening remains essential. The next step is to make prevention more personal, drawing on an individual’s genetic profile, medical history and measurable changes in their health to determine where earlier action could make a difference. That ambition is reflected in To Sense is to Predict, the theme of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, taking place from October 20 to 22. For patients and families, its meaning is practical: recognising the signals of disease sooner and turning that information into care. Future Health - A Global Initiative by Abu Dhabi’s longevity whitepaper places healthspan, the years a person lives in good health, at the centre of this shift. Its focus is on helping people remain well and independent for longer by connecting scientific advances with prevention and everyday care. For UAE families, that means thinking about health across generations. Earlier recognition of risk could help a parent manage a developing chronic condition, support an older relative’s independence or give a child access to specialist care sooner. Genomics can reveal inherited susceptibility. Biomarkers, measurable indicators such as blood glucose or cholesterol, can help clinicians assess what is happening in the body. Medical records add the history of previous tests, diagnoses and treatment. AI can help analyse these sources of information and identify patterns that warrant clinical attention. The value comes from interpreting those signals together. A genetic finding is one part of a person’s health picture; its significance depends on clinical evidence, family history and other risk factors. Predictive care aims to give clinicians a stronger basis for deciding who needs closer monitoring, which screening is appropriate and when to intervene. Earlier insight must lead to better care. Abu Dhabi’s priority is to translate advances in genomics, data and AI into evidence-based decisions that help people stay well. For patients and families, this means understanding their risks, receiving appropriate screening and having a clear pathway to support or treatment. Abu Dhabi has established infrastructure that supports this approach. Malaffi, the emirate’s health information exchange, connects records across public and private healthcare providers, giving authorised clinicians access to a patient’s medical history. This helps them assess new findings alongside previous results and coordinate care across different settings. At the population level, the Department of Health’s Population Health Intelligence platform, unveiled with Microsoft in 2025, brings together clinical, lifestyle and environmental data. It is designed to help identify emerging risks and inform targeted prevention, with obesity and cancer among its initial focus areas. The longevity white paper also stresses the importance of helping people act on health information. Understanding a risk is useful when it leads to appropriate follow-up, support with healthier habits or a treatment decision. That requires prevention to become part of routine care, with progress assessed over time. Abu Dhabi’s Newborn Genetic Screening Programme offers a concrete example. Launched by the Department of Health in August 2025, its first phase was implemented at Kanad Hospital in Al Ain and Danat Al Emarat Hospital, in partnership with M42. Using cord blood collected at birth with parental consent, the programme applies whole genome sequencing to screen for more than 815 treatable childhood genetic conditions. These include disorders that may not be apparent at birth but could affect a child’s health if treatment is delayed. The announced expansion aims to reach all maternity hospitals in Abu Dhabi, covering UAE nationals and children of Emirati mothers born in the emirate. For families, the opportunity is earlier knowledge and a clearer route to care. Where screening identifies a concern, clinical assessment and genetic counselling help explain what the finding means and whether treatment or monitoring is needed. Future Health’s genomics and rare diseases whitepaper examines the next scientific challenge: understanding how genetic variants disrupt biology and using that knowledge to develop targeted interventions. It also explores how rare diseases can reveal biological mechanisms relevant to more common conditions. For patients, this reinforces the importance of connecting discovery with clinical care. Identifying a variant is a starting point. Its value depends on accurate interpretation, specialist expertise and access to an appropriate intervention. As the summit brings together healthcare leaders, researchers, policymakers and innovators, the test of predictive prevention will be what changes for families: a condition recognised sooner, a better-informed care plan or more years lived in good health.

title: In the new world order, expect fewer alliances and more ‘pop-up partnerships’
description: “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation o
content: “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation of the new world order taking shape. For much of the past century, international relations were organised around relatively permanent alliances, geographical blocs and established institutions. Countries joined international organisations, aligned themselves with major powers and accepted long-term commitments that extended beyond their immediate interests. Today, that architecture is being supplemented by something more fluid: temporary, purpose-driven coalitions that I would call “pop-up alliances”. The emerging geopolitical advantage may no longer be choosing the right side, but retaining the ability to work with several sides. India illustrates this new geopolitical a la carte menu. It participates in the Quad alongside the US, Japan and Australia, maintains defence relationships with Russia, belongs to Brics and deepens economic ties with Europe and the Gulf. The UAE similarly combines Brics membership with extensive western security partnerships and growing commercial relationships through more than 30 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements across Europe, Asia and Africa. These arrangements are not necessarily contradictory. They reflect a world in which countries increasingly choose their partners according to the issue rather than their permanent geopolitical affiliation. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave this thinking a powerful expression at Davos earlier this year, arguing that middle powers must co-operate more deliberately because, as he put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu”. His proposed approach of “variable geometry”, involving different coalitions for different issues, captures an important shift in how international influence is exercised. Traditionally, great powers built alliances while smaller countries joined them. Increasingly, middle powers are becoming coalition entrepreneurs, bringing together countries around shared capabilities and interests. Influence depends not simply on military strength or economic size, but on the ability to mobilise capital, technology, energy, natural resources and market access. For countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Canada, India and Indonesia, this creates opportunities to shape international co-operation rather than merely participate in structures designed elsewhere. The logic also challenges the geographical foundations of traditional alliances. The EU, GCC and the Association of South-East Asian Nations were largely built around regional proximity , whereas emerging partnerships increasingly reflect strategic interdependence. Semiconductor supply chains connect Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and the US, while critical minerals, artificial intelligence and cyber security create overlapping interests across continents. The next geopolitical map may therefore be drawn less around borders and more around the supply chains, technologies and resources that countries cannot afford to lose. Britain’s evolving relationship with Europe offers another revealing example. Brexit represented a decisive departure from institutional integration, yet the subsequent rebuilding of economic and security co-operation demonstrates that geography and mutual dependence cannot simply be legislated away . The debate over closer relations, including possible, eventual re-entry, reflects a broader movement towards more selective forms of international co-operation. This is not necessarily the end of globalisation, but rather its rewiring. Countries are reconsidering who they depend on, for what purposes and under which conditions. Strategic resilience increasingly means maintaining options rather than placing every national interest within a single alliance. In the future of international relations, every country will be permanently looking for new and better friends. This is an emerging model that can be described as “pop-up governance”: flexible partnerships formed around specific challenges, designed to achieve defined outcomes, and time-bound and designed to possibly dissolve when their purpose was fulfilled. Traditional institutions such as the UN, EU, GCC and Asean will remain, although some may lose influence as governments seek faster and more targeted arrangements. Alongside them, we are likely to see a growing layer of pop-up alliances, organised around shared interests rather than geography, with clear objectives and sometimes explicit time limits. Some will address defence, geopolitical tensions or economic security . Others will be more forward-looking, bringing together countries to develop water technologies, secure critical raw materials, co-ordinate specialised manufacturing capabilities or accelerate industrial innovation. A coalition formed to develop water desalination technologies, for example, might unite Gulf countries, Singapore, Australia and technology providers without requiring a broader political alliance. Such flexibility carries risks. Temporary coalitions can weaken accountability, exclude smaller economies and undermine established international rules. Their effectiveness will depend on whether they complement permanent institutions rather than simply bypass them. Nevertheless, the direction of change is becoming clearer. The emerging international system may resemble a network of overlapping partnerships, some permanent and others temporary, in which countries co-operate where interests converge while accepting differences elsewhere. Kissinger ’s famous principle remains relevant, but its application is changing. National interests may be enduring, yet the alliances through which countries pursue them need not be. The next measure of diplomatic influence may be less about which alliances a country belongs to, and more about which alliances it has the capacity to create.

title: UAE weather: Speed limits reduced after morning fog alerts in Abu Dhabi and Dubai
description: Police in both emirates urge motorists to drive carefully amid heavy fog
content: Heavy fog led authorities to reduce speed limits in Abu Dhabi on Friday morning, with a safety warning issued in Dubai . Alerts were sent to motorists in parts of Abu Dhabi, warning them that speed limits had been reduced to 80kph, while drivers were urged to exercise caution on the roads in Dubai due to poor visibility. " Abu Dhabi Police call on motorists to exercise caution due to reduced visibility during the fog," the force wrote on X. "They are urged to follow changing speed limits displayed on electronic information boards." A similar message was issued by police in Dubai, where motorists were told to drive carefully in the heavy fog. "With the formation of fog and reduced visibility in some areas of the emirate of Dubai, and in the interest of your safety, we remind you of the importance of reducing speed in accordance with road conditions, and exercising caution and care while driving," Dubai Police said on X. The National Centre of Meteorology predicted the foggy conditions would continue until at least 9am on Friday.

title: Naseer Shamma returns to UAE National Orchestra with bigger ambitions for the oud
description: Iraqi virtuoso brings new orchestral arrangements as the ensemble enters its second season
content: When Naseer Shamma joined the UAE National Orchestra for its inaugural concert in January, the performance was a celebration of what the newly formed ensemble could become. Nine months later, the Iraqi oud virtuoso is returning to an orchestra with a full season and more than two dozen concerts across the emirates behind it, and a more ambitious programme ahead. At Friday's Harmony concert at NYU Abu Dhabi's Arts Centre, Shamma will perform four of his compositions in new orchestral arrangements, including a concerto for oud and orchestra. “The first concert was different. It was a celebration. We were saying, here we are, we are together. But now we have a concrete programme. We have something much deeper, with different pieces,” he tells The National . “I think the orchestra is clearly at another level now compared with the first concert. The first show was very good, and if you notice, each concert since then has been about going deeper and finding new forms of creative expression. I am so glad to be part of that journey.” For Shamma, one of the Arab world's most influential oud players and educators, the collaboration continues nearly four decades of experimentation with the instrument's sound, design and repertoire. He has helped to develop a family of ouds covering different musical registers, composed for film and theatre, and founded Bait Al Oud in Cairo in the late 1990s, later expanding the conservatory to Abu Dhabi, Alexandria and Baghdad. His interest in oud-inspired orchestral music is long-standing, having led a 70-member Eastern Orchestra at Abu Dhabi Festival in 2008. Friday's programme includes Concerto for Oud and Orchestra , which Shamma says has been developed through extensive rehearsals and discussions with musicians. Despite previously performing orchestral works, including an adaptation of Vivaldi's Mandolin Concerto for the oud, he describes it as the ideal concerto for the occasion. “I hope it will be a good work because we have taken time with the composition, with rehearsals and with discussing the ideas with different musicians. Now I think it is ready to be presented on stage with the orchestra,” he says. Shamma acknowledges the contributions of earlier Arab composers, including Iraqi oud musician Jamil Bashir, who wrote for the instrument in orchestral settings. He now hopes to expand the repertoire available to future generations of oud players. “For that reason, I think it is time to compose differently. To compose one concerto every year would be great, because this would create a repertoire for other musicians who come after us,” he adds. “Of course, many Arab composers have written concertos for the oud, qanun, nay and other instruments. But when I compose something for the oud as an oud soloist myself, it will be different from what another composer writes. Because that composer may only be a composer, not an oud player.” Writing for a symphony orchestra also means balancing its instrumental range with the oud's distinctive sound and characteristics. “I think the oud has its own special characteristics. Its sound, its power, its chords, its quarter-tones and many other things,” he says. To keep the instrument from getting lost in the orchestra, “we have to preserve the oud's identity ”, Shamma says. “Not in a traditional way but in a contemporary way. It must remain an oud in the middle of the orchestra.” Shamma's collaboration with the orchestra has also developed through his relationship with its musicians. He recalls their curiosity during January's rehearsals about his oud's clarity of sound and his playing style, and how the experience helped to establish a rapport. “It was a beautiful experience. I felt that we had covered a great distance through a single piece of music. “It is a distance that might take two years to cover in ordinary life, just to create a friendship. But we achieved it through one piece lasting eight minutes.” Some of the orchestra's musicians have an earlier connection to Shamma through Abu Dhabi's Bait Al Oud, which he set up with clear expectations. “When I established it in Cairo in 1998, and then the second in Abu Dhabi in 2007, I had a clear idea that one day the UAE would need professional musicians. So I began preparing these musicians.” Several Emirati musicians who trained at the institution have joined the UAE National Orchestra, according to Shamma. “So this is a collaboration. We complement one another. We complete one another's projects,” he says. “We are working to become bridges that lead to the other side, to professional music.” Harmony by the UAE National Orchestra: Friday, October 16 at The Arts Centre, NYU Abu Dhabi. 8pm. Tickets start from Dh100

title: How Abu Dhabi is revealing the roots of the UAE’s global outlook
description: New museum exhibitions show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term existed
content: The Gulf has sometimes been portrayed in the West as, until recently, a remote corner of the world, a place defined largely by its desert environment and the relative isolation of its communities. Two new exhibitions in Abu Dhabi museums suggest a different and more compelling account of the history of the region, namely, that far from being a peripheral place, the Gulf was a crossroads of commerce and culture – much like it is today. At Louvre Abu Dhabi , a major exhibition about how the Indian Ocean connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia explores a millennium of maritime exchange through more than 200 objects. In December, the Zayed National Museum will explore more than 7,000 years of the camel’s place in the life on the Arabian Peninsula. Together, these exhibitions tell a story of land and sea that helps explain the UAE ’s enduring role in connecting people and places. The Louvre exhibition makes this history tangible. Six detailed ship models evoke the vessels that carried goods across the Indian Ocean. A third-century Buddha sculpture from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan, offers another reminder that religious and artistic traditions travelled alongside commercial cargoes. The Gulf’s pearl industry was part of this wider network, linking its waters to markets and communities far beyond Arabia. The camel exhibition will turn the focus inland. Bones dating to between 4500 and 4000BC, discovered at Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, provide evidence of an extinct wild camel species. Remains from Dubai ’s Saruq Al Hadid illustrate the later relationship between humans and domesticated camels. Meanwhile, recordings of Taghrooda poetry and Alheda’a, the traditional practice of calling camels, demonstrate how deeply the animal remains embedded in Emirati cultural expression. These exhibitions will present a reminder of how the people of the Gulf participated in networks of exchange and developed traditions suited to their environment. Such connections are still evident today. Ports remain vital to the UAE’s international trade, but are now complemented by aviation and rail links. The camel also endures with the animal featuring in racing, competitions and poetry – its place as part of the Emirates’ national identity is irreplaceable. There is also a wider significance in the way these exhibitions tell their stories. Preserving heritage should mean more than celebrating familiar symbols or indulging in nostalgia. Understanding how the past shaped the present helps us today to recognise the complexity of the societies that preceded our modern times. For anyone seeking to understand the UAE, exhibitions such as these are a good place to start. They represent a vital reminder that the country’s cosmopolitan outlook is not a recent invention, but part of a much longer history of exchange and encounter. In other words, they show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term even existed.

title: Why it’s important to deepen our understanding of AI
description: Our readers have their say about the safe use of artificial intelligence, Sheikha Shamma’s appointment, support for Saudi Arabia and Lebanon’s generators
content: Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week Promoting AI awareness I write in reference to the article titled Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI (October 14): this is a commendable initiative. As AI continues to transform various aspects of our lives, it is essential to ensure that children understand both its benefits and its potential risks. Parents play a crucial role in helping their children navigate this rapidly evolving digital world by encouraging responsible usage, protecting their privacy, identifying misinformation and developing critical thinking skills. The UAE has demonstrated a keen interest in embracing and expanding the use of AI across various sectors. This initiative clearly reflects the country’s long-term vision of promoting AI awareness, digital literacy and technological advancement while prioritising the safety and well-being of younger generations. Equipping parents with the necessary knowledge and guidance is an important step towards building a society that can confidently and responsibly embrace emerging technologies. Such initiatives will not only benefit families but also contribute to preparing future generations for an AI-driven world. A commendable step by Dubai towards ensuring that technological progress goes hand in hand with awareness, responsibility and the safety of children. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India A little knowledge ... With regard to the article headlined Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills (October 7): raising awareness about AI is a great thing. What is not so great is when people attend a few workshops and emerge believing they have become AI experts. That is where things can become dangerous and counterproductive. AI projects can be costly and complex, requiring technical expertise, sound judgment and a depth of understanding that simply cannot be acquired in a week-long workshop. There is a significant difference between understanding what AI can do and having the expertise to design, implement and manage AI projects successfully. – Muhammad A, Dubai Taking the longview I refer to the video captioned Speaking at the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Dubai, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence said trust in agentic AI systems would be difficult to rebuild if they caused harm (October 14): precisely and certainly, but the UAE leadership is foresighted. They want their people to be happy and prosperous. – Muhammad Naeem Ul Fateh, Pakistan An unsurprising decision Regarding the news that Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan has been appointed as an executive fellow by the World Economic Forum, raising her growing international profile in sustainability and climate action (October 14), I will say “bravo”, for she is a true embodiment of deep knowledge, unsurpassed intellect and pure talent. And God is a granter of success. – Dr Aisha Bilkhair Our second home This is regarding the video clip captioned ‘There is no way that somebody will break our back,’ Saudi Arabia’s energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said following a series of deadly attacks on Riyadh international airport (October 12): we in the Filipino community stand firmly in solidarity with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We are deeply grateful to this nation, which has become our second home, providing us with opportunities, security and a place to build a better future for our families. In times of challenge, we stand united with the kingdom and its people. We are ready to offer our support in any lawful and appropriate way, contributing to the safety, peace, stability and prosperity of the nation we proudly call our second home. May peace, unity and protection always prevail throughout the kingdom. Long live Saudi Arabia. – James Rey Romero, Jizan, Saudi Arabia Citizens suffer I write in reference to Nada Maucourant Atallah’s article Lebanon’s power failure: Diesel generators, $300-a-month bills - and a corrupt system milking the profits (October 14): thank you for this report on the less visible impact of war. Lebanon is in a stranglehold, and as usual, those paying – literally and figuratively – the highest price are the citizens themselves. – Miguel Quintana, Switzerland Lebanon should be looking at solar and wind power. These diesel generators are making cancer cases rise dramatically. – Kay Francine

title: Gazans prepare to return home from Abu Dhabi's Emirates Humanitarian City
description: Thousands of Gazans remain at the centre receiving medical treatment
content: Dozens of Gazans who have been receiving medical treatment at Emirates Humanitarian City in Abu Dhabi are to return to their home country. The humanitarian centre has been a refuge from the Israel- Gaza conflict for thousands of Palestinians since 2023, but many long to be reunited with their families back home. Among them is 59-year-old Ibtisam Salout. She is preparing to return to Gaza in the coming days, after three years in the UAE. Ms Salout is a mother of nine and has 45 grandchildren. “The first thing I’ll do is gather them all and hold them tight. Yes, all of them," she says. She checks her suitcases before checking them again: the dresses for her daughters, the chocolates for her grandchildren. “The sneakers are for the boys. They sent me a photo and asked for these brands specifically," she says. Ms Salout is from Deir Al Balah. She arrived in the UAE in 2023 for treatment. She had breast cancer and her treatment had been interrupted after October 7. The UAE has provided medical treatment and comprehensive health care for 1,000 cancer patients and 1,000 injured children from the Gaza Strip. “When I arrived, they began treatment immediately and discovered the cancer was also in my lymph nodes. They saved my life,” Ms Salout says. Every patient is allowed an escort, but she does not have one. “I didn’t bring anyone with me. My husband said, ‘You are in the safest country in the world, with the kindest people taking care of you. I would be more worried about you in Gaza. Get better and come back to us. I’ll stay with the children and wait for you.' ” Today, she is cancer-free and ready to go back home to Gaza. “I’ll kiss its ground before running to my family," says Ms Salout. Her house has been partially destroyed, but her husband and children continue to live there. “We fixed it up like we will fix Gaza,” she says. Ms Salout is one of dozens of Palestinians who have completed their treatment and are heading back home. There remain close to 3,000 Gazans at the UAE’s Humanitarian City under treatment. “The plan was always that they would return home once they completed their treatment, but it is hard to part with them after so many years. They have become our family," says Falah Al Qahtani, spokesperson for EHC. A few Gazans have married at EHC, and others have had children. Younger children are enrolled in schools and nurseries, while adult Gazans are enrolled in online universities. Almost every week, there is a celebration at the complex: a birth, a birthday or a graduation. “This is a bittersweet farewell. We are happy that they are heading back home. We are happy that they are happy and can go back, but they have also formed deep connections with us and the country.” For Ms Salout, this is not goodbye. “You have to come to Gaza. I’ll make you fatteh, and I make the best maftool. You can ask anyone,” she says with pride. There are 30 people living with her but, she says; “I’ve told them to keep a clean room always ready for 'the Emirati'. Without them, I wouldn’t have been alive today.” The EHC has served as a sanctuary for many of those affected by the violence of the war. The centre is part of the UAE's continuing humanitarian operations in solidarity with the Palestinians. About medical 150 appointments are carried out each day within the vast complex, not including admissions to hospitals in Abu Dhabi for complex surgery. A building at EHC has a pharmacy, clinics, a ward with hospital beds staffed by doctors, paediatricians, an internal medicine doctor, psychiatrists, dentists and a rehabilitation specialist. The complex has a medical team of more than 50 doctors, nurses, therapists and administrators. There is also a school serving more than 400 children.

title: Russian bots and influence operations 'weren't disrupted by Ukraine strikes'
description: People started to 'see what they wanted to see' in data after Ukraine drone attack, experts say
content: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that last weekend's attacks on Russia 's Yandex data centres led to a drop in Pro-Russian bot operations is causing debate. The situation highlights the need to differentiate between bots, social media trolls and sophisticated influence operations , experts say. Prof Olga Belogolova , director of the emerging technologies initiative at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, wrote a long LinkedIn post to try to give context. Prof Belogolova, who previously led policy at Meta against influence operations, said that too many people saw "what they wanted to see" with data from network and cloud infrastructure company Cloudflare. "The story went viral when people started sharing a Cloudflare screenshot as proof of the silenced troll farms, as it showed a severe drop in bot traffic," she said. "Their motivated reasoning made them see that the internet was cleaner, more friendly, less toxic. "As someone who investigated and disrupted numerous malign influence operations and troll networks, I can also tell you that they do not often host their infrastructure on Yandex ." Prof Belogolova also said that far too many people were confusing and misusing tech terminology. "Bots are importantly not trolls ... as many tech researchers have already pointed out, Cloudflare labels any non-browser, automated script as a bot," she said. She said that when a data centre is taken offline, "its automated web-crawling and indexing traffic cuts out too". Cloudflare Radar, a branch of the company, agreed that nuance was needed when looking at internet traffic data. "Bot traffic refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms," a post from Cloudflare Radar read, casting doubt on claims that Russia's social media trolls and disinformation campaign had been disrupted. On Thursday, Cloudflare provided more clarity on the Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centres. "Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks," the company posted. "There was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the internet." Yet Prof Belogolova said that there were probably still ramifications faced by Russia after the data centre strikes. "Kinetic strikes on Russian tech infrastructure may disrupt Russia's digital economy and cloud services," she said. "They are not exactly a precise tool for stopping foreign influence operations."

title: US extends sanctions waiver on Russia's Lukoil until 2027
description: Treasury also authorises certain transactions for oil giant's entities over same period
content: The US on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil giant Lukoil , allowing its service operations outside the country to continue until April 2027, the Treasury Department announced. Under the new general licence, Lukoil petrol stations will be able to serve customers until April 25, 2027. This includes petrol stations in the US, the department said. The waiver replaces a previous licence that was set to expire this month. The licence prohibits the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”, it reads. It also excludes transactions involving Russia 's central bank, its national wealth fund and the Ministry of Finance. In a separate licence, the Treasury Department also authorised certain transactions for Lukoil Bulgaria's firms in the same time period. The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would allow Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global markets. The agreement deepened a rift between the US and its European partners, including Ukraine, and within Mr Trump's Republican Party. Mr Trump said Russia would immediately release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes released in November and a million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. He also said Russia would release three million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time” depending on the condition of the country's diesel refineries. Oil prices remain high during the seven-month Iran war, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is significantly well below its prewar levels and as Iranian attacks continue in the waterway. Futures for Brent global benchmark crude fell 0.27 per cent to settle at $105.8 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate futures gaining 2.76 per cent at $97.71 a barrel. Diesel prices also remained elevated at $6.31 a gallon, compared to the average of $3.65 a gallon at the same time last year. The International Energy Agency's governing board on Thursday said it would quicken the release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel and the remaining volumes of the 400 million barrels of emergency stocks of crude and other oil products previously agreed to in March. The IEA said on Wednesday it expects oil market balances to remain in a deficit well into 2027. “As the remaining buffers in the system continue to erode, in the absence of a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027,” it said.

title: Rubio speaks to Lebanon’s Aoun about explosives seized from Hezbollah
description: US Secretary of State also criticises Lebanon’s 1955 Boycott Law
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to ensure explosives seized from Hezbollah are not returned to the group, while calling for direct military communication between Lebanon and Israel to reduce the risk of clashes. In a call with Mr Aoun on Thursday, Mr Rubio discussed the confiscation of several hundred kilos of explosives from Hezbollah, a State Department official said. He called for accountability for those who ordered, financed and directed the shipment, and said returning the explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question. Mr Rubio also criticised Lebanon’s 1955 Boycott Law, which the US official said was used for politicised prosecutions that deter efforts towards peace with Israel. He "emphasised that the law is impractical and urged direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces for deconfliction", the official said. This would help to reduce miscalculation and to advance sequenced implementation of the Trilateral Framework, the official added. Signed in June, the framework sets out a phased process for the Lebanese army to restore state authority and disarm non-state militias including Hezbollah, and for Israel to progressively withdraw from Lebanese territory

title: Trump accuses Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Muslim Brotherhood ties
description: Democrat denies the allegation as Trump repeatedly calls him 'Mohammed'
content: US President Donald Trump has accused Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, a claim the Democrat denies. Mr Trump also repeatedly referred to Mr El Sayed as “Mohammed” as the race in the key battleground state heats up. “I call him Mohammed Al Fayed. His name is Abdul, but I think I call him Mohammed Abdul El-Sayed, and he's a Muslim Brotherhood guy, 100 per cent,” he said at the White House on Thursday. The Brotherhood accusation comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as the race in the swing state intensifies. Michigan is home to about 300,000 Arab Americans, and Mr Trump has won the state twice. Polls show Mr El-Sayed narrowly ahead of his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, an ally of Mr Trump. Throughout the campaign, Mr Trump has referred to Mr El-Sayed as a radical and a “jihadist lunatic”, among other Islamophobic insults. The November 3 elections will determine control of Congress, and Michigan is among the most closely watched Senate races. If Mr El-Sayed wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. US media reports this week have quoted social media posts by Mr El-Sayed’s half-sister that allegedly refer to his mother as a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood. Mr El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, has denied the accusations and at times dismissed them. His parents were divorced when he was a child, and he was raised by his American stepmother. “I have no ties. We have no ties,” Mr El-Sayed said in an interview with NBC that aired on Thursday. “I have never had these conversations with my mother. I wasn’t raised by my mother. “You’re using hearsay evidence from a tweet. It’s just not serious.” Mr El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health official, has also faced questions about his credentials. During a heated debate last week, Mr Rogers called Mr El-Sayed a “con man” and accused him of having ties to armed groups in the Middle East. “He can't condemn Hamas. He can't condemn the Muslim Brotherhood. He says his home is Egypt,” Mr Rogers said. He later suggested that concerns about surveillance could be personal for Mr El-Sayed because he or someone in his family might be suspected of terrorism. “Go ahead and say it,” Mr El-Sayed interjected. “You've been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”

title: Marco Rubio accuses Cuba of helping Iran and other 'malign actors' to attack US
description: Washington imposes sanctions on state-owned Cuban bank, claiming it provided financial services to Iranian lender
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday accused Cuba of helping Iran and other adversaries to attack the US, as he announced sanctions against a Cuban state-owned bank claimed to have provided financial services to an Iranian lender. Banco Internacional de Comercio has provided services to Iran’s Karafarin Bank since at least 2022, Mr Rubio said in a statement. The US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Karafarin Bank in 2020. “For too long, Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups – including the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said. The designation was announced alongside Treasury Department measures against Iranian financial networks, as the US administration of President Donald Trump seeks to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance. Mr Rubio said Washington would continue to identify and dismantle Cuba’s financial and security links with Iran and other states, and those it considers hostile.

title: US imposes Iran-related sanctions on Iraq Development Bank
description: Latest 'Economic Outcast' moves also aimed at Iran-linked entities and people
content: The Iraq Development Bank, among dozens of other targets, was hit with sanctions by the US on Thursday for its relations with Iran , the Treasury Department said in a statement. The bank was one of 10 entities and 16 people hit in the latest round of sanctions under Washington's “Economic Outcast” programme. US President Donald Trump's administration has warned countries and companies that continue to do business with Iran would face significant consequences. “Working with partners across the US government, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said. The Treasury has previously imposed sanctions on banks in Turkey and a Bank Melli branch in the UAE, among others. The UAE Central Bank last month banned Bank Melli Iran from conducting transactions between its branches in the UAE and Iran after an investigation. Mr Trump's administration has hoped its “Economic Outcast” programme would sever Iran's remaining economic lifelines and force the regime to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. “The noose is tightening around Iran’s economy, and not even Iran’s so-called allies can save it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Iraq in 2024 banned the IDB and seven other local commercial banks from engaging in US dollar transactions. The Treasury said the IDB has abused the now-dissolved dollar wire auction and maintains ties to Iran government entities and militia groups in Iraq. It is one of dozens of Iraqi banks that have been cut off for years due to concerns over sanctions evasion, money laundering and illicit finance. The US holds significant influence over Baghdad's financial policies because its international oil revenue is held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has sought to work with US authorities on the country's banking sector , which for years has been marred by corruption. Hiba Abdulwahib, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, said Thursday's move should not be viewed as a punishment for Iraq and it does not necessarily indicate that the US believes Mr Al Zaidi's government is unwilling to reform its banking sector. "Authority in Iraq is fragmented," she said. "The government does not have effective control over every institution or economic actor operating inside the country. I believe Washington understands those limitations, especially when it comes to Iran’s networks in Iraq." Ms Abdulwahib also said she expected the pressure of sanctions to lead to more co-ordination on closer oversight, monitoring of suspicious activities and penalties for breaches. "Baghdad has an incentive to address these problems before Washington imposes further sanctions, and the banks themselves have to take that risk seriously," she said. In July, the Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence outlined a years-long plan that would eventually allow restricted Iraq banks to be reintegrated into the US dollar system. The process would include an initial phase of reforms from the Central Bank of Iraq, with the second phase consisting of a restricted bank completing the entire reform and licensing process. This would involve successfully undertaking a third-party audit of their compliance function, securing a qualified investor and meeting international standards. The department at the time said “no banned banks have regained access to foreign currency transactions”. "The United States will not tolerate the abuse of Iraqi banks by Iran-aligned militia groups and will take independent action, if necessary, to target such activity,” it said. The move coincided with Mr Al Zaidi's visit to the US, where he had pledged to disarm militia groups in the country by September 30. In an interview with The New York Times in September, Mr Al Zaidi pushed that timeline to June 2027. The disarmament is a crucial part of how he is expected to manage Iraq's relations with the US and Iran.

title: Trump abandons plan to stream execution of Fort Hood gunman after backlash
description: Idea drew condemnation from religious leaders and criticism from within US President's own circle
content: US President Donald Trump on Thursday called off plans for a live-stream broadcast of the execution of a former US army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009. The plan to broadcast the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan was this month proposed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, but was withdrawn after condemnation, including from within Mr Trump's own political circle. In a post on Truth Social, Mr Trump said the execution by firing squad would proceed as planned but would not be broadcast live. “I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the world to witness how America deals with terrorists and scum like Hasan,” he wrote. “But many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming or through any other visual device. “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.” Mr Trump said the victims’ immediate families could witness the execution in person if they wished. Hasan, a former major, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. He later described his shooting spree as retaliation for US wars in the ⁠Muslim world. Now 56, the son of Palestinian immigrants was scheduled to be ​sent to Afghanistan before the shooting. Hasan was left paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair after being shot ​by police during ‌his arrest. Mr Trump initially said he had not been involved in the decision to broadcast the execution but understood its rationale. “They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision,” he said last week. But the proposal drew scepticism and condemnation, including from figures in Mr Trump’s own circle. Vice President JD Vance expressed reservations, saying he doubted the Pentagon would go ahead with the plan and that he would not watch if it did. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Archdiocese for the Military Services, issued a statement questioning the morality and purpose of broadcasting the execution. He warned that it could cause “moral injury” to the service members carrying it out and called on Catholic soldiers assigned to the firing squad to seek an exemption. “Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries? The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” he wrote. The controversy has raised questions about the administration’s judgment and its approach to capital punishment, legal experts said, as Mr Trump faces increasing political pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections . Mr Trump is dealing with low approval ratings as Americans increasingly blame him for rising costs and express disapproval of his handling of the war in Iran. On November 3, voters will decide which party controls Congress. “It's nonsensical, the way this has developed. The administration is not playing with a full deck,” said Eugene Fidell, a military law expert at Yale Law School. “This is totally tone deaf. It's very revealing of how out of touch this administration is, and seemingly how little supervision there is.” Mr Fidell also said a public execution would have gone against international human rights standards. The proposed use of a firing squad adds to the controversy. The US military has not carried out an execution by firing squad since 1945. The debate comes as capital punishment and execution methods face renewed scrutiny. Last month, Christa Pike, who was convicted of killing a friend in the 1990s, survived a botched execution attempt in Tennessee involving lethal injection. She was left badly injured. Daniel Urman, a constitutional law expert at Northeastern University, said Mr Hegseth and Mr Trump may have regarded the proposal as a way to project American strength but miscalculated the reaction it would provoke. “It does capture the Trump administration in the second term, where it looks like there's been an impulsive plan set out that might get walked back and might end up being embarrassing for them,” he said. “I think it's a headache he doesn't need. I think he's heard from members of his own party that it's a bad idea. And he needs his own party to stand by him.” Hasan's execution is scheduled for December 3, and it is unclear if any legal challenges could delay it.

title: Israel says entry of commercial goods into Gaza halted amid dispute between traders and Hamas
description: Hamas says $3,200 fee it is charging merchants is actually voluntary contribution to fund the needy
content: Lorries carrying commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza amid a dispute between traders and Hamas over taxes, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in the Palestinian territory has said. Cogat said the traders had decided to stop co-ordinating with it on shipments across the Israeli-controlled border in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed ​by ⁠Hamas on each lorry entering ‌the territory and a demand that 30 per cent of sales should be conducted in cash. Hamas denied the accusation in a statement released by the Gaza government's media office, which said the 10,000-shekel fee was, in fact, a contribution to a “voluntary community initiative” to support those in need such as widows and orphans. It also said the demand for cash payments was an “absolute necessity to address the severe imbalances in the Palestinian market, most notably the acute shortage of cash liquidity ”. Cogat said the traders' decision would cut the total ⁠number of lorries entering Gaza , bringing both humanitarian and commercial goods, by half, to around 300. The majority of Gazans are dependent on aid following three years of war, repeated displacement and restrictions imposed by Israel on aid deliveries. A global hunger monitor warned in July that more than two-thirds of Gazans could face acute hunger by the end of the year. Most of the territory's two million population live in makeshift shelters following widespread destruction of buildings and forced displacement during the war. Nahed Shhaibar, the head ​of the private transport union in Gaza, said that not ‌a single lorry carrying commercial ⁠products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, lorries carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had lorries carrying commercial ​goods from ‌Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing, he told Reuters. Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 lorries normally enter Gaza each day. Mr Shhaibar said the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods. Under the US-mediated ceasefire that halted full-scale fighting in October last year, Israel is obliged to allow a minimum of ​600 lorries carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. Nickolay Mladenov, high representative of the Board of Peace overseeing Gaza's recovery under US President Donald Trump's peace plan, said the dispute showed the need to move on to the next steps in the process, which has stalled over Israel's insistence that Hamas must first disarm. “These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), supported by the International Stabilisation Force, is urgently needed,” Mr Mladenov said in a post on X. “Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference.” The NCAG is a committee of Palestinian technocrats that was formed in January but has not been allowed to enter Gaza so far.

title: How is Europe helping Saudi Arabia? France begins deploying military means
description: Britain and Italy also offer military help as kingdom attacked by Houthis
content: France said on Thursday it had begun deploying military means to help Saudi Arabia as the kingdom comes under attack by Houthi rebels. Britain and Italy have also offered modest military help as Yemen's heaviest fighting in years spills over to Saudi Arabia. There is wariness in Europe of becoming too involved in the Middle East conflict, although the effect of the conflict on energy prices is also a consideration. Here is what major military powers in Europe have said about supporting Saudi Arabia: France ​is ​starting ⁠to put ⁠into action operational ​elements of an ⁠agreement to help protect Saudi oil ⁠facilities, Foreign Ministry ​spokesman Pascal ⁠Confavreux ‌said on ​Thursday. He declined to elaborate on what military means were being sent to Saudi Arabia. President Emmanuel Macron said last month France would send troops ​and ‌defence systems ⁠to ​Saudi Arabia ​to ‌help protect the Red ⁠Sea port city ⁠of Yanbu, which is vital for energy transport. Mr Macron is set to visit the UAE , Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar on a Gulf tour next week. A summit of EU and Gulf leaders in Riyadh has been postponed from its planned date of October 24. Britain has provided an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi operations in Yemen. It has also offered air defence equipment. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the Voyager aircraft had completed 14 “operational missions”. He said the UK would consider any further requests “as and when they come in”. Mr Burnham has made reducing the cost of living a major theme since taking office in July and indicated last month that this was a factor in approving the RAF Voyager deployment. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told The National last month that Italy had provided equipment such as radars and anti-missile batteries to Saudi Arabia before the regional war broke out in February. Italy also offered the kingdom “technological assistance in defending itself against Iranian attacks … and capable of assisting it also against attacks when they came from the Houthis,” he said. Last month an Italian F-2000 aircraft was hit at the Taif airbase in Saudi Arabia, where some Italian forces had been stationed on a separate mission. No personnel were injured. Germany has not declared any military support. Chancellor Friedrich Merz offered solidarity in a call with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, but there were no concrete announcements. The German parliament did vote on Thursday to extend the country's involvement in an EU naval mission to protect shipping in the Red Sea, which is under threat by the Houthis. Past German governments had blocked the sale of Eurofighter jets to Saudi Arabia, but the veto was declared lifted in 2024 due to the kingdom's “stabilising role”. Poland has one of Europe's largest militaries but has not announced any military aid to Saudi Arabia. Many Polish resources have already gone to supporting Ukraine's war effort against Russia. Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman spoke to his Polish counterpart Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on Tuesday. He said the two countries had “reviewed their defence co-operation” and discussed ways to support regional security. It is not known if any military aid was discussed.

title: Gianni Infantino apologises to Fifa Council over World Cup sell-off plan
description: Swiss head of world football's governing body grilled during three-and-a-half-hour meeting in Zurich
content: Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council about his failed attempt to sell off stakes in its competitions to private investors. But the president of Fifa also faced continuing questions about his role in the $4.2 billion Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme during a three-and-a-half-hour meeting in Zurich. Infantino was also asked to provide more information regarding the suspension of United States attacker Folarin Balogun's ban during this summer's World Cup in North America and the Fifa Peace Prize controversially awarded to US President Donald Trump. English and German football chiefs said they remained unconvinced Infantino was fit to ⁠continue as the head of football's world governing body. The apology from Infantino again came with the caveat that the FFE plan had been only a proposal and “in no way a done deal”. “First of all I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise project which led to many consequences,” said Infantino. “But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal and in no way a done deal, that actually intended to enable Fifa to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources.” The FFE plan involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, and selling ⁠a minority stake to private investors. Infantino said it was intended to generate additional funding for Fifa’s 211 member associations. While Infantino appeared to retain strong support among ​African officials, ⁠opposition from some of Europe’s most influential football associations remained ‌pronounced. German FA president Bernd Neuendorf called for a “complete restart” at Fifa, saying the governance reforms the organisation needed could not be delivered with Infantino in charge. “The first thing ​is we need reforms. That's true. And everyone knows that,” Neuendorf said. “The old administration has to be reformed, and the whole governance has to be reformed. But I'm pretty clear here in this that this is not possible with Gianni. “So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart.” English FA chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, insisted that too many questions remain unanswered after what she called the “most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting” she had experienced. “One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested – for example getting the papers from FFE,” Hewitt said. “I asked the question 'why not?' – and we were asked to submit those questions in writing. “I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president – and that was what was shared in the meeting. “I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them. “It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize. “The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate. “That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change.”

title: IEA oil supply pledge to exceed target as it boosts release of remaining stocks
description: Agency's members agree to boost the roll-out of the remaining 100 million barrels, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel
content: The International Energy Agency (IEA) has said that its March pledge to release crude oil stocks will exceed its target, and will be accelerating the release of the remaining supplies as global efforts to tame soaring energy prices continue. Members of the Paris-based agency have so far released 330 million barrels of oil, and the remaining 100 million barrels – which includes more than 20 million barrels of diesel – will be released in a “timely manner consistent with national circumstances”, it said in a statement on Thursday. That would make the total releases exceed the initial 400 million barrels the IEA had pledged in March, at the onset of the war between US and Israel and Iran. “Some IEA members have released higher volumes than initially pledged in March while other members intend to do so,” the IEA said after a meeting. Specific plans are already in place ... [to release the stocks] as soon as possible.” Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies. Earlier this month, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by rolling out 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA to help to stabilise markets. And in a surprising move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions on Russia to enable the latter to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The Opec + group, meanwhile, kept its oil production targets unchanged for November, extending the pause it started in October after six months of gradual increases. Oil prices rose after the IEA's announcement. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, added 0.15 per cent to $106.20 a barrel at 8.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, jumped 3.28 per cent to $98.21 a barrel. Thursday's IEA statement said it has “encouraged those IEA members holding oil production and refining capacities to boost supply of crude and refined products, particularly diesel”. The IEA said it will continue to monitor the progress of the completion of its March pledge, “and will inform G7 leaders as requested and the IEA governing board on further actions needed, based on an updated oil market assessment, focusing on diesel”, it added.

title: Yemen's Houthi rebels hit presidential palace in Aden
description: Attack caused deaths and injuries among security personnel but government members said to be unharmed
content: Yemen ’s Houthi rebels attacked the presidential palace in the southern city of Aden with five missiles on Thursday, the country's Information Minister Moammar Al Eryani said. He added that the Prime Minister and government members were safe, but two security guards were killed. It was the first attack on Aden since the Houthis and government forces resumed fighting last month after a four-year lull in the civil war. The southern port city has been the seat of Yemen’s government since the Iran-backed Houthis took over the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military intervention by a Saudi-led coalition a year later. “We reassure the children of our Yemeni people that the Prime Minister, and all members of the government are safe and well,” Mr Al Eryani said in a statement. He described the attack as a terrorist act. A statement from the Council of Ministers said the attack involved missiles as well as drones and caused deaths and injuries among security personnel. It said the attack "clearly exposes the militia’s inability to confront the Yemeni people’s resolve to restore state authority across the entire national territory and to put an end to its Iranian-backed subversive agenda". The cabinet said the attack would not weaken the government’s resolve or deter it from carrying out its national and constitutional responsibilities. “Aden will remain the hub for the operations of state institutions as they carry out their duties towards citizens,” the statement said. The Houthi-run Saba News Agency reported earlier that the target was a military operations headquarters at the palace, allegedly run by Saudi officers, and associated weapons depots. The agency quoted a military source as saying the headquarters had been hit. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said that the attack "falls within the framework of the declared policy to strike Saudi troop concentrations wherever they may be, and to treat any military presence of the Saudi enemy as a legitimate target for our forces, wherever it is located".

title: UK charity trustee belonged to sanctioned Iranian morality council
description: Supreme leader representative Ahmad Vaezi appeals Charity Commission ban
content: A member of a sanctioned Iranian morality body is taking legal action in the UK to appeal a ban which would prevent him from being a trustee of a charity for 12 years. Ahmad Vaezi is also the head of an Iranian propaganda body but has sought to cover up his links to the regime, a tribunal heard. Mr Vaezi is the head of the Islamic Propaganda Office (IPO), a member of Iran’s Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution (SCCR) and the representative of Iran’s supreme leader on European student affairs. The SCCR was sanctioned in 2023 for its role in enforcing morality laws following the death of Mahsa Amini in prison after she was accused of breaking laws on wearing a headscarf. Mr Vaezi is appealing against a decision by the Charity Commission to disqualify him from serving as a trustee of the Al-Tawheed Charitable Trust. In a submission to a tribunal hearing the case in London, the commission’s lawyer, Adrian Francis, said Mr Vaezi’s close links to the Iranian regime “in themselves render him unfit to be a charity trustee”. Mr Vaezi has attended events in support of Hezbollah and Hamas, both of which are proscribed as terrorist organisations by Britain, said Mr Francis. “The commission’s case is that it is self-evident a charity should not associate itself with a regime of such ill-repute and that doing so brings it, and the charity sector generally, into disrepute,” he said. Mr Vaezi sought to obstruct the watchdog’s inquiry “by deliberate suppression of such links”, said Mr Francis. He also sought to “mislead and obstruct the commission” on events that took place at Al-Tawheed’s premises in West London “and has, at the very least, turned a blind eye to the extremist activities that students and others connected to the London property can be shown to have engaged”. Mr Francis said the Iranian “has dishonestly sought to withhold information about his links to the Iranian regime; then, when confronted with his failure to disclose them, lied about the reasons for doing so”. The tribunal was told that a group called the Islamic Student Associations of Britain (IASL), which is part of the Union of Islamic Associations of Students in Europe, reportedly organised a remembrance event for Qassem Suleimani, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force, who was assassinated by the US in Baghdad in 2020. The student group allegedly live-streamed events featuring current and former IRGC officers, including Gen Saeed Ghasemi, in 2020 and 2021. Gen Ghasemi falsely claimed the Holocaust was “a lie and a fake” and said British students could “bring an end to the life of the oppressors and occupiers, Zionists and Jews across the world”. The video was shared at the time with the BBC by the US-based campaign group United Against Nuclear Iran. Mr Francis said this “demonstrates the British student group has engaged in extremist activity” and given Mr Vaezi’s 20-year association with the charity, it is “inconceivable he was not aware of the near-permanent presence and activities of the London student group”. The regulator is investigating the charity itself over the event and says it “is aware that speakers praised Suleimani and could hear anti-Semitic chants being made during the event”. Mr Vaezi, who also uses the surname Vaeijezei, remains a trustee while he appeals against the 12-year disqualification order imposed on him in January. He did not attend the hearing but details of his defence were provided in the commission’s submission to the tribunal. Mr Vaezi claims there is nothing inappropriate in being a member of the SCCR, despite its designation. He dismisses the designation as a political act and says his role is purely academic. He similarly contests that his leadership of the IPO, which he has held since February 2011, is incompatible with his trusteeship, insisting it is a non-political, educational, scientific and cultural institution that does not engage in propaganda. Another trustee, Seyed Moosavi, has appealed against his four-year disqualification for his role with Al-Tawheed and the Islamic Centre for England, one of the UK’s largest religious and cultural centres. A Charity Commission representative said it was “currently overseeing the remaining trustees’ progress on improving the charity’s governance and we put in place a protective order prohibiting a third party from using the charity’s premises”. “Decisions to suspend or disqualify trustees or senior managers of a charity are not taken lightly and are based on clear evidence it is necessary to protect charities,” the representative said.

title: Earliest evidence of human ancestor killed with wooden spear found in Iraqi cave
description: Violent death ended more than year of suffering for Neanderthal known as Shanidar A
content: Remains of a Neanderthal found in an Iraqi-Kurdistan cave reveal he died a violent death after more than a year of being cared for in agonising pain, a study has shown. The killing 75,000 years ago involved a sharpened wooden spear and may be the earliest example of lethal violence using such a weapon, archaeologists believe. A 15mm circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests a “heart shot”, in which the spear was thrust downwards to pass completely through the body, bringing rapid death. Tiny shards of displaced bone were pieced together to reveal how the spear would have penetrated the body. A spear tip or flint would have left a different shaped hole, researchers said in the study, published in the journal Scientific Reports . Other remains, notably damaged teeth, suggest the unfortunate individual – thought to have been around 45 years old when they died – had suffered a brutal facial injury at least a year earlier, and would have needed looking after. “It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual,” said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St John’s College, Cambridge, who led the excavation. The Neanderthal has been named Shanidar A by researchers, after the cave on the Bradost Mountain in Erbil where the remains were found. The scapula bone, or shoulder blade – broad, flat and so thin in places it is almost translucent – was preserved intact under rock and sediment, along with a mostly complete right hand and two ribs. “It’s extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don’t get complete scapulae from modern burials,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge’s Department of Archaeology. “We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight metres of rock and sediment.” The earliest known rounded wooden spear, pulled from the sea in Clacton-on-Sea, England, in 1911, is more than 400,000 years old. But very few wooden objects from prehistory survive due to the inevitable decomposition. Some waterlogged examples of spears dated to around 200,000 years ago – when early Neanderthals roamed Europe – were found in Schoningen, Germany, in the 1990s. They were around two metres long and used for throwing, like modern javelins, to hunt large game. The researchers believe a similar weapon caused Shanidar A’s death. “Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula,” said Dr Pomeroy. “What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A.” She said it was possible the death might have been in a hunting accident, but the evidence suggests deliberate violence was more likely. “Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries,” she said. “The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart.” It is possible that the fatal blow was struck by an early human, as they had evolved by that time, but violence between Neanderthals seems a more straightforward explanation. “All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal’s life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear,” said Prof Barker. One of the seven teeth that were found had been split lengthways with only half remaining, with the others twisted inward. The half tooth had significant tartar build-up along the exposed root canal, suggesting it stayed in the mouth for some time after a blow to the face. Surviving a trauma that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for at least a year would have required care and support from other Neanderthals,” said Dr Pomeroy. Shanidar A may have been fed soft food. Previous research on sediment in Shanidar Cave shows that plants were being soaked before cooking around the same time. “There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time,” said Prof Barker. “The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognise as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime.” The vast cave in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan known as Shanidar is one of the world’s most famous Neanderthal sites. Excavations in the 1950s led by Ralph Solecki found remains from 10 individuals, including a “cluster” of four in the same spot despite dying at different times, suggesting the Neanderthals had returned to inter their dead. Remains of a Neanderthal from another part of the cave, who lived thousands of years later, showed evidence of a paralysed arm, arthritis, deafness and partial blindness. Yet they had lived a long life, so must have been cared for. Shanidar A is one of five Neanderthals unearthed in 2020 in a part of a cave just 1.5 metres long and one metre deep, directly behind a large vertical boulder, thought to be a “prominent marker”. The body was positioned on its back, head facing east. “These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest,” said Dr Pomeroy. “Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades.”

title: UK arm of Iran's 'hate' TV channel reported to police under national security law
description: HispanTV has ties to another Iranian broadcaster that was banned from the UK
content: The UK government has come under fire for failing to tackle an Iranian TV company registered in Britain for the past 15 years, despite links to the banned channel Press TV. HispanTV, focused on the Spanish-speaking world, is part of state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (Irib) and has faced accusations of acting as Iran's “long arm of hate”. Its UK arm was this week reported to police under national security laws by a senior British politician. Alicia Kearns, the UK's shadow Home Office Minister, told The National she had complained to the Met Police that HispanTV was allegedly breaching the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme. Records show the current and former owners of the UK entity had close ties with Press TV , Iran’s English-language state broadcaster, which broadcast from London studios until 2012 when its licence was revoked by the UK’s media regulator, Ofcom. According to Companies House, HispanTV has been registered as a business in the UK since January 2011, with its current address given as a unit on an industrial estate in north-west London. Seyedmehdi Mirtaleb, who is listed as the director and majority shareholder, was an executive producer at Press TV in London from 2009 until 2020, according to his LinkedIn profile. The 48-year-old is listed as a British citizen on Companies House but in a previous entry his nationality was given as Iranian. The records show that HispanTV was originally registered by a Hamid Khairoldin, 68, but he resigned as a director and gave up his ownership of the company in 2014. When PressTV was registered as a company in the UK, Mr Khairoldin was listed as a director from 2007 to 2010. Ofcom told The National that HispanTV has never been licensed to broadcast in the UK and so it had not acted on its presence as a company. Press TV's licence to broadcast was removed by Ofcom in 2012 after it failed to pay a £100,000 fine imposed for broadcasting an interview with imprisoned journalist Maziar Bahari, which the regulator said had been conducted under duress. Ofcom also said it had breached several broadcasting licence rules over editorial control of the channel. Shortly before PressTV was banned, it shared a Companies House-registered address with HispanTV in a west London office block. The umbrella Irib is sanctioned by the US and EU, while some of its directors were listed by the UK for overseeing the programming decisions that led to human rights violations. HispanTV's global remit is broadcasting news, documentaries, movies and Iranian films 24 hours a day. Its activities in the UK are unclear. It does not appear to make programmes or broadcast from the UK, but its footprint is aimed at Latin American nations. The UK is a global media hub where the industry clusters for business and talent, as well as broadcast assets. When The National visited its current registered UK address, the unit was occupied by another business which said it had never heard of HispanTV. Businesses in nearby units said the lock-up had previously been empty for a number of years. Since a change in the law this summer, the UK requires anyone carrying out political influence activities in the UK at the direction of any foreign power to register their arrangements. The law came into effect in 2025 under the National Security Act to increase transparency and protect the UK from covert state-backed interference. “There is no question that it is not conducive to national security to have these types of outlets operating in the UK – they are cut-outs of the Iranian state,” Ms Kearns told The National. The Tory politician, whose brief includes national security, said she has previously raised the presence of media linked to Iran and its allies with both the police and government. Ms Kearns recently raised the issue of the Houthi TV station Al Masirah TV in the House of Commons. The company's presence in the UK was revealed by The National earlier this year and raised concerns over alleged illicit funding, visa facilitation and intelligence gathering on political rivals. “I feel like I'm sitting in this limbo where I'm screaming and shouting and neither the police nor the government are doing anything at all,” she said. “It's preposterous. We’ve got to get them shut down.
