What I do not understand is how the government doesn't understand these cut-outs are risks to our society.” Mr Mirtaleb and Mr Khairoldin have been approached for comment. HispanTV'S UK arm was founded with £1 in share capital and has filed limited accounts under rules for small businesses that exempt it from providing details of its turnover. It has been listed as dormant since 2012 and its accounts state its assets have remained at £1 throughout its existence. HispanTV's Spanish-language service went on air from Tehran in October 2011 and was officially launched by President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in January the following year. “The new channel will limit the ground for supremacy of dominance-seekers,” Mr Ahmadinejad said during a ceremony marking the inauguration. “It will be a means for better ties between people and governments of Iran and Spanish-speaking nations.” The channel was launched on the back of Iran’s attempts to establish strong commercial, political and strategic links with South America at a time when it had been hit with tough sanctions for its nuclear programme. For a time it had a base in Madrid, but it was closed down in 2013 by the Spanish government as part of broader EU sanctions against Iran. In a report earlier this year, HispanTV was described by the Anti-Defamation League as the “leading platform peddling anti-Semitic hate and disseminating anti-Israel prejudice and incitement across Latin America and the wider Spanish‑speaking world”. The study found that HispanTV has significantly ramped up its rhetoric over the last two years through its satellite, cable and live-streaming broadcasting, as well as its website. It has more than a quarter of a million followers on social media. An earlier ADL study called HispanTV: “The Iranian Regime’s Long Arm of Hate in Latin America.” United Against Nuclear Iran (Uani) says HispanTV “serves as an arm of Iran’s public diplomacy outreach to Latin America, a region in which Iran has invested significant political capital”. “The UK continues to harbour a permissive environment for these media arms of the Iranian regime,” Jason Brodsky, Uani’s policy director, told The National . “HispanTV is part of the Irib, which is under US sanctions for its ties to the Iranian intelligence services. “PressTV has those ties as well. Former Irib executives are under UK sanctions. At a time when the Islamic Republic is plotting terror on UK soil, the UK government should be cracking down on these networks' freedom of movement on British soil. There must be a reassessment as to how these networks are using UK soil as a platform.” The continued presence of HispanTV in the UK comes amid an escalation of attacks which Iran is believed to be behind. These include arson attacks on Jewish volunteer ambulances, a synagogue and Iran International TV, a broadcaster critical of the regime. Responsibility for the attacks was claimed by a group named Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, or Ashab Al Yamin. It is widely believed to be a creation of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) .

title: Syria sentences two to death over coastal sectarian violence
description: Military court in Aleppo hands prison terms to three other defendants
content: A Syrian military court has sentenced two men to death over sectarian violence along the country's coast in March 2025, state news agency Sana reported on Thursday. Three other defendants received prison terms and two were acquitted at the Military Criminal Court in Aleppo. Al Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali were convicted of seeking to incite civil war and sectarian fighting, and leading armed gangs with the intent of attacking public forces. Both were sentenced to death. Maher Othman was sentenced to 12 years in prison for complicity in the two offences, while Mohammed Bakour received a 20-year sentence for intentional murder and Ammar Abdul Aal was sentenced to three years for torture. The court acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammed Zarzouri. Public hearings began at the Palace of Justice in Aleppo on November 18, 2025. The latest verdicts follow rulings on September 17 in cases involving four other defendants accused of violations during the violence, in which pro-government fighters killed hundreds of members of the Alawite minority. At that hearing, one was sentenced to death, another to life imprisonment and a third to 20 years in prison, while the fourth was acquitted. The violence followed attacks on army and security facilities on March 6, 2025. A national investigative committee reported on July 22 last year that remnants of the deposed regime of Bashar Al Assad had carried out widespread attacks that killed 238 military and security personnel. The committee also documented violations against civilians in the days that followed the attacks. It concluded that the abuses were not organised or systematic, but were committed by individuals and small groups for various motives. Separately, Syria’s General Intelligence Service has arrested Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, a key suspect in the 2013 Baniyas massacre , as he attempted to flee across the border, Sana reported. Mr Kayali formed an armed militia that fought alongside forces of the deposed Assad regime during the Syrian civil war. The militia was implicated in mass killings in several parts of the country, including Al Bayda and Ras Al Nabaa in Baniyas. According to the Syrian Network for Human Rights, 264 civilians, including 36 children and 28 women, were killed in Al Bayda, while 195 civilians, including 56 children and 43 women, were killed in the Ras Al Nabaa. Reports and testimonies described summary executions using firearms and bladed weapons, as well as the burning of homes and bodies. Militias affiliated with Kayali were also accused of carrying out massacres in the countryside of Latakia, Aleppo and Idlib, leaving hundreds dead or wounded. He is also the main suspect for the twin bombings in Reyhanli in Turkey’s southern Hatay province in 2013, killing 52 people, according to Anadolu Agency. Earlier this month, Turkish intelligence arrested Omar Al Khatib, one of the alleged planners of the Reyhanli bombing, as he attempted to flee by sea to Europe. He had co-ordinated between the attackers and members of the deposed regime’s intelligence services, according to the report. On October 4, Syrian security forces arrested Jamal Tarabulsi, Kayali’s deputy. The Interior Ministry has said it is continuing to pursue those accused of violations against civilians during the Assad regime as part of efforts to advance transitional justice and hold accountable those responsible.

title: UAE 'better prepared' for war than when US conflict with Iran began, says official
description: Hundreds of members of Iranian sleeper cells arrested, says chairman of FNC's Defence, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee
content: The UAE is "better prepared" for a resumption of full-scale war should it happen, a senior official said on Thursday, amid a US-Iran diplomatic deadlock and growing signs of a potential return to major confrontation between the two countries. Dr Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defence, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the Federal National Council, was speaking to journalists in Dubai. Asked by The National about the possibility of war resuming and the country's level of preparedness, Dr Al Nuaimi said the UAE is “better prepared than it was on February 28”, when the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran, which sparked the regional war . “The war can resume, yes,” he said, adding that “the readiness” in the UAE was in “all aspects” and that “whatever is needed to protect the country and the people, we will do it”. A ceasefire began in June when the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding intended to pave the way for a final peace settlement. US President Donald Trump declared the truce and MoU “over” in early July after renewed Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and retaliatory American strikes. Both sides have indicated in recent weeks that they are preparing for a resumption of hostilities. At the peak of the war, Iran attacked the UAE and other Gulf states with ballistic missiles and drones, attempting to strike civilian infrastructure, including energy sites and airports. The UAE was the most heavily attacked country, facing more than 550 ballistic missiles and 2,265 drones, most of which were intercepted or destroyed before reaching their targets. In April, the UAE State Security Department said it had dismantled a terrorist organisation operating inside the Emirates. The department sanctioned the arrests of the group's members over suspected involvement in activities aimed at undermining national unity and carrying out planned sabotage operations inside the country. The organisation was discovered to be holding secret meetings inside and outside the UAE, surveillance reports said. The group was also found to be trying to recruit young Emiratis by spreading “misleading ideas” in the hope of gaining their support for “foreign allegiances”. The UAE also announced the dismantling of a “terrorist network” funded and operated by Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iran and the arrest of its members. The network was said to have been operating in the UAE using a fake commercial cover and had tried to infiltrate the national economy and conduct “external schemes” against the country’s financial stability. Dr Al Nuaimi said “hundreds” of members of Iranian sleeper cells were arrested, including several Emiratis, after they were “caught guiding Iranian [attacks using] missiles and drones” to hit targets in the UAE. “They wanted to undermine and destroy this model,” he said. Despite this, he said, dialogue remains a priority for the UAE . He added that if Iran took one step towards rebuilding trust, the UAE would take further steps in response, but stressed that, for now, “we don't trust them”.

title: What are Saudi Arabia's options to deter the Yemeni rebels?
description: Senior US official tells The National that Trump administration has no plans to announce new military operations in Yemen
content: Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar problem in Yemen: having the military resources to strike the Iran-backed Houthis hard, but no guarantee that a campaign will stop the heavily armed militant group from threatening the kingdom again. The latest wave of missile and drone attacks has brought that dilemma into sharper focus, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi airports and threatening critical energy infrastructure, including Saudi Aramco ’s headquarters in Dhahran. While Saudi Arabia ’s challenge is restoring deterrence, analysts say Riyadh’s options are narrow. They include intensifying air strikes, bolstering Yemeni government forces on the ground, strengthening air defences and seeking renewed diplomatic engagement. “Saudi Arabia should apply military pressure on the Houthis inside Yemen to deter further attacks,” Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre, told The National . “A key priority is to limit their ability to launch cross-border attacks, particularly by degrading their missile capabilities.” Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to escalate in July, when an air strike hit Sanaa International Airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia. Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government claimed responsibility, saying it had hit the runway to prevent an unauthorised Iranian aircraft from landing. The strike tested a fragile period of calm that had largely held since a truce took effect in 2022. The Houthis subsequently launched missiles towards Saudi Arabia, while fighting between the group and Yemeni forces intensified. Mr Sager said that the kingdom had accepted the principle of a ceasefire with the Houthis and remained committed to de-escalation. “However, renewed military pressure may be necessary before agreeing to another ceasefire to secure credible commitments that attacks will stop,” he added. The Houthis have been fighting the Yemeni government since seizing Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 at the head of a coalition of regional allies to support the government against the rebels. Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s largest military budgets and a sophisticated arsenal, including American warplanes, missile-defence systems and other advanced weapons. However, Aziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said defeating the Houthis militarily would require more than air power. The kingdom has demonstrated its ability to conduct air operations, but he explained that a successful campaign would also require effective ground forces capable of changing the balance of power in Houthi-held territory. Maritime forces would be needed to restrict the movement of supplies reaching the group through the Red Sea and from the Horn of Africa, he added. That combination could be difficult to assemble. Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis have improved their capabilities, but continue to face problems of competence and political fragmentation. “The reason why the Houthis may hold what they have is not because of their strength, but really the weakness of the other ground operation,” said Mr Alghashian. “A state-building approach would also be needed.” The Houthis, once regarded as a relatively poorly equipped militia, have developed into a formidable fighting force. Their arsenal includes missiles and drones that can strike targets more than 1,000 miles away. Since the war in Gaza erupted in 2023, the group has launched hundreds of drones and missiles towards Israel . Most were intercepted, but some reached their targets, including a drone strike in Tel Aviv that killed a man in 2024 and a missile strike near Ben Gurion Airport last year. The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Washington and Tehran have not yet reached a lasting peace agreement . In recent weeks, they have exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy shipments, but negotiations have not resumed. Some observers argue that a broader agreement between the US and Iran offers the most viable path to ending Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Under such a deal, the US could seek Iranian commitments to rein in the Houthis and secure an end to their attacks as part of a regional settlement. But whether the group would comply with such an arrangement is not known. The US supports Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthis through arms sales, military advisers, intelligence sharing and targeting assistance, though it has avoided direct military combat operations. President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining strikes against the Houthis, as the rebels attack a US ally and threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have warned that any US strikes could prompt them to attack American personnel and interests across the Middle East, potentially drawing the US deeper into the seven-and-a-half-month war. But a senior US official has told The National that the Trump administration has “no announcements to make regarding US support for new military operations” in Yemen. The official added that the administration remains in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. “We will always fulfil our commitments to our partners,” said the official without elaborating. Mr Alghashian believes American firepower could deter the Houthis, at least initially. But he cautioned that the rebels may be prepared to absorb the strikes and wait for US resolve to weaken. “The Houthis feel they will try to weather the storm. Their calculation seems to be that they have withstood many storms before,” he added. “The Saudis still need their allies and still need to focus on alliances for defence.” Mr Trump ordered a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but declared a swift victory after the US expended weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone, according to US media reports. “Saudi Arabia should mobilise the international community to respond to this aggression against the kingdom. Strengthening Saudi defensive capabilities and securing support from regional and international partners are essential to protecting its territory and deterring further attacks,” affirmed Mr Sager.

title: The global water conversation is changing – now the UAE and the world must act
description: Our objective at the UN water conference in Abu Dhabi this year should be to build momentum around investment, international co-operation, innovation and implementation
content: One of the defining characteristics of UN conferences is the opportunity to bring together perspectives and stakeholders whose paths might otherwise rarely cross. During the high-level week at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, I engaged to technology leaders on artificial intelligence, investors on infrastructure, policymakers on climate resilience, business leaders on opportunity, and researchers and development institutions on sustainable development. These conversations reflected different priorities, yet increasingly converged around a common question: how can we build a future that is more resilient, more prosperous and better equipped to withstand disruption? Time and again, the conversation came back to water. This was not simply a matter of increased attention to water as a standalone issue. Rather, it reflected a growing recognition of its fundamental role in addressing the interconnected challenges facing communities, countries and economies. Food security depends on water . The energy transformation depends on water. Economic strength depends on water. And thriving communities require reliable access to safe water. For many years, those working to advance the global water agenda have emphasised the importance of integrating water into discussions on climate, food, energy, infrastructure, economic growth and development. Increasingly, however, water is being recognised as an integral part of these discussions in its own right. This shift reflects an important evolution in how the international community understands the relationship between water and sustainable development. We are increasingly recognising water not only as a resource we need to conserve, but also as a strategic asset we need to invest in – one that underpins resilience, enables opportunity and supports long-term prosperity. The scale of the challenge is clear. Agriculture accounts for about 70 per cent of global freshwater withdrawals, while millions of livelihoods depend on water-intensive sectors. When water becomes unreliable, the consequences extend well beyond the water sector, affecting food prices, employment, businesses, communities and investment. Yet the human impact is even more significant. When water is scarce or unsafe, women and girls often carry a disproportionate burden. Globally, women and girls are responsible for fetching water in more than 70 per cent of households. Instead of receiving an education, learning a new skill or joining the workforce, women and girls are collectively spending 200 to 250 million hours every single day collecting and hauling water. Water security is fundamentally about people. It is about peace, stability and human dignity. When water systems are disrupted, livelihoods are disrupted. When scarcity puts pressure on communities, resilience is tested. And when countries share rivers, aquifers and water systems, co-operation becomes essential . Water can be a source of pressure. But it can also be a reason to co-operate and collaborate. That matters even more at a time when faith in international co-operation is under increasing pressure. We are living through a period of profound global change, when trust between countries and confidence in multilateral institutions cannot be taken for granted. Yet there are challenges that no country can solve alone – and water is one of them. Every country depends on water, every economy depends on it, and every family needs it. That gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that international co-operation can still deliver something tangible: solutions that improve lives, strengthen resilience and create opportunity. Here in the UAE, we understand this connection particularly well. We live in one of the world’s most water-scarce regions . For us, water has shaped how we think about our cities, our economy and our future. This understanding also informs our approach to international co-operation. At Cop28, hosted by the UAE in 2023, the adoption of the historic UAE Consensus by 198 Parties demonstrated the importance of collective action in addressing interconnected climate challenges. It reinforced the need to advance climate ambition through practical solutions, international co-operation and implementation. Beyond that event, we have spent years talking about climate, energy, food, technology and water as separate agendas. But now those boundaries are disappearing. Climate change is intensifying droughts, floods and water variability around the world. Extreme weather is placing greater pressure on economies, infrastructure and communities. At the same time, the world is rapidly electrifying, investing in new technologies, expanding digital infrastructure and seeking pathways to sustainable growth. Water systems require energy. Energy systems require water. Food production depends on both. And the rapid growth of AI and digital infrastructure is creating a new set of demands on these interconnected systems. This is why we recently launched the Crosscurrents Report , examining the growing relationship between AI, water and energy. The report highlights a dual challenge. As digital infrastructure expands, its demand for energy and water will grow. But there is another side to the story: AI is also helping us manage water better – from detecting leaks and improving irrigation to forecasting drought, optimising infrastructure and strengthening decision-making. The significance of this extends beyond AI itself. It points to a broader truth: the systems that underpin our economies can no longer be planned in isolation. Decisions about energy affect water. Decisions about water influence food production , industry, communities and economic growth. Climate adaptation affects all of them. The future will not be built by solving one issue at a time. It will depend on how effectively we understand these connections and plan for them together. What gave me optimism during our discussions in New York was the scale of the coalition engaging with these challenges and opportunities. The most encouraging discussions were not confined to governments or traditional water stakeholders – instead, they involved investors, technology companies, financial institutions, entrepreneurs, researchers, young leaders and development organisations. There is growing recognition that resilience is a shared responsibility. But awareness alone will not close the gap. We know many of the solutions. We have better technologies , better data and better tools than we did a decade ago. We know more about reuse, storage, loss reduction and efficient desalination. The challenge is getting those solutions out of the pilot phase – to translate ideas into impact. How do we connect capital to projects? Innovation to deployment? Technology to communities? And international commitments to action on the ground? These are the questions I heard often in New York . And they are the questions that will matter most at the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December. The conference, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal, will bring these conversations together. The event will hold special significance as the first UN Water Conference to be co-hosted by two nations from the Global South, reflecting their role as active partners in shaping solutions and driving international action on water. It is also the first UN conference focused on accelerating the implementation of SDG 6, which addresses clean water and sanitation services. Our ambition is to build momentum around investment, international co-operation, innovation and implementation – and to keep that momentum going long after December. That means bringing governments together with investors, development institutions with the private sector, technology companies with communities, researchers with policymakers. And, critically, giving youth a seat at the table – not simply asking them to listen to the decisions of today, but empowering them to help shape the solutions of tomorrow. We understand that the future of water will not be solved by one government, one institution nor one technology – it will be solved by what we do together. The strongest lesson I took away from the General Assembly last month was that for the first time the global conversation is truly changing. Water is moving from the margins to the centre – of economic planning, climate and humanitarian resilience, sustainable development, technology, food and energy transformations, and international co-operation. At a time when global confidence in international co-operation is being tested, water gives us a practical opportunity to prove what it can achieve. If we get water right, the benefits will be boundless – healthier communities, greater opportunity for women and girls, stronger economies, more resilient food and energy systems, stronger digital infrastructure, and greater peace and stability. The conversation has shifted. Now, the water conference will turn that momentum into action. Together, we invite everyone, no matter where they may be in the world, to join us in reimagining water’s role in creating a better future for all, driving co-operation, growth, resilience and opportunity.

title: Robbery, harassment and fraud rise across England and Wales
description: Robberies against businesses had biggest increase after change in the way UK police record theft and violence in shops
content: Robbery, harassment and fraud are among the offences that rose in England and Wales in the year to March 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. The broader Crime Survey for England and Wales estimated 9.6 million incidents overall, which reveals no major statistical change from the previous year. However, as some crimes fell, others rose. Police recorded 87,362 robberies, up 10 per cent. That rise came from business robberies, which increased 91 per cent to 29,669. The ONS says this was mainly because police were told to record shop thefts involving violence or threats as robbery from April 2025. Robberies of personal property fell by 9 per cent. Recorded rapes rose 4 per cent to 74,727. Violence without injury edged up 2 per cent, while violence with injury fell 3 per cent. The ONS cautions that police figures for these offences are not a reliable guide to trends, as they can be affected by changes in recording and by more victims coming forward. Harassment rose 6 per cent, according to police records, but the ONS says those figures are not a good indicator of trends. Its survey found a statistically significant rise in repeated harassment: from 2.3 per cent to 3.5 per cent of adults aged 16 and over, or about 1.7 million people. The estimates are interim. The survey also found that the number of adult fraud victims rose 10 per cent to 3.8 million. Bank and credit account fraud incidents increased 15 per cent to about 2.8 million. Total fraud incidents reached 4.5 million, with no statistically significant change.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed offers condolences to Saudi King after airport strikes
description: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed and Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi also expressed their sympathies
content: UAE leaders have sent condolences to Saudi Arabia's King Salman bin Abdulaziz following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which left several people dead and hundreds injured. President Sheikh Mohamed expressed his sincere sympathy for the victims of the attacks and wished the injured a speedy recovery. Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, sent similar condolences to King Salman. Sheikh Dr Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, also sent his condolences to the Saudi King. King Khalid International Airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, the deadliest on the kingdom in more than ​a decade. On Sunday, another strike killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The Houthi rebels have launched attacks other airports in Saudi Arabia in the past week, hitting sites not only in the capital but in Abha, Jazan and Najran, with a projectile also damaging the airport serving Dammam. The strikes have disrupted air travel across the region, including flights from the UAE. Emirates, flydubai and Air Arabia have cancelled a number of flights to Saudi destinations, while Etihad Airways has cancelled services between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 18.

title: Riyadh Fashion Week postponed to next year in latest Saudi event shake-up
description: Other gatherings that have been rescheduled include the Red Sea International Film Festival and Soundstorm
content: Riyadh Fashion Week has been postponed until next year, organisers said late on Wednesday, a day before the event was scheduled to begin in the Saudi capital. The fourth iteration of the annual fashion event was to run from October 15 to 20, bringing together local and international designers for six days of runway shows and industry meetings. The changes come amid heightened regional tension and Saudi security concerns, although organisers of Riyadh Fashion Week have not publicly linked their decision to the situation. The decision is the latest in a series of changes to Saudi Arabia's cultural and entertainment calendar, after the postponement of the Red Sea International Film Festival and the cancellation of this year's Soundstorm music festival. The Red Sea International Film Festival, originally scheduled to take place in Jeddah from December 3 to 12, has been pushed back to the last quarter of 2027. Organisers said the decision followed a review of the event's timing and logistical requirements, but did not give a more specific reason. Meanwhile, the Joy Awards , which are usually held in January and have attracted leading Arab and international stars to Riyadh, are reportedly set to be scrapped in 2027 amid a broader reassessment of spending on major entertainment events. The General Entertainment Authority and MBC Group, organisers of the ceremony, have yet to officially confirm the move. First held in 2023, Riyadh Fashion Week was launched as part of efforts by the Saudi Fashion Commission to promote the kingdom's growing fashion industry and provide a platform for local designers to reach international audiences. The event has since grown in prominence, attracting major international labels alongside established and emerging Saudi talent. Last year's edition featured British fashion house Vivienne Westwood , which opened the event, while Stella McCartney made her Saudi debut with a runway show that brought the week to a close. The programme also highlighted regional designers, reflecting the event's ambition to establish Riyadh as a destination on the international fashion calendar. Organisers have yet to announce the dates or programme for the 2027 edition.

title: DFSA fines immigration firm Hayman-Woodward Dh1.67m for unlicensed services
description: Breaches were committed for more than six years
content: The Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA) has fined the Dubai unit of Hayman-Woodward Global Mobility Services (HWW DIFC) $454,367 (Dh1.67 million) for providing unauthorised services for more than six years. HWW DIFC was found to have carried out client services in or from Dubai International Financial Centre without being registered as a designated non-financial business or profession (DNFBP), DFSA said in a statement on Thursday. The company is incorporated in the DIFC, but its business activities are only permitted for management consultancies and document clearing services. The DFSA found that HWW DIFC breached DNFBP regulations, specifically by acting as a formation agent of legal persons, and providing a registered office, business address, correspondence and administrative address for companies and legal persons. The unauthorised services were provided to 71 clients between August 2018 and February 2025. HWW DIFC also signed agreements with three free zones outside the DIFC to assist in company set-ups and other customer service provider transactions. The penalty comprises the fine and a disgorgement, or the surrender of any profits obtained from unlawful acts. The fine, however, was reduced by 30 per cent, from $522,047.05, after Hayman-Woodward agreed to settle the case. “The DNFBP regime is a key component of the DFSA's framework for mitigating money laundering and other financial crime risks within the DIFC,” said Alan Linning, managing director for enforcement at the DFSA. “Businesses that provide company service provider and other DNFBP services can present elevated financial crime risks and are therefore subject to appropriate regulatory oversight and supervision.” Authorities in the UAE have been vigilant in cracking down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the Emirati financial system's integrity and reliability. Earlier this month, the DFSA imposed a Dh401,000 fine on wealth management services firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation. Last week, the Registration Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM imposed fines totalling $100,000 against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers over regulatory failings. The UAE Central Bank has also imposed fines on lenders that have violated rules, especially those on anti-money laundering. “The DFSA remains committed to developing, administering and enforcing world-class regulation of financial services within the DIFC,” the authority said. It added it will continue to take “appropriate enforcement action to protect users and prospective users of financial services and to preserve confidence in the DIFC’s regulatory framework”.

title: Sheikha Latifa hosts women leaders' majlis in Dubai to discuss innovation and opportunities
description: Dubai Culture chairwoman leads discussions on women's role in shaping future of leadership
content: Sheikha Latifa bint Mohammed has hosted an international gathering of women leaders in Dubai , bringing together voices from 22 countries to explore the future of leadership and innovation. The Women Leading the Future majlis was organised as part of the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which was delivered through a partnership between the UAE Government, the World Economic Forum and the Dubai Future Foundation. The majlis, on Wednesday, brought together 29 women leaders from government, entrepreneurship, science , technology, finance and culture. Discussions considered the choices, responsibilities and collaboration required to create opportunities for the next generation, with a focus on women's contributions to public leadership, innovation, investment and social change. Sheikha Latifa, chairwoman of Dubai Culture and Arts Authority, emphasised the UAE's commitment to investing in women's capabilities and equipping them with the knowledge, skills and experience to drive sustainable change. She highlighted the growing importance of diverse perspectives as artificial intelligence and emerging technology reshape industries, working practices and everyday life. She also noted the critical roles women play across sectors in fostering integration, harnessing technology to create opportunities and strengthening social cohesion. Shaping humanity's future, she said, was a shared responsibility requiring broader participation and practical, sustainable solutions to tomorrow's challenges. This first Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders brought together more than 700 leaders and experts from 100 countries, including ministers, officials, 300 Young Global Leaders and 150 UAE government leaders. It served as a forum for international dialogue on developing responses to future challenges.

title: Hezbollah claims ownership of explosive-laden vehicle seized by Lebanese army
description: MP says weapons were intended to confront Israeli forces and accuses Lebanese PM of 'sowing internal discord'
content: Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah ⁠said ​on Thursday an explosive-laden vehicle ​seized by the Lebanese Armed Forces last week belonged to the Iran-backed group. Mr Fadlallah said Hezbollah had contacted Lebanese authorities to claim ownership of the vehicle as soon as it was intercepted. Its contents were intended “to confront the Israeli occupation” and Hezbollah's weapons were “pointed exclusively at the [Israeli] enemy”, he added. Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said there would be “no leniency” in the investigation and the government “will not tolerate anyone who dares to toy with the country's security, safety and stability”. About 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4 were discovered in a vehicle bound for Beirut when it was stopped at an Internal Security Forces checkpoint at Dahr Al Baidar in the Bekaa Valley. Then on Monday the Lebanese Armed Forces on Monday said it had seized 200kg of explosives, foiling a smuggling attempt from Syria through the Hermel border region. The Dahr Al Baidar seizure – one of three such interceptions in a matter of weeks – comes as pressure is mounting on the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah and bring all weapons in the country under state control. The seizure also caused widespread uproar in Lebanon. While the case is being investigated by a military court, some ministers at a cabinet meeting on Thursday are expected to push for it to be heard by Lebanon's Judicial Council, which deals with serious state security threats. Meanwhile, Hezbollah has remained defiant in rejecting disarmament and says any talks on the fate of its weapons can take place only after Israel halts attacks on Lebanon and withdraws from occupied Lebanese territory. Israel and Hezbollah have engaged in several bouts of fighting since the onset of the Gaza war in October 2023. The latest conflict began on March 2, when Hezbollah fired missiles at Israel in support of Iran in the regional conflict. Israel responded with a devastating military campaign, killing more than 4,000 people and flattening dozens of villages in southern Lebanon, where it continues to occupy vast areas of territory . Direct US-brokered talks between Israel and Lebanon have done little to move the needle, with no real progress on Hezbollah's disarmament or Israel's withdrawal. The interception of the explosive-laden vehicle has prompted fears of renewed political assassinations in Lebanon, a country with a grim history of such killings. In a second incident, about 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of the explosive C4 were discovered in a lorry bound for Beirut. “I understand the anxiety gripping the Lebanese people upon the news of this truck's interception and the materials it was transporting, especially since C4 has been used in several of the infamous political assassinations in modern Lebanese history,” Mr Salam said in a post on X on Monday. Mr Fadlallah dismissed the Prime Minister's words as an “inflammatory campaign aimed at sowing internal discord” and said it would not “deter” the group from “continuing its efforts to defend and liberate their land”. He said Hezbollah had demanded the release of the two men “and the return of the vehicle and everything inside it”. He also castigated the government's decision earlier this year to ban Hezbollah's military activities. “For our people, this decision is null and void, has no existence, and has no effects on the ground that we recognise.” In the 2000s and early 2010s, several high-profile opponents of the Assad regime in Syria and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah were killed or had attempts made on their lives using explosives. Former prime minister of Lebanon Rafic Hariri was killed along with 20 others when a one-tonne lorry bomb was detonated as his convoy was driving through Beirut on February 14, 2005. Hezbollah members were convicted of that attack by the UN's Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

title: Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ new Dubai hub highlights bold plans for regional growth
description: Founded in 1961, the group expanded from its initial activities in the field of pharmaceuticals
content: Dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical giant Pierre Fabre Laboratories Group has underlined its ambitions for growth in the Middle East and beyond with the opening of a new regional hub in Dubai. The company is a global player with its dermo-cosmetics brands Avène, Ducray, A-Derma, Klorane, and René Furterer, as well as its entire medical division specialising in oncology, dermatology, and rare diseases. Eric Ducournau, chief executive of Pierre Fabre Laboratories, officially inaugurated the new premises in the Landmark Group building near Dubai Marina. It is the headquarters of the French company’s Middle East, Africa, Russia, Turkey (MEART) subsidiary and will play a central role in its strategy to double its sales in six years. Ducournau said the move confirmed Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ bold expansion route, which also involves leveraging local expertise. “This investment clearly illustrates our desire to expand in this region, and Dubai is ideal for recruiting international talent from the UAE,” he told The National. Ducournau also said the country’s political stability, its investment in science, and its strong commitment to health care were the main reasons for choosing Dubai as the regional centre. Pierre Fabre Laboratories aims to continue its research into “the medicines of the future” while potentially adapting existing medical treatments and dermo-cosmetic products to regional needs. “We work closely with healthcare professionals to understand patients’ needs,” Ducournau said. “Here, the country invests in its hospital infrastructure, equipment, and training for doctors to treat patients. Our expertise, combined with that of healthcare professionals, will enable us to provide medicines and dermo-cosmetic care tailored to the needs of the local population.” Ducournau said: “What is important for a pharma company is to develop products, and to develop products you need scientific partnerships. “And in this area, countries are really investing; the level of hospitals is very high … the equipment, the training, the presence of highly experienced doctors. “The country is investing in good facilities to treat the population…that’s very important because you can’t develop the company more in the field of oncology or dermatology or rare diseases without this footprint in science.” A proud history Founded in 1961 by pharmacist Pierre Fabre, the group expanded from its initial activities in the field of pharmaceuticals to include dermo-cosmetics, investing heavily in research and development - as it continues to do today - particularly in the fields of oncology and dermatology. Upon his death in 2013, Pierre Fabre finalised the donation of his majority stake to the Pierre Fabre Foundation, which he had created. The foundation, recognised by the French government, works to improve access to essential medicines and doctors, particularly in Africa and East Asia. In Lebanon, for example, it has helped Syrian refugee populations in camps by providing them with care. Ducournau said the company is fully committed to caring for patients and its employees, as well as for the environment. Also a botanist by training, Fabre had a strong desire to respect nature, minimise his footprint, and support local communities. Pierre Fabre Laboratories invests in CSR (corporate social responsibility) initiatives and sources many of its active ingredients from plants. Today, the company operates directly in 44 countries and markets its products in all geographies. It is the world’s second-largest player in the dermo-cosmetics market and France’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical company, with an already significant presence in the Middle East. “We have grown significantly in Europe in recent years,” explained Ducournau. “Today, we are continuing our development in this region, as well as in China, Asia at large, and the United States. These regions are very important for the medicines of tomorrow.” In the Arabian Peninsula, Pierre Fabre Laboratories is renowned for its Avène brand - in sun protection and anti-ageing care - and for A-Derma in eczema care. The same is true for Ducray and René Furterer in the field of hair and scalp care, dandruff and hair loss, where the brands rank first in sales. Pierre Fabre Laboratories said it wants to forge scientific partnerships with key healthcare professionals and hospitals in the region to understand the needs of patients here and offer dermo-cosmetic care addressing their specific skin issues. It is also committed to supporting research in oncology and dermatology and wants to support clinical programmes in these areas with innovative partners. “To establish our brands, we seek to build long-term relationships with dermatologists and dermatology clinics, in particular by showing them how these formulas are formulated to be highly tolerable and clinically proven through clinical trials,” said Ducournau. He also confirmed digital technology as another priority area for investment. “We need to develop the online presence of our products and brands,” Ducournau continued. “To do this, we need to recruit talent with real digital and international expertise. “Dubai is an international city with a mix of different cultures. This is a real strength when we want to develop our presence across an entire region such as MEART. “You have a lot of people not from this area, but living in Dubai. And that creates a sort of international framework, which is very important, because we have a different culture mix here, and you want to reach very different parts of the population.” The chief executive said Pierre Fabre Laboratories plans to raise its revenue from €3.1 billion (Dh13.37 billion) in 2024 to a minimum of €5 billion (Dh21.8 billion) by 2032, ensuring a balanced split between its dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical activities. The company is investing heavily in developing new, increasingly targeted treatments for patients with cancer or rare diseases requiring targeted therapy. The same applies to dermo-cosmetic care. Ducournau said: “Each region has its own specific characteristics, whether in terms of skin types, lifestyle, or climate. “To establish ourselves, we need to understand these specific characteristics so that we can commercialise products locally that are tailored to them. “Patients in Europe or in the Middle East are not the same as those in America or Asia. So we really need to combine global scale and local grasp to do what’s right for patients, consumers and customers everywhere we operate.” While Ducournau has ruled out developing new brands locally for now, the Pierre Fabre Laboratories boss acknowledged need for localised manufacturing in the future. “Today, we are doing 71 per cent of our revenues internationally, but still manufacturing 95 per cent in France,” he said. “Tomorrow, we will have to manufacture closer to the area where the products are sold and consumed.” Ducournau highlighted that Pierre Fabre Laboratories has been present in this region since the 1980s, and its growth trajectory will continue to be deployed on the basis of the strong regional ties it has built. “I want to emphasise that we found good partners to establish our business here…we believe that this chain of distribution will extend in the region,” he said, re-confirming the Dubai hub’s role as part of the broader strategy to dramatically increase global footprint and revenues. Ducournau added: “We took 40 years to establish a certain level of revenue…and we want to double this in only six years. So, that’s the objective of this opening and this presence here.” This page was produced by The National in partnership with Pierre Fabre Laboratories.

title: Adnoc says decade-old contingency plan kept oil flowing throughout Iran war
description: Years of crisis drills built 'muscle memory' for staff when disruption hit
content: State-owned Adnoc began preparing for major disruption to energy supplies 10 to 15 years ago, building contingency plans and backup infrastructure that helped it maintain oil production throughout the Iran war. “We actually prepared for this scenario in our playbooks 10 years ago, 15 years ago,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, a board director at Adnoc and chairman of Abu Dhabi energy event Adipec, said on Thursday. Mr Al Kindy, who previously served as executive director of Adnoc's upstream directorate, said the company invested heavily in backup facilities and interconnections that allowed it to switch supply sources and delivery destinations. “[We] built projects at great expense, even though at the time they didn’t make any commercial sense,” he said. “When the time came, we actually kept the lights on.” The company's preparedness extended beyond physical infrastructure to years of emergency drills and scenario planning, giving employees “almost muscle memory” when the crisis struck, he said. Adnoc has increased its oil production capacity by almost 75 per cent over the past decade to 4.85 million barrels per day and is targeting five million bpd by 2027. Last November, Adnoc approved a Dh551 billion ($150 billion) spending plan for 2026 to 2030 to maintain operations and expand production capacity to meet rising global energy demand. Mr Al Kindy was speaking at a press conference ahead of Adipec 2026, which Adnoc will host in Abu Dhabi from November 2 to 5, as energy security takes on greater urgency following months of disruption to global oil and gas flows. “2026 has demonstrated a fundamental truth – energy security is economic stability,” he said. The event will draw its largest Asian participation yet, with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea. Organisers expect more than 239,000 visitors from at least 170 countries, with international visitors accounting for 56 per cent of the total attendance. Three quarters of the 2,250 exhibiting companies are expected to come from outside the UAE. The conference will feature more than 16,500 delegates and 1,800 speakers across 13 programmes. Rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and industrial growth is bringing “energy security, economic stability and competitiveness” closer together, said Thomas Loffler, executive vice president at organiser dmg events. Demand for exhibition space has prompted organisers to move the opening ceremony to the Abu Dhabi Energy Centre and expand the exhibition's AI and robotics zone. Confirmed speakers include Suhail Al Mazrouei, Minister of energy and Infrastructure; Katherina Reiche, Germany's Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy; Meg O'Neill, chief executive of BP; Richard Jackson, president and chief executive of Occidental Petroleum; Wael Sawan, chief executive of Shell; and Roland Busch, chief executive of Siemens. Last year's Adipec generated $53 billion in business deals across 49,131 transactions, the first time organisers tracked the value of agreements reached during the event. It also contributed $420 million to Abu Dhabi's hospitality and tourism economy, Mr Loffler said.

title: David Dastmalchian was told to change his surname to succeed in Hollywood
description: Street Fighter actor reflects on his Middle Eastern heritage, early rejections and the opportunity that brought him to the screen
content: Early in David Dastmalchian’s screen career, one Chicago casting director saw two possibilities for him: a cab driver or a terrorist. The American actor, whose father was Iranian, had been playing a much wider range of characters on stage to that point, but the auditions coming his way offered little opportunity to do the same on camera. “I remember in the beginning of my career being told, ‘You’re gonna have to change your last name,’” Dastmalchian tells The National . But despite needing the work, he resisted racial typecasting again and again. “I don’t want to do that. I want to be able to go after every role that I could possibly swing for,” he continues. Nearly two decades after his film debut, Dastmalchian has become one of Hollywood's most versatile performers. In his latest starring role, he plays M Bison in director Kitao Sakurai’s new Street Fighter adaptation . The villain joins a career spanning superhero films, science fiction and horror, all under the surname he was advised to change. Set in 1993, the film follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) for the World Warrior Tournament. Behind the competition is a conspiracy that draws them back into conflict. Dastmalchian's route into that career began with director Christopher Nolan’s The Dark Knight , released in 2008, in which he played one of the Joker’s accomplices. Casting director John Papsidera brought him in to audition for what would become his film debut. “And thank God for John Papsidera, who came into Chicago and he was casting a movie, and he was willing to see everybody,” Dastmalchian says. “And he saw me as something that other people hadn’t given me a chance to do on camera. “On the stage I always felt like I had an opportunity to swing for the fences with all different types of roles.” Even appearing in one of the biggest films of the decade did not guarantee steady work. In an interview with Backstage , Dastmalchian recalled arriving in Los Angeles without an agent or manager. Despite having The Dark Knight on his CV, he was turned down by the small agencies and management companies he approached. “It was devastatingly humbling to continue to be told, ‘No, we don’t want to work with you,’” he said. He continued auditioning for short films and music videos and attending casting workshops. Few of those auditions produced jobs, but they introduced him to people and helped him build the professional relationships on which his career would come to depend. Nolan later cast him again in Oppenheimer , while director Denis Villeneuve championed his work in the meantime, casting him in Prisoners , Blade Runner 2049 and Dune . Dastmalchian also took a leading role in the Abu Dhabi-produced runaway hit Late Night with the Devil , playing Jack Delroy, a television host whose Halloween broadcast spirals out of control. “I swim in such a giant pool of gratitude, honestly, because it was the people who were willing to see me and see the potential for what’s the human underneath, right?” he says. “That’s the story that you’re always trying to tell.” The actor recognises that nationality and ancestry can be central to how a character is written and performed. His objection, however, is to those factors limiting the roles an actor is allowed to pursue. Having found people willing to give him that freedom, he wants others to have the same opportunities. “I want everybody out there who’s an actor that feels like they want a chance to embrace the art, no matter what they look like, where they’re from, where their parents are from, what language they were raised speaking, to know that all the things we’re dealing with in acting are universal.” Street Fighter is in cinemas now across the Middle East

title: Abu Dhabi F1 Grand Prix: 'Unprecedented demand' and preparations on track with 50 days to go
description: Saif Al Noaimi, chief executive of organisers Ethara, tells The National he was always confident F1 season would finish at Yas Marina Circuit
content: Planning for the 2026 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix “never stopped for one day”, according to Saif Al Noaimi, chief executive of organisers Ethara. The F1 season finale is now 50 days away, and preparations for the race have clicked up a gear at Yas Marina Circuit. Eleven artists, including Andrea Bocelli, Lewis Capaldi and The Script, have been booked for the after-race concerts, with the final headline act set to be announced next week. Doubts were raised earlier this year when the Grands Prix in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled because of the Iran war. However, F1 president Stefano Domenicali has said they intend to finish the season as planned, with “everything confirmed for [us to stay in] Qatar and Abu Dhabi”. The season finale will take place in the UAE capital from December 3-6, and Al Noaimi spoke to The National at Yas Marina Circuit as the days tick down to the 18th Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. Q: Given some of the speculation we have seen about the race, what assurances can you give about the 2026 event? A: We are delivering the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at the same high standard we deliver every year. We are delivering a safe event, just like we do every year. We are planning and preparing ourselves just like we do every year. And from a readiness point of view, we are 100 per cent ready to deliver the Grand Prix this year. Everything is on schedule, the date has not changed. We're really excited to be hosting the season finale on December 6. Q: You are used to seeing a rise in demand every year, so how have ticket sales been this year? We are 50 days away from the Grand Prix, and if you compare where we were last year, 50 days away, we're actually ahead in terms of ticket volume and sales. So, demand is unprecedented. We are fortunate our customers know they're going to come because it's such an important event. Every year, early on, as soon as we go on sale, we see a huge spike in sales. And, you know, the last few weeks we've seen a spike in international sales also. So, interest in inbound tourism is growing, and we're starting to see that in the sales numbers. Q: Considering what happened with the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia Grands Prix, was there ever a fear that this wasn't going to go ahead? To be honest, we haven't stopped planning for the 2026 Grand Prix for one day. We've been full speed ahead since the beginning of the year. Since we delivered the Grand Prix last year, we've been completely full speed ahead. Obviously, being the last race of the season, early on in the year, we were in the planning period and the planning phase. September is when we start to see the venue transform and the build start. But this is our schedule every single year. We haven't had to make any changes to the planning and the execution. Q: Can you give a message to fans thinking about buying a ticket? Come and see Abu Dhabi, come and visit Abu Dhabi. We are seeing a huge growth in international visitations over the last few months. As you can see, everything's functioning normally over here. It's an exciting time to be here. And yeah, we're very, very happy to start welcoming the world back. Q: Are you a little bit worried that Kimi Antonelli is going to win the title before we get to Abu Dhabi? It was very fun last year … It was fun last year; we had the three-way fight. I mean, look, we can't have a three-way fight every year. But what I can assure you is these guys are going to fight till the chequered flag in Abu Dhabi, regardless of the championship. It's great to see someone young like Kimi taking that position. But also, like I said earlier, you can't write off the championship yet. You have Max Verstappen winning the last two races out of nowhere. Six different drivers have won races in 2026. So, regardless, it's still going to be an exciting race. Q: Can you talk about the enhancements the venue has undergone this year? So, we are upping the capacity for the event this year. We have unprecedented demand. We are expanding our Paddock Club (hospitality) offering. We already have the biggest Paddock Club, but we're actually increasing it to surpass 12,000 in 2026. There's a completely new Paddock Club offering that we're building on the west side also. And, you know, every year we look at additions and enhancements. We have a few new exciting products that we have launched already for 2026. And, you know, from a hospitality point of view, we have 16/360 (hospitality) expanding. We launched it last year for the first time, and we're making some additions to that product, which has been very, very popular. And then, in terms of other branded hospitality offerings, we announced our partnership with Nammos at Turn 9. And then we have a few other new branded hospitality experiences that we're launching this year. Q: Today we heard that Rashid Al Dhaheri will race in F3 next season. How long until we see him here? It's really exciting having Rashid and Keanu [Al Azhari] now both representing the UAE in the FIA Formula 3 championship. It really shows how strong our grassroots motorsports programme and our academy are. Both of them came through the Yas Heat Academy. They both raced in Formula Four UAE for Yas Heat. They're both Yas Heat ambassadors. And today they're both participating in the FIA Formula 3 World Championship. It's a huge, huge achievement for us. Huge achievement for them and for their families, who have dedicated so much over the years. And look, it's very, very promising, you know, maybe one or hopefully both of them could be in Formula One in as little as two years. So we're excited to see that. Congratulations to them.

title: Abu Dhabi shuts down cafe over repeated food safety violations
description: Business will remain closed until food safety issues resolved
content: An Abu Dhabi cafe has been temporarily shut down for repeated food safety violations that posed a public health risk . Let's Talk Riz Corner Cafe's licence was suspended by the emirate's food regulator after it failed to take effective corrective action over the issues. The Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority said it had intervened immediately to protect food safety and consumer health. The closure will continue until the outlet addresses the violations and receives approval to resume trading, the authority added. The closure is part of the authority's work to strengthen Abu Dhabi's food safety system. Food regulators regularly inspect cafes , restaurants and products to ensure compliance with safety standards. The authority urged residents to report any violations they notice in cafes, restaurants or grocery stores, including suspected food contamination, by calling the Abu Dhabi Government’s toll-free number 800555.

title: Gulf-EU summit in Riyadh postponed amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
description: Brussels 'remains committed' to relationship with new date to be announced in due course
content: A summit of Gulf and EU leaders planned for next week in Riyadh has been postponed. Jasem Al Budaiwi, Secretary General of the Gulf Co-operation Council, said on Thursday that attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels in Yemen, and the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport, meant the meeting would be rescheduled. Mr Al Budaiwi said the decision was taken to ensure the safety of participating delegations amid continued threats to civilians. The meeting "will be rescheduled to a later date to be agreed upon in due course by the GCC and EU sides", he said. In a separate statement, the European Council said it remained committed to "deepening this partnership." Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman , who travelled to Brussels for the first GCC-EU summit in late 2024, was scheduled to co-host the summit with European Council President Antonio Costa, in the presence of the EU's 27 leaders. This would have been the second time that the leaders gathered in this format, designed to boost ties between the two regions. Houthi missile strikes have also damaged the kingdom's energy and maritime infrastructure. Speaking earlier in the day, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he expected the postponement of the summit "maybe for security reasons". "We highly appreciate the dialogue between the EU and the Gulf countries, especially Saudi Arabia," he said. Mr Radev said his country was pushing to develop a railway corridor to export Saudi oil through Syria, Turkey, Bulgaria and onwards to Europe, to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, currently under an Iranian blockade. "I believe that this new route will find a place in our discussions and solutions and decisions within the European Union," he said. Gulf states had hoped that the summit would pave the way for the harmonisation of Schengen visa waivers. There are different rules depending on states, with the UAE benefiting from an exemption, while citizens from Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman are granted five-year multiple entry visas. EU states have strengthened their relationship with the Gulf since the start of the Iran war, portraying themselves as a reliable ally. Countries like France and Italy have sent air defence systems to the UAE and more recently to Saudi Arabia.

title: Three dead in Istanbul as torrential rain floods Turkish city
description: Residents told to stay at home as record rainfall 'turns roads into lakes'
content: Torrential rainfall has killed three people and caused chaos across Istanbul, as the Turkish city recorded its highest rainfall in more than 80 years. Istanbul Governor Davut Gul instructed the city’s 16 million residents to stay at home unless outings were absolutely necessary, closed schools and banned motorbikes as 8,000 emergency service workers were sent out to deal with the effects of days of downpours. “Rainfall in Istanbul will continue for another two to three days. Do not go outside unless absolutely necessary,” Mr Gul told a press conference on Thursday morning. He said it was “the highest level of precipitation recorded in Istanbul since 1942”, when records began. About 3,000 people were rescued from flooded areas, he said. Many areas of the city had received more than 100kg of rain per square metre, equivalent to 100mm, since early on Wednesday, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said. Rainfall in the Beykoz area of north-eastern Istanbul had reached 242kg per square metre, the authority said. An investigation has been launched following the death of a 14-year-old boy who died from electrocution after he stepped into a puddle in the Fatih district, the Istanbul governorship said. He was taken to hospital unconscious but could not be saved, the statement added. A 34-year-old died after slipping and hitting their head on a pavement, and authorities are trying to identify the body of a man found near the banks of the Kagithane Creek, according to the governor’s office. Footage published by state media showed cars drifting down streets, flooded homes and mosques, and passengers trapped in a bus with dirty flood water up to their knees. “Roads turned into lakes in many parts of the city,” state broadcaster TRT reported. At Istanbul Airport, 51 flights were diverted to alternative airports and another 19 flights were cancelled, Mr Gul said. The unusually heavy rain began on Tuesday and continued into Wednesday. Streets began to flood as drainage systems were overwhelmed. Istanbul residents received text messages from disaster management services on Wednesday evening warning them to stay away from riverbanks and flooded roads. Residents of basement apartments were told they “should take precautions”, while power cuts halted water supplies to homes and businesses in parts of the city, despite the torrential rain falling outside. Emergency services received more than 1,200 reports of flooding, 15 of landslides, 47 of people trapped and two of roofs blown off, the governorship said. Heavy flooding also made streets impassable in the city of Antalya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The state meteorological service issued warnings for more heavy rain and wind across the country on Thursday. Turkey has been experiencing an unusually wet 2026, the service said in a climate report released in September. Rainfall between January and August was 54 per cent higher than the 30-year average between 1991 and 2020. A third of the extreme weather events in the first eight months of the year were heavy rainfall and flooding.

title: Hormuz matters but UAE has more than one gateway, economy minister says
description: Country's tourism also set for a rebound, Abdulla bin Touq tells The National
content: The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism. “ Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai . “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.” It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years. Before the Iran war , roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28. But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said. The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains. It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah , outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman. If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said. Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added. However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy. With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”. In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity. The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict. With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year. The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”. The International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted. The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.” For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital. On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”. As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

title: Sharjah Police arrest 33 in crackdown on $2.4bn global money-laundering scheme
description: Suspects accused of being part of gang network involved in cyber fraud and violent crime
content: Sharjah Police have arrested 33 people from 12 countries accused of cyber fraud , digital wallet theft, money laundering and violent assault. Police said they were members of an organised criminal network who targeted individuals and companies through cyber attacks, stolen data, cryptocurrency transactions and physical intimidation. The arrests were the result of an international operation and carried out in the UAE and abroad. The suspects are accused of operating as four separate gangs, each specialising in one area. The first group carried out cyber attacks and stole customer information and databases, police said. The second gang specialised in laundering money through virtual assets and other financial channels, and the third used social engineering to manipulate victims and steal digital wallets. Members of the fourth group are accused of violent assaults, allegedly targeting victims to force them to disclose passcodes to their digital wallets. Lt Gen Abdullah Mubarak bin Amer, commander-in-chief of Sharjah Police, told a press conference on Thursday that more than 30 companies and institutions were targeted by the criminal network, with the operation securing the assets of companies worth Dh65 billion. More than Dh200 million in cash was seized, with about 3,000 digital wallets audited and verified. “What distinguished this gang was that it did not rely on a single type of criminal activity,” he said. The Sharjah Police Digital Crime Combat Department “uncovered the highly complex and concealed infrastructure of the organisation, whose members had made the deepest reaches of cyberspace a home for their activities”, he said. The suspects are accused of hiding their activities behind sophisticated layers of encryption, moving through closed networks. In public, they “cultivated an image of wealth, travelling between world capitals and displaying a lavish lifestyle that concealed a framework managed secretly, and they appeared to be legitimate businesspeople and investors, while their illegal activities extended across countries”. Sharjah Police said initial inquiries alerted them to one suspect in particular, a 15-year-old boy. “We traced the networks and their locations until we reached the teenager,” said Brig Dr Khalifa Balhai, director of Sharjah CID. “He had a digital wallet with huge amount of cryptocurrency. We traced all the suspects through the teenager.” It was discovered the gang had set up a group on social media, which was locked by a code that changed every eight hours. “What has been achieved in this case is the result of integrated institutional work, continued security efforts, and close co-operation and co-ordination with federal, local and international authorities,” Lt Gen bin Amer said. “These efforts led to the dismantling of these networks and groups, the arrest of their members and the thwarting of their plans. “This confirms the efficiency of the UAE's national security system and its ability to handle various cases, regardless of their complexity or whether they extend beyond its geographical borders, and to keep pace with security challenges efficiently and competently.” The security operation, called End of Battle, has also served to protect interests and assets, he added. Anwar Al Harmoudi, Attorney General of Sharjah, said the investigation “revealed a cross-border criminal organisation with integrated criminal roles, beginning with seizing victims’ funds through fraud and hacking”. The suspects are accused of converting stolen assets into property and other investments to give the appearance of legitimacy.

title: New Dubai footbridge and Sharjah buses to improve access to Etihad Rail stations
description: A 400-metre bridge connects Jumeirah Golf Estates Metro station and Dubai Al Yalayis rail station
content: New transport links in Dubai and Sharjah are making it easier to reach Etihad Rail stations, with a pedestrian footbridge opening in Dubai on Thursday and three connecting bus routes launching in Sharjah. Passengers can now switch more smoothly between Metro and train services in Dubai using the new footbridge linking Jumeirah Golf Estates station with Etihad Rail’s Al Yalayis Station . Before the elevated 400-metre footbridge opened, a shuttle bus operated between the stations. Passengers can use a Nol One-Day Pass ticket, which offers unlimited travel on the emirate's public transport network and is valid until midnight. Using digital QR codes on phones eliminates the need for a single-use red paper Nol ticket. In the coming years, Dubai Al Yalayis Station will become a transport super-hub with an interchange between the Metro Red and Gold lines planned for 2032. The station opened to passengers on September 30 for the first rail service to Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Fujairah. Due to increased demand, extra services were added on some weekends. Variable pricing has been introduced on several routes due to demand, with some tickets increasing by up to Dh69. The F38 bus also serves Dubai's rail station, operating a circular route to Dubai Sports City and Dubai Production City. Sharjah 's Road and Transport Authority on Wednesday announced three new bus routes connecting Sharjah's first rail station in Al Dhaid. ER1 connects Al Madam Bus Station to Al Dhaid Station, stopping in Mleiha and Al Dhaid and taking one hour. ER2 connects Al Sajaa Bus Station with Al Dhaid Station, stopping in Al Batayeh and Al Dhaid, and takes about 43 minutes. ER3 links Jubail Bus Station in Sharjah city with the rail station on a non-stop service, taking about one hour and 42 minutes. These services are vital for connecting some of the smaller towns in Sharjah emirate that previously had limited public transport connectivity to other emirates. Bus journeys are timed to train arrivals and departures, and you can buy tickets with cash or a Sayer Card.

title: Nissan Patrol marks 75 years with limited-edition model exclusively for Gulf
description: Model is limited to initial run of 1,951 vehicles
content: Nissan has announced a limited-edition Patrol to mark the SUV’s 75th anniversary, with an initial production run of 1,951 vehicles exclusively for the GCC region. The number marks the nameplate's debut in 1951.
