Based on the flagship Platinum V6 Twin Turbo grade, the anniversary edition features copper-gold exterior accents, a Bordeaux red interior and special anniversary detailing. AWR Automotive, Nissan’s dealer in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, introduced the model on Thursday. It costs Dh439,900 ($119,780) including VAT. Nissan says its bespoke copper-gold finish is inspired by desert landscapes. The detailing appears across the grille bars, fog lamp surrounds, fender vents, shoulder line and emblems, paired with dark chrome finishes and black alloy wheels. Anniversary signatures feature on the front grille, shoulder-line graphic and rear emblem. An illuminated carpet light projects a “Patrol Since 1951” graphic and a sand-dune motif. Nissan lists five exterior colours for the Gulf edition, while AWR Automotive has confirmed four options for its customers: grey, white, black and two-tone white with a black roof. Inside, the cabin features copper-gold steering wheel detailing and ambient lighting alongside dark chrome trim. Anniversary detailing appears on the passenger-side dashboard, seat headrests and floor and luggage mats. Other additions include illuminated anniversary kick plates and a deep red leather key fob case. Thierry Sabbagh, Nissan and Infiniti’s divisional vice president and president for the Middle East, Saudi Arabia, India and CIS, said: “To mark 75 years of the Patrol, we wanted to deliver something lasting for our customers, a special product that serves as a memorable token of our shared history.” The anniversary edition keeps the Platinum V6 Twin Turbo’s 3.5-litre twin-turbocharged engine, which delivers 425hp and 700Nm of torque. It is paired with a nine-speed automatic transmission and adaptive air suspension with Intelligent Dynamic Damping. The cabin includes a 28.6-inch Monolith display, a Klipsch audio system and quilted leather seats with heating, ventilation and massage functions. The model also features Biometric Cooling, ProPILOT driver assistance and advanced visibility systems. In the UAE and Saudi Arabia, NissanConnect 2.0 with Google built-in provides navigation , voice assistant functions and connected car services. The anniversary edition joins a regional Patrol range that includes the Platinum, PRO-4X and Nismo. AWR Automotive says the model is available through its Nissan showrooms in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, and can also be viewed at its City Walk location in Dubai.

title: Iran may not order every Houthi attack, but backing Yemen's rebels carries consequences
description: The immediate question is how the militia has been able to threaten airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links
content: Attacks by Yemen 's Houthi rebels on Riyadh 's international airport and Saudi Aramco have exposed the strategic threat posed by a militia whose growing missile and drone capabilities have become a key part of Tehran's regional reach. The attacks have brought the war in Yemen directly into Saudi Arabia's capital and its oil-producing heartland, raising the stakes for the world's largest oil exporter and testing its ability to protect critical infrastructure. A weekend attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said. A further strike on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. On Tuesday, an attack targeted an administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran, causing a fire but no reported casualties. Debris from intercepted missiles injured four people in Riyadh. The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi targets and threatened further strikes after Saudi-led coalition forces bombed an oil facility in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa . These latest exchanges mark a sharp escalation in a conflict that had increasingly become intertwined with the wider confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the US. The immediate question is how the Houthis have acquired the capability to threaten major airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links across Saudi Arabia. UN investigators and American military assessments have documented extensive links between Iranian military technology and Houthi weapons systems. A February 2024 report by the US Defence Intelligence Agency identified similarities between Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones. UN experts have also investigated foreign weapons supplies, technical assistance, training and procurement networks supporting the organisation. Such evidence does not establish that Tehran ordered every attack. But it makes Iran's role in strengthening the Houthis' military capabilities central to understanding the threat now facing Saudi Arabia. The militia has its own political leadership and domestic objectives. It emerged from Yemen's internal conflicts and seized Sanaa in 2014, before the Saudi-led military intervention began in 2015. Its independence in decision-making, however, does not negate the strategic importance of external assistance. For Iran, the Houthis offer a partner positioned near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a vital shipping corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Their ability to threaten Saudi infrastructure and disrupt maritime traffic gives Tehran an additional source of pressure on regional adversaries without requiring publicly demonstrable Iranian command over every operation. The attacks also carry consequences beyond the immediate damage. Disruption to Saudi aviation, heightened risks to oil facilities and uncertainty over regional security threaten not only the kingdom's efforts to establish Riyadh as a centre for international business but also the global economy that relies on Saudi oil flows. It also threatens the millions of Muslim pilgrims who go to Saudi Arabia as a key tenet of Islam. Saudi Arabia has responded with further strikes on Houthi-held targets in Yemen, including fuel infrastructure in Sanaa, increasing the danger of a wider cycle of retaliation. Tehran has repeatedly rejected the characterisation of the Houthis as a proxy force, despite evidence to the contrary, and it repeats rhetoric that Yemen's crisis requires a political settlement. But the latest attacks sharpen the question of whether Iran is prepared to use its influence to restrain an ally whose military operations have direct consequences for Gulf security. The issue is no longer simply whether the Houthis take orders from Tehran. It is how Iranian assistance has helped build a military capability that can threaten Saudi Arabia's most important economic and transport assets – and whether diplomacy can prevent that capability from driving a wider regional conflict.

title: At least 34 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse
description: Authorities launch investigation after roof collapses on to classrooms, causing both storeys to cave in
content: At least 34 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said. Most of the students killed were under 13 years old, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department. At least ​45 people ⁠suffered major and minor injuries, ‌he added. Rescue workers spent hours pulling children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of ⁠their loved ones. The incident took place at 8.48am local time, and the rescue operation lasted four to five hours, Mr Khattak said. Victims of the collapse were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesman Mohammad Asim. “The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher,” Mr Asim said. Three children remained in critical condition, with head injuries, he said. Most of the injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home. A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor had collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in. Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said excessive weight from construction on the school roof had caused the collapse. “It was a weak building structure,” he ​said. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, ‌which caused the collapse.” Mr Saeed said ⁠the school's owner had been arrested ​and authorities had opened an investigation. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in. Distraught relatives accused the ​school of ‌ignoring safety concerns about the building's condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson ⁠for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make ⁠money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif promised “a thorough investigation” into the incident. “My heart is with the families grieving the loss of their children and a teacher in the tragic roof collapse at a school in Peshawar. No parent should have to endure such pain,” he wrote in a statement on X. “I extend my deepest condolences and pray for strength for every family affected. I have directed that the injured receive the best possible care. We will ensure a thorough investigation into this tragedy and take every necessary step to protect the safety of children in schools across the country,” he added. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse. “In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the President’s office posted on X.

title: Aldar enters Sharjah with Dh1.1bn residential acquisition
description: Abu Dhabi developer will acquire nine residential buildings in Aljada development as part of deal
content: Aldar , Abu Dhabi ’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio. The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion. Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community. “Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio. The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi- Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island. Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria. Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE . The new project, with an undisclosed value, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London this week. The move comes as the UAE property market continues to perform strongly despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. The Emirates was ranked as the world’s leading real estate investment destination in a property market league table released in June. Arada’s UAE Property Investment Index – conducted on behalf of the Dubai developer by US-based Penta Group – found that 56 per cent of global investors have serious interest in the UAE’s property market. The latest acquisition will broaden Aldar’s geographic exposure while adding residential rental assets aimed primarily at end users and long-term tenants seeking housing at accessible price points, the company said. Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said Aldar’s decision to make its first investment in Sharjah at Aljada reflected confidence in both the development and the emirate’s residential market. “To have a developer of Aldar’s calibre and track record choose Aljada as its first investment in the emirate reflects the quality of what we have built here, and the scale of the opportunity that Sharjah represents,” he said. Aljada spans 2.2 million sq m and is expected to comprise about 25,000 homes at full buildout, with an anticipated gross sales value of Dh35 billion. Residential handovers at the development began in 2021, with more than 8,800 homes delivered across multiple districts, according to the statement. The community also includes schools, hotels, student accommodation, retail space and the Madar family entertainment district. Aldar said the acquisition adds to its strategy of expanding its portfolio of income-generating properties, as the developer seeks to diversify its revenue streams. The Abu Dhabi developer, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, is expected to hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company’s launch, with the deliveries going up to 4,500 next year, according to Mr Emery.

title: Abu Dhabi revokes doctor's licence for violating controlled medication rules
description: Second doctor's licence suspended after breaches including missing medical records
content: Abu Dhabi health authorities have revoked a doctor's licence and suspended another's over violations of controlled medication rules. The breaches included incomplete clinical assessments, a lack of proper follow-up care and missing medical records, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi found. In some cases, the two doctors failed to record the medical reasons for prescribing controlled medications. The health department said it took the action to protect patients and ensure doctors followed medical rules and professional standards. The violations were identified through routine inspections, digital monitoring and co-ordination with other authorities. The health department said it would continue monitoring healthcare facilities and carry out inspections to identify violations and ensure compliance with the rules. Controlled medications are subject to strict regulations because they carry a risk of misuse or dependence. They typically include strong painkillers such as morphine and fentanyl, medicines used to treat anxiety and sleep problems, and drugs that affect mood and behaviour. They also include certain medications for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Only licensed doctors are allowed to prescribe controlled drugs in the UAE and should provide documentation to prove the need for a patient. The medicines have to be administered by a registered nurse. Healthcare facilities must comply with all regulations, laws and policies related to narcotics, controlled and semi-controlled drugs. Storing, distributing, dispensing, administering or handling narcotics, controlled or semi-controlled drugs without approval from the Ministry of Health and Prevention and Dubai Healthcare City Authority-Regulatory is prohibited.

title: Love Is Blind on Netflix: Every international edition ranked as US season 11 arrives
description: Reality show that made its debut in 2020 has spawned 13 international spin-offs
content: Is love really blind? Since 2020, couples around the world have been trying to prove as much – mostly unsuccessfully – in Netflix's hugely popular reality show Love is Blind . Following its debut, set in the US, the show has spawned 13 international versions, including Love is Blind: Habibi , the Arabic spin-off that premiered in October 2024. A second season is coming later in the year. The format is similar across all. A group of single men and women looking for love are introduced to each other through “pods”, where they can interact but not see the other person. Once participants have chosen their prospective partners, the couple meet for the first time and become engaged. They are then flown to a luxury resort where they spend time and get to know each other better. In the final stage of the experiment, the couples who are still together go back to their respective lives where they meet each other's families and friends, and are given 10 days to prepare for their wedding. From Brazil to the UK and Japan, each edition of Love is Blind has proved to be a hit, turning some of its cast members into overnight celebrities. Love is Blind: Habibi , for instance, was viewed more than 1.3 million times in the first seven days after its debut. It also ranked No 8 globally among Netflix's non-English shows. With Love is Blind: South Africa set to debut later this year, here are all the editions so far ranked by fan ratings on IMDb. Watch out for spoilers from reunion episodes Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.4/10 Viewership in first week: 1.3 million Hosts: Khaled Saqer and Elham Ali The Arabic version of Love is Blind became a massive hit, dominating social media chats and debates for weeks after its premiere in October 2024. Featuring 20 singles – 10 women and 10 men – from across the Arab world and North Africa who are all residents of the UAE, the series was filmed in Lebanon, Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Six couples progressed to the next stage and were flown to a luxury resort in Lebanon, where their relationship was further tested. Eventually, out of two couples who made it to the wedding day, only one – Safa and Mohammed – exchanged vows. Speaking to The National a few weeks after its debut, cast members shared how their lives had changed thanks to the popularity of the show. “This experience didn’t just transform me, it shaped me into a person I never imagined I could be,” Mohammed said. “It opened up a whole new world and revealed aspects of myself I hadn’t recognised before. Beyond discovering ‘the one’, I found myself.” Season two will have celebrity couple Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi taking over hosting roles. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.4/10 Viewership in first week: 1.2 million Hosts: Omar and Lucy Chaparro One of the most dramatic editions, Love is Blind: Mexico debuted in August 2024. Of the nine women and nine men taking part, six couples progressed to the next stage and only one couple, Karen and Fernando, made it to the altar. In the reunion episode, which aired three weeks later, the couple confirmed they were still together and had even started a business. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.5/10 Viewership in first week: Data unavailable Hosts: Dario Barassi and Wanda Nara Launching in November 2024, Love is Blind: Argentina featured two couples getting married. In a break from format, Florencia Fernandez and Jose Luis Farina, who did not get engaged during the pods segment, returned to the show as a couple during the honeymoon phase. They are also the couple who have managed to stay married, a fact revealed in the reunion episode. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.6/10 Viewership in first week: 1.3 million Hosts: Steffi and Chris Wackert-Brungs Hosted by German TV presenter Stephanie “Steffi” Brungs and her husband, the show had its premiere in January last year with 30 singles. Only one couple, Alina and Ilias, have remained married. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 5.9/10 Viewership in first week: 1.7 million Hosts: Nicolette van Dam and Bas Smit Dutch celebrity couple van Dam and Smit shepherd 30 single men and women in search of love in this spin-off, with only one couple, Mika and Jurriaan, tying the knot in the final episode aired on October 14. Number of seasons: 4 IMDb rating: 6.2/10 Viewership in first week: 2.1 million (season four) Hosts: Camila Queiroz and Klebber Toledo The first country to get its own version, Love is Blind: Brazil debuted in October 2021, with production for season five in progress. Hosted by celebrity couple Camila Queiroz and Klebber Toledo, this spin-off is as dramatic as reality shows can get. In season one, for example, there was a massive twist in the fairy tale: Nanda – who originally chose Thiago over Mackdavid – revealed in the reunion episode that she and Thiago had separated and that she had got back with Mackdavid. Nanda and Mackdavid welcomed baby Ben in 2022. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 6.2/10 Viewership in first week: 1.3 million Hosts: Teddy Riner and Luthna Plocus Debuting in September last year, the first season of the show's French version featured 15 men and 15 women. It was hosted by French Judo champion Riner and his wife Plocus, and filmed in Tangier, Morocco. Of the six couples who made it to the next round, Jonathan and Cynthia, called it quits following several arguments. The remaining decamped to Paris to test how well they mesh in everyday life, after which another couple, Yannick and Tatiana, decided to end their relationship, leaving four couples to plan their wedding. On the big day, two Alexandre and Chloe, and Charles and Julie eventually said “I do”. But the reunion episode, which aired in October, revealed none of the couples have remained together. Number of seasons: 11 IMDb rating: 6.2/10 Viewership in first week: 2.5 million (season ten) Hosts: Nick and Vanessa Lachey All seasons of the original US series have been hosted by celebrity couple Nick and Vanessa Lachey. The latest, season 11, premiered on October 14 and is set in Boston, where six couples have found potential partners. However, episode five ends on a cliffhanger, as Jax and Stew, whose first face-to-face meeting did not go particularly well, agree to meet again to talk things through. The next batch of season eleven episodes will stream on October 21. The show has won Critics' Choice Real TV Awards, which recognise achievements in non-scripted shows, three times – in 2020, 2022 and 2023. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 6.3/10 Viewership in the first week : 1.3 million Hosts: Benedetta Parodi and Fabio Caressa The Italian version of the show had its premiere on December 1 last year, featuring 12 men and 12 women. Hosted by journalist couple, Parodi and Caressa, the show revealed only two couples made it to the altar. Fan sites have noted that both couples – Karen Norman and Nicola Botticini, and Hyoni Song and Alessandro Bianchin – have remained together. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 6.3/10 Viewership in first week: Data unavailable Hosts : Zofia Zborowska-Wrona and Andrzej Wrona Poland's version had its premiere on May 6, 2026, with 30 singles looking to meet their ultimate partners. Hosted by actress Zofia Zborowska-Wrona and her husband, volley ball star Andrzej Wrona, five couples made it to the next stage, with three of them failing to say I do. Two couples – Marta and Damian as well as Daria and Filip – said “I do” and were still married when the cast members reunited to share their relationship statuses in an episode that aired on May 24, 2026. Number of seasons: 2 IMDb rating: 6.5/10 Viewership in first week: 1.7 million (season one) Host: Jessica Almenas Sweden's version had its premiere in January 2024, with five couples moving to the next stage of the relationship. Three couples celebrated their wedding, out of which Krisse-Ly and Rasmus recently revealed the former is pregnant. Amanda and Sergio's first child, a boy named Ralph, was born in May last year. The second season, which had its debut in March, had three couples eventually exchanging vows, of which Karin and Niklas announced they were expecting their first child in the reunion episode. Number of seasons: 2 IMDb rating: 6.9/10 Viewership in first week: 3.6 million (season one) and 2.6 million (season two) Hosts: Matt and Emma Willis Matt Willis, co-founder of English pop-punk band Busted, hosts this show with his wife, broadcaster Emma Willis. Debuting on August 7 2024, the show featured seven couples who found their prospective partners. Out of these, three made it to the altar. The reunion episode revealed Steven and Sabrina have called it quits after saying “I do”, leaving just two couples who successfully found love – Benaiah and Nicole, and Bobby and Jasmine. Season two debuted on August 13 last year with five couples moving on to the next stage. While this season received lower buzz and viewership than the first, the UK version of the reality show is still one of the most popular globally. Five couples met their match, but three made it to the altar – Billy and Ashleigh, Kieran and Megan, and Kal and Sarover. Of the three, only Kieran and Megan have remained together. Number of seasons: 1 IMDb rating: 7.0/10 Viewership in first week: Data unavailable Hosts: Takashi Fujii and Yuka Itaya The second spin-off after Brazil, Love is Blind: Japan had its premiere in February 2022 and featured eight couples who found their potential true loves. Six couples separated before their wedding day, leaving Wataru Mizote and Midori, as well as fan-favourites Ryotaro and Motomi, to get hitched. The couples are still married with both pairs now becoming parents. A second season was announced in March, but later cancelled.

title: Emirati racer Rashid Al Dhaheri takes major step towards F1 dream with Formula 3 move
description: UAE will be represented on F3 grid for first time with two drivers landing contracts for 2027
content: Rashid Al Dhaheri will compete in FIA Formula 3 in 2027 after signing with Van Amersfoort Racing. The Dutch team announced a deal with the 18-year-old Emirati on Thursday in a move that will see him step up in class after finishing fourth in this year’s Formula Regional European Championship. “I’m very proud to be taking the next step into FIA Formula 3 with Van Amersfoort Racing,” said Al Dhareri, a member of the Mercedes Junior Driver Programme since March 2025. “It is an important milestone in my journey, but I know the hard work is only beginning. I’m proud to represent the UAE and the wider region at this level, and I’m looking forward to learning, improving and giving everything I have on and off the track. “Every step has to be earned, and my focus now is on preparing as strongly as possible for 2027. I’m grateful to everyone who has supported me and helped make this opportunity possible.” The move means that the UAE will have two drivers on the grid next season after it was also announced that Keanu Al Azhari had signed for Hitech. No Emirati has previously competed in F3. Brad Joyce, team principal for Van Amersfoort Racing, added: “We’re looking forward to welcome Rashid to [the team]. He has had a very strong season in Formula Regional, with three wins and eight podiums, finishing in fourth place in the championship. “He has shown his pace throughout the year and has been able to fight at the front of a very competitive field. That gives us a good starting point as he steps up to Formula 3. We’re looking forward to working with him during the post season tests and preparing for his first F3 season together.” Al Dhaheri's journey in motorsport began at the age of three, and he quickly rose through the ranks, winning the WSK Super Master Series and the South Garda Winter Cup in the 60 Mini category. In 2023, he made his single-seater debut with Prema Racing in the Italian F4 Championship, finishing 10th overall and taking P3 at Macau. He continued to impress in 2024, competing in the Formula 4 UAE Championship and the Euro 4 Championship. In March 2025, it was announced that Al Dhaheri had joined Mercedes as part of their Junior Driver Programme, becoming the first Middle East driver to be selected for their F1 development initiative. He described the move as “a dream come true” as he took the next step towards his ultimate goal of becoming the first driver to represent the UAE in F1. George Russell, who has raced for Mercedes in F1 since 2019, is also a graduate of the programme. Al Dhaheri has just finished the FIA Formula Regional European Championship campaign with a podium finish at Hockenheim, ending the weekend fourth in the overall standings, 38 points behind title winner Emanuele Olivieri of Italy. It caps an impressive season for the teenager who claimed three victories, eight podiums, one pole position and a fastest lap. Driving for French team R-ace GP, Al Dhaheri recorded victories at the Red Bull Ring, Monza and Hungaroring across the eight-round championship. He became the first Emirati to lead the standings and sat 21 points clear at the halfway stage and, despite some challenging weekends later in the season, arrived at the Hockenheim finale as one of four drivers still able to win the title.

title: Saudi coalition hits back at Houthis with strikes on 120 mountain depots in Yemen
description: Alliance responds to Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport that have killed 17 people and injured hundreds
author_name: Amr  Mostafa, Mina Aldroubi, Nada AlTaher
content: A Saudi-led coalition has hit back at the Houthi rebels with strikes on more than 120 mountain depots in Yemen , it revealed on Thursday. The strikes came in response to a wave of Houthi attacks on Riyadh, where King Khalid International Airport has been attacked 20 times with missiles and drones, the coalition said. Inside Yemen, the government's headquarters in Aden came under attack by Houthi missiles on Thursday, with some security personnel killed. Fears were growing for the population of Taiz, with that city encircled by the Houthis. Attacks on Riyadh's airport have killed 17 people and injured 333 others, the coalition said. It said Houthi attacks on Abha airport, in south-western Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, had killed three people and wounded 28. UAE leaders, including President Sheikh Mohamed , have sent condolences to Saudi Arabia's King Salman. A summit of Gulf and EU leaders planned for next week in Riyadh has been postponed, as has a $5 million Saudi golf tournament. The airport attacks were part of a wider campaign against Saudi civilian facilities such as airports, ports and oil facilities, said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. Maj Gen Al Malki said 127 mountain storage facilities used by the Iran-aligned Houthis, as well as several launch platforms, had been destroyed in recent days. The announcement came as a Yemeni government minister vowed to continue the fight against the Houthis. Mustafa Al Noman, Yemen's Deputy Foreign Minister, told The National that the government had no option but to “go all the way” with the battle. “If the government stops at this point, that'll be a disaster for the population and give the Houthis a much higher hand in the situation. It will be a disaster,” he said. Mr Al Noman said there was no hope of a political process with the Houthis. “The only solution is a military solution because the Houthis have not left an option for the government to adhere to,” he said. Riyadh has come under heavy fire as Yemen's heaviest fighting in years has spilt over into Saudi Arabia. Four attacks have caused fatalities at King Khalid Airport, with the deadliest on Saturday killing 12 people and injuring 309 others, according to the coalition's toll. Maj Gen Al Malki condemned what he called “cowardly terrorist acts” by the Houthis against civilians. The airport attack, which took place during peak hours, threatened the safety of Saudi citizens, visitors and travellers of other nationalities, including pilgrims visiting Makkah and Madinah, he said. He said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with assistance from outside, allowing them to use ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and explosives-laden speedboats. The coalition said it would continue operations to deter Houthi attacks. “We reaffirm our support for Yemen’s legitimate government and armed forces on all fronts, and our commitment to providing air support to units on the ground around the clock,” Maj Gen Al Malki said. “As a final message, the terrorist Houthi militia must stop its attacks on civilians in the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. It must read the coalition’s statement carefully and read between the lines,” he added. In response, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that his group had the right to act until Saudi Arabia ended what he described as its aggression and blockade against Yemen. Mr Saree accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out more than 274,000 air strikes over the past 12 years, allegedly including more than 2,350 during the current escalation. “Anyone who attacks our country should not expect us to salute him,” he said. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in ⁠support of the government in 2015, fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring ⁠sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace in place until this year. Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept along the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab Al Mandeb strait. The EU has urged the Iran-backed Houthi rebels to lift their siege of Taiz, as the Yemeni government appealed to the UN for urgent action to avert a humanitarian catastrophe. Taiz, in south-western Yemen, is controlled by government troops but has long been attacked by the Houthis and remains the main front line in the civil war. In recent weeks, fighting between the rebels and government forces has intensified and the rebels have encircled the area. The EU called on the Houthis to allow desperately needed food, water, medicine and fuel to enter the city . It stressed that civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected and humanitarian partners must be permitted to deliver essential aid. On Wednesday, the Yemeni government sent a letter from Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba to senior UN and humanitarian officials, outlining a sharp deterioration in conditions in Taiz governorate amid a new Houthi escalation. Ms Al Zouba warned that the tightening of the siege on Taiz and surrounding villages could trigger a humanitarian disaster affecting more than four million people. They include residents trapped inside the city and displaced families in districts such as Al Shamayatayn, Al Mawasit and Jabal Habashi. The government urged the UN to apply direct pressure on the Houthis to lift the blockade immediately, reopen all access routes for civilians and supply chains, and ensure sustained, unhindered delivery of food, fuel and drinking water. It also called for stronger monitoring and documentation of violations to preserve evidence, hold perpetrators accountable and prevent impunity. Humanitarian agencies have voiced concern over low food and medical supplies, as well as hospitals' ability to care for thousands of injured people. Wheat flour stocks in the city are nearly exhausted, ‌the UN World Food Programme said. The WFP said remaining food supplies may not last long if access constraints ​continue. At least 600,000 people in Taiz depend on aid, including more than 200,000 children. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said front-line hospitals in areas such as Marib, Taiz and Yemen's ​Red Sea coast ‌are taking in unprecedented numbers of patients wounded by weapons, with some admitting more than 700 casualties in one week. More ⁠than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting began in ⁠recent weeks, the UN's International Organisation for Migration said. “Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” said Feras Abusamra, ICRC health co-ordinator. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health centres can provide comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people and shortages of ​surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicine. The siege of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has been in place since 2015 and has long been a severe humanitarian flashpoint, with aid agencies warning that shortages of basic goods and medical supplies are pushing civilians towards crisis conditions.

title: AI is changing us as humans, says pioneering Arab scientist
description: Fadel Adib, who won UAE's Great Arab Minds award, further sees powers outside the US and China getting in on the AI race
content: AI will help humans operate at a "higher intellectual level", even if that means ditching some of the life skills we once had, a leading Arab scientist has said. Fadel Adib, an MIT professor and successful AI start-up founder, said it was not necessarily bad that people are coming to rely on large language models such as ChatGPT. "We first augment humans and increase their productivity, and then eventually we also augment humans with robots, not just with AI ... increase productivity there as well. AI is changing who we are as humans," he told The National at a World Economic Forum event in Dubai. His company, Cartesian, uses AI technology to help robots navigate hundreds of warehouses and retail stores in 15 countries, tracking and collecting thousands of different products. "Some of us cannot operate without asking ChatGPT the question, and that might not necessarily be bad," he said at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which he co-chaired. "I'm a professor. So I remember when people used to say 'oh, students are not memorising anymore in schools, and we're losing the ability to memorise.' "What's the point of memorising if you can Google everything? And maybe AI is going to help us operate at a higher intellectual level. "And as humans, we've repeatedly managed to do that. We don't learn how to make fire anymore, and we don't need to. "As humans, we've managed to repeatedly figure out how we operate at a higher level of abstraction, and I think we're going to do that again." Dr Adib, who grew up in Tripoli, Lebanon and was given a Dh1 million Great Arab Minds award in 2023 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, also predicted further challenges to US tech firms' dominance of AI. Speaking earlier at the same event in Dubai, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's AI minister, said that superpower dominance of AI was not appealing, and that middle powers and sovereign governments would want an alternative. "AI is moving at an accelerated pace. It is moving from the digital into the physical world," said Dr Adib. "If you look at the 1990s, where the internet was growing... that was a US-led world. "Today, there is the race between the US and China on AI. What role is Europe and Africa and Latin America and the rest of Asia going to play? The answer is not clear that just the US or China is gonna win this race." He added: "Our first prime adopters were in Europe. And if you look at the United Arab Emirates, there's a lot of investment. There's a lot of AI investments here in Dubai, and they are deploying it. They're seeing real change. And in Abu Dhabi, with the creation of G42, and the investment in data infrastructure. "And as a scientist, I love challenges, and as a technologist, I love the optimism of it. There is an opportunity for real change and impact."

title: Make peace, Iran reformist urges, as hardliners rule out surrender
description: Conflict has weighed heavily on country's 90 million people, former Tehran mayor Gholamhossein Karbaschi says
content: A former Tehran mayor has urged Iran to reach an agreement with the US to end the war, as internal divisions widen over how to respond to Washington amid a deepening economic crisis. Gholamhossein Karbaschi, a reformist politician, made the remarks on Iranian state television last on Wednesday, warning that a prolonged conflict would deepen domestic hardship. “We cannot take on America’s power and diplomacy,” Mr Karbaschi said. “We must make a non-emotional assessment of the situation." Mr Karbaschi said there was no clear end in sight and that officials should consider the consequences of continuing the fighting. “We were never volunteers for war,” he said, adding that families faced uncertainty over whether hostilities would resume. Iran is facing soaring inflation and pressure on household finances, while restrictions on oil exports have contrained a key source of government revenue. Long petrol queues have also been reported. Mr Karbaschi also criticised the Iranian attacks in June on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, saying they had derailed the peace process and given Washington a pretext to breach the interim accord. “If the Islamabad agreement had been implemented as it should have been, the incident involving the targeting of the three ships would not have happened,” he said. “We must distinguish between the reason for violating the agreement and a pretext for violating it.” The attacks he was referring to appear to have occurred about 10 days after the US and Iran signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding on June 17. Mr Karbaschi said the interim agreement had been advantageous to Tehran and had surprised observers because Washington accepted its terms while Israel opposed them. He argued that the subsequent attacks on the ships gave the US an opportunity to breach the agreement. He also questioned who had ordered the strikes, adding that nobody had publicly claimed responsibility. “Everyone says, ‘We don’t know who attacked the three ships,’” he said. Referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian, he asked: “Can it be that the president doesn’t know?” Mr Karbaschi's comments were reported by other media outlets on Thursday morning, including the Entekhab newspaper. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded sharply. Its spokesman, Hossein Mohebi, rejected suggestions that the attacks were unauthorised or carried out without the approval of senior officials. Mr Mohebi described the strikes as a “decisive and crushing response” to what he called the third US breach of its commitments. He accused Washington of breaking its commitments twice during negotiations and a third time after signing the memorandum. “In the armed forces, no action is taken without observing the chain of command and co-ordinating with senior officials,” he was quoted as saying by the reformist Shargh newspaper on Thursday. The dispute has also prompted attacks by Hossein Shariatmadari, editor-in-chief of the ultraconservative Kayhan newspaper, on former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, former president Hassan Rouhani and politician Hossein Marashi. Mr Shariatmadari accused the three of advancing positions on ending the war or preventing renewed fighting, which allegedly serve US and Israeli interests. He described Mr Marashi’s proposal for a "tactical retreat" to avoid another war as a surrender and rejected Mr Rouhani’s suggestion of a referendum on whether military attacks should continue. “Although the US has no embassy in Iran, some political figures effectively act as Washington’s ambassadors through their positions,” Mr Shariatmadari wrote in an editorial. The comments reflect the level of disagreement among Iranian politicians over the terms of a possible settlement, the conduct of the war and the risks of renewed hostilities.

title: Oil transfers off India's west coast surge as Gulf shipping congestion worsens
description: Gulf producers are cutting prices and absorbing transit risks to retain Asian buyers as shipping costs climb
content: Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack . Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. " Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm Vortexa The expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs. Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict. "The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said. A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes. The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale. South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa. In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data. Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally. "The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst. The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed. Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east. Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island. Moving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf. "The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said. Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said. Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata. Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers. A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said. "If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil. The disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply. Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad. The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict. Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase. QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document. “In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said. Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz. "Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it." The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad. For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa. The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing. Gulf producers are increasingly taking on transit and security risks themselves to keep Asian customers. Adnoc, Aramco, Iraq and Qatar now offer STS deliveries outside Hormuz, and Kuwait has adopted the same approach to attract buyers, according to Mr Choudhary. These arrangements let buyers receive cargoes without sending their own tankers through the strait. The UAE has also moved to lock in Asian demand. Adnoc agreed in May to explore raising its crude storage in India to as much as 30 million barrels, from about 5.9 million at Mangalore. Aramco, which sold more than 60 million barrels for transfer off Sohar for September and October deliveries, is negotiating term contracts for next year involving loadings outside Hormuz, Mr Choudhary said, signalling that buyers and sellers alike expect the arrangement to last.

title: Saudi Pro League's big money signings: Who's shining and who's struggling?
description: We take a look at the impact made by the kingdom's most expensive imports this season
content: The 2026-27 Saudi Pro League season is now well under way and the latest influx of talent is already influencing the title race. This summer’s recruitment was concentrated on investing heavily in established internationals still in their prime. Several of the most expensive arrivals have wasted little time in justifying their price tags while others have faced criticism. Al Hilal lead the standings on 21 points, two clear of Al Qadsiah and defending champions Al Nassr. Below, we take a look at how the competition’s latest wave of imports have performed. English Premier League side Arsenal recorded their record sale when Martinelli signed for Al Hilal in September for £60 million, with the Brazilian highlighting his pride at joining a club that countryman Neymar played for. Martinelli, though, will clearly be hoping for a far more successful stint at Hilal than the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain attacker, who had his contract terminated after an injury-ravaged 18 months in Riyadh. After a subdued debut off the bench against Al Shabab , Martinelli conceded he might need “some time to adapt” to his new surroundings having been with the Gunners since 2019. Those concerns appeared to be unfounded as the 25-year-old bagged a hat-trick little over a week later as Hilal demolished Al Taawoun 6-0, ending his seven-month goal drought. He then opened the scoring in the Saudi Clasico win over Al Ittihad on Saturday, taking his league tally to four in four appearances. “He’s a big player and we are lucky to have Martinelli,” manager Simone Inzaghi noted after Tuesday’s 2-0 AFC Champions League win at Al Sadd . Reijnders was honest about his motives after completing a £52m move from Manchester City . “Me a money grabber? I can't deny that,” he said. “By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?” Qadsiah manager Brendan Rodgers has given him the box-to-box role he prefers and he responded by scoring in his first start in the 2-0 win over Neom. The 28-year-old then scored a double in the 3-2 defeat of Al Ahli at the beginning of September and opened the scoring in Friday’s 5-0 victory over Al Kholood. Three of his four league goals have come from outside the box, more than any other player in the SPL this season. Summerville joined in a £60m switch from West Ham United who had just been relegated to English football's second tier. The 24-year-old's first goal arrived against Al Khaleej in his third appearance when he scored the fourth goal with a dinked finish as Hilal ran out 5-1 winners. Summerville also supplied his first two assists in that game. He was on target again the following week, this time driving home a low finish from a tight angle and also scored a fine winner against Al Ittihad. Summerville has registered three goals and three assists in eight league appearances. Al Nassr signed Costa from Mallorca for €22m at the request of new coach Ange Postecoglou, with the 25-year-old Portuguese midfielder recruited to replace Marcelo Brozovic. He was bought to give the reigning champions greater energy in midfield but his early performances have attracted criticism. Speaking on TV, former Al Nassr defender Hussein Abdulghani called the signing of Costa “disastrous”, and dismissed comparisons with Brozovic, claiming Cristiano Ronaldo had encouraged management to sign his countryman. But it has not all been bad with Costa scoring three times in seven SPl appearances, including Friday's 3-0 win over Diriyah, while it was his cross that Anvar Gofurov turned into his own net to seal a 3-1 Champions League win over Neftchi on Monday. Former Barcelona attacker Trincao insisted “the passion of Al Ahli supporters was one of the main reasons” he moved to the Jeddah club in a €40m deal from Sporting. But passionate fans are also demanding and the player tasked with replacing the much-loved Riyad Mahrez has struggled at times as Marino Pusic’s side lost three of their opening six games. But the 26-year-old Portuguese appears to be finding his feet, scoring four times in his last four SPL matches, including a double against Al Fateh on Friday that earned him the man-of-the-match award. Trincao then scored one and supplied another as back-to-back Asian title winners Al Ahli defeated UAE outfit Al Wasl 3-1 in Dubai in the Champions League three days later. Al Hilal forked out £50m to Aston Villa for England striker Watkins who the club had been monitoring since last season, according to Inzaghi. The 30-year-old scored on his debut against Al Ahli and was delighted by the reception he was given. “The fans were calling my name. From minute one, it was amazing,” he said. He later described Saudi football as being of “Premier League quality”. Watkins has already registered five goals and four assists from his six appearances for Hilal and played a role in all three goals in their 3-2 win over Al Ittihad. He was on target again on Tuesday after opening the scoring in Tuesday's win away to Qatari side Al Sadd.

title: Fire, sinking and reported scramble for cargo: what we know about ship lost in Strait of Hormuz
description: Singapore-flagged GFS Pride goes down amid reports Iran changed tactics against commercial shipping on US-backed route
content: A Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by an unidentified projectile. All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were evacuated safely and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority has said. The sinking was confirmed on Wednesday, after the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the attack on Tuesday. A sister ship, the GFS Giselle, was damaged in the same wave of attacks but made its way to anchorage. Singapore condemned the strikes as a breach of international law. The incident highlights how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies. Photos and videos on social media appeared to show a container ship listing heavily under thick black smoke, with containers and their contents floating nearby. Pakistan’s maritime authority warned mariners of floating containers in the area. Other clips added a stranger note. Posts on X suggested small boats converged on the scene to scoop up cargo, and one described sellers doing business on the spot, calling out offers of phones and perfumes. Another post said paying Iran’s unilaterally declared transit toll, which has faced international opposition, would beat losing everything on board. The footage is unverified. It could not be confirmed where or when any clip was filmed, or whether it relates to the GFS Pride. AI-generated images were also widely shared around the sinking, including claims that thousands of iPhones were found floating in the water. The GFS Pride had the capacity to carry 2,824 standard containers, it was reported. It was not clear how many it was carrying when it sank and no manifest was published. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the ship had more than 2,500 containers, including alleged contraband. The claim could not be substantiated. The IRGC also warned local vessels and fishermen to avoid the floating boxes. Quoting two senior Iranian officials, Reuters reported on Wednesday that Tehran was changing its tactics against shipping to keep oil prices high and influence the November 3 US midterm elections. One warned such vessels “would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz”. Another said a complete closure of the waterway would come soon. The IRGC claimed the ship struck a naval mine while using an “unauthorised” route. Tehran has described the US-backed route hugging the Omani coast as dangerous. Maritime security firm Marisks said there was no independent evidence that a mine sank the vessel and described Iran’s claims as consistent with a psychological operations campaign. The available evidence does not establish that the southern route near Oman has been mined.

title: What Gulf economies need to watch out for as potential bond crisis looms
description: In a sufficiently stressed market, even investors who believe government debt will ultimately be repaid may sell
content: Much has been heard recently about the risk of a bond market crisis, with US government bond yields this month reaching their highest levels since 2002, and some warning of 6 per cent US Treasury benchmarks. Yields in several advanced economies globally have also hit multi-decade highs on the back on inflation fears amid soaring energy costs. However, a crisis related to investors losing confidence in governments’ ability to control inflation and debt levels is only part of the story. The next bond-market crisis could start with more technical factors, an increase in issuance, a wave of selling that pushes prices lower, sparking further losses and forcing more investors to sell. Investors demand higher returns when inflation threatens to persist, governments borrow heavily or interest rates are expected to remain elevated. But markets can also move for reasons that have little to do with a sudden deterioration in economic fundamentals. When bond prices fall, leveraged investors can face margin calls or tighter financing conditions. Funds may need to sell assets to raise cash, while institutions managing interest-rate exposure adjust their hedges. Those transactions can put further downward pressure on prices, pushing yields higher and generating new losses. In a sufficiently stressed market, even investors who believe government debt will ultimately be repaid may sell simply because they cannot afford to hold their positions. The US Treasury market is particularly important because its securities underpin global borrowing costs, provide collateral for financial transactions and serve as a benchmark for corporate debt. A disorderly sell-off can therefore spread well beyond Washington. The market has already demonstrated its vulnerabilities. During the disruption of March 2020, US Treasuries experienced severe dysfunction despite their status as one of the world's safest and most liquid assets. Meanwhile, the OECD's Global Debt Report 2026 estimates that governments and companies will borrow $29 trillion from markets this year. The growing role of price-sensitive investors, alongside the retreat of central banks from bond holdings, adds to concerns about the market's capacity to absorb shocks. The AI boom could also complicate that equation. Technology companies and infrastructure developers are competing for capital rapidly. Bloomberg reported this month that major AI-related borrowers had issued nearly half a trillion dollars of debt in 2026. The Dallas Federal Reserve estimates that AI-related investment-grade bond issuance could reach about $300 billion this year, adding significant long-term borrowing to US financial markets . If borrowing rises sharply to finance data centres and other AI infrastructure, investors may demand higher returns, particularly if future revenues appear insufficient to justify the investment. A deterioration in profitability expectations could also undermine the value of AI-related debt, reduce financing and force companies to postpone projects, with losses and tighter credit conditions spilling into other markets. The interaction with government borrowing matters. Heavy Treasury issuance, substantial corporate financing needs and a reassessment of AI investment returns could coincide, putting pressure on all borrowing costs. If that happened alongside leveraged positions being unwound, an initial repricing could become more disruptive. A sharp reversal in the yen carry trade could amplify this dynamic for example, while higher Japanese bond yields may encourage domestic investors to repatriate funds rather than buy US Treasuries. For Gulf economies, the implications extend beyond investment portfolios. US Treasury yields influence international borrowing costs, and a sustained increase can make it more expensive for regional governments and companies to issue debt, refinance obligations and finance infrastructure and economic diversification projects. The effect is direct for Gulf economies whose currencies are pegged to the US dollar, because their monetary conditions are closely influenced by US interest rates. Gulf governments and investors are committing resources to data centres, computing capacity and digital infrastructure. If markets begin to question the returns on AI investment, financing conditions could tighten just as regional projects require more capital. That would not necessarily derail these ambitions. Strong sovereign balance sheets and long investment horizons provide resilience. But higher funding costs and a more selective investor base could change the economics of specific projects. AI could also generate substantial productivity gains, while higher bond yields can attract buyers and eventually stabilise prices. Neither heavy borrowing nor market volatility alone signals a systemic crisis. But the real concern is the possibility that several pressures coincide: heavy government issuance, rising corporate borrowing, doubts about AI returns and leveraged investors forced to unwind positions. For policymakers and investors, the priority should be to monitor market functioning as well as headline yields. Are transactions becoming harder to execute? Are funding pressures rising? Are investors demanding larger premiums to hold assets that would ordinarily be considered liquid? The next bond-market crisis, if and when it comes, may not begin when investors decide governments are insolvent. It may begin when a crowded financing cycle meets a sudden reassessment of risk, and investors who believe in the underlying assets still find themselves forced to sell.

title: Global Village reopens in Dubai: What’s new for the 31st season?
description: Family-friendly multicultural festival will run until May
content: Global Village has reopened in Dubai for its 31st season, with new restaurants, live shows and a rollercoaster added to the popular multicultural festival park . The outdoor destination welcomed visitors back on Wednesday and will remain open until May 2027. Running under the theme A More Wonderful World, the season features 29 pavilions representing more than 90 cultures, plus more than 3,500 shopping outlets and more than 250 dining options. Opening-night celebrations included a choir performance, the Parade of the World and the destination’s signature confetti shower at the Gate of the World. A display featuring 600 drones also marked the season's start. Among the additions is Tokyo Rush, a rollercoaster scheduled to open later in the season, featuring sharp turns and a loop. It will join returning attractions including Dragon Kingdom, The Horror Hotel, Secrets of the Lost City and Exo Planet City. The Festival Wheel returns with refreshed carts offering panoramic views of the destination, while the Gardens of the World has also been updated. Across the cultural attractions, visitors will find refreshed experiences at the Sri Lanka pavilion and the Russia and Azerbaijan areas. The Syria and Kuwait pavilions have new facades. A redesigned Season 31 passport and a new passport for children allow visitors to collect stamps as they explore the pavilions. Fernando Eiroa, chief executive of Dubai Holding Entertainment, said: “Global Village holds a special place in people’s lives because of the connections they make here, with their own roots, with other cultures and the people they visit alongside. It has become a much-loved tradition for families and friends, reflecting the welcoming, multicultural spirit of the UAE.” Restaurant Plaza, beside Carnaval and overlooking the Falcon Stage, has several new additions, including Trabzon Turkish Restaurant, Robo Al Sham, Hawawshi Al Rabie and Chicking. New cafes include Vinci Dolci, Emir Bey Gourmet and Uzungol Cafe. Dessert District also returns with a refreshed facade and a selection of sweet treats. The venues join a wider dining offering of more than 250 options, spanning international street food, restaurants and cafes. Global Village will host 40,000 shows throughout the season, with a programme spanning music, dance, acrobatics and family entertainment. New productions include Fast Live 2: The Police Strike Back , a stunt show featuring driving manoeuvres and action sequences. Bollywood Idol and Bank Heist also join the programme, alongside returning show Slam . For younger visitors, characters from Care Bears and PJ Masks return to the Kids Theatre. Upgrades to amenities include a new VIP parking self-payment system, improved directional signage and expanded ticketing capacity at Happiness Gate. Additional family washrooms have been introduced, including accessible areas for people of determination. Other updates include bilingual signage at the Gate of the World, upgraded lighting at Cultural Gate and a new theme for the Sharjah tunnel. A new WhatsApp chatbot will provide visitors with information and assistance during their visit. Global Village is open from 4pm to midnight on Sunday to Wednesday, with extended hours until 1am on Thursday to Saturday and on public holidays. Tickets cost Dh30, or Dh25 from Monday to Thursday excluding public holidays. They are available through the Global Village website, app and gate counters. Tuesdays are reserved for families, couples and women, except on public holidays.

title: Lionel Messi’s Champions League records tumble as Mbappe, Haaland and Kane make history
description: Argentine superstar sees three of his personal benchmarks surpassed in two nights of European action
content: Lionel Messi holds so many records that there’s a good chance he’s not even aware of half of them. Many of those records relate to the Champions League , a competition he won four times with Barcelona between 2006 and 2015, but has not played in since PSG’s last-16 defeat to Bayern Munich in 2023. For example, Messi scored the most goals for a single club (120 for Barcelona), the most hat-tricks (eight, shared with Cristiano Ronaldo ) and scored in the most consecutive seasons (18, alongside Karim Benzema). But this week, three of his personal benchmarks were surpassed - each by one of this generation’s three elite goalscorers: Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Erling Haaland . Back in September 2015, Messi became the youngest player to reach 100 Champions League appearances when he featured in a 1-1 draw against Roma at the age of 28 years and 84 days. On Wednesday night, he saw that record fall when 27-year-old Mbappe made his 100th appearance in the competition. However, there was at least a sense of symmetry, as it came against the same opposition. Real Madrid came back from 3-1 down to beat Roma 4-3 at the Stadio Olimpico. Mbappe celebrated with a goal, his 72nd in 100 Champions League appearances. As if that wasn’t enough, Messi simultaneously lost another of his records over in Manchester, at the Etihad Stadium, where City were hosting defending champions PSG. The visitors put on a first-half clinic but had to survive an Erling Haaland-inspired fightback after the break. By scoring twice on the night, Haaland became the fastest player to reach 60 goals in the competition, doing so in just 60 games. His second goal took his tally to 61 in 60 appearances. Messi had previously held the record, having reached 60 goals in 80 games. On Tuesday night, it was widely reported that Kane had broken Messi’s record for Champions League goals scored after turning 30. More accurately, Kane moved ahead of Messi on the list. The record is held by Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored 68 times in the Champions League after his 30th birthday. However, Messi, who scored 35 times after turning 30, did find himself pushed further down the list as Kane’s double against Viking for Bayern Munich took his tally to 36. Given the way the Englishman is making up for lost time, perhaps he could yet threaten Ronaldo’s mark.

title: Houthis make ‘major leap’ building advanced missiles with greater Middle East range
description: Arms investigators believe Iran-linked group is making its own missiles indigenously with smuggled specialist parts
content: Yemen's Houthis have made a “major leap” in locally producing sophisticated ballistic missiles using components imported from China , an arms intelligence report has revealed. Experts have also told The National that the militia's manufacturing was becoming increasingly sophisticated. Its engineers have developed the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre during its terminal stage at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It was allegedly responsible for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport attack that killed 13. Attacks by the Houthis have significantly increased in the past month and are designed to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to end its blockade of the Yemen rebels. The Houthis have been significantly helped by specialist parts for missiles imported from China, according to the Conflict Armament Research report passed to The National . Its teams examined weaponry from an intercepted shipment that had been heading to the Houthi-held port of Hodeida. The haul included highly specialist machined parts for rockets such as stabilising fins and equipment for hypersonic flight. “The discovery points to a major leap in the group’s domestic production ambitions and has major regional security implications at a time when Houthi forces are intensifying their deep strike campaign against critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia,” the report said. The components, discovered in containers on a cargo ship from China, demonstrate that the Houthis are now advanced in their work to manufacture the Iranian-made Kheibar Shekan series of ballistic missiles. Their Palestine-2 variant has a range of 1,800km, bringing much of the Middle East into their sights. The findings also demonstrate that the rebels, who are under a UN arms embargo, have expanded their supply chains beyond their traditional Iran-linked networks, the paper said. “The documented components suggest that, in terms of longer-range ballistic missiles, the Houthis have moved beyond simply reassembling Iranian systems,” it stated. “Only a few countries in the world have the capacity to manufacture missiles of comparable ranges domestically.” While the Houthis have “not yet mastered” the technology for the Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile, Iranian expertise on the ground is “accelerating their progress”, said Dr Nawaf Obaid, of Kings College London. “Their principal constraint is time, not technical impossibility,” he told The National . While it is understood the airport attack involved several projectiles in a swarm attack, the Houthis currently cannot build significant numbers, he added. “Scale remains their weakness,” he said. Analysis by Kings College's department of war studies showed that 85 to 90 per cent of missiles were intercepted by Saudi Arabia’s advanced defence system, he added. It is understood that the Houthis exploited a gap between Saudi Arabia’s lower and middle air defence layers in the airport attack, rather than a “technological breakthrough”, said Dr Obaid. He added that the kingdom’s air defences were “performing exceptionally well under sustained wartime conditions”. Documents show the contents from four shipping containers arrived in the Aden Free Zone in Yemen in June and October 2025 from China. The shipments contained custom-made metal parts including components of the airframe and a solid-propellant rocket motor for a Kheibar Shekan missile. They were made by a Chinese precision-metal producer “that advertises itself as a specialist manufacturer of custom aerospace parts”, the report said. It demonstrated that the Houthis were buying “more specialised parts for the construction of missiles, apparently independent of Iran-linked supply networks”. According to UN reports, Chinese companies form the biggest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis and they have been importing components for solid-fuel missiles from China for at least two years. China has stated that it adheres to the UN Houthi arms ban. Asked by The National what action the UK government might take against Chinese companies allegedly supplying components, the prime minister’s official spokesman said Britain “strongly condemns Houthi attacks and remains committed to supporting the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”. Saudi Arabia's ambassador to London told a meeting of parliamentarians on Tuesday that the UK's support in the face of the Houthi missile menace was welcomed by his government. Prince Abdullah bin Khaled held discussions focused on “recent Houthi attacks against the kingdom, regional security, and the importance of international co-operation in safeguarding stability and supporting peace in Yemen”, an embassy post on social media said.

title: Asian markets fall on tech stock rout as high US inflation weighs on Wall Street
description: South Korea's Kospi slumps more than 7 per cent on Thursday
content: Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector. South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent. Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com. In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom. Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains. "The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region. "A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added. The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September. "Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said. The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added. US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year. "US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. "The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper." The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.

title: Mariah Carey to bring Christmas hits to Abu Dhabi in December
description: American singer returns to UAE capital for festive concert at Etihad Arena
content: Mariah Carey is returning to Abu Dhabi for a Christmas concert at the Etihad Arena on December 12.
