The American singer will bring her Christmastime show to Yas Island, with a programme expected to include festive favourites such as All I Want For Christmas Is You, Santa Baby and Christmas (Baby Please Come Home). Tickets for the Saturday concert are already on sale, with prices starting at Dh249. The performance will mark Carey's second appearance in the capital this year, after her Saadiyat Nights concert in February. She also performed at the outdoor concert series in January 2024. Carey has become closely associated with the festive season thanks to the enduring popularity of All I Want for Christmas Is You . Released in 1994 as part of her album Merry Christmas , the song has become an annual fixture on music charts around the world. It reached No 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for the first time in 2019, 25 years after its original release. The five-time Grammy winner is among the best-selling recording artists of all time, with 19 No 1 singles on the Billboard Hot 100, including We Belong Together, Fantasy and Hero. Her coming concert also continues a long history of UAE performances. Carey previously appeared in Dubai in 2004, 2017 and 2019, with the latter concert taking place as part of celebrations marking one year before Expo 2020 Dubai. Carey's concert joins a busy December calendar on Yas Island. Andrea Bocelli will perform at Etihad Arena on December 2, before the Formula One Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 3 to 6. The weekend's after-race concerts will feature Lewis Capaldi, Imagine Dragons, The Chainsmokers and The Script. Etihad Arena will also host a series of film concerts including Encanto on December 18, Frozen and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York on December 19, and The Lion King on December 20. Mariah Carey performs at Etihad Arena, Yas Island, on December 12. Tickets start at Dh249 and are available through the venue's official website.

title: PSG show class to hold off Man City as Guardiola looks on, Real Madrid launch stunning comeback
description: Goals flow in Champions League as holders provide timely reminder they are still the team to beat
content: Manchester City's 4-2 defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Uefa Champions League told only part of ​the ​story of Enzo ​Maresca's first loss at the helm, with ⁠his men staggering through the first half before roaring ⁠back after the break. ⁠City were staring at a rout when a rampant PSG raced to a 3-0 lead with a first-half masterclass. Then they woke up. Maresca's side tore into the visitors after half-time, pouring forward with ⁠an intensity and urgency that had been entirely absent in the opening 45 minutes. Erling ​Haaland spearheaded ⁠the fightback, scoring twice to ‌become the fastest player to reach 60 Champions League goals, hitting the mark in ​just 60 games, 20 quicker than Lionel Messi. City kept coming. They finished with nearly twice as many shots as PSG and around three times as many touches in the opposition box, while recording a higher expected goals figure at both half-time and full-time. PSG, though, were more ruthless. “I think we start quite good until the first goal [from Desire Doue in the 13th minute] and then we concede the second one (Ousmane Dembele) after one minute. That created some bad feelings,” Maresca told TNT Sports. “Second half, we were much better and probably deserved something more.” City had arrived on the back of a 3-0 thrashing of Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday and Maresca felt they generated enough chances to salvage something even ​after digging themselves a three-goal hole. “Even with 3-0 in the first ‌half, with the amount of ⁠chances we created in the second half, ​we deserved more,” he said. “Luis (Enrique, PSG's manager) said at the end of the ​game that ‌they were quite lucky today. “You have to be clinical but not lose the balance,” Maresca said. The ⁠defeat unfolded against a backdrop of turmoil stretching far beyond City as an independent commission found City guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period. City have denied any wrongdoing and have appealed. On the pitch, they remain three points clear of Arsenal atop ​the Premier League table ahead of Saturday's home game against Ipswich. Asked if he had a message for supporters, Maresca said: “We are sorry for the first half for sure. Saturday is a Premier League game and we need to continue our run.” Former City manager Pep Guardiola watched from the stands in Manchester alongside chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and senior executives Ferran Soriano and Hugo Viana. On a breathless night of Champions League football featuring 46 goals, Real Madrid staged a stunning comeback to beat AS Roma 4-3. At the ‌Stadio Olimpico, Real Madrid scored three times in the closing stages to overturn a two-goal deficit. Marten de Roon gave Roma the lead ⁠in the 20th minute before Kylian Mbappe equalised five minutes later, but Donyell Malen struck twice in the 51st ⁠and 57th minutes to put the hosts in control. The visitors mounted a remarkable comeback as Carlos Espi pulled a goal back in the 82nd minute before Endrick levelled three minutes later. Former Roma defender Antonio Rudiger then completed the turnaround in the 90th minute, holding off his marker to steer home Arda Guler's corner from close range and snatch victory for ​the Spanish giants. Meanwhile, Bradley Barcola scored a hat-trick in Liverpool's ⁠6-3 thrashing of LASK. Barcola scored his first goals for the club during the rout of Champions League newcomers LASK in Austria. Ronald Araujo, Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas also scored for Andoni Iraola's side, who bounced back from Sunday's 3-0 Premier League defeat by City. Florian Flecker struck twice for the hosts.

title: IMF official says Iran war price shock buffers are narrowing
description: Renewed disruptions threaten region's 'highly uncertain' outlook, Jihad Azour says
content: A senior International Monetary Fund official has said prewar buffers are helping countries in the Middle East to limit the economic impact of the Iran war, but the region's outlook remains highly uncertain as it faces threats of renewed disruption. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's energy supplies was shipped before the war, has rattled markets, as have Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway and key sites in neighbouring countries. “The impact was more contained than the scale initially suggested,” the fund's regional director, Jihad Azour, told reporters during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand. While the price of Brent crude is 47 per cent higher than its prewar levels, it has yet to hit the $200-a-barrel mark that was previously feared. The IMF this week maintained its 2026 global growth projection at 3.1 per cent and slightly raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. Higher oil prices were partially attributed to the fund lifting its 2026 inflation forecast to 4.7 per cent. The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been exploring alternatives to send their supplies to markets, while International Energy Agency members agreed in March to release up to 400 million barrels of reserve stocks. Output from non-Gulf producers and an adjustment in energy demand have also mitigated the war's impact, Mr Azour said. “These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments,” he explained. Iranian attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz this week. At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the waterway in the past week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. On Wednesday, Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters . Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz , Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said in a statement. The IEA said crude oil exports from Gulf producers, led by Saudi Arabia, jumped by 4.4 million barrels a day in September to reach more than 75 per cent of prewar levels. Iran's escalatory attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker traffic threaten to derail those gains, the agency said. Brent crude rose 0.36 per cent at $106.1 a barrel on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 1.08 per cent at $95.16 a barrel. The IMF said its 2026 forecasts show a sharp divergence for oil exporters and importers, with the latter being assisted by remittances, tourism and government support. Regional economies are forecast to see a sharp divergence in trends due to the war. The IMF projected economic contractions of 11.3 per cent for Bahrain, 16 per cent for Iraq, 16.7 per cent for Kuwait, 15.6 per cent for Qatar , 3.3 per cent for Saudi Arabia and 3.9 per cent for the UAE this year. Growth is expected to rebound in 2027, but the conflict has inflicted a "long-lasting scarring impact" on regional economies, Mr Azour told journalists on Thursday. The economic recovery will take time and will require additional spending on infrastructure to boost resilience. "If we compare to the [growth] trajectory before the war, in 2030, we will be below it," he said. A more prolonged conflict remains the most significant risk for the region's highly uncertain outlook, with further disruptions likely to weaken economic activity, inflame inflationary pressures and place extra strain on fiscal positions across the region, he said. Mr Azour also said tighter financial conditions could deepen vulnerabilities in economies with large sovereign financing needs. He urged the region's economies to prioritise price stability, rebuild their fiscal buffers and build capacity to withstand future shocks. The IMF will release its outlook for the Middle East next week in Dubai. On Wednesday, UAE central bank governor Khaled Balama noted the region's experiences have shown that resilience depends on how quickly economies adapt to changing circumstances while building their fiscal buffers, state news agency Wam reported. Mr Balama was addressing the region's central bankers and finance ministers during a meeting alongside the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok. He also said the UAE economy has shown resilience, supported by its robust fiscal buffers, low levels of public debt and its vast sovereign assets, helping to reinforce investor and market confidence. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening international co-operation frameworks amid geopolitical tension. Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan was due to hold a media conference with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday. The International Monetary Finance Committee, which is the fund's policy advisory panel, announced this week it had extended Mr Al Jadaan's position as IMFC chair by another year after his term ends on January 3, 2027.

title: Israel accused of imposing media blackout on occupied south Lebanon
description: UN peacekeepers unable to arrange visits as press freedom groups accuse Israel of censorship
content: UN peacekeepers have been blocked from arranging journalist visits to Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon for weeks, a spokesman told The National, amid accusations of a media blackout. Journalists have embedded with the UN Interim Force for Lebanon ( Unifil ) several times since a June ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Those visits provided one of the few means of accessing the occupied territory, which Israel designates as a buffer zone. The visits allowed journalists to report on the handful of predominantly Christian villages that remain inhabited , as well as the systematic destruction of depopulated Muslim villages inside the zone. “At the moment, we cannot conduct media visits south of the so-called yellow line,” said a Unifil spokesman. “This has been the case for the past few weeks.” He added that Unifil did not know when visits would be permitted to resume. Elsy Moufarrej, president of the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told The National that the union had received several complaints from journalists denied access to the zone in recent weeks. She accused Israel of a “media blackout” that prevents independent reporting on “potential crimes and violations”. “It also deprives these communities of a voice and violates the public's right to know,” she added. Israel occupied an area extending 10km to 12km into Lebanon during its war with Hezbollah, which reignited in March. The Israeli military launched a ground invasion and forced people to leave the south before establishing its so-called security zone. Since then, Israel has severely restricted movement in and out of the occupied area, enforcing control through military positions, strikes, forced displacement orders and restrictions on access. The charity Reporters Without Borders has condemned restrictions on journalists entering the zone, accusing the Israeli military of turning co-ordination mechanisms intended to facilitate safe access into tools of censorship. “It is unacceptable that Lebanese journalists are denied access or prevented from entering Lebanese territory,” said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF’s Middle East office. “Ceasefire agreements and military considerations must no longer serve as a pretext to obstruct the right to information and threaten the safety of journalists.” While some communities such as the Sunni Muslim village of Kfarshouba can still be reached from the Lebanese sid e, predominantly Christian villages deeper inside the territory are effectively besieged, with movement in and out subject to Israeli permission. Travelling with Unifil had offered journalists rare opportunities to reach these communities. The media restriction appears to have begun in late-September, following visits to the occupied zone by journalists from international news organisations. Téa Ziade, a French-Lebanese freelance journalist, was scheduled to enter the zone with Unifil on September 25 for an assignment with a European news outlet. Her trip was cancelled that morning, just minutes before the convoy was due to depart. “We had submitted all our papers to Unifil. Everything was in order,” she said. “A Unifil lieutenant told us: ‘It’s the journalists. No journalists are allowed in the convoy.’” She was given no explanation at the time. She was later told by Unifil that a proper deconfliction process had not taken place. There have been no Unifil journalist embeds since. The Israeli military confirmed to The National that it had raised the issue of journalist access with Unifil. “Following incidents in which journalists entered the security zone without prior co-ordination and published footage revealing the locations of troops, the issue was discussed with Unifil,” a military spokesperson said. But another Israeli military official went further, alleging that journalists had entered the occupied zone concealed within convoys and “shared photographs, which showed the location of our troops, with Hezbollah operatives or people connected to Hezbollah operatives”. The official did not identify the journalists or news organisations involved, or provide evidence to substantiate the allegation. When questioned about the accusation, an Israeli military spokesperson appeared to backtrack on the claim that journalists had shared information with Hezbollah or affiliates, instead saying that publicly available information about Israeli troop positions could be exploited by the group. Pictures of Israeli positions inside southern Lebanon are widely available online. Israel, which has been accused of targeting journalists, has routinely portrayed them as militants. In October, it published a list of 170 people killed in the Gaza war who it said were militants posing as media workers. Israeli forces have killed at least 16 journalists and media workers in Lebanon since October 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Among them was Reuters journalist Issam Abdallah , killed by Israeli tank fire in October 2023 in an attack that wounded six other journalists and which Human Rights Watch described as an apparent war crime. In April 2026, Al Akhbar journalist Amal Khalil was killed in an Israeli strike while reporting from the security zone during a ceasefire, while her colleague Zeinab Faraj was seriously wounded. Unifil was not the only means of accessing the occupied territory. Humanitarian and civilian convoys had also offered journalists a route into the occupied zone. Those routes, too, have become increasingly restricted in recent weeks. Sources within Unifil and other organisations say access requires “prior deconfliction arrangements, usually through humanitarian convoys”, Ms Moufarrej said. Deconfliction with the Israeli army usually involves speaking to Unifil or a US and French-led committee established to monitor the ceasefire. The process is intended to arrange safe passage through the area . “However, Israeli forces have reportedly begun preventing these convoys from entering if journalists accompany them,” she added. A humanitarian worker who regularly travels into the occupied territory told The National that Israeli soldiers have significantly tightened checks at checkpoints, inspecting every vehicle to ensure no journalists were on board. Such checks were not previously routine, the worker said. “Israeli soldiers now come out of their base and check every person inside the car to make sure their identity matches the approved list.” An Israeli army spokesperson said the military reviewed journalists’ requests to enter the occupied zone on a “case-by-case basis”, without clarifying what procedures must be followed for approval. “Areas where military operations are taking place pose genuine security risks, requiring measures to protect the lives of journalists on the ground, as well as the safety of [Israeli] troops,” the Israeli army spokesperson added. “This policy is intended to enable journalistic coverage to the extent possible, without endangering human lives or compromising the safety of troops and their operational activities.” However, Israeli military operations are an inherent feature of the occupation, meaning any area could be cut off. Ms Ziade rejected the Israeli army’s security justification. “If we cannot go to the south, how are we supposed to tell the story of the occupation?” she asked. “We lose part of the meaning of this profession, the ability to build trust and intimacy with people. Without journalists on the ground, there is also a question of accountability and impunity.” Access for journalists has always been challenging. In July, a vetted humanitarian convoy, which included The National , was barred at the last minute by the Israeli army, despite having obtained prior approval. At the time, Unifil said the decision was probably made because of media presence. It has now become practically impossible. Since the end of September, no journalists have been allowed inside the security zone. “What worries me is that this justification could come to be accepted by the international community, and that we, as journalists, will simply be expected to accept it too,” Ms Ziade said. “And that is how, little by little, a territory becomes closed to journalists.” The restrictions have also had consequences for civilians living under Israeli occupation. Israeli forces suspended convoys to Debel and Rmeish for three days after journalists entered the occupied zone , according to a humanitarian worker who regularly travels to the area. Residents of both villages confirmed they had been prevented from entering or leaving during the three-day closure. They said Israeli military officials had accused journalists of entering the territory without authorisation. The Israeli military official denied having a policy of punishing civilians or villages for hosting reporters, saying troops had temporarily paused the convoy to investigate the incident. “It is unacceptable that a civilian area is isolated for three days simply for having hosted journalists,” said Mr Dagher from RSF. The suspension temporarily cut off a lifeline for the besieged communities, whose residents depend on the convoys for travel and supplies. The closure sparked fears about speaking to the media. “It was indirect, but the message was received by all the villages: ‘There are a lot of mistakes happening, be careful. If there are more mistakes there won't be any more convoys,'” said a locally elected official from Debel, who requested not to be named to avoid retaliation by Israeli forces. “People got scared. They need these convoys to access hospitals, doctors and supplies.”

title: Why Europe's reading habits should concern the Arab world
description: Encouraging children is only the beginning of building lifelong reading habits, Frankfurt Book Fair is told
content: Even with some of the world's oldest and most prestigious publishing houses, extensive library networks and a celebrated literary culture, Europe is struggling to keep successive generations reading. That was among the takeaways from a presentation by the Federation of European Publishers, which represents national publishing associations across the continent, at Frankfurt Book Fair last week. While the federation reported that print book sales had fallen by about 6 per cent over five years in the markets surveyed, equivalent to a 110 million decline in copies, more revealing was its examination of reading habits. Drawing on Eurostat research from 2022, the report highlighted that 47.2 per cent of European Union residents aged 16 and older had not read a book in the preceding year. Among those aged 16 to 29, nearly four in 10 had not read one. The reasons reported by non-readers warrant attention. Among those aged 16 to 29, a lack of interest was cited by 58 per cent, compared with 21.8 per cent who said they lacked time. Across all age groups, 2.4 per cent identified cost or access as the obstacle. The figures add to gnawing concerns that predate Frankfurt, with research published in February by Britain's National Literacy Trust finding that 46.9 per cent of children aged eight to 11 enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 29.5 per cent of those aged 11 to 14. Among boys aged 14 to 16, the figure was just 18.8 per cent. Europe's experience offers a reminder against taking the Arab world's considerable investment in introducing children to books for granted. As educators and parents know, that desire to turn the page can change as they grow older, with education, social media and entertainment compete for attention, followed eventually by the growing pressures of professional and family responsibilities. Reading habits are not set in stone simply because children were encouraged during childhood. That is merely the first chapter of an ongoing story. The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing the reading bug. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. An impact study conducted in partnership with Unesco reported increased reading frequency and more books completed by participating students. Meanwhile, the Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, is more concerned with encouraging children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested on what they have consumed. Researchers are evaluating its effects and the longer-term affects remain unknown. Beyond the classroom, UAE libraries are also finding ways to keep books part of people's everyday lives. Sharjah's House of Wisdom and Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Library have become places to work, study and attend cultural events, as well as read books. The latter houses nine specialised libraries, including sections for children and young adults. But reading habits cannot develop through osmosis alone and both libraries continue to encourage younger audiences through workshops, holiday programmes and exhibitions. The quality of that content is critical, particularly when young Arabs themselves are questioning the appeal of the cultural content available to them. At the Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi in September, a survey of 4,092 people aged 18 to 25 across 10 Arab countries found that 71 per cent preferred media in Arabic, yet 67 per cent considered much of the available Arabic content outdated compared with English-language alternatives. The findings covered media broadly rather than books specifically, but they should give publishers reason to consider whether their books are resonating with younger audiences. Cairo's Diwan Publishing is one example worth noting, having reintroduced Naguib Mahfouz's novels through contemporary cover designs and graphic-novel adaptations, including The Thief and the Dogs . As previously reported by The National , co-founder Ahmed Qarmalawi said the project, developed with the Mahfouz family, sought to introduce the Nobel laureate's work to a generation familiar with his reputation but not necessarily his writing. At the 2024 Abu Dhabi International Book Fair, a large interactive pavilion dedicated to Mahfouz showcased the new editions. Qarmalawi recalled young visitors responding enthusiastically to the books, suggesting that an author some might regard as a literary cultural heirloom could still speak to a younger generation. And in that regard, social media is also playing a role in building a love of books during adolescence. As The National has reported, BookTok and BookTube communities have emerged in the region, with members recommending titles, sharing punchy reviews and introducing fellow readers to new authors. While the footfall at such events and the viewing figures online deserve to be celebrated, more work is needed to turn that enthusiasm into lasting reading habits and make reading books a normal part of life rather than homework. Authors and publishers must also take risks and create content that resonates. With its young population, eclectic cultural sensibilities and governments that view culture as an investment, the Arab world has a chance to lead in keeping people reading. That would be an achievement for a regional publishing industry still regarded as evolving by some of its European counterparts, provided the same commitment that encouraged children to pick up books in the first place is sustained.

title: Why trust in AI is hard to earn and easy to lose
description: AI's lasting value will depend on whether it improves people’s lives without asking them to surrender their confidence in the technology
content: Trust, it is often said, is earned in drops but lost in buckets. When it comes to realising the potential of artificial intelligence , trust is arguably as important as computing power or economic returns. Just how much ordinary people are willing to trust this technology is a critical question – and one that is difficult to answer quantifiably. Nevertheless, it is a pertinent question for the UAE , a country that has positioned itself at the forefront of this technology. Dubai ’s announcement yesterday to offer a $1 million (Dh3.6 million) prize in collaboration with the World Economic Forum for meaningful AI innovation is another expression of that commitment. However, as the technology becomes more capable, its success will depend on more than just the ability to build it. To this point, speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders yesterday in Dubai, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Omar Al Olama suggested AI has to earn trust before being granted broader decision-making powers. His observation deserves to be central to the debate about the technology’s future. It is a future that offers the possibility of a substantial economic prize. Research presented alongside the WEF gathering suggests that AI could unlock more than $1 trillion in value across the Middle East and North Africa by 2030. For a region in which many countries want to diversify their economy, this is an opportunity to be taken seriously. However, projections such as these should not gloss over some important caveats – and the human factor. An AI system that makes a demonstrable contribution to productivity is valuable. One that people feel they cannot trust with their personal data, their finances or important decisions will struggle to succeed. Trust has to be earned through clear accountability and tangible safeguards. When AI makes mistakes, people need to know who is responsible and how errors will be corrected. These protections gain importance in step with the greater authority granted to automated systems. Dubai’s gathering of established and emerging leaders is an opportunity to consider these questions in depth and across generations. Future generations will inherit the consequences of the decisions being made today. It stands to reason that they should also have a meaningful voice in determining how AI moves forward. The UAE has demonstrated that early investment and a willingness to experiment can establish a country as a serious player in a new industry. The next stage requires a comparable determination to get the governance right. AI may transform the Middle East’s economy and help prepare it for a rapidly changing world with many challenges. However, its lasting value will depend on whether it improves people’s lives without asking them to surrender their confidence in the technology. In the long run, success will belong to those who give people good reason to trust them.

title: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons consider leaving UK as tax concerns mount
description: UAE has emerged as leading destination for UK’s migrating millionaires
content: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found. The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth. Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth. The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The mass departure of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE , Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US. The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs. CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says. Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai -based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”. “UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National . Under the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains. Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules. The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon. Enquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds. Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent. Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows. “ Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits. Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon. Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows. For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity. “The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.

title: Reconstruction in north-east Syria key to refugee returns from Iraq, UNHCR official says
description: Many Syrian refugees have found work and access to services in Iraq's Kurdistan Region, making the decision to return home more difficult
content: Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National . Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle. “We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added. Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said. Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey. “When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war. Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”. “I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added. However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community. “I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said. He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said. He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees , Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee. “But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees. To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said. Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.” A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said. Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants. "What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said. Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014. Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq. ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces. “I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said. He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas. In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis , with UN support. However, its implementation has largely stalled amid disputes over who should control the area and appoint a mayor. The Popular Mobilisation Forces , an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar. Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK , and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.

title: Dubai Police arrest group over fake reviews: Can bad review land you in trouble?
description: Even factual statements that damage a reputation can be defamatory
content: Posting a negative online review of a business could land UAE residents in legal trouble if their comments are deemed defamatory or deliberately damaging to the business's reputation, experts have warned. The warning follows the arrest of a group by Dubai Police accused of posting fake reviews on a company’s Google Maps page in an attempt to harm its business. Police said an investigation launched after the company filed a complaint revealed that several commercial shops had formed groups to publish false and damaging comments. While customers are entitled to share their experiences online, their comments must not harm others or their interests, said Maj Yasser Juma Mohammed, head of the Social Media Crimes Section at Dubai Police. He warned social media users that there is a difference between leaving an honest negative review and posting comments that could amount to an insult or defamation. Nikhat Sardar Khan, a litigation lawyer in Dubai, said that insulting, misleading or malicious reviews can expose the writer to legal action. "Online defamation is considered more harmful as it can cause lasting damage because it can be saved, shared and viewed long after it was first published." Ludmila Yamalova of law firm Lylaw said: "Deleting a review does not automatically eliminate legal liability. Once a statement is published, the offence may have occurred. Screenshots, platform records, or other electronic evidence may preserve the original content." For small businesses, a few negative or fake reviews can bruise their reputation and leave a lasting online imprint. For Apple Gawaran, a Dubai-based content creator who runs a personalised 3D-printed gifts business, the issue is personal. "One fake review can create unnecessary negativity and potentially influence people who have never even experienced the business," she said. Ms Gawaran said customers should share honest feedback, positive or negative, but there is a clear difference between genuine criticism and deliberately posting false information to damage a business. Amreen Iqbal, founder of jewellery brand Piece of You, said fake reviews can create doubts among potential customers who rely on online feedback when choosing gifts. "When someone posts a review about an experience they never had, it creates confusion and doubt," she said. The team at Mövenpick JLT raised a similar concern, saying fake reviews can mislead families planning holidays and business travellers booking accommodation, while unfairly affecting the staff behind the service. Constructive criticism or opinions based on genuine experiences generally do not constitute defamation if they are not insulting or made with malicious intent. However, even factual statements that damage a reputation can be defamatory. Ms Yamalova said: “Negative reviews are not illegal in the UAE. However, the distinction between legitimate criticism and unlawful defamation is not always clear-cut, and is more nuanced.” Simply put, saying a restaurant's service was slow or a product didn't meet expectations is different from accusing a business of fraud or insulting its employees. "These reviews, while critical, aim to provide constructive feedback without making false statements," said Ms Khan. In contrast, a defamatory review contains false statements. Such reviews go beyond mere opinion or criticism, which can lead to legal consequences. According to Ms Khan, "Businesses and individuals can sue for defamation if they can prove that the statements have caused harm or tangible damage. Reviewers must ensure their feedback is honest and not insulting or defamatory, causing reputational harm or tangible damage." Under Article 43 of the UAE Cybercrimes Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 34 of 2021), online insults and statements that expose others to punishment or public contempt can carry criminal penalties. The penalties can include fines ranging from Dh250,000 to Dh500,000 and/or imprisonment. Depending on the circumstances, the affected party may also pursue a separate civil claim for compensation where legally recognised damage can be applied. However, a complaint does not automatically establish an offence. Criminal liability depends on the particular statements, circumstances, and applicable legal requirements. The UAE cybercrime law strictly prohibits spreading false information and imposes severe penalties. Violators may face imprisonment for at least one year and a fine of at least Dh100,000. The penalty increases to two years in jail and a minimum fine of Dh200,000 if the crime was committed during an emergency or crisis. Ms Yamalova's advice to consumers is simple: "Focus on the facts, not accusations. Criticise the product or service, not the individual. Avoid inflammatory language, personal insults and unsupported allegations. Consider whether the review aims to share a genuine experience or cause harm. "Negative reviews are a legitimate part of consumer feedback. But in the UAE, approach them thoughtfully, recognising that even an honestly held grievance does not automatically protect you from legal liability." If a consumer has a bad experience, they can exercise their rights under Consumer Protection law. This law protects consumers and gives them the right to fair treatment, accurate information, and compensation for damage caused by defective products or poor services, holding businesses accountable for their actions. Seeking compensation under this law is more effective than posting negative reviews because it provides a formal process for resolving grievances.

title: Dubai's shared housing rules will lead to better quality of life for those on low incomes, says official
description: Landlords have until September 2027 to comply with new regulations
content: Dubai's crackdown on overcrowded and illegally sub-let apartments will result in a better life for residents on low incomes, a senior official from the emirate's municipality has said. The Dubai Municipality's shared housing guide sets standards for building design, occupancy, health and safety, shared amenities and approved locations. It gives landlords until September 1, 2027, to comply with the new requirements across 43 designated areas of the emirate. Nasser Al Shaibani, structural control section manager at Dubai Municipality, said most tenants living in shared accommodation previously did not have any contracts "or any legal backbone to their residential status”. “With this law, tenants can have a one or two-month contract, which gives them the flexibility to change, to go and come back while having legal support," he said. “This will have a big impact on Dubai, as we'll see people moving to better housing and a better quality of life.” The new regulations address unregulated residential practices , prevent rooms from being subdivided, and protect the privacy and rights of owners and occupants. The new law requires buildings to be designated as either individual or family-shared housing. “Each building should be designated only for individuals or only for families; you cannot mix both permits within one building,” Mr Al Shaibani said. “Within this year, we are giving the building owners time to get the necessary approval from Dubai Municipality, Dubai Land Authority, Civil Defence and Rera. “During this time, Dubai Municipality will keep on monitoring those buildings. We will continue visiting and we will do the inspections. This period does not exempt them from unpermitted building modification." The municipality has received six applications for shared-housing permits so far. Three of them have been approved through the Build in Dubai platform. Apartment blocks designated for shared accommodation are close to public transport and workplaces to reduce commuter traffic and encourage people to walk or cycle. A 2025 Dubai workforce report by Edenred UAE found that 60 per cent of workers earned less than Dh5,000 ($1,361) a month, creating strong demand for affordable housing. While the new regulations aim to improve housing standards, industry operators caution that higher costs could make it harder to provide affordable accommodation for all. Rayan Hanna, founder and chief executive of Next House, an affordable housing platform in Dubai specialising in short-term rentals, backed the regulations but said the sector still faces challenges. “Although subdividing apartments into smaller rooms, commonly known as partitions, and operating shared rooms in residential units was prohibited, this type of accommodation has existed across Dubai for years,” Mr Hanna told The National . “A clearer legal framework for shared housing creates opportunities for experienced operators, property owners and institutional investors. “I also believe we will see stronger enforcement against illegally subdivided and overcrowded apartments in premium residential areas, with shared housing gradually moving towards designated locations.” Next House caters to professionals visiting Dubai who are looking for short to medium-term rental agreements. Under the new standards, shared accommodation must include kitchens, sanitary facilities and designated areas for dining, recreation, laundry and clothes drying. Bedrooms must be at least five square metres per person. There must be at least one toilet for every four occupants and one shower for every six people. Kitchen space must provide at least one square metre per person, and buildings must provide bicycle parking for at least 10 per cent of residents. Landlords found in breach of the regulations can be fined up to Dh500,000 ($136,147) for a first offence, with repeat offenders facing a maximum penalty of Dh1 million. Mr Hanna, who has amended his business model to comply with the latest rules, said affordability remained the biggest challenge for many people moving to Dubai for work. He said operators may need to generate about Dh2,000 to Dh3,000 per rentable room per month to make the model financially attractive for investors and property owners. “Many people relying on bed spaces simply cannot afford more than Dh700–Dh900 a month,” he said. “The new regulations introduce minimum space requirements, which are important improvements, but they also increase operating and development costs. “The real challenge is finding the balance between making housing safe and compliant, and making it attractive for investors. I don't think these regulations alone will solve Dubai's affordable housing problem, but they're certainly a step in the right direction.” Dubai is one of the world's fastest-growing cities , with its population of about 4.8 million forecast to increase to six million by 2040. The city's infrastructure is expanding alongside its population, with extensions to public transport networks and existing communities.

title: Elon Musk shifts responsibility to Trump over satellite restrictions affecting Ukraine
description: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Starlink service had been deliberately disrupted
content: Elon Musk on Wednesday sought to distance himself from the satellite communications restrictions over Ukraine that have disrupted Kyiv's military operations, suggesting that US President Donald Trump is ultimately behind any changes. There has been growing tension between Washington and Kyiv after Mr Trump's agreement with President Vladimir Putin to resume buying Russian diesel, which critics have called a betrayal of Ukraine . Since the deal was announced last week, Ukrainian officials have said restrictions on satellite terminals have disrupted drone operations as Russia continues to attack Ukrainian energy sites. Kyiv has also reported difficulties in receiving advance warnings of Russian missile attacks, although it is unclear whether these are connected to the satellite restrictions. In a post on X, Mr Musk drew a distinction between Starlink, which is the satellite internet company owned by SpaceX, and Starshield, a national security and military subsidiary. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Mr Musk said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the President of the United States]." He was responding to a post minutes earlier by former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that some of the satellite connectivity was being restored. “Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” he said. Mr Musk added that use of Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company". Mr Musk's post leaves key questions unanswered, including who authorised the restriction and whether SpaceX acted on instructions from the US military or from Mr Trump. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A source told Reuters that SpaceX had limited terminal connections, complicating Ukrainian drone interceptions and mid-range strikes. In an interview on the Piers Morgan Uncensored YouTube channel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Mr Trump and Mr Musk of restraining Kyiv’s military access to SpaceX’s satellite technology, deepening the rift between Washington and Kyiv. “I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely,” Mr Zelenskyy said when asked if Ukraine’s use of the satellite service had been intentionally disrupted. “I think he is not right. It’s a big mistake.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ukraine also depends on US intelligence assistance for early warning of Russian missile launches. White House officials are actively discussing the possibility of cutting that arrangement with Ukraine, although there is no consensus on what to do, Semafor reported on Wednesday, quoting an unidentified administration official. Mr Trump said on Tuesday that the US continued to share intelligence with Ukraine. His deal with Russia has drawn bipartisan criticism. On Tuesday, 12 senators wrote him a letter asking him to rescind it. One of the signatories, Republican Senator Thom Tillis, on Wednesday asked Mr Musk to clarify what was happening with Starlink. "Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a grey area for the US government or for American corporations. Can you clarify the SpaceX position?" he wrote on X. The suggestion that Mr Musk's company had ⁠limited Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf. "Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister ⁠Radoslaw Sikorski posted on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you." There was no immediate response from Mr Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man".

title: AI plans 'have not changed' in Middle East despite Iran conflict, Nvidia says
description: Ruth Berry says company remains committed to region's AI appetite
content: Despite the continuing conflict with Iran , Gulf countries have not abandoned their AI ambitions, and demand for the infrastructure needed to develop the technology remains strong, a senior Nvidia official said on Wednesday. “The imperatives these countries see have not changed, they still see it as an opportunity to diversify their economies,” Ruth Berry, who leads global policy on Nvidia’s government affairs team, said during a discussion at the Washington-based Middle East Institute . “Infrastructure is really sticky,” she added, referring to continued global demand for Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs), which power much of today’s AI infrastructure. Ms Berry said countries in the region continue to have a "clear vision for where they want to go on AI", which bodes well for future plans. The UAE, which has developed several investment partnerships with the US technology giant, is among the countries pressing ahead. In May, the first shipments of Nvidia's highly sought CPUs and GPUs arrived in the UAE, the country's ambassador announced. In recent years, the UAE has sought to buy and use Nvidia's chips for its AI plans. Stringent export controls aimed at protecting the US lead in AI made such purchases difficult. Washington eventually approved the shipments after the UAE provided security assurances intended to prevent the chips from being accessed by unauthorised parties. But the Iran conflict has raised questions about the Gulf's growing AI infrastructure, particularly after Iranian attacks in the region. Mohammed Soliman, a technology analyst and senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said that the threat of conflict could have an inverse effect, causing countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia to increase their AI investments. Mr Soliman said that Ukraine's ability to withstand Russia's invasion for more than four years could largely be attributed to Ukraine's AI investments and innovations. The country has used AI to improve drone strikes, troop logistics and other facets of battle. "Without AI, Ukraine would have lost the war … war is a function of compute," he said. Governments throughout the Middle East, Mr Soliman continued, have taken note of that. "If you’re thinking about how you’re going to be able to sustain against Iranian aggression, you also have to be thinking about compute," he said. The discussion largely focused on whether US AI technology products would remain influential throughout the Middle East. Mr Soliman said it and China were the two major contenders in this area. He said the recent attacks from Iran would count when it comes to buying decisions, working in favour of the US. "It's been widely reported that China has assisted Iran," Mr Soliman said. He said that the Middle East remains incredibly appealing to the US companies and government as the race for AI dominance heats up. He also said that countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia have an abundance of energy, which is a significant AI prerequisite, along with a geographic advantage. "You need a nearby compute hub that's capable of supporting multiple markets," he said. "They're able to make a financial bet on this infrastructure." Nazak Nikakhtar, an international trade and national security lawyer, said China what could have an advantage in the race against the US. "They're really fast," she said, referring to the speed at which decisions are made in Beijing at the highest levels of government.

title: Sally Rooney can no longer sell books in the UK due to Palestine Action support
description: Award-winning author had pledged to donate proceeds from her books to the banned group
content: Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold ​in ​the UK after she said she planned to use her royalties to ⁠support the banned campaign group Palestine Action. The bestselling author, who is known for novels including Normal People ⁠and Conversations with Friends , has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action , which was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year. Ms Rooney had previously said that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in the UK , in a witness statement to London's High Court that challenged the government's ban. Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Ms Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format". However, it will continue to sell her works elsewhere. "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement. "To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher." Ms Rooney said in a statement: "I ​have made every effort to be honest with ‌the public about my ⁠beliefs and intentions and I ​am wholly prepared to accept the consequences." Palestine Action's sources of funding came under scrutiny after the government suggested it was backed by Iran, but the group has rejected the allegations. The group has continued to seek donations online despite being banned in the UK. Its co-founder Huda Ammori will challenge the decision to ban the group at the Supreme Court next month. The High Court had previously ruled that the ban on the group was unlawful, but the Court of Appeal then overturned this in favour of the Home Office's decision. Thousands of campaigners have been arrested in the UK for expressing support for Palestine Action after the ban. They include Robert Del Naja of the band Massive Attack, who was arrested for the second time last month. Ms Rooney has criticised the arrests, some of which have affected Irish citizens in the UK. Last year she wrote in The Irish Times that they were "selective enforcement of anti-terror law". She highlighted the activities of supporters of another proscribed organisation, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), who had repainted a loyalist mural in north Belfast after it was damaged by a storm last year. “No arrests were made on that basis, nor has the mural been taken down, though the UVF is a proscribed terrorist organisation responsible for the murders of hundreds of civilians," she said. “Palestine Action, proscribed under the same law, is responsible for zero deaths and has never advocated the use of violence against any human being. Why then are its supporters arrested for wearing T-shirts, while murals celebrating loyalist death squads are left untouched?” Ms Rooney is not the first high-profile donor to Palestine Action. James "Fergie" Chambers, an American communist and heir to a multibillion-pound conglomerate, said in a 2023 interview that he was paying Palestine Action’s legal fees.

title: 'Trust the process': Republicans struggle for closing argument before midterms
description: President Trump's checklist of promises now looks more like a litany of liabilities
content: Times are tough for Republican strategists. With the November 3 midterm elections looming, they are desperately seeking a closing argument that explains why Americans should give US President Donald Trump and his party another two years in charge of Congress. In 2024, Mr Trump campaigned on lowering energy prices and inflation, ending “forever” wars, putting America first and clamping down on immigration. Two years on, his checklist of promises looks more like a litany of liabilities. Republicans are now trying to convince Americans that soaring fuel costs will be worth it in the long run, and that the US is enjoying a “Golden Age”, as inflation rises. Even one of Mr Trump's signature achievements – slashing illegal immigration – has become a liability, as voters react with horror to mass round-ups of suspected migrants and the killings of US citizens by masked federal officers. And then, of course, there is Iran. Mr Trump has yet to find an exit from the war he started, and he has turned to none other than Russian President Vladimir Putin for help. A diesel purchase deal with Moscow, which critics say will do little to bring down fuel prices, will also put money into the Kremlin's coffers to help finance its war machine in Ukraine. And a bipartisan group of US senators has warned that the revenues could also aid Russia's security co-operation with Iran – you know, the same country that America is at war with. The not-very-America-First vibe doesn’t give Republicans a lot to work with. They've tried blaming former president Joe Biden for everything amiss in the world. But Mr Biden has been out of office for nearly two years, and by some measures the economy was performing better at the end of his term than it is today. Which brings us to the White House's latest midterms marketing masterstroke. The message: “Trust the process.” “Bottom line, it’s all gonna work out. You know why? It always does," the White House said on X. In other words, the Republican strategy for winning the midterms essentially comes down to magical thinking: Trust us, everything will be fine … because we say it will. It is a curious pitch to make for a president who has often promised better days are just around the corner. People don't want a process, they want results. Mr Trump's promises that Americans would win so much they would become "sick and tired of winning" appear to be falling flat for a critical mass of voters. Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s. In the 2018 midterms, during his previous term in office, the Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives and surrendered 40 seats. Mr Trump's approval rating then was generally in the low 40s. Republicans insist such surveys overcount Democratic support and speak of some epic polling blunders, including the prediction that Hillary Clinton would win the White House when she ran against Mr Trump in 2016. But while polls definitely can get things wrong, that does not amount to a campaign strategy in and of itself. Mr Trump, who has railed against Democrats as "socialists", has promised a $5,000 "dividend" cheque to every adult American, should the Republicans retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives. He doesn't have the independent authority to order such payments, which would cost about $1.2 trillion, and some scholars contend that the offer amounts to a political bribe. Many remember Elon Musk's promise of a $5,000 rebate cheque from all the money the US was going to save through his slashes to the federal workforce, or Mr Trump's vow that tariffs would generate $2,000 reimbursements for citizens. What ended up happening, of course, is the national debt ballooned despite Mr Musk's cuts, while tariffs fuelled a jump in costs for US consumers. Fewer people seem as willing to believe the "cheques are in the post" promises as they were in the past. Meanwhile, Mr Trump still sees himself as the kingmaker who is adored by his party. Yet signs of trouble abound, as vulnerable Republicans quietly try to put some distance between themselves and their leader. In Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed , is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly." It's a striking contrast from the Republican talking point that the economic pain from the war is worth it. Other Republicans are playing down their association with Mr Trump. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for Florida governor, removed eight references to the President, a photograph of the pair together and an “Enact the Trump Agenda” section from his campaign website last month, according to Forbes . Polls also suggest that voters are preoccupied with the economy and the cost of living, with many holding Mr Trump responsible for how those issues are being handled. Aside from its "trust the process" argument, the Republican Party wants to persuade voters that the midterms are a choice between common sense and the Democrats' radical agenda of "men in women's sports" and an "open border". Those old culture war tropes may still resonate for many voters, but they don't help people at the petrol pump or at the supermarket checkout. If the polls are to be believed, and judging by the sorry state of Republican messages, Mr Trump's party is on course for a "shellacking", to repeat the expression Barack Obama used in 2010 after his own midterm losses. Trust the process? For a party struggling to explain why its promises have fallen short, it sounds less like a winning strategy than an admission that it has run out of answers.

title: El Sisi says no changes planned for Egypt's constitution amid rumours of fourth term
description: President's comments will curb speculation that he plans to stay in power beyond the end of his final term in 2030
content: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi said on Wednesday there were no plans to change Egypt 's constitution, after calls by some supporters for him to stay in office after the end of his final term in 2030. But Mr El Sisi appeared to leave the door open for a possible amendment to allow him to stay at the helm, saying Egyptians were the only ones who would decide on any initiative. "The nation has a constitution that we adopted. No one can touch it, no one can touch it," he told a televised gathering of cabinet members and army officers. "So, don't let anyone mess with your heads. The people alone will decide the success or lack thereof of anything that's done." Calls for Mr El Sisi to stay in office beyond 2030 have been made publicly by loyal politicians and social media accounts linked to the government. The campaign has picked up steam in recent months as opposition figures abroad intensified criticism of his policies. Mr El Sisi's comments on Wednesday were his first on the question of constitutional amendments. In office since 2014, the Egyptian leader's final term ends in 2030, by which time he would have served for 16 years. Egypt's constitution is a relatively progressive document adopted in a nationwide referendum in 2014, three years after autocratic president Hosni Mubarak was removed by a popular uprising after nearly 30 years in office. Mr El Sisi owes his current term in office to previous constitutional amendments in 2019, which were adopted in a national referendum. Before the changes, the constitution stipulated that no president could serve more than two four-year terms. The amendments kept the two-term cap but extended the term to six years and, in a clause added for Mr El Sisi's benefit, considered the first of his two terms in office to have begun in 2018, not 2014 when he was first elected. And as was the case in 2018, when he ran against an obscure politician, Mr El Sisi – the latest in a line of military men who ruled Egypt since the monarchy was overthrown in the 1950s – ran again in 2023 against three little-known politicians, winning 89.6 per cent of the vote. Many Egyptians see him as a safe pair of hands at a time when the Middle East is roiled in conflict, with unresolved wars in Gaza, Egypt's neighbour to the east, Sudan, its southern neighbour, and political instability in Libya, on its western border. The fallout from the Iran war – from the on-and-off closure of the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on Tehran's Arab neighbours and strikes on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis – has affected Egypt's economy, increasing its already high energy import bills and badly blocking revenue from the Suez Canal. Supporters of Mr El Sisi praise the stability of Egypt during those challenges, while he repeatedly urges Egyptians to endure their economic hardship and praises their resilience. But critics insist the government's policies are at the root of the country's economic woes, due to what they regard as excessive foreign and domestic borrowing and spending on infrastructure projects that will take years to generate revenue. They also blame the government for not dealing effectively with a decade-old water dispute with Ethiopia that could reduce the country's vital share of the Nile waters. Mr El Sisi rejects the criticism, saying the billions of dollars spent on infrastructure and modern transport, such as a Cairo monorail, a cutting-edge electric train and a new capital, prepare the nation to attract sizable foreign investments. He says Ethiopia saw in the turmoil in Egypt that followed the removal of Mubarak in 2011 a chance to start construction of a massive dam on the Blue Nile, the river's main tributary and source of more than 80 per cent of the water reaching downstream.

title: Alaska LNG project becomes $54bn flashpoint for would-be Asian buyers
description: Trump promotes foreign investment before midterms but investors remain cautious
content: A massive liquefied natural gas project in Alaska has emerged as an unlikely focal point in purported foreign investment, as Asian buyers rush to diversify their supply imports amid disruptions from the Iran war. On Tuesday in Wasilla, a town 70km north of Anchorage, US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 per cent of the LNG from the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Taiwan had committed to investing $4.4 billion to develop the pipeline. The terms of the deal were not immediately clear. Last week, Mr Trump announced a $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska LNG as part of a $200 billion energy package and $350 billion trade deal the two sides struck last year to lower tariffs on Korean imports. South Korea has rejected the claim, saying it has given no firm commitment on the project. “There's no investors other than the US government, and there are no buyers who have committed to signing any sales and purchase agreements,” said Ira Joseph, a global fellow at the Centre on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University. The project hopes to make a final investment decision on the pipeline this year, with a separate one on the export terminal in 2027. One of the dominant factors in the publicly promoted claims are the November 3 midterm elections . Alaska has become a battleground state for control of the US Senate. Mr Trump’s appearance in Wasilla on Tuesday underscored the race’s importance as he seeks to promote energy exports and foreign investment. At the same time, the Alaska LNG project holds big promises, as South-East Asian buyers are seeking to diversify their energy supplies as the Iran war cut off shipments from the region . If Alaska LNG becomes operational, it would drastically reduce the time for delivery of LNG shipments. The journey from Alaska to Japan is more than 9,600km shorter than from the US Gulf Coast, the project's developer said in a 2023 report. For all the promise that Alaska LNG holds, it remains a far-off venture. Development is expected to begin in phases, with targets for the first exports in 2031. Glenfarne Group estimates the project will cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. That means about $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion a tonne a year of capacity, according to a Reuters analysis. “This is an expensive project that's going to take at best a lot of years to sort of come to fruition,” said Rachel Ziemba, founder of risk advisory firm Ziemba Insights. Another possible sticking point is the about 106cm-diameter pipeline that would stretch 1,300km from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, south of Anchorage, running parallel to the existing Trans Alaska Pipeline System for oil. LNG sites in Nikiski would produce 20 million tonnes a year for export and hold a daily capacity of 3.3 billion cubic feet. The pipeline itself – Phase One – is likely to cost between $13.2 billion and $16.9 billion, according to company estimates. “If the gas is sitting right next to the LNG facility, this thing would have been built 40 or 50 years ago, but it's not, and … that's the difference maker in this project,” Mr Joseph said. Investors remain cautious. As of January this year, only six non-binding offtake agreements have been signed totalling 13 million tonnes a year. Another point of friction is competition, with LNG projects in Canada and in America's Gulf Coast also attracting attention. Major players in the Middle East have continued to increase their interest in LNG, but through the Gulf Coast. This summer, Adnoc's XRG boosted its stake in NextDecade's LNG site in Rio Grande, Texas. QatarEnergy began LNG exports from its joint venture with Exxon at the Golden Pass project in March. “It is notable to me that at a time where you know Trump is looking for all the finance he can for this project, that he's not turning to these sources of capital,” Ms Ziemba said.

title: Six Kings Slam tournament in Saudi Arabia featuring Alcaraz and Djokovic postponed due to attacks on Riyadh
description: Star-studded exhibition has been pushed back until late December
content: The Six Kings tennis tournament featuring the likes of Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev in Saudi Arabia has been postponed due to the recent attacks on Riyadh. The exhibition event, where the world's top men's players were due to compete, was scheduled to take place from October 21-24 and shown live on Netflix. But the continuing attacks on Riyadh's airports by Iran-backed Houthi rebels has resulted in the Six Kings Slam – held at the ANB Arena which is around 30km away from the King Khalid International Airport – being pushed back until December 27-30. The other players due to take part were Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Learner Tien. “The decision ⁠reflects Riyadh Season's commitment to ‌delivering sporting events to the highest ‌standards, following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges ⁠associated with hosting ​the tournament ​and their potential ​impact on the ⁠quality of the audience experience,” ⁠organisers said in ​a statement. The tournament, which is in its third edition and awards £1.2 million per player and an extra £3.5m for the winner, was previously won by Jannik Sinner with the Italian beating Alcaraz in the final on both occasions. The decision comes in the same week that three Saudi Pro League fixtures were postponed due to “logistical considerations” after Al Hilal and Nassr, who are based in Riyadh, and the Jeddah teams Ahli and Al Ittihad, were all involved in AFC Champions League matches. Al Nassr's match against Uzbek side Neftchi Fergan – which saw Cristiano Ronaldo score in a 3-1 victory for Ange Postecoglou's side – on Monday was delayed due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence. The match kicked off 20 minutes after it was scheduled to start.
