On Tuesday, golf's Asian Tour said that it is monitoring the ⁠security situation ahead of the Saudi International due to take place ​in Riyadh from November 18 to 21. “Any changes to the schedule will be announced as soon as we have determined the right course of action for our players, fans and partners,” the Asian Tour told Reuters in a statement. “The PIF Saudi International is incredibly important to the Asian Tour as our season finale, however the safety of our players, staff and service teams is always our number one priority.”

title: Sheikh Mohammed and Sheikh Mansour meet to discuss UAE's national development priorities
description: Senior UAE leaders convene at Al Marmoom to review major initiatives and strengthen country's global standing
content: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President, Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai, and Sheikh Mans our bin Zayed , Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, held high-level talks in Dubai on Wednesday, focusing on the UAE's development agenda and future priorities. The meeting at Al Marmoom, Dubai, was also attended by Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance. The leaders reviewed a range of issues of national importance, including major development initiatives aimed at advancing the UAE's comprehensive growth, strengthening its global standing and reinforcing its leadership across sectors. Discussions also covered the latest national developments and priorities, with a focus on improving government performance and accelerating progress to meet the UAE's long-term aspirations and enhance quality of life for its citizens and residents. The leaders emphasised the importance of co-ordinated national efforts in driving the country's progress and prosperity. They highlighted the need to anticipate future trends and convert emerging opportunities into new avenues for growth. The meeting further underscored the importance of building on the UAE's existing achievements and reinforcing its position as a global model for development and leadership, while continuing to advance national priorities and promote the well-being of its people.

title: Zelenskyy in London as Burnham promises delicate Trump diplomacy
description: Ukrainian leader wants stronger European backing as White House and Starlink moves raise doubts over US commitment
content: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London on Wednesday as he attempted to shore up European support for the war . Despite battlefield advances by Ukrainian forces this year, coupled with heavy Russian losses, that position could be undermined after President Donald Trump called for Mr Zelenskyy to be replaced and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel. US intelligence sharing has also appeared to waver. New restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet network disrupted Ukrainian military operations, including its air defence systems on Tuesday night. But Mr Burnham was expected to promise Britain would go “further and faster” in providing financial and military assistance, including accelerating the delivery of lightweight multirole missiles designed to intercept Russia jet-powered drones that travel at 600kph. An escort of Irish Guards stood to attention outside Downing Street as Mr Zelenskyy posed for pictures with the Prime Minister before heading inside for talks. The meeting is possibly the most challenging foreign affairs moment for Mr Burnham early in his premiership as he has to support Ukraine while not angering Mr Trump, as US intelligence support is vital to Kyiv’s war effort. Earlier in parliament he offered “unwavering” support for Ukraine during Prime Minister’s questions. But Mr Burnham was then asked if the US President’s announcements were “yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security”. The Prime Minister replied that this is a “very dark and difficult moment” for Mr Zelensky, who he said was “carrying the heaviest of weights”. But he declined to criticise Mr Trump directly, stating that “what I have to do in my role is try to repair bridges so that the support comes back”. The tricky diplomatic moves came after SpaceX introduced overnight restrictions limiting the speed of some devices connecting to Starlink to 160kph, a move that disrupted a number of Ukrainian military missions, according to presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. Starlink is a critical component of Ukraine’s drone warfare which allows soldiers to guide weapons towards Russian targets, and is also vital to its air defences. Kyiv had allegedly not been informed of the restrictions. Mr Beskrestnov said that “this cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation”. SpaceX has not commented on the apparent restrictions. A barrage of overnight missiles and drones killed three people in Kyiv, while six died in a separate Russian drone strike on a warehouse in Lutsk, in north-western Ukraine.

title: Sheikh Hamdan meets World Economic Forum president to strengthen UAE partnership
description: Deputy PM discusses future leadership and global collaboration with Alois Zwinggi
content: Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, met the president of the World Economic Forum on Wednesday to strengthen ties between the UAE and the global body. Sheikh Hamdan met Alois Zwinggi at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders 2026 in Dubai. Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed also attended the meeting. Discussions centred on the longstanding partnership between the UAE government and the WEF, as well as their shared commitment to shaping the future through international dialogue and collaboration. Sheikh Hamdan reaffirmed the UAE's dedication to expanding international dialogue among experts, innovators and decision makers. He highlighted the significance of more than 700 participants – including decision makers, officials, specialists and young leaders – attending the annual meeting in Dubai, saying it reflected the shared vision of the UAE and the WEF to empower the next generation of leaders. Sheikh Hamdan said the gathering also further reinforced Dubai's standing as a global centre for international initiatives aimed at equipping future leaders to make a greater impact on the world stage. The meeting was attended by senior UAE officials including Mohammed Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs; Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications; Ohood Al Roumi, Minister of State for Government Development and the Future; and Khalfan Belhoul, Chief Executive of the Dubai Future Foundation. The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders brings together emerging leaders from across the public and private sectors to engage with global challenges and opportunities, forming part of the World Economic Forum's broader agenda to foster inclusive and sustainable growth worldwide.

title: Aldar to launch major Dubai villa and townhouse project by end of year
description: Abu Dhabi-listed company to hand over more than 3,000 units in 2026 and up to 4,500 next year, says senior executive
content: Aldar plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. The new project, whose value is not disclosed, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London. It will be the fourth project in Dubai for Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, following the launches of the Haven, Athlon and The Wilds. “It’s another partnership with Dubai Holding , and it's a very large villa community [with] townhouses and also sits above the Blue Line extension,” Mr Emery said. In February, Aldar and Dubai Holding expanded their joint venture announced in 2023 by adding two plots in Dubai to deliver almost 14,000 new homes with a combined gross development value of more than Dh38 billion. The first plot of four million square metres, is along Dubai’s eastern growth corridor opposite Nad Al Sheba. The second plot, on Palm Jebel Ali, will be an ultra-luxury waterfront development of branded and non-branded residences. The new developments are coming even as buyers become cautious due to regional uncertainty driven by the Iran war. Transaction volumes and values fell in the third quarter. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year, while the number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, according to the latest report from Cavendish Maxwell. “The customers are still there for the right product. Now, clearly, the international side of the market is the one that's just slowed a little bit. There’s uncertainty and people are taking their time to have a look. But we still believe in the fundamentals … the products that we have brought to the market have all done really well,” Mr Emery said. Aldar, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, will hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company's launch. The deliveries will go up to 4,500 next year, he said. Among the projects that are expected to be delivered this year are the Sustainable City on Yas Island, and the Grove and Louvre Abu Dhabi residences on Saadiyat Island. The Abu Dhabi-listed company will also hand over its first homes in Dubai next year, at its Haven project near Dubailand. In September, Aldar and Sharjah-based Arada announced a partnership to build housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, with a combined value of about Dh15 billion. The partnership involves a master plan joint venture to create a large-scale mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border and Arada’s acquisition of three residential plots on Yas Island. Aldar will continue to look for new partnerships with established developers, Mr Emery said. “Partnerships is a way that we believe we can diversify the customer offer, because you know if we pick the right partner that has a great proposition, maybe they have a great following with their customers … then it’s good to be able to introduce that to our customers as well,” he said.

title: Calls on UK government to 'come clean' as 4,500 prisoners are set for early release
description: Opposition claims government scheme leaves more criminals laughing at victims
content: UK authorities are using AI tools to drive a controversial early prisoner release scheme that will see some 4,500 people leave before the sentence end date. The scheme has already seen the release of 1,350 people in two tranches in October and will see additional monthly releases through to next summer. The National Audit Office reported on Wednesday on the key role the efficiency gains of AI is playing. It said Justice Transcribe was speeding up probation service decisions in the early release process. The Institute for Government think tank said this weekend the flagship government policy was in endangered by chokepoints in probation. Opposition spokesmen have criticised the government for pursuing the overcrowding policy saying it had left hardened criminals laughing at victims. "Labour said all the prisoners they are freeing would be tagged," said Nick Timothy, the Conservative Party justice spokesman. "Now they refuse to say how many have been, and are covering up the data. I forced them to come to Parliament yesterday but they still wouldn’t answer. "I have called on the Justice Secretary to come clean." In its report the IFG warned that early-release exemptions and shrinking cell margins could "wipe out capacity buffers, forcing emergency measures before new cells are built". "Recent policy changes have put prisons back at risk of running out of spaces, while probation is struggling to manage offenders in the community," it said. The framework of the policy relies heavily on the work of sentence management changes. According to the IFG those released after serving a third of their sentence in prison will be subject to ‘intensive supervision’ in the community for the second third of their sentence. This includes rules on wearing an electronic monitoring tag until they are three fifths of the way through their sentence. It is only in the final third of their sentence that the offenders will not be actively supervised. The NAO report said the AI introduction across the service had left more time available for activities that directly contribute to managing the exiting prisoners and their impact on society. "This makes more time available for activities that directly contribute to public protection and rehabilitation," the statement said.

title: Dubai's Al Satwa Roundabout replacement to halve journey times
description: RTA completes junction and upgrades infrastructure in bid to reduce queues
content: Dubai’s busy Al Satwa Roundabout has been converted into a traffic light-controlled junction to improve vehicle flow and halve journey times. The Roads and Transport Authority has completed the junction and related infrastructure upgrades. These are expected to reduce waiting times and traffic queues by up to 60 per cent during peak hours. The authority said the new design provides a smoother experience for road users and improves traffic flow through the junction. It serves traffic travelling along 2nd December Street towards the Trade Centre and Al Satwa, as well as in the opposite direction, easing movement between key roads and the area’s smaller streets. The design also improves bus journeys, reduces delays and strengthens integration between the road network and public transport. The junction has an important role in connecting Al Satwa with nearby districts such as Al Bada’a, Al Jafiliya, Al Hudaiba and Jumeirah. The new junction is part of other road improvements in the area, including the World Trade Centre Roundabout Development. Together, these projects will improve the road network, and connect Dubai World Trade Centre, Sheikh Zayed Road and nearby routes, and help spread out traffic to reduce congestion at busy locations.

title: Families seek justice as trial of English Channel tragedy mastermind opens in Erbil
description: Relatives of Iraqi Kurds who died trying to reach Britain in 2021 attend proceedings of alleged smuggler linked to crossing
content: The trial has begun in Erbil of an alleged Iraqi-Kurdish people smuggler accused of involvement in the 2021 English Channel disaster, in a case linked to investigations and prosecutions in France and the UK. Bashdar, whose real name is Hajar Mina Abdullah, is accused of playing a role in the smuggling operation behind the November 2021 crossing, during which 31 people died attempting to reach Britain from France. He was led into the courtroom in handcuffs by police officers and seated at a stand on the right-hand side. Wearing a beige shirt and a yellow vest marked “Erbil Police” on the back, he appeared well groomed and walked confidently. “Why have they fattened him up like that?” one woman sitting with the families at the back of the courtroom asked as he entered. Another woman, dressed in a black veil and black dress, began to cry at the sight of him. The case in Iraq follows proceedings in France against 14 men accused of involvement in organising the fatal crossing. A Paris court convicted 13 defendants in September, handing down sentences for offences including manslaughter and migrant smuggling. The disaster was the deadliest migrant shipwreck in the English Channel. Most of those who died were Iraqi Kurds, and the tragedy prompted renewed scrutiny of the criminal networks organising dangerous journeys to Britain. The UK’s response to the disaster was examined by the Cranston Inquiry , an independent public inquiry that published its final report in February 2026. It concluded that some of the deaths were avoidable, citing failures in the response by British and French authorities. It revealed the systemic problems in the search-and-rescue response, including communication failures and missed opportunities to intervene. Bashdar was arrested in Iraq in October 2022. His case is part of wider efforts to pursue those suspected of organising the dangerous crossing between France and the UK. Bashdar is being tried according to Article 8 of Iraq’s law on human trafficking. According to the law, if an act of human trafficking results in the death of the victim, the offender is punished by death. The Kurdistan region, UK and France have co-operated on efforts to tackle the smuggling networks responsible for Channel crossings, with investigations into the 2021 disaster spanning multiple countries. The UK has sought to tackle Channel crossings further upstream through an international working group involving Iraq and the Kurdistan region, focusing on disrupting smuggling networks before migrants reach Europe. The issue has become increasingly prominent in British politics, with small-boat arrivals a major focus of debate over border security and immigration. The trial in Erbil brings the case back to the Kurdistan region, where many of the victims and their families came from. Zana Mamand Mohammed, whose brother Twana made the journey and whose body was never found, has been leading the efforts by family members in the pursuit of justice. “The trial currently under way in Erbil is precisely the reason why Bashdar has not been prosecuted in France – the same person cannot be tried twice for the same crime in two different countries,” French lawyers Matthieu Chirez and Thomas Ricard told The National in a joint statement. “The victims' families there are following the proceedings very closely and remain deeply affected by what is yet another step in this legal process, which began almost five years ago,” they added. Before entering the courtroom, Mr Mohammed and the other family members gathered in a circle, encouraging one another ahead of the proceedings. He reminded them why they had come, as several women wept while he spoke. Mr Mohammed has emerged as the families’ main advocate, leading their fight for justice and accountability for the deaths of their loved ones. Inside the courtroom, the judge called the relatives forward one by one, forming a line just metres from the man they accuse of being responsible for their loss. When they had all taken their seats, Mr Mohammed returned to the front of the court to set out the case against Bashdar, recounting how he lost his brother and other relatives in the Channel disaster. Beside the pillar that partially obscured Bashdar from the audience sat his two lawyers. None of his family members attended the hearing. One row of seats was filled with university students, young people studying for a future at home as the court heard how others of their generation had risked everything to find a better one abroad. Their presence offered a stark contrast between those preparing to build a life in the Kurdistan region and those who had left in search of economic opportunities elsewhere, never to return. Mr Mohammed told the judges the story of how his brother ended up involved in the tragedy as the woman in black began to cry more loudly. Originally from Hajiawa, a town in Ranya district, Twana was 18 when he got in touch with Bashdar, also known as Bashdar Ranya at the time. Mr Mohammed said he left $3,200 as a deposit at a money shop, as instructed by Bashdar. On August 10 he left Erbil for Istanbul by plane after obtaining a Turkish visa. On October 8, he left Italy by yacht and arrived on October 12. He arrived in France on October 25, and on the night of November 23-24, when he was crossing from France to Britain, the incident occurred. “They told them they would use a good boat,” Mr Mohammed told the court. The boat they were put on was only supposed to hold up to 25 people, but there were 34 on board, he added. The life vests they were provided with were also inadequate. Rasul Farka told The National that his son Pshtiwan and the others on board had their life vests torn when the boat capsized. Pshtiwan was 18 when he left, and his body is among the four that were never found. Mr Farka said his son had gone to try to earn money for his sister Srwa’s heart surgery. His youngest daughter had been born with a heart defect. “Here, he was an innocent man and didn't have problems with anyone. God willing, he will return,” she said, appearing to hold on to hope that her brother may still be alive. Mr Farka and his wife brought photos of their son to show the court. The judges did not sentence Bashdar on Monday, and no date has been set for subsequent sessions. However, proceedings were initiated against the money shop that Mr Mohammed had mentioned, which demonstrated the link between him and Bashdar. Mr Mohammed told the prosecutor they had never spoken personally. Bashdar’s defence does not deny his involvement as a smuggler but says he did not place the victims on the boat . As he was escorted out of the courtroom, he appeared to be angry and mumbled to himself. After the session, Afrasia Ahmed Mohammed's parents arrived, too late to catch the hearing. “She just got out of surgery and she is like this because of the loss of her son,” Mr Farka said of Afrasia's mother, who is elderly, is unable to walk or stand by herself and had a bandage on her eye. His father showed a photo of his son, who was 27 at the time, as Mr Farka broke down in tears. Pshtiwan, Twana and Afrasia had travelled together. The National’ s previous reporting has traced the smuggling networks linked to the Channel tragedy to Ranya, a town in Iraqi Kurdistan that has emerged as a hub for people-smuggling operations. An investigation last year showed how money-exchange businesses in the town, known as hawalas, were used to facilitate payments between migrants and smuggling networks operating across Europe. “Today, we are very happy that the smuggler was tried at the Erbil court. We are very happy, and we hope that he will face a severe punishment,” Srwa said. Sunniva Rose contributed from Paris

title: 'World’s oldest known shipwreck' lost more than 4,000 years ago found off Turkey
description: Ceramic jars recovered near Kekova Island indicate trade links with the Levant during the age of Egypt’s pyramids
content: Archaeologists have identified an ancient shipwreck off Turkey's Mediterranean coast, dating back as far as 4,700 years, which they believe could be the oldest yet discovered. More than 30 ceramic storage jars and three stone anchors have been found near Kekova Island in Antalya, about 30 metres beneath the surface. The pottery suggests the vessel dates to between 4,400 and 4,700 years ago, during the Early Bronze Age. Although none of the ship’s wooden structure has survived, the team of archaeologists has been able to estimate its age by comparing the shapes and decoration of its pottery with objects discovered at other archaeological sites. Without surviving timber, radiocarbon dating cannot be used to establish when the ship sank. Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Turkey’s Culture and Tourism Minister, announced details of the continuing excavation on Wednesday and spoke of the world’s oldest known shipwreck. The vessel is believed to have been about 10 metres long and used to transport goods across the Mediterranean. The wreck was first documented during an underwater survey by Akdeniz University in 2024. Two jars were recovered for examination in 2024 and 2025, before further excavations began this year under the Antalya Museum Directorate. A preliminary study published in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology in July by archaeologists Hakan Oniz and Ceyda Oztosun suggested the ship had been travelling from east to west when it sank. The study also noted that the three anchors found in the surrounding area had not yet been conclusively linked to the vessel. The oldest previously known shipwreck was discovered near the Greek island of Dokos in 1975. The Hellenic Institute of Marine Archaeology dates its ceramic cargo to around 2200BC, later than the dates proposed for the Kekova finds. The Kekova discovery could also provide evidence of trading connections between the Levant, Egypt and Anatolia during the Early Bronze Age. “Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were probably produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley,” Ersoy said. Similar vessels have been discovered near the Egyptian pyramids at Giza, Saqqara and Abusir, as well as at Troy and on the island of Crete. Archaeologists believe the ship may have departed from a port on the Levantine coast and been travelling towards Troy or Crete. Some of the recovered jars contain residues that could help establish what the vessel was transporting. Karin Sowada, an archaeologist at Macquarie University in Australia who examined the finds, told the BBC she was surprised by how much material had survived inside them. Some jars were still intact and contained a glossy, viscous residue. Analysis is continuing to determine whether the containers held olive oil, wine, tree resins or other goods. Sowada said the jars could also have been emptied and reused, so the surviving material may come from more than one use of the containers. Another jar, marked with nine symbols and featuring two holes in its body, may have served a different purpose. Ersoy said it could have been used as a churn for making cheese or butter, suggesting sailors may have produced some of their own food during lengthy voyages. Turkey’s Mediterranean coast has previously yielded several important Bronze Age vessels, including the Uluburun shipwreck , which sank around 1300BC carrying copper, tin, glass and other commodities. The artefacts recovered from Kekova are undergoing conservation and further scientific examination. Ersoy said the finds would be displayed at the planned Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya.

title: Dubai's rainwater drainage capacity to increase by 700 per cent on completion of Tasreef project
description: City also aims to plant 3.5 million trees to increase green space
content: Dubai’s rainwater drainage capacity is set to increase sevenfold under a Dh30 billion infrastructure project designed to protect the emirate from extreme weather and serve its growing population for the next century. The new system will be capable of handling more than 20 million cubic metres of water a day and will include more than 6,500km of drainage networks, alongside more than 5,000km of sewage networks, according to plans outlined by Dubai Municipality. Marwan bin Ghalita, director general of Dubai Municipality, said the Tasreef scheme was launched in 2024 after the country experienced widespread flooding caused by unprecedented rainfall in April of that year. Rather than simply repairing the damage, authorities opted for a long-term solution to strengthen Dubai’s resilience against future storms. “Dubai did not simply stop to assess the damage or look for solutions. It took a swift and bold decision to begin a drainage programme designed to serve the city for the next 100 years,” Mr bin Ghalita said. In June 2025, the municipality completed a Dh277m sewerage and rainwater drainage network in Nad Al Sheba, while in April this year, the drainage network in Al Quoz Creative Zone was completed . The Tasreef project, which is due to be completed in 2033, is a continuation of drainage projects launched by Dubai in 2019, covering the Expo Dubai area, Al Maktoum International Airport City and Jebel Ali. The new projects will serve vital areas including Nad Al Hamar, and around Dubai International Airport, Garhoud, Rashidiya, Al Quoz, Zabeel, Al Wasl, Jumeirah and Al Bada’a. Speaking at the Mohammed bin Rashid Leadership Forum, Mr bin Ghalita outlined how Dubai was investing in infrastructure, AI and modern construction methods to improve residents’ quality of life and prepare for further urban expansion. The presentation also featured Saeed, Dubai Municipality’s virtual spokesman, who outlined a vision for the emirate’s infrastructure and public services in 2033 by adopting technologies such as 3D printing, robotic construction systems, modular building methods and AI. Its Integrated Waste Management Strategy 2040 includes converting waste into energy, while the municipality is moving towards smart operational systems that use robots for cleaning operations and autonomous cleaning vehicles in collaboration with the Roads and Transport Authority. Dubai is also developing a comprehensive digital twin of the city and a control centre that uses real-time data to monitor operations and support decision-making. Mr bin Ghalita said the city’s achievements are driven by the vision of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai. “Dubai is a city of action” is the philosophy that has enabled the emirate to continue delivering results, he said. Dubai’s greening programme aims to plant 3.5 million trees and increase green and cultivated areas to 187 square kilometres by 2040. The municipality expects annual visits to parks to reach 95 million as it expands public spaces for walking, exercise and recreation. Food safety is another priority. The presentation said municipal teams inspected more than 577,000 food consignments annually, representing approximately 2,706 million food products. Co-operation with government entities, including Dubai Customs, is helping make inspections faster and more precise, it said. Initiatives including DM Check and 'Montaji' use digital tools and artificial intelligence to support food safety monitoring. Mr bin Ghalita said the progress outlined in the presentation reflected the combined efforts of municipal teams and the emirate’s leadership. “Everything you have seen today is the result of the combined efforts of our teams,” he said, adding that a clear vision and collective commitment are essential to delivering Dubai’s long-term ambitions. “What we are building and developing today is what Dubai will be in the future. Our aim is to make Dubai a city with advanced infrastructure, smart and ready to face challenges.”

title: Addison Lee taxi founder takes near 50% hit on London mansion sale
description: John Griffin bought property near Regent’s Park for £20.7 million but has sold it for £11.5 million 13 years later
content: The founder of London taxi company Addison Lee has sold a mansion overlooking London’s Regent’s Park for little more than half the price he paid 13 years ago, as prime London property sales dry up. John Griffin, who sold his business to the Carlyle Group for about £300 million ($464 million) in 2013, offloaded the property on the park’s western perimeter for £11.5 million at the beginning of October, people with knowledge of the transaction told Bloomberg . Mr Griffin, who last month lost a drawn-out battle with UK tax authorities, paid £20.7 million for the property in 2013, filings show. The six-bedroom home, part of a Regency-era terrace designed by architect John Nash, has repeatedly been offered for sale in recent years. A 2021 listing, describing the home as among the grandest and most prestigious in London , priced the property at £32 million. Following a series of reductions, the property was subsequently withdrawn from the market before being re-listed this year for £13.5 million, Bloomberg 's sources said. Earlier this year, the mystery owner of another grand property in Regent's Park , The Holme, sold it for a profit of about £56 million ($75 million) less than two years after bringing it out of receivership for £139 million. However, that “flip” was at odds with the rest of the UK capital's prime market. The cut-price sale of Mr Griffin's property is the latest sign of the malaise gripping prime London real estate, which has seen the city’s priciest properties buffeted by a series of tax changes, and economic and political shocks. The recovery of nominal price growth for London’s most expensive properties is not expected to take place until 2028, according to a forecast by Savills. Estate agent JLL’s residential research data showed that between July and September, 457 homes worth more than £5 million were sold in central London, 11 per cent fewer than in the previous quarter. It found that the prime London sales market remained subdued, with prices declining 7.2 per cent over the past 12 months. It said that the UK capital’s prime houses had lost a quarter of their value since a peak in 2014. Property analysts LonRes found there had been a summer slowdown in the prime London market, with average sale prices 7.9 per cent lower in July than the previous year and 5.7 per cent lower than the pre-Covid period. Transactions in the market above £5 million were 20 per cent lower in July than the same month last year. New instructions in this market decreased by 30.3 per cent over the same period, with the number of prime homes on the market 5.2 per cent lower than a year earlier. LonRes said standout property sales over the summer included a £40 million five-bedroom home in Belgravia and a £25.9 million six-bedroom property in Notting Hill. Nick Gregori, head of research at LonRes, said July’s activity was low even for the time of year. “Adding a new prime minister and continuing global uncertainty to the mix has resulted in a subdued prime London market, with the super-prime segment particularly affected,” he said. “The key indicator is simply the number of transactions relative to new instructions, under offers and existing stock – it remains stubbornly low. Uncertainty and a lack of urgency, driven in part by low expectations of future price growth, continue to hinder any potential recovery. “At the top end of the market fewer people need to buy or sell so the issues are amplified. Last year we saw a prolonged slowdown as pre-budget tax speculation started in the summer and carried on all the way to the end of the year. “This year, new PM Andy Burnham has attempted to quash speculation around property tax reforms, but it may not be enough to boost sentiment in the super-prime market.” Mr Griffin has been in a long-running battle with His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs over his tax residency, with the entrepreneur arguing he should qualify for non-domiciled status between 2013-2020 that would have exempted overseas earnings. Non-dom status has since been scrapped by the government. A provisional agreement was reached with the buyer of the Regent’s Park property this summer, before the tribunal ruling in September, one of the people familiar with the process said. The sale eventually closed less than a month after the tribunal’s verdict. It is not clear whether the decision to accept the cut-price offer was linked to the tax ruling. A representative for Mr Griffin declined to comment.

title: Diesel shortage to persist into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA warns
description: Depleted inventories and weak Middle East exports threaten to prolong fuel squeeze
content: The global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war is set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories unlikely to recover until the second half of 2027, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday. Supplies of gas oil, which contains diesel and heating oil, will fall short of demand in the fourth quarter, even as refineries increase output towards the yea's end, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly oil market report. Without a recovery in refined-product exports from the Middle East, further cuts in consumption and the “heavy economic costs these will entail” may be needed to balance the market, it warned. Wholesale diesel prices surged to record highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US last month and exceeded $200 in Singapore. Prices have since eased but remain nearly double crude benchmarks and prewar levels. US diesel pump prices topped $6 a gallon for the first time in September, up about 70 per cent since the Iran war began, the IEA said. The shortage reflects a sharp decline in shipments from two major suppliers. Combined net gas oil exports from the Middle East and Russia plunged more than 60 per cent annually to 820,000 barrels per day last month, a loss of 1.3 million bpd. Gulf export routes remain constrained, while Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged Russian oil refineries. Higher shipments from the US and China have failed to offset the losses. Inventories offer little relief ahead of winter. US diesel stocks ended September at a 14-year seasonal low, while European commercial gas oil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July. On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflict. Gulf crude exports rebounded sharply last month, rising by 4.4 million bpd to 13.9 million bpd, more than three quarters of prewar levels. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz climbed to 10.9 million bpd, supported by increased ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. However, refined products and liquefied petroleum gas shipments have recovered much more slowly, remaining below half their prewar volumes. The IEA warned that the recovery remains fragile following the bombing of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline on September 11 and an escalation in Houthi attacks on regional energy infrastructure and shipping throughout this month. North Sea Dated crude, a physical oil benchmark, was trading near $134 a barrel when the report was prepared, reflecting mounting supply risks and record freight costs. Global observed oil inventories stood 509 million barrels below prewar levels at the end of September, leaving markets increasingly exposed to more disruption. The IEA cut its 2027 oil demand forecast by 630,000 bpd and downgraded its global economic growth outlook by 0.4 percentage points to 3 per cent, as central banks raise interest rates to contain war-driven inflation. Global oil consumption is now expected to rebound by two million bpd next year, but remain 620,000 bpd below 2025 levels. For 2026, demand is forecast to fall by 2.6 million bpd to 102.4 million bpd, with diesel accounting for about a quarter of the decline. The agency also trimmed its global supply forecast for this year by 60,000 bpd to 100.7 million bpd, a decline of 5.8 million bpd from 2025. Output is projected to rebound by 7.7 million bpd in 2027, although recovery remains vulnerable to renewed disruption in the Gulf.

title: 'Minimise catastrophes': UAE's AI minister highlights dangers of autonomous arms
description: Omar Al Olama says major powers must come to consensus on regulating use of AI in destructive systems
content: The UAE's artificial intelligence minister has said there must be worldwide consensus on the use of AI in controlling weapon systems. Omar Al Olama , Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, said there was an urgent need for countries such as the US, Russia and China to agree whether AI should be used when it comes to the deployment of autonomous weapons. “If you're going to talk about AI deploying a rocket or a bomb or sending a fighter jet to destroy a school or do certain things, we haven't been able to come to a global consensus to stop that,” he said. “There are certain fronts of AI that need to be regulated and globally everyone's calling for it again, autonomous systems that are being used in the military to kill people. That's something that we should all agree [needs to be regulated].” Mr Al Olama was speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, hosted by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and the government of Dubai. He said it is important that AI companies are accountable for ensuring sufficient guardrails are in place to prevent the military misuse of the technology. “It's important for us to put the right systems, to invest in understanding what could possibly go wrong,” he said. “We won't get everything right, but we need to make sure that we minimise the catastrophic events and we try to work with each other to ensure that we know exactly what's going to come out of this.” In July, The National reported that UK foreign secretary at the time, Yvette Cooper, said AI could become the “greatest security challenge of the next decade” and called for international co-operation to stamp out the risks. Her call was backed by UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres. Ms Cooper drew parallels between AI and efforts around nuclear safety in the wake of the Second World War and the atomic bombing of the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Referring to sentiments shared in a new book by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, Mr Al Olama said trust is the backbone and true currency of the UAE – and should be the same for AI. “The challenge that we have is it's going to be extremely easy for us to lose trust, but very hard for us to gain it back when it comes to agentic systems,” Mr Al Olama said. “If the government takes one wrong decision, you lose a lot of that currency – you lose a lot of that trust. Once we have one breakthrough event where AI exits the sandbox and goes and harms people, I think it's going to take a long time for us to regain that trust.” He said the UAE is doing what it can to maintain public trust in its use of AI, for example through a government-wide control tower. “We have an agentic control tower on the federal UAE side and every agent [in the country] needs to log in and plug into the control tower,” he said. This provides oversight of agentic AI used in government bodies and constantly assesses the value of the service. The UAE has participated in high-level discussions such as the G20, the G7 and the UN General Assembly but the conversations about AI have yet to lead to any conclusive global action on applying guardrails, said Mr Al Olama. "We haven't invested enough, as governments collectively, to create a global system of consensus that ensures that we all agree to put guardrails. There needs to be action." Countries have been working on securing their own AI infrastructure to be self-reliant, building local data centres and servers. Mr Al Olama sees countries building their own models in the future. “Governments are not going to be at the mercy of a company or at the mercy of a specific group of people,” he said. “The challenge is if everyone can deploy AI on their own infrastructure in their own way, that would create a lot more avenues of things going off the rails and harming people. But it also means that they're going to understand exactly what they can and cannot do with these tools, and they are responsible for it.”

title: UAE-backed GlobalFoundries to run two chip plants under $21bn US-Japan deal
description: US government to take additional 4% equity stake in company
content: Japan is set to invest up to $21 billion in two chip-production plants in New York state that will be operated jointly by GlobalFoundries and the US government, the semiconductor manufacturer said on Wednesday. In a separate agreement, the Commerce Department will take a 4 per cent equity stake in the company, bringing the US government's stake to 7 per cent, chief executive Tim Breen told Reuters. The company is majority owned by Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company. The move is part of a deal struck last year, under which US tariffs on Japanese imports were lowered from 25 per cent to 15 per cent while Japan will invest $550 billion in the US economy . “This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the United States and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” Mr Breen said. Shares in GlobalFoundries were trading 4.9 per cent higher at $48.99 each as of 10am ET. Under the agreement, Japan will provide all the capital while GlobalFoundries will input its technological and manufacturing expertise, and operational capacities. The company makes integrated circuits on silicon wafers designed to help support AI and high-performance computing, communications infrastructure, and applications for aerospace and defence. The deal comes with an initial investment of about $10 billion to boost the construction of a new 300mm semiconductor manufacturing plant – or “fab” – expected to come online in 2029, with an additional $10 billion to fund a second fab. The company said the first fab will add about 900,000 of the 300mm wafers to annual US manufacturing capacity when fully operational, with a second factory adding about the same. GlobalFoundries also agreed with the Commerce Department to amend its existing award under the Chips Act to reallocate $955 million and accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium and advanced packaging at its sites in the US states of New York and Vermont. The announcement comes about a week after GlobalFoundries announced a $2 billion manufacturing agreement with TSMC.

title: How this year’s Nobel Prize in economics helps us understand the Gulf economies
description: The key to the region’s post-oil future lies in millions of individual choices
content: This year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded to an American duo – Prof Robert Hall of Stanford University and Prof Michael Woodford of Columbia University – for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their research emphasised that keeping the economy on a steady path requires understanding how ordinary businesses and consumers make decisions at an individual level rather than treating them as a homogenous whole. The insights provided by their work could help us understand the potential trajectory of the Gulf economies as they continue to diversify away from oil. In fact, the energy policies pursued by Arab oil-exporting countries during the 1970s contributed to the genesis of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work, but the story begins much earlier. Before the interwar period of the early 20 th century, the kind of macroeconomic policy that is pursued by governments around the world today to stabilise their economies was essentially absent. Policymakers perceived the role of economic authorities very narrowly: balance the state budget and ensure liquidity in the financial system by managing the money supply and overseeing banks. A key reason for this limited, self-imposed mandate was the lack of macroeconomic data, such as gross domestic product, consumer price inflation and unemployment figures. In other words, even if governments had a theory of how to intervene in the economy to soften the boom-and-bust cycle, they lacked the information needed to put it into practice. Things changed between the First and Second World Wars for two reasons. On the one hand, the deepest economic crisis in modern history struck in 1929, making it essential for scholars and policymakers to develop methods of stabilising the economy. On the other hand, governments began collecting macroeconomic data systematically, equipping themselves with the tools needed for active macroeconomic management. This process accelerated during the 1960s and 1970s, as the substantial expansion in data availability was complemented by advances in computing technology that enabled sophisticated statistical analysis. As a result, on the eve of the first oil shock in 1973 , economic authorities around the world were well-versed in collecting macroeconomic data, as well as using fiscal and monetary instruments to smooth the economy’s peaks and troughs. Crucially, policymakers relied on historical statistical relationships to guide their interventions. One influential example was the Phillips Curve , which linked higher inflation to lower unemployment. Suppose historical data showed unemployment averaging 6 per cent when inflation was 2 per cent, but only 4 per cent when inflation was 4 per cent. Accordingly, when unemployment was actually 6 per cent and this was considered undesirably high, policymakers might loosen monetary policy through interest rate cuts to push inflation towards 4 per cent, expecting unemployment to fall towards 4 per cent as well. This approach assumed that the historical relationship would remain reliable when policymakers deliberately tried to exploit it. However, the oil crisis of the 1970s exposed the inadequacies of this approach and set the stage for Prof Hall and Prof Woodford to contribute to a paradigm shift in economics. The tipping point was the phenomenon of “stagflation”: inflation and unemployment rising simultaneously, in direct contradiction to the conventional interpretation of the Phillips Curve. This left economic authorities in oil-importing countries bereft of ideas. Prof Hall and Prof Woodford were part of a new cohort of economists who went back to basics. Rather than taking historical relationships between macroeconomic variables at face value, they recognised that each macroeconomic variable represents an aggregation of millions of microeconomic decisions. For example, aggregate consumption across an economy is the sum of individual households’ consumption decisions. Accordingly, to understand how a macroeconomic variable behaves and how it relates to other macroeconomic variables, we must first understand the relationships between the underlying microeconomic variables from which these aggregate measures are derived. Unemployment provides a good illustration. Economists must not treat economy-wide joblessness as the starting point for their statistical analysis. Instead, they must understand how individual members of the labour force and businesses make employment decisions and then build their analysis from the ground up. The result of this novel way of thinking was a new generation of economic models with two features that their predecessors lacked. First, they helped explain the phenomenon of stagflation and provided clear reasons for its occurrence, including the role of the energy shocks of the 1970s. Second, they offered governments a new set of tools for stabilising the economy. As the global financial crisis of 2008 demonstrated, the problem was by no means solved. Nevertheless, Prof Hall, Prof Woodford, their contemporaries and their successors have continued to advance our understanding of these issues. In the context of the Gulf economies, the legacy of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford can be seen clearly in several aspects of macroeconomic policy. One of the most salient is the challenge of maintaining a sustainably high rate of economic growth. There is growing recognition that aggregate economic expansion depends on innovation at the level of small and medium-sized enterprises . Gulf governments understand that they must work from the bottom up rather than rely on fleeting relationships between observed economic growth rates and other macroeconomic variables. In this regard, the subsequent work of other Nobel laureates – such as Paul Romer, Peter Howitt and Philippe Aghion – has been instrumental in shaping the region’s growth-enhancing policies, including subsidies for research and development and support for venture capital. Another illustration of the influence of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work is the Gulf currencies’ pegs to the US dollar (with the exception of the Kuwaiti dinar). These arrangements reflect the belief that investors and consumers are forward-looking decision-makers who value the certainty afforded by fixed exchange rates. They might be far more reluctant to spend and invest if Gulf currencies were to adopt a free-floating regime that exposed them to exchange-rate risk. For the regional economies , the enduring lesson of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work is that effective macroeconomic policy begins with understanding how households and businesses make decisions. As diversification progresses, policymakers will do well to ensure that their reforms encourage people to invest, innovate and create jobs while providing a credible framework for economic stability. The region’s success will ultimately depend on translating ambitious national strategies into millions of individual decisions that collectively sustain prosperity beyond oil.

title: Gold worth millions seized in three smuggling bids on UAE-Delhi routes
description: Seized goods were hidden in bags and socks and under aircraft seats
content: Three separate gold smuggling attempts from the UAE to India have been foiled in recent weeks by customs officials at Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi. Officials recovered gold concealed inside trolley bag linings, hidden in passengers' socks and disguised as silver chains. In the biggest case, officials seized 6.5kg of gold valued at around Dh3.8 million. The accused sprayed the gold chains with silver and black paint and hid them under seats on Emirates flight EK-514 from Dubai to Delhi. Airport police arrested eight passengers and remanded them to judicial custody. On October 10, customs officers intercepted a passenger arriving from Sharjah and recovered 241g of 99.31 per cent pure gold. The passenger moulded the gold and hid it as wire linings in the corners of two trolley bags. A video posted by Delhi Customs shows an official cutting through the seams of the passenger's red bags to extract the rod-like gold. The recovered gold was valued at approximately Dh149,000. Customs seized the gold, and further investigation is under way. On the same day, customs officers at Terminal 3 intercepted an Indian passenger arriving from Muscat on Oman Air flight WY-241. The passenger had travelled from Dubai to Muscat on connecting flight WY-612 on October 9. A personal search found two rectangular pouches containing gold paste concealed inside his socks. The pouches weighed 725g gross, including wrapping and concealment material. After finding gold in his socks, officials also recovered a 587g gold bar. A karatometer test confirmed 100 per cent purity. Customs assessed the gold’s tariff value at approximately Dh323,000 and its market value at approximately Dh364,000. The passenger told investigators the gold was brought from Dubai and concealed to avoid declaring it and paying customs duty. Customs seized the gold under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962. Delhi Customs has reiterated its vigilance against smuggling and its commitment to strengthening enforcement at the country’s busiest international airport. According to a Reuters report in July, unofficial gold inflows in India have risen since the government raised import tariffs on the precious metal earlier this year. The World Gold Council said grey market inflows and the disruption they cause are hurting organised players. India, the world's biggest gold consumer after China, more than doubled import tariffs to 15 per cent on May 13 to curb demand, cut the trade deficit and ​ease pressure on the currency. India's net gold imports fell 23 per cent year-on-year to 98.1 tonnes in the June quarter, the lowest quarterly level since September ​2020, when Covid lockdowns curbed demand, the WGC said in ​a report.

title: Khaldoon Al Mubarak meets China's Wang Yi to strengthen bilateral ties
description: UAE presidential envoy holds talks with Chinese foreign minister in Beijing to boost co-operation
content: Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Presidential Special Envoy to China and Chairman of the Executive Affairs Authority, travelled to Beijing this week for high-level talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. Mr Al Mubarak met Mr Wang in the Chinese capital on Tuesday, as part of a trip aimed at deepening the UAE-China Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two delegations reviewed bilateral relations under the framework of the partnership, which has served as the foundation for growing co-operation. Both parties exchanged views on issues of shared interest, with particular emphasis placed on the importance of sustained co-ordination and close consultation between Abu Dhabi and Beijing. The talks were attended by Hussain Al Hammadi, UAE ambassador to China, along with senior officials from both sides. China remains one of the UAE's most significant trading partners, and the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, established in 2018, has provided a structured platform for co-operation spanning trade, investment, technology and energy.

title: Saudi Crown Prince meets Iraqi PM in Riyadh after deadly Houthi airport attack
description: Ali Al Zaidi's visit is the first by a foreign leader since attack on King Khalid International Airport
content: Saudi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman received Iraq's Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi in Riyadh on Wednesday, in the first visit by a foreign leader to the Saudi capital since a deadly Houthi attack on its airport . The Saudi Press Agency (Spa) published footage and pictures of the meeting between the Crown Prince and Mr Al Zaidi. It said they “discussed regional developments and co-ordinated efforts to address them in a way that strengthens regional security and stability.” “The Crown Prince reaffirmed the Kingdom’s commitment to strengthening co-operation between the two countries across various fields, particularly security co-ordination,” it said. Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people. The airport has come under attack four times, ​including Saturday's attack, which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade. Authorities have closed the airport until October ​17, and airlines have cancelled ‌flights to Saudi Arabia. It is not known how Mr Al Zaidi travelled to the country. Mr Al Zaidi expressed the Iraqi government’s condemnation of the attack on King Khalid Airport and all harm inflicted on civilians, describing such acts as a threat to regional security and stability, his office said in a statement. He reaffirmed Iraq’s position that its territory should not be used as a launch pad for any attacks on Saudi Arabia or other countries. The kingdom said drone attacks in July had come from Iraqi territory. The meeting also reviewed Iraqi-Saudi relations and ways to strengthen co-operation across various fields, notably on security matters. The Saudi Crown Prince offered the kingdom's support for the Iraqi government’s efforts to promote dialogue and achieve stability in the region. In an opinion piece published in the Saudi-owned Al Sharq Al Awsat newspaper on Tuesday, Mr Al Zaidi said Iraqi-Saudi relations hold particular strategic importance, given the political and economic weight of both countries, their Arab ties and their shared security interests. The two countries have made tangible progress in rebuilding trust and opening channels of co-operation, providing a foundation for a more advanced phase of bilateral relations, he said. Iraq and Saudi Arabia can now usher in a new phase of closer ties and move towards partnership and joint planning, he added. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in ⁠support of the government in 2015, fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring ⁠sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year. Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept along the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab Al Mandeb strait. The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war ​casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines. The UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month. “WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children,” the WFP said in a statement.

title: Under siege: Taiz isolated and afraid as Houthis and Yemeni forces fight over city
description: Wheat and flour could run out in less than three weeks, the UN has warned
content: Medical warehouses are unsafe and inaccessible, fuel is not arriving, fleeing is not an option, and food is simply running out. The 800,000 people in the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen are largely isolated, with all roads leading in and out blocked for the past three days. Taiz was already struggling for food before full-scale war returned to Yemen, and the UN has warned that wheat and flour could now run out in less than three weeks. Speaking to The National , an aid worker in the suburbs who tracks violations by the Houthi rebels and Yemeni government forces said people were unable to flee. “People cannot leave. They are afraid, even of speaking,” he said. “Whatever little does manage to enter is being taken over by bandits.” As supplies dwindle, prices have skyrocketed. Saeed Saif, a co-ordinator for Taiz and Yemen's west coast with the UN Population Fund, said traders had “hiked up prices” during the crisis. “Food prices have gone up by more than 50 per cent since the escalation,” he told The National from Aden. The UN and other international organisations have pulled staff out of the province due to security risks. Mr Saif was in Taiz until September 18. People have been asking family and friends outside the city for help. But some of these requests cannot be met, and the situation is only becoming more desperate. “We had sent some fuel to people who needed it two weeks ago. It still hasn't arrived because of the siege,” one source said. Taiz is the third-most populous city in Yemen. It has remained largely under government control until the Houthis began waging battles in recent weeks, aiming to capture the city and the wider province. Victory would pave the way for the rebels to seize areas further south, towards the government's interim capital in Aden, and expand their already substantial territory. Taiz province is also home to the Kahboub Mountains , over which the two sides have been fighting. The mountain range overlooks roads leading to the Bab Al Mandeb strait, where Houthi threats could disrupt up to 15 per cent of global shipping. The World Food Programme warned that the situation could quickly turn into a “humanitarian catastrophe” if aid continues to be blocked. In the suburbs where the Houthis are in control, there is slightly more access to supplies, but witnesses say the situation is complicated in different ways. “As a woman, it's not safe. I can't even go to the souq without facing issues,” another aid worker told The National . “Someone told me that she was harassed with her daughters by the militias. This is becoming increasingly problematic.” The National could not independently confirm the source's claims. Overall, the sentiment seems to be one of desperation, fear and isolation. Mr Saif said that many Yemenis feel “let down” by aid organisations that were supposed to, but are unable to, help them. “People lost trust. They make us feel like we disappointed them. I felt guilty (leaving).” Others have simply given up. They feel that being displaced several times as front lines change is no longer viable, sometimes because they can't afford the move. Most people are terrified, Mr Saif said. “They need immediate psychological support.” One of the many fears is that the fighting will be protracted, as the battle for control continues.

title: Lebanon's power failure: Diesel generators, $300-a-month bills - and a corrupt system milking the profits
description: The state utility now provides less than a third of the country's electricity, a victim of chronic under-investment. Why? Because the people with the power to fix it are profiting from the racket that's replaced it
content: Lebanon now relies on diesel-powered generators for about half of its electricity supply, further exposing the crisis-hit country to financial, environmental and operational risks, according to data for an upcoming report. Behind that alarming figure lies a deep-rooted crisis decades in the making. Interviews with officials, as well as government statistics, studies and testimonies gathered by The National reveal how a largely unregulated industry has been lining the pockets of high-ranking officials and neighbourhood generator owners alike. The electricity sector has been regarded as one of the most corrupt parts of Lebanon’s sectarian system of government since the end of the civil war in 1990. Those who benefit from the dysfunction have allegedly resisted efforts to repair the sector, preserving a system that lets them continue profiting from its failures. Figures being compiled by the Lebanese Centre for Energy Conservation for their upcoming report show that private generators accounted for 50 per cent of Lebanon’s electricity supply at the beginning of 2026, while Electricite du Liban, the state utility, provided only 31 per cent. EDL's share is likely to have shrunk even further over the summer, according to the LCEC, a national agency affiliated with the Energy Ministry. Meanwhile, the Lebanese people are left to foot the bill. The country's dependence on expensive diesel imports to run generators has sent energy bills rocketing in recent months amid rising global oil prices due to the Iran war, further straining households and businesses already struggling after years of economic crisis. Among a dozen people interviewed by The National , the median generator bill was $310 in August. Dependence on generators increased dramatically after a severe economic crisis began in 2019, driving the final nail in the coffin of the dilapidated electricity sector . As the bankrupt state struggled to secure fuel for its power plants, EDL production fell by nearly 80 per cent between 2018 and 2023, from 15.4TWh to 3.37TWh, according to a 2025 report by the LCEC. Over the same period, diesel-powered generators' share of Lebanon's electricity supply more than doubled, from 23.1 per cent to 51.5 per cent. Beirut’s roughly 9,300 generators have barely stopped their relentless humming since then, spewing polluting exhaust into the air and wrapping the capital in a yellowish smog, as they supply electricity to those who can afford it. “We can’t go on like this,” said Ayman, manager of a shawarma restaurant in Beirut’s vibrant Hamra neighbourhood, who gave only his first name. With state electricity available for only a few hours a day, and at unpredictable times, the restaurant is almost entirely reliant on a private generator, he said. The small restaurant’s electricity bill for August alone came to almost $20,000. “We’re losing money,” Ayman sighed. The usually bustling summer season, which he had been banking on to shore up the restaurant’s finances, proved disappointing. With the war between Hezbollah and Israel resuming in March, tourists and even Lebanese expatriates largely stayed away. “If nothing is done, we will have to close. And not just us, everyone else too,” said Ayman. While generator bills vary considerably from one area to another because of limited state oversight, data from New Energy Consult and The National 's interviews with residents show that monthly bills often exceed $300 – roughly equivalent to the entire monthly minimum wage of 28 million Lebanese pounds. By comparison, the average household electricity bill in the UK is about $95 a month for a medium-sized household of two to three people. In one neighbourhood of the capital, a 25-amp generator subscription cost as much as $750 in August, according to New Energy Consult, a consultancy founded by Lebanese energy expert Jessica Obeid. Ms Obeid said some generator operators had taken advantage of the global surge in oil prices to increase their profit margins. “The problem is that nobody has provided state electricity over the past three decades, and nobody has implemented any serious reforms,” she explained. “Generators eventually just reflect the failure of the state, the failure of policies and the failure of institutions. So it’s time for state institutions to stand up and do what they’re supposed to be doing: provide electricity.” People strolling along Hamra’s main street express their exasperation over soaring energy costs. “It’s insane,” said Karim Agha, 33, who recently returned from Dubai. He said his parents’ electricity bill reached $600 in August, three times what he used to pay in the Emirates. “I’m scared to look at the bill,” said Talal Fayed, a 67-year-old driver who paid a $300 generator bill in August. Asked what he expected from the Lebanese state, he sighed and replied with a faint smile: “What state?” Such vast sums flowing each month from consumers’ pockets into the private generator industry raise the question: why have the Lebanese authorities failed to implement energy reforms that would redirect that money to the state? Energy experts say vested interests and a lack of political will have prevented a transition towards cheaper, cleaner energy and locked the country into a dangerous dependence on generators. The diesel generator industry is lucrative: Ali Ahmad, a World Bank expert, estimated its value at around $3 billion in 2020, with roughly $1 billion going to the generator market and $2 billion to diesel importers. Opposition MP Paula Yacoubian said the generator “cartel” benefitted politically connected individuals and companies that had little incentive to give up their bread and butter. Generator owners are part of Lebanon’s clientelism networks, she argued, able to offer benefits such as forgiving unpaid bills in exchange for political support. “It's a mass bribe system,” she told The National. A systemic lack of investment and squandering of public funds have left Lebanon’s energy sector in shambles. About 40 per cent of electricity entering EDL's network is lost between technical distribution and commercial losses such as theft and illegal connections, according to a 2024 EDL report. With its battered financial sector and unstable security situation, Lebanon has struggled to attract foreign capital since 2019. But lack of investment in the energy sector is not new. The state has not built a major power plant in decades. Its newest large plants, Deir Ammar and Zahrani, date back to the late 1990s. “With $1 billion, you can build a 1,000MW power plant. It's nothing. People are already paying for it with their generator bills,” Ms Yacoubian said. EDL has about 3,000MW of nominal installed capacity, but in 2023 it supplied electricity equivalent to just 13 per cent of its theoretical maximum output. The country needs about 3,000MW of electricity to meet daily demand. Only two of Lebanon’s seven thermal power plants are operational, because the cash-strapped state cannot buy enough fuel and badly maintained infrastructure limits production. A 1,000MW plant operating at an 80 per cent capacity could produce about 7TWh annually, more than twice EDL’s total electricity supply in 2023, which stood at roughly 3.4TWh, according to LCEC. “This is not a technical problem,” Ms Yacoubian said. For over two decades, political bickering has stopped all major investment projects in Lebanon. “Power plants are routinely built everywhere else in the world. Anyone, my aunt Salma included, could bring electricity,” she said. “But there are no politically affiliated politicians who were able to do it in Lebanon.” Energy Minister Joseph Saddi said he was well aware that the remedy to the country’s dependence on generators was in investment in electricity generation. “We are now engaging with the private sector,” he told The National . The Energy Ministry has given the International Finance Corporation, the private-sector arm of the World Bank, a mandate to secure the necessary private-sector investment. “There are investors who are interested, but they require a certain number of financial guarantees. So what we are focusing on now is how we can provide those guarantees,” Mr Saddi said. The IFC’s role is notably to act as the lead transaction adviser on a public-private partnership for a new 825MW combined-cycle gas turbine plant, a project that has been in the pipeline for years. Meanwhile, the World Bank has approved a $250 million loan to EDL to upgrade its infrastructure. Experts say that, even more than generator owners, diesel importers wield significant influence over policy decisions, thanks to their close connections with politicians. A 2022 investigation by Beirut-based research centre Triangle revealed direct links between several of Lebanon’s 13 licensed fuel-importing companies and current or former politicians. For energy expert Marc Ayoub, who has investigated the sector for years, Lebanon’s diesel importers form an oligopoly with far-reaching political connections. Rather than competing with one another, he said, they collaborate to maximise their margins, sharing the cost of vessels and associated shipping fees before dividing the imported quantities among themselves. They then sell the diesel, locally known as mazout, according to the price set by the Ministry of Energy, currently about $30 for 20 litres, which Mr Ayoub said allowed them to make comfortable margins. The tariff “contains a lot of hidden profits for importers, in addition to margins for distributors, lorry owners, petrol stations and everyone else involved”, he said. The Energy Ministry could reduce additional premiums it pays to importers, which he said could lower diesel tariffs by at least 15 per cent. But instead, he said, the state kept “protecting the interests of these private players”. There is also an issue on the generator side. While the Energy Ministry sets generator tariffs – which have risen by almost 60 per cent in six months – many operators do not comply with them, or even bother to install mandatory electricity meters. Instead, they charge residents a fixed monthly rate based on the amperage of their subscription, which determines how many appliances consumers can run at the same time. Despite occasional government crackdowns for overcharging customers and failing to install electricity meters, generator operators have largely been able to set prices at their discretion. One silver lining of the near-collapse of state electricity supply is that solar panels have soared in popularity, accounting for 19 per cent of electricity production in 2026, up from just 0.4 per cent in 2018, according to LCEC. None of the people interviewed by The National said they had installed solar panels. Mr Fayed, the taxi driver, said this would be the only way to move beyond dependency on generator owners and the state, neither of which he trusts. But, like many Lebanese living from pay cheque to pay cheque, he does not have the upfront capital to install solar panels. “Too expensive,” he sighed. With Lebanon experiencing one of the fastest-growing cancer rates in the world, experts have urged the country to move to cleaner sources of energy. According to a 2024 study led by scientists from the American University of Beirut, the level of carcinogenic pollutants from diesel generators in the capital's air has doubled since 2017, increasing the risk of developing cancer by 50 per cent. “It’s suffocating, it’s killing us, it’s loud, it’s expensive … And we know that it is all due to corruption,” Ms Yacoubian said. “I'm telling the Lebanese people to wake up – wake up, and smell the mazout.”

title: Sharjah turns to AI to identify foreign investment opportunities in seconds
description: Invest in Sharjah's new platform Najm will initially help investors locate industrial and commercial properties, with plans to expand into healthcare and education
content: Sharjah is using artificial intelligence to help foreign investors identify investment opportunities within seconds, as the emirate seeks to attract more foreign direct investment despite mounting geopolitical uncertainty . A new AI-powered platform, called Najm, will initially help investors find sites for factories and warehouses across the emirate. It was launched by the emirate's investment promotion agency, the Sharjah FDI Office, also known as Invest in Sharjah. The AI agent is designed to help investors make “informed investment decisions”, Mohamed Al Mushrrakh, chief executive of Invest in Sharjah, said at the Sharjah Investment Forum on Wednesday. For the introductory phase, Invest in Sharjah has teamed up with property portals Bayut and Property Finder, as well as e-commerce platform Dubizzle . Najm will use commercial and industrial real estate data from the online portals and will provide instantaneous information to investors. “Investors could struggle to find information they need to make an investment decision, so we asked ourselves a simple question: how can we deliver the right information at the right moment, when they need it,” Mr Al Mushrrakh told delegates at the Sharjah Investment Forum. “Najm is the answer to that question. It is Invest in Sharjah's new tool for global investors.” The launch of the AI agent is driven by the need to cut the noise around the investment ecosystem in Sharjah and find new ways to bring foreign direct investment to the emirate. Sharjah, the third largest emirate in the UAE after Abu Dhabi and Dubai, is home to 33 industrial zones. Sharjah’s real estate sector recorded more than 16,000 transactions during the first half of this year, with the emirate’s Muwaileh commercial area accounting for the highest value and volume of deals in the first six months, according to Invest in Sharjah data. Sharjah received Dh7.74 billion in FDI last year, an 8.8 per cent increase on an annual basis. The count of projects in the emirate that received FDI also soared by 45 per cent year-on-year, to reach 142 developments, data showed. In the second phase, the Najm platform will expand its sector horizon to cover a broader range of assets and investment opportunities in the healthcare and education sectors, Mr Al Mushrrakh said. “What you have seen today is just the beginning ... Najm stands to cover investment opportunities across multiple sectors from industry to education and technology and beyond,” he said. “We will continue to invest in human capital, technology, infrastructure and partnerships between the public and private sectors. "Through these efforts, we can build a resilient economy, attract new investments into opportunities that we will build together."

title: State Street plans 100 jobs for Emiratis at Al Ain hub as it aims for July 2027 opening
description: Company linking up with UAE universities to recruit graduates
content: US financial services group State Street plans to employ about 100 Emiratis at its Al Ain operating centre as it targets a July 2027 opening date. The new centre is expected to have 300 staff by 2030, with technology, artificial intelligence, operations and client services among its main areas. About a third of the workforce will come from State Street’s global centres, another third will be recruited from the UAE talent pool and a third will be Emiratis, said Jack Keshishian, State Street’s head of Middle East and North Africa (excluding Saudi Arabia and Bahrain).
