Preparations are under way, including arranging links with UAE universities through its partnership with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office. “We are looking at the go date of the first of July,” Mr Keshishian said. This is earlier than the “end of next year” start date outlined at the Al Ain Future Business Forum in September. State Street announced the centre in January. Mr Keshishian said the current focus was on building a workforce of 300 over three years to 2030, with the possibility of future expansion if there was sufficient demand. “Obviously, we have ambitions to grow because [the] Middle East is a growth market for us, and we take a long-term view,” he said. The company expects to identify potential graduate recruits in the first quarter of next year. The “talent pool” in Al Ain is a key reason the company chose to set up there, alongside the potential to sustain and grow the business, Mr Keshishian said. AI and technology will help automate work and improve the use of data, while employees will also provide operational and client services. Mr Keshishian said technology and staff would work together to improve efficiency for clients. He did not provide an investment figure for the centre and said spending would continue over the coming three years. State Street’s decision is based on its assessment of the available workforce and the potential to sustain and expand an operation in the city, Mr Keshishian said. The company has had a presence in Abu Dhabi since 2018. Its new centre will broaden that operation beyond the capital and support clients across several markets. “I think despite the tension in the region, we are seeing global institutions establishing their presence here in the UAE and the wider region, and we haven't seen any sort of a change in that,” he said. The company has also submitted an application to expand the services it can offer at Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM. Subject to approval, these would include safeguarding clients’ financial assets and providing administrative services for investment funds.

title: Spices, shipwrecks and ancient trade routes: Louvre Abu Dhabi explores 1,000 years of Indian Ocean history
description: Museum's new exhibition brings together 240 objects to reveal how trade, navigation and religion connected civilisations across continents
content: Visitors to Louvre Abu Dhabi's latest exhibition begin their journey in darkness, lights above mimicking a star-filled sky. It's a reminder of a time when sailors relied on the heavens to navigate the Indian Ocean, carrying spices, precious stones and textiles between distant civilisations. Such voyages connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia, establishing commercial and cultural relationships that developed over centuries. Their history is explored in Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean, opening at Louvre Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, October 14, and running until February 14, 2027. Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders, covering maritime exchange from antiquity to the 17th century. Among them are archaeological discoveries, jewellery, religious artefacts and objects recovered from shipwrecks. Six detailed models of historic vessels and specially created maps illustrate how sailors crossed vast waters and transported goods between continents. The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's historical role in these networks. “The story is told from here, and that is something we consider very important at Louvre Abu Dhabi: telling the story from the region,” says Guilhem Andre, the museum's director of scientific, curatorial and collections management “This has never really been done on this scale before.” The exhibition features loans from institutions including the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore, the National Museum of the Philippines and the Al Sabah Collection in Kuwait . Pierre Baptiste, director of collections and curatorial staff at the Guimet in Paris, says the exhibition explores how people established relationships through commerce and spiritual exchange. The Arabian Gulf's pearl industry provides a significant regional example. Pearls harvested from its waters travelled to markets in India and beyond, while materials such as carnelian were traded across the ocean from ancient times. Later networks expanded the circulation of gemstones, jewellery , furniture and textiles. Andre said the objects revealed how discoveries of new sources of gold, spinels, rubies and emeralds influenced jewellery production. Diplomatic gifts also feature, demonstrating how valuable objects helped establish relationships between rulers and communities. Beyond the goods themselves, the exhibition examines the techniques that made these journeys possible. Its opening gallery recreates the darkness experienced by ancient navigators, who relied on stars and coastal landmarks to determine their position. “The main idea was to give visitors a sense of what people at the time experienced,” Baptiste says. Subsequent galleries explore navigational instruments, including the kamal, used in Arab and Indian maritime traditions, and the astrolabe. Twenty-four maps created specifically for the exhibition trace the routes connecting ports across the ocean. Six large ship models represent Arabian, South-East Asian, Chinese, Portuguese and Spanish maritime traditions. Andre says they were constructed in South Africa over the course of a year, drawing on extensive historical research. The models are accompanied by objects recovered from shipwrecks, offering evidence of the cargo these vessels carried. Baptiste says advances in underwater archaeology since the 1990s have enabled researchers to recover significant quantities of material from sunken ships, including objects originating in China, India, Spain and Mexico. Among the most valuable commodities were spices, which commanded high prices alongside luxury products such as jewellery and textiles. Cultural exchange is another central theme. A Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan, loaned by the Guimet, reflects the influence of ancient Greek and Roman artistic traditions on Buddhist sculpture. The final gallery examines four religious traditions that spread across the Indian Ocean, showing how beliefs travelled along the same routes as commercial goods. Andre says merchants and pilgrims often crossed these waters for different purposes, carrying objects and practices that became part of life in distant communities. “Religion was not separate from trade,” he says. “They were all part of the same relationships and exchanges.” The exhibition also offers a perspective on maritime history that predates the expansion of European influence in Indian Ocean commerce during the 17th and 18th centuries. Baptiste says the decision to conclude the historical narrative in the 17th century was deliberate, allowing visitors to understand the networks that existed long before European powers became prominent in the region. These earlier connections, he says, laid the foundations for the expansion of international commerce in subsequent centuries. “We wanted to approach the history of commercial relationships from a multicultural perspective,” he says. “Europe was only one part of this story.” Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean runs at Louvre Abu Dhabi from October 14, 2026, until February 14, 2027. The exhibition will subsequently travel to the Guimet in Paris, where it will be presented from May 12 to September 6, 2027.

title: Investors in collapsed jeweller Vashi 'could be compensated' after watchdog ruling
description: Financial Ombudsman says banks should pay out under fraud protection scheme
content: A financial watchdog has ruled that investors who lost money when the jeweller Vashi collapsed can receive compensation under an anti-fraud scheme. The company folded in April 2023 with debts of £170 million, and investors, many from the Middle East , believed its diamond stock would be used to reimburse them if the company failed. But when the safes were examined, the stock was worth £114,000. Its founder, Vashi Dominguez, vanished as his UK firm was wound up, and an investigation by The National revealed he was able to raise millions to fuel his global ambitions using the diamond stock and inflated sales figures. Some investors have been seeking compensation under the authorised push payment (APP) scam reimbursement scheme that was operated by banks at the time. The UK’s Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) initially rejected a claim by a group of investors that banks were not liable for losses in Vashi under APP But it has now overturned its decision regarding the claim of a couple for around £100,000 ($132,000). In his ruling, the Financial Ombudsman, Stephen Dickie, said that Vashi’s “supposed business model was simply a falsehood and that it was most likely a deliberate fraud”. The decision now clears the way for the couple, referred to as Mr and Mrs C, to get their money back from their bank, NatWest. Millions of pounds could also be returned to other investors under the APP scheme. In his ruling, Mr Dickie said neither Mr and Mrs C nor NatWest could have known that Vashi was a “fraud” and a “facade” overstating the value of its accounts and diamond stocks. Given the bank’s obligations under the APP scams code, NatWest should have done more, especially when two payments totalling £50,000 were sent to Vashi from the couple’s account in the space of 24 hours. “NatWest ought to have been on the lookout for out-of-character and unusual transactions and other indications that its customer might be at risk of financial harm from fraud,” said Mr Dickie. Michael Moszynski was among a group of Vashi investors urging the FOS to reconsider its initial ruling, made at the beginning of this year. He told The National he welcomed the new decision. “This is what we've been fighting for,” he said. “The amount of detail we presented meant that we put them in a position where they couldn't continue not upholding our complaints against the banks.” Stuart McFadden, co-founder of fraud-recovery experts Refundee, has been pursuing claims on behalf of investors, including Mr and Mrs C as well as those from overseas. “This is a significant outcome for investors who were wrongly denied reimbursement,” he told The National . “While this was a sophisticated scam in its delivery, once it collapsed it was clear that investors had been defrauded. We believed the evidence was clear and continued to fight on their behalf, and we’re pleased the FOS has now found NatWest should have done more to stop these payments.” An FOS representative said it would not comment on individual complaints but “allegations of large-scale investment fraud are among the most complex cases we deal with”. “They can involve thousands of pages of evidence, investigations by multiple agencies including the police and regulators, and a picture that constantly evolves,” said the representative. “Ultimately, it’s not our role to prosecute fraud; it’s to decide if a bank should be held liable for an investor’s losses.” The Metropolitan Police complex fraud team has launched an investigation, called Operation Palisade, into the collapse of Vashi. NatWest has been approached for comment.

title: Dubai and Abu Dhabi among top destinations for next-generation wealth, Savills says
description: Emirates benefits from government initiatives that support economic growth
content: Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tensions, according to Savills. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, the London-based consultancy said in its Spotlight on Wealth Trends report on Wednesday. Next-generation wealth refers to individuals under 40 who have inherited significant wealth or have accumulated it through entrepreneurial success. Dubai and Abu Dhabi benefitted from a slew of government initiatives that support economic and societal growth, including favourable tax environments, business-friendly policies and significant infrastructure investment “with a sophisticated luxury offering”, Savills said. In particular, Dubai's entrepreneurial ecosystem, global connectivity and lifestyle appeal attract international talent and capital. Abu Dhabi complements this with its growing financial centre, a rising number of family offices, expanding economic opportunities and a high quality of life, the study said. Those are “reinforcing the UAE's position as a compelling destination for globally mobile wealth”, Kelcie Sellers, associate director for world research at Savills, wrote in the report. In the wider Gulf, “economic diversification and succession planning are becoming more prominent, with growing focus on family governance, next-generation involvement and the long-term deployment of capital within the region”, Ms Sellers said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as for global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as institutional partners. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a report this week by Boston Consulting Group found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report said. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. New York topped the Savills list, followed by Miami, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Singapore, Hong Kong and Monaco at ninth. Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide. Cities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa accounted for 16 of the index’s top 30 locations, driven by lifestyle and sporting events, which include major golf and tennis tournaments and Formula One races. In terms of the number of sporting events, Dubai was number one in the Emea region, while Abu Dhabi, home of the season-ending F1 race, was sixth. “The defining characteristic of Emea is the diversity of its wealth proposition. Global business centres, leading educational institutions, major sporting and cultural events, coastal retreats and mountain resorts are all within reach,” Ms Sellers said. Global wealth continues to grow rapidly. Total personal wealth jumped by nearly 11 per cent in 2025 to create about one million more millionaires, according to industry tracker Altrata. More than 510,800 are now ultra-high net worth individuals, or those with a net worth of $30 million or more, holding around $60 trillion in combined wealth – which is greater than the combined economies of the US and China, Altrata said. “Location decisions are becoming a core component of wealth planning … at the same time, new fortunes generated by technology and artificial intelligence are reshaping global wealth hubs,” Ms Sellers said. “As a result, many wealthy families are adopting multi-jurisdictional lifestyles, balancing residence, education and wealth structures across multiple markets.”

title: Aldar's international unit plans to deliver 9,000 homes in next five years
description: New homes will be built on 30 sites, says company official
content: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company targeting buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. More than 3,600 homes will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be in the affordable segment, in which government provides grants to registered developer to help it lease to tenants at affordable rental rate. London Square plans to start work on 12 sites this year with 65 per cent of those affordable, said chief executive Adam Lawrence. “There's always demand for affordable housing, it is a huge market and a huge need,” he told The National. There is also international demand from buyers in Turkey, Hong Kong and Middle East countries, he added. “Turkey is really strong at the moment. We've opened an office in Turkey, in Istanbul, recently, and we're seeing, within days of opening, we're into double-digit sales there. Hong Kong's been very quiet, but that looks like it's coming back.” The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010. “Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.” London Square, which regenerates former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space. It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures. The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026. “Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year. London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of 2026, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director. “International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.” London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher. In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society. However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE. “There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said. “London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.” It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

title: Keanu Al Azhari to represent UAE with 'immense pride' after landing F3 contract for 2027
description: Yas Heat graduate named in Team Hitech's three-man line-up for 2027 championship
content: Keanu Al Azhari says he can't wait to test himself in Formula 3 after being named in Hitech's three-man line-up for the 2027 championship. The 18-year-old racer joins as a rookie alongside the returning Kanato Le and Michael Shin, having progressed through the ranks with the team. After two years in Formula 4, in which he finished runner-up in the Spanish F4 championship, Al Azhari joined Hitech’s GB3 team in 2025, claiming one victory, six podiums and three pole positions to finish sixth in the championship. Al Azhari, a member of the Alpine Academy since March 2025, said he was proud to represent the UAE on the F1 support programme. No Emirati driver has ever raced in F3 before. He said: “I am proud and honoured to continue my journey with my family at Hitech as we step up together into the 2027 FIA Formula 3 Championship. “To become the first driver from the UAE to compete in FIA F3 is a milestone I carry with immense pride. “Representing my nation at this level is the greatest honour, and I’m humbled by the support of the UAE behind me. I hope this journey inspires the next generation of drivers across our region to dream without limits.” Paul Bellringer, Hitech’s F3 team manager, said: “We’ve worked closely with [Keanu] over the last two seasons and have seen first-hand how much he has developed in that time.” Al Azhari is the son of Karim Al Azhari , a German-Emirati businessman and multiple UAE karting champion. He is the older brother of Adam Al Azhari , who he raced against in Spanish F4. After some success in karting, Al Azhari began his racing career in the 2023 Formula 4 UAE Championship for Yas Heat Racing Academy before moving up through the ranks. Last season, he competed in Eurocup 3, winning the Spanish Winter Championship title. He is currently third overall in the Eurocup-3 standings.

title: Gaza committee signs recovery assistance deal with Germany’s GIZ in Cairo
description: Implementation of committee's mandate has been hampered by Israeli restrictions
content: The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s international development agency GIZ to support the coastal strip's postwar recovery and reconstruction, although Israeli objections continue to prevent the body from entering the territory. The pact, signed on Tuesday at the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza’s temporary headquarters in Cairo , establishes a framework for technical assistance on reconstruction, public institutions and essential services, the committee said. It was formed in January under US President Donald Trump's peace plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Mr Trump's plan brought about a shaky ceasefire between Israel and Hamas last October after two years of fighting and also established a Board of Peace to oversee its implementation. Led by Ali Shaath, a former Palestinian Authority deputy minister, the committee is intended to restore public services and oversee civilian administration and reconstruction under the supervision of the Board of Peace. Mr Shaath and GIZ country director Alexander Zschocke signed the agreement at the committee’s temporary headquarters in Cairo. Bulgarian diplomat Nikolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, attended alongside German officials. Under the agreement, GIZ will provide technical expertise, advisory services, needs assessments and training to strengthen the committee’s planning and implementation capabilities. Co-operation will cover municipal services, social protection, education, employment, water, agriculture and energy. The statement did not mention a funding commitment, specific projects or a timetable for implementation. Mr Shaath called for the agreement to be translated into practical measures that improve living conditions. He said the committee would lead its implementation according to Gaza’s urgent needs and in co-ordination with Palestinian institutions. However, Israel refuses to allow the committee to enter Gaza or to proceed with the second stage of Mr Trump's peace plan until Hezbollah disarms. Its restrictions on the entry of equipment and supplies are also hampering recovery efforts. Gaza needs extensive reconstruction of homes and infrastructure. A European Union and UN assessment released in April estimated the cost of recovery and rebuilding at $71.4 billion over the next decade.

title: ‘You can’t swim’: The rejection that fuelled Maha Al Shehhi’s Olympic journey
description: Emirati athlete was told there was no pathway for girls like her to compete in the pool. Now she is determined to make the journey easier for the next generation
content: Maha Al Shehhi was only 13 when she realised there was no established pathway for an Emirati girl who desired to swim competitively. But being told she was unable to train and swim lit a fire inside her that ultimately led her to the Olympics. “When I found out that I couldn’t swim in the first three years because I was a female, that hit me really hard. They were like, 'You can’t swim. We won’t give you a pool; it’s impossible'. I was like, 'What do you mean? I can'.” Her family searched for a pool that would allow her and her sisters to swim and train alongside boys. The absence of a clear pathway became the reason for her determination to create one. “I feel like that was the time when it hit me. I should be a change,” the 20-year-old told The National in an interview at Middlesex University's 'Dubai Women in Sport' series. In 2024, Al Shehhi represented the UAE at the Paris Olympics , where she swam a personal best time of 2:17.17 in the 200 metres freestyle. For her, progress is about removing that sense of novelty surrounding female athletes. “The way we talk about females is always a surprise. We never say, 'Great, she’s a female; she did it like how a man would do it',” she says. Instead, she argues, there’s so much surprise when a woman competes. “My goal is to make it normal. For everyone,” she adds. For Al Shehhi, normalising female athletes participating in all disciplines is the only way to ensure progress. Maha’s family encouraged her and her two sisters to pursue whatever made them happy. “They always told me that whatever you’re going to pursue, make sure you finish it. You can’t start something without finishing it,” she says. And so she, alongside her twin sister Mahra and their younger sister Mira, took up the sport together. They became known as 'M3', the three Al Shehhis. All of them went on to represent the UAE. Sport runs in the family. Born to a Polish mother and an Emirati father, Maha’s mother had once participated in athletics in her youth. Their father initially needed time to adjust to the idea of his daughters training in an environment he had largely associated with men. However, their commitment to the sport eventually won him over. “He did have a rough time trying to understand but then he saw the 4am training and the 5pm training and he saw how dedicated we were so he was like, ‘You know what, I’ll always support you. I’m your father. I’m here for you. Just know I’ll be the backbone of everything’,” says Al Shehhi. “Our mother is the support system. She makes sure that every training session I go to, I smile. Everyone has this thing with me that if you don’t see Maha smiling, it’s a bad thing; it’s the end of the world. “She always makes sure I’m happy. She makes sure that I’m doing it for myself and if I feel low, she's like do it for me and it motivates me. “She always reminds me that I’m also doing it for the younger generation; that's my priority and I really want to just make a clear path.” That’s not to say there haven't been times when she didn’t contemplate walking away. Having a strong support system was key to keeping her on track, as is her fierce competitive nature and the desire to rebel against those who tell her 'no', something she attributes to her heritage. “When it comes to swimming and when it comes to fighting in the pool or racing, it’s the Polish blood coming out,” she says. Emiratis often speak with pride of Eyal Zayed, the sons of Zayed, named after the nation’s founding father. Al Shehhi wants the same reverence for ‘Banat Zayed’, his daughters. She wants future generations to find it easier to access pools, sponsorship and equipment. “My goal is to make sure the girls that are coming right after me or in any other sport feel like they shouldn’t go through the challenges I went through because I would never wish that on my worst enemy, honestly,” she says. Al Shehhi estimates that 90 per cent of parents she meets still discourage their daughters from entering the sport, whether it be on account of wearing a swimsuit, mixed training, or the belief that sport is simply a distraction from studies. Al Shehhi says she often offers to speak to parents to ease their concerns. “Let her enjoy what she wants to do. You can't force her to just study and then spend the day doing nothing. If she feels like she wants to do a sport, let her. Let her run, let her jog, let her do anything. But let her experience what she wants to experience,” she says.

title: Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI
description: New educational platform designed to help families navigate artificial intelligence tools responsibly
content: Dubai has launched a digital platform designed to help parents guide their children in using artificial intelligence safely and responsibly. The Dubai Centre for Artificial Intelligence announced GenDubAI in collaboration with the Community Development Authority and Dubai Future Foundation, state news agency Wam reported on Wednesday. The platform aims to nurture creativity, protect privacy and strengthen family engagement, supporting the objectives of the Dubai Social Agenda 33 and the UAE's Year of the Family. Available in Arabic and English, GenDubAI is designed for families with children aged 8 to 15 and is accessible through a dedicated mobile-friendly version. The platform offers interactive content rooted in UAE values and culture, addressing key questions around AI use while helping children develop critical thinking and creativity. It also introduces parents to the fundamentals and tools of AI, highlighting its opportunities and challenges. Hessa bint Essa Buhumaid, director general of the CDA in Dubai, said the platform placed families at the heart of AI learning. "This initiative reflects Dubai's commitment to preparing future-ready generations by empowering young people to embrace technology with confidence and responsibility while preserving their values and identity," she said. Khalfan Belhoul, chief executive of Dubai Future Foundation, said the UAE was among the world's leading countries in AI adoption, and smart-device use among children continues to rise. "Knowledge of safe and responsible AI use is one of the greatest gifts parents can give their children to help them thrive in the age of AI," Mr Belhoul said. Saeed Al Falasi, executive director of the DCAI, said the platform was built around the concept of "family moments", offering content that can be integrated into everyday life and encouraging meaningful conversations about AI within the home. Mr Al Falasi added that GenDubAI will evolve continuously through new content, tools and educational pathways to keep pace with rapid advances in AI and the changing needs of families.

title: US decries 'embarrassing' case against Lebanese envoy over contact with Israel
description: Nada Hamadeh Moawad spoke to Israeli counterpart after his son was injured in ramming attack
content: The US government has criticised Lebanon's handling of a complaint filed against the Lebanese ambassador to Washington, Nada Moawad. The case stems from contact the envoy made with Israel's ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter, to inquire about his son, who was critically injured in a car-ramming attack at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank. A representative said the US State Department was aware of the complaint lodged by Hassan Adel Bazzi, whom Washington described as a “pro-Hezbollah lawyer”. The State Department said it was “embarrassing” that Lebanon's military court was handling the case. The US government, along with Israel, has exerted intense pressure on Lebanon to disarm Hezbollah, the influential Iran-backed Lebanese political party and armed group. Lebanon’s public prosecutor referred the complaint to the government commissioner to the military court, a procedural step that does not itself constitute a prosecution or referral for investigation, according to Lebanese media. The two ambassadors have been at the forefront of direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which have technically been in a state of war since 1948. The talks were supposed to pave the way for Israel's withdrawal from south Lebanon and the disarmament of Hezbollah , two goals that have been almost entirely unsuccessful. Some in Lebanon, including Hezbollah and its supporters, have been deeply critical of the government for engaging in negotiations with Israel and the agreements reached as a result of those talks. “The Lebanese military judiciary should use its limited resources to prosecute Hezbollah operatives plotting against the Lebanese government and people instead of those working on their behalf,” the State Department said. “Laws and practices that enable this kind of politicised targeting of civilians and diplomats, while systematically shielding Hezbollah operatives, must be repealed. We have no patience for obstruction.” While Ms Moawad and the Lebanese government have not officially commented on the complaint, she has received backing from her supporters and Hezbollah critics. Michel Moawad, a member of parliament who is unrelated to the ambassador, described it as an “empty complaint” of a kind “that was routinely referred to the military court”. He called for an end to “using the judiciary as a tool for domination, intimidation, and settling political scores”. Lebanon's military court has in the past been accused of being influenced by Hezbollah. The court is investigating two men whose vehicle was stopped last week with half a tonne of explosives bound for Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah holds sway.

title: Palestinian faction leaders gather in Cairo to renew bid for long-elusive reconciliation
description: Talks sponsored by Egypt set to begin on Thursday
content: Leaders of Palestinian factions were gathering in Egypt on Wednesday for a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas , sources told The National. They said the talks were scheduled to begin Thursday and will continue until the end of the month, but not necessarily at leadership level. The gathering in Egypt represents eight factions, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, a pro-reform faction of Fatah, and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The talks will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine. Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Officials from its spy agency have led efforts, taking responsibility for key foreign policy files traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry. The sources said Khalil Al Hayya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads the pro-reform faction within Fatah, were among those taking part in the talks. Also participating are Jebril Rajoub, a top official of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and Mohammed Ashtiyah, a former Palestinian prime minister and top Fatah official. Among the main topics to be discussed are how to narrow ideological gaps between their factions, the inclusion of Hamas and Islamic Jihad in the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and charting a political role for armed groups like Hamas and Islamic Jihad. “These are preliminary contacts that will precede negotiations that bring together everyone in the same room, which is expected to happen towards the end of the month,” said one source. The talks in Egypt will take place at a time when prospects for the Palestinian cause are looking dimmer than at any time perhaps since the mass displacement of Palestinians around the time of Israel's creation in 1948. A year since a US-sponsored Gaza ceasefire was announced to pause two years of fighting, the strip lies in ruins, Israel's military controls more than 60 per cent of the enclave and shows no intention of withdrawing as provided by American President Donald Trump's peace plan. Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing frequent violent attacks on their homes and farmland in what increasingly looks like a concerted, state-backed campaign to displace them. Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced last weekend that the legislative vote would be postponed until next September next, when the presidential election is also due to take place. Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place. The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas , triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the Palestinian Authority. Mr Abbas, 90, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term. The deeply unpopular president, according to recent polls, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption. An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down. Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”. However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives. “The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it explained in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Mr Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.” The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

title: Crunch SPL fixture involving Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr postponed due to ‘logistical considerations’
description: Grudge match against Asian champions Al Ahli is one of three league fixtures to be rearranged
content: The Saudi Pro League clash between Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr and Asian champions Al Ahli has been postponed. The fixture, which was due to be played on Thursday, is one of three SPL games that have been rearranged. The league cited “logistical considerations” related to rest period for players, rather than the security situation in Riyadh . Alerts were sounded in the Saudi capital on Wednesday, as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. An SPL fixture in Abha that was due to be played on Sunday had been postponed, as a direct consequence of the situation. It was the day after 12 people died and more that 300 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Riyadh. Abha is around 200 kms from the Yemen border. Matches in Riyadh did go ahead. Each of Nassr , who were playing at home, and Ahli were in Asian Champions League action on Monday night. While Ahli’s fixture in Dubai against Al Wasl went ahead as planned, Nassr’s game in Riyadh was delayed for an hour because of an alert. In postponing three matches planned for this week, though, the league said the reasons were related to “the mandatory minimum rest period between matches”. The three matches all involve sides who were involved in the Champions League. That is Al Hilal and Nassr, who are based in Riyadh, and the Jeddah teams Ahli and Al Ittihad. “The [SPL] has rescheduled three Roshn Saudi League Matchweek 9 fixtures for logistical considerations, taking into account the mandatory minimum rest period between matches” the league wrote in a statement. “Two fixtures; Al Riyadh against Al Hilal and Al Ittihad against Al Shabab will now be played on Saturday, December 19, 2026, while Al Ahli versus Al Nassr will be played on Saturday, March 6, 2027. “The remaining games in Matchweek 9 will be played according to the previously announced schedule with no changes. “In making the decision, the SPL took into consideration the mandatory minimum rest period between matches in addition to organisational and operational requirements for the matches. “The changes are made in accordance with approved regulatory procedures for managing the competition's schedule, factoring in clubs' various logistical considerations for matches.” The Ahli-Nassr clash, in particular, was keenly anticipated. It was to be the first meeting between the sides since their acrimonious clash at Al Awwal Park last season. There, Nassr refused to give a guard of honour to their visitors, just days after Ahli had secured a second successive AFC Champions League title. Tempers boiled over in the game, with Ronaldo pointing out he has won five (Uefa) Champions League titles to goading Ahli fans. Merih Demiral, the Ahli centre back, also brought along his Champions League winner’s medal, and used it to taunt Nassr with in the melee which followed the game.

title: Diplomacy's changing footprint as told by mission openings and closures
description: An increase (Damascus) or decrease (Kabul, Khartoum) in the number of embassies can be a barometer for a country's international standing
content: Over the past few years, global politics have been reshaped by sudden shifts in power. The Taliban retook control in Afghanistan in August 2021 after US-led forces withdrew, and rebel forces in Syria toppled the Assad regime in December 2024. Those shifts are being reflected in diplomatic networks, and our latest chart of the week shows this clearly. Some cities are gaining missions as countries deepen or restore ties. Others have lost posts amid conflicts, political upheaval or isolation. The number of missions a country sends or hosts offers a glimpse of its diplomatic reach and priorities. But a reopening does not, on its own, prove that relations have fundamentally changed — or that the change will last. “Reopening an embassy is a political signal, but it does not necessarily indicate a lasting shift,” says Jasmine El-Gamal, founder and CEO of Founder and CEO of Averos Strategies, an advisory firm that operates across geopolitics and conflict resolution “A reopening is therefore better understood as a sign of renewed engagement than a guarantee of lasting alignment.” The reverse can also happen: a mission may remain open, close or move even after the political circumstances that prompted the decision have changed. As El-Gamal says, such decisions “can outlast the administrations that made them even when the original intent does not necessarily apply”. Syria has seen one of the biggest changes. After the fall of the Assad regime, several countries reopened embassies in Damascus that had been closed for years. Turkey and Qatar resumed operations in December 2024, followed by Spain in January 2025 and Germany in March 2025. Damascus recorded 12 openings between December 2024 and December 2025. Embassies returned to Pyongyang after pandemic-era closures. From 2024 onwards, Reuters reported that many European countries began sending delegations and missions back to North Korea. Brazil, Sweden, Poland, India and Nigeria were among the countries to resume operations, while Ukraine opened a series of new missions in African cities in 2024, including Kinshasa, Abidjan, Maputo and Kigali. Closures have been concentrated in a smaller number of cities. Kabul lost 19 diplomatic posts between 2017 and 2025, many after the Taliban returned to power in 2021. Governments evacuated staff and suspended operations amid the security crisis following the takeover, and others left due to uncertainty over how to engage with the new authorities' policies. The Taliban’s restrictions on women and girls have since further complicated diplomatic relations. Khartoum had the second-largest loss, with 14 diplomatic posts closing in the eight years to 2025. Most closures followed the outbreak of Sudan's civil war in April 2023, with governments evacuating staff and suspending operations amid security fears. Despite the closures, the figures suggest an expanding diplomatic footprint across more regions overall particaurlly into the Middle East and Africa, which have seen the biggest gains.

title: OpenAI employee and Saudi suspect ‘came to the US with a dream’, lawyer says
description: Abdulrahman Alfozan is accused of hiding recording device in company's headquarters
content: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and OpenAI employee, has been arrested over accusations that he hid a recording device at the company's offices in San Francisco. The Justice Department said Mr Alfozan hid the device – a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3, manufactured by a company in China – behind a television in a conference room. The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. According to a court motion filed by prosecutors on October 8, actions taken by Mr Alfozan indicated he planned to quickly depart the US. "Indeed, the defendant, his wife, and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) .. and defendant has the means and the incentive to flee the US sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the court filing reads. California lawyer William Pernik said that he is still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client, and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court. “Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik told The National via email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why.” He emphasised that his client has been charged with breaching a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent. “There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us,” he said. Mr Pernik implied that his client is already facing bias because he was not born in the US. “It is regretful that this is the one factor that seems to have caught the most attention,” he wrote. “Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origin is – and always should be – a protected status under our system of laws.” According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP. Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from MIT in 2016 and then earned his master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley. According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He is scheduled to appear in court on October 19 for a detention hearing. “If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department reads. OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations that it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.

title: India's Bank of Baroda to 'defend interests' after BR Shetty's $15bn lawsuit
description: NMC Health founder alleges lender and employees helped facilitate fraud
content: India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court. Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters. The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion. Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.” The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him. The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said. Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported. The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC. Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures. He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.

title: Trump threatens renewed military action against Iran
description: Tehran has rejected Washington’s latest response to proposal to end conflict
content: US President Donald Trump has warned of further action against Iran, saying Washington will decide its next move “very soon” as Tehran steps up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Mr Trump, speaking outside the White House late on Tuesday, described Iran as a “failed country” and said its economy was collapsing under severe inflation and financial pressure. “They have no economy … they have no money,” Mr Trump said. “We’ll make a decision on Iran very soon.” The US President later struck a more threatening tone at a campaign event in Alaska, warning of further action against Tehran. “Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We’re going to do a number … wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we’ve sort of had it,” he said. “The big thing is, they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. That’s buried under thousands of tonnes of rock.” The remarks came after Reuters reported two Iranian officials said Tehran was using new ⁠tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. The officials declined to ​provide ⁠details but one ‌said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about ​10 days ago, leading to an increase in attacks on such ships. At least 12 vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has said. Six were struck on Sunday alone – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage. “The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one was quoted as saying. A second official said Tehran would prevent Washington from lowering oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. The US military rejected a claim by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that it is in control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it does not possess an actual naval force. “US forces and their regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz . Just yesterday, US forces assisted their Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait,” said Central Command, which oversees US military operations across the Middle East. Officials in Tehran have rejected Washington’s latest response to its proposal to end the conflict , which began with US and Israeli strikes across Iran on February 28. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the US response as “insufficient” and warned of possible attacks on regional digital infrastructure if hostilities resumed. Washington has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports and expanded sanctions, while seeking an agreement. The Pentagon has also directed US Central Command to complete preparations for possible major combat operations, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. Mr Trump said last week the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, citing progress in negotiations. Israel is also considering its options. Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran, Axios reported, as the Israeli leader prepared for a general election on October 27. Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran’s response to a US counterproposal.

title: UAE orders recall of face mask batch over possible contamination
description: Local distributor instructed to retrieve all quantities supplied to the market
content: The UAE has ordered a recall of a batch of face masks because of concerns about possible contamination of the material used in its manufacture. The Emirates Drug Establishment issued the recall for Nin 160 FMB-NML Facemask C G blue, batch number 20251015. It is described as blue in colour and three-ply in structure. The Dubai Health Authority also issued a circular on Monday instructing healthcare centres to comply with the recall. Officials said Ningbo ETDZ Holdings Ltd in China manufactured the masks, and Globemed Care LLC distributed them in the UAE. The drug regulator said the recall was ordered after a quality complaint. Inspections identified foreign material or contamination in units from the affected batch. Healthcare professionals, hospitals and clinics and pharmacies must immediately stop selling, supplying, distributing or using the affected batch. They must identify and quarantine all available stock, then arrange for its return to the local supplier or distributor, Globemed Care LLC. They must also maintain records of quantities identified, quarantined, and returned. Residents who purchased the affected product should stop using any packs with batch number 20251015 and return them to the point of purchase or supplier. Healthcare providers must report any product quality complaints or adverse incidents related to the masks through EDE-approved reporting channels. Globemed Care LLC has also been ordered to retrieve all distributed quantities from the UAE market. It must also provide the regulator with details of quantities imported, distributed, returned, and remaining in stock, as well as a complete UAE distribution list. The regulator also urged people to report any quality concerns or adverse incidents involving the product directly to the authority.

title: UAE offers $1 million prize for winners of global AI challenge
description: 10,000 entrants from around the world will take part in competition
content: The UAE announced a prize of $1 million for the winners of a global competition aimed at improving the quality of life through the use of agentic artificial intelligence . Mohammed Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs, announced the award on Wednesday at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, organised by the UAE Government and the World Economic Forum (WEF). The competition, a collaboration between Dubai Municipality and the WEF, will feature 10,000 entrants working to improve quality of life through artificial intelligence. The winner of the Agentic AI Award will be announced at next year's event, with organisers hoping it will become a "model for hundreds of cities worldwide". "This is an annual $1 million prize involving over 10,000 global changemakers across 150 countries to develop smart solutions that enhance urban services and quality of life," Mr Al Gergawi said. It was also announced that the Centre for Global Future Opportunities will be established between the Dubai Future Foundation and the WEF, which will "turn technological and economic opportunities into policies, legislation and projects that can be implemented". Also unveiled was the Future 20 initiative, which showcases the effective work of 20 emerging leaders under the age of 30 "capable of driving major global transformations". The first cohort, chosen from around the globe, was in attendance at Wednesday's meeting in Dubai

title: Barefoot calm in the Baa Atoll: A family review of The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo
description: Set within a Unesco Biosphere Reserve, this intimate island combines well-being experiences with a relaxed, family-friendly feel
content: The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort sits on a coral island in the heart of the Baa Atoll. Surrounded by a vibrant house reef and the protected waters of a Unesco Biosphere Reserve, this pocket-sized hideaway recently received its first Green Globe certification, a mark of its focus on sustainability and biodiversity protection. Positioning itself as a family-friendly escape with a focus on well-being, the resort uniquely incorporates subtle Japanese design influences, via minimalist architecture, water features and anchored by a distinctive Japanese-style tree at its centre. I visited with my husband and our toddler daughter and found that, while it's not the most ultra-polished property in the Maldives , nor does it try to be, it offers a quietly confident island stay and slower pace that suits its scale. Arrival is direct to the hotel via seaplane or by a domestic flight to the nearby Dharavandhoo Airport, followed by a 20-minute speedboat transfer. We opted for the former, and the welcome begins before we step on to the island, with resort staff lining up to smile and wave as our seaplane taxis to the jetty. A short buggy ride delivers us to an open-air lobby, where a chilled welcome drink awaits and check-in is handled unhurriedly as we drink in the ocean views. We stayed in a Beach Villa, a category that works particularly well when travelling with a young child. Our room opens on to a terrace with steps down to the sand and a narrow path through dense greenery leading straight to the beach, ideal for early-morning walks and sunset strolls. Inside, the design is relaxed rather than glossy, with dark wood finishes and soft neutral tones. It feels natural and lived-in rather than overtly staged, and I wasn’t worried about letting my daughter run around and make herself at home. The spacious bathroom comes with a delightful open-air shower, there is something unmistakably indulgent about rinsing off under warm water with palm leaves blowing overhead. A Westin Heavenly Bed lives up to its sleep-inducing reputation. A small highlight is the Kids Sleep Manual, designed in collaboration with paediatric sleep specialists and packed with dream-promoting activities like beachside bedtime stories and stargazing walks, alongside a sleep-focused children’s room service menu. All 70 accommodation units have private pools, but note that, at least in our room category, these are not temperature controlled and the water is noticeably cold – so much so that I never managed a proper swim, only braving a quick leg dip. More premium options exist, including the two-bedroom Heavenly Beach Residence or Heavenly Overwater Villa with Pool. Dining centres around four venues, so the choice isn’t vast, but each has a clear identity. The standout is The Pearl, a Japanese restaurant set over the water, with sweeping ocean views and a live kitchen. The sushi and sashimi are exceptional, order the sushi boat for a beautifully prepared platter that ranks among the best I’ve had in the Maldives. Service runs firmly on island time, but the setting, particularly at sunset, is divine. Island Kitchen pairs all-day dining with healthy international dishes, overlooking the pool and sea beyond. This is where the resort’s Eat Well concept comes into play, with nutritious options alongside a dedicated children’s menu. For casual evenings, Hawker brings a lively open-air feel, and the seafood barbecue was one of our highlights, with chefs grilling freshly caught tuna and squid under the stars, accompanied by live music. Sunset Bar is the best vantage point for golden hour, with squishy beanbags perfectly positioned for sundowners. Breakfast at Island Kitchen is a highlight. The buffet is kept behind glass, a simple but effective solution to the fly issue common at island resorts, and the spread is generous but not excessive. There are well-being shots and local options like mas huni, a fresh tuna and coconut dish, alongside a strong Asian selection, plus a separate station for made-to-order fruit platters. For a small island, the range of facilities is impressive. Alongside the main swimming pool, there are tennis courts, running tracks and a fitness studio with TRX and functional training equipment, plus a comprehensive programme of free daily fitness classes. The watersports centre offers everything from scuba instruction to snorkelling trips and dolphin-spotting cruises. We partook of the latter and enjoyed views of shoals of spinner dolphins cruising alongside the boat. Trips also tap into the wider Baa Atoll Biosphere, including to nearby Hanifaru Bay, famous for hosting the world’s largest gathering of manta rays. The Heavenly Spa is one of the resort’s most tranquil spaces. Housed in overwater villa-style treatment rooms, the beds are positioned so guests can gaze directly into the ocean below while enjoying a massage. Watching colourful marine life drift past as a therapist worked her magic was particularly soothing. The resort is family-friendly without being overtly family-centric. The Kids Club features an impressive outdoor area with a swimming pool and a large wooden pirate-ship playground, alongside an indoor play space where staff run workshops and craft sessions. It caters only to children aged four and above, and while younger children may be permitted entry if accompanied by a parent, this is subject to daily capacity and staffing, meaning the space may not always be accessible to families travelling with babies and toddlers. Some staff go the extra mile, from a Sunset Bar bartender creating a custom mocktail for my daughter to the excursion team staging an impromptu Baby Shark- themed disco on a boat trip to local island Eydhafushi. Late restaurant hours – with most venues opening for dinner at 7pm – mean evenings may require forward planning for families with young children, including arranging babysitters in advance. That said, for those with children beyond toddler stage seeking calm surroundings rather than constant entertainment, the balance works. However, while the child-focused sleep manual is a good idea, it perhaps needs some tweaking. When we tried to use it to settle a jet-lagged toddler, we were told, after several back-and-forth phone calls, that most of the Kids Sleep Well menu items were unavailable later in the evening. Sustainability is embedded in the resort’s day-to-day operations, with a focus on energy, water and marine conservation. Solar power plays a central role in operations, alongside an on-site desalination and bottled water plant and the resort team leads coral restoration, sea turtle monitoring and reef-safe tourism initiatives. There are no designated accessible rooms, and as with many coral islands, pathways, overwater villas and boat transfers may present challenges for guests with limited mobility. Rates start from $750 per night. Check-in is from 3pm and checkout is at noon; westinmaldives.com. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Ukrainian ex-officer on trial over Nord Stream bombing argues it was not a crime
description: Serhii Kuznetsov accused of leading group in 2022 attack that ruptured crucial gas pipeline
content: A Ukrainian former military officer went on trial ​in Germany on Wednesday, accused of organising the secret operation that blew ⁠up the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022, severing western Europe from a vast source ⁠of Russian natural gas. The suspect, Serhii Kuznetsov , 50, is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents, including divers and an explosives expert, to mount one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of ⁠modern times. He ​has denied ⁠any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200km-long ‌Baltic Sea pipeline. His lawyers argued on Wednesday that blowing up the pipeline may not have been a crime. Moving to have the case dismissed, Mr Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini said the pipeline – which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's ⁠invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 – was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target. “Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?” Mr Canestrini asked. Mr Kuznetsov said he could not mount a proper defence because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets. “He has to mount a defence with his hands tied,” said Mr Canestrini. The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the crime. Prosecutors have alleged that Mr Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant ⁠in Italy last year, worked with other members of the military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities. The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military ​aid. The Russian government said it expected a “just verdict” that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation. German prosecutors say the actions of which Mr Kuznetsov is accused – attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services – would amount to a war crime. The alleged aim was to disrupt a major source of foreign revenue for Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched earlier that year. Protesters gathered outside the court in Hamburg, Germany in support of the accused, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?” “Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one dozens of protesters outside the court. Mr Kuznetsov is the only person on trial but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers in the team. The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's long-standing dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Germany previously received half its natural gas imports through the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, by far the biggest and most modern Russian conduit serving western Europe, which allowed Russia to bypass Soviet-era pipelines crossing Ukraine. The supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, which was already built, although Berlin cancelled approval to start operations shortly before Russia's invasion. The trial, expected ​to continue into February, could also have domestic political implications. Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in ‌opinion polls for more than a year, has called for ⁠an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ​ties with Moscow. In the initial months after the pipelines were attacked, western officials mainly pointed fingers at Russia. Moscow has always denied ​any involvement and called ‌the suggestion it would blow up its own pipelines absurd. It also rejects charges that it has more recently targeted western infrastructure with so-called “hybrid” sabotage and drone attacks. The ⁠Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 metres under the Baltic and built by Russian energy corporation Gazprom ⁠to supply up to 110 billion cubic metres of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries. On September 26, 2022, several blasts were detected by Swedish seismologists over 17 hours. The explosions sent huge plumes of methane gas into the atmosphere, as three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines were ruptured. Prosecutors allege Mr Kuznetsov travelled to Germany through Poland about three weeks before the attack, using ​a forged Ukrainian passport. They say he and his group used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialised military-grade explosives fitted with timers to the sea floor. The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on September 6 and returned on September 23, 2022.

title: Houthi attack hits Aramco's historic nerve centre in Saudi Arabia
description: Dhahran complex houses key research facilities, thousands of employees and their families, and the site of the kingdom's first commercial oil discovery
content: A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry , sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties. The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families. People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. "This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack. While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations. Aramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988. Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families. The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development. The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling. The area also includes Ithra, the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, which was built by Aramco as a cultural and creative destination for the public. The centre has attracted more than four million since its opening in 2018. The Dhahran area was attacked on February 25, 1991, during the Gulf War, when an Iraqi Scud missile struck a US Army barracks, killing 28 American soldiers and wounding 110. Aramco’s other sites in the Eastern province have also faced attacks in the past. Several drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing centres on September 14, 2019, knocking out about 50 per cent of the country’s crude oil production. The 17-minute strike by 18 drones and three low-flying missiles, claimed by the Houthis, caused a surge in oil prices and shut down more than 5 per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said about two weeks later that it had fully restored oil output. In March 2022, an Aramco plant in Jizan was also attacked by the Houthis with a drone laden with explosives, with a gas station in Khamis Mushait and a power station in Dhahran also hit. In early March this year, after the start of the Iran war, a fire broke out at Aramco’s Ras Tanura refinery , the kingdom’s largest, with 550,000 barrels per day of capacity, due to drone attacks. Operations were halted for 16 days. Ras Tanura, on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports. Other sites hit this year include Satorp in Jubail, a joint venture between Saudi Aramco and TotalEnergies processing 465,000 bpd and one of the world's largest export refining platforms, as well as Samref in Yanbu, a 400,000 bpd Aramco-ExxonMobil joint venture. Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser said ​the company had ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required. Aramco can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million bpd available ⁠within days, ​he ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “Our system is intact,” he added. Aramco, which is listed on the Tadawul exchange, is majority owned by the Saudi government. It is due to release its third quarter financial results on November 3.

title: UK loses 'leverage' to prevent atrocities in global wars
description: Human rights lawyers fear aid cuts and weakness leave Britain unable to play leading international role
content: Cuts to the UK’s foreign aid and diplomatic arms are hampering Britain's ability to prevent atrocities as global conflicts increase, experts have warned. Yasmine Ahmed, senior director at Amnesty International , said the UK government was not acting fast enough to prevent war crimes, such as those allegedly committed in Sudan and Gaza . “Often atrocity prevention is not prioritised sufficiently in terms of a whole of government policy response,” Ms Ahmed told The National. Last year, Britain’s overseas aid budget was slashed from 0.5 per cent of its gross national income to 0.3 per cent, at a time when conflicts are increasing worldwide. These cuts were issued by former prime minister Keir Starmer in January last year and Britain's spending on overseas aid is expected to fall by 42 per cent, or £6.5 billion ($8.6 billion), over four years, according to the Independent Commission for Aid Impact. One of the first Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office units to feel the impact of the cuts was international humanitarian law cell monitoring war crimes in Gaza. The FCDO has insisted these aid cuts would not affect the department’s ability to conduct human rights assessments of a conflict – but Ms Ahmed was sceptical. “If you’ve got a huge percentage – 20 per cent of the Foreign Office being cut – there’s no doubt this is going to have a significant impact across the board,” she said. “The question is how well will the Foreign Office continue to be equipped to conduct these assessments.” In the past few weeks there has been an escalation of conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, and the possibility of all-out war between Eritrea and Ethiopia has developed. Yet the UK's ability to enforce the laws of war and human rights on the world stage was dwindling. “What we’re finding now is that the UK and certainly other European states and other western states don’t have as much leverage as they used to,” Ms Ahmed said. This was leading to a visible decline in the protection of civilians in conflict. “They [the UK and European governments] are operating in an increasingly volatile political world and it’s increasingly transactional,” she said. “There is less space to be values driven.” On Tuesday, a group of British human rights lawyers and experts in global conflict called on the UK to loosen jurisdiction rules, so British courts can prosecute on a wider range of war crimes as well going after as companies accused of involvement. The group warned that the UK was currently “ill-equipped to identify and respond effectively to the warning signs of genocide and other atrocity crimes”, and that this had “serious implications” for “national security, stability and economic prosperity”. The Atrocities Standing Group, which includes Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk and Baroness Helena Kennedy, published the results of its 18 months of inquiry and parliamentary hearings on Tuesday in a report. It called for a tougher global policing role by using more “Magnitsky-style sanctions”, targeted punitive measures. Frozen sovereign assets from such sanctions could be repurposed to compensate victims of war crimes, by introducing relevant laws to do so, the report suggested.
