The UK government is seeking to re-establish Britain’s role in the world as conflicts escalate globally. “As the international rules-based order is facing fragmentation and significant challenges, it is key that the UK uses its global position to lead and support efforts to secure justice and accountability for international crimes,” the report said. Former British prime minister Gordon Brown, who has endorsed the report, said the UK needed to take serious foreign policy steps that go well beyond “condemnation” and “sympathy”. “Sympathy is not prevention, condemnation is not policy,” he said ahead of the report's launch. “The question before the United Kingdom and other democratic states is simple and grave. “Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully and in time?” The upholding of human rights risks being further eroded by the US decision to sanction the International Criminal Court in The Hague. While the UK has made “strong statements” of their continued support for the court, their next step could be putting in place a “blocking statute” that would make the sanctions unenforceable in the UK, Ms Ahmed said. The wars in Sudan and in Gaza have featured clear examples of the UK government’s inability to intervene in time, Ms Ahmed said. She questioned why it had taken the UK months to apply a partial suspension of around 30 out of about 350 arms export licences to Israel for military use in Gaza, which the British government eventually announced in September 2024. Export licensing was one area in which the government could act quickly, by referring to its own criteria and the Arms Trade Treaty, she said. “They have the duty to prevent genocide and other crimes, but that’s very hard to enforce. But when you have the export-licensing criteria, that’s where we find there’s a space where the government themselves has processes to evaluate. “I was going in on a weekly basis with either ministers or high-level officials and sometimes middle-ranked officials. We were presenting the evidence. It certainly took longer than it should have,” she said. “It did so on the basis that Israel couldn’t be found to have a commitment to comply with international law because it was restricting aid.” Likewise, the UK’s response to the Sudanese civil war had failed to activate “the full plethora of government machinery”, despite its key resolutions on Sudan at the UN Security Council. With cuts to overseas aid anticipated for the long term, Ms Ahmed – who previously worked as a legal adviser to the FCDO – outlined options that would reinforce the role of human rights in UK foreign policy. The units involved in human rights and atrocity prevention needed to be “supported at the highest-ministerial level, prioritised, given resources and given the power within the bureaucratic system to have a say when policy decisions are being made,” she said. Instead, government advisers on human rights policy were often sidelined. “So often, what I have found, is that the human rights directorate aren't key stakeholders in key political decisions,” Ms Ahmed said. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's declaration last month that settler “terrorists” were responsible for “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank was a major step, Ms Ahmed said. “That was a really huge development and important to note because it's the first time the government has ever made any such determination and it's clear, given the magnitude of the forced displacement of Palestinians from their land in the West Bank,” she said. Questions remain about how the UK will implement its most significant foreign policy shift in months – the move to impose sanctions on the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. Foreign Office officials have suggested a six to nine month time frame for initial measures to be implemented but campaigners including Ms Ahmed say this is too long. “As I understand it, there is a commitment to implementing it in a way that’s effective,” she said. “The devil will be in the detail to ensure that they in fact do that.” Amnesty International and other organisations are calling on the government to make sure the ban extends to banks and financial services that work with companies involved in illegal settlements. “It’s not just about goods and services to settlements. It’s also about the financial enabling of the occupation … which are involved in continuing the financial stability of the settlements,” Ms Ahmed said.

title: UAE weather: Rainy weekend expected in east of country
description: Winds of up to 50kph expected
content: Rain is expected in parts of the UAE across much of the weekend, according to the latest update from the National Centre of Meteorology (NCM). Wet weather is forecast in the south-east of the country on Wednesday, with winds reaching up to 50kph. On Friday and Saturday, clouds in the east are likely to bring rain, while wet weather is forecast in the north-east. The NCM's website says rain is expected on Wednesday in Fujairah and in Al Ain on Thursday. At the weekend, the highest temperature in the country will be 41°C in Sweihan on Saturday. The temperature will reach 39°C in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, with Dubai's temperature cooling slightly from 37°C on Wednesday and Thursday to 35°C on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Zayed National Museum's first temporary exhibition to explore 7,000 years of camel history
description: Opening in December, Tracks Through Time will feature rare archaeological discoveries, ancient rock art and enduring Emirati traditions
content: Zayed National Museum has announced its first temporary exhibition, exploring more than 7,000 years of camel history and the animal's significance in Emirati culture. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art will open in early December, coinciding with the Abu Dhabi museum's first anniversary. The exhibition will trace the camel's role in trade, society and artistic expression, from its presence in the region thousands of years ago to contemporary traditions such as racing and beauty competitions. Among the highlights will be the first public display of archaeological evidence of an extinct wild camel species. These include bones discovered in Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, from between 4500 and 4000BC, and Bronze Age remains from Al Sufouh in Dubai, dating to between 2000 and 1300BC. Domesticated camel bones from Saruq Al Hadid in Dubai will also be displayed, offering some of the world's earliest evidence of the transition from wild camels to domesticated animals. The artefacts are on loan from the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority. “We are excited to present our first temporary exhibition, which celebrates the camel's profound significance in Emirati culture and the broader story of the UAE,” says Peter Magee, director of the Zayed National Museum . He says the exhibition draws on archaeological research to explore the relationship between humans and camels, from early domestication to the prestige of Al Hejin racing and Mazayna beauty competitions. Other objects include camel rock artwork from Fujairah dating back 3,000 years, a rare children's book from the 1840s detailing camel species and their uses and UAE postage stamps featuring the animal. Archival photographs, film footage and oral testimonies from camel herders will offer further insight into the animal's place in daily life. Recordings of Taghrooda, a form of Bedouin poetry, and Alheda'a , the traditional practice of camel calling, will also feature. Both are recognised by Unesco as intangible cultural heritage. The exhibition will be accompanied by workshops, guided tours and activities as part of the museum's first anniversary celebrations, alongside a dedicated retail offering inspired by the exhibition's themes. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art opens at Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi in early December

title: Four Syrian troops killed in ambush on Hama motorway
description: Incident happened on edge of desert area that has witnessed attacks by ISIS and other militant groups
content: Four Syrian security personnel were killed when two patrols were ambushed in the countryside of Hama province on Tuesday night. Nour Al Baba, spokesman for Syria's Interior Ministry, condemned the attacks on the Salamiya-Athriya motorway and said authorities would pursue those responsible. “With deep sorrow and grief, we mourn the loss of four of our brothers – road security personnel – who were killed when two of their patrols were targeted in the Hama countryside,” he said. “The crime will not deter us from continuing to pursue the perpetrators and bring them to justice,” Mr Al Baba said, adding that the incident would strengthen the security forces’ resolve to protect civilians and safeguard lives. Internal security forces said they were continuing efforts to track down those involved. The attack took place on the road linking Salamiya, east of Hama city, with Athriya, an area farther east on the route towards the Syrian desert. The motorway forms part of a transport corridor connecting central Syria with the country’s eastern regions. The area is on the edge of the Syrian desert, where armed groups and ISIS militants have carried out attacks. The ministry did not provide further details about the circumstances of the attack, including the weapons used.

title: To the Ramparts: New missile shield 'protects warships from drone swarms'
description: Laser-guided rockets offer lower cost-to-kill ratio than Patriots
content: A cost-effective missile system to defend civilian and military sites from drone swarms has been unveiled in France . Rampart, developed by Naval Group , can create a defensive shield around warships using large numbers of low-cost laser-guided rockets rather than expensive interceptors such as Patriot, that were expended at high rates in the Iran war. It has completed successful sea trials in the Mediterranean, including a French Navy counter-drone exercise off Toulon. “It is designed to build a defensive shield around a warship in drone warfare,” said Stephan Meunier, a former French navy commander involved with the programme. Naval Group expects to produce up to 10,000 Rampart systems by 2028. In tests, the system struck an aerial drone as well as unguided rockets trained on surface targets. The system fires laser-guided 68mm rockets fitted with proximity fuses and has a range of up to 6km. The launcher consists of four modules, each carrying 20 projectiles, giving a maximum load of 80 rockets. It can be loaded with a combination of weapons, including surface-to-air and surface-to-surface missiles, decoys or precision missiles. An experienced crew can reload a single 20-round module in about 10 minutes. The system weighs about four tonnes, allowing it to be fitted to relatively small warships including corvettes. During the recent Iran war, western forces used large numbers of expensive interceptors against relatively cheap drones. Patriot missiles costing more than $4 million each were used to take out Shahed-136 drones costing just $35,000, roughly the same price as a guided 68mm rocket. “The cost-to-kill ratio is very effective and it can tackle a drone swarm attack,” Mr Meunier said. “Rockets are cheaper and more efficient.” There is growing evidence that shipping in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea could face “saturation attacks” by drones fired from Iran or the rebel Houthis. Naval ships equipped with Rampart would be able to provide significant close-in protection, Mr Meunier said. Rampart can also be deployed as a ground-based system to protect airports, military bases and civilian areas. “This system would provide good defences for fixed installations such as airports and to protect urban centres or military camps in the Gulf as well as on board warships,” Mr Meunier said. Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia’s main airport came under attack from Houthi rebels, with 13 people killed in two incidents. Missiles were also intercepted in Riyadh and Dammam. Naval Group has also developed a single Rampart module for its Sirenha unmanned surface vessel, allowing an autonomous drone boat to provide an additional defensive layer. The French company is also working with Emirates' defence group Edge to conduct trials of the UAE-developed SkyKnight air-defence missile, beginning with land trials before maritime testing next year. SkyKnight can engage aerial threats at ranges of up to 10km, potentially giving Rampart a more capable missile option alongside its 68mm rockets. There is also a possibility that Rampart could be battle-tested in Ukraine where Kyiv is getting desperately short of air defences against daily Russian drone and missile attacks. If successful, then it could well provide a major step in defending key military and civilians sites from the threat of drone saturation attack at low cost.

title: Geeing up for 6G: What the next mobile standard promises and challenges it faces
description: With AI growing more powerful, reliability and security are priorities
content: Over the past weeks, UAE telecom operators etisalat and du have announced further progress in their march towards 6G, the next generation of wireless communication. The industry is accelerating its preparations for the technology that being presented as vital to the world becoming more connected, underpinned by increasingly intelligent devices and services . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi's etisalat – which recently rebranded back from e& – said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. 6G promises faster speeds and efficiency than the current 5G mobile phone technology, which also has more advanced forms under names such as 5G+, 5G Advanced and 5.5G. Historically, new generations of wireless technology have emerged with every new decade, suggesting 6G could become available in the early 2030s. This is a widely shared industry expectation. The US introduced the third generation in 2002, the fourth in 2010 and 5G in 2018. The second and first generations were in the 1980s and early 1990s, respectively, with the “zero G” before that. While a 6G rollout is predicted in the early 2030s, not all of its features are expected to be available at launch, as the industry would continue testing its deployment. 5G's maximum transmission speed is 20 gigabits per second, which is already 20 times faster that 4G's 1Gbps rate under ideal circumstances. However, 6G's theoretical maximum compared to 5G, has varied from anywhere between 50 times faster, or 1 terabit per second, to 1,000 times, or 2.5 terabytes per second. One can only imagine how much that will increase transmission speeds. A multi-gigabyte file that used to take seconds or a few minutes to download could be done in a snap. The consumer proposition of 6G will always be front and centre, especially as digital consumption and reliance on connected devices will only become more widespread. But on an industrial scale, 6G is expected to power advanced iterations of immersive and mass communication, ubiquitous connectivity, integrated sensing and communication, low-latency and hyper-reliable communication and artificial intelligence communication, according to the International Telecommunication Union, which leads the framework and standards-setting of wireless communications. Communications, business and economic gains aside, the power of 6G will also play a critical role in society by enabling affordable, resilient and energy‑efficient networks for health, education, agriculture and disaster response, the Geneva-based UN agency said. “Advanced networks also present a way to close the persistent digital divide that today leaves many people in low-income countries behind,” it added. Transport, home appliances and security, payment networks, financial transactions and a host of other products and services expected to be highly connected in the future will also rely on the speed 6G would offer. There are a number of issues that need to be addressed to ensure the reliability of 6G networks. Arguably the biggest challenge is to build 6G networks resilient to any AI-induced compromises. Networks of the future should be able to detect threats and adaptive enough to respond to them, according to the EC-Council University in New Mexico. Encryption, especially that which can protect against quantum threats, and integration to blockchain would also be important to avoid unauthorised data access and manipulation, the university added.

title: 'We expect more from the top': Lisandro Martinez takes aim at Manchester United hierarchy
description: Defender says club bosses failed to strengthen squad sufficiently after loss at Atletico Madrid extends poor start to season
content: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez did not hold back as he criticised the club's hierarchy ​after ​their ​Champions League defeat to ⁠Atletico Madrid on Tuesday. United slipped to a 2-0 defeat, which means Michael Carrick 's team have now gone winless for five consecutive games across competitions. Martinez, however, attempted to highlight issues outside the pitch, stating that he ⁠expected greater investment to help ​the team compete at the highest level. The Argentina international singled ⁠out director of football Jason Wilcox, saying United needed more signings to compete with their rivals. “I expect more from ​our ⁠technical director. I have ‌to be honest. And also, as players, we ​have to do more,” Martinez told Amazon Prime. “Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas.” Atletico took the lead through Pablo Barrios inside the opening minute at the Metropolitano, before Ademola Lookman secured victory in the 79th minute, shortly after United defender Leny Yoro was sent off. United are on three points in the Champions League league phase, having opened their campaign with a 4-0 win over ​Sabah FK . United are returning to the ‌Champions League after a ⁠two-season absence, having finished ​bottom of their group in their previous appearance ​in ‌the competition in 2023/24. “We had a fantastic season last season ⁠and now we expect more from the top, from ⁠upstairs, to bring in more players to compete, because many teams have brought in many players as well,” Martinez added. “Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today. “I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.” United, who are 13th in the Premier League , ​visit Leeds United on Sunday before travelling to Como for their next Champions League fixture on October 21. Former Manchester United star Wayne Rooney said Martinez's comments were unwarranted and could throw the dressing room into chaos. “It is disrespectful to his teammates,” Rooney was quoted as saying by the BCC. “He is saying his teammates aren't good enough. “Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens – but that interview isn't going to help. “[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way.” Barcelona recovered well to defeat Galatasaray 4-1. Barca overturned a first-half deficit with Lamine Yamal supplying two assists. Galatasaray went ahead as Alexey Batrakov scored in the 28th minute. The hosts thought they had doubled their lead through a Baris Yilmaz header, only for VAR to identify an offside ​in the build-up. Joao Cancelo equalised just before half-time and Yamal then set up Fermin Lopez and Anthony ‌Gordon to score in the 50th and 53rd minutes. ⁠Karim Adeyemi completed the victory. Also, Arsenal scored three times in seven minutes to defeat Lille 3-0. Arsenal had to wait until the 64th minute for Jurrien Timber to break Lille's resistance from Noni Madueke's pass. Substitute Bukayo Saka then set up Eberechi Eze's goal before Kai Havertz supplied Saka for the ​third in the 71st minute.

title: Ollie Watkins on target for Al Hilal while Sardar Azmoun bags double as Shabab Al Ahli win in Jeddah
description: Iranian striker scores twice as UAE club extend perfect start to AFC Champions League
content: Sardar Azmoun struck both goals as Shabab Al Ahli picked up a superb away win at Al Ittihad in the AFC Champions League on Tuesday night. The victory took the UAE club to a perfect six points from six, while Saudi Pro League Al Ittihad have just a single point after opening their campaign with a draw against Al Shamal SC of Qatar last month. Backed by a full house in Jeddah, the home side started positively with Ahmed Al Julaydan forcing Matheus Donelli into a save from a tight angle in the sixth minute. Shabab Al Ahli , however, struck in the next phase of play when Guilherme Bala powered down the left before teeing up the unmarked Azmoun to slot home. Al Ittihad looked for an immediate response, with Steven Bergwijn testing Donelli from distance in the 13th minute, but the visitors doubled their advantage three minutes later. Reza Ghandipour, who had only just replaced the injured Bala, released Azmoun with a through ball and the forward outpaced his markers before converting from a tight angle. “We conceded two goals because of easy mistakes, which made the task difficult afterwards,” said Al Ittihad coach Jens Wissing. “My job as a coach is to work with the players. We were better in the second half and we reached the opponent's goal, but we were not successful.” He added: “We played with three forwards because we had more crosses, and it was possible to make use of one of the crosses. We did not play the game well. We had many chances and we could have been better.” Elsewhere, Al Hilal recorded their second successive victory after defeating Al Sadd 2-0. Ollie Watkins put Saudi Pro League leaders Hilal ahead in the first half before a Ruben Neves spot-kick confirmed the points as Qatar’s Al Sadd suffered a second consecutive defeat. “I am happy with the players' performance,” said Hilal boss Simone Inzaghi. “We produced a big performance and controlled most of the game, and I saw a wonderful display from the team.” The Italian also praised Gabriel Martinelli after the former Arsenal man gave the Al Sadd defence a difficult evening. “He is a big player and we are lucky to have him with us,” added Inzaghi. “He always proves his high quality and his ability to serve the team and benefit it in more than one different position.”

title: Man United ratings vs Atletico Madrid: Yoro off and Baleba promising on another tough night for Carrick
description: Pressure builds on Old Trafford boss after Champions League defeat in Spain
content: Atletico Madrid needed only 50 seconds ​to punish Manchester United's high defensive line on their way to a 2-0 victory in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night. Alex Baena broke clear down the left before squaring for Pablo Barrios ​to finish and it looked like being a long night for the visitors. United threatened through ‌ Bryan Mbeumo , who shot narrowly wide and later forced a close-range save from Jan Oblak, while Marcus Rashford also squandered an opportunity. Atletico had a Johnny Cardoso ⁠effort disallowed for a Marcos Llorente handball before the break and Julian Alvarez volleyed against the post early in the second ⁠half. United's task became harder when Leny Yoro was sent off in the 74th minute for denying Jonathan David a goalscoring opportunity. Five minutes later, Ademola Lookman tapped into an empty net after David's shot was saved. "I don't see it being a red card, I have to say. I really don't agree with the decision," said United boss Michael Carrick. "I don't know whether I'm allowed to say or not, but I just don't agree with the decision. "He wasn't really moving in a quick direction to goal. Whether it was or wasn't a foul, or not a foul, it was very soft and slow and [to get] a red card for that, especially to be taken to VAR. I just don't understand it." Senne Lammens – 6: Awful start, not that he was at fault, as he conceded to the excellent Barrios after 50 seconds. Then beaten by a Cardoso shot which Atleti thought was a goal, but it was handball. Good save from David before the second. One clean sheet in eight games. Ayden Heaven – 6: Nightmare start for the makeshift left-back despite his best efforts as a simple ball over United’s defence split it. Actually unlucky not to block Barrios’ shot. Some nice turns. Grew in confidence. Lovely ball towards the corner as United attacked on 79 minutes. Lisandro Martinez – 6: Left centre-back and drifted a lovely ball towards Rashford on 14 minutes. Clumsy challenge on Barrios conceded a free-kick. His post-match criticisms of Manchester United will be headline news. Leny Yoro – 6: Right centre-back after playing well on Saturday at right-back. Didn’t realise how much time he had on the ball at times as he ballooned it back towards Atletico or gave up possession. Started second-half well but sent off after 74 minutes – he was the last line of defence. But it was harsh, especially as the referee was so close. It was not a clear and obvious error. Diogo Dalot – 5: Right-back and kept very busy by the excellent Baena and Grimaldo on that flank. Poor on goal as Baena caught him out as the ball came over. He was up against better players. Andrey Santos – 6: First start since the opening day of the season and steady in the middle alongside Baleba. Found his feet, played deeper and played the full 90. There might be something there with him and Baleba. Carlos Baleba – 7: Tame header from an unmarked position eight yards out went straight at Oblak. Beaten by Barrios who then crossed for Alvarez in a superb bit of Atletico play. Otherwise good energy and decent passing in his first United start. Youri Tielemans – 6: Played higher – at least in theory – up behind Mbeumo, whom he played a smart one-two with on 24 minutes, but barely featured in first half. More advanced in second and brilliant vision for a ball to Fernandes. Bruno Fernandes – 5: On the right and less of an impact on the game. Stunning turn to beat Grimaldo – three times in total – as United pushed to equalise on 39 minutes but he didn’t cross. He did at the start of the second – and nearly equalised on 57 minutes as his volley bounced just wide of the post. Moved into his usual role after the subs and was better. Hit crossbar on 70 minutes with a right-foot shot. Bryan Mbeumo – 6: Swept a deflected shot wide in United’s first attack on 11 minutes after he took out two defenders and did a number on Romero. Came close again on 23 minutes – well saved by Oblak. Marcus Rashford – 5: Scored against Atletico last season. Good duels against Llorente. Made a run on goal but couldn’t get on the ball enough before he switched right. Didn’t really get in the game. Ineffective. Booked. Joshua Zirkzee (for Tielemans, 65') – 5: Should have scored in stoppage time when he had time. Floats around. Frustrating. Mason Mount (for Baleba, 65') – 5: No impact Amad Diallo (for Rashford, 65') – 5: See above Matheus Cunha (for Fernandes, 80') – N/A: Outrageously pulled back in a yellow card incident. Shot was well-saved by Oblak. Harry Maguire (for Heaven, 80) – N/A: Late sub.

title: Britain must settle its Brexit argument before seeking an EU return
description: The road back to Europe is fraught with political obtacles
content: Confusion reigns where the UK and EU is concerned. Having been dormant for so long, avoided and ducked by successive recent prime ministers, Britain’s future relations with the EU has suddenly become a major political and diplomatic issue. The uncertainty stems from how far Andy Burnham wants to go and at what speed. He gives every impression of wishing the UK to rejoin and quickly. But then he will say in the next breath that the British public must decide. That raises the possibility, make it probability, of a bitter, protracted Brexit battle all over again. He is pinning much on the forthcoming UK-EU Summit, scheduled for November 20, and has set out his wish-list of what he would like that meeting to achieve – including free trade of food and drink products, greater movement of young people – while giving the impression of this only being the first step. That in itself, though, is radical compared with where the UK and EU were. And, as Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch has rightly observed, it’s a curious way to proceed into a negotiation, showing your hand at one go. It is clear to everyone, not least the EU that he sees this as merely the beginning not the end. How though, can he get there, without resurrecting the old battle-lines and splitting the country? He began by being inflammatory, by suggesting the referendum verdict was improperly obtained. No sooner did Mr Burnham signal his desire for the UK to form closer ties with the EU, with a view possibly to rejoining, than the Prime Minister appeared on a podcast saying there was incontrovertible evidence that Russia interfered in the referendum campaign . Bearing in mind the decision to leave was won by just 2 per cent of the vote, the suggestion that it was some way Russian influenced has the ability to invalidate Brexit, to throw the authenticity of the UK’s departure into doubt (Remainers would argue it was already questionable as part of the Brexiteers’ campaign was based on hyperbole and falsehood). So, we actually didn’t choose to exit after all, which could help our efforts to gain readmission. Except Mr Burnham’s was not a new claim. It had been made repeatedly in the past and had always been denied by government ministers and security officials. Nevertheless, here was Mr Burnham maintaining that upon arriving in No 10 he asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 ballot and stating: “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was.” Fine, if he has the proof. At the time of writing, none is forthcoming. Indeed, well after Mr Burnham made his comment, Stephen Doughty, the Foreign Office minister, was challenged by the BBC to produce it, and replied he wouldn’t “get into specifics”. Instead, Mr Doughty resorted to vague accusations that “Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes. They’re engaged in information warfare, they’re spending £1.5 billion [almost $2 billion] this year alone on disinformation and propaganda”. Cue Nigel Farage, the Brexit architect, denouncing Mr Burnham as “a liar”. Cue too, a feeling of deja vu, that we’ve been here before, many times, that nothing has really changed, that the old wounds have never healed, but still exist, waiting to be reopened. All this row – and it quickly erupted into a war of words, with Mr Farage, who has been accused in the past of enjoying close ties with Russia, sensing his honour and reputation had been impugned sounding most indignant – served to show was that the UK is nowhere near ready to rejoin, not collectively with a consensus, that EU leaders starting to take Mr Burnham at his word might wish to reconsider. The question they should ask themselves is, does Mr Burnham speak for the nation? He may wish to come back but does the electorate, how certain can they be that the same mixture of disregard, often tipping into open contempt, for the EU and its ideals, won’t simply rear its head again? It’s true that a majority of the British people, far greater than the percentage who chose to quit, now believe Brexit was a mistake . The polls put the figure slightly above 70 per cent. In democratic terms, that’s substantial. But it’s an opinion poll, not the real thing, and however the cake is cut, a significant portion of the populace still argue we were right to go. That slice is inspired by committed and noisy agitators. Mr Farage has already said Mr Burnham’s public ambition has regalvanised his Reform UK party’s support base. Until the senior pro-Brexit players in the epic drama of a decade ago come out and admit they were wrong, those of a suspicious nature in the EU are fully entitled to worry the UK would become the renegade member it was before – harrying, obstructing and yes, insulting, at every turn. It would require former prime minister Boris Johnson to recant, and ideally, Mr Farage. Even better still, for the pair of them together to fall on their anti-EU swords. Well, that will never occur . Rather, what will happen is that they will unpick the scars and a whole new anti-EU front will erupt. In the same way that Britain withdrew by the thinnest of margins, this perception matters. Because should we pursue readmittance, we must clear several hurdles, any one of which could block our path. Mr Burnham clearly would like to make it an election issue, to be included in the Labour manifesto. If he wins that popular mandate, in theory, there ought to be no requirement for a re-run of a separate EU vote. That is the view of the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, among others. But the EU is likely to insist upon a second referendum as a precursor to commencing membership negotiations. Their argument is that they would want to be persuaded the decision is non-party political, and that a vote for a manifesto covers all manner of issues, only one of which is the EU. A re-run could make the case that recommencing membership would last beyond the lifetime of the newly elected government and extend across successive governments. Virtually all countries joining have done so only after holding a public ballot. So, the UK could not realistically seek special dispensation. The European Commission, which would lead the process, would also need to vote its agreement. So too would a majority of the members of European Parliament. Critically, as well, the 27 member countries would have a say and it is by no means guaranteed they would approve the UK resuming. Traditional anti-Britishness could re-surface and they could have agendas of their own – skilful diplomacy by the UK government and Foreign Office would have to be deployed. That said, British diplomats are indicating privately they think simply going back in and taking up where we left off is a tall, if not impossible, order. The EU too would be right to examine Britain’s motives – why now, why the sudden change of heart, why after all this time, 10 years and counting, do we wish to return? The answer, and one Mr Burnham is correct to proclaim, is because Brexit has not delivered . At a stroke, we ditched a free trade bloc of 450 million people. British businesses too found themselves bereft of skilled EU labour. Nothing we’ve done since has come remotely close to replacing what was lost. The Bank of England estimates a loss to our gross domestic product of 6 per cent to 8 per cent – this at a time of increased global competitiveness, rising protectiveness and sovereignty, energy crisis, supply chain difficulties, rising cost of living, threat of AI to jobs, when just adding 1 per cent is a tough bar. Here was the UK saying goodbye to 6 per cent. Just like that. As welcome as they are, trade deals have helped plug the gap, but they only go so far. We had a huge customs-free market on our doorstep, and we blew it. Business investment post-Brexit also fell, down, according to estimates, by 12 per cent to 18 per cent. That’s what we’d like again and if not through full membership, through a much greater rapprochement, possibly through the Customs Union. We’d love also to be able to stem the tide of illegal immigration, which we have failed to do on our own. But the EU is aware of our need and it realises too, that is a prize worth having and is not something to be awarded easily. Not if it comes with the baggage of anti-EU rhetoric and the likelihood that at any moment, a new administration, one led by Mr Farage, say, could again up sticks. That said, there are those in the EU who would like to see Britain’s return in some form. We bring with us 69.5 million people and we could provide an economic as well as political fillip. In a world dominated by two superpowers, a united EU would be a match for them. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech to Davos earlier this year, in which he called for the “middle powers” to combine, continues to resonate loudly. The fact Mr Carney has followed that up with a suggestion of “associate membership” of the EU has met with a warm response. Mr Carney and Canada, they can do business with. Are they able to say the same with certainty for an unclear, impatient Mr Burnham and his Perfidious Albion? Therein lies the rub.

title: Aramco building attacked after Saudi-led coalition hits Houthi site
description: Videos show huge orange fireball erupting above Yemeni capital Sanaa as troops take on rebels
content: An administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco was attacked by a missile on Tuesday night, causing a fire but no casualties, as fighting intensifies between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The kingdom's Energy Ministry said the missile strike happened in Dhahran, in the Eastern Province. Authorities responded to the attack, with no deaths or injuries reported, the Saudi Press Agency reported. People living near the Aramco compound described terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. “This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life,” one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area. “They couldn't go outside to check what had happened because the smoke was everywhere,” she said. Debris from two cruise missiles intercepted and destroyed over the capital Riyadh injured four people – two women, a man and a child – state television quoted the Saudi Civil Defence as saying. A Civil Defence representative said the falling debris also damaged 15 residential homes in the Saudi capital. Authorities implemented established procedures in response. Bloomberg reported that the site was Aramco’s executive headquarters, while a company source quoted by Reuters identified the target as an Aramco headquarters complex. Neither Aramco nor Saudi authorities had officially confirmed which building was hit. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen separately said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Dhahran, with debris falling in a residential area. It also reported intercepting a missile targeting Haradh and three drones north of the capital, Riyadh. The coalition said late on Tuesday that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including the Al Sabahah station in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and piers used for loading fuel at the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki accused the Houthis of using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. “It has been established that the Houthi terrorist militia uses civilian objects and vital resources to sustain its war effort," he said on X. "These include the Al Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground strategic fuel reserves and storage facilities and fuel and dedicated fuel-loading and unloading berths in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.” Video posted on social media appeared to show a huge orange fireball erupting above Sanaa, followed by a towering column of thick black smoke. The strikes came after the coalition had warned civilians near the oil facility to leave “for their safety”. The scale of the damage to the site and the impact on fuel supplies were not immediately clear. The Houthis said fuel reserves had been dispersed before the attack, a claim that has not been independently verified. Saudi energy infrastructure has been been hit before. A refinery in Jazan, in the kingdom's west, was shut after a strike, and a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast was also targeted. A cross-country pipeline used by Aramco to transport crude to export markets was temporarily shut in September following an attack launched from Iraq. The pipeline is strategically important because it offers an alternative route for Saudi oil exports when shipping through the Gulf faces disruption. Oil prices rose on Wednesday after news of the attack on the Aramco building, as traders weighed the risk of further disruption to regional energy supplies. It is unclear how the latest incidents could affect production, refining or exports. Dhahran lies at the centre of Saudi Arabia’s oil industry, close to major oil fields in Eastern Province and the Gulf.

title: Chinese companies seek Gulf partnerships as physical AI takes shape
description: LinkerBot is exploring UAE partnerships as region increases advanced manufacturing
content: Chinese robotics companies are looking to the Gulf as a possible manufacturing centre for the next generation of AI-powered machines, as the region's capital, energy resources and industrial ambitions create opportunities for partnerships. Beijing-based robotics company LinkerBot is among those exploring opportunities in the UAE, where it is in talks with major institutions on potential partnerships, Weber Su, the company's vice president and head of global markets, said during the AIM Summit in Dubai on Tuesday. One model being considered would involve Chinese companies supplying advanced robotics parts, while the UAE provides capital-intensive assembly and automated production. Such an arrangement could allow Gulf countries to take part directly in making advanced robots, rather than mainly buying the technology. “That could be the business model that we are exploring with Middle Eastern countries, particularly in UAE,” Mr Su said. LinkerBot specialises in dexterous robotic hands, enabling machines to grasp and manipulate objects. It has expanded into components including reducers and micromotors that control robotic movement. The potential collaboration reflects a broader trend in which Asian companies seek international manufacturing partners, while Gulf economies use their capital, energy and infrastructure to build higher-value industries. In September, Chinese electric and extended-range vehicle maker ROX Motor began producing vehicles in Abu Dhabi . The UAE, meanwhile, is also boosting manufacturing and under its Operation 300bn strategy aims to increase the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to Dh300 billion by 2031. The country's industrial exports rose 25 per cent last year to a record Dh262 billion, with medium and high-technology exports increasing 42 per cent to Dh92 billion, according to the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. The UAE is also investing in automation to improve manufacturing competitiveness. Mr Su said Chinese companies could increasingly focus on specialised robotics parts, while Gulf partners develop the capital-intensive assembly operations needed to bring those technologies to market. Turning that potential into commercially successful partnerships will require investment agreements, viable production models and sustained demand for AI-powered machines. The potential partnerships come as the technology industry moves towards what investors and developers describe as the next stage of artificial intelligence: physical AI. Chinese AI developers including DeepSeek , Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI are becoming increasingly competitive with their US rivals, offering advanced models at lower costs, according to Joseph Zeng, founder and chief investment officer of Hong Kong-based Arcadia Fund Management Group. While generative AI has focused on chatbots, content creation and software applications, the next phase is expected to bring intelligent systems into the physical world. Physical AI combines advanced AI models with robotics, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings, make decisions and perform tasks traditionally requiring human intervention. Unlike conventional industrial robots, which are generally programmed for repetitive movements, the ambition is to develop machines capable of adapting to different situations. Applications could include robotic hands manipulating unfamiliar objects, autonomous machines working across production lines and robots assisting hospital patients. Mr Su said advances in computing power and AI models were making these capabilities increasingly possible. LinkerBot is developing robotic hands with built-in movement ability that could eventually be combined with sophisticated AI systems to perform a wider range of tasks. “We're going to have skill stores similar to the app stores,” Mr Su said. China's manufacturing scale could give its companies an advantage as the technology shifts towards commercial production. The country installed about 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, accounting for 54 per cent of global installations, according to the International Federation of Robotics . The figures refer to factory robots rather than humanoids, but demonstrate the scale of China's industrial automation industry and supporting supply chains. SK hynix held 50 per cent of the global high-bandwidth memory market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung accounted for 33 per cent, according to Counterpoint Research data reported by the Yonhap news agency. "Physical AI provides a lot of opportunities for investors,” said Mr Zeng, whose investments include ByteDance and Zhipu AI in China, as well as South Korea's SK hynix and Samsung. The next stage of AI would require advances in computing hardware and infrastructure, he added. He identified high-bandwidth memory, optical transceivers and robotics components among the technologies benefitting from rising investment. Health care could also become an important market. During a recent visit to Suzhou, near Shanghai, Mr Zeng said he encountered a company developing a voice-controlled robot designed to assist bedridden patients with repositioning and personal care. Mr Su said humanoid robots could eventually help to care for elderly people and children in smaller communities, where shrinking populations make it difficult to attract doctors and maintain healthcare services. While fully autonomous, general-purpose robots are still being developed, their potential to ease labour shortages, reduce care costs and extend essential services to underserved communities illustrates the social and economic impact physical AI could have beyond factories. For the Gulf, opportunities could include using autonomous systems in established industries. Mr Zeng highlighted electric and autonomous heavy-duty trucks for mining and industrial operations, alongside energy storage and cleaner power technologies. Energy is also becoming increasingly important to AI investment. Global data-centre electricity use is expected to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency . The forecast highlights the importance of electricity generation, storage and cooling infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates. For Gulf countries with substantial energy resources and growing renewable power capacity, this creates another potential area of collaboration with Asian technology developers.

title: Roma v Real Madrid: Mourinho struggles to solve Vinicius Jr conundrum amid Bernabeu chaos
description: Portuguese coach heads back to former club in Champions League days after out-of-form Brazilian attacker was sent off for pulling opponent's hair
content: The idea that Jose Mourinho was the man to restore order to the mayhem that is Real Madrid and prevent a third successive campaign without a major trophy appears to be unravelling fast. Last season was a turbulent one for Los Blancos that saw managers sacked, players jeered by their own fans, teammates fighting each other, all topped off by bitter rivals Barcelona securing a second successive La Liga title. To control a dressing room of rampant egos, Madrid president Florentino Perez turned to the biggest coaching ego of them all, brining Mourinho back for his second stint at a club who sacked him back in 2013. But just nine matches into the new season, all is not well in the Spanish capital. On Saturday at the Bernabeu, Madrid were labouring towards a 1-0 win over Villarreal – courtesy of teenager Yan Diomande's first goal for the club – when Vinicius Junior scored with a clinical first-time finish. It sparked ferocious celebrations from the attacker, with Mourinho sprinting across the pitch to join in. But the joyous scenes were cut short when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera Escuderos was asked to view the pitchside monitor by VAR, where he saw Vinicius clearly pulling the hair of Nathan Saliba in the build-up to the goal. Just 20 minutes after coming off the bench to replace Trent Alexander-Arnold, Vinicius was shown a red card and the scene quickly descended into chaos as furious Madrid players surrounded the referee, while the Brazilian had to be dragged away by teammates. An incandescent Mourinho, who had already spent the entire game berating officials, earned himself a yellow card, then refused to appear for the post-match press conference. The player himself has since issued a brief apology on social media – saying “sorry to the team and the fans” – but could now receive a three-match ban that would see him miss the Clasico on October 25 against a table-topping Barca team that has won eight from eight in La Liga so far. While Mourinho continues to rant and rave about perceived refereeing agendas against his team, the fact remains they are not playing well. They find themselves in fourth place, six points shy of Barca, having lost to Real Betis and the derby against Atletico Madrid, where Mourinho was again left bemoaning refereeing decisions . And the biggest puzzle facing the veteran Portuguese is coaxing Vinicius – who signed a bumper new six-year contract extension over the summer – back into top form. The 26-year-old has managed just one goal in 672 minutes of action this season prompting questions as to why Mourinho has not turned to other attacking options in his squad. “Some players need time to get back to their usual level … and I’m not going to hide from that,” he insisted ahead of the Villarreal game. “I never criticise the Madrid fan base; I only respect it. It breaks my heart to see a boy like him suffer. He wants to become that Vinicius again who wins matches and makes the difference … Vini deserves support.” Mourinho has also found himself defending top-scorer Kylian Mbappe – who has eight goals in nine games, taking his Madrid career tally to 94 in 112 matches – after the French attacker was criticised for making trips to Paris and Switzerland while still recovering from a minor knee injury picked up on international duty. “What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to … They won't have the chance to whistle, because they'll be at home,” said the 63-year-old, who dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous” while also accusing the media of trying to turn Madrid fans against Mbappe. After starting their Uefa Champions League campaign with a 2-1 win over Inter Milan – with Mbappe and Federico Valverde on target – they now face another of Mourinho's former clubs in Roma at the Stadio Olympico on Wednesday. The Italian side are currently third in Serie A after drawing 0-0 at Como on Sunday, when they had top-scorer Donyell Malen shown a straight red card for a reckless tackle on home defender Kaiki. The Giallorossi's opening European game saw them draw with Fenerbahce in Turkey. Mourinho's three-year spell in the Italian capital was a trademark mix of success and controversy that ended in the sack. He guided Roma to their first major European crown when they defeated Feyenoord 1-0 in 2022's inaugural Europa Conference League final, which also meant Mourinho became the first manager to win all four major European trophies, having previously lifted the Uefa Cup, Champions League and Europa League. “I knew the moment I arrived what it meant to the people,” said Mourinho after the match in Tirana. “They had been waiting for something like this. This was not work tonight, this was history. We had to write history. We wrote it.” But 12 months later, Mourinho was once again left ranting at officials after Roma were beaten by Sevilla on penalties in a Europa League final that witnessed a tournament record 13 yellow cards. His infamous foul-mouthed tirade at referee Anthony Taylor in the car park after the game earned him a four-match ban. The following season, Mourinho was sacked after a poor run of results, but the Portuguese insists his love for the club remains intact. “I think the bond between me and the Roma fans was created by the fact … they understood that for me there was only Roma and the Roma fans. I fought for them, I gave everything,” he said last week in an interview with Corriere dello Sport. “What do I expect from the Olimpico? I do not expect banners. I do not expect anything. I expect respect. ”

title: Cody Rhodes calls for WWE return to Abu Dhabi, before Street Fighter release
description: Co-star Andrew Schulz shares his love for the UAE, which he says has 'some of the best comedy audiences in the world'
content: It's been nearly nine years since WWE last staged a show in Abu Dhabi. Three-time WWE champion Cody Rhodes thinks it's time the wrestling company returned. “Love Abu Dhabi,” Rhodes tells The National . “I only get to stop in for a brief moment usually, but I feel like it’s been a minute because WWE has been over in the Middle East, but we haven’t really hit Abu Dhabi. And we should.” WWE last staged shows in the UAE capital in December 2017 , when Roman Reigns was among the stars who performed at Zayed Sports City Tennis Stadium. The company has since increased its presence in Saudi Arabia, where its next major event, Crown Jewel , takes place in Riyadh on November 7, with Reigns set to face Sami Zayn. Rhodes is speaking alongside American comedian Andrew Schulz, his co-star in the new Street Fighter film. Schulz is no stranger to the emirate as he has performed at Etihad Arena twice, first in October 2023 and again in May 2024 during the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week. “Abu Dhabi’s great. Some of the best comedy audiences in the world,” Schulz says. In director Kitao Sakurai's adaptation of Capcom's fighting-game series, Rhodes plays US Air Force fighter Guile, while Schulz portrays Dan Hibiki. Set in 1993, Street Fighter follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter the World Warrior Tournament. Schulz came to the film with two decades of stand-up comedy experience, although some of the habits he had developed on stage proved less useful when working alongside other actors. “We’re not getting a big pop or a big laugh,” he says. “So I think in some ways it’s like training yourself out of waiting for the reaction. “This character’s not even looking for a laugh. He’s dead serious about what he’s saying. It might be ridiculous and absurd, but to him, it’s the most important thing in the world. It’s kind of unlearning some things that we’ve both been doing for the last 20 years.” Rhodes found more familiar territory during a tournament scene involving hundreds of extras gathered around the fighters. With Guile surrounded by competitors and spectators, there was an opportunity to draw on the showmanship he has developed throughout his wrestling career. “There is an element of peacocking to what Guile was doing,” he says. “I mean, I even challenged Schulz to an arm-wrestling contest.” Director Sakurai and representatives from Capcom were also on set, providing some of the feedback Rhodes was accustomed to receiving from wrestling audiences. Their encouragement helped him judge whether his interpretation of Guile was working and remained faithful to the character. There was also room to experiment, particularly when Schulz and Rhodes began suggesting ways to add humour to the action. During one scene, Schulz was fascinated by the aerial performers suspended above the set, some of whom were hanging by their hair. “They literally just tied a knot to their hair, and they’re just spinning around,” he says. The sight inspired an idea. Schulz and Rhodes suggested that one of the performers could descend upside down during a conversation involving Guile, interrupting the exchange before disappearing back towards the ceiling. The filmmakers liked the gag enough to include it in the finished film. “They were very willing to just hear our absurd ideas,” Schulz says. Beyond those contributions, Schulz was working within a production in which the broader creative decisions were in other people's hands – an unfamiliar position after two decades building his own comedy career. “It was very cool to be in something where you trust the creators and you just go, ‘OK, for the first time in my career, I completely submit to what your creative is, and I’m going to try to execute that to the best of my ability',” he says. Rhodes is joined in the film by fellow professional wrestlers Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma, and Hirooki Goto, who portrays E Honda. WWE has helped promote the adaptation, with Rhodes wearing Guile-inspired ring gear during his SummerSlam entrance in August. The crossover between wrestling and film offers an opportunity to reach an audience already familiar with their work, while showing fans something they haven't seen before from all three. “What I love is that when they see Roman, when they see Goto, when they see me, they won’t be seeing what they’re used to, which is a credit to what we’ve been able to do and the skills that we were able to develop before we got into this, in terms of creating a brand new character, another layer for us,” Rhodes says. Street Fighter releases in UAE cinemas on Thursday

title: Toxic Trump? President makes midterms all about him but some Republicans are inching away
description: President portrays elections as referendum on his agenda, but party colleagues distance themselves on economy, immigration and Iran
content: On November 3, Americans will elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot but he has sought to make the midterm elections all about himself . “I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. Just one more time,” he said at a recent rally. “Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth.” At recent rallies, Mr Trump has campaigned on what he says are his administration’s accomplishments and made the election a referendum on his presidency. He said voters turn out in greater numbers when he is running and that Republican control of Congress is necessary to preserve his agenda. He even pledged $5,000 cheques to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, calling it a “Trump dividend”. Previous similar promises related to tariffs and cuts in government spending have come to nothing and he cannot unilaterally authorise such payments. But amid low approval ratings, rising costs of living and an unpopular war with Iran, some Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him on major issues, raising the question of whether Mr Trump has become toxic. John Feehery, a Republican strategist, said the war with Iran presents a particular challenge for the President because it conflicts with his central message of non-intervention in conflicts abroad. “The war is very unpopular, even though it’s probably for a good cause. It hasn’t been really well explained. It’s not the Trump brand," Mr Feehery said. "And so, all these people who voted for Trump because they wanted an end to no more endless wars – it’s kind of a betrayal." Mr Trump has said that the war, which he initially claimed would last only a few weeks, would end after the midterms , and that fuel costs would go down shortly after. Control of Congress is likely to hinge on a relatively small number of contested races in Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Historically, the party of the sitting president loses seats in the House. “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states. But it’s all about 35 different contests – not states, contests,” Mr Trump said at a recent rally. Midterm elections also typically draw fewer voters than presidential polls, and experts say Mr Trump's base is less motivated to vote in the midterms than Democratic supporters. “This is not going to be a high-turnout election, so you have to be very careful – you can’t run against Trump," Mr Feehery said. Still, some Republican candidates have been trying to distance themselves from the President's stance on Iran and other issues. Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed in Michigan, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.” Polling also suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming Mr Trump for his handling of the issues. In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, focused her message on the economic impact of the war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said in a statement. Heavy-handed immigration enforcement is another possible vulnerability for Republicans, with polling showing that many voters believe the Trump administration has crossed the line. In a campaign advertisement, Maria Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman running for re-election in Florida, said Mr Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts “have gone too far”. “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Mr Trump has also dismissed criticism from lawmakers from both parties over a recent deal with Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with President Vladimir Putin. The move appeared to be an attempt to slow the rising prices of diesel, but Republican senators said the deal may violate US restrictions imposed after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators released a statement at the weekend opposing Russian diesel fuel imports. Senator Thom Tillis, one of the signatories to the statement, told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that "there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law". “Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious,” Mr Trump said on Monday when asked about the criticism from his own party. Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval ratings in the low 30s nationally, a historic low, and his disapproval ratings above 60 per cent. Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey who ran against Mr Trump twice for the party's presidential nomination, highlighted the growing unease of politicians in his party. “With his current approval rating, Republicans are going to treat Trump like he has malaria by the time we get to October,” he wrote in a post on X. Mr Trump, however, appears convinced that his stamp of approval is a boost for candidates rather than the proverbial albatross. "I think we're going to do very well. I think that the rallies I'm doing are really changing around," he said on Tuesday. Mr Trump pledged to visit a different state most days until the election, and forgo playing golf on the weekends.

title: Even during wartime, the UAE is budgeting for the future
description: Latest federal budget is best understood as expression of ambition and investment in resilience
content: There is no denying that for many regional economies, these are uncertain times. Strikes on oil tankers and airports highlight the unresolved nature of the conflict between Iran and the US, and its ripple effects. However, a look at how the UAE is planning its future in this environment is illuminating. The country’s latest federal budget is a reminder that long-term economic ambitions cannot be put on hold every time the region faces a crisis. The decision to commit Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion) over the next three years is a serious statement of intent. Of particular note is its emphasis on social development, which has been earmarked as the largest area for spending. Economic strength largely depends on the people who sustain it, particularly their education, skills, health and ability to participate in a changing economy. Investing in citizens is an essential part of the UAE’s long-term competitiveness and is recognition that its most valuable asset is its people. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged…” Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai , said on Monday. “Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen.” Somewhat counterintuitively, despite the months of violent and dangerous conflict in the region, the UAE is confident in its future. This is borne out by some independent projections; a report on Monday by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group suggested that wealth in the Emirates is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade. This reflects the Emirates’ enduring appeal to investors and its accumulation of assets. The country’s long policy of diversifying its economy beyond hydrocarbons has been supported by international capital and a reputation for stability. This is not to be complacent. The International Monetary Fund’s recent decision to downgrade its growth forecasts for regional economies highlights the seriousness of continuing challenges. Even countries with substantial financial reserves and diversified sources of income are not wholly immune from regional shocks of the magnitude being experienced right now. The UAE’s budget can be best understood as an expression of ambition and an investment in resilience. The current regional turmoil actually supports the case for more medium and long-term planning. Funding resilience only when a crisis arrives is not the most effective strategy. It is the decisions that governments make today that will count when the chips are down. Long-term planning and strategic foresight are strengths of the UAE, and essential ingredients for its current and future success.

title: 'He irrigated the tree with his blood': West Bank olive farmers set for another deadly harvest
description: Palestinian growers face extreme settler violence even before the season has officially begun
content: Abdul Latif Al Bazzari, 59, moved slowly and deliberately as he battled through pain to recount the last moments of his cousin, Ali Al Bazzari, at an olive grove in the pale green, dusty hills around the city of Nablus. On Monday, the scattering of olive trees among which he stood was serene. Accessible through a rough dirt track, the only sign of a world outside the grove was a light breeze that travelled through the valley. That peace was shattered last week, on October 7, when the family was subjected to the only settler attack they have faced in that area in 60 years. “He irrigated the tree with his blood,” Mr Al Bazzari said, standing near the trunk where his relative bled to death. “It will forever be the real estate of this attack by Jewish terrorist settlers.” His face barely showed emotion as he described the death of his cousin, a 44-year-old father of four. Perhaps it was too painful: his face was still bruised and covered in a fresh white dressing. Mr Al Bazzari said the settlers shot at them, beat them with metal and wooden objects and threw stones. Eight people were injured, two by gunfire. One of his cousins is still in the hospital. “They don’t want us to stay on any land, or take any of our crops. They are telling us to stay in our villages and cities, and not to go down to our trees,” he said. Palestinian olive farmers across the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing another harvest season marred by settler violence . Unlike last year, when the crop was poor, the weather this year has been good and the trees are full. The settlers, however, are still as violent, if not more so. The harvest season officially begins on Thursday but the farmers have been out in their groves for weeks, fearing thefts from Israeli settlers who are posting social media campaigns encouraging people to steal their olives. Already, two Palestinians have been killed by settlers since farmers started heading to their trees in late September, and many more injured. The entire harvest season is in danger – a major blow to the Palestinian economy , which has been significantly damaged by violence and severe restrictions in the occupied West Bank during the three years since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on southern Israel. The olive harvest is not only crucial to the economy but also symbolic of Palestinians' deep connection to the land. “The olive groves and the harvest are the soil of the Palestinian people. This is a strategic crop," Mr Al Bazzari said. "It’s not like wheat or barley; it’s the identity of the Palestinian people. Some of the trees are more than 500 years old, hundreds of years before Israel was established.” Farther south, in the village of Usarin, Warda Adeli, 63, was also nursing wounds from a settler attack, with her arm in a sling and stitches stretching across her bruised right cheek. She was beaten as she rushed towards family members who were ambushed by settlers in the tiny grove outside their house 10 days ago. “I was screaming. I was scared for my son. Then they threw me to the ground and I couldn’t feel anything,” she said. Family members said her entire body is blue with bruising. One of her sons is still in the ICU in Nablus with a severe brain injury after being beaten with a metal bar. Another son, Ghassan Ahmed Adeli, seated next to Ms Adeli, has a broken shoulder and a back injury. He spoke on her behalf during most of the interview because she was still too weak and traumatised. The views from their home are spectacular, but also reveal a bleak situation: vast groves in the valley that farmers have not been able to access for years because of Israeli violence. There are also new settler outposts visible, established amid the blitz of settlement construction since the Gaza war broke out . The empty groves are a reminder of the long-term nature of the problem facing Palestinian olive cultivation under Israeli occupation. This year, however, there has been a worrying new development. The attacks on the Al Bazzari and Adeli families took place in Areas A and B, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to have either full or partial control. In previous harvests, the attacks focused on Area C, where Israel has full security and civil occupation. In Ms Adeli’s case, the attack actually happened inside her village, in the narrow groves and streets between the homes of this close community, which turned out in great numbers to listen to her describe her ordeal. Some in Israel talk of there being a loss of control in the occupied West Bank , which has accelerated during the tenure of the far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Palestinian olive farmers who have been attacked, as well as some of the few Israeli-Jewish activists who try to support them during the harvest, disagree. There has never been more Israeli military and civilian power in the territory. Military vehicles are everywhere, rushing about to open and close various checkpoints and gates installed in the past few years, while settlers travel and build at will. With Israel's general election just weeks away , there is also a heavy presence of candidates' campaign posters. Opposition candidates such as Gadi Eisenkot are visible shortly after passing the separation wall that separates East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. That changes deep inside the Palestinian territory, where the only posters visible are of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right members of his government, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Many of them and their supporters laud the “revolution” this government has achieved during its tenure. For them, the unpicked Palestinian olive trees are a sign of progress; the violence inflicted on Mr Al Bazzari, Ms Adeli and many others is not something Israel has to apologise for, but to praise.

title: Haaland vs Mbappe: The race to break Cristiano Ronaldo’s historic Champions League goals record
description: Manchester City striker and Real Madrid forward both have realistic hopes of setting a new benchmark but it will be far from easy
content: Erling Haaland’s two goals against Porto on the opening matchday of the 2026/27 Champions League maintained the Manchester City striker’s incredible scoring rate in the competition. Haaland has scored 59 goals from 59 games at the elite level of European club football, giving him the best goals-per-game ratio of any notable player in its history. In fact, he is the only player to have scored a significant number of goals at a rate of at least one per game. It’s also the best scoring rate of the three active players among the Champions League's all-time top scorers: Haaland, Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe. The benchmark, however, is still some way off for all three. Cristiano Ronaldo is out in front with a staggering 140 goals from 183 appearances in the competition. So, this raises the question: Can one of this generation’s elite goalscorers actually beat Ronaldo’s record? Kane has an impressive haul of 54 goals in 70 games, but at 33, the England captain can almost certainly be ruled out of the race. Sadly for him, he stayed at Tottenham Hotspur for too long. That leaves us with Haaland and Mbappe. Both are in action on Tuesday night, with Manchester City hosting PSG and Real Madrid visiting Roma. Below is an appraisal of each man’s chances of going down as European club football’s greatest-ever goalscorer. Haaland, 26, made his Champions League debut for RB Salzburg against Genk on September 17, 2019, and scored a hat-trick. Of course he did. Since then, as stated above, he has scored at a rate of a goal per game in the competition. His best return came in 2022/23, when he scored 12 times in 11 games and ended up with a winner’s medal . He currently sits seventh on the all-time list. This season will be his eighth in the Champions League. Among those, there is an outlier – 2021/22 – when he played just three games, scoring as many goals, as his then club, Borussia Dortmund, made an early exit. Every other season, he has played at least eight games. If we remove that campaign and the current one, then he has a tally of 54 goals in 55 games across six seasons, at an average of nine goals per season. By that calculation, he will need another 9.1 seasons (including the current one) to get the 82 goals he requires to break Ronaldo’s record – form, fitness and participation willing, of course. That means Haaland needs to continue scoring at the same rate until the 2035/36 season. The Norwegian star, born in July 2000, will be 35 by then. It’s a big ask to be so consistent for so long, but in this era of supreme athleticism, it’s far from inconceivable. There’s also the frightening prospect that he could still get better and increase his goal output. Mbappe, 27, has 71 goals in 99 Champions League games following his strike in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter Milan in their opening game of the 2026/27 competition. That took him to joint-fifth with Raul in the all-time list. He made his UCL debut on September 27, 2016, with a 13-minute cameo off the bench in Monaco’s 1-1 draw with Bayer Leverkusen. He is now into his 11th season of Champions League football. Mbappe has managed at least eight games in each of his first 10 seasons, making his average a pleasingly concise seven goals per season, with 70 goals across the 10 completed campaigns. At that rate, he will need exactly 10 more to chalk up the 70 goals he requires to surpass Ronaldo. Mbappe will be 38 heading into the back end of the 2036/37 season. It's clear he needs to speed up, and there's ample evidence to suggest that he has. His goals-per-game rate has spiked sharply since he moved to Real Madrid in 2024. The France striker managed an incredible 15 goals in 11 games last term – his best return – while he has a total of 22 in 25 games in his two completed seasons at the club. At an average of 11 per campaign, he would need another six-and-a-half seasons to potentially put him within striking distance of the record by the 2032/33 season, when he will be 34, turning 35 in December. The numbers suggest that both Haaland and Mbappe stand a reasonable chance of surpassing Ronaldo’s mark if they can stay fit and play in the majority of matches for their respective clubs. Both will be helped by the extra games offered by the competition’s new format, with teams now guaranteed eight league phase games as opposed to the six group games Ronaldo used to get before the knockouts. If anything, this exercise really underlines Ronaldo’s incredible longevity and potency in front of goal. Interestingly, he scored goal number 140 on his 183rd and final Champions League appearance in a 2-0 win for Manchester United over Villarreal on November 23, 2021. He was 36 years, nine months and 18 days old at the time. Should Mbappe manage to stay at Madrid into the twilight of his career, then you would have to give him a shot, given the number of goals he has scored since his move to Los Blancos, and their consistency in reaching the latter stages of the competition year after year. Ronaldo was 33 when he left Madrid, while Mbappe's compatriot, Karim Benzema , stayed there until he was 35. That said, averaging 11 per season to get there by the time he is 35 is a big ask, and he may need to keep playing into the second half of his 30s to eventually top the list. Haaland, 19 months younger than Mbappe, will feel that 141 is an achievable target if he can regularly play 10 or more games per season in the competition. As the younger man, and with the better goals-per-game ratio, you'd have to make the Manchester City striker a firm favourite. The X-factor is, of course, Mbappe's Real Madrid form. His 15 last season was the third most ever behind Ronaldo in 2015/16 (16) and 2013/14 (17). Either way, it seems certain that both men will finish their careers considered among the finest goalscorers in modern football history. If either eventually stands alone as the best, remains to be seen.

title: 'There are no dreams left': Families of two sailors missing after drone attack off Oman speak of their grief
description: Relatives await news days after drone hit and fire ripped through part of ship
content: Two families are “sick with grief” waiting for news of two young sailors missing days after an empty tanker was struck by a drone off Oman. The oil tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was hit near the Sohar anchorage on Sunday.
