Relatives in two northern Indian villages are waiting for information on Amit Singh, 20, and Bir Bahadur Yadav, 25, who were on the main deck when the drone struck and fire spread. Of the 12 crew on the Nicaraguan-flagged tanker, nine Indians and one Bangladeshi national were rescued and two seafarers are missing, India’s External Affairs Ministry has said. It was the first sailing job for both men, and their relatives have described the incomprehensible loss they felt on learning of the attack. “Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh. “It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?” Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil. There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation. An experienced seafarer , Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival. “The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.” Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.” Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment. His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars. Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together. “Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?” Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family. “Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them. “This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.” The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing , but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television. “I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred. “In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?” The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract. “We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.” Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank. “Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav. The family continues to hold on to hope. “We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir. “What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.” Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations. “It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.” Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues. “This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.” India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”

title: AI could be worth $1 trillion to the Mena region, new research suggests
description: Global Future Leaders in Dubai puts AI in the spotlight
content: Artificial intelligence could be the key to unlocking about $1 trillion in the Middle East and North Africa region by 2030, if used efficiently, research by the World Economic Forum has shown. Two reports have been published as the WEF and the Government of Dubai host the inaugural Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders this week. The three-day event brings together hundreds of leaders and experts from around the world, who will hold intergenerational conversations aimed at tackling the problems of the future. If the region uses AI for growth in the sustainability and economic sectors, the WEF sees great potential for value by 2030. Across sectors, this could mean up to $200 billion in sustainable financing through the financial sector, $370 billion in sustainable investment flows enabled by the public sector, $250 billion in long-term asset losses avoided, $90 billion in increased valuation through improved sustainability performance for the energy sector and $100 billion in sustainable projects launched through cross-sector partnerships. Altogether, this is valued at more than $1 trillion. The region is ripe for this growth, experts say, but it will require cross-sector collaboration. "Mena has the resources, investment capacity and ambition to become a major centre of AI-led growth,” said Maroun Kairouz, managing director of the WEF. “Turning that ambition into reality will require innovation across data-centre infrastructure, energy and water systems, and the application of AI to drive sustainability solutions." Case studies showed how different UAE and regional companies used AI for sustainable initiatives, from First Abu Dhabi Bank in sustainable finance to Adnoc in the energy sector. The UAE has been at the forefront of AI investment, with the US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership resulting in an AI campus in Abu Dhabi and a $1.4 trillion investment plan over the next 10 years. Abu Dhabi is betting big on AI, with a $3.54 billion investment to integrate the technology into the government's public services by next year. The second report gave a warning about the consumption of resources such as energy and water through data centres, to power AI infrastructure, especially given that the region faces extreme heat and water scarcity. Data-centre cooling, which uses large amounts of water, was flagged as one of the priority areas for innovation and the incorporation of sustainable methods for long-term efficiency and resilience. The opportunities for data centres in the region, however, are plentiful, experts said. Connecting new data centres to the grid can be much quicker in the region, taking between two and five years compared with other mature markets. “Mena is uniquely positioned to lead the next wave of digital infrastructure by bringing together its energy capabilities, investment capacity and technological ambition,” said Nedaa Almubarak, managing director of SRMG Think. “The opportunity lies in aligning intelligent infrastructure with efficient resource use to build resilient, sustainable and competitive digital ecosystems that drive long-term economic growth and innovation.” The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai continues until Thursday.

title: Emergency order by US to 'prevent blackouts' could affect data centres
description: Move authorises distributor to direct 'large-load customers' to back-up power resources, if needed
content: The US Department of Energy has issued an emergency order to try to prevent power cuts amid increasing demand. Monday's order prompted PJM Interconnection , a corporation that transmits electricity in parts of the US, to " direct data centres and other large-load customers to switch to back-up generation resources, if necessary". Data centres in the US are commonly blamed for a surge in electricity prices and have driven public opinion on AI to sour, according to polls. In issuing its emergency order, the Energy Department also gave "a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season" as a possible cause of blackouts. The order remains in effect until October 16. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was confident in his decision to order utility companies and others to take emergency measures. "This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including back-up power, available to use as needed," Mr Wright said. The Department of Energy said in a statement that the US had 35 GW of unused back-up generation available nationwide. PJM issued a maximum generation alert for October 13 and 14: "Emergency procedures took place as above-normal temperatures are forecast across much of the PJM region. Additional emergency procedures may be necessary pending system conditions." The company said the alert does not "require any action from customers". The warnings come before the US midterm elections, where energy policy, AI and data centres are key issues. Any blackouts or failure to adequately address them could add to friction between residents in the US and utility companies, as well as AI firms. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed critics of AI in recent weeks and accused them of "hoaxes". But in February he tried to ease the strain data centres were putting on the grid by signing a non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which technology and data centre companies would provide their own electricity to operate. Meanwhile, the Department of Energy has pushed for the construction of more nuclear reactors to address AI energy needs.

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer diagnosed after surgery, Vatican says
description: Medical experts must still assess size of tumour ​and whether disease has spread
content: Pope Leo XIV has had lung cancer diagnosed after surgeons ⁠removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said. The Pope , 71, has adenocarcinoma, ​a common form of lung cancer , with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the Vatican said. He was admitted to Rome's ⁠Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health check-up. The Vatican said earlier on Tuesday that the operation had been successful, before providing a more detailed update from the Pope's lead surgeon and personal physician. "In order to make the procedure ⁠curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making it clear that the aim was to eliminate ​all cancerous ⁠tissue. Medical experts said that in order to assess the Pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour ​removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes. Pope Leo is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru starting from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. The Vatican has cancelled all of his audiences until October 21 to give him time to recuperate. The American-born pontiff revealed during his regular Sunday blessing on October 11 that doctors had discovered the nodule. The late Pope Francis, Pope Leo's predecessor, was admitted to hospital several times as he grew frail in his later years. He ​died aged 88 in April ‌2025. Pope Leo was elected leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Roman Catholics in May 2025. He has left his mark on the papacy by addressing the social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence and has grown increasingly critical of US military actions, challenging the administration of President Donald Trump's argument that God was on the side of the US in its conflict with Iran.

title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over claimed sanctions breaches
description: US lender also reaches settlement over 'apparent violations' of sanctions against 'Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism'
content: Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the US Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday. The authority said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC. The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “ Russia , Belarus, Iran , Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”. Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law." The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it willfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering. Bank of America said it has "invested billions of dollars" to tackle financial crime, and that it is "far along" in its remediation efforts with US regulators. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right", a Bank of America representative said. The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks "indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border." The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes. “The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comptroller of the Currency. Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade. Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. The bank said its third-quarter results will include a $1.2 billion non-tax deductible charge, reducing income by roughly 17 cents per share. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," a bank representative said.

title: US envoy says next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit, not rotation or gender
description: Security Council works to select successor to Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31
content: US President Donald Trump ’s special envoy for global partnerships said on Tuesday that the next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit rather than regional rotation or gender, as these are “political traditions” rather than “legal rules” under the UN Charter. “The world should choose the best person for the job – based on merit, reform and results,” Paolo Zampolli said on social media. “After 18 years at the United Nations , I believe this is a moment to think bigger about the future of the institution.” The Security Council is to select a successor to Secretary General Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31. The Trump administration has so far kept its preferences private, leaving uncertainty over who it might support in a contest that has drawn seven candidates , including Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s Rafael Grossi. Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan has emerged as the front-runner, but her support has shown signs of weakening. In the fifth round of informal straw voting on October 7 , Ms Grynspan received nine “encourage” votes and six “discourage” votes, with no council members expressing “no opinion”. That was a setback from the previous round, on September 29, when she won 10 votes in favour, three against and two with no opinion. To secure the post, a candidate must win at least nine votes in the Security Council without a veto from any of its five permanent members – the US, Britain, France, Russia and China. The selection process has long been shaped by unwritten diplomatic conventions, including the expectation that the post should rotate among the world’s regions. Since 1946, the position has been held by leaders from Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America, although no formal rotation system exists. The organisation has also never been led by a woman in its 81-year history, despite repeated calls from member states for more women's representation. The final decision rests largely with the Security Council’s five permanent members, each of which can block a candidate regardless of how much support that person has. “The UN Charter only offers limited guidance about the process for selecting a new UN Secretary General. It requires the Security Council to recommend an individual for the General Assembly to appoint to the role,” said Daniel Forti, head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group. Much of the process, he said, had evolved through changes to council procedures and agreements with the General Assembly. The expectation of regional representation developed through decades of diplomatic practice and non-binding General Assembly resolutions. A 1997 General Assembly resolution called for regional rotation and gender to be taken into account when selecting a secretary general, while a 2015 resolution encouraged member states to nominate women. Neither resolution is legally binding. Another long-standing convention has excluded citizens of the five permanent Security Council member states from the post, reflecting concerns that a major power could exert undue influence over the institution. “Many other factors, whether the demand for regional rotation, the push for the UN to select its first woman secretary general, or commitments about the SG not being a P5 national, are all informal conventions,” Mr Forti said. "They are not binding on the Security Council even if they weigh heavily in the court of public opinion." The veto is a different matter. “The UN Charter is indirect, but unequivocal, about the permanent members’ veto privileges in the Secretary General selection process,” Mr Forti said. “No one questions that the recommendation of a new UN leader is a substantive decision, so the permanent members’ veto authorities are inconvenient but undisputed.”

title: US senators ask Trump to rescind 'disastrous' Russian diesel deal
description: Bipartisan group of a dozen senators suggests Moscow will use diesel money to help Iran's war effort against the US
content: A bipartisan group of US senators on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to rescind his deal allow Russian diesel exports, saying it will prolong the Ukraine war and put at risk the lives of American troops in the Middle East. Mr Trump last week said that during a call, Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The deal comes amid growing domestic political pressure on Mr Trump to lower diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries , before the November 3 midterm elections. A letter signed by 12 senators, including former Republican senate leader Mitch McConnell, said granting Moscow the ability to freely sell diesel damages American security interests. It "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies. It should be rescinded", the letter reads. They also claim that Mr Putin will use the money to help Iran's war effort against the US. US intelligence sources, senior European officials, the UK government and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have accused Russia of helping Iran . US media reports, quoting officials, have said Moscow provided Tehran with information on American military assets in the region. The deal "will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security co-operation with China, Iran and North Korea. It will also endanger service members operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury". Mr Trump on Monday acknowledged that Russia and China may be helping Iran "at a very low level" but said he does not "believe" they are. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said Mr Putin has failed to respect a purported truce on energy infrastructure attacks. "Zelenskyy has agreed. Putin continues bombing. Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool and hoping to weaponise a freezing, starving, bloody winter against Ukraine," Mr Blumenthal said on X. The Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allows Mr Trump and future American presidents to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major importers of Russian energy meeting specified criteria. The US Treasury Department has issued a special exemption as part of Mr Trump's deal with Mr Putin, but some elected officials have questioned the legality of that special licence. And a 2022 law prevents the US importing Russian energy unless a president consults with Congress and observes a 90-day waiting period. “Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato allies," a different group of senators wrote in a statement at the weekend.

title: Saudi-led coalition and Houthis trade threats over oil installations
description: Saudi Arabia announces more missile interceptions, days after deadly strikes on airports
content: The war between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated further on Tuesday, as the two sides traded threats against oil installations. The coalition announced that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including Al Sabahah station in the capital Sanaa and piers used for loading fuel at the port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the Houthis had been using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. He added that the operation had been focused on neutralising the Houthis’ ability to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the Red Sea and international shipping lanes. Earlier in the day, the coalition had urged civilians to leave Al Sabahah, owned by the Yemen Petroleum Company, before what it described as a “special operation”. The order was published on social media by Maj Gen Al Malki, alongside a map of the area. In response to the strikes, the Houthis announced that oil installations in Saudi Arabia would be considered legitimate targets and that any civilians working at those sites should stay away. The coalition also said it had intercepted three missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia on Monday evening and yesterday. One of the projectiles was aimed at Riyadh, while the others were heading towards the city of Khamis Mushait, Maj Gen Al Malki said. In the past weeks, Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and 308 injured. However, although the attacks have disrupted travel and forced schools in Riyadh to switch to remote learning, the city’s roads remained crowded yesterday, offices were open and sporting events took place as planned, residents told The National . “The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen who lives in the Saudi capital. “I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.” Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi yesterday, during which he pushed for an immediate halt to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, his ministry said in a statement. Mr Abdelatty was quoted as saying that there could be no justification for the attacks.

title: 'Yallah!': Whoop chief celebrates debut of app's Arabic option
description: Members can now access health insights in Arabic
content: Whoop 's decision to provide an Arabic option on its platform is part of a broader commitment to the Middle East, its Egyptian-American chief executive Will Ahmed has said. Arabic has joined English, French, German, Latin American Spanish, European Portuguese and Italian as languages available on the wearable fitness tracker company's app. Mr Ahmed said the addition of Arabic was meaningful for him. “My father is Egyptian and immigrated to the United States, and when I was younger I had the fortune of being able to travel with him throughout the Middle East,” he told The National . “I think the first time I visited the UAE was when I was 14 or 15, and I’ve been coming back to the region ever since.” He added that the Gulf was “our fastest-growing market globally” and said the company viewed the expansion of wearable use in the region as “a critical footprint for growth”. “Launching the Whoop experience in Arabic is part of our wider commitment to residents of the GCC, giving native speakers access to personal health insights in the language they use every day,” Mr Ahmed said. Though some technology companies have struggled to implement the nuances and diversity of Arabic , Mr Ahmed said that Whoop spent a lot of time working closely with Arabic-speaking members to ensure that the launch would be seamless. “Their feedback helped us identify where we could improve and get the details right,” he said. The Arabic language option will be rolled out gradually and will be available in the most recent version of the company's app. Whoop's co-founder also said he viewed the region as quick to embrace the idea that technology can empower people to take care of their health. His Boston-based company shares that vision, he added. “Our continued commitment to the GCC comes from a deep respect for the leadership in the region and what they’re trying to accomplish,” he said. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the Arabic option with a video posted to its social media accounts showing users throughout the Middle East working out while wearing Whoop devices . “Yallah!” posted Mr Ahmed as he shared the video. He launched Whoop in 2012 into a crowded wearable technology market. The company has grown steadily, amassing a loyal following, particularly among professional athletes. In a recent interview with The National , Dr Ami Bhatt, who joined Whoop as its first chief medical officer in July, said she was encouraged to see that more women across the Middle East were turning to the company's devices as a way to better understand their health. “Across the GCC , female member growth has increased more than 90 per cent year-over-year, with strong growth across every market we track,” she said. Her comments about the Middle East echoed the sentiments of Mr Ahmed, who in August said the fitness-tracker company would open a second office in the UAE, calling the move “critical for growth”. In March, Whoop announced $575 million in funding from a group of international investors led by Abu Dhabi and Qatari sovereign wealth funds. The Series G round was led by three Gulf investors: Mubadala Investment Company, 2PointZero Group and the Qatar Investment Authority. Whoop partners with fitness initiatives such as the Dubai Fitness Challenge and Doha Marathon. It also “serves as the official health and performance wearable” of UAE Team Emirates-XRG and Al Nassr Football Club. The company was at the centre of controversy during this year's Australian Open when officials made tennis players, including Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, remove their Whoop devices. “Data is not steroids,” Mr Ahmed posted on his X account in protest. In April, Mr Ahmed hailed announcements that Whoops can be worn in the French Open, Wimbledon and US Open.

title: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid announces Dh2.1 trillion of projects under way in Dubai
description: Ruler of Dubai says emirate is building 'city within a city' in next phase of growth
content: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, has announced a Dh2.1 trillion portfolio of active projects in the emirate that cover housing, transport, aviation and infrastructure. Speaking at the Mohammed bin Rashid Leadership Forum at Dubai World Trade Centre, Sheikh Mohammed said the emirate was “building a city within a city” with further projects set to be announced. The annual forum brought together 1,000 government and private sector leaders, alongside experts, decision-makers and academics. “Our momentum is continuous and our achievements are ongoing. This is a remarkable period for growth and development; the ideal time to invest in Dubai and its infrastructure,” Sheikh Mohammed said. He said the emirate was investing heavily in housing, transport and infrastructure to prepare for a new phase of economic growth. “Cities that aspire for progress act before others,” he said, calling for leaders capable of translating ideas into tangible outcomes. The projects include Dh1.1 trillion allocated for real estate development to 2030, with about 350,000 residential units planned. Aviation investment also features prominently, with Dh128 billion for Al Maktoum International Airport – designed to handle up to 260 million passengers annually, alongside Dh328 billion to expand the Emirates and flydubai fleets and Dh18.7 billion for a new Emirates engineering and maintenance complex. Infrastructure spending includes Dh100 billion for road upgrades and the Dubai Metro Blue and Gold lines, Dh151 billion for new power and water grid infrastructure and Dh80 billion for the Dubai Strategic Sewerage Tunnels system. A further Dh100 billion has been set aside to develop Phase 2 of the Dubai International Financial Centre.

title: Home health tests aim to tackle disease before it strikes
description: Dh599 blood test offers comprehensive analysis of personal markers and illness risk
content: At-home blood tests that can identify potential health risks years before symptoms emerge are to become more easily available in the UAE as healthcare providers shift their focus from treatment to prevention. Health assessments starting from about Dh200 can offer patients insights into their future risk of disease and the lifestyle changes they can make to potentially prevent or delay its onset. More comprehensive services analyse hundreds of biomarkers, while DNA testing costing several thousand dirhams can provide a directory of detailed genetic information. The growing market reflects a wider push towards preventive healthcare in the UAE, with new government initiatives in Dubai and Abu Dhabi encouraging residents to take greater control of their long-term health. Dubai recently launched the Dubai Longevity Authority to encourage people to live healthier lives, free of chronic disease and mental decline. Abu Dhabi has also put preventive healthcare and pre-emptive screening at the forefront of multiple initiatives implemented by the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre and the Department of Health Abu Dhabi. Private operators have also stepped up their focus on wellness rather than on responding to ill health. For Dh599 ($163), Aster promises a home assessment that can help identify health risks based on more than 120 biomarkers extracted from a blood test and a urine sample. The test promises a comprehensive, personalised health assessment that could help people make more informed lifestyle decisions. “Once the system has your genetic code and understands what's happening with your microbiome, along with your blood work, it can give a very comprehensive view on where your predispositions may be or some vulnerabilities,” said Alisha Moopen, managing director and chief executive of Aster DM Healthcare. “It can show how you can address them way earlier to delay or prevent them becoming a problem. But in the wider longevity, 80 per cent of the work needs to be done by the individual. “If you have the sleep, nutrition, movement and stress management under control, you can benefit from all the other exciting things science is offering. “People can't go in and sit in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber or talk about doing stem cells or cleansing the blood if you don't have the basics right. Longevity can get you to an amazing health outcome, but just doing the shiny things is throwing away money.” The service is the latest in a long line aiming to capitalise on the booming demand for longevity medicine. Medcare Hospitals offer a Lab at Home service where qualified technicians visit homes to collect blood and diagnostic samples across Dubai and Sharjah. Elsewhere, Vesta Care and Health 24/7 offer full-body check-ups, vitamin, hormone and thyroid panels, and routine blood tests at your doorstep, delivered by qualified nurses, with results in 24 hours. The tests form part of a wider switch in attitudes towards a more preventive health strategy. Ms Moopen said insurance companies are also beginning to change their approach and support disease prevention. “My father started off the Aster business being reactive to ill people, but today we can't just be a sick care company,” she said. “There are companies that sponsor enhanced insurance plans which think about prevention, we do see employers being a lot more pro-employees' health and managing that much more closely. We're seeing that shift, especially in the UAE.” The recently formed Dubai Longevity Authority is aiming for 31 per cent annual growth in the longevity sector and a Dh35 billion ($9.53 billion) economic boost over the next decade. Experts, however, said it could be difficult for some to buy into the reality of wellness programmes and avoid being blinded by slick marketing campaigns that fail to deliver results. The House of Longevity is a research and community platform hoping to capitalise on demand. The platform translates clinical and scientific research into practical guidance across seven pillars of sleep, movement, nutrition, mental health, preventative care, healthy environments, and purpose. Alex Zagrebelny, founder and CEO of R.Evolution, the company behind the project, said where we live can have a significant impact on how long we live. “Longevity itself is not an industry,” he said. “As prevention, wellbeing and quality of life become greater priorities, existing industries will need to develop new services, products and infrastructure around them. “The sheer volume of claims, often based on different levels of evidence, makes it difficult for consumers to understand what is genuinely supported by science and what is simply good marketing.” Researchers at the non-profit Global Wellness Institute said property focused on health and wellness was on the rise. Global investment has increased from $151 billion in 2017 to $$876 billion in 2025, the report says. While longevity may have become a buzzword in healthcare and real estate, Dr Eli Abirached, an expert in recovery and biohacking at Dubai’s Restore Fitness, said consumers should do their own research into what works for them. “Whenever there is demand, there's always a clever entrepreneur somewhere coming up with the next problem solving and devised path you must take,” he said. “If you do not have it, you are behind everyone else. Fear of missing out is a great selling, anchor. However, when it comes to biohacking (in health), the equation is incredibly simple. “When you get a longevity device or sign up to a programme, if you do not have a reason for getting it, then you’re the sucker.” “If you have a reason, but you're also trying to track the changes that are happening, you've moved from the sucker to adding real value to your life.”

title: UAE universities must change to equip students in AI age, say leaders and students
description: Minister says evolving jobs market must be reflected in courses and teaching methods
content: UAE universities must overhaul their courses and teaching methods to keep pace with artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing demands of the jobs market, the acting Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research has said. Dr Abdulrahman Al Awar called for closer collaboration between universities and industry. He warned that emerging technologies were transforming the skills employers require and creating an urgent need to rethink how students are taught. He was speaking at the Zayed Education Foundation’s Partnerships for the Future event, in Abu Dhabi, where 12 institutions came together to strengthen collaboration and expand opportunities for home-grown scholars. “Economies and job markets are undergoing a radical and rapid change, and it is happening at a very rapid pace,” Dr Al Awar said. “New technologies, including artificial intelligence, are creating new opportunities and changing the skills that the market needs. “Fundamental changes must happen in engaging higher education institutions and economic sectors and redesigning the curricula and the skills of both faculty and students.” He said the ministry’s Outcome-Based Evaluation Framework was challenging universities to meet those demands and become more competitive in shaping the future of higher education in the UAE. “The UAE vision for higher education is centred on creating a vibrant higher education ecosystem that is future-ready, globally competitive and connected to the needs of our students, our economy, and our society,” he said. An updated guidebook for the framework was released earlier this year following consultations involving 735 representatives from higher education institutions across the country. Change has not just been called for from the top, but also by students. The National spoke to two Ruwwad Zayed Scholars about their hopes for the future of higher education. Noor Odeh, a UAE resident from Jordan, is a member of the first cohort of the masters scholars and is studying computational data science at Khalifa University. She scrapped her plans to study at an Australian university to stay in the UAE. “I want to be a changemaker. So it's not just the degree that I got excited about when I was accepted [for the scholarship]. It was more that will get to do something for my community because I will receive guidance,” she said. She believes the future of higher education will rely on hands-on experiences and skills rather than grades and metrics. “We need to put less focus on numbers like GPA [grade point average], and more about the skills that you're learning. What has helped me the most was not just the knowledge that I got from my degree, but the skills that I gained,” Ms Odeh said. Fellow Ruwwad Zayed Scholar Jassem Alkhoori is studying digital transformation at Zayed University. He agrees that higher education needs to be agile and keep pace with technological development. “I think currently the education system follows guidelines that are very outdated. Now that AI is actually overtaking most simple tasks such as screening papers, I think there should be more education on how to use these tools to help with research,” he told The National . The push for a competitive higher education sector has accelerated in recent years and has taken major steps since the founding of the country's first university, the United Arab Emirates University, 50 years ago. Zayed Education Foundation hopes to create opportunities for 100,000 students by 2035 and recently announced the first cohort of 50 Ruwwad Zayed Scholars – exceptional Emirati and Arab students who will pursue master’s degrees at universities in the UAE. Saeed Al Nazari, secretary general of the Great Arab Minds initiative – which recognises and empowers exceptional Arab scholars, scientists and innovators – told The National that the talented minds from the region must be nurtured. “With whatever happening around us – conflicts, news, social media, AI – sometimes we even forget to look up to our people in this region who are doing brilliant stuff,” he said. “This region has always been part of the momentum to move educational research forward globally. The good thing is that we have so many people who are willing to invest in knowledge economy. We just sometimes need to connect the dots.”

title: Housekeeper cleared of stealing Jordanian princess’s jewels
description: Colombian worker had been accused of theft from Princess Firyal's home in London
content: A long-serving housekeeper has been found not guilty of stealing expensive jewellery from her employer, a Jordanian princess. A jury in London took less than two hours to clear Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, of theft. She had been accused of stealing several items from the home in Belgravia when Princess Firyal, 81, flew to Jordan at the outbreak of Covid in 2020. Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978. She had told Southwark Crown Court that she had been alerted that items from her jewellery collection were missing when a jeweller friend called to tell her they had appeared for auction in Canterbury. The items included a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring. The court heard police found Princess Firyal’s wedding ring, a pair of earrings and a necklace during a search of Ms Taborda Henao’s home in Fulham. The princess thought the wedding ring had been lost years earlier. Ms Taborda Henao, who is from Colombia and had worked for Princess Firyal for 11 years, told the court, through a Spanish interpreter, that the princess had called her a thief and made similar accusations against other people. Ms Taborda Henao’s nephew, Julian Ramirez, was said to have acted as a conduit for the sale of the items. He was also arrested but fled to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail.

title: Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K: What to know about smart hub and updated console
description: New HomeView device available from November 13 in English only
content: Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home. A video posted to Apple 's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders. “Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple 's AirTag. In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”. The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall. Before Apple's HomeView announcement, Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint , said that such a device would help the US technology giant strengthen its consumer product offerings. “The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. Apple also seems prepared to allow devices made by other companies to work with HomeView. “Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories – including smart cameras, thermostats and a door lock – are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home,” the company posted to its site. It added that the collection of devices would arrive at a later date. Mohit Agrawal, research director with Counterpoint, said that this aspect was intriguing. “Rather than buying its way in, as Amazon did with Ring and Google with Nest, Apple is partnering with LG and Schneider Electric,” he explained. “This lets it fill out the home quickly, from the front door to the thermostat, while keeping control of the experience through Siri and the Home app.” Apple seems to be positioning the forthcoming HomeView product as a device that is used passively in day-to-day life. “HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house,” a description reads. “And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos and calls look and sound amazing … meet the new heart of your home.” According to technology news outlet, The Verge , HomeView will be initially available in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and India. Also on Tuesday, Apple announced its HomePod mini speaker devices would be getting an upgrade. “Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the centre of your home,” the company said. “Once set up with your iPhone or iPad , Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.” The HomePod 2 will be available on October 30, with prices starting at $149. Apple touts improved sound, touch controls, a mesh design and a woven power cord among the HomePod's improvements. “With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. “Still, shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year over year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles.” Apple's TV console has gone several years without an update, but that changed on Tuesday with the unveiling of Apple TV 4K. The company says the updated console has an A19 processor that assists in delivering 4K video quality, and it will also have a Siri remote. Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13, with prices starting at $299. “Apple TV 4K delivers the ultimate cinematic experience, from shows and movies to games and workouts,” the company said. “With the new, more powerful Siri AI and built-in microphones, enjoying what you love is as easy as using your voice.”

title: US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns amid controversy
description: Ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr says claims she asked donor for $100,000 to pay credit card bill are 'false'
content: Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece , resigned on Tuesday amid accusations she had asked for favours from donors and others in exchange for influence. The ​White ⁠House first announced President Donald Trump had asked her to step down, with new press secretary Katie Zacharia describing Ms Guilfoyle as “a ⁠wonderful ​asset to ​the ‌team”. “From my first day as ambassador, I have worked tirelessly to advance President Trump’s America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people,” Ms Guilfoyle said in a post on X following the announcement. She thanked Mr Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support. It came a day after Mr Trump said his administration was scrutinising Ms Guilfoyle following allegations of unethical conduct, and reports he was considering removing her from the diplomatic post. A Wall Street Journal report alleged that Ms Guilfoyle had solicited or accepted money or other benefits from private individuals while offering to use her influence and connections with administration officials to help further their interests. Mr Trump's son, Donald Jr, had been engaged to Ms Guilfoyle before they broke up in 2024. “Kimberly Guilfoyle was not a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago. I didn't like what I read,” Mr Trump told reporters outside the White House. The newspaper reported that in one instance Ms Guilfoyle had asked a long-time Trump donor for $100,000 to help pay off an American Express credit card bill before her 2025 confirmation hearing in exchange for access to officials. Ms Guilfoyle said that the allegations against her were false. Her lawyers have disputed key parts of The Wall Street Journal ’s reporting. The US embassy in Athens told the newspaper she had followed State Department ethics and all gift-reporting requirements. “I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”

title: The US targeting the International Criminal Court is a slippery slope to nowhere good
description: Sanctioning intergovernmental agencies will undermine the important work the world needs them to do
content: The US government’s moves to sanction the International Criminal Court represent an unwelcome distraction that sets a dangerous precedent for the rest of the world. The ICC is certainly an elitist organisation, and it is intrusive in certain areas to the point of justifying reforms and new safeguards. But that should not disguise the wider harms that come from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s latest pushback against the court. Mr Rubio has warned that Washington will demolish the ICC “brick by brick” unless it ends the overreach of prosecuting US citizens for alleged battlefield crimes. “Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members or political leaders,” he said earlier this month. “America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it.” Washington is undoubtedly entitled to resist the wildest demands of the court, but it is in principle setting a precedent that the US and the rest of the world could come to regret. Overarching global bodies perform a necessary function in a world where scores of nations are growing and interacting in pursuit of common development. There is a well-established set of benefits that stems from having a common point at which countries establish rules and guidelines on how to co-operate better together. The people who work in these international systems are more often motivated to carry forward the principles and ideals of global co-operation than the pursuit of a narrow agenda or ideology. In any event, the need for this architecture is the most important element to remained focused on. It is not just courts and the highest echelons of international law that come under a shadow when the US takes this sort of action. There is also the UN, which has a number of agencies under its umbrella, such as the World Bank Group. There are also a number of private and public institutions that are dedicated to a “force for good” impact. There are even areas of scientific and research co-operation to tackle issues such as health, metrological developments and geographic changes. To some critics, this is an archipelago of the legal industry that has become a historical aberration. Calling out poor performances or abuses of powers is, therefore, a natural effort that restores balance in the international system. As an unchallenged superpower, the US had an outsized role in judging how the far the balance had tilted one way or another – even in situations where it had not subscribed to the international body, such as the ICC. But President Donald Trump has gone even further across his two terms. For a sample of his view on global institutions, his reaction to the Nobel Peace Prize given last week to Navi Pillay – the jurist who has carried out inquiries for the UN – was tellingly dismissive. “In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me,” he said. Leaving aside the record of settling or initiating wars, you have in Mr Trump’s statement the fundamental starting point of the US administration. The problem is, when the fabric of global co-operation starts to get worn down by sanctions, it has to rely on the willingness of people to volunteer to undertake any given mission. That is a wider point than suggesting that people will no longer work for free or give their backing to appeals that are led by international institutions. The campaign amounts to an attack on those who offer their professional skills, talent and dedication to the inner workings of the world. For many, the difference between signing up for good works and suffering the penalties of a powerful system that turns against international work is a dividing line they would not cross. Just for personal reasons, including to insulate themselves and their families, they will find that the appeal of making a contribution has diminished or been extinguished. The ethos that dies, then, becomes impossible to replace. What come next are the cynical and the exploitative instincts of those with an agenda. That sets the international system on a collision course within itself and among the nation-states that have a clear need for good rules of the road. Also, as frustrating as it might be for the US to suffer constant challenges, there is a reflection of its own strength across the international system. Undermining that extension of its own powerful role in the world is, ultimately, not in its interest. It is the quiet death of the best people not turning up that will be the consequence of applying system-wide sanctions. Mission creep will follow, too, as sanctions tend to be addictive for policymakers with few tools as easy to embrace in a world of grey choices and negative developments. Other countries might even emulate the US government’s actions, which would lead to the worst sort of competitive dynamic. Within the global system, the leadership is bound to go into defensive mode. Co-operation could succumb to confrontation. Reform could become an illusory platitude. There is little positive to say about what might follow. A bad idea begets worse ones, so don’t be surprised if the world ends up in the worst possible situation.

title: UK intelligence chief warns of 'major shift' after Iran attacks military bases
description: MI5 director Ken McCallum says he is on edge over efforts to contain rising threats facing the country
content: Iran has raised the stakes in its sabotage efforts against military bases in the UK with Tehran behind multiple plots, the head of the UK's domestic intelligence service warned. Authorities have arrested scores of people suspected of working for Iran, as the level of state-backed threats against the UK exceeds terrorism and extremist activity, Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, revealed on Tuesday. “Over the last 12 months, our Iran-linked operations have led to more than 50 arrests in the UK,” he said. “The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tehran was "highly likely" behind a suspected plot against RAF Fairford on Monday. The base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran since the war was launched in February. The plot prompted a security alert and led to US President Donald Trump withdrawing planes from the air base. Seven people have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident. Two more suspects were arrested last week at the RAF Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, which is known to be used by US intelligence agencies. Mr McCallum warned an even greater threat existed elsewhere, raising the prospect of more "aggressive and sophisticated" tactics spreading to the UK. "Clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary ​Guard Corps] has quite ‌deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology," he said. Iran has previously attempted attacks at UK bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and Akrotiri in Cyprus. The UK has prosecuted dozens of people for carrying out attacks on Jewish sites and on dissidents active in London and other parts of the UK. Mr McCallum's last national security update a year ago revealed that there were 15 active plots disrupted within the UK. In his latest his annual report he added that all state threats, including from Russia and China, had quadrupled. He referred to interconnected financial systems, energy grids, supply chains and manufacturing bases – designed during simpler times for maximum efficiency – as key vulnerabilities to disruption and coercion by foreign actors. Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign affairs minister, expressed solidarity with the British government on Tuesday, following Mr Burnham's statement. "UK has now concluded that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind the threat to Fairford airbase," she said. "Iran’s campaign of intimidation and chaos extends well beyond the Middle East. "The EU has already designated the Revolutionary Guard as a terrorist organisation. We have sanctioned Iranian officials for undermining freedom of navigation and serious human rights violations. The UK is a close partner, and we stand firmly with them."

title: New robot that can prepare your meal in under four minutes arrives in Abu Dhabi
description: Circus Group’s CA-1 is being tested at First Clique in Paragon Mall
content: A new kitchen robot in Abu Dhabi can cook four hot dishes at once, with each meal ready in about four minutes. Circus Group’s CA-1 is being tested at First Clique in Paragon Mall with the catering company Royal Prestige. The German company says the Abu Dhabi installation is its first in the UAE and that it hopes to expand to hospitals, universities, shopping malls, petrol stations and airports, where fresh food can be harder to find. “The goal is to help people have great food in places where they normally don’t have food,” Michael Bassler, Circus Group shareholder, told The National. The CA-1 has 36 silos for solid and liquid ingredients, four induction plates and two robotic arms: one cooks and the other serves. Its current menu has 10 dishes, including chicken fajita, chicken biryani, lentil soup, chicken curry and pasta. Depending on the menu, the machine can make up to 50 hot meals or 100 cold meals an hour. One load of ingredients can produce up to 200 dishes with the current menu configuration. Ingredients are kept in temperature-controlled silos and usually replaced within 48 hours. “If you already have a restaurant, it’s a very good question: why do you need the CA-1?” Mr Bassler said. “The best locations we focus on are places where you have no food or really bad food.” The company is looking at 24 hour sites such as petrol stations, central stations and airports. Mr Bassler said Abu Dhabi Airport’s VIP terminal would be a good fit. The Paragon Mall site is being used as a showroom where customers can try the meals. Mr Bassler said customers have been eating there for about two months. Sana Pathan, 24, from India, tried the quinoa salad and chicken biryani. “For something made by AI, I think this biryani is really fresh and it feels like it’s made with love,” she said. “It does really taste human-made.” She said she would like to see the technology in restaurants and public places, including beaches, sports centres and university campuses. Meals start at Dh40, with a chicken curry at about Dh48. Mr Bassler said the machine costs about Dh1 million. “The big goal is to find the best locations where the clients can make the money back,” he said. Circus Group has 50 machines operating in Germany, including at Mercedes-Benz and Meta sites, and at a supermarket chain. It was founded five years ago and spent about four years developing the CA-1 before entering the German market around a year and a half ago. It also makes a smaller machine, the CA-A, for smoothies and protein shakes. “It’s like a small vending machine, just for fresh smoothies,” Mr Bassler said. The company is developing a larger version for military use. Circus Group is updating the CA-1’s software and visual recognition system to improve cooking and detect when food may be burning. Customers in Germany can order through touchscreen or, or speak to the machine for meal recommendations based on their dietary needs. Those options remain to be tested in Abu Dhabi. The robot does not remove the need for people to load ingredients, handle orders and serve meals. Dylan Frayne, Circus Group’s culinary research and development chef, develops and tests recipes before they are programmed into the machine. Asked whether the robot could replace his job, Mr Frayne said: “It hasn’t replaced my job. It’s given me a another job.” Mr Bassler said the CA-1 was meant to give people another way to get a quick, freshly cooked meal, rather than replace restaurants. “You will always have restaurants. You will always have chefs in restaurants,” he said. “We don’t replace anyone in this scenario. We offer an additional option for people to have fresh food that didn’t exist before.”

title: Riyadh keeps moving after deadly strikes, but schools go online and travellers reroute
description: Traffic remains heavy even as airport closures disrupt travel
content: Riyadh’s roads remain crowded, many offices are open and sporting events are continuing, residents say, even as deadly attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport have disrupted travel and forced schools to switch to remote learning. King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest after King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah, will remain closed until midnight on October 17, according to a Notice to Air Missions issued on Monday, following a series of attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants. Operations at the airport have been suspended since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Another attack on Sunday killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The strikes have caused one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding pressure to an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits. Despite the repeated attacks, Salman Al Dosary, Saudi Minister of Media, said on Monday life was continuing as normal. The National spoke to five Riyadh residents about how the attacks had affected their daily lives. “The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen working in Riyadh on an events management project. “I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.” Tony, another foreign resident, said his company has given employees the choice of working from home or going into the office. Some of his friends, however, have been told to work remotely. “We could hear loud explosions from time to time, but the situation was worse for those living near the airport,” he said. Several events, summits and conferences are scheduled to take place in Riyadh over the coming weeks, with most appearing set to proceed as planned. However, the Misk Foundation, a non-profit organisation established by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to empower young people in Saudi Arabia, announced on Monday that this year’s Misk Global Forum would not go ahead, citing organisational and logistical challenges. Saudi Pro League football matches are also expected to continue and the Riyadh Racing Season is due to begin on Friday. Ahlam, a Saudi journalist, highlighted Saturday night’s Saudi Clasico between Al Hilal and Al Ittihad at the Kingdom Arena in Riyadh. The match took place as scheduled before a crowd of about 22,800, she said. Schools in Riyadh have been ordered to switch to remote learning for a week, according to an email sent to parents on Sunday citing instructions from the Education Ministry. It is the second time in less than a month that schools in the capital have moved online . The Houthis have warned of further strikes on Saudi airports. Late on Monday, they said they had targeted Riyadh’s international airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a missile fired towards the capital by the militant group. The attacks represent a sharp escalation in the conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia , which has long backed Yemen’s internationally recognised government. Riyadh has vowed to respond, while US President Donald Trump has said Washington is considering joining Saudi strikes against the rebels. Mr Trump condemned the Riyadh attack, saying it was unacceptable. “The Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” the President said. He added that he would be speaking to Prince Mohammed. The airport closure has forced travellers to find alternative routes out of Saudi Arabia. Ahmed, who needed to travel for work, said he drove from Riyadh to Dammam, flew to Jeddah and then caught a flight to Paris. “The [King Khalid] airport is closed and I was travelling for work, so I had to take the longer route,” he said. Rami, another Riyadh resident, said he was concerned about the apparent gap in public alerts before the latest attacks. He said he had not received one for weeks, until they resumed on Monday. “I received one yesterday,” he said. “Before that, the last one I got was on September 19. And I’m not the only one who noticed the gap.” His account could not independently establish whether alerts had been issued to other residents. Messages seen by The National suggest public alerts had resumed by Monday. Early on Tuesday, residents also received a Civil Defence message urging them to update their mobile phone operating systems to the latest available version “to ensure that warnings are received”. The contrast between busy streets and the disruption to schools and air travel reflects the uncertainty facing residents as Saudi Arabia braces for further attacks, and the possibility of a wider conflict that could draw in the US. The interviewees’ surnames have been withheld at their request because of the sensitivity of the situation

title: President Sheikh Mohamed receives phone call from Russia’s Vladimir Putin
description: Leaders discuss regional issues of concern
content: President Sheikh Mohamed and Vladimir Putin have spoken by phone, with the two leaders reaffirming the strength of ties between the UAE and Russia. Sheikh Mohamed and the Russian President held the call on Tuesday and discussed ways to deepen their countries' strategic partnership and advance shared interests, state news agency Wam reported. The two leaders reviewed regional and international issues of mutual concern, with developments in the Middle East featuring prominently in their discussions. Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Putin underscored the importance of reinforcing security and stability across the region, emphasising that such efforts are essential for the benefit of all countries and peoples in the Middle East. The call reflects the continued engagement between Abu Dhabi and Moscow at the highest levels of government, as both nations look to strengthen bilateral co-operation across key areas of shared interest. The UAE has maintained active diplomatic channels with Russia, with Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Putin having met on several occasions to discuss bilateral relations and pressing global issues. Tuesday's phone call signals both sides' commitment to sustaining that dialogue in an evolving regional and international landscape.

title: WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh: Start time, matches, tickets and how to watch in the UAE
description: Roman Reigns, Sami Zayn, Liv Morgan and Chelsea Green are among stars confirmed for November event
content: WWE is set to return to Saudi Arabia for Crown Jewel, with the annual wrestling event scheduled to take place in Riyadh on November 7, despite recent missile attacks on the Saudi capital. The show will feature some of WWE's biggest stars, including Roman Reigns, Sami Zayn , Liv Morgan and Chelsea Green , with two championship matches confirmed during Monday Night Raw on October 12. WWE has continued to promote the show, with no changes to the venue or date announced. Crown Jewel is part of Riyadh Season and continues WWE's partnership with Saudi Arabia, a partnership that began in 2018. The kingdom is also preparing to host WrestleMania 43 in 2027, which will be the first time WWE's flagship event has taken place outside North America. Here is everything you need to know about Crown Jewel 2026. Crown Jewel will take place on November 7 at Riyadh Season Stadium in the King Abdullah Financial District. The main show is scheduled to begin at 10pm Saudi Arabia time, which is 11pm in the UAE. Tickets went on sale on October 2 through Webook. Prices range from 80 Saudi riyals to 600 Saudi riyals, depending on seating category. Availability and prices may change closer to the event. Crown Jewel will stream live on Netflix in the UAE and other international markets covered by WWE's streaming agreement. In the US, the event will be available through the ESPN app with an ESPN Unlimited subscription. World Heavyweight Champion Roman Reigns will face WWE Champion Sami Zayn for the men's Crown Jewel Championship. Zayn won his first WWE Championship at Night of Champions in Riyadh in June, before losing it only nine days later. However, he recaptured the title for the second time on September 11. Women's World Champion Liv Morgan will take on WWE Women's Champion Chelsea Green for the women's Crown Jewel Championship. Their rivalry developed on Raw when Morgan dismissed Green's championship reign before Green lost a non-title match to Roxanne Perez. Both contests follow Crown Jewel's champion-versus-champion format, with separate titles awarded to the winners rather than either wrestler's existing championship being defended. Seth Rollins and Stephanie Vaquer won the respective men's and women's Crown Jewel titles at last year's event in Perth, Australia. More matches are expected to be announced in the coming weeks.

title: Du and etisalat unveil new services boosting UAE push towards 6G
description: Latest commercial technology to enhance network capacity and upload speeds
content: UAE telecoms operators du and etisalat have unveiled new services to boost mobile phone communications as the nation accelerates its push towards 6G technology . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . U6GHz – the new spectrum for the next generation of mobile connectivity – is expected to enhance the cloud, artificial intelligence, digital experiences and connected environments. The U6GHz band was identified for international mobile telecoms in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, several Asian countries, as well as China, Brazil and Mexico, according to global technology advisory Omdia. U6GHz combines a wide contiguous spectrum bandwidth with characteristics closer to that of existing bands than that of other higher candidate bands, making it the “sweet spot” that balances capacity and coverage, the UK-based research firm said. Placing U6GHz “into the hands of customers … [will be] unlocking new opportunities for consumers, businesses and emerging digital applications”, Saleem Alblooshi, chief technology officer of Dubai-based du, said in a statement. Separately, Abu Dhabi's etisalat said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. The company – which recently rebranded back from e& – is using 2x2 Mimo, a wireless technology that allows the transmission of two data streams between mobile devices and cellular base stations. That new capability is exclusive on compatible smartphones on etisalat UAE’s 5.5G network and will be useful in sending high-resolution photos, videos and large files faster, in addition to harnessing the abilities of AI-powered applications, the company said. “Mobile experiences are changing,” said Marwan bin Shakar, chief technology officer of etisalat UAE. “Smartphones are no longer primarily consuming content – they are creating, sharing and increasingly sending richer data to AI and cloud applications in real time. That changes what we need from the network. By bringing this capability … we are increasing upload capacity where it matters.” Last month, etisalat claimed it had launched the world’s first mobile network operating on U6GHz. Mr bin Shakar said this was key to “accelerating the nation's transition to the 6G era”. Sixth-generation technology , or 6G, will offer faster speeds and data transfers for users of smartphones, tablets, laptops and other devices. Though the announcement does not mean 6G cellular technology has officially arrived, the UAE telecoms company's U6GHz mobile network makes use of several innovations that “elevate the 5G-advanced experience” and pave the way for it to become standard. The announcements from du and etisalat are the latest in a series of developments in the UAE related to the eventual adoption of 6G. Last month, du and Khalifa University said they had carried out field trials for the new technology. In 2024, the UAE's Telecommunications and Digital Regulatory Authority announced plans to allocate 600MHz and 6GHz bands, a move that helped accelerate the development of 6G services in the Arab world's second-largest economy. South Korea's Samsung, one of the world's largest manufacturers of smartphones, has predicted widespread adoption of 6G networks by 2030, with “completion of standards and early commercialisation by 2028".

title: Solenn review: Come for the setting, stay for the Wagyu lasagne
description: Chef Gregoire Berger’s first Abu Dhabi restaurant offers relaxed Mediterranean dining, although some dishes deliver better value than others
content: Known for his work at some of Dubai’s most acclaimed restaurants, chef Gregoire Berger now has his sights on Abu Dhabi. Solenn, which opened in August at The Arcades at Al Khail Square and overlooks Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club , is Berger's first restaurant in the capital. A departure from the fine dining for which he is known, the relaxed Mediterranean eatery is built around the idea of long lunches, quality produce and a slower pace. The Arcades at Al Khail Square is busy on a Friday evening, with people strolling along its corridors and between cafes, but Solenn is surprisingly quiet when we arrive, leaving us free to choose a table. Inside, colourful sofas and chairs, terracotta walls and pale pink tables give the space a warm and relaxed feel, like sitting in a cosy living room. Tall arched windows overlook the equestrian area, making the window seats a good spot to watch the activity outside over a meal. Chef Gregoire previously described his vision for Solenn as a “beautiful springtime in the South of France, there's great music outside and an amazing fragrance of lemon trees, and you just chill over a long lunch”. The inviting surroundings make it easy to settle in. The extensive menu offers plenty of choice, from breakfast dishes such as eggs, sandwiches and baked-to-order filo, to bowls, bakery items and manakish. My dining partner and I are here for dinner, so we turn our attention to the mains, although with so many options it makes deciding what to order a bit daunting. We are persuaded to try the Solenn Passion (Dh39) and Blanc Lychee (Dh38), two mocktails that we find quite refreshing, especially after coming in from the heat. Our meal starts with the burrata “Puglia” illusion (Dh95), a dish that is recommended by Gregoire himself. Adapted from one of his signature creations, it features a delicate tomato shell created from white chocolate and cocoa butter filled with a tomato salad and locally made burrata. It’s creamy, with the shell of the tomato offering a touch of sweetness. There is a long list of choices when it comes to mains to try. After some time, we decided on the marrow melt Wagyu burger (Dh160), whole sea bass (Dh220), truffle Wagyu lasagne (Dh85) and, after some persistence from our server, the Solenn baby chicken (Dh135). We’re told the lasagne regularly sells out, and we can see why. Generously portioned and full of flavour, it quickly becomes a favourite at the table, setting a high bar for the other mains. The sea bass is another highlight. Although I am not the biggest fan of seafood, I’m impressed by its tenderness and colourful presentation.
