It comes on a plate with two sauces – miso beurre blanc and curry – offering different flavours to accompany the fish. Unfortunately, the Wagyu burger is less successful. Neither of us feels it justifies the Dh160 price tag. The patty is small and with fries on the side it feels like an item that doesn’t really fit with the rest of the menu. However, the baby chicken fares better, although by the time we turn to it, we’re already rather full. We finish with two desserts. The caramel millefeuille (Dh55) combines baklava with crunchy vanilla pastry and cinnamon cream caramel, served with vanilla ice cream. The noisette velours (Dh65) is a more chocolate-heavy option, pairing sponge with mousses and hazelnut crunch for texture. It comes with vanilla ice cream and a milk chocolate spray finish. By this point, we’re already full, so the manageable portions are welcome. The millefeuille is the less sweet of the two, while the noisette velours will hit the spot for anyone craving a sugary finish. For us, the truffle Wagyu lasagne royale is the standout, with distinct layers that allow each component to come through. The rich flavour of the Wagyu beef also comes through clearly in each bite. Big enough to share, it also offers better value than some of the pricier mains. A three-course meal at Solenn can cost between Dh178 and Dh547. At the high-end of the price spectrum are the beef carpaccio “truffle vinaigrette” (Dh120), solo meuniere “Turkish Riveira” (Dh355) and luxe mango (Dh72). Meanwhile, those who would like to save can order the black lime hummus (Dh48), crispy chicken burger (Dh75) and caramel millefeuille (Dh55). Solenn is an easy place to settle in for an unhurried meal with friends or family, with its comfortable seating and views of the equestrian area adding to the appeal. The extensive menu could benefit from a tighter focus, and some dishes offer better value than others, but the Wagyu lasagne and sea bass give us reasons to return. Solenn is located at The Arcades in Al Khail Square at the Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club. It’s open Monday to Thursday, 8am to 10pm and Friday to Sunday, 8am to midnight. Reservations can be made by calling 54 328 9899. This review was conducted at the invitation of the restaurant

title: Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan appointed WEF executive fellow for science and innovation
description: UAE official named to lead key pillar at Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai
content: Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan has been appointed as an executive fellow by the World Economic Forum, raising her growing international profile in sustainability and climate action. The WEF named Sheikha Shamma to lead the Science, Discovery and Innovation pillar at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which is taking place in Dubai until October 15. The appointment is one of six core theme fellowships at the event, which is held in partnership with the UAE Government. Sheikha Shamma, who chairs Frontier25, The Climate Tribe, Aurora50, the Alliance for Global Sustainability and Reset Mena, said the WEF role offered a vital opportunity to accelerate climate solutions. “It's an honour to be selected by the World Economic Forum and to have the opportunity to engage with other distinguished experts in their respective fields,” she said. “I have always believed that the knowledge and stories we exchange shape the future we are building. This is more important now than ever before in the context of climate action, where the question is how fast we can scale solutions and how fairly we support others. “I look forward to sharing what we're learning from our work in the UAE with the world, and to using this platform to help more people, from classrooms to boardrooms, see themselves as part of the solution.” The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders is one of the flagship initiatives of the strategic partnership between the UAE Government and the WEF. This year's gathering brings together more than 700 leaders and experts from 90 countries, including ministers, senior government officials, 300 Young Global Leaders and 150 UAE government leaders. The meeting focuses on six strategic themes. As well as science, these cover artificial intelligence, geopolitics, economic growth, leadership, and climate. Executive fellows serving in the future track roles will hold their positions for a one-year term, during which they will provide thought leadership, strategic guidance and convening power around their respective themes. The initiative is designed to build stronger connections between current decision-makers and the next generation of global leaders. Sheikha Shamma was first recognised by the WEF when she was selected as a member of its Young Global Leaders community in 2023, joining approximately 100 exceptional young leaders acknowledged for their achievements in diverse fields.

title: UAE food aid reaches Gaza through Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge
description: Millions of meals being delivered to Palestinians as part of major UAE humanitarian initiative
content: Food aid from the UAE has entered the Gaza Strip through the Rafah crossing under a plan to deliver more than 10 million meals to Gazans in need. The delivery was made as part of the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative, named after Sheikh Ahmed, brother of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, who died on September 21. The initiative was launched to recognise Sheikh Ahmed's generosity and philanthropic work. The aid was transported from Al Maktoum International Airport to the Gallant Knight 3 team, operating from the UAE Humanitarian Aid Logistics Centre in the Egyptian city of Al Arish. The team prepared, loaded and transported the supplies to the Rafah crossing before they were moved into Gaza. The operation is part of broader, sustained efforts to support Palestinian civilians and alleviate the humanitarian crisis in the territory. The 10 million-meal target reflects the scale of need and the UAE's continued commitment to addressing it through organised, large-scale relief operations. The Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge is one of several continuing UAE-led initiatives directly assisting Gaza residents. Since the launch of Operation Gallant Knight 3, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid directed to the enclave since 2023. That assistance has included 130,708 tonnes of relief, medical and food supplies delivered by 796 aircraft, 25 ships and 14,483 lorries. By channelling aid through established logistics networks and co-ordinating with Egyptian authorities at the Rafah crossing, the operation aims to ensure supplies reach those most in need in a structured and efficient manner. Meanwhile, Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, the region's largest humanitarian and community development foundation, recorded expenditure of more than Dh2.3 billion in 2025, positively impacting approximately 165 million beneficiaries across 122 countries. Its humanitarian aid and relief programmes alone exceeded Dh625 million in expenditure, benefiting more than 53 million people worldwide.

title: IMF warns UK of risk of inflation ahead of government’s first budget
description: Economies such as Britain should sparingly use cost of living relief, fund says
content: The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday. The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget. It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies , said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023. “The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported. Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported. The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported. The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal. Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter. The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy. Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility. In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back. The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month. Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned. “Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels. The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added. “The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs. “Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.” Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said. The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

title: F1 announces 10-year deal for African Grand Prix in Rwanda from 'early 2030s'
description: Ferrari star Hamilton among those to campaign for sport to return to continent
content: Formula One has announced a 10-year agreement to bring the sport back to Africa, with Rwanda set to host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s. The agreement sees the sport head back to the continent for the first time since 1993, when the South African Grand Prix left the calendar. Racing will take place at a new circuit in Bugesera, which is expected to be completed early in the next decade. The circuit will be located approximately 40 kilometres south of the capital, Kigali. The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board. “Today is a landmark moment for Formula One ,” said Stefano Domenicali, president and chief executive of F1. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe. “Africa has always been part of Formula One’s future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.” The announcement is expected to be well received by Ferrari star Lewis Hamilton , who has long been an advocate of the sport returning to Africa. Hamilton reaffirmed his stance on the need for an African F1 race in Singapore at the weekend. “I’ve always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa. It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, and the most beautiful continent,” said Hamilton. Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement. Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa.” Mohammed ben Sulayem, FIA president, said: “The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport.”

title: Qatar's government revenue fell 42% in first half due to Iran war, Emir says
description: Doha plans investment opportunities valued at $60.7 billion over next five years as it bolsters non-hydrocarbon economy
content: Qatar's revenue fell 42 per cent in the first half of this year, as exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) dropped due to the impact of the Iran war, Emir Sheikh Tamim said during a Shura Council meeting. LNG exports from Qatar, the world’s second-largest supplier before the conflict, has fallen sharply due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz as well attacks on its Ras Laffan complex . “The crisis naturally had an adverse impact on public finances, with total revenues falling by 42 per cent during the first half of the year, while public expenditures decreased by 14 per cent – all without compromising essential services or development priorities,” Sheikh Tamim said. “We decided against curtailing essential services and chose not to alter development priorities, aiming to sustain the economic momentum Qatar is experiencing.” Measures taken before the crisis, such as strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, adopting conservative oil-price assumptions in the budget and developing non-oil revenue, helped Qatar absorb the economic fallout, he said. About 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG capacity is offline after Iranian strikes damaged two of its 14 export trains, removing 12.8 million tonnes a year from the market. QatarEnergy has said repairs will take three to five years, meaning even a safe reopening of Hormuz would restore access to only part of Qatar’s prewar supply. Gas prices have soared globally due to the disruption. Disruption to Qatar's energy sector affects markets and consumers worldwide, the Emir said on Tuesday. “The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, along with direct damage to some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, has disrupted a significant portion of the country's exports,” he said. However, the economic fallout is concentrated mainly in the energy sector, while non-hydrocarbon industries continue to grow, accounting for about 80 per cent of real gross domestic product, he added. “This reflects the national economy's ability to withstand and continue growing under exceptional and complex circumstances,” Sheikh Tamim said. Economies across the Gulf are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue, the World Bank said last week. Qatar's economy is estimated to be hit the hardest among all countries in the region, facing a 20.9 per cent contraction this year, compared to 1.8 per cent growth in 2025, the World Bank said. The estimate would represent the country's weakest economic performance in five decades, after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund in its update this week said it expects Qatar's economy to contract by 15.6 per cent this year, before rebounding to growth of 18.8 per cent in 2027. However, Qatar will emerge from the regional crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes, Sheikh Tamim said. “We have a portfolio of projects and investment opportunities valued at approximately 221 billion riyals [$60.7 billion] over the next five years,” he said. Planned investments will cover infrastructure, public-private partnerships and private-sector projects in real estate and hospitality, he added. Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had faced three simultaneous responsibilities during the crisis: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy and economic security, and keeping diplomatic channels open. “Our strategy for shouldering these responsibilities consisted of four main elements: first, firmly defending the homeland without being drawn into war; second, maintaining services, supply chains and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and open waterways; and fourth, encouraging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful solutions to the conflict,” he said. Sheikh Tamim said the goal is “not merely to return to the pre-crisis status quo, but to use recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities”. “God willing, Qatar will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes,” he added.

title: Dubai inflation eases even as fuel costs rise
description: Consumer prices fall slightly from summer highs
content: Dubai's inflation rate eased slightly in September from the previous month, even as rising oil prices pushed up the cost of petrol. Inflation on an annual basis stood at 5.03 per cent, down from the 5.54 per cent recorded in August and the 5.7 per cent peak for this year reached in June. The figures were released by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Dubai’s General Monthly Consumer Price Index decreased by 0.05 per cent month-on-month in September on falling airfares and cheaper holiday packages. Airfares on a monthly basis fell by 23.44 per cent and holiday packages dropped 12.47 per cent from the August level. However, on an annual basis, the transport division was the biggest contributor to the rise in consumer prices in September, climbing 14.7 per cent. The increase in transport charges was driven by a 37.52 per cent rise in the cost of fuels and lubricants for personal transport, as well as a 13.48 per cent rise in passenger transport by air, according to the latest government data. The transport segment, which accounts for 9 per cent of Dubai’s Consumer Price Index basket, has been the main driver of inflation in the emirate over the past several months amid a rise in prices petrol prices . The UAE lifted fuel subsidies in 2015 and prices are evaluated on a monthly basis, based on movements in global markets. Petrol prices in the Emirates rose for a third consecutive month for October as prices in global oil markets remain elevated amid escalating geopolitical concerns in the Middle East. Global crude prices, which surged by nearly 109 per cent during the peak of the war, now in its eighth month, are still more than 70 per cent higher on concerns of a possible resumption in fighting between the US and Iran . Brent crude, which hovered around the $110 per barrel mark in September, has largely remained above $100 over the past few weeks. The West Texas Intermediate benchmark passed $105 a barrel in September as the Strait of Hormuz remained a flashpoint. Increasing attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the Red Sea by the Houthi rebels in Yemen have added another layer of risk to energy supplies from the region. Despite economic headwinds, Dubai's economy has largely skirted the deeper slump experienced by some neighbours. Non-oil private sector business activity in the emirate, which is one of the largest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, indicating a “solid improvement” in Dubai, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026, S&P Global Markets Intelligence said earlier this month. The boost to the emirate’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven by a “sharp and accelerated increase in output” as new orders also rose markedly and employment in the emirate rose, according to the PMI survey data. The tourism and retail sectors in the emirate have also bounced back from the initial shock of the war. Property, among the top contributors to the emirate’s economy, has also held up relatively well. The food and drinks category increased by an annualised 8.05 per cent last month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and domestic fuel rose by almost 6.23 per cent, “as a result of the growth of the average residential rental prices in most areas of the emirate during September”, the latest government data shows.

title: Tiny dragons of Darjeeling: How a small community became the last hope for the Himalayan salamander
description: Long before scientists arrived, a few hill people of Darjeeling were quietly saving the amphibian from the pressures of change
content: Towards the end of summer in the emerald-green tea estate of Margaret's Hope, the weather cannot make up its mind. One moment, drizzle comes soft and steady through the tall pine trees. Next, mist rolls in and swallows everything as the hills play hide-and-seek with the sky. A steep tarmac road drops from the main hill cart path through rows of tea bushes. At the bottom, about 11 kilometres north of Kurseong town, a pond sits hidden in the mist. Sedge, a dense waterside plant common to Himalayan wetlands, stands along its edges like a barricade. In the hill villages of Darjeeling, India , these ponds have long been more than bodies of water. “Local communities have been protecting this species long before any funding or international recognition,” says Barkha Subba, a Darjeeling conservation biologist. “These wetlands are deeply intertwined with local culture and religious beliefs.” What they have been protecting is one of India's last remaining breeding grounds for the Himalayan salamander, known locally as gora or pani chepara in Nepali . They are sometimes described as a tiny dragon that swims quietly in mountain ponds. Growing up to 20 centimetres long, they are also called crocodile newts, for the ridges along their dark bodies. Scientifically known as Tylototriton himalayanus, it is listed as vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List of Threatened Species , with a declining population trend. Ramesh Rai, 55, moves around the pond in a white cotton T-shirt and rubber gumboots, parting the sedge and scanning the water. He is searching for eggs tucked into submerged vegetation. Ramesh is the munshi of Margaret's Hope tea estate, head of the workforce that keeps the 160-year-old site running. His grandfather and father worked this land. He was born and grew up here and has known the gora since childhood. “There is a place called Gorabari not far from here,” he says, pointing at the tea bushes above the pond. “In the past the gora used to be found throughout the garden fields up there. The place was named after them. That is how many there once were.” Gorabari translates as the garden of the salamander. In 1993, Ramesh noticed the gora losing ground. While planting tea, he saw ponds shrinking, eggs dying and habitat being consumed by human activity and a shifting climate. He began protecting the salamanders without formal conservation training. In 2005, he wrote about the vanishing creature in the first issue of Sahityashri , a Nepali literary journal printed within the estate. MK Rai, 52, farms land around the estate. “In June, July, August, you would see them on the road,” he says. “We called them baby dragons then. We did not know their value.” Now tourists arrive with cameras and picnics, often leaving plastic on the bank. The two men have helped build the nursery pond with estate management and join clean-up campaigns run with Subba's organisation, the Federation of Societies for Environmental Protection, or Fosep. “Saving the salamander,” MK says, “means saving our culture, too.” Subba grew up in these hills, hearing stories of tigers, forests and mountain spirits from her grandmother. She studied biological sciences, completed a doctorate on high-elevation amphibians and returned to Darjeeling to work on conservation. In 2014, researcher Kartik Vasudevan of CCMB Hyderabad mapped 38 salamander habitats across Darjeeling. When Subba returned to check them, most were gone or severely degraded. Wetlands had dried up and invasive species had moved in. “Climate change is no longer a myth or a mystery,” she tells The National . “It is a fact we are seeing in everyday life. And the salamander is one of the clearest signs of what is being lost.” A peer-reviewed study published in Atmosphere in December 2024, analysing Darjeeling's temperature and rainfall records between 1991 and 2023, found that total rainfall has increased while maximum temperatures have also risen significantly. The rains are coming harder and shorter, not steadier. The salamander's entire life cycle is tied to the monsoon. With the first rain, it emerges from hibernation and returns to the same pond in which it was born; behaviour scientists call this site fidelity. Destroy that wetland and the species has nowhere else to go. At Margaret's Hope, 1,500 metres above sea level, salamanders mate and lay 60 to 90 eggs in submerged vegetation. But if the rain stops after two days, the shallow pool dries quickly and the clutch desiccates before hatching. “They lay eggs thinking there will be rain for another month,” Subba says. “Then suddenly the rain stops, the sun comes out, the pool dries up. The whole generation dies off.” The threat to the species doesn't stop there. Carp and guppies, which have been released into the main pond by local religious communities, eat eggs and larvae. Invasive phragmites grass has choked the banks. But, above all, it is climate change. In a bid to help the species, Ramesh, with members of the community and estate management, built a 1.8m-by-3m nursery pond with a vegetated island close to the main pond. Every March and April, he searches for clutches and moves them away from fish, herons and snakes, monitoring them for 12 to 15 days until they hatch. He is not paid for this work. Subba grew up in these hills and has been coming to Margaret's Hope since childhood. However, 2020 was the first time she came as a scientist, specifically to map the district's salamander habitats. What she found when she arrived surprised her. The community had already been doing the work without her. Around 2015, when the pond had nearly dried up and invasive grass had taken over, residents and estate management cleared it by hand. The salamanders returned. When Subba met Ramesh, she found something harder to teach than biology: decades of watching. “For him,” she says, “the salamanders are like his children.” Their collaboration now has formal backing. This year Subba received the 2026 Whitley Award, a prestigious British conservation prize, presented by Princess Anne at London's Royal Geographical Society. She was recognised for protecting seven critical breeding sites across Darjeeling. Margaret's Hope is one of them. Subba plans to extend the work to Nepal and Bhutan, creating a transboundary framework for a species that knows no borders. An estimated 5,000 individuals survive in the wild, with about 80 per cent living outside protected areas on tea garden land and private holdings. As the mist thickens again, Ramesh moves on, steady and unhurried. What began in 1993 as one man's effort to protect a disappearing species has grown into a wider conservation movement, bringing together local knowledge, community action and scientific expertise. But at the water's edge, his work remains much the same: watching, waiting and protecting what is left.

title: Iran accused of waging 'systematic campaign' against UK
description: Tehran's actions should be met with offensive measures, former army officer says
content: Iran is conducting a “ systematic campaign ” against UK interests that should be met with offensive action by security services, a politician and former British Army officer has said. Mike Martin, who served on several tours with the Intelligence Corps in Afghanistan , urged Britain's Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to take much tougher action against the regime, which has been blamed for several attacks and plots, including the recent incident at RAF Fairford, a base that had been used by US aircraft . Seven men have been arrested and released on bail while inquiries into a potential bomb plot continue, with the US withdrawing its B-1 bomber aircraft in the meantime. Two Iranians have been arrested for allegedly planning a lethal attack on Manchester’s Jewish community. Ms Mahmood announced on Monday that the government has created a specialist counter-terrorism section to tackle state threats from countries such as Iran. However, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he suspected the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the Fairford incident, Mr Martin told parliament during an urgent debate on UK national security: “I think it’s safe to say that there’s a systematic Iranian campaign on British soil.” The Liberal Democrat MP, who sits on the defence committee, said the government’s measures against Iran, which included imposing sanctions on the head of counter-espionage operations in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and summoning the Iranian ambassador in London, were “largely defensive in nature”. “Sometimes offence is the best form of defence, and I wonder whether the Home Secretary has considered that perhaps we need to increase the costs on the Iranians for their actions and considered signalling that fact to the Iranians to deter them from future activity?” Mr Martin said. Former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden told parliament on Monday that Iran considered the UK its enemy and “ smells weakness ”. He said Iran had attempted attacks at bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, Akrotiri in Cyprus and Fairford in Gloucestershire. The UK introduced sanctions on the IRGC in July, after the first two incidents and a series of attacks against dissidents in previous years. Ms Mahmood said the threats from Iran have been discussed with Britain’s allies. “We will always make sure we take both collective action to deal with the threats we all face, but also make sure we are always protecting the British national interests,” she said. She said she would not provide “a running commentary on wider discussions”, but added the government “will always take every appropriate step to keep our people safe”. In her statement, Ms Mahmood outlined how the new National Security Act gives the government “powerful new tools to tackle state threats”. She announced her department was “building a specialist mission in counterterror policing to disrupt state threats and tightening security around military bases”. Britain will also establish a National Centre for Information Defence to tackle disinformation from states and will give “intelligence agencies and police stronger powers to bear down on cybercriminals”. In addressing the threat posed by states such as Iran, she said: “Make no mistake: our police and security services are on permanent watch.” Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France ​and Germany, issued a statement on Monday condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts ‌of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber attacks, and other ⁠hybrid activities against us and our partners”. “The UK has also ​concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks ​and proxy actors,” ‌the statement added. Mr Burnham said: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity if Iran and the IRGC do us harm.”

title: Egypt and Sudan investigate after two Egyptians shot dead in Khartoum
description: Gunman claims shooting was revenge for brother who was among scores of goldminers killed in air strike near Egyptian-Sudanese border
content: Egypt and Sudan say they are investigating the deadly shooting of two Egyptians in Khartoum, an attack that followed the weekend death of scores of Sudanese goldminers in an air strike near the Egyptian border. Police in Sudan said they have apprehended the gunman whom they identified as Ibrahim Abdullah Adam, 23. They say he has admitted carrying out the attack, in which a third Egyptian was wounded, to avenge the death of his brother in Saturday's air strike. They said all three Egyptians were lorry drivers. A Sudanese police officer was also wounded in an exchange of fire before the gunman's arrest. “The investigation is continuing to establish the circumstances of the incident and its motives,” police said late on Monday night. “We will firmly deal with the matter under the law.” Neither Egypt nor Sudan publicly have said who was behind the air strike. The Egyptian military issued a statement saying troops and police were continuing to counter “illegal” gold prospecting in the country's Eastern Desert. It said it had dropped flyers on what it called criminal elements, warning them they must stop illegal mining “so that full sovereignty is safeguarded inside the Egyptian state's borders”. Egypt's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, said it was closely following the “regrettable” shooting in Khartoum. It said Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Sudanese counterpart in the military-backed government, Mohieldin Salem, spoke on the phone on Monday evening. It added that the ministers “emphasised the mutual respect that binds the two nations, including respect for each other's sovereignty, and the safety and integrity of their territories and borders”. The air strike near the border was initially reported by human rights and watchdog groups in Sudan, including the Emergency Lawyers, the civilian-led Somoud alliance and the Sudan Doctors' Network. They gave widely varying death toll figures, from 13 to 72. Some media reports in Sudan put the figure as high as 200. “We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somoud said. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bears the responsibility for what happens in areas under their control.” Sudan's military-led Sovereign Council said the air strike took place in the border region with Egypt. “The leadership in the two brotherly nations have been in contact since immediately after the incident took place to guarantee the protection of lives and safeguarding relations between the two peoples, find out the circumstances of the incident and give public opinion ownership of the facts,” it said. Images ​and video shared online, which The National has been unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn across rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s. There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative sources of income. Egypt 's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drugs and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested. Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign parties seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011. The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold in Sudan. Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million. Official figures place Sudanese government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion but experts say smuggling and the use of gold outside official channels account for far more. Last year, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated primitive localised refineries. Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

title: Dubai plans new underground transport network
description: Future of mobility extends beyond roads, says head of emirate’s Roads and Transport Authority
content: Plans have been unveiled for an underground transport network in Dubai. The proposed integrated underground system is part of wider efforts to reshape mobility above and below ground, said Mattar Al Tayer, director general of Dubai’s Roads and Transport Authority. At the Mohammed bin Rashid Leadership Forum on Tuesday, Mr Al Tayer said an RTA team was examining the proposed network, which could form part of a broader transformation of the city’s transport infrastructure. He described a future in which mobility extends beyond conventional roads and public transport to encompass three dimensions: the ground, the sky and underground. “The Dubai of the future will be a city that moves in three dimensions," said Mr Al Tayer. "Journeys in the sky that cut travel times to a matter of minutes; smooth movement at ground level through flexible roads and wider green spaces for walking, social interaction and enhanced quality of life. "And an innovative underground system that moves people, goods and services, redefining how space is used, creating new opportunities for investment and prosperity, and enabling more efficient and sustainable mobility. “Through this transformation, we are redefining how space is used, opening up new opportunities for investment and prosperity, while enabling mobility that is more efficient and sustainable,” Mr Al Tayer said. A video included with Mr Al Tayer's presentation showed an ambitious vision of the future for Dubai, with air taxis swooping across the skyline as buses travel on an underground road network and metro trains and futuristic pods glide into pristine stations. Mr Al Tayer said Dubai records more than 11 million journeys on its roads each day, equal to more than 7,000 a minute. More than six million people move around the city during daylight hours, a figure he said is expected to double by 2040. He said the emirate’s approach to transport planning was shaped by a principle instilled by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai: rather than wait for the future, Dubai should create it. The RTA also has a goal for one in every four journeys in Dubai to be autonomous by 2030. Driverless taxis have travelled more than four million kilometres in the past year, Mr Al Tayer said. Dubai is moving towards commercial urban air mobility, with the opening of its first air-taxi station planned for this year. He said the emirate’s infrastructure investments had delivered savings exceeding Dh319 billion ($86.8 billion) and added Dh156 billion to its economy. Tuesday's announcement was the latest in a line of recently unveiled transport projects focusing on the city's underground. Earlier this year, The National reported how construction was under way on the Dubai Loop , a high-speed underground transport network led by the government in partnership with Elon Musk's Boring Company, aimed at cutting congestion in the city. The RTA said in February that the first phase of the underground project would cost Dh565 million and connect DIFC with Dubai Mall as using autonomous Tesla cars. The first four stations are to be in Burj Khalifa, DIFC 2, Zabeel Dubai Mall Parking and ICD Brookfield Place. The network will eventually cover 22km and consist of 19 stations. The final cost is estimated at about Dh2 billion. The emirate's transport chief is exploring options to meet the demand created by Dubai's increasing population, which had crossed 4.5 million by the end of last year. The emirate's population reached 4.58 million, representing an increase of 7.5 per cent year-on-year, government statistics revealed. Last month, The National reported how the Boring Company was planning to build 150km of tunnels in the Emirates after it raised $3 billion in a funding round, led by the UAE. This was followed by last week's announcement that Elon Musk's firm had signed an agreement to explore underground transport, utility tunnels and related infrastructure opportunities in Abu Dhabi .

title: ‘My mum is my fire’: UAE Olympic sprinter Maryam Al Farsi’s mission to give back
description: Inspired by the strong women in her life, the Emirati athlete is determined to pay back her mother's many sacrifices
content: On the mirror in Maryam Al Farsi’s bathroom are coloured Post-it notes carrying the promises she makes herself every morning. “I will provide for my mum. I am strong. I will do this.” On the days she doubts herself, she reads them, walks out of her room and sees her mother working on her laptop, a reminder of why she must continue pursuing her dreams. Al Farsi is now 18, but two years ago in Paris, at just 16, she became the first Emirati sprinter to compete at the Olympic Games . One would presume her pursuit is for herself, but it’s not. “It’s my lifelong mission to provide for my family,” she told The National . Al Farsi was a speaker at Middlesex University Dubai’s Women in Sport series, launched through its London Sport Institute. The series brought together Emirati women to speak about identity, heritage and the next generation. And while she hopes to pave the way for the younger generation, her main purpose in life is to provide for the women who made her. Her inspirations are her mother, Leila, and Leila’s twin sister, Elham. “They’re both like my mothers. They are the strongest pillars in my life and they are my why. They’re the reason I chose track in the first place. They’re the reason why I didn’t give up,” she said. Then Maryam catches herself. “Actually, I did give up.” At around age 14, the pressure she piled on herself became too much, and Al Farsi walked away from athletics for almost a year. She kept much of what she was feeling to herself, but Leila and Elham sensed it anyway. “My mum said, 'Just give it one more try ... just for me.' And I was like, ‘Only because it’s you.' And that was the best decision I made because if I didn’t do that, I wouldn’t have gone to the Paris Olympics.” Al Farsi’s parents are divorced. Her father is Emirati and her mother is Iranian. Leila raised Maryam and her brother as a single mother, with her twin sister, Elham, and the rest of the family close beside her. “She has six sisters and they’re all so amazing. It’s like basically a family full of women, which I love, a house full of women,” Al Farsi said. Her appreciation and gratitude to her mum and her aunt are so profound they almost lendthemselves to guilt. She watched as her mother toiled and laboured to ensure Maryam could make her Olympic dreams come true. Leila paid for school, training, physiotherapy and everyday costs that came with raising two children. “She financed my whole life; no one else was helping. Her and my aunties were the only people there.” She recalls one memory that left her in tears after she dropped her mum off at work one day. “I just started sobbing after, and I was like, 'I want to provide for my mum. I don’t want her to work a nine-to-five. I want to pay for her house, I want to pay for her bills.' “I don't want her to ever worry about money. I never want her to worry about her job. I want to retire her. When I say her, I mean both of them, like the twins – one person. I just want to make them happy,” Al Farsi explains tearfully. She admires her mother’s character and her disinterest in all things material. “She doesn’t care about money. My mum does not care. She cares about health, she cares about happiness, about love.” What the mother sacrificed, the daughter wants to repay. Leila fought for her daughter’s right to compete when others questioned whether she should continue pursuing sport. “My mum is my fire.” Maryam continues, “My whole essay for university was that my mum was a fire in my life. Because she said no to someone. Because they didn't want me to compete in sport and she said no, she is competing and the second I saw her say that it felt like because she was able to do that, I'm able to do anything.” Success always comes at a cost, and Al Farsi remembers all the weekends and birthday parties she had to miss. “I lost a lot of friends,” she added. Education remains a priority. Al Farsi put athletics “a little to the side” while completing A-levels in economics, business and maths. “I love track, and I really want a future in it. But I also need to prioritise my education. And for my mum, it's education, education, education. But thank God I graduated with a great grade.” Attending Harvard Business School is the ultimate goal. “I really want that picture in front of the banner of me posing in front of Harvard Business School.” Al Farsi is also an aspiring entrepreneur. She has launched a company that focuses on parent engagement for schools and aims to bring all the information needed into one place. The idea was inspired by watching her mother’s struggles with her own children’s education. “I saw my mum struggling with trying to even paint a picture for me and my brother’s education. Even though she has so much information, it’s just fragmented.” Athletics remains part of her future. She admits that she "kind of thought I was fast but I wasn’t naturally fast.” Then her competitive nature came into play. “I need to get better at this. I will die if I don’t become the best.” Al Farsi has her sights set on qualifying for the LA2028 Olympics and competing in as many Diamond League meetings as possible. She’s proud to represent the UAE. “I get to represent such an amazing country and amazing people, so I definitely won’t stop with that.” Dr James Doty, a Stanford neurosurgeon and neuroscientist, says manifestation is most effective when it’s driven by compassion and the wish to improve other people’s lives. Al Farsi's instinct to look after people extends beyond just her own family. “I just love it, seeing the happiness in someone else’s eyes, just taking the pressure off of them. I’ll do it, even if that puts pressure on me.” Her advice to young girls is to find their niche, their fire that will spur them to succeed. “It could be something like I want to prove this person wrong, or I want to make this person happy, and if I can make this person happy, that will make me happy. That's really it.” Asked to choose among another Olympic opportunity, attending Harvard or owning a successful company, Maryam doesn’t hesitate. “I would choose whichever provides for my family.”

title: UAE weather: Rain expected across parts of country in coming days
description: Morning fog forecast on Wednesday and Thursday
content: Rain is expected to fall across parts of the UAE in the coming days, according to the latest forecast by the National Centre of Meteorology. The NCM is forecasting wet weather in Al Ain from Tuesday until Thursday this week, while rain is expected to fall in Fujairah on Tuesday and Wednesday. The highest temperature this week is expected in Sweihan, where it is tipped to reach 42°C each day until Friday. The highest temperature in Abu Dhabi is forecast to be 39°C on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday, while in Dubai the thermometer will peak at 38°C on the same days. The NCM also predicted there was a probability of foggy weather on both Wednesday and Thursday mornings. The rain, particularly in the eastern parts of the country such as Al Ain, is being caused by a low-pressure system from the south-east bringing moisture-laden air from the Arabian Sea. These systems then meet the mountains on the UAE’s east coast, wherer the air rises and meets a relatively cooler layer abovem, and this can lead to the formation of convective clouds and rain.

title: Abu Dhabi court sentences teacher to two years in prison for assaulting pupils
description: Educator to be deported after completing sentence
content: A male teacher has been sentenced to two years in prison for assaulting four pupils, the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department said on Tuesday. He was found to have assaulted the four pupils in a classroom at a private school in Abu Dhabi, according to a statement by the ADJD on Tuesday. The assault resulted in the pupils suffering injuries that left them unable to attend school. The teacher admitted the charges during the investigation and in court, the ADJD added. He admitted to “assaulting the students, claiming he did so to prevent them from causing chaos and disruption during the lesson, and in an attempt to discipline their behaviour”. CCTV footage corroborated the confession, capturing the violence inflicted on the pupils without justification, the ADJD said. Committing the offence inside a school during lessons meant the teacher was guilty of a breach of public security and order. Protecting public order aims to safeguard the fundamental values of society, ensure the safety of its members and maintain respect for the law – principles that directly apply to the case at hand, the court heard. The teacher will be deported after serving his sentence and will have to cover all the legal costs of the case, Abu Dhabi Criminal Court ruled. The court was told the defendant’s behaviour represented a blatant breach of existing laws and regulations, underlining the necessity of firm legal enforcement to protect public safety, uphold individual rights and deter violations that subject people to harm or undermine their security and stability.

title: France’s angry youth are demanding a future – not just better schools
description: With Emmanuel Macron nearing the end of his final term, the country’s far right is waiting to grab a disgruntled vote bank
content: Last week, on my way through the Latin Quarter, a neighbourhood in Paris, I passed the gates of Lycee Henri-IV. It is one of the most elite schools in France, the kind of place that produces philosophers, scientists and presidents – the equivalent of getting into Harvard or Yale universities, but for high-school students. A cluster of teenagers in hoodies stood outside holding signs. They were very young and very annoyed. Today, near Boulevard Raspail, I came across more students. “If we are old enough for you to use violence against us, we’re old enough for you to listen to us,” said a 17-year-old marching through the leafy district of the French capital. Violence has not reached this wealthy neighbourhood bordering the Jardin du Luxembourg. But students at the Institut Catholique, which Pope Leo XIV visited two weeks ago , are joining in solidarity and resistance against President Emmanuel Macron’s government, calling for change . The protests began on September 21 at Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, a suburb in the Val-de-Marne, south-east of Paris. Many other schools in the Ile-de-France region quickly joined, followed by Marseille, Lille, Rennes and Strasbourg. As the days pass, the students’ demands have grown. At first, the protests were about the lack of resources in public schools: teacher shortages, classes of 35 or more, leaking buildings and long days that start at 8am and run into the evening. Now the rallying cry is about a generation that feels unheard and is inheriting a dysfunctional world it did not create. I have spent three decades watching young people take to the streets: in Cairo, in Aleppo, in Belgrade, in Ramallah, in Kyiv. Some, like in Belgrade, were successful – the students overthrew Slobodan Milosevic. My first year as a new mother in France, 2005, brought the riots triggered by the electrocution of two teenagers. They later spread across the country’s suburbs, with burning cars and real violence . The deaths of the teenagers were the trigger, but the real causes were unemployment, discrimination and broken relations with the police. The first thing I learnt about the protests in France is that the stated grievance is rarely the whole story. What is happening now is no exception. The French are exceptional at protesting. Their protests are effective, and the protesters know they work. The country has a culture of dissent that goes back to the French Revolution, and taking to the streets is seen as a civic duty rather than a disruption. That legacy runs through May 1968, when a general strike drew in between seven and 10 million workers. It all began with a handful of students at Nanterre, whose early grievances included dormitory rules. The grievances behind this latest movement should embarrass the government. On October 1, according to the Interior Ministry, 1,027 of France’s roughly 3,700 lycees were affected, 222 of them blockaded. Bins burned in Toulouse and Rennes. There was tear gas in Strasbourg and Lille, and a school in Nantes was firebombed. The Justice Minister, Gerald Darmanin, says about 2,000 people have been arrested since the movement began, the majority of them minors. More than 400 schools were closed the following day. The student who lives with me and studies at Institut Catholique just came home disgruntled because protesters were blocking the streets. The government’s response is predictable: condemnation, a crisis meeting, protest bans outside closed schools. Next come the endless TV and radio shows looking for a scapegoat. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ’s office called it a manoeuvre organised by La France Insoumise, the hard-left party. LFI’s Manuel Bompard replied that the government was sliding into conspiracy theory. Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis and France’s answer to New York City’s Zohran Mamdani, put himself between riot police and students and was tear-gassed for it, an amazing moment caught on camera and widely shared this week. Remember that all this is happening in the run-up to a presidential election that fills most of us with dread. Mr Macron, whom I voted for, is on his way out. He is barred from running again next May, because Article 6 of the Constitution limits a president to two consecutive terms. Personally, I like Mr Macron, but I’m in a minority. He is credited with being strong on foreign policy, less so on domestic issues. Meanwhile, the National Rally, the far-right party founded by the late Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, is on the rise. With Mr Macron close to the end of his term next year, the RN believes the Elysee is finally within reach. Jordan Bardella , its 31-year-old president, has spent years cultivating young voters even as he faces allegations, which he strongly denies, of anti-Semitic messages from the 2010s. LFI is finding a niche, particularly among the young. It’s no coincidence that the protests came to a head in the same week the government unveiled a budget built on spending cuts and tax rises to bring down France’s deficit. The teenagers did not miss the timing, and neither should we. “Most of all, we’re fed up with the high cost of living,” an 18-year-old political science student told me. She ran through the cost of food, cell phones, metro transport and drinks in a cafe. It’s not Manhattan or London, but salaries in France are lower. I expect the protests to be put down fairly soon, but it will be telling to see who benefits most. Marine Le Pen , daughter of Jean-Marie, blamed LFI for stoking the unrest, and her officials have demanded damage reports and crisis meetings. RN supporters aren’t on the streets, and they don’t need to be. They are content to watch France lose control of its schools and its young. This plays nicely into the party’s education platform, which promises a “big bang of authority”: phone bans, uniforms and sanctions that reach families’ benefits. They are standing back, watching the left fall on its face. It remains to be seen whether the RN will win young supporters once the protests actually end. But the real story here is generational, and it began long before the protests. In 2023, Mr Macron forced through pension reform raising the retirement age from 62 to 64. Millions marched against it, many of them young people who saw that the changes meant they would have to work longer. I remember watching French TV and being amazed how many young people were protesting against pensions . But they saw it as their future being crushed. France’s wealth sits disproportionately with older owners of property and savings. Its debt, and now its austerity, will fall on the young. Whether French teenagers are reading budget tables and spread sheets, or not, they do understand that their classrooms are cold because a radiator has not been fixed for a year. They do understand that their teachers are exhausted and cannot give them the time or attention they need. They do understand that they are being handed a world threatened by war in Eastern Europe, with Russia’s latest hybrid war, a mounting national debt and high unemployment for recent graduates. Mr Macron came to power in 2017 as the young man who would modernise France. It was his youth that attracted so many of us: youth and energy which the older politicians lack. But he is leaving office a middle-aged weary man with teenagers in the streets demanding a better world. At the very least, he has to listen to them before deciding who to blame.

title: Saudi Arabia vows to remain strong after deadly Houthi attacks
description: Coalition fighting against Iran-backed group warns civilians in Yemen's rebel-held capital of imminent 'special operation'
content: Saudi Arabia has vowed to remain strong in the face of repeated attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels on its civilian infrastructure. Speaking at a government press conference in Riyadh on Monday, Minister of Media Salman Al Dosary praised the Saudi security forces and military, saying the kingdom would “remain strong and united” behind its leadership and continue its development efforts despite the attacks. “We strongly condemn the Houthi terrorist attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities in the kingdom,” Mr Al Dosary said. The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government said it intercepted a Houthi missile launched at Riyadh on Monday night, while the rebels claimed to have achieved a “direct hit” on the capital's King Khalid International Airport. The airport's operations have been suspended until midnight on October 17 after Houthi missile strikes on Saturday and Sunday killed 14 people and injured more than 300. On Tuesday, the coalition intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched towards Khamis Mushait in the south-west of the kingdom. A brief statement issued by spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki did not say where the missiles were launched from or whether the incident had caused any casualties or damage. The Iran -backed group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, repeated its warning “to all international airlines, experts, employees, workers and passengers from all countries of the world against flights to Saudi airports, as they are unsafe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah”. He also claimed a drone launched at the Khamis Mushait airbase resulted in a “direct hit”. Later on Tuesday, the coalition urged civilians in Yemen's rebel-held capital Sanaa to evacuate the area around the Yemen Oil Company’s Al Sabahah central station ahead of a “special operation”. The Houthis warned any attack on Sanaa would be met with a harsh and painful response. Meanwhile, pro-government forces and the Houthis are battling for control of the key city of Taiz. Human rights groups have raised the alarm on the humanitarian situation inside the city, where people are cut off from food, water, medical and energy supplies amid what some organisations described as a “siege”. “Within five days, the city lost its main supply route for goods and commodities: Taiz-Al-Turbah-Lahj-Aden, following the Houthi group’s takeover of areas west and south of Taiz,” the Studies and Economic Media Centre in Yemen said in a report this week. The government also closed the eastern route used by civilians for security reasons, it added. The International Organisation for Migration estimates that more than 216,000 people have been displaced since the escalations in Yemen began in August. At least 172,000 of them are from Taiz. The UN said it was providing assistance to those in need but that reaching them was proving difficult, especially with key roads closed. That has disrupted “civilian movement, commercial supplies and humanitarian access”, the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in a briefing on Monday. At least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children, the agency said. “A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children,” it added.

title: Strait of Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping
description: At least 12 tankers have been attacked in the strait in the past week, tally of UKMTO warnings shows
content: At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage. The UKMTO reclassified the Sohar incident from suspicious activity to an attack after confirming a tanker had been struck by a drone. Local authorities assisted in evacuating the crew. In a separate incident, an outbound tanker was damaged when it was hit on its port side, although all crew members were reported safe. The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”. The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources. The International Maritime Organisation recorded nine vessel-related incidents in the same period, reflecting differences in verification and reporting. Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off. Shipping analyst Sal Mercogliano said video circulating with the claim did not appear to show a mine strike, as the vessel was stationary and there was no underwater explosion. The IRGC claimed any tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait would face a similar fate. Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said. On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. The incident not been confirmed. Earlier this month, a crude tanker was struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, but the threat to commercial shipping has also extended beyond the waterway. A vessel reported being hit by projectiles about 95km north of Madinat Ash Shamal in Qatar, with casualties reported. The Panama-flagged crude carrier Gem No 2 was struck by a drone, with reports placing the vessel about 25km west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. The resulting fire was extinguished and Indian officials said the vessel’s 22 crew members were safe. The attacks and warnings have sharpened the divide between Tehran’s claims of control over the waterway and Washington’s assessment of shipping conditions. Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC's commander, said Iran would close routes it considered to be illegal, including passages along Oman’s coast. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mr Naqdi was quoted as saying by the Fars news agency. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected that assessment last week, saying commercial oil flows had largely recovered despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt shipping. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he said. “So they’ve lost complete control of the strait.”

title: Al Ahli coach Marino Pusic calls for action after 'dangerous' bottle throwing at Al Wasl
description: Visiting players pelted with plastic projectiles during 3-1 win in Dubai
content: Marino Pusic said something needs to be done to stop fans throwing bottles at players, terming it “dangerous”. The Al Ahli Saudi coach was speaking after his side’s 3-1 win over Al Wasl in Dubai on Monday night. The AFC Champions League Elite group match was played in an electric atmosphere created by 4,500 supporters at the Zabeel Stadium. Emotions boiled over at points, though, with many plastic bottles and cups being thrown onto the pitch. In particular, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, became a target after irritating supporters with his antics. First, he invoked ire after being perceived to feign injury in an altercation with Adryelson, the Wasl defender. When he was playing on the wing near Wasl’s diehard supporters in the second half, he was pelted with bottles. He responded by gesturing to them to throw more. Later in the game he was stretchered off on a medical buggy with a shoulder injury. The injury did not stop him from goading the home supporters, and celebrating when he went past the away section. That led to more aggravation, with even a couple of bottles being lobbed his way from the Wasl bench – leading to a confrontation between the opposing sets of substitutes. The issue of bottle throwing is not unique to Wasl. Most high profile fixtures in the region see instances of projectiles being thrown at moments of tension in the game. With matches played in high temperatures, clubs make water readily available to supporters. At Al Ain , for example, that now takes the form of paper cups alongside large water coolers at the back of stands. Other clubs provide small bottles or plastic cups of water. Sometimes these are thrown by irate fans, targeting players, coaching staff, or match officials. It happened at the AFC Champions League Elite final last season, which Ahli themselves ended up winning. High profile international fixtures between Qatar and the UAE have also been notable for it happening. Pusic joined Ahli, the two-time Asian champions, ahead of this season after leaving Abu Dhabi club Al Jazira. He said he does not want the passion of supporters to be diluted, and pointed out that the fixture against Wasl ended with cordial relations between the two sides. But the Croatian-Dutch coach said players and officials should not have projectiles thrown at them. “It could be a problem with people throwing very dangerous things on the pitch, because players and staff members [could] be hurt by these kind of things,” Pusic said. “I feel always pity about things when that happens. The passion and the support must be always there, and that's good. I like that part as well. “But as you can see, after the game, it was everything was nice, fine, like it should be. “In the heat of the moment, things can happen. But it's dangerous when you throw too much. It shouldn't happen, of course. But we are professionals; we are used to a lot of things.” The result leaves Wasl without a point after two matches in the Champions League, with many supporters voicing their frustration with coach Rui Vitoria. Roger Ibanez, who scored the first goal for Ahli, said his side were glad to get out of Dubai with the three points. “We knew it would be a tough game,” said the Brazil centre back, who was the player of the match. “We played here two years ago when we also got the result, and today was again a really tough match but we got the result. “We did a good job. Inside of the pitch, the players who started and the players who came in helped a lot. “Now let's go home and recover because we have a tough match [in the Saudi Pro League against Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr on Thursday].” Al Ain maintained their sparkling start to the Champions League and they sit at the top of the 16-team table. The UAE double winners followed up their opening day thrashing of Al Nassr with a 4-1 win over Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basra.

title: Dubai Design Week 2026 announces programme spanning architecture and craft
description: Emirati palm trimming, Japanese woodwork and a reimagined Abwab exhibition feature in the programme running from November 3 to 8
content: Dubai Design Week has unveiled its 2026 programme, with installations drawing on Emirati palm craft, traditional Japanese woodwork and the reuse of concrete rubble. The event will be held at Dubai Design District from November 3 to 8, bringing together exhibitions, public installations, talks and workshops. Downtown Design, its contemporary design fair, will take place from November 4 to 8. Abwab, the event's commissioning programme, will move from individual pavilions to a group exhibition. Called In Other Words, it will bring several practitioners together to explore how people communicate through gestures, signage, symbols, oral histories, and spoken and written language. Dubai-based practice Nao Architects, founded by architect Reem Nassour, has won this year’s Urban Commissions competition with Three Gardens and a Room . The annual competition focuses on design for public spaces. Responding to this year’s theme, Atmospheres, Nassour’s proposal uses vegetation, colour, shade and filtered light to create three distinct gardens around a shared central space. The arrangement forms a room between the gardens where visitors can gather. Elsewhere, Emirati architect Rasha Saffarini’s Taqleem will draw on the traditional practice of palm-tree trimming to create a communal space. Palestinian-Turkish practice aestudio will use reclaimed concrete rubble to make new architectural forms in InBetween What Was and What Will Be . Japanese firms Nikken Sekkei and Sobokuya will return with Chatai 2.0 , an expanded timber structure combining traditional craftsmanship with spaces for gathering and collaborative craft. Their Japanese teahouse was among last year’s installations. Other installations will draw on games and domestic life. Indian practice Alter’s Playing Field will turn Ludo into a space for shared play, while Bahrain’s Palm and Palazzo will explore the balance between privacy and social connection in the traditional Bahraini home through Bayn . The UAE Designer Exhibition will return under the theme Inherited Futures, with architect and designer AlZaina Lootah as this year’s design collaborator. Supported by Dubai Culture, it will bring together UAE-based designers exploring how inherited materials, rituals and technologies can inform contemporary design. Craft will also feature in an exhibition by L’Ecole, School of Jewelry Arts, supported by Van Cleef & Arpels, presenting experimental archaeological research into lost goldsmithing techniques from the Second Iron Age. Al Jalila Cultural Centre for Children will return with an exhibition of ceramics by young practitioners. Downtown Design will showcase work developed through UAE training and mentorship programmes, including Tashkeel’s Tanween Design Programme and Abu Dhabi’s Athath Fellowship. The latter’s 2026 cohort will present furniture prototypes developed for the market. Carpet and textile specialist Iwan Maktabi will present new work by UAE-based designers Nadine Kanso and Omar Al Gurg. Kanso’s designs draw on Arabic calligraphy and symbols of the UAE, while Al Gurg’s reflect memories of the traditional majlis. An exhibition dedicated to Memphis Milano will explore the design movement’s graphic patterns, unconventional forms and continuing influence. British-Nigerian artist and designer Yinka Ilori will create the fair’s Veuve Clicquot lounge. Alongside the displays, interior architect and designer Tristan Auer will be a keynote speaker at the fair’s Forum in a space designed by architecture and interiors studio Bone. The wider festival’s workshops will take place at a dedicated Maker Space, with sessions led by practitioners from institutions including the University of the Arts London and SAE University College. The programme is open to participants of all ages and experience levels. The outdoor Marketplace will be held on November 7 and 8, bringing together independent makers selling homeware, jewellery, fashion and handcrafted goods, alongside children’s activities and live performances.
