title: Sports events in Saudi Arabia to go ahead despite Houthi attacks
description: Saudi Pro League matches scheduled to go ahead with Riyadh Racing Season also set to begin
content: The situation in Saudi Arabia has been tense for many weeks, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensifying their attacks on the kingdom. Over the past week, attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports in Riyadh, Abha, Jazan and Najran caused multiple deaths and major destruction. As the kingdom faces a major security challenge, the crisis is casting a shadow over live sports. Here we take a look at where things stand in Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Pro League continued on Sunday even as Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport endured deadly attacks over the weekend, leaving 13 dead and hundreds injured. Al Shabab’s match against Al Taawoun in Riyadh went ahead, with Shabab completing a comfortable 3-0 win. Al Fayha and Al Riyadh played out a draw, but the game between Abha and Al Faisaly was postponed until later in the month. The SPL continues this Thursday. Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr hosted Uzbek side Neftchi in their AFC Champions League Elite match in Riyadh on Monday. There was uncertainty surrounding the match , especially after training for the game at Al Awwal Park was called off. Kick-off was delayed due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence, but the match went ahead and Nassr eased to a 3-1 win . Fellow SPL heavyweights Al Ittihad are all set to take on Shabab Al Ahli in Jeddah on Tuesday. The world's top men’s tennis players are scheduled to compete in the third edition of the Six Kings Slam, to be shown on Netflix from October 21-24. Carlos Alcaraz , Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Alex de Minaur and Taylor Fritz are set to compete at the ANB Arena. However, defending champion Jannik Sinner has been replaced by Learner Tien in the line-up. Tickets for the tournament have gone on sale, with no changes announced so far. Earlier in the year, it was announced that the 2026 WTA Finals had been relocated from Riyadh to Indian Wells, California, after Saudi Arabia relinquished the right to host the tournament. Boxing great Saul "Canelo" Alvarez is scheduled to take on Christian Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title in Riyadh on October 31. There was uncertainty over the bout after several days of deadly strikes on the city. However, organiser Turki Alalshikh said Canelo would fulfil his commitment and compete in the Saudi capital. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Alalshikh posted on X. “He fears nothing.” World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE)'s Crown Jewel event is set to take place on November 7 at Riyadh Season Stadium. It is the 16th event that WWE will hold in Saudi Arabia under a 10-year partnership. At the event, Roman Reigns will face Sami Zayn, while in the women’s category, Liv Morgan is scheduled to fight Chelsea Green. The 2026/27 racing season in Riyadh is scheduled to start on Friday and end April 17 next year. As things stand, the season is set to last six months and include 69 races. The total prize pool on offer is 197.8 million Saudi riyals. ⁠Golf's Asian Tour said on Tuesday that it is monitoring the ⁠security situation ahead of the Saudi International ​in Riyadh. The PIF ​Saudi ⁠International, which serves as the Asian Tour's ‌season-closer, is scheduled to take place at the Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 to 21. "Any changes to the schedule will be announced as soon as we have determined the right course of action for our players, fans and partners," the Asian Tour told Reuters in a statement. "The PIF Saudi International is incredibly important to the Asian Tour as our season finale, however the safety of our players, staff and service teams is always our number one priority."

title: Morocco's first female prime minister secures deal to form government
description: Authenticity and Modernity Party to lead coalition of four parties
content: Morocco's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), led by the country's first female prime minister Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri , has ⁠reached a deal with three other parties to form a coalition government. The coalition, which includes moderate socialist parties ⁠and the nationalist Istiqlal, together hold 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority. PAM, which won last month's parliamentary election, was founded in 2008 by a royal adviser and has positioned itself as an advocate of social modernisation. It is led by Ms El Mansouri, who in September was named Morocco's first female prime minister , marking the latest chapter in a career that has taken her from Marrakesh's city hall to the top levels of the country's political establishment. Ms El Mansouri, 50 was urban planning and housing minister under prime minister Aziz Akhannouch since 2021. The coalition deal "produces a ⁠strong political government, made up of components marked by ​ideological ⁠and political proximity, ‌united in, and committed to, a shared reformist vision", ​the parties said in a joint statement. The next step is to propose a cabinet. They are to propose the names of male and female ministers "who possess competence, political acumen, integrity and probity, as part of a cohesive and strong government capable of implementing the government programme, which will be drawn up as quickly as possible". Ms El Mansouri's party has pledged to protect purchasing power by raising incomes and regulating markets, while making youth employment a priority. Its 2027-2031 programme aims to support one million young people, amid 29.2 per cent unemployment among people aged from 15 to 24. Other priorities include improving health care, education, housing and digital services, strengthening water, food and energy security, embracing artificial intelligence, and driving inclusive economic growth while protecting public finances. The new government is to oversee the final stages of preparations for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Portugal and Spain.

title: Galatasaray v Barcelona: Lamine Yamal and Co aim to make it perfect 10 in Champions League clash
description: Flick's La Liga table-toppers have won all nine matches this season but face Turkish test on Tuesday
content: Despite a three-week international break and the absence of La Liga's current top scorer, there was no stopping Barcelona's perfect start to the campaign at the weekend. Hansi Flick's table-toppers secured their eighth win in eight La Liga matches when they brushed aside Getafe 3-0 on Saturday – with Anthony Gordon, Gabriel Jesus and Jules Kounde on target – equalling their best start to a domestic campaign. And European football 's form team managed that without 12-goal forward Raphinha, who missed the game after picking up a thigh injury while away with the Brazil national team. Win at Real Betis next weekend, and Barca will have matched Real Madrid's Spanish top-flight record of nine consecutive wins at the start of a season, achieved in 1968. After also thrashing Feyenoord 5-1 in the opening round of the UEFA Champions League last month, Flick recorded nine victories across all competitions, breaking a club record set a century ago. That is a flying start that even legendary Barca coaches Johan Cruyff, Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique could not match. Strength in depth meant Flick could hand rare starts to the likes of Kounde, Gavi and Jesus against Getafe, with all three making valuable contributions at Camp Nou. “In every position, we have two or three players performing at an outstanding level,” said the German coach. “There is a great atmosphere in the team. That is what I like most. Everything is about the team, not one player or the coach. “The important thing is the team, and they have to understand that sometimes they need to be on the bench. That’s what’s important to win titles. “Everyone has to contribute in attack and defence. Everyone feels a responsibility to help the team and stay connected. Gabriel Jesus is a great player; you saw his goal. He’s different from Raphinha, yes, but today he showed his quality and I’m very happy for him.” Barcelona return to Champions League duty on Tuesday, when they face Galatasaray in what is sure to be a white-hot atmosphere in Istanbul, where the Catalans will again be without Raphinha. Having secured back-to-back La Liga titles, Flick's young side will now attempt to transfer that success onto the European stage, which saw them reach the semi-finals in 2024/25 and the quarter-finals last season. The five-time European champions last ruled the continent when Luis Enrique's side defeated Juventus 3-1 in the 2015 final. This is a Barca squad being built for long-term success. The starting XI against Getafe had an average age of less than 25, with only Rodri, 30, into his third decade. The five players brought off the bench – Fermin Lopez (23), Marc Bernal (19), Pedri (23), Karim Adeyemi (24) and Hamza Abdelkarim (18) – averaged just 21.4 years old. Leading the charge for European domination for the foreseeable future will be Ballon d'Or favourite Lamine Yamal, who continues to shine for both club and country. In four Uefa Nations League matches during the international window, the 19-year-old scored four and assisted another as world champions Spain stretched their unbeaten run to 43 games. “Lamine never stops surprising us,” said Spain coach Luis de la Fuente after Yamal scored in Spain's 3-1 win over Czech Republic. “He has so much talent and so much quality … Lamine is on the path to becoming a legend.” Against Getafe, Yamal added a seventh assist of the campaign to go with his eight goals across nine matches. “We all know Lamine’s level. He’s fantastic. He’s very difficult to stop, even when you take precautions,” admitted Getafe manager Jose Bordalas. “He’s excellent in one-on-one situations, finishing and passing. He’s a magnificent young player, and he shows the level he has … He will improve much more and can win the Ballon d’Or. I have no doubt.” Before the Getafe match, Flick made clear the talent Yamal had at his disposal. “He will be the best player in the world, if he isn't already,” said the German. “With his attitude, his mentality, his will to improve every day … That is the right mentality. For now, he is on that path and I am very happy.” Yamal's next test will be against Turkish Super Lig leaders Galatasaray at Rams Park, with an atmosphere Flick described on Monday as "one of the best in the world". Okan Buruk's team have won four successive domestic league titles and go into the match on the back of a 3-1 win over Kasımpasa on Friday – despite having Uruguayan midfielder Lucas Torreira sent off in the 65th minute – but started their Champions League campaign by losing at Portuguese side Sporting by the same scoreline. And Ismael Garcia, Galatasaray's assistant coach, acknowledged the challenge facing his side. “Yes, of course. In the end, playing against Barca is like going to the dentist: you know it's going to hurt, but you have to go and take it as well as possible,” the Spaniard said. “Hopefully things go well. We know that they are possibly the most in-form team in Europe, but we are confident that we can put them in trouble.” And Garcia also insisted they had the “perfect” man to hurt Barca in fit-again Nigerian striker Victor Osimhen, whose five games this season have produced six goals, while his Galatasaray record stands at 65 in 79 matches. “The top players do well in every game, but perhaps, because of Barcelona's way of defending, so aggressive and with the defensive line in the middle of the field, Osimhen is the striker who ... is perfect against that type of defence,” he said. “Beyond the fact that he is an extraordinary striker, we hope that he can do a lot of damage to Barcelona with the way he plays.”

title: Bryan Cranston leads tributes to Breaking Bad co-star RJ Mitte: 'I’ll miss you, son'
description: Actor, who played Walter White Jr, has died aged 34
content: RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad , has died aged 34. The American actor died on Monday in Brownsville, Texas. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," a representative for Mitte said. The actor appeared in all five seasons of hit drama Breaking Bad , which ran from 2008 to 2013, playing the teenage son of Bryan Cranston ’s chemistry teacher turned drug dealer. Mitte and his character had cerebral palsy. The role brought him international recognition and provided a platform for his work advocating for people with disabilities, including greater representation in the entertainment industry. Cranston was among those who paid tribute, remembering Mitte’s enthusiasm for acting and the years they spent working together. “I’ll miss you, son,” he wrote on Instagram. Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman in the series, also expressed his sadness. “RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed,” he said. Dean Norris, who played Hank Schrader, recalled looking out for Mitte as a young actor on set and said he would be greatly missed. Tributes also came from his co-stars on Switched at Birth , including actress and disability rights advocate Marlee Matlin. “My heart is shattered. There will never be another like RJ Mitte,” she wrote on Instagram. Lea Thompson, who also worked with Mitte on the series, remembered him as “joyous, professional and kind”, and said his work had inspired many people. Born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi, Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at the age of three. He moved to Los Angeles in 2006 and took small television roles before joining Breaking Bad as a teenager. He appeared in 56 episodes and was part of the cast that won the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding ensemble in a drama series in 2014. His other TV credits include Now Apocalypse and The Guardians of Justice . On film, he appeared in The Recall and The Oak Room , among other projects. In the 2021 drama Triumph , he played a high school student with cerebral palsy determined to become a wrestler, continuing his work portraying characters whose experiences reflected aspects of his own. Away from acting, Mitte served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, as well as leading the Mitte Foundation and supporting philanthropic and community initiatives. His representatives highlighted his efforts to challenge stereotypes and improve opportunities for people with disabilities.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League
description: Kick-off against Neftchi Fergana was delayed after Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence issued a security alert
content: Cristiano Ronaldo was on the scoresheet as Al Nassr got their AFC Champions League Elite campaign back on track with a comfortable win over Neftchi Fergana. Ronaldo scored the second of Nassr's goals just before the break after Angelo Gabriel had given the hosts a 33rd-minute lead. Alishev Odilov had reduced the deficit in the 51st minute before an Anvarjon Gofurov own goal sealed a 3-1 victory for Nassr. Kick-off was delayed at Al Awwal Park due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence. Riyadh has suffered a series of ​deadly ​attacks ‌by the ⁠Iran-aligned Houthis over the past week. Supporters were allowed to remain in their seats as authorities carried out safety protocols before the match kicked off 20 minutes after it was scheduled. Ronaldo, 41, was spotted kissing the badge on his shirt during the warm-up. He was also pictured holding the shirt up to his face to cover his eyes in an emotional moment. The Portuguese superstar scored the 981st goal of his career in the 42nd minute, latching on to a knockdown from Ayman Yahya in the area before firing past Neftchi goalkeeper Botirali Ergashev. "Important win tonight. We keep building," Ronaldo posted in a message on his social media channels after the match. Angelo broke the deadlock in the 33rd minute, meeting a cross inside the box and turning the ball into the net to give Al Nassr the lead. Odilov capitalised on a Nawaf Boushal blunder to spark life back into the Uzbek champions in the 51st minute, but a red card shown to Ali Bayev for violent conduct after he caught Nassr defender Mohamed Simakan swung momentum back in Nassr's favour. Nassr made the extra man count on 78 minutes. Bojan Cecer turned the ball into his own net, handing the Saudi champions all three points and their first win in this season's competition after they were routed 4-0 in their first match at Al Ain . Ange Postecoglou revealed after the match that he had been worried about his players' mental state before the match following the deadly attacks on Riyadh. “I was worried about the players during the match because I care about them, but I was very happy with the professionalism they showed,” the Australian told reporters. Postecoglou said the club will monitor injuries to Kingsley Coman and Mohamed Simakan. French forward Coman was forced off injured after only 13 minutes, while Simakan was withdrawn following the red-card challenge by Bayev. Al Ain maintained their 100 per cent start to the league phase with a thumping win over Iraq's Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basrah. Houssine Rahimi struck twice as Al Ain raced to a 4-0 lead at the break, as the former champions cruised to a second successive win in emphatic fashion. Alejandro Romero had opened the scoring in the 13th minute before Saed Al Rodsan turned into his own net to double Al Ain's advantage. Rahimi, who struck twice for Al Ain in their victory over Nassr in September, grabbed another brace against Al Quwa before half-time to kill the contest. Mohammed Jawad grabbed a consolation goal in the 89th minute. “We know what we can do, and the players did their job excellently until the end. They deserve this victory," Al Ain coach Vladimir Ivic told reporters. “We sent a message to ourselves about what we can do, and that is the most important thing for me.” Victory took Al Ain top of Group B ahead of Esteghlal on goal difference. Tijjani Reijnders was on target as Al Qadsiah were held to a 1-1 draw at Pakhtakor.

title: Pakistan detains Imran Khan ally in stronghold province
description: Chief Minister held after government suspended and state of emergency imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
content: Pakistan has detained an aide to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and several cabinet members, the government said on Monday, a day after it suspended the provincial government. President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday, saying the administration had failed to tackle Islamist militancy. Azam Nazeer Tarar, Minister of Law and Justice, said a governor would take charge. Khan's ​Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ⁠party rejected the move, saying it was ‌intended to deter his supporters from marching on the capital to demand his release. The detentions took place on Sunday at the chief minister's residence in Peshawar, where police and paramilitary forces sealed off the area using shipping containers, witnesses and officials said. Khan's three sisters and hundreds of supporters were also detained ahead of the planned march. Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, a Khan ally, and several cabinet members were taken into custody, the government said. “Yes, I can confirm that the Chief Minister and some of his cabinet members have been taken into preventive custody,” Junior Interior Minister Talal Chaudhry told Reuters. The imposition of emergency rule and suspension of the provincial government have led to a sharp rise in tension between Khan, 74, a former cricket star, and Pakistan's powerful military. The move came a week after Khan's supporters had rallied for days in the province, preparing to march on Islamabad to demand his release and access to medical treatment. Mr Chaudhry said those facing charges would be prosecuted, while the others would be released. He added that the detentions occurred on Sunday at the provincial chief minister's house in Peshawar, the provincial capital. Khan aide Shaukat Yousafzai demanded the release of all those held. The PTI's last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces. Khan's arrest in 2023 also sparked nationwide riots during which some of his supporters attacked military installations. Pakistan's constitution allows the government to assume control of a provincial administration during an emergency. The government and PTI have held several rounds of talks since the party called for the march on Islamabad last month. The government was ready to accept all the PTI's demands, including permission for the march, Mr Chaudhry said. “We asked for just one thing, that the party should publicly condemn militancy and join us in the fight against militant groups,” he added. The PTI refused and the talks broke down, he said.

title: How the Gulf can turn threats into shared purpose
description: Unjustifiable attacks may build a more aligned approach that unites neighbours facing common challenges
content: Yesterday’s call for stronger collective defence in the Gulf by Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, comes at a moment when a beleaguered Iran and its remaining armed proxies have decided to escalate and target the Arab world's largest economy. As the Iran-backed Houthis’ repeated strikes on travellers at Riyadh’s King Khalid airport show, the human cost of failing to deter attacks or intercept missiles is steep. Such attacks also strike at the region's prosperity, something that depends on transport networks, energy infrastructure, the environment and the confidence that connect active economies and those who benefit from them. A threat to an airport or a shipping route has consequences well beyond the country directly targeted. Airlines reassess risks to flights and businesses are forced to reconsider other supply chains. Investors also have to debate the costs of operating in a volatile region. Even the mere threat of disruption can come with a heavy price tag. As we have seen since the Iran conflict began in February, aviation is particularly vulnerable. The Gulf’s position as a global hub depends on reliable connections between Europe, Asia and Africa. Attacks, such as those seen in Riyadh, can force airlines to reroute flights, increasing costs and disrupting travel. From this tourism, trade and international connections are imperilled. Environmental security presents another shared challenge. Attacks on oil centres, tankers and other energy infrastructure risk causing pollution that crosses international borders and presents a generational problem. The region's marine environment is already under pressure, while the concentration of energy infrastructure and shipping in a relatively confined Strait of Hormuz makes the consequences of a major spill particularly serious. Economic security is equally inseparable from the wider crisis. Arab states may be competitors in some markets, but their economies are also linked. Disruption in one country can ripple through its neighbours. Joint environmental response arrangements and plans to protect critical infrastructure could also improve the region’s joint ability to withstand the kind of shocking events witnessed in recent days in Saudi Arabia . This does not mean individual Gulf countries suddenly dropping their individual national priorities or resolving every difference of opinion. It is more a question of building on the long-standing ties that unite Gulf societies and recognising the that although economic interdependence can create shared prosperity it can also come with common responses to threats. At a time when ideological actors are lashing out at those around them, the eventual outcome may just be a more aligned approach by Arab neighbours to the challenges that face them.

title: The Middle East's biggest archaeological discoveries in 2026
description: From a Bronze Age tomb in the UAE to a lost Egyptian city, these finds are shedding new light on the ancient world
content: The Middle East continues to reveal traces of its ancient past, with discoveries offering new insight into how early civilisations lived, worshipped and organised society. Since January, archaeologists have uncovered ancient burial chambers, royal monuments and prehistoric artworks. Some finds may answer long-standing historical questions, while others are challenging what we know about the region's earliest communities. Here are six of the most significant discoveries announced over the year so far. A burial chamber uncovered at the Qattarah Necropolis in Al Ain has revealed evidence of funerary traditions that endured for at least 1,000 years. Announced by the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi in July, the chamber was 11 metres long and 2.5 metres wide. Dating back to the Wadi Suq period, it remained in use into the Iron Age, suggesting successive generations continued to bury their dead at the same site. Archaeologists recovered weapons, vessels and personal ornaments, providing clues about the customs of the communities that inhabited the region. The chamber's entrance faces the East, potentially allowing the rising Sun to illuminate its interior, although whether this carries symbolic significance remains uncertain. The discovery adds to Al Ain's archaeological importance, with its Unesco-listed sites already documenting thousands of years of settlement, burial practices and technological development. An inscription bearing the name of a long-lost Egyptian city may finally help settle an archaeological mystery dating back almost 140 years. Discovered at Tell Abu Seify, near the Suez Canal, the sandstone lintel bears the royal titles of Ramses II, who ruled Egypt during the 13th century BC. It also records the restoration of a statue of Horus, described as Lord of the City of Masn . Announced in August, the find strengthens the possibility that Tell Abu Seify was the ancient settlement, although further investigation is required to confirm its identity. Excavations have also revealed a temple complex, defensive walls, roads and evidence of Roman military occupation. Establishing the city's whereabouts could help researchers reconstruct Egypt's eastern frontier, particularly the Horus Military Road, which connected the Nile Delta with Sinai and territories farther east. More than 2,600 years since the reign of King Ashurbanipal, archaeologists have uncovered a monument documenting the ambitions of one of Assyria's most powerful rulers. The two-metre stone stele was discovered in June at Shamash Gate in Nineveh , once the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. It features cuneiform inscriptions and relief carvings associated with Ashurbanipal's reign from 668BC to 627BC. The inscriptions offer further evidence of how the king developed Nineveh and commemorated his achievements through public monuments. The discovery also carries significance for the city's modern history. Nineveh's archaeological remains suffered extensive destruction during ISIS's occupation of the Mosul area between 2014 and 2017. Recovered by a joint Iraqi-American archaeological mission, the stele contributes to efforts to document and preserve one of the ancient Middle East's most important cities. An ancient bronze ring recovered from the Mediterranean Sea bears a rare depiction of one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was announced last week that the signet ring had been discovered during underwater excavations at Antirhodos, a submerged island that once housed a royal palace in Alexandria's Great Harbour. Its engraving depicts the Lighthouse of Alexandria and resembles representations found on Roman-era coins. Archaeologists have yet to establish the ring's precise date or identify its owner, but it is believed to be the first known depiction of the monument on a signet ring. Constructed during the third century BC, the lighthouse guided ships into Alexandria's harbour for centuries before successive earthquakes brought about its destruction. The discovery adds to the limited surviving visual record of the structure, whose appearance is known largely through ancient descriptions and representations. A human face carved into a limestone pillar is providing new evidence of artistic expression among some of the world's earliest settled communities. Unveiled in November 2025, the discovery was made at Karahantepe in south-eastern Turkey, a Neolithic site dating back about 11,000 years. The 1.4-metre T-shaped pillar features deep-set eyes and a prominent nose. It is the first known example of a human face represented directly on this type of pillar at the region's prehistoric sites. Similar structures have been found at nearby Gobeklitepe, with archaeologists suggesting their forms may represent stylised human figures. The discovery at Karahantepe lends weight to that interpretation. Alongside other sculptures and monumental structures uncovered at the site, the pillar reveals the sophistication of prehistoric artistic and ceremonial traditions thousands of years before the emergence of writing or cities. Paintings, engravings and inscriptions spanning thousands of years have been documented at a previously unknown archaeological site in South Sinai . Announced by Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities in February, the discovery was made on the Umm Iraq Plateau, where researchers identified a natural sandstone rock shelter extending more than 100 metres. Its walls contain prehistoric paintings depicting animals and other figures, alongside later engravings and inscriptions. Archaeologists have also documented pottery fragments and material associated with different periods of human activity. Some of the earliest artwork is believed to predate the emergence of the ancient Egyptian state, although further research is needed to refine its chronology. The site is particularly valuable for its unusually long archaeological record. Its changing imagery and inscriptions suggest communities returned to the same location across vastly different historical periods, leaving evidence of their environments, beliefs and artistic traditions.

title: Hold your horses: Therapeutic riding programme helping people build confidence and skills
description: Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club launches initiative for children, disabled people and senior citizens
content: In Abu Dhabi's city centre, the stables at the Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club are an oasis where time slows down, and the clip-clop of hooves can soothe the effects of even the most stressful day. It is here that horses are being used to help children, people of determination and senior citizens build confidence and improve their well-being through a new therapeutic riding programme. The initiative, launched at Abu Dhabi Equestrian Club at the end of September, has already attracted 45 participants and aims to harness the bond between humans and horses to support some of the community’s most vulnerable members. Funded and supported by Mubadala Investment Company and the Authority of Social Contribution – Ma’an, the programme offers participants the chance to interact with horses in a safe and calm environment, with activities designed to develop confidence and encourage social interaction. “The programme will give people of determination, vulnerable children and elderly citizens the opportunity to learn about horses,” said Dayle Brown, chief sports and equestrian officer of Al Khail Square. “Horses are very intelligent, they're very used to working around people and relating to people where there is a need. It's well known around the world.” Faye Galvin, a therapeutic riding instructor, is in her element at the club. With her horse Ally – one of three she brought over from Ireland this summer – by her side, she said she has witnessed first-hand the difference that working with horses can make. “Horses have been a big part of my life, and working in different elements of care and with children and seeing the difference that horses can make to people’s lives and the connection is beautiful,” Ms Galvin told The National . “To bring the two together is the dream job.” The National spoke to Faisal Alsuwaidi, who brought his nephew Ghaith, 7, to the stables for his session. The young boy spoke in Arabic and English until he was two years old, when he became non-verbal. “He was talking, playing with us. Sometimes you will see him looking at the sky, looking at things and thinking. We want him to continue this thinking, and say what is inside his mind; we try our hardest to push him to talk,” said Mr AlSuwaidi. The family, who live in Ras Al Khaimah, have tried many things to help Ghaith find his voice again – from playing with animals on their farm to going to the swimming pool to enrolling him in a specialised school. Mr Alsuwaidi said that Ghaith looked forward to the twice-weekly sessions, and had seen some progress, which gave the family hope. It was clear that he felt comfortable on the horse – his mood changed when he mounted Doolin. “We try to let him have lots of contact with the animals, and we try to improve his motivation to talk to anyone. Today he tried with the horse to push him to move forward,” he added. Ms Galvin's three ponies were brought from Ireland for the therapeutic riding programme and had to acclimatise to the desert conditions. “They've been out in a big field in Ireland, so it's quite a contrast coming to Abu Dhabi,” she said. “We've had to get them desensitised, because when you're working in the therapeutic environment, there's a lot of different variables and different sounds, which takes time.” Each lesson is tailored to the rider, and can involve playing games, working on co-ordination or balance, and doing exercises that engage motor skills. The instructor has seen the impact horses can have on people, and she believes they can connect with anyone. “They are very spiritual, empathetic and sensitive, so they can connect with people in so many ways,” she said. “Their gait mirrors that of a human, so for people with physical disabilities, it can be very good for their whole physical development as well, and it gives them that feeling and experience.” The programme is open for volunteer applications in addition to session applications.

title: Airports forced to review security as missile and drone threats rise
description: Industry experts at Dubai Airport Show convene as conflicts expose civilian aviation vulnerabilities
content: Airports are being forced to rethink how they protect passengers and keep flights running as missile and drone attacks pose an increasingly serious threat to civilian aviation, industry experts have warned. Repeated attacks by Houthi rebels in Saudi Arabia, alongside months of disruption caused by the war in Iran, have exposed the vulnerability of airports to modern warfare and the difficulty of maintaining operations during prolonged security crises. Industry leaders gathered at the Dubai Airport Show on Monday said airports were investing in new technology and contingency planning to withstand threats from military strikes to cyber attacks, while acknowledging that no facility could ever be completely secure. Tim Walder, chairman of the British Aviation Group, said the changing nature of global conflicts had created unprecedented challenges for airport operators. “What we’re seeing today is a completely different set of challenges being faced geopolitically,” he said. “Resilience isn’t something that’s 100 per cent, it’s always going to fail on occasions, but we learn faster. “The key thing is the airport can be a leader in terms of understanding where the threats can come from, such as cybersecurity and climate change.” Mr Walder, whose company offers expertise on meeting the challenges of the global aviation industry, said supporting passengers during a crisis was critical to retaining confidence. “If something goes down, you lose passenger confidence and you can lose that for a long time,” he said. “Cyber-attacks are obviously high up there when talking about risk and we are seeing different levels of that. “A few months ago in the UK and Europe, hackers attacked the software that supports the check-in process and that impacted a number of airports in Europe, including London and Brussels. “These attacks aren't going to be just necessarily hitting an individual airport or airline, they're going to hit a network. The question is how do we make the network more resilient as well.” Critical Gulf transit hubs and other major infrastructure are increasingly connecting site security with dedicated anti-drone and air defence measures to improve protection at airports. International gateways to the region have increased perimeter screening and police patrols near airports, while others have implemented terminal entry checkpoints in response to raised threat levels in the Middle East. Exhibitors at Dubai World Trade Centre displayed the latest countermeasures and showed how drone technology was rapidly advancing to help secure airspace. Udi Lowy, sales director for the Gulf Co-operation Council and India at D-Fend Solutions, said his company’s EnforceAir Plus system was capable of taking over unidentified drones and bringing them under control. “Drones are quite a new threat in the world, so most of the technologies just adopt [existing] air-defence mechanisms for drones,” he said. “We are using cyber systems that detect the communication of the drone and we have the ability to retract the relevant information from the drone itself.” Rather than jamming a drone’s signal to bring it down, potentially causing damage or injuries on the ground, the EnforceAir Plus system takes over its controls and lands it safely nearby. It can then verify from where the drone was deployed and by whom. The system can even be programmed to deal with a swarm attacking airspace simultaneously, Mr Lowy said. “Sometimes, a kid can fly a drone and create mayhem. Rather than jamming all signals, we cherry-pick the signal we want to interfere with and actually take the drone itself. “We don't interfere with any other signal, so there is no interference with airplanes.” The Ministry of Defence has reported a total of 2,265 drone attacks on the country since February 28, when the Iran war broke out, with Dubai International Airport handling 111 aerial threat alerts. Future airport developments, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, will feature blast-proof designs and hardened concrete shells to bolster defences against aerial attacks. Speaking on a panel at Dubai Airport Show on operational resilience under pressure, Binu Gopal, chief operating officer at Ras Al Khaimah International Airport, said the priority in a crisis was to maintain operations as safely and efficiently as possible. “We prepare for multiple kinds of disruption which may occur at the airport,” he said. “Resilience is the ability to continue our operations even when we face some kind of disruption, maintain critical activities and respond to the disturbance, and get back to normal safely and efficiently. “This cuts across the entire ecosystem, be it set operations, terminal operations, airlines, ground-handling operations, customs and immigration. However, during a crisis, it becomes more and more interdependent. For us it is not about having a contingency plan, it's about how well we are able to respond as a team.”

title: IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies due to prolonged Hormuz closure
description: Fund pushes back forecast for strait's reopening and warns global economy's resilience is waning
content: The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz , and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening. In its latest World Economic Outlook , released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year. The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 to 3.4 per cent. “This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom. The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices. The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly. Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.” The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs. Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada. Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan. The IMF projects the UAE 's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. The new projections for the Arab world's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast. Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia , but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year. Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent. The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year. Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year. Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade. Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon. The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures. Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points. Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter. “This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said. Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury , a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs. Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

title: Al Ahli overcome Al Wasl in fiery AFC Champions League clash
description: Back-to-back Asian champions win 3-1 in Dubai but were made to fight by UAE side
content: Al Ahli Saudi left Dubai with three points towards their bid for a hat-trick of Asian Champions League titles after a fiery meeting with Al Wasl. Roger Ibanez and Francisco Trincao, two big-money imports to Saudi Arabian football, scored, before Feras Albrikan clinched a 3-1 win in stoppage time. The margin of defeat was harsh on a spirited Wasl side, who deserved more than the lone strike by Pedro Malheiro in first-half stoppage time. Given the gap they were bridging to the high-spending Saudi Pro League side, the home players fully merited the backing they got from their fans on a hostile night in Zabeel. Before kick-off, Ahli’s players stood on the 18-yard line and were serenaded with their club anthem by the travelling supporters. Around 200 had made the trip from Jeddah, but they were drowned out by the noise of the home faithful. The Ultras Junoon are always loud, but they were particularly rowdy when the Ahli anthem was being sung. The home players responded. Wasl’s start was bright, and they fashioned the first opening, only for Siaka Sidibe to blaze over from the edge of the box. Home optimism was dissipated in the 20th minute, though, when Ibanez headed in the opener for Ahli. The Brazil centre-back, who was called into the Selecao squad by Carlo Ancelotti for the World Cup this summer, is renowned for his leap. Despite common knowledge of his aerial prowess, he was unchallenged at the back post to make it 1-0. The visitors nearly doubled their lead 10 minutes later, but were saved by the post as Eduard Spertsyan’s shot bounced away to safety. Wasl’s defence was being cut open with greater regularity, and they were lucky not to be a long way behind by the break. Their fortune continued when Adryelson, the Wasl defender evaded a red card. After a confrontation in the box, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, went down. Replays showed Adryelson had squared up to him, and lightly pushed his forehead towards his opponent. Shamat tumbled to the floor and rolled around as if he was mortally wounded. It was enough of a show to persuade VAR to recommend the referee take a second look at the monitor. Usually, that is ominous for the perceived offender. Justice was served, though, as Abdulrahman Al Jassim, the Qatari official, decided he was right the first time, and stayed with a yellow card. Adryelson nearly provided the perfect riposte; from the ensuing free-kick for Wasl, he bundled the ball into the net, only for it to be ruled out for offside. The hosts were level by the break, though. In stoppage time at the end of the half, a long range effort from Malheiro, Wasl’s right back, found its way into the net after some limp goalkeeping. Shamat had fully established himself as public enemy No 1. At the start of the second half, he was playing on the wing in front of the hardcore or Wasl’s supporters. They frequently lobbed plastic water bottles in his direction. Rather than fuss, he waved a hand at them, encouraging the fans to bring it on. Just before the hour mark, Trincao ruined the home fans’ fun. The Portuguese forward finished clinically to restore the away side’s lead. Wasl should have levelled shortly after following a rapid counter-attack, but Serginho hit the post with the goal at his mercy. Even when he went off, Shamat caused rancour. After an innocuous incident, he went down clutching his shoulder. He looked in genuine pain, and had to be stretchered off on the back of the medical golf buggy. It turned out that his injury was not so severe that he could wave with both arms as he was taken past the Ahli supporters. That added to the fury of the home fans, and even the players were so incensed they threw bottles in his direction as the buggy went past the home dugout. Ahli’s bench sprung to his defence, and the two sets of replacements and substituted players had to be separated. Wasl had their chances as they chased the game, but their hopes were finally dashed when Albrikan scored Ahli’s third in stoppage time.

title: Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis fire on Saudi Arabia
description: At least 20 people have been killed and hundreds injured since Yemen's Houthi rebels escalated attacks last week
content: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched fresh attacks against Saudi Arabia on Monday, following deadly missile strikes on Riyadh's international airport that killed passengers, some of whom were preparing to board flights to perform Umrah. Saudi authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport until midnight on October 17 following an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, and another on Sunday in which one person was killed. The King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also hit on Sunday evening, Saudi Arabia 's General Authority for Civil Aviation said, with the damage being assessed. A missile launched at Riyadh by the Yemeni Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed, the Saudi-led coalition said. The interception was announced shortly after authorities sounded a threat alarm, followed by three explosions, in the Saudi capital on Sunday night. The strikes came as Yemeni government forces, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, clashed with Houthi rebels on the outskirts of the strategic south-western city of Taiz, repelling fresh attacks amid warnings that a tightening rebel siege is worsening conditions inside the Yemeni city. A military spokesman said on Monday that air strikes prevented the Houthis from sending reinforcements to Taiz. At least 20 people have been killed in a series of attacks since last week on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the Abha international airport in Saudi Arabia’s Asir province. Saudi state TV broadcast footage of the moment a missile struck the passenger terminal in Riyadh on Saturday, with flashes of light filling the screen as travellers, including pilgrims in white robes, scrambled for cover. Ali, from Hyderabad, was travelling with his family on an Umrah pilgrimage when he was injured in Saturday’s attack. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed his death on Sunday and said it was in contact with his family to help arrange the repatriation of his remains. Etihad Airways cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until Monday, October 19, extending disruption to services between the UAE and the Saudi capital into next week. Flydubai has also cancelled Riyadh flights until Wednesday, October 14, while Emirates and Air Arabia services have been affected. The Saudi-led coalition said it responded to drone and cruise missile threats against the kingdom on Monday, as hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthis continued despite diplomatic efforts, including a phone call between the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Iran, which supports the Houthis . The coalition said a missile launched at Riyadh by the Houthis on Monday night was intercepted and destroyed. The interception was announced shortly after authorities sounded a threat alarm, followed by three explosions, in the Saudi capital. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan that Tehran was ready to "provide assistance" to start talks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to reach a "political solution", Iranian state media reported. "The Foreign Minister of our country, expressing concern over the escalation of tensions, emphasised that insisting on a military approach and ignoring political solutions would complicate the existing situation," Mr Araghchi was quoted as saying. Amid the continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence . In his statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible". He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added. He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges. US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper said the US and its regional allies were deploying the “largest air-defence umbrella in the world” to deter Iranian attacks, describing the effort as part of an “enduring security architecture” in the Middle East. “It was a vision we discussed with our regional allies and partners,” he told the audience in a recorded message at Trends Global's sixth annual conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. “Earlier this year, during Operation Epic Fury, we validated at full scale and in actual combat the Middle East Air Defence network known as Mead. “Through our combined efforts, we transformed a concept into the most sophisticated and largest air-defence umbrella in the world,” he added. “For the first time in history, US air defenders stood shoulder-to-shoulder with allies and partners across the Middle East, linking national systems in real time. And so together we intercepted thousands of Iranian attack drones and missiles with an integrated shield built on mutual trust. This is partnership in action.”

title: UAE teacher injured in Riyadh airport attack assured she can complete Umrah
description: Saudi health minister visits teacher and colleague in hospital
content: A teacher from the UAE injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been assured she will be able to complete her Umrah pilgrimage once she recovers. The teacher, whose name was not released, was travelling with a colleague from Abu Dhabi to Makkah via Riyadh when the airport came under attack on Saturday. Saudi Health Minister Fahad Al Jalajel visited the two women in hospital on Sunday when he went to see people injured in the attack and find out about their medical care. One of the teachers told the minister how their journey had been interrupted, according to Saudi state-run television channel Al Ekhbariya. She praised the doctors treating her. Mr Al Jalajel said King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had instructed officials to ensure the women received full support throughout their recovery. “You’re not part of what happened. We know that. For that reason, King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are telling us to take full care of you, even the recovery, and that you continue on your Umrah,” he told her. Saudi Arabia has extended the suspension of operations at the airport following the deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels at the weekend. The General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Monday that the suspension would continue while checks on the safety and operational readiness of airport sites were completed. It did not give a date or time for the reopening. Etihad Airways has cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 19, extending disruption to services between the UAE and the Saudi capital into next week. Flydubai has cancelled Riyadh flights until Wednesday, while Emirates and Air Arabia services have been affected. Services to other Saudi destinations have also been impacted. Etihad cancelled four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam on Monday, with all services on the route cancelled on Tuesday and Wednesday. Selected Jeddah flights have been cancelled until Thursday.

title: Iraq should not pose threat to Gulf states, President of Kurdistan region says
description: Nechirvan Barzani endorses Iraqi PM's call for all weapons in the country to be under state control
content: President Nechirvan Barzani of Iraq's Kurdistan region has said weapons must be held by the Iraqi government and warned that the country must not threaten Gulf states, as Baghdad enters a new phase following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces. “Iraq should not be a threat to Gulf countries. Iraq should never do that, that is not sovereignty,” Mr Barzani said at the annual Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil on Monday. “Weapons should be in the hands of the government,” he added, arguing that Iraq needed to strengthen its ability to exercise sovereignty and take responsibility for its own security. The remarks come as Iraq faces pressure to bring armed factions under state control following attacks by Iran-aligned groups on targets in Iraq and across the region. The US-led coalition against ISIS completed its military withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, with security co-operation between Baghdad and Washington now moving towards a bilateral framework. In a statement marking October 1 as the day of full Iraqi sovereignty following the withdrawal, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the serious work of dealing with weapons outside state control began now. Mr Barzani said Iraq no longer needed such a large international coalition after 12 years of its presence, adding that the country should develop bilateral security relationships with partner states. “We thank them, but we are happy today that Iraq stands on its feet,” he said. However, he stressed that the Kurdistan region still needed air defence systems to protect itself, following repeated drone and missile attacks. On the wider regional situation amid the Iran war , Mr Barzani said the changes unfolding across the Middle East presented both opportunities and threats for the Kurds, but he believed the opportunities could outweigh the risks. The greatest threat to Iraq, he said, was economic uncertainty, particularly the country's dependence on oil exports . “If the Strait of Hormuz is not resolved, it will be a long-term challenge,” he said, referring to the vital waterway through which a significant share of the world's oil supply passes and which has been effectively blockaded by Iran since the war began. He also warned that Iraq and the Kurdistan region faced challenges in maintaining stable relations with neighbouring countries while navigating the shifting regional landscape. Mr Barzani was more critical of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, saying their actions during the war had placed the Kurdistan region in a difficult position. “The opposition Iranian forces unfortunately behaved irresponsibly and put the Kurdistan region in an embarrassing position,” he said. He said the Kurdistan region's position had been clear from the beginning and that it would not become involved in the war. Reports that Iranian Kurdish opposition fighters were preparing to cross into Iran emerged in early March, after the Iran war broke out. Several media outlets reported that Washington had contacted Iranian Kurdish groups based in Iraq about a possible ground operation, with some fighters said to be on standby near the border. However, the groups denied that their forces had crossed into Iran. Iraqi Kurdish officials also rejected reports of an incursion, amid fears that any involvement could draw the Kurdistan region into the conflict and provoke further Iranian attacks. “It was not our war,” Mr Barzani said. The Kurdistan region shares a border of more than 600km with Iran. Mr Barzani said it was impossible for Erbil to allow its territory to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbour. He said the regional government had closed the border during the early days of the conflict and deployed forces along it, making clear that it would not allow anyone to use the Kurdistan region to attack Iran.

title: ‘Iran smells weakness’: Burnham challenged over IRGC after airbase plot
description: UK announces sanctions on two Iranians involved in plots to attack Britain
content: Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham was urged on Monday to take direct action against Iran if it succeeded in attacking a British airbase. The UK ​announced sanctions against ⁠two Iranian nationals who ⁠the ‌government ​said had been involved in Iranian plots to ​attack ‌Britain, which Mr Burnham blamed on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps . He was told by former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden that Iran considered the UK its enemy and “smells weakness”. He said Iran had attempted attacks at bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, Akrotiri in Cyprus and Fairford in Gloucestershire. The UK introduced sanctions on the IRGC in July, following the first two incidents and a series of attacks against dissidents in previous years. A successful attack would require direct action, suggested Mr Dowden, who also asked for a pledge of “enhanced support and assistance to allies under constant attack”, noting the targeting of Saudi Arabia in recent days. Mr Burnham said Britain was providing the “most robust response” to the situation and “playing its part”. Under Monday’s sanctions, the head of counter-espionage operations within the IRGC, Ruhollah Bazghandi, will be subject to an asset freeze, travel ban and prevented from running any companies in the UK. The government believes he was directly involved in threatening, planning or conducting attacks against in the UK or against its allies. A key organiser of the Zindashti criminal network, Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, who the government said had been involved in several plots against Iranian dissidents, has also been sanctioned for supporting planned attacks. Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France ​and Germany issued a statement condemning "Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts ‌of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other ⁠hybrid activities against us and our partners". "The UK has also ​concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks ​and proxy actors," ‌the statement said. The developments were announced as Mr Burnham told the House of Commons that it was highly likely that the incidents at RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the US to launch attacks on Iran, were co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. Seven men have been arrested, and released, over a suspected attack on the base in Gloucestershire. Police said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans near the base, and detectives said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved. The US decided to remove its B-1 bomber aircraft from ​the base after the attack, giving mixed messages over whether there had been direct intelligence of a plot to carry out a drone attack, or whether it had been done out of caution. The British authorities have accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots in Britain. In July, Britain used new powers designed to stop the use ​of state-sponsored proxies to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group accused of being behind attacks at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities and Persian-language media. Mr Burnham said: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity if Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Iran’s continued attempts to undermine the security of the UK and its allies “through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable”. The Iranian ambassador was summoned for a foreign office dressing down but the Tehran state news agency afterwards described the British allegations as baseless. Iran's ​Ambassador ⁠to ⁠Britain, Seyed ​Ali Mousavi, ⁠denied any Iranian role ⁠in a ​suspected ⁠plot, saying Tehran was willing to cooperate with British ​authorities ‌in ⁠investigating the ​issue. “We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," Mr Miliband said. “This government will never waiver in our commitment to tacking Iran’s unacceptable actions and protecting our national security. We have already designated the IRGC under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran's malign activity.” The Foreign Office said the UK had identified at least 15 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals in the UK between 2022 and 2023, rising to more than 20 in 2025.

title: US immigration agents raid Democratic politician Ilhan Omar's home
description: Search reportedly follows criminal fraud investigation into legislator's immigration paperwork
content: US federal agents conducted a predawn raid on the home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday. The search followed a criminal fraud investigation into Ms Omar's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by the Somali-born politician's late father when she was a child, Fox News reported, quoting unidentified sources. A Justice Department representative told AP that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) had authorised a search warrant, adding that the action was part of a continuing federal investigation. Ms Omar has repeatedly denied allegations of wrongdoing, describing them as false and politically motivated. “This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies,” Jacklyn Rogers, communications director for Ms Omar's office, said in a statement. “For a decade, [US President] Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back. Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid.” The Justice Department did not immediately return The National 's request for comment. Ms Omar was taken to the US as a child, fleeing the civil war in Somalia. She became a US citizen at the age of 17 in 2000 and, in 2018, was elected to Congress to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis. Ms Omar is seeking another term for the seat in the midterms on November 3. An outspoken critic of Mr Trump, he has previously suggested she should leave the country. In February, he said Ms Omar and fellow Democrat Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” after they criticised his remarks during the State of Union address. Mr Trump has also recently attacked Abdul El Sayed , who is aiming to win a US Senate seat in Michigan. Should he win, Mr El Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. The US President has used anti-Muslim language in online attacks against the Democrat, calling him a “jihadist lunatic”.

title: PKK withdraws from Turkish border area in Iraqi Kurdistan
description: Turkish security sources confirm move as part of militant group's dissolution process
content: Militants from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) have withdrawn from four camps in northern Iraq , Turkish security sources said on Monday, as part of a drawn-out disarmament process that could eventually include the return of former militants to Turkey . Fighters from the PKK withdrew from “four shelters” in the Metina area near the border with Turkey in Iraq’s Kurdistan region, security sources told state news agency Anadolu. The PKK last week said it had evacuated four “war tunnels” in the Metina area and withdrawn fighters from Turkey in the days before that. The moves showed it had “fulfilled” its strategy “to end the armed struggle against Turkey”, the group said. The Turkish sources did not mention withdrawals from Turkey but said the PKK's departure from the locations in Iraq’s Kurdistan region was part of efforts to evacuate locations that “pose a risk of conflict to Turkey’s security”. Neither Turkey nor the PKK said where the militants went next. The group is known to have locations in both federally-controlled Iraq and the Kurdistan region, including its headquarters in the Qandil Mountains. The PKK said last year it had withdrawn from other areas near the border with Turkey . The moves are part of a process of dissolution of the PKK, whose insurgents fought a 40-year conflict with the Turkish state until the group’s jailed leader, Abdullah Ocalan, last year called for it to dissolve and disarm . The conflict killed at least 40,000 people on both sides, spilt across Turkey’s borders with Syria and Iraq, and left an indelible mark on Turkish society , where up to one-fifth of the 86 million population is ethnically Kurdish. Turkey has long regarded the PKK as its main national security threat, and, alongside the EU and US, has designated the group as a terrorist organisation. Turkey’s parliament in August passed legislation that provides a legal framework and procedures for the PKK’s dissolution. It allows for the suspension of some prison sentences and the postponement of other trials and investigations, depending on the severity of the alleged offences. PKK members who live abroad, many in the group’s base in the Qandil Mountains, could be allowed to return home and reintegrate into society, although Turkish veterans’ groups have vehemently opposed such measures. The aim is to eventually ensure “social reconciliation” to end more than four decades of internal strife, Anadolu reported on Monday. But measures under the legislation can only take effect once Turkey's National Security Council is convinced that the PKK has completely dissolved and surrendered all its weapons – something that has not yet happened. Mehmet Ucum, a senior adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan , said last month that the NSC would confirm the PKK’s dissolution and disarmament complete “by the end of this year at the latest”. Tuncer Bakirhan, co-chair of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), said last week that some former militants could return as soon as this month, but a lot depended on the confirmation of their legal status. “People return not to a place where they don't know what will happen to them tomorrow, but to a place where their law, status, and security are defined,” he told the independent leftist Evrensel media outlet in an interview. Kurdish politicians, who do not belong to the PKK but have liaised between the group and the Turkish government, have criticised the peace process for moving too slowly and failing to provide Turkey’s Kurdish minority with greater access to cultural, political and social rights. Elected Kurdish mayors in the country’s south-east, whom the Turkish government replaced with political appointees, have not been reinstated, and people dismissed from their jobs over alleged PKK links have not been allowed to return to work. “Even the simplest steps are not being taken,” Mr Bakirhan said in separate remarks to MPs last week. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz told state media on Wednesday that the PKK’s dissolution process requires “patience”. The PKK has demanded that Turkey release Ocalan, who has been in prison for more than two decades, as part of the dissolution process, but Turkey has made no such pledges: the move would be highly unpopular among much of Turkish society after the decades of unrest and loss of life caused by the conflict between the PKK and the state. Ocalan could have a role on a disarmament committee as part of the dissolution process but would not be released from prison, presidential adviser Mr Ucum said last month.

title: Young content creators to be trained in water awareness before UN conference in Abu Dhabi
description: Programme aims to equip young people with skills to communicate links between water, human health, food, energy and development
content: The UAE is recruiting 50 content creators to produce digital material on water sustainability before a major UN conference in Abu Dhabi this December. The National Media Authority, in partnership with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Federal Youth Authority, has launched the Blue Content Creators Programme, with applications open from October 12 to 30. The initiative will train 50 Emiratis and UAE residents to produce digital content raising awareness of water issues and highlighting the country's sustainability and innovation efforts. The programme comes as the UAE prepares to co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from December 8-10. It aims to equip young people with skills to communicate the links between water, human health, food, energy and development to audiences at home and abroad. Abdulla Balalaa, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said the programme would bring new perspectives to water issues. "The decisions we make today about water will shape the world inherited by future generations," Mr Balalaa said. "It is essential that young people's voices and ideas help guide these decisions. "As the UAE prepares to welcome the world to Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, I look forward to the fresh perspectives and innovative ideas young content creators will bring to water issues, the questions they will raise, and the stories and experiences they will highlight. "Their participation will enrich the conference with new ideas and ambitious creative contributions, encourage us to examine challenges from different perspectives, and reinforce our shared responsibility to translate the discussions in Abu Dhabi into practical action that delivers tangible benefits to individuals and communities." Mohammed Al Shehhi, secretary general of the National Media Authority, said the UAE places water at the heart of its sustainable development efforts. "Raising awareness of these issues strengthens public understanding of the challenges and encourages community participation in addressing them," he said. The programme includes three weeks of training in November, covering water issues, storytelling, video production, digital publishing strategies and the use of artificial intelligence tools in content creation. Participants will then apply these skills to produce content related to the UN conference in December. Applications are open to UAE citizens and residents aged 18 to 35 with an interest in content creation, media, water, the environment or sustainability, with selections made to reflect the diversity of UAE society.

title: Britain faces looming energy crisis as gas reserves dwindle
description: Operator threatens to close UK's largest gas storage site early next year
content: Britain faces a deepening energy crisis as a result of dwindling reserves and the possible closure of its largest storage site. With a 150 per cent surge in European gas prices before the seasonal dip in temperatures, the prospect of another inflationary shock is casting a shadow over the October 28 Budget. The prospect of losing Rough, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, threatens to further weaken the country's ability to withstand supply disruptions as Europe heads into winter with depleted reserves. Underground gas storage in Britain was only 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to only 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity equals about seven days of average winter demand. The problem of limited UK reserves is compounded by uncertainty over the future of Rough, which could close next year unless the government backs a £2 billion redevelopment proposed by its owner, Centrica. Chris O'Shea, chief executive of Centrica, which also owns British Gas, stepped up pressure on the government on Tuesday, warning that the site, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, would close at the end of the first quarter without a plan to support investment. "The commercial decision will be that this facility will close at the end of the first quarter," Mr O'Shea told the BBC, rejecting the government's position that Rough's future was a commercial matter for the company. He said Centrica was seeking a regulatory framework similar to those available to other critical infrastructure operators, providing more predictable returns in exchange for lower investment risk. Mr O'Shea described Rough as "the biggest battery in the UK", saying the proposed investment could create up to 5,000 jobs while safeguarding almost 1,000 existing positions. The company has also offered to make the site available as a temporary strategic gas reserve this winter but has yet to receive a response from the government, he said. "Our system is not resilient. Without energy security, we have no national security," Mr O'Shea said, pointing to increasingly frequent electricity supply margin notices. Britain’s grid operator sought emergency assistance from France on Monday, requesting as much as 1,200 megawatts of additional electricity through an undersea interconnector to help maintain the security of the power system.
