Britain will probably not run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House. “The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said. Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”. European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group. “It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters. Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels. EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves. A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further. Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high. The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

title: Saudi Arabia faces challenge of repeated and simultaneous attacks
description: Demand for Patriot and Thaad rises in defending Houthi attacks
content: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have demonstrated that its build-up of batteries of air defence must stretch to all corners of the country. Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest Patriot operator, said Nawaf Obaid of King’s College London’s Department of War Studies. “Saudi Arabia does not lack air defences,” he told The National . “It possesses one of the world’s most sophisticated integrated air and missile defence architectures, protecting a country larger than Western Europe. “The fundamental challenge is that no existing system, including those protecting the United States, can guarantee the interception of repeated, simultaneous attacks involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.” The kingdom is buying seven batteries of Thaad (Terminal High Altitude Area Defence), the largest programme outside the US, he added. The extensive use of missile interceptors during the Iran war has meant there is a need for renewed stocks, experts have told The National. Despite having the world’s second-largest air defence system, 13 people were killed when King Khalid International Airport was struck by what are thought to have been ballistic missiles, causing widespread damage and leaving 308 wounded. Countries around the world will now be looking at how to defend airports, but experts suggest close-in defence will be nearly impossible, given the number and size of civilian and military sites that could be attacked. “An attack like the one we saw on Saturday on Riyadh Airport would in normal circumstances have been met with lavish application of Thaad at high altitude and Patriot on incoming,” said Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer. “But what is clear is that Thaad and Patriot are not available in quantity and we’re seeing leakage.” Military analyst Francis Tusa said the scale of interceptor expenditure during the war had put significant pressure on American stocks, with consequences for allies globally. During one attack on a US airbase in Jordan, it is estimated up to 80 Patriots were fired in one night, leading to a rapid dwindling of the stockpile, he said. “The generals have told Trump that ‘we haven’t got the rounds left’.” There is also the issue of the rebel Houthis' improving arsenal that includes manoeuvring ballistic missiles. The Iranian-derived Palestine-2 has a range of about 2,000km and hypersonic capabilities, including manoeuvrability, making interception more difficult during its terminal phase. The US has expended an estimated 1,500 Patriots and has about 800 left. Saudi Arabia had more than 1,800 Patriot interceptors and has used a large number defending itself from Iran and the Houthis. Other defences include the South Korean KM-SAM, a medium-range system also owned by the UAE that is designed to intercept aircraft and incoming missiles. Saudi Arabia requested further defensive support from Britain's ministry of defence in the weeks leading up to the current attacks but the requests failed to secure ministerial approval. Saudi Arabian counterparts were left frustrated at the UK inaction. The UK has contributed, with its Sky Sabre system providing a medium-range defensive layer using Common Anti-Air Modular Missiles, surveillance radar and integrated command-and-control systems, Mr Obaid said. British industry can offer other options, which can be used for “point defence”, to stop close-in threats. “The UK has got the Starstreak high-velocity missile, with 8km to 9km range, and is unjammable,” said Mr Tusa, editor of Defence Eye . “It’s also probably £100,000 [$132,300] a shot.” The £40,000 Martlet missile, which uses a high-explosive warhead rather than Starstreak’s three tungsten darts, is another comparatively inexpensive option, he said. As a vast country with considerable infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s commanders have to decide where best to position radars and interceptors without being able to protect everywhere. The resources for a single site are significant. “For Patriot, you’d normally get one, maybe two radars, two command systems, and four to six missile launchers,” Mr Tusa said. Dr Nusbacher also questioned why commercial airports in the Middle East should be expected to have dedicated close-in air defence when comparable facilities in the West do not. “Heathrow doesn’t have close-in air defence, and why would you expect King Khalid Airport to have close-in air defence?” she said. Until recently, there was little expectation that Gulf states would face sustained attacks, she added. But the changing picture is now forcing a “major reassessment” of how civilian infrastructure should be protected. Robert Tollast, a military analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said defending one site could also leave others exposed. There is a risk of “putting so much resource into interceptors around that facility that you leave other critical areas uncovered”, he said. Destroying energy infrastructure outside the summer months “could also be disastrous”. One response would be to improve intelligence and attack missile launchers before they fire, as Saudi Arabia depends heavily on US satellite intelligence. Given the scale of the emergency, US manufacturers are attempting to increase interceptor production – an estimated 2,000 Thaad and Patriots have been fired this year – but replenishing stocks could take up to 30 months. Dr Nusbacher said defence planners had not anticipated the “profligate use of high-value, exquisite air defence systems” during a war “lasting more than a few weeks”.

title: African NGO forum urges Sudan to open sites to chemical weapons inspectors
description: Rights groups call on African Commission to pressure Sudanese Armed Forces over allegations
content: African civil society groups have called on Sudan to allow international inspectors into the country to investigate accusations that the Sudanese army used chemical weapons in its war against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. In a resolution adopted at the end of a three-day forum in Senegal's capital, Dakar, on Saturday, NGOs urged the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights to demand that Sudan allow the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) to send technical teams. The commission began a session in Dakar on Monday. The NGO forum called for Sudan to declare any chemical weapons production sites and the whereabouts of munitions, and to let the OPCW verify and destroy them. The resolution also condemned "massive war crimes and crimes against humanity committed by the two parties to the conflict". It called for a ceasefire monitored by an independent international body and an end to foreign weapons, funding and diplomatic backing for the warring parties. Washington found in April last year that Sudan's government had used chemical weapons in 2024 and imposed sanctions. A second round of sanctions took effect in July. Sudan denies the charges. In July, its Foreign Ministry said the country "neither produces, possesses nor uses chemical weapons" and called the US sanctions "unilateral and unlawful". In an interim report circulated at an OPCW meeting in July, a Sudanese national committee said that it had found no evidence. After the meeting, the US representative said that "domestic bureaucratic mechanisms are not a substitute" for independent verification. Both sides in Sudan's war have faced sanctions over breaches of international law. The US found in January 2025 that the RSF and allied militias had committed genocide in Darfur, while UN investigators said in February that the paramilitary's group's capture of El Fasher last year bore "hallmarks of genocide". The NGO forum noted that about 16 million people have been forced from their homes and more than 20 million face hunger since the war began in April 2023.

title: Future leaders to convene in Dubai to tackle the next generation's challenges
description: World Economic Forum and Dubai government are to host inaugural Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders
content: Hundreds of leaders and experts from around the world will gather in Dubai this week at the inaugural Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, hosted by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and the government of Dubai. The three-day event will feature panels and collaboration among multiple generations to prepare for the challenges of the future. Fifteen ministers and more than 100 chief executives will participate in the event, but the spotlight remains on young leaders, who should have a say in governing and decision-making, say the organisers. "The decisions we make today will shape the world the next generation inherits. Emerging leaders should have a voice in those decisions, not just live with their consequences,” said Alois Zwinggi, president and chief executive of the WEF and principal chairman of the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders. “This inaugural meeting will bring different generations and perspectives together to look beyond immediate challenges and work together on practical ideas for the decades ahead." Six themes have been chosen for the meeting, with the hope of advancing dialogue on pressing issues. Themes include geopolitical uncertainty, technological disruption, economic resilience and prosperity, leadership, science and innovation, and climate and nature. AI will be a major talking point, with new research on its application for sustainable development in the region. "At a time of rapid technological, economic and geopolitical transformation, preparing future leaders is more important than ever,” said Mohammed Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and principal chairman of the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders. “By bringing together emerging voices from around the world, we aim to equip them with the insights and tools needed to turn challenges into opportunities for innovation, growth and sustainable development.”

title: Powerful short film drives vital new pulmonary fibrosis awareness campaign
description: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis are lung conditions that can have a profound impact on patients’ everyday lives
content: Pulmonary fibrosis is on the rise and is being brought into sharp focus by a new short film alerting more people in the UAE to the disease. The video is central to a major awareness campaign by leading research-driven pharmaceutical company Boehringer Ingelheim, explaining the effects of the condition and how seeking urgent intervention can prevent further suffering. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis are lung conditions that can have a profound impact on patients’ everyday lives, on their families, and can prove fatal if left untreated. The Boehringer Ingelheim film, launched during an event titled “A Breath of Hope”, will stream across the company’s social media channels, delivering a motivational yet simple message about a complex disease. It follows a man with a persistent dry cough as he shares an elevator ride with a young girl and a medical professional. They ask about his health and help him confront the issue by urging him to see a doctor about his symptoms. Boehringer Ingelheim describes pulmonary fibrosis as a “serious condition that remains under recognised”. IPF and PPF are characterised by progressive scarring of the lungs, which causes an irreversible decline in lung function. Common symptoms can also include shortness of breath, fatigue, and weight loss. The film brings a different perspective and understanding about people living with pulmonary fibrosis, but not necessarily knowing they have it. Ousama Alhaj, general manager and head of human pharma at Boehringer Ingelheim, Near East and UAE, said it is “part of a journey” built on its legacy of more than 100 years in respiratory care. “Talking about the disease is something, but living with it is something else,” he told The National. “We see that it is under-diagnosed; people don’t know exactly what IPF is, so we decided we needed this campaign. “Part of our responsibility is to educate the patient, so we are going to continue that in order to raise awareness.” This includes recognising the symptoms and not delaying visiting a doctor so a timely diagnosis can be obtained, said Alhaj. IPF and PPF are actually considered rare, but figures show that together they are believed to affect up to 9.2 million people globally. Their progressive nature makes early recognition particularly important. However, studies have suggested diagnosis can be delayed by one to two years, meaning potentially more damage is done. Alhaj added: “This is the message: getting an early diagnosis and starting treatment is critical in slowing disease progression and supporting a better quality of life.” Not least in the UAE, where recent developments in pulmonary fibrosis care have brought important progress for patients and healthcare professionals working to improve disease management, following the approval of a new treatment option. The Boehringer Ingelheim awareness initiative, therefore, comes at a pivotal time. Dr Bassam Mahboub, vice president of the Emirates Thoracic Society, said case numbers are rising, partly due to increased detection. “There might be also another explanation why…because of the prevalence of smokers and environmental hazards,” he said. “But I think the main reason is awareness and us doing a better medical screening job, picking up these things earlier.” This, however, can only happen if people take prompt action when they show symptoms. “If you are dealing with the disease itself, it is pretty much easier than dealing with its consequences,” said Mahboub. “Just get it checked - 80/90 per cent of the time it’s not PF, it’s something else we can sort out. But if it is, let’s do something about it. Better to be safe than sorry.” While contributing factors can also be occupational, PPF can develop in people living with other conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis. Mahboub explained that it is characterised by progressive scarring of the lung interstitium - the lining of the lungs - making them stiff, reducing their ability to expand. This makes it increasingly difficult for the body to take in oxygen, and as PPF progresses, everyday activities become tougher and the risk of death increases. However, in IPF, the cause of this scarring “They cannot breathe all the way out because of the scarring,” Mahboub explained. “And when we examine them, we hear what we call Velcro-like crackles” The condition is more common in older adults, smokers and former smokers. Causes may also include medication and genetic factors, but can also be unidentifiable. Speakers at the film launch said early screening is particularly important for people with autoimmune conditions, persistent symptoms or relevant exposures. However, symptoms are sometimes mistaken for ageing, tiredness, lack of fitness, allergies, infection, or other conditions including asthma. “We are telling the public that it’s a bad disease…you cannot cure it,” continued Mahboub. “So we need to diagnose it early, and there are good medications that will make them live in a healthy way…instead of going all the way downhill. “We ask them to stay healthy in terms of not smoking. We encourage people to do exercise and to stay fit because in all diseases, not just lung fibrosis, people who are physically active do better than people who are not. "Having good muscles will make the muscles use less oxygen and put less burden on the lungs.” Dr Shamma Al Nokhatha, president of the Emirates Society for Rheumatology, highlighted how interstitial lung disease could be associated with other conditions such as systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory myositis, lupus, Sjögren’s disease and mixed connective tissue disease. “Rheumatoid arthritis is a very common condition in rheumatology,” she said. “It’s more affecting the joint, but might have lung involvement too. “Inflammatory myositis will present with a weakness in the shoulder and a head rash, but it also can involve the lung. We have also lupus … it can affect many organs, including the lung.” Founded in 1885, Boehringer Ingelheim has worked to advance respiratory health, pioneering treatments across conditions including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and PPF. It builds on its scientific expertise through research, development and strategic collaborations aimed at advancing new therapies and improving outcomes for people living with serious lung conditions. Alhaj further emphasised “the importance of bringing greater visibility to a condition that is often under-recognised and can significantly affect quality of life”. He added: “I do believe that raising awareness is a journey … that raising awareness is an important part of our responsibility. “We know that scientific progress must go hand-in-hand with greater disease awareness and timely diagnosis. Earlier recognition of symptoms and timely conversation with healthcare professionals can help support earlier diagnosis and better inform patient journeys.” Al Nokhatha also suggested people who are already diagnosed “might help other colleagues or family to understand the concept of the disease”. “The next chapter in pulmonary fibrosis care should be defined not only by scientific progress, but by how effectively we translate that progress into earlier recognition and better patient journeys,” she added. "That means strengthening awareness across patients, families and healthcare professionals, and making sure people with persistent symptoms are connected to the right care at the right time.” Mahboub added: “The takeaway message is: pulmonary fibrosis is a bad disease, but we are telling you now, today, that there is hope, and the hope gets even better if you diagnose early…diagnose it correctly, and we manage it the right way.” This page was produced by The National in partnership with Boehringer Ingelheim

title: EU launches support mission for Lebanese army as Unifil deadline looms
description: Three-year mission to focus on military surveillance and counter-smuggling
content: European foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Monday agreed to establish a support mission to the Lebanese army with an initial mandate of three years. The mission will work to strengthen the capacity of the Lebanese army and the Internal Security Forces, as well as to support maritime security, the European Council said in a statement. The training mission is part of a European effort to retain an international presence in Lebanon after the UN Interim Force withdraws on December 31. Unifil has been deployed on the southern border with Israel since 1978, at the start of a 22-year Israeli occupation of south Lebanon. “Europe is invested in Lebanon's future,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. “With this new mission – a major update of our security ties – we continue to support the country’s institutions in restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people.” The European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, will co-ordinate closely with the UN and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector, the European Council said. Support for the army will include land border surveillance and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-smuggling and operational co-ordination. The ISF will be trained in areas such as combating cybercrime and smuggling . French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the EU mission would replace the army to support the Lebanese police in their day-to-day duties, so that it could focus on its core work. Dylan Macchiarini Crosson, EU researcher at think tank International Crisis Group, said that while EUSM Lebanon would not replace Unifil, it would be a centrepiece of the bloc's engagement in the country. He called on the EU to deploy quickly, building on the €160 million in military assistance it has provided over the past three years. “Yet the mission does not directly address the core security concern for Lebanon and its international partners: maintaining an international presence in the south to support the Lebanese state, prevent Hezbollah’s military resurgence and deter further Israeli intervention,” Mr Crosson said. “The initiative nevertheless gives the EU more entry points. It should use its channels and leverage to press Israel and Hezbollah to abide by the ceasefire, advocate for a reconstituted international force in the south – perhaps one led by some EU member states – and expand humanitarian and development assistance.” France and Italy are looking into establishing a separate mission to help the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah, but this has yet to take shape. European states have no intention of directly being in charge of disarming the pro-Iran militia, which kept its weapons after the end of the civil war in 1990 to fight the Israeli occupation. The hope is that disarming Hezbollah would encourage the withdrawal of Israel, which currently occupies roughly 7 per cent of southern Lebanese territory and has destroyed a number of villages to establish a so-called buffer zone. US-brokered peace talks have stalled as Israel says it will withdraw only if Hezbollah disarms but Lebanon wants Israel to withdraw first. Western states have long pressured the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah, which they consider a terrorist organisation. But Lebanese politicians have lacked the political will – with Hezbollah represented in parliament – to pit the historically weak Lebanese army against the regional militia's powerful military arsenal. Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said the recent seizure of large quantities of explosives in Lebanon showed why the Lebanese government's efforts to bring all weapons under state control were essential. "The Lebanese state must have the exclusive authority to use force throughout its territory," Mr Prevot said on X. "For these efforts to succeed, the Israel-Lebanon Framework Agreement must be fully respected. Hezbollah's disarmament must go hand in hand with full respect for Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity."

title: Riyadh airport closure: Etihad cancels flights until October 19
description: Flydubai services also cancelled until Wednesday, with no confirmed reopening date for Saudi capital's airport
content: Saudi Arabia has extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport after deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels at the weekend. The General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Monday that the suspension would continue while checks on the safety and operational readiness of airport sites were completed. It did not give a date or time for when the airport would be reopened. Etihad Airways has cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until Monday, October 19, extending disruption to services between the UAE and the Saudi capital into next week. Flydubai has also cancelled Riyadh flights until Wednesday, October 14, while Emirates and Air Arabia services have been affected. The disruption continues beyond Riyadh, with flights to and from other Saudi destinations, including Dammam, Jeddah and Abha, also cancelled. Aviation analytics company Cirium said 46.4 per cent of scheduled flights across Saudi Arabia had been cancelled as of 4pm UAE time on Monday. Etihad has cancelled all Abu Dhabi–Riyadh services until October 19, according to its latest travel advisory. The airline said the situation remains dynamic and further changes are possible. Services to other Saudi destinations have also been affected. Etihad cancelled four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam on Monday, with all services on the route cancelled on Tuesday and Wednesday. Selected Jeddah flights have been cancelled through Thursday, October 15. Passengers are advised to check their flight status directly with Etihad before travelling. Emirates ' flight status website shows all six services between Dubai and Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday. These include outbound flights EK815, EK817 and EK819, along with returning services EK816, EK818 and EK820. Four flights remain cancelled on Tuesday, including EK815, EK817 and EK819 from Dubai to Riyadh and the return service EK816. Return services EK818 and EK820 have not yet been listed as cancelled, although this does not confirm they will operate. Flydubai has cancelled all flights between Dubai and Riyadh up to and including Wednesday, October 14. Services to Abha and Dammam have also been cancelled until that date. “Flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh have been cancelled up to and including October 14,” a flydubai representative told The National . “We continue to monitor the situation closely and we will update our customers through our official channels regarding any amendments to our flight schedules.” According to Air Arabia's official flight status website, flights G9151 and G9154 from Sharjah to Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday and Tuesday. Flight G9195 from Sharjah to Abha is also listed as cancelled on both days. Those with plans to travel should confirm their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport and check notifications about changes to their booking. Passengers whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about rebooking and refund options. Travellers with onward connections should also confirm whether changes are needed to the rest of their journey.

title: Lebanon's dark history of assassinations raised after half tonne of explosives seized
description: Package of TNT intercepted last week contained nails and ball bearings, security source says
content: The seizure by Lebanese security forces of half a tonne of explosives bound for Beirut - one of three such interceptions in a matter of weeks - has sparked uproar in Lebanon , where the country's grim history of political assassinations has risen to the fore again. On Monday, the Lebanese army said it had seized 200kg of explosives that was being smuggled in from Syria through the porous Hermel border region. The smugglers fled back to Syria, it said. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Monday that there would be “no leniency” in the investigation and that the government “will not tolerate anyone who dares to toy with the country's security, safety and stability”. About 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4 were discovered in a lorry bound for Beirut when it was stopped at an Internal Security Forces checkpoint at Dahr Al Baidar in the Bekaa Valley, officials said. It is the most popular route from Bekaa to the coast, and the road is usually very busy. Two men travelling in the vehicle were detained and the explosives handed over to the army, with the investigation now in the hands of a military court. "It's still under investigation but it is not something that we will accept. We will investigate this until the end," a senior government official told The National. A senior security source told The National the explosive package contained nails and ball bearings. The source said such seizures “were not common” and that there was added concern after the army intercepted a similarly sized package of explosives near the border with Syria two weeks ago. “I understand the anxiety gripping the Lebanese people upon the news of this truck's interception and the materials it was transporting, especially since C4 has been used in several of the infamous political assassinations in modern Lebanese history,” Mr Salam said in a post on X on Monday. In the 2000s and early 2010s, several high-profile opponents of the Assad regime in Syria and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah were killed or had attempts made on their lives using explosives. Former prime minister Rafic Hariri was killed along with 20 others when a one-tonne lorry bomb was detonated as his convoy was driving in Beirut on February 14, 2005. The UN's Special Tribunal for Lebanon has convicted Hezbollah members of that attack. Some in Lebanon are already linking the explosives seizures to Hezbollah , even though officials stress that the investigation is continuing. An official of the Iran-backed political party and armed group declined to comment. Mr Salam said Lebanese could “rest assured that we will not relent in pursuing the investigation and expanding it, to identify every individual involved in this criminal operation, those behind them, uncover their plans and objectives, and bring them all to justice to receive the punishment they deserve”. Hezbollah is under intense pressure both internationally and domestically amid a push to disarm. The government banned its military wing earlier this year after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel as part of the wider regional Iran war. Mr Salam's government has also declared its intent – under pressure from the US and Israel – to bring all weapons under state control. The explosives seizures have stirred memories of Lebanon's past political violence. May Chidiac, a journalist and former government minister who survived an assassination attempt in 2005, said her attackers had tried to kill her with a combination of C4 and TNT. “I survived by a miracle, but many of my friends who deserved to live were killed,” she said.

title: Huupe wants to make almost every basketball hoop in the world 'smart'
description: Tech company hopes to sell at least a million of its newest product
content: Huupe , a California company, says it wants to use its technology to make every basketball hoop in the world " smart ". The sports start-up, which offers several products including AI-using basketball hoops, says that its Huupe Arena Upgrade Kit fills an important gap in the market. "It's our biggest launch since the Huupe Mini 1 ," Huupe chief executive Paul Anton told The National of the $699 Arena Upgrade Kit, which consists of an attachable sensor hub and lights that connect to most backboards. The attachable device syncs with smartphones and allows players to automatically track shots, measure performance, and play against other users around the world. "We believe it is the biggest game-changer in the world of basketball hoops," Mr Anton continued, adding that it "enables every existing hoop to remain, while offering a simple smart upgrade". The company's chief executive said Huupe has introduced the Arena Portable, which starts at $995. The Arena Portable is described as a complete, full-size but movable basketball hoop that has all the AI and technology features on the Huupe basketball software platform. This is Huupe's latest offering in a deep bench of products since June, when it introduced the Arena, which is available at a base price of $2,995. The Arena provides players with rim impact charts, AI-powered shot form analysis, three-point percentages, field goal stats and interactive shot charts. Huupe was founded in 2015 by Mr Anton and Lyth Saeed, both originally from Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and both insatiable basketball fans. It took several years to co-ordinate the right technology, tools and financing for their vision of creating a better hoop. In 2022, the company introduced the world's first smart basketball hoop, Huupe Pro, which uses a display and apps to enhance the basketball experience. Two years later, Huupe introduced a smaller version of the product, Huupe Mini, for use in the home. Huupe Mini allows users to play with others around the world and can also be used, through an HDMI port and built-in Wi‑Fi, to connect to streaming services such as YouTube or Netflix. The Mini, like the Pro, can track and analyse shooting performances through the use of advanced radar as well as light detection and ranging (lidar) technology. Huupe announced in 2025 that retired NBA all-star Tracy McGrady would be joining in the capacity of chief innovation officer, and that hall-of-famer Vince Carter would be coming on board as a strategic adviser. Mr Anton is setting ambitious goals for the company's next steps. "Next for Huupe is growing the Upgrade Kit to one million units sold," he said. "There are over 100 million basketball hoops that exist in the world today." According to a Future Data Stats market report, in 2024 the global basketball hoop market "was valued at $2 billion" and is projected to expand to $3.5 billion by 2032.

title: Drivers warned of lower speed limit on Fujairah to Khor Fakkan road
description: Top speed reduced from 120kph to 100kph from Tuesday
content: The speed limit on the road between Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, in Sharjah, is being reduced to 100kph from Tuesday. Police in Fujairah announced the reduction from the previous speed limit of 120kph. “Fujairah Police urges all road users to observe the posted speed limits and comply with traffic signs and instructions to ensure everyone's safety,” the force said in a post on X on Sunday. Only Umm Al Quwain ranks lower than Fujairah for road safety among the seven emirates , according to analysis released last month. Fujairah’s low ranking in the index, released by Dubai-based Bin Yaber Driving Institute, was primarily due to its low provision of driver education with only two driving schools. The emirate’s roads are not the safest, with above-average death rates and hit-and-run incidents, and the highest average driving speed in the UAE, the analysis found. The same index rated Sharjah top for road safety, with the lowest death rate (1.78) on the roads and hit-and-run incident rate (5.33) per 100,000 residents. The average driving speed of 31.6kph in Sharjah is also at the safer end of the spectrum, which may be due to heavy traffic but also indicates more cautious driving behaviour.

title: US and regional allies shielded by ‘world's largest air-defence umbrella’, says Centcom chief
description: Adm Brad Cooper's remarks come after deadly Houthi attack on Saudi airport
author_name: Fatima Al Mahmoud, Mohamad Ali  Harisi
content: The US and its regional allies are deploying the “largest air-defence umbrella in the world” to deter Iranian attacks, US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper said, describing the effort as part of an “enduring security architecture” in the Middle East. The senior US commander was speaking in a recorded message at Trends Global's sixth annual conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday, days after a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s main airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Adm Cooper said the combined missile defence effort throughout the Iran war, which once seemed a “distant goal”, was now “military partnership in action”. “It was a vision we discussed with our regional allies and partners,” he told the audience at the Ritz-Carlton. “Earlier this year, during Operation Epic Fury, we validated at full scale and in actual combat the Middle East Air Defence network known as Mead. “Through our combined efforts, we transformed a concept into the most sophisticated and largest air-defence umbrella in the world,” he added. “For the first time in history, US air defenders stood shoulder-to-shoulder with allies and partners across the Middle East, linking national systems in real time. And so together we intercepted thousands of Iranian attack drones and missiles with an integrated shield built on mutual trust. This is partnership in action.” Military partnerships between the US and its regional allies were key to achieving sustainable security in the Middle East, said the Centcom chief. “Sustainable security is not the absence of conflict. It is having robust systems, partnerships and interoperability in shared leadership firmly in place to manage threats before they escalate into a crisis,” he said. Adm Cooper said the US forged military partnerships through “training, working shoulder-to-shoulder and operating alongside regional partners because we're stronger together and sustainable security requires strength”. “Modern threats like advanced missiles and drones, as well as attacks from space and cyber, don't respect geographic boundaries or national borders, meaning no nation alone can counter these threats effectively,” he added. While the US positions itself as a pillar of the Middle East's security architecture, Iran is facing growing isolation, said Mike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN. “Iran wanted a ring of fire around Israel and instead it sealed its own fate,” Mr Waltz said at Trends in a recorded message. Countries in the Middle East such as Lebanon, Iraq and Syria “refuse to ever again be treated like Tehran's pawns on an Iranian chessboard”. The US officials' remarks come amid growing signs that Tehran and Washington are bracing for a renewed confrontation after weeks of fragile calm. The Iran war, which erupted in late February, has engulfed the Middle East for almost eight months, with no immediate end in sight. Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. However, President Donald Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and warned military operations could intensify after the US midterm elections. The conflict's regional spillover has also widened, with the latest escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen adding to mounting instability across the Middle East. Mr Trump said this week he was considering joining Saudi Arabia in retaliating against the Houthis following deadly attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, despite initially declining Saudi requests for military intervention, according to reports. When asked whether the Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport would change his previous decision not to attack Iran until after the midterms, Mr Trump said: “Well, we're going to take a look.” The situation reflects the US administration’s reluctance to open another front, as efforts to end the Iran war prove elusive and the Strait of Hormuz crisis persists. Yet the appetite for war appears to be growing on both sides. The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tehran was no longer responding to the US amid stalled negotiations, describing Washington's response to its proposals as “insufficient”. Meanwhile, Mike Pompeo, former CIA director and US secretary of state, said the only solution was to “crush the Iranian regime … there is no solution short of that. “We could not all be foolish to think that the regime in Iran is going to comply with any agreement,” he said at the Abu Dhabi event.

title: 13 comedy shows coming to Abu Dhabi, from Russell Peters to Whitney Cummings
description: International stand-up stars and regional favourites are heading to the capital, with performances in English, Arabic, Hindi, French and Tagalog
content: Sunday was the first day of Abu Dhabi Comedy Season, as Morgan Jay made a stop in the capital as part of his The Goofy Guy Tour. Bringing his TikTok on-screen humour to the stage at Etihad Arena, he set the standard for a season of comedy still to come. Russell Peters, Mo Amer, Maz Jobrani and Whitney Cummings are among the performers heading to the capital between October and January. The programme offers a mix of international stars and regional favourites, from the storytelling of Scottish comedian Kevin Bridges to the political satire of Maz Jobrani and the improvisational humour of Egyptian performer Mina Nader. Most shows will take place at Etihad Arena in Yas Island as part of the third Abu Dhabi Comedy Season, which has previously welcomed Dave Chappelle, Kevin Hart, Trevor Noah and Bill Burr. Smaller venues are also getting involved, including The Club, which will host a special anniversary programme of The Laughter Factory. Here are the comedy performances announced for Abu Dhabi between October and February. Long before social media became an essential tool for comedians, Russell Peters was attracting millions of viewers through clips of his stand-up routines. The Canadian, whose parents emigrated from India, became internationally recognised for his observations about immigrant families, accents and misunderstandings between cultures. His specials include Outsourced ; Red, White and Brown ; and Deported . Audience interaction remains central to his performances, with Peters frequently turning conversations with spectators into some of the evening's biggest laughs. Tickets from Dh275 ($75) Palestinian-American comedian Mo Amer has taken his experiences of displacement and immigration from the comedy stage to television. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents and raised in Houston, Amer created the semi-autobiographical Netflix series Mo with Ramy Youssef. The series won a Peabody Award in 2023 and concluded with its second season in 2025. His stand-up similarly draws on questions of belonging, family and identity, subjects he approaches through humour informed by his experiences of navigating different cultures. Tickets from Dh325 When the Axis of Evil Comedy Tour emerged in the 2000s, it offered American audiences a different perspective on the Middle East at a time when regional identities were frequently reduced to political stereotypes. Iranian-American comedian Maz Jobrani was among its founding performers, using humour to challenge assumptions about Arabs and Iranians. He has since built an international career spanning television, film and stand-up specials, with politics, parenting and contemporary society continuing to provide material. He appeared at the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week in 2024. Tickets from Dh275 The UAE's stand-up scene looked considerably different when The Laughter Factory was launched in Dubai in 1996. International comedy clubs were uncommon and arena-sized performances by visiting comedians had yet to become regular fixtures. Three decades later, the organisation is celebrating its 30th anniversary with a UAE tour that includes Abu Dhabi. 30 Years of Laughs continues its tradition of bringing established and emerging comedians to smaller venues, offering the intimacy and spontaneity of a traditional comedy-club evening. The show starts at 7pm; tickets from Dh140 Moroccan comedian Amine Radi brings a distinctly North African flavour to Abu Dhabi's comedy programme. His performance moves between French and Arabic, drawing on the humour of everyday exchanges, social expectations and the complications of modern relationships. Radi has developed an audience across the francophone world through performances built around animated delivery and increasingly elaborate stories. His appearance will also be phone-free, with electronic devices secured in pouches during the performance, keeping the focus firmly on the stage. Tickets from Dh150 A seemingly ordinary anecdote can become an elaborate comic adventure in the hands of Indian stand-up performer Anubhav Singh Bassi. His relaxed delivery gives stories room to develop, with friendships, student life and questionable youthful decisions supplying much of his material. Bassi's performances have attracted millions of views online, introducing his Hindi-language humour to audiences beyond India. His latest show, Kisi Ko Batana Mat , meaning Don't Tell Anyone, continues this approach, finding absurdity in situations that often begin innocently enough. The show starts at 6pm; tickets from Dh125 Few comedians can switch between famous impersonating personalities as convincingly as Aries Spears. The American performer spent eight seasons on the sketch comedy programme Mad TV , where his impressions of entertainers and public figures helped establish his reputation. Michael Jackson, Eddie Murphy and Shaquille O'Neal are among the celebrities he has imitated. Beyond impersonations, Spears has developed a more confrontational approach to stand-up, exploring race, entertainment and American social attitudes. His Abu Dhabi performance offers a mixture of observational humour and the character work that made him famous. The show starts at 10pm; tickets start at Dh120 Generations of Filipino television viewers will recognise Jose Manalo and Wally Bayola from the long-running variety programme Eat Bulaga!. The comedy partners are particularly known for their sketches, recurring characters and ability to improvise around the unexpected. Their Abu Dhabi production, The Ultimate Dabarkads Comedy , brings that chemistry to the stage through sketches, live music and audience participation. Presented in Tagalog and English, the afternoon show is also among the few family-friendly performances in the comedy calendar, with no minimum age restriction. Tickets from Dh99 Lebanese-American comedian NEMR brings his Rampant Disorder show to Abu Dhabi as part of the Wagef stand-up comedy road tour, presented by MBC Group. Having grown up between Lebanon and the US, he has frequently drawn on the contradictions of those experiences, particularly the expectations placed on young people by their families and communities. His latest production takes a wider look at relationships, culture and the disorder of modern life, delivered through the energetic storytelling that has helped him attract audiences across the Middle East and internationally. Tickets from Dh150 No two Mina Nader performances are quite alike. The Egyptian comedian builds much of his Arabic-language stand-up around conversations with spectators, transforming unexpected answers and personal anecdotes into improvised material. With more than 16 years of experience, Nader has performed across the Middle East, Europe and North America. Organisers credit him with more than 500 sold-out shows, a reflection of the following he has developed through his interactive approach. His Abu Dhabi appearance continues that format, with the audience helping shape the evening's direction. Doors open at 8pm; tickets start from Dh195 Scottish comedian Kevin Bridges has a talent for extracting humour from the ordinary frustrations of life. Growing up in Clydebank, near Glasgow, provided much of the inspiration for his early routines, which examine working-class experiences and the peculiarities of everyday behaviour. His distinctive Glaswegian delivery has become part of his appeal, helping him build a substantial following across Britain and internationally. Bridges has also written two books, including his autobiography We Need to Talk About … Kevin Bridges , documenting his journey from aspiring comedian to arena headliner. The show starts at 8pm; tickets from Dh295 Creating one successful American sitcom is difficult enough, but Whitney Cummings helped launch two during the same television season. In 2011, she created and starred in NBC's Whitney while also co-creating the CBS comedy 2 Broke Girls . She has since continued working across television, stand-up and podcasting, hosting Good For You and releasing several comedy specials. Her routines frequently examine relationships, gender expectations and contemporary social habits. Her Big Baby tour brings her to the UAE for the first time. Show starts at 6pm; tickets from Dh215 Liverpudlian comedian Paul Smith has found international success by making the audience a central part of his performances. Clips filmed at the city's Hot Water Comedy Club have attracted millions of views, largely because of his ability to build jokes around unpredictable exchanges with spectators. His latest show, HAPPY , combines that spontaneous approach with stories about finding humour in the frustrations and complications of daily life. The performance also marks his first appearance at Etihad Arena, closing January's comedy line-up with an emphasis on improvisation. The show starts at 9.30pm; tickets from Dh275

title: Are Pakistan turning over a new leaf in T20 cricket?
description: Captain Sahibzada Farhan leads from front in series win over Sri Lanka, adding to a growing sense of positivity around team
content: Pakistan completed a T20 series win against Sri Lanka on Sunday, securing an 82-run victory in the second match of the three-game series in Rawalpindi. New captain and opener Sahibzada Farhan hit a quick 73, his second straight fifty, and young middle order bat Maaz Sadaqat smashed 96 from 51 balls to help Pakistan post 215-3. Sri Lanka batters did not even come close, restricted to 133-7. On paper, it is a routine result in a bilateral series well away from a T20 World Cup cycle. But for Pakistan , it was a significant milestone. Pakistan have tried to hit the reset button in white-ball cricket for quite some time. After successive misses at ICC tournaments and a growing trend of failing to even qualify for the semi-finals, the team needed a fresh set of eyes to look at the issue. In 2026, they have started to get more things right than wrong. If you look at the bigger picture, Pakistan did not win any major titles – either the T20 World Cup or Asian Games. However, they lost just four out of 15 completed matches this year and two of those losses were against double world champions India, including in the Asian Games gold medal match. Pakistan thrashed Australia 3-0 at home ahead of the T20 World Cup and were largely competitive in the main tournament, losing to India and England (by 2 wickets). So what has changed? For starters, Pakistan are putting more faith in T20 specialists. Farhan – top scorer at the T20 World Cup and ranked third in the world among T20 batters – was named captain for the ongoing Sri Lanka series. There was no space for tried and tested fast-bowler Shaheen Afridi or all-rounder Salman Agha. Babar Azam and Mohammad Rizwan are almost certainly out of the T20 scheme of things for good. The selectors and team management have backed players who live and breathe the 20-over format. Hasan Nawaz is one such name and almost snatched the T20 Asian Games gold medal from India’s grasp with a destructive 96 in the final. Left-arm fast bowler Salman Mirza has played more T20Is than first-class matches and should get an extended run, albeit at the age of 32, now that Pakistan seem to have had enough Afridi the T20 bowler. Mirza picked up 2-28 from three overs against Sri Lanka on Sunday. There are many more waiting in the wings. There always have been. It was just that some players were turned into multi-format players for the sake of it, which took away precious spots in the T20 side which could have easily gone to specialists. One can sense change in the air. Captain Farhan made it clear what he wants from his team, especially the batters. “We have been a different T20 side in 2026 as our six-hitting ratio has improved and our batters are scoring at more than 150 [strike rate]. If we continue this way, we will end up scoring more than 200 every time,” the opener said after the Sri Lanka series win. That is a significant statement because it is the only way successful teams operate. And also because those words came from a player who is a genuine trend setter in the country. Farhan is one among only five batters to hits four T20 centuries in one year. Also, Farhan is the first Pakistan batter to hit a six against India’s Jasprit Bumrah – after a staggering 400 deliveries bowled by the Indian ace. That alone broke the shackles that had gripped the minds of many Pakistan players and supporters after successive defeats against their neighbours at ICC events. India still obviously hold the upper hand but Pakistan are beginning to believe that the gap with the world champions and other leading T20 teams is probably not as vast as it was a couple of seasons back.

title: From missing pets to new homes, Microchipped’s mission to help UAE cats
description: Event at Rosewood Abu Dhabi also aimed to raise awareness of animal welfare and responsible pet ownership
content: From uncertain futures to a home of their own, eight rescued cats found new families at an adoption event in Abu Dhabi on Sunday. Another four adoptions are pending following the gathering, which encouraged residents to consider the long-term commitment of taking in a pet. Hosted by microchip database service Microchipped.ae and the Rosewood Abu Dhabi hotel, the event brought together animal rescuers, prospective adopters and families, and 56 cats available for adoption. Alongside helping the animals find permanent homes, the event also highlighted responsible pet ownership and the importance of trap-neuter-return programmes to manage stray cat populations . The event also drew strong support through Volunteers.ae, with all 80 volunteer places filled and others joining a reserve list. For Dave Appleby , founder of Microchipped.ae, seeing the community come together was an emotional moment. “It went beyond what we hoped,” he tells The National . “Seeing rescuers, adopters, families and our community all in one room at Rosewood, with ... real conversations around adoption, it felt like everything we’ve been working for over the last four years finally came together. It was emotional but also full of hope.” The initiative has its roots in Appleby’s own experience of losing pets. In late 2022, he and his wife Jacqueline began searching for three missing cats in Khalifa City: Monty, Blacky and Winnie. As The National reported in February 2023, Monty was eventually reunited with the couple after 100 days, when a resident recognised him from a photograph shared online. The search prompted Appleby to develop Microchipped.ae, a free online platform that allows owners to match their pets’ microchip numbers with those of animals found or taken to vets and shelters. His experience of pets going missing continues to shape the initiative’s work. “That pain is why Microchipped.ae exists – so no other family has to go through not knowing.” Sunday’s event extended that mission to help rescued cats find permanent homes, while encouraging visitors to adopt rather than buy animals. Appleby says he wanted people to leave with a greater appreciation of the stray cats they encounter and the difference small acts of care can make. “If people left today thinking twice before ignoring a community cat, then we did our job,” he says. “Every cat has a story and deserves to be seen. Microchipping, keeping a pet passport, taking that extra minute to scan a lost cat – those small actions are what bring cats home. Also, adoption is not a transaction; it’s a lifetime commitment.” For residents interested in animal welfare but unsure where to begin, Appleby’s advice is to choose something manageable. Helping does not have to mean taking on several animals or becoming a full-time rescuer. “Start small and start local. You don’t have to rescue 50 cats. Offer to foster for one week. Volunteer to drive a cat to a vet. Learn how to scan a microchip. Share a genuine adoption post instead of scrolling.” People who encounter a lost cat can take a photograph, arrange for its microchip to be checked at a vet and share the information on the Microchipped website, he says. “That one post could be the reason a family is reunited.” Appleby also encourages residents to recognise the work rescuers undertake beyond public events. While an adoption day can bring people together and help cats find homes, their care depends on continued support. “If you can’t adopt, support the rescuers who do it every day,” he says. “They are the backbone of animal welfare in the UAE and they burn out because they do it alone. Even just saying thank you goes a long way.”

title: Pilot, flight attendant and widowed mother among victims of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia
description: Strikes on kingdom’s airports have killed at least 20 people and injured hundreds
content: At least 20 people were killed in a series of attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid and Abha international airports in Saudi Arabia ’s Asir province last week, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels stepped up attacks on the kingdom. The victims include a Saudi airline pilot, an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widowed mother of four. Saudi and foreign citizens were among the dead, while hundreds of people have been injured, Saudi authorities say. Among those killed in Saturday’s attack in Riyadh were four Saudis and eight foreign citizens. The death toll from that strike rose to 13 after an injured Indian citizen was confirmed dead. A Pakistani citizen was killed in a separate attack on Sunday, Saudi authorities said, while 11 were injured. The foreign victims included two Bangladeshis and citizens of the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. More than 300 people were wounded on Saturday, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade. This marks a sharp escalation in the war in Yemen , where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government in its battle against the Houthis , raising fears the fighting could widen and draw in American forces. US President Donald Trump ​said on Saturday his country was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Details about some of those killed have emerged through official statements, diplomatic missions and reports from their families. Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami , a pilot with Saudi Arabia’s national carrier Saudia, was among three Saudi citizens killed in attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport last Thursday. The airline confirmed his death in a statement. Saudi authorities said airport facilities and a Saudia aircraft had been struck. Azza Ramzy, 28, worked as a flight attendant for Saudi airline flynas. She died from injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty directed the Egyptian embassy and the general consulate in Riyadh to expedite the transfer of her body to Egypt. Egyptian media reported that she was from Beheira governorate, in the north of the country. Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, a widowed mother of four, had lived in Saudi Arabia for five years and was based in Makkah. She lost contact with her family on Saturday while returning from Riyadh, where she had been visiting her sister. Her brother told Syria’s state-run news agency Sana that the Syrian consul later informed him of her death, citing official confirmation from the Saudi government. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh said she was killed in an attack on King Khalid International Airport. Talal Al Dani was among those killed in Saturday’s attack, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry. The Palestinian embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was handling arrangements concerning his body and providing support to his family. Mohammed Yusuf Ali, from Hyderabad, was travelling with his family on an Umrah pilgrimage when he was injured in Saturday’s attack. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed his death on Sunday and said it was in contact with his family to help arrange the repatriation of his remains. Mahmoud Al Barqawi, 33, a Jordanian father of two, was killed in the Houthi-claimed attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday. He had lived in Saudi Arabia for about two years and worked at a cafe at the airport. His body was returned to Jordan, where he was buried in Amman on Monday. His father, Hassan Al Barqawi, said the family was struggling to cope with the loss. Footage released by Saudi state television of the attack on ‌the Riyadh airport on Saturday showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites, Makkah and Madinah. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, ​while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation has since extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

title: Veteran politician calls for Kurdish rights to be enshrined in Syria’s constitution to prevent tension
description: Ilham Ahmed says integration has brought progress but women’s participation and representation in state institutions is in decline
content: Syria's constitution must guarantee the rights of the Kurdish community, the country's largest ethnic minority group, a veteran politician has said, warning that the move towards a more centralised state risks fuelling tension. Damascus has worked to integrate Kurdish-led troops into the military. Ilham Ahmed, a Syrian Kurdish leader, told the Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil, Iraq, that the integration process had made significant headway, but remained a work in progress as the Kurds stake out a claim in the new Syrian political dispensation under President Ahmad Al Shara. Ms Ahmed, a senior figure in the former Kurdish-led autonomous administration in north-east Syria, is now a member of the foreign relations committee in the Syrian parliament. She said the process of merging the Syrian Democratic Forces with the military had helped to relink cities, reopen border crossings and create conditions for greater stability following the fall of Bashar Al Assad’s regime. The experience of self-administration had demonstrated the importance of women’s participation in public life, Ms Ahmed added. But she warned that their role in institutions and decision-making was now diminishing despite the integration process. “Today, we are seeing that despite the merging process, there is a regression in the role of women and in their roles and participation in institutions and in decision making process,” she said. Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi announced in August from the city of Qamishli that the integration of the Kurdish administration into Syria’s state institutions was complete. The move built on an agreement struck between Damascus and the SDF in January. The deal was mediated by Washington and Paris and endorsed by Ankara. It sought to end hostilities between Kurdish forces and the new Syrian authorities, while establishing a road map for incorporating the north-east into state institutions, while offering specific linguistic and cultural rights as well as political representation. In January, Mr Al Shara issued a decree , after weeks of violence, offering concessions designed to foster goodwill with Syria's Kurdish population. They included recognising Nowruz as a national holiday and recognising Kurdish as a national language that may be taught in public and private schools in Kurdish-populated areas. He also granted Syrian nationality to previously stateless Kurds. Ms Ahmed described the presidential decree recognising Kurdish identity, language and the community’s place in Syria as a historic achievement. But she said the measures remained incomplete, particularly regarding the right to education in the Kurdish language. Kurdish existence had been acknowledged for the first time in Syrian history, she said, but mechanisms were still needed to fulfil the decree on the ground. She said the government was responsible for establishing those mechanisms and ensuring stability. Tension has risen in north-east Syria over the future of Kurdish-language education, with students protesting against restrictions imposed by the new authorities in Damascus. The Education Ministry's decision to limit instruction in Kurdish has prompted demonstrations in areas including Hasakah, Qamishli and Kobani, where pupils and teachers are demanding the right to study in their mother tongue. Ms Ahmed said recurring hostilities were linked to discrimination, adding that the integration process remained at a stage of testing and observation. She also challenged the negative perception of decentralisation in Syria, arguing that it was too often portrayed as a threat to the country’s territorial unity. “In general, when we talk about decentralisation in Syria, it’s like we’re talking about the devil,” she said. Last year when The National sat down to speak to Ms Ahmed in the run up to the integration, she spoke of the importance of federalism as the main priority for Kurdish leaders. "It appears as if decentralisation would divide Syria but it’s not like that. We are moving into a more centralised state which will cause more tension,” she said. “Speaking and learning more languages does not lead to dividing the country or segmenting it. It strengthens the Syrian culture."

title: Jon Rahm to make Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship debut as he gets set for LIV Golf exit
description: Spaniard confirmed for finale to DP World Tour season in the UAE
content: Jon Rahm will continue his reintegration into golf’s established tours when he tees it up at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship for the first time next month. The Spanish Ryder Cup star has been confirmed for the penultimate competition of the DP World Tour season, taking place at Yas Links from November 5 to 8. As a previous Race to Dubai winner, Rahm has enjoyed some of his finest successes in the UAE. He has won the season’s finale, the DP World Tour Championship at Jumeirah Golf Estates, three times – in 2017, 2019 and 2022. And yet this will be his first time in the capital. “I’ve had some of the best weeks of my career in the UAE, so I’m really looking forward to playing in Abu Dhabi for the first time,” Rahm said. “I’ve heard great things about Yas Links, and I’m looking forward to playing there. It’ll be great to get started in Abu Dhabi before heading to Dubai the following week.” He will join a field that will include fellow stars like Rory McIlroy and Patrick Reed, who are vying with each other to win the Race to Dubai. Reed signalled at the start of this season he was ending his association with the breakaway LIV Golf tour. After winning the Dubai Desert Classic and heading to Bahrain, he said he hoped to play his way back on to the PGA Tour in the United States via Europe’s tour. The top 10 players in the Race to Dubai rankings are eligible for PGA Tour cards. Rahm is now also in the throes of exiting LIV. The rebel tour is set to be restructured after losing funding from Saudi Arabia. Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European Tour in 2027. Players have been told they have to make a choice regarding where they play. Many of LIV’s leading stars, like Reed and Brooks Koepka, have already made for the exit. Rahm has also signalled he will not be part of the new-look series. In May, he reached an agreement with the DP World Tour to maintain his membership, and ensure his availability for the Ryder Cup. Participation in certain DP World Tour events was part of that, leading to him playing in the two-legged play-off finals in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai. While his schedule for next season is unclear, he might pursue a similar route back to the PGA Tour in the US which Reed has taken this season. Rahm could yet finish in the top 10 of the Race to Dubai standings this season. He is currently 46th in the standings, but could leap up with strong performances in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. However, he would not yet be eligible for a return to the PGA Tour. Rahm won the individual LIV title for the third time in August. There is an automatic year ban for LIV players, so he would not be able to play there until August 28, 2027.

title: Zelenskyy urges US to act to ensure Russia abides by 'energy ceasefire'
description: Ukrainian President says he learnt about Trump deal through media reports
content: Ukraine is ready to agree to a deal with Russia to halt attacks on each other’s energy supplies, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. Mr Zelenskyy was responding to US President Donald Trump’s announcement that there would be an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine . Speaking by video at the Warsaw Security Conference, the Ukrainian leader said he learnt about the proposed truce from the media, after Mr Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social platform on Sunday. “If the Americans need it, we are ready to sign these guarantees to make sure they can be trusted. It’s important that we all see this situation in the same way,” Mr Zelenskyy said. But he said Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t read Truth Social” and that Ukraine continued to come under attack. Mr Zelenskyy added that “if Russia doesn’t agree to energy ceasefire, we will respond”. He urged Washington to step in to ensure that Moscow abided by the terms of the putative agreement. "There were ​Russian ⁠violations ‌of the energy ceasefire announced ​by President Trump," he said. "We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take. "This energy ceasefire, it ⁠can work, and it can ⁠become a major step towards ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and ​make sure Russians respect it." As Mr Trump made his announcement, large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water as repair crews struggled to restore power after Russian strikes. A power plant in Kharkiv, in the north-east, also came under attack. “All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered Shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities,” said Mr Zelenskyy, referring to Iranian-supplied drones used by Russia in the war. “We shoot down many of them and, if we didn’t, there would clearly be even more damage to our energy infrastructure.” Mr Zelenskyy ended his address by urging Ukraine's allies to dedicate their time to making sure the US gets "one clear message". "An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social,” he said. “We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together, Europe and the United States." At the weekend, Mr Zelenskyy held talks with key allies, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte. French President ​Emmanuel Macron ​said ​on Monday that ⁠he had not ⁠seen any ​signs in the past ⁠48 hours of Russia respecting an energy ceasefire. "We can only reopen the debate on ​the energy ‌situation if there ⁠is real ​ceasefire which is ​respected ‌by both sides," Mr Macron said at the Paris ⁠Autoshow. "I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from ​the Russian side." Mr Burnham told Mr Zelenskyy that he recognised "the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” and stressed his “complete solidarity” with Kyiv, according to a Downing Street readout of the call between the two leaders. The pair discussed the “importance of maintaining pressure on Russia” and Mr Burnham made it clear that the UK “would continue to strengthen its sanctions on Russia and take further action to constrain the Russian war machine”. Mr Carney’s office said he had spoken with Mr Zelenskyy about Mr Trump’s “diesel deal” with Russia, which aims to immediately release 300,000 tonnes of the fuel to global markets in an effort to curb rising costs. The Canadian leader said the agreement was in "direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe". Mr Zelenskyy has proposed a 60-day ceasefire to allow his country to hold presidential elections, but that was immediately rejected by Russia. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said his country wanted a long-term peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.

title: Boehringer Ingelheim premieres short film to raise awareness of pulmonary fibrosis in the UAE
description: Debut in Dubai brings together leading pulmonology and rheumatology healthcare professionals
content: Boehringer Ingelheim, a leading research-driven biopharmaceutical company, has premiered a new short film as part of a campaign to raise awareness of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis, two progressive lung conditions that can have a profound impact on patients’ everyday lives. Hosted in Dubai, the premiere brought together leading pulmonology and rheumatology healthcare professionals, including Dr Bassam Mahboub, vice president of the Emirates Thoracic Society, and Dr Shamma Al Nokhatha, president of the Emirates Society for Rheumatology, to raise awareness of pulmonary fibrosis and the importance of recognising its signs earlier. IPF and PPF are characterised by progressive scarring of the lungs, which causes an irreversible decline in lung function and makes it increasingly difficult for the body to take in oxygen. In IPF, the cause of this scarring is unknown, while PPF can develop in people living with other conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis. Common symptoms include a persistent dry cough, shortness of breath and fatigue, which are often mistaken for ageing, tiredness or lack of fitness. As PPF progresses, everyday activities become increasingly difficult and the risk of death increases. “We have been working in respiratory health for generations, and we know that scientific progress must go hand in hand with greater disease awareness and timely diagnosis," said Ousama Alhaj, general manager and head of human pharma at Boehringer Ingelheim, Near East and UAE. "Recent developments in pulmonary fibrosis care in the UAE represent important progress for patients and healthcare professionals working to improve disease management. We want to build on this momentum by helping more people recognise the signs of IPF and PPF and seek medical advice earlier, while continuing to advance science and access to innovative healthcare solutions.” While IPF and PPF are considered rare, together they are estimated to affect up to 9.2 million people worldwide. Their progressive nature makes early recognition particularly important, yet studies suggest that diagnosis can be delayed by one to two years. “Pulmonary fibrosis care is at an important point of transition. We are moving towards a future where recognising the disease earlier, strengthening multidisciplinary assessment and acting sooner can become a more consistent part of the patient journey," said Dr Bassam Mahboub, vice president of the Emirates Thoracic Society. "The challenge now is to make sure that a symptom as easily dismissed as breathlessness becomes a prompt to investigate, rather than a reason to wait. The more we recognise these changes earlier, the better positioned we are to move patients towards the right assessment and appropriate care." The awareness initiative comes at a pivotal time for pulmonary fibrosis care following the recent approval of a new treatment option for IPF and PPF. The milestone follows more than a decade without a new treatment demonstrating efficacy in IPF, representing important progress for people living with these progressive diseases. "The next chapter in pulmonary fibrosis care should be defined not only by scientific progress, but by how effectively we translate that progress into earlier recognition and better patient journeys," said Dr Shamma Al Nokhatha, president of the Emirates Society for Rheumatology. "That means strengthening awareness across patients, families and healthcare professionals, and making sure people with persistent symptoms are connected to the right care at the right time. This is where innovation can have its greatest impact for patients." For more than a century, Boehringer Ingelheim has worked to advance respiratory health, pioneering treatments across conditions including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and pulmonary fibrosis. Today, the company continues to build on its deep scientific expertise in respiratory disease through research, development and strategic collaborations aimed at advancing new therapies and improving outcomes for people living with serious lung conditions.

title: US says Hormuz oil flows recover to 14 million bpd despite Saudi attacks
description: Energy Secretary Chris Wright condemns Houthi strikes on Riyadh
content: Up to 14 million barrels of oil a day are moving through the Strait of Hormuz , with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said. Additional supplies from the Gulf are also being transported through pipelines bypassing Hormuz, Mr Wright said on Monday, addressing the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh remotely. "The crude problem we talked a lot about – it's still there but it's mostly handled," he said, offering a more optimistic assessment than ship-tracking data suggests. Figures from analytics firm Kpler show oil exports through Hormuz averaged slightly under nine million bpd in September, the highest monthly level since the war began, but only about 44 per cent of the 20.6 million bpd recorded in February. About 22 vessels crossed the strait daily in the 30 days to October 12, about two thirds of them tankers, according to Kpler. The data is provisional and subject to revision as tracking information is updated, reflecting movements registered by 2pm UAE time on October 12.
