Laden crude tankers leaving the Gulf carried about 8.9 million bpd over the past month, mostly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq. The figures are not directly comparable with Mr Wright's broader recovery estimate, which includes supplies transported through bypass pipelines. Kpler's September data nevertheless suggests lower volumes through Hormuz than those cited by the US official. Mr Wright's comments came after an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured about 300, underscoring the security risks facing the world's biggest oil-exporting region. "I want to start out by strongly condemning the cowardly attacks by the Houthis on the people of Saudi Arabia, on civilian infrastructure," Mr Wright said in addressing the energy congress on Monday. He reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the kingdom as energy ministers and industry executives gathered in Riyadh despite heightened security concerns. "We are here as your partners," he said, reiterating the US's "unwavering support for Saudi Arabia". Mr Wright warned the recovery in crude supplies had yet to ease pressure on fuel markets, with diesel prices remaining "very high", and jet fuel and petrol prices also elevated. "The challenge is still here and the challenge is still ahead of us," he said.

title: UAE wealth set to hit $6 trillion in 2030 despite short-term war volatility
description: The number of ultra-high-net-worth individuals in the Emirates set to grow to 800, BCG says
content: Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a new report has found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said. The sharp projected increase, driven by a rise in real assets and financial wealth, “points to the UAE's long-term wealth creation potential”, BCG said in its Global Wealth Report 2026: The Great Reordering report on Monday. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030. The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG. “While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.” Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said. BCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed. The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners. The UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said. The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030. Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030. The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found. The UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year. Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030. Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.

title: 'Being allowed to leave does not erase injustice': Former Dubai resident leaves Iraq after years of detention
description: Robert Pether reunited with family after being jailed along with colleague over contract dispute involving their employer
content: A former Dubai resident detained in Iraq for more than five years said being allowed to return to his family shouldn't mask the injustice he was forced to endure. Australian engineer Robert Pether, 50, was reunited with his family in Ireland on Monday after being allowed to leave Iraq having been sent to jail over a contract dispute involving his employer. Mr Pether was released from prison last year but had to remain in Iraq because he was barred from leaving due to financial claims linked to the case. Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, both of whom lived in Dubai at the time, had travelled to Iraq for what they expected to be a routine business meeting but ended up being jailed in August 2021 and fined $12 million over a contract dispute between their employers and authorities in Baghdad. Mr Radwan has now also left Iraq. “I was an engineer,” said Mr Pether, speaking at a press conference on Monday. “I was an employee doing my job. I had a wife and children waiting for me at home. I was there because I made a choice to help a war-torn country rebuild. I never came home.” The travel ban Baghdad had imposed on Mr Pether and Mr Radwan led to the office of the US Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs to push for their release. That followed a call from Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, calling for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family. Since his release, Mr Pether had stayed either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family. During his detention, Mr Pether's health deteriorated, which led to the office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issuing a statement in June, highlighting the “particularly alarming” situation, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”. Mr Pether said that “coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected. It wasn't. Not even close. Coming home is not exoneration and being allowed to leave is not justice. “Our convictions have not been overturned. Neither of us has been exonerated. We were innocent when we were taken on April 7, 2021 and we remain innocent today.” Mr Pether said that when he was released from prison he was only hours from death, with his body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, only to find that he remained trapped in Iraq. “I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital,” said Mr Pether. “Travel bans prevented me from returning to my family and from accessing the medical treatment I desperately needed outside Iraq.” Mr Pether said he was forced to sign a waiver before being allowed to leave Iraq and return to his family. “I signed it because I wanted to go home. There was no choice. After more than five years, with my health deteriorating and my family waiting for me, there was no meaningful choice between signing a document and remaining trapped in Iraq,” he said. “So, I want to be very clear about something. I am incredibly grateful to be standing here. I am overwhelmed to finally be home. But gratitude for being home does not erase what happened to me for even one second. Freedom should never have been something that had to be bargained for.” He also spoke of the emotional impact felt by his family and praised his wife for her campaigning on his behalf. “My wife and my children have lived this every single day with me. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try to bring me home,” said Mr Pether. “They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances no child should ever have to carry. I am so thankful for my wife Desree, always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her, too.” Ms Wong released a statement on Monday morning. “The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government's decision to allow Robert Pether to leave Iraq today,” she said. “I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family. “Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country. “I thank the Australian officials whose tireless work helped achieve this outcome, as well as the Irish authorities for their close co-operation throughout this process. I wish Mr Pether and his family all the very best as they reunite,” Ms Wong said.

title: Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief
description: Russian strikes were carried out within hours of the announcement
content: US President Donald Trump's declaration of an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement. The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes. Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent. The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel. “Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes. “Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.” The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets. But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said. That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said. Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow. He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said. Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added. Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt. Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production. Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India , Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed. The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease. S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said. Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said. About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery. Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe. That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said. Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes. Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict. “Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

title: MEP Raphael Glucksmann wins centre-left primary to run for French presidency
description: Pro-Ukrainian candidate, 46, has distanced himself from Emmanuel Macron's pro-business policies
content: Raphael Glucksmann, a pro-Ukraine defender of liberal democracy, has won a centre-left presidential primary, paving the way for him to run next year in the race to succeed President French Emmanuel Macron . Mr Glucksmann won with 66 per cent of the vote. He will now seek to unify the left in the hope of winning next year's election in which far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite. “We are going to put an end to the psychological, cultural, political and ideological hegemony of brutes over the French left,” Mr Glucksmann, 46, told radio France Inter on Monday. “Finally, we have a democratic left that is regaining momentum and can win the presidential election.” Mr Glucksmann is co-president of centre-left political party Place Publique. He has been a member of the European Parliament since 2019 and is a prominent supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and of the Uighur minority in China. His campaign has highlighted the role of his partner, Lebanese-French journalist Lea Salame, who has had to step back from presenting the evening news on national broadcaster France 2 to avoid accusations of any conflict of interest. Ms Salame, the daughter of prominent Lebanese diplomat Ghassan Salame, will continue to anchor a weekly non-political talk show. “Thinking of Lea Salame,” Valerie Trierweiler, a journalist and former partner of former socialist president Francois Hollande, wrote on X immediately after the announcement of Mr Glucksmann's victory late on Sunday. Mr Glucksmann faces an uphill battle to be elected, with recent polls projecting Ms Le Pen to win more than 30 per cent of the vote, and hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon and centre-right former prime minister Edouard Philippe trailing at around 15 per cent. Mr Glucksmann is sitting at about 9 per cent. The first round of the election takes place in April 2027. Divisions on the left are viewed as the main obstacle to defeating Ms Le Pen's far-right political party, the National Rally, which has never governed in France. Founded by her father Jean-Marie Le Pen and Nazi sympathisers in the 1970s, its popularity has skyrocketed in recent years as the party has campaigned to demonstrate more moderate views. The centre has so far struggled to make its voice heard in the presidential campaign. Mr Glucksmann has rejected the possibility of an alliance with Mr Melenchon. A controversial topic of the left's campaign has been the Gaza war . Mr Melenchon describes Israel's military campaign as genocide, while Mr Glucksmann uses expressions such as “war crimes” and “crimes against humanity”. His critics have attempted to portray him as holding similar views to the sitting president, Mr Macron, who has used comparable rhetoric on the Israel-Palestine conflict, while also remaining staunchly pro-Ukraine. However, Mr Glucksmann has distanced himself from Mr Macron's pro-business policies by championing measures such as increasing taxation on inheritance. In power since 2017, Mr Macron cannot run again next year. Since losing a majority in parliament last year after a snap election, Mr Macron's government has struggled to implement new policies and has had to freeze what many regard as much-needed pension reforms. Many residential candidates, such as Mr Philippe, have distanced themselves from Mr Macron's legacy as France struggles with a debt crisis, social unrest and nationwide school protests .

title: UAE approves 2027-2029 budget with Dh292.5bn in spending
description: Allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to previous three years
content: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday. The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion. Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement. The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X. The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle , focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency. It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services. The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week. The Iran war has tipped the Middle East into one of its worst geopolitical crises in decades. The conflict, which began on February 28, led to Iranian strikes on its Arab neighbours and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, continues to grow despite the conflict. Ratings agency Fitch said on Monday that the UAE non-oil growth model is broadly resilient to the war baseline. The non-oil growth model of the UAE has leveraged a role as a hub between Asia and Europe “backed by a favourable operating environment, supportive government policy, and the ability to attract and retain foreign labour and visitors”, it said in a report. It added that it expects further measures to “improve the operating environment along with a smoothing of administrative procedures” for corporates and residents, backed by higher spending and other sources of financial support at the sovereign and government-related entity level. “Fitch sees structural strengths that will support the resilience of the non-oil economy. However, a persistent period of regional insecurity will call into question logistical advantages and perceptions of the country as a commercial and financial centre and tourism destination,” said Paul Gamble, senior director at Fitch Ratings. The approval of the budget confirms the UAE government’s “keenness to achieve a balance between current development requirements and investment in future opportunities, and to establish a government financial system characterised by flexibility, efficiency and sustainability”, the media office said on Monday. It enhances the UAE’s position among the most advanced and prosperous countries in the world, it added. Budget breakdown for 2027: Dh34.6 billion (38.4 per cent) – Social development and social benefits Dh29.1 billion (32.3 per cent) – Government affairs Dh17.8 billion (19.7 per cent) – Federal expenses Dh5.6 billion (6.2 per cent) – Financial assets and investments Dh3 billion (3.4 per cent) – Infrastructure and economic resources

title: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
description: Kingdom's capital hosts WPC Energy Congress this week amid escalating security fears
content: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier. “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress . “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.” The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack. But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time. “Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.” The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added. He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline , which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd. The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added. “Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said. At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”. The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

title: UAE teenager Mariam Kareem’s stunning rise from school runner to Asian Games champion
description: Diamond League, World Championships and LA 2028 all on the agenda for 18-year-old hurdler after breakthrough in Japan
content: After a dream summer that saw her place fourth in the 400m hurdles at the World Athletics U20 Championships and clinch gold at the Asian Games, Emirati teenager Mariam Kareem is still trying to wrap her head around everything she has accomplished over the past couple of months. The 18-year-old hurdler started her season running 57.39 seconds at a Grand Prix in Addis Ababa in April and finished it with a stunning 54.31s to top the podium at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, two weeks ago. The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record. In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium. She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold. “I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National . “After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction. So I was expecting a very fast time, but not that fast or a gold medal. In Japan, I had a lot of ups and downs there. I really struggled with the time zone change. “I was tense, I was scared. I was a bit sick, but thank Allah for everything. I just had to put everything behind me and focus on my personal events.” Kareem’s success in Nagoya made headlines, not just in the UAE , but across the region, and she was given quite the reception when she returned to the Emirates, both at the airport and at a special event held by her sponsors 'On' to celebrate her historic gold medal. “I'm still taking everything slowly. There's a lot of people around, a lot of messages, a lot of congratulations, a lot of places I've been to. It's my first time being in this situation, so I'm taking it easy,” said Kareem. “It really took me by surprise. I’m just trying to wrap my head around all the news, the messages, and to keep on doing the good work. I really hope I can keep up with the work and continue.” Things have been happening fast for Kareem. It was just three years ago that she was scouted by the UAE Athletics Federation, which saw potential in her when she was competing at her high school in Dubai and at her local club. Kareem, who liked running but wasn’t really into competing, was encouraged by a coach from the federation to take athletics seriously. She was barely 16 at the time. “He was really a great mentor for me,” Kareem recalls. “He advised me; he talked to me like a father. He told me, ‘Continue training; I believe you have a potential in you. You can go far. There's a bright future ahead’. “I was not really into athletics. I just loved running, but not really that passionate to compete at the high level. So he talked me into it.” Kareem initially ran 200m and 400m flat, but urged by her coach, who saw she had the height and flexibility, switched to the 400m hurdles, which has become her signature event. “Representing my country with pride, it was something that I really wanted to do. So I was happy to. I'm going out there, coming back with medals, representing my country, raising the country flag,” she said. “So I was really happy and excited and I love doing it. So I'm going to continue doing it and keep on the good work.” Kareem is achieving what no Emirati woman has achieved before, and she is well aware that there is the potential to make history every time she steps on the track. “For now, there is no pressure, but it's still giving me motivation to go forward, to do more and so that at least our country can be up in the world,” she explained. “My aim is to continue raising the national flag up and keep making names for the country before anybody can come and take the place from me. Because I cannot be here forever. So, there's still going to be young athletes that can still come from here.” Kareem is the fifth of six siblings, none of whom are athletes. She jokes that they all want to start running now that they’re witnessing her success. Her mother has been her biggest supporter from day one, and she remembers her father being sceptical of her running career at first. That scepticism has since dissipated, and her father was the first to call to congratulate her when she took gold in Nagoya. “After I collected the medal, my dad called and he was so proud of me, was so excited,” she revealed. “Coming from a family like that, and I'm making names, going far, he’s like, ‘Ah, I should have supported her when I had the chance’. I was like, ‘It's OK, you still have the chance, I'm very young, you can still support me’,” she added with a laugh. Kareem is now enjoying some well-deserved downtime during this offseason before she starts training again for her upcoming goals. “Getting the gold medal in the Asian Games and the Games record has given me the confidence that I can still achieve a lot in the future. So I want to improve my performances and go to compete at the higher level,” she said. “I'd like to go the Olympics , the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hard. Not just to compete, I want to go there and have fun, be the best, and be at the podium. So, that's just my aims for the future.” Before the LA 2028 Olympics, Kareem is hoping she can compete in the Diamond League in 2027 to line up against the world’s best for an entire season. She immediately lights up when asked which athlete she'd most like to meet if she makes the Olympics. “Sydney [McLaughlin-Levrone]. I'd love to meet her. She's a role model to me,” she says with a grin. “The fact that she can do anything. She can play in 400 flat, 400 hurdles; she can do multiple events. And she doesn't look like she's doing more, but she's giving all her best. It feels like she's not doing anything. “I want to be like her, at least make names, have a lot, the world records, six-time world record. I really hope to be at the LA Olympics, so that at least I can see her and compete with her at the lanes. So that's my biggest dream right now, to compete with her, yes.” In the span of three years, Kareem went from being a kid who loved running but was not too keen on competing to being an Asian Games champion and Asian U20 record holder. What were her biggest lessons during this transformation? “Athletics taught me a lot. Taught me discipline, taught me patience, taught me consistency. I think I've learnt a lot,” she says. “I've learnt how to stay consistent in what I'm doing and keep doing what I love and keep making names, keep going forward. From one minute to another, now I'm [running] 54, so that is consistency. “I keep on training, I keep on believing in myself, my coach, my teammates, our training. I know I can go further, I can run very fast. So I just have learnt that consistency is the key.”

title: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027
description: IFC Oman working on legal framework, rule book and registry system
content: Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year. IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday. A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules. A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added. “IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business." IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre. The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said. Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil , with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country. It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy. Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

title: Dozens of gold miners killed in Sudan strike, rights and political groups say
description: Civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold
content: Dozens of gold miners were killed in an air strike in northern Sudan at the weekend, near the border with Egypt, watchdogs said. Emergency Lawyers, a human rights monitor, the civilian-led Somoud alliance and the Sudan Doctors' Network all reported the strike and accused the military-aligned government in Sudan of not doing enough to protect its people and the country's territorial integrity. “We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somoud said. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bear the responsibility for what happens in areas under their control.” Sudan's military-led Sovereign Council said the air strike took place in the border region with Egypt. “The leadership in the two brotherly nations have been in contact since immediately after the incident took place to guarantee the protection of lives and safeguarding relations between the two peoples, find out the circumstances of the incident and give public opinion ownership of the facts,” claimed the council. Egypt's military issued a statement late on Monday evening saying its troops and police were continuing to counter "illegal" gold prospecting in the country's eastern desert. It said it had dropped flyers on what it called criminal elements, warning them they must stop "so that full sovereignty is safeguarded inside the Egyptian state's borders". "The Egyptian armed forces emphasises the depth of bonds between the Egyptian and Sudanese nations on the political and popular levels. The peaceful coexistence that millions of Sudanese enjoy while on Egyptian territory is the best proof of that," said the statement. It warned both Egyptians and Sudanese against believing "rumours" . Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and the Sudanese Foreign Minister in the military-backed government, Mohieldin Salem, also spoke on the phone on Monday evening, according to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry. It said the pair “emphasised the mutual respect that binds the two nations, including respect for each other's sovereignty and the safety and integrity of their territories and borders”. Images ​and videos shared online, which The National was unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn in rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s. There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative sources of income. Egypt's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drug and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested. Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign interests seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011. The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold . Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million. Official figures place government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion, but experts say smuggling and local use of gold outside official channels account for far more. In 2025, for example, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes, but only 20 tonnes were exported formally, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated locally in primitive refineries. Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

title: Morgan Jay in Abu Dhabi: Why the viral comedian is at his best off-script
description: US comic brings musical humour to Etihad Arena, but his spontaneous crowd work delivers the biggest laughs
content: “Are you a goofy guy?” It’s a question I’ve heard repeatedly on Instagram and TikTok, where comedian Morgan Jay’s face seems to appear whenever I scroll. On Sunday, I headed to Etihad Arena to find out whether I was, indeed, a “goofy girl” as he brought The Goofy Guy Tour to the capital to open Abu Dhabi Comedy Season . The show was phone-free , with attendees required to secure their devices in pouches. It’s a familiar policy at comedy gigs, but there was a certain irony in putting away the screen through which I’d discovered him. For once, I would be watching an entire performance rather than whichever snippets my algorithm decided to show me. Looking around, the audience was mostly Gen Z and millennials , perhaps a sign of how Jay became so popular thanks to social media. I suspect I wasn’t the only person whose introduction to his comedy had come through a short clip while scrolling . Those viral videos often show him moving through the crowd, turning exchanges with audience members into pure comedy. Watching them, I’d wondered how that spontaneity would translate to an arena show in Abu Dhabi – and whether the moments that made me laugh on my phone could sustain a full evening. The show opened with Emirati-Omani comedian Abz Ali, who delivered a locally focused stand-up routine, drawing laughs with observations about the UAE’s residents and the stereotypes surrounding them. With the crowd warmed up, he introduced Jay to an enthusiastic audience. The US comic emerged in a white T-shirt and jeans to cheers, immediately running through the arena, high-fiving fans and pausing to chat along the way. Spotting a man in a kandura wearing AirPods, he stopped to ask what he was listening to – drawing laughter from across the arena. Music also formed a substantial part of the performance. With his acoustic guitar, Jay sang songs including Friend Zone and Would You Be My Dad? The latter, delivered with Auto-Tune, mixed comedy with the sadness of growing up after losing his father to cancer at a young age. He also adapted his Lol Haha Lmfao Jaja bit for the Abu Dhabi audience, replacing “jaja” with “As-salamu alaykum” – a playful touch that connected his familiar material to the local audience. The show, which lasted more than an hour, was enjoyable, with crowd work its strongest element. Although the musical moments were funny, I found myself wishing he spent more time interacting with the audience. His quick, witty responses, facial expressions and ability to find humour in unexpected situations were what I had come to see – and what made me laugh most. Perhaps that expectation came from the clips I’d seen online. Seeing the full show gave me a broader sense of his act, but it also confirmed which part I enjoyed most. It was a strong start to Abu Dhabi Comedy Season, with Russell Peters, Mo Amer, Maz Jobrani and Whitney Cummings among the names still to come. Jobrani’s appearance will also mark a farewell as he has announced it will be his final Abu Dhabi show, saying he is slowing down to focus on his health and spend more time with his family. Did I leave knowing whether I was a goofy girl? Perhaps. But I’d happily have traded a few songs for more of the spontaneous exchanges that brought me there. Abu Dhabi Comedy Season runs until January 31

title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
description: World Bank says 'small AI' could generate ​enormous ​opportunities for developing countries
content: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

title: Military superiority cannot guarantee peace in the Middle East
description: The solution lies in confronting the political interests that keep conflicts alive, and giving the Gulf states a greater say in regional security
content: The deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday was another reminder of how vulnerable civilian life and economic activity have become to the region’s wars. At least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured and air traffic was disrupted. The consequences extended well beyond the airport itself. The attack also illustrated a larger strategic problem – an armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone else. This has become one of the defining features of conflict in the Middle East. Military power remains decisive in determining what happens on the battlefield, but it has proved far less effective in deciding what happens afterwards. The ability to inflict damage is increasingly detached from the ability to impose a political settlement. In some cases, preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives has become a strategy in its own right. The war involving Iran, the US and Israel has brought this problem into sharp focus. Washington and Israel enjoy military and technological advantages that Tehran cannot match. Iran has suffered extensive military and economic damage. Yet it retains the means to prolong the confrontation and threaten interests far beyond its borders, particularly through its ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. This is not a balance of military power. Iran cannot impose losses on the US comparable to those it has sustained. However, it can complicate Washington’s calculations , raise the economic cost of continuing the war and make a satisfactory political conclusion harder to achieve. American military superiority, meanwhile, has not been sufficient to compel Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. The result is a confrontation in which military pressure continues without producing the political outcome either side seeks. What we are witnessing might be described as the emergence of a “veto over peace”. Certain states and armed groups have acquired the means to obstruct settlements even when they lack the power to impose their own. Their influence comes from the damage they can threaten, the agreements they can undermine and the violence they can resume. Such a veto requires no formal recognition. A group capable of attacking an airport, disrupting a shipping lane or reopening a military front can make its effective consent necessary for a settlement to endure. There is, of course, an important distinction between opposing an unjust agreement and deliberately sabotaging peace. A settlement that ignores legitimate rights or leaves the causes of conflict unresolved may create the conditions for another war. The problem arises when actors use the threat of renewed violence to preserve political influence or economic privileges that might be diminished by a return to stability. This points to a distinction often overlooked in discussions about ending wars. Some conflicts continue because the parties cannot bring them to a conclusion. Others persist because influential actors have little interest in doing so. In the first case, the obstacle lies in the balance of power and the difficulty of agreeing on enforceable terms. In the second, the obstacle is political. War may protect established interests, strengthen military institutions, postpone domestic decisions or provide leverage that would be lost in peacetime. Both conditions can exist within the same conflict. Iran illustrates the complexity . The national interest in ending isolation and restoring economic activity does not necessarily coincide with the interests of every institution that has gained influence during decades of sanctions and confrontation. Greater openness could benefit Iranian society while unsettling entrenched centres of power. That does not mean these actors necessarily oppose every settlement. But any agreement that alters the internal distribution of power may encounter resistance. This raises a question that goes beyond the terms negotiated with Tehran: can Iran’s political leadership ensure that all those who possess the means of escalation will comply ? An understanding over the Strait of Hormuz, for example, could be negotiated through diplomatic channels and then undermined by a single maritime incident. The problem is especially difficult when those capable of wrecking an agreement do not bear the full political or economic consequences of doing so. Similar difficulties are apparent elsewhere. Israel’s military superiority has not resolved the political future of Gaza or the Palestinian question. In Lebanon, durable stability remains tied to the state’s authority over decisions of war and peace, the future of Hezbollah’s weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory. In Yemen, weakening the Houthis militarily would not, by itself, resolve the divisions that have undermined the state. These conflicts are different in their causes and responsibilities. What they share is a widening gap between the ability to stop fighting temporarily and the ability to prevent its return. Who, then, can actually end these wars? In many cases, the necessary authority is divided among several actors. One has the military power to halt hostilities. Another has the political authority to negotiate and make concessions. Others may hold the means to enforce an agreement or undermine it. A government can sign a peace deal without being able to bind the armed groups operating within its territory. An external power can enforce a ceasefire without resolving the political grievances that threaten it. Even the most capable guarantor will struggle if those able to restart the fighting believe the benefits outweigh the costs. This is also where the limits of American power become apparent. The US remains the most consequential external security actor in the Middle East. No other country can match its regional military capabilities and intelligence resources. Yet Washington's ability to change the military balance does not give it equivalent control over the political decisions of every actor involved. Additional mediation by China, Russia or European powers may help create opportunities for compromise. It cannot substitute for political authority capable of delivering on an agreement. For the Gulf states, these questions are particularly consequential . Their economies depend on reliable maritime access, functioning airports, secure energy infrastructure and the confidence of international investors. Even limited military disruptions can have effects that extend far beyond the immediate target. The challenge is therefore not confined to preventing another major war. It also involves reducing the ability of hostile actors to keep Gulf economies under the persistent threat of disruption. The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem. Any agreement that restores navigation would be welcome, but its terms matter as much as its immediate results. Reopening the waterway in exchange for recognising an Iranian right to determine which vessels may pass would merely institutionalise a new source of insecurity. Co-operation among the states bordering the strait on navigation and maritime safety is both legitimate and necessary. Granting any one state discretionary political control over an international shipping route is a different proposition. Gulf states must therefore have a substantive role in shaping the regional security arrangements that follow the war. Their security cannot be dependent on understandings negotiated by others, particularly when those understandings could leave the sources of future threats intact. Military deterrence remains essential, but it must be accompanied by stronger economic resilience, diversified trade and energy routes, and diplomatic arrangements that make renewed aggression costly. Above all, the interests of states exposed to the consequences of war must be represented in the negotiations intended to end it. The Middle East’s wars are not necessarily impossible to resolve. History offers many examples of conflicts that resisted military victory but eventually ended through political compromise. What changed was not always the balance of military power. Often, it was the calculation of those who had previously found reason to continue fighting. That is the political challenge facing the region today. Ending wars requires more than persuading adversaries to accept a ceasefire. It requires changing the interests that make renewed conflict attractive. As long as societies bear the greatest costs of war while some of those with the power to reignite it continue to benefit from its continuation, peace will remain fragile. The real measure of a settlement is not whether it stops the fighting today, but whether it deprives those who would resume it tomorrow of the incentive and the means to do so.

title: Mohamed Salah sets Turkish Super Lig record with 10 goal contributions
description: Egyptian forward has reached the milestone in only seven matches
content: Mohamed Salah set a new Turkish Super Lig record over the weekend, becoming the fastest player to register 10 goal contributions. The Egyptian laid on an assist for teammate Francolino in Trabzonspor's 3-0 win over Samsunspor on Saturday; it was his third assist of the campaign. Added to his seven goals since his summer move from Liverpool , Salah has reached double figures in goal contributions in only seven games for his new club. Salah leads the Super Lig scoring charts alongside Gift Orban of Umit Sortif. Victor Osimhen (Galatasaray), Vedat Muriqi (Fenerbahce) and Eldor Shomurodov (Istanbul Basaksehir) have all scored six goals. His assist against Samsunspor also took him level at the top of the assists chart. Trabzonspor are fifth in the Turkish Super Lig, three points behind league leaders Galatasaray, whom Trabzon beat 4-0 before the recent international break. A return to domestic action comes after Salah endured a turbulent time with his national team during the international break. Salah left Egypt's camp ahead of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan after a reported falling out with coach Hossam Hassan . Salah was substituted in Egypt's previous match against Angola after only 60 minutes, with Pharaohs coach Hassan saying Salah was taken off for "technical reasons". News then broke that Salah had left the national team camp, with the Egypt captain also said to have taken exception to Hassan's comments about injured goalkeeper Mohamed El Shenawy. The Egyptian Football Association released a statement saying that the plan, made before the Angola game, was always for Salah to sit out the match against South Sudan in Juba as the game would be played on an artificial pitch, before rejoining the rest of the squad for the friendly against South Africa in Cairo on October 4. Salah did not return, and Egypt lost the match 1-0. Several news outlets reported that he travelled to England before returning to Turkey to begin training with Trabzonspor ahead of the league's resumption on October 10.

title: Canelo Alvarez 'fears nothing' and will fight in Riyadh despite security concerns
description: Saudi Arabian promoter Turki Alalshikh says October 31 bout against Christian Mbilli to go ahead as planned
content: Boxing legend Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez is set to defy security concerns and go ahead with his bout against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh, according to organiser Turki Alalshikh. Alvarez is slated to face Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title in the Saudi capital on October 31, but the event has been thrown into doubt after several days of deadly strikes on the city. One person was killed and 11 injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, according to Saudi authorities. That came a day after a Houthi-claimed strike killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Alalshikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority and a global boxing power broker, said in a social media post that the event would go ahead as planned, and that Alvarez had confirmed he was happy to proceed. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Alalshikh posted on X on Sunday night. “He fears nothing. “My country is home to the two Holy Mosques, land of peace, safety, rich civilisation, deep history, and kind-hearted people. Thank you to everyone who checked in and showed support. Hard times reveal true friends.” The Saudi Pro League postponed Sunday's match between Abha and Al Faisaly, while it remains unclear whether Monday's Asian Champions League match between Al Nassr and Neftchi Fergana will go ahead. “The SPL confirmed the decision was made following a review of the circumstances surrounding the match,” the league said. "[The decision was taken] in accordance with approved regulatory procedures, ensuring that situations beyond the clubs' control are addressed while maintaining the continuity of the competition.” Abha is around 900km south-west of Riyadh and approximately 200km from the Yemen border. Saudi sport has seen several major events cancelled this year, including April's Formula One Grand Prix and next month's World Rally Championship. The October 31 boxing card at Kingdom Arena is dubbed “Mexico vs the Rest of the World” and is headlined by Alvarez's attempt to recapture a version of the 168lb world title. The 36-year-old (63-3-2) has not fought since losing to Terence Crawford last September . It was reported by The Athletic on Sunday night that Alvarez remained eager to press ahead with the Riyadh bout, and that broadcaster DAZN was advancing in its plans to cover the event on the ground in Saudi Arabia.

title: Gargash calls for stronger Gulf security and collective defence
description: Adviser to UAE President says attacks on Saudi Arabia undermine security of all Gulf states
content: Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, has called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence, warning that threats against one Gulf state put the entire region at risk. In a statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible". “Since the start of the aggression against the Gulf Arab states, based on the aggressor's mistaken assessment that they were the weakest link in a war we sought to avoid, it has become clear that we are all targeted and that our security is indivisible,” he said. He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added. Dr Gargash called for renewed regional co-ordination, particularly in security and defence, and stronger collective security arrangements. “There is a need to revitalise joint Gulf action, particularly in its security and defence dimensions, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he said. He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges. “This is the dimension in which there has been a serious shortcoming, which encouraged others to overstep against us,” Dr Gargash said. “Gulf security is a shared responsibility that cannot tolerate neglect or delay."

title: UAE’s ODI status under threat after dismal series in United States
description: National team will be playing for survival at World Cup Qualifier Play-off after three defeats in Dallas
content: The UAE’s leading cricketers started their tour of Dallas for their latest Cricket World Cup League Two tri-series conflicted by feelings of a potential loss of earnings. Now they face the prospect of having to play for survival as one-day international cricketers altogether after a dismal sequence of performances. The national team suffered a third loss in a row on Sunday as they were soundly beaten by the United States by five wickets. They lost with over 11 overs to spare. So consigned to their fate were they, they did not even bother bringing up the field to prevent the single that was needed to win the game. It leaves them last placed in CWCL2, and in a fight to retain their status in ODI cricket. It is a sorry state for a side who have underachieved for years, and now face the threat of relegation to the third tier of 50-over international cricket. Even with one more tri-series still to play, involving the Netherlands and Oman in the UAE later this month, they are now guaranteed to be playing in the World Cup Qualifier Play-off in December. They had started the trip to Dallas with fanciful ambitions of playing their way into the top four of CWCL2. That would have avoided the need to participate in the play-off, and advancing straight to the global qualifier in February. More pressingly, it would have made the players available for the ILT20 in December. Six of the 15-player squad had earned contracts to play in that competition, on deals ranging from $10,000 to $95,000. To avoid the scheduling clash, they would have had to have won all eight of their remaining matches, and hoped results elsewhere went their way. Instead, they saw one match washed out, and lost the other three. Finishing in the top six of CWCL2 now looks beyond the UAE, too. To do that, they would have to win all four matches against the Netherlands and Oman, and hope sixth-placed Nepal lost all their remaining three matches. So now ODI status – and the vast tranche of ICC funding that it unlocks – is in jeopardy. The rules governing ODI status are complex, and have yet to be publicly confirmed by the ICC. The play-off is an eight-team tournament involving the bottom four sides from CWCL2, plus two sides each from the two feeder Challenger Leagues that make up the third tier of ODI cricket’s competition structure. It is likely the UAE will likely have to finish above both sides who won those feeder leagues for them to retain their ODI privileges. Italy – who have former UAE coach Dougie Brown on their coaching staff - finished top of Challenge League B, and came up to the play-off with Uganda. Challenge League A will conclude in Kenya this month. Jersey are top of the table, with Kuwait in second. If the UAE are to continue in ODI cricket via the play-off, they will have to find a remedy to their chronic batting failings. After making 330 in their first match in Dallas, they crumbled to 134 against Namibia, then 213 in the last game against the United States. “It was tough luck for us on this tour,” Harpreet Bhatia , the UAE captain, said after defeat on Sunday. “I hope the boys will learn from this series. We were always short of runs in the last couple of games. We will work things out and see what we can do from here. “The way we played the first game, it was close. We scored 330, then after that there was a problem with scoring runs in the last two games. “We were always short. I feel we were 40 or 50 runs short today and if we could have got 280 I think it could have been a good game for us.”

title: Timeline: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi airports
description: Riyadh has been struck four times in five days, killing at least 20 people
content: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports in the past week, hitting sites in Riyadh, Abha, Jazan and Najran, with a projectile also damaging Dammam's airport. The strikes have disrupted air travel and caused civilian casualties, with Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport bearing the brunt of the aggression. The escalation included a missile attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured hundreds, Saudi authorities said. A further attack on Riyadh airport on Sunday killed one more person. October 6 : Saudi authorities reported attacks on King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, in the south. Three people were injured. Saudi air defences also intercepted a ballistic missile fired at Khamis Mushait. October 7 : Strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport killed three foreign citizens and injured 36, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks. October 8 : At least one attack hit King Khalid International Airport. Three Saudi citizens were killed, including an airline pilot , and several people were injured. An aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia was damaged and smoke was seen rising from the airport. October 10 : A Houthi missile struck King Khalid International Airport, initially killing 12 people and injuring 309, Saudi authorities said. The dead included Saudis and citizens of Bangladesh, the US, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Syria and Sudan. The toll rose to 13 on Sunday after an injured Indian citizen died. Airport operations were suspended and flights were cancelled or diverted. October 11 : A projectile struck Terminals 3 and 4 at Riyadh airport, killing a Pakistani citizen and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition also said a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and that the damage was being assessed. The Houthis claimed responsibility. Riyadh's airport has been struck four times in five days, and at least 20 people have been killed. The Houthis have said Saudi airspace is a military zone. The coalition has vowed to “respond decisively” and says it is continuing strikes on Houthi launch sites.

title: Ivan Toney in outstanding form but UAE’s Al Wasl can cause upset: AFC Champions League talking points
description: Two-time Asian champions Al Ahli Saudi face Dubai side, while Al Ain and Shabab Al Ahli each look to build on strong starts
content: UAE clubs might have been battling to bridge the gap to their star-studded Saudi Arabian rivals in recent seasons. But there are signs that sides from the Emirates could challenge for honours in the AFC Champions League again this term. Al Ain made a major statement when they thrashed Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr 4-0 on the opening day of the AFC Champions League Elite season last month. Now Al Wasl have their chance to make a mark against celebrated Saudi Arabian opposition, too, when Asian competition returns this week. Over the past two seasons in continental competition, Wasl have twice been beaten 4-0 by Nassr – with Ronaldo scoring in each fixture. And yet they will have reason for optimism when they host another expensively assembled Saudi club, Al Ahli , in Zabeel on Monday night. On the surface, it seems like a daunting task for the Dubai side. Ahli have been champions of Asia in each of the past two seasons. Ivan Toney, their English striker, has scored 11 goals in eight games at the start of the Saudi Pro League season. That is quite the haul, given Ahli have not exactly dominated: they have lost three of those eight matches. Plus, many of Ahli’s players are returning to club commitments buoyed by success with the Saudi Arabia national team in the Arabian Gulf Cup. That includes Feras Al Buraikan , the Ahli striker who scored in the final win against the UAE. But Wasl have made a bright start to the season themselves. They have lost just once in the UAE Pro League and are the division’s leading scorers. They also had an uplifting three matches in the Adib Cup while many stars were away on international duty, winning all three. Wasl can pick at the fragile confidence of their guests, who are in the early stages of a rebuild following the departure of some influential figures this summer. Marino Pusic, the new coach, had big boots to fill when he joined the Jeddah giants ahead of this season. His predecessor, Matthias Jaissle , was wildly popular. As well he should have been, seeing as he guided them to successive AFC Champions League titles. Pusic arrived fresh from an indifferent spell with Al Jazira in Abu Dhabi, where he underachieved with an enviable playing squad. When he arrived at Ahli, he inherited a squad that was newly shorn of key players such as Franck Kessie and Riyad Mahrez , who was the difference between the two sides when they played in Dubai two seasons ago. With Iranian striker Mehdi Taremi leading the line, Wasl will hope they can heap more pressure on Pusic. Al Ain might have started the Champions League campaign with the most spectacular display, crushing Ronaldo’s Nassr at the Hazza bin Zayed Stadium. In the meantime, though, they have had a reality check. Their lengthy unbeaten run in domestic football – they won the double last season undefeated – ended during the international break. They lost twice in two games in the Adib Cup, first to Wasl, then more surprisingly, Ajman at home. While that competition is the least valued among UAE’s major tournaments, and many of the side’s stars were away with their national teams, coach Vladimir Ivic was not happy with what he saw. He will be hoping a return to the big league, with a game against Iraq’s Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basra, will help resharpen the focus. Shabab Al Ahli, the third UAE side in Champions League Elite action this week, are going to have a taste of what might have been on Tuesday night. The 2024/25 UAE double winners are facing Al Ittihad at King Abdullah Sports City in Jeddah. They were within an ace of playing at that venue in the biggest fixture in continental club football last season, only to be deprived of a place in the Elite final by a shocking VAR controversy . The player who was central to that heartache has since played at that 62,000-capacity venue – only to taste yet more woe. Guilherme Bala, whose late equaliser against Machida Zelvia was ruled out by that VAR call in the semi-final last season, was part of the UAE side that played in the Gulf Cup final on Tuesday. They were soundly beaten by Saudi Arabia. Now Bala and his club colleagues will be hoping they can exact some semblance of revenge when they face Ittihad.

title: Dubai resident leaves Iraq after being detained for five years
description: Robert Pether and co-worker were jailed over contract dispute involving their employer
content: Update : 'Being allowed to leave does not erase injustice', says Pether A Dubai resident detained for five years over a contract dispute has left Iraq to be reunited with his family. Australian engineer Robert Pether, 50, was released from prison in Baghdad in June last year but had remained in Iraq because he was barred from leaving owing to financial claims linked to the case. Mr Pether arrived in Dublin Airport on Monday afternoon, where he was reunited with his family who now reside in Ireland, public broadcaster RTE reported. "The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government's decision to allow Robert Pether to leave Iraq today," said Penny Wong, Australia's Foreign Minister. "I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family. Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country. "I thank the Australian officials whose tireless work helped achieve this outcome, as well as the Irish authorities for their close co-operation throughout this process. I wish Mr Pether and his family all the very best as they reunite." Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, who both lived in Dubai at the time, were jailed in August 2021 and fined $12 million after a contract dispute between his employer and authorities in Baghdad. Mr Radwan has also left Iraq. They were released from prison last year. In 2025, the office of the US Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs pushed for his release. That followed a call from Ms Wong for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family. Since his release from prison, Mr Pether had stayed either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family. UN experts expressed “grave concern” earlier this year over the health of Mr Pether. The office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issued a statement in June, highlighting the “particularly alarming” situation given Mr Pether's declining health, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued a report in 2022 describing Mr Pether’s detention as “arbitrary and in contravention of international law”. A ruling in 2023 by the International Chamber of Commerce's International Court of Arbitration said Iraq's central bank was to blame for the contractual dispute. Mr Pether and Mr Radwan were arrested when they travelled to Iraq for what they thought was a routine business meeting. Employed as an engineer in Dubai for CME, Mr Pether was contracted to work on the central bank's headquarters near the Tigris River. The men were detained during the meeting. They each received a five-year jail sentence and were ordered by an Iraqi court to pay $12 million. The dispute was over a $33 million contract awarded to CME in 2015. The project was put on hold a year later, with plummeting oil prices and Iraq’s war against ISIS given as the main reasons. Operations resumed in 2018, with CME working for 39 of the 48 months as set out in the contract. Payment was received for 32 of those months before it was withheld. CME was asked by the central bank to extend the contract by three months to make up for work suspended because of the coronavirus pandemic. The Australian government said previously that it recognised the significant impact Mr Pether's detention had on him and his family and pledged to continue to offer consular support in an effort to enable him to leave Iraq.

title: The best EVs to buy in the UAE for every budget
description: From pocket-friendly hatchbacks to luxury SUVs, here are 12 electric vehicles worth considering
content: As recently as five years ago, it seemed unimaginable that electric vehicles would find any traction in the UAE. Given that fuel was relatively cheap in our region and the EV recharging infrastructure was still in its infancy, the business case for battery-powered vehicles seemed tenuous, at best. However, times change and so do buyer demands. Petrol prices are now edging towards Dh4.50 a litre; filling up even a compact Toyota Corolla can cost more than Dh200. For drivers of larger SUVs, the expense is considerably higher – a full tank in the latest Nissan Patrol costs more than Dh400, while older models can guzzle Dh600. In this context, an EV makes financial sense, particularly for people with access to a wall-mounted home charger. Even without one, the savings can be considerable. Depending on the vehicle's battery size, a full charge at a Dewa or Adnoc charging station typically costs little more than Dh80 ($22). Alongside rising petrol prices, the UAE's public EV charging network has continued to expand, with about 2,800 charging points across the country and more expected in the coming years. As electric vehicles become an increasingly practical option for motorists, here are some of the best models currently available in the UAE.
