They had a very good, technically sound plan to try to press us, which was difficult to play out of. Then, at half-time, you could see we made some tactical changes, and a couple of players came on who helped us out as well. Then you could see that we pulled the game towards us, and you had the feeling you were in control of it. Next time, we need to try to start the game like that straight away. Especially here, we need to be able to press their team and control the game. Can you speak a bit about those players coming in, like Carlos Baleba? It's very important. One of the good things about today was that they came on and helped us out a lot - everyone could see it. We needed that extra spark towards the end, those fresh legs. I'm very happy for them as well that they could show themselves, but that's what we've been seeing in training every day, so for us, it's nothing new. We know we have a very deep squad. Those players are going to have to step up this season as well, and I'm happy they were able to do that today. Can I ask about your reflections on the defence so far this season? It feels like there have been a few occasions when there have been errors or miscommunications. I'm wondering how you see it from your position and what conversations you've had. I agree. I think sometimes, in the end, it comes down to a mistake here or there from someone, but it doesn't really start with that. I think it's a team thing. The manager has been hammering home the message about defending as a team and being able to put pressure on the opposition, especially when it comes to crosses. I think today was better, but then you see that, in the end, one good cross and one good header can cost you the game, or the win can slip away like that. So I understand what you're saying, but I think we've been trying to make a difference there, and I think it's already been better. It's a pity that today, especially at the end, the win slipped away from us. Looking at the schedule, it's not great. You've got three really tough away games coming up. You said it felt like a loss in a way. How do you stay positive? I mean, you can look at it both ways. We know there are a lot of games coming up very quickly. After a disappointment, you can carry that disappointment with you, or you can move on quickly and focus on the fact that there's another game coming up soon. For me personally, if I haven't had the best game, I'm looking forward to the next one to get that sour feeling out of my mouth. So I think that's the mindset we need to have. We know we showed a lot of good things today as well, so we need to take those positives and learn from the bad things. As you say, there are a lot of very important games coming up, but we also love playing those games. We fought last year to be in the Champions League, so we're very happy to be there. And if you want to go far in that competition, you have to win those games as well.

title: Oscars 2027: All the Arab films submitted for Best International Feature
description: Algeria, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Palestine have entered submissions for the 99th Academy Awards
content: Eight Arab regions have selected the films that will represent them in the Best International Feature Film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. Iraq, Morocco, Palestine, Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan and Saudi Arabia have selected the films that will represent them. Their subjects range from the legacy of Algeria’s civil conflict and Lebanon’s financial crisis to the battle against ISIS in Iraq, the treatment of Moroccan seasonal workers in Spain and daily life during the war in Gaza. The Academy’s September 30 submission deadline has now passed, with the films entering the next stage of consideration. The 15-film shortlist will be announced on December 15, followed by the five final nominees on January 21. The 99th Academy Awards will take place in Los Angeles on March 14, 2027. This year, Tunisia reached the final five with Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Voice of Hind Rajab , after a record four Arab films made the 15-film shortlist . Alongside The Voice of Hind Rajab , the shortlisted films for 2026 were Iraq’s The President’s Cake , Palestine’s Palestine 36 and Jordan’s All That’s Left of You . Ben Hania’s film ultimately became the only one of the four to reach the final nominations . Here are the Arab films to know for 2027. Lebanon has selected Rami Kodeih’s Furies , a heist thriller inspired by the country’s banking crisis. The film follows sisters Maro and Dalia, who plan to break into a bank to recover their savings because they are unable to access the money, partly to pay for Dalia’s life-saving surgery. Kodeih and his wife and co-writer, Nora Mariana, told The National that the premise grew out of their own experience after Mariana needed surgery but was unable to access savings held in a Lebanese bank. Furies , Kodeih’s first feature, has its premiere in the Venezia Spotlight section of this year’s Venice Film Festival, and is backed by George Clooney and Grant Heslov’s Smokehouse Pictures. Lebanon’s selection committee chose the film unanimously. Saudi Arabia has selected Anas Ba Tahaf’s A Matter of Life and Death as its submission for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards. Set in Jeddah, the film stars Sarah Taibah as Hayat, a woman convinced she will die on her 30th birthday. She meets Youssef, played by Yaqoub Al-Farhan, a heart surgeon with an unusually slow heartbeat. Taibah also wrote the screenplay. The film mixes romance, dark comedy and fantasy, using its central relationship to explore mortality and the fear of what comes next. A Matter of Life and Death is set to hit streaming this month, releasing on MBC Shahid on October 22 across the Middle East. Algeria has selected Yanis Koussim’s Roqia , a horror film rooted in the country’s violence during the 1990s. The film centres on an ageing raqi – a spiritual healer – who is living with Alzheimer's disease, alongside an amnesiac man who returns to his village. Moving between the 1990s and the present, it connects supernatural horror with memories of Algeria’s civil conflict. Koussim told The National that the story was informed by his own memories of growing up during the period and by research into roqia. His first feature, Roqia, had its premiere in the Critics’ Week section of the Venice Film Festival in 2025. Algeria previously received five nominations in the category, winning for Z in 1970. Iraq has selected No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman , an action drama by Kurdish-Norwegian filmmaker Halkawt Mustafa. The Kurdish-language film follows Vyan, a sniper who has learnt to suppress her emotions after years of war. When she discovers that her younger sister, believed to have disappeared during a 2014 ISIS assault, may still be alive, she returns to Mosul to find her. Mustafa has said the film was inspired by Kurdish women who fought ISIS and by his encounters with women Peshmerga fighters on the front line in 2014. Starring Kurdish actress Avan Jamal and Norwegian actor Thorbjorn Harr, the film is scheduled to have its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival this week, where it is screening in the Venice Open section, out of competition. The film is a Norway-Iraq-UAE-Sweden co-production, giving this year's Iraqi submission a UAE connection. It is Mustafa's second film to represent Iraq at the Oscars, following El Clasico in 2016. Morocco will be represented by Laila Marrakchi's La Mas Dulce , also known internationally as Strawberries . The film follows Hasna and Meriem, two young Moroccan women who travel to Andalusia to work as seasonal strawberry pickers in the hope of improving the lives of their families. They instead encounter exploitation, harassment and poor working conditions, eventually facing the decision of whether to speak out against those employing them. The film had its premiere in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival in May. Marrakchi has said the project developed after she learnt about Moroccan women working in Spain's strawberry industry and travelled there to understand their experiences. Morocco 's selection committee chose La Mas Dulce unanimously on September 2, citing its subject, technical and artistic qualities as well as its distribution prospects. It was selected from four films under consideration. The film marked Marrakchi's return to Cannes two decades after Marock , her 2005 debut about young people in Casablanca, and followed her 2013 feature Rock the Casbah . Palestine has chosen Ahmed Hassouna's documentary Citizen Osama , filmed in northern Gaza during the war. The 69-minute film follows Osama Al-Ashi, a former artistic photographer who becomes a war documentarian, recording the devastation around him while trying to protect his wife and newborn child. The film has already emerged as one of the Palestinian highlights of this year's Venice Film Festival line-up. When the programme was announced in July, Citizen Osama was one of two Palestinian features selected, alongside Muayad Alayan's Conversation With the Sea . It had its world premiere at Venice earlier this month, screening out of competition. Moving between Al-Ashi's work and his family life, the documentary offers an intimate account of survival in northern Gaza amid hunger, loss and displacement. Palestinian Minister of Culture Imad Hamdan announced the Oscar selection on August 31 following a recommendation by an independent committee of film professionals. The selection makes Citizen Osama Palestine's 19th submission in the category since 2003. Egypt has selected The Stories, a 2025 semi-autobiographical anthology drama written and directed by Abu Bakr Shawky. It follows the cross-cultural romance between an aspiring Egyptian pianist and an Austrian woman, tracing their lives against the backdrop of Egypt from the late 1960s to the 1980s. The cast includes Nelly Karim, Ahmed Kamal, Amir El Masry, Sabry Fawaz, Amr Abed, Sherif El Desouky and Ahmed El Azaar. The film was selected after two rounds of voting by Egypt's selection committee, which considered 36 films produced between September 2025 and September 2026. It is the second time Egypt has selected a film by Shawky in the category, after Yomeddine in 2018. Jordan has chosen Zain Duraie’s Sink as its submission. The drama stars Clara Khoury as Nadia, a mother struggling to respond as her teenage son, Basil (Mohammed Nizar), experiences a worsening mental health crisis. Duraie described the film as deeply personal and said she wanted to explore mental health through a Jordanian family rather than the kinds of stories Arab filmmakers are often expected to tell internationally. Sink , Duraie’s first feature, had its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025 and was later screened at the BFI London and Red Sea film festivals. The Royal Film Commission said Jordan's selection committee made the choice independently.

title: Fujairah shows why resilience is the Gulf’s greatest energy asset
description: The Indian Ocean port has emerged as a crucial hub for the world economy, sustaining the UAE’s energy exports despite the Hormuz crisis
content: For a city sometimes unfairly described as “sleepy”, Fujairah is keeping the global energy industry awake these days. The Indian Ocean port has emerged as a crucial hub for the world economy, sustaining the UAE ’s energy exports despite the Hormuz crisis. Last week, Fujairah’s importance was highlighted when Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, and chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), attended the UAE Energy Markets Forum in the city. This continued a hectic run of conferences as the global energy industry emerges from a sticky summer and tries to find a way through conflict and disruption. The biennial WPC Energy Congress takes place in Riyadh this week, its first time in the kingdom and only the second time it has taken place in the Middle East , after Doha in 2011. The event has gone ahead despite the fatal attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport . Then, at the start of next month, executives take on the final boss, at Adipec, the world’s biggest energy event. Probably the most popular word in Fujairah last week was “resilience”. The UAE has managed to sustain, and possibly even increase, its oil exports through the conflict, as well as maintaining its essential imports. The Indian Ocean ports of Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and the others have been crucial. Rather than hasty workarounds, this rapid shift builds on years of preparation. The Habshan-Fujairah oil pipeline, with capacity up to 1.8 million barrels per day, was opened in 2012. Preparation for a second line had begun before the war, with the announcement in May and planned completion next year. Massive oil storage in caverns hewn out of Fujairah’s rugged brown mountains began construction in 2018. Adnoc Logistics and Services has amassed a large fleet of tankers and other ships, which has proved essential for moving oil. Supertankers are now in desperately short supply – it costs more to hire one, $80 million, than to launch SpaceX, a bargain at $74 million. Work on the impressive, modern new railway to Fujairah started in early 2020. The Barakah Nuclear Power Plant, an important part of assuring electricity even when gas facilities came under attack, began splitting atoms in August of that year. Beyond the UAE, we could highlight similar regional examples of preparedness, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council electricity grid, Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline , and the new port, refinery and oil storage facility at Duqm on Oman’s south-east coast. Like Adnoc, Saudi Arabia – with Bahri – Kuwait and Qatar have their own sizeable tanker fleets. Physical assets are only one part of resilience. Adnoc has over several years built a strong trading capability. That was profitable in the years of peace. In months of war, it has been even more important by salvaging supply to customers, and seizing attractive commercial opportunities. These assets were not accumulated with precise foreknowledge of the current conflict. Of course, blockade of Hormuz, or general trouble in the Gulf, has been a known risk since the Tanker War of the 1980s, if not before. In general, though, having a broad set of deployable national assets, whether in one company or several, whether in state or private hands, enables a country to cope with crises of all kinds. That could be regional political unrest as in 2011, a price crash such as that of 2014, a pandemic such as 2020, or a far-off war as in 2022. We do not know what the next challenge may be: a natural disaster, a big climatic upset, an energy technology breakthrough, an international market meltdown over AI or government debt. But combining physical, institutional and human capabilities with a flexible and proactive mindset is the best way to come through such storms. Resilience alone, though, is not enough. When the bombers thundered through the sky on February 28, politicians and observers alike thought it would be a short war. It has now ground on for more than seven months, though most direct strikes on Gulf and Iranian territory have stopped. Other theatres – Yemen, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq – have become entwined. Every regional country, even the non-involved such as Turkey, Egypt and Cyprus, have seen some unwelcome visitor land on their soil, and have suffered disruption to their airspace and trade routes. On Friday, US President Donald Trump announced proudly that Russia’s Vladimir Putin had promised to provide some diesel to ease the growing global fuel crisis, a product of the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine. The Gulf energy industry must build on the resilience established so far, establish new options to respond to future crises, and accelerate creating value. Of course, that is not easy to do while the spectre of renewed violence hovers over the region, and while shipping routes are still not functioning freely. The regional countries were, overall, investing heavily and sensibly in their energy industries before this year. They were solidifying their oil upstream, making the downstream more sophisticated, accessing gas for the domestic economy and for export, generating more value from commercial ingenuity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, electrifying their economies and seizing on transformational new technology in the AI space. Those remain excellent aims, even if specific projects have to be reprioritised for the new regional reality. Regional energy companies can do more. Becoming true international players fills a capital gap, builds their capabilities and somewhat reduces their near-total reliance on the Gulf. They can do more in inventing and deploying truly game-changing hard technologies. These often struggle in the rest of the world because of lack of visionary capital, overregulation and difficulty in co-ordinating diverse interests. Regional energy companies can work together more. Huge gains are possible from networking physical infrastructure – pipelines, ports, electricity grids and data cables. Greater achievements can come from soft integration, such as commercial joint ventures, cross-border investments and technology partnerships. The energy industry, one of the first truly globalised businesses, needs more than most to reimagine or construct institutions that govern its world by laws and not by the missile. The power to convene the world’s leading energy doers and thinkers, as at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, brings positive influence. Finally, at recent events elsewhere, the energy business has sometimes given the impression of being relieved the issue of climate change has been dethroned by that of war. That is a mistake. Conflicts will, by some smart application of strength and diplomacy, be resolved. Climate change, bad or worse, will be with us for the rest of the century and beyond. It will reshape everything we do in energy and itself can inflame war.

title: Al Nassr Asian Champions League clash in doubt over Riyadh security situation
description: Ronaldo's side due to face Uzbek outfit Neftchi Fergana on Monday night at Al Awwal Park
content: The AFC Champions League Elite fixture between Al Nassr and Neftchi Fergana is in doubt because of the security situation in Riyadh. At least 12 people died and 309 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Riyadh on Saturday afternoon. The attack was the third on King Khalid International Airport this week by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. Riyadh-based Nassr, who are captained by Cristiano Ronaldo, have a home match against Uzbek side Neftchi scheduled for Monday night. The Asian Football Confederation and the clubs involved have yet to comment on the status of the match. However, one of the Saudi Pro League fixtures scheduled for Sunday evening has been postponed. The game between Abha and Faisaly will be rearranged for later in the month. “The SPL confirmed the decision was made following a review of the circumstances surrounding the match,” the league wrote. “[The decision was taken] in accordance with approved regulatory procedures, ensuring that situations beyond the clubs' control are addressed while maintaining the continuity of the competition.” Abha is around 900 kms to the south-west of Riyadh , and around 200 kms from the Yemen border. Whether the Champions League fixtures will be similarly affected is unclear. There are four matches involving Saudi Arabian clubs in the continental competition scheduled for the next two days. Nassr are the only club playing a home fixture. They are due to host Neftchi at their home ground of Al Awwal Park on Monday. The Uzbek side were already in Riyadh when the attack on the airport happened. Fergana travelled via a direct charter flight, while around 100 fans of the side are also reported to have travelled to Saudi Arabia ’s capital for the fixture. The situation is also likely to affect Al Hilal. The four-time Asian champions went ahead with the “Saudi Clasico” against Jeddah’s Al Ittihad on Saturday night. They won 3-2 at the Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, to strengthen their position at the top of the SPL. Simone Inzaghi’s side are due to fly to Doha to face Qatar side Al Sadd, for their fixture scheduled for Tuesday. Qadsiah flew from Dammam to Tashkent on Sunday. The Brendan Rodgers-coached side will face Pakhtakor on Monday. Al Ahli Saudi, the two-time defending champions of Asia, will face Al Wasl on Monday evening. They travelled from Jeddah to Dubai on Saturday.

title: UAE waives IP registration fees under new rules for student inventors and people with disabilities
description: Cabinet resolution exempts two groups from costs to boost innovation
content: The UAE is waiving intellectual property registration fees for student inventors and people with disabilities, removing a key barrier to innovation protection. The Ministry of Economy and Tourism began implementing Cabinet Resolution No 136 of 2026 on September 14, providing full exemptions across 29 services related to patents, industrial designs, utility certificates and integrated circuit layouts. Student inventors and people of determination both benefit from exemptions on 11 shared services, including patent and industrial design registration applications, utility certificate examinations and annual protection fees covering years two through five. Those fees previously ranged from Dh100 to Dh1,000. People of determination receive additional exemptions on nine further services, with original fees of up to Dh9,000, while student inventors are exempt from nine separate services previously costing up to Dh4,500. Abdulrahman Al Muaini, Assistant Undersecretary for the Intellectual Property Sector at the Ministry, said the resolution reflected the UAE's commitment to building a comprehensive legislative environment aligned with international standards. "The Cabinet resolution affirms the UAE's vision of fostering creativity and innovation by supporting student inventors and People of Determination, enabling them to register their innovations with ease and protect their rights," Mr Al Muaini said. The move comes against a backdrop of rising demand for intellectual property protection in the UAE. The ministry recorded a 9 per cent increase in patent applications during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, while utility certificate applications grew by 21 per cent over the same period. Total patent applications in 2025 reached approximately 4,300. The cumulative number of patents, utility certificates and industrial design applications registered in the country has reached 22,184, reflecting growing interest among innovators and businesses in securing industrial property rights. The ministry said it continues to develop its digital infrastructure for IP services in line with the objectives of the We the UAE 2031 vision.

title: Sudan's Al Burhan accused of political scheming as war puts children at risk
description: Army chief faces accusations of Islamist influence as activists warn war is exposing the young to military recruitment
content: Political figures and analysts have accused the head of the Sudanese Armed Forces, Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, of political manoeuvring and remaining under the influence of the Islamist movement. They have also warned the prolonged civil war is depriving Sudan's children of education and exposing them to forced recruitment. In an interview with Sky News Arabia, Mohamed Abdel Hakam, a leader of the Sumoud alliance, Sudan’s largest civilian coalition, said Gen Al Burhan had full control over the army and the levers of power, but faced constraints on decision-making because of the influence of allied groups, including those within his own office. Mr Abdel Hakam alleged Gen Al Burhan had made significant concessions during his meeting with Massad Boulos , US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, in Egypt on October 5. Those talks took place on the sidelines of the African Union ’s co-ordination meeting, less than two weeks after Washington withheld a visa for Gen Al Burhan ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York. The move was reportedly linked to the army-led administration’s resistance to a US proposal for a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire, followed by political negotiations aimed at ending the war and restoring a transition to civilian rule. Sudan has said it did not reject the proposal but instead submitted comments on it. Political analyst and military expert Hashem Abu Rannat also accused Gen Al Burhan of political scheming, saying the army chief had accepted certain conditions but was reluctant to disclose them to his allies. Mr Abu Rannat said Gen Al Burhan had returned to his allies to inform them that he was prepared to make concessions, while continuing to pursue his objectives in Darfur, including driving out the Janjaweed militia. He claimed the Islamic Movement has a decisive role in shaping political and military decisions, alongside affiliated army officers. “Al Burhan is a tool in the hands of the Islamic Movement,” Mr Abu Rannat said. Meanwhile, Sudanese activist Nagisa Hagar has warned the conflict is depriving an entire generation of Sudanese children of education. She said many children who should have been attending kindergarten or primary school have lost these critical years, leaving them outside of the education system. Ms Hagar also warned that children faced the risk of recruitment by the warring parties, particularly the Sudanese army and groups affiliated with it. She said videos published by these groups showed children being recruited, warning of the serious threat posed by forced recruitment and the imposition of responsibilities on children that should instead be borne by adults and state institutions. The war broke out in April 2023 after a power struggle between the army and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary over the transition to civilian rule and the planned integration of the rival bodies. Repeated diplomatic initiatives have failed to secure a lasting ceasefire. The conflict has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, according to the UN World Food Programme .

title: Palestinian factions to meet in Egypt for reconciliation talks after election postponed
description: Mohammed Dahlan's pro-reform Fatah faction delivers scathing criticism of Abbas's decision to defer vote
content: Egypt has invited leaders of Palestinian factions to meet in Cairo in a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas , sources told The National on Sunday. The meeting proposed for next week will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine. The sources said Khalil Al Hayya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads a pro-reform faction within Fatah, the main group in the Palestinian Authority, were among those invited by the Egyptians. As is customary, there has been no official announcement by the Egyptian government on the proposed meeting. Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced on Saturday that the vote would be postponed until September next year, when the presidential election is also due to take place. Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place. The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank. The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas , triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the PA. Mr Abbas, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term. The deeply unpopular Mr Abbas, who is 90, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption. An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down. Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Its efforts have been led by officials from its spy agency who have taken responsibility for key foreign policy files over the years, traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry. Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”. However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives. “The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it said in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.” The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

title: US warplane knocks out ship breaching Iran blockade as tankers burn in Hormuz
description: Fourth vessel disabled since July as projectile strike and mass rescue take place in troubled Gulf waters
content: A US fighter jet knocked out a cargo ship trying to breach Washington’s blockade of Iran, as a tanker caught fire in a Strait of Hormuz lane that has come under attack from Tehran’s forces. US Central Command (Centcom) said the jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged Ocean Molika, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday after its crew had ignored repeated warnings. The ship had left an Iranian port and was trying to transit regional waters in defiance of the blockade. No crew members were harmed, Centcom said in a statement on Sunday. Video footage released by Centom showed an explosion erupting from the ship, sending a plume of smoke into the air, obscuring the vessel. It is the latest escalation in a campaign that began with ships being turned away and is now being enforced with live fire. Since resuming the blockade on July 14, US forces say they have disabled four commercial vessels and turned around 135 more. The restrictions cover ships entering or leaving Iranian ports. The strike on the Ocean Molika comes as commercial vessels in the same waters are being hit by projectiles, fires and, by Iran's account, mines. The cause of the incidents remains unconfirmed but they underline the increasing danger in the vital waterway. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz at 11.20pm UAE time on Saturday, causing a fire on board. All crew were reported safe. UKMTO also reported an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman. The advisory, issued on Sunday, gave no further details, with the time of the incident still to be confirmed. Authorities were aware of the incident and investigations were ongoing, it said. Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Navy claimed a supertanker carrying crude oil caught fire after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel had entered a designated high-risk area before a powerful explosion, the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iran’s Fars news agency. The account could not be independently verified. Separately, the UAE National Guard Command said 22 people had been rescued from an oil tanker in the Arabian Gulf after a fire broke out on board. A specialised coastguard team responded to a report from the crew, located the vessel and rescued those on board. The 22 people, all Asian citizens, received first aid before being transferred to the relevant authorities. All were in stable medical condition, the command said.

title: Diplomats or Quds Force? Zarif's blunt question rattles Iran's old guard
description: Former foreign minister's resurfaced remarks on deterrence have drawn fury from hardliners
content: A growing rift over Iran's security strategy has emerged after footage showed former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif questioning Tehran's reliance on military threats and arguing that diplomacy and economic opportunity should take priority over confrontation. The video, which appeared online on Saturday, has triggered a wave of criticism from hardline media as Iran faces mounting economic pressure from a US blockade and renewed uncertainty over the prospect of another conflict. “The balance of power has changed – nuclear weapons do not create deterrence, just as they did not protect Israel or the Soviet Union,” Mr Zarif said in remarks delivered in May last year, shortly before the 12-day war with Israel. Mr Zarif said Iran lacked sufficient uranium to build a nuclear weapon at the time. He argued that Tehran's security-first outlook had distorted its nuclear strategy and regional diplomacy, limiting opportunities to pursue economic and diplomatic interests. The former minister drew a direct contrast between treating neighbouring countries as threats and viewing them as potential partners. “If we see the region as a threat, our ambassadors must be representatives of the Quds Force [but] if we see it as an opportunity, our ambassadors must be businesspeople and diplomats,” he said, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps unit responsible for overseas operations. He also criticised the tendency to frame domestic social issues in security terms. “We even see hijab as a trench line,” Mr Zarif said, calling for a shift away from a threat-based approach. The remarks have drawn a sharp response from Iran’s hardline establishment. The ultraconservative Kayhan newspaper accused Mr Zarif of undermining national security and helping Washington. “Why, precisely at moments when the US finds itself deadlocked and helpless in the face of Iran’s power, do you give the enemy breathing room by launching a suicidal attack on the arms of national security?” a line read. The hardline Tasnim news agency published an editorial attacking Mr Zarif’s comments and demanding an apology, while Raja News questioned whether the judiciary would act against him. No formal judicial action has been established. The backlash comes as Iran’s leadership confronts difficult choices over how long the country can sustain its confrontation with Washington while absorbing the effects of economic restrictions and the US blockade on Strait of Hormuz shipping. Pressure on trade and revenue has intensified concerns about Iran’s economic resilience, adding urgency to arguments that Tehran should seek a diplomatic settlement rather than risk further damage through renewed hostilities. Reformist politician Hossein Marashi, secretary general of the Executives of Construction Party, warned that Iran must avoid decisions that could trigger another war. “Whatever political or military measures are necessary, including any tactical retreat, must be taken to protect Iran and prevent its people from facing even greater and mounting pressure,” Mr Marashi said. He argued that Tehran could not simultaneously preserve all its nuclear ambitions, maintain its military posture, resolve its economic crisis and force the US out of the region. Iran’s leaders, he said, must prioritise national survival and economic recovery. Omid Memarian, senior Iran analyst at the democracy and human rights organisation Dawn, sees the debate as reflecting a broader division over whether continued resistance will strengthen Tehran’s negotiating position or leave the country increasingly vulnerable. “There is a profound and growing divide within Iran, from the highest levels of political decision-making to different segments of society, over how to prevent another war with the United States,” he told The National . Iran’s leverage over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could become a liability if prolonged disruption prompts Washington to intensify military and economic pressure, Mr Memarian said. “A tactical advantage can become a strategic liability when leaders fail to recognise the moment to cash it in,” he said. The economic consequences could extend beyond immediate trade disruption, with prolonged uncertainty complicating the management of food supplies, fuel reserves and recovery efforts. Foreign attacks, meanwhile, may foster national solidarity without erasing public grievances over domestic conditions. The approaching US midterm elections on November 3 add another consideration. Some Iranian pragmatists say Tehran should make meaningful concessions and pursue a settlement before the vote, rather than assume mounting economic costs will eventually force US President Donald Trump to retreat. Mr Trump has said the US will not resume military strikes before the elections , citing productive discussions with Iran. Washington has nevertheless continued preparations for possible military operations, leaving fundamental disagreements unresolved. Mr Zarif’s remarks have exposed the political sensitivity of questioning Iran’s deterrence strategy at a moment when its leadership faces pressure on several fronts. The central dispute is whether Tehran should use its remaining leverage to negotiate a sustainable settlement or continue a confrontational approach that could deepen economic hardship and increase the risk of another war.

title: Al Ain Airport renamed as Tahnoun International Airport
description: Move honours the late Sheikh Tahnoun bin Mohammed's decades of service to the UAE
content: President Sheikh Mohamed has ordered the renaming of Al Ain International Airport to Tahnoun International Airport. The name change, which takes effect immediately, honours the late Sheikh Tahnoun bin Mohammed's decades of service to the country. Sheikh Tahnoun was the Ruler's Representative of the Eastern Region of the emirate of Abu Dhabi from the country's founding until his death in 2024. Tahnoun International Airport is the second international airport in the emirate of Abu Dhabi, situated about 18km from the oasis city of Al Ain. The airport currently has scheduled flights for two airlines and serves more than 100,000 passengers annually, according to Abu Dhabi Airports. Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 shows two scheduled flights today: Pakistan International Airlines flight PK144 from Islamabad and Air India Express flight IX336 from Kozhikode. The name change comes two years after Abu Dhabi's main international airport was renamed to Zayed International Airport, in honour of UAE Founding Father, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan.

title: Saudi Arabia presses on with global energy summit after deadly Riyadh airport attack
description: Media access to ministerial meeting will be limited to invited journalists only
content: Saudi Arabia pressed ahead with a major gathering of global energy ministers and industry executives on Sunday, hours after an attack by Yemen's Houthis on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and injured 309. The International Energy Forum's 17th ministerial meeting, hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria, is being held alongside the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together policymakers and industry leaders. Media access to the ministerial meeting will be restricted, with only journalists invited directly by the IEF permitted to cover the opening remarks, according to a Saudi Energy Ministry spokeswoman. “As you are aware, the ministerial plenary will be held behind closed doors,” she said. No live broadcast pool arrangements were in place, she added. The event is proceeding despite mounting security concerns after repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport , which have forced airlines to cancel flights and complicated travel arrangements for delegates. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said on Friday that he would participate in the IEF meeting by video link rather than travel to Riyadh. The WPC Energy Congress, which runs from Sunday until Thursday, is also proceeding as scheduled. Organisers have directed delegates to alternative routes into the Saudi capital, including by road from Dammam on the kingdom's east coast. A projectile landed near King Fahd Airport in Dammam on Saturday, a representative for the Saudi coalition said. Saturday's strike was the third on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in a week and the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, which killed four Saudis and eight foreign citizens, including one from the US. Two attacks on the airport this week killed four people and caused extensive damage to a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac. The latest strike caused widespread disruption to aviation, with about 260 flights cancelled and another 219 delayed on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The attacks have heightened security concerns, as Saudi Arabia seeks to maintain its calendar of high-profile international gatherings despite the war's growing regional spillover. Riyadh is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative from October 26 to 29, with organisers saying the event will proceed as planned, with additional security arrangements put in place.

title: Saudi-led coalition vows to ‘respond decisively’ to deadly Riyadh airport attack
description: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis blamed as attack draws widespread condemnation and raises fears of regional escalation
content: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to “respond decisively” to a Houthi attack on Riyadh that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malik condemned Saturday’s strike on King Khalid International Airport as “a full-fledged war crime according to the customary international humanitarian law”. “It is a heinous act that contradicts all principles, values, and ethics,” he said on Sunday morning, adding that the coalition would respond in accordance with international humanitarian law. The airport was closed as a precaution on Saturday. Authorities on Sunday extended the shutdown by 24 hours, until 1am local time on Monday, flight-tracking platform Flightradar24 said. Passengers were advised to check with their airlines for updates. US President Donald Trump said Washington could join Saudi Arabia in strikes against the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, following the attack , which killed an American citizen. Asked whether the US would participate in any Saudi action, Mr Trump said: “We may. We're going to look at it.” “We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he added. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the strike, saying it had taken “numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen”. “These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Mr Rubio wrote on X. “We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families.” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by the attack and called for an immediate halt to strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure, warning that such attacks violate international law. UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg described the latest series of attacks as a “grave escalation”, saying it threatened regional security, perpetuated violence and further complicated efforts to secure peace in Yemen. He urged the Houthis to cease the attacks and respect international humanitarian law. Governments in the region and beyond rallied behind Riyadh. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “completely unacceptable”, reaffirming Islamabad’s “unwavering solidarity” with the kingdom and its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security. Qatar described the strike as a “grave violation” of Saudi sovereignty, stressing that the kingdom’s security was integral to its own and to that of Gulf Co-operation Council states. Jordan also condemned the attack, reporting that one Jordanian was was killed and four wounded. Kuwait condemned what it described as a “blatant assault” by the Houthis, according to the state-run Kuwait News Agency. It renewed its “absolute solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and called on the international community to take a firm position to protect civilian sites and hold those responsible to account. The Netherlands also condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on multiple airports that caused casualties. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen expressed condolences to victims’ families, saying the Netherlands stood in “full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and our Gulf partners”. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the attacks “abhorrent”, saying there could be no justification for attacking civilian infrastructure. US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy was among those to criticise Mr Trump, writing that the situation now represented “a full regional war” and the US President had started the conflict. "This is now a full regional war. Started by Donald Trump. For no good reason," he wrote on X. "It’s a civilian airport that should never, ever be a target. This campaign of terror by the Houthis must stop immediately," he added.

title: Saudi Clasico: Watkins, Martinelli and Summerville all fire as Al Hilal go top
description: Riyadh giants open up two-point advantage after Premier League recruits deliver against Al Ittihad
content: Al Hilal's three-man former Premier League strikeforce all scored as they beat Al Ittihad 3-2 on Saturday to reclaim top spot in the table. The Riyadh giants spent big to reshape their forward line over the summer, bringing in Ollie Watkins ($60m from Aston Villa), Gabriel Martinelli ($70m from Arsenal) and Crysencio Summerville ($80 million from West Ham) from the English top-flight. All three came good at Kingdom Arena as Al Ittihad were well beaten despite a strong effort and the close scoreline. Former Gunners winger Martinelli opened the scoring on 11 minutes before Al Ittihad striker Youssef En-Nesyri pulled his side level. But parity didn't last long as England striker Watkins struck on 30 minutes to make it 2-1. Summerville then stretched the lead to 3-1 just after the hour mark. Steven Bergwijn scored a penalty in the dying stages to reduce the arrears and complete the scoring. Watkins was pleased with the three points, but felt he should have had another goal, with him having one chalked off for a questionable handball. He said: “It was a high-level match, especially as we had just returned from the international break. We trained for many days, but nothing compares to playing a match at full strength. “It was a top-of-the-table clash, and you can see how important it was to everyone. There is a lot of noise and celebrations, but the most important thing is that we took the three points, and I am very happy. “Honestly, I scored another goal, but unfortunately it was disallowed,” he added. “I know it was a difficult decision, and I will not comment on it, but I felt it was a valid goal.” Al Hilal are now two points clear at the top of the table ahead of Al Qadsiah and Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr , who beat Diriyah 3-0 on Friday night.

title: UAE IPOs and credit markets primed for growth once war ends, Morgan Stanley executive says
description: Investment bank's co-president Dan Simkowitz discusses AI and midterms
content: The UAE is expected to see a rebound in initial public offerings once the US-Iran conflict ends, and the country’s credit market is also set to boom, according to a senior Morgan Stanley executive. While there have been no listings in the UAE so far this year, the investment bank is bullish about the capital market prospects despite the uncertainty caused by the war. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. “I think long term, as the conflicts get resolved or hits some level of stabilisation, you will definitely see a rebound in the IPO marketplace in the UAE,” Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley told The National . “So, we are investing in and have high confidence in that. And we've been so impressed with the leadership on the sort of financial infrastructure in the country all the way around,” he said. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased uncertainty across the Middle East. After the US-Israeli bombing of Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on its Arab neighbours halted in early April, peace in the region has teetered on a fragile ceasefire. A report from the World Bank released last week said Gulf economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. While the International Monetary Fund also anticipates that the Gulf economy will contract this year, the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping, the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said. "I think it [the war] clearly creates a slightly higher and hopefully temporary risk premium in the region, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest," Mr Simkowitz said. The investment bank's commitment to the region is "as strong as it's ever been". "We continue to be thinking about how to invest in growth. Our corporate clients, FDI clients, are still very focused on the demographics in the region, the potential for GDP growth, the diversification that is coming in the marketplace,” he added. There is extreme resilience that has been built in the region, the Morgan Stanley executive said. “There is also real capital strength in the region, and so as they need to either rebuild or redirect energy infrastructure, for example, there is the capability to do so. And … there is international capital ready to help do that,” he explained. Morgan Stanley, which is headquartered in the US and has more than $10 trillion in assets, has been present in the region for the past 20 years. It also opened a new office in Abu Dhabi in 2024. The bank currently has well over 100 employees in the region and it plans to expand its operations further. "We're going to stay very committed to growing that. I think wealth and asset management will be a part of that,” Mr Simkowitz said. The company's current pipeline of deals in the region is still active, he said. "Some element is on pause, and I think it would change a little bit in that people will have to re-underwrite maybe some of their resiliency supply chain and diversification. But I would argue most of it that was on is underway." The Morgan Stanley executive is also bullish about growth in credit markets in the UAE and across the region, with global trends also positive. Credit markets cover bonds, government debt, private credit and bank loans. Globally, asset managers and owners, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, are playing a key role in the credit market, he said. “The credit market has become more important because we're entering into a period where high capex manufacturing is back ... and in that context, you need to spend money, and you need to bridge this ‘build to revenue, build to profitability’ gap … and it is not just banks or governments.” Economic tailwinds from the AI buildout and "surprisingly enduring demand" have bolstered credit conditions in many major economies this year, S&P Global Ratings said in a report this month. But the positive momentum of overall credit stability seen over the past few years will become more difficult to sustain, it said. Heading into the fourth quarter, "risks are building amid the sharp rise in benchmark borrowing costs, including yields on government debt, as investors bet that major central banks have a complex challenge in their fight against inflation", the ratings agency said. In the UAE and the Gulf, the credit market “is coming, and I think that's encouraging”, Mr Simkowitz said. Gulf debt capital markets reached $1.2 trillion outstanding at the end of the first half of this year, according to Fitch Ratings. Even in mature markets like the US, the credit market is evolving and building, Mr Simkowitz said, adding that the growth of a fixed income market or a bond market is "incredibly important”. “Over the last several years, the conversations we've had throughout the Gulf with finance ministries, stock exchanges, and other leadership … has been skewing more and more towards bond markets and credit markets, as we've had some great success with ADX [Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange] and with other exchanges in the Gulf around equities, it's a natural progression,” he said. More than $100 billion has been raised in debt markets in the region this year, he said. "That is really important to continue to satisfy the growth, diversification and resiliency ambitions, it can't all be done with equity, and so you need some element of credit and bond markets.” The big economic theme is AI, which is "incredibly transformational", Mr Simkowitz said. "It's going to require a lot of capital today to drive an immense amount of productivity in the future. "Certainly, the UAE has been at the centre of that. As relative to GDP or even wealth or market cap, the UAE is one of the most important AI players in the world." A recent report by Bain found that the AI industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed for data centres. Revenue from new product development is projected to become the biggest contributor to the industry, and is estimated to generate about $4.2 trillion to fund the technology's global market within the next half-decade. "We're reasonably bullish on AI-related revenue," Mr Simkowitz said. "There's a timing mismatch in that you need to build compute a little ahead, but that timeframe is shrinking ahead of the productivity and the revenue impact." Ultimately, the technology will prove beneficial. "Anything this transformative and large is .. not going to always be linear, and not everyone's going to win. But I would say the users will win, and then I would say there's going to be a group of winners who deliver it, who will win big from an investment perspective." From the political standpoint, investors are keenly watching the US midterm elections early next month. However, Mr Simkowitz stressed that while everybody in the markets will be focused on the midterms, "it's not nearly as consequential" as presidential elections, such as upcoming ones in Brazil or France. Looking ahead, there remains uncertainty in the markets over the US-Iran war, the Ukraine-Russia conflict and economic indicators such as inflation. Mr Simkowitz's outlook for next year? "I think intense and don't be complacent. No one can be complacent. It may not be as dramatic [as this year], but it's going to be intense."

title: Lionel Messi scores twice for Inter Miami in first game since Argentina farewell
description: Luis Suarez also on target with a brace in comfortable win over DC United
content: Luis Suarez and Lionel Messi each recorded a brace to help Inter Miami emphatically snap ​a ​five-match winless streak ​with a 4-0 shutout of DC United ⁠on Saturday night in Miami. Messi was playing his first club game since his emotional final match for Argentina in midweek. Suarez also had an ⁠assist for one of Messi's goals ​as Inter Miami (13-5-10, 49 points) moved up to second place in Major League Soccer's ⁠Eastern Conference and one point ahead of the Chicago Fire. German Berterame also recorded two assists while Sergio Reguilon and Rodrigo De Paul each had one. "We had to win again, and we did it convincingly ," said Inter Miami coach Kily Gonzalez, satisfied with his team's collective performance. DC United (6-9-12, 30 points) fell further ⁠out of the playoff picture and are now six points behind FC Cincinnati ​for ⁠the conference's final post-season play-in berth. Suarez ‌scored his 14th and 15th goals before he was substituted off in ​the 61st minute. Inter Miami brought their MLS-leading team goals total to 68, and recorded a fifth clean sheet overall and first in 10 matches. DC United mustered 14 shots overall, but only two on target including a close shot by Matti Peltola that sailed just high and over the crossbar in the second half. Suarez found the mark in the third minute when he converted a long cross from Berterame past DC United goalkeeper Sean Johnson. Reguilon recorded the second assist as he fired the ball ahead to Berterame, allowing him to send a high-arching ball that appeared to be ​redirected right to Suarez. Suarez scored his second in the ‌39th minute after Berterame controlled ⁠a rebound and headed it to him ​right in front of the goal. The goal followed a great chance ​by Messi, ‌who fired a close-range shot that Johnson blocked high into the air, allowing Berterame ⁠to track it down. Messi found his way on to the scoresheet in the ⁠47th minute for his MLS-leading 22nd goal to give Inter Miami a 3-0 edge. The Argentine first fired a shot at the top of the box that was deflected. Suarez controlled the deflection and lobbed a cross to Messi, who ​tapped it past Johnson. Messi recorded his second in the 60th minute when he controlled a back heel from Rodrigo De Paul, jinked past DC United's Lucas Bartlett, and fired the ball just inside the far post.

title: Manchester United ratings vs Tottenham: Mbeumo strikes but late Solanke goal frustrates Carrick
description: Draw at Old Trafford offers little respite for home boss after poor start to season
content: Manchester United looked set for a much-needed victory but Dominic Solanke scored in stoppage time to salvage a point for 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford on Saturday. Both teams were in dire need of a win, and when Bryan Mbeumo broke the deadlock in the 73rd minute it seemed as though the pressure would ease on United boss Michael Carrick . Things got worse for Spurs when Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off for a headbutt on Luke Shaw, but Solanke headed home Sandro Tonali's cross deep into stoppage time to earn the visitors a point. “I'm not happy with the amount of points we've got so far, for sure, you know,” said Carrick. “I'm not hiding, there's no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we've got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain.” Senne Lammens – 5: Mistake gave away possession after two minutes. Solanke spared his blushes. Tottenham had so many chances, yet United again conceded to 10 men. The Belgian fronted up to talk to the media again, but it’s one win from six for United so far, something he didn’t see coming this season. Leny Yoro – 7: In for Dalot who dropped to the bench. Made two last-ditch tackles in the first half, the best of them stopped Van Hecke. Encouraging at right back. As was his performance for France midweek. Lisandro Martinez – 5: Stopped yet another early Spurs attack, but couldn’t get near Solanke, who really should have scored on 51 minutes. A couple of poor passes. Booked for a rash tackle near halfway line. Then poor defending as he looked at his man and not the ball – which went in for Spurs’ equaliser. Harry Maguire – 6: Heavily involved as United struggled to clear their lines in a frantic, dreadful start. A pirouette on 29 minutes lifted the crowd and proved to be a turning point as the team moved higher. Luke Shaw – 6: It all kicked off on 78 minutes. Outraged by a tackle, he pushed Bentancur to the ground. He was then headed by the Argentine, who got a red. Shaw got a yellow. Before that? United were too slow in the first half and struggled to get the ball from Spurs. But he started the second half brighter and crossed on 47 minutes. Shaw was involved in the build-up for the goal. Smart interception on 84 minutes. Kobbie Mainoo – 6: Lammens left him stranded and Solanke should have scored at the start. Pushed up in second half. Strong block to stop Savio hitting the target on 68 minutes. Youri Tielemans – 5: Slow with the ball and that meant United struggled to connect higher up the pitch. Did put the ball in the net but was offside. Amad Diallo – 6: First start of the season and he was pushed back in front of Yoro as Spurs attacked and attacked. Managed first shot on target on 33 minutes. Ran into a few dead ends. Wild shot over on 48 minutes and came off, as expected, shortly after. Bruno Fernandes – 5: Quiet first half. Worryingly so. Better in second – he moved towards the Stretford End goal after nutmegging Senesi. Shot wide on 63 minutes as he got a lot more of the ball. Booked for a challenge on Van Hecke. Bryan Mbeumo – 7: Got the key goal which put United ahead. Super finish. Before that, a good ball in for Amad after 19 minutes as United managed an attack. Ran and set up Amad on 33 minutes. Showed his pace to get ahead of Senesi on 85 minutes and shoot on target. Matheus Cunha – 7: Striker was more on the left and won possession back in a rare United attack. Urged the fans on in the first half as he asked for more support. Brilliant move after 56 minutes but it was offside. Attacked down the left to set up Mbeumo. Smart use of the ball as United tried to hold on. Swept a shot on target on 89 minutes. Diogo Dalot (for Yoro, 58') – 6: First thing he did was get a cross in. Booked in stoppage time. Carlos Baleba (for Tielemans, 58'): Debut for the 22-year-old. Lovely first pass, tackled strongly and incredible pass towards Mbeumo. Impressive technique and running. Joshua Zirkzee (for Amad, 58') – 7: Got a chance from the bench after scoring for the Netherlands in midweek. Effort blocked on 61 minutes. Made a difference with good touches. Defended well at the end. Marcus Rashford (for Cunha, 90') – N/A: Late sub. Ayden Heaven (for Shaw, 90') – N/A: Late sub.

title: Why international publishers are overlooking Arabic books
description: At Frankfurt Book Fair, Egyptian publisher Sherif Bakr discusses the barriers facing Arabic literature abroad and how to address them
content: For Arabic publishers trying to sell translation rights abroad, the first challenge is getting foreign buyers to consider their books. Many international publishers have little idea of the range available, says Sherif Bakr, general manager of Cairo's Al Arabi Publishing and Distributing. “They don't know what to expect. They don't know what we have. This is why we as an industry needed to extend the variety,” he tells The National from the Frankfurt International Book Fair. Bakr hopes to narrow this gap through the newly launched Arab Voices website, which showcases contemporary literature from across the Arab world. The initiative began in 2020 with a printed catalogue of 32 Egyptian books before expanding online this year. Funded by the EU and launched in July, the platform introduces foreign publishers to books including Palestinian author Bassem Khandaqji's A Mask, the Colour of the Sky – winner of the 2024 International Prize for Arabic Fiction, Egyptian novelist Adel Esmat's At the End of Time and Nora Nagi's The Fuel House . “We now have fantasy, crime, women writing crime novels, women's literature, chick lit, literary fiction and award-winning books. We've also expanded across the Arab world, with 200 titles from 22 countries. We need to give more exposure to writers from across the region, not just the known ones or the famous ones,” Bakr says. Arab Voices joins initiatives such as Leila , an EU-funded European project launched in 2021 to promote contemporary Arabic literature. Based in France, it offers a curated catalogue and resources for publishers and translators, with a focus on Arabic-to-French translation. Meanwhile, the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre is marking the first anniversary of its From Kalima to the World initiative at the book fair on Thursday, announcing 14 new translation and international co-publishing partnerships. For Bakr, the range of books is important, but the selection must also reflect what international publishers are looking for. An open directory would give buyers more titles to sift through without helping them to identify books suited to their markets. “Publishers need a selected, curated list. Something that they know is going to work with them. You can't just put anything,” he says. Literary prize shortlists and winners offer a starting point, although he also considers books that have not received such recognition. A book's success at home is no guarantee of international appeal. “Maybe it's very good locally, but it doesn't travel, or maybe it travels,” he says. Bakr also believes Arab publishers need to be more active at international book fairs, where the emphasis is on networking, rights negotiations and showcasing titles rather than the consumer sales that dominate many regional fairs. He acknowledges the additional costs but believes the investment can pay off. “You have to talk to the publishers and convince them that this book stands up with the others,” he says. International publishers, however, are not always receptive. At a separate Frankfurt discussion on publishing industry challenges, Bakr described how publishers from the Middle East can be overlooked by their foreign counterparts. “We would feel publishers don't reply to us, don't think of us as important,” he said. Foreign publishers and agents can also underestimate the logistical challenges facing regional publishers, including contractual obligations that are far more expensive to fulfil in some markets. Requirements to send free copies to authors, agents and rights holders in several countries can leave Egyptian publishers facing shipping bills greater than the cost of producing the books. Bakr recalls attending fairs with suitcases packed with copies, relying on travelling colleagues to help to deliver them. He also recalls agreeing a $100 advance with a Nordic literary agency, only to struggle to transfer the money because Egyptian bank officials at the time did not understand the purchase of publishing rights. He eventually paid in cash at a book fair. Although restrictions have eased, he says a $100 transfer can still incur about $40 in fees. “We don't have the same banking system,” he says. “We have to be flexible and understanding.” Bakr plans to increase Arab Voices' international outreach after Frankfurt and to expand the platform into a hub carrying publishing news and links to other initiatives. He is reluctant, however, to judge its progress solely by the number of translation deals. “It's not that we have to have a KPI of how many translated books,” he says. “You're building something. It's like soft power. It's about expanding the visibility of what's out there in Arabic literature. There are so many great stories out there, and we just want to help in that effort.” Frankfurt International Book Fair ends on October 11

title: The Inside Brief: Menzies chief on aviation’s recovery and a lifetime of navigating crises
description: From becoming a refugee during Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, Hassan El Houry reflects on resilience and leadership
content: When you look out of the aircraft window on the apron, the people turning your flight around probably work for Menzies . Its chief executive, Hassan El Houry, manages 65,000 of them across 65 countries and joined me for the launch edition of season two of The Inside Brief . This was days after the security incident on flydubai flight FZ1073 , which diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia on September 30 and is now under investigation by UAE authorities. He said the industry's next task is clear. “Airlines need to reinstall confidence in the general public,” he said. What most people do not know, he explained, is how thoroughly staff are screened. “After September 11, airports and airlines introduced an array of security measures for passengers,” Mr El Houry said. “While there are security measures for people that work at airports and airlines, they’re not so much in the spotlight like taking off your shoes and your belt.” That is about to change. “I think what we’ll end up seeing is that a lot of the security measures that are applied to pilots, to cabin crew, to our staff, to airport staff ... will come to the spotlight because it is quite thorough actually.” Every Menzies employee is background-checked and passes through “the same security measures that a passenger does”. And no new bill is coming. “All those security measures are already there,” he said. The bigger pressure is cost. Jet fuel has risen by 50 per cent or more since the war began, and ticket prices are “two, three, four times more expensive than they were pre-crisis”, Mr El Houry said. Asked whether fuel prices would fall straight away if a lasting peace reopens the Strait of Hormuz, he replied: “Every time there’s been an aviation crisis, we’ve recovered fairly quickly”. After September 11, “it was just a year and a half or two years, and aviation recovered”. Covid-19, the longest crisis, took “about three and a half years”, he said. “When there is some sort of peace and more clarity, I think we’ll recover fairly quickly.” The reason is demand. “Every airline that I’ve been talking to has been telling us that there isn’t a demand problem," he said. “Passengers are still flying. There’s a cost problem.” About five billion passengers will fly this year. “Five billion, that’s a record,” Mr El Houry said. Yet airline profits are expected to halve, from $50 billion last year “to about 25 billion this year”. Mr El Houry learnt about risk early. His privileged childhood in Kuwait ended with the Iraqi invasion in 1990. “We were made refugees literally overnight,” he said. The family drove to Baghdad, then Amman, and spent two years in Cyprus. “At any moment you can have a black swan event. You can have a binary event from one to zero literally overnight, and you just have to be resilient enough to overcome it.” Compulsory military service in Lebanon followed. “I would spend 10, 12, 14 hours a day on my feet, and the one idea that kept going through my mind was the pain, the discomfort is temporary, but quitting is permanent.” His tolerance for complaining today? “It’s very low. It’s very low.” Wharton had been his dream since he was 19. It taught him to ask when he does not know. “You have to be humble. You’re not expected to know everything about everything.” Then came the choice: a New York investment bank, with the draw of “walking down Wall Street every day, going up to the 50th floor”, or Agility in Kuwait. “It wasn’t a cash decision,” he said. He chose Agility. “It was probably one of the best decisions I’ve made in my life.” At 28, he was running National Aviation Services, with 200 employees in one country. “Leadership is not a right that you have. You have to earn it.” Today, the combined business is the largest of its kind in the world, and Mr El Houry has the Gulf in his sights. “We don’t need to IPO,” he said. “The barriers to entry in the region are pretty high, but our resolve is much higher.” The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and other major platforms.

title: Arsenal vs Leeds player ratings: Odegaard 8, Guimaraes 7; Calvert-Lewin 7, Trafford 4
description: Gunners overcome slow start to take all three points at Emirates Stadium
content: Goals from Riccardo Calafiori and substitute Bruno Guimaraes saw Arsenal come from behind to beat Leeds United 2-1 on Saturday. Leeds, who were on top for an hour, had led through James Justin's 55th-minute opener, and it looked like being another difficult afternoon for the champions after their 3-0 defeat to Brighton immediately before the international break. However, Calafiori's equaliser proved the turning point, and was quickly followed by a triple substitution by home boss Mikel Arteta to cement the shift in momentum in favour of his side. One of those subs was Guimaraes , and the Brazil midfielder started and finished a flowing team move to complete the turnaround and secure all three points. “It feels unbelievable. I felt in the last game against Brighton we were not at the level. Today the mentality was bouncing back,” said Guimaraes. “This is my first official game at home. It feels unbelievable to score and it's an important goal, three important points. Great finish and I am very happy.” David Raya – 7: Great save to thwart Gudmundsson at end of first half. Kept busy by Leeds, and generally up to challenge. Ben White – 6: Nodded back into a good area for equaliser that Arsenal scarcely deserved at the time. Ezri Konsa – 7: Had his hands full with Calvert-Lewin but had a strong game and distribution improved as match went on. Gabriel – 6: Few sloppy moments from Brazil defender and trademark set-piece threat was absent. Riccardo Calafiori – 7: Gambled and made great run into box to score equaliser and get his team back in the game. Myles Lewis-Skelly – 5: Difficult day after positive start to the season and impressive performances for England. Slow on the ball and ineffective passing. Declan Rice – 7: Enjoyed a rare rest over the international break but struggled as Leeds pressed and disrupted. Became more prominent after Arsenal's leveller and it was his sublime flick that teed up Guimaraes to score. Noni Madueke – 6: Given a start on the left. Created a decent chance for Havertz on 20 minutes with smart wing-play. Arsenal's sparkiest forward in stodgy first half, but bar was very low. Martin Odegaard – 8: Frustrating opening half then scuffed contact with first sight of goal early in second. Grew into game and also orchestrated fine team move for second goal. Bukayo Saka – 6: Completely anonymous in first 45 as Leeds denied him and Arsenal's other attackers space. Was part of fine passing sequence for goal that made it 2-1. High and wide with effort on 74 minutes. Kai Havertz – 5: Headed tame effort straight at goalkeeper on 20 minutes. Peripheral figure before being replaced by Gyokeres. Viktor Gyokeres (for Havertz, 63') – 5: Big Swede struggled to get into the game but did feed Saka for chance with virtually last touch of the afternoon. Jurrien Timber (for White, 63') – 6: Dutch defender still feeling his way back but showed a few nice touches. Bruno Guimaraes (for Lewis-Skelly, 63') – 7: Immediately breathed life into Arsenal midfield and scored excellent second goal. Piero Hincapie (for Calafiori, 82') – N/A: Replaced goalscorer Calafiori late in game. Mikel Merino (for Odegaard, 90') – N/A: Late sub. James Trafford – 4: Didn't have much to do before fumbling Calafiori's shot into his net. Should have done much better with it, and leveller proved turning point. Went walkabout late on. Poor afternoon for England hopeful. James Justin – 7: Not far off target with superb curling effort on 50 minutes. Scored opening goal with brilliantly controlled side-foot finish. Nico Elvedi – 6: Won plenty of duels as the middle man in Leeds' trio of centre-backs. Tarik Muharemovic – 6: The giant Bosnian has impressed so far this season and had another steady game. Booked for mistimed tackle on Saka. Jayden Bogle – 6: Unwittingly blocked Stach's volley and then saw effort saved by Raya as Leeds had decent spell midway through first half. Ao Tanaka – 7: Neat and tidy in possession and worked hard off the ball. Replaced midway through second half as energy levels dipped. Ethan Ampadu – 6: Worked hard, occasionally loose in possession. Almost scored with looping header in first half. Anton Stach – 7: Consistently impressive set-piece delivery. Might have scored in first half but saw volley blocked by teammate Bogle. Gabriel Gudmundsson – 7: Terrific cross on 24 minutes created chance for Stach. Thumping close-range volley brought save from Raya on stroke of half-time. Showed great tenacity to provide assist for opening goal. Noah Okafor – 6: Narrowly off target with early effort that look destined for the corner. Poor pass when could have played Stach through on goal. Trickery caused problems but end product was lacking. Dominic Calvert-Lewin – 7: Led the line expertly in first half with some silky touches and intelligent link-up play. Continually got Leeds up the pitch and won several smart fouls. For all his quality, didn't get too many looks at goal. Harry Wilson (for Tanaka, 71') – 5: Entered just as Arsenal got on top and failed to make an impact. Brenden Aaronsen (for Okafor, 71') – 5: See above. Felix Nmecha (for Justin, 78') – N/A: Late replacement for goalscorer Justin. Jaka Bijol (for Elvedi, 86') – N/A: Late change. Jean-Matteo Bahoya (for Bogle, 86') – N/A: Late change.

title: Max Verstappen criticises Singapore track after claiming sprint and pole double
description: Red Bull driver continues strong form with productive day at Marina Bay Street Circuit
content: Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed a double in Singapore on Saturday as he won a chaotic sprint race before clinching pole position for Sunday's Grand Prix. The Dutchman has largely endured a frustrating campaign but will now be fancied to make it back-to-back race victories after his triumph at the Bahrain Grand Prix, hosted in Malaysia last weekend. That breakthrough followed a run of three successive podiums for the four-time world champion. Verstappen will have Ferrari's Charles Leclerc alongside ​him ‌on the ⁠front ​row while ​Lewis ‌Hamilton was ⁠third-fastest. Championship leader ⁠Kimi Antonelli was only fourth-fastest for Mercedes. The result means Verstappen will be on pole for his 250th F1 race and for the first time at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Earlier in the day, Verstappen, 29, had showcased his pace by winning an eventful sprint race staged in tricky conditions. Russell was leading, with the track still wet from an earlier downpour, when he drifted a little wide at the final corner of the first lap and lost control. His Mercedes flew across the track and into the wall. Ferrari's Hamilton took second place, having made a flying start from sixth on the grid with teammate Leclerc taking third. A late collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri lifted Antonelli into fourth place. The result, combined with Russell's retirement, stretched the Italian's overall lead in the championship to 89 points. Rain had delayed the start of the inaugural sprint at Marina Bay, and with overtaking nearly impossible, the only drama came in the form of collisions and a record nine retirements. “I think ⁠we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass,” Verstappen told ​reporters after ⁠notching his first victory at ‌the circuit. “I'm fine, I just do my thing … but it's not what I like. The overtake ​mode, it barely does anything here. You don't really gain a lot on the straights … we need to have a longer straight or like more of a proper hairpin to overtake.”
