He says the South Bank tends to attract a younger more creative clientele than other areas popular with the world’s super-rich, such as Mayfair, due to its culture and “place of identity”. He cites the main selling points as its “best-in-class” design and furnishing, as well as the building’s amenities including 25 metre pool, yoga studio and gym. Being on the 12th floor, “it’s not too windy” and as the only apartment on that storey it comes with privacy built in. Plus, “some people just love a penthouse” and there are not that many to choose from with “views of iconic, quintessential London”. Despite the dent that has been done to London’s reputation for safety in recent years, unfairly so, according to Mr Wood, he believes top-end properties will still achieve top prices. The difference is that now buyers are likely to be thinking long term, generational, rather than just a two or three-year investment. “This has been a 10-year journey and the penthouse is the final piece of the jigsaw,” he said. “It’s been an interesting decade, a challenging time for global geopolitics, but people still want to buy best in class. And with its education, culture and law, I believe London is still the best city in the world.”

title: Why banning children from social media may not be enough to keep them safe online
description: Experts say co-ordinating strategies between countries and educating parents crucial to reducing risks to young people
content: Barring young people from social media platforms may not be enough to keep them safe unless it forms part of a wider online protection plan, experts have told The National . A co-ordinated strategy that takes into account the need for education on best online practices for young people and their parents would be much more effective in addressing issues around digital safety, the experts said. Several countries have imposed bans on people under a certain age using social media. The UAE is among those seeking to enhance online protection, with plans to prevent under-15s from using social media from June 2027. "The challenge is different countries have different approaches to this. There needs to be joined-up thinking," said Wayne Denner, co-founder of Beat the Cyber Bully, an initiative that helps educate parents and children on digital safety across the UK, Ireland and UAE. "Some approaches may be more effective than others. The challenge is legislation often only covers certain apps, games or platforms and there are others that fall outside of this. It means that bans might not completely close loopholes around inappropriate content, exploitation or abuse. That's why we still want parental involvement and schools guiding young people on appropriate and responsible use of technology." The UAE's ban, announced in June, is to come into force after a one-year grace period, during which social media companies must bring their services in line with the protocols. Australia was the first country to introduce a social media ban. Anyone under the age of 16 is barred from using platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, X and Reddit. But that does not mean that young people are unable to access other forms of social media. Lemon8, which is owned by TikTok's parent company ByteDance, surged in popularity in Australia after it emerged that it was not included in the initial list of banned apps for under-16s. It was later added. "There are lesser-known platforms that parents and teachers aren't aware of," Mr Denner said. "There could be bad actors operating on those platforms who know they might not be as moderated as heavily as elsewhere. This presents a safeguarding risk. "It can be something of a whack-a-mole scenario. As soon as you bring one of these platforms under the umbrella, another will emerge." Other countries have also announced social media measures. The UK's ban for under-16s is also to come into effect from June next year. Under-15s will also be stopped from using social media in France from next year. Nations including Spain, Denmark, Greece, Norway, Indonesia and Canada have also announced proposals for similar bans. The EU announced the EU Kids Act last month, which proposes social media bans for under-13s, with limited accounts for those aged between 13 and 15. Educating parents on the dangers around young people having access to the online world is a crucial step in bolstering safety, Mr Denner said. "You should not be handing your child a phone if you haven't received some kind of education on the risks involved," he said. "You shouldn't be able to buy a smartphone for your child without some sort of education on it. You wouldn't be allowed to let a young person drive a car without being qualified. It should also be illegal to introduce technology to children without safeguards in place." Last month, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, agreed on a major settlement over allegations about the addictiveness of its social platforms for children. According to court filings, the social media company could pay up to $17.1 billion, after action from 47 US states and Washington, DC, and other American territories. The success of efforts to bar young people from social media platforms will depend on how such restrictions are implemented, said Prof Nathalie Martial-Braz, chancellor of Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi. "An age limit works best as one element of a wider approach," she said. "The most promising measures act on the product itself – private accounts by default, no contact from unknown adults, no advertising based on profiling, and limits on features designed to hold attention, such as infinite scroll and autoplay. "Education matters as much as regulation, and schools and universities have a part to play. Children who will open an account at 15 need to be prepared for it beforehand. "A single global rule is probably out of reach, since countries have chosen 13, 15 or 16 [years of age]. Shared principles and compatible age-verification standards look more achievable." Another important factor is ensuring young people are protected against the risks lurking around the corner, as technology advances amid the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence. "AI has changed the nature of the risk," Prof Martial-Braz said. "It drives the recommendation systems that decide what a young person sees. It can also produce harmful content that did not exist before, such as fabricated images of real people, and a child does not need an account to be affected by that. At the same time, AI is part of the solution. "I would plead for a sense of proportion. AI offers real benefits for learning, and a university engaged in AI research would be the last to deny it. The question is which uses are appropriate at which age, and with what safeguards. We are better placed to ask it early than we were with social media." But not everyone is in agreement about the efficacy of imposing blanket bans on young people using social media. In December last year, Unicef called for "governments, regulators and companies to work with children and families to build digital environments that are safe, inclusive and respect children’s rights". The agency warned that "social media was not a luxury for many children, especially those who are isolated or marginalised – it is a lifeline providing access to learning, connection, play and self-expression". When British authorities announced plans for the ban in June, Kerry Moscogiuri, chief executive of Amnesty International UK, described it as the "right diagnosis but the wrong prescription". She said the onus should fall on social media companies to do more to keep young people safe. "Too many social media companies have built products and business models that prioritise keeping children engaged for longer, often at the expense of their well-being, privacy and rights," she said at the time. “But the problem is not that children exist on social media, it’s that social media companies have built platforms that are unsafe by design. Banning under-16s risks treating children as the problem rather than addressing the companies and systems that create the risks in the first place." Dr Katherine Kemp, associate professor at the faculty of law and justice at UNSW Sydney, told The National that broad bans raise issues about data protection and privacy. For some young people, social media could actually provide a lifeline and help them connect with others, she said. "There are some teenagers who successfully use social media to take part in political debate and advocate causes that are important to them," she added. "Social media can also provide vital connections for young people who feel isolated because of their gender, sexuality, neurodiversity or ethnic background, especially where they lack connections in their nearby community."

title: UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’
description: More than 200,000 people have been displaced across country since beginning of August
content: The UN special envoy for Yemen warned the Security Council on Friday that the country has returned to all-out conflict, with fighting spreading across several fronts and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to deepen regional instability. “In the past few weeks, Yemen has slid back into full-scale war, with hostilities spreading across multiple front lines,” UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the 15-member council . The Iran-backed Houthis had earlier advanced towards Mokha and the coast along the strategic Bab Al Mandeb strait , while Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had recaptured territory nearby in a counteroffensive launched this week. The conflict has increasingly spilt into Saudi Arabia. Three Saudi citizens, including an airline pilot, were killed in attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a Saudi aircraft on Thursday, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks on the airport. Mr Grundberg condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure, including Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport. He also warned that threats against Saudi-linked commercial vessels in the Red Sea risked further destabilising international shipping and energy markets. “These threats are becoming enmeshed with the broader confrontation over control of maritime trade routes and the stresses on the international energy market,” he said. According to the UN, more than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since the beginning of August, the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce. In addition, nearly 4,000 people have fled across the Bab Al Mandeb strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia. Despite escalating hostilities, Mr Grundberg urged the warring parties to pursue negotiations. “Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now,” he noted.

title: US failure to prepare for rise of quantum computers could be 'catastrophic' for economy, GAO warns
description: Government Accountability Office report echoes recent concerns raised by cryptography and cybersecurity experts
content: The development of Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) capable of breaking just about any encryption might be "catastrophic" to the US economy and security, a new federal report says. The recently released analysis from the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) echoes concerns from technology and cyber security experts in recent years about a hypothetical scenario known as “Q-Day" , in which quantum computers fall into the wrong hands and are used to crack billions of passwords and break down other encryption methods, resulting in a wave of financial crimes. Conventional computers process data in bits and have a binary value of zero or one, whereas quantum computers can process digits simultaneously using a two-state unit called a qubit. What that means is that data crunching for research can now be done in a fraction of the time, potentially yielding new breakthroughs in science and medical research. Unfortunately, as the report points out, it also could have tremendous ramifications for cyber security. The non-partisan federal watchdog said that it recently made 89 recommendations to more than 20 federal agencies to develop inventories of potentially vulnerable cryptography that would help in identifying funding for "post-quantum cryptography." It published only the broad recommendations that it had conveyed to officials, and details of the others are unknown. "We have omitted the original agency comment letters reprinted in the sensitive report due to sensitivity concerns," it said. Though 12 government agencies agreed with the GAO's recommendations, one agency disagreed with several of them, and the US Department of the Interior failed to provide a response. "We continue to believe that all of the recommendations made in the sensitive report are warranted," the GAO's analysis explained. Though the GAO's evaluation about US government preparedness for CRQCs makes for sobering reading, it did point out a silver lining. "Experts say that the probability that a CRQC will be built in the next 10 years is low," the GAO report reads, though it adds that there's a significant risk that bad actors, governments or organisations might be harvesting large amounts of encrypted data right now, and are simply waiting for CRQCs to become available to decrypt it. "The loss of even a small amount of important sensitive information could have a severe effect on federal operations." The World Economic Forum touched on worries related to quantum computers in its Top 10 Emerging Technologies Report for 2026. It listed lattice-based cryptography as being among the more important technologies. Lattice-based cryptography is based on the idea of preserving encrypted data on computers and devices by relying on a series of mathematical problems consisting of complicated grids, also known as lattices, that are impossible for even quantum computers to solve.

title: US sanctions entire ICC for first time in Trump escalation
description: Action comes on same day former ICC judge awarded Nobel Peace Prize
content: The US imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, sanctioning the entire tribunal for the first time as the Trump administration escalated its campaign against the institution in The Hague. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with “this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us." “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Mr Rubio said in a video posted on social media. The sanctions are expected to restrict the ICC's ability to use the US financial system, with a transition period before most prohibited transactions become unlawful. Previous US sanctions were imposed on individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over investigations involving American and Israeli officials . “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Mr Rubio said. He also warned US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to bring the tribunal under control or face further American efforts to dismantle it “brick by brick”. The US action came the same day that ⁠former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The ICC “strongly” rejected the sanctions, calling them an attack on international justice and warning that “history will judge this moment”. “It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement. ICC President Tomoko Akane urged its member states to defend the institution against mounting US pressure. “The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. The Rome Statute is a collective promise that the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” she said. The EU called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work”. The latest confrontation follows Mr Trump's call last month for all ICC member states to withdraw from the tribunal, which he called “out of control” and a “rogue institution”. Established in 2002, the ICC has 125 member states, although major powers, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members. Under its founding Rome Statute, the court can prosecute people for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide only when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so themselves. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned the sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to carry out its work. Human rights groups condemned the US sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to pursue justice for victims of atrocities around the world. “By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director of Dawn, a US-based human rights organisation. “US sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine, all to shield Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide from justice.”

title: El-Sayed and Rogers trade personal attacks in bitter Michigan Senate debate
description: Candidates clash over Iran, Israel and the economy ahead of November's midterm elections
content: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, the two candidates vying for a US Senate seat in Michigan, have traded bitter personal attacks during a hostile debate over Iran , Israel and the economy. Their first televised exchange late on Thursday was marked by acrimonious jibes and fundamental disagreements, with tensions spilling over into the commercial break. “I want to take a quick aside and tell you that in 30 years of doing debates, I've never seen it continue during the commercial,” said Rick Albin, the debate's moderator. “But it did.” The heated debate comes during a tight race in the swing state, with less than four weeks until the midterm elections. Michigan is home to about 300,000 Arab Americans, and President Donald Trump has won there twice. The November 3 elections will determine who controls Congress, and Michigan is among the most closely watched Senate races. If Mr El-Sayed, a Democrat, wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Mr Rogers, a Republican, is an ally of Mr Trump. “Under this guy who's going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp, you're going to continue to pay way more out the nose because he works for corporations and Donald Trump,” Mr El-Sayed said. Recent polling suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming the President for his handling of the issues. His approval rating has sunk to the low 30s. Mr Trump has said the war would end after the midterms and that fuel costs – which rose after Iran put a chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz – would go down shortly after. But the war has been particularly unpopular among voters, and the Trump-endorsed Mr Rogers has run an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.” Mr Rogers questioned his opponent's credentials, calling Mr El-Sayed a “con man” and accusing him of having ties to armed groups in the Middle East. “He can't condemn Hamas. He can't condemn the Muslim Brotherhood. He says his home is Egypt,” he said. Mr Rogers later suggested that concerns about surveillance could be personal for Mr El Sayed because he or someone in his family might be suspected of terrorism. “Go ahead and say it,” Mr El-Sayed interjected. “You've been tiptoeing around it the whole time.” The candidates also traded accusations over their wealth and property. Mr El-Sayed accused Mr Rogers of owning a home in Florida and two yachts. Mr Rogers countered that Mr El-Sayed's wife owned a home in the UAE and might own one in Egypt. They actually own two rental properties overseas – one in Bangalore and the other in Dubai, but not in Egypt. Although the moderator at times struggled to keep the debate focused on policy, the candidates also clashed over their positions on the Middle East. Asked whether any action by Israel would lead him to withdraw support for US military assistance, Mr Rogers said: “I support just as staunchly their right to exist, the right to exist for the Jewish state, and the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood.” Pressed on what might change his position, he said that if Israel were to talk about using nuclear weapons, he would shift stance. Mr El Sayed also faced repeated questions about which country posed a greater threat to the US, Israel or Iran. He called it a “ridiculous hypothetical”. “Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he said. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So, this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part.” When pressed for an answer, he said: “I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One at risk of attacking us. One getting us into wars we have no business fighting.” Highlighting the Islamophobia that Mr El Sayed has been subjected to throughout his campaign, after the debate, Mr Trump attacked Mr El-Sayed in a racist social media post, calling him a “Jihadist lunatic” and referring to him as “Mohammed”. “Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the US fail,” he wrote. The candidates are scheduled to meet for a second and final debate on October 21 in Detroit.

title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 9/11-style attack on Tel Aviv and trained for cockpit fight
description: UAE's Attorney General reveals Omani co-pilot confessed to terror plot
content: A flydubai co-pilot attempted to seize control of a passenger jet and crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport in a premeditated suicide attack , UAE prosecutors have said. The UAE's Attorney General, Hamad Al Shamsi, announced on Friday that an investigation into the September 30 incident involving flight FZ1073, bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai , found that the aircraft's Omani co-pilot carried out a terrorist plot to cause mass casualties at the Israeli airport. The suspect, aged 29, was inspired by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and had pursued a career in aviation specifically to carry out a similar operation, according to his confession. Dr Al Shamsi said investigators traced the suspect's radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Melbourne, Australia. During that period, he was exposed to extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. He also attended a mosque affiliated with the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology, where he allegedly came into contact with people connected to a centre managed by a Lebanese man known as Abu Hamza, said to have links to the Muslim Brotherhood. He also said that he had prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing with a private coach. Investigators found that the suspect had used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv to reconnoitre the route and airport ahead of the attack. The suspect worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, then briefly for Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. The investigation also examined the procedures under which the suspect had been recruited by flydubai. The findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot’s licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot. During the incident, he allegedly struck the aircraft's captain, Smit Machchhar, with an emergency axe inside the cockpit. A pilot travelling as a passenger on the return flight noticed the cockpit door behaving unusually, gained entry, and, with the help of crew and passengers, restrained the suspect and rescued the injured captain. The aircraft was diverted and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. The suspect confessed to acting alone, though investigations are continuing to verify that claim. The Public Prosecution also heard statements from the captain, the return flight pilot, his co-pilot and members of the crew. The forensic medical report established that the captain’s injuries were concentrated on the head and consistent with the timing of the incident. The findings were also consistent with the statements made by the suspect and the captain, as well as witness testimony. The Public Prosecution is reviewing recordings, technical reports and possible connections to accomplices.

title: Dubai Orchestra Foundation established by law to boost emirate's cultural ambitions
description: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid issues decree creating body to develop orchestral music and support local talent
content: Dubai has a new dedicated body to champion orchestral music after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, signed a law establishing the Dubai Orchestra Foundation. Sheikh Mohammed issued Law No. (20) of 2026, creating the Foundation to advance the arts and orchestral music across the emirate. The body is tasked with strengthening Dubai's regional and international cultural standing, preserving local artistic heritage and showcasing the UAE's musical excellence. Among its core responsibilities, the Foundation will establish a local orchestra, stage performances both within the UAE and abroad, and promote Emirati musical heritage. It will also support emerging talent, including People of Determination, develop an annual calendar of musical events and host international orchestras. The Foundation will build local and global partnerships, support music education and production, and foster collaboration with cultural institutions worldwide. The Law outlines a governance structure headed by a Board of Trustees, comprising a Chairman, Vice Chairman and members with relevant expertise, all appointed by the Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai. The Foundation is expected to contribute to Dubai's broader creative economy, reinforcing the emirate's position as a leading destination for cultural tourism and encouraging investment in the music and performing arts industries.

title: Dubai Cashless Strategy contributes Dh8bn to economy as it exceeds goals ahead of schedule
description: Transactions index also surpasses 90% target as access to digital payment methods continues to grow
content: The Dubai Cashless Strategy has contributed more than Dh8 billion ($2.18 billion) to the economy, surpassing its goals ahead of its two-year timeframe. The emirate's cashless transactions index hit 90.1 per cent, exceeding the 90 per cent target set for 2026, the Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Friday, quoting figures from Dubai Finance. The Dh8 billion figure was also the target set when the strategy was launched in October 2024 . The digital enablement index for the government sector reached 100, reflecting the availability of digital payment methods across institutions and businesses, it said. The initiative achieved strong results across the strategy’s three pillars, with 97 per cent achieved in governance, 95 per cent in society and 93 per cent in innovation, it said. “Operational business continuity was also maintained to ensure the sustainability of these results and maximise their long-term impact,” the report said. Additionally, the community happiness index also hit 90.1 per cent, also surpassing the 90 per cent target. “The strategy reflects the success of Dubai’s model, which is built on a clear vision, integrated roles between the government and private sectors, and the expanding use of technology and innovation to serve people and enhance economic competitiveness,” the DMO said, citing Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence. The Dubai Cashless Strategy was unveiled in October 2024 as the emirate seeks to solidify its standing as one of the world’s top digital cities . The initiative seeks to enable seamless and secure digital payment solutions across both government and private sectors, the media office said. It aligns with the objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda , the initiative also known as D33. In a separate statement on Friday, top Dubai officials said the achievement marks a new milestone and reinforces Dubai’s position as a leading global hub. “The transition towards a cashless society is not a technological objective in itself. It is part of a broader vision for an interconnected digital city that provides individuals and businesses with easier and more efficient experiences and enables innovation to translate into economic and social value,” said Hamad Al Mansoori, director general of Digital Dubai, which spearheaded the cashless strategy. Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, noted that the efficiency of transactions is a vital element of the experience of businesses, residents and visitors. “The wider range of payment options enriches the visitor experience, enhances Dubai’s competitiveness and reinforces its position as one of the world’s most accessible and connected cities,” he added.

title: What's behind the postponement of Palestinian elections and what happens next?
description: Mahmoud Abbas has overstayed his term by 17 years and rules by decree
content: Under intense pressure to reform, President Mahmoud Abbas vowed 2026 would be the year of diplomacy, announcing that Palestine would hold legislative elections in November and Presidential elections next year. Many doubted they would happen, given past experience. Their fears became reality this week, with sources telling The National that the elections are to be delayed again. The last time this happened was in 2021, when Mr Abbas announced that legislative elections were cancelled after hope had been ignited that the Palestinian government might be revived. “This was not a postponement, this was a cancellation,” said Palestinian-Canadian lawyer Dania Buttu, who is the former spokeswoman for the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO). Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree. “This is called authoritarian rule,” she added. This time, the postponement comes at a crucial period, weakening the Palestinian Authority's credibility in the face of a mountain of challenges, including a right-wing Israeli drive to make it impossible to establish statehood, a war that has not stopped in Gaza, and international obligations that have not been fulfilled. Israel has occupied more than half of the Gaza Strip, and its army has killed 70,000 Palestinians there over the course of the three-year war since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks have become more rampant and intense, and conditions inside Israeli prisons are described as torture by Israeli and international rights groups. The conditions for free and fair elections are unlikely to be met in Palestine in the near future, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu 's government survives Israel's own vote set to take place at the end of this month. However, Mr Abbas has also not secured any type of future for Palestine. “When Abu Ammar [Yasser Arafat] was alive, we knew what would happen after he was gone. There would be elections, and Abbas would win. Today, we have no idea,” Ms Buttu said. Palestine's parliament has not met since 2007, the last time since legislative elections, and Mr Abbas has issued at least “three times” more decrees than parliament has passed laws, she added. Despite creating the role of Vice President, Mr Abbas has also bolstered the position of his own son, and a clear plan of action is not in place for when the 90-year-old President dies. Sources from different factions said the roots of the delay are mainly tied to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. But attempts to unite notorious factions within the Palestinian political scene have often failed, stemming from disagreements about the way forward for Palestine. Systemic and endemic problems mean that Palestine has lacked the right environment for elections for decades. Under an occupation that has become more fierce and deadly in recent decades, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed. High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling support circle. Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign. This confirms “the persistence of exceptionally high dissatisfaction with his leadership”, the PSR said in its findings. Driven by what seemed like a crucial moment for change after Mr Abbas's announcement earlier this year that elections would be held, momentum began to build, preparations were set in place and alliances began to form. First, municipal elections were held in the West Bank and in one area of Gaza, Deir Al Balah, because the remainder of the strip is simply too destroyed to host an organised vote. The vote went ahead, and despite some criticism, was viewed as a step forward towards larger elections. Then, he held elections in Fatah's Central Committee, where the cracks began to form. Several sources told The National that the vote was clearly “rigged”. People who once seemed to be guaranteed winners were sidelined, while others, like Mr Abbas's son Yasser, gained enough votes to secure a seat on the committee. “In my estimation, this is one of the most significant reasons [for the postponement],” an official with Palestinian Islamic Jihad told The National . “There is internal disarray within the Fatah movement regarding the formation of its electoral list and the distribution of power centres following the movement's Eighth Conference.” Additionally, Fatah is not viewed as a single party. Splits over the years from the group's main members by people who can, in today's political climate, play a significant role, such as Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Kidwa, mean that Fatah no longer represents one single vision. Mr Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of Fatah called the Democratic Reform Party, was the Fatah representative in Gaza before being exiled from the group. Similarly, Mr Al Kidwa, who is the nephew of former Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was expelled from the Fatah party and joined forces with one of Palestine's most prominent political figures, Marwan Al Barghouti, for the elections in 2021 that Mr Abbas also “postponed”. Mr Dahlan recently met the head of Hamas's politburo, Khalil Al Hayya, in Cairo. Both Mr Dahlan's party and Hamas issued a statement confirming that they had met, cementing further what many had suspected before: that efforts were probably being made to unite against Mr Abbas in upcoming elections. There were also talks that Mr Barghouti himself would join one of the parties running against Mr Abbas – causing the chances of the President's political survival in a poll to shrivel. Only 14 per cent of people would vote for him if Mr Barghouti and Mr Al Hayya ran against him. “New alignments have emerged over the past few months, including a rapprochement between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the faction led by Mohammed Dahlan. This creates the possibility of an electoral map reshaped in a way that makes it difficult for the current leadership to control the outcome,” the PIJ official added. “Thus, postponement becomes a means to realign alliances before heading to the polls.” A lot of this was expected, and did not come as a surprise for many. In fact, the same public opinion poll showed that 44 per cent of Palestinians did not believe the elections would take place on time. So did many Palestinian experts and watchers. Mr Abbas postponed the 2021 elections under the pretext that Israel would not allow people to cast their vote in occupied East Jerusalem, after it became increasingly apparent that he would lose. Today, the circumstances are significantly more dire. The framework within which the November vote will be postponed is important. In 2021 there was simply an announcement, but if Mr Abbas issues a decree, this should make it legally binding. Additionally, pressure from Europe may also mean that a vote is not “postponed” indefinitely, but takes place later, within a set timeframe. Eyes will now be on France and other European countries that have made reform a condition of their provision of assistance to the Palestinian Authority, now that the decision to postpone has been made but not officially announced.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed and Canadian PM Mark Carney discuss UAE-Canada economic ties
description: Leaders reaffirm commitment to stronger investment partnerships
content: President Sheikh Mohamed spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday, with both leaders pledging to deepen bilateral ties across vital sectors, with a particular focus on strengthening economic and investment ties. Advanced technology and AI also featured prominently in the discussions, reflecting both nations' ambitions to position themselves as leaders in emerging industries. The two leaders identified these sectors as central to the development priorities of both countries and pledged their commitment to advancing UAE-Canada relations through long-term, sustainable partnerships. In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement ( Cepa ) with Canada . The trade ​agreement with Ottawa aims to reduce trade barriers to goods, services and ⁠investment, and follows a $50 billion investment commitment from the UAE last November. The Cepa gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest market for Canada's exports to the Middle East, and could help attract capital into energy, mining, artificial intelligence and ports. Friday's call also touched on a number of regional and international issues of mutual concern. The two leaders exchanged views on developments in the Middle East, with both expressing support for continuing efforts to promote security, stability and peace across the region. The emphasis on AI and advanced technology signals a forward-looking agenda, aligning with the UAE's broader national strategy to diversify its economy and cement its status as a global hub for innovation.

title: UAE worshippers answer President Sheikh Mohamed's call to pray for rain
description: Salaat Al Istisqaa performed by worshippers on Friday around the country
content: Worshippers gathered at mosques across the UAE on Friday to perform Salaat Al Istisqaa , the Islamic prayer for rain. Earlier in the week, President Sheikh Mohamed had called on Emiratis and UAE residents to perform the prayer. The call came as the level of rainfall declines across parts of the Middle East. Through most of 2025, cumulative rainfall in the UAE was significantly below average – about 38 per cent less than the historical baseline and nearly three times lower than in 2024. At Sheikh Hazza bin Sultan Mosque in central Abu Dhabi on Friday, people were hopeful that rain will come soon. Egyptian resident Ibrahim Hamouda, 30, has attended Friday prayers at the mosque for six years. “It is a way for us to call upon our Lord through prayer; specifically, during times of drought,” he said. “It is how we ask God for what we need.” Jordanian Hussam Ali Hamdan was born in Abu Dhabi and has frequented the mosque since 2017. He said that the prayers are not just for humans, but for all living beings. “It is sunna of Prophet Muhammad, where we supplicate and we make duaa to the Almighty Allah to have mercy upon us and to send the rain for us as humans and for the living beings, like the trees and the animals,” Mr Hamdan told The National . Mohammad Arif from India participates in the rain prayers annually, and finds enjoyment in coming together to ask for blessings. “Inshallah Allah will give us rain. It's not only in the UAE, it should be everywhere in the world. We are very lucky to be in this country, but like other places ... I belong to India, this year there are lots of droughts over there in many places. I'll be praying for that also, throughout the world rain should come,” he said. Ahmed Sabir, from Egypt, said that the prayers are a way to ask God for the needs of the people. “It is essential; we must pray and supplicate to God so He may show us mercy, improve our conditions and the weather, ensure our agriculture thrives, and keep everything running smoothly. God’s bounty is vast,” he said. Samir Ashaar, from Egypt, has been coming to the mosque for nine years. He believes this ritual is one that everyone should follow. “May God show us mercy through the rain,” he said. “Everyone ought to attend today, as this prayer – whether considered an obligation or a Sunnah – invites forgiveness and mercy from Allah. God willing, there will be supplication and a favourable response; hopefully, the rain will fall today, by His leave.”

title: Iraq expects to start transporting crude oil by lorry to Syria from mid-October
description: Latest agreement further boosts co-operation between Baghdad and Damascus
content: Iraq is expecting to begin transporting crude oil via a route to be provided by Syria starting in mid-October, a development that is expected to boost its energy exports that have been hampered by flare-ups in the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in Iran . The crude products will be moved to a port in the Mediterranean Sea using lorries after Iraq requested assistance from Syrian authorities , Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of the state-owned Syrian Petroleum. The agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is “almost done”, and the Iraqi oil exports are expected to “start as soon as possible ... hopefully, by mid-October the first chain of trucks with crude will come to Syria”, he said. The impending move follows a similar energy trade-related co-ordination between the two Middle East nations in late September, in which Iraq began importing petrol through Syria . In April, Syria became the main route for Iraqi fuel oil exports, partially compensating for the disruption to shipments caused by the war in Iran. At least 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi fuel oil have also flowed by lorry to Syria's Baniyas since then. An Iraqi Oil Ministry official had told The National that the first cargo of imported petrol, comprising 32,000 tonnes, was being unloaded at the Baniyas refinery, to be transported to Iraq on lorries. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals. The agreements between Iraq and Syria also mark a significant deepening of ties as Baghdad deals with disruption to its trade through the Strait of Hormuz , and as the US pushes for closer relations between the two countries. The strait, through which about a fifth of the world's energy exports passed before the war, remains a flashpoint in the eight-month conflict. The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. The figures include shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and by other methods. Iraq is a major crude oil producer, but faces petrol shortages because of problems with its refineries and the management of its energy infrastructure. Last Sunday, the state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company transported two million barrels of its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades. The move was intended to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, director general Ali Qais said, adding that the company is also in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”.

title: French lender Natixis CIB expects double-digit growth in Middle East and Asia despite war uncertainty
description: The bank plans to hire more staff across the business in markets such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia
content: French lender Natixis Corporate and Investment Banking expects double-digit growth in its Middle East and Asia business this year and next, despite the uncertainty driven by the Iran war and contracting economies. The lender, which has grown in double digits over the past five years in the region, has not been deterred by the geopolitical headwinds . It plans to hire more bankers across the business in markets such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia , said Bruno Le Saint, chief executive of Natixis CIB for Asia Pacific and Middle East. “In the overall region, we want to grow in double digits on average. This is what we've been doing over the past years and going forward we'll keep that pace,” he told The National . “It means that, overall, we hope to be close to 20 per cent in the next two to four years, but it also depends on how quickly we grow the rest of the business.” For the broader Middle East, Natixis CIB expects its business to grow by at least 10 per cent next year, despite the economic challenges caused by the war. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are the two largest regional markets for the French lender. Part of Groupe BPCE, the eurozone's fourth-largest banking group, Natixis CIB is expanding its footprint in the UAE, where it operates from the Dubai International Financial Centre. The Paris-based company has 80 personnel working out of Dubai and it plans to bring more resources, “expanding our workforce and our capabilities on the ground", Mr Le Saint said. “I think it's important because, in the context of the current situation, I don't think there have been many international banks growing staff in this region,” he said. It also plans to further boost its presence in Saudi Arabia, where Natixis CIB operates through its banking subsidiary , Natixis Saudi Arabia Investment Company. “We want to keep growing this,” Mr Le Saint said. “We still think that we are underinvested in Saudi Arabia.” The kingdom's Vision 2030 agenda also aligns well with Natixis CIB’s core financing and investment banking expertise in sectors including telecoms, energy, infrastructure, metals and mining. The bank is also considering expansion into Turkey, "which is also a big economy in the region", Mr Le Saint said of Natixis CIB’s expansion beyond the Arab world. “How do we grow there? It's under exploration for now, but these are the questions we are asking ourselves.” The company currently provides services to clients in markets including Oman and Turkey in the region and covers Central Asia from its Dubai hub. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed. The World Bank said this week that Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects oil-rich economies in the region to contract this year, before enjoying a strong recovery next year – subject to shipping operations returning to normal, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. But Mr Le Saint said he was “quite confident” about Natixis CIB’s growth prospects in the Middle East. “I still think that, even though some economies in the region, from a GDP perspective, are contracting, we have not yet reached our natural market share,” he said. “It's more difficult to reach our natural market share in a market that is contracting, but when we see that our franchise and our expertise fit well with the needs of the client, especially in the current situation, I still think that we can keep growing at this pace.” That projection, however, could change if the Iran war does not end soon, he added. “Of course, if the conflict stays for the next two to three years, what I say might at some point be revisited. But for the foreseeable future, for the next year, I'm very optimistic that we will be growing 10 per cent at least." “We are expanding, we are investing, so we are capturing market share at a time where not everyone has full attention on growing the business here, which I think is quite exciting.” Although Natixis remains bullish about the long-term economic environment of the Middle East, as well as the bank’s own growth prospects, it has seen a slowdown in the regional debt capital market this year. The volume of deals so far has dropped by about 10 per cent, but the market is “relatively resilient”, Mr Le Saint said. The slowdown is not due to the lack of access to liquidity, but is instead caused by borrowers who "don't want to access it now because they see the yield and the rates are too high”, he said. Borrowers can wait and have several options to raise funds, as well as their own liquidity. “Chinese banks are coming back in the region and are investing massively, especially to support probably, the need to source and help the flow of energy to China,” he said. “I don't think that our clients are in any stress to find liquidity. Many of them are just waiting to see better conditions or to tap a new pool of liquidity." Natixis CIB, which is celebrating its 20th anniversary, combined its Asia and Middle East operations at the beginning of last year. The lender offers structured financing solutions, large-scale project funding, leverage and acquisition finance, funding for event-driven transactions as well as trade and structured financing. It primarily focuses on sectors including infrastructure, energy, transport, metals and mining, and technology and aviation. “They are global sectors where you've got investors, capital seekers and capital providers from [all parts] of the world. We connect the dots,” Mr Le Saint said. The bank also offers advisory, investment banking and corporate banking, as well as capital markets services. Currently, the Asia and Middle East platform accounts for more than 15 per cent of Natixis CIB’s overall business and “we want to grow that to 20 per cent and perhaps more", Mr Le Saint said. By combing the geographies, the bank is better placed to capture opportunities arising from the growing business and trade links between them, he said. “It also makes sense because our Asia Pacific set-up today, compared to what it was 20 years ago or even 10 years ago, is much more established and comprehensive so now we can offer our Middle East clients access to this market,” Mr Le Saint said. Natixis CIB’s clients in Asia also have access to funding pools in oil-rich countries in the Middle East, he added. “There is geopolitical and economic rationale, but there is also a business rationale."

title: Binance expands financial super app offering with launch of bStocks in the UAE
description: bStocks give users access to tokenised securities representing select US stocks and ETFs
content: Binance, the global blockchain ecosystem behind the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume and registered users, today announced the launch of bStocks for eligible users in the UAE, marking another milestone in the company’s vision of becoming a financial super app. The launch expands Binance’s growing ecosystem beyond digital assets, enabling users to access select US stocks through tokenised securities within a single platform. As Binance continues to bridge traditional finance and blockchain technology, bStocks provide users with a more accessible and flexible way to diversify their portfolios while benefiting from blockchain-native capabilities. Users in the UAE can already access a wide range of financial services, including crypto trading and earning products. The addition of bStocks further strengthens Binance’s ambition to bring multiple financial opportunities together into one seamless ecosystem, making it easier for users to manage different asset classes through a single platform. bStocks are tokenised securities designed to mirror the price of select US stocks and ETFs. Issued by BTech Holdings Limited, a Binance group affiliate, each bStock is intended to track the price of a corresponding underlying share held with a regulated custodian. While bStocks do not represent actual ownership of the underlying stocks, they are designed however to combine traditional finance with blockchain technology. They offer eligible users a simpler and more flexible way to access U.S. equity markets. These securities allow eligible users to : Corporate actions, including stock splits and dividend-related adjustments, are processed automatically in accordance with the applicable product structure, helping users maintain continuous exposure without requiring manual action At launch, eligible users will have access to tokenised securities representing: In addition to the above, many other bStocks are available on Binance and are expected to be introduced progressively, subject to applicable approvals. Commenting on the launch, Tarik Erk, head of MENAT said: “At Binance, we’re building much more than a cryptocurrency platform, we’re building a financial super app designed to give users seamless access to a growing range of financial opportunities through one trusted ecosystem. The launch of bStocks in the UAE marks another important step in that journey. "By bringing tokenised US equities onto blockchain infrastructure, we’re making access to US equity markets, more flexible and better aligned with how today’s digital-first users want to manage their finances. As we continue expanding our ecosystem, our focus remains on simplifying financial access while connecting traditional finance with the innovation of blockchain technology.” * Prices outside traditional market hours may be especially volatile, and trading during these periods carries additional risk. bStocks are designed to track the price of the corresponding underlying asset, but are not guaranteed to reflect its real-time market price at all times.

title: Agricultural city being developed in Abu Dhabi to aid UAE's food security efforts
description: The desert will turn green in country's latest agricultural mega-project
content: In the era of smartphones and social media, in which people simply order groceries through a delivery app, the disconnect between humans and farms has never felt so pronounced. This may be about to change, as the future of farming takes shape in Abu Dhabi . An agricultural community, known as Qitaf City, twice the size of Monaco, is being developed in Abu Dhabi to help boost the country's efforts to tackle food security. At four million square metres, the coming project will include villas, townhouses and Emirati housing with farms alongside AgriTech projects. Shamsa Alfahim, chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Investment and Development and managing director of Qitaf Holding, said she hopes to attract those interested in taking up farming while incorporating the latest technologies. “We're hopefully trying to target different university students or people who are interested in agriculture, and be able to give them this farm for their own use and giving them to the market,” she told The National at Global Food Week. In a rapidly modernising country which has put AI at the forefront, the hope is the project will bring Emiratis back to their roots and allow them to contribute to the country's growing food ecosystem. “There's something very humble about being in this kind of ecosystem because it does ground you to your roots. It's not just agriculture any more – there's also aquaculture and agritech,” she said. The first project starting in the agriculture city will be growing potatoes using solar panels as part of the laboratory process. Months of supply chain instability with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz underlined the importance of food security for the UAE, a country that imports a majority of its food from abroad. The goal is to create a strategic hub for food security in Abu Dhabi. “We wanted to launch Qitaf to battle these new circumstances because we want to be resilient and self-sufficient within the UAE,” said Ms Alfahim. Qitaf City will be about 40 minutes from Abu Dhabi city, Al Ain and Dubai's Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC). The area, known as Al Haffar, is part of a wider master plan that includes a sports city. Etihad Rail's track runs alongside it, and in the future, she says, freight rail access will play a key role in logistics. “The new Etihad railway is going to pass by the area where Qitaf is located within Al Haffar city. So in terms of logistics it's going to be very strategically located because there's a very easy route of being able to transport the produce from Qitaf to other places in the UAE." Qitaf Holding has recently been established as the agricultural arm of ADID to “create an environment for food security” in the country. The agriculture city project is slated to launch in February. “The bigger master plan is actually creating a sustainable city that encompasses lots of different health points,” Ms Alfahim said. “A part of it is going to be a sports city, another is going to be a medical city, and the large majority is going to be housing and estates for the local community.” Qitaf Holding is also working with AG Groups on large-scale projects across countries in Africa and Asia. They launched a green corridor between Tanzania and the UAE during Global Food Week. “We can connect with farmers in Tanzania, give them a platform for exchanging their products, bring the their products to the UAE for processing and manufacturing, and re-export it from here,” said Ms Alfahim. “It's going to create a whole system. We want to do the same thing with Madagascar where we can bring vanilla from Madagascar into the UAE.”

title: UAE's revised suicide law can 'reduce mental health stigma and improve support'
description: Specialist services continue to expand as new hub opens in Dubai
content: Access to mental health support is poised to continue to improve following legal amendments to decriminalise attempted suicide, experts have said. The UAE announced the removal of criminal liability in an amendment to the country's Crimes and Penalties Law on Thursday. Previous legislation in 2020 gave judges the discretion to offer mental health treatment as an alternative to prison, although there had been confusion over the legal ramifications for people who tried to take their own lives. The change is expected to improve the chances of early intervention, ensuring care and support is given when needed to bolster suicide prevention. Dr Tina Mistry is a clinical psychologist and corporate wellbeing director at AlKalma Health and Wellbeing, a mental health platform in the UAE and Saudi Arabia. She said the legal change was a positive step. “The recent amendment decriminalising attempted suicide shows a real commitment to supporting people with mental health difficulties,” she said. “Until now, fear of a criminal case stopped many people from saying they were having suicidal thoughts. “Removing that fear should make it easier for people in distress to speak up and get help early.” Early intervention is viewed as critical when signs of depression and anxiety appear, to prevent symptoms from deepening or developing into suicidal thoughts. Mental health services have been steadily improving in recent years. As more mental health and workplace wellbeing programmes have appeared in the corporate world, insurers have added mental health care to their coverage. Saudi German Hospital Dubai is one of the providers launching an on-site specialist mental health and wellness hub to coincide with World Mental Health Day on October 10. It is designed to end the fragmented experience many families face when navigating mental health care by bringing specialists together around a single shared care plan. Dr Ahmed Eissa, a psychiatrist and group chief executive officer of Saudi German Health UAE, hopes the centre can help with early intervention. “There are a lot of people suffering without having the right support, drug diagnosis or services,” he said. “Part of it is related to the stigma itself of going into mental health facilities, the affordability and the number of healthcare providers in the field of mental health. For some, they have days of anxiety, stress, work burnout or marital and relationship, challenges. “If we can provide the service that will help the whole family as a unit of the community, this is the core objective of the hub itself.” Services for adults and older people include psychiatric assessment, medication management and individual therapy. It also offers treatment for depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and related conditions, as well as geriatric psychiatry, addiction support and family counselling. Recruitment of mental health specialists for the hub had been a challenge. “If we are talking about integrating the mental health team here, most front lines are related to nursing, so they should be trained very well," said Dr Eissa. “There is scarcity in mental health personnel, so we need to train most of the healthcare providers in all levels so that they act like filters. “Recruiting psychiatrists and specialists to come here was a little bit challenging, especially in different subspecialties. Ideally, in the future we'll recruit from our own trainees.” A recent Global Mental Health Care Access and Affordability Benchmark report assessed access to care in 15 nations, including the UAE. The report compiled by Australian service provider TherapyNearMe.com assessed coverage, timeliness, availability, mental-health-specific unmet needs, provider fees and affordability. Eleven countries had compatible observations for psychologists, psychiatrists and mental health nurses. Five national mental health programmes were psychologist-led, five, including the UAE, were majority nurse-led, and one in Jordan was psychiatrist-led. Dr Mistry said plans to train 2,000 Abu Dhabi family doctors in mental health were a positive move towards improving access to care. “Official figures show around two thirds of the UAE's mental health workforce are nurses, which isn't quite the same as nurses leading care,” she said. “Nurses are a real strength, and often the healthcare professional a patient sees most. The risk is that they carry complex cases without enough supervision or specialists to turn to when needed.” Clear directives under the UAE’s Crimes and Penalties Law should help relieve some of the prejudice against people living with mental illness, professionals said. In 2024, Dubai authorities dropped charges of attempted suicide against Irish citizen Tori Towey, an Emirates flight attendant. Charges stemmed from a domestic incident involving Irish national Ms Towey, 30, and her South African husband. The case attracted international media attention after being raised in the Irish Parliament, with an intervention by Taoiseach Simon Harris. Any threats of prosecution for similar cases should disappear under recent amendments. Marie Byrne, a therapist from Ireland who runs positive psychology sessions in Dubai for workplace wellness, said the legal amendments can help reduce the bias still associated with certain mental health conditions. “Prior to the Iran conflict, workplace wellness was really on the agenda, the sense now is that productivity and achievement has taken over,” she said. “With the amount of uncertainty for occupational security, there is a need for people to feel they have support. “Anxiety is more prevalent with uncertainty for the future, and people are in a kind of loop; they get exhausted with worry, and they're not sleeping properly either. “It's easy to see how someone could start to think, 'it's all getting on top of me'.” Ms Byrne was one of a cohort of mental health professionals who volunteered their services for the Emirates Foundation during the pandemic. They offered free support for those in crisis or living in isolation, anxiety and depression. It was a sign of changing attitudes towards mental health, she said. “There are now similar, more permanent support structures in place with the health authorities,” said Ms Byrne. “This legal amendment could be a real incentive for people to go for early intervention, before they get to where they're even thinking to end their own life.” “I really do think this can help remove some of the stigma that is still associated with mental health.”

title: Community mourns NYUAD post-doc researcher after fatal car accident
description: Dr Xiangyu Wang was 'quietly brilliant' and an inspiration to his colleagues
content: The New York University Abu Dhabi (NYUAD) community is mourning the loss of Dr Xiangyu Wang, who tragically died in a car accident in Abu Dhabi at the end of September. Mr Wang was regarded as a brilliant researcher and spent eight years working for the university at the Advanced Materials and Building Efficiency Research Laboratory (Amber Lab) under Professor Kemal Celik. “Xiangyu joined my laboratory in 2018 as my first doctoral student and spent eight years with us, growing into one of the most talented young researchers I have known,” Prof Celik, associate professor of civil and urban engineering, told The National . Dr Wang was a co-recipient of the inaugural Bescher Award for Breakthrough Potential in CSA (calcium sulfoaluminate) Research last year. “His work on sustainable, low-carbon construction materials – from concrete made with local desert resources to 3D-printed low-carbon cement – earned international recognition,” Dr Celik said. Dr Wang pursued his bachelor's and master's degrees in China and joined the university shortly after. He earned his PhD in Civil Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering and NYUAD in 2023, after which he continued his work in the Amber Lab as a postdoctoral associate. In September 2024, he became a postdoctoral associate within NYUAD's Shores Centre, where his research focused on sustainable development challenges in desert environments. His colleagues remember him not just as a smart mind, but as someone who made an impact on the lab at a human level. “What we will remember most is the person: quietly brilliant, endlessly generous, the colleague everyone could count on, with a warm smile that lifted the whole lab. “He exemplified everything we hope science can be, and everything we hope a colleague and friend can be. His loss is immeasurable, and his work and spirit will continue to inspire our laboratory for years to come,” Prof Celik said. University leaders Fabio Piano and Marta Losada expressed their sorrow in a statement issued campus-wide. “Xiangyu exemplified the best of NYUAD – bringing an international mindset, high potential to become a world leader in his field and dedication to finding solutions for local and global challenges. Our community has lost an exceptionally talented early-career researcher who worked to advance sustainable and innovative construction technologies.” Fellow researchers and community members are organising a memorial service for Dr Wang.

title: Abu Dhabi Police share video warning about dangers of reversing on busy roads
description: Motorists must not reverse if they miss their intended exit, authorities say
content: Police in Abu Dhabi have shared a video to emphasise the risks involved in reversing on busy roads. The footage, shared on X, shows accidents caused by " drivers dangerously reversing their vehicles", police said. The Traffic and Security Patrols Directorate issued a warning about the "dangers of reversing vehicles, especially when passing exits or changing lanes, confirming that sudden stopping and reversing on roads may lead to confusion among approaching drivers, and result in dangerous collisions that may cause injuries and human and material losses". Police told motorists to continue driving if they miss their exit and to refrain from attempting to reverse. They should use another exit to reach their destination safely. Motorists caught reversing dangerously will face a fine of Dh500 ($136) and receive four black points. They will be given a further fine of Dh2,000, 23 black points and have their vehicle impounded for 60 days if found to have risked people's safety.

title: EU to increase monitoring of Muslim Brotherhood financial flows
description: 'We must know who gets EU money,' says EPP group after parliament backs motion on entryism
content: The European Parliament has urged the bloc's executive arm, the European Commission, to increase the monitoring of financial flows to the Muslim Brotherhood on the continent. The 10-page resolution calls on the Commission to provide a "comprehensive overview" of all EU funds delivered to entities suspected of links with the Muslim Brotherhood . The resolution demands the overview specify details such as the amounts received and the "failure of control" that led to the awarding of such funds. Examples given of such failures include the youth group Femyso, the European Network Against Racism, Al Sharq Forum, Islamic Relief Worldwide and the University of Gaziantep. They are described as having received EU funding "in sensitive areas such as youth, anti-discrimination, education, culture, research, humanitarian action, intercultural dialogue or university programmes, despite having raised serious questions regarding their ideological, institutional or financial links with networks linked to the Muslim Brotherhood or political Islam." The Commission, which is headed by Ursula von der Leyen , was urged to ensure full traceability of funding, including sub-grants, financial intermediaries, implementing partners and final recipients. The Parliament also encouraged it to develop new control and assessment tools "adapted to entryism strategies and network structures". The Muslim Brotherhood is described in the resolution as orchestrating an "unacceptable form of cover and malicious interference aimed at weakening democratic institutions". The resolution passed by a vote of 381 to 167. It was spearheaded by the Parliament's largest group, the right-wing European People's Party (EPP), and supported by others including the centrists at Renew. It was rejected by the left. "The European Commission and member states must duly check who receives EU funding before it is granted," said MEP Tomas Zdechovsky, the EPP spokesman for budgetary control. "We must know who gets EU money, how much and through which programmes, and be able to trace every euro, flag the risks and stop funding where the rules are not met." Resolutions are not legally binding, but they give a signal of the political mood on the continent. The Commission has three months to reply to requests made by Parliament but is not bound to follow up with a legislative proposal. The National has contacted the Commission for comment. In June, the EPP adopted a resolution at its factional political assembly in Vienna, Austria, titled “Interference of Political Islam in European democratic processes." "We are concerned with Islamist entryism as a structured political strategy that promotes an ideological project in which the religious, the social, the legal and the political are conceived as inseparable," it said at the time. The European debate on the Muslim Brotherhood was relaunched by the French government announcing last year it would take new counter-measures , including the disbanding of endowment funds and a new asset-freeze mechanism. The resolution calls for the listing of some Muslim Brotherhood supporters as terrorists. It highlights that several EU states had recently banned entities linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. "Where rules allow, the Council should list individuals and organisations linked to the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist entities," said MEP Celine Imart, who led the EPP Group’s work on the topic. "European money must not fund groups that threaten our rights and freedoms." Earlier this year, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez revealed the government prefers to act on a case-by-case basis to address the concerns raised by a French Parliament vote to endorse a resolution calling on the EU to add the Muslim Brotherhood to its list of terrorist groups.

title: UAE art guide: 13 exhibitions to see, from Indian Ocean history at Louvre Abu Dhabi to Revelation at 421
description: Plus, Unseen Script at Rizq to Revelation at 421
content: Galleries and institutions across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah are presenting a diverse programme of exhibitions as the UAE's autumn art season gathers pace. Current highlights include Revelation at 421 Arts Campus , Emirati artist Juma Al Haj's first institutional solo exhibition exploring seclusion and self-reflection; Paul Guiragossian : 100 Years of Art at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation, celebrating the centenary of the Lebanese modernist's birth; and Taking Form at The Third Line, where Rana Begum explores colour, geometry and material through a new body of work. Elsewhere, exhibitions examine cultural identity, environmental change and the relationship between people and their surroundings, with works spanning painting, photography, sculpture, textiles and moving image. Here are 13 exhibitions to see across the UAE. In Unseen Script , curated by Meena Vari, works by 10 artists explore the patterns people form through repetition, from familiar journeys and domestic objects to changing landscapes and gestures that become so ingrained they often go unnoticed. The exhibition brings together art by Najat Makki, Nujoom Alghanem, Nasir Nasrallah, Abdulla PA, Ana Escobar Saavedra, Fadi Balhawan, Ismail Al Rifai, Joanna Barakat, Neveen Abu Samra and Simrin Mehra Agarwal. Across painting, sculpture, assemblage and mixed media, the artists return to recurring subjects within their practices, revealing how personal habits and ways of seeing become a kind of visual script. Several works draw on the relationship between people and their surroundings. Abdulla reflects on abandoned homes and the ways nature reclaims human-made spaces, while Saavedra transforms seashells into delicate assemblages. Nasrallah draws on memories of his grandfather’s antique shop, Makki extends her abstract practice into steel and Alghanem examines the cityscape as a contemporary horizon. While the exhibition touches on the way technology can identify and predict human patterns, its focus remains on subjective experience, asking what memory, consciousness and observation can reveal that data cannot. Until October 28; Abu Dhabi Taking Form is Rana Begum’s fifth solo exhibition at The Third Line, bringing together new works across textile, linen, wood and paper that continue her exploration of light, colour, geometry and material. Large wool tapestries suspended from the ceiling form the centre of the exhibition. Woven with geometric patterns, their appearance shifts as visitors move around them. Elsewhere, diluted acrylic has seeped into linen, while smaller works on paper and wooden panels explore interactions between colour and surface. The exhibition introduces a greater sense of softness to Begum’s practice while retaining the abstraction and geometric structures that have long shaped her work. Until November 10; Dubai Two exhibitions at Leila Heller Gallery consider Emirati identity and heritage through the work of Azza Al Qubaisi and Karima Al Shomely. Al Qubaisi’s Between Land and Sea, curated by Aysha Al Hemeiri, surveys a multidisciplinary practice spanning intimate jewellery and large-scale public works. Her use of natural resources and materials connects the UAE’s desert and coastal environments with ideas of memory, identity and place. In Between a Fold and a Memory, Al Shomely turns to the clothing, textiles and objects associated with Emirati women. Photography, sculpture, textile and video explore how materials such as the burqa and traditional fabrics can carry memories of labour, social change and cultural knowledge across generations. Until November 10; Dubai Kenyan artist Maggie Otieno transforms reclaimed materials into vessels of memory in Sojourner: The Difference is the Same, her first solo exhibition with Efie Gallery. Otieno’s practice has centred on distressed and discarded materials for almost three decades. The exhibition includes works made from 150-year-old railway sleepers, whose histories are tied to East Africa’s colonial railway network, alongside sculptures incorporating fragments of wooden canoes produced during a residency at El Anatsui Studio in Ghana. By cutting, assembling and reconfiguring these materials, Otieno shifts objects once associated with movement and infrastructure into forms concerned with stillness, memory and passage. Until November 13; Dubai Emirati artist Eman Al Hashemi examines the changing rhythms of urban life in the UAE in The Horizon We Inherit, her first solo exhibition with Iris Projects. Working across ceramics, printmaking and mixed media, she considers how cities shape attention, memory and everyday routines. The sun, street lights, buildings and roundabouts recur throughout the works, turning familiar features of the UAE cityscape into forms that can appear both recognisable and strange. Al Hashemi is particularly interested in the routes people repeatedly travel and the traces left behind as places are altered through construction and redevelopment. Rather than treating the built environment as a backdrop, the exhibition considers it as an active force in daily life and asks what remains when familiar places survive only through photographs, maps, memories or repeatedly travelled routes. September 26 to November 26; Abu Dhabi Vantage Point 13 marks a new chapter for Sharjah Art Foundation's long-running photography platform as it moves into the institution's dedicated photography gallery.
