Selected through an international open call, six artists present commissioned photographic series developed with the foundation's curatorial and production support. The exhibition features work by Adam Rouhana, Guanyu Xu, Latifa AlBokhari, Luisa Dorr, Maheder Haileselassie and Sathish Kumar. Together, their projects demonstrate the breadth of contemporary photography, reflecting the programme's evolution from a platform for UAE-based photographers into an international exhibition embracing diverse approaches. Introduced in 2013, Vantage Point has become one of the UAE's key photography initiatives. This edition also reflects the foundation's expanded commitment to supporting new work, with participating artists receiving production funding to create original projects specifically for the exhibition. Until November 29; Sharjah Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve brings together eight UAE-based women artists whose practices are rooted in the Global South, exploring how ceramics can give physical form to emotions and experiences that are difficult to express through words. Curated by Shafeena Yusuff Ali, founder and executive director of Rizq Art Initiative, the exhibition examines the relationship between the body, clay and emotional expression. The exhibition features sculptures by Nujoom Alghanem, Mirna Bamieh, Moza Al Falasi, Malavika, Parneet Pahwa, Zahra Shafie, Laiba Sherin and Haseena Suresh. Working on an intimate, domestic scale, the artists use processes of pressing, building, breaking and firing clay to explore memory, grief and lived experience. Presented at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery's Project Space, the exhibition also considers the long-standing relationship between ceramics, women's labour and practices of care. By focusing on the physical act of making, it positions clay as a medium through which personal experiences and emotions can take shape. October 22 to December 13; Abu Dhabi The exhibition brings together works by Shahana Rajani, Rohini Devasher and Sarker Protick to explore how land, water and the cosmos can act as archives of memory and history. Through photography, moving image and installation, the exhibition considers how ecological change and human intervention leave traces on the environment that can persist across generations. Rajani’s three-channel film Lines That World a River focuses on communities displaced from the Indus Delta, where paintings and murals reconstruct villages submerged following the construction of dams and barrages. Devasher turns towards the cosmos with Latent Fields , monumental silk panels inspired by sunspots and other solar phenomena, while Protick’s Dhaka 1217 documents 15 years of transformation around the neighbourhood in Dhaka where he was born and continues to live. Drawing together perspectives from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, the exhibition considers ecological decline across national borders, and the ways landscapes can preserve histories of displacement, destruction and resilience. Until December 15; Dubai Emirati artist Juma Al Haj explores seclusion, reflection and personal transformation in Revelation, his first institutional solo exhibition. Developed through 421 Arts Campus's Artistic Development Programme, it brings together painting, engraved glass, text, light, shadow and installation to consider how moments of uncertainty can lead to greater self-understanding. The exhibition unfolds as a physical journey, beginning with Balaa , a painting concerned with trials and the ways people measure their lives, and Traces , a series of engraved glass panels whose inscriptions shift with light and shadow. It culminates in Hijr , a darkened, carpeted space centred on a water feature, where visitors remove their shoes and are encouraged to slow down and contemplate. Al Haj's approach draws on journaling, philosophy and spiritual texts, extending the layered marks of his paintings into an environment visitors can move through. Rather than presenting revelation as a final answer, the exhibition treats it as one stage in an continuing process of reflection and discovery. Until January 10, 2027; Abu Dhabi Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art celebrates the centenary of the Lebanese artist's birth, bringing together significant works from his estate at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation in Abu Dhabi. Developed in collaboration with the Paul Guiragossian Foundation, the exhibition offers an overview of the life and legacy of one of the leading figures of modern Lebanese and Middle Eastern art. Known for his expressive use of colour and distinctive depictions of the human figure, Guiragossian (1926–1993) developed a visual language concerned with family, identity and the human condition. His paintings frequently explored themes of displacement, belonging and everyday life, reflecting both personal experiences and the wider history of the region. Drawing primarily on works from the artist's estate, the exhibition traces the development of his practice and considers his enduring influence on modern Arab art. October 17 to January 17, 2027; Abu Dhabi Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean explores 1,000 years of maritime trade and cultural exchange, tracing the routes that connected communities across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, India, China and South-East Asia. Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders. The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's pearl trade and the movement of spices, precious stones, textiles and religious artefacts. Highlights include six detailed models of historic vessels, objects recovered from shipwrecks, ancient navigational instruments and a third-century Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan. Through specially created maps and immersive displays, the exhibition examines how sailors navigated using stars and coastal landmarks, while merchants and pilgrims carried goods, beliefs and artistic traditions between distant societies. Its historical narrative concludes in the 17th century, drawing attention to the extensive trading networks that existed before European powers came to dominate Indian Ocean commerce. Until February 14, 2027; Abu Dhabi A Board Game Adventure transforms Louvre Abu Dhabi into a giant playground, using some of the world's oldest games to explore how people have connected across cultures for thousands of years. Designed for children but engaging for all ages, the exhibition traces the journey of games including chess, Mancala, Ludo and Carrom as they travelled between ancient civilisations and evolved into the games still played today. The exhibition combines immersive installations with rare artefacts borrowed from international museums, including some of the earliest known board game objects from ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Iran and India. Highlights include centuries-old chess pieces carved from ivory and rock crystal, engraved backgammon pieces, ancient six-sided dice and one of the earliest known predecessors of Ludo. Interactive displays encourage visitors to solve puzzles, challenge artificial intelligence, play on oversized game boards and discover how strategy, chance and storytelling have always been part of human play. Throughout the exhibition, historical figures ranging from Queen Nefertari and Achilles to samurai Hatakeyama Shigetada are reimagined through playful “player profiles”, linking games to the personalities and cultures that shaped them. Rather than presenting games as simple entertainment, A Board Game Adventure reveals them as cultural objects that have crossed borders, adapted to societies and brought people together for millennia. Until April 25, 2027

title: Among the world's megaprojects, the Gulf is building big
description: Four of ten ambitious developments valued at $100 billion or more are being constructed in the region
content: Building a new city or regional rail line is expensive, but that has not put a halt to developments in the Gulf. In a ranking compiled by Statista, four of the ten megaprojects with estimated costs of at least $100 billion were in the region. They include Saudi Arabia’s Neom and King Abdullah Economic City, Kuwait’s Silk City and a railway project to connect the six GCC member states. Together, those megaprojects show the scale of the region’s ambitions to build new industries, cities and transport links. Neom, announced in 2017 with an initial $500 billion price tag, is perhaps the most well-known. The development in the north-west of the kingdom encompasses several projects, including The Line, a city originally envisaged as stretching 170km between mirrored walls. The Gulf railway project is intended to make it easier to move people and goods across the region. The GCC Railways Authority has said the line is to span 2,117km, with the network scheduled to be fully operational in December 2030. The costliest entry in the Statista ranking, however, lies outside the Gulf. Europe’s Trans-European Transport Network is listed with an estimated $600 billion. It brings together railways, roads, ports and other infrastructure across EU states, with various aspects of the project to be completed between 2030 and 2050. But comparing those megaprojects requires some care. Building a transport network across several countries is different to constructing a new city. The figures in the ranking also represent estimated costs, rather than the money already spent, and those can change as plans evolve. The chart captures the size of those ambitions. Whether they are delivered at the scale, cost and pace first promised is another story.

title: UAE economy grew in first half of 2026 despite impact of Iran war
description: Growth was heavily driven by non-oil sector, which contributed 79% of GDP
content: The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the GDP during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said in a statement on Friday. The results "reflect the continued diversification of the UAE's economic base and the growing role of non-oil activities", the FCSC said. Trade topped contributions to non-oil GDP at 16.2 per cent, followed by financial and insurance (15.2 per cent), construction (13.1 per cent), manufacturing (11.8) and real estate (7.9 per cent). Meanwhile, activities in the financial and insurance sector posted the highest growth rate in the six months through the end of June, rising by 14.8 per cent, the FCSC said. That was followed by information and communication (7.3 per cent), health and social work (6 per cent), construction (5.1 per cent), government (3.6 per cent) and real estate (2.3 per cent). The non-oil sector's "expanding contribution to economic activity demonstrates the diversity of growth drivers and supports sustainable and balanced growth across a broad range of economic sectors", the FCSC added. The UAE's GDP last year grew 6.2 per cent year-on-year to hit Dh1.9 trillion, as non-oil GDP jumped 6.8 per cent to Dh1.5 trillion. In the second quarter of the year, the UAE's real GDP hit Dh476.9 billion, a decline of 2.1 per cent annually. Non-oil activities also contracted by 1.1 per cent, as several economic sectors, particularly tourism, transport and trade, were affected by regional developments and disruption to travel. However, the non-oil sector has started to rebound. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index remained stable at 55.3 in September, the same as August, and well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. That reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, S&P said. Business activity in September increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month, the index found. Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years, in response to higher input costs, the report found.

title: Anthony Vaccarello exits Saint Laurent after a decade
description: Belgian designer hailed for  elevating house to 'forefront of desirability and image'
content: Following weeks of rumours, global luxury fashion group Kering has confirmed that creative director Anthony Vaccarello has exited Saint Laurent. The label's parent company said he had "played a key role in Saint Laurent's development, helping to strengthen its identity and influence across the worlds of fashion and culture". Saint Laurent president and chief executive Cedric Charbit praised Vaccarello for his decade-long "dedication" to the company. "During his tenure, Anthony took Saint Laurent on a remarkable trajectory, elevating the house to the forefront of desirability and image, while accomplishing exceptional work both creatively and through his cultural impact,” he said. Kering chief executive Luca de Meo added: "Through his creative vision and exacting standards, [Anthony] has contributed to strengthening the enduring influence of one of France's greatest couture houses, as we embark on a new chapter in its history." Vaccarello leaves behind a legacy with the label. With a keen eye for the dramatic, he understood the role of spectacle, staging shows beneath the Eiffel Tower that showcased razor-sharp tailoring, sheer mini dresses and dramatic eveningwear, and creating a vision of Paris after dark that helped propel the French house to the top tier of global luxury. The Belgian designer's final show with Saint Laurent, held in Paris on September 29, was filled with gilded looks that faded into darkness, and at the time, was widely regarded as his farewell to the house. Appointed in 2016 to succeed Hedi Slimane , Vaccarello introduced greater colour, volume and sensuality to the house’s monochromatic codes. Building on Saint Laurent's signature codes, from towering heels to elegant silk trench coats, he helped shape a distinctive aesthetic that proved both creatively and commercially successful. Under his direction, the house's revenue tripled to €3.3 billion, before falling to €2.6 billion in 2025 amid a wider slowdown in luxury spending. His influence also extended beyond fashion, with Saint Laurent launching its own film-production arm in 2023. His departure comes at a time of wider change for Kering . Under new chief executive De Meo, the luxury group is undergoing an 18-month overhaul aimed at reviving its brands, with plans to expand Saint Laurent's menswear and jewellery collections. Whoever succeeds Vaccarello will face the challenge of taking Saint Laurent in a new direction while preserving the distinctive glamour that defined his decade at the house. Kering has yet to announce a replacement, although Chemena Kamali, currently creative director of Chloe, is already being mentioned as a possible successor.

title: Small stamps, big ambitions: A history of Middle East progress
description: Vintage postage stamps offer a window into how many of the region's countries marked their progress and future
content: I recently came across an article published by the Data Visualisation Society's Nightingale magazine that captures a niche but wonderful corner of a largely bygone era of stamps, graphic design, and data visualisation as political communications. Its author, Julie Peasley, assembled 180 stamps from around the world featuring charts and other data visuals from 88 countries. Among them are examples from across the Middle East and North Africa. Together, they offer a shed light into how the region's governments chose to illustrate growth through future projections and economic indicators. I reviewed a set containing 38 entries from 14 countries from 1940 to 2015. Looking into the stamps, I uncovered a rich snapshot of the time the stamp was issued and the context behind the beautiful graphics, colours and charts. Here are a few of the most striking and informative stamps. Census stamps were a common feature in the database. At the turn of the last century, many Middle Eastern countries' populations were exploding, and the administrative task of keeping track was a huge national undertaking. Many countries chose to mark these occasions with special commemorative stamps. Iraq 's 1987 census stamp is a busy composition highlighting the diversity of the country, with illustrations representing rural and urban workers. Behind them, a line graph presents a population count through the visual language of a modern government. But it's important to remember another context. According to Human Rights Watch, “the machinery of genocide was set in motion” against Iraqi Kurds in March 1987, and that year’s census became part of it ahead of the Anfal campaign. In that context, the stamp is a reminder that counting a population can also be a means of documenting who is wanted – and who isn't. Egypt ’s 1976 population and housing census stamp brings people and their surroundings into the same frame. Combining the height of the construction boom showing a city scape in a turquoise backdrop, figures gather along the bottom and lines traverse a grid marked with years and numbers. It was issued during president Anwar Sadat ’s infitah , or “open-door” policy, introduced in 1974 to attract Arab and foreign investment. Egypt was changing its economic direction and the stamp’s buildings and statistical grid can be read as a small picture of that ambition to modernise. Kuwait ’s census stamp shows a family of four in traditional dress, beside a pink outline of the country and beneath a rising line chart, combining both a family portrait and statistics. Issued in 1965, only four years after independence in 1961, it captures a country changing quickly. Kuwait’s population had more than doubled since 1957, reaching about 467,000 by 1965, with non-Kuwaitis making up slightly more than half of its residents. Behind the simple family illustration was a much bigger story of oil, migration and the building of a modern state. The UAE ’s 1980 population census stamp is beautiful in its illustrative simplicity. A family stands against a pink grid, in traditional dress. The UAE was still less than a decade old at the time and this count followed its first general census in 1975. In Abu Dhabi alone, the population more than doubled between those two counts, from about 212,000 to 452,000. Qatar marked the Mena Economic Conference of 1997 with a stamp featuring an artistic line chart, turning the visual language of economic growth into a commemorative and memorable design. Held in Doha in November 1997, the conference belonged to a series launched in the wake of the Oslo Accords, with hopes that closer economic ties would support regional peace. The stamp’s optimism sits against a much more complicated political moment. Marking 100 years of the Egyptian stock exchange, the design combines a rising graph with a sweeping curved arrow. This shows a colourful composition of movement, fluctuation and forward momentum. The anniversary reaches back to the exchange’s establishment in 1903. This UAE stamp, with “Growth Monitoring” written in Arabic and English, was issued as part of Unicef’s Child Survival Campaign, reflecting a major public-health push of the 1980s. Unicef promoted simple, affordable measures – regular growth monitoring, breastfeeding, immunisation and oral rehydration therapy – to help more children survive their early years. It is a strong example of data visualisation serving a practical purpose. Growth charts are still used today to track children’s development and spot when they might need help. Sudan ’s World Statistics Day stamp takes a broader view of what data can do. Colourful triangles and circles accompany the phrase “Better Data, Better Lives”, putting the emphasis on how statistics can improve people’s lives. The timing matters. In 2015, the UN adopted the Sustainable Development Goals, setting targets on poverty, health, education and much more. Reliable statistics were essential to knowing where countries stood and whether they were making progress. Sudan’s stamp carries the theme of that year’s World Statistics Day into a small, colourful design.

title: Dubai Miracle Garden reopens for 15th season with more than 200 million flowers
description: Outdoor attraction to welcome visitors until May 31
content: Dubai Miracle Garden has reopened for its 15th season, welcoming visitors back with more than 200 million flowers and a new programme of weekly themed events. The outdoor attraction, which spans 72,000 square metres, will remain open until May 31, 2027. The latest season is being held under the theme Fifteen Years, Blooming Together. For the first time, the garden will introduce a different theme every week, with activities and celebrations inspired by the UAE's national and cultural calendar. The opening months will feature events marking Pink October, United Nations Day, UAE Flag Day and Diwali, alongside musical performances, family entertainment. Fitness activities will be organised as part of the Dubai Fitness Challenge. Special programmes are also planned for Commemoration Day and Eid Al Etihad. Visitors can explore more than 150 varieties of flowers, alongside the garden's elaborate floral installations and structures, several of which have been celebrated as Guinness World Records. Sheikh Theyab bin Tahnoon, chairman of Miracle Group, inaugurated the new season. “For 15 seasons, Dubai Miracle Garden has grown alongside Dubai and its people,” he said. “This season is dedicated to the community that made it possible, particularly the families and residents who return year after year.” Since opening in 2013, the attraction has welcomed millions of visitors and become one of the city's best-known outdoor attractions, particularly during the cooler months. Last season , the garden featured more than 150 million flowers and introduced a children's area with a miniature train and bumper cars. Returning favourites include the Guinness World Record Emirates A380 floral installation, made from more than 500,000 flowers and plants, as well as the Smurfs Village and Floating Lady sculpture. Dubai Miracle Garden is open daily from 9am to 9pm. Tickets are priced at Dh80 for children aged between 3 and 12 and Dh100 for those older than 12; children under 3 can enter free of charge

title: Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival returns to Abu Dhabi with message of renewal
description: Event at NYU Abu Dhabi explores humanity's relationship with nature and the efforts to repair it
content: Cinema cannot save the environment, but it can change the way we see it. That is the idea behind Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival, which returns to Abu Dhabi with a programme examining humanity's relationship with nature and the ways that relationship can be repaired. Now in its fifth iteration , the festival runs from Friday to Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi, bringing together international documentaries, fiction, animation and conversations with filmmakers, scientists and conservationists. Organised in collaboration with Environment Agency Abu Dhabi, the festival this year has the theme Mend, which takes its name from the Arabic verb rammim, meaning to repair or restore something of value. Artistic director Nezar Andary says the theme reflects a philosophy that has guided the festival since 2020. He believes environmental cinema should encourage curiosity rather than overwhelm audiences with alarming statistics or instructions on how to live. "I don't want an environmentalism that believes in some pristine, perfect version of nature," he tells The National . "Mending is something we're constantly doing, and it's something the Earth itself does." Al Sidr was inspired by a small environmental film festival that Andary attended at Princeton Public Library in the United States. He was impressed by its preference for creative documentaries over conventional environmental campaigning. "The more creative, artistic documentary isn't force-feeding you an environmental ideology, but is actually creating a sense of intimacy and questioning," he says. Al Sidr has since welcomed more than 5,000 attendees and engaged 2,000 students from more than 20 schools across Abu Dhabi. This year's selection approaches ecology through scientific exploration, cultural heritage and conservation. Among the headline screenings is Ghost Elephants , a documentary by German filmmaker Werner Herzog . The National Geographic production, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, receives its Arabian Gulf premiere on Friday. Another highlight is Fire of Love , the Oscar-nominated 2022 documentary by Sara Dosa, which chronicles the lives of French volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft, whose fascination with volcanoes shaped their work and relationship. "It's about two lovers who are studying volcanoes. And it's about love. It's about love of science," Andary says. Dosa's 2026 documentary Time and Water , which premiered at Sundance, will screen at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi on Friday, accompanied by a free museum tour, and again on Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi. The programme also includes Fungi: Web of Life , narrated by Icelandic musician Bjork, and Chuuraa , a short film by Evgenia Arbugaeva that premiered at this year's Berlin International Film Festival. Beyond documentaries, Andary is particularly enthusiastic about the restored 4K edition of Manthan , the 1976 Indian film by Shyam Benegal, which screens on Saturday. The film examines the formation of a dairy co-operative in rural India, connecting agriculture with questions of class, collective action and social change. Andary says environmental storytelling can extend to subjects that might not immediately appear to be ecological. At a previous edition, he screened Ken Loach's Kes , a British drama about a working-class boy and his relationship with a kestrel. He says both films address class and solidarity, issues that can also resonate with audiences in the UAE. Closer to home, the festival will premiere episodes of Conservation Diaries , a five-part documentary series produced by Connect with Nature, the youth environmental movement established by the Environment Agency Abu Dhabi and Emirates Nature–WWF. Filmed across the UAE's wadis, mangroves, coastlines and rural communities, the series follows scientists, volunteers and conservationists protecting biodiversity. It offers a practical interpretation of Mend , highlighting the patient work required to understand ecosystems and protect vulnerable species. "They're the heroes on the ground who are tracking animals, who are working with citizen scientists," Andary says. A panel on Sunday will examine ecological restoration in the UAE, while other sessions explore water, fungi and environmental science. Saturday's family programme features international animated shorts alongside Fungi: Web of Life and an introduction to fungi by Dima Al Srouri, founder of Dubai venture MycoSphere, which develops materials using mycelium and agricultural waste. Andary hopes the festival encourages people to question their relationships with the natural world. Previous editions experimented with audience-led discussions instead of conventional expert panels, while one screening was accompanied by a meal prepared using food waste. Although he wishes this year's programme offered more interaction, Al Sidr will continue its educational activities through school visits across Abu Dhabi. Andary recalls how working on a documentary involving an ancient burial site in the UAE changed his perspective on wildlife. Learning that people used Socotra cormorant feathers in burials made him more attentive to the birds and their historical relationship with people. "I listen more, I'm more attentive," he says. He believes such changes in perception can be as important as the practical lessons audiences take from a screening. The festival should begin conversations that continue beyond the cinema. "Cinema is not going to heal the environment. We are," Andary says. Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival runs from October 9 to 11 at the Blue Hall, NYU Abu Dhabi. Tickets and the full programme are available at alsidrfestival.com

title: 'I had to keep lifting myself up': Breast cancer survivors offer hope as screening push boosts health fight
description: Former patients emphasise need to stay strong after diagnosis, amid calls to ensure early detection
content: Breast cancer survivors in the UAE have delivered a message of hope to others as crucial screening drives are expanded to help save lives and transform "awareness into action". To mark Breast Cancer Awareness Month, two Emirati women have shared their stories of battling back from adversity and refusing to allow the disease to define their lives. Sara Al Sheebani and Meera Al Ameri underwent operations and gruelling chemotherapy sessions on their road to recovery – but were determined not to be ruled by fear, even in the toughest of times. They have now highlighted the importance of regular check-ups to ensure any issues are detected early. Breast cancer remains the most common form of the disease to affect women around the world. It is the leading cause of premature death among women, with annual cases expected to rise from 2.3 million in 2023 to more than 3.5 million by 2050. In October last year, breast cancer screenings in Abu Dhabi surged by 377.5 per cent compared with the same month in 2024. The exact numbers of screenings were not made available. The Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre is seeking to build on that momentum by offering free mammograms around the emirate throughout October. For Ms Al Sheebani, now 47, a pain in her chest led her to seek medical advice. She was 34 when doctors diagnosed her with stage two breast cancer. She had no skin changes and could not feel a lump. “I accepted the news. I wasn’t frightened,” she said. “I kept praying that they would be able to operate and that it hadn’t spread elsewhere in my body.” She underwent surgery, chemotherapy and about 20 sessions of radiotherapy. She also had hormone treatment for more than seven years. At times, she was in so much pain that she could barely raise herself up. “Sometimes I would open my eyes, see the sun and say, ‘Thank God, I’m alive,’” she said. “There were moments when I wondered if I might die. But I knew God was with me, and I had to keep lifting myself up.” Ms Al Sheebani was determined to live life to the fullest and attended a family wedding during her treatment, despite her mother pleading with her to rest at home. Her feet were so swollen from treatment that she wore the largest men’s slippers she could find and asked a make-up artist to apply false eyelashes as she dealt with hair loss. “I’m still going,” she told her parents. “Why should I hide? Why should cancer patients continue to hide in their homes? Why should I be ashamed of something I wasn’t responsible for? It is an illness like any other. So what if I lost my hair? Why should I be judged?” Ms Al Sheebani recovered and has since had a son through IVF. She now advocates early cancer screening and encourages other patients to share their experiences. “Cancer has changed me in so many ways. I won’t deny it was hard, but it is also manageable and you get through it,” she said. Meera Al Ameri, a marathon runner, weightlifter and mother of five, thought that paying close attention to her health would protect her from the disease. Her diagnosis in 2024 came as a shock. “I ate healthily, lifted heavy weights and participated in marathons,” she said. “You think that because you are healthy, it cannot happen to you. But cancer can happen to anyone.” She underwent chemotherapy and a double mastectomy, but continued to exercise during her treatment. “After chemotherapy, I would go and lift weights,” she said. “I treated myself as a message for others. Why should we be shy? Why should we be embarrassed?” Ms Al Ameri also drew strength from art, which offered her an opportunity to express her emotions on paper during her cancer fight. She chose not to hide the physical effects of treatment. “I loved myself bald,” she said. “I would actually stand in front of the mirror and admire myself. I enjoyed the wigs, too.” Dr Rashed Alsuwaidi, director general of Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre, emphasised the importance of Breast Cancer Awareness month, but wants efforts to catch the disease early to be in sharp focus all year round. “The increase we saw in breast cancer screenings last October shows what can happen when awareness turns into action,” he said. “Our priority, not just in October but for the rest of this year, is to build on that progress and make preventive screening a sustained part of how people look after their health.” Dr Mouza Al Ameri, assistant professor at the United Arab Emirates University’s College of Medicine and Health Sciences and a consultant breast surgeon, said fear can hold women back from seeking out help. “Fear can make the disease feel bigger than it is,” she said. “Once it is diagnosed, it becomes something we can deal with. That is why courage is the first step towards taking action.” Dr Aala Al Nuaimi, consultant psychiatrist at Sakina, Abu Dhabi's mental health network, said support from others could help women manage the fear and anxiety surrounding screenings and diagnosis. “Awareness is about providing information, psychological safety helps them act and human connection helps them sustain the journey,” she said. Dr Stephen Grobmyer, head of Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi's Cancer Institute, said screening remained crucial to catching cancer early and improving patient outcomes. Studies at Cleveland Clinic found that about a quarter of breast cancer patients were under 40 when they had the disease diagnosed – a younger patient profile than in the US or much of Europe. Researchers are investigating why and how screening might be improved for younger women. Abu Dhabi's Department of Health has awarded Centre of Excellence status to specialist breast cancer services at the Burjeel Breast Centre at Burjeel Cancer Institute, as well as Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi. The designation matters for patients because a team of specialists is often required to assess, diagnose and plan treatment together, Dr Grobmyer said. “A Centre of Excellence really brings all of those things together into one place and improves communication between doctors and patients, and doctors and doctors,” he said. “It makes care safer, more efficient and we think it leads to happier patients and safer care.” Dr Dima Abdul Jabbar, consultant medical oncologist and director of the Burjeel Breast Centre, said care is "not one size fits all". “Genetics is also only one part of the picture," she added. "We need to look at clinical, lifestyle, social and population data to develop a more complete understanding of each patient.” Dr Grobmyer said advances in understanding breast cancer and the results of clinical trials had helped doctors reduce treatment for some patients while improving outcomes. He also said artificial intelligence was being used to support radiologists assessing mammograms, help estimate risk and improve the analysis of pathology samples. “In the early days, back in the mid-90s, we pretty much treated all patients the same,” he said. “At that time, we didn’t know who needed chemotherapy and who didn’t.”

title: 'Why would you need courage to speak the truth': Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
description: Committee says South African judge has shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure war crimes are prosecuted
content: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to ⁠South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure that war crimes and genocide were prosecuted and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. It also said she had demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career. The former UN human rights chief led the world body's Commission of Inquiry into the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year. The commission determined that war crimes had been committed by both Hamas and Israel in the wake of the attacks on October 7, 2023. In her first reaction to the announcement, Ms Pillay discussed the importance of that finding. "The last thing I did is deliver the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," she said to friends gathered in the German city of Nuremburg. "One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage and you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision making." She later dedicated the award to "all the survivors of international crimes, as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign". In a message to world leaders, she said: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war." Israel ‌condemned the Nobel Committee for giving her the award. "The decision of the Nobel Committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of anti-Semitism, like Pillay herself," said Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron. "As the chair of ​the Commission of Inquiry, she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence, campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda." The Nobel judges said Ms Pillay had enlarged the scope and impact of international law as a judge in the High Court in South Africa and at the International Criminal Court. "A common thread runs ⁠from her early work defending ​Nelson Mandela ⁠and ‌others who stood up against ​apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said. Ms Pillay has "held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict", they said. "Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time," the committee added. "Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world." The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented ​in ‌Oslo on ⁠December 10, the ​anniversary of the ​death ‌of Swedish industrialist ⁠Alfred Nobel, who founded the ⁠awards in his 1895 will. Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Ms Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988. She was the first non-white judge of the High Court of South Africa. The ​UN ⁠human rights office ​on Friday ⁠welcomed the award to Ms ⁠Pillay, ‌acknowledging ​her long-standing advocacy for human rights. "It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human ​rights," ‌Shabia ⁠Mantoo, ​spokeswoman ​for ‌the UN ⁠human rights office. “The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. “Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.” He said the committee wanted to remind the world that "the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently”, adding that peace "requires justice”. Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist. Last year’s peace prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her prize to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts ​in Venezuela. Mr Trump has again suggested he should be the recipient of the prize , although he acknowledged it was unlikely. Mr Trump, who this year has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on ​Wednesday: "They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me." Since his ​return to the White House last year, Mr Trump has repeatedly ⁠said he deserves what may be the world's most prestigious award. "It is about ​that time," Mr Trump said in the Oval Office. "But I was very honoured ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump." The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Mr Trump, though there is no way of verifying that. Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, with the Swedish Academy recognising her experimental approach to writing and her ability to bring ancient Greek literature into the modern world. The 76-year-old author ’s best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox. The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. Francis Halzen won the physics prize for contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. The Chemistry prize went to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for work in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

title: Saudi airline pilot among three killed in attacks on Riyadh airport
description: Missiles hit airport facilities and aircraft owned by ⁠state carrier Saudia
content: Three Saudi citizens were killed in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Friday. The missile attacks took place on Thursday and hit a Saudia aircraft and airport facilities. A number of people have been injured, it added, without specifying the number. An airline captain named Hamoud Ali Alkalthami was among those killed. Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed they hit the airport with two cruise missiles. The Iran-backed group also said it attacked an airport in the south-western city of Najran, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed, and launched ballistic missiles at an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The latest casualties come ⁠after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people ⁠were killed in earlier strikes this week on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the south-west. Saudi Arabia has been attacked repeatedly after the Houthis made advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the Yemeni government launching a counter-offensive supported by coalition strikes. On Thursday, the kingdom said it would “punish” the Houthis after the deadly attacks on airports in Riyadh and the south, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile causing damage to civilian areas in the capital. “The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom … will not go unpunished,” said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. The coalition’s joint forces had destroyed dozens of Houthi military targets across Yemen, he added. In another development, services from King Khalid International Airport were gradually returning to normal on Friday, after days of delays and cancellations. Flights were initially suspended on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks, with disruption continuing into Thursday.

title: Iran's supreme leader calls for greater use of AI to strengthen security
description: Push to integrate AI into defence systems accelerated after confrontation with Israel in 2024
content: Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has called for greater investment in artificial intelligence and advanced technology to strengthen the country's security forces. In a message marking National Police Week, he said Iran needed to bolster its police force through improvements in personnel, equipment and technology, particularly the use of AI in data analysis. "A comprehensive strengthening of the forces responsible for safeguarding security in all respects, including human resources, hardware and software – particularly through the advancement of technology, such as the purposeful use of artificial intelligence in data analysis – plays an important role in improving the ability of the police force to carry out their missions and facilitates their work," he said. Mr Khamenei also praised the country's security forces for maintaining order despite repeated US and Israeli attacks . He accused the US and Israel of deliberately targeting police commanders and personnel, but said the attacks had failed to undermine the ability of security forces to carry out their missions. The National revealed late last year that Iran planned to use AI in its armed forces and security apparatus – nearly three months before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February, sparking the regional war. Despite restrictions on its access to advanced AI chips owing to sanctions, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said last year during military exercises that it was using AI in domestically developed drones, including in missiles capable of autonomously locking on to moving targets. The announcement highlighted Tehran's determination to keep pace with the global AI race. Under an official strategy, Iran aims to rank among the world's top 10 AI powers by 2032, with AI contributing 12 per cent of its GDP. The push to integrate AI into Iran's defence systems accelerated after its first direct military confrontation with Israel in 2024. In April, Brig Gen Kioumars Heydari, commander of the army’s ground forces at the time and now deputy chief of staff, described AI as "one of our priorities to maximise our defensive power”. The US has also used AI in its war against Iran. In March, Admiral Brad Cooper , commander of US Central Command, said AI systems “allow us to analyse large volumes of data within seconds, enabling our leaders to make the right decisions faster than the enemy amid the noise”. He said advanced AI tools had reduced processes that would typically take hours, and sometimes days, to mere seconds. “However, the final decision is always made by a human: what to strike, what not to strike, and when to strike,” he added. But the US bombing of an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on the first day of the war – an attack that killed more than 150 people, many of them schoolgirls – raised questions about AI's role in military operations. A September report by Bloomberg said an overreliance on AI tools, alongside outdated intelligence and imagery, contributed to the strike. The full findings of a Pentagon investigation into the attack have not yet been made public.

title: UFC: Sean Strickland says he may quit over pay dispute and pursue a boxing match with Jake Paul
description: UFC middleweight champion cited the amount stars like Conor McGregor as a factor and that his heart 'isn't in MMA anymore'
content: UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland said he is considering his future with the world's lead MMA promotion over pay, citing the amount of stars like Conor McGregor earn. Strickland aired his grievances on social media, saying he is considering giving up his title, moving up to light heavyweight to "speed run" through the rest of his contract and then pursue a lucrative boxing match with Jake Paul. The American, 35, pointed to McGregor's reported payday for his comeback against Max Holloway in July. The Irishman took home a reported paycheque of $30 million for a fight that lasted 69 seconds after he blew out his knee in the opening seconds of the fight. Although McGregor largely transcended the sport of MMA into the mainstream, his star power has been on the wane for several years. The Holloway fight was his first in five years and resulted in his fourth defeat in his past five UFC bouts. "I gotta be honest unless things ​change with the UFC I'm kinda over it," Strickland wrote on X on Wednesday. "McGregor makes 30 million to fight for 30 second and they don't want to pay us a fraction of it." Strickland regained the middleweight championship in May with a split-decision victory over previously unbeaten Khamzat Chimaev at UFC 328. He has yet to schedule the first defence of his second title reign. A potential matchup with Nassourdine Imavov had been discussed for later this year, but Strickland reportedly turned it ​down, previously indicating that compensation was an ‌obstacle in negotiations. "The thought ⁠of just giving up ​my belt going to 205 and speed running ​my contract ‌to fight Jake and make what these guys are making ⁠sounds pretty damn appealing," Strickland wrote in a separate post. Paul ⁠responded on social media Wednesday, inviting Strickland to contact his company, Most Valuable Promotions, once he becomes a free agent. In another post, Strickland said injuries meant his heart "just isn't in MMA anymore" and that a switch to boxing appealed because "there is more money and it's significantly easier." Strickland, who has a record of 31 wins against seven losses, also referenced boxer Conor Benn's reported $15 million, one-fight agreement with ​Zuffa Boxing. Benn, the celebrity son of former middleweight champion Nigel Benn, suffered a brutal second-round stoppage at the hands of Ryan Garcia in September, earning a lucrative payday despite the obvious mismatch. Strickland has previously criticised the UFC's pay structure despite regularly describing himself as loyal to the promotion. It is unclear how many fights remain on his current UFC contract.

title: Former refugee gives ‘This is Britain’ speech after defeating Greens' Zack Polanski in London byelection
description: Sagal Abdi-Wali retains seat for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour party
content: The UK’s ruling Labour party saw off the challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski in a by-election caused by former prime minister Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP. Labour’s candidate, local council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, delivered a powerful victory speech about diversity in Britain. She arrived in the country as a child refugee from Somalia and said she hoped the result of the vote would help people like her to feel like they also “belong here”. Labour’s decision to choose a British Somalian had been criticised by Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf. The final days of campaigning were also overshadowed by the Green Party conference, at which a motion was passed declaring “Zionism is racism”. Mr Polanski , who increased the party’s share of the vote, has been accused of failing to show leadership over the ”dangerous” and “divisive” motion by not taking part in the debate. He was pressed about the motion in media interviews after the result and refused to say directly whether he supported the right for Israel to exist. “I believe everyone deserves a safe home,” Mr Polanski, who is Jewish, told the BBC. “I believe Israelis and Palestinians should have equal rights in a democracy. I don't believe that any state has a right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide.” The failure to win a seat in the House of Commons represents a major setback for his party. Mr Polanski said he intended to stay on as leader. While he has been credited with tripling the Greens’ membership to more than 200,000 people since he became leader about a year ago, his popularity ratings have dipped in recent months. "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion," he said. Ms Abdi-Wali received 45 per cent of the vote in Holborn and St Pancras, ahead of Mr Polanski, who came in second with almost 33 per cent. The seat was vacated by Mr Starmer after he was replaced as the country's leader by Andy Burnham, in part because Labour MPs hoped he could do a better job countering the Greens. In her acceptance speech, Ms Abdi-Wali praised Mr Starmer and said she wanted to work with Mr Burnham on issues such as housing. “This moment means something deeply personal to me – to represent the place that gave me a home, and my family a home, gave me opportunity and helped shape the person I am today,” she said. While in its northern reaches, Holborn and St Pancras contains some of the most affluent parts of London, several of its neighbourhoods are included among the most income-deprived in England. “I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong, for people who look like me," Ms Abdi-Wali added. "I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain. “We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built, and pass it on. Hope is not naive. Without hope there is nothing to build on, and nothing to build for. People need to believe that politics can make their lives better and that their communities can thrive and that tomorrow can be better than today.” In a message issued before the vote, Mr Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.” Labour had been expected to win, having occupied the seat since its 1983 inception, and party strategists are likely to take the result as a sign Mr Burnham is re-energising the progressive voter base that splintered under Mr Starmer. Mr Polanski, a former actor and hypnotherapist, had tried to persuade the liberal constituency’s voters that they would be better served by electing the leader of a party who could push Mr Burnham further to the left, instead of giving Labour another backbencher to boost its majority in the 650-seat House of Commons. Mr Polanski currently serves as a member of the London Assembly and was looking to transition to the Parliament in Westminster, where his party is represented by a contingent of five MPs. He said that he was disappointed not to ​win the seat but that the party would continue to grow despite the setback. "No politician runs in a by-election and doesn't want to win," he added. "But at the same time, to see the growth in what was supposedly a safe Labour seat … is now a marginal Labour seat. That's clearly growth, and next time we can get it over the line.” He told broadcasters that "so many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance ... let's see what he does with it". Labour’s nationwide popularity had slipped since Mr Starmer led it to a majority in 2024, but polling shows the party is enjoying a bounce under Mr Burnham. The by-election is the first to be held since he became the UK leader in July. He has refocused his party on an unabashedly left-wing agenda that prioritises public ownership. He has proposed trimming rises in the state pension to fund a care service for the elderly that operates along the same principles as health care, which in the UK is free at the point of use. Missing out on a seat in the House of Commons will be a blow for the Greens, even while officials managing expectations in advance of the vote pointed out that Nigel Farage, leader of right-wing Reform, stood unsuccessfully in seven parliamentary elections before gaining a seat. “Any ideas of a return to the cosy two-party system is just wishful thinking on the part of the establishment,” the Green Party said in a statement after the result.

title: Eight family-friendly half-term staycations in the UAE
description: Organised by the type of trip you enjoy
content: You might not be jetting off with the family for cooler pastures this half-term holiday, but that doesn’t mean you can’t have a change of scenery. Research shows the demand for staycations in the UAE is booming, with dnata Travel reporting a 31 per cent increase in bookings compared with the same period last year, with Dubai accounting for 78 per cent of that. Thankfully, options for domestic vacations abound, so here are eight Emirates-wide options, organised by the types of activities your family might enjoy. Dubai Parks and Resorts , which has just reopened, is the obvious draw, but Abu Dhabi's Yas Island still edges in for sheer variety. These two hotels put the rides within easy reach and wrap tickets into the package. Rove At The Park, Dubai Book direct through Rove Hotels until October 31 and the deal works out at Dh590 net for two – with two Dubai Parks and Resorts tickets included and one complimentary night added on top. Extra tickets are available at Dh295 per person. Yas Plaza Circuit, Abu Dhabi Available via dnata Travel from Dh545 per person per night, this four-star Yas Island address includes breakfast, theme park access and complimentary stays and meals for two children under 11 for one Queen Family Suite Plaza View. Think the world’s fastest roller coaster at Ferrari World or the most waterslides in any waterpark worldwide at Yas Waterworld. If a half-term spent entirely at the pool and/or shore sounds right up your street, Fujairah's east coast offers a slower pace than Dubai. Then again, Dubai’s Centara Mirage adds a waterpark and a fifth-anniversary weekend to the mix for families who want something more. Le Meridien Al Aqah Beach Resort, Fujairah On the east coast, Le Meridien Al Aqah, via dnata Travel, is allowing guests to book a Deluxe Sea View King room from Dh695 per person per night, breakfast included. Fujairah's calmer coastline makes it a natural choice for families who want a proper change of pace from the city, with the Hajar Mountains as a backdrop. Centara Mirage Beach Resort, Dubai Islands UAE residents can access a discounted rate until October 31 using promo code UAERES, which covers daily buffet breakfast, unlimited waterpark, pools, lazy river and private beach access, kids' club time, plus 25 per cent off on rooms, dining, drinks and spa. The resort marks its fifth anniversary on October 14 with face painting, a bubble show, Cinema Under the Stars and a kids' disco. For families who want the city on their doorstep, Palm Jumeirah and Sharjah's beautiful Aljada district both work as a change of scene without a long drive. Hilton Dubai Palm Jumeirah This sprawling resort at Palm Jumeirah has a deal on offer via dnata Travel from Dh545 per person per night. It includes breakfast for all guests and one complimentary stay and meals for children under 11. It's a straightforward package for families who want the beach, the pool and the Dubai skyline in one place. Vida Aljada, Sharjah A new opening in Sharjah's Aljada district, Vida is offering 20 per cent off its best available rate for direct bookings made until December 20. The deal includes early check-in from 11am, late check-out until 4pm and a complimentary room upgrade, subject to availability. Rather spread out than check-in? Think four bedrooms, a private pool, golf course views and a chef who comes to you. Elara Villas, Dubai Creek Resort Four-bedroom private villas with a pool and golf course views start from Dh4,200 per villa (excluding taxes). The 36-Hour Escape, available Sunday to Thursday, gives families a confirmed 9am check-in and 9pm check-out the following day, with padel, mini golf and kids' club access included. The Weekend Villa Retreat runs Friday to Sunday from Dh4,600 with the same access. A private in-villa chef dinner for up to 10 is available at Dh2,500, booked 48 hours in advance. Both offers are valid until October 31. Alzorah Beach Resort, Ajman It’s less than an hour’s drive from Dubai, but this stunning, sprawling property feels like a world away from the hustle, as it's set within one million square metres of protected mangroves and a white-sand beach. The Seaside Staycation package includes daily breakfast for two, a 20 per cent discount on dining and spa, a complimentary Ocean View room upgrade (excluding suites and villas), early check-in and late check-out, subject to availability, and welcome drinks at Vinesse Bar on arrival.

title: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
description: Powerful storm forces US oil companies to significantly scale back their operations, adding to supply concerns
content: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations. Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel. From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent. “Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

title: Audit firm fined $100,000 by Abu Dhabi's ADGM regulator
description: PKF Accountants and Business Advisers and registered audit principal hit with penalties
content: The Registration Authority of ADGM has imposed fines totalling $100,000 on an audit firm at Abu Dhabi's financial centre over regulatory failings. The action was taken against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers, an ADGM-registered audit firm, and its registered audit principal, Saranga Lalwani, the authority said in a statement on Friday. It has imposed a fine of $65,000 on PKF and $35,000 on Ms Lalwani. The decision was taken after an on-site inspection conducted by the authority to assess PKF’s compliance with ADGM's auditor rules and the quality of its audit work, the statement added. During the inspection, the authority said it identified "significant deficiencies" in an audit conducted for an ADGM-registered entity by PKF and Ms Lalwani. The deficiencies included "failures to conduct the audit and prepare the audit report in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (ISA) as required by the Companies Regulations (Auditors) Rules 2023 and failure to exercise due skill, care and diligence in carrying out the audit", the authority said. The inspection identified that PKF "rebutted the risk of fraud in management override of controls, which is a mandatory fraud risk and cannot be rebutted under ISAs". The firm was also accused of failing to assess fraud risks, failing to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence, inadequate audit documentation, and insufficient evidence demonstrating the audit principal's involvement in the audit process. "Registered auditors and registered audit principals are expected to conduct audits in accordance with applicable professional standards and exercise appropriate skill, care and diligence," the authority said in the statement. "This action reinforces the importance of robust audit practices and demonstrates that failures to meet regulatory requirements will result in appropriate enforcement action." Authorities in the UAE have cracked down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the financial system's integrity and reliability. The Dubai Financial Services Authority this month imposed a Dh401,000 ($109,200) fine on wealth management firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation.

title: Riyadh airport flights broadly back to normal after days of disruption
description: Several services are listed as cancelled on Friday
content: Services from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport are gradually returning to normal following days of delays and cancellations. On Friday morning, flight tracking website Flightradar24 reported that 63 flights (18 per cent) have been delayed, with 44 cancelled (13 per cent) since midnight. This is compared to a total of 164 delays (42 per cent) and 167 cancellations (43 per cent) on Thursday . From 8am Friday morning, flights are broadly projected to depart on time. Flights were initially suspended on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks, with disruption continuing into Thursday. There are several cancellations listed from King Khalid International Airport, including Emirates flight EK820, which was delayed by several hours on Wednesday and Thursday. The Dubai-bound flight is cancelled on Friday, but is currently listed as scheduled for Saturday. Etihad Airways has also confirmed the cancellation of eight flights between Abu Dhabi's Zayed International Airport and Riyadh due to operational disruption at the Saudi airport. Six flights have been cancelled on Friday – EY551, EY555 and EY559 from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh, and EY552, EY556 and EY560 in the opposite direction. Two further flights, EY551 and EY552, have been cancelled on Saturday. The airline said the situation remains fluid and further schedule changes are possible, advising passengers to check the latest flight status on its website. Also cancelled is flydubai flight FZ848, which faced delays on Thursday but is scheduled to resume its service on Saturday. "Flights to Riyadh and Yanbu have been cancelled up to and including October 10, while flights to Abha have been cancelled up to and including October 11," a flydubai spokesperson said. "We are monitoring the situation closely and remain in close coordination with the relevant authorities. We will update our customers through our official channels regarding any amendments to our flight schedules." Several flights from Riyadh to India – including Air India flight AI2214 and IndiGo flight IGO74 to Mumbai, and Air India Express flight IX896 to Bengaluru – are also cancelled. Low-cost Saudi airline Flyadeal has cancelled several domestic flights, including F3111 to Jeddah and F323 to Abha. The disruption follows drone and missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, which killed three people and injured 36 others, according to the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation. Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attacks, which also caused damage.

title: Enzo Maresca says 'feeling is fantastic' at Man City as Haaland urges fans to 'stick together'
description: Game at Liverpool will be club's first since an independent commission found City guilty of breaches of Premier League's financial rules
content: Enzo Maresca insists Manchester City are embracing the challenge of returning to Premier League action at Liverpool on Sunday, with the team's perfect start providing a welcome distraction from the storm surrounding their landmark financial case. City travel to Anfield with five wins from five league matches and top the table, but their first game since an independent commission found them guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period will be played against an unprecedented backdrop. The club have lodged an appeal against the verdict and continue to maintain their innocence, arguing that the commission's decision contains “clear material errors” and that City have evidence supporting their position. For Maresca , however, the focus inside his dressing room is firmly on what City can control. “Personally I’m very calm to be honest. The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club,” Maresca told City 's in-house media on Thursday. “The feeling is fantastic, to be honest. The players are excited for the next two games [they host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday], but especially they are excited because in this moment, we are top of the league, so the players are just focused on that. “They know that what we can control is the football side. They know they are professionals. They know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise. “They are just focused on this moment, how we can beat Liverpool , how we can, together with the fans, try to win at Anfield." Maresca's sentiments were echoed by star striker Erling Haaland. The Norwegian, fresh from scoring three times in four Uefa Nations League matches during the international break, has called on City fans to show their support at Anfield. “We have to stick together. We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive," Haaland said. “No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile. We have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game. “We have to stick together, and we have to spread the love to each other. “So yeah, stick together, enjoy the ride and smile.” Anfield has long been one of the most intimidating venues in English football, and City's visit comes at a particularly charged moment, with the verdict likely to dominate the atmosphere around the game. City's players, though, have so far shown little sign of allowing the uncertainty away from the pitch to affect their football. They have won all five of their league matches and sit three points clear of defending champions Arsenal, with Maresca's side having made an emphatic early statement of intent. Liverpool, by contrast, have endured a less convincing opening to their title defence. They have won twice and drawn three times in their first five matches and sit sixth heading into Sunday's fixture. A victory would provide Andoni Iraola's side with a significant lift and, more importantly, halt City's perfect start. But the result will inevitably be viewed through the prism of the financial case. Every City appearance now brings questions about what consequences could eventually follow the verdict. The appeal process remains ongoing and sanctions have yet to be determined. For now, City must attempt to separate that uncertainty from their pursuit of another title. Anfield represents perhaps the most difficult environment in which to do so. The rivalry between the clubs has been one of the defining contests of the past 10 years, with City and Liverpool repeatedly battling for supremacy at the top of the table.

title: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
description: Comparing H-1B visa holders to 'indentured servants' raises spectre of colonial-era abuse
content: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive". A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India ’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”. "The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service. The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant. "When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country." The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers. As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards. The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients. In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg. In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans. Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella , the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration. Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students. J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

title: Golan Heights dilemma: Israel's new military line blurs engagement and confrontation
description: The Sufa 53 line expands occupation, but unlike Gaza or Lebanon, Damascus is more accommodating in pursuit of peace
author_name: Khaled Yacoub Oweis, Thomas Helm, Nada Maucourant Atallah
content: On a clear day, Israeli soldiers on the Golan Heights can see Damascus with the naked eye, underlining the strategic advantage Israel has held for almost six decades since it occupied the plateau. Now Israel is seeking to add a layer of protection to the occupied area by building a military line known as Sufa 53 , a few kilometres inside Syria in Quneitra and Deraa governorates. It is one of three new occupation lines created by Israel in the three years since the start of the Gaza war, comprising roads, barriers, trenches and other fortifications and infrastructure. Israel built the first, called the Yellow Line, in Gaza in October last year after a ceasefire that on paper ended two years of war with Hamas . It has set up another Yellow Line in south Lebanon, the main theatre of the latest Israel-Hezbollah war that began in March.
