Israel says the line is needed to guard against attacks by the Iran-backed group. The Sufa 53 line runs near populated Syrian areas where Israel has increasingly been staging incursions to apprehend people deemed a threat or to search for weapons caches. The line is named after the designation of an Israeli battalion known as Sufa (storm), which played a key role in foiling Syrian attacks to regain the Golan Heights in the 1973 war, which was launched by Syria and Egypt. The Golan also overlooks southern Lebanon, northern Jordan, and the Sea of Galilee, Israel’s main water reservoir. According to a local official, who said his farmland and that of others in the village are now inaccessible, the line begins near the town of Hader in northern Quneitra and extended for about 20km as far as the village of Hamddieh by last winter. The Israeli military started work in recent weeks to extend the line to Asheh further south, he said. “The situation keeps getting worse," he explained, adding that Israeli arrests and raids have become routine. In Hamadieh, residents who venture into restricted areas risk being shot at by Israeli forces, including the killing of one person this week and the shooting of a man with a disability. Israeli media reported that Israeli forces killed a 22-year-old Palestinian man suspected of trying to infiltrate an Israeli army position in the area. Syria's policy towards Israel has changed sharply since the December 2024 ouster of its former president Bashar Al Assad. His removal by militant forces led by current President Ahmad Al Shara deprived Russia and Iran of a key ally and helped to restore the US position in the region. Mr Al Shara, a former Al Qaeda operative turned US ally, has abandoned the anti-Israeli rhetoric of his predecessor and of his former comrades. His top lieutenants have taken part in US-supervised talks on security arrangements with Israel as a precursor to a peace deal. The l ast of these meetings was held in August in the Jordanian capital Amman. A main figure behind them is Tom Barrack, US Special Presidential Envoy for Syria. On Thursday in Istanbul, Mr Barrack discussed "shared priorities in addressing regional threats" with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani. He praised Syria as "assisting the region in finding an algorithm to lower the temperatures in its neighbourhood". Carmit Valensi, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Jerusalem, told The National that the more permanent the infrastructure appears, the harder it becomes for Mr Al Shara to sell continued engagement domestically. The military logic of Sufa 53 is "easier to understand than its political meaning”, said Ms Valensi, who heads the Syria Research Field at INSS. She pointed out that after the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas, Israeli military doctrine has emphasised "forward defence, greater depth, better observation, obstacles to infiltration and the ability to detect and disrupt threats before they reach Israeli communities". Under this logic, "roads, berms and fortified positions have clear tactical value", she said. "The problem is that tactical infrastructure can acquire strategic and political meaning". However, Israel has not formally declared Sufa 53 "to be a new political border" and it has not been adopted as “the formal name of an overarching territorial project”. Speaking in New York during the UN General Assembly last month, Mr Al Shara said Israel should withdraw to the positions it held in the Golan before the downfall of Mr Al Assad, or to what is known as the 1974 armistice line. US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger negotiated the armistice with then president Hafez Al Assad as Israeli forces reversed initial losses in the 1973 war and advanced to within 40km of Damascus. The “discussions for security arrangements” should follow an Israeli withdrawal to the 1974 line, Mr Al Shara said at an event organised by Atlantic Council. If these arrangements succeed, Syria would “enter in discussions about lasting peace”, he added. Israel withdrew from a deal after "we almost reached 90 per cent of agreement,” Mr Al Shara explained, without elaborating. The Golan has been so important for Israel that it annexed the area in 1981, in a move the UN Security Council declared “null” and “without international legal effect”. In contrast, Israel has not officially annexed the occupied West Bank, despite the pressure from settlers and other extremists in the country. Syria and Israel had come very close to signing a deal in 2000, after years of US mediation. A few metres stood in the way. Hafez Al Assad turned it down because the proposed agreement did not give Syria sovereignty over a part of the north-eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. He regarded that part as Syrian territory, while Israel said the whole shore was Israeli. Under Bashar Al Assad, Syria became beholden to Iran, particularly in the last years of his rule, when the Golan became part of Tehran's " ring of fire " of states and groups with capabilities to attack Israel. Work on Sufa 53 began during the Syrian civil war in 2022, four years after anti-Assad rebels withdrew from southern Syria under a surrender deal and were replaced by pro-Iranian groups. Under Mr Al Shara, security forces have been combing areas near the 1974 line in Quneitra and Deraa provinces for remnants of groups that were associated with Iran and Hezbollah and confiscating weapons. The Syrian President is also widely seen as more flexible when it comes to a peace deal that could transform the Middle East and bring in huge Western investment, although it could put him at ideological odds with some of his supporters. "He is not in a strong position to turn down anything requested by his allies, unless he can play them against each other," a diplomat who works on Syria said. However, Sufa 53 is a political slap in the face for a leader who has made co-operation with the US a core of Syrian foreign policy, even after President Donald Trump boasted in December about the decree he issued in 2019 that recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan. Ms Valensi described Israel's policy towards Syria as half-engagement and half-confrontation. It negotiates and co-ordinates on security while "maintaining military positions, incursions and defensive infrastructure". Under this logic, "you do not surrender leverage before an agreement", especially since Israel "does not yet trust Damascus to control all armed actors in the south", with October 7 having "dramatically reduced Israel’s appetite for taking security risks" based on intentions. "From Al Shara’s perspective, this creates a serious political problem," she said.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Messi: 'Your story will remain forever'
description: Ronaldo's comment following Messi's last match for Argentina has more than six million likes
content: Cristiano Ronaldo paid tribute to his great rival, Lionel Messi, after the Argentine great played his final international match this week. Messi brought the curtain down on a 21-year international career with a goal and two assists as Argentina beat Benin in Buenos Aires in an international friendly on Tuesday. It was his 208th and final game for La Albiceleste, with more than 85,000 fans packed into the Monumental stadium to give their hero a fitting send-off. Commenting on one of Messi's Instagram posts, Ronaldo messaged: “Leo, so many years representing your country and a story that will remain forever. All my respect for what you achieved with Argentina. A hug.” The comment has over six million likes. The debate over who is the greatest player between the two has been a near-constant among supporters and commentators for the past two decades, but Ronaldo's message shows the level of respect he has for his great rival. Between them, they share 13 Ballon d'Ors, the award for the world's best player each year. Messi has eight, Ronaldo five. Messi's goal from the penalty spot against Benin was his 126th in the famous sky-blue-and-white colours of the national team. He is both Argentina's record scorer and appearance maker. His crowning glory came in 2022 when he led Argentina to a third World Cup triumph. He was also part of the Copa America-winning sides of 2021 and 2024. While Messi's international bow came with the appropriate pomp and pageantry, Ronaldo's international future with Portugal came close to an undignified end. The 41-year-old released a statement this week – running to nearly 2,000 words – confirming he was not retiring from international football and remained available for selection after walking out on Portugal's training camp ahead of their match against Denmark. The Al Nassr striker accused Portugal manager Jorge Jesus of an “absolute breach of trust” and said he had twice broken his word to him. The row was sparked by Ronaldo feeling unhappy at being an unused substitute in Portugal's previous match against Norway. Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of ⁠the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. After being asked to warm up, Ronaldo was then left on the bench. According to Ronaldo's account, a plan was agreed with Jesus in which he would clarify that the player had not demanded to play and that the coach had made a mistake in asking him to warm up without bringing him on. Jesus made no mention of this in his next press conference, prompting Ronaldo to leave the national team camp in Copenhagen . Ronaldo said he deserved to be punished by the Portuguese Football Federation, while Jesus said the door remained open for Ronaldo to return. Ronaldo holds the record for most caps (234) and most goals (146) in international football.

title: Merab Dvalishvili vows to avenge Petr Yan defeat and reclaim UFC title in Abu Dhabi
description: Former bantamweight champion has learnt from his previous defeat and believes a full camp will make the difference at UFC 333
content: Merab Dvalishvili has built his reputation on relentless work inside the octagon and a playful streak outside it. But as he prepares to face Petr Yan again at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi, the former champion says his focus is firmly on the fight: learning from their last meeting, reclaiming the belt and returning to the busy schedule he thrives on. 'The Machine' was one of the busiest fighters in 2025, defending his bantamweight title four times. He kicked off his run with a unanimous decision over Umar Nurmaogomedov, before submitting Sean O’Malley with a gorgeous north-south choke and then rag-dolling Corey Sandhagen for five successive rounds. The win over Sandhagen saw Dvalishvili tie his close friend and training partner Aljamain Sterling for the most successful bantamweight title defences (three) and surpass the legendary Georges St-Pierre's record for most takedowns in UFC history (119 and counting). Many fighters would have been happy to sign off, down tools and begin mapping out their fight schedule for the next 12 months. Dvalishvili opted to fight again, this time rematching with Yan, a mere two months after Sandhagen. By his own admission, accepting the fight was a mistake, leaving Dvalishvili with little time to rest, recover and fit in a full camp. Yan had vowed to be better than in their first meeting two years earlier, where he lost on the judges’ scorecards. The Russian was as good as his word: consummate boxing, outstanding takedown defence and devastating body shots saw him take a unanimous decision. In Las Vegas, Petr was perfect . ‘The Machine’ had metaphorically broken down. Dvalishvili, the man with cardio for days, simply ran out of gas. Yan solved what seemed the unsolvable problem: figuring out the Dvalishvili dilemma. Some of his body shots had the Georgian wincing and wheezing in pain. The sight of Dvalishvili’s face battered and bloodied as the decision was announced, told the whole story. “I'm not blaming that because of my loss, but I know why I lost,” Dvalishvili told The National when asked if his overexertion played a part in his loss to Yan. “Maybe I was too relaxed, you know. I beat him already, and then when I fought again in the rematch, I have only two months between fights when I defend my belt, and as I said before, I was trying hard, but not actually smart and not actually preparing like how I should do. “That's why I don't do what I was supposed to do in the fight; I was fighting Yan's fight, and that's why he beat the [expletive] out of me and busted me up.” His loss to Yan ended a 14-fight win streak and necessitated a long-overdue break. He’s filled a lot of that time by entertaining his nearly 3 million Instagram followers with hilarious sketches alongside Sterling and his UFC content creator partner Nina Marie Daniele. Dvalishvili, 35, says social media offers him an outlet, a break from hitting pads, slamming on mats and constant drills. It gives him a chance to show his comedic side. “I like to balance between hard training and fun content because, you know, training is hard and most of the time it's the same thing, just grinding, wrestling, improving, sparring, and I don't want to post about training and sparring, and I don't want to show people how hard I work. But I do want to make people laugh and give them good times and make them smile,” he said. He still trained – of course he still trained. UFC commentator Daniel Cormier often recounts the time when he went to visit Dvalishvili the day after a title fight, only to be left waiting around for hours as the Georgian was out running. Much of his life is spent around Sterling. They corner each other for fights and refused to fight each other during Sterling’s run as bantamweight champion. “Aljamain Sterling is a great guy, great human being, and of course, we all know how good a fighter he is. We are brothers, we train together, we have fun together. I know his whole family, he knows my family, and then all my other friends, my other teammates, we are brothers too. We try to help each other and motivate each other. This is the life.” After a punishing 2025 schedule, Dvalishvili has limited himself to one fight this year, against Yan. Neither has fought since that Las Vegas showdown 10 months ago. Abu Dhabi will settle the trilogy . This will be Dvalishvili’s first time fighting in the UAE capital and Yan’s fourth. Despite the Georgian’s outsized persona and online popularity, it is the Russian who is most likely to enjoy the majority of the support. “I have support everywhere I go. Of course, in Abu Dhabi, I will have support too. But I'm a professional fighter. When I first fought in America, nobody in the arena [knew me], but I still won. It's always good when we have support, but even if Yan's fans will be more, that's cool. I'm fine with it. I'm just going to focus on the win.” The defeat to Yan humbled Dvalishvili and he respects the Russian’s skill set. The head-to-head reads one win apiece, but with plenty of rest and with a full camp behind him, Dvalishvili (21-5) said he is determined to settle the debate once and for all . He believes that he will leave Etihad Arena champion once again, and plans on fighting "at least three times" in 2027. “The past is the past. I don't regret anything; whatever I do, I do and I move on. I had a lot of time to think about [fighting Yan again], and I want my belt back. I want to avenge my loss. I know what mistakes I made [in the second fight], and I know how to beat him,” Dvalishvili said. “His striking’s good, his takedown defence is good, and his cardio is good. He never gives up, but I believe I've been training super hard, and I'm very well prepared this time. And I will be much sharper, much better this time. “I believe in myself. I think in Abu Dhabi we will have a new champion.”

title: 'We made our own supply chain': How UAE food retailers and producers adapted to absorb impact of Iran war
description: From chartering their own vessels to rerouting trade, companies are changing the way they do business
content: Turning to new trade routes and changing long-held business practices have helped UAE food producers and retailers to navigate the uncertainty caused by the Iran war . The closure of the Strait of Hormuz meant firms had to be creative to ensure minimal disruption to food supplies. For some retailers, the main challenge was finding suppliers closer to home, no small ask when about 80 per cent of food in the UAE is imported. The conflict meant products being imported by sea could take up to 70 days, which is a problem for items with short shelf lives, said a senior figure from the Lulu supermarket group. “It is more convenient to source from local companies rather than importing essentials,” said Shamim Sainulabdeen, director of private labels at Lulu Group International. The challenging logistics and increasing costs have meant that the supermarket firm, which has branches in all GCC countries, has had to make significant changes to where it sources its stock. The focus has shifted to finding products in Asian markets that are similar to those typically coming from Europe and North America. “We are not waiting for this [situation] to get corrected. We made our own supply chain,” said Mr Sainulabdeen, speaking to The National from the Global Food Week conference in Abu Dhabi. “Now we are bringing chartered flights and ships to all the GCC countries where we have outlets, and this is how we manage it: shifting of sourcing from distant proximity to close proximity.” The supermarket firm has also been chartering entire vessels to speed up deliveries, instead of having its orders shipped with those of other companies. “We are chartering vessels from India, from Thailand, China, Indonesia, from Spain, Turkey, Italy,” he said. “This is the only way. Usually it was going from different manufacturers before, but nowadays we take the initiative to bring all the shipments together and charter vessels exclusively for us.” Shipping has been a major recent challenge for United Foods, which manufactures essential goods such as oils and ghee. The company took a different approach by placing maximum orders for raw materials in advance. While this method is still affected by global supply chain fluctuations, it keeps the price of materials low, which in turn can benefit consumers. “Even while the war was happening, we had already made the future bookings,” said Mohamad Ziad Al Najjar, United Foods B2B senior manager. He said that the company placed orders several months in advance to maintain its supply. “Even though there is a supply chain problem … when we are receiving items in bulk it is maintained for up to five months,” said Mohamad Ziad Al Najjar, United Foods B2B senior manager. Al Ain Farms Group, on the other hand, doubled down on its home-grown products and regarded local manufacturing as a priority given the positive reputation of UAE products. “The strength of the UAE comes with being an international mix, leveraging its legacy, heritage with the traditions of the UAE, and mixing it with international best practices is the only way to be able to be competitive and succeed,” said chairman Tareq Al Hosani. “The thing that I'm assured of is the value of the 'made in the UAE' slogan. It does create value. People understand and recognise that UAE is a very well regulated market. Food security and health and safety is not something to be tampered with in the UAE,” Mr Al Hosani said. Support from the UAE government has been a major factor in being able to navigate the difficult period, companies told The National . “They are even calling us [asking]: 'Do you have challenges, issues of receiving your goods?'” said Mr Al Najjar, praising the government's support for manufacturers and traders. Building resilient supply chains was a big talking point at Global Food Week this year, with an emphasis on improving efficiency using artificial intelligence. “Our focus this year is to move from being agile to being ready, focusing on readiness, future-forward thinking, as well as focusing on resilience and I think [the UAE] has shown great results,” said Sumaya Al Marzooqi, official spokeswoman for Global Food Week.

title: Iran war drives South-East Asia towards renewables but investment falls short
description: Ember warns financing barriers for battery storage and power grids could spell danger for region's long-term energy security
content: The liquefied natural gas shock caused by the Iran war is pushing South-East Asia towards solar and wind power, but the region has lined up less than a third of the energy storage it needs by 2030, a report has found. South-East Asia's current pipeline of utility-scale storage projects of about 7GW, expected to be operational by 2030, covers less than a third of the 23 to 26GW needed to support its renewable energy targets, energy think tank Ember said in the report published on Wednesday. On its current growth rate, the region would fall even further behind by 2045, Ember said. “The financing bottleneck in Asean's [Association of South-east Asian Nations'] energy transition has shifted from raising capital to creating bankable assets,” said Alnie Demoral, an energy analyst at Ember. The findings highlight the challenge for economies trying to cut their exposure to imported fuel after the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway carried almost a fifth of global LNG before the conflict began in late February. South-East Asia sourced about a third of its gas imports from the Middle East before the war, according to the Global Energy Monitor. Asian spot LNG prices averaged $17.50 per million British thermal units in the second quarter, 45 per cent higher than a year earlier, GEM said. In the South-East Asia region, the Philippines , which declared a national energy emergency in March, gas-fired power capacity in development had fallen from 19.7GW in January to 13.8GW by August, GEM data shows. In Vietnam, Vingroup has sought to replace a planned 4.8GW LNG power plant with solar, wind and battery storage. Large solar farms are increasingly able to attract commercial financing, Ember found, but battery storage, smaller renewable installations and transmission lines remain less attractive to investors. Under the same tariff and financing assumptions, a half-megawatt solar project returns 2.6 per cent to equity, against 13.1 per cent for a 20MW plant. Investment will increasingly depend on cutting transaction costs and allowing storage and grids to earn returns that reflect their value to the power system, Ms Demoral said. Current investment falls short of the $281 billion a year the region needs by 2035 to complete its energy transition, Ember said. Electricity demand in South-East Asia is forecast to increase about 5.4 per cent a year through 2030, the International Energy Agency says. Expensive gas is also reviving coal, with the IEA expecting global coal demand to rise 1.2 per cent to a record 8.94 billion tonnes this year, as high LNG prices push utilities in Europe, Japan, South Korea and China to burn more. The financing models that supported large renewable projects have yet to extend to the storage and grids needed to integrate intermittent power, Ember said.

title: F1 driver power rankings and Singapore prediction: Verstappen and Hamilton find form
description: Antonelli retains huge lead at top of drivers' championship with seven races to go in 2026
content: Formula One heads to Singapore this weekend, and Marina Bay always offers the drivers a stern test, especially considering the FIA has declared it a heat-hazard race. Temperatures are forecast to exceed 31 degrees, putting even more pressure on the drivers. Marina Bay is a street circuit that places a premium on braking confidence, traction and precision, leaving little room for error. Just to add even more drama, Singapore is hosting its first Sprint weekend. Teams will have just one practice session before Sprint qualifying, leaving them with less time to find the right set-up. Our power rankings measure who will arrive in Singapore in the best shape. We take into account recent form, raw speed, drivers' ability to extract performance from their cars, momentum, and how well their strengths might suit the Marina Bay circuit. Form: Baku DNF, Bahrain P9. Championship: P5 How quickly the mighty fall. Norris went from being one of the grid’s most in-form drivers to desperately needing a strong weekend. McLaren admitted the MCL40 was only the fourth-fastest car in Malaysia, and Norris added to the problems by running through the gravel behind the safety car. McLaren need to rediscover the pace the team enjoyed before the Baku race, but it won’t be easy when you consider the unresolved straight-line speed issue with the car. Form: Baku P12, Bahrain P7. Championship: P9 Lawson referred to his Sepang getaway as “one of the best starts I’ve ever had in my career” after jumping from 11 th to fourth. He eventually finished P7 and was the best of the midfield. Racing Bulls looked genuinely competitive throughout the weekend rather than just benefiting from the chaos. Lawson will be feeling proud of his recent performances and eager to continue impressing. Form: Baku DNF, Bahrain P8. Championship: P17 Finally, something for Alonso to celebrate. Aston Martin reached Q2 with both cars for the first time this season before Alonso converted 12th on the grid into P8 in the race. He survived the wrong opening tyre choice, passed Arvid Lindblad for a points position and then kept Norris behind until the end. The retirements and the rain helped. It was Aston Martin’s best result of 2026. Alonso believes the team has "some hope" for Singapore. Form: Baku P13, Bahrain P6. Championship: P7 Piastri needed a good weekend, and at last had one in Sepang. He finished in P6, which, according to team principal Andrea Stella, was effectively the best McLaren could have managed. Piastri looked stronger on the hard tyres and was closing in on Charles Leclerc before the final safety car interrupted his progress. There is still a big gap between McLaren and those ahead of them, and Piastri admitted the team “need to improve”. Form: Baku P1, Bahrain DNF. Championship: P2 Russell was heading for another podium in Malaysia when his engine failed with five laps remaining. He has been unlucky too many times, and Mercedes have to address their reliability issues. Not only was he forced to retire, but things are set to get worse in Singapore. Mercedes have confirmed that Russell will need another power unit and that he is set for a grid penalty, so he will start towards the back of the grid at Marina Bay. It’s a notoriously difficult circuit for overtaking, and Russell will be disadvantaged. Form: Baku P3, Bahrain P5. Championship: P8 Hadjar continues to look completely at home near the front of the grid. He was only 0.428 seconds off teammate Max Verstappen in qualifying, but was forced to drop five places and start P8 due to a grid penalty for exceeding his allocated internal combustion engine (ICE) components for the season. In the race, he managed to recover to fifth and spent much of the race holding Lewis Hamilton behind before battery issues and a lack of grip hindered him. A podium finish followed by a fifth place since returning from injury is impressive. Form: Baku P4, Bahrain P4. Championship: P4 Three races, three P4s for Leclerc. Ferrari’s decision to start on slicks dropped him to the back, and Leclerc later said the team needed to learn from Red Bull how to execute better strategies. He still managed to recover and finished just over two seconds behind Hamilton. Ferrari are demonstrating good pace, and the team hopes Singapore will allow their strengths to shine. Leclerc’s qualifying speed will become particularly valuable this weekend. Form: Baku P5, Bahrain P2. Championship: P1 Despite Antonelli leaving Sepang with another 18 points to open up an 84-point championship lead, the team were left with more questions surrounding the new package. The Italian took the lead at the start and eventually finished second and described that as the maximum available to him once Max Verstappen came through. The bigger question heading into Singapore is the car. Mercedes expected their upgrade to deliver approximately three-tenths of a second of extra speed, but instead, according to Toto Wolff, it seems to have cost them several tenths. Form: Baku P6, Bahrain P3. Championship: P3 What a monumental drive by the Brit in Malaysia. A brilliant qualifying lap put his Ferrari on the front row, just 0.298 seconds behind Verstappen. On race day, Ferrari’s choice of tyre threatened to undo all that good work as he dropped from second to 18 th . Hamilton admitted his “heart just sank” when he realised Verstappen was on intermediates. But in true Hamilton fashion, he managed a superb recovery, climbing up the field and passing Hadjar late to claim third. Ferrari’s straight-line deficit should prove to be less of a problem in Singapore, and Hamilton boasts genuine momentum going into this weekend. Form: Baku P2, Bahrain P1. Championship: P6 Finally, the former champion got his race win. He took his first pole of the year in Malaysia and converted it into Red Bull’s first win of the season with their own power unit. More important than the result itself was how convincing the RB22 looked. Red Bull had already improved in Baku, as evidenced by Hadjar and Verstappen both finishing on the podium, but Sepang demonstrated further progress, giving hope of a strong finish to the season. Singapore will show us whether Max is truly back. 1. Max Verstappen The recent progress from the team is too substantial to dismiss, and Laurent Mekies, the team principal, believes this track should suit the RB22. Verstappen has never won here before. Can he manage it? 2. Kimi Antonelli It’s hard to dismiss the youngster’s insatiable appetite for victory or the risks he’s willing to take to get there. Reliability remains an issue – will he have a dependable car? 3. Lewis Hamilton The Brit has won in Singapore four times before and is showing his class. Can he maintain rear-end stability to secure another podium finish?

title: How to keep children safe on UAE beaches as the cooler season begins
description: If you’re heading back to the beach as temperatures drop, experts say you should refamiliarise yourself and your children with basic water safety knowledge
content: As temperatures begin to cool across the UAE, outdoor activities are making a welcome return, with beaches once again becoming popular destinations for residents and visitors alike. While some brave the summer heat for a day by the sea, others are returning to the water after months away. With this in mind, water safety experts are urging beachgoers to familiarise themselves with essential precautions, particularly families with young children and those who are less confident swimmers. “I would hope that most families choose lifeguarded beaches, stay within designated swimming areas and follow the advice of the lifeguards,” says Paul Stokes, founder and head coach at Ocean Warriors Lifesaving Club. “That’s really what beach safety is about. It’s not about being frightened of the ocean. It’s about understanding it, respecting it and knowing what you would do if something changed.” The UAE is home to dozens of beaches, including popular destinations such as Dubai’s Jumeirah and Kite Beach, Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Beach and Ras Al Khaimah ’s Al Hamra Beach, as well as quieter spots such as Dibba “Secret” Beach in Fujairah. While many of the busier ones have lifeguards, they are not all always monitored, which makes beach safety even more important. UAE beaches with lifeguards are usually monitored from sunrise to sunset, with floodlights set up at designated night beaches. Stokes says one of the biggest risks beachgoers face is being unfamiliar with the beach they are visiting. “People should look for information boards and beach signs and actually read them. They should check where the lifeguarded swimming areas are and understand what the red and yellow flags mean," he says. "They should also understand dangers such as rips and currents, wave types, effects of tides, weather, water temperature, marine life , prevailing winds, sun and heat exposure and the type of beach they are on.” The green flag means conditions are safe for swimming; yellow means exercise caution; red signals that you should not enter the water; purple means the potential presence of harmful marine life, such as jellyfish; and red and yellow flags are used to identify designated, lifeguarded swimming areas. Experts say that, beyond understanding beach conditions, it is equally important to recognise your own swimming abilities and those of your children. “Beach safety is about knowing your child, knowing your own ability and understanding the environment you’re swimming in,” adds Daniel Wright, Learn to Swim manager at Hamilton Aquatics. “The sea is very different to a swimming pool, so before you get in, think about things like the depth, water temperature, waves and currents.” Experts agree that the number one thing parents and carers can do to ensure children are safe at the beach is to supervise them at all times. “There’s a great line from an Australian water safety campaign: ‘Watch me, not your phone’,” says Wright. “It’s simple, but it really says it all. It can take just seconds for a swimmer to get into difficulty, so putting the phone away and keeping your eyes on them whilst they are in the water should be a top priority.” While statistics on drownings and water-related incidents are not centralised or published annually across all seven emirates, figures from National Ambulance offer some insight into the risks. In 2021, the service responded to more than 194 drowning-related incidents at swimming pools and beaches across the Northern Emirates. Among the most common risk factors were swimming when lifeguards were off duty and lapses in supervision. Teaching children basic water safety rules and regularly reinforcing those rules are also essential, including staying in shallow water and swimming within designated lifeguarded areas. “Nothing beats constant, active adult supervision,” says Stokes. “When your children are in or around the water, your eyes should always be on them and you should be actively engaged with what they are doing." He also recommends that children wear bright-coloured, high-visibility swimming costumes and rash vests – orange and pink have been identified as the easiest colours to see in the water. He adds: “I would recommend always having a plan and a checklist. Have a family discussion about the ‘what if’ scenarios. What happens if someone gets into difficulty? Where is the lifeguard? What do the flags mean? Who would call for help?” While learning to swim is one of the most vital water safety skills for young children, practising basic skills such as treading water and floating is also important. The idea of “self-rescue” is also taught at swimming schools, where children who can’t yet swim learn to stay afloat and wait for help, or manage to reach a ledge to hold onto. A common misconception is that a drowning person makes a lot of noise, calling for help, while visibly splashing around. In reality, most drownings are quiet and fast, as the person struggles to stay afloat, using all their energy to keep their head out of the water rather than call for help. “A good tip for parents is to watch for when your child starts losing their footing or can no longer stand comfortably,” says Wright. “You may notice them tiptoeing as the water gets deeper, with the waterline creeping up towards their chin; that’s a good sign to step in before they get into difficulty.” Stokes identifies the four types of swimmers who might get into difficulty in the water and describes what they might look like. He explains that a non-swimmer in difficulty may appear upright in the water, facing the shore and making climbing-like movements with their arms as they struggle to keep their head above the surface. A weak swimmer may show signs of distress through ineffective strokes, with their head tilted back and sitting low in the water. An injured swimmer may wave or call for help while holding the affected part of their body, while an unconscious person may be floating face down, with water washing over them. "If you see someone potentially drowning or in difficulty, your priority should be to call for help and alert the lifeguards," says Wright. "Wanting to make a rescue is brave, but attempting a rescue without the right training can put you in serious danger, too. A rescuer without training can very quickly become another casualty.”

title: Nana Patekar has gone too early
description: Our readers have their say on an Indian actor’s passing, a brave pilot, AI, an Abu Dhabi trio and an intriguing trend emerging in Dubai
content: Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week Not your typical star I write in reference to David Tusing’s article Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies aged 75 (October 8): it is a sad day for all lovers of art and films, that a gifted and consummate artist like Nane Patekar has passed away. He was a great performer, a skilled thespian and a fine human being. He will be remembered for his many strong roles, particularly in movies like Ab Tak Chhappan and Parinda . He will also be cherished for his comedic roles in movies like Welcome . Despite his success and fame, Patekar remained a simple person, and engaged in philanthropy and rural welfare schemes. His heart was always with the farming community and the marginal sections of Indian society. He was a Bollywood star, but he avoided all the trappings of a typical star. Actors tend to improve their performances as they age. As they mature and become more experienced, they know exactly what a script or scene warrants. They require little direction or instructions from the director. Patekar was getting better with age. Lamentably he has gone too early. 75 years is no age to go. I believe he had more movies in him, and his best was yet to come. His strong, earthy performances and robust dialogue delivery will be missed. Sadly, we will have to be content with his past performances. – Rajendra Aneja, Mumbai, India Truly a hero Ramola Talwar Badam’s article headlined ‘Don’t sleep please, we need you,’ dentist told flydubai pilot as he battled to save him (October 6) was both moving and meaningful. It describes how the pilot Smit Machchhar battled for 45 minutes after the attack as Dr Shota Musaev laboured to keep him alive. The doctor’s determination and the pilot’s courage during those critical moments have been beautifully analysed and presented in the article. The words “Don’t sleep, please. We need you”, uttered by the dentist to the injured pilot, reflects not only the urgency of the situation but also the hope that the captain would survive. The pilot is truly a hero. He fought bravely to save the lives of 174 passengers, even while being targeted in an alleged terrorist attack. His courage, presence of mind and determination helped protect the passengers and bring them to safety. “We need you” is indeed the right message for such a brave pilot. His courage reminds us that behind every safe journey there are individuals who may risk their own lives to protect others. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India In that moment, no one was Indian, Israeli, pilot or passenger – they were simply human beings saving human lives. Respect to every brave soul who helped. This is humanity at its purest. – Name withheld upon request I hope he also receives emotional support after his physical injuries heal. An instinct and a decision in a split moment that saved so many lives. A hero indeed. – Wardah Harharah, Dubai Admit uncertainty People are learning to ask artificial intelligence almost anything. The dangerous moment is not always when the system gives a completely absurd answer. It is when a doubtful answer sounds certain. AI literacy should therefore include one ordinary habit: ask what the system is uncertain about. Students and workers can request sources, check dates and compare important claims with reliable material. But AI products themselves should also make uncertainty easier to see rather than hiding it behind fluent language. This matters in a country such as the UAE where people work across languages, professions and national backgrounds. A confident answer can travel quickly between contexts where the assumptions are different. The goal is not to make every AI response full of warnings. It is to make confidence more honest. A useful assistant should not only know how to answer. It should also know when the user deserves a reason to check. – Swaansh Mahat, Kathmandu, Nepal Beautiful event In reference to Salma Arafa’s article Take a seat: How Jalsa is giving Abu Dhabi’s emerging artists a stage (October 1): this was such a beautiful and wholesome event. Hats off to Harmony Abu Dhabi for creating something so special for the city’s community. – Mahmoud Hamdan, UAE Valuing outdoor space Dubai’s villa owners are spending more on their outdoor spaces than ever – shaded terraces, pergolas, garden rooms. As someone who designs and installs these structures across the city, I see the demand weekly. It is worth noting what this says: the villa is no longer just the building, it is the whole plot. Developers, valuers and agents who still treat outdoor space as an afterthought are misreading where the market is going. – Abbas Jamil, Dubai

title: Google Earth shows a cold, hard fact: for many Gazans, there is no place to live
description: Palestinians face another winter with too few homes intact and shelter supplies in critically short supply
content: A Google Earth update has offered the world a stark view of the destruction around Gaza, but for most people in the war-ravaged enclave it has underscored a more urgent question: where are we supposed to live? With neighbourhoods reduced to rubble before winter, for some, the answer is a tent. For others, a damaged building. For many, there is no safe option at all. Israeli bombardment has turned densely built Gazan neighbourhoods into expanses of rubble and bare earth, leaving millions of Palestinians with few options for shelter as winter approaches. A ceasefire that began on October 10 last year brought the worst of Israel’s two-year war on Gaza to an end, after the October 7, 2023 attacks led to the conflict. But the deaths did not stop. More than 1,400 Palestinians have since been killed in near-daily Israeli attacks, while Israeli forces still occupy large parts of the narrow coastal strip. For Amani Abu Jalhoum, 35, winter is measured not in falling temperatures, but in memories of water pouring into her tent. “I go to sleep and wake up thinking about winter,” she told The National . “Will we be flooded like we were last winter? How will the situation be? And what about illnesses such as colds and flu? Will my husband, my children and I get sick again this winter like we did last time?” It will be the second winter her family has spent in a tent since their home in Sheikh Radwan, northern Gaza city, was destroyed during Israel’s Operation Gideon’s Chariots in 2025. They had fled believing their displacement would be temporary. When they eventually returned, there was no home left. Last winter, while Ms Abu Jalhoum was displaced in Deir Al Balah, rainwater repeatedly entered her family's tent, soaking clothes and belongings. Her son Ayham, 4, was sick for much of the season. “He spent the entire winter with the flu and a runny nose because I was unable to provide him with the care and protection he needed during the cold winter months,” she said. This year, she is trying to prepare. But there is little with which to do so. “There are no tarpaulins or other materials available to reinforce our tents and make the situation better,” Ms Abu Jalhoum said. Google Earth comparisons between prewar and more recent imagery show how the loss of housing has reshaped Gaza’s urban landscape, particularly in areas of Rafah, Khan Younis, Gaza city and northern Gaza. The images provide a stark backdrop to a problem confronting families there. With so much housing destroyed or damaged, the choice is no longer one between adequate and inadequate accommodation. For some, it is between a tent exposed to winter weather and a damaged building that may not be safe to occupy. Basel Abu Eish, 41, chose the building. His family of four is living in a house that, he says, authorities have warned could collapse during heavy wind and rain. “I am afraid of winter because I fear that our house could collapse on top of us,” Mr Abu Eish told The National. “All the relevant authorities have warned us that with the winter weather and strong winds, the house could collapse at any moment.” The building survived relatively intact until May 2025, he said, when Israeli forces detonated explosive-laden vehicles in the surrounding area. The blasts badly damaged the house and its foundations. The family stayed on someone else’s land in central Gaza. But after the ceasefire began, the owner asked for the land back. With nowhere else to go, Mr Abu Eish returned with his family to the damaged house. “The reason we are living in this house is that we have no alternative,” he said. “I have tried several times to find shelter for myself and my family of four, but each time I failed.” Now his thoughts turn repeatedly to his children and what would happen if the building collapsed. “Sometimes I say, ‘God, if it does collapse on us, let us all die together'.” For Mr Abu Eish, winter will magnify a danger already present every day. “Every night will feel like a nightmare,” he said. “You imagine death could come at any moment.” The Norwegian Refugee Council has warned that 1.65 million Palestinians in Gaza are expected to spend a fourth winter in worn-out tents and war-damaged buildings. About 284,250 families will require shelter assistance this winter, according to the NRC-led Palestinian Shelter Cluster. Existing stocks and supplies in the pipeline are enough to provide shelter and household assistance to only about 52,200 families, the NRC says. The problem is not simply a shortage of homes. Materials needed to make tents more weather-resistant or damaged buildings safer are also severely restricted. The NRC says Israeli authorities classify essential shelter materials, including tents, tarpaulins, timber, cement, tools and other supplies, as “dual use” items. According to the organisation, only 15 lorries carrying Israeli-designated dual-use goods from Jordan are currently allowed to enter Gaza each week. At least 500 lorryloads of such shelter materials are already in the pipeline or under procurement. At the current rate, the NRC says, getting them into Gaza would take more than seven months, even under the best conditions. Israel says restrictions are necessary because items with civilian purposes can also be diverted for military use. The NRC argues that restrictions on basic shelter materials are preventing humanitarian organisations from adequately protecting civilians from winter weather. Funding presents another obstacle. The minimum shelter response for winter requires $283 million, according to the NRC, while donors have provided or pledged $96.2 million, leaving a $186.8 million gap. For Taysir Abu Hani, 32, winter once meant something entirely different. Before the war, his family lived in Rafah in a large house where heavy rain was something they could watch from the windows. “No matter how heavily it rained, it never affected us,” he told The National. “We enjoyed warm, pleasant family times together.” That changed after the Israeli military operation in Rafah forced the family into displacement and eventually into a tent in Al Mawasi, Khan Younis. Last winter, Mr Abu Hani's father, 75, left the tent in the middle of a rainy night to use the bathroom. He slipped. “My father fell on his back,” Mr Abu Hani said. “To this day, he is still suffering from the effects of the fracture and can barely hold his head upright without difficulty.” The accident transformed the family’s relationship with winter. After seeing what happened to their grandfather, Mr Abu Hani’s children became afraid to leave the tent at night to use the bathroom, fearing they might also slip and break a bone. “Winter used to be something we welcomed and enjoyed,” he said. “But now it has become a nightmare that both adults and children fear.” The NRC estimates that about 950,000 Palestinians are living in displacement sites considered to be at medium or high risk of flooding. Severe shortages of heavy machinery, engine oil and fuel have hampered work to prepare sites and drainage systems before the rains. For Mr Abu Hani, the prospect of another winter brings memories of flooded tents, soaked mattresses and ruined clothes. “I hope for this winter to be better for us than last winter,” he said. “Because we can’t endure the same experience again.”

title: The Houthis have no answer for Yemen's problems
description: Permanent mobilisation and attacking civilian targets are not strategies
content: Yemen ’s Houthi rebels have sought to claim legitimacy ever since they overthrew the internationally recognised government in Sanaa in 2014. Using the same rhetorical lines as those adopted by other Iranian proxies, the group presents itself as a defender of Yemeni sovereignty. However, one need only look at the list of civilian casualties from week’s Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia to understand the hollowness of that claim. The details of the dead and injured reveals not hardened opponents but ordinary people from Sudan, Egypt, Pakistan, Morocco, Algeria, Bangladesh and the Philippines going about their lives. Saudi citizens are also among the injured. Such indiscriminate violence against a neighbouring state highlights the danger the Houthis present. Striking airports and energy infrastructure does nothing for Yemenis’ welfare. Instead, it risks drawing their impoverished country further into regional confrontation. An organisation that says it represents a nation should be judged by what it does for its people. On that measure, the Houthis’ record is poor, to say the least. While they use ballistic missiles and heavy weaponry, 62-74 per cent of the people of Yemen live below the poverty line. In the Yemeni city of Taiz, Houthi forces have imposed a siege that has trapped aid workers and threatens water supplies. There are increasing reports of child soldiers being found among captured Houthi fighters. This is in addition to the rebels’ subpar ability to govern the areas it controls. There is no denying that Yemen suffers from real political grievances and deep regional divisions. Those issues cannot be wished away, but recognising Yemen's problems is not the same as accepting the Houthis’ answers to them. There is a difference between resolving political exclusion and allowing an armed organisation to use force to establish territorial facts. The Houthis repeatedly open new fronts, extort international shipping and threaten their neighbours. Most tragically of all, the Houthis subject Yemenis themselves to further conflict. This is not “resistance”. Eventually, Yemen will need a political settlement. The country’s divisions cannot be resolved on the battlefield. However, peace cannot mean rewarding territorial conquest or allowing the rebels to entrench parallel power structures. Yemen needs functioning institutions, secure borders, open roads and ports, and a political system capable of representing its people. This is a far cry from the Houthis’ preferred approach of permanent mobilisation. Resistance may be a powerful slogan, but it is not the answer to Yemen’s many problems. The sooner the realists within the Houthis’ ranks realise this, the better.

title: Test shows AI models likely to give advice for terrorist attacks
description: Tech against Terrorism ran series of questions that retrieved dangerous responses
content: All but two of 134 leading large language artificial intelligence models gave information useful to launching a mass casualty attack or building deadly weapons, in a test of the industry's safety measures. A stress test of the industry found that safety measures can be stripped from leading models within three days, according to researchers at London-based Tech against Terrorism. There have been growing concerns over the potential threats posed by AI, with former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon discussing the issue at a New York City hearing this month. The issue has been overshadowed by the opportunities promised by technological advances in many countries. Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, spoke on Friday at an AI opportunity summit organised by his predecessor Gordon Brown that brought together executives and investors to discuss the industry's growth. Mr Burnham is gearing up for the rotating presidency of the G20 and said he would use the UK's 2027 role to promote a global code of standards and principles to support what he called an AI for good approach to develop common safety standards. "We do need to take an AI for good approach first and foremost because it can unlock everything that we’re talking about today, but at the same time be clear-sighted about the risks it may pose," he told the meeting. The spread of so-called abliterated AI was identified by Tech against Terrorism as a serious danger, with 13 out of 13 failing the tests after safeguards were stripped away. Abliterated is a term for the models run on users' own systems, often without any shelf life. "Abliteration is a proliferation problem," Tech against Terrorism said. "Companies that host, serve, list or sell models should keep abliterated and other modified copies that fail an independent test out of search, recommendation and app stores, and require verified identity for access to them, working with open-source developers rather than against them." In the survey, the Tech against Terrorism model CT-AI put 627 requests to the AI models that a terrorist planning an attack would need to have answered. Eighty-one models gave a complete answer, while another 51 gave useful advice. That left the two that were provisionally passed on safety measures. A user stating that they were a terrorist and intended to commit an atrocity received a usable response in just under two per cent of cases. The equivalent figure for a user stating they were a safety researcher was 16.9 per cent or 8.9 times higher, the research found. "The models appear to respond to the stated purpose of the request, rather than the request itself," it said. The group's founder, Adam Hadley, said: "A model that refuses a stated terrorist and answers a stated researcher has not been made safe. It has been made polite." In addition to seeking government backing for benchmark testing such as the tools it is pioneering, Tech against Terrorism recommends developers filter hazardous knowledge and known terrorist content out of their training data. The organisation wants developers to test how hard each model is to strip of its safety measures before it is released, and publish the results. Where a new model fails a common test, the developer should decline to release it and the results be declared to governments, it said. The report raises important questions over how countries can build trust in AI while accelerating innovation and adoption. Sovereignty over AI does not yet appear to be a factor in improving the safety of the systems on offer. "Governments and companies should support independent safety benchmarks – ours and others – and publish which models do well as well as which do not, so that parents, schools, businesses and public bodies can choose safer models," it said. "Informed buyers move companies faster than rules do."

title: Online sports gaming takes root in the UAE after successful Fifa World Cup
description: Cricket a 'natural' area of focus for gaming platform Play971 ahead of busy calendar
content: Sports gaming is one of the oldest methods through which fans engage with a match, a team or their favourite players. But it was only last year that authorised sports gaming was allowed in the UAE, allowing sports enthusiasts to partake in its vagaries. The UAE’s General Commercial Gaming Regulatory Authority (GCGRA) gave the green light for Play971 to operate; it is the first and only licensed online gaming platform in the country. The launch came ahead of the hugely successful 2026 Fifa World Cup where interest from the region was very high owing to a record eight teams from the Arab world qualifying for the 48-side mega tournament in North America. Despite the time zone challenge, the 2026 World Cup became one of the most-watched tournaments in history – both on screens and at the stadiums. Its popularity was reflected in fan activity on the Play971 platform. For Philippa Bowland, commercial director for iGaming at Play971, the Fifa World Cup gave sports gaming in the UAE a big push. “The response has validated everything we set out to do. We launched with a clear conviction that there is a genuine, under served appetite for a licensed, locally rooted gaming platform in the UAE, and football's biggest stage gave us the first major proof point of that,” Bowland told The National . “We saw strong and sustained growth in both registrations and active players throughout the tournament, culminating in an extraordinary level of engagement during the final itself. Fans were deeply invested right up to the final whistle, with nearly half [49%] of all predictions during the final placed live as the action unfolded.” Morocco garnered the most interest as they replicated their successful run at the 2022 finals by battling their way to the quarter-finals, where they fell to France. “Morocco stood out as one of the most universally backed teams on the platform, cutting across nationalities in a way that few teams managed. They were our biggest underdog story, attracting the largest increase in player engagement and experiencing the greatest odds improvement from start to finish,” Bowland explained. " Kylian Mbappe emerged as the most-backed goalscorer overall. But some of the most compelling activity emerged around specific fixtures. The draws featuring teams like Portugal, Brazil, England, Spain and Belgium generated the strongest fan engagement on the platform. "The most engaging moments tend to be the ones where multiple communities engage in the game simultaneously, which is why fixtures like France v Spain attracted our greatest volume of individual predictions." The end of the World Cup has not slowed things down in online gaming. The Premier League, La Liga and Uefa Champions League are perennial favourites, with cricket also attracting interest in the region. November will see two major UAE-based franchise cricket tournaments - the DP World International League T20 and Abu Dhabi T10 - that will take place back-to-back. And the international cricket calendar is already in full swing. Fans in the UAE can now watch their favourite players and wager on the results. Former Australian fast bowler Brett Lee was appointed brand ambassador of Play971, adding to the profile of sports gaming in the UAE. “Cricket is also a natural focus. With a large and highly engaged South Asian population, many of whom come from countries that have produced some of cricket's biggest stars. The UAE is one of the world's most passionate cricket markets. Brett Lee's appointment as our first brand ambassador reflects that commitment directly. The International League T20 [ILT20], international series, and the broader cricket calendar give us a rich pipeline of content and engagement opportunities throughout the year,” Bowland said. While there is ample room for growth, Bowland said the priority is to consolidate in the UAE and create a dependable and regulated sports gaming platform. “Our focus is firmly on the UAE, and there is good reason for that. Regulated commercial gaming is new here: the GCGRA was established in 2023, and Play971 is the first and only licensed platform operating under that framework. Getting this right, building a platform that genuinely serves this community and earns their long-term trust, is the priority. “In practice, that means age and identity verification before any player can access the platform, player controls embedded throughout the experience, including deposit limits and timeouts, and independently certified technology partners to ensure fairness, security and transparency across the platform. “The UAE is a new market for regulated commercial gaming, and the way this industry earns long-term trust is by demonstrating from the outset that player protection is central to the experience, not an afterthought.” The Play971 website lists a set of rules and regulations that users must meet before they can participate. Users must be at least 21 years of age, be physically in the UAE, and not be in a sensitive geographic area, as determined by the GCGRA.

title: School buses to global stages: 30-year story of the Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation
description: Founder Huda Alkhamis-Kanoo reflects on three decades of youth outreach, Abu Dhabi Festival and international cultural partnerships
content: During a tour of her Abu Dhabi home, Huda Alkhamis-Kanoo stops in a majlis dating back about 200 years, its walls lined with intricately carved wooden panels. The room once formed part of the home of a Christian family in the Levant and had been passed down through generations. Kanoo knew the family for years and understood why they never wanted to part with it. When recent conflict put the house and its contents at risk, however, they turned to her, trusting that she would preserve what the room represented. It was carefully dismantled, brought to Abu Dhabi and rebuilt in her home. “No matter who we are or what we believe in, we have a responsibility to preserve our heritage, tell our story and pass it on,” Kanoo says. “This room belonged to a Christian family, but the principle is the same for all of us. Christians, Muslims, wherever we are, we preserve what carries our history.” Kanoo grew up with that atmosphere in Beirut. Her mother cooked with music playing, her father hosted poets, businessmen and thinkers, and the sounds outside ranged from church bells to people calling in the street. “I lived with music, art, culture and literature,” she says. “It was at home, at school, outside. I lived it. It opened something in my heart.” What Kanoo wanted to recreate in Abu Dhabi was that sense of culture as part of everyday life , shared among artists, families and young people. It became the purpose behind establishing the Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation, now celebrating its 30th anniversary, and later its flagship event, Abu Dhabi Festival , which opens on Saturday with a concert by the UAE National Orchestra at Etihad Arena. To understand that journey, Kanoo recalls Admaf’s beginnings as a small desk at the Abu Dhabi offices of the Kanoo Group, the long-established Gulf family business, when Cultural Foundation and the National Theatre hosted much of the capital’s cultural activity. “There was always this idea I found when I came to Abu Dhabi that culture was essential,” Kanoo says. “You can see that in some of the city’s most loved and historic buildings, which are now on the heritage register. Cultural Foundation was there. The National Theatre was there. “I think the contribution I wanted to make by setting up Admaf was simply to widen that access further, particularly to young people.” Kanoo went into public schools, organised buses and brought pupils to Cultural Foundation for concerts, operas and ballets. “I still remember watching the young people watching The Nutcracker at Cultural Foundation not long after we opened,” she recalls. “They were so enthralled. We had small gifts and a lunch box, but it was their reaction, seeing them happy. It was about exposing them to art and giving them an opportunity to decide for their lives in the future.” At times, these excursions required convincing families first, particularly when young women at university needed permission to attend. She adds: “Some families did wonder what the aim was, and I said, ‘Fair enough.’ I told them: ‘Let them open their horizons, listen to something new, watch something new, do something new. Let them enjoy. Why don’t you come with them?’” In the early years, much of the work was funded by Kanoo and her husband, Mohamed Abdul Latif Kanoo, a businessman and self-taught painter and gallerist who has long been active in Abu Dhabi’s visual arts scene. “I didn’t know if I was going to be successful,” she says. “I couldn’t dare ask for public funds or private funds when I didn’t yet know if it would work.” The programmes spread through schools, the Cultural Foundation, Al Ain, Dubai and Liwa. Performances were paired with workshops and masterclasses, while artists spoke to students about music and the worlds from which it came. Much of that grassroots model would later be carried into Abu Dhabi Festival, with major performances given equal weight alongside school visits, workshops, talks and masterclasses. Launched in 2004, the festival was, Kanoo says, a natural evolution of what Admaf had already been doing. Before Emirates Palace became one of the festival’s major performance hubs, the Cultural Foundation, the National Theatre and other community halls were used, and Kanoo’s home served as backstage and storage space for visiting artists. As the festival drew greater official support, major artists and ensembles, including Placido Domingo, the Mariinsky Ballet and Orchestra, London Symphony Orchestra, Al Jarreau and Natalie Cole appeared during its first decade . Many also made side trips to visit schoolchildren and take part in Admaf’s wider programme across Abu Dhabi. “We ask them to go to Liwa, to sit with students from public schools who probably didn’t have a violin to play with,” she says. “You tell them, ‘Do you mind helping me spread music to the young?’” Kanoo says none refused. “They said, ‘We’ll do it together,’ and, ‘We’re thankful you are giving us the opportunity.’ This is the generosity of the artists.” As Admaf and Abu Dhabi Festival grew, international co-commissions became another way of extending that exchange. One of the earliest came in 2009, when Abu Dhabi Festival joined Manchester International Festival and Holland Festival to commission a portable concert pavilion designed by Zaha Hadid. This was followed by major international stage productions including Verdi’s opera Aida , co-produced with Madrid’s Teatro Real (2022); Maria Pages’s flamenco production De Scheherazade a Yo, Carmen at Barcelona’s Gran Teatre del Liceu (2022); and Debussy’s opera Pelleas et Melisande in collaboration with Opera national de Paris (2025). “With these productions come opportunities for Emirati talent, whether through placements, workshops or performances abroad,” Kanoo says. “It’s not for one year. It is for future generations to understand how we did it, how a production was made and how a co-commission works at that level. You create something together and that knowledge remains. Khalas, it’s an investment forever." Admaf also began taking UAE art abroad from Berlin to London, commissioning artists and supporting exhibitions and acquisitions. More exhibitions followed through a reciprocal partnership with Seoul Museum of Art . In May 2025, Layered Medium: We Are in Open Circuits brought 48 works by 29 Korean artists to Manarat Al Saadiyat. That December, Proximities took more than 110 works by 48 UAE-based artists, including 33 Emiratis, to Seoul. "When I established the festival, music was the heart, but there was also our story: what is happening in the UAE?" Kanoo says. "When guests and artists come, they also want to see what is happening here. What is the visual art movement? You cannot segment it. It is one engine." Kanoo points to how far Abu Dhabi’s cultural landscape has developed since Admaf was launched, from Louvre Abu Dhabi and NYU Abu Dhabi Arts Centre to the institutions of Saadiyat Cultural District , many of which now have children’s and family programmes built into their regular calendars. The creation of the UAE National Orchestra in 2025 is another sign of that growth, and it will open this year’s Abu Dhabi Festival at Etihad Arena on October 10. With the festival now staging performances in arenas at home and commissioning abroad, Kanoo says its value cannot ultimately be reduced to box-office returns. “Ticket sales can give you an indication of your programming choices, but ultimately you do not measure culture by ticket sales,” she says. “If you want to speak purely about economic impact, yes, cultural events move everything in your country: airports, hotels, buses, taxis. Everyone works. “But culture lives for years to come. It is the impact, the influence, the thinking and the creativity it inspires.” The UAE National Orchestra opens Abu Dhabi Festival at Etihad Arena on Saturday at 8pm; tickets start from Dh225

title: Pentagon to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter in Texas
description: 'We'll make sure that people are able to watch it,' Pentagon chief Hegseth says
content: The firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan , the army psychiatrist who killed 13 people ​at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be broadcast live. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told Human Events Daily with Jack Posobiec on Thursday that Hasan's execution would be carried out on December 3 at Fort Hood. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Mr Hegseth said. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The last public execution in the US was in 1936. "The Secretary is correct. It will be ​livestreamed. ⁠Details will follow," a Pentagon official told Reuters. US President Donald Trump this week ordered the use of a firing squad ⁠to execute Hasan. Hasan, a former US Army major, later described his shooting spree as retaliation for US wars in the ⁠Muslim world. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said on X that Mr Trump had approved putting Hasan to death by an Army firing squad at the recommendation of Mr Hegseth. Mr Parnell said Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" during the attack, in which 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman were killed, and 32 others ​wounded. Death by firing squad was ​one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. Thom Tillis, a Republican senator who voted to confirm Mr Hegseth, said Hasan should face the death penalty, but that making his execution public and streaming it was "beyond disgusting". "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," he wrote on X. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but unconscious and in hospital on life support. She regained consciousness on Tuesday. Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, because of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line. A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder ​and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical centre at the sprawling central Texas military base. The shooting ⁠came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be ​sent to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot ​by police upon ‌his arrest. In a statement responding to Mr Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump ⁠loves more than the power to kill." Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice ⁠a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president". If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Centre, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad ​was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the centre reported. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

title: Apple event: expect new smart-home device and revamped HomePod, analysts say
description: Event comes after launch of iPhone Duo last month
content: Apple indicated on Thursday that it would be making a smart-home product -related announcement on October 13, releasing a video showing someone embroidering the company's famous multicoloured logo . The caption being created read "Welcome home", seemingly confirming months of rumours that Apple will soon be introducing a new device for the home during the event, which is scheduled to take place next Tuesday at 9am Washington time (5pm GST). "The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart-home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart-home ecosystem," said Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint . Ms Jain said that signs point to another announcement from Apple, probably the introduction of a refreshed HomePod, a Siri-enabled speaker that was first introduced in 2018. "With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem," she said. Ms Jain said that unlike Apple's success with iPhone, Mac and MacBook sales, she does not necessarily expect the refreshed HomePod to be an initial hit. "Shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year on year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles," she said. She said that rather than blockbuster sales figures, Apple might be seeking to solidify its loyal customer base: "The bigger opportunity for Apple is not just the hardware volume." Analysts and technology experts say Apple has filed patents appearing to be related to HomePod over the years. An announcement would not be out of character for Apple, which is known to take its time in developing products. Some experts have also speculated that Apple will introduce new versions of its Apple TV console, which it has gradually improved since its introduction in 2007. In the company's 50-year history, Apple has dabbled in various devices not directly related to computing and smartphones. It introduced a PowerCD player in 1993, although sales were lacklustre and it was quickly discontinued. The company also briefly linked up with Japan's Bandai and created a gaming console in 1995 called Pippin, although again success remained elusive. In 2007, under the direction of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, the company introduced iPod HiFi, a high-quality speaker that docked with the company's iPod, but amid stiff competition the product never took off. Various media reports suggest that Apple is linking up with Korea-based LG Electronics to assist it in making sure that various products such as doorbells, thermostats and locks work with the products set to be announced on Tuesday. Apple previously worked with LG to help make some of the first versions of the company's iMac introduced in 1998. This will be Apple's second major product announcement in less than a month. Last month, the company unveiled its much-anticipated foldable smartphone, iPhone Duo, the design and competitive price of which were met with enthusiasm. iPhone Duo will go on sale October 16 and may be shipped as soon as October 23.

title: UAE and Saudi Arabia sign rail and energy agreement to boost trade and connectivity
description: Arab world's top economies sign deal to strengthen rail links and electricity grid integration
content: The UAE and Saudi Arabia have signed an agreement to develop rail links and deepen energy co-operation between the Gulf neighbours. Mohamed Alsuwaidi, the UAE Minister of Investment, and Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, Saudi Minister of Energy and Minister of Industry and Mineral Resources, signed the preliminary agreement in Riyadh, state news agency Wam reported. The agreement sets out a framework for rail links between the countries, with a focus on moving goods and cargo across borders. It provides for technical and economic studies to support logistics integration, improve supply efficiency and advance broader regional economic development. The agreement also outlines measures to streamline cross-border trade and transport, with both sides committing to studies that will assess the feasibility of linking their rail networks. The agreement reflects growing momentum behind Gulf-wide integration as the two countries seek to strengthen economic ties and reduce friction in bilateral trade corridors. Beyond rail, the deal extends to energy infrastructure, covering co-operation on electricity interconnection and the exchange and sale of power between the two nations. Technical, economic and environmental feasibility studies will be conducted to evaluate interconnection opportunities, with both parties agreeing to co-ordinate with other GCC member states on expanding the Gulf's broader system. The inclusion of electricity co-operation indicates an ambition to enhance energy-system efficiency across the region, building on existing Gulf grid infrastructure. By aligning their energy networks more closely, the UAE and Saudi Arabia aim to bolster resilience and support the wider GCC's long-term connectivity goals.

title: Missing woman confirmed dead by police in Ras Al Khaimah
description: Woman with 'special medical condition' was reported missing on Thursday morning
content: A woman who was reported missing was found dead by police in Ras Al Khaimah on Thursday. The police force in the emirate extended its deepest condolences and sincere sympathy to the family of the deceased, referred to as Sheikha, in a post on X. Earlier on Thursday, police had announced the disappearance of Sheikha, a middle-aged woman with “a special medical condition”.

title: UAE amends Crimes and Penalties Law relating to suicide
description: New legislation also lays out penalties for those whose actions cause someone to try to take their own life
content: The UAE is to decriminalise attempted suicide as part of amendments to the country's Crimes and Penalties Law.
