Eritrea is “deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea”, he told AFP. Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara last Thursday and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing them of threatening national security. Eritrea responded by cutting ties. The US has warned that “the Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis”. In a statement on Saturday, it urged both countries to exercise “maximum restraint”. Eritrea's move also puts the spotlight on Egypt, which has its own dispute with Ethiopia over its share of the Nile, in addition to the latter's Red Sea ambitions. Cairo has spent the past few years building ties with Asmara. In October 2024, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi and his Eritrean counterpart Isaias Afwerki agreed with Somalia's President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on a framework for strategic co-operation that includes Red Sea security. Ahmed Moussa, a prominent pro-government Egyptian television host, said on Saturday that Egypt and Eritrea have a joint defence agreement, though no text has ever been made public. With Cairo and Addis Ababa trading blame over the Nile dam and also expelling each other's diplomats last week, the question now is how far Egypt would go if its ally faces a serious Ethiopian attack.

title: UAE and Thailand conclude Cepa talks to boost trade and investment
description: Non-oil bilateral trade hit $10.2 billion in first half of 2026
content: The UAE and Thailand have concluded negotiations for their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement , which is expected to remove trade barriers and boost bilateral relations. The countries began talks on the deal in 2023 and launched a joint business council the same year. As part of the negotiations, they discussed avenues to enhance trade, investment and opportunities to expand co-operation, the ministry of Foreign Trade said in a statement on Thursday. In the coming phase, the UAE and Thailand will finalise the legal and technical procedures required for the agreement to be signed and implemented, it said. The Cepa is expected to accelerate trade flows, unlock new investment opportunities and strengthen private sector co-operation in priority sectors, including advanced manufacturing, logistics, food security, digital trade, renewable energy and precious metals. “The conclusion of negotiations … embodies our shared commitment to building stronger economic bridges between South-East Asia and the Middle East,” said Minister of Foreign Trade Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi “Thailand is one of the most dynamic and diversified economies in the region, and this agreement will open new avenues for companies, investors and entrepreneurs in both countries to expand and access high-growth markets.” The Cepa builds on strong ties between the UAE and Thailand. Bilateral non-oil trade in the first half of 2026 jumped by more than 75 per cent year-on-year to $10.2 billion. Trade last year also grew more than 65 per cent to $12.3 billion. The UAE's key non-oil exports to Thailand include gold, aluminium and other industrial goods. “These figures reflect the growing integration of the two economies and the scale of opportunity the agreement can unlock,” the ministry said. “By reducing trade barriers, enhancing market access and stimulating investment flows, the Cepa will support our long-term economic objectives and generate new opportunities across a wide range of strategic sectors,” Dr Al Zeyoudi added. The UAE has signed 38 Cepas with trading partners as it seeks to boost investment ties, expand its non-oil economic base and broaden exports. The Cepa programme is a key pillar of the UAE's foreign trade agenda, which aims to increase non-oil foreign trade to Dh4 trillion ($1.1 trillion) by 2031.

title: Russian plague scare: Everything we know as health chief calls for information
description: Russian authorities have sought to allay concerns after death of laboratory worker in Siberia
content: The World Health Organisation has demanded more information following the death of a laboratory worker at a Russian plague research laboratory. Danya Shipilova, 28, a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Shelekhov, Siberia, died on October 2 after developing pneumonia of undetermined cause. Russia has placed more than 200 people in quarantine after the incident. The circumstances surrounding her illness, and the nature of the research conducted at the institute, have raised international concern about the potential threat of a plague outbreak. However, Russian authorities have denied reports of a confirmed case of pneumonic plague in the region. The World Health Organisation has asked Moscow to provide more details about the incident, including laboratory test results for Ms Shipilova and those placed in quarantine. At a media briefing on Wednesday, WHO director general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Russian authorities had held a meeting on October 2 after a resident of Irkutsk Oblast in Eastern Siberia was suspected of having contracted a dangerous infection. “WHO has asked the Russian Federation for more information in accordance with the International Health Regulations,” Dr Tedros said. “The Russian Federation responded, saying that no case of plague had recently been reported in the Irkutsk Oblast and that they had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.” The WHO has requested additional information about laboratory testing, the reasons for the public health measures and the health status of those who were quarantined. It has also asked Russia to clarify media reports about a second employee who allegedly developed pneumonia of undetermined cause. Dr Tedros said the WHO had offered technical support on plague and laboratory biosafety and biosecurity but had not been able to conduct a full risk assessment or establish a complete picture of what had happened. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he said. The US and the EU have also urged Russia to be transparent about the incident. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had rejected media reports about the suspected plague case. The US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said it was monitoring developments. “We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the CDC said. “While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognised and treated early. “At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the US,” the CDC said. The CDC added that pneumonic plague can spread through respiratory droplets during close contact. Rapid identification and treatment of infected people, together with monitoring of potentially exposed individuals, are important public-health measures. Pneumonic plague is a severe lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is the most serious form of plague. Close contact: Pneumonic plague can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes and someone else inhales the respiratory droplets. Infected animals: Rarely, people can be exposed to respiratory droplets from animals with pneumonic plague, including domestic cats. Secondary infection: Bubonic or septicaemic plague can progress to pneumonic plague if the bacteria reach the lungs. Symptoms usually appear quickly, within three days of exposure, but sometimes as long as a week after contact. They include sudden fever, chills, headaches, weakness and shortness of breath, similar to some seasonal illnesses such as influenza. These symptoms can be followed by rapidly worsening pneumonia and chest pain with coughing that frequently produces bloody or watery mucus. Yes. Plague can be treated with antibiotics, particularly when treatment begins promptly. Because pneumonic plague can progress quickly and can be fatal without treatment, suspected cases require urgent medical assessment, isolation and appropriate antibiotic dosage. Antibiotics used to treat plague can include gentamicin, doxycycline, ciprofloxacin and moxifloxacin, depending on the clinical circumstances and medical guidance. Arizona, US, July 2025: A man died from pneumonic plague a week after exposure to sick cats. Despite receiving antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to hospital. Global endemic areas: The bacterium Yersinia pestis is active in wild rodent populations in about 26 countries. Seasonal cases are reported most frequently in Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Peru. There are about seven cases a year in the US, mainly in the western part of the country.

title: Saudi-led coalition vows to 'punish' Houthis after attacks on airports and civilian facilities
description: UAE expresses 'full solidarity' with Saudi Arabia and support for 'all measures' taken in response
content: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to “punish” Houthi rebels after deadly attacks hit airports in Riyadh and Saudi Arabia's southern region, and debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaged civilian facilities in the capital. “The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom … will not go unpunished,” said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. He said the coalition’s joint forces had destroyed dozens of military Houthi targets across Yemen. Authorities at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh urged passengers to check with their airlines and confirm their flight status before heading to the hub, as flights continued to be affected. The Saudi Civil Defence said debris from the missile caused damage to a nursery and a medical clinic on Thursday, and two Riyadh residents reported hearing explosions. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the Iran-backed group had attacked the airport in Riyadh repeatedly. The UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs “condemned in the strongest terms” the attacks, adding that they “constitute a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and a threat to its security and stability”. The ministry, in a statement, reaffirmed the UAE’s “full solidarity” with the kingdom and its support for “all measures” taken in response. It also expressed its “solidarity and sincere condolences and sympathy to the families of the victims, as well as its wishes for a speedy recovery for all the injured”. Drone and missile strikes on King Khalid airport and Abha International Airport in the south killed three people and injured 36 others, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation announced late on Wednesday. Attacks by Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia come amid renewed fighting after the rebels made advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and a Yemeni government counter-offensive supported by coalition air strikes. “The targeting of civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable,” the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement, expressing condolences to the families of those killed and wishing a speedy recovery to those injured. It also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said it stood with the kingdom’s people and government. France also condemned the Houthis’ repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia and expressed its “full solidarity” with the kingdom's defence of its territory and infrastructure, the Foreign Ministry in Paris said. Last month, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan called for a comprehensive political solution in Yemen and condemned Houthi missile and drone attacks against his country and commercial vessels, as well as threats to navigation in the Red Sea. He told the UN General Assembly that a comprehensive agreement was needed to bring stability to Yemen and called for diplomacy over the bigger conflict between the US and Iran. Communication channels between the two countries remain open, with new messages exchanged through mediators, diplomats and sources have told The National , as efforts to reach a lasting agreement to end the nearly seven-month-old war remain elusive. The push to establish a fresh diplomatic path following the failure to achieve a breakthrough in New York during the UN General Assembly last month comes amid growing signs that both sides are preparing for a major confrontation . Last week, a source in Tehran told The National that Iran was preparing for a “major round of fighting”. Days later, US media reports suggested that US President Donald Trump's administration was considering renewed strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that the Pentagon had ordered preparations for possible major combat operations. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said his country was reviewing Washington's response to its proposal, under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days, and could reply within days. “The ⁠diplomatic process is still continuing,” he said.

title: UFC star Arman Tsarukyan added to RAF Abu Dhabi card
description: Armenian will take on Neiman Gracie in a catchweight crossover clash at Etihad Arena on November 14
content: UFC star Arman Tsarukyan of Armenia will face Neiman Gracie in a catchweight crossover matchup at the inaugural Real American Freestyle (RAF) Abu Dhabi tournament next month. Tsarukyan, the No 1-ranked contender in the UFC's lightweight division boasting an 11-2 record in the world's lead MMA organisation, heads to the UAE capital with a 7-1 RAF record, including five wins by technical fall. He faces Brazilian Gracie, a three-time World BJJ bronze medallist in a contest that will test both athletes under freestyle wrestling rules. The contest leads five new additions to the Middle East’s first RAF event. American Kyle Dake will defend his cruiserweight championship against Turkmenistan’s Alp Arslan Begenjov. Dake is unbeaten in six RAF appearances. The two-time Olympic bronze medallist and four-time world champion is also the only wrestler to win NCAA titles in four weight classes. His challenger Begenjov is a U20 world champion, three-time Asian U23 medallist, and 2026 senior Asian bronze medallist. Kennedy Blades puts her women’s middleweight title on the line against fellow American Bella Mir, daughter of former UFC heavyweight champion Frank Mir. Blades has recorded six technical falls in RAF without surrendering a point. Her illustrious resume includes a 2024 Olympic silver medal and 2025 world bronze medal. Blades faces 2026 NCAA champion Mir, who also holds a 4-1 professional MMA record. Russia’s Zabit Magomedsharipov takes on Giga Chikadze of Georgia in a welterweight crossover bout, while Team USA Olympic gold medallist Jordan Burroughs meets Belarusian Azamat Nurykau at Middleweight. Magomedsharipov enters RAF with an 18-1 professional MMA record, including a perfect 6-0 UFC run and a 14-fight winning streak. His opponent, Chikadze, is an experienced MMA featherweight and accomplished kickboxer, with two world kickboxing titles and multiple world and European karate championships. RAF Abu Dhabi will be headlined by the UAE's Khamzat Chimaev . The former UFC middleweight champion takes on Colby Covington for the Cruiserweight Crossover Championship when they meet at the Etihad Arena on November 14. Last week, former UFC bantamweight title contender Umar Nurmagomedov was also added to the card . The Dagestani will take on Uriah Faber, who returns for his third RAF match. Faber is a former MMA champion and the founder of Team Alpha Male. Also joining the card is reigning RAF light heavyweight champion Kyle Snyder, who will face Shamil Erdogan. The inaugural RAF Abu Dhabi event marks the start of a five-year partnership between Real American Freestyle, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi (DCT Abu Dhabi), and the UAE Wrestling Federation. It follows RAF’s international events in Tbilisi, Georgia and Moscow.

title: Dubai school plans scholarship in memory of teacher after 33 years of service
description: Anjana Sanalkumar was a teacher and exam officer at Gems Education school
content: Gems Education plans to honour the life and legacy of Dubai teacher Anjana Sanalkumar with a scholarship in her memory, recognising her 33 years of service with the school group . Ms Sanalkumar, a teacher and examination officer at the Westminster School in Dubai, died on Wednesday. The cause of her death has not been disclosed. The school announced her death on social media and in a letter to the Gems community from group chief executive Dino Varkey. He paid tribute to Ms Sanalkumar's decades of teaching and the relationships she built with colleagues. “Her passing is a profound loss, particularly for her family, friends and the entire community at the Westminster School,” Mr Varkey wrote. Gems Education intends to establish the Anjana Sanalkumar Memorial Scholarship at the school. "We are currently finalising the details of the Anjana Sanalkumar Memorial Scholarship at The Westminster School, including its scope, eligibility criteria and selection process, and will share further information with our community in due course," Carl Roberts, executive principal, CEO and brand ambassador for Westminster Schools, told The National . The Westminster School invited former and current pupils, teachers and colleagues to pay tribute to Ms Sanalkumar. “As we come together to remember and celebrate the life of Ms Anjana, we invite everyone who knew and loved her to share a heartfelt message, memory, or a few words in her honour in the comments,” the school said in an Instagram post. A memorial service was live-streamed at 3pm on Thursday so those unable to attend in person can take part remotely. “Your words, memories, and presence – near or far – mean more than we can express. Thank you for helping us honour and celebrate a life that touched so many,” the school said. Hundreds of students, teachers and alumni have posted messages of remembrance on the school’s social media. Juliet Carolyn, a former biology teacher and department co-ordinator at school, stated that she had the privilege of knowing and working with Ms Sanalkumar for 11 years. “She was such a beautiful soul, kind, compassionate, and deeply empathetic. Hearing of her passing is truly heartbreaking. May the Almighty God comfort and console her family and loved ones during this difficult time of grief,” she wrote. Former student Ahmed Azab described Ms Sanalkumar as one of the teachers he was always happy to see. “Whenever we met her regarding school issues, she always met us with grace and compassion, helping us find a solution. Never did she make me feel judged or add to the stress I was in,” he wrote. Another former student, Faisal Mushtaq, said Ms Sanalkumar taught him computer science in the early 2000s. “Very helpful, caring and smiling. I was fortunate enough to meet her two years ago at the school alumni event,” he wrote, sending his condolences to her family and the school community.

title: Saudi Arabia flights: Airlines including British Airways and KLM suspend or cancel routes
description: Regional and international carriers adjusting operations as regional tensions disrupt travel
content: Flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport continued to face disruption on Thursday morning following Wednesday's Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia . The latest disruption comes amid wider regional uncertainty , with several international airlines already suspending or reducing services to destinations across the Middle East. Here's how major airlines have adjusted operations and when flights are expected to resume. It announced on Friday that it has temporarily suspended flights to Riyadh "in view of the situation in the Middle East". The airline asked passengers to contact the PIA call centre to check the latest status of their flights. The airline has cancelled its scheduled Dubai to Abha services. Air Arabia cancelled flights between Sharjah and Abha on Wednesday and Thursday, with services expected to resume as normal on Friday. British Airways discontinued flights to Jeddah on April 24, as part of a wider reduction in its Middle East operations. The airline is scheduled to resume a reduced service to Riyadh on November 3, operating one flight daily. The Hong Kong-based airline has extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh until January 31. The Dutch airline has cancelled all flights to Riyadh and Dammam until October 24. It has also said it will avoid flying through the airspace of Iran, Iraq, Israel and several surrounding Gulf areas. Air France has suspended flights to Riyadh until October 24. The Singapore Airlines-owned low-cost carrier has suspended flights between Singapore and Jeddah until December 2.

title: Jordanian princess 'discovered jewellery had been stolen when it appeared at UK auction'
description: Princess Firyal's former housekeeper on trial accused of stealing items from London home
content: A Jordanian princess discovered a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring had been stolen from her London home by her housekeeper when it appeared at auction, a court has been told. Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, is accused of stealing items of jewellery from her former employer, Princess Firyal. Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978. She is a humanitarian and philanthropist and became a Unesco Goodwill Ambassador in 1992. The princess, 81, told London's Southwark Crown Court that she had received a phone call in November 2020 from a partner at high-end jeweller JAR, who told her that two items of jewellery were being sold at an auction in Kent, south-east England. The Jordanian royal had left London in March 2020 during the Covid pandemic, but Ms Taborda Henao remained to look after the Belgravia house, the court was told. She had been the princess's housekeeper for 11 years before the alleged thefts and was the only person who had permission to access the princess's belongings in her absence. The princess realised that a “unique” JAR sapphire and diamond ring, which had been made for her, was being sold by Canterbury Auction Galleries, the prosecution said. Prosecutor Oliver Wellings said the princess thought she had lost her wedding ring and would never have given away such an important personal item. She then obtained copies of the auction house catalogue and set about proving she was the true owner. After seeing more of her jewellery for sale, along with items that had already been sold by the auction house, Princess Firyal phoned the police. Officers then arrested Ms Taborda Henao and searched her house. They found a wedding ring in a coat, a jewelled metal necklace in a kitchen cupboard, and an envelope containing earrings belonging to the princess, the court heard. Ms Taborda Henao denies taking the items. Some of the items allegedly stolen were sold at auctions by the defendant's nephew, Julian Ramirez, who acted as a “key conduit” for their sale, said Mr Wellings. The court heard that Mr Ramirez first attended Canterbury Auction Galleries in March 2019 for a valuation day. He allegedly visited the auction house again in 2020, when items he had brought were listed for auction. Mr Ramirez had been arrested at an address in Rochester, Kent, on the same day as his aunt and was later released on bail. The court heard he was believed to have flown to Colombia in October 2023 and had not returned. The case continues.

title: Etihad Rail confirms variable pricing as some tickets increase by up to Dh69
description: Inter-emirate train services remain in high demand as transport network expands
content: Etihad Rail has confirmed variable pricing is in place on a number of its routes amid sustained demand for train travel since the long-awaited launch of passenger services - with some tickets increasing by up to Dh69. Fares for the inaugural route between Abu Dhabi and Fujairah were initially set at Dh55 ($15) for Comfort class and Dh109 for Premium class when services began on June 30. Tickets for the routes between Abu Dhabi and Dubai were priced at Dh39 for Comfort Class and Dh109 for Premium class when it opened to the public on September 30. The online timetable shows an increase in prices, typically for afternoon and evening services, and at weekends, across the network. On Thursday, Etihad Rail's website showed Comfort class tickets for the Abu Dhabi-Dubai line priced from Dh39 to Dh59, depending on departure times, while Premium tickets for the same route were Dh109 to Dh149. Meanwhile, tickets for train travel between the UAE capital and Fujairah are now Dh55 to Dh79 in Comfort class and Dh120 to Dh189 for Premium. Ticket for trains from Sharjah's Al Dhaid station – which also opened on September 30 – vary from Dh19 in Comfort class to Dh79 in the Premium class. The operator told The National fares depended on several factors including when passengers choose to travel and book their tickets. “Prices vary based on selected service, time and date of trip, ticket class and category, and time of booking,” an Etihad Rail representative said. “Ticket categories are designed to cater to diverse passenger needs, whether for daily commutes, business trips, visiting family, or enjoying a weekend getaway at one of the country’s destinations.” Many journeys – between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, and Abu Dhabi and Fujairah – are already sold out in advance. Passengers can view fares, compare options and book ahead through the Etihad Rail app, website and ticket vending machines at stations. Passenger services connecting Abu Dhabi and Dubai began on September 30 as part of the expansion of the national rail network. Etihad Rail added more than 2,000 tickets across six extra train services between Abu Dhabi and Dubai last weekend. The additional services were made available after the new passenger rail route connecting the UAE's biggest cities attracted “exceptional early demand”. Etihad Rail's network is set for more expansion in the coming months. New stations in Al Dhafra region are scheduled to open on November 30 and December 30, extending connectivity to areas beyond the capital. The highly anticipated University City Station in Sharjah is expected to open on March 30, broadening the network's reach across the Northern Emirates.

title: Syrian official denies Saudi Arabia asked Damascus to deploy troops in war with Houthis
description: Media adviser to Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara describes reports as 'lies'
content: A Syrian official has denied reports that Saudi Arabia asked Damascus to send troops to support the kingdom against the Houthis in Yemen. Ahmad Zaidan, media adviser to Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara, described reports in recent days of plans to send troops to Saudi Arabia or Yemen as “lies”. Mr Al Shara met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ​in Riyadh during ‌an ​official visit ⁠on ​Tuesday. “The security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and the security of the Gulf, is inseparable from the security of Syria,” Mr Zaidan wrote on X. Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted by Houthi rebels who have stepped up escalation in Yemen. “But what some media outlets are promoting about the kingdom's request to send Syrian forces to Saudi Arabia or Yemen is a lie and has no basis in truth,” he added. The denial was also backed by Syrian Response, the official English-language account of Syria’s Foreign Media Department on X. “Syria’s position is clear: we stand firmly with Saudi Arabia against threats to its security and stability. At the same time, Syria’s policy in the region is focused on stability, peace and co-operation, not opening new fronts,” Syrian Response wrote. “Our priority is Syria: rebuilding the country, strengthening its institutions, working with our partners on reconstruction and improving the lives of Syrians. Any military co-operation with partner countries would take place only through official channels and existing bilateral frameworks,” it added. Reuters reported on Wednesday that Syria was considering providing military assistance to Saudi Arabia, citing a US official and a Syrian military official. It reported that options being considered included defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, ​or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis. The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have brought the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between the kingdom, Pakistan and Turkey into focus, raising questions about how the collective security alliance could be realised on the ground. Earlier this week, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to provide “military forces and capabilities” to Saudi Arabia. The text of the Makkah pact has not been made public but a joint statement from the three countries when it was signed in August said it was intended to strengthen collective deterrence. Similar to Nato's Article 5 on collective defence, an attack on one country would be considered an attack on all. Syria on Thursday “strongly condemned Houthi militia attacks targeting vital facilities and civilian sites in Saudi Arabia”, including this week's attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport that killed three people and injured 36 more. Syria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said “the attacks on civilian facilities and infrastructure and the endangerment of civilian lives constitute a blatant violation of international law and relevant international rules and conventions”, warning that “such attacks pose a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and the stability of the region”. The ministry also reaffirmed “Syria’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its support for all legitimate measures taken by the kingdom to protect its security and stability and ensure the safety of its citizens and residents”. The Saudi Press Agency said Mr Al Shara and the Crown Prince discussed bilateral relations on Tuesday during their meeting in Riyadh and “promising opportunities for developing these relations in various fields”. They also discussed the latest developments in the region.

title: Nana Patekar's most memorable roles, from Krantiveer to Dubai-shot Welcome
description: One of Indian cinema's most recognisable performers, acclaimed actor brought  an intensity to his characters that few actors could match
content: Indian actor Nana Patekar , who died on Thursday aged 75, leaves behind a remarkable body of work spanning nearly five decades, from intense crime dramas and hard-hitting social commentaries to some of Bollywood 's most beloved comedies. Known for his distinctive voice, explosive dialogue delivery and commanding screen presence, Patekar was one of Indian cinema's most recognisable performers. Whether playing a ruthless gangster, an uncompromising police officer or a vulnerable father, he brought an intensity to his characters that few actors could match. Born Vishwanath Patekar in Maharashtra in 1951, he began his career in theatre before making his film debut in Gaman in 1978. He went on to become a major force in both Hindi and Marathi cinema, winning three National Film Awards and receiving the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, in 2013. Patekar's career also had a strong connection to the UAE, where he filmed two of his most popular comedies, Welcome and Welcome Back , with locations across Dubai and Abu Dhabi. As tributes pour in for the veteran star, here are 10 of his most memorable performances. Patekar played Baba Golub, a drug dealer, in Mira Nair 's acclaimed debut feature, which offered an unflinching portrayal of life among Mumbai's street children. The film follows Krishna, a young boy struggling to survive on the city's streets, where he encounters sex workers, drug dealers and other marginalised characters. Patekar's Baba is one of the adults whose troubled lives intersect with the boy's journey. Although the story centres on Krishna, Patekar played a significant supporting role, bringing a menacing presence to a film celebrated for its gritty realism and largely non-professional cast. Salaam Bombay! earned international acclaim and was nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the 1989 Academy Awards, becoming only the second Indian film to receive a nomination in the category after Mother India (1957). Patekar's portrayal of Anna, a ruthless underworld gangster in Vidhu Vinod Chopra's crime drama, remains one of his most celebrated performances. Starring alongside Anil Kapoor, Jackie Shroff and Madhuri Dixit, Patekar played a violent and unpredictable crime boss whose actions drive the film's tragic events. His performance was particularly striking for the way he moved between quiet menace and sudden outbursts of violence, creating a villain as psychologically complex as he was terrifying. The role earned Patekar the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor and helped establish him as one of Hindi cinema's most formidable character actors. Patekar took on both directing and acting duties in this military drama, playing Major Pratap Chauhan, a fiercely disciplined army officer who trains young recruits for combat. The character's uncompromising sense of duty gave Patekar ample opportunity to showcase the fiery intensity that would become his trademark. It was also an unusually personal project for the actor, who underwent military training in preparation for the film. Few films are as closely associated with Patekar as Krantiveer , in which he played Pratap Narayan Tilak, a disillusioned man who becomes a crusader against corruption, injustice and communal hatred. Directed by Mehul Kumar, the action drama became famous for Patekar's powerful monologues, delivered with an anger and conviction that made them instantly memorable. His character's transformation from a seemingly aimless gambler into an outspoken voice against social injustice gave the actor one of his most defining roles. The performance earned him the National Film Award for Best Actor and cemented his reputation as an actor capable of carrying a film through sheer screen presence. In this psychological drama, inspired by Julia Roberts' 1991 film Sleeping with the Enemy , Patekar played Vishwanath, an abusive and obsessive husband whose wife, played by Manisha Koirala, attempts to escape his control. The film explored domestic abuse and the devastating consequences of possessiveness, with Patekar delivering one of his most disturbing performances. The role earned him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor and demonstrated his willingness to take on deeply unlikeable characters. Patekar showed a very different side of his acting abilities in Sanjay Leela Bhansali 's directorial debut. He played Joseph Braganza, a deaf father whose daughter Annie, portrayed by Manisha Koirala, dreams of pursuing a career in music. The role required a quieter, more physically expressive performance and is one of the strongest examples of Patekar's versatility, showing that Patekar could communicate powerful emotions without relying on his famously forceful voice. Patekar returned to the crime genre with this gritty thriller, playing Sadhu Agashe, a Mumbai police officer specialising in encounters with suspected gangsters. Inspired by the world of police encounter squads, the film follows Agashe as he navigates the blurred lines between law enforcement, organised crime and personal vengeance – his understated performance making the character's capacity for violence all the more unsettling. The film became a cult favourite and was followed by Ab Tak Chhappan 2 in 2015, with Patekar reprising the role. In Prakash Jha's crime drama, Patekar played Tabrez Alam, a powerful gangster whose influence extends into the worlds of politics and organised kidnapping. Set against the backdrop of Bihar's criminal underworld, the film follows a young man, played by Ajay Devgn, who becomes entangled in the kidnapping business. Patekar's Tabrez is a calculating and intimidating figure, using his political connections and criminal influence to maintain control. The performance once again demonstrated his ability to play morally corrupt characters with a combination of charisma, menace and authority. After years of playing intense and often intimidating characters, Patekar surprised audiences with his comic turn as Uday Shetty in Anees Bazmee's Welcome . The film follows two gangsters, Uday and Majnu Bhai, played by Anil Kapoor, who are desperate to arrange a respectable marriage for Uday's sister. Patekar's hilarious exchanges with Kapoor, particularly his character's increasingly unsuccessful attempts to control his temper, became some of the film's most memorable moments. He reprised the role in Welcome Back (2015), in which the two gangsters attempted to leave their criminal lives behind, only to become entangled in another series of chaotic misunderstandings. Both films also have strong UAE connections. Much of Welcome was shot in Dubai, including at Grand Hyatt Dubai, while its sequel featured locations across Dubai and Abu Dhabi, including Jumeirah Zabeel Saray and Emirates Palace. Welcome Back also premiered at the Dubai International Film Festival in 2014. The films introduced Patekar to a new generation of viewers and cemented Uday Shetty as one of his most beloved characters, proving that his famously intense screen persona could be just as effective when played for laughs. One of Patekar's most acclaimed later-career performances came in this Marathi-language drama, adapted from the celebrated play by V V Shirwadkar. He played Ganpatrao Belwalkar, an ageing theatre actor who, after retiring from a successful career on stage, struggles with changing family relationships, loneliness and the loss of his former identity. The role allowed Patekar to draw on his theatrical background, moving between grand Shakespearean-style monologues and deeply intimate moments of vulnerability.

title: ‘My country deserves this’: UAE Asian Games champions Al Hosani and Al Shehhi on gold and World Pro dreams
description: Having defended their continental jiu-jitsu titles in Japan, next target is November's global finals in Abu Dhabi
content: Asma Al Hosani was moved to tears when she draped herself in the UAE flag after successfully defending her jiu-jitsu gold medal at the Asian Games in Japan last week. The 23-year-old was one of five Emiratis to top the podium in jiu-jitsu at the Games, and was thrilled she was able to retain the -52kg gold medal she first claimed in Hangzhou three years ago. The UAE claimed eight jiu-jitsu medals in total in Japan, the most among all participating nations, and Al Hosani assures it is no coincidence. “Honestly, I was really moved when I held the flag after my fight because I felt like my country deserves this achievement,” Al Hosani told The National upon her return to Abu Dhabi. “It’s important to thank God for the things we have. When we travel abroad, we thank God for the UAE for providing us with coaches and training centres and everything we need. It makes me feel like I need to give my best for the sake of the UAE. Because it deserves it.” Like scores of Emiratis across the country, Al Hosani was introduced to jiu-jitsu at school from a young age, thanks to the sport’s inclusion in public school curricula – a process that began nearly two decades ago, championed by President Sheikh Mohamed, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince at the time. “Jiu-jitsu was something new for us. We were more used to basketball and football, but a contact sport like this, a martial art, it was a bit strange for us,” Al Hosani recalls. “We also wear the hijab, which is something different in this sport. But when I got into it, I felt that it has something special. “It helped me leave my comfort zone. I was a bit introverted in school; I had a specific group of friends, but in jiu-jitsu, you see people of different ages, different nationalities; it brings together people of all nationalities in one place. That’s what attracted me to this sport; it’s that it has diversity. I felt that it changed me a lot. I became more sociable. I felt like it gave me another family.” Al Hosani grew up in Al Dhafra and had to go back and forth to Abu Dhabi to train when she was still at school. Upon graduation, she moved to Abu Dhabi to study mechanical engineering at Khalifa University, and it was then that she felt she could really build a career in jiu-jitsu. “When I moved to Abu Dhabi, I felt that I could be a champion in this sport and that I could give more to this sport. I felt that things changed for me and this sport became very close to my heart,” she added. Al Hosani carved a path for herself in jiu-jitsu, and in 2024 became the first Emirati woman to reach the finals in the brown/black belt categories at the World Pro in Abu Dhabi. At the Asian Games in Hangzhou three years ago, Al Hosani became the first Emirati woman to win a gold medal in martial arts, and she says returning to the continental stage as the reigning champion came with higher expectations. “In the Asian Games, the first time I trained for it, I was there to help the girls who were participating in it, because I was still underage,” she reflected. “So when I started training for it as an athlete competing in the event, it was different. I thought to myself, ‘This is the chance Asma; take all the chance, and give 100 per cent for that chance. We don't know what will happen next’. This is what I thought: I have to take advantage of every opportunity I have. The UAE did everything for us, it's just a five-minute fight, so go for it. “I tried to give my best, everything I had, in the Asian Games to retain my title. And thank God, I was able to do it.” Al Hosani’s journey doesn't end here. The Baniyas club fighter has her eyes set on clinching gold at next month’s Abu Dhabi World Professional Jiu-Jitsu Championship , and she has dreams she hopes to achieve both on the mat and off it. One is to see the sport added to the Olympic programme. “Jiu-jitsu is a great sport. It's very exciting. You feel it has several martial arts rolled into one. It has judo, it has wrestling, it has grappling, it has striking, it's so interesting to see,” she explained. “People deserve to see it. It has everything. Jiu-jitsu requires physical skills and a great deal of mental skills too. You have to be smart with the scoreboard, know when to score points, when to concede points. I hope one day it will be in the Olympics.” No Emirati woman has ever taken gold in the black belt at the World Pro, and Al Hosani is keen on changing that. Separately, she wants to help usher in the next generation of Emirati fighters and has already begun coaching in her spare time. “My next ambition is to be a coach. I started with this, but I want to have my team. I want to have the feeling of being a coach, seeing my team fighting. Especially the kids, it's so nice to see them fighting. It's so nice when you teach them something and then you see them doing it,” she said. Khaled Al Shehhi has similar ambitions. Like Al Hosani, Al Shehhi returned from Japan having successfully defended his Asian Games gold medal in the -62kg event. The 23-year-old says the first gold “was hard, but the second one was harder”, knowing he went there with all eyes on him in his weight class. But conquering Asia is not Al Shehhi’s endgame. “Since I started in jiu-jitsu, I had a goal that I focused on, which is to win the world title in the black belt. That is my main goal and I haven't achieved it yet. But the championship is in a month and I hope to get it done,” said Al Shehhi, who has reached the final twice. “The reason I am hungry to achieve more and more and more is because I haven’t achieved the one goal I set out for myself from the beginning yet.” Al Shehhi initially trained in judo with his older brother, but when he was introduced to jiu-jitsu as a 10-year-old in school, he liked the fact that it involved more grappling, which played to his strengths. He wasn’t too committed in his first couple of years of training but started getting serious about jiu-jitsu and won a silver at the World Pro in 2015. “My coach at the time had full confidence in me and he told me that I would become a great player one day. I didn't believe him. I just said, insha’Allah,” Al Shehhi recalled. “Since then, whenever I win a big tournament, I remember his words.” Al Shehhi sees jiu-jitsu as a healthy outlet – a tool to step away from the stresses of life and a positive environment in which he can expend his energy. He believes he has what it takes to win gold next month and, like Al Hosani, has already started dabbling in coaching, first at Al Ain Club, and now through a team called Namoos, which he created with a friend in Abu Dhabi. He still sees himself competing for at least another decade, though. “Jiu-jitsu changed my life,” he says. It might change even more if he gets that world title next month.

title: Asian football chief backs Gianni Infantino's Fifa presidency bid
description: AFC president Sheikh Salman says regional body 'united in support' of Fifa chief
content: Asian football's governing body has said it will support Gianni Infantino's bid for reelection as Fifa ⁠president, having earlier opposed his proposed plans to sell commercial rights to world tournaments. Earlier in July, the Asian Football Confederation had in a statement said that “AFC stands in solidarity with Uefa and Concacaf in expressing serious concerns over Fifa’s proposal to introduce private investment into [its] flagship competitions”. Infantino later apologised for mistakes “in relation to the communication and consultation process” for the World Cup sale plans. On Friday, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said the regional body is backing Infantino. “I think that we reaffirm our ​full commitment, ⁠of course, to supporting you and ‌your leadership as you seek a new mandate as a Fifa president,” Sheikh Salman said in comments directed ​at the Swiss-Italian, who was present at the AFC's extraordinary congress in ⁠Tokyo. Later, in an AFC statement, Sheikh Salman added: “Our greatest strength lies in our unity, and we have all seen the historic heights Asian football can achieve when we stand together. The Asian game’s remarkable journey and historic achievements are deeply rooted in the strong partnership, trust, and shared vision that we share as one united family. “As we look towards a brighter and more competitive future, our solidarity remains our greatest strength. We are ready to move forward, united in support of Fifa president Gianni Infantino.” Infantino is up for reelection in March as he seeks a fourth term until 2031. Potential candidates must submit their nominations by November 18. Several key AFC members had publicly declared their support for Infantino. Infantino ‌also gave Sheikh Salman his backing in his address to delegates. “You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in ⁠the last 13 years, my dear Salman,” he said. “You will do fantastically as well for ⁠the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years.” While Africa has also backed Infantino's reelection, ​he continues to face opposition from European football's governing body . Uefa has sent a letter to Fifa seeking answers about his presidency, including questions over the World Cup rights sale project and the Fifa Peace Prize. Football's world governing body had revealed plans to sell a 20 per cent stake in a subsidiary company set up to run Fifa's competitions, attracting widespread criticism. Japan Football Association president Tsuneyasu Miyamoto said on Friday that the association was aiming to align with the AFC but ⁠that they had not made a decision.

title: Oil prices rise as Houthis launch another wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia
description: Crude set to end week higher, with supply disruption in Libya also impacting prices
content: Oil prices rose on Friday as Yemen’s Houthi rebels launched another wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia, stoking concerns about further disruption to supplies from the Middle East. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.1 per cent higher at $114.50 a barrel at 10.21am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 1.3 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Brent, which on Thursday settled at its highest level since May 4, is ⁠set to close higher for a third successive week, while WTI ​is ⁠on track to finish ‌lower. “Oil prices remain supported by geopolitical risks with Brent futures and WTI ... both holding on to large overnight gains,” said Edward Bell, head of research at MUFG, and Soojin Kim, research analyst at the group. “Houthi militants claimed an attack on the oil loading port at Yanbu in Saudi Arabia, along with attacks on Aramco facilities and the Dammam airport in the past several days. Production and export flows through the Strait of Hormuz are still holding at close to pre-conflict levels, though at elevated shipping rates.” Saudi Arabia has faced regular attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, with the group last month making rapid advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a key waterway for global crude supplies. The Houthis have claimed attacks on the Saudi Defence Ministry headquarters in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an Aramco site in Yanbu and Abha International Airport over the past 48 hours. Developments in Libya, an Opec member, are also affecting oil prices. Production was curtailed in the country after the closure of an oil pipeline valve connecting Al Zawiya refinery with the Hamada and Tahara oilfields. People entered the crude receiving station near the refinery and closed the valve, Libya’s National Oil Corporation said in a statement published on Facebook. The pipeline belongs to the Arabian Gulf Oil Company, an NOC subsidiary. Libya’s crude has been valuable to global markets as supply disruptions continue owing to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Many European countries import crude from Libya, with the country’s production estimated at about 1.4 million barrels per day.

title: AstraZeneca and Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi team up for $50 million clinical trials action plan
description: Studies to start this year aimed at boosting research into cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases
content: Global biopharmaceutical company AstraZeneca is to invest $50 million to carry out dozens of clinical trials in Abu Dhabi in a major partnership with one of the emirate's leading hospitals. The company is joining forces with Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi in a long-term drive to address pressing healthcare challenges, with the first studies expected to start before the end of the year. About 30 trials will be conducted in the emirate in the coming years, focusing on advancing treatment for patients with cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases. According to the UAE Ministry of Health and Prevention, cardiovascular disease is responsible for 34 per cent of all deaths in the country, highlighting the need to strengthen medical care. “The investment is around $50 million over the next few years," Iskra Reic, international executive vice president for AstraZeneca, told The National on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit this week. "We have already finalised the feasibility work for six studies and are planning to start the first by the end of this year.” Ms Reic said the initiative, which is being supported by Abu Dhabi's Department of Health, is poised to benefit patients and the wider medical community in the emirate. “The expansion of clinical research may allow more patients from here to be included in global clinical trials. It will expand and enhance the collection of data that is relevant to the local population and the local healthcare system. “Equally, it will allow the local research community and healthcare professionals to be more connected and to become part of the global clinical research network. At the end of the day, it helps the researchers and it helps the patients.” AstraZeneca also announced a global collaboration with Oracle. Its first programme, taking place in Abu Dhabi, will focus on hypertension care and clinical research with M42, using AI and real-world data to explore earlier diagnosis, clinical-trial recruitment and safety monitoring. “All the partnerships we have signed today are related to two main things: how we can combine clinical development and healthcare expertise with AI and the opportunities that technology offers,” Ms Reic said. “On one side, we want to improve patient outcomes. On the other, we want to support healthcare systems to become more sustainable and resilient.” She said the aim was to use available data and harness AI to identify diseases more quickly, enabling earlier intervention to improve patient care. “If the early detection of hypertension proves to work, we will be able to identify patients who are at risk of developing hypertension much earlier,” she said. “That means they will have an opportunity to receive treatment early and improve their outcomes. Both partnerships are very much focused on supporting local patients and the local healthcare system.” Investing in health Ms Reic said the UAE was an ideal partner for its projects due to its robust data collection, research network and the government's commitment to bolstering the health sector. “The UAE is one of very few countries presently suited for these partnerships,” Ms Reic said. “On one side, we have very well-connected medical records and Emirati genomic data. By using AI, that allows you to predict specific diseases. “When you add very engaged and fast regulators, and a knowledgeable and committed clinical research and academic network, you have almost the perfect ecosystem to revolutionise this area.” Earlier detection and treatment could improve outcomes for patients while making healthcare systems more financially sustainable, she said. “By treating patients too late, we are not helping patients, and we are not helping the healthcare system from a sustainability and financing perspective,” Ms Reic added. “If we intervene early and treat patients earlier, that will also help the healthcare system retain more funding for investment and innovation.” The pharmaceutical industry’s role has changed as AI, health data and other technologies have developed, she said. “The future is already here,” Ms Reic said. “Previously, from the pharmaceutical industry’s perspective, we looked at our business as developing and delivering medicine to patients. I would argue that today, and even more so in the future, that is not enough. “As a responsible, innovative pharmaceutical company, you need to transform care for patients. You need to look at every step of the patient pathway to see how you can reduce the barriers and intervene earlier.” She said collaboration between companies, governments, hospitals and research organisations was essential. “Every stakeholder in a healthcare system should act, and we should act together,” she said. “I don’t think any industry or organisation can change the healthcare system on its own. Bringing different industry players together with government and healthcare stakeholders actually makes a difference.”

title: US warns citizens that Houthi attacks 'have potential to escalate rapidly'
description: Travel advisories issued for 13 Middle East countries after recent strikes by Iran-backed group
content: The US has warned citizens against travelling to Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Qatar, Syria, Yemen and Israel. All of the advisories referred to the threat of "terrorism". Washington urged people to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia owing to threats including the "risk of drone and missile targeting of American interests by Iran and the Iranian-supported Houthis", as well as armed conflict and terrorism. "Do not travel to the Yemen border due to terrorism," it added said in the advisory for the kingdom. The US said the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area". A State Department official said after the announcement that the advisories were "not indicative of new capabilities from the Houthis, but reflect the strikes we have seen over recent days, including on the airport". That was a reference to attacks by the Iran-backed group on the Riyadh, Dammam, Najran and Jazan airports in recent weeks. The deadly strikes caused disruption to air travel. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport only partially reopened after it was closed this month and international services have not yet been fully restored. The latest Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the Eastern Province, killed two people and injured eight, Saudi Arabia's Civil Aviation Authority said on Wednesday. Fears are growing of a renewed escalation between the US and Iran. On Friday, US President Donald Trump said Washington may ⁠carry out another military operation against ​Iran if a deal was not reached. "We may do another little Epic Fury," Mr Trump told a rally in Florida yesterday, ⁠using the US military's term for its war on ​ Iran . ⁠ "If they're smart, they'll just say, 'Let's get down to business.' But, you know, I doubt they'll do that because perhaps they're not smart." Earlier this month, he said the US would not strike Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. Iranian officials have vowed to carry out an even more widespread response to any new attack than the strikes Tehran launched across the region after February 28. Cables, data centres and artificial intelligence sites could be attacked by Tehran , Iran's National Security Council chief Maj Gen Mohsen Rezaei told Iranian media this week. The US continues to impose a naval blockade on Iran’s ports, while Tehran regularly attacks ships in the Strait of Hormuz .

title: Swift response key to limiting environmental impact of UAE oil spill, experts say
description: Marine specialists say containing the slick at sea is preferable to removing oil from shoreline
content: Rapid containment of an oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is essential to limit potential damage to the UAE’s marine ecosystems, experts have warned after authorities confirmed the spill off its coast . The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the spill on Friday after residents in Dubai and the Northern Emirates reported a strong fuel-like smell earlier this week. Rob Mortimer, chief executive of Dubai-based Fuelre4m, which supplies substances used to disperse oil slicks, said the initial priority should be “to keep it all together” using floating barriers known as booms, allowing as much as possible to be recovered from the sea surface. “It’s reasonably easy to do it while it’s all together,” he said. “Once it’s spreading and moving around, it’s more difficult. Even with the dispersant, you have to cover a greater distance … The longer you leave it, the more the oil gets dispersed.” Another early measure, Mr Mortimer said, is to use dispersants, substances that break oil into tiny droplets. Dispersants break oil into tiny droplets, making it easier for naturally occurring microorganisms to break it down into simpler compounds, including carbon dioxide, water, and other harmless products. However, using these substances requires careful assessment because some can harm marine organisms, including corals, fish, crustaceans and plankton. “You have got to look at how toxic these dispersants are themselves,” Mr Mortimer said. “Some of the chemicals that are used, they’re not very nice. You have to weigh up whether the treatment is better. Sometimes it’s quite marginal.” The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirms the UAE’s technical monitoring and environmental assessment system detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches. Odors noticed in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain pose no health risks to residents. Teams… pic.twitter.com/KKIP45k1Dj — ‎وزارة التغير المناخي والبيئة (@MoCCaEUAE) October 22, 2026 When dealing with oil slicks, preventing pollution from reaching the coast is typically a top priority. If that happens, clean-up becomes harder, and habitats can suffer lasting harm. “Once it hits the shoreline, you have to do a lot of clean-up and remediation,” Mr Mortimer said. Clean-up operation Prof Richard Thompson, director of the Marine Institute at the University of Plymouth, said cleaning a wide, sandy beach would typically be a less complex task than dealing with a rocky shoreline. “If you have intertidal habitats with a large range of organisms, it’s going to make it more difficult to clean than if you can capture it [the oil] at the sea surface,” he said. “If it’s among rocks or mangroves or seagrass, it’s going to be very difficult to clean … Ideally what you’re trying to do is catch it before you get the encounters between the creatures and the oil.” The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has highlighted the trade-offs in using dispersants, including the benefits of removing oil from the sea surface and reducing the risk of shoreline contamination, weighed against potential effects on plankton and other organisms in the water column. “Part of the work of planning the response to potential oil spills is the difficult task of evaluating these trade-offs, which requires careful consideration of the resources and issues involved,” the agency said in an online briefing document. Mr Mortimer said Fuelre4m supplied vegetable-based substances intended to disperse oil and was seeking approval from UAE authorities to use them. The risks associated with some oil-spill treatment chemicals were highlighted after the Torrey Canyon tanker ran aground off south-west England in 1967 while transporting oil from Kuwait to Wales. Some of the chemicals used to disperse the resulting slick were reported to have been more toxic to marine life than the oil itself. Taking action Umm Al Quwain Municipality said on Friday it was working to contain the pollution and to reduce any harm to marine and coastal environments. The source of the oil has not been officially confirmed. This oil spill is the latest in a series of incidents that have raised concern about the “unprecedented” environmental effects of this year’s US-Iran war. In response to the spill, beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain were closed, while Sharjah’s Al Hamriya Beach was also shut. Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace Mena, said timely containment was particularly important because the Gulf’s semi-enclosed geography limited the exchange of water with the open ocean, potentially allowing pollutants to persist. “We acknowledge the UAE authorities’ ongoing efforts to contain the reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain and address its immediate effects,” she said. “As these efforts continue, understanding the potential environmental impact will be important to protecting the area’s marine ecosystems.” Ms Benzaki said the coastline formed part of a wider marine environment where shallow coastal waters, mangroves, seagrass meadows and lagoons provided important habitats for marine life and supported coastal livelihoods. She warned that even after visible oil was removed, residues could remain in coastal sediments and sensitive habitats, prolonging the spill's effects. If oil reached the UAE coastline, it could “threaten sensitive marine and coastal ecosystems”, she said. Continued environmental monitoring and assessment would help establish the extent of any damage, identify areas requiring further attention and guide recovery measures, she added. Protecting these ecosystems matters not only for marine biodiversity but also for coastal communities that depend on healthy seas. Prof John Burt, director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, previously warned that if oil reached the coastline, remediation could be expensive and a full recovery could take years. Millions of barrels of oil were released into the northern Arabian Gulf during the 1990-91 Gulf War. Prof Burt said submerged habitats, including coral reefs and seagrass beds, were not as severely affected in some areas because oil generally floats on the water’s surface. However, coastal areas in the northern Gulf that oil reached suffered considerable damage. Mangroves and mudflats used by feeding birds were among the affected habitats, while footage from the period showed birds covered in oil. The latest incident has renewed attention on the importance of rapid containment, careful selection of clean-up methods and sustained environmental monitoring to limit potential damage to the Gulf’s marine and coastal ecosystems.

title: Who are the key figures in Israel's election and what are their stances on Palestinian statehood?
description: Israelis to vote on October 27
content: Israelis will head to the polls next week in one of the most important elections in their country's history , with potential implications for the entire region. As international recognition of Palestinian statehood grows, who are the main figures and what have they said about the issue? Benjamin Netanyahu Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been the most famous, capable and divisive politician in Israel for decades. As with so many recent Israeli elections, Tuesday’s vote is not fundamentally about left versus right. It is about whether Israelis choose to be led by “Bibi” Netanyahu once again. He is not projected to even come close to a majority in mainstream polls – but no one is writing him off. He survived pressure to stand down after the massive security failure of the October 7, 2023, attacks, even though many predicted that his departure was imminent at the time. Many analysts say that he could come into his own in complicated coalition negotiations stages, if Tuesday’s elections result in a stalemate. His supporters, be they fervent or reluctant, say that only he is truly qualified to lead Israel, given his decades-long experience as a statesman, his perfect English and his relationships with world leaders, in particular US President Donald Trump . His opponents say he has driven Israel into global isolation, undermined its security with aimless and endless wars after the disaster of October 7, and empowered the far-right and the ultra-Orthodox, which could put Israel on a path to becoming a theocracy. What he says about the two-state solution : Today, Mr Netanyahu is vehemently opposed to a Palestinian state and regularly says that it has been his life’s work to prevent one. His latest government unleashed a massive wave of illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank. Israeli settlements have long been considered one of the main obstacles in achieving the two-state solution. His coalition partners also want to resettle the Gaza Strip. Gadi Eisenkot A former military chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot is trying to bring military efficiency to the hapless campaign to unseat Mr Netanyahu. His straightforward brand has propelled him to the top of the opposition, far ahead of much more experienced candidates, including former prime ministers. His party, Yashar, means “honesty” in Hebrew. His brand is more about who he is than his policies. His family are Mizrahi Jews from Morocco, not Ashkenazim from Europe, who typically dominate Israel’s political elites. He lost close family members during the Gaza war. He is from Israel’s periphery, not the posh neighbourhoods of Tel Aviv or West Jerusalem. He says a lot less about his policies and has run a very cautious election campaign. He is not shy when it comes to military force. He pioneered the Dahieh doctrine , the use of disproportionate force in war, including against civilian infrastructure, an approach that shaped Israel’s campaign during the Gaza war. He does not oppose illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank. Nonetheless, his promise for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and an end to draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Israelis put him at substantial odds at home with Mr Netanyahu, of whom he is just ahead in most polling. What he says about the two-state solution : In August, Mr Eisenkot said in a post on X that no Palestinian state would arise if he was in government. In a post earlier in October, he criticised Mr Netanyahu for speaking “in favour of two states dozens of times”. Itamar Ben-Gvir National Security Minister Ben-Gvir is a convicted criminal who has been in charge of Israel’s police for four years. He is arguably the second most prominent face of Israel’s coalition, after Mr Netanyahu. He regularly gloats about the destruction of Gaza, dramatically worsened conditions for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and the huge rise in illegal settlements. He has growing support from Israel’s increasingly populist right wing, much of which is young and full of political energy. Opponents of Mr Netanyahu often lambast the Prime Minister for giving Mr Ben-Gvir a path to power. They hope that a responsible opposition government can put the Ben-Gvir genie back in the bottle. Even if the Netanyahu bloc that put him in power falls, good polling numbers, a booming brand and a massive social media following mean that he is probably here to stay. What he says about the two-state solution : Mr Ben-Gvir is deeply opposed to a Palestinian state, calling instead for Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank and resettlement of the Gaza Strip , alongside the expulsion of its Palestinian residents. Last year he said that Palestinian Authority officials should be assassinated if the UN advanced the recognition of a Palestinian state. Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid Both Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid were prime ministers in the government before Mr Netanyahu’s current coalition. Their steady decline in the polls over recent months after combining forces in April to form the “Together” party sums up why so many of Mr Netanyahu’s opponents feel depressed by the state of Israel’s opposition. Despite a great deal of political experience, neither could drum up inspiration and are now overshadowed by Mr Eisenkot, who says very little, giving the impression that Israel’s opposition is neither dynamic nor energised, but instead a cautious exercise in crisis management. What they say about the two-state solution : Mr Bennett, a former settler leader, is opposed to a Palestinian state. He said in July that if “someone comes along and says that ‘we need to withdraw [from the occupied West Bank]’… they’ll just kill us”. Over his career, Mr Lapid has been more open to the prospect of the two-state solution than his running partner, often speaking of some form of “separation” between Israelis and Palestinians. He has hardened his rhetoric since the October 7 attacks, however, calling the UK, Canada and Australia's recognition of a Palestinian state in 2025 a “diplomatic disaster, a terrible step and a reward for terrorism”. Mansour Abbas He is chairman of the Arab-Israeli Ra’am party and a potential kingmaker. Despite many Jewish-Israeli politicians vowing never to stand with parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian citizens, expectations of higher-than-usual voter turnout in the Arab community could lead to Palestinian politicians commanding an important number of seats in the Knesset. The community has faced a devastating wave of organised and violent crime since Mr Ben-Gvir took over the police. They are frequently attacked by Israel’s growing right wing as a threat to the country. Motivation to go to the polls after very tough times at home, as well as the trauma of seeing what is happening to fellow Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza, could make leaders such as Mr Abbas a lot more powerful. What he says about the two-state solution : Mr Abbas called on Israel to recognise an “independent Palestinian state” in August. “We want [Israel and the US] to recognise it, and we’ll work to achieve peace, rapprochement and an end to the occupation and conflict,” he added.

title: Dana White on why Abu Dhabi is ‘a very special place’ for UFC as Usman Nurmagomedov waits in wings
description: UFC president talks about the enduring relationship with the emirate ahead of UFC 333
content: Dana White is no stranger to Abu Dhabi. The UFC president has visited the emirate regularly for almost two decades. His enthusiasm shows no sign of waning. As the UFC returns to Etihad Arena for UFC 333 on Saturday, White says Abu Dhabi remains one of the most important destinations on the organisation’s global calendar. “Abu Dhabi is a very special place to us,” White tells The National . “We always try to deliver here.” The UFC’s relationship with Abu Dhabi dates back to 2009, while the extraordinary Fight Island series during the Covid-19 pandemic cemented the emirate’s place in the organisation’s history. White still looks back on that period with particular fondness. “Fight Island was really special for us,” he says. “We had a blast over here during probably the scariest time in human history. It was incredible. It was a great experience, and there’s always going to be a special place in our hearts here at the UFC for Abu Dhabi.” With a stacked card featuring two title fights, there is plenty for fans to get excited about. Etihad Arena is sold out, although White managed to find a few extra tickets for one particularly eager young Emirati fan at Thursday’s press conference. The youngster had offered to let White shave his head in exchange for tickets. White handed them over for free – meaning the fan got his UFC seats and kept his hair. White believes Abu Dhabi’s attraction extends beyond the fights themselves. “The thing about putting on events, fights, concerts, whatever it may be, it’s about destinations – the hotels, the restaurants, all the other things to do here, and then the fight.” The UFC’s business also grew dramatically during the pandemic, with Abu Dhabi playing a central role in keeping mixed martial arts alive while other sports were on life support. “Our business grew like 77 per cent during Covid,” White says. “Fans from all over the world were watching what was going on here in Abu Dhabi.” The UFC president believes that experience helped create a lasting connection between the world’s leading MMA organisation, its fighters and the UAE capital. “It was a special time,” he says. This is the second time since the Iran war kicked off that the UFC has returned to Abu Dhabi following UFC Fight Night in July . Between that and helping stage live events during the pandemic, Abu Dhabi’s relationship with the UFC is one defined by overcoming adversity. Expanding on the close ties, White said: “Relationships are based on how do you react when bad things happen? And Abu Dhabi’s been very good to us, and we reciprocate.” Looking back on UFC 321 That relationship has also survived some painful nights. At the last numbered event in Abu Dhabi 12 months ago, fans were left disappointed as the main event turned into a damp squib. The bout was ruled a no-contest after Tom Aspinall was unable to continue after receiving a knuckle-deep eye poke , ruled unintentional, by Ciryl Gane. The prevailing sense among many fight fans was that the UFC owed Abu Dhabi a memorable event to make up for it. White laughed off the suggestion. UFC 321 in pictures “I don’t know if UFC ‘owes us one’. I mean, this is a contact sport. Anything is possible. These things happen,” he says. “But, you know, Abu Dhabi is a very special place to us. We always try to deliver here.” Asked for an injury date on Aspinall, White said his staff were in contact with the Englishman and his team but gave no update on when he might be ready to return from his injuries. “When he's ready, he's going to let us know.” Gane has since been promoted from interim to full champion without having to fight, something unprecedented in the promotion’s history. Why the exception? “I mean, he's been here forever. He's fought everybody; we knew Tom wasn't coming back anytime soon.” Gane will defend the belt for the first time next month at Madison Square Garden against Josh Hokit. Nurmagomedov to the UFC? One fighter linked with a move to the UFC is Usman Nurmagomedov . He is officially out of contract with rival organisation the PFL following his win over Archie Colgan at PFL New York in July. He is locked into a 90-day exclusive negotiating period with the PFL, meaning he cannot officially sign or negotiate with other promotions like the UFC until this window expires. That window is closing soon. A switch to the UFC has long been mooted. There is already a familial connection: Usman’s brother, Umar, already fights there while their famous cousin, Khabib, is regarded as one of the UFC’s greatest champions of all time. When asked if any talks had been held with the Dagestani, White gave little away. “Well, contractually, I don't know where he's at right now, but obviously, when he's a free agent, and he's able to talk to us, we're interested.” RAF and boxing a threat to UFC? Another hot topic is crossover between disciplines and organisations. The UFC is happy to let stars such as Khamzat Chimaev and Arman Tsarukyan compete in RAF wrestling. Both are slated to compete at RAF’s inaugural Abu Dhabi event next month . While wrestling is an important part of MMA, so too is boxing. One fighter particularly keen to chance his arm in the latter is UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland. The American went on an epic social media rant recently , threatening to quit the UFC as he voiced his frustration at the disparity between what the promotion’s top stars earn and the rest of the roster. Never one to miss an opportunity to step into the ring with a fighter capable of killing him, Jake Paul urged Strickland to reach out and set up a boxing match. White hasn’t commented on Strickland’s situation, which is not without precedent. Conor McGregor took part in a boxing match against Floyd Mayweather in 2017, while several former UFC stars who are no longer under contract have also swapped the octagon for the squared circle. So why is White happy to allow his fighters to cross over into one discipline but is seemingly less enthusiastic about boxing? Does he see it as a threat to the UFC’s product? “I’m trying to think off the top of my head. Tell me one good experience where a UFC fighter or an MMA fighter has crossed over into boxing and it’s ended unbelievably well?” He’s got me. I can’t. UFC 333 predictions As for UFC 333, White refuses to predict the outcomes of a card featuring two championship fights: Alexander Volkanovski defending his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev in the main event, and Petr Yan facing Merab Dvalishvili in their bantamweight trilogy bout. “I never give predictions,” White says. “I predict a great fight. That’s what I predict.” He expects plenty of intrigue in both title bouts, particularly given the contrasting styles. “I think that’s the fun of both of those fights: the co-main and the main,” he says. “ Merab is going to be shooting for the takedown, and if he doesn’t get him down, it’s going to be a long night. “And I think the same thing goes for Volkanovski.
