He said yesterday, ‘He [Evloev] thinks he’s going to be able to take me down, but he won’t, and he’s going to have to stand and strike with me’. So both the co-main and main event sort of have the same theme to them.” The focus is firmly on Abu Dhabi, a destination that White believes has become an integral part of the UFC story.

title: UAE Property: 'Should I sell my off-plan Dubai apartment amid uncertainty or wait?'
description: Investors should consider selling if something fundamental has changed
content: Question: I bought a two-bedroom apartment in February from Emaar at Expo City, in Terra Gardens. It’s a first-floor unit of around 1,100 sq ft, for which I paid Dh2.237 million ($609,000). So far, I’ve paid 20 per cent towards the property , plus the 4 per cent Dubai Land Department fee. I’ve been feeling a bit nervous recently given the current geopolitical situation and uncertainty around property prices. I’m currently considering whether I should continue making payments and get to around 40 per cent to 50 per cent before potentially selling, even if that means taking a loss, or whether I should simply hold the property until completion around 2030 and see how the market develops. Given the current situation, I’m second-guessing myself a little. What should I do? Ghery, Dubai Answer: I can understand why you're questioning your decision to invest at the moment. It's obvious that when you buy something and then the world becomes considerably more uncertain six months later, it's very easy to start looking back and wondering whether you should have waited. I wouldn't panic, though. You spent four to six months researching the purchase, you bought the property , but not with the intention of selling it six months later. So I would remind myself of why I bought it in the first place before allowing today's geopolitical situation to change what was originally a long-term decision. Your purchase works out at roughly Dh2,030 per sq ft. Looking at Terra Gardens today, the figures don't suggest you've suddenly bought something that's fallen dramatically out of the market. Current two-bedroom pricing numbers are at around the Dh2,100 – Dh2,200 per sq ft level, although individual units obviously vary considerably according to the building, floor, layout and of course the view. On the secondary market , some sellers are asking anything from Dh2.09 million to Dh2.5 million for similar-sized units, so I wouldn't confuse an anxious market with your property suddenly being worth substantially less. I wouldn't sell now. You're only 20 per cent into the payment plan. Selling now because you're nervous potentially means paying selling costs, accepting a discount to attract another buyer and giving away an investment before the main reason for buying Expo City has really had time to develop. You haven't bought a completed apartment in a mature community where we already know exactly what the area is going to become. You've bought into the future development of Expo City and that part of Dubai. If your investment was based on Expo City developing over the remainder of this decade, judging it in September 2026 is far too early. I'd only consider selling if something fundamental has changed and by this I mean either in your own finances or in the investment itself. Otherwise you're simply choosing a different date on which to make the same decision. What I would be asking myself is much more practical: Can I comfortably continue making the payments without this property putting me under financial pressure? If the answer is yes, I'd be inclined to continue with the investment. If reaching 40 per cent, 50 per cent or eventually completion is going to stretch your finances or keep you awake at night, that's different. No investment is worth putting yourself into financial difficulty for and in that situation I'd start planning an orderly exit rather than waiting until I was forced to sell. I'd also keep an eye on the actual evidence rather than the headlines. Watch what comparable two-bedroom units in Terra Gardens are actually transacting for, not just what sellers are advertising them at. Watch the progress of Expo City, infrastructure, new commercial activity and what Emaar continues to deliver around you. One other point to consider, you've already paid the 4 per cent DLD fee . If you sell and buy something else because you're nervous, you've crystallised that cost and potentially selling costs as well. The replacement investment therefore has to be sufficiently better to justify getting out of this one. If this were my investment and I could comfortably afford the remaining payments, I would be inclined to hold and give the original investment time to play out rather than sell because of the uncertainty we're experiencing today. That doesn't mean I'm telling you Terra Gardens will definitely be worth more in 2030, nobody can honestly promise you that. Dubai will have considerably more residential supply by then and Expo City still has to mature as a residential destination. But let's look at the facts, you bought from a major developer, at a price per square foot that doesn't look obviously out of line with today's data, in an area where there will be more activity in the years to come. Therefore, I wouldn't necessarily ask myself, “Am I concerned today?” I'd ask, “Has anything happened that fundamentally changes the reason I bought this property in February?” From what you've told me, I'm not sure that it has. So perhaps the biggest mistake you could make now would be turning a long-term investment decision into a short-term emotional one. Q: I have lived in the same two-bedroom apartment in Dubai for three years and my tenancy is coming up for renewal. For the past two renewals, my landlord increased the rent , which I accepted because rents everywhere seemed to be rising. This year he has offered to renew at exactly the same rent, Dh145,000, and initially I thought that was reasonable. The problem is that I've started looking online and there are now several similar apartments in my building and nearby for around Dh130,000 to Dh135,000. One even appears better upgraded than mine. My landlord says I should be happy that he isn't increasing my rent, but I feel I'm now paying above the market. Can I insist that he reduces the rent, or do I have to move out if he refuses? JB, Dubai A: This is a situation we're going to hear more and more about because the conversation between landlords and tenants is definitely changing. For several years now, tenants facing renewals were mainly concerned about how much their rent might increase by but in most parts of Dubai today, tenants are beginning to ask a different question. The important distinction is that a softer market doesn't automatically give you a legal right to a rent reduction. Your existing tenancy is a contract between you and your landlord. Just as a landlord cannot simply increase the rent by what they want, a tenant cannot unilaterally decide that the rent should fall because cheaper properties have appeared online. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't try to negotiate either. My advice would be to do some proper homework. Firstly, don't rely on just one unusually cheap portal listing. Find a few genuinely comparable apartments in your building or immediate community. Look for those with a similar size, condition, view, floor and furnishing status. There's a big difference between an asking price on a portal and the rent at which a property will actually transact, so recent rental evidence is even better if you can get hold of this information. Once obtained, this is when you should try to have a sensible conversation with the landlord. Don't underestimate yourself because you are actually bringing something valuable to the negotiation. You've been there for three years, presumably paid on time and looked after the property. If you leave, the landlord potentially faces a vacant period, possibly some agency commission, cleaning or maintenance costs and the very real chance that the next tenant pays less anyway. Let's say you pay Dh145,000, while a genuinely comparable apartment can now be rented for Dh135,000. Moving might save you Dh10,000 a year, but once you've paid the movers, deposits, connection charges, the agency commission and endured the inconvenience of relocating, the saving becomes much less attractive. Equally, your landlord needs to do the same calculation. Losing a good tenant and leaving the property empty for just one month costs roughly Dh12,000 at your current rent before any other expenses. Suddenly reducing your rent by Dh5,000 or Dh7,000 to keep you doesn't look unreasonable. That's where I'd try to find the middle ground. I wouldn't necessarily approach the landlord saying, that rents are falling so you must reduce mine but I believe it would be easier for you to get your point across if you showed him the evidence of what is available. Explaining that you'd genuinely prefer to renew , but the difference between your rent and today's market is becoming difficult to justify. And be prepared for him to say no. At that point, this becomes a financial decision rather than an argument about who's right or wrong. Work out the true cost of moving versus the true saving over the next 12 months. For quite a few Dubai tenants this year, I suspect renewal negotiations will be less about fighting against an increase and more about deciding whether renewing the contract will still be worth paying a premium for. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

title: Sole DXB music guide, from Lola Young to Nia Archives and Fatoumata Diawara
description: What to know about the three-day festival as it moves to a new location
content: British singer Lola Young, electronic music duo Overmono and Malian musician Fatoumata Diawara are among the acts to be announced for Sole DXB, which will take place from December 11 to 13 at The Square in Nad Al Sheba. Moving from its previous home in the Dubai Design District, the festival will feature three days of concerts and DJ sets alongside fashion, art and street culture. Here are some of the notable artists performing at this year's event. Friday, December 11 Overmono (Main Stage) British brothers Tom and Ed Russell are to perform in Dubai, mixing UK garage, breakbeats and techno with soulful vocal samples. The duo gained wider recognition with their 2023 debut album Good Lies , featuring the single Is U . They return with their new album, Pure Devotion , released in August, featuring tracks including Lockup and Even Angels Ghost . Saturday, December 12 Lola Young (Main Stage) The British singer-songwriter arrives following the international success of Messy , from her acclaimed 2024 album This Wasn't Meant for You Anyway . Her smoky vocals move between soul, rock and R&B, with other notable tracks including One Thing and Spiders . Nia Archives (Main Stage) The British DJ, producer and singer mixes rapid jungle breakbeats and heavy bass with her own melodic vocals. Her 2024 debut album Silence Is Loud earned a Mercury Prize nomination, while its follow-up, Emotional Junglist , released in July, features Jorja Smith on Get Me Down and Sampha on Tender . Matthew Herbert (Stage 2) The British producer has spent more than three decades making music from disparate elements, including household objects, animal samples and sounds from food production. His work ranges from house and jazz to experimental compositions. His latest work, theukhasmorefoodbanksthanbranchesofmcdonalds.com , was released this month and uses recordings of food and household products to address poverty in Britain. Sunday, December 13 Hajaj (Main Stage) The Saudi singer-songwriter performs English-language alternative R&B and soul, with relaxed grooves and intimate vocals. Having lived in Jeddah, Switzerland, the US and Spain, he has earned a cult following across the region with his indie-pop sensibility, including in his 2021 EP Last Call for Coco , featuring Love to Last and Place to Call Home . Fatoumata Diawara (Stage 2) The Malian singer is a familiar performer in the UAE, known for energetic shows featuring West African blues and percussion. Her 2018 album Fenfo earned two Grammy nominations, while her latest solo album, Massa , released in June, explores family history and her Malian heritage. Peter Cat Recording Co (Stage 2) The New Delhi band moves between psychedelic rock, disco, jazz and cabaret, led by Suryakant Sawhney's deep, crooning vocals. Their catalogue includes Bismillah (2019) and their latest album, Beta (2024), featuring People Never Change and Suddenly . Gia Fu (Stage 2) The Hong Kong DJ specialises in salsa and Afro-Caribbean music, drawing on vinyl from the 1960s and 1970s. Her interest in Latin music began through breakdancing and led to Canton Mambo, a project examining musical connections between Chinese and Caribbean communities. She also worked with salsa musician Angel Melendez and Big Band Maquina on a 2021 recording project. Maii and Zeid (Stage 2) View this post on Instagram Egyptian singer Maii Waleed and Lebanese producer Zeid Hamdan pair Arabic vocals with guitar and electronica. Hamdan, who formed the pioneering Lebanese duo Soap Kills with Yasmine Hamdan in the 1990s, began working with Waleed after meeting her in Alexandria. Their early album Moga (2013) established their dream-pop sound, while recent recordings include Fashi (2025) and Manhoos (2026). Sole DXB runs from December 11 to 13 at The Square, Nad Al Sheba, Dubai, from 4pm to 2.30am; three-day tickets start from Dh495

title: Overseas Israelis mobilise for 'change' in election that could end Netanyahu era
description: Packed airlines are flying in potentially crucial voters who told The National that they are seeking a new direction for the country
content: Thousands of Israelis from overseas are flying into the country to vote for a “change” of government and end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s time in office, voters have told The National . There has been a huge surge in overseas arrivals, with an estimated 67,000 Israelis living in the US and Europe having entered the country to vote in Tuesday’s election . This 25 per cent surge above the figures expected could well have a dramatic impact in a very tight election, with their numbers accounting for the equivalent of two seats in the 120-seat Knesset. “We may disagree on what needs to change but we all on the flight agreed that it needs to change and that 20 years of the current leadership has been ineffective and counterproductive,” said Ben, who had just flown in from Maryland, in the US. “You see so many people coming in from overseas, and you don't cross the world if you're happy with the current outcome. You're motivated because you are unhappy.” The American-Israeli, who did not want to give his last name, said he works in the travel sector and has been closely watching the numbers coming into Tel Aviv. “Passenger loads in the week leading up to the election are just astronomical – you would think it's tourist season and it's not. This is the off season.” The flight The National took from London to Tel Aviv on Thursday had a week earlier been just over half full, the seat bookings showed, but by take-off it was fully booked. While there were many orthodox Jews, the majority were secular Israelis, and it is understood this is causing deep concern in the Netanyahu camp. In part, that is because Israelis outside the country have been exposed to the widespread international unease at Israel’s actions in Gaza, where 74,000 people have been killed in the last three years. That followed the October 7 Hamas killings in which more than 1,200 Israelis died, many of them in the town of Sederot, where on Friday you could still hear gunfire. The distant ruins of Gaza, where there is supposed to be a ceasefire, are also visible. It is unclear what impact that major security lapse will have on Mr Netanyahu’s vote share but it is apparent that those flying in from abroad want a new approach. “These elections now are very critical, and it's really important that we change the government and make a change in Israel … especially after what happened in the last few years, since October 7,” said Shirley Segal, whose brother had just flown in from the US. She agreed that Mr Netanyahu had failed the country “big time” and that it was “very sad what happened in Gaza”. “But we need to find a way to live next to Gaza,” she added. Change is required, said her brother Danny Segal, because Israel needs “a different direction, a different understanding of what this country needs to look like in the next five, 10, 20 years”. He believes current policies threaten the idea of a Jewish homeland in Israel. “I don't know if we would be around for the next 10, 15, 20, or forever” on the current trajectory, he said. “We need it to be diverse and strong, and that's one of the reasons that I came to vote.” Israelis must learn to live with Palestinians because “we have to, there are no two ways about it”, he said. “We are surrounded by Arab countries, so we need to understand what they need. We need to coexist in this neighbourhood”. But Mr Segal, who will vote for the centre-right party of former prime minister Naftali Bennett, suggested that, given the October 7 attacks, “it will take a bit of time before we can see a Palestinian state”.

title: T-Rex Glamping Dubai review: A Jurassic Park-inspired staycation
description: Dinosaur-themed getaway with cosy cabins offers plenty for adults and children
content: Jurassic Park is a work of fiction, but T-Rex Glamping at Dubai Parks and Resorts is probably the nearest you'll get to experiencing it in real life. As a child, I was obsessed with t he movie, so I was just as excited about a dinosaur-themed getaway as the little ones. The campsite offers two-storey cabins surrounded by moving dinosaur models, with some of Dubai's biggest theme parks just a short distance away. The welcome Located directly off the Sheikh Zayed Road, T-Rex Glamping is easily accessible by car. The experience starts as soon as you drive into the park. Dinosaur illustrations line the walls, giving you a little preview of the prehistoric world you're entering. A huge Tyrannosaurus rex welcomes you as you arrive. These aren't just giant dinosaur statues; they move their heads, wag their tails, blink their eyes and even roar. The movements seem so realistic that even as an adult, you can't help but stop and watch. At reception, I noticed a little girl who was completely fascinated by one of the dinosaurs. I watched her for a little while before realising I was probably just as amused. The room The best part of T-Rex Glamping is that you spend the night surrounded by these dinosaurs. The two-storey cabins combine the feel of camping with the comforts of a hotel room. Inside, you'll find double beds and a modern bathroom. The space is compact but well designed, with everything you need for a relaxing night. I found the beds particularly cosy, and having air conditioning on both floors was another plus. The layout works particularly well for families. Children can sleep upstairs while parents stay downstairs, or the other way around. One of my favourite features was the upstairs balcony, where you can sit with a coffee and look out over the grounds. There's also a private garden area with a barbecue and outdoor dining space, giving you plenty of room to unwind. And despite having your own little corner to yourself, you're never far from the action. One moment, you hear a dinosaur roaring in the distance. The next, it's people screaming on a nearby roller coaster. The food and facilities Roaring Dinosaur, the on-site restaurant, offers a selection of casual dining options. I stopped here for lunch and ordered a burger and fries. As well as guests having barbecue facilities outside the tents, breakfast is included in the booking. One of my favourite parts of the campsite was the outdoor cinema, where you can settle into a beanbag with some popcorn and watch a movie under the stars. There's also a large outdoor pool and plenty of play areas for children. Theme parks on your doorstep What makes T-Rex Glamping even more interesting is that you're not just booking a night in a cabin. You're staying at Dubai Parks and Resorts, which means there's plenty to explore at Motiongate Dubai, Real Madrid World, Legoland Dubai and the Legoland Water Park. I'd recommend arriving late morning, dropping off your bags and heading straight to the parks. As an adrenalin junkie, I was naturally drawn to the roller coasters and rides, but there's something for everyone. Motiongate Dubai has plenty of movie-inspired rides, including the indoor DreamWorks area, which is perfect when it gets too hot outside. An unexpected highlight was the Submarine Adventure ride at Legoland Dubai, where I spotted a tiger shark for the first time in my life. Real Madrid World's Hala Madrid roller coaster is definitely worth trying if you love a thrill. Approximately 34.5 metres tall, it was the first wooden roller coaster to open in the Middle East. At Riverland Dubai you'll find cafes, restaurants and other immersive experiences. After a day of exploring the theme parks, I'd suggest heading back to T-Rex Glamping in time to enjoy the evening. The following morning doesn't need to be rushed either. Enjoy breakfast, spend some time by the pool and relax before checking out. You can always return to Dubai Parks and Resorts afterwards to explore any attractions you missed the previous day. T-Rex Glamping is at Dubai Parks and Resorts on Sheikh Zayed Road. Check-in is from 3pm and checkout is at noon. Nightly rates start at Dh720 for two adults. This review was conducted at the invitation of the resort and reflects standards during this time

title: Harrow Abu Dhabi to open next year as plans for capital's first boarding school take shape
description: Headmaster at newest branch of prestigious UK-based institution pledges to bring Harrow's culture and ethos to the capital
content: As one of the world's most prestigious schools opens a branch in Abu Dhabi, its principal is banking on attracting families from the UAE and Gulf region that would normally send their children overseas to study. Harrow Abu Dhabi is expected to begin operating in August 2027, after the opening was delayed earlier this year. Families can expect to pay fees between Dh80,000 and Dh106,000 per pupil, and even more if they opt for boarding. Adrian Frost, its founding headmaster, compared bringing the 450-year heritage British school’s education to the UAE to buying a Rolls-Royce overseas: some features would change to suit the country, while the thinking behind it should remain the same. “You could buy a Rolls-Royce in the UK, and you can buy a Rolls-Royce here, and you'll notice that there are certain differences,” he told The National. “It's a different regulator. It's a different location. It's quite plausibly a different demographic that will be interested in the school, but yeah, the ethos and culture is very, very much the same.” For parents, that will be reflected in an extended school day with activities, shared mealtimes, supervised homework, along with an emphasis on reading and handwriting, and reduced reliance on screens. Families looking for boarding options will have to wait beyond its first year, Mr Frost said. Food will be regulated on campus, with pupils not allowed to bring lunch boxes from home. There are several dining halls that serve an array of meals and snacks throughout the day, focusing on the nutritional value of meals while ensuring pupils learn proper etiquette and table manners. “It is a very different education offering,” he said, “one that is not really replicated in quite the same way in any school in Abu Dhabi.” The Saadiyat Island campus will initially admit children from Foundation Stage 1 to Year 6. Boarding will be considered as the school expands into its next phase. The opening date or fees for accommodation have not yet been confirmed. “It’s a few years away though, and we will obviously need to set up the first phase, which is FS1 to Year 6,” said Mr Frost. That timeline puts Abu Dhabi's first boarding school at least two years away. Half the building would not be needed for at least a year after the school opens, Mr Frost said. The school was initially planned to accommodate 1,800 pupils on a site of about 70,000 square metres, which is 30 per cent larger than the Dubai campus, which opened earlier this year. Alternative to boarding abroad Mr Frost hopes families in the UAE and the wider Gulf region who might otherwise send their children overseas will consider Abu Dhabi. Having attended boarding school himself, he recalled studying alongside children whose families lived in countries including Jordan and Bahrain. He intends to bring his experience and knowledge of boarding schools to Abu Dhabi’s first one. “There are parents who want boarding. I hope that they will look to us as an alternative option,” he said. He sees Saadiyat’s cultural institutions, including the Louvre Abu Dhabi and Guggenheim museums, as well as proximity to New York University Abu Dhabi, as part of the appeal, particularly for a school that intends to place importance on music and performing arts. “That location is not just an address, it’s a teaching resource,” he said. Mr Frost previously worked as vice-principal of Brighton College Abu Dhabi and has experience in British day and boarding schools, and in establishing a boarding school in Portugal. He said work was still under way with regulators, school operator Taaleem and Harrow to establish the policies and arrangements for boarding. The school intends to align with standards set by the Boarding Schools’ Association, Mr Frost added. Although being a boarding advocate himself, he warned against treating the option as the right choice for every family. “All the children are different, every single one of them,” he said. “There are some children that thrive in that type of environment, and there are some that can find it a struggle.” What parents will pay for Mr Frost said annual school fees are expected to range from Dh80,000 for FS1 to Dh106,000 for Year 6. He added that although some schools charge extra for after-school activities, Harrow intends to include sport, performing arts and other activities within the premium fee range, but the arrangements with external providers in Abu Dhabi have not been finalised. The extended day would begin with activities, followed by breakfast, continue through lessons, and finish with tea and supervised homework, known as prep. Teachers are called “beaks”, following Harrow tradition. “That is all part of the provision that comes within that price,” he said. At the Dubai school, where Mr Frost was completing his induction, about 96 clubs and activities were running for 400 pupils. Boarding will carry an additional charge in Abu Dhabi but that price has not yet been finalised. “There will obviously be a higher cost associated with it,” he said. “But it’s important to us that we don’t price ourselves out of the market.” British families form a large proportion of the Dubai school’s intake, which Mr Frost said is “unsurprising”. Why the opening was delayed The Abu Dhabi campus was initially expected to open this year. Mr Frost said the postponement to 2027 was due to operational constraints on Saadiyat Island, including infrastructure requirements and approvals from authorities. “It was nothing from the school's side, they were ready to go,” he clarified. He said those obstacles had been overcome and construction had reached the third and final floor, allowing work to move towards the windows and interior fittings. The Abu Dhabi campus would broadly reflect the Dubai school, although the shapes and sizes of the sites are different, he said. During the visit, he highlighted Dubai’s early-years spaces, an auditorium, music rooms and sports amenities as examples of the provision planned for the capital.

title: Touchscreen MacBook: Will Apple's upcoming event contradict Steve Jobs?
description: Technology giant expected to introduce laptop that uses organic light-emitting diode display with touchscreen option
content: Apple 's “pro and tell” event will take place next week, and a significant upgrade to the MacBook line-up is likely to be announced – potentially going against something that Steve Jobs once said. News outlets have reported that the technology giant will introduce a MacBook that uses an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display with a touchscreen option. It would be the first MacBook to contain a touchscreen, and the expected debut starkly contrasts with Apple-cofounder Mr Jobs 's stance on portable computer touchscreens. “We've done tonnes of user testing on this, and it turns out it doesn't work,” the late Apple chief executive said in 2010 during a product launch event, discussing why trackpads worked well with laptops and touchscreens didn't. “Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, and it gives a great demo but after a short period of time, you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off. It doesn't work, it's ergonomically terrible.” Apple's current MacBook line-up uses mini-LED displays. But there is a lengthy list of products that have made debuts years after Apple, and even Mr Jobs, dismissed their concepts. Those products include video-capable iPods, stylus pens, larger iPhones and medium-sized iPads. “Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell have already helped bring OLED screens to premium notebooks, but Apple’s entry could be a turning point,” said David Naranjo, associate director for technology market analysis firm Counterpoint Research. He also pointed out that Apple's expertise in establishing dominance in supply chains could help it significantly, and even help other companies. “Not unlike smartphones, when Apple adopts OLED, it boosts manufacturing capacity, improves yields, and lowers panel costs, making OLED more affordable for a wider range of products,” he explained. Mr Naranjo said that he believed a 14-inch MacBook with an OLED display, based on the price of materials, might cost between $2,799 and $2,999. “This higher price would cover the cost of advanced tandem OLED technology, possible touchscreen features, and ongoing memory expenses,” he said. But he cautioned that although Apple's products tend to exceed expectations, new MacBooks are arriving at a time when overall PC sales are starting to slow, giving the California technology company an additional hurdle to overcome. View on Threads According to Bloomberg, Apple will also be changing the MacBook Pro's name to MacBook Ultra. As has been the case with the company's events in recent years, some are expecting new iMac and iPad models with simple upgrades consisting of faster semiconductors, improved displays and slightly tweaked designs. Regardless of what transpires at the event on Wednesday, it will cap the busiest Apple product introduction seasons in recent years. In September, the company announced the keenly awaited foldable iPhone Duo. Weeks later, it introduced a new device, HomeView , which incorporates AI, Siri and the company's iOS to allow people to interact with various products in their home. It also announced the Apple TV 4K, the first significant upgrade to the product in several years.

title: European and Middle Eastern foreign ministers urge restraint at Istanbul talks
description: Foreign ministers from eight countries call for diplomacy as regional war threatens to widen
content: Regional and European powers on Friday urged parties to war in the Middle East to avoid further military escalation, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. “Military intervention is not a solution, and nobody approves this at the moment,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told journalists in Istanbul after a meeting with counterparts from across the region and Europe. Foreign ministers from the UK, France, Germany and Italy met with counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt at a hotel alongside the Bosphorus strait on Friday afternoon, in the first meeting of its kind between all the ministers. The countries represented had agreed to “give the message to all parties” that diplomacy needed to prevail over more war, Mr Fidan said. “A repeated attack on Iran could spread the war and conflict in the region further,” said Mr Fidan, who maintains dialogue with both the US and Iran. “On the other hand, the opening of the Strait of Hormuz is needed, and the attacks on Saudi Arabia shall also stop.” A new escalation between Tehran and Washington “would create nothing but losers”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told journalists after the talks on Friday. Ministers from the eight countries discussed the “urgent need” for diplomacy to resolve regional challenges, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement. Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar briefed his counterparts on Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and prevent a resumption of hostilities, it added. Ministers discussed the “parameters” for preventing the conflict from spreading across the Middle East, Mr Fidan said, declining to elaborate. The US and Israel have reportedly discussed launching a new major military operation against Iran, potentially involving strikes on missile and nuclear sites as well as oil installations, although US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that he would not strike again before the US midterm elections on November 3. Iranian officials have vowed an even more widespread response to any new attack than the strikes Tehran launched across the region after US-Israeli military operations began on February 28. Cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities could all be attacked by Tehran , Iran's National Security Council chief Maj Gen Mohsen Rezaei told Iranian media this week. The US continues to impose a military blockade on Iran’s seaports, while Tehran regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation. 'Constructive discussions' After “very constructive discussions”, the eight countries around the table had decided to meet regularly, “to address issues related to a lasting resolution of the Iranian regime’s actions”, Mr Barrot said. They are also seeking to ensure freedom of navigation in Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea, where suspected Russian drone attacks have struck ships near Bulgaria and Romania in recent weeks, raising fears of another chokepoint on global maritime transport. A ceasefire and peace agreement in Ukraine were also needed “as soon as possible”, Mr Fidan added. Attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia were also a central agenda item, and Mr Fidan said he had discussed them in a meeting with the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Egypt before the talks with their European counterparts. Three of those nations – Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey – signed a collective defence pact in August, and Islamabad and Ankara have vowed to defend Saudi Arabia. Turkish officials have made it clear they draw a line at offensive actions against the Houthis in Yemen, whose fatal attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to cancel major events and furthered the turmoil in global energy markets. Saudi Arabia confirmed Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan’s attendance at the Istanbul meetings but did not provide details. Mr Dar held a bilateral meeting with Mr Farhan, in which he expressed Pakistan’s “full support” for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, according to a post on X from Islamabad's Foreign Ministry. The talks in Istanbul also come against a backdrop of growing unrest in Europe, partly over a cost-of-living crisis exacerbated by rising fuel prices resulting from the Middle East war. France has been buffeted by weeks of protests that began around education but which have expanded to encompass demands over the high cost of living, while Italians have taken to the streets over soaring fuel prices and living costs. Mr Barrot underlined efforts to secure energy supplies during President Emmanuel Macron's tour of the Gulf this week, which included a surprise stop in Saudi Arabia. France has also confirmed it was sending military capabilities to protect the key Yanbu oil export terminal in western Saudi Arabia. Violations of freedom of navigation, whether in the Black Sea or Gulf region, have “extremely concrete consequences for us”, Mr Barrot said. “They significantly drive up transportation costs, which ultimately leads to inflation – that is, rising prices – and thus a reduction in the purchasing power of French citizens.”

title: Are you ready for retirement? Because it's not just a question of having enough money
description: Giving up work entails sacrificing more than just a salary
content: Many people I speak to could stop working tomorrow if they chose to. The income from employment stopped being the obstacle some time ago. And yet many keep going. Sometimes, that's because they love what they do, and there's nothing wrong with that. More often, when we talk it through, something else is holding them in place. They lack clarity and aren't sure what the next stage looks like, or who they'll be once the job title goes. That hesitation deserves attention. Work gives far more than just an income . It gives your week a shape, puts people around you, makes you feel useful and hands you real problems to solve. Most of us don't notice how much we rely on that until it's gone. Other people have the opposite problem. Their retirement date arrives because they've had enough. Sometimes it comes suddenly, after a particularly hard year. Sometimes it builds over years of deadlines and long days, until their patience finally runs out. They leave to get away from something, which is a perfectly good reason to go, of course. I've seen capable, financially secure people leave this way with everything in order on paper. Then they find themselves unsure what to do with a Tuesday morning. Some stay too long and others leave too fast, but both are wrestling with the same question. Am I ready for what comes next? Readiness comes down to whether you've built something to step towards. Everything a career gave you can come from somewhere else, provided you set it up. Structure can come from any standing commitment you take seriously. A fixed morning with a coach or trainer, a residential programme at a university you've long admired, a weekly lesson towards your pilot's licence, or a protected day each week with the grandchildren all give the diary its shape back. Connection takes more effort than it did at work, where clients and colleagues filled your diary without you lifting a finger. A club where you see the same faces each week, a regular dinner with former colleagues and clients who've become friends, or a sailing syndicate can fill that gap. So can more unhurried time with family, who'll be glad to see more of you. Purpose is often the hardest to replace. Many executive leaders draw their sense of worth from being the one others call when it matters. That can carry forward through a non-executive role, chairing a charity or an endowment , advising founders in your field, or taking an active hand in how your family's wealth is governed and given away. These roles nearly always come through your existing network. That makes them far easier to secure while your title still opens doors than after you've left. Stimulation matters too. Your work has kept you addressing genuinely hard problems for decades. Serious study can do the same, whether that's a master's in a subject you set aside at 20, learning a language well enough to argue in it, or mastering an instrument, a craft or a sport. It works best when it keeps stretching you and puts you among peers. None of this falls into place overnight. It takes some trial and error, and the people who settle best tend to start years before their last day. So, if you've been putting off a date you could have afforded some time ago, it may be worth asking what you'd be stepping towards, and starting to build it now. The advice provided in our columns does not constitute legal or financial advice and is provided for your information only. Readers should seek appropriate independent legal and financial advice from a regulated professional

title: I'm having a baby, not opening a nursery: The pressure to buy everything before becoming a mother
description: From colour-coded spreadsheets to gadgets promising to solve problems I don't know if we’ll have, preparing for a first baby has introduced me to a whole new world of consumerism
content: I have never considered myself a minimalist. I like nice things, enjoy shopping and can easily convince myself that a purchase is an investment rather than an indulgence. But since becoming pregnant with my first child, I have found myself navigating a level of consumerism unlike anything I have experienced before. It started with a spreadsheet. A friend sent over a document curated by a well-known influencer and businesswoman. It was a comprehensive list of everything one could possibly need for a newborn . There were tabs, categories, colour-coded cells and links to products. It was a work of type-A art. But it was also overwhelming. Troubling research describes how social expectations about being a good mother can be reinforced through marketing Rita Figueiredo, managing director of Peninsula Psychology With the lists come the new words – Artipoppe, Isofix, Owlet – all of which come with a sizeable price tag, designed to solve problems I didn't know existed. On the subject of the fabled Artipoppe, I asked friends on Instagram whether a baby carrier could really justify a Dh1,650 ($450) price tag. The replies were split: people either swore by it or couldn't fathom spending that much money on something that straps a baby to your chest, even if it does come in leopard print. The suggestion to shop for one second-hand came up more than once. My friends without children are looking on bemused, asking how much stuff one tiny person could possibly need. It's a fair question. Part of the problem is that, as a first-time mother, I am entering an entirely new market. I consider myself a reasonably informed consumer, but when it comes to babies, I have no frame of reference. Until recently, I couldn't have told you the difference between a travel system and a pram (I am still not 100 per cent sure I now know), or why one bottle steriliser might cost three times as much as another. When you don't know what you need, it is remarkably easy to be persuaded that you need everything. Rita Figueiredo, managing director of Peninsula Psychology, says this is something brands can exploit. "Marketing, particularly on social media, can introduce a concern parents had not even considered and then present a product as a way of reducing that risk," she says. “Research on consumption during the transition to motherhood describes how social expectations about being a good mother can be reinforced through marketing … This is perhaps the most troubling part: the suggestion that buying a particular product makes someone a better, more caring parent." There is, of course, the excitement of it all. Having a baby is a huge milestone and buying things is one of the few tangible ways to prepare for something that still feels abstract. Choosing a cot, organising tiny clothes and imagining the little person who will eventually use them is lovely. But I am also acutely aware that being able to browse, compare and deliberate over these purchases is a privilege in itself. For many expectant parents, the challenge isn't deciding what not to buy, but finding the money for the essentials. Maryanne Peacock, host of the Mother Tongue podcast, believes that it is enthusiasm that drives the urge to overbuy, rather than external influences. “With your first, you don’t really know what you’ll need, so you’re more likely to buy things just in case. Social media, recommendations from friends and brands all feed into that. When you keep seeing something described as a must-have, you start to think you should probably have it too,” she says. Adding, “We need more reassurance that you can have the basics ready and figure other things out once your baby is here.” Alongside my excitement are the intrusive thoughts. What if the baby won't sleep? What if feeding is difficult? What if I find myself lost in the middle of the night, desperately needing something I could have bought months earlier? Preparing with products can become the one part of parenting that feels controllable. "You can’t practise the 3am feeds or know what your baby’s personality will be like, but you can buy the bassinet," says Anna Baker, founder of SleepBaker sleep consultancy. "The tricky part is that the stuff doesn’t make you ready. Knowledge does, support does, and a good night’s sleep definitely does," Baker adds. A bassinet, or Moses basket, is another polarising product. To some, they're an essential; others dismiss them as a waste of space and money, something you'll only use for a handful of months. This has made me more interested in products that grow with my child – cots that convert into beds, high chairs that can be used for years, and car seats that have a purpose long after the newborn stage. Babies do not need an elaborate collection of equipment to begin exploring the world around them Hossam Gamal, specialist in baby travel safety at Britax Romer Arabia It's a philosophy echoed by Karishma Rajput, brand lead at Stokke Middle East. “I would challenge the idea that being prepared means having everything bought, assembled and perfectly organised before the baby arrives," she says. "The best purchases are not necessarily the newest, most talked-about or most expensive. They are the ones that genuinely meet a need and continue to be useful as circumstances change." As well as looking for products with longevity, I have been exploring second-hand options. Babies grow so quickly that plenty of equipment and clothing is barely used before being outgrown. Buying pre-loved or accepting hand-me-downs from friends makes financial and environmental sense. And there is something satisfying about giving a beautifully made piece of furniture a second life, rather than assuming everything needs to be bought brand new. This is not an argument against shopping for the essentials, particularly when safety is involved. But I am trying not to lose sight of the difference between items that genuinely protect a child and unnecessary gadgets sold with a safety spin. "For car travel, a suitable and safe car seat is an essential rather than an optional extra," says Hossam Gamal, specialist in baby travel safety and product training at Britax Romer Arabia. But even here, more expensive does not automatically mean more appropriate. Gamal stresses that parents should choose a seat that fits their child and vehicle and understand how to install and use it correctly. "Babies do not need an elaborate collection of equipment to begin exploring the world around them," Gamal says. It is also an area where I would be particularly cautious about sourcing second-hand, unless I could be certain of a car seat's history, condition and suitability. Ultimately, I am trying to separate what a baby genuinely needs from products I am being encouraged to want. Something another parent considers indispensable might never be opened in our house, while a product we have dismissed could turn out to be the best thing we buy. The most useful advice I have received, and something I am trying to remind myself daily as I browse Next, Amazon and Mamas and Papas, is the simplest: you can always buy things later. Amid the spreadsheets, shopping lists and targeted advertising, that is surprisingly easy to forget.

title: ‘Suluk’: What the Arabic word for behaviour has in common with Dubai’s Salik toll system
description: Its root also connects everyday conduct with physical paths and spiritual journeys
content: Our Arabic word of the week, suluk, means behaviour and describes how we conduct ourselves at home, school, work and in relationships with others. Husn al-suluk means good behaviour, while su al-suluk refers to bad behaviour or misconduct. Suluk al-tifl describes a child's behaviour, while suluk mihani means professional conduct. The word comes from the Arabic root letters seen, lam and kaf, associated with entering or following a path. The verb salaka means to travel along a route, while maslak can refer to a physical pathway or a person's approach to a situation. In personal relationships, suluk can describe someone's general conduct rather than an isolated action. This differs from another Arabic word, tasarruf, which generally refers to a particular action or response. A person may behave rudely on one occasion, for example, without that incident reflecting how they usually treat others. UAE residents will recognise another root word in Salik , Dubai's road toll system. The name means “open” or “clear”, suggesting travel without barriers. In Sufism , suluk takes on a spiritual meaning, describing the journey towards closeness to God. Someone following this path is also known as a salik. The concept is explored in the 11th-century work Al Risala Al Qushayriyya , or Al Qushayri's Epistle on Sufism , which examines stages of spiritual practice, including repentance, patience and trust in God. The related adjective suluki means behavioural and appears in the psychological term al-ilaj al-suluki al-marifi, or cognitive behavioural therapy, which addresses patterns of thinking and behaviour. Sulukiyat, meanwhile, refers to individual behaviours or behavioural practices. The term also appears in UAE schools , where the Ministry of Education uses al-suluk al-ijabi to mean positive behaviour and includes conduct as part of student assessment. From our everyday conduct to our spiritual pursuits, suluk reflects how we live and the paths we choose to follow.

title: Grosvenor House Dubai review: Refined five-star luxury and stellar service
description: With its acclaimed restaurants, newly renovated spa and consistently attentive staff, this Dubai Marina favourite holds its own among the latest openings
content: Dubai is not short of five-star hotels. With new ones opening all the time, some of the city's more established names face a different challenge: how do you keep standing out when you are no longer the latest hotel on the block? The twin towers of Grosvenor House, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Dubai, have been a big part of the city's Marina skyline for years. And there is something reassuring about the fact that the hotel does not seem to try to reinvent itself to compete with every new opening. It is traditional five-star luxury, and it knows how to do it well. A lot of that comes down to getting the details right. My husband and I checked in for a weekend without our children, with very little planned beyond eating well, having a massage and, most importantly, switching off for a couple of days. The welcome There is plenty to impress at Grosvenor House, but what stayed with us most was the service. You get a sense of that from the moment you arrive. The valet takes care of the car, huge bouquets of fresh flowers fill the foyer, and there always seems to be someone there when you need them. The staff seemed to move effortlessly around us. Everyone knew what they were doing and what needed to happen next. Check-in was quick and easy, and the staff were warm and attentive without being overbearing. That became a theme throughout the weekend. Small requests were remembered and staff would ask us later how dinner, the spa or another part of our stay had gone. They paid attention. The room We stayed in the Deluxe Guest Room with views across the marina and towards the sea. Fruit, macarons and refreshments awaited us as we entered the room. The room wasn't enormous, but we didn't need it to be. There was plenty of storage, an extremely comfortable bed, soft towels and a good-sized bathroom. Grosvenor House is an established hotel, and the design reflects that. This isn't the minimalist look of some of Dubai 's newer hotels. There is wooden cabinetry, marble throughout the bathroom and touches of Art Deco. It feels traditional, in a very elevated way. For a weekend when the whole point was to switch off, the most important things were there: a great bed, a good bathroom and plenty of quiet. The food You could easily spend the whole weekend eating your way around Grosvenor House. Our first dinner was at Rhodes W1 . I started with the watermelon salad which was nice, although I couldn't quite get my head around the almond and orange dressing with fresh za'atar and tarragon. For me, it was one herb too many and needed balancing with something more salty. My husband was much happier with his duck rillette fritters. I followed with a rib-eye steak, and he went for the braised lamb shank: great mains that were traditional and well made. Again, the service made a difference. Staff took the time to talk us through dishes and let us sample drinks before deciding what to order. Breakfast at Sloane's the following morning was busy, but incredibly well run. Everything you would expect from a five-star Dubai breakfast was available: eggs, pastries, Arabic dishes, fruit and plenty of Asian and Indian options. Dinner on our second night was at Toro Toro , which was probably my favourite meal of the stay. The interiors of restaurant are beautiful, but also fun. Staff talked us through the Pan-Latin American influences behind the dishes without making the whole thing feel too formal. The standout for me was the cachapas, a Venezuelan sweetcorn pancake with whipped halloumi, sour cream and pico de gallo, assembled at the table. It reminded me a little of cornbread, but creamier, warmer and sweeter. I followed it with the encocado, with black cod, prawns, squid, coconut, aji mirasol and rice. We had already started with the smoked guacamole, so by this point we were completely stuffed. There were still plenty of things we wanted to try, though, which gives us an excuse to go back. Spa and wellness A weekend away without the children was always going to involve a trip to the spa. Our couples massage at the newly renovated Sanara Spa was one of the highlights of the weekend. We had our consultation earlier in the day and came back later for the treatment. Before the massage we were taken to the separate male and female changing areas, each with a sauna, steam room and Jacuzzi, for some time apart to unwind. For a city hotel, the spa is huge. There is also a hammam and plunge pools at different temperatures, including an ice plunge. I loved the interiors too. There are Japanese influences throughout, including the textiles, particularly two beautiful kimonos hanging as wall art, one behind the reception desk and another in the women's changing room. Then came the massage. Both therapists were excellent and knew exactly where more pressure was needed. I nearly fell asleep, although my husband's snoring from the other side of the room hampered that. By the end, I realised just how tense I had been beforehand. The service There is no shortage of luxury hotels in Dubai. Beautiful rooms, restaurants , spas and pools come with the territory, but good service is harder to get right consistently. From reception and housekeeping to the restaurants and spa, the staff were attentive without constantly hovering around us. More importantly, it never felt scripted. There were fresh roses left on our pillows and a welcome letter in the room, but it was the smaller interactions that I noticed more. Someone remembering where we had dinner and asking how it was. A member of staff recalling something we had mentioned earlier. Not having to repeat a request. None of these things is huge on its own. Put together, though, they mean you don't spend your weekend thinking about logistics or chasing things up. Everything just works. The verdict Grosvenor House isn't Dubai's newest hotel, but it doesn't need to be. There will always be a newer hotel, a bigger room or another spectacular opening around the corner. But what is much harder to replicate is a hotel where the service feels this consistent, confident and luxurious. It worked particularly well for a weekend away for us as a couple. We ate far too much, spent a few hours doing very little at the spa and, for a couple of days, had almost nothing that needed organising. The bottom line A weekend at Grosvenor House made it easy to enjoy the Dubai Marina skyline, attentive service and a good mix of dining, with time to unwind at the spa. Rates currently start at about Dh540 a night, including VAT, though they vary by date and room type. Check-in is from 2pm and checkout by noon. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time

title: Lupin part four: The story so far ahead of Netflix return
description: Omar Sy returns as gentleman thief Assane Diop, whose plans for a quieter life are disrupted by a mysterious copycat
content: With elaborate heists, convincing disguises and a revenge plot that puts an entire family in danger, Netflix ’s Lupin has taken its gentleman thief from the Louvre to a prison cell over three parts. The French mystery thriller follows Assane Diop (played by Omar Sy ), who draws inspiration from the adventures of Arsene Lupin, the fictional thief created by French author Maurice Leblanc. What begins as a mission to clear his father’s name develops into a struggle to protect Assane’s own family from the consequences of his crimes. Alongside the thefts and escapes, the series is centred on Assane’s relationships with his estranged wife Claire, their teenage son Raoul and his closest friend and accomplice, Benjamin. His schemes repeatedly test their loyalty, even when he believes he is acting in their interests. Part four finds Assane behind bars, apparently ready to leave his criminal life behind. But a new thief operating as 'Lupin' threatens those plans. As the series returns for its latest season, here is a refresher on what happened in the first three parts. What is Lupin about? As a teenager, Assane’s life changes after his father Babakar, a Senegalese immigrant working for wealthy businessman Hubert Pellegrini, is accused of stealing a valuable diamond necklace. Babakar dies in prison, leaving his son to grow up with the consequences of an accusation he believes was false. Years later, Assane sets out to uncover what happened and expose those responsible. Taking inspiration from Leblanc’s stories, he uses disguises, sleight of hand and elaborate deception to outwit his opponents. But his pursuit of Pellegrini also attracts police attention and places Claire and Raoul in danger. The story so far (spoilers ahead): What happened in Lupin part one? The series begins with a robbery at the Louvre , where Assane steals the necklace his father was accused of taking years earlier. The heist is the first step in a wider plan to expose Pellegrini. As Assane investigates, he uncovers the businessman’s insurance fraud and the involvement of corrupt police commissioner Dumont in framing his father Babakar. Assane joins forces with investigative journalist Fabienne Beriot, who has been looking into Pellegrini’s dealings. But their efforts to bring him down take a deadly turn when his henchman Leonard murders her. Meanwhile, detective Youssef Guedira begins to recognise a pattern in Assane’s methods. A fellow fan of Leblanc’s books, he realises the thief is drawing on the adventures of Arsene Lupin. Part one ends during a family trip where Leonard kidnaps Raoul. As Assane discovers his son is missing, Guedira catches up with him. What happened in Lupin part two? The search for Raoul brings Assane and Guedira together, with the detective ultimately rescuing the teenager. Although Raoul returns safely to Claire, the kidnapping makes clear how dangerous Assane’s pursuit of Pellegrini has become. With Benjamin’s help, he uncovers Pellegrini’s diversion of charitable donations into an offshore account. Assane then confronts him and records his confession to framing Babakar and ordering Beriot’s murder. However, Assane continues his efforts to expose the businessman, reconnecting with Pellegrini’s daughter Juliette and devising a plan centred on the family foundation’s charity concert. The evidence leads to the arrests of Pellegrini and Dumont, finally exposing the conspiracy against Assane’s father. But Assane’s identity is now public, leaving him unable to return home without risking arrest. Part two ends with him saying goodbye to Claire and Raoul before disappearing. What happened in Lupin part three? After going into hiding, Assane returns to Paris to steal the Black Pearl and carry out an even more ambitious deception: faking his own death. He hopes his apparent demise will allow Claire and Raoul to escape the attention surrounding him. But the plan unravels when Keller – a dangerous figure from his past – kidnaps his estranged mother, Mariama. Using her captivity as leverage, Keller forces Assane to carry out further thefts, drawing him back into the life he had been trying to escape. Assane eventually saves his mother and defeats Keller, but recognises that his freedom comes at a continuing cost to those around him. To give his loved ones a chance at a quieter life, he makes a deal with Guedira and turns himself in. During the final scenes, Assane receives an envelope from the neighbouring prison cell, revealing that Pellegrini is being held next door. What to expect in Lupin part four? Netflix says the new instalment begins four years later, with Assane still serving his sentence. He intends to fulfil his promise to Raoul and join his family in Senegal after his release. However, a string of simultaneous museum robberies – announced in Lupin’s name – makes him a suspect once again. Footage appears to show him at one of the thefts, during which police captain Belkacem is seriously injured. With someone apparently impersonating him, Assane must escape from prison to identify the copycat and clear his name. Lupin Part Four is now streaming on Netflix.

title: 'I feel like it’s meant to be': Eight-year-old Emirati acrobat finds her feet in the air
description: Jawaher Essa Sharafi followed her mother into aerial arts and is encouraging other children to join her
content: Jawaher Essa Sharafi wears an outfit splashed with pink, turquoise, lime green and yellow in a brushstroke pattern. Suspended from a hoop, she twists, twirls and drops as she practises at Aerial Lab in Arjan, Dubai. The eight-year-old has already taken her skills to the international stage, winning bronze in aerial hoop at the IAAA Grand Open Cup in Belgrade, Serbia, in September. The youngest competitor among more than 100 athletes from 11 countries, she became the first Emirati to compete internationally in aerial athletics – only two years after she began formal training. View this post on Instagram An aerialist is an acrobat who specialises in performing on suspended apparatus, such as hoops, trapezes and silks. The discipline combines acrobatics and artistic performance, drawing on strength, flexibility and co-ordination as athletes move through holds, spins and drops, often set to music. Jawaher trains on hoop and hammock, a suspended fabric sling, but asked which she prefers, there is little hesitation. “Hoop, hoop, hoop. It's the best. First of all, I like hoop because it's hard. I like to challenge myself in aerial,” she tells The National . The hoop shape and texture also set it apart. It's the “only one that's a circle made out of metal … because the rest [of the aerial equipment] are made out of same thing: fabric”, she says. “Hoop is made out of something different. That made me fall in love with it.” Her enthusiasm is equally apparent when she talks about training. “Whenever I do it, I get all my excitement out,” she says. “I feel like it's meant to be.” Following her mother Aerial arts was familiar to Jawaher long before she attended her first class. Her mother, Fatma Almadani, practised and taught the discipline. Almadani says: “She used to watch me train and she would attend all my trainings and be like, ‘I want to try, I want to try,’ So my trainer would put her up there since she was a baby.” Later, Jawaher began accompanying her mother to the children’s classes she taught. Participants had to be at least nine, and Jawaher was only four or five at the time. Watching from the sidelines did little to diminish her interest. She wanted to help, demonstrate and prove that she could keep up with the older children, her mother says. “I’d come home and she'd be like, ‘Mama, can you please come into the gym room? I want to show you that I can do what you were teaching the kids and I'm good enough to join your classes,’” Almadani recalls. The age restriction prompted her to look for somewhere that offered classes for younger children. Jawaher then began training at Aerial Lab when she was six. “Other than simple things we used to teach her at home, proper training was at Aerial Lab,” Almadani says. Watching other students perform gave Jawaher another goal. When Almadani took her to students' aerial showcases, she began asking when it would be her turn on stage. Finding her confidence Enthusiasm does not mean every new aerial skill comes easily. Jawaher describes the uncertainty of learning a trick that requires her to turn upside down, and wondering what might happen if she falls. However, she tries to reassure herself before attempting a move. “I can do this, no need to be worried, my teacher is here. She'll protect me, she knows what's right for me,” she tells herself. One drop proved particularly difficult after she fell while learning it. Returning to the movement took time, beginning slowly and gradually building speed as her confidence returned. Developing that control matters in competition, where judges assess difficulty, execution and artistry. For Jawaher, one detail requires particular attention: pointing her toes. “I've also been doing karate and in karate you don't point your toes,” she says. “It's been a challenge for me to try and remember.” Jawaher attends aerial classes on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays, with more training when a competition approaches. But she recognises the importance of taking a break. “Maybe not [training] every day, because I need rest days . It's important to have rest days,” she says. She sometimes practises at home on days when she does not have a class. The family’s gym room was originally Almadani’s space. “I actually set it up for me and now she took over,” she says. There, Jawaher has room to experiment as well as rehearse. Almadani adds: “She loves coming here and just she puts on music and does her own routines. She tries to imagine new moves.” From classes to competition Almadani did not initially see her daughter’s progress. Parents were asked not to sit in on group classes, so she would drop Jawaher off and collect her afterwards. Then the teachers began approaching her about private training. A competition planned in the UAE offered an opportunity, and Jawaher was selected to represent the studio. Almadani says she was the only child chosen from her age group. But that event was cancelled, and the competition in Serbia became Jawaher's international debut. Her mother was struck by her progress as she watched her prepare. “From seeing her in her first showcase on stage, compared to this year, doing a routine for the competition, I was surprised by how much she advanced in just one year,” Almadani says. Jawaher says she feels both nervous and excited before performing, but finishing her routine brings relief. “I'm like: finally I can get all that energy out of me. And I don't need to worry any more about my routine,” she says. Bigger ambitions What most impresses Almadani is her daughter’s willingness to work towards goals she has set herself. “I find her personality very inspiring. Her confidence is very inspiring,” she says. “It gets hard sometimes to train every day. Sometimes she's exhausted. Sometimes she wants to stay up at night and the weekends. But I'm inspired by how she's very committed to the goals she has.” Still, she wants her daughter to have the freedom to explore other interests. Jawaher has mentioned karate competitions, horse riding and parkour, adding to an already busy schedule. “She wants to try everything,” Almadani says. “But we don't have enough days of the week to do after-school [activities] every day.” Whatever Jawaher eventually chooses, her mother hopes the experience will leave her with habits and confidence that extend beyond competition. “It builds personality, it builds character and gives you skills that you need in life,” she says. For now, Jawaher is preparing two routines for her next showcase, one on hammock and another on hoop, and looking ahead to a competition in Italy next year. She would like more young athletes from the UAE to join her. Almadani recalls her daughter hoping that photographs from the competition in Serbia might encourage friends to enter future contests and help to build a bigger team. Jawaher invites friends to try aerial arts at home and has already encouraged one to begin classes. While keen to share her enthusiasm, she knows not everyone will feel ready to give it a go. “If you tried it, you would love it and you would keep going again and again,” she says. “But if you don't want to, I won't force you.”

title: Beirut commuters switch to motorcycle taxis as rising fuel prices push up fares
description: With even ride-sharing cabs becoming unaffordable, more and more people are turning to unregulated 'moto-taxis' to get around the Lebanese capital
content: Adam cannot afford to say no. Unlike most drivers of Beirut’s “servees ” – shared taxis, the most common form of public transport in Lebanon 's capital – he picks up almost anyone looking for a ride, even if it is for less than the set rate. “A lot of customers can’t afford the fare , so they offer 200,000 lira ($2.20) or less,” he told The National as he drove downtown. “People won’t ride if the price is too high.” His need to pick up every commuter is also driven by growing competition from the cheaper motorcycle taxis, commonly called “moto-taxis”, that more people are turning to as they endure a prolonged economic crisis now in its seventh year. Beirut’s servees drivers raised their fares from 200,000 to 300,000 lira after the government imposed a fuel tax in February, only nine days before the Iran war began. Fuel prices have nearly doubled since, according to the Syndicate of Gas Station Owners, as the war disrupted shipments from Gulf producers. The servees drivers now charge “as they see fit”, according to Zainab, who spoke to The National after dismounting a motorcycle taxi that she had booked through a ride-share app. The journey from her neighbourhood in Ras Al Nabaa to Jisr Al Wati cost her 200,000 lira, she said – “cheaper and faster than flagging a taxi in the street and then haggling with a chauffeur”. Ten years ago, it would have been almost unthinkable for a woman to ride on the back of a motorcycle with a strange man. But Lebanon's economic collapse has made financial necessity a priority over social norms. The crisis, which began in 2019 and which the World Bank has described as among the worst in modern history, has left most of the population struggling. Lebanese depositors were locked out of their savings and the national currency lost more than 98 per cent of its value against the US dollar, eroding salaries and severely diminishing purchasing power. That, combined with the higher fuel prices caused by the Iran war, have made traditional taxis increasingly unaffordable in a country where the monthly minimum wage is only $300. Meanwhile, motorcycles have come to dominate the streets of Beirut, with imports surging as commuters seek cheaper alternatives to cars and conventional taxis. Even car owners are choosing to forgo driving and take motorcycle taxis. “I used to fill up my car for $45. Now it costs almost $90 to $100, or sometimes even more. So we've started turning to slightly cheaper options,” said Moussa, a paramedic in his 30s who took a motorcycle taxi to a doctor’s appointment in Clemenceau, a busy Beirut neighbourhood notorious for its traffic gridlock. Moussa said he hails motorcycle rides by sending his pickup location to a “dispatcher” on a WhatsApp group. Motorcycle taxis “are cheaper and more economical considering how much petrol prices have risen recently. Everyone is trying to save money,” he said. More than a dozen servees drivers interviewed by The National voiced frustration over dwindling passenger numbers, as increasing numbers of commuters like Zainab and Moussa turn to motorcycle taxis, or cheaper but slower alternatives such as vans and buses. Adam, who drives a Nissan Sunny – known for its fuel efficiency – shrugged. “It’s why I take everyone. I can’t afford to pick and choose. But at the same time it’s tough, and sometimes after hours of working I barely break even.” And motorcycle taxis are not the only players in Beirut's informal transport market. There are also the “white-plate” taxis – private cars operating as taxis through ride-hailing apps and WhatsApp groups. A red number plate, which serves as the licence to operate a taxi, costs about $16,000 in Lebanon. Along with the cost of the vehicle itself, this represents a significant upfront investment. Some drivers rent a licensed taxi and pay the owner about $20 a day. With petrol prices so high, drivers say they cannot afford to lower their fares. “Someone with a cheap motorcycle comes along, picks up passengers and drives off like he’s a taxi. It’s not safe. It's not legal. If there's an accident, there's no insurance or anything,” said Ibrahim, a taxi driver parked at the Cola intersection as he waited for customers. He accused motorcycle taxi operators of competing without the licensing and insurance requirements imposed on conventional taxi drivers. I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business Wael, Beirut taxi driver “Our cars cost money. We have to repair them, we work hard and we still can't make ends meet. Motorcycles are our biggest [competition].” But Ibrahim also recognised the financial pressures driving passengers to cheaper alternatives. While some servees drivers have started charging 400,000 lira or more per journey to compensate for rising fuel prices, he said he has continued to charge 300,000. “We're being considerate of the public,” he said. “We also can't raise fares for passengers because everyone's situation is difficult.” Other taxi drivers, unable to deny the economic reality, have simply decided to join the motorcycle phenomenon. By day, Wael ferries commuters around Beirut on a motorcycle. At night, he switches to his licensed taxi. His motorcycle uses less petrol, is easier to manoeuvre through daytime traffic and allows him to complete more trips in less time – meaning a higher profit. At night, lighter traffic, airport runs and Beirut’s nightlife make driving a taxi more feasible. “Everyone with a motorcycle now thinks it’s a fast and easy way to make money,” Wael told The National . He belongs to two WhatsApp groups that co-ordinate motorcycle taxi rides, each with more than 350 riders. He said the growing competition has taken a major toll on conventional taxis. “I’d be making a lot more money as a taxi driver if it weren’t for the motorcycle competition. They’re taking half our business,” he said. “But I don’t think they’re the problem. It’s the state, which has done nothing to regulate the taxi-motos or fix the economy. People are turning to motorcycles because they have to, not because they want to endanger themselves.” The dangers are clear to see. Motorcycles weave around potholes and through Beirut's notoriously chaotic traffic unpredictably, rarely a helmet in sight, and often pass through red lights. Beyond the occasional crackdown on unregistered motorcycles, Lebanon’s government has done little to regulate the growth of the informal motorcycle taxi industry. Asaad, another motorcycle taxi operator, thinks state regulation would be the best possible outcome for the moto-taxi phenomenon. “Because motorcycle taxis aren’t going away. They're the future,” he said.

title: Wealth expert Becky Fatemi: Tax the rich, but don’t scare them away from UK
description: With decades of deals under her belt, the Iran-born businesswoman has a message for PM Andy Burnham
content: It was an advertisement for a tele-sales job in the mid-1990s that set Becky Fatemi on the path to success. It meant standing on her feet all day, cold-calling hundreds of people, and talking, talking, talking while knowing she was under pressure to seal a deal in minutes. A role at which many people would baulk came naturally to the self-starting whirlwind of energy, who moved to London from Iran as a baby and was mostly brought up in a single-parent family. It forced Ms Fatemi to rely on her natural people skills, honing her ability to read what people wanted. She went on to use those skills for more than a decade as a top operator at estate agent Foxtons, a similar amount of time at her own property firm Rokstone, and now as a partner at Sotheby’s International Realty where she has evolved into a wealth adviser. Along the way she has worked as a hip-hop DJ, at McDonald’s, in Selfridges, sold tables at nightclubs, been a stylist to celebrities, worked for a children’s charity, founded a charity and launched a social media platform. “Any type of work that I felt that could fortify my CV, I did,” said Ms Fatemi, 50. She spoke to The National during lunch near her office in Marylebone, and over Zoom while she spent the summer in Portugal. Having spent the best part of three decades learning how people are willing to spend their money, and where they wish to invest, she is well positioned to know how those with wealth will respond to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s leadership, as he and Chancellor John Healey head towards their first budget, on October 28. Taxing The Labour government has already made significant changes to the tax regime: scrapping the non-domicile status, raising employer national insurance contributions, increasing capital gains, applying VAT to private school fees and toughening property taxes. More changes are expected, with the middle classes and wealthiest expected to take the brunt. Ms Fatemi has more confidence in Mr Burnham than she had in his predecessor Keir Starmer, but still does not think he is the right person to steer the UK’s economic fortunes. Trying to please everyone, an accusation immediately laid at Mr Burnham’s door as he entered Downing Street seemingly happy to respond positively to requests for funding, simply will not work, she believes.
