She is in no doubt those with money need to pay their fair share of tax, to “address the disparity in wealth”, but should not be squeezed too hard. “A lot of my clients are working far longer hours than I've ever seen, and working much harder,” Ms Fatemi says, adding: “Politically, we cannot alienate wealth. It helps support the [country’s] infrastructure and, at the moment, our infrastructure is failing.” Exodus She is well aware of the exodus of the ultra-wealthy from London, especially after the decision to scrap non-doms , the status to ensure only money earned in Britain was taxed. The number of non-dom taxpayers in the UK in the final year before it was scrapped dropped by 1,200 , statistics show, as the wealthy geared up for the change. About 16,000 millionaires were predicted to leave the UK last year as the taxman’s grip tightened. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index suggest about half of the UK’s billionaire wealth – £120 billion ($160.7 billion) – has been lost. It is too soon to tell the true impact of such decisions, says Ms Fatemi, but there is no doubting the direction of travel. The government is avoiding addressing the issue of “a mass exodus of our uber-wealthy who are our biggest taxpayers”. Inheritance tax and being taxed on global wealth has “driven a lot of people out”, but she says: “I don't think we have seen the ramifications of exactly how that has affected the economy. "Someone employing over a thousand staff, who has personal staff, chefs, security guards, physiotherapists, tutors, teachers – all of these things have a domino effect to another workforce, like black cab drivers. I don't think we're going to understand these figures for a good five to six years.” Hidden quitters More than a dozen people with multibillion-pound fortunes have left or loosened ties with the country in favour of more favourable tax regimes, the Bloomberg index showed, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and telecoms investor Shravin Bharti Mittal. The UAE has been the preferred destination for many of the billionaires, along with Monaco, Switzerland and Italy. But for the UK, all is not lost. “Is there money still coming into London? Yes. Could we be more tax-smart? Yes. Do they need to be taxed? Yes,” Ms Fatemi says. She says there is a need for transparency on how any wealth coming into the UK is taxed, with anything enveloped in a company structure paying “ridiculous” taxes. “That’s where the government is missing a really big trick,” she says. The people really making money from the current situation are tax advisers, Ms Fatemi says, as there are so many moving parts. She suggests the government gets a grip on the situation by speaking to wealth advisers like her “who are looking at where that tax position is and speaking to the people at every level to understand exactly what is going on”. Immigrant mindset Ms Fatemi puts her irrepressible work ethic down to her immigrant background, which created a determination to succeed. Born in 1976, with a father who was a pilot with Iran Air before the revolution deposed the Shah, she spent time growing up in Kuwait and Bangkok, but mostly London. She was even a "baby boarder" at the Norland Nursery in London for a year, which she recognises was a bizarre start to life in a new country. “Both my parents felt it was imperative that my brother and I were educated,” she says, adding her father in particular fitted the immigrant stereotype of hoping she would study medicine or law, even though her passion was to work in the music industry. “My mother really wanted us to live in the UK. We came at the time of [Margaret] Thatcher, having to work very, very hard. Nothing was for free, you should be grateful to be here and you're going to work very hard in order to stay here. “It took 10 years to get my passport.” Her father was rarely around, and her mother had multiple sclerosis, so she learnt to fend for herself. Her mother returned to Iran as her health deteriorated, meaning Ms Fatemi left home at 15 and surfed sofas until she found somewhere permanent to live, “on one of the roughest council estates in north London”. She dealt with racism, prejudice and inequality but felt determined that she was going to “make a difference” by being a disruptive force. Ms Fatemi had made her way through university when she saw the tele-sales advert. “It said: ‘Are you good at talking? If you're a good salesperson, come and join us. You'll make a lot of money’. I got to number one in that company.” Still in her early 20s, she then had to deal with both her parents, plus her boyfriend and best friend, dying in quick succession. She needed a change, so she threw herself into her career. She badgered estate agent Foxtons for a job as a receptionist but ended up selling homes. “I came from a tele-sales job of cold-calling over 400 people to this job where people would call me to spend millions. “The Park Lane office, which is where I ended up in the late '90s, early 2000s, was where the real money was. International money was pouring into Mayfair.” Speaking several languages and being well-travelled was an advantage as it gave her an understanding of people. “I know culturally how these people live,” Ms Fatemi says. It was still not easy. “You were just in this pit of sales. Each for their own. It was very cut-throat, very male, very chauvinistic. Very hard to navigate. “But I was just born with this inherent female strength, being Iranian, Persian, but just being an immigrant. When you're an immigrant you're fighting just to be included, to survive. You don't know where your next meal's coming from and you're grateful just to be there.” Wrong side of the tracks Her personal situation also made things difficult. “I was leaving Mayfair and going home to the worst estate in Kilburn, or sofa-surfing in the worst parts of north or south London, living in hostels, while still working at Foxtons. “I was living in two worlds, which allowed me to see the other side of the track how people were really trying to survive. That allowed me that street-smart mentality. It led her to set up a charity years later, called Shadow to Shine, to give opportunities for young people from underrepresented, diverse backgrounds to break into tech, fashion, construction, law or creative industries. Perception When Foxtons was sold, she set up her own conglomerate, Rokstone, inspired by Richard Branson’s multi-pronged business empire. “He did Virgin Brides, Virgin Trains, Virgin planes, Virgin Holidays. And I thought, why can't I do that? So I set up this company called Rokstone.” It allowed her to promote her love of music and entertainment with bricks and mortar, plus tech and philanthropy – all from her living room. Ms Fatemi started travelling the world, running parties and events, amalgamating brands and styling for celebrities such as Rihanna and Beyonce. A phone call from a former client asking her to act as a property buying agent returned her to London. “I didn’t even know what a buying agent was,” she says, not entirely convincingly. She found a £500,000, one-bedroom flat after about 100 viewings on a small commission. Through word of mouth, she gained a few more clients before opening an office in Devonshire Street, Marylebone, the neighbourhood where she still operates. It was all about perception, Ms Fatemi says. If she could persuade customers that Rokstone was a luxury real estate firm, it would live up to her exaggerations. “We had one property to start, then got a house in Mayfair for £5 million and then I was selling two flats in Camberwell for £220,000. All referral, referral, referral.” She would go out on viewings with other agents and pretend she was looking for a place for herself while learning their trade secrets. “I was fearless,” Ms Fatemi says. “I was that ‘Persian princess’, because I had been at one stage, and my mother had been. I believed that I had a right to be there and because of that conviction I think people believed that I was one of them.” She ensured she was “in every conversation, in every restaurant, at every opening” and even got a Hummer that was Rokstone-branded, which kept conveniently breaking down on Park Lane, where it could be seen by everyone. At the time Ms Fatemi also became a single mother herself, so knew she had to make it work “because there was no other option”. Networking After 13 years of running her business, achieving a profit every year from £6 billion worth of sales, even through Covid, it was time to look for the next challenge. During a viewing of a £30 million property in Piccadilly, an old colleague suggested she meet George Azar, who was assembling an "Avengers team" after buying the Sotheby’s franchise. They agreed after a 10-minute Zoom call that she should become a partner, with support for her charity and the wriggle room to set up a tech platform called Blackbook part of her conditions. Blackbook is the culmination of 30 years of networking for Ms Fatemi and is intended as a sort of LinkedIn/Instagram for creatives, to allow them to display and monetise their skills in one place by connecting them with other "talent". But her day-to-day is spent speaking with lawyers, tax advisers, compliance and most importantly, clients. She has just been advising a client in New York, a "prominent billionaire", about bricks and mortar investments. “I am a global wealth adviser, which includes real estate, but really it's looking at their life position, how they're living, what's in their best interest for quality of life as well as investment. “The conversations I'm having now are with the most powerful, leading people in the world.” She says she deals with lots of Middle Eastern royal families and has clients in the UAE and across the GCC. “I make sure I'm in Abu Dhabi and Dubai three or four times a year, in Qatar, in Saudi, and supporting them with the investment that they're bringing into London and globally.” London calling Despite its troubles, she is likely to recommend London as a place for long-term investors to place their money due to its “durability” and “tenacity”. “The market is going to stay firm if you invest in best-in-class and super prime," she says. “And really, the people that I told to do that have made a lot of money.” After three decades of deals, she now has a sixth sense for spotting long-term opportunities. “I'm sad that I never pushed myself into investment banking because I think I would have been one of the best investment bankers in the world,” Ms Fatemi says. But at the very least she can appreciate what she has achieved for herself. “I'm going to be a better billionaire at 50 than I would have been at 30,” she says.

title: Erbil’s historic houses find new life as centre for Kurdish art and heritage
description: Kurdistan Centre for Arts and Culture is creating an archive for rare manuscripts while supporting artists and documenting Kurdish contributions to the region’s cultural history
content: In Erbil’s old quarter, Kurdish history is held in family manuscripts, works of art and memories passed down through generations. Now, four historic houses near the city’s ancient citadel are being brought back to life to give those stories a place to endure. The Kurdistan Centre for Arts and Culture (KCAC) is working on turning the homes into spaces for safeguarding manuscripts, supporting contemporary artists and documenting Kurdish contributions to the region’s cultural history. “One of the houses is dedicated to the archive, as a state-of-the-art storage facility … fireproof, waterproof, bulletproof – as you need here: everything-proof,” said Spede Mizuri, director of public impact at KCAC. The houses were evacuated in 2012 during moves by the regional government to improve the area around the historic landmark, but plans were put on hold when ISIS emerged two years later. The properties have remained vacant ever since. Most predate the Iraqi monarchy, while one is an Ottoman-era house with British influences, Ms Mizuri said. The archive building will be home to a partnership with the city's Salahaddin University to make its manuscript collection accessible to researchers and the public. Ms Mizuri said the collection had remained largely inaccessible since being moved to the university in the 1960s, with little cataloguing or academic study. The second house will become a permanent exhibition space, opening next month with the first solo exhibition in Kurdistan by a Kurdish artist living in exile. The remaining two properties will host workshops and longer-term training programmes in the arts, heritage and cultural sectors. The restoration builds on the organisation’s work to preserve vulnerable collections across Iraqi Kurdistan . Launched in 2024, its initial mobile archiving project used scanners inside a Toyota van to travel between villages, religious schools and private libraries, digitising material and making it freely accessible online. The collections range from political documents and religious manuscripts to personal journals, astrological material and modern printed works. Some were hidden underground during periods of conflict to protect them. “We have a major, major issue in Kurdistan for precious materials and artworks that have been purchased. They've been taken into stewardship, so to say, and nobody really knows what happened to these materials,” Ms Mizuri said. “Some of them are under really, really bad conditions as well, so digitisation is the first immediate crisis response to something like that.” Kurds are spread across Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Syria , with a large diaspora beyond those countries. Despite sharing a distinct cultural identity, Kurdish communities have developed under different political systems and national borders, so their language, literature and traditions play an important role in preserving a sense of shared history. For Ms Mizuri, the work addresses a broader problem: the lack of resources for Kurdish history and its contributions to the region to be documented and studied. “We have left our mark … on the world entirely, but there's very little to showcase that.” That effort to make Kurdish history more accessible extends beyond Erbil. In Sulaymaniyah, KCAC is working with the British Library and the University of Exeter on a project involving the library of the Ministry of Religious Endowment, which holds some of the oldest manuscripts in Kurdistan. The initiative, due to be announced next week, aims to make the collection the first Kurdish library represented in the British Library’s cataloguing system, bringing its manuscripts into a wider international research network. Ms Mizuri said the project was significant given Kurdistan’s history under British imperial rule, and the continued absence of a Kurdish library from the institution’s catalogue. From preserving manuscripts to promoting contemporary artists, KCAC is also seeking to ensure Kurdish culture has a stronger presence across the region. For Kurds, whose history has often been preserved through oral traditions and family accounts, making these collections accessible offers a tangible record of their cultural and intellectual contributions. Manuscripts, artworks and personal documents can help establish connections between generations, while giving researchers and communities material evidence to study and share. Ms Mizuri said the archive could also provide a sense of security by ensuring that Kurdish history was not dependent solely on memories or oral accounts, which can be difficult to substantiate or preserve over time. It also offers a way to understand Kurdish identity within the wider history of the region, recognising the contributions of Kurdish artists, writers and scholars that have not always been acknowledged as such. “We are known for being at the midst of war and continuously the spoils of wars that sometimes maybe we were part of, and other times we're really not,” Ms Mizuri said, adding that having tangible history helps to “introduce ourselves beyond conflict”. 'Ambassador for Kurdish artists' Preserving Kurdish heritage is also a way of bringing it into a wider cultural conversation, ensuring that Kurdish artists and their work are represented even beyond the Kurdistan region. The centre has been building relationships with cultural institutions in Iraq and across the Middle East, including through its participation in the first edition of Art Basel Qatar. Later this year, it will take part in the Sharjah Art Foundation’s art book fair , where it plans to host a workshop and talk and present its publications. Artist and resident Walid Siti was also recently presented at Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai. KCAC’s work extends beyond preserving historical material to exploring contemporary social issues through art. Its first exhibition, held in Akre in 2024, transformed the town’s old Qishla, an Ottoman-era fortress, into an exhibition space for digital artist Kaiwan Shaban. The exhibition was extended three times at the request of the local tourism office, Ms Mizuri said. A subsequent exhibition, Being Lost, was held in a public park in Ranya , a town near the Iranian border, associated with people-smuggling networks and young people attempting to reach Europe. The park, where The National has previously reported from, is known to be a location where those attempting to migrate seek out smugglers. The exhibition brought together memorabilia connected to families whose relatives had left or disappeared, exploring the uncertainty and pain experienced by those waiting for news. Visitors could record messages on phones attached to a transparent wall, with the recordings intended for broadcast on the radio in the hope of reaching those who had left. Seminars were held in nearby Raparin University, in the same district as Ranya , which used to be one the highest performing universities in the Kurdish region, which Ms Mizuri described as the “dichotomy” that exists in the city. “Heritage is collective,” she said of Kurdistan's place in the region. She added that the main priority was to “preserve and then to promote”. For Ms Mizuri, the work is ultimately about giving Kurdish communities the means to understand and share their own history, while recognising the connections between them and their neighbours.

title: The US will remain central to Gulf and Arab security, but the terms must change
description: A more secure region will depend on diversifying partnerships, building resilience and doubling down on diplomacy
content: The wars of recent months have exposed a troubling reality: despite a substantial American military presence and decades of close defence co-operation between the US and Arab countries, the security partnerships have neither deterred Iran nor fully shielded the region from its attacks. Two shortcomings stand out. The first is technical: traditional air defences that the US and its partners used have grappled with Iran’s asymmetric use of large numbers of missiles and inexpensive drones. The second is political: Washington embarked on a war that some of the region’s leaders had warned could have devastating consequences for their countries. They raise two questions. Can the US and its partners repair the gaps in the security umbrella? And will another costly Middle Eastern war weaken American public and political support for a sustained regional role? The answers remain uncertain. But enduring US interests make a wholesale withdrawal unlikely. And Arab states are likely to maintain a central strategic partnership with the US while strengthening their own capabilities, adding partners and pursuing diplomacy to reduce the danger of renewed conflict. Military history is marked by moments when new technologies overturn established assumptions. The widespread use of inexpensive drones, alongside large missile inventories, in Ukraine and the latest war with Iran, has highlighted another such shift. The American umbrella did not fall short because it was not equipped. It did so because it had not anticipated or prepared for the nature of these evolving threats. Saturation attacks can exhaust interceptors and overwhelm defences; the cost of shooting down a cheap drone may vastly exceed the cost of launching it. The US retains formidable offensive capabilities, as demonstrated by its and Israel’s ability to strike targets in Iran. But the ability to punish an adversary is different from the ability to shield cities, energy installations, airports and ports from retaliation. American military planners and defence firms are intensifying work on cheaper interceptors, counter-drone systems, directed-energy weapons and AI-assisted detection and targeting. The outcome of that technological race is impossible to predict. In the near term, however, Iran and its partners are likely to retain the capacity to inflict damage, even against sophisticated defences. In the medium term, new technological advances may once again shift the regional balance of power or give regional countries more effective defences. The military vulnerabilities were compounded by political decisions. The region’s leaders understood that a war perceived as existential by Tehran could prompt attacks on their territory and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz . They warned against that scenario. Yet US President Donald Trump, encouraged by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, chose a military course that exposed America’s partners to precisely those risks. Mr Trump has subsequently appeared more attentive to regional concerns and has explored a negotiated outcome. But diplomacy has yet to produce a durable settlement, and the risk of renewed large-scale fighting is emerging once again. For the regional governments, the lesson might be concerning: close relations with Washington do not necessarily translate into influence over decisions with existential implications for their security. There is also a longer-term question. After Iraq and Afghanistan, could another costly Middle East war turn US voters and future presidents against maintaining a substantial regional presence? Washington is likely to reassess its regional posture, favouring a leaner, technologically advanced and less vulnerable deployment, but retrenchment is not the same as disengagement. The US has enduring interests in keeping Gulf energy flowing to world markets and critical waterways open; preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons or dominating the region; protecting Israel; and sustaining partnerships with Gulf states whose importance now extends beyond hydrocarbons to investment, defence industries, advanced technology and artificial intelligence. Even an energy-producing America remains vulnerable to a global recession caused by a prolonged Gulf supply shock . Many American politicians from both parties disagree sharply about how the war was launched and prosecuted. Yet disagreement over methods does not amount to a consensus for abandoning these interests. Interestingly, the positions of potential presidential candidates from both parties confirm this view. Future administrations may adopt different strategies, but are unlikely to pull out wholesale from the region; indeed, they will grapple with many of the same dilemmas that have shaped US-Gulf policy since 1979. The regional states face a demanding agenda. Politically, they are justified in asking why exceptionally warm relations with Washington did not prevent a war they considered dangerous. They will need stronger mechanisms for consultation and greater input into decisions affecting regional escalation, as well as a serious role in shaping any settlement with Iran. Militarily, there is no other great power currently able to replace the US as most Arab countries’ principal strategic security partner. Hence, they will work with Washington as it rethinks the shape of its future security presence and relationships in the region. But the American partnership, while necessary, is no longer sufficient. The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system The answer is less a matter of hedging against America than of adding layers to what is likely to remain an American-centred system: stronger national armed forces and industries; more effective intelligence-sharing and integrated air defence; and additional security relationships. Saudi Arabia’s engagement with Turkey and Pakistan points in this direction, as do opportunities to draw on European, Ukrainian, South Korean and other expertise in equipment, training and counter-drone innovation. Some countries will draw closer to Israel. It is not America or other partners, but America and other partners. The Gulf is understandably focused on building further resilience into its economies. Protecting energy, water, power, transport and digital infrastructure will require redundancy, dispersed facilities, rapid-repair capacity and strategic reserves. Alternative pipelines, ports and overland corridors – which are already in the works – can reduce dependence on vulnerable maritime chokepoints , even if geography cannot be wished away. Finally, Arab countries understand that defence needs to be accompanied by energetic diplomacy. Iran is a permanent neighbour, and Gulf states have every reason to pursue de-escalation, crisis-management channels and arrangements that lower the risk of repeated wars. Military deterrence and diplomatic engagement are complementary, not contradictory. The outcome of the current confrontation remains uncertain. Whether it moves towards another round of escalation or arrives at a limited agreement, the region is likely to be facing years of insecurity. The emerging regional order is unlikely to be a clean rupture with the American security architecture. More plausibly, it will be an evolution towards a flexible, multilayered system: the US still central, but reinforced by stronger Gulf and Arab capabilities, better GCC co-ordination , wider regional and international partnerships, economic resilience and sustained regional diplomacy. For the region, the challenge is not to replace the American umbrella. It is to make security less dependent on any single umbrella – and to gain greater control over the decisions that determine whether the region goes to war or moves towards de-escalation and co-operation.

title: From inshallah to ojala: Havana museum explores Cuba's hidden Arab history
description: Community of immigrants from Arab world has left 'indelible print' on island
content: The Casa de los Arabes in Havana is easy to miss, hidden in one of the ubiquitous colonial-era manses that line the winding streets of the Cuban capital. But inside the “Arab House” the stories of the island's Arab immigrant community and the formative role it played in the country's history is revealed. One room displays traditional Arab weaponry such as swords and rifles, some of which were presented as gifts by foreign dignitaries to Fidel Castro , who led the Cuban revolution in the 1950s. Another room recreates a Bedouin tent in the Kuwaiti desert. And another features photos of early immigrant families, along with letters and personal possessions illustrating their stories. Jackeline Diaz Fuentes, director of Casa de los Arabes, told The National that before Cuba was discovered by European explorers, the Arab world had an influence on Spanish-speaking people through Muslim rule in Spain that lasted more than 700 years. “There are many Arabic words that came into Spanish, even our expression 'ojala' – 'hopefully' – comes from the Arabic phrase 'inshallah' ,” she said. Spanish architecture, heavily influenced by Islamic rule in the country, also made its way to Cuba . Cuba has historically been a major hub for international trade, its ports full of ships shuttling sugar, cotton and manufactured goods between the Americas and Europe. People from all over the world – either of their own free will or as slaves or indentured servants – came to Cuba over the centuries, and most people on the island can claim indigenous roots, alongside African, European, or Asian. Arabs came to Cuba in the second half of the 19th century. The first Arab immigrants came to the island, as well as other parts of the Americas, from the Levant, which was undergoing severe upheaval at the time. Economic depression, high taxes and fears of military conscription under the Ottoman Empire, as well as shrinking available farmland and the collapse of the regional silk trade, pushed many in Levantine countries to seek opportunities in other parts of the world. The ultimate destination for many who came to Cuba from Lebanon , Syria and elsewhere was the US, but the island was a key point of entry to the West, Ms Diaz Fuentes explained. “First, young [Arab] men came alone and got into street vending, eventually establishing stable import businesses,” she said, highlighting that while initially the men would bring families and brides from their home countries, members of the community eventually began marrying into the local population. Over time, this community integrated more and more into the culture of the island. Arab Cubans even took up arms during the war of independence from Spain in 1895. “There are memorable examples of Arabs that were incorporated, that identified themselves with the Cuban people and with their fight to achieve improvements in their standard of living,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. The community has largely assimilated into wider Cuban culture, but descendants of the first immigrants formed the Arab Union of Cuba in the 1970s to preserve and promote Arab culture and contributions to the island. Today, Cuba is still a magnet for people from the Arab and Muslim world, particularly for the hundreds of students that come to study. Casa de los Arabes used to be the site of the only mosque on the island, which was used exclusively by foreign diplomats and their families. But that changed when another mosque, funded by Saudi Arabia, was built across the street from the museum in 2015. Arab influence can be found everywhere – even the island's distinctive guayabera, a lightweight summer men's shirt, was redesigned and popularised by a Lebanese textile merchant. “There is an inextricable link between Cubans and Arabs,” Ms Diaz Fuentes said. “They left an indelible print on Cuba's national history.”

title: How a hero principal who saved hundreds of pupils from the Nepal floods is rebuilding broken lives
description: Rajendra Dawadi has set up makeshift classrooms in tents and under stairs for survivors of the August 26 disaster
content: The principal of a government school in flood-hit Nepal has set up tents to ensure hundreds of children he guided to safety two months ago can continue their education. Rajendra Dawadi, head of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, one of the areas hit hardest by the flash floods, was hailed as a hero when his swift actions helped to save the lives of 900 children, before a torrent of water crashed into the school compound on August 26. He has made it his mission to enable classes to continue, using 20 tents and the shaded sections of a local sports academy. His goal is to provide some normality to families who lost their homes and livelihoods in the flooding that killed at least 1,455 people, with 5,285 listed as missing. “People lost everything. But the children are still eager to study,” Mr Dawadi told The National . “There was a big celebration on the first day – I thought most children would not come back to the school, but more than 95 per cent came back, they cheered, they exchanged happiness. "I was very happy. My school family, the teachers, students, their smiling faces made me more happy.” A video from September 21 shows children cheering as classes resume in tents set up on higher ground. Mr Dawadi, 47, said it could take at least two years to rebuild the school. As thousands across Nepal look to pick up the pieces after the disaster – which was caused by glacial ice and rock collapsing into a Himalayan river – the UN has said funding is urgently needed. Fractured lives The raging waters that cut through the school compound have since receded. Only the roof of a three-storey building is still visible, with the rest submerged in thick mud. Other buildings were swept away. The devastation across six districts has left deep scars in the school. One child became an orphan and 12 pupils lost one parent. “Many children need our support. They lost their father, some their mother,” Mr Dawadi said. “The students had counselling sessions, music classes. We try to motivate them, we make it like a family environment in school. I tell them it was a black day but we saved our lives and had a rebirth for me, my colleagues, my students. It was a rebirth from the great disaster.” Attendance is strong, with 1,621 pupils showing up for class. They sit on the floor in tents and share benches and desks under the stairwell of a sports centre. The tents, books and furniture were provided by Unicef and private foundations. School authorities await a decision on new land where they can rebuild. Until then, there are other pressing matters – pupils will need a library and science labs. Two more buses are also required to help children get to lessons at the tent site. Parents whose children had attended private schools are now sending them to free government institutions. “People are in trauma but they are doing their work, they are trying to be normal,” Mr Dawadi said. “Parents are worried about studies so they send children here, even if it’s in tents.” Critical moments It took only 11 minutes from the time Mr Dawadi first raised the alarm to when floodwater crashed into the school. Two school staff were killed in the flood. Mr Dawadi was teaching when he heard two staff members shouting about heavy flooding in the nearby Rasuwa district. He quickly told teachers to take pupils from each class to higher ground, urging them not to panic. Mr Dawadi turned away a bus with young children that was entering the compound and anther bus was also alerted about the danger. Older pupils who had motorbikes and bicycles were asked to help take other children to safety. “People were saying, 'Flood, flood,' but the sun was shining here,” he recalled. “But I decided to close the school. First, I told my staff to ring the bell. Then I told class teachers to go to separate classes to say school is off due to the flood, to go to a safer place … three girls fainted. When we left the school, the water had already entered. It was 11 minutes.” But Mr Dawadi praised his staff. “I am not the real hero,” he said. “My team worked together, this was my duty. For this, I was recognised all over the world.” Heart of community The school is a vital part of the community and parents have welcomed the return of classes. “We had tears in our eyes when school started – all parents felt it,” said Sharmila Shreshtha, 46, whose home and stationery shop were destroyed in the disaster. “We have nothing. Our homes are gone, our shop is gone, we are so tired. But the school makes everyone happy.” Pupils have appealed for books, computers and lab equipment. Aspiring software engineer Saswot Shah, 14, worries about how a lack of equipment will affect his studies. "Earlier we had smartboards, computers, maths and science laboratories. Now we are just surviving. We work together but we need a proper computer and maths lab,” he said. Pradakshina Shreshtha, 16, lost her home and now lives in rented accommodation. She hopes to be a doctor, but worries about exams. “I’m really happy to study in my own school, meet my friends and learn from my own teachers,” she said. “Before the floods, I thought I would pass the exam and join a science college. My dream is the same but it’s more difficult to study now. We need books. Our study materials are all gone.”

title: Arab and international leaders condemn deadly funeral attack at church in Jordan
description: King Abdullah II describes incident as terrorist attack
content: Regional and international leaders have condemned a shooting at a church in Jordan that killed seven people and injured 34, sending shockwaves across the kingdom. Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, expressed the Emirates' full solidarity with the kingdom during a phone call on Friday with Ayman Safadi, Jordan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates. He affirmed the UAE’s support for Jordan's measures to safeguard its security and stability and protect the safety of its citizens, residents and visitors. Sheikh Abdullah also extended his condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery. In a separate statement, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs reiterated the country's strong condemnation of terrorist and criminal acts, reaffirming its rejection of all forms of violence, extremism and terrorism aimed at undermining security and stability. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah El Sisi expressed his "unequivocal condemnation of these heinous acts, which violate all human values" in a statement on X. He stressed his country's solidarity with Jordan "in confronting this deplorable attack and all forms of violence and terrorism". Saudi Arabia also condemned what it described as a "cowardly terrorist attack" in the strongest terms. It expressed its solidarity with Jordan and rejected all acts of terrorism aimed at undermining the country's security and stability, the kingdom's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. Iraq condemned "all forms of terrorism and violence, which threaten the security and stability of societies and seek to sow division and incite discord among their communities". It also called for "enhanced regional and international co-operation and solidarity to combat terrorism and strengthen security and stability". Syria stressed its "unwavering support in confronting any threats to Jordan's security, stability and national unity", while rejecting "all forms of terrorism that threaten the safety and security of civilians", the Foreign Ministry said. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun said the attack on a place of worship "violated the sanctity of death and mourners" and "all religious and humanitarian values". He said “terrorism has neither a religion nor a homeland" and warned that such actions sought to undermine co-existence and sow discord. Qatar said it rejected "violence, terrorism and criminal acts, regardless of their motives or causes", as well as "attacks on places of worship and the terrorisation of innocent people". Bahrain's Foreign Ministry affirmed its support for Jordan's efforts to "safeguard its security, combat terrorism and extremism, and apprehend those responsible for the attack". Oman and Kuwait also condemned attacks on "places of worship and acts that terrorise civilians", expressing solidarity with Jordan and extending condolences to the families of the victims. International reactions The US embassy in Amman said Washington stood with King Abdullah II against those seeking to sow division and harm people practising their faith. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney described the attack as a terrorist act and condemned the violence. Germany's Foreign Office expressed shock over the attack and emphasised the importance of protecting peaceful co-existence between religions. The EU condemned the "cruel attack" and offered its "full support to the ongoing security investigation by the Jordanian authorities". UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also strongly condemned the terrorist attack. "It goes without saying that an attack not only on a place of worship, but during a funeral procession is especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. The shooting took place during a funeral at Hamoud Church in Karak governorate, where gunmen opened fire. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said 27 of the injured were receiving treatment in hospitals, while security forces continued to search for the attackers. King Abdullah II described the incident as a terrorist attack and said the attack would be met with force. He vowed to crack down on those responsible and said the shooting would not undermine national unity. “Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation,” he said. Opened fire on mourners Gunmen arrived in a vehicle and opened fire on mourners before fleeing, a relative of one of the deceased told The National . They continued shooting for about five minutes, according to a witness quoted by Al Mamlaka TV. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70. A video broadcast on Al Mamlaka that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. A member of the Halasah family in Karak told The National that three doctors were among those killed. “This was a direct attack on the church. Christians were the target,” the relative said.

title: Iran sent bomb-making manual as it organised plots in the UK
description: Salam Ahmadyan and Rahman ⁠Salehi to face trial for alleged plot to attack synagogue
content: An Iranian plotter transferred bomb-making instructions to the UK as it sought agents to carry out an atrocity in a major city. A court heard on Friday that investigators uncovered steps for making a “powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb” in a document prepared in Iran. Prosecutors alleged that a terrorism suspect was found to have instructions on his phone for making a home-made bomb to attack Jews in the UK. Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman ⁠Salehi, 34, are accused of plotting acts of terrorism at the behest of a regime agent believed to be in Iran . The targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed. Mr Ahmadyan, who had a Kurdish Sorani interpreter, and Mr ⁠Salehi, were told they would face trial in June in Manchester, charged with terrorism offences relating to the alleged plot. Both deny the charges. At a preliminary hearing at the Old Bailey in London, prosecutor Lydon Harris told the court that Mr Ahmadyan was asked by a third party to buy components for a home-made bomb around September 8 this year. Ten days later he recruited Mr Salehi to help him. He subsequently purchased various materials online, Mr Harris said. “On September 20, that being the date of the Jewish celebration of Yom Kippur, both defendants were seen by police officers driving around areas of Manchester, taking photographs and video recordings of various areas,” the prosecutor said. “The Crown’s case is that this was reconnaissance conducted for the purposes of a future attack on the Jewish community in Manchester.” Mr Harris told the court that the “police investigation has revealed Mr Ahmadyan was in contact with a third party who appears to be located in Iran”. “Analysis of his mobile telephone shows that it contained a file, the title of which, when translated into English, is steps for making a powder chlorine and rake oil fluid bomb.” Both suspects were interviewed by police and Mr Salehi denied any involvement in a terrorist plot, said Mr Harris. He said that Mr Ahmadyan made no comment on the questions he was asked. At a previous hearing, the court was told both suspects had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Mr Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Mr Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding.

title: Initial shipment of Russian diesel heads to the US after Trump-Putin deal
description: Russia has agreed to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports and supply the fuel to global markets
content: A Malta-flagged tanker carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of Russian ⁠diesel is heading towards New York following an agreement with US President Donald Trump , LSEG data showed on Friday. Mr Trump has made several moves to try to ⁠bring down diesel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections ​, including waiving ⁠parts of a new ‌sanctions law against Russia and threatening Europe with a US diesel export ​ban unless countries release more from their emergency reserves. The medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the US on November 7. Russia agreed to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports and supply the fuel to global markets, including the US, after the agreement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Mr Trump. Mr Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 ​tonnes in November and one million tonnes "immediately thereafter". Russia ‌will be able to increase ⁠diesel exports to between three million ​tonnes and 3.5 million tonnes per month by the end of the year, ​the country's ‌usual export volume of the fuel, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said last ⁠week. Last week, export diesel cargoes were loaded in the Russian Baltic ⁠port of Primorsk, but their final destinations are not clear, with most vessels signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, according to LSEG shipping data. Since the full EU embargo on the import of ​Russian oil products came into effect in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Brazil and Turkey, as well as to African countries.

title: UAE researchers win award for AI tool that helps surgeons during operations
description: Janus AI draws on footage of previous robotic surgeries to give doctors real-time visual guidance
content: Researchers in Abu Dhabi have won an international award at a robotic surgery conference in Italy for an AI tool designed to assist surgeons during operations. The team at Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) in Abu Dhabi won the accolade for developing Janus AI, which will show surgeons footage of similar past procedures. The technology analyses video footage captured during robotic surgery and selects a 30-second clip from a previous operation that matches the current stage of the procedure . The system works like a Google search for robotic surgery clips, letting doctors access relevant examples while operating. The footage can help surgeons see how other doctors approached the same task and guide them through subsequent steps. “While performing robotic surgery, we can have superimposed a number of small videos that show similar procedures, successful procedures, good procedures, in the exact same moment, so there is a guideline to follow,” said Cesare Stefanini, a professor of robotics at MBZUAI, who oversaw the technology’s development. “Sometimes surgeons may need some assistance; they would like to discuss with a colleague what they are doing, but they are not there, so this is a way to bring some human content to another human.” Janus AI takes its name from the Roman god Janus, depicted with two faces: one looking to the past and the other to the future. The name reflects the system’s aim of using previous surgical experience to help doctors make decisions during current procedures. The technology won the Robotic Urology Breakthrough Innovation Challenge award at Erus 26, a robotic urology surgery conference held in Padua, Italy, in September. “It’s very rewarding to be acknowledged by a community which is not only the computer science, AI, and robotics community, but also the medical community, [as it shows] that we are doing something that can be useful in the future,” said Prof Stefanini. The project was developed in collaboration with surgeons at the University of Illinois Chicago, and the University of Turin in Italy also contributed. Edoardo Fazzari, a postdoctoral researcher at MBZUAI, carried out much of the system’s development over about five months this year, following initial discussions with doctors. He said the project was particularly rewarding because it offered practical benefits beyond academic research. The system can show surgeons footage from three previous operations at the same stage of a procedure, letting them compare different approaches. “Why it’s helpful for the resident, for the surgeons, is that you can look at the future. We are using past experience to help humans make the next steps,” he said. “It should be very quick – we try to make it in milliseconds. You just click your button, make your query, and it pops up with three previous experiences that you can learn from.” The current video library covers robotic urology procedures, including nephrectomies, in which a kidney is removed. The researchers hope to expand the system to other surgeries, particularly robotic procedures, as the library grows. However, Janus AI is not yet ready for use in live operations. The technology needs further refinement and regulatory approval before it can enter clinical practice. When development is complete, the researchers hope to secure a commercial partner to bring the system to market. Prof Stefanini, whose group plans to recruit new postgraduate students, including Emiratis, said the project is a source of pride for the UAE. He said MBZUAI had created an environment in which AI researchers can exchange ideas and develop new technologies. “We’ve proven we can produce world-class results in the UAE, with the talent and vision that we have here. It’s encouraging for the future,” he said. “It’s not just something that individually we are proud of, but it can become a platform for future developments here.”

title: Melania Trump says she negotiated ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city
description: Oleshky in southern Ukraine is 'on the brink of disaster', US first lady says
content: US President Donald Trump's wife Melania Trump has secured a ⁠localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled ⁠city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, the White House announced on Friday. The ceasefire will begin on ​October 29. Oleshky has been occupied by Russian forces since February 2022 and residents there have reported a deepening food crisis. In a statement, the first lady described the situation in Oleshky as “dire” and on “the brink of disaster”. The White House said that Russia and Ukraine agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter ⁠and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water,” Ms Trump said. “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads and endure regular military attacks.” She added that it was “abundantly clear” that without her intervention, the possibility of bringing humanitarian aid into the city and evacuating the elderly would have been “impossible”. The development comes as ‌Mr Trump appears to be increasingly on Russia's side in its war against Ukraine. He has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a peace deal and has waived sanctions to allow the US to import Russian diesel as he tries to lower prices ahead of the November 3 midterms. Of his wife's announcement, Mr Trump said it was “not the worst idea I've ever heard.” “What she wants to do is save children ... It was her initiative, and they contacted both sides, and both sides wanted to do it,” he told reporters. Ms Trump has been active in trying to have Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families. Last year, she said she and Russian President Vladimir Putin had an “open channel of communication” to discuss the welfare of children caught up in the war. Oleshky, which is across the Dnipro River ​from Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people – ​primarily elderly residents ‌along with about 50 children – down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White ⁠House said. About 90 per cent of the city was flooded following the destruction ⁠of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House. The White House said Ms Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and ​transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine,” Ms Trump said. The suffering in Oleshky came to Ms Trump’s attention during a private discussion at an event during the UN General Assembly in New York, the White House said.

title: UK power supply forecasts warn of 'tight winter days' as costs soar
description: Energy operators confident of enough gas and electricity for peak demand
content: The UK’s power supply could have “some tight days” in December and January, despite energy prices more than doubling, one of the country’s energy operators said on Friday. At the same time, a last-minute deal with a Belgian interconnector firm would provide for an additional five per cent of forecast demand, maintaining gas import capacity and allowing more flexibility for the grid at times of demand strain. Supply agreements should mean there is enough gas and electricity to meet peak demand through winter, according to forecasts published by National Gas and National Energy System Operator (Neso). Front-month gas and power prices have risen about 180 per cent and 120 per cent since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February of this year, and this is set to have a rising impact on consumer bills. Neso predicts a “small number of low surplus days”, which balances supply and demand across the grid in real time. This would require routine balancing tools such as electricity margin notices, and did not indicate a risk to electricity supplies, Neso said. Peak gas demand is expected to reach 493 million cubic metres per day this winter, 2 per cent higher than last year, according to a separate report by National Gas, also published on Friday. This is largely due to stronger demand from power stations. Overall gas demand is expected to fall by 1 per cent as a result of consumer switching. Peak gas supply capacity is estimated at 592 mcm/day, leaving a buffer of 99 mcm/day but a “highly unlikely” stress scenario, such as the failure of the largest single part of the transmission system, would shrink the buffer to 18 mcm/day. National Gas said its forecasts were improved by a deal it reached on Thursday with a Belgian Interconnector pipeline to boost gas import capacity. Gas imports to the UK through interconnectors with Europe declined in recent years because of their maintenance costs, including the capacity of the two-way Belgium- Britain Interconnector. Yet lower levels of gas storage in Europe – also as a result of the war – would probably restrain imports. The British energy regulator Ofgem said it would launch a consultation on how to recover the costs of this capability, as it approved the agreement on Thursday. Disruptions in the global liquefied natural gas (LNG) market could also still affect supplies. “Our ​analysis shows that Great Britain is expected to have sufficient gas ‌supply capability to meet demand throughout winter ⁠2026/27, even under a range of ​very unlikely high-stress scenarios,” said Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, National Gas's director of energy systems and ​resilience. The UK's gas storage levels were estimated to be the lowest in Europe – at 48 per cent of its capacity – according to analysis by the European network of transmission systems for gas (Entsog) earlier this month. On the power side, there will be spare capacity of 5.9 gigawatts above peak demand – the equivalent of 9.5 per cent of peak demand – during a typical cold spell, according to Neso. That margin is similar to recent winters, and is wider than during the 2022 energy crisis. Higher peak demand has largely been offset by additional battery storage, gas-fired generation and wind power, Neso said. The margin is also higher than its June estimate because it now expects more wind generation to be available during ​peak periods. Neso said some days in December and January could be tight and require routine balancing tools such as electricity margin notices. It stressed that such notices signal a need for additional generation and do not indicate a risk to electricity supplies.

title: Tense Shabbat in Israel as pivotal elections approach
description: During the final days before what many call the most important elections in Israel’s history, tensions are high at home and abroad
content: Unless there is a major emergency, many of the far-right politicians who have set the tone in Israel for the past four years will put down their phones and log off for Shabbat on Friday evening. The country’s secular community will keep campaigning to some extent, but might also opt for a moment of rest before the crucial final days until polls open on Tuesday morning. After a week as frantic as this one, whether anyone can relax at the weekend is a whole other question, even with their phones turned off and with a brief respite from travelling around the country. There have been massive attacks in the occupied West Bank , which now appears to be under a total lockdown. There are fears of an imminent new round of fighting with Iran. Polls are deadlocked. There have been street brawls between supporters of rival parties. Settlers continue to maraud through the occupied West Bank, threatening the vital Palestinian olive harvest. That is the tense reality in which Israel finds itself, less than a week before polls open. On Friday morning, Israel awoke to the news that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the “full closure” of the occupied West Bank after five people were injured in a shooting at a military checkpoint near the city of Hebron. Palestinian media reports named the attackers as family members Mohammad Jaaba and Firas Jaaba, both 27 and from Hebron. The military said the men had planned to carry out a “large-scale” attack on Israelis. There are a number of illegal Israeli settlements in Hebron. After the attack, Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who lives in the illegal Hebron settlement of Kiryat Arba, called for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled. It is supposed to control parts of the West Bank. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, another radical settler, ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”. Israeli defence officials reportedly warned of a surge in settler violence in the occupied West Bank after the elections, as ultranationalists prepare for the possibility that a different government might demolish some of the many illegal settlements that have been established during the tenure of the current government. Inside Israel, candidates from across the spectrum have been rushing around as polls continue to point to a stalemate. Some of those events turned violent. Michael Illouz, the father of Guy Illouz, an Israeli hostage killed in captivity in Gaza after being abducted in the October 7 attacks, said he was assaulted by supporters of Mr Netanyahu in Tel Aviv on Thursday evening. “I came to protest against the Prime Minister for abandoning my [son], and shameless citizens with no moral conscience resorted to violence against me,” he said in comments reported by the Israeli outlet Haaretz . “It is a disgrace that a bereaved father is beaten by fellow citizens.” In Jerusalem, someone threw a glass bottle at Mr Netanyahu’s motorcade after a visit to a market, drawing a swift response from security forces. No one was injured. Elsewhere, supporters of the Prime Minister attacked a man who heckled him about allowing the transfer of “billions of dollars to Hamas”. Death threats were also sprayed on a billboard showing the leader of the left-wing Zionist party The Democrats, Yair Golan. Defence Minister Israel Katz was widely criticised for saying that opposition leaders would be responsible for future attacks on Israel. “Any attack on Israel and all the next terrorist attacks will be attributed to Yair Lapid, Naftali Bennett, Yair Golan and their opposition partners,” he said. The statement came as he and the Prime Minister warned that Israel’s enemies might be trying to undermine its elections. Opposition leaders have been warning of the prospect that Mr Netanyahu would launch a new round of fighting against Iran for political reasons, to remain in power as he struggles to gain momentum in the polls.

title: King Abdullah condemns 'terrorist attack' at Jordan church that killed seven
description: Seven people were killed and 34 wounded when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan ’s Karak governorate on Friday, the country’s Public Security Directorate said, with King Abdullah II describing it as a “terrorist attack”. In a statement on Saturday, Jordan's Health Ministry sai
content: Seven people were killed and 34 wounded when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan ’s Karak governorate on Friday, the country’s Public Security Directorate said, with King Abdullah II describing it as a “terrorist attack”. In a statement on Saturday, Jordan's Health Ministry said that 27 people were still receiving treatment in hospital. The directorate's head, Maj Gen Abdallah Al Maaytah, said the search for the attackers was continuing. Twenty-seven of the wounded were receiving treatment in hospitals, he added. Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in Karak before opening fire, the directorate had earlier said in a statement. Karak, about 100km south of Amman, is home to a Christian minority in the Muslim-majority kingdom. King Abdullah said the attack would be met with force. He vowed to crack down on those responsible and said the shooting would not undermine national unity. “The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation,” he said in a post on X. “Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity. All Jordanians, from north to south, are partners in land and fate, and nothing stands between them. “Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation.” The King visited the injured in hospital and spoke with them to check on their condition, according to footage aired by the state-owned broadcaster Al Mamlaka TV. Queen Rania said the "heinous crime against worshippers in Karak" had affected all Jordanians. “Our hearts are with our people of Karak,” she wrote in a post on X. 'Group of extremists' Jordan's Interior Minister, Mazen Al Faraya, said the attack was carried out by a "group of extremists" and that the government is doing all it can to find the culprits. "Jordanians reject this cowardly terrorist act. It will strengthen the country's push to combat terrorism in all its forms," he said during a press conference alongside Maj Gen Al Maaytah. "Jordan is immune to all attempts to drag it towards extremism and terrorism," he said. Gunmen arrived in a vehicle and opened fire on mourners before fleeing, a relative of one of the deceased told The National . They continued shooting for about five minutes, according to a witness quoted by Al Mamlaka TV. Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70. A doctor who was attending the funeral told The National that mourners were struck by bullets around him as gunfire erupted. He then saw that his father and uncle had been shot. His uncle died, while his father was taken to hospital. A video aired on Al Mamlaka that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. A member of the Halasah family in Karak told The National that three doctors were among those killed. “This was a direct attack on the church. Christians were the target,” the relative said. There was no immediate claim of responsibility ​for the attack. Such incidents are very rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable but has come under Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. The kingdom is home to ​several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.

title: How AI is driving the future of clean water and energy at WETEX 2026
description: Exhibitors on day two of the Water, Energy, Technology and Environment Exhibition shared their views on AI – and most of them were building something with it
content: Artificial intelligence was the main topic of conversation for almost everyone on day two of Dubai’s Water, Energy, Technology and Environment Exhibition (WETEX), which is taking place this week at Dubai World Trade Centre. Ask whether AI belongs at a green energy event, and almost everyone agrees that while it currently consumes too much water and drives up electricity demand, the answer is not to stop using it, but to keep pursuing new solutions AI itself can help generate. The more interesting question – the one that companies from Lucy Electric to PwC Middle East and Thermax Limited were all working on – is what AI looks like when it is designed specifically to make the energy and water system work better rather than harder. The central challenges surfacing at WETEX are the speed of AI deployment and the pace at which energy infrastructure can be built to support it. The human in the loop Wissam Mahfouz, partner for technology consulting at PwC Middle East, spent his morning leading a roundtable on resilience asset management that brought together representatives from the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA), Abu Dhabi's Emirates Water and Electricity Company (EWEC), TAQA, Siemens and Hitachi. The session, he said, produced the kind of conversation that the day-to-day professional world rarely allows. "Usually in day-to-day life, we don't have that opportunity to bring them all together," he said. One point raised by DEWA stood out: "Let's work all into partnership together to find the right solution." Mr Mahfouz believes AI enhances humans. "If, as a consultant, a year ago, before AI, I was to do an analysis, it would have taken me one week, two weeks to run the analysis, come up with the report. Today, with certain models, I can do that analysis with the help of AI in two hours, three hours. It didn't replace me. I'm still there." The technology will improve on its own terms, he added. "Technology always accelerates through adoption. Today AI consumes a lot of energy and water. But in two or three years down the road, it will be more efficient." Particularly with the UAE's plans to feed data centres through solar power, he said. Predicting failure before it happens At Lucy Electric's stand, general manager Charbel Zouein was explaining a system called Synapse to a steady stream of utility visitors. The platform monitors underground power cables. "Through machine learning and digital twin simulation it mirrors what the hardware is going through," Mr Zouein said, "and lets a company like DEWA know that there's a 90 per cent chance in the next two weeks this cable will fail – so go do preventive maintenance rather than let it fail and you run for an unplanned shutdown." The company is also using WETEX to showcase its next-generation switchgear range – compact medium-voltage distribution units using a proprietary atmospheric gas instead of sulphur hexafluoride (SF6), whose global warming potential is several thousand times greater than carbon dioxide. "The new technology has zero risk of causing global warming because of accidental leakage," Mr Zouein said. The case for inevitable progress Ashish Bhandari, managing director and chief executive of Thermax Limited, arrived at WETEX with a broader brief. The company operates across clean energy, clean water and air pollution control. "When we talk about the Middle East right now, we're talking about resources, stability, energy conservation, resource availability,” Mr Bhandari told The National . “At the heart of it are two things, which are energy and water. And this event, in a way, is central to both of those dialogues." Thermax is showcasing its Edge Live platform – a digital solution using machine learning and AI to help customers extract more performance from existing assets in energy, water and air pollution infrastructure. But the detail that drew most interest from visitors, Mr Bhandari said, was a newer application in desalination. Standard desalination produces clean permeate and the brine reject pumped back to sea. Thermax's argument is that the reject stream contains commercially valuable salts that can be recovered and sold to chemical industries. "We are making a case that you should do advanced processing of desalination rejects," Mr Bhandari said. "Recover the salts and start to use it in chemical industries." On the broader AI debate, Mr Bhandari said, “Progress is something you can't stop. Just the way you can't say stop driving cars or stop using air conditioning – AI is not something that we can stop. It's the nature of human progress." The more useful question, he argued, is how to make AI less resource-intensive. "Investment in AI will happen. You just have to make sure that it happens in a way that you are hurting the environment in the least way possible." The infrastructure question The companies building the physical layer beneath the AI economy were making the same point. Chris Ren, chairman of Sunten Electric Equipment Co, which supplies transformers to DEWA, said AI has entered the product development roadmaps of almost every major manufacturer. Siemens, he noted, has integrated AI into automation systems to the point of cutting labour requirements by roughly half in some applications. "That's very impressive," he said. Sunten is investing in research and development focused on transformers designed specifically for AI data centre requirements. “It's the future. AI is coming. We have to face it," he said. The clean energy alignment, for him, is structural: data centres can sit anywhere, while renewable energy is often generated away from urban centres, so putting the two together makes geographic sense. "Clean energy is a 100 per cent match with AI. AI needs power, and clean energy.” Chirag Patel, managing partner and director at Emirates Transformer & Switchgear, which has supplied DEWA and regional utilities for more than 40 years and is now expanding into data centres and renewable energy, described the exhibition as the place where long-term investment strategy gets tested against customer reality. "Customers actually drive the direction we need to go," he said. "We invest for the long run." Investing in the long run is what each of these companies is doing, through the Synapse system, the new switchgear, the salt-recovery desalination unit, the AI data centre transformer. Each is a response to a demand of the future. As Mr Mahfouz put it: "We're focusing on AI as a negative, but there are lots of positives in terms of decarbonisation, clean energy targets to reduce emissions. And if people can take that away from the various companies that are here, it will be good." This page was produced by The National in partnership with WETEX and WGES .

title: Ramy Youssef’s A24 directorial debut Martha & Muhammad: What we know
description: Amanda Seyfried joins Sharon Stone and the Egyptian-American comedian in the forthcoming comedy
content: Ramy Youssef’s first feature film as director is taking shape, with Amanda Seyfried joining him and Sharon Stone in the cast of Martha & Muhammad . The Egyptian-American comedian will also write and star in the A24 comedy, with Seyfried’s involvement reported by Deadline . The project brings together several of Youssef ’s long-standing collaborators, including The Bear creator Christopher Storer, alongside Uncut Gems and Marty Supreme filmmaker Josh Safdie. Youssef has already built a directing career through his own series, Ramy , and The Bear . His move into feature filmmaking follows years developing stories about faith, family and the contradictions of Muslim-American life – subjects that also feature in the new film’s reported premise. Here is what we know so far. What is Martha & Muhammad about? The comedy follows a white, widowed New York socialite who develops a relationship with a younger Muslim man, according to The Hollywood Reporter , which first reported the project in August. The story will reportedly explore class, religion, immigration and the couple’s age difference. A24 has not commented on those details and a full official synopsis has yet to be released. Who is in the cast? Youssef and Stone were the first stars attached, with Seyfried the latest addition. Details of Seyfried’s character have not been disclosed. Stone is best known for films including Basic Instinct and Casino , while Seyfried’s recent work includes the thriller The Housemaid , opposite Sydney Sweeney, and the title role in the musical The Testament of Ann Lee . Supporting characters are also beginning to emerge through casting notices. Backstage reported this month that the production was seeking actors to play Mamadou, a Muslim immigrant and close friend of Muhammad, and Amina, Mamadou’s cousin and a lawyer who handles immigration cases. Casting for those roles has not been announced. What has Ramy Youssef directed before? Youssef’s work behind the camera includes episodes of Ramy , the series in which he plays a young Egyptian-American navigating his religious beliefs, relationships and family expectations. He also directed Honeydew , the Copenhagen-set episode of The Bear ’s second season, earning an Emmy directing nomination in 2024. That episode follows pastry chef Marcus, played by Lionel Boyce, as he travels to Denmark to develop his skills while worrying about his seriously ill mother back in Chicago. In a 2024 interview with The National , Boyce described walking around Copenhagen with Youssef to discuss Marcus’s relationships. Their preparation helped shape an episode in which the pleasure of discovering a new city is accompanied by the persistent fear of bad news from home. “Ramy was really thoughtful about crafting that. He’s such a team player, always there to support us all,” Boyce said. Youssef has also spoken about the influence of Poor Things director Yorgos Lanthimos, with whom he worked as an actor. In a 2024 GQ interview, he said Lanthimos had encouraged him to make films, and described his long-standing interest in spending more time within a single, self-contained story. Who is producing the film? A24 is financing the project, with Youssef producing through his company Cairo Cowboy. The producing team also includes Eli Bush, Ronald Bronstein and Josh Safdie through Central, and Christopher Storer and Tyson Bidner through American Light & Fixture. The film extends Youssef’s relationship with A24, which has worked with him on Ramy and his stand-up specials. Cairo Cowboy and A24 also collaborated on #1 Happy Family USA , the animated series he co-created with Pam Brady about a Muslim-American family navigating life after September 11. When will Martha & Muhammad be released? A24 has not announced a release date. The production is recruiting supporting actors for work in New York City between November 23 and January 20, according to the casting notice reported by Backstage . Those dates indicate the anticipated work period for the advertised roles, rather than a confirmed schedule for the entire shoot.

title: Dubai sends winter relief supplies to Gaza through new air bridge
description: First flight carrying thermal blankets arrives in Egypt
content: Dubai Humanitarian has launched a new air bridge to deliver winter relief to Gaza. The first flight, carrying essential humanitarian supplies including thermal blankets for Unicef, arrived in Al Arish, Egypt, before being transferred to Gaza. The initiative is being carried out under the directives of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai . The air bridge involves multiple flights operated by the Dubai Royal Air Wing using C-130 aircraft, each carrying approximately nine metric tonnes of humanitarian supplies. At least three more flights are scheduled in the coming days to deliver blankets for children and other vulnerable groups as families prepare for the approaching winter. Marwan Ahmed bin Ghalita, chairman of the Dubai Humanitarian Authority , said the winter months pose additional challenges for families already enduring difficult conditions, particularly children. “The first facilitated shipment of this new air bridge arrived in Al Arish , ahead of its onward transfer to Gaza. This operation reflects Dubai Humanitarian’s long-standing role as a trusted global hub that brings humanitarian partners together, supports their efforts and enables aid to reach those in need,” he said. The shipment also represents the first co-ordinated sourcing order under the UN80 Integrated Supply Chain Approach, which brings together UN agencies to strengthen joint sourcing and delivery of humanitarian supplies. Enabled by Dubai Humanitarian in collaboration with its partners, the initiative aims to improve co-ordination, speed up relief operations and make aid delivery more efficient. Since 2023, Dubai Humanitarian has supported relief efforts in Gaza through air bridges, land convoys, and sea shipments, working with international humanitarian partners to keep essential supplies flowing through multiple transport routes.

title: Russia and Ukraine exchange 540 captives after latest UAE mediation
description: UAE has conducted 27 mediations with a total of 8,537 detainees exchanged
content: Russia and Ukraine agreed to release 540 captives following a new round of UAE-led mediation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Friday. Each side agreed to exchange 270 captives, the ministry said. This brings the total number of captives exchanged between the two countries through the Emirates' efforts to 8,537. The ministry thanked both countries for co-operating with the UAE as a trusted international mediator and for appreciating its commitment to supporting work to resolve the crisis. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy shared several photos of the released detainees and wrote: "National Guard members, including Azov warriors, border guards, warriors of the Territorial Defense Forces, the Navy, the Land Forces, the Airborne Assault Forces, and the State Special Transport Service, as well as nine civilians, are returning home. Most of them had been in captivity since 2022." He added: "We remember one and all and continue searching for everyone. I thank everyone who works to make these exchanges possible." This is the 27th detainee exchange between Russia and Ukraine through UAE-led talks. The ministry said the Emirates would continue to support initiatives for a peaceful resolution to the war and to address the humanitarian impact on refugees and prisoners.
