The two countries last exchanged captives in August, when 206 were released.

title: Showjumping leaps forward with Global Champions Tour at Giza Pyramids
description: Sport makes spectacular debut in Egypt with 50 of the best riders in the world
content: A perfect breeze swept through the arena as Italian rider Emanuele Gaudiano jumped the first fence of the Global Champions Tour (GCT) stop in Cairo atop his horse Chabrello PS on Thursday afternoon. It marked a historical moment as the tour kicked off its inaugural event in Egypt, with the Pyramids of Giza providing the perfect backdrop for the one-of-a-kind show. Taking place this weekend, the GCT in Cairo features 50 of the best riders in the world, competing for a €1.75 million prize purse. It is the penultimate stop on the tour before next week’s Finals in Rabat and drew a sellout crowd on opening night on Thursday. The GCT was founded in 2006 by Dutch Olympic champion Jan Tops. What started as a six-event showjumping tour has evolved into a global championship spanning 17 destinations across 15 countries in 2026. From Miami to Mexico City, Shanghai to Cairo, the tour has taken riders to all corners of the globe. But they all agree that competing in front of the Pyramids is an unrivalled experience. None more so than Egyptian rider Sameh El Dahan, who got back to representing Egypt earlier this year after five years flying the British flag. This GCT event serves as the perfect homecoming for the 41-year-old, who received massive roars from the Cairo crowd when he went clear in round one of the team competition on Thursday. “When I first heard that the event is coming here, take away the Pyramids on the side for a minute, but just that there is a five-star event that will be in Egypt with this calibre, I was very excited as soon as I heard the news,” El Dahan told The National . Hosting an event at the Pyramids of Giza requires a huge amount of planning and lots of red tape to clear, so El Dahan was understandably sceptical but extremely hopeful it would happen. “Lots of the riders asked me 'what do you think the show will be like?' I said, if they are able to make it, they'll make an amazing show. And then add the backdrop, where in the world would you be jumping underneath thousands of years of history like this? “So for me as an Egyptian coming back, I've competed all over the world, different continents, championships, this, that, the other. But I haven't competed on home ground for 16, 17 years. The buzz just coming to the show, like everybody's ringing me, asking me for tickets, 'we want to see you', people I haven't heard from for years. It's been great, honestly. “I hope people don't mind me saying that, it's socially exhausting, but I love it. I really, really love it, and I love the buzz that the people have, and they're proud to have us here, and I'm proud to perform in front of them.” Saudi rider Abdulrahman Al Rajhi, fresh off taking team gold and individual silver at the Asian Games in Japan, could not stop smiling as he sat for an interview with the Pyramids lit up behind him as nightfall descended on the Egyptian capital. View this post on Instagram “Whenever we talk about Egypt, the Pyramids is something special. And I've always dreamt to come and visit it and experience such a historical place,” said the Saudi Olympian. “And guess what? We're here at one of the most historical places in the world, at the most prestigious sport in the world, and one of the biggest shows and events, and with the most important riders from all over the world. And to be part of it and to be part of this amazing event definitely is such an amazing experience.” Qatari rider Sheikh Ali bin Khalid Al Thani described staging a GCT at the Pyramids as “a win for the sport” while Tops, the founder and president of the GCT said the tour’s arrival in Cairo is “an important milestone” on the 20-year anniversary of its launch. New heights “When we launched the Tour in 2006, our ambition was to take show jumping to new heights,” said Tops. “Twenty years later, seeing the world's best riders competing against the backdrop of the Pyramids of Giza is an incredibly proud moment and a reflection of how far we have come. “From six events to a championship reaching audiences around the world, we have continued to push boundaries and create new opportunities for riders, teams and fans. “Our ambition has always been focused on the future. Cairo marks another important milestone in our journey, and as we look ahead to the next 20 years, our focus is firmly on further innovation, expanding the global reach of the sport and inspiring a new generation of fans around the world.” The action continues on Friday afternoon with a CSI5* 1.45m show followed by CSI5* 1.55m in the evening, before the €1,000,000 Grand Prix of Cairo closes out proceedings on Saturday.

title: Six arrested after Dubai resident loses years of savings in online shopping scam
description: Police say gang used fake website to steal bank card details and transfer money
content: Dubai Police arrested six suspects in connection with a bank fraud scheme that used a fake online shopping website to gather card details and steal money from victims' accounts. Police said the investigation and arrests followed complaints from victims who noticed sudden deductions from their bank accounts despite not making or authorising the transactions. One victim, identified by her initials SN, said she woke up to text messages about a large sum withdrawn from her account, wiping out savings she had accumulated over several years. Shocked by the unexpected transactions, the woman, who works for a private company, contacted Dubai Police for help. “I wasn’t even using my phone or making any purchases. I was fast asleep while someone unknown was draining money from my account,” she said. The complaints prompted the General Department of Criminal Investigation at Dubai Police to launch an investigation that led to the arrest of a six-member fraud gang known as the "unexpected deduction" gang. The investigation revealed that the suspects had set up a fake online shopping website to obtain victims’ bank card details. They later used this information to make unauthorised purchases and transfer money into digital wallets to receive the stolen funds. Police said the gang also opened bank accounts and digital wallets to move stolen funds. According to the investigation, the gang sold some compromised bank card details to other people for money, allowing further fraudulent transactions. Digital wallets and bank accounts Dubai Police formed a specialised team to investigate the complaints. Through surveillance and investigative efforts, officers identified all six gang members, found where they were living and carried out a co-ordinated raid. During the operation, police recovered bank cards belonging to victims that the gang allegedly intended to sell to other fraudsters, as well as chequebooks believed to have been used to assist their illegal activities. The investigation also found that the suspects had exploited digital wallets provided by a telecoms company to receive proceeds from the alleged fraud. Dubai Police urged residents to be careful when shopping online and to verify website authenticity before entering personal or banking information. The force warned the public against sharing bank card details or other sensitive financial information with untrusted people or organisations. Residents who discover unfamiliar deductions or suspect fraudulent activity should report it promptly through the Dubai Police contact centre on 901, the Police Eye service, or the eCrime service available through the Dubai Police smart application and official website.

title: UAE petrol prices expected to rise again in November
description: Recovery in Middle East crude supplies does not mean energy market has returned to normal
content: Petrol prices in the UAE are expected to rise again in November, as the recovery in Middle East oil supplies does not immediately translate into a return to normality for the energy market, according to analysts. Costs at the pump rose for a third consecutive month in October due to lingering uncertainty around a potential US-Iran truce . At present, Super 98, Special 95, E-Plus 91 and diesel cost Dh4.40 ($1.20), Dh4.28 ($1.17), Dh4.21 ($1.15) and Dh4.80 ($1.31) per litre, respectively – up by more than 70 per cent since March, the first full month of the war in Iran. They are still significantly lower compared to markets such as Britain. The Petrol Prices UK website shows that this week unleaded petrol and diesel cost an average of £1.75 (Dh8.61) and £1.99 (Dh9.79) per litre, respectively. In the US, petrol prices, which vary by state, are mostly higher than in the UAE. AAA Gas Prices shows that petrol ranges from $4.29 to $5.20 per gallon, which is equivalent to $1.13 to $1.37 when converted to litres. Diesel is at $6.32 per gallon, or $1.67 per litre – markedly higher than in the Emirates. Oil prices also recorded a sharp rise this month, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia, causing crude to hit five-month highs this week . On Friday, Brent was trading 1.65 per cent higher to hit $115 a barrel at 5.26pm UAE time, while West Texas Intermediate climbed 1.89 per cent to $101.30 a barrel. With Brent this month exceeding September's peak, “the risk of another increase in UAE petrol prices for November is elevated”, said Jordan Lawrence, chief executive and co-founder of London-based financial services firm Damisa. “October’s fuel rates already rose significantly, and the committee’s end-of-month review will reflect the full month’s international averages, refined-product prices and costs,” Mr Lawrence told The National . Oil movements across the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, are gradually picking up, according to ship tracking data. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week that up to 14 million barrels of oil a day were moving through the strait, with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels. However, while October has shown a recovery in Middle East oil exports, that does not necessarily mean the market has returned to normal, said George Pavel, general manager at Naga.com Middle East, a capital markets firm operating in Abu Dhabi's ADGM. “Ongoing threats to shipping and persistent uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz continue to support prices. The key change is that the market is increasingly pricing the risk of further disruptions, instead of simply assessing current production and export volumes,” he told The National. “ Even when supply flows recover, the cost and reliability of transporting crude remain important constraints … if exports remain resilient and diplomatic progress reduces the threat to shipping, prices could retreat quickly. “The next decisive factor will be whether October's security risks translate into lasting physical supply losses.” Ahmad Assiri, a research strategist at financial services firm Pepperstone, noted that even if barrels continue reaching markets through the Strait of Hormuz, uncertainty over the reliability of future deliveries gives buyers a reason to pay a significant premium for now. “Many buyers have become price-insensitive due to elevated uncertainty … a diplomatic breakthrough could provide some ease and a pullback,” he told The National . “However, a sustained decline would require confidence that infrastructure and shipping routes can operate securely, which is a hard thing to see in the current environment,” he said. “October has strengthened the conviction that the geopolitical premium will be persistent, and this in turn makes the eventual growth and inflation consequences more concerning.”

title: UAE art guide: 15 exhibitions to see, from Indian Ocean history at Louvre Abu Dhabi to Paul Guiragossian
description: Plus, Provisional Sanctuaries at Tashkeel to Revelation at 421
content: Galleries and institutions across Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Sharjah are presenting a diverse programme of exhibitions as the UAE's autumn art season gathers pace. Current highlights include Provisional Sanctuaries at Tashkeel, where Malaysian artist Shamin Sharum explores the overlooked prayer spaces that offer a sense of belonging in the UAE; Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve at NYU Abu Dhabi, which brings together eight women artists using ceramics to explore emotion and lived experience; and Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean at Louvre Abu Dhabi, tracing 1,000 years of maritime trade and cultural exchange. Elsewhere, exhibitions examine memory, migration, identity and environmental change, with works spanning painting, photography, sculpture, textiles and moving image. Here are 15 exhibitions to see across the UAE. 1. Unseen Script at Rizq Art Initiative In Unseen Script , curated by Meena Vari, works by 10 artists explore the patterns people form through repetition, from familiar journeys and domestic objects to changing landscapes and gestures that become so ingrained they often go unnoticed. The exhibition brings together art by Najat Makki, Nujoom Alghanem, Nasir Nasrallah, Abdulla PA, Ana Escobar Saavedra, Fadi Balhawan, Ismail Al Rifai, Joanna Barakat, Neveen Abu Samra and Simrin Mehra Agarwal. Across painting, sculpture, assemblage and mixed media, the artists return to recurring subjects within their practices, revealing how personal habits and ways of seeing become a kind of visual script. Several works draw on the relationship between people and their surroundings. Abdulla reflects on abandoned homes and the ways nature reclaims human-made spaces, while Saavedra transforms seashells into delicate assemblages. Nasrallah draws on memories of his grandfather’s antique shop, Makki extends her abstract practice into steel and Alghanem examines the cityscape as a contemporary horizon. While the exhibition touches on the way technology can identify and predict human patterns, its focus remains on subjective experience, asking what memory, consciousness and observation can reveal that data cannot. Until October 28; Abu Dhabi 2. Taking Form at The Third Line Taking Form is Rana Begum’s fifth solo exhibition at The Third Line, bringing together new works across textile, linen, wood and paper that continue her exploration of light, colour, geometry and material. Large wool tapestries suspended from the ceiling form the centre of the exhibition. Woven with geometric patterns, their appearance shifts as visitors move around them. Elsewhere, diluted acrylic has seeped into linen, while smaller works on paper and wooden panels explore interactions between colour and surface. The exhibition introduces a greater sense of softness to Begum’s practice while retaining the abstraction and geometric structures that have long shaped her work. Until November 10; Dubai 3 & 4. Between Land and Sea, and Between a Fold and a Memory at Leila Heller Gallery Two exhibitions at Leila Heller Gallery consider Emirati identity and heritage through the work of Azza Al Qubaisi and Karima Al Shomely. Al Qubaisi’s Between Land and Sea, curated by Aysha Al Hemeiri, surveys a multidisciplinary practice spanning intimate jewellery and large-scale public works. Her use of natural resources and materials connects the UAE’s desert and coastal environments with ideas of memory, identity and place. In Between a Fold and a Memory, Al Shomely turns to the clothing, textiles and objects associated with Emirati women. Photography, sculpture, textile and video explore how materials such as the burqa and traditional fabrics can carry memories of labour, social change and cultural knowledge across generations. Until November 10; Dubai 5. Sojourner: The Difference is the Same at Efie Gallery Kenyan artist Maggie Otieno transforms reclaimed materials into vessels of memory in Sojourner: The Difference is the Same, her first solo exhibition with Efie Gallery. Otieno’s practice has centred on distressed and discarded materials for almost three decades. The exhibition includes works made from 150-year-old railway sleepers, whose histories are tied to East Africa’s colonial railway network, alongside sculptures incorporating fragments of wooden canoes produced during a residency at El Anatsui Studio in Ghana. By cutting, assembling and reconfiguring these materials, Otieno shifts objects once associated with movement and infrastructure into forms concerned with stillness, memory and passage. Until November 13; Dubai 6. The Horizon We Inherit at Iris Projects Emirati artist Eman Al Hashemi examines the changing rhythms of urban life in the UAE in The Horizon We Inherit, her first solo exhibition with Iris Projects. Working across ceramics, printmaking and mixed media, she considers how cities shape attention, memory and everyday routines. The sun, street lights, buildings and roundabouts recur throughout the works, turning familiar features of the UAE cityscape into forms that can appear both recognisable and strange. Al Hashemi is particularly interested in the routes people repeatedly travel and the traces left behind as places are altered through construction and redevelopment. Rather than treating the built environment as a backdrop, the exhibition considers it as an active force in daily life and asks what remains when familiar places survive only through photographs, maps, memories or repeatedly travelled routes. September 26 to November 26; Abu Dhabi 7 . Provisional Sanctuaries at Tashkeel Dubai-based Malaysian artist Shamin Sharum explores the overlooked prayer spaces found across the UAE in Provisional Sanctuaries , his solo exhibition at Tashkeel. Drawing on the small, often temporary musollas established in warehouses, industrial areas and workplaces, the exhibition examines how modest architecture can provide a sense of familiarity and belonging in a city shaped by migration. The exhibition grew from Sharum's experience of encountering a makeshift prayer room shortly after moving to Dubai. Working across painting, drawing, architectural models and axonometric studies, he reconstructs these spaces through memory, focusing on improvised minarets, hand-painted signs, prayer mats and other details that reflect the communities using them. Trained as an architect, Sharum considers how temporary structures can acquire lasting emotional significance through shared rituals and everyday use. One model recalls a prayer space he encountered during his first days in Dubai that has since been demolished, turning an architectural study into an act of remembrance. Developed following his participation in Tashkeel's Critical Practice Programme, the exhibition connects the impermanence of these spaces with wider experiences of displacement, identity and belonging. Until November 27; Dubai 8. Vantage Point 13 at Sharjah Art Foundation Vantage Point 13 marks a new chapter for Sharjah Art Foundation's long-running photography platform as it moves into the institution's dedicated photography gallery. Selected through an international open call, six artists present commissioned photographic series developed with the foundation's curatorial and production support. The exhibition features work by Adam Rouhana, Guanyu Xu, Latifa AlBokhari, Luisa Dorr, Maheder Haileselassie and Sathish Kumar. Together, their projects demonstrate the breadth of contemporary photography, reflecting the programme's evolution from a platform for UAE-based photographers into an international exhibition embracing diverse approaches. Introduced in 2013, Vantage Point has become one of the UAE's key photography initiatives. This edition also reflects the foundation's expanded commitment to supporting new work, with participating artists receiving production funding to create original projects specifically for the exhibition. Until November 29; Sharjah 9 . Fellow Travellers at Tabari Fellow Travellers brings together six artists whose practices span Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas, exploring themes of movement, memory, kinship and cultural exchange. Conceived and curated by artist, author and cultural historian Professor Omar Kholeif, the exhibition draws on nearly two decades of research, writing and personal relationships with artists. The exhibition features works by Sonia Balassanian, Jai Chuhan, Luísa Correia Pereira, Lalitha Lajmi, Irene Scheinmann and Kholeif himself. Bringing together landmark pieces and rarely seen works, it traces artistic journeys across different geographies, considering how experiences of migration, cultural encounters and personal histories shape creative expression. Accompanied by a limited-edition publication featuring original poetry and a curatorial essay, the exhibition also reflects Kholeif's long-standing interest in the relationships between artists and the connections that emerge across generations and borders. Until November 30; Dubai 10. Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve at NYU Abu Dhabi Project Space Bodies that Make, Bodies that Grieve brings together eight UAE-based women artists whose practices are rooted in the Global South, exploring how ceramics can give physical form to emotions and experiences that are difficult to express through words. Curated by Shafeena Yusuff Ali, founder and executive director of Rizq Art Initiative, the exhibition examines the relationship between the body, clay and emotional expression. The exhibition features sculptures by Nujoom Alghanem, Mirna Bamieh, Moza Al Falasi, Malavika, Parneet Pahwa, Zahra Shafie, Laiba Sherin and Haseena Suresh. Working on an intimate, domestic scale, the artists use processes of pressing, building, breaking and firing clay to explore memory, grief and lived experience. Presented at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery's Project Space, the exhibition also considers the long-standing relationship between ceramics, women's labour and practices of care. By focusing on the physical act of making, it positions clay as a medium through which personal experiences and emotions can take shape. October 22 to December 13; Abu Dhabi 11. The Sky Held It, The Earth Remembered at Ishara Art Foundation The exhibition brings together works by Shahana Rajani, Rohini Devasher and Sarker Protick to explore how land, water and the cosmos can act as archives of memory and history. Through photography, moving image and installation, the exhibition considers how ecological change and human intervention leave traces on the environment that can persist across generations. Rajani’s three-channel film Lines That World a River focuses on communities displaced from the Indus Delta, where paintings and murals reconstruct villages submerged following the construction of dams and barrages. Devasher turns towards the cosmos with Latent Fields , monumental silk panels inspired by sunspots and other solar phenomena, while Protick’s Dhaka 1217 documents 15 years of transformation around the neighbourhood in Dhaka where he was born and continues to live. Drawing together perspectives from Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, the exhibition considers ecological decline across national borders, and the ways landscapes can preserve histories of displacement, destruction and resilience. Until December 15; Dubai 12. Revelation at 421 Arts Campus Emirati artist Juma Al Haj explores seclusion, reflection and personal transformation in Revelation, his first institutional solo exhibition. Developed through 421 Arts Campus's Artistic Development Programme, it brings together painting, engraved glass, text, light, shadow and installation to consider how moments of uncertainty can lead to greater self-understanding. The exhibition unfolds as a physical journey, beginning with Balaa , a painting concerned with trials and the ways people measure their lives, and Traces , a series of engraved glass panels whose inscriptions shift with light and shadow. It culminates in Hijr , a darkened, carpeted space centred on a water feature, where visitors remove their shoes and are encouraged to slow down and contemplate. Al Haj's approach draws on journaling, philosophy and spiritual texts, extending the layered marks of his paintings into an environment visitors can move through. Rather than presenting revelation as a final answer, the exhibition treats it as one stage in an continuing process of reflection and discovery. Until January 10, 2027; Abu Dhabi 13. Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art celebrates the centenary of the Lebanese artist's birth, bringing together significant works from his estate at Bassam Freiha Art Foundation in Abu Dhabi. Developed in collaboration with the Paul Guiragossian Foundation, the exhibition offers an overview of the life and legacy of one of the leading figures of modern Lebanese and Middle Eastern art. Known for his expressive use of colour and distinctive depictions of the human figure, Guiragossian (1926–1993) developed a visual language concerned with family, identity and the human condition. His paintings frequently explored themes of displacement, belonging and everyday life, reflecting both personal experiences and the wider history of the region. Drawing primarily on works from the artist's estate, the exhibition traces the development of his practice and considers his enduring influence on modern Arab art. October 17 to January 17, 2027; Abu Dhabi 14. Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean at Louvre Abu Dhabi Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean explores 1,000 years of maritime trade and cultural exchange, tracing the routes that connected communities across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, India, China and South-East Asia. Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders. The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's pearl trade and the movement of spices, precious stones, textiles and religious artefacts. Highlights include six detailed models of historic vessels, objects recovered from shipwrecks, ancient navigational instruments and a third-century Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan. Through specially created maps and immersive displays, the exhibition examines how sailors navigated using stars and coastal landmarks, while merchants and pilgrims carried goods, beliefs and artistic traditions between distant societies. Its historical narrative concludes in the 17th century, drawing attention to the extensive trading networks that existed before European powers came to dominate Indian Ocean commerce. Until February 14, 2027; Abu Dhabi 15. A Board Game Adventure at Louvre Abu Dhabi A Board Game Adventure transforms Louvre Abu Dhabi into a giant playground, using some of the world's oldest games to explore how people have connected across cultures for thousands of years. Designed for children but engaging for all ages, the exhibition traces the journey of games including chess, Mancala, Ludo and Carrom as they travelled between ancient civilisations and evolved into the games still played today. The exhibition combines immersive installations with rare artefacts borrowed from international museums, including some of the earliest known board game objects from ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, Iran and India. Highlights include centuries-old chess pieces carved from ivory and rock crystal, engraved backgammon pieces, ancient six-sided dice and one of the earliest known predecessors of Ludo. Interactive displays encourage visitors to solve puzzles, challenge artificial intelligence, play on oversized game boards and discover how strategy, chance and storytelling have always been part of human play. Throughout the exhibition, historical figures ranging from Queen Nefertari and Achilles to samurai Hatakeyama Shigetada are reimagined through playful “player profiles”, linking games to the personalities and cultures that shaped them. Rather than presenting games as simple entertainment, A Board Game Adventure reveals them as cultural objects that have crossed borders, adapted to societies and brought people together for millennia. Until April 25, 2027

title: Sheikh Theyab holds talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi
description: Discussions focused on efforts to advance bilateral ties
content: Sheikh Theyab bin Mohamed , deputy chairman of the Presidential Court for Development and Fallen Heroes’ Affairs, held talks on Friday with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. Sheikh Theyab and Mr Modi explored ways to expand deep-rooted bilateral ties within the framework of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in place between the nations. The high-level meeting was held on the sidelines of the two-day NDTV World Summit. The two reflected on central themes of the conference, including shifts in the global economy, the role of artificial intelligence and technology in driving development and the importance of building international partnerships to address pressing challenges. The discussions demonstrate the strength of relations between the long-standing allies, which date back to the formation of the Emirates. ذياب بن محمد بن زايد يلتقي ناريندرا مودي، رئيس وزراء جمهورية الهند، على هامش قمة "NDTV" العالمية 2026، حيث ناقش الطرفان أهمية تعزيز الشراكات الدولية لمواكبة المتغيرات العالمية وتحويل التحديات إلى فرص للنمو والازدهار. pic.twitter.com/YlommOsrCo — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 23, 2026 Flourishing friendship On Monday, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed , Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, met Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar , India's Minister of External Affairs, in Mumbai as part of a working visit to the country. Sheikh Abdullah said the UAE-India partnership was continuing to gain momentum, helping to reinforce the countries as vital drivers of global economic growth. The UAE is home to about four million Indian citizens, the largest expatriate community in the country. In May, Mr Modi made an official visit to the Emirates, during which he met President Sheikh Mohamed. Sheikh Mohamed made a working visit to New Delhi in January, where he and Mr Modi pledged to deepen co-operation in sectors including artificial intelligence, the economy and food security, during discussions at the Prime Minister's residence. Mr Modi made a two-day visit to the UAE in 2024, where he addressed a crowd of 40,000 Indians at Zayed Sports City Stadium. He also spoke at the World Governments Summit in Dubai, before inaugurating the first Hindu temple in Abu Dhabi.

title: UK Telegraph staff face cuts after Axel Springer takeover
description: New round of job losses as editor spearheads reorganisation
content: Staff at Telegraph Media Group received notice on Friday of a round of job cuts just months after the German company Axel Springer took control. The British newspaper publisher was bought out earlier this year on the promise of fresh investment, but after examining the business the newspaper is to start a consultation period. Staff at risk received an email by midday, Telegraph editor Chris Evans and chief executive Carolin Hulshoff Pol said in an email to staff on Friday, which was seen by Bloomberg News. “These are difficult choices that we believe are necessary for the future of the business,” Ms Hulshoff Pol wrote in the memo. It didn’t say how many cuts were being made. The cuts signal a shift for the newspaper group under Axel Springer, which acquired TMG for £575 million ($766 million) in June. In April, it completed the purchase of the publisher of The Daily Telegraph by acquiring a call option held by RedBird IMI in a deal notified to the UK government. RedBird IMI had acquired the Telegraph titles as well as The Spectator magazine in 2023, but a retrospective change in British law forced the consortium to find a new buyer. The deal united two of Europe’s most influential media brands on the right of politics. The buy-out was led by Axel Springer’s billionaire chief executive, Mathias Doepfner. At the time, the German media group, which also owns Business Insider and Politico , pledged to back an investment programme “to grow and expand the business to enable it to become the leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”. Axel Springer subsequently parachuted in its own top managers to the UK group. Ms Hulshoff Pol, formerly head of the German title Bild , became chief executive, while long-time executive Patrick Wehrmann was appointed as finance chief. Mr Evans will remain in his position. Under the changes, the publication plans to merge the comment and analysis teams, and combine features and lifestyle workers, Mr Evans told staff at a meeting on Friday at which the cuts were announced. “We will look to develop new revenue streams, and we will look to expand into overseas markets,” he said.

title: Iran 'deliberately undermining Iraq’s security', says Al Zaidi adviser
description: Iraq has closed several border crossings with Iran
content: Iran is committing serious violations against Iraq, including security breaches, economic disruption and drug trafficking, said an adviser to the Iraqi Prime Minister, as Baghdad closed some border crossings over security issues. Abdelamir Taiban, a senior adviser to Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi , told local media that Iran had “deliberately undermined Iraq’s security”, alleging that Iranian-linked people were entering the country without authorisation and causing “chaos” along the border. Mr Taiban said Tehran must take “strict legal measures” against those responsible. His remarks this week appeared to be an unusually direct public criticism by an Iraqi government official of Iran’s influence over Iraqi state affairs. Iraqi citizens had been kidnapped after crossing into Iran, particularly near the Shalamcheh and Al Sheeb border points, he said. The government must expand new electronic monitoring and automation systems to all crossings with Iran, he added. Mr Taiban said Iraq’s most serious border problems involved Iran. One of the biggest challenges was the flow of drugs and counterfeit currency from Iran, which he said had inflicted economic damage “greater than what ISIS caused”. The terrorist group has been responsible for widespread violence and human rights abuses. Mr Al Zaidi, who took office in May, has sought to maintain balanced ties with both Tehran and Washington while moving to bring armed factions under state control. Some Iran‑aligned groups have complied, while others have resisted. Mr Taiban said the government’s efforts to tighten border controls were part of a broader push to stabilise the economy and strengthen state authority. In September, Iraq closed the Shalamcheh crossing as a precautionary security measure after drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. His comments came as protests erupted in the southern city of Maysan over the closure of Al Sheeb crossing. Dozens of lorry drivers and workers demonstrated on Thursday, calling on the government to reverse its decision to shut the crossing, a strategic land route used by commercial and civilian vehicles. Protesters said their livelihoods depended on cross‑border traffic. The shutdown has disrupted trade and daily activity in the province. It is expected to impact the prices of basic goods, especially fresh produce and Iranian building materials that dominate southern markets. Mr Al Zaidi called on security forces to ensure a safe environment for demonstrators. The Prime Minister chaired a meeting of the Ministerial Council of National Security that underscored the need to “secure peaceful demonstrations” and to treat protesters with respect, his office said in a statement. All security agencies must prioritise humane treatment and guarantee a safe space for citizens to voice their demands, he said. Iraq and Iran share a 1,599km border and there are nine official border crossings linking Iran to Iraq and the Kurdistan region.

title: Saudi Arabia flight cancellations: Which airlines are suspending services and until when?
description: UAE and other international services remain suspended despite airport reopening
content: Flight cancellations across Saudi Arabia continue as airlines extend suspensions amid ongoing regional tensions and attacks by Yemen's Houthis . Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has partially reopened following its closure earlier this month, but international services remain heavily disrupted. Etihad Airways has extended cancellations on routes to Riyadh and Dammam into November, while flydubai has suspended several Saudi services until October 29. The disruption has also spread beyond the capital, with an attack on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport on Wednesday adding to concerns over aviation safety in the kingdom. Here is how major airlines have adjusted their operations and when flights are expected to resume. Etihad Air ways Etihad Airways has cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5 owing to the regional disruption. All services to and from Riyadh and Dammam are affected, along with four Jeddah services – EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604. Emirates Emirates has suspended all of its flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until October 25. Flydubai The airline has cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha up to and including October 29. Air Arabia Air Arabia has cancelled services between Sharjah and several Saudi destinations including Riyadh, Abha, Dammam and Taif. No resumption date has been announced. Qatar Airways The airline has temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam up to and including October 24. Meanwhile, its services to Jeddah have been reduced from seven daily flights to four. Gulf Air Gulf Air has said flights after Sunday, October 18 are currently proceeding as scheduled, following its previously announced Riyadh cancellations. Oman Air Oman Air has announced that all flights to and from Riyadh are suspended until October 31. SalamAir The Omani low-cost airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until October 31, citing regional security developments. Air France The French airline has extended its suspension of flights to and from Riyadh up to October 24. British Airways British Airways is scheduled to return with a limited service to Riyadh on November 3, operating one flight daily, according to previously announced plans. The airline discontinued flights to Jeddah in April as part of wider changes to its Middle East operations. Air India and Air India Express Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam until October 24. Akasa Air The Indian low-cost airline has suspended flights to and from Riyadh until October 24 and Jeddah until October 21. Cathay Pacific The Hong Kong airline has extended its suspension of flights to Riyadh up to January 31, 2027. Pakistan International Airlines The airline announced a temporary suspension of flights to Riyadh on October 9, without setting out a resumption date. The Pakistan Airports Authority said at the time that its other Saudi services were continuing as usual. Delta Air Lines The US airline has postponed the launch of flights between Atlanta and Riyadh until March 2027. Services had been scheduled to begin on October 23. IndiGo The Indian airline has cancelled flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah up to October 24. Lufthansa The German airline has suspended flights to Riyadh until November 18, extending its previously announced October 16 deadline. The Lufthansa Group’s advisory also lists Dammam services as suspended through November 30. Eurowings, part of the group, is scheduled to resume flights to Jeddah on November 12. Malaysia Airlines Malaysia Airlines has announced that flights to and from Jeddah and Madinah will resume on October 18 after a safety review. KLM The Dutch airline has extended cancellations of all flights to Riyadh and Dammam up to October 31. Philippine Airlines The Philippine flag carrier has suspended Riyadh flights PR654 and PR655 until November 29, citing the security situation at King Khalid International Airport. Scoot The Singapore Airlines-owned low-cost carrier has cancelled flights between Singapore and Jeddah until December 2.

title: Terror investigation launched after deadly drive-by shooting near Paris
description: Racist motives believed to be behind 39-year-old suspect's attack, which killed one and injured five
content: A gunman opened fire from a car outside Paris on Friday, killing one person ⁠and wounding five others, including a 12-year-old girl, ⁠French authorities said. “We ‌would like to thank our law enforcement agencies, ​which have already taken the suspect into custody. The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has taken over the case,” President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on X in which he expressed deep sorrow over the killing. Speaking from Trappes, one of two cities west of Paris where the shootings took place, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described it as an “extremely serious act”. “This morning, an individual went on a deadly rampage, shooting and killing one person and wounding five others – three of them very seriously, with their lives still considered to be in danger as we speak,” Mr Nunez said. Local media reported the shooter's apartment was booby-trapped with gas canisters. “That is indeed what we have heard; the investigation will determine whether it is true,” Mr Nunez said. The shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France, after nationwide protests turned violent last Saturday and ahead of possible unrest this coming weekend. Some on the far right had blamed immigration for last weekend's violence. Racist shooting? The anti-terrorism prosecutor's office said lines of inquiry included examining whether the ​shooting was a terrorist act or if it was racially or religiously motivated. While this has yet to be established by the investigation, Ali Rabeh, the ​mayor of Trappes, described the incident as “likely one of the first attempts at a mass crime with Islamophobic and racist overtones ”. “[The killer] failed to cause more casualties despite the weaponry that would have allowed him to do so, thanks to the police,” Mr Rabeh said. He said the deceased had been killed near a playground, where he was visiting family, and was of “African origin”, while one of the injured is “of Maghrebian origin”. The killer allegedly used a Second World War-era Sten submachine gun for his attack. Five policemen succeeded in stopping his car and arresting him in the city of Coignières, roughly a quarter of an hour after he started shooting. He did not try to shoot at police, local officials said. Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of neighbouring La Verrière, said the killer was of “European appearance” and lived in the city of Plaisir, also in the Yvelines department. The killer started his shooting spree in La Verrière and ended in Trappes, according to Mr Dainville. Locals told him that the killer got out of his car to shoot at two male cleaners working in a school. “It is a waking nightmare, it is sheer terror,” Mr Dainville told BFMTV. “The individual continued his murderous spree by heading to another neighbourhood in a different municipality – Orly Parc – where he targeted a 12-year-old girl,” Mr Dainville said. “Eight bullets, eight impacts: it’s truly chilling.”

title: UK government advises stockpiling water and food
description: Households told they should be self-sufficient for three days in case of emergencies
content: The UK government has published guidance urging households to “be ready” in the event of a national emergency by stocking up on essentials and signing up for government support. The new advice that households should ensure they could be self-sufficient for three days in an emergency was posted on a government website on Thursday, along with a written ministerial statement to Parliament by Security Minister Dan Jarvis. He also posted on social media about the campaign. The UK has been facing threats from bad weather, drought and flooding, as well as AI and hostile activity from Russia and Iran. The campaign for Britons to step up their preparations had been planned for earlier in the year by Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer. However Mr Burnham delayed the launch due to concerns that it could be seen as an overly pessimistic start to his premiership, Bloomberg reported. Mr Burnham has spent his first three months in office trying to build optimism across the UK. Policy announcements have focused more on feel-good steps such as bus fare caps and greater devolution than on thorny issues such as defence spending and the threats facing the UK. But the decision to publish guidance telling households to “take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted” suggests the government is now seeking to build voter awareness of the difficult decisions facing John Healey in his budget next week. The Chancellor is weighing the need to increase defence expenditure against other government spending priorities. “Individual households can play their role in making sure that they’re more resilient, but government has a role in making sure we’ve got the right defences,” Paymaster General James Murray told Sky on Friday morning. “The big focus, rightly for many years and into the future, is on our military capability, our defensive capability.” The online checklist advised Britons to stock up on three days’ supply of bottled water and non-perishable foods, as well as hand sanitiser, a torch and batteries, and a radio. It also advised them to keep cash at hand, copies of important documents, and blankets and warm clothing. “The storms last winter and the wildfires this summer have shown how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, like phones, power, water and the internet,” Mr Jarvis said in his statement. They “are a reminder that we can all play our part to keep ourselves, our loved ones and our communities safe in times of emergency.” Ministers are under pressure to take significant steps to modernise infrastructure and prepare for the future. Hotter summers and plans for data centre construction are increasing demand for water, but the UK has not built a reservoir since 1992, shortly after the privatisation of the water sector. Britain has also been warned by leading defence experts that it needs to invest heavily in its military, as it is unprepared to defend itself in the event of a full-scale war. Mr Healey quit as defence secretary under Mr Starmer in a row over military spending. Now, as Chancellor, he faces the challenge of getting defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035. The way the advice has been rolled out highlights the government’s determination not to overdo the worries, with memories of supermarket shelves being emptied in the early days of the Covid pandemic still relatively fresh. Mr Jarvis said the move “brings the UK into line with many of our European peers who also have the three-day message at the heart of their campaign”. No government ministers had been scheduled to speak on the launch of the resilience campaign this week. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting only revealed that the launch was imminent when questioned by journalists at the opening of weapons factory in the West Midlands on Thursday. He said the public needed to be prepared for supply chain disruption caused by “hostile state actors or terrorists” and later added, in an appearance on BBC’s Question Time , that he wanted “people to be alert but not alarmed”. Speaking in front of the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee last week, Jim Bligh, corporate affairs director of the British Retail Consortium, said he was concerned about being too alarmist. “Panic buying is quite easy to generate, particularly if you tell people to buy a particular type of product – they will go out to buy it,” he said. “If the government were to say to you, ‘Go and buy x litres of water,’ would we run out of water? I do not know.” UK shoppers rushed to stockpile essentials in March 2020 as the Covid-19 pandemic stoked fears of lockdowns and shortages. Toilet paper, pasta and cleaning products vanished from shelves in many stores, forcing supermarkets to step up restocking. Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons joined the BRC that month in urging shoppers to buy only what they needed, warning that panic buying risked leaving others without essentials.

title: Michael Carrick does not have support of all Man United players but manager alone can't be held responsible
description: Outbursts from Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes have worsened crisis at Old Trafford, with club weighing up other managerial options
content: AFC Bournemouth visit Old Trafford on Sunday buoyed by a European win against seven-time continental champions AC Milan. Bournemouth, who were a third-tier club with average crowds of 5,500 the last time Milan won the Champions League in 2007, drew 4-4 at Old Trafford last season and won 3-0 in two visits before that. They will meet a United team reeling from a dreadful start to the season, the low point of which was Wednesday’s 4-1 Champions League hammering by Milan’s tiny neighbours, Como. Michael Carrick’s United side have not won in seven games and while the manager is set to be in charge against Bournemouth, his position is perilous. Carrick has long needed wins but they have not come. In the Premier League, United are 13th after seven matches and while Bournemouth are on a high, they too have won only one league game. The addition of European football isn’t helping the domestic form of either side and two United players have blown up the dressing room with their post-match comments after the last two European defeats, in Madrid and now Como . Lisandro Martinez , who wants a new contract but has made no headway towards getting one, was critical of the club’s technical director Jason Wilcox among others after the defeat to Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes was critical of his boss Carrick and his staff after being substituted in Como. The Portuguese, who had done no interviews since August, offered to speak to the media and said: “It’s the decision of the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball. But sometimes when you give the ball too much to these teams, they get confidence.” Asked if Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: “That’s on the manager and staff to see it, not me.” This is an affront to the name of Manchester United. — Andy Mitten (@AndyMitten) October 21, 2026 Criticism 'for the dressing room' Fernandes was correct in what he said. Whether he should have said it publicly is another issue. United looked passive, not just against Como but in too many games this season. United played to Como’s style and strengths and the team have struggled to press all season. Como’s model of extreme possession with penetration by playing through opponents diagonally was a recipe for disaster for United. Martinez struck a chord with fans, while Fernandes, despite being the club’s best player and captain, saw his actions questioned. “You do not criticise your manager in public if you are the captain because no good can come from that,” one former Premier League captain told The National . “This is stuff for the dressing room. As captain, if you smell things are changing on the pitch then you change things. If what the manager wants you to do isn’t working, you can feel it as a player. So you adjust. It’s what leaders do.” Fernandes normally chooses his words carefully since he is aware of the global impact of them. But these criticism were meant to make headlines. As a result, it doesn’t look like all United players are with the manager Carrick right now. Onus on players as well Yet in a rain-lashed Como on Wednesday night, Carrick was right to say that those players should be playing for Manchester United, not him. When the unity goes, players get defensive and lash out. They blame anyone but themselves. United fans will get behind their team on Sunday. The Stretford End want their players to maintain the standards expected at Manchester United and will make that clear. This isn’t the weight of history crashing on the shoulders of current players once again. Yet, it is another reminder of how things were once great and now they are not. It’s not the fault of those who wear the red shirt in 2026 that they are not as good as legends of yore who were some of the best in the English league and beyond. It's just a reminder that certain standards are expected and the players fell short of the expected levels in Wednesday’s atrocious defeat in Italy. "I 100% take responsibility for the overall team and the performance. That's where it stops. It stops with me." Michael Carrick reacts to Manchester United's "unacceptable" display against Como. 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/agXYEERLGq — Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) October 21, 2026 United's leaders want it to work for Carrick and there is little appetite for yet another managerial change. But it’s whether the club have the faith that Carrick can turn fortunes around. This run cannot continue and the club are privately weighing up other managerial options, just as they did before Carrick got the job permanently after the excellent work he did in guiding his team into the Champions League. Sadly, this is the time of year that United managers lose their jobs. Erik ten Hag was dismissed in October 2024, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in November 2021, Jose Mourinho in December 2018. Sir Alex Ferguson took control of United 40 years ago in November 1986. Carrick has remained calm amid the chaos, but he is struggling to get a tune from the very same players who couldn’t stop winning under him last season. To make matters worse, United’s injuries are extensive, there is no recognised centre forward and the fixture list is unrelenting. Manchester United’s problems go well beyond the first team manager. The club operate under the cloud of a vast and continuing debt placed on it when the Glazer family took over in a controversial and highly leveraged takeover in 2005. Fans have consistently protested this, even when the team are winning. But the problems always come into sharper focus when United are on a losing streak, like they are on now.

title: Dubai Fashion Week opens with dazzling couture by Yousef Al Jasmi, Sara Pedram, Pallavi Puri and Kresha Bajaj
description: Regional designers make strong showing on first day of spring/summer 2027 collections
content: Dubai Fashion Week opened its spring/summer 2027 season with a reminder that the region’s fashion ambitions extend well beyond the runway. Before the first models took their places on Thursday, a showroom in Dubai Design District previewed emerging talent from around the world and introduced several designers to the UAE market. Among them was Bahrain’s Touchless, whose 3D-printed handbags have already attracted the attention of British Vogue , Selfridges, Level Shoes and Fashion Trust Arabia, as well as making an appearance in the Bridgerton universe. Egyptian jeweller-turned-eyewear designer Amr Saad brought a precious touch with bespoke gold and silver frames finished with jewellery-like detailing along the arms and bridge. Tunisian footwear label Balga drew on traditional metalworking techniques for its sculptural heels. Leather mules featured hand-hammered metalwork, including a tapered heel etched with graphic lines reminiscent of baklava. Kuwaiti designer Kochylia, whose name means seashells in Greek, offered a considered take on wardrobe classics, from reworked trench coats to tuxedo jackets finished with handmade porcelain buttons fashioned from Kuwaiti mud. Yousef Al Jasmi The evening’s runway programme opened with Kuwait’s Yousef Al Jasmi, a designer well-versed in dressing for the spotlight. Having created looks for Lady Gaga, he understands the appeal of theatrical excess, and this collection delivered it in abundance. Crystal-encrusted dresses skimmed the body, long strands of crystals cascaded from shoulder to floor, and sculpted bodices were paired with sheer, close-fitting skirts. Moving from barely-there nude to dramatic black, the collection was designed to catch the light from every angle. Sara Pedram Next came self-taught designer Sara Pedram, whose collection, Simurgh, drew inspiration from The Conference of the Birds , the 12th-century epic poem by Attar of Nishapur. Exploring transformation, spirituality and Persian cultural heritage, Pedram translated the story into a series of sculptural silhouettes. A ballerina opened the show, followed by sheer creations with wing-like extensions at the shoulders. A richly embellished burnt-umber column gown gave way to a shimmering cascade of swaying paillettes, while a Prussian-blue velvet gown featured a Swarovski-crystal Tree of Life traced across its train, symbolising growth and renewal. Most arresting was a voluminous, full-skirted creation in rough hessian, hand-painted with a scene inspired by Persian poet Hafez , whose work, Pedram explained, was “close to my heart”. “Simurgh is a legendary bird that represents rebirth, transformation and rising again,” Pedram explained backstage. “This collection is very personal to me, especially this year. Fashion is more than a beautiful dress; I love to explain the story behind each piece.” Pallavi Puri Indian designer Pallavi Puri followed with Beyond Borders, a collection exploring cultural exchange through a wardrobe designed for women across the region. Drawing inspiration from family and friends, their tastes and the way they dress, Puri reworked traditional Indian beadwork for a contemporary audience, citing Emirati, Asian and Moroccan women among her most inspirational clientele. Horses were another recurring motif, reflecting both the designer’s long-standing fascination with the animals and Dubai’s enduring equestrian culture. Indian model Lisa Haydon opened the show, while Lebanese actress Cyrine Abdel Nour closed it wearing an embellished bridal look. “Did you realise one is from India and one is Arab?” Puri said, highlighting the collection’s cross-cultural message. “My show is Beyond Borders, so it is about mixing and coming together.” It was Haydon's first appearance for Puri and a return to opening a runway show after a lengthy break. “When you open a show, you set the tone, so I was extra nervous,” she admitted. “This is [Puri’s] debut show [at Dubai Fashion Week], so it was quite a special moment to be part of. I have walked in Dubai Fashion Week before, but today was a lot of firsts.” Kresha Bajaj Closing the evening was Kresha Bajaj, who returned with a collection showcasing the designer’s signature beadwork. Applied to daywear, it trailed across delicate crocheted tops, framed the necklines of street-style tank tops and formed striking zebra-skin patterns. As the collection moved into evening wear, the embellishment became increasingly elaborate, forming latticework across torsos, looping around hips and swaying across legs with every step. It was glamour with an edge.

title: Lebanese and British troops conclude three-week joint exercise with mock helicopter assault
description: The National was granted access to Operation Pegasus Cedar 2026, held at a pivotal time for the LAF
content: Lebanese and British troops have concluded a three-week joint exercise in Lebanon aimed at enhancing co-operation between the two militaries. Operation Pegasus Cedar 2026 was held at a pivotal time for the Lebanese Armed Forces, which have been given the formidable challenge of disarming Iran-backed Hezbollah and extending state control across the country. The task has been made more difficult by Israel’s occupation of parts of southern Lebanon and its bombardment of the country. British army commander Lt Col Alex Phillips said the exercise was an opportunity for the two militaries to learn from each other. The National was granted access to the drills, which took place at Hammana Barracks, east of Beirut. “It's incredibly important to build our relationship of mutual support and to develop our professionalism as militaries in the region,” he told reporters. Soldiers from Lebanon's elite Air Assault Regiment and the UK's 4th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, trained together over three weeks of drills. Six other countries, including the US , Qatar and Jordan , were also involved. It culminated in a mock assault, with LAF helicopters swooping through the valley before placing British and Lebanese soldiers on the roof of a building to launch attacks. Observers included LAF Chief of Staff Maj Gen Hassan Audi, the army's second most senior officer. بحضور قائد الجيش بالنيابة اللواء الركن حسان عوده، أُقيم حفل اختتام تمرين PEGASUS CEDAR 2026 الذي امتدّ لثلاثة أسابيع، نفّذه فريق بريطاني من الفوج الملكي الاسكتلندي والفوج المجوقل في الجيش اللبناني، بمشاركة عناصر من جيشَي الولايات المتحدة وإيطاليا وحضور عناصر من جيوش فرنسا وقبرص… pic.twitter.com/IFxHsXtPqZ — الجيش اللبناني (@LebarmyOfficial) October 22, 2026 The British contingent is normally based at Dhekelia Garrison in Cyprus. The exercise built on a joint drill held in September 2023, which was described as the largest exercise involving UK and Lebanese troops. The latest exercise was the first joint drill between the countries to take place since Israel launched its war on Gaza, after the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023. Lebanon has repeatedly been dragged into the wider regional war, with Hezbollah and Israel exchanging fire. Israeli troops occupy a large part of southern Lebanon, where residents have been ordered to flee and villages have been demolished. A US-backed peace process called for the Lebanese military to reassert control and disarm Hezbollah, in exchange for the withdrawal of Israeli troops. But that process has largely ground to a halt. Hezbollah , which was not party to the agreement signed in June, has rejected it. The LAF, while highly respected in Lebanon, is poorly funded and equipped and relies largely on foreign support.

title: Global Hamas fundraising network shut down after 'Gaza aid diverted'
description: Charities in France allegedly worked with suspected Hamas financier charged in US
content: A global network that raised funds for Hamas by allegedly diverting financial donations intended as humanitarian aid for Gaza has been closed down by a series of arrests. The fund-raising operation for the militant group was controlled by Saleem Alzaq, 45, a senior Hamas propaganda official, according to prosecutors. US authorities claim that Mr Alzaq's network raised $2 million for Hamas, of which $1.5 million was received after the 2023 October 7 attack on Israel . Arrests have included founders of two charities based in France, who are alleged to have worked with Mr Alzaq. One of the charities, Association Baraka, was set up by Faouzi Barika, a 35-year-old Algerian, just days after October 7 to allegedly act as the vehicle to raise funds for Hamas. The charity has been closed down following the swoop by France's security service, the General Directorate for Internal Security (DGSI). Two weeks after the US notices, the charity website was still operating an apparent link to an international payment system. PayPal told The National it was not processing payments for either the individual or the organisation. Days later the website closed. Mr Alzaq, Mr Barika and Association Baraka have been placed under sanctions by the US under the Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) designation. Code words Mr Alzaq has been charged for his alleged role in the social media fund-raising under the guise of aid for Gaza. If convicted, he faces a 20-year prison sentence in the US, although he is currently in Gaza. The indictment filed against Mr Alzaq in a New York court states that he and his “co-conspirators have solicited donations from around the world” which were “purportedly to provide humanitarian aid to the people of Gaza”. Mr Alzaq's activities allowed Hamas to “exploit the sympathy and generosity of the international public at the expense of the Palestinian people”, it adds. In a conversation with an undercover US law enforcement officer, Mr Alzaq is alleged to have used coded language for his activities. Hamas was referred to as “the Green”, and he boasted that he could deliver monthly donations to “them” using terms such as “buy bread” or “give it to the bakeries”. US arrests Three men have been arrested in the US for allegedly donating funds to Hamas through the financing network. Abdel Adhami, 35, and Omar Adhami, 33, from Louisiana, and Raed Yousef, 56, from Florida, were arrested for allegedly donating a total of $155,000. The Adhamis and Mr Yousef face a number of charges, including providing material support to a foreign terrorist organisation. They face 20 years in prison if convicted. Mr Alzaq's alleged fund-raising activity fits into a pattern in which Hamas has benefited from organisations purporting to be charities, the US authorities say. French network Included in the French round of arrests and accused of being part of Mr Alzaq's financing network is Amel Oualid, 39. She was also arrested by the DGSI. The Algerian citizen and her charity, Ensemble C Mieux, have also been sanctioned under an SDGT designation for allegedly raising money for Hamas. Mr Barika and Ms Oualid are also accused of sending hundreds of thousands of dollars in cryptocurrency to Mr Alzaq. The “investigations and arrests spanned multiple jurisdictions in the United States and across international borders”, said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A Eisenberg. “Money is the lifeblood of terrorist organisations, and the arrests disrupted a global financing network that was supplying Hamas with the funds needed to continue its campaign of destroying innocent lives,” he added. The US Department of Justice describes Mr Alzaq as being a battalion deputy in the Al Qassam Brigades , Hamas’s armed wing. He serves in the photography department of its media office, a Hamas propaganda operation. In this role, he has photographed Hamas events, including those led by senior leaders such as the late Ismail Haniyeh and Yahya Sinwar .

title: Sheikh Khaled tours cultural spots in Athens during official visit
description: Abu Dhabi Crown Prince visits National Gallery of Greece and National Archaeological Museum
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, toured two of Greece's leading cultural attractions on Friday as part of his official visit to the country. Sheikh Khaled viewed the extensive collection of artwork at the National Gallery of Greece and also visited the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. He was briefed on the creative works at the gallery that reflect the rich history and heritage of Greece and the evolution of its art scene. Officially known as the National Gallery – Alexandros Soutsos Museum, it was founded in 1900 and is home to more than 20,000 exhibits, including paintings, sculptures and prints from the post-Byzantine period to the modern era. Picturing the past Among the artworks adorning the walls of the National Gallery is Street Market, a painting by Greek artist Panayiotis Tetsis that captures the bustle of everyday life in the capital. Measuring more than 12 metres wide and nearly 2.5 metres high, the oil-on-canvas triptych depicts a crowded open-air market, with shoppers and vendors filling the scene. The painting was inspired by a weekly market on Xenokratous Street in central Athens, where the artist maintained his studio. The archaeological museum, the largest of its kind in Greece, was established towards the end of the 19th century and contains a treasure trove of antiquities. خالد بن محمد بن زايد، ولي عهد أبوظبي، يزور المعرض الوطني اليوناني في أثينا، وسموّه يطّلع على أعمال توثّق تطوّر الفن اليوناني، وتعكس دور الفنون في التعبير عن هوية الشعوب وتاريخها وتعزيز التواصل والتفاهم بين الثقافات. pic.twitter.com/J3BPV1BWPu — مكتب أبوظبي الإعلامي (@ADMediaOffice) October 23, 2026 Landmark visit Sheikh Khaled had on Thursday held talks with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis as major deals were agreed on between the countries. Discussions between at the Prime Minister's Office centred on efforts to bolster collaboration across sectors including energy, infrastructure, health care, advanced technology and health care. Sheikh Khaled emphasised the UAE's desire to strengthen long-standing relations with Greece to support the aspirations of both nations. It was also announced during the visit that the UAE is to invest a further €15 billion ($16.8 billion) in Greece as part of a joint initiative between the countries.

title: US stresses there is no military solution to Sudan war in Geneva talks
description: Trump adviser warns of increased instability in region, as countries call for humanitarian truce
content: There is no military solution to the civil war in Sudan, where the fighting is fuelling further instability in the region, a senior US official said. Massad Boulos , President Donald Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, said Washington officials this week joined representatives of 27 countries in Geneva for the sixth Consultative Meeting on Sudan. "Every day that this war continues comes at a devastating cost to Sudanese civilians and risks spreading further instability to the region," Mr Boulos said in a post on X on Thursday. The impact of the conflict on the wider region was underscored this week when a drone strike killed four people in Chad, near Sudan's western border. At least 14 were injured, an official from Chad's Wadi-Fira province said on Thursday. Sudan’s civil war , which began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has repeatedly spilled over into Chad. International efforts aimed at ending the conflict have so far been unsuccessful. Mr Boulos voiced strong support for the efforts of the Quintet – which comprises the African Union, Arab League, UN, EU and Intergovernmental Authority on Development – to enable an inclusive and credible Sudanese-led political process to take place. He added that those efforts complemented US engagement with the Quad, which also includes the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, to press for a humanitarian truce that could pave the way for a permanent ceasefire. During the Geneva meeting, participants called on all parties to the conflict to engage in good faith to pursue de-escalation, protect civilians and commit to a humanitarian truce. The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the UK, Chad, China, France, Germany, Russia, Switzerland and South Sudan were among the nations represented. "The members of the Quad had highly productive meetings in Geneva on how we can continue to work together towards urgently bringing an end to Sudan’s conflict through a humanitarian truce and path to permanent ceasefire, ensuring humanitarian assistance can reach those in need, and supporting the Quintet’s critical efforts to facilitate inclusive dialogue in Sudan," he said in a post on X. Mr Boulos thanked Switzerland and the UN for hosting the meeting and said participants had collectively raised their voices in support of ending the conflict. In Geneva, the U.S. joined 27 partner countries and international organizations at the 6th Consultative Meeting on Sudan. Our message was clear: Sudan's war must end, and there is no military solution to the conflict. Every day that this war continues comes at a devastating cost… pic.twitter.com/HfVLnWbAEn — U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs (@US_SrAdvisorAF) October 22, 2026 African civil society groups this month called on Sudan to allow international inspectors into the country to investigate accusations that SAF used chemical weapons in the war. In a resolution adopted at the end of a three-day forum in Senegal's capital Dakar, the groups urged the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights to demand that Sudan allow the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to send technical teams into the country. Both the SAF and the RSF have been accused by the UN of war crimes and rights breaches. The conflict has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, the UN World Food Programme has said.

title: Netanyahu orders West Bank lockdown after Hebron checkpoint shooting
description: Five injured in attack in occupied territory, as far-right minister Ben-Gvir calls for Palestinian Authority to be 'dismantled'
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the “full closure” of the occupied West Bank after five people were injured in a shooting at a military checkpoint near the city of Hebron. “I have instructed the [military] and the security forces to immediately impose a cordon around the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire [ West Bank ], effective today,” Mr Netanyahu’s office said in a statement. Israel’s military said it killed two suspects armed with a rifle and a handgun. Two of those injured were reported to be in a critical condition. Palestinian media reports named the pair as family members Mohammad Jaaba and Firas Jaaba, both 27 and from Hebron. The military said the men had planned to carry out a “large-scale” attack on Israelis. There are a number of illegal Israeli settlements in Hebron. Settler and military violence against Palestinians has swept across the West Bank during the olive harvest season, while Israel is preparing to hold elections that could unseat Mr Netanyahu’s ultranationalist coalition government, which has been in power for four years. Mr Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would demolish parts of Hebron in response to the attack, referencing earlier operations in which Israel levelled entire refugee camps in the north of the occupied West Bank and displaced their populations. “We will implement the successful, offensive model we employed in the refugee camps, this time within the cities. The [Israeli army] will enter the neighbourhoods from which the terrorists emerged, evacuate the residents, go house-to-house and dismantle the terror infrastructure. We are prepared for an extensive operation in [the occupied West Bank].” “A few weeks ago, we warned of attempts by our enemies to strike at us − at our citizens and our soldiers − in the lead-up to the elections. That is what they attempted to do here,” he added. “Concurrently, we are imposing a closure on the cities of Hebron and Halhul … the Defence Minister and I have overseen the planning of a very extensive [army] operation in [the occupied West Bank] on a scale not seen since the Six-Day War. The [military] is prepared to carry it out; we will determine the timing, but it is coming.” Shortly after Mr Netanyahu’s words, Defence Minister Israel Katz elaborated on the operation, in a post on X. “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron,” he wrote, referencing the now-destroyed camp in the north of the occupied West Bank. “Every [tribal] clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents, and the terror infrastructure in the neighbourhood will be addressed and dismantled,” he added. “This is the only language that jihadist terrorism understands. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.” Hamas praised the attack but did not claim responsibility. After the attack, Israel's far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who lives in the illegal Hebron settlement of Kiryat Arba, called for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled. It is supposed to control parts of the West Bank. “We have to act before it’s too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” he said. Israel’s military chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir described the attack as “serious” and said a “large quantity of ammunition was found in the vehicle in which the terrorists arrived at the scene ... which was intended to be used to carry out a larger-scale attack”.

title: Abu Dhabi private schools to hire 2,000 Emirati teachers in next five years under education push
description: Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge is joining forces with private school groups to integrate local talent
content: Abu Dhabi on Friday unveiled plans to hire 2,000 Emirati teachers at private schools over the next five years under a major push to champion local talent in the education sector. The Emiratisation Policy for Private Education will seek to provide training and qualifications for a new generation of Emirati educators to encourage them to play a leading role in developing the next generation of learners. It is being supported by the Ministry of Human Resources, the Emirati Talent Competitiveness Council - also known as Nafis - and private education operators, Gems Education, Taleem, Sabis, International Community Schools, and Liwa Education. Private schools in the capital will be asked to meet new recruitment targets specific for teaching roles in an expansion of the government's Emiratisation strategy. Adek said the plans would complement existing Emiratisation goals, while establishing a dedicated approach to boosting Emirati representation in the classroom. Private schools are already subject to Emiratisation employment targets, with the new scheme aiming to sharpen focus on hiring citizens in teaching positions rather than in administration roles within schools. It will initially focus on Social Studies, Arabic, and Islamic Studies roles, with recruitment and integration taking place progressively over the coming five years. Teacher training plan As part of the strategy, Adek is working with Emirates College of Advanced Education to launch a teaching programme to develop a long-term pipeline of qualified Emirati teachers. The programme will provide specialised training, practical classroom preparation and employment opportunities within the private education sector. It is open to Emirati jobseekers and those seeking to transition into education careers, subject to approved eligibility requirements. It will offer two dedicated pathways for teachers and teaching assistants, creating flexible entry routes for Emirati talent at different qualification levels to pursue careers. Through the Nafis programme - which was introduced in September 2021 to ensure 10 per cent of all skilled jobs in private companies are taken up by citizens by the end of 2026 - participants will be eligible to receive a monthly financial incentive of up to AED4,000 throughout the training period. Making the grade The policy will provide schools with access to a pool of national talent and will offer funded qualification pathways, practical school-based training and structured routes into employment. Private schools are already making significant progress on a mission to integrate Emirati employees within their teaching workforce. Adek signed an agreement with Aldar Education in May to create more than 300 opportunities for Emirati teachers within its schools.
