The education authority has now entered into further strategic partnerships with Sabis, Taaleem, GEMS Education, International Community Schools and Liwa Education, Taaleem has committed to recruiting more than 200 Emirati educators, Sabis more than 150, Gems Education more than 120. International Community Schools and Liwa Education have pledged to create teaching positions for at least 77 and 61 Emiratis respectively. Emiratisation plans take shape Employers in the UAE with at least 50 members of staff - including schools - are required to raise their Emirati workforce by 1 per cent every six months under the Emiratisation scheme. They must hit a 10 per cent target by the end of this year, with companies who fail to hit targets or flout rules facing significant fines. The initiative has proved crucial in encouraging large numbers of citizens – who have typically preferred to take up jobs in the public sector – to join the private sector. Government figures released in July showed more than 190,000 Emiratis were employed by 32,000 private sector companies. In April, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed , Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, on announced the extension of the landmark Emiratisation strategy Sheikh Mansour unveiled a series of updates to the programme, include the expansion of the children's allowance for Emiratis, removing the previous cap on the number of eligible children. A salary support programme for children of Emirati women in the private sector and the wives of citizens working for private companies will also be introduced.

title: UAE tackles oil spill, Yemen warns of Houthi child recruitment and Oman strengthens UK investment ties

title: Israel's elections: What would a new government change?
description: PM Netanyahu faces a tight race as frustrations surface over his government’s response to the October 7 attacks
content: Israelis will vote on Tuesday in the first national election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and subsequent war on Gaza . Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s Likud party could win, but polls are showing that opposition candidates also have a good chance. No single party is likely to secure a majority. Whoever wins will almost certainly have to form a coalition. Israelis will be casting their ballots with security and the economy among their main concerns. Palestinians, who cannot vote, are also waiting to see whether a new, potentially less right-wing government will be elected. Under Mr Netanyahu, the West Bank has experienced increasing settler violence and land grabs. In Gaza, a post-ceasefire plan has mostly stalled as Israel refuses to withdraw and Hamas has yet to disarm. In this episode of Beyond the Headlines , host Nada AlTaher asks whether there is any meaningful alternative to Mr Netanyahu and his party and what it could mean for Israelis and Palestinians if he does win. She speaks to non-profit Rand's distinguished chair for Israel policy, Shira Efron, and Palestinian political scientist Xavier Abu Eid.

title: UAE confirms oil spill off coast and temporarily closes Umm Al Quwain beaches
description: The spill was causing the strong fuel smell reported by residents in Dubai and the northern emirates
content: UAE authorities are working to contain an oil spill from a supertanker in the Arabian Gulf, with Umm Al Quwain Municipality intensifying efforts to limit pollution and protect marine habitats. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirmed the incident early on Friday morning. It said the spill is causing a strong smell that residents of Dubai and the northern emirates have reported in recent days. The ministry did not name the vessel, but international maritime agencies say the Gem No.2 was struck in a suspected Iranian drone attack on October 9 to 10. Twenty-two Indian sailors were rescued from the 330-metre vessel at the time. The extent of the oil slick is unclear, but the incident was confirmed amid growing concerns about the environmental impact of the Iran war on the Gulf and the Arabian Sea. On Friday afternoon, Sharjah authorities closed Al Hamriya Beach as a precautionary measure after Umm Al Quwain temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas. Umm Al Quwain Municipality said it was carrying out field operations to contain the effects of the spill and minimise damage to marine and coastal environments. The municipality will monitor conditions, identify affected areas and support clean-up and treatment work as part of those efforts. Specialists will also help to assess the impact of the spill and determine appropriate measures. Acrid and strong fuel smell People in the UAE have in recent days reported an acrid and strong fuel smell in the air. The ministry said there was no health risk from the odour, but advised the public to stay away from any oil that washes ashore. "The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment confirms the UAE’s technical monitoring and environmental assessment system detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches," it said in a statement. "Odours noticed in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain pose no health risks to residents. "Teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation with local and federal authorities to limit environmental impacts. Precautionary coastal surveys, monitoring and assessments continue to gauge impacts and protect the marine environment. "With relevant authorities, the ministry has temporarily closed all Umm Al Quwain beaches and coastal areas until technical teams complete assessments and identify safety and marine protection measures. Fishermen and sea users are urged to follow authorities’ instructions and avoid fishing in affected areas." Lingering effect Dr Diana Francis, an associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences Lab at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said oil spills caused by the regional conflict could create odours. A VLCC-size tanker is leaking oil 25 km off Umm Al Quwain. Currents are setting it southwest toward the coast, and Windward’s drift model shows it reaching Sharjah’s and Ajman’s desalination intakes and ports by 22–23 Oct if the leak isn’t stopped. More maritime intelligence… pic.twitter.com/OY8Vq9W2aB — Windward (@WindwardAI) October 20, 2026 “When an oil spill happens, it continues to move with the currents unless it is removed and cleaned completely,” she told The National before the ministry confirmed the oil slick incident. “Several spills can also move with the currents and accumulate in favourable gyre [rotating ocean current] areas. Then with time, heat and winds, they evaporate into the air and give off fuel-like odours. “Oil doesn't mix with water. It continues to float until it is removed or evaporate with time.” Prashant Kumar, professor of air quality and health at the University of Surrey in the UK, said air pollution – and the smells that it brings with it – can travel over long distances. “The smell can travel tens of kilometres,” he said, in comments also made before the ministry's statement on Friday. “It depends on the meteorological conditions, it depends on the wind speed and the wind direction. You can easily have the longer-range transport of pollutants from one place to another.” Dealing with oil spills When it comes to reducing the effects of oil spills, containment is key because “prevention is better than cure”, Prof John Burt, director of NYU Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said after it was confirmed that the smell was caused by an oil spill. “If floating booms can be put out to contain the spill and collect it before it reaches a coastline, this would be the ideal scenario,” he added. “Remediation is timely, cost intensive, and full return to normal can take years in the event that a spill reaches a coastline.” He said that the Gulf War of 1990-91 offered lessons on the potential impacts of oil spills in the region. Then, millions of barrels of oil were released in the northern Arabian Gulf. “Because oil is buoyant and floats, there were minimal impacts on subtidal habitats such as coral reefs and seagrass beds at that time,” he said. “And as it was volatising to the atmosphere as it drifted down the Gulf, the oil slick back then only made it as far south as Qatar before dispersing fully. “That said, where it reached coastlines in the northern Gulf, particularly around Kuwait and northern Saudi Arabia, it caused considerable impacts in the intertidal zones.” In these areas, Prof Burt said, tar mats formed in the sands of beaches that persisted for years, and there were significant impacts in mangrove areas and on mudflats where many birds feed.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed and Syria's Al Shara discuss regional security in call
description: Leaders reflect on implications of conflict in the Middle East
content: President Sheikh Mohamed and Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara stressed the need to bolster security and stability in the region during a phone call on Thursday. The two leaders discussed the implications of the latest developments in the Middle East and underlined the importance of serving the interests of all people in the region, state news agency Wam reported. The discussions come amid heightened tension in the Gulf after drone and missile attacks on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia killed three people and injured 36 others, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said. Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the strikes, which have also raised concerns about the impact of the conflict on air travel. Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Al Shara also discussed bilateral relations and explored ways to further expand co-operation , with a focus on economic and development sectors. The two sides have taken significant steps to strengthen ties between their nations. In September, Sheikh Mohamed and Mr Al Shara held high-level talks in Abu Dhabi as part of the Syrian leader's working visit to the Emirates, where he took part in the in the 24th Arab Media Summit in Dubai . Central to their discussions was a recent visit by a UAE economic delegation to Syria, which both sides highlighted as a significant step towards establishing frameworks for economic recovery. The leaders said the visit had helped lay the groundwork for strategic partnerships and projects aligned with both countries' development goals. Abu Dhabi-based Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria including a residential and tourism development as part of a framework agreement the company has signed with the Syrian government. Total investment in the two projects in Damascus and Latakia has not been disclosed but Syria 's Arab News Agency reported they will create more 40,000 jobs. The Central Bank of the UAE last week agreed to deepen bilateral co-operation with regulators in Syria and Morocco, focusing on key areas to boost financial stability and technology. The preliminary agreement with the Central Bank of Syria includes a framework for building technical expertise for payment systems, monetary policy, cash management and financial technology, the CBUAE said in a statement on Friday. On Friday, Latakia Racecourse in Syria will host the UAE President's Cup for Purebread Arabian Horses, in a further demonstration of the robust links between the countries. The showpiece race will be held as part of the two-day UAE-Syrian Festival, which gets under way on Friday and features 15 races for purebred Arabian horses.

title: Middle East flights: Singapore Airlines, Scoot and Wizz Air extend suspensions
description: Carriers continue to adjust operations as regional tensions disrupt travel
content: International airlines continue to adjust schedules for Middle East flights as airspace restrictions linked to the Iran war persist. Against the backdrop of continuing geopolitical uncertainty across the region, here's how airlines are adapting their operations. Wizz Air has postponed the planned restart of its Abu Dhabi and Dubai routes, cancelling all flights to and from both destinations for the winter season. “Regional airspace restrictions extended on September 30 require significantly longer routings to these destinations, increasing flight times and costs and making both A321neo and A321XLR operations commercially unviable under current conditions,” the airline told The National . Wizz Air also said flights to and from Amman are affected by the EU Aviation Safety Agency's latest conflict zone information bulletin, which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace at any altitude. Singapore Airlines flights to Dubai were scheduled to resume on August 2, but the suspension has been extended until December 1. “As the situation remains fluid, other flights may be affected,” the airline said on its website. “Customers affected by cancellations will be reaccommodated on alternative flights or can seek a full refund of the unused portion of their ticket.” The low-cost subsidiary of Singapore Airlines has suspended its flights from Singapore to Jeddah until December 2. Customers affected by cancellations may request a full refund if they choose not to continue with their travel or rebook on alternative Scoot flights, the airline said. Air Canada has extended the suspension of its flights to Tel Aviv and Dubai until the end of March 2027. Passengers affected by the cancellations are advised to check directly with the airline for rebooking and refund options as schedules continue to be adjusted. “If you are in either of these regions, please do not head to the airport unless you have a confirmed flight with another airline, and your flight is operating as scheduled. Your safety is our top priority,” the airline said on its website. Air France has resumed its regular flights to Tel Aviv and Beirut. Flights to Riyadh and Dubai are however suspended until October 24. “Affected customers are being contacted individually. Air France reiterates that the safety and security of its customers and crew are its absolute priority,” the airline said. The Hong Kong carrier has extended its suspension of flights to Dubai and Riyadh until January 31, 2027. “Affected travellers will be offered the flexibility to rebook, reroute or refund their tickets. Cathay will continue to closely monitor the evolving situation in the Middle East,” the airline said. Kazakhstan's national carrier had earlier suspended flights from Almaty and Astana to Dubai until September 30. But flights between the cities are now available to book for travel on October 1 onwards. British Airways has revised its schedule for several Middle East destinations, with flights to Dubai set to resume on November 3. The airline will initially operate one daily flight between London and Dubai during the winter season, before increasing to twice-daily services for the summer. Flights to Abu Dhabi will remain suspended for considerably longer, with services scheduled to resume during the winter 2027-2028 season. Elsewhere in the region, BA's Doha service resumed on September 1 at a reduced frequency of one flight a day, down from twice daily. Flights to Tel Aviv are scheduled to resume on October 25 with one daily service, while Riyadh flights will restart on November 3, also at one a day. Amman services are due to resume on November 4 with four flights a week. Flights to Bahrain will remain suspended until the end of March 2027. Lufthansa Group airlines will gradually resume flights to Dubai from late October, restoring connections from several European cities. Lufthansa will restart services between Munich and Dubai on October 25, followed by flights between Frankfurt and Dubai on October 26. The German airline will operate up to five weekly services on the routes. Swiss will resume daily flights between Zurich and Dubai from October 27, while Austrian Airlines will restart its Vienna-Dubai service on December 12, operating up to five flights a week. Eurowings will also restore three routes between Germany and Dubai. Daily flights from Berlin will resume on November 1, alongside four weekly services from Stuttgart. Three weekly flights from Cologne Bonn Airport will follow from November 3. The Lufthansa Group is also restarting services to other destinations in the region, including Tel Aviv, Beirut and Amman. The group said it “continuously monitors and evaluates the situation in the Middle East” and remains in close contact with relevant authorities. “The safety of passengers and crew is always the top priority for the Lufthansa Group,” it said, adding that the continuing volatility in the region means short-notice changes to individual routes may still be necessary. American Airlines has extended its travel alert for passengers flying to, through or from Tel Aviv, with flexible booking options now covering travel into March 2027. Affected customers who bought tickets by March 28, 2026, can make a one-time change without a fee for journeys scheduled up to March 26, 2027. Rebooked travel can take place through April 2, 2027. For Doha, the existing alert covers travel scheduled between February 28, 2026, and January 6, 2027, with rebooked journeys permitted through January 13, 2027. Passengers must keep the same origin and destination, and rebook in the same cabin or pay any difference in fare. Eligible travellers can also cancel their trip and request a refund. Delta has extended the suspension of flights between Atlanta and Tel Aviv until December 18. The launch of flights between Boston and Tel Aviv has been delayed until further notice, although services between New York-JFK and Tel Aviv resumed on September 6. Customers affected by the Atlanta suspension can rebook their journeys or request a refund for the portion of their trip that has not been flown. Virgin Atlantic flights to Dubai remain suspended until October 2027, with tickets for the resumed service to go on sale later this year, the airline said in a notice on its website. “If you're looking to travel sooner, you can still book a Dubai holiday with Virgin Atlantic Holidays, flying with Emirates,” it added. Finnair has extended the suspension of its flights to both Dubai and Doha until March 27, 2027. “Finnair continuously monitors the security situation in different regions and, when necessary, makes changes to flight routes or operations. The security situation in the Middle East has remained unstable, with no clear signs of improvement,” the airline said. KLM has adjusted its flight schedule across the Middle East and continues to avoid the airspace of Iran, Iraq and Israel, as well as parts of the Arabian Gulf. The airline has resumed services to Tel Aviv, with flights stopping in Larnaca, Cyprus, where the crew will rest overnight. “We always check the situation and adjust our flights to keep you safe and give you the best options,” the airline said. Flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam and Dubai remain suspended until October 24. Passengers affected by cancellations can rebook their journeys for a later date or request a refund, depending on their ticket conditions. Turkish Airlines has resumed flights to Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Damascus, Beirut and Amman as the carrier continues to restore services across parts of the Middle East. But flights to Tehran remain suspended. The airline also warned of further disruption due to the latest escalation. “Some of our flights to and from Iran and the surrounding region have been cancelled. The current situation in the region's airspace is being monitored in real-time, and additional flight cancellations may occur,” the airline posted on its website. The national carrier of Italy has resumed flights between Rome and Riyadh, but flights to Dubai are suspended until October 24. “Passengers can request rebooking on an alternative flight or a refund of their ticket,” the airline said. Flights operated by the Latvian flag carrier between Riga and Dubai remain suspended until October 24. Korean Air's regular service between Incheon and Dubai remains suspended, with no date set for flights to resume. “As limited airspace capacity related to the conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran continues, the suspension of the Incheon-Dubai route will be extended until further notice,” the airline said. “A decision on when to resume flights will be made at a later date, following a comprehensive review of Dubai Airport's normalisation and market demand recovery.”

title: Wizz Air cancels winter season flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai
description: Airline blames airspace restrictions for the move
content: Wizz Air has postponed the planned restart of its Abu Dhabi and Dubai routes, cancelling all flights to and from both destinations for the winter season, running from October 25 to March 27. The low-cost airline said last month that it was resuming flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, alongside routes to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan. Earlier this week, it said it would delay the launch of some routes to Abu Dhabi until January, following security updates from Europe's aviation regulator. "Regional airspace restrictions extended on September 30 require significantly longer routings to these destinations, increasing flight times and costs and making both A321neo and A321XLR operations commercially unviable under current conditions," the airline said in a statement to The National . It also confirmed that flights to and from Amman are affected by the EU Aviation Safety Agency's latest conflict zone information bulletin, which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace. "We regret the disruption to travel plans and will continue to monitor developments, reassessing operations as safety guidance and operating conditions evolve," Wizz Air said. International airlines have been forced to adjust schedules for Middle East flights in the aftermath of the US-Iran war as airspace restrictions persist. Wizz Air suspended its European-operated services to the Middle East in late February due to the regional conflict. The UAE services were part of a wider restoration of 12 routes and 49 weekly flights to the Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Jordan over the winter, providing 470,000 seats across services to nine European cities. The airline was set to resume operations after its low-cost subsidiary, Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, ceased operations in September 2025.

title: The US and Israeli elections are making the Middle East wars worse
description: They are also undermining, and not advancing, the democratic values both countries claim to uphold
content: While proponents assert that the spread of democracy is essential to securing peace, two allied democracies – the US and Israel – are engaged in wars that are actually being exacerbated by the fact that both countries are in the midst of elections. From the beginning, in the American mind, democracy has been seen as more than just a form of governance. Both liberals and conservatives have idealised and elevated the idea of democracy into the equivalent of religious doctrine, making exaggerated claims about the benefits that accrue to societies that are democratic. We have been told that democratically elected governments can claim to be more tolerant, more respectful of minority rights, more accountable for their actions, and less likely to start wars. Given this mindset, several past US administrations have made the spread of democracy a foreign policy priority, arguing audaciously that it was essential for world peace. While the US and some of its allies flaunt these attributes, boasting that their democracies place them above societies with other forms of governance, in reality, their claims of purity and adherence to ideals do not hold up to scrutiny. The glaring contradiction between the values that the US and other democracies espouse, and their actual behaviours, have been clear since America’s founding. After all, the American experiment with democracy was built on the backs of slave labour and the genocide of native Americans. And more recently, when the George W Bush administration launched its campaign to promote democracies worldwide, it did so while blundering through a devastating “war of choice” in Iraq and torturing prisoners in “black sites” they had suborned other countries to make available to US interrogators. Much the same can be said of Israel , which Americans tout as “our closest ally” and the “only democracy in the Middle East”. Like the US, Israel claims that its democracy elevates it above its neighbours, making its actions more just and its behaviour more moral. And like true believers in any ideology, when it is pointed out that reality doesn’t agree with their claims, they deny it and criticise whoever has pointed out the disconnect. The fact that democracies hold elections provides them with yet another reason to boast. However, as the rest of the world sees playing out in both Israel and the US, instead of providing a cleansing moment, elections are often used by contesting parties to justify bad behaviours and exacerbate social tensions. US President Donald Trump, for example, needs a way out of his no-win war with Iran, especially because of its negative impact on the economy and consumers, and the insecurity and instability it’s fomenting in the Gulf. But he is loath to look weak by ending the war without some claim of victory, because of the negative impact that might have on his legacy and his hold over his base voters – whom he needs to turn out in November to deliver a victory for the governing Republican Party. And so, he continues his bellicose language and threats towards Iran. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have assumed that he could manage a governing coalition of parties even more extreme than his own. But his partners have used their positions to aggravate tensions with Palestinians in both Israel and the occupied lands. And when Mr Netanyahu felt compelled to sign on to ceasefires that were supposed to stop the bombing in Gaza and Lebanon, his agreement proved hollow . In the face of criticism from his opponents and even his coalition partners that he was compromising Israel’s security by not “finishing the job”, his government has continued to violate both ceasefires with impunity, while doing nothing to rein in the widespread violence in the West Bank being fomented by his political allies. He feels he must do this because he cannot afford to lose any of his governing partners, or he’ll be out of office. The bottom line is that in both instances, instead of implementing the values claimed to be the attributes of democracy, in practice these elections do the opposite. Political discourse becomes coarser and more divisive, social tensions are aggravated and warlike behaviours are promoted. Especially troubling is that while reporters and commentators know that the words and actions of both Mr Netanyahu and Mr Trump are directed more at appeasing their constituents than they are at the realities in Palestine, Lebanon or Iran, too often they sin by omission and treat the political posturing as if it were real. For example, instead of being honest and treating Mr Netanyahu’s claims that villages in southern Lebanon need to be demolished to fend off his opponents’ accusations of weakness, they report it as if levelling whole Lebanese villages is needed for Israel’s security. This is what has become of two of the world’s allied democracies, as they cultivate and then prey on the worst instincts of voters, instead of providing solutions and challenging voters to make better choices.

title: UK keeps Jerusalem mission open despite Israeli closure order
description: Dispute follows Britain's announcement of measures including ban on imports of goods produced in illegal settlements
content: Britain will keep its diplomatic mission in East Jerusalem open despite an Israeli order to close the consulate, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Thursday, averting an immediate escalation between the two allies as talks continue over the dispute. Mr Miliband said the building would remain independent and operational under a new name, UK Mission, Jerusalem , and continue serving Palestinians in the city and the wider occupied Palestinian territories. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Israel had implemented measures announced last month, but that the two sides had agreed to continue dialogue. He said the British consulate had ended its role in the city and that 19 diplomats would leave Israel , while a task force of seven British diplomats would be allowed to continue operating from the building with a limited remit. “Following discussions with the Israeli government, our consulate general building will not be closing,” Mr Miliband said. “It will be known as UK Mission, Jerusalem, and will be independent and operational.” The dispute follows Britain's sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank . “We have been clear that we do not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years,” Mr Miliband said. “The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.” His announcement came hours after workers removed signs and plaques identifying the building as the British consulate general. Signage identifying the mission was still missing on Thursday, although the British flag remained flying above the building. Officials that remain are believed to retain the diplomatic protections that governs their work and residence in the city. It is not thought they are accredited through the embassy in Tel Aviv, a long-run aim of the Israeli government. Documentation and status remains as before the recent impasse erupted. The changes implemented on Thursday should not expose the other diplomatic missions in East Jerusalem to further repercussions. The UK government appears determined to preserve its diplomatic presence for Palestinians while avoiding escalation with Israel. “The mission is a fudge, not a downgrade. The UK has a mission to the UN in New York and to the UN in Geneva,” a diplomatic source told The National. Though the implications for the UK's recognition of Palestine were unclear, “a working arrangement is better than none,” they said. UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty rejected suggestions that the arrangement represented a political fudge allowing Britain to say the mission remained open while Israel could claim it had closed. “The building remains open. We continue to have staff able to do important work, engaging with the Palestinian Authority, supporting British nationals, and we are engaged in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter,” he said. Regardless of the name change, Mr Doughty said, Britain’s presence needed to remain. Mr Miliband said: “We will work to build back up our presence in the coming months.” Britain has withdrawn several diplomats, staff and family members in recent weeks. The Foreign Secretary said the withdrawal had been necessary because Britain had not received sufficient security assurances. “Without an understanding, we would not have the necessary assurances for the security and protection of our staff and premises. Accordingly, the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security,” he said. The consulate handles Britain's relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza and provides consular services to Palestinians. Britain's diplomatic presence in Jerusalem dates back almost 200 years, well before the establishment of Israel in 1948. Israel ordered the consulate to close within 30 days after Britain announced measures including a ban on imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements and sanctions against individuals and companies supporting settlement activity. The UN and most countries consider the settlements illegal under international law, while Israel disputes that position. Mr Doughty said the UK remained engaged in dialogue with the Israelis and would push on with the sanctions on illegal settlements. He said the move, along with Britain's accusation that the Israeli government was turning a blind eye to “ethnic cleansing”, had enraged the Israeli government and led to its decision to close the consulate. Mr Saar said all four measures he announced on September 8 had been implemented, including removing British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre in Kiryat Gat, ending British activity to train Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank, and barring 12 British officials and other citizens from entering Israel. He said Israel had agreed to continue dialogue with Britain, but warned: “Any country that acts against Israel must know that there will be a price for doing so.” Mr Miliband also sought to dampen speculation that Britain would retaliate by expelling Israeli diplomats. “We will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are under way and credible,” he said. Britain had been considering expelling Israeli diplomats if Israel forced the consulate to close, sources told Reuters earlier this week. Such a move would have represented a highly unusual escalation between two countries that remain close security and intelligence partners. The confrontation marks another sharp deterioration in UK-Israel relations after Britain repeatedly criticised Israel's conduct in Gaza and Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's government has accused Britain's Labour government of hostility towards Israel. “This will ensure that we maintain our long-standing British presence and the UK's role in support of [a] two-state solution,” Mr Miliband said. With the UK reserving its position to hold further negotiations, political ties with the Palestinians will be maintained following the reduction of almost three quarters of the staff posted to the mission.

title: Indian in Al Ain wins $1 million draw after trying for 11 years
description: Shaheen Mohammed hits Dubai Duty Free jackpot a week before his birthday
content: Shaheen Mohammed has been buying Dubai Duty Free tickets since 2015, in the hope of finally hitting the jackpot. Just before turning 39 on October 16, he secured an early birthday gift after being named a $1 million winner on Wednesday. The Indian engineer, an Al Ain resident for six years, bought winning ticket 3097 on September 11. A father of one, he works as a senior estimation engineer for a construction company in Mussaffah. “This really gives people an opportunity to make their dreams come true and helps them achieve their goals,” he said. “This is an early birthday gift to me too.” Mr Mohammed wishes to buy a house back home in Kerala and save the rest for his daughter's education. He is the 285th Indian national to have won $1 million in the Millennium Millionaire promotion since its inception in 1999. The Dubai Duty Free draw is held every other Wednesday, so there are normally two draws a month. The number of Millennium Millionaire winners in each draw depends on ticket sales. There can be one, two or more. Arya Mustafa, who lives in Iraq, won a BMW car with ticket number 1762 in the Finest Surprise Series 1963, which he purchased online on August 20. Seeyali Shamsudheen, 65, an Indian living in Dubai, won an Aprilia Tuono motorbike with ticket number 0270 in the Finest Surprise Series 680. The father of three works in a phone accessories shop in Karama.

title: Riyadh airport flights delayed and cancelled after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
description: Dozens of departures were affected at King Khalid International Airport on Thursday
content: Flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were suspended for more than an hour on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, with disruption continuing into Thursday. Flight tracking website Flightradar24 reported that 58 departures, or 15 per cent of the day's scheduled services, were delayed at Riyadh airport as of Thursday morning, while 11 flights, or 3 per cent, were listed as cancelled. The airport was experiencing an average departure delay of 45 minutes, with its disruption index standing at 4.2 out of five, a level classified by the platform as indicating major disruption. Flights affected on Thursday morning included Saudia's SV311 service from Riyadh to Cairo, which was delayed by more than two hours, and Yemenia's IY533 service to Aden, which faced a delay of more than three hours. Saudia's SV562 bound for Dubai and Turkish Airlines' TK145 bound for Istanbul were among flights cancelled. The disruption follows drone and missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, which killed three people and injured 36 others, according to the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation. Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for the attacks, which also caused damage. The latest disruptions have raised concerns about the impact of the escalating conflict on air travel, with the US embassy in Riyadh warning that the fighting could lead to flight cancellations. “US citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport,” the embassy said. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia: Get all the latest updates here

title: Attacks on British mosques intensify in wave of 'sustained harassment'
description: Rise in hate showing no sign of slowing down, says British Muslim Trust
content: Attacks on British mosques are becoming more severe, while reports of lower-level types of intimidation of Muslims has decreased, a report has found. There were 78 attacks and incidents against mosques in the UK and Channel Islands from the year ending in July 2026, amounting to an incident every five days, according to the campaign group British Muslim Trust. The research found a reduction in lower-level threats to mosques and buildings owned by Muslim organisations, such as the drawing of crosses, flags and hateful slogans on mosque walls, desecrating objects left outside mosques and property damage. But more severe incidents involving arson, weapons, threats to kill and violence have increased. This includes foiled plots for mass casualties, of which there were none the previous year. The report included “sustained harassment” and online campaigns in its assessment of more severe threats. The attacks took place across 64 mosques and buildings on their premises, with almost one fifth of those premises experiencing multiple attacks in the same year. The BMT, which was set up last year as the government’s watchdog for anti-Muslim hatred and threats, said the fluctuations showed “unchecked” low-level incidents had paved the way for more serious crimes. “This data tells an incredibly sombre story about the rise in anti-Muslim hostility that British Muslims are living with. Today, a mosque is vulnerable purely because it’s a mosque,” said the BMT’s chief executive Akeela Ahmed . “Security needs are increasing as a direct response to the severity of attacks that mosques are under. British Muslims are under attack due to the polarisation that is building and many Muslims are scared to go about their everyday lives.” The Home Office has allocated £40 million ($52.8 million) of funding to protect mosques and Muslim community organisations in the UK. The BMT had previously reported some mosques had experienced delays of up to 18 months in obtaining that official funding. The trust campaigns for a wider effort to tackle the underlying issues behind the security threats. “If we want to bring down the costs for protecting British Muslims in the UK, then we need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities,” Ms Ahmed said. “The rise in hate that we are witnessing is showing no signs of slowing down and until it does we need to make mosques a safe place for Muslim communities.” There was an increase of attacks on mosques during Ramadan, with a man in Ayr, Scotland, repeated using a heavy object to hit a window in a room where women and children had gathered to break their fast. A man was charged with terrorism-related crimes after allegedly stabbing worshippers outside a mosque in Edinburgh . Last year, a mosque was set on fire in Peacehaven, East Sussex. Twelve people were arrested for plotting an “extreme right wing terrorism-related” attack directed at an Islamic event in Ipswich in July, according to Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London. The report's authors faced questions over the inclusion of an attack on the former buildings of the East London Central Synagogue as one of the 78 attacks. The BMT said the attack followed an online hate campaign towards the local Somali community, members of which had announced their intention to buy the building and turn it into a mosque. The cause of the attack has not been identified, while two men were arrested on suspicion of involvement. “The community received a significant amount of online hate. When the arson attack happened, many local Muslim communities felt affected, alongside Jewish communities,” the BMT report said.

title: Oil prices rise on potential US strikes on Iran before midterm elections
description: Crude has been hovering above $100 a barrel despite a lull in hostilities
content: Oil prices jumped on Thursday after reports about Pentagon plans for US strikes on Iran that could be launched before the midterm elections amid continued Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, climbed nearly 3.86 per cent to $104.1 a barrel at 1.49pm UAE time, after falling below the $100 mark earlier this week. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, rose 3.78 per cent to $91.62 a barrel. Crude prices have been hovering above the $100 per barrel mark despite a lull in the US military campaign. US President Donald Trump, who is facing domestic backlash over the war, earlier indicated that the US would resume strikes only after the midterms. However, rising Iranian attacks in recent weeks on oil and gas tankers in the strait may force Mr Trump’s hand. The Atlantic on Tuesday reported that the US Defence Department was identifying targets for attacks in Iran. The size of potential strikes, if the US administration were to proceed with hostilities ahead of polls, was still being discussed, it said, quoting unnamed US officials. The US may choose to conduct a limited military campaign and follow it with a larger operation after polls conclude next month, The Atlantic reported. Axios quoted officials as saying potential operations could involve extensive US-Israeli strikes on Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets. “President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States,” the US news outlet quoted a White House official as saying. Israeli officials said the chances of renewed combat before the elections remain low but could rise significantly afterward, with escalation potentially triggering a major Iranian missile response, according to the report. "Renewed tensions — or, rather, the increasingly crowded headlines surrounding existing and persistent Middle East tensions — weighed on market sentiment," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. "Oil fluctuated, and Brent is extending gains above $102 per barrel." Traffic through the strait, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas flowed before the conflict broke out, has remained thin. The number of vessels transiting the strait fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months, according to shipping data from analytics firm Kpler. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data showed. Strikes on tankers climbed to their highest weekly rate since the conflict began on February 28. In the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's civilian and energy infrastructure are also adding to market jitters. Saudi Arabia's maritime blockade in the Red Sea by the Houthis and consistent strikes on Saudi Airports, ports and oil pipelines as well as refining facilities are stoking fears as an all-out war that would further crimp supplies energy supplies through the Bab El Mandeb strait. "The risks of multi-front escalation in the region and the war heading toward further fragmentation are boosting the risk premium in pricing," Samer Hasn, senior market analyst at XS.com said. "Nothing suggests a possible return to diplomacy; rather, all signs point to the situation in the region heading toward further deterioration at existing flashpoints and expanding into new ones."

title: The fight beyond the cage: Zamzam Al Hammadi’s promise to her mother
description: Emirati trailblazer opens up about her mother’s cancer battle, her Iraqi heritage and her ambition to become a world MMA champion
content: Zamzam Al Hammadi had just become a world champion when she saw her mother cry for the first time. She was befuddled by the tears. She had won; this was supposed to be a time for celebration. “I saw her crying for the first time, even though I was winning. I really didn’t understand if she was happy or sad. Then I asked her, ‘Mum, why are you crying?’ She told me, ‘I’m happy because you won, but I want to tell you something.’ I was like, ‘What?’ She told me, ‘I have cancer’, and I was like, ‘Mum, you’re kidding me, right?' She was like, ‘No.'" Al Hammadi became emotional recalling that moment. The smile that had barely left her face faded momentarily. “I told her, 'Mum, I’m going to fight with you. No matter what happens, I’m going to be by your side. I’m going to be with you and believe me, with me, I’m going to see your smile, I’m going to see your smile 24/7'.” Fighting is what Al Hammadi knows best. The 18-year-old is a two-time IMMAF youth world champion and the first Emirati woman to sign with the Professional Fighters League. She made a winning PFL Mena debut in Dubai in May in an amateur strawweight bout. Al Hammadi is bright, animated and a jolt of electricity in conversation. She’s gloriously expressive, extremely witty and incapable of harbouring a modest ambition. She’s shooting for the moon and at the very least hoping to land in the stars. Such was her ascent that she was invited to speak at Middlesex University Dubai’s Women in Sport Series, launched through its London Sport Institute. The opening discussion brought together Emirati athletes to speak about identity, heritage and the next generation. She agreed to speak to The National on the sidelines. What really shines through is her love for her mother, Nada Al Nuaymi, who serves as both her inspiration and the reason for her fierce ambition. Her mother was born and raised in the UAE but possesses Iraqi roots, two identities that she’s particularly proud of. Mention Iraq and Zamzam’s eyes light up. When she discovered during our conversation that I was Iraqi, she immediately called for her mother:. “Mum! Come here! She’s Iraqi! Can you believe it? She’s Iraqi!” The delight spread from her face to her mother’s as they conveyed their admiration for the country, explaining their ancestry. Iraq is a country that she has yet to visit, but Al Hammadi dreams of travelling there. “My blood is there, my blood is there. I always talk about it, and I’m really proud because I have the blood of real history makers. "My mum always talks about Iraqi history and to be honest, every day I’m learning new stuff about it and that makes me even prouder of it.” She indulges in her mother’s stories and the Iraqi cuisine she’s learning to cook. She’s already got quite good; she said her mother already considers her the best Iraqi cook in the house, which she considers both a blessing and a curse. “I can’t really cook it [Iraqi food] when I have to diet. When I’m on a diet, I just cry and think I’m losing my skills.” Al Hammadi has also developed a deep interest in the history of the country and spoke excitedly of studying Hammurabi, the former ruler of the first Babylonian dynasty, famed for creating the code of Hammurabi, the oldest and most complete written legal system in history. A lecturer once asked her why she was so interested. “I told him, because I have Iraqi blood, why not?” Despite being captivated by her maternal roots, she lives to serve her country, the UAE, the flag she carries into competition. “I’m not representing myself only. I’m not representing my family only. I’m representing my country. Before my name appears, it says Emirati,” a fact that makes her immensely proud. Al Hammadi is a trailblazer in UAE MMA. She is the first Emirati woman to sign for the PFL and aims to turn pro soon. Grander ambitions include becoming a world champion and to fight in the UFC. Still only 18, she is in her second year of studying for a degree in international relations, political economy and development and serves on the student council at Abu Dhabi's Zayed University. She once considered studying media because she likes broadcasting and, by her own admission, thought it would be an easier course. Her mother instead pushed her towards a degree that would help her serve her country. “She’d be like, 'Zamzam, what you’re doing is great, but I still think this is nothing. You need something bigger.'" Nada says she has been likened to a lioness for her ability to breed competitive fighters. Her younger daughter, Ghala, is also a decorated mixed martial artist and already owns one advantage that Zamzam is determined to challenge. Ghala once finished a fight in five seconds; Zamzam's quickest finish is six. “And now we’re really competing on this. I was like, ‘Ghala, I’m not stepping down until I get it in four seconds. You’re going to see Ghala, I’m coming for four seconds,'” Zamzam says with a grin. Asked whether their mother ever worries about raising so many well-trained fighters, Al Hammadi replies, “To be honest, we’re the ones scared of mum.” Al Hammadi refers to her mother as a cancer warrior. A single mother who has devoted her life to her children, she is full of admiration for her . Grateful for this, Al Hammadi is encouraged to keep competing and progressing as she feels it motivates her mother to continue treatment. “She’s fighting for her life, to survive. So why don’t I fight for her? So she feels that there’s someone with me who’s fighting as well?" Al Hammadi is also focused on helping the next generation of girls enter combat sports. She remembers a time she and her sister were the only girls from their group competing at the world championships She says more women are seriously considering a similar career, and much of that is down to representation. Athletes like Al Hammadi have helped create a pathway that many never thought possible. The jiu-jitsu and martial arts club that Zamzam established had few members in its first year. She says it now has 51 members, with fathers now actively approaching her to ask about opportunities for their daughters. Al Hammadi hopes that more Emirati women will come to represent the country in every sport. “At least one Emirati girl in every global organisation,” she said.

title: Hormuz traffic hits lowest level in two months as tanker attacks surge
description: Seven commodity vessels passed through strait on Tuesday, the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, Kpler data shows
content: ​The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest in more than two ⁠months after attacks on tankers in the key waterway reached their highest last week since the start of the ​ Iran war , shipping data showed. Seven commodity ships passed through the strait on Tuesday, for the ⁠lowest figure since July 23, data from analytics firm Kpler showed. “Crude crossing the strait fell ​27 per cent ⁠from a wartime high the week ‌before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” Kpler analysts Emmanuel Belostrino and Yui Torikata ​wrote in a note on October 6. “That is back to its September average, but 74 per cent of its prewar level.” Most of the fall was in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes move between tankers, they added. However, exports from the Gulf of Oman coast and the Red Sea rose to 6.7 million bpd, more than twice prewar levels, analysts said, making up for lost supply from Hormuz. This helped keep overall exports of Middle East crude at the prewar level, they said. The number of vessels transiting the strait edged up to 10 on Wednesday, but was well short of the daily tally of more than 20 on Sunday and Monday, the data showed. More vessels entered the strait than exited in the past two days. The figures exclude vessels crossing with their ​Automatic Identification System transponders turned off to avoid detection. LSEG data of all ‌vessels crossing the strait showed eight ⁠on Tuesday, evenly divided between entries and exits, ​down from the previous day's 14. These included five oil tankers and the liquefied ​natural gas tanker ‌Al Mafyar which loaded at Ras Laffan in Qatar and was set to head for Port Qasim ⁠in Pakistan, LSEG added. Attacks on tankers sailing through Hormuz hit their highest last week of ⁠any week since the Iran war began, maritime security sources tracking incidents said, as Gulf producers made a bigger export push. In the latest incident, projectiles struck a tanker 94km north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal, with casualties reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said ​on Wednesday. Before the February 28 start of the Iran war, about 125 large commercial vessels went through the strait each per day, comprising tankers, gas carriers, bulkers and container vessels. Their cargoes accounted for a fifth of global supplies of crude oil and liquefied natural gas.

title: Jon Rahm to quit LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
description: An attorney for the Spaniard told a US bankruptcy court the two-time major champion had reviewed details of LIV’s proposed next phase but had decided not to take part
content: Jon Rahm is quitting LIV Golf after deeming the proposed terms for LIV 2.0 "unacceptable", depriving the breakaway circuit of one of its biggest stars as it attempts to emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy and reshape its future. Rahm’s attorney, John Beck, told a US bankruptcy court hearing on Wednesday that the two-time major champion had reviewed details of LIV’s proposed next phase but had decided not to take part. “Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 … and has determined that those terms are unacceptable as to him,” Beck told the court. Rahm, a former world No 1, joined LIV in late 2023, eight months after winning the Masters to claim his second major title. He has since dominated the circuit’s season-long individual standings, winning three consecutive titles. Rahm’s departure is a major blow to a league already facing its biggest financial upheaval since its launch in 2022. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced in April that it would end its financial backing of LIV after the 2026 season , following an investment of more than $5 billion into the circuit. The decision prompted LIV to scale back operations, lay off most of its workforce, and ultimately file for Chapter 11 protection in New Jersey in September. PIF has agreed to provide a further $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing while the bankruptcy proceedings continue. The league’s bankruptcy filing listed several high-profile players among creditors with millions of dollars in unsecured claims, with Rahm’s claim the largest at $7.5 million. He is not the only player seeking an exit. Attorneys for Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith, An Byeong-hun, Marc Leishman, Cameron Tringale and Matthew Wolff asked the judge to allow their clients to terminate their existing LIV contracts and to clarify their ability to negotiate with other tournament organisers and sponsors. LIV has already agreed to terminate Sergio Garcia’s contract after determining it would not honour its terms. The requests do not necessarily rule out players joining LIV 2.0, with sources familiar with the league saying discussions over participation remain on track. Earlier this week, LIV secured up to $300 million in financing from BC Partners to help fund its emergence from restructuring and prepare for the 2027 season. The proposed new model would see players become equity owners in both LIV Golf and its teams, although the financing remains subject to court approval and customary conditions. Rahm’s decision, however, leaves LIV without one of its most recognisable faces as it attempts to secure its next chapter.

title: Oil’s long goodbye – what it means for the Gulf
description: The global shift away from oil could produce two opposing effects
content: Even as global oil demand continues to grow, albeit gradually, it is broadly understood that technological developments could eventually drive that demand to zero by the end of the 21st century. However, the latest economic research shows that such a fall in oil demand won’t necessarily mean a fall in oil production – in fact, in the short run, we may paradoxically see higher levels of oil consumption. This has important implications for Gulf countries . For the time being, setting aside the disruptions associated with the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz, oil demand is buoyant and growing at a steady pace. But there are strong forces in the background that are making analysts predict a terminal decline in the demand for oil starting in the middle of this century. These include sustainability commitments, the emergence of alternative technologies such as electric cars and solar power, and the desire by oil-consuming countries to achieve higher levels of energy security. If these forecasts are borne out, it is natural to imagine that falling demand for oil will lead to falling production. Yet this reasonable assumption may turn out to be misleading, as evidenced from recent research by University of Chicago professor Ryan Kellogg. Using simulations to predict what will happen to oil, Prof Kellogg identifies two forces that are pulling in opposite directions, making it unclear whether failing oil demand will indeed bring about a contraction in oil supply, or if it will motivate oil-rich countries to increase their production. Starting with the more intuitive scenario, Prof Kellogg notes that the production cycle for oil is both long and requires a lot of up-front capital expenditure. For example, when a new well is discovered, the process of mobilising the extraction equipment and initiating operations typically takes about five years with a large proportion of the spending occurring during that initial phase. In light of this, if producers forecast an impending significant contraction in oil demand, it makes sense for them to hold off on investing in new wells. After all, the market for their output might be gone (or at least severely curtailed) by the time operations start to run smoothly, while the bill for the setup will still need to be paid. Accordingly, under these conditions, oil production will simply follow its natural lifecycle of gently tapering off as existing operational fields dry up, resulting in global oil supply mirroring the decline in oil demand. Under such a scenario – which Prof Kellogg terms the “disinvestment” case – we would expect oil prices to be relatively stable. The more unusual scenario is what Prof Kellogg labels the “green paradox”, whereby policies that are ostensibly friendly to the environment cause a decrease in oil demand, but cause a sharp increase in oil supply that results in more oil being consumed during a transition period. This happens if oil-rich countries decide they want to avoid having their reserves turn into “stranded assets” , meaning that they try to get as much oil out into the market as possible today before the currently valuable resource becomes commercially non-viable in the future. This is somewhat analogous to stock markets: if you own stocks and you are suddenly informed that their price will fall next month, you will rush to call your broker and sell your stocks now before you suffer a capital loss. Notably, under the green paradox scenario – and unlike the disinvestment scenario – global oil prices will fall sharply as a supply glut collides with falling demand. Prof Kellogg also noted how the behaviour of the oil-producing group Opec can reinforce the green paradox. The bloc has for decades co-ordinated oil suppliers through production quotas to prevent oversupply, thereby implying a lower total volume in the market compared to a scenario where production decisions are decentralised and not co-ordinated. If an anticipated decline in oil demand leads to lower quota adherence by the group, the green paradox will be accentuated as a laxer output configuration becomes the norm. In practice, the world will not neatly fit into either the disinvestment or the green paradox scenario. The forces associated with each will materialise to some degree, meaning that either they cancel each other out, or whichever is stronger prevails. Given the strategic significance of oil, predicting what actually happens has important implications for carbon emissions, supply chain logistics, resource-related conflicts, and even economic planning, as in the case of the Gulf states’ visions. With this in mind, Prog Kellogg analyses the past behaviour of oil-producing countries to build a sophisticated model of the effect of an anticipated contraction in long-term oil demand on production and prices. His simulation suggests that the most likely outcome is for the disinvestment effect to be stronger than the green paradox effect, meaning that falling oil demand is broadly mirrored by falling oil supply, and oil prices will be relatively stable. A key reason for the model’s prediction is that – historically speaking – oil producers have demonstrated a significant preference for the present over the future, and with it an aversion to the large up-front investments needed for the green paradox effect to dominate. Environmentalists will surely be happy if this prediction plays out as it means that they need not worry that green policies – which check oil demand – result in a temporary boost to oil consumption. For most oil producers in the Arab world, such a path would also be preferable to oil markets devolving into a Hobbesian state of nature, as prices would remain higher for a longer time. Their status as low-cost producers would afford them a “last hurrah” as the global economy permanently shifts away from oil as it once did from coal. It is important to note that for producers, low production costs provide time, not immunity. They make the region’s oil likely to be among the last barrels produced, but they cannot guarantee either high prices or stable revenues. Economic diversification – and, more specifically, diversification of government revenue and exports – therefore remains indispensable. Its purpose is not to predict the precise date of peak oil demand, but to ensure that the region’s prosperity no longer depends on getting that prediction right. Policymakers in the region understand this well.

title: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar dies aged 75
description: Acclaimed star of Hindi and Marathi films was reportedly found unresponsive at his home in Goa
content: Acclaimed Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his work in Bollywood and Marathi cinema, died on Thursday aged 75. Patekar, who last appeared in the Bollywood film Housefull 5 , released in June, was found unresponsive at his home in Goa , hospital sources told Indian broadcaster NDTV. Dr Shekhar Salkar, chief of the oncology department at Manipal Hospital, told news agency ANI that doctors performed CPR for 45 minutes but were unable to revive the actor. He was pronounced dead at 5.20am. Patekar's family is yet to release a statement. Known for his commanding screen presence and distinctive dialogue delivery, Patekar portrayed a wide range of characters, from volatile and morally complex figures to comedic roles. He enjoyed success in both Bollywood and Marathi cinema. Patekar made his film debut in 1978 with Gaman, but his breakthrough role was with Mira Nair's Oscar-nominated film Salaam Bombay! . Patekar played Baba, a drug dealer and pimp, in the drama centred around Bombay's street kids. He went on to win a spate of awards for his roles in films such as Parinda (1989), in which he played a ruthless crime lord, and Krantiveer (1994) , in which he played a gambler turned fierce anti-corruption crusader. A monologue in Krantiveer , in which Patekar's character delivers a powerful message about Hindu-Muslim unity, is widely regarded as one of Hindi cinema's most memorable speeches. The role earned him a National Film Award for Best Actor. His other memorable performances came in films such as Agni Sakshi , Ab Tak Chhappan and Apaharan , showcasing his versatility across villainous, comedic and dramatic roles. In Khamoshi: The Musical , he played the deaf father of Manisha Koirala's character, a role that earned him wide acclaim. In 2013, he was awarded the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, for his contribution to cinema. He is survived by his wife, Neelakanti, and son, Malhar Patekar.

title: Juma Al Haj finds new meaning in seclusion with first institutional solo show in Abu Dhabi
description: Emirati artist’s exhibition considers reflection, uncertainty and moments that shape an inner journey
content: Juma Al Haj’s new exhibition arrives at a turning point in his life. Last June, after 15 years in a corporate career, the Emirati artist left his job and returned to university to fully commit himself to art. Revelation, now on view at 421 Arts Campus in Abu Dhabi, grew out of this period of reassessment. The exhibition – which is also Al Haj ’s first institutional solo show – was developed through 421’s Artistic Development Programme. Running until January 10, the show brings together painting, glass, text, light, shadow, water and installation in a meditation on seclusion, reflection and the idea that personal revelation is part of an continuing process rather than a final answer. Al Haj says the decision to become a full-time artist came relatively late. He studied visual communication before completing a master’s degree in international relations and moving into government work, following a path familiar to his family. His father is a diplomat, while his siblings also work in government and diplomacy. While art remained present, it was something separate from his professional life. “I always thought of it as a practice that I do in my spare time,” he says, describing that as a familiar regional attitude towards creative work. The assumption was that art could be pursued seriously, but not necessarily as a livelihood. That changed when he began posting his work online during the Covid-19 pandemic. The response encouraged him to take his practice more seriously. Between 2020 and 2021, he started to see art as a possible career rather than a parallel pursuit. Revelation grew from that shift. When Al Haj joined the Artistic Development Programme about two years ago, he initially wanted to explore seclusion and the idea of a maze, asking why people withdraw from the world when trying to understand difficult experiences. His thinking was shaped by journals, philosophy, poetry and spiritual texts from the three Abrahamic religions. Over time, however, the exhibition became less concerned with presenting a fixed narrative and more interested in creating a space where viewers could arrive at their own understanding. That is reflected in the way the works are installed. Glass panels carry text, but their meaning changes according to light, shadow and reflection. Al Haj says the object itself is only one part of the work. The surrounding conditions are equally important. He compares the panels to floppy disks that contain information revealed only when activated. Light performs that function in the exhibition, bringing inscriptions into view and casting shadows that become part of the experience. “The artwork is also the placement of the light, the placement of the panel and the reflection of the shadow,” he says. The installation gradually leads visitors towards Hijr , a darker and more enclosed space designed for contemplation. At the centre is water, which Al Haj uses as a symbol of movement and renewed energy. “Revelation is not an ending point; it’s just a checkpoint,” he says. The idea is that a person gathers what they need, reaches a moment of understanding and continues. The ripples in the water reinforce that sense of movement, with each disturbance creating another moment that quickly passes. That cyclical thinking also appears in Balaa , one of the exhibition’s early works. The title refers to the Arabic concept of trial or affliction. Al Haj uses it to think about the way people count and measure their lives, whether through time, emotions, deeds or individual moments. The tension comes from uncertainty: the constant questioning of whether choices are right or wrong, and whether progress can ever be measured with confidence. The exhibition is also designed to be physical rather than purely visual. A thick carpet covers the space, requiring visitors to remove their shoes. Al Haj connects that action to the experience of entering a sacred space such as a mosque, where removing footwear can signal respect and change a person’s awareness of their surroundings. The softness underfoot, along with subdued lighting and dark walls, is intended to slow the pace of the room. “The artwork is the atmosphere as opposed to the items within the room itself,” he adds. Black is used deliberately. Al Haj sees it as a contemplative colour that can bring certain elements forward while allowing others to recede. The room is meant to feel enclosed, but not oppressive. “It’s supposed to hug you like a cocoon, like a blanket,” he says. That approach extends ideas already present in his painting. Al Haj says his canvases can contain between seven and 14 layers, most of which are invisible once a work is complete. Revelation effectively opens up those layers and spreads them across a room, allowing viewers to move through a process that would normally remain compressed on a flat surface. “A lot of my work is about turning the intangible into something visually tangible,” he says. Al Haj is currently thinking more seriously about where his practice sits within the wider Emirati art scene. He describes himself as part of a third generation of Emirati artists , following an earlier period when institutions and opportunities were fewer. Today, he says, younger artists can begin earlier, experiment more freely and build careers with greater institutional support. At the same time, he believes exposure beyond the UAE remains important. He has just moved to Paris, partly motivated by a desire to understand the international art world from within, rather than only encountering it when major institutions and artists arrive in the Emirates. He warns younger artists against confusing international exposure with imitation. His advice is simple: “Leave the comforts of home but take home with you.” Al Haj’s visual language partly grew from Arabic handwriting exercises he practised as a child while attending an American school. This later fed into the gestural marks that appear across his work. The goal, he says, is not to remain bound by tradition, but to develop something recognisably personal. “Find your own language, stick to your roots, but don’t be confined by your roots.” Revelation by Juma Alhaj is on at 421 Arts Campus in Abu Dhabi until January 10

title: Premier League predictions as Arsenal host Leeds and Man United face Spurs
description: Picking out the winners and losers as the English top-flight returns after the international break
content: The Premier League returns on Saturday after one of the longest international breaks in memory. Below we try and pick the results from what looks like being a pivotal weekend of action. Arsenal saw their perfect start to the season end before the break as they fell to a 3-0 loss at Brighton, leaving the Gunners three points behind leaders Manchester City. Kai Havertz is an injury doubt after picking up a hamstring problem on international duty with Germany. Leeds go into the match unbeaten with two wins and three draws, the last of which was a stalemate at home to Crystal Palace. The Yorkshiremen are three points and three places shy of Arsenal in the table. Prediction: Arsenal 2 Leeds 0 Villa dragged themselves out of the bottom three when they defeated Spurs 3-2 in what was their first league win of the campaign, with Johan Manzambi, Nicolas Jackson and Emiliano Buendia scoring the goals. Brentford are one of five teams yet to lose a league game this season and were convincing 3-0 winners over Chelsea last time out – which saw Igor Thiago open his league account for the season – lifting the Bees to fourth in the table. Prediction: Villa 2 Brentford 1 Chelsea have dropped down to 10th place after taking one point from three matches and have the worst defensive record in the top flight, conceding 12 goals. Marco Rose has yet to win a game as Bournemouth manager, with the Cherries having drawn three and lost two so far. They will also be without key midfielder Alex Scott for two months after he picked up a thigh injury on his England debut. Prediction: Chelsea 3 Bournemouth 1 Ipswich have lost three of their past four matches, the last of which was a 1-0 defeat at Everton. The Tractor Boys still have six points on the board, though, and are in 11th place. Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa is still waiting for his first league win, but the Spaniard's side has shown signs of improvement after starting with three successive losses, as they drew with Liverpool and then Manchester United. The Cottagers are level on two points with bottom club Spurs. Prediction: Ipswich 2 Fulham 2 Sunderland are looking to avoid a third league loss on the spin after defeats by Arsenal and then Manchester City. The Black Cats are on four points, one place above the bottom three. Brighton are flying high in third place following wins over Coventry and Arsenal that saw Fabian Hurzeler's side score eight and concede none. Prediction: Sunderland 2 Brighton 2 United needed a last-minute deflected Matheus Cunha strike to avoid defeat at Fulham last time out, and the Red Devils have won only once in five league games. Spurs are rock bottom, without a win, and have scored just twice in five games, with those proving to be late consolations in the defeat at home to Villa. Prediction: Man United 2 Spurs 1 Palace have just one win so far, having drawn at Leeds before the break, leaving the Eagles one point and three places outside the bottom three. Forest are one point and two places above Palace, and have one win from five games, but fell to a surprise home loss to Coventry last time out. Prediction: Palace 1 Forest 1 Hull's fine unbeaten start was ended by a narrow loss at Newcastle, but the Tigers remain in the top half with eight points on the board. Everton are one point above Hull, with Thierno Barry's goal earning them a home win over Ipswich, their first victory since the opening weekend of the season, following three successive draws. Prediction: Hull 1 Everton 1 Liverpool are sixth in the table with three draws and two wins after Alexander Isak's goal earned manager Andoni Iraola a victory at his former club Bournemouth. Manchester City have won all seven games since losing to Arsenal in the Community Shield and top the table, but are back in action for the first time since being found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules . Top scorer Erling Haaland is also an injury concern. Expect a bear-pit atmosphere at Anfield. Prediction: Liverpool 3 Man City 1 Coventry secured their first top-flight win since April 2001 by beating Forest thanks to Jay Dasilva's second-half goal, ending a run of four successive defeats in which Frank Lampard's side had failed to score. Newcastle recovered from their 4-1 thumping at Leeds by edging Hull at St James' Park, with Joe Willock and Lewis Hall scoring the goals. The Magpies are in ninth place but are just one point off the top four. Prediction: Coventry 1 Newcastle 3

title: Ronaldo row and a top-of-the-table showdown as Saudi Pro League returns
description: We look at the main talking points as the Saudi top-flight returns to action following the international break
content: The Saudi Pro League returns to action following a three-week international break. The national team enjoyed success in the Arabian Gulf Cup, beating UAE 2-0 in Tuesday's final in Jeddah. Other SPL players also made headlines – not all of them good. We take a look at the main talking points ahead of the weekend's fixtures. Cristiano Ronaldo made headlines during the international break for all the wrong reasons. The Al Nassr striker abruptly walked out on Portugal ahead of a Uefa Nations League match in Denmark last week. On Tuesday, the 41-year-old released a lengthy statement, giving his version of events, saying he was not retiring , remained available for selection, while accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an “absolute breach of trust”. The row erupted after Ronaldo was an unused substitute in Portugal's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Norway on September 29, the first time in 18 years he had sat on the bench for an entire match for his national team. According to Ronaldo's account, Jesus had agreed the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of ⁠the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. “Everyone ​knows the ⁠rest. I warmed up from ‌half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager ​had broken his word to me.” The statement added that in a subsequent meeting between player and coach, mediated by Al Nassr sporting director Simao Coutinho, the parties agreed that Jesus would clarify events ahead of the Denmark match. According to the plan, Jesus would say that Ronaldo had never demanded to be played and that asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Jesus did not mention any of this when he spoke to reporters but later denied he had made any such agreement. “The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting,” Ronaldo explained. When Ronaldo learnt he would not play against the Danes, the player packed his bags and left the team's camp in Copenhagen. Ronaldo has said the Portuguese Football Federation should punish him accordingly, and said that he would make himself available for selection after any suspension that may come his way. Jesus, too, left the ​door open ‌for his return. Whether bridges can be rebuilt before the November internationals remains to be seen. When approached by reporters on Wednesday, Jesus said: "I read the statement, and now, as I do every day, I go to the federation to work, to think about the team and the national team.
