I have nothing more to say." It's all a far cry from the jubilant scenes just a few months ago when Jesus and Ronaldo celebrated leading Al Nassr to the Saudi Pro League title. Ronaldo will have been banking on the extra games with his country in his pursuit of 1,000 goals (he currently has 979). One hundred and forty-six of them have come for Portugal. Depending on how his Portugal future pans out, Nassr could end up the main beneficiary. Nassr resume their Saudi Pro League campaign on Friday against Diriyah. They sit in third place, two points behind leaders Al Hilal, with Al Ittihad sandwiched in between the two Riyadh clubs. A chastening defeat at UAE champions Al Ain in their first match of the AFC Champions League Elite saw Nassr get their league phase off to the worst possible start. Nassr welcome Uzbekistan's Neftchi Fergana to Al Awwal Park on Monday. Nassr coach Ange Postecoglou may have some sympathy for Jesus. The Australian has himself had to deal with Ronaldo taking issue with his team selections; Ronaldo felt snubbed after Postecoglou substituted him in the comeback win against Al Ettifaq on August 25. Nassr trailed 2-0 in that game when Ronaldo was subbed off in the 46th minute. By the end of it, they had won 3-2. Postecoglou, Jesus and Ronaldo have all said he should only be picked on merit, but it's hard to think that a player who has accomplished so much doesn't expect to be treated differently from his teammates. Managing Ronaldo used to be every coach's dream. Now it seems to be one of football's most difficult jobs. A top-of-the-table clash sees first-placed Al Hilal take on second-placed Al Ittihad at Kingdom Arena. Hilal suffered a first league defeat in 47 matches when they fell 2-0 to Neom on September 7, ending their 100 per cent start to the season. It was Hilal's first league defeat under Simone Inzaghi since he took the reins in the summer of 2025. They bounced back in spectacular style, thumping Al Taawoun 6-0 to head into the break on top of the pile. Saturday's opponents are the only unbeaten team left in the league, having won five and drawn two of their seven matches. The Jeddah club sit a point behind Hilal. Champions in 2024/25, Ittihad look like a team transformed under Jens Wissing, with Houssem Aouar one of the team's leading lights so far. The Algerian playmaker was part of that championship-winning side, and believes the Jeddah club are capable of pushing for honours again this season. “This season we want to achieve big things. I always say that when you play for a club like Al Ittihad, you have to win something every season,” he told the SPL's official website. “And it's in what we have to improve. To win things, you have to be focused, dedicate yourself to the club, to the pitch, and to make a lot of sacrifice. “The league is going up every season. You can see that now there is a lot of competition. You never know who's going to win the league until the end, until the very end of the game.” All kick-off times UAE time Friday Al Kholood v Al Qadsiah, 5.50pm Al Fateh v Al Ahli, 6.55pm Al Nassr v Diriyah, 10pm Saturday Al Hazem v Neom, 5.50pm Al Ettifaq v Al Khaleej, 6.55pm Al Hilal v Al Ittihad, 10pm Sunday Al Fayha v Al Riyadh, 5.40pm Abha v Al Faisaly, 7.25pm Al Shabab v Al Taawoun, 10pm

title: AI works best when everyone is able to use it
description: A new training programme in Abu Dhabi could be the first step in redefining citizens’ and residents’ relationship with artificial intelligence
content: For more than a decade, the UAE has been setting itself ambitious targets when it comes to artificial intelligence , embracing the technology at the highest levels of government, commerce and education. However, a key test of AI’s impact is not just the sophistication of the technology but by how many people are able to use it. For many ordinary people, AI is still something of an unknown quantity – and one that is being promoted by powerful and remote tech company owners. Despite excitement about potential AI-led breakthroughs in medicine and scientific discoveries, high-profile stories about jobs being lost to AI or autonomous digital agents hacking rival companies have raised questions about its uses. With that in mind, the launch in Abu Dhabi this week of AiNative, a new training programme, could be the first step in redefining citizens’ and residents’ relationship with AI. Developed by the emirate’s Department of Government Enablement in collaboration with OpenAI, Microsoft and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, AiNative aims to give 20,000 government employees access to training by the end of this year. Plans to eventually make the programme freely available to citizens and residents could prove to be even more consequential. Technology can widen inequalities as easily as it can reduce them. Those who understand new tools quickly can gain an advantage. Those who lack access to AI or confidence in using it, risk being left behind. This has been an issue with other game-changing technologies – many older people can still struggle with personal banking or medical appointments as more services migrate to online platforms. That is what makes the public element of AiNative particularly significant. The programme is intended to show people how AI adoption can help with practical matters, from finding a job, managing personal finances, running a small business or creating content responsibly. This recognises that the arrival of increasingly capable systems will affect just about everyone, whether or not they work in technology. The UAE has invested heavily in the AI era, and Abu Dhabi has emerged as a major centre for computing, tech investment and research. Partnerships such as those between Abu Dhabi’s G42 and France's Mistral AI announced last year are helping to build the foundations for the next iteration of AI – but human capability is just as important as infrastructure. Giving as many people as possible the opportunity to understand AI means giving them a better chance of recognising its strengths and weakness, and using it responsibly. The aim should not be to make everyone in society a computer scientist but to give them the chance to participate in the digital era confidently. Knowledge often dispels doubt and creates opportunities – by building an AI-enabled society, the potential for success becomes even greater.

title: Gaza has no MRI scanners or fully functioning hospitals one year after ceasefire, says Israeli rights group
description: World Health Organisation reports 128 attacks on medical facilities since Donald Trump-backed deal last October
content: Gaza is without a single fully functioning hospital a year on from the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas , an Israeli human rights group has said. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said Gaza also had no MRI equipment for its population of more than two million. It said, in a new report, that only a marginal improvement could be reported in Gaza's overall healthcare situation. The World Health Organisation says there were 128 attacks on medical facilities during the first seven months of the ceasefire. Intensive care capacity “has increased by one bed only – from 103 to 104”, PHRI said. Dialysis is less available than before, provided by 12 per cent of medical facilities compared to 17 per cent in October 2025. An Israeli blockade of Gaza's borders means only a fraction of Palestinians in need of medical treatment abroad have been able to receive it. Gaza's Ministry of Health reports that at least 1,570 patients have died, including 264 children, while waiting for medical evacuation. The ceasefire that began on October 10 last year ended the worst of Israel's two-year onslaught on the strip, which was triggered by the October 7 attacks of 2023 . But more than 1,400 people have been killed in near-daily attacks by Israel, which still occupies much of the territory. PHRI said Israel's restrictions on medicine and equipment, failure to allow patients to be treated abroad, and obstruction of efforts to repair Gaza's healthcare system were part of the pattern of alleged genocide. The international definition of genocide includes “the deliberate infliction of conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the Palestinian population”. “A year of ‘ceasefire’ should have brought meaningful relief and rehabilitation to Palestinians and allowed the recovery and reconstruction of the decimated healthcare system,” said Milena Ansari, a PHRI director who wrote the new report. “The data show that the ceasefire did not stop the genocide – it changed the way it is being carried out. Israeli policy continues to create conditions that prevent Palestinians in Gaza from recovering and surviving.” The ceasefire was agreed last October in a peace plan backed by US President Donald Trump . It was meant to be the beginning of restoring and rebuilding life in Gaza through reconstruction, aid and reversing many of the devastating effects of Israel's two-year war on the enclave. The war was triggered by a Hamas -led assault on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which militants killed nearly 1,200 people and took about 250 as hostages. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military response, which left most of the territory in ruin. The majority of Gaza's residents have been displaced and now live on a narrow area near the enclave's Mediterranean coast. With continuing attacks, and life largely distant from normality, many Gazans have wondered if the ceasefire only exists on paper , rather than reality.

title: UAE drive to cut sugar, salt and fat in food to make healthy choices easier, experts say
description: New regulations mark new milestone in drive to improve public health
author_name: Shireena Al Nowais, Alexander Christou, Nick Webster
content: The UAE’s new limits on salt, sugar and fat in packaged foods are an important shift towards changing the food environment itself, rather than placing the responsibility for healthier eating entirely on consumers, health experts have said. The new rules , approved on Tuesday, place caps on levels of sodium, sugar and fat in packaged foods, whether locally manufactured or imported. The rules are to be implemented in phases, with the final limits taking effect by December 31, 2030. They form part of a much wider effort across the UAE to tackle obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and other lifestyle-related conditions by changing the types of food people encounter every day. Dr Ahmed Al Khazraji, Executive Director of Healthy Living at the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, said the Cabinet resolution represented a major milestone for public health. “By focusing on commonly consumed products and introducing these changes progressively through 2030, we can improve their nutritional profile while giving manufacturers time to reformulate responsibly and maintain the taste and quality consumers expect,” he said. Dr Al Khazraji said the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre and the Ministry of Health and Prevention worked together to advance the food reformulation agenda. “The logic is simple: improve the nutritional profile of products that people already buy and enjoy, rather than placing the responsibility entirely on individuals to make a different choice every time,” he said. “This is part of our work across the food ecosystem, collaborating with government, producers, retailers and food service providers to improve what is available, how it is promoted and placed, and the information people have when making choices.” The move builds on years of measures aimed at improving public health. The UAE introduced excise taxes on tobacco, energy drinks and fizzy drinks in 2017, before expanding the system to e-cigarettes, vaping products and drinks containing added sugar or sweeteners. The country also introduced a sugar-based tax system for drinks, under which products with higher sugar content per 100ml face a higher tax rate. Abu Dhabi has introduced a parallel series of measures under its Healthy Living Strategy, including restrictions on where foods high in fat, salt and sugar can be displayed in large supermarkets, tighter controls on fast food advertising, stronger nutrition standards in schools and healthier menu requirements in hotels and restaurants. Doctors and dietitians say the changes could have an important cumulative effect because many people consume more salt, sugar and fat than they realise. Dr Safa Hegazin, staff physician at the Digestive Disease Institute at Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, said reducing excessive levels of those ingredients in commonly consumed foods could help support healthier dietary patterns over time. “Making healthier choices should not be difficult, and policies like these help ensure that the healthier option becomes the easier option,” she said. “As these changes are introduced over time, even modest reductions can contribute to meaningful long-term health benefits.” “Sustained improvements in diet can help reduce the risk of conditions associated with obesity and poor nutrition, including type 2 diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease,” she added. However, clinicians stressed that products meeting the new limits should not automatically be considered healthy. Heenana Mustaheena, clinical dietitian at LLH Hospital, Mussaffah, said much of the salt and sugar consumed by people is already present in packaged foods and can easily go unnoticed. “Most people consume far more salt, sugar, and unhealthy fat than they realise because much of it is already present in everyday packaged foods,” she said. “In the UAE, this is especially important given the high prevalence of excess salt intake.” She said consumers should continue to check nutrition labels and compare products, particularly by looking at nutritional values per 100g. “The limits represent maximum levels, and the actual amount consumed still depends on portion size,” she said. “Excess salt can raise blood pressure and increase the workload on the heart and kidneys, while excess sugar and fat can make blood glucose and weight more difficult to manage.” Dr Leila Kay Karimpoor, Consultant in Internal Medicine at Burjeel Medical City, also said the significance of the policy lay in addressing population-wide exposure rather than relying solely on individual behaviour. High sodium intake is associated with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, kidney problems and fluid retention, while excess added sugar can contribute to weight gain, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, she said. “Consumers should read labels and consider their overall diet, as meeting a regulatory limit does not necessarily make a processed food healthy,” she said. Food manufacturers have already begun responding to the wider health drive. Al Ain Farms Group previously announced reductions of 10 to 20 per cent in added sugar across some juices, flavoured milk, flavoured yoghurt and laban products, saying the reformulations were aligned with Abu Dhabi’s Healthy Living Strategy. United Foods Company, which produces edible oils and assorted food products, and distributes name brands like Oreo and Cadbury, said the new standards are something they feel prepared for. “We are following the international standards even while supplying to 62 countries worldwide,” said Mohamad Ziad Al Najjar, United Foods senior manager B2B. “When it comes to the healthy standards that Abu Dhabi and the UAE are implementing, it is not something that we have ever faced any challenges with. There is no risk to quality. We are caring for the customer by having all the options.” The Danish company Arla is a major international dairy co-operative that has had a presence in the UAE for decades. Berta Zammar, head of corporate affairs, communications and sustainability for UAE, Oman and Qatar, told The National at Global Food Week that the regulations are welcome and will succeed with private and public collaboration. “This circular is totally aligned with our position,” she said. “As our health strategy, it's aligned with our ambition. We are working a lot to move all our products to make them healthier and to be a part of national strategies. It's always a good thing to provide the consumer with healthy food.” Restrictions on the salt, sugar and fat content of food have been brought in around the world. Several European nations, including Denmark, Finland, Belgium, Croatia, the Netherlands, Hungary, Greece and Portugal, already have limits on how much salt can be used in bread production, ranging from 1.3g to 2g per 100g. Some countries in Europe extend those limits to cereals, cheese and processed meats. Elsewhere, countries require producers to add warning marks to labelling for foods that exceed strict thresholds for sugar, salt and saturated fat. Chile pioneered black octagon labels warning consumers about high content, as well as school marketing bans which have been replicated in Mexico, Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Venezuela and Uruguay. Similar warning flags or contrast colours on labels are used in Canada, Singapore and India to help guide consumers.

title: Hero flydubai captain was always ‘two steps’ ahead when on duty
description: Capt Smit Machchhar’s former colleague speaks of training and experience that helped his friend pull off a ‘miracle’
content: The experience and instinct of flydubai's Capt Smit Machchhar to prepare for any eventuality helped to prevent an “unimaginable” suspected terrorist attack, a friend has said. The flydubai captain saved the lives of 174 passengers when he opened the cockpit door of Flight FZ1073 despite life-threatening injuries from an emergency crash axe attack by a co-pilot. The mid-air attack began a few hours into a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight on September 30. Passengers overpowered the attacker, and reserve pilots diverted the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight to land safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Dharav Gosalia, a former colleague of Capt Machchhar, shed light on the fortitude of his friend of 14 years. “When you’re in the cruise phase all you have to do is ensure that the flight is being monitored, but Smit always had the habit of staying at least two steps ahead of the aircraft,” Capt Gosalia, 33, told The National . “He would prepare for what could happen to the aircraft, or what could happen to the weather, or what is the situation at the runway. This is instilled within you when you have been flying for so many years – to think a little ahead of the aircraft because it's a fast-flying machine and whatever can go wrong goes wrong in a fraction of a second. He had this habit of staying ahead, ready with a prompt reaction.” Capt Machchhar has been praised as a hero for his quick thinking and bravery, and is recovering from deep wounds to his head and hands in an Abu Dhabi hospital. UAE authorities are investigating the motives of the attempted terrorist attack in which the co-pilot tried to take control of the aircraft. The two men lived in the Ghatkopar suburb of northern Mumbai, completed flight training at the same academy in New Zealand and later flew Boeing 737s at India’s SpiceJet. Capt Machchhar was a commander with SpiceJet for 11 years and moved to Dubai with flydubai four years ago. Capt Gosalia then shifted to Air India. “It was a miracle that he came out of this,” Capt Gosalia said. “It was because of his presence of mind. It all boils down to all the experience and intuition built over the last 15 years of flying. “One thing is very clear for Smit or any captain – no matter what happens, the aircraft has to land safely with all the souls present on board. That would have been the only thing in his mind, that's what we have been taught.” Both captains had undergone training with retired senior Air Force commanders in India. But Capt Gosalia said no amount of training could prepare a captain for an attack from a co-pilot. "We have been trained for hijack protocols, incapacitation, security threats or abnormal scenarios, but an attack from a first officer sitting next to you who is your trusted wingman, it's impossible," he said. "I don't think in all years of flying anybody would have thought of this.” Rehearsing emergency procedures, visualisation or "chair flying" and the right attitude as a commander were key. “It all boils down to those small ‘chair flying’ or visualisation techniques, your nature before the flight that makes you the best in the cockpit,” Capt Gosalia said. “Chair flying is about going through a sequence of actions during maybe an engine failure or depressurisation. This is useful for an abnormal situation in the cockpit. "When your motor skills and muscle memory are good, it helps rehearse procedures and your hands automatically move to the right direction, like automatically putting in the right squawk [emergency] code.” Capt Machchhar’s approach was to treat the crew as his team, his friend said. “People want to fly with him,” Capt Gosalia said. “Whether it’s a crew member, loader or engineer he never treated anyone differently, he is that kind of person. He would carry the whole crew as a unit, as a team. Nobody felt left out. Smit is humble, warm and jovial.” When working for the Indian carrier, the men played cricket in a Mumbai suburb during their breaks and sometimes co-ordinated off-duty time overseas during layovers. “We used to fly a lot together. Apart from flying, we would check the roster to see where we could do our layovers and we would also meet for sports at home,” Capt Gosalia said. He said his long-time friend needed time to heal . “For other people, this is a story but not for him,” Capt Gosalia said. “For him, it’s a real thing that happened. His family needs space. What he went through inside the cockpit is just unimaginable. "The aircraft plunging with a heavy rate of descent, it's almost vertical, he is trying to reach the door while completely wounded. Hats off to what he pulled off. He will definitely come out strong. And every one of us is proud to know him.”

title: London phone theft crackdown leads to 700 arrests
description: Met Police officers chase thieves on specially adapted motorbikes
content: Police have arrested hundreds of people in their biggest operation against mobile phone theft in London, as figures show the number stolen is at a four-year low. Met Police officers chased suspects at high speed to reunite victims with their phones and searched second-hand phone shops suspected of handling stolen devices. The force says it has arrested more than 700 people as part of Operation Reckoning and has seized hundreds of mobile phones suspected of being stolen in one month. In recent years, London has been plagued by mobile phone thefts, harming its image at home and abroad as a safe place to visit and work. The Met has faced criticism for its apparent inability to find stolen phones, even when tracking apps directed officers to their location. In response, the force began dedicating resources to tackle the problem, including the use of specially adapted motorcycles and drones. Major successes include breaking up a gang responsible for trafficking up to 40,000 stolen iPhones from the UK to China in 2024 and 2025. Officers say the haul accounted for about 40 per cent of all phones stolen in London during that period. New data released today by the Met shows phone theft and robbery offences have fallen to their lowest August level since 2022. In August, 3,963 offences were recorded across London compared with 3,311 offences in August 2022. Commander Andy Featherstone, the Met’s lead for tackling phone theft, said figures were a reflection of the “Met’s relentless campaign to crack down on these criminals”. “This was our biggest operation yet, with officers targeting every stage of the organised criminal chain, including street thieves, handlers and exporters," he said. “Our message to these criminals is clear: London is becoming a much harder place to steal phones. The risks are increasing, the opportunities are shrinking, and we are coming after you.” The Met has released CCTV and body-cam footage that captured the moment a suspected phone thief who had fled on an e-bike jumped into a pond, discarding several phones in an effort to avoid arrest. Officers chased him on high-powered Sur-Ron e-bikes and waded into the park to fish out six phones wrapped in foil, a tactic used by thieves to block signals and hinder tracking. He was arrested moments later. The operation, which took place in September, also included arrests on suspicion of robbery and handling stolen goods. Officers also seized drugs, knives, firearms, tens of thousands of pounds in cash, and more than 110 illegal e-bikes. The Met says the arrests underline how organised criminals involved in phone theft are often linked to wider offending, including drug supply. Officers also visited 220 second-hand phone shops across London to gather intelligence and build positive relationships with legitimate businesses. The results come as the Met and Apple continue to share intelligence on stolen devices, helping officers to track phones in the UK and abroad. Early data also indicates that as security on phones has improved, criminals are increasingly using new “social engineering” tactics to hack into devices. By posing as trusted organisations, they contact victims on other devices, trying to obtain passwords and account details that can be used to unlock devices. In some cases, criminals use threats to pressure victims into handing over information.

title: UAE report examines how to power AI in a water-scarce world
description: 'Integrated governance' needed amid fears of widespread shortages, Foreign Ministry says
content: Artificial intelligence has become a major focus for global water and energy, bringing significant new demands while offering tools to improve water management, a report from the UAE Foreign Ministry has said. The report, Crosscurrents: Navigating the AI-Water -Energy Nexus , highlights that integrated planning and governance are essential to ensuring the technology advances sustainably without contributing to water scarcity . "The extraordinary rise of artificial intelligence has brought with it a paradigm shift in both the nature of the global water crisis and our ability to address it," Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed , Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, said in the executive summary of the report. Sheikh Abdullah said that as water scarcity intensifies alongside the expansion of AI, governments and industry must manage water, energy and digital infrastructure as a single interconnected system. The report maps water use across the AI value chain, including semiconductor manufacturing , electricity generation and cooling infrastructure, while also emphasising that indirect water use, particularly in power generation and chip production, often exceeds direct consumption at data centres themselves. It added that policymakers have overlooked the implications of the effect of AI's rapid expansion on resources. Data centre water use is projected to about double by 2030, reaching 9.32 trillion litres. In January, the UN said that parts of the world have entered water bankruptcy , meaning depletion that cannot realistically be reversed. The report also highlights that a key constraint on future AI growth is political. Using examples from the US, Malaysia, Chile and Ireland, the report points to how community concerns about water access, electricity demands and other issues are delaying or reshaping large data centre projects. To address these concerns, the report highlights significant opportunities for AI to improve water management. It points to projects in the UAE , such as MaiWater, that have integrated AI with renewable energy and water planning, including advanced data centre cooling and strategic water storage. "AI is opening possibilities that could scarcely have been imagined only a few years ago," Sheikh Abdullah said. "Used wisely, it could help us solve one of humanity’s oldest and most fundamental challenges: ensuring safe and reliable access to water for all." The report gives five recommendations for future AI development: establishing international co-operation on responsible AI water use; integrating AI infrastructure into water and energy planning; requiring transparent resource-use reporting; promoting low-water and low-energy technologies; and embedding water and climate risk into corporate strategy. "The priority is integrated governance: planning water, energy, infrastructure, and data as mutually dependent systems," the report says. The UAE and Senegal will host the 2026 UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December. The report called the event a "premier opportunity to turn responsible AI development into a shared global agenda".

title: Jordanian-American woman's body identified after being pulled out of Texas river
description: Rana Nofal Soluri's roommate has admitted killing her after he 'snapped' during argument
content: The body of a Jordanian-American flight attendant who disappeared a year ago has been identified after being pulled out of a Texas river. Rana Nofal Soluri's body was found in June by a fisherman under a bridge in Montague County, about 40km from Fort Worth, local media reported. Her remains were taken to the University of North Texas Health Centre for Human Identification, where DNA testing confirmed her identity, police told NBC News. Ms Soluri, 47, worked for a subsidiary of American Airlines and was reported missing in March last year after she failed to return to work following time off for a medical procedure. Her roommate, Dennis William Day, 67, was arrested and charged with murder in June after he confessed to killing her and throwing her body off a bridge. Police said Mr Day admitted he had “snapped” during a dispute with Ms Soluri and strangled her, according to an arrest warrant quoted in media reports. Law enforcement agents said home video from Mr Day’s property showed him dragging what appeared to be a body from the house into the backyard on March 21, 2025. Mr Day is currently awaiting trial. An “inadvertent call” and voice mail on another woman’s phone appeared to capture Mr Day asking for help with moving the body. The woman, Joni Thomas, was arrested on charges of tampering with evidence. Ms Soluri's sister, Nez, told NBC the months after the disappearance were “torture”. She said her sister had been a proud Jordanian-Palestinian and a “firecracker”. “She might've been in a small frame but she had a big personality,” she added. A GoFundMe page has been set up for Ms Soluri's daughter, Lulu, to help with burial costs and other expenses.

title: Will Trump's data centre reckoning boost Democrats in the midterms?
description: US electorate growing increasingly agitated by tech executives as midterm elections loom
content: A major issue in the coming US midterm elections is data centre construction – and according to polls, that's good news for Democrats and bad news for Republicans. President Donald Trump has continued to say that data centre and AI fears are a hoax , but recent polling shows that his decision to double down on unregulated artificial intelligence might cost his party the House and Senate. Recent surveys show that in the US, concerns about AI causing widespread labour disruption and data centres' high energy needs are growing. In some parts of the US, data centres have popped up in once-tranquil residential neighbourhoods, causing audible and visual nuisances. Critics have alleged that data centres also have a negative impact on the environment. These issues have led to protests, anger at town halls and, in some cases, new laws. Democrats, seen by many voters as being more likely to regulate the private sector, have benefited from the current climate. About 73 per cent of voters, regardless of party, oppose the building of AI data centres in their community, a recent Quinnipiac University poll indicated. Other surveys have essentially told the same story. Though most polls have indicated the economy and the cost of living are top concerns as the midterm elections near, that, too, plays into AI and data centre fears, experts say, with the general public seeing technology companies as greedy. In Tennessee, Democratic state legislator Justin Pearson has made his opposition to data centres a focal point of his campaign for Congress. Mr Pearson has called out technology tycoon Elon Musk, whose company xAI operates Colossus, one of the largest data centres in Memphis. Colossus has been the subject of countless community meetings amid allegations of pollution, a sharp rise in electricity bills and an overall disregard for the well-being of residents. The Democratic politician has been a frequent speaker at public meetings on the issue, demanding more accountability from xAI and pushing for a moratorium on data centre construction. “Tech oligarchs and Elon Musk are targeting our community because they believe that our community is somehow the path of least resistance,” Mr Pearson says in one of several campaign videos. Timothy Kneeland , a political scientist and public policy historian at Nazareth University in western New York, says there is plenty of data to suggest there is electoral substance behind the AI and data centre concerns. “A lot of Americans simply don't think President Trump is taking these concerns seriously,” he said. A backlash against technology executives and a perceived disregard for community concerns is being felt at just about every level of government, he added. “It's causing quite a stir in the US midterm elections and even in some state legislative races across the US.” There has been a rise in political adverts portraying a dystopian future in which technology executives call the shots. Michigan Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed has drawn attention to his Republican opponent Mike Rogers's investments in data centre firms and ties to various technology companies. “You can't have your privacy violated if you don't know your privacy is violated,” a quote from Mr Rogers plays throughout one of Mr El-Sayed's adverts. The video also shows headlines covering the growing anger in the US related to Flock cameras, which have come under intense scrutiny over their use of automatic licence plate reading technology, motion and sound sensors, and a vast database aimed at tracking criminals and assisting law enforcement. But rights groups such as the American Civil Liberties Union say Flock cameras violate privacy laws, are sometimes misused by law enforcement and build a nationwide surveillance network. “If there are Flock cameras in your city, they are tracking, logging and sharing your movements without a warrant,” ACLU's Flock website awareness message reads. Mr Kneeland said in some parts of the US, opposition and anger towards Flock cameras is so intense that it is actually causing some elected officials to change their views. “These concerns are now shaping Republican candidates for the Senate, the House of Representatives and in state races,” he said. “This is a clear break with the de facto head of the Republican Party, President Donald Trump, who has called for unregulated AI development, the expansion of data centres, and is strong on law and order which Flock cameras are often associated with.” In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the US Senate following his 2024 re-election loss, focusing on holding data centre companies more accountable. “Ohio's electric grid is being treated like a game by gobbling up energy to feed their data centres,” Mr Brown says in one advert targeting incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, of whom Mr Brown says has repeatedly sought more data centre construction in the state. “I'm Sherrod Brown and I'll require the data centres to pay the full cost of their electricity, not you.” Even in Republican states like Texas, as Mr Kneeland points out, the Republican Governor Greg Abbott has shifted his stance on data centres. “He once suggested Texas should become a hub for AI development and activity, but has since has backed away from this and sponsored a bill to tighten up regulation,” he said. The midterm elections will take place on November 3.

title: Under-pressure Araghchi defends Iran's war diplomacy
description: Foreign Minister says Iran making 'serious' efforts after impeachment motion
content: Iran 's Foreign Minister Abbas Arachghi on Wednesday defended his efforts to end the war with the US amid criticism from within political circles. Mr Araghchi fielded three hours of questions from members of Iran's parliament, the Islamic Consultative Assembly, which could in theory hear a motion on his impeachment after it was filed by a critical MP. The case relates to claims that Mr Araghchi overstepped by holding a meeting with US officials in New York without the permission of Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei . MPs also informed Mr Araghchi of "public concern" about Iran's unity and cohesion, state media said. It is the latest hint of division within Iran's political circles, which have been reshaped by the war and the killing of senior figures such as Ayatollah Ali Khamenei . Mr Araghchi said the delegation he led at the UN General Assembly in New York had "explained Iran's positions in the most eloquent and authoritative manner possible". He said his team had followed the instructions of "competent authorities" in Iran. "Iran showed in New York that it is tough in defending itself and serious in using diplomacy to ensure national security," state media quoted Mr Araghchi as saying. Mr Araghchi is proposing a "seven-day plan" that would count down to reopening the Strait of Hormuz in a week if the US accepts Iran's conditions. US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran's offer. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control” of the strait, saying oil flows through the waterway had returned to near prewar levels. The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler. The figures include shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and by other methods. Mr Rubio said Iran was facing “crippling sanctions” and that its economy was in “total and complete free fall”. He predicted its economy “is about to reach a point that few countries in the world have experienced in terms of how bad it is going to get”.

title: Saudi Arabia suspends four companies for putting Umrah pilgrims in unlicensed housing
description: Ministry of Hajj and Umrah says four foreign agents also disciplined
content: Four companies offering Umrah pilgrimages to Makkah have been suspended after visitors were provided with unlicensed housing, Saudi authorities said. Saudi Arabia 's Ministry of Hajj and Umrah said the companies, as well as four agents, were disciplined for violations that “affected a number of pilgrims”. It said the breaches “involved the accommodation of pilgrims in unlicensed facilities”. The companies have been referred to a Committee for Reviewing Pilgrims' Complaints, which could issue penalties. The ministry warned companies providing Umrah services they are subject to “field and digital monitoring” to check they meet requirements. The so-called Pilgrim Experience Programme to improve services for religious visitors is one plank of Saudi Arabia's economic modernisation plan as it aims to become a tourism centre. Umrah is a pilgrimage to Makkah that can be performed at any time of year, unlike Hajj, which takes place during a specific window in the Islamic calendar. Although not mandatory like Hajj , Umrah holds great spiritual significance for Muslims around the world. The ministry this year introduced a new Umrah visa allowing pilgrims to visit Saudi Arabia several times in one year, with a maximum cumulative stay of 90 days. Hajj packages usually include accommodation and transport as part of wider pilgrimage arrangements, while Umrah travellers have more flexibility to book hotels directly. The current Umrah season runs until April 7, about five weeks before Hajj is expected to begin in May 2027.

title: UAE seeks to boost Gulf industrial integration and supply chain resilience
description: Delegation participates in GCC Ministerial Meetings in Bahrain
content: The UAE is seeking to boost industrial integration with Gulf states, as the region explores ways to strengthen supply chain resilience at high-level meetings in Bahrain. A UAE delegation led by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, is participating at the GCC Industrial Co-operation Committee and the Ministerial Committee for Standardisation Affairs meeting being held in Bahrain. The UAE’s participation focuses on “strengthening industrial integration among GCC countries, building more resilient and competitive Gulf supply chains, accelerating the deployment of advanced technology and artificial intelligence in the industrial sector, and enhancing the role of the private sector in building partnerships and joint industrial opportunities”, the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology said in a statement on Wednesday. The meetings, which began Tuesday and will continue until Thursday, highlighted the need for co-ordination in standards. Dr Al Jaber emphasised the importance of advancing joint efforts to develop a more advanced industrial sector that supports the diversification of national economies and strengthens the GCC's position as a global hub for industry and innovation. “Industrial integration is a cornerstone of Gulf competitiveness,” he added. The meetings took place on the sidelines of the inaugural Made in GCC Forum and Exhibition 2026 being held in Manama. The event is aimed at boosting collaboration and partnerships across investment, manufacturing, supply chains and technology. Key outcomes of the meetings include the launch of the Gulf Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution and its digital platform aimed at enhancing the digital maturity of factories and supporting industrial transformation, the GCC Council said in a statement. The evaluation period for the amended rules on exempting industrial inputs from customs duties was extended until the end of 2027. The UAE’s participation comes amid a strong push towards domestic manufacturing in the country. The industrial sector plays a key role in the national economy, with its contribution having reached Dh200 billion ($54.45 billion) – an increase of 70 per cent. Its industrial exports reached Dh260 billion last year, including Dh92 billion in medium-and high-technology industrial exports. The Emirates also launched its industrial strategy, Operation 300bn , in 2021, to position itself as a global industrial hub by 2031. The UAE’s overarching agenda is focused on priority industries including chemicals, electrical, construction, machinery and equipment, food, transport, metals, pharmaceuticals, rubber, plastic and fibreglass, and wood and paper. The Emirates has in recent years also invested heavily in advance technology and AI, with multibillion-dollar projects being built. In May, the UAE launched the Dh1 billion National Industrial Resilience Fund to support the industrial sector and announced a national strategy to secure supply chains and boost local food, medicine and industrial production. Meanwhile, the country's National In-Country Value (ICV) programme has redirected more than Dh473 billion into the national economy. The UAE is pushing for deeper industrial co-operation across the Gulf as countries seek to localise supply chains and reduce their reliance on imports following disruption exposed by the Covid-19 pandemic and other global shocks, Dr Farah Al Zarouni, assistant undersecretary for the Standardisation Affairs sector at the ministry, told The National . “We need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries,” she said. The Made in GCC event is expected to involve the signing of a number of initial pacts between UAE entities and Gulf companies, the ministry said. The UAE is participating with 23 Emirati companies spanning sectors including basic industries, pharmaceuticals, defence and spare parts. “We no longer look at industry as simply traditional manufacturing. We are moving our national industry towards more advanced manufacturing,” Ms Al Zarouni said. “Technology is a very important and fundamental component of our national industrial sector.” The experience of the six years since the pandemic has highlighted the vulnerability created when countries depend heavily on overseas suppliers for relatively small components for manufacturing. “If I had been able to source that small component locally, the component that enabled me to produce the final product, I would not have been affected to the same extent,” she said. The priority now should be to identify which raw materials and components can be produced within the UAE or elsewhere in the GCC, she said. “Supply chains are long, so you need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries.”

title: Dubai launches Create AI Agents Championship with prize money exceeding Dh2.5m
description: New competition offers grants of Dh550,000 per category with top prize of Dh1m
content: Dubai has launched the Create AI Agents Championship, replacing its successful app development competition , as the emirate accelerates its push to lead global innovation in artificial intelligence . Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, announced the event at an awards ceremony honouring winners of the third Create Apps Championship at Emirates Towers Boulevard on Wednesday. Sheikh Hamdan said the initiative would make Dubai “the first city to lead innovation in this field”, shaping future approaches to service delivery and placing people at the centre of technological advancement. The new championship shifts focus from digital application development to the creation of autonomous AI-agent systems designed to address real-world challenges. Open to all ages and backgrounds from around the world, it accepts entries ranging from innovative ideas and early-stage prototypes to minimum viable products. Fully commercialised solutions are not eligible. Participants will compete in four categories: Best Societal AI Agent, Best Personal AI Agent, Best Business AI Agent, and Best Youth AI Agent, the latter open to those under 21. Each category winner will receive a grant of Dh550,000 ($150,000), with one overall winner awarded the AI Agent of the Year title and Dh1 million. Total prize money exceeds Dh2.5 million. Registration is now open, with workshops and a Digital Academy offering advanced training courses and mentorship sessions planned throughout November and December. At the same ceremony, winners of the Create Apps Championship were announced. POP by Kwelio, a smart medication-adherence app using behavioural science and predictive analytics, claimed both the Longevity App of the Year award and the title of Dubai's App of the Year. Since it was launched in 2023, the Create Apps Championship has attracted 15,564 apps from 153 countries and supported the launch of more than 140 apps.

title: IEA members support faster release of reserve oil stocks
description: Agency says members agree to prioritise release of diesel stocks
content: Members of the International Energy Agency (IEA) expressed support on Wednesday for accelerating the release of roughly 100 million barrels of reserve oil stocks previously agreed to in March. About 325 million barrels of oil have been released under the March agreement to ease oil markets after the onset of the Iran war led to a surge in energy prices. The IEA also said members had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks. Member countries still hold roughly 1.1 billion barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel. “The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required,” executive director Fatih Birol said in a statement. “Participants in the meeting expressed strong appreciation for the IEA’s response to the energy impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis." Mr Birol said members also welcomed last week's statement by G7 leaders on global energy and security, and agreed to assess and review the situation at the IEA governing board meeting next week. G7 member countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA, following pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have triggered a global surge in fuel prices, adding to pressure on Mr Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. On Monday, he signed an executive order waiving restrictions on cheaper red-dyed diesel, which could ease price pressures for lorry drivers, who are facing higher costs at the pump that could be passed down to consumers. Diesel prices have risen to more than $6 per gallon in recent weeks, compared to the average price of $3.60 per gallon this time last year. The White House said the federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fuel. Europe is also facing higher diesel prices, which hit a record of €2.24 per litre, compared to €1.59 before the Iran war began on February 28. The US is currently in the process of a 172-million-barrel drawdown from its strategic petroleum reserve. Once completed, the SPR is projected to fall to its lowest levels since 1982.

title: What happens if the UN cannot agree on Antonio Guterres’s successor?
description: Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica led fifth straw poll on Wednesday
content: Less than three months before UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres's term expires, the Security Council has not decided who will succeed him, and the rules offer little guidance on what happens if the panel cannot agree on an applicant. Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica led the fifth straw poll on October 7 with nine “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes with no council members expressing “no opinion.” The result, however, marked a setback from the previous round on September 29 , when she received 10 “encourage” votes, three “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes. Her support slipped in the latest ballot, while opposition to her candidacy increased. She remains short of a clear consensus. A candidate needs at least nine votes in the 15-member Council and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members. The Council has not yet moved to a colour-coded ballot, which would reveal whether any of the five veto-wielding members had voted against a candidate. Ben Cohen, who focuses on international organisations at the Foundation for the Defence of Democracies, said Ms Grynspan was unlikely to be Washington’s first choice. But she could emerge as a compromise candidate if the five permanent members of the Security Council reject the other leading contenders and agree that they could accept her, he said. The selection carries particular significance this year. In its 81-year history, the UN has never been led by a woman, and several women are among the candidates seeking the post. Should none of the publicly named contenders have a veto-proof way forward in their applications, other names have been unofficially suggested as possible candidates, including Nickolay Mladenov , head of the Board of Peace, and UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh , who has not publicly commented on the race. Diplomats have suggested that new candidates or a “dark horse” could enter the contest as the permanent members seek consensus. Esther Brimmer, former US assistant secretary of state for international organisation affairs in the administration of president Barack Obama, said she thinks it is possible a new candidate will emerge. “That variable I think is also keeping everyone concerned about what the outcome will be,” Ms Brimmer told The National. Some diplomats have also raised the possibility that the US could push for a candidate from the business world, reflecting Washington’s concerns about the UN’s finances and bloated bureaucracy. “I did hear about that as well,” said Mr Cohen. “They could parachute in a capable businessperson with a good record of balancing books and doing budgets.” He said such a candidate could appeal to Washington because of its concerns that the UN is financially wasteful, duplicates functions and is burdened by an oversized bureaucracy. But Mr Cohen questioned whether such a candidate could win the support of Russia and China, both of which hold vetoes over the selection of the next secretary general. “Is it going to fly with the Russians and the Chinese?” he asked. Under the UN Charter, the General Assembly appoints the Secretary General on the recommendation of the Security Council. But the Charter does not state what happens if the Council fails to agree on a candidate. Experts say several scenarios could emerge. Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group's global issues and institutions programme director, said he believed Mr Guterres had little appetite to remain in office beyond the expiry of his second five-year term. He said Washington appears opposed to an extension anyway. “I don't think Guterres wants to stay on even one more day and he is not going to volunteer to be a lame duck indefinitely,” Mr Gowan said. The General Assembly, which usually ratifies the council's choice as a formality, might press for a bigger voice. “Nobody is very clear what happens if the secretary general's chair is empty on January 1,” said Mr Gowan. “Some member states are cooking up plans for the General Assembly to install a new UN chief without a recommendation from the Security Council. But that could get very messy indeed, as I think the veto powers might refuse to recognise the legitimacy of anyone who does not have Council endorsement.” The UN has never let a secretary general's term lapse without a successor or an extension in place. It has, however, come close. In 1981, the Council deadlocked for weeks as China backed Salim Salim of Tanzania and the US opposed him, while Austria’s Kurt Waldheim sought a third term. After 16 rounds of voting, the Council turned to Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru in mid-December, less than three weeks before the term expired. The 1996 selection was nearly as tight. Washington vetoed a second term for Egypt’s Boutros Boutros-Ghali, and African governments resisted alternatives for weeks. Ghana’s Kofi Annan was recommended in mid-December and appointed days later. The closest precedent for a gap came in 1950, when the Soviet Union vetoed a second term for Trygve Lie of Norway and the Council could not agree on anyone else. The General Assembly extended Mr Lie's term by three years on its own, without a Council recommendation. Moscow called the move illegal and refused to deal with him, and he resigned in 1952. A more likely temporary solution, said Mr Gowan, would be for a group of senior UN officials to oversee the organisation, with one official serving as its senior administrative officer without formally assuming the title of acting secretary general. Mr Gowan said he still expected the five permanent Security Council members to reach a last-minute compromise rather than allow the post to become vacant. “I do not think the P5 actually want this car crash,” he said. “They know it would make them look very silly and raise questions about their competence to steer the UN more generally. So I think a last-minute compromise is still more likely than an empty chair.” “But with the big powers in their current state, a car crash is possible.”

title: Iran has 'lost complete control' of Strait of Hormuz', US claims
description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says 'almost as much oil flowing out as before conflict', as IRGC insists sea lane is closed
author_name: Amr  Mostafa, Kyle Fitzgerald, Jennifer Gnana
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz, saying oil flows through the waterway had returned to near prewar levels. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began. So they’ve lost complete control of the strait,” Mr Rubio told a press conference in Athens. He said Iran was facing “crippling sanctions ” and that its economy was in “total and complete free fall”. He predicted its economy “is about to reach a point that few countries in the world have experienced in terms of how bad it is going to get”. The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler. The figures include shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and by other methods. Mr Rubio accused Iran’s leadership of spending state revenue on Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias and the Houthis, rather than on infrastructure or improving the lives of Iranians. “Every dollar and every penny that regime gets, they don’t spend it on roads or bridges or helping improve the lives of the Iranian people,” he said. “They spend that money on Hezbollah and Hamas, on militias that fire rockets out of Iraq and on the Houthis. That’s who they spend their money on. They should have spent their money on their people. Instead, they spend their money on terrorism and weapons.” Brig Gen Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the IRGC commander-in-chief, maintained Iran’s stance that the strait is closed and that its armed forces have “full control” over it. He said this would continue until Iran’s “legitimate demands” are met. He added that transit routes in the strait deemed illegal by Iran would soon be closed, apparently referring to the southern route flanking Oman’s coast. Brig Gen Naqdi said the “few routes” had been created by blasting and damaging rocky passages in the strategic waterway and were being used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring it to tankers”, challenging the narrative that Gulf oil exports are returning to prewar levels. US Vice President JD Vance has said Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to meet Washington’s demands and end the seven-month war. Mr Vance, in an interview with Reuters, said any agreement could not rely on Iranian assurances of future nuclear drawdowns, arguing that Tehran must take concrete steps to reduce its enrichment capacity. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 per cent enriched fuel?” Mr Vance said, calling it a “very basic threshold issue”. “I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he said. The head of the International Monetary Fund said the energy-price shock driven by the US-Iran war has been large but contained. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to market. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline, which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through its own East-West Pipeline. Meanwhile, Middle East refining capacity is now recovering rapidly from disruption caused by the conflict, Tom Baker, managing director for Vitol in Bahrain, said at an industry forum in Fujairah on Wednesday. About two million barrels a day of refining capacity has been knocked out in Russia, while the Middle East suffered similar issues and capacity in China has also been down, he said. “We had similar [refinery disruption] in the Middle East but it’s recovering very rapidly now,” Mr Baker said. Iran and the US have exchanged proposals aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz but US President Donald Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer. Mr Vance said Washington remained open to a deal but would demand concrete Iranian concessions. “We’re not going to trade words for actions,” he said.

title: Crown Prince of Jordan and European leaders discuss energy crisis caused by Hormuz blockade
description: Energy prices, diplomacy with Iran and migration high on agenda of talks
content: Crown Prince Hussein of Jordan joined a European leaders' meeting on Wednesday in Croatia to discuss the energy crisis caused by Iran. Leaders of the MED9 group – Croatia, Cyprus, France, Greece, Italy, Malta, Portugal, Slovenia and Spain – were searching for a response to moves blocking the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of Houthi forces restricting maritime passage in the Red Sea. The working lunch was devoted to the crises in the Middle East. “Acting on energy prices and securing our supplies, working towards stability in the Middle East, preparing for the next European Council: these are all the stakes of the summit of Mediterranean countries of the European Union gathered in Croatia,” French President Emmanuel Macron said. “We are building together the future of Europe and the Mediterranean, to invest in our competitiveness and strengthen our sovereignty, while protecting our natural spaces.” Attendees included European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen , European Council president Antonio Costa and Albert II of Monaco. “The priority, within a Mediterranean framework, is to discuss all contacts with the US President and Iranian authorities in order to foster a resolution to the crisis and contribute to stability and security in the region, as well as to [maritime] transit,” an adviser to Mr Macron said before the meeting. Faced with mounting discontent in Europe over high fuel prices caused by tensions over maritime routes in the Gulf, some European heads of state, including Mr Macron and Italy's Giorgia Meloni, are expected to lobby EU institutions for extra spending. The G7 group of nations recently announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel would be released to ease prices. Speaking last week, Mr Macron, who currently heads the G7, said routes were opening up slowly but that transport costs remained high . Yemen's Houthi rebels on Monday secured control of the Bab Al Mandeb strait , the Dhubab area overlooking the sea lane and the strategic port city of Mokha. They had previously said they would block passage to Saudi vessels. This comes months into Iran's separate blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. European leaders are expected to continue pushing for alternative routes to Hormuz, including working on developing oil pipelines via Syria, as well as to accelerate the implementation of the Great Sea Interconnector, a planned 1,300km subsea power cable to connect Greece, Cyprus and Israel, funded in part by the EU. Southern Mediterranean states are also particularly concerned by the implementation of new measures adopted earlier this year by the EU to discourage the arrival of illegal migrants. Last week, the European Commission moved to strengthen EU border controls ⁠in the ​wake of mass arrivals this summer in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in North Africa. The plan, which requires the approval ​of member states, would strengthen the mandate of Frontex, the EU border protection agency, and give it a ​standing corps ready for immediate deployment. The adviser to Mr Macron said the EU needed a new framework that addressed the exploitation of migration by third countries and also increased border protection and surveillance. “The priority is to have a comprehensive plan” that can be discussed next week by the EU's 27 leaders at a meeting in Brussels, they said.

title: Israeli National Security Minister hands out pro-death penalty pins at high school
description: Itamar Ben-Gvir has touted tough stance against Palestinians in bid for re-election this month
content: The mayor of an affluent Israeli city condemned a senior minister for distributing pins depicting a hangman’s noose, as the government’s push to expand the use of the death penalty against Palestinians gains momentum in Israel. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir distributed the pins to students at Handasaim Herzliya High School during a visit on Monday, according to The Jerusalem Post. Herzliya's mayor, Yariv Fisher, said the “ugly incident […] represents the crossing of an educational, ethical and moral red line”. "There are things that simply cannot happen within school walls, where many students are under the age of 18," he added. School officials had told Mr Ben-Gvir’s representatives that distributing the pins would not be allowed, and instructed staff to confiscate them after they were handed out, according to the report. The incident comes in the midst of Mr Ben-Gvir’s election campaign, during which he has boasted of his far-right agenda in videos that show him abusing Palestinian detainees and celebrating the destruction of Palestinian homes. Israel has used the death penalty only twice in its history. Mr Ben-Gvir has pushed to use it against Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks. Mr Ben-Gvir’s party, Otzma Yehudit, defended his distribution of noose pins. "Otzma Yehudit is proud to demonstrate to the young generation in schools the importance of deterrence against terrorism, without fear and without blinking," it said in a statement cited in The Jerusalem Post ’s report. "A terrorist who comes to kill a Jew must die, period.” In August, Mr Ben-Gvir unveiled plans to build an execution facility in a new wing for death row inmates at a prison in central Israel.

title: Four deputies, one son-in-law: Iraqi PM’s cabinet deal exposes price of consensus
description: Possible appointment of militia figure Laith Al Khazali as deputy PM and Nouri Al Maliki’s son-in-law as Interior Minister sparks backlash as Iraq considers austerity budget and dinar devaluation
content: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi is close to finalising his government, but the process to get there has already drawn fire – for the cost, their surnames and what it says about who really governs Iraq. Mr Al Zaidi , a businessman who was nominated by the largest Shiite parliamentary bloc, the Co-ordination Framework, was sworn in in mid-May after parliament endorsed most of his proposed cabinet members, ending months of political deadlock. Then, parliament voted in favour of 14 of the 16 ministerial nominees he presented, leaving Mr Al Zaidi with nine posts to fill. The ministers for defence, interior, labour and social affairs, culture, planning, youth and sport, migration and displacement, reconstruction, and higher education have yet to be appointed. After months of deadlock, political blocs have agreed to fill and finalise the formation by creating four deputy prime ministers: two Shiites, one Sunni and one Kurd, according to three political sources involved in the negotiations. The most significant – and controversial – name for deputy prime minister is Laith Al Khazali, brother of Qais Al Khazali, leader of the Iran-backed Asaib Ahl Al Haq (AAH) movement, one of Iraq’s most powerful paramilitary and political forces. Laith Al Khazali’s appointment was initially rejected by Washington, which has pressed Baghdad to keep militia leaders and senior members out of top executive posts, two Iraqi and one western source said. The group is designated a terrorist organisation by Washington, as a central actor in attacks on US forces and a pillar of Iran ’s influence in Iraq. One of the sources close to the talks said Mr Al Zaidi managed to convince the Americans to drop their objection. The other two sources could not confirm it. The agreement to create four deputy prime minister posts at a time when Iraq is struggling to pay salaries to contractors and farmers has sparked widespread condemnation in parliament. Critics say the move shows the pressure Mr Al Zaidi faces from parties and suggests he is unable to say no. “These four posts alone will cost the state trillions of dinars per month in salaries, offices, advisers, protection and benefits, at a time we are telling people there is no cash,” an MPs' finance committee official told The National . The controversy comes as the Finance Ministry and parliament’s finance committee are locked in negotiations over the 2027 budget. Iraq, Opec’s second-largest producer, is facing a cash crunch not seen since 2020, triggered by regional instability since the outbreak of the Iran war that has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and its spillover into energy shipping and investor confidence. Since the war started, Iraq’s oil revenue has fluctuated, while spending on security, subsidised fuel and emergency imports has risen. The government has delayed salary payments to public employees in several provinces, deferred payments to contractors and wheat farmers, and drawn heavily on its Central Bank reserves, according to Finance Ministry officials and two advisers to the committee. To close the gap, Iraq has officially devalued its currency again, setting a new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, starting from Wednesday, according to a document seen by The National. The Council of Ministers approved the move late on Tuesday, based on a recommendation from the Central Bank of Iraq, the bank said in a directive sent to all licensed lenders, electronic payment companies and exchange houses. According to the directive, the new structure is: the Central Bank will purchase from the Ministry of Finance at the price of 1,500 dinars. The sale price to banks is set at 1,510 dinars and to the public at 1,520 dinars. The dinar was last devalued in 2020 from 1,182 to 1,450 to the dollar. That was later adjusted to 1,320 as the official rate under the previous government, though the market rate often hovered higher. The Ministry of Finance has also proposed adding 100,000 new public-sector jobs demanded by parties as part of power-sharing deals. Half of these will be in the defence and interior ministries, as well as the Counter-Terrorism Service. Against that backdrop, the decision to expand the top echelon of government is seen by many Iraqis as tone deaf. “This is irresponsible and reckless behaviour,” said Majeed Ali, a taxi driver in Baghdad. “We are at the height of the crisis today, We desperately need every single dinar today, and the Prime Minister and the political parties are appointing four deputies to him. “They keep saying we are having problems in securing the needed cash, and eye our pockets through imposing more taxes and tariffs, while they seek to siphon off more money from the budget for their parties,” he said. A second flashpoint is the Interior Minister role, one of Iraq’s most sensitive security portfolios, overseeing police, federal police, border guards and intelligence. State of Law Coalition leader and former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki is pushing his son-in-law, Yassir Al Maliki, for the post, according to three Shiite political sources. The move has sparked heated debate in Iraq. Yassir Al Maliki is a former MP with no background in security or policing. Critics say the nomination entrenches family rule in Iraqi politics. Supporters of Mr Al Maliki argue the Interior Ministry has traditionally been held by the State of Law bloc and that he is a trusted figure who can manage its vast patronage network. The agreements are not final, sources cautioned. Horse-trading over deputy minister and director-general posts continues, and any candidate for the Interior Ministry must still pass a parliamentary vote and vetting. Parliament is expected to hold a session on Thursday to vote on the remaining cabinet, including the deputies and interior, if the final deal is reached. For Mr Al Zaidi, a compromise figure who emerged after months of stalemate, the deals illustrate the tightrope of Iraqi leadership: to govern, he must appease the blocs that nominated him – even if that means expanding a government that Iraqis increasingly see as too big, too expensive and too familial. As one finance committee member put it: “We are hiring more ministers to manage a budget that says we have no money.”

title: How UAE and US students could take the next giant leap together
description: A new research partnership in Abu Dhabi aims to advance lunar exploration through international co-operation
content: Landing the first astronauts on the Moon remains one of the US’s greatest achievements. Its enduring images are of American astronauts, an American flag and mission control in Houston. The reality is even more remarkable. Behind them was a communications network spanning California, Spain and Australia. An antenna near Canberra relayed the television pictures of Neil Armstrong’s first steps to the world. Engineering expertise also came from beyond US borders. Canadian engineers helped design the lunar module and develop the heat shield that protected the returning astronauts. Scientific knowledge and technical ability travel more widely than the familiar images of national achievement suggest. That international contribution remains essential. When Artemis II carried astronauts around the Moon in April this year, its crew included Canadian Jeremy Hansen. Orion’s European Service Module provided propulsion, electricity, air and water. Co-operation was present in both the crew and the systems keeping them alive. As we mark World Space Week, these achievements offer a wider lesson about how technology advances. Progress depends on people sharing knowledge and building on discoveries made across institutions and borders. Bringing that expertise together allows humans to solve increasingly difficult problems, with results that can create opportunities far beyond the original purpose of the research. At NYU Abu Dhabi, we are preparing to lead a new collaboration with the US State Department. The 18-month project begins in November and will bring together 15 graduate students from the UAE and 15 from the US to design and build small lunar rovers. Their work will draw on research into a challenge familiar to the Apollo astronauts: Moon dust . Fine, abrasive and prone to clinging to equipment, it makes operating machinery difficult. A rover that performs well on a laboratory floor still has much to prove before it can travel across the lunar surface. Our laboratory has developed the Emirates Lunar Simulant , using rock found in the UAE to reproduce important properties of lunar soil. We matched the mineral composition and grain size of soil from the lunar highlands around the South Pole, where Artemis and the UAE’s future missions are headed. We began developing it because importing simulants was expensive, particularly in the quantities our experiments required. It is also a strategic asset: the ability to test lunar hardware at home, on our own schedule, for our own missions and for our partners. Our planetary simulation chamber also lets us test equipment under extreme temperatures and vacuum conditions. These capabilities give international partners a reason to work here. US students will join their UAE counterparts in our laboratory, while the UAE-based students will visit the Colorado School of Mines, our partner with expertise in lunar exploration and space resources. Each team will develop a rover with a specific scientific objective, taking it through design reviews, construction and testing. We plan to involve specialists with Artemis experience and to work closely with the UAE's national space institutions, including the engineers behind the Rashid rovers. The aim is to develop proposals for lunar missions that advance the UAE's goals in lunar exploration. The teams will have to defend their designs, revise assumptions and bring different kinds of expertise to bear on the same problem. For the UAE, this is a practical way to deepen its contribution to exploration. Facilities developed locally can support both national missions and international research. The experience gained through those partnerships then helps us undertake more demanding work. Lunar exploration also pushes those involved in this sector to rethink how technology is designed. The extremely high cost of transporting equipment to the Moon demands lighter designs and more efficient use of energy. Batteries that store more energy for their weight, or instruments that operate on far less power, could make more ambitious missions possible. Advances developed to meet these demands could also have substantial commercial value on Earth, with applications in electric vehicles, energy storage and consumer electronics. There is a precedent. Nasa ’s work on silver-zinc batteries during and after Apollo helped lay the foundations for rechargeable hearing aid batteries commercialised decades later. Further development by industry was essential. Scientific progress can create opportunities whose eventual applications take years to emerge. We are beginning discussions about commercial uses for our own expertise. Future industries will need people who can turn an idea into working technology, and facilities where they can test it. Research partnerships help develop both. Students may go on to join space agencies, work in established companies or create businesses of their own. They are already discovering the pleasure of making something work. Students in our lab have designed rover components , 3D-printed them, fitted motors and written software. When something failed, they changed the design and tried again. They now have a functioning rover. They are excited about what comes next, even as they discover how demanding this work can be. World Space Week celebrates the contribution of space science and technology to improving human life. That purpose should guide how we judge our efforts. A mission’s legacy includes the people it trains, the discoveries others can build upon and the practical uses that follow. For the students preparing to work together in Abu Dhabi, those possibilities are still unfolding. Giving them the expertise, facilities and international relationships to pursue them is an investment whose value can extend far beyond the Moon.

title: Mubadala to maintain annual investment of $39bn with Asia in focus
description: China, South Korea, India and Japan among countries where it plans to increase investment
content: Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Company plans to maintain annual investment of $39 billion with a focus on Asia, its chief financial officer said on Wednesday. “Last year, we invested about $39 billion, which is roughly 10 per cent of our portfolio, and our aim is to continue doing that through all cycles. Every year, we want to deploy that same amount,” Carlos Obeid told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. Asia will be “important” as the fund continues to boost its investment around the globe, he added.
