China, the world’s second-largest economy, South Korea, India and Japan will be the main countries where it plans to ramp up investment in Asia. “We’ve been trying diligently over the last few years to increase our exposure to Asia,” Mr Obeid said. “Three years ago, the share of the portfolio invested in Asia was about 10 per cent, it is now about 13 per cent, and we want to do more.” “We’ve been present in China, South Korea, Japan and India, and want to grow those exposures because we believe there are a lot of opportunities across all the strategies and themes.” Energy transition, “technology everywhere”, the recreation of global supply chains and the evolving consumer are four areas Mubadala wants to focus. “Our strategy has been aligned with the objectives of the government: generating returns, but at the same time integrating the economy into the global economy,” Mr Obeid said. “The way we do that is by partnering with the best companies through our private equity investments, both direct and indirect.” Mubadala, which invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government, has been steadily expanding its global investment portfolio with a focus on sectors including renewables, mobility, advanced technology, AI and life science. The sovereign investor’s portfolio spans six continents across asset classes. Last year, it reported a 17 per cent annual rise in assets to $385 billion, driven by growth sectors in the UAE and abroad. Last month, it announced a significant minority investment in Chinese coffee chain Luckin Coffee alongside its controlling shareholder, Centurium Capital, in a deal worth about $1 billion. Mubadala is betting on confidence in China’s consumer sector with demand for freshly brewed coffee continuing to grow in the country. It has investments in India, including Reliance Industries telecom arm Reliance Jio and other companies. It is also investing in India through Investcorp, in which Mubadala has a 20 per cent stake.

title: Iran war disruption creates ‘huge’ oil trading opportunities, Vitol says
description: World’s largest independent oil trader sees rapid recovery in Middle East refining capacity
content: The Iran war is creating “huge” arbitrage opportunities across global energy markets as disrupted trade flows stretch tanker fleets to capacity and send oil on longer journeys, according to Vitol Group, the world’s largest independent oil trader. “There’s huge arbitrage opportunities going on,” Tom Baker, managing director for Vitol in Bahrain, said at an industry forum in Fujairah on Wednesday. The disruption has also pushed the global tanker fleet to full utilisation. “When you see the shipping fleet at 100 per cent utilisation”, shipping becomes “very interesting”, Mr Baker said. Tanker rates have surged as restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait force vessels on longer journeys and increase ship-to-ship transfers. Average spot earnings for very large crude carriers approached $642,000 a day globally in late September, according to Clarksons Research. The upheaval has also changed where Vitol sends its barrels. “It’s been fascinating to see that barrels from our Western or European refineries have found their way around to the east under these conditions,” Mr Baker said. Refining has been another source of market dislocation, although Mr Baker said Middle East capacity is now recovering rapidly from outages caused by the conflict. About two million barrels a day of refining capacity has been knocked out in Russia , while the Middle East suffered similar outages and capacity in China has also been down, he said. “We had similar [refinery outages] in the Middle East, but it’s recovering very rapidly now,” Mr Baker said. Middle East refinery runs were forecast last month to average about eight million barrels per day this year, 1.6 million bpd below 2025 levels, according to S&P Global Energy, as outages tightened supplies of petrol, diesel and jet fuel. The turmoil is also changing how Vitol assesses energy infrastructure investments, with the trader generally backing assets that can generate returns immediately over projects that take years to develop. “Today, you can buy a ship and make an immediate return on it,” Mr Baker said. A pipeline that will not be ready for another two or three years has to be assessed against the possibility of further “black swan events”. Some projects may also be driven by “national strategic reasons” rather than the returns sought by private investors, he said. “We’ve gone from being more of a trader of a third-party barrel to really seeing the need to be part of the infrastructure chain,” Mr Baker said. Vitol views the Middle East and East Africa as an increasingly connected energy market, with the Gulf’s surplus fuel supply and short shipping distances making it a natural source for countries short of products, Mr Baker said. During the crisis, Vitol helped landlocked Uganda diversify fuel imports beyond Kenya’s pipeline system, routing supplies through Tanzania’s port of Tanga. Uganda is also expected to begin exporting about 230,000 bpd of crude through its heated export pipeline to Tanga “at some point next year”, Mr Baker said. Those barrels “will easily get bought” in Europe, the Middle East or Asia.

title: Dubai gives building owners 12 months to comply with shared housing regulations
description: New guide covers building design, occupancy, health and safety, shared facilities and permitted locations
content: Landlords have been given a year to bring their buildings into line with new shared accommodation regulations after Dubai earmarked 43 areas for shared housing. The move came as the city cracks down on overcrowding and the illegal subletting of multi-occupancy apartments. Dubai is grappling with a major population rise; more than 200,000 people moved to the emirate this year, despite the impact of the war in Iran. Most approved shared housing areas are located outside major tourist hubs, such as Al Souq Al Kabeer, Al Ras, Al Warqa 1, Al Barsha 1, Al Muraqqabat, and Al Rigga. Additional areas may be approved in the future. For many residents, sharing a home is an affordable and practical way to live in Dubai. The concern is what happens when an apartment designed for a limited number of residents is turned into a much more crowded arrangement. For example, a two-bedroom apartment may be divided into multiple rooms, with more people sleeping in living areas, on balconies, or in other spaces never intended as bedrooms. That can put pressure on kitchens, bathrooms, ventilation and electrical systems. Unauthorised partitions can also affect fire safety and escape routes. In June last year, a fire in a residential block in Dubai Marina that was home to more than 3,800 people exposed fire traps in illegally partitioned homes. The Dubai Municipality's shared housing guide sets standards for building design, occupancy, health and safety, shared facilities, and approved locations. These regulations address unregulated residential practices and protect the privacy, safety, and rights of owners and occupants. Ahmed Elnaggar, founder of Elnaggar & Partners, a legal firm, said the law identifies six types of property that may be approved for shared accommodation: residential apartments, stand-alone houses, residential complexes, mixed-use buildings, adjoining houses and multi-storey buildings. Taimur Khan, head of research for the Middle East and Africa at JLL noted that unauthorised partitioning occurs throughout Dubai, not in a single area, and expects enforcement to focus on specific buildings rather than neighbourhoods, emphasising “the asset, not the location.” Each building must be designated as either individual or family accommodation. Bedrooms must provide at least five square metres per person. Family units require a separate bedroom with an en suite bathroom. The guide specifies requirements for shared facilities and services based on accommodation type and occupancy. Buildings must include kitchens, sanitary facilities, and designated areas for dining, recreation, laundry, and clothes drying, as appropriate. The law excludes labour accommodation, which is governed by separate legislation. Property owners have one year from the law’s effective date, September 8, 2026, to bring shared housing buildings into compliance. Owners, property managers, and leasing companies should use this period to assess properties and make the changes needed to meet the new standards. Mr Khan anticipates the property market will respond before the September 2027 deadline, given the significant penalties for non-compliance. Although there is time to comply, Dubai Municipality has already begun inspections in identified problem areas. Violations may result in fines from Dh500 to Dh500,000. Repeat offences within a year can double the penalty, up to a maximum of Dh1 million. Buildings and villas may be designated for shared housing only after obtaining the required permit. Permit applications and renewals are available through the Build in Dubai platform. Maryam Al Muhairi, chief of the Building Regulation and Permits Agency at Dubai Municipality, said the guide provides a clear reference for property owners and management and leasing companies. “It sets out planning, building, technical, health and public safety requirements, as well as the areas where buildings may be allocated for shared housing,” she said. “This will contribute to providing a safe, healthy and well-regulated residential environment for different segments of the community, while translating the provisions of the Shared Housing Law related to protecting rights and enhancing public health and safety.” She stated that the objective is to raise awareness, strengthen oversight, and help owners standardise their buildings, while preserving Dubai’s urban and aesthetic character.

title: Mubadala's Solutions+ expects to double Dh1.5bn contribution to Abu Dhabi GDP
description: The business management services firm is now a billion-dollar company with more acquisitions planned
content: Mubadala's business management services unit Solutions+ contributed about Dh1.5 billion ($408.4 million) to Abu Dhabi's economy in 2025 and expects this to double this year, its chief executive has said. The figure forms part of Mubadala's wider Dh45 billion portfolio contribution to the emirate's GDP. Solutions+ has been able to grow by 53 times since it was formed as Mubadala Business Management Services in 2014, Nasir Al Nabhani told The National on the sidelines of the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday. “We invested in people and technology, and we have grown significantly. We have healthy cash [flow and] healthy net profit, so we have a healthy organisation,” he told The National in an interview. The privately held company, which does not disclose its financials, has also been able to exceed its goal of becoming a billion-dollar company, which it first revealed in 2023 , as it accelerated its acquisitions strategy. The company grew by about 20 per cent in 2022, an achievement that was “beyond its targets”, Mr Al Nabhani previously said. Solutions+ is in the midst of a five-year growth plan that was introduced during its rebranding in 2023. During that span, it welcomed seven companies into its fold, with three more to be acquired “very soon”, he said. “All the acquisitions that we have done in the last three years, based on the [five-year] strategy, will give us also another 100 per cent of growth.” Solutions+ provides digital business services for sectors including business process outsourcing, finance, procurement, facilities management, and environmental, social and government. Initially, its services were dedicated to companies under Mubadala, the sovereign wealth fund of Abu Dhabi. Solutions+ has more than 50 government and enterprise clients, and its services have helped them save more than Dh300 million, according to its website. It has also developed Weave, a software-as-a-service solution designed to simplify HR and enterprise management. The company is also increasingly improving the use of AI on its services. Mr Al Nabhani said Solutions+ and its partners are testing new large language models, the underlying algorithm of generative AI. They are expected to introduce a new one by the first quarter of 2027, he added. At AI Everything, the company signed agreements with Tahaluf Al Emarat Technical Solutions to boost AI collaboration and Saal.ai to accelerate the adoption of enterprise data platform solutions. These are part of a broader strategy to grow Solutions+'s business locally and abroad, Mr Al Nabhani said. The company currently has a presence in countries including Saudi Arabia, Algeria, Pakistan, Tunisia and Uganda. “We are trying to explore what could be or what could add value to us and to our clients,” Mr Al Nabhani said. Meanwhile, Mubadala, whose $385 billion portfolio spans six continents across asset classes, also continues to build its AI portfolio. Last week, it signed an agreement with the US company Together AI to explore investment opportunities in AI infrastructure in the UAE.

title: Why staff using ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for work could create problems for employers
description: Employees using 'shadow AI' can leave firms open to data breaches, experts warn
content: Cyber security experts have urged companies to be vigilant against the risks posed by employees using outside AI applications including Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini in the workplace. The practice, known as using shadow AI, can lead to important data being leaked and, in some cases, malware and viruses being uploaded into companies' internal systems. Firms are urged to ensure they are aware of what AI tools are being used by employees when it comes to sensitive company information, as it could lead to problems with customer information and intellectual property. Pasting documents into an outside AI application, or even asking it to tidy up an email, means that sensitive information is being sent to a cloud tool outside the company. If the person's personal accounts are hacked, their company's data could end up in the wrong hands. “Staff might see the benefits of completing work faster, but employers are likely to have no record of the systems they were using or the information those systems received,” said Vladislav Tushkanov, research and development group manager at the cyber security company Kaspersky. “You cannot send personally identifiable information in the cloud.” This means employees will need to be educated on the need to ensure that only internal AI systems are used to process information, added Mr Tushkanov, who spoke to The National at the Ai Everything summit taking place this week in Abu Dhabi. The rapid advancements in AI mean it is crucial that companies take a fresh look at business workflows and ensure security is built in from the start, said another expert, Premchand Kurup, chief executive of the cyber security firm ParamountAssure. “Companies should first identify unapproved AI use that could expose customer information or intellectual property through external tools, then establish approved alternatives and clear access limits,” Mr Kurup said. The scale of the risks companies face from data breaches was laid out in IBM’s 2026 Middle East Cost of a Data Breach Report, which found 26 per cent of malicious breaches were AI-enabled. The average breach cost in the region was $8 million. The research included organisations in the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Another challenge firms will face is keeping a closer eye on AI agents that play a more advanced role as technology improves. Agentic AI is likely to carry out more tasks with less human supervision, raising questions of who is accountable when something goes wrong. “We can't put AI agents in jail, so ultimately it will always have to be a human [who is accountable],” said Costi Perricos, Deloitte’s global generative AI leader. Businesses need to manage agents as a digital workforce, with performance checks and decisions about how much responsibility each system is given, said Mr Perricos. Their behaviour could change over time as they pursue their goals, he said. Companies need to track what agents are doing, establish when they are ready for use and know when to switch them off. An example of how quickly AI capability is increasing is provided by the UAE government, which has set a target to introduce agentic AI across 50 per cent of federal sectors and operations within two years, under a framework announced in April. Companies should set access limits and require AI-assisted security investigations to draw on verified internal records, said Mr Kurup. He added that analysts need evidence they can check before approving sensitive actions. “The same discipline should guide wider AI adoption, with employees trained to challenge outputs and records kept for review,” he said. Ahmed Hafez, director of solution engineering for the Middle East, Turkey and Africa at the data company Snowflake, said businesses need trusted information and controls over what AI agents can access. “Extensive testing in controlled environments, with governance and security built in from the ground up, becomes increasingly important as these systems take on more complex work,” he said.

title: Libya replaces parliamentary speaker Aguila Saleh after 12 years
description: Al Salhin Abdulnabi speaks of 'shared responsibility' as he takes over the role
content: Libya's eastern-based parliament has ousted its long-serving speaker Aguila Saleh after 12 years at the helm, amid tensions within the House of Representatives over his tenure. He was replaced by Al Salhin Abdulnabi, who comes from the same tribe as Mr Saleh, 82, and represents the eastern city of Tobruk. “Libya is greater than our differences and more precious than our individual interests, and the future of its sons is a shared responsibility that falls on all our shoulders,” Mr Abdulnabi said in a speech on assuming the post. Mr Saleh was replaced a day after 98 of the chamber's 190 MPs ⁠approved limiting the speaker and deputy speakers to a single 12-month term, ending a system that had been ⁠in place since he was elected in 2014. He denounced the session as “not official” and one that “does not have any legal effect”. “The magic backfired on the magician,” said a Benghazi-based politician, referring to the power Mr Saleh accumulated over the years, as well as his ability to remain at the forefront of Libyan politics for more than a decade. Mr Saleh has been one of the most prominent Libyan figures since the 2011 uprising that ended with the killing of long-time ruler Muammar Qaddafi. He grew close to and helped raise the profile of the Haftar family, which dominates eastern Libya. It is led by Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, the military commander of the eastern region. FM Haftar's son, Lt Gen Saddam Haftar, generally regarded as his likely successor, said after the new speaker's election that Libya's path towards a stable and unified state “begins with building effective national institutions capable of renewing and assuming their responsibilities”. The source in Benghazi said one of the reasons for Mr Saleh's removal was a divergence with Saddam Haftar, whose ascent in recent years has been rapid even in comparison to his many brothers who hold positions of power in eastern Libya. Lt Gen Haftar, who is the youngest of his father's children, has backed an initiative by senior US adviser Massad Boulos that would unify Libya's west and east. Libya, a major oil and gas producer , remains deeply divided, with effectively two seats of power in the east and west – the ⁠internationally recognised Government of National ​Unity is based in the capital Tripoli. In August, rival factions signed an agreement at the headquarters of the UN Mission to Libya calling for presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months and seeking to settle disputes over electoral laws and restructure the country's election commission. However, it follows a long list of failed attempts to unify the country and optimism remains muted that it will succeed.

title: Iraq to ban Waze navigation app over Israeli links
description: Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad suggests alternatives such as Google Maps
content: Iraq has announced it will ban the navigation app Waze from next year because it was developed in Israel . Speaking to journalists in the Iraqi Kurdistan region, Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad said Waze is widely used in Iraq but that alternatives are available. Asked what was behind the move, he said: “The reason is because it is made in Israel, therefore we will ban it at the beginning of 2027. The app is widely used in Iraq but there are alternatives, like Google Maps.” In a separate post on his Facebook page, the minister said he would bring the ban forward to the end of this year, after a wave of online mockery. Known for providing live, crowdsourced traffic information, Waze was founded in Israel in 2008 before expanding globally. In 2013, Google acquired the app for about $1 billion, operating it as a subsidiary. It continues to maintain a presence in Tel Aviv. It is one of the most widely used navigation apps in Baghdad and other cities in Iraq, where drivers rely on its real-time alerts. After criticism, Mr Sanad used his Facebook account to defend the decision, linking it to the war in Gaza. Waze is to be banned “because it is a famous Israeli app and is still managed by them” and because “such apps help [with] scanning Gaza, and the app provides the company with money and information”, he wrote. The announcement follows a series of calls by Iran-aligned politicians and groups in Iraq to boycott Israeli-linked products and services since the start of the war in Gaza in October 2023. Iraq does not have diplomatic relations with Israel and Israeli-linked companies are prohibited from operating in the country, though some digital services with Israeli origins are now owned by US companies and remain accessible in Iraq. It was not immediately clear how the ban will be enforced. Telecoms companies could be ordered to block Waze servers, or it could be removed from app stores in Iraq. The minister’s Facebook page was flooded with hundreds of comments within hours, many mocking the decision and pointing out that Google Maps, which he cited as an alternative, is owned by Google, which also owns Waze. “Waze benefits us more the minister himself,” Ali Al Askari wrote. “Since you are so concerned about Iraq and the interests of its people, create an Iraqi app that can benefit all of Iraq before you think of such a step,” another commentator, Duraid Al Saffar, said.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed calls for rain prayers on Friday
description: Salaat Al Istisqaa will be performed half an hour before Friday prayers
content: President Sheikh Mohamed has called for rain prayers to take place in all mosques in the UAE this Friday. Sheikh Mohamed called for Salaat Al Istisqaa to be performed half an hour before Friday prayers. The President called upon everyone to pray to God for rain and mercy, in line with the traditions of the Prophet Mohammed. Last October, worshippers gathered in mosques across the country following Sheikh Mohamed's call to perform rain prayers. The tradition is performed across the Gulf when rainfall is delayed. Although parts of the UAE have seen scattered rains, most areas remained dry. Additional rainfall is crucial for agriculture, helping farmers grow healthy crops in tough conditions and strengthening groundwater reserves. The country usually gets around 150mm of rainfall each year. During the rite, worshippers stand together, facing the qibla, for two rak'ahs led by an imam, as they seek forgiveness and make supplications for divine mercy and rainfall. This is followed by sermons. The imam speaks about the prayer's importance, reminding the worshipers about the role of rainfall in enabling agriculture and bolstering groundwater reserves.

title: Ambassador meets British couple detained in Iran’s Evin prison after months without contact
description: Engagement marks shift since staff were moved out of Tehran in July
content: A British couple detained in Iran’s Evin prison have been allowed their first consular visit in months, weeks after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband raised their case with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. Craig and Lindsay Foreman last met British ambassador Hugo Shorter on 15 June, shortly before embassy staff were told to leave Tehran due to escalating hostilities between the US and Iran. British embassy officials returned to Tehran in late August. The couple’s children in the UK said the latest visit on Monday brought “desperately needed reassurance” to the family. They were expecting a phone call from their detained parents on Wednesday, which was promised to them by Evin’s prison authorities following the visit, they said. Mr Miliband met Mr Araghchi at the UN General Assembly in September, where he repeated the British Government’s call for the Foreman’s immediate release. Tension between the UK and Iran is at an all-time high following a suspected terror attack at a British airbase containing US military planes last week. This followed a series of attacks on Jewish businesses and Iranian dissidents in the UK , which police suspect were ordered by Iranian officials. The couple were travelling through Iran on a motorcycle trip around the world when they were arrested in early January 2025 and subsequently sentenced to ten years in prison for espionage. UN experts have described the couple’s detention as a “state hostage taking for political leverage”, citing “irregularities” in their trial last year. During the meeting with Mr Shorter, it emerged that Ms Foreman was still waiting for medication that had been prescribed to her. She had also been unable to call her lawyers in the UK, the family said. The couple had previously been allowed to make nearly daily phone calls to their families, but their phone cards were cut off in May after Ms Foreman gave an interview to British media from prison. Mr Foreman is said to have regained 10kg of the 17kg he lost during a hunger strike in the summer to protest the barring of phone calls. The couple are said to be “trying to cope” with their detention by supporting fellow prisoners. Ms Foreman is giving yoga lessons while Craig is helping with cooking and distributing the few vegetables available within his prison wing. The family said this was “entirely in keeping with who they are” but warned that this was not a sign that their situation was improving. Ms Foreman’s son, Joe Bennett, said that he welcomed Mr Miliband’s move, but that more action was needed from the UK government following the meeting to secure their release. “I welcomed Ed Miliband raising Mum and Craig directly with his Iranian counterpart at the United Nations. That matters,” he said. “It is important that the British Government is publicly saying they should be released. Now we need to see ‘immediately’ being put into practice,” he said. During Mr Shorter’s visit, Lindsay showed a written document dated June 3 containing a series of conditions she understood had been agreed with the prison authorities. This included telephone contact, consular access, access to her lawyer and basic welfare provisions. “Months later, many of those issues remain unresolved,” the family said. Mr Bennett said the family wanted to see better treatment for their parents while in prison and feared Mr Miliband’s meeting with Mr Araghchi would be ineffective without further pressure from the UK government. “I don’t want another assurance that a phone call should happen. I want the phone to ring,” Mr Bennett said. “I don’t want to hear that medication can be provided. I want medication prescribed by a doctor to reach my mum.” “And I don’t want ‘immediate release’ to become another powerful phrase that changes nothing about where they wake up tomorrow morning.”

title: New image of an ancient wonder: Divers find ring showing Lighthouse of Alexandria at sunken palace
description: Lighthouse, one of Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, is depicted on bronze ring discovered off Egypt's Mediterranean coast
content: Underwater archaeologists have discovered a bronze signet ring depicting the Lighthouse of Alexandria at a submerged Egyptian palace, in what has been hailed as an important find. The ring was found on Antirhodos, an island once part of the royal quarters in Alexandria’s Portus Magnus, or Great Harbour. The European Institute for Underwater Archaeology announced the discovery on Wednesday. Carved into the ring is an image of the lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The image is similar to those found on coins from the second century AD, although the institute did not give a firm date for the ring or details on who might have owned it. The excavations have been led by French underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, whose work off Egypt’s Mediterranean coast has helped bring submerged cities , temples and shipwrecks back into view. “The discovery of the signet ring is even more important as it has been excavated in the legendary palace of the Island of Antirhodos, that once was a centre of power,” Mr Goddio said. He said it suggested the palace had housed administrative offices, including functions connected to the lighthouse. Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry described the find as the first known depiction of the lighthouse engraved on a signet ring. The Lighthouse of Alexandria was completed around 280BC during the reign of Ptolemy II. Built on the island of Pharos to guide ships into the city’s harbour, it is thought to have stood more than 100 metres tall, making it one of the ancient world’s tallest structures. A succession of earthquakes reduced it to ruins during the Middle Ages. In the late 15th century, the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on its site, incorporating stone from the fallen lighthouse. The Antirhodos palace was described by the Greek geographer Strabo, who visited Egypt between 29 and 25BC. The new find provides a clue to how the complex may have been used. Excavations on the island are revealing architectural remains across several thousand square metres which are yet to be completely examined. Mr Goddio said excavations this year cover four sites in Alexandria’s Eastern Harbour: the temple of Isis, the palace and western mound on Antirhodos, remains of an obelisk, and the Timonium, a palace associated with Mark Antony. Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy and his assistant, Ahmed Rehema, visited the team aboard its research vessel on Monday to observe the underwater excavations and inspect the ring. The mission is taking place in collaboration with the ministry and is supported by the Hilti Foundation, which has funded Mr Goddio’s work since 1996. After completing its current work in the Eastern Harbour, the team will begin excavations in Abu Qir Bay, the ministry said. It was there that Mr Goddio’s team located the submerged city of Thonis-Heracleion in 2000. Excavations there have already yielded monumental statues, inscriptions and dozens of ancient vessels, offering an unusually detailed picture of a port that disappeared beneath the sea. Among the more striking discoveries were 2,400-year-old wicker baskets that still contained doum palm fruit and grape seeds. Announced in 2021, they were found among funerary offerings, alongside imported Greek ceramics. That year, the team also uncovered a rare Ptolemaic galley about 25 metres long. Its construction combined Greek shipbuilding techniques with features suited to navigating the Nile and its delta, including a flat bottom. Researchers said it sank when part of the nearby temple of Amun collapsed in the second century BC. In 2023, excavations at the temple revealed silver ritual instruments, gold jewellery and fragile alabaster containers for perfumes and ointments. A Greek sanctuary dedicated to Aphrodite was also discovered nearby, containing imported bronze and ceramic objects. In 2025, a quartz sphinx statue with the sigil of Rameses II, a granite figure and a white marble statue of a Roman nobleman were among a large haul from the area. Together, those finds have helped document the close interaction between Egyptian and Greek communities along the ancient coast.

title: French government offers olive branch to student protest movement
description: Students and pupils complain of long hours, overcrowded classrooms and collapsing infrastructure
content: The French government has made a series of conciliatory moves towards a student protest movement amid public uproar over police violence during demonstrations. Several teaching unions on Wednesday called for another day of action on Thursday, while Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the “voice of high school students is precious and must be heard” and would feed into “a concrete action plan”. He said dialogue would be held in every school, but must come with pupils returning to class. After weeks of school blockades, protesters took to the streets across the country for the first time on Tuesday, with 266,000 participants, including 56,000 in Paris, the Interior Ministry said. They largely featured secondary school pupils , university students, teachers, parents and left-wing political representatives. Some protests ended in violence, with 488 arrests and 43 injured among security forces as police resorted to using tear gas. French schools are blighted by dilapidated infrastructure, including overcrowded classrooms, inadequate heating and cooling systems and collapsing ceilings. France has a high number of pupils per class – 29 compared to an average of 26 in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development – and among the longest hours due to a condensed teaching schedule, with longer holidays. School days start at 8am and end at 6pm, often with gaps during the day. Yet the cabinet has little leeway to respond with financial incentives, as tough parliamentary debates on the budget begin this week. State expenditure to service the national debt surpasses what is spent on education. An online consultation platform has now been launched alongside a promise to simplify complicated university application procedures . The government has suggested a half-day of dialogue is held in secondary schools, a proposal rejected on Wednesday by the main union for school principals, which supports the protest movement, along with a number of other workers' unions. The school principals' union called for more resources and teachers. Some school and university blockades continued on Wednesday, including at Sciences Po University in Paris, where police dispersed people with tear gas. However, 86 per cent of schools were operating normally, according to Education Minister Edouard Geffray. Speaking to RTL radio , Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said he has banned the use of stun grenades after a 15 year old had his hand blown off last week. “For the moment, I am suspending its use – only for the high-school student movement – for the time it takes to understand what happened,” Mr Nunez said . Student protests are not new to France but the level of violence in recent clashes with police has shocked the public. Former political leaders, including then-president Nicolas Sarkozy, urged police to avoid physical confrontation with teenagers during 2006 protests. Some parents, who joined student demonstrations wearing white bands round their arms, said they were there to protect their children from the police. The mother of the teenager who had his hand blown off has rejected rumours he had tried to pick it up to throw at security forces. “His life was stolen from him, it's over – he no longer has a hand,” she told BFMTV. Mr Lecornu has blamed hard-left political party France Unbowed for stirring the crisis. Speaking in parliament on Tuesday, he rejected the phrase “police violence,” saying it “would suggest that there are political instructions for police repression”. He said the police response had been proportionate despite some “accidents”. Mr Nunez defended security forces, highlighting violent attacks by protesters against them, which have left hundreds injured. “It’s not simple when you have some people telling you we’re too soft, that we aren’t being forceful enough, that it’s chaos and things are getting out of hand everywhere, while others tell you the police are intervening with extreme brutality and violence,” he said. In a signal of the urgency of the situation, Mr Nunez was among the ministers convened on Tuesday evening at the Elysee Palace by President Emmanuel Macron, who for the first time held a meeting with a restricted number of ministers to address the student movement. Mr Nunez said Mr Macron had asked his ministers to “do a bit more explaining” and to “show empathy”. “Above all,” Mr Nunez said, the President asked them to “explain our doctrine regarding interventions by security and internal affairs forces – specifically, when serious violence occurs.” He added “there is no reason for police intervention” as long as “protests are peaceful”.

title: Mine-clearance workers trapped in besieged Yemeni city of Taiz
description: Houthi siege could lead to water crisis and increase civilian casualties from unexploded bombs
content: A British charity has warned that dozens of its aid workers are trapped in Taiz , south-west Yemen, which has been under siege by the Iran-backed Houthis since Sunday. The rebels have cut off the city's supply routes from Aden, weeks after their takeover of the key port city of Mokha on Yemen’s west coast. Yemeni government forces – backed by Saudi Arabia – said they had recaptured Mokha on Monday. But Taiz remains closed off, with the demining charity Halo Trust raising concerns over an estimated 30 staff members there. Though some Halo staff fled to Aden, those who remained are now trapped until the roads reopen. “Some fled from Taiz to the south. Some decided to stay, it was an incredibly difficult decision for them,” said Mara van der Kamp, Halo's Yemen director. Displacement shelters in the city of Lahj, on the road from Taiz to Aden, are packed with civilians. “There has been a lot of movement in the last 24 hours. People moved to Aden and other displacement camps,” she told The National. There is uncertainty over Taiz’s water reserves, as the city imports it from the capital, Sanaa, because of its own poor networks. Conflict in 2021 severely restricted the supply of drinking water in Taiz. The renewed fighting on the west coast has forced the charity to abandon its mine and explosive clearance projects in the area. The Halo Trust is not registered to work in Houthi-controlled areas. Teams have been redeployed to Lahj and Ad Dhale, in southern Yemen, with uncertainty as to when they can resume their work in Taiz. Yemen has recorded the world’s third-highest number of landmine casualties over the past decade. Ballistic missiles, rockets and mortars are common sights in and around cities. The most severe danger from unexploded devices in Yemen was around Taiz and Mokha. The toll on children is particularly severe. In 2024, landmines and ordnance killed or injured 260 civilians, including 44 deaths of children. Youngsters frequently encounter lethal hazards during daily activities, such as farming and herding, or by mistaking explosives for toys. The fighting around Taiz is likely to lead to a “severe” surge in casualties. “We’re hearing of weekly accidents from landmines and explosives,” Ms Van der Kamp said. “ Renewed fighting risks creating new contamination on top of an already enormous problem. ” People displaced from Mokha weeks ago had sought refuge in Taiz, mainly in buildings in previously abandoned parts of the city. These areas are closer to the front line, increasing the risk of exposure to unexploded devices.

title: Will Israelis ever find out what failures led to October 7 rampage?
description: Lost evidence, confused testimony and even foul play become more likely the longer Israel waits for a state commission of inquiry, say government critics
content: Three years since the October 7 attacks, Israel has still not formed a state commission of inquiry into the deadliest day in its history. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blames everyone in the security apparatus at the time, except himself. His opponents lay the blame fundamentally at his feet. Until there is a state commission of inquiry, the highest and most powerful level of investigation that Israel can conduct, the bitter debate will continue to pull at the loosening threads of an already divided society. The absence of an investigative body is astonishing for a country that obsesses over security. After the disaster of the 1973 Yom Kippur War, in which Israeli forces were taken by surprise and suffered heavy initial losses, it took only three weeks to establish one. An inquiry into October 7 would look into the security failures that led up to the killings, as well as the chaotic and ineffective response. There have been small military investigations into pockets of fighting that day but nothing near the scale of a state commission of inquiry into the collective failure and the divisive period that led up to it, critics say. They believe Israel needs the broad scope and power of such a body, which is independent from political leadership and can summon anyone to give evidence. Rather than being appointed by politicians, members are chosen by the president of the Supreme Court. Their investigations have in the past led to recommendations for further action against certain people, opening the possibility that Mr Netanyahu himself could be held directly responsible. Setting up a state commission is a key campaign promise of many of Mr Netanyahu’s opponents in the October 27 general election. In an interview with The Times of Israel on Wednesday to mark the third anniversary of the attacks, Mr Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , said he would establish one “immediately” if elected. With so much time having passed since the attacks, there are fears that evidence might have been compromised or lost. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara warned in August the delay could “undermine the effectiveness of a future investigation and result in the loss of evidence”. However, she supported postponing the issue until after the election, fearing the process could undermine the vote. The Israeli news outlet Haaretz , whose editorial board has long called for a state commission of inquiry, last week published testimony from experts that the effectiveness of one could diminish over time. Eyal Eshel, a leading campaigner for such an investigation, told the outlet a delay “gives those under investigation time to co-ordinate their testimony [and] memories fade, evidence can be concealed and other damage can be done”. Her daughter, a soldier, was killed at the Nahal Oz base as Hamas-led militants poured across the border and attacked communities, military outposts and a music festival early on October 7, 2023, leaving about 1,200 people dead and taking about 250 hostage. As memorials are held across the country, less than three weeks before people head to the polls, trauma is mixed with anger. A Gaza ceasefire has been struck, even though Israel continues deadly attacks on the strip, all of the hostages taken during the attacks have been returned, and almost all of the security officials in senior positions during the October 7 attacks have resigned, apart from the Prime Minister. There are still no answers.

title: Move to limit sugar, salt and fat in food is latest step in UAE drive to boost nation's health
description: Tobacco, vaping and fizzy drinks previously targeted in drive to tackle disease and obesity
content: The move to cut the amount of sodium, sugar and fat in packaged foods is the latest in a range of policies the UAE has introduced to promote healthier diets and tackle lifestyle-related diseases. The new rules, approved on Tuesday, affect packaged foods sold in the Emirates, whether locally manufactured or imported. The caps on levels of sodium, sugar and fat will be introduced in phases, with the final limits taking effect by December 31, 2030. They apply to packaged food manufacturers and businesses that handle those products, including companies operating in free zones. Companies that fail to comply face penalties including fines of up to Dh500,000 ($136,147), closure for up to six months and cancellation licences. The UAE used taxation as a public health tool in 2017, introducing excise taxes of 100 per cent on tobacco and energy drinks and 50 per cent on fizzy drinks. The government said the measures were intended to reduce consumption of harmful products, prevent chronic diseases and encourage healthier choices. This “sin tax” was expanded in 2019 to cover e-cigarettes and vaping products , while drinks containing added sugar and sweeteners were also subject to the 50 per cent rate. The strategy has now shifted to requiring manufacturers to modify products to increase their nutritional value and to target certain ingredients. At the beginning of 2026, the UAE introduced a new sugar tax system for drinks , The higher the sugar content per 100ml, the higher the tax cost per litre, in a move away from the previous flat fee. Authorities said the system was designed to encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar levels while helping consumers to make more informed choices. Abu Dhabi has also developed a broader Healthy Living Strategy, announced in November 2025, focused on increasing physical activity, improving diet and nutrition and strengthening health awareness. Sleep and mental well-being are also among its priorities. Dr Ahmed AlKhazraji, executive director of Healthy Living, said: “Our mission is clear: to make healthy living the easy choice for every citizen and resident in Abu Dhabi.” The strategy has led to measures designed to change the food environment around residents rather than relying only on individual choices. From January 1 next year, supermarkets larger than 4,000 square feet in Abu Dhabi will no longer be allowed to place foods and drinks high in fat, salt or sugar in prominent areas such as entrances, checkouts and the ends of aisles. The restrictions will also apply to online shopping platforms, where unhealthy products will no longer be allowed prominent placement on home pages, in search results, promotional pop-ups or checkout pages. Consumers can still buy the products, but they will not be prominently displayed. Schools are another focus for building a healthy community and supporting well-being. Abu Dhabi is monitoring children's school lunches for unhealthy foods such as deep-fried falafel or fries . A food “Red List” identifies products that cannot be consumed on school premises. The list includes high-fat and high-sugar foods, unhealthy drinks and some processed meals. Cakes, doughnuts, croissants, sweet pastries, marshmallows, lollipops, ice creams, slushies, chocolates (less than 50 per cent cocoa) and other high-fat and sugary desserts are also on the restricted list. Abu Dhabi has also introduced restrictions on fast-food advertising as part of a wider campaign against obesity, diabetes and other chronic diseases. The health drive ranges from new food labels through Nutri-Mark and tighter advertising rules to changes in supermarket layouts, expanded community fitness programmes, and stronger nutrition standards in schools and workplaces. The aim is not to force people to behave differently, but to change the environment around them and at the same time raise their health awareness so they make the right choices. Restaurants in hotels and tourist areas in Abu Dhabi must have at least one healthy item in each menu category under rules taking effect on October 1. At least half of the items on children's menus must meet approved SEHHI criteria, which include being lower in fat, sugar and salt, and higher in nutritional value. Food manufacturers are starting to reformulate their products. Al Ain Farms Group has announced reductions of 10 to 20 per cent in added sugar across some juices, flavoured milk, flavoured yoghurt and laban. The company said the changes conformed to Abu Dhabi's Healthy Living Strategy. The UAE's public health measures also continue to target smoking. In September, the Ministry of Finance imposed a minimum excise price of Dh1/ml for liquids used in vapes and electronic cigarettes . Products sold below that threshold will still have their excise tax calculated using the minimum value.

title: Jaguar Type 01 revealed as controversial reinvention becomes reality
description: British marque unveils its first car of a new era, a 1,015hp electric grand tourer
content: After almost two years of teasers, controversy and considerable debate about what a Jaguar should be, the car intended to answer that question has finally arrived. Jaguar has unveiled the Type 01, an all-electric four-door grand tourer and the first production model created under the British marque ’s radical reinvention. Revealed in New York, it is the road-going evolution of the Type 00 concept shown in Miami in December 2024 – and, crucially, retains much of that car’s deliberately provocative design. The car has the same enormously long bonnet, low roofline, and cab-rearward silhouette, and sits on 23-inch wheels. At the back, there is no conventional rear window; instead, a camera feeds the view behind the car to a digital rear-view display inside. The production car gains four doors, but Jaguar has resisted the temptation to significantly soften the proportions of the concept. At 5.2 metres long and only 1.4 metres high, this is a very large car. Yet Jaguar says it is also the most aerodynamic road car it has made, with active vanes, a three-stage deployable spoiler and a drag coefficient of 0.23. That contradiction – imposing but aerodynamic, extravagant but technically driven – is central to what Jaguar is trying to do. Underneath the body is Jaguar’s new dedicated electric platform, known as Jaguar Electric Architecture, or JEA. Its tri-motor powertrain produces up to 1,030ps (1,015hp) and 1,365Nm of torque, making the Type 01 the most powerful Jaguar road car yet. It will accelerate from zero to 100kph in 3.2 seconds, while Jaguar says the car can go from 100kph to 180kph in another four seconds. It has 50:50 weight distribution, all-wheel steering and torque vectoring, with expertise from Jaguar’s Formula E programme feeding into its development. But Jaguar appears keen not to turn the Type 01 into another exercise in EV acceleration statistics. The company describes it first and foremost as a grand tourer, intended to combine large reserves of power with the sort of long-distance comfort historically associated with some of its best cars. That means range is important. Jaguar quotes up to 720km under the WLTP testing cycle. Its 850-volt architecture allows up to 200 miles of range to be added in 13 minutes when connected to a 350kW charger. The Type 01 matters because Jaguar has in effect spent the past two years betting the company on it. Its transformation began publicly in November 2024 with the controversial Copy Nothing campaign and an entirely new visual identity. The Type 00 concept followed weeks later, offering the first indication that the changes went much deeper than a new logo. Jaguar’s aim was to move further upmarket, repositioning itself as a more exclusive, design-led luxury marque rather than competing in the premium market as it had before. The Type 01 is the first opportunity to judge that strategy as a physical product rather than a marketing exercise. And whatever one thinks of the result, it is difficult to accuse Jaguar of playing it safe. There are echoes of the marque’s past – particularly the extravagant bonnet-to-cabin proportions of the E-type and XJS – without attempting to remake either car. Even the name is intended to draw a line between old and new: “Type” references Jaguar’s historic models; “0” represents zero tailpipe emissions; and “1” denotes the first car of the new generation. Jaguar chose New York for the world premiere, projecting the Type 01 across digital displays in Times Square, Dumbo and the Lower East Side before the car arrived at Storied in West Chelsea. British actress Florence Pugh was also announced as the first brand ambassador of the marque’s new era. The choice of city feels significant. Jaguar’s ambitions are no longer simply about restoring a storied British car company. It wants to place itself within a broader world of fashion, architecture, art and contemporary culture and attract a new generation of customers in the process. Whether those customers will follow is the considerably harder question. Prices will start at £130,000 (Dh635,000), pushing Jaguar into a very different market from the one occupied by its previous saloons and SUVs. Orders open in early 2027, with the first customer deliveries expected during the second half of the year. There will be time to decide how successfully the Type 01 drives, how convincing its luxury credentials are and whether Jaguar can translate the enormous attention surrounding its reinvention into sales. For now, though, the most important thing about the Type 01 may be that Jaguar has followed through on a bold and controversial promise.

title: Five highlights to look out for at Christie’s first Abu Dhabi fine art auction
description: Mawasim brings more than 70 pieces to the capital on November 1
content: Christie’s first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi will offer more than 70 works spanning six decades of modern and contemporary Middle Eastern art. Mawasim : 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art will be held at the Abu Dhabi Edition hotel on November 1. It marks 20 years since Christie’s held its first UAE auction in Dubai in 2006. The sale includes artists from across the Arab world, Iran and Turkey, with works drawn from collections including Beirut’s Dalloul Collection and Sharjah’s Barjeel Art Foundation. The sale is taking place during a busy period for Abu Dhabi’s art scene, with Frieze art fair following later in November and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening on December 11. Christie’s Middle East and Africa chairman Ridha Moumni previously told The National that the auction house intended to become “more present and more visible in the city”. Among the works are an early Fahrelnissa Zeid abstract piece, a royal Egyptian portrait completed months before the monarchy fell and a monumental Paul Guiragossian . Here are five works to look out for. Estimated at $500,000 to $700,000, Composition is among the most valuable works in the sale and comes from a decisive period in Fahrelnissa Zeid ’s development. Painted in 1948–49, the work captures her move towards the kaleidoscopic abstraction that would establish her international reputation in the following decade. Interlocking passages of blue, red, yellow and orange are divided by dark lines, creating a visual language shaped partly by Zeid’s experience of seeing cities and landscapes from the air. The painting also has a strong personal history. After her husband, Prince Zeid Al-Hussein, became Iraq’s ambassador to Britain, Zeid established a studio at the Iraqi Embassy in London, where Composition was displayed. The work remained with her through later stages of her life, including her years in Amman, making it both an important early abstraction and a witness to her own movement between cities and countries. Mahmoud Said’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia , estimated at $400,000 to $600,000, carries one of the most personal provenances in the auction. The sitter is Princess Fadia, the youngest daughter of King Farouk I and Queen Farida of Egypt. Said was her great-uncle, making the painting as much a family portrait as a royal one. Its timing gives it added historical weight. Painted in 1952, it was completed only months before Egypt’s monarchy came to an end. Saïd gave the portrait to Queen Farida before it passed to Princess Fadia and remained within the family. According to the catalogue, it was among the possessions Fadia took with her into exile. What began as a portrait of royal childhood became a lasting connection to a life that had abruptly changed. Said had also painted Queen Farida as a child decades earlier, giving the work a link to two generations of the same family. At almost 2.4 metres wide, Noces is one of the largest works by Paul Guiragossian to come to market. Estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, the painting predates the mature figurative style for which the Lebanese-Armenian artist became widely known. A seated bride anchors a gathering of musicians, dancers and guests, while the compressed space and elongated figures anticipate the more expressive direction his work would take. One detail is especially personal. Among the musicians is a blind figure recalling Guiragossian’s father, who was blind and remembered as a violinist and singer. The painting was acquired directly from Guiragossian by Lebanese architect and collector Farid Trad and was shown at the artist’s 1959 exhibition in Beirut. Moumni has described it as one of Guiragossian’s most exceptional works. Its return to the market is also timely, with 2026 marking the centenary of the artist’s birth and Bassam Freiha Art Foundation in Abu Dhabi presenting an exhibition devoted to his work. Ahmed Mater ’s Golden Hour examines the transformation of Makkah through one of the most recognisable views in the Islamic world. Estimated at $80,000 to $120,000, the monumental photograph belongs to Mater’s Desert of Pharan project, which looks at the changing relationship between the holy city’s sacred history and its rapidly evolving urban landscape. The Kaaba and pilgrims performing tawaf sit at the centre of the image, surrounded by cranes, construction equipment and new infrastructure. Mater places the cyclical movement of a centuries-old ritual against the constant momentum of development. The result is less a simple contrast than a layering of different ideas of time: religious continuity, ancient landscape and modern construction all occupying the same frame. There are four prints of Golden Hour in total: three numbered edition copies, plus one artist’s proof. Christie’s is selling the single artist’s proof. Another example from the edition is held by Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art in Doha. Hassan Sharif ’s Press Conference No 2 brings satire into the sale. Painted in 2008 and estimated at $50,000 to $70,000, the work presents a distorted public speaker whose open mouth, misaligned eyes and exaggerated appearance undermine the authority normally associated with political spectacle. The objects in front of him resemble microphones but also spoons and ladles, giving the scene an absurd edge. The painting connects to Sharif’s early career as a cartoonist for Akhbar Dubai , where he addressed political and social subjects before becoming one of the central figures in the development of conceptual and experimental art in the UAE. That influence continued well beyond his own practice. Moumni previously told The National that Sharif would appear in the sale alongside younger Emirati artists shaped by his legacy. Press conference No 2 was also included in Christie’s 2023 exhibition, Emirati Art Reimagined: Hassan Sharif and the Contemporary Voices.

title: Dubai home sale transactions fall in third quarter amid regional uncertainty
description: Buyers more cautious, with deal volumes and values declining, report finds
content: The volume and value of residential property transactions in Dubai fell sharply in the third quarter of this year as buyers became “more cautious” amid regional uncertainty over the Iran war, according to a new report. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year. The number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, which reflected “the impact of reduced activity as the lag in property sales registrations begins to clear”, the report by property consultants Cavendish Maxwell said. “The Q3 2026 data captures a mix of recent and earlier buying activity, reflecting the time between a purchase being agreed and formally registered as a sale,” Ronan Arthur, director and head of residential valuation at Cavendish Maxwell , said. “Purchasing activity became more measured, with buyers being more cautious in the weeks and months following the start of the conflict.” The off-plan sector continued to dominate residential sales during the quarter, accounting for 65 per cent of total sales values and 72 per cent of property purchases. Dubai's property market has boomed in recent years, benefiting from government initiatives such as residency permits for retired and remote workers, expansion of the 10-year golden visa programme and overall growth in the UAE’s economy on diversification efforts. However, the market started to cool during regional tensions triggered by the Iran war that began in late February. The war also affected hospitality, tourism and aviation as the US and Israel attacked Iran, and Tehran retaliated by striking energy sites and civilian infrastructure across the Gulf region and Iraq. “While the fundamentals driving Dubai real estate demand remain, near-term activity will continue to be shaped by a number of factors, including the frequency and number of launches, regional uncertainty and a broader normalisation in buyer activity,” Mr Arthur added. Residential sales transactions fell for the first nine months of the year, Cavendish Maxwell data showed, with total volumes down 23 per cent on annual basis to 112,580 and values declining 27 per cent to Dh292 billion. A report by S&P Global Ratings also found a significant drop in Dubai's residential property transactions as a result of the war. Citing Dubai Land department data, the ratings agency said total real estate sale transactions averaged 12,644 per month between March and September 2026, a drop of 26 per cent from 17,198 in January and February 2026. It also said prices declined by 5 per cent to 15 per cent between the end of 2025 and September 2026, quoting industry reports. S&P Global Ratings expects a “gradual” price correction in Dubai’s property market. “Over the medium term, we anticipate that the UAE and Dubai governments will remain focused on developing the emirate's attractiveness through reforms and large-scale infrastructure projects. That is why, for the residential real estate market, we expect a gradual price correction rather than a rapid price decline,” it said. The ratings agency expects secondary-market transactions to become more prevalent as price declines prompt investors to offload their properties. The greatest impact could be on investor sentiment and demand within the luxury and ultra-luxury segments, it added. Emaar Properties founder Mohamed Alabbar also indicated an “adjustment of 5 per cent to 10 per cent” in Dubai’s broader real estate sector because of the war. “But then again, you know, if the situation settles, God knows what could happen in this market. It could become pretty fast [paced],” he said last month at AIM Congress in Dubai.

title: Iraq devalues currency as war and Hormuz closure squeeze cash
description: Cabinet approves central bank recommendation to set new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar
content: Iraq has officially devalued its currency again, setting a new official exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, according to a document seen by The National . The Council of Ministers approved the move late on Tuesday, based on a recommendation from the Central Bank of Iraq, the banking regulator said in a directive sent to all licensed banks, electronic payment companies and exchange houses on Monday. According to the directive, the new structure is that the central bank will purchase from the Ministry of Finance at the price of 1,500 dinars. The sale price to banks will be at 1,510 dinars, and then to the public at 1,520 dinars. All institutions were ordered to update their systems, notify branches, stop using the previous rate, and adopt the new price from the start of business on Tuesday, the document says. It is Iraq’s second major devaluation in six years. In December 2020, during the Covid-19 oil crash, the central bank cut the dinar rate from 1,182 to 1,450 per dollar to cover a crippling deficit. That rate was later adjusted to 1,320 as the official rate under the previous government, though the market rate often hovered higher. This time, the decision is driven by a deepening cash crunch since the outbreak of the Iran-Israel war in June 2025 and the intermittent closure and threat to the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq earns more than 90 per cent of its budget in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through Hormuz – the narrow waterway carrying a third of the world’s seaborne oil. Since the Iran war broke out on February 28, shipping insurance costs have soared , tanker traffic has been disrupted, and Iraq’s oil loadings from its southern terminals at Basra have faced delays and discounts. The result: Iraq gets fewer dollars, and when it converts those dollars into dinars to pay nearly eight million public employees, contractors, farmers and pensioners, it needs more dinars than it has. In recent months, Baghdad has delayed salary payments in several provinces, deferred payments to wheat farmers and construction firms, and relied on short-term borrowing from state banks. The country's finance ministry warned parliament that without adjustment, it could not fund the 2026 budget, which includes 100,000 new public jobs demanded by political blocs as part of government formation talks. Devaluation is the fastest fix. By lowering the dinar’s value from 1,320 to 1,500, the government gets about 13 per cent more dinars for every dollar of oil it sells – enough to print salaries without printing dollars it does not have. But the cost is passed to Iraqis. A weaker dinar makes imported food, medicine, cars and construction materials – almost everything Iraq imports – more expensive. After the 2020 devaluation, inflation jumped and triggered protests in southern provinces.

title: Arabian Gulf Cup: UAE have plenty to work with despite final defeat in Jeddah
description: Hammam Al Hammami was standout performer for Saudi Arabia but national team too showed promise ahead of next assignment – Asian Cup
content: The UAE were outplayed in the final of the Arabian Gulf Cup by hosts Saudi Arabia in Jeddah on Tuesday night, but new UAE coach Zlatko Dalic was still able to reflect on a positive first assignment. The former Croatia manager saw his new charges succumb to early goals from Hammam Al Hammami and Feras Albrikan, as Saudi Arabia emerged deserving winners . The eight-team regional tournament stirs high passions – as shown by ugly skirmishes between fans and players, plus UAE captain Khalid Essa’s reaction to jeers during the national anthem. But Dalic has been brought in with a view to bringing success on a broader scale than a local stoush. The next significant challenge is rapidly heading into view. The Asian Cup, which will also be staged in Saudi Arabia, starts in January. Under Dalic’s guidance, it is hoped the UAE will go deep in that competition. Looking ahead to the first game in that, against Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, here is what he will have learnt from the Gulf Cup. In terms of talent, there is plenty to work with. The pool of players available for Dalic has been expanded by naturalisation. There might be even more outstanding UAE Pro League players who are becoming eligible before the Asian Cup. That is a double-edged sword. For some while now, it has been unclear what the best XI is for the national team. The side might look good in one international window, but then by the next there could be two or three more players eligible for selection who dilute what went before. At the Gulf Cup, for example, Dalic handed out a number of debuts to players who now look inked into the best XI. Players like Yuri Cesar, Mamadou Coulibaly, Ousmane Camara and Guilherme Bala . But even they might not be guaranteed starters if the likes of Matias Palacios, the Al Ain schemer, and Federico Cartabia, Shabab Al Ahli’s playmaker, are available. What the deeper player pool does allow for is tactical flexibility. The two early goals in the final against Saudi Arabia meant the game had gone by the time Dalic was able to respond effectively. But his substitutions did show how personnel changes can rectify issues. Al Hammami, the jet-heeled Saudi left-winger, was the difference between the two sides in the first half of the final. Marcos Meloni, the right back who has been a key figure under successive UAE coaches, could not keep up. Dalic responded by switching Ruben Canedo – the left back who, like Al Hammami, is diminutive but fast – to the right, and bringing on the powerful Richard Akonnor to play on the left. Not that the UAE were able to overturn the deficit, but at least they were able to regain parity in terms of the run of play. Dalic reasoned – logically – that it was the nightmare start which cost the UAE. “The first goal and second goal killed us,” he said. “I told my players when we were preparing for the game, the first 20 minutes will be the key to the game; please be careful, be patient and focused. We cannot concede a goal. “After conceding two, it is not easy to come back into the game.” His team had looked spooked by the frenzied atmosphere inside the King Abdullah Sport City Stadium. The official attendance was touching 63,000, and by the way all the gangways were filled, there might even have been a few more in than that. An impressive chunk of that – around 12,000 – were travelling UAE supporters. Both sets of players were amped by the atmosphere, but it was the home side who kept their cool the best. That is an issue because it is a recurring one for the UAE. When World Cup qualification was on the line in Doha last year, amid a similarly wild atmosphere in Doha, the players were also distracted, and lost out as a result. It is difficult to think how the Gulf Cup could have gone any better for Saudi Arabia. They won the title – for the first time in 25 years – without conceding a goal. Even before the final , Dalic pointed out they were the best side in it. They looked like a side transformed from that which had traipsed out of the World Cup in North America in the summer without landing a punch. They were without their talisman, Salem Al Dawsari , and yet his replacement, Al Hammami, announced himself as a real attacking threat. For Georgios Donis, it was validation. He had only been appointed as coach at short notice before the World Cup . To judge him on that would have been unfair. The Gulf Cup was a greater reflection of his worth, and he is already excited about what they can do at the Asian Cup. “There are players who played a lot of minutes over two weeks, and we delivered a great performance and deserve this achievement,” Donis said. “I'm happy with what we've accomplished, and now we'll start focusing on the Asian Cup.”

title: Cheers for hardliners on Israel's campaign trail as security drowns out social and economic problems
description: Candidates make their pitch to Anglo-Israeli voters in Jerusalem
content: In a normally quiet corner of upmarket West Jerusalem , almost 300 members of the city’s Anglo-Jewish community joined a raucous election debate three weeks before they will cast their ballots in Israel's general election on October 27. The crowd at the sold-out event was partly secular but mainly religious. The VIP front seats hosted politicians, their aides, doyens of the city’s pro-Israel PR industry and a British-Israeli rabbi and pundit whose wife and two daughters were killed in a Palestinian attack in the occupied West Bank in 2023. They were there to cheer and, on rarer occasions, jeer the 10 candidates from across the spectrum of Zionist politics on stage. Their reactions gave a clear indication of where this influential Israeli community stands, one that plays a disproportionately important role in how Israel is viewed abroad at a time when its international popularity is in sharp decline . Israel’s problems are not merely external. Three years of war have pushed the economy into uncertainty and stress is palpable on the streets during a short walk to the shops, even before you see the price of milk. Yet the panellists had little to say about the cost of living and nothing about the crisis in the country’s education system. The message for politicians by the end of the evening was clear: to grab the attention of voters by talking incessantly about security, enemies, settlements and the need for defiance in the face of Israel’s sliding popularity abroad. The first loud cheers were for Israeli settler and social media personality Yishai Fleisher, a party colleague of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir . Mr Fleisher praised Mr Ben-Gvir over the deteriorating conditions for Palestinians in Israeli jails, increasing Jewish worship at Al Aqsa Mosque compound and lowering his car insurance bill, which he linked to a decrease in vehicle thefts. Leading Israeli rights group B’Tselem has described Israel’s prison system for Palestinians as a “network of torture camps”. Displays of Israeli nationalism at Al Aqsa draw criticism from the international community, which fears changes to the decades-long status quo could cause major unrest. Other crime statistics have worsened under Mr Ben-Gvir’s tenure – the murder rate among Arab Israelis in particular. “Is Ben-Gvir hurting our international reputation? The genocide [in Gaza] narrative is, but is that Ben-Gvir? No!” Mr Fleisher said. “They find enemies all the time and try to take us down around the world. Here comes one guy who is talking straight and strong, who the enemies are afraid of – and that’s a good thing. “Ben-Gvir, you can like him or not like him, but you don’t have to marry your daughter to him, you don’t have to invite him over for Shabbos lunch. He’s a hammer. He gets things done.” The most left-wing candidate in attendance, Moran Zer Katzenstein of The Democrats, received moderate applause for her work on women’s rights. She was also the candidate who received the loudest jeer, which came when she challenged audience members who appeared to support expelling the population of Gaza . “You can clap if you think this is what Jewish morality is,” Ms Zer Katzenstein said after the jeering. The audience did exactly that – what followed was one of the longest and most passionate bursts of applause of the night, with bellows of support across the room. Another of the panellists, Moishe Feiglin of the Zehut party, recently called for the total expulsion of Gazans by any means necessary in an interview with The Jerusalem Post . He suggested even Gaza's infants were enemies: “The baby that will be born in Gaza tomorrow will do exactly the same, God forbid, to your baby that will be born tomorrow in Jerusalem. There’s no other way. That’s the reason they live for. That’s what they learn with their mother's milk.” A bounce in opinion polls suggests Mr Feiglin’s party could win five to six seats in the 120-member Knesset. The faction is in a right-wing alliance with the Religious Zionist Party led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who was recently filmed boasting about Israel’s occupation of a huge part of southern Lebanon , saying “the world is not stopping us”. Although many parties were present, the event did not paint a complete picture of Israeli politics. The two main ultra-Orthodox parties spurned their invitations. The bitter debate around enlisting ultra-Orthodox young men into the Israeli military was raised but received surprisingly little attention given dire warnings about a lack of manpower. Israeli-Arab parties, which were recently battling disqualification in the Supreme Court, were not represented. The only Palestinian mentioned at length was Yoseph Haddad of Amcha Israel, a combative pro-Israel influencer. Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party, currently the most powerful opposition party, is accused by the far right of being a backdoor for Arab parties to enter an opposition coalition. At the event, Amichai Chikli, from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, accused Mr Eisenkot of dangerously viewing Syria ’s President Ahmad Al Shara as an “opportunity” for Israel. Much of the energy of the opposition parties was taken up defending the record of their candidates, many of whom have been in the Israeli political system for years. Mati Gill of Naftali Bennett’s party was asked why voters should trust its members after its leader’s turbulent political career. That career has attracted accusations of hypocrisy and broken promises, including from the settler community, which he used to represent as head of a settlers' group called the Yesha Council. Mr Gill said Mr Bennett’s ideals had not changed since he entered politics. The message does not appear to be cutting through. With so little time until elections, the former prime minister continues a steady decline in the polls. Despite bitter moments, the conclusion was a festival of politeness, featuring a resounding rendition of the national anthem and far-right candidates praising even Ms Zer Katzenstein. Those in attendance who wanted to learn more about plans for the economy, education, the environment and infrastructure would have left disappointed at the end of the two-hour session. They did not seem downcast, however, despite the challenges Israel faces in all those areas. Once again, it seems Israeli voters will head to the polls with security on their minds and the many extreme aspects that priority has come to embody.

title: Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills
description: AiNative initiative will equip citizens, residents and government employees with vital tech skills
content: Abu Dhabi on Wednesday set out plans to equip thousands of government employees and the wider public with artificial intelligence skills under a major drive to advance responsible use of the rapidly evolving technology . The Abu Dhabi government and the emirate's Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence have joined forces with global tech giants OpenAI and Microsoft to launch the AiNative training programme. The key strategy will provide 20,000 government employees with cutting-edge support by the end of the year and is central to Abu Dhabi's mission to become the world's first AI-native government by 2027. The initiative – announced at the Ai Everything conference in the capital by Abu Dhabi's Department of Government Enablement – will seek to encourage citizens and residents, government workers and department leaders to unlock the potential of AI to drive progress. Under the initiative, employees will be given help to build up expertise with ChatGPT, Codex and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Specialised, function-specific certifications, including areas such as coding and data, will follow in later phases of the project.
