Citizens and residents will be able to access the training programme via Tomouh, DGE's AI-driven learning app, which can be accessed through the UAE Pass government app. The scheme will cover practical applications of AI in everyday life, including managing personal finances, running a small business, finding a job, studying and creating content responsibly online, and will be delivered through the free version of ChatGPT. DGE owns the curriculum, which has been developed with OpenAI, Microsoft and MBZUAI. “AI will only create lasting value when people have the knowledge and confidence to use it well,” Wesam Lootah, director general of GovDigital at DGE, said. “AiNative puts that capability at the heart of Abu Dhabi’s AI journey, giving government employees and the wider community practical skills to use AI responsibly in their work and everyday lives. “By bringing together government, industry and academia, we are building a common foundation for an AI-enabled society and government.” Eric Xing, president and professor at MBZUAI, emphasised the importance of ensuring access to AI for all as it shapes the future. “Championing a culture of lifelong learning ensures that the benefits of new technologies are understood and realised responsibly by all,” he said. “Through AiNative, people can gain practical knowledge alongside the judgment to apply AI thoughtfully in a way that it becomes a partner for progress. “Developing this capability at scale will be an important part of Abu Dhabi’s transition to an AI-native government and society.” AiNative is being rolled out in phases. An initial pilot within government is already under way, before it will be made public. The launch of AiNative follows the roll-out of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 35,000 Abu Dhabi government employees through the Frontier Employee Programme, announced in July. Abu Dhabi unveiled its vision to be the world's first AI-powered government last year, as part of its Digital Strategy 2025-2027. Led by the DGE, the programme will allocate Dh13 billion ($3.5 billion) to boost digital infrastructure, automate 100 per cent of government processes, and integrate sovereign cloud computing across all operations. The strategy is expected to contribute more than Dh24 billion to Abu Dhabi’s economy by 2027 and create more than 5,000 employment opportunities supporting Emiratisation efforts.

title: Guyana: The tiny country with big ambitions fast emerging as a global oil producer
description: Surging oil production is making South American nation one of the fastest growing economies in the world
content: A tiny South American country is emerging as a reliable oil supplier globally as flows from the Middle East face disruptions and European nations seek alternatives to Russia. Guyana's rapid increase in crude production, from zero in 2019 to about 900,000 barrels per day in the first half of the year, is catapulting the country to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, lifting thousands of people out of poverty with newfound wealth. The non-Opec country's oil output is expected to reach 1 million barrels per day (bpd) imminently, with the country targeting 1.7 million bpd by 2030. “With disruptions in the Middle East, Guyana’s oil is becoming strategically more important to global markets,” Stephanie Rivera, research analyst at S&P Global Energy told The National. “Guyana’s light-to-medium, low-sulfur crude is not exposed to Middle Eastern shipping chokepoints, providing refiners with an attractive option for diversifying away from Middle Eastern supply. As the conflict in the Middle East continues, Guyanese crude can help enhance energy security in an increasingly tight market.” The Middle East conflict, which broke out on February 28 after the US and Israel attacked Iran, has roiled global markets, with prices jumping to an intraday high of about $120 per barrel in April. Tehran carried out retaliatory strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure leading to curtailment of production, with 10 million bpd of Gulf output remaining shut as of August amid heightened security risks, according to the International Energy Agency report last month. The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than 20 per cent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies used to pass before the war, has been a restricted route since the war began, raising supply concerns. Countries in Europe, North and South America have been the main importers of Guyana’s oil, but the Middle East crisis has also prompted some Asian countries to look towards Guyana for oil. Europe imported up to 57 per cent of Guyanese crude between March and August this year, Kpler data shows, with the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, the UK, Italy, Poland and Spain being the main buyers. The Americas took about a third, while Asian nations, including China, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, imported about 6 per cent of Guyanese crude during the period. Turkey bought roughly 5 per cent. Another factor that is contributing to a rise in demand for Guyana's crude is the Ukraine war. European nations are looking for alternative sources of supply as they seek to reduce dependence on Russian crude and squeeze off Moscow’s oil revenue as it continues to wage war against Ukraine. Guyanese crude is also highly valued for its low sulfur content, high yields of middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel, and competitive break-even costs of $30–$40 per barrel that "make it particularly attractive to refiners, especially in Europe", Ms Rivera said. An oil boom is a recent phenomenon in Guyana, with production starting only seven years ago following the discovery of oil in 2015. An ExxonMobil-led consortium – including Chevron, and China’s CNOOC have been dominating production, with total investment estimated at between $55 billion and $60 billion at the Stabroek Block. The group hit a milestone last month by producing its billionth barrel of oil at Stabroek less than seven years after production began in 2019. “With an estimated resource base of just under 11 billion oil-equivalent barrels and plans for up to eight offshore developments by 2030, the Stabroek block is helping meet demand across the Americas, Europe and Asia, contributing to global energy security and market stability,” ExxonMobil said in a statement last month. More projects are expected to come online, with Uaru expected to start up by the end of 2026, Whiptail expected to start up in 2027, and Hammerhead expected to begin production in 2029, it added. Last year, France’s TotalEnergies, QatarEnergy and Malaysia’s Petronas also signed an agreement with the Guyanese government to explore a shallow block off the coast of Guyana for oil production. Oil revenue, spurred by a rise in production and higher prices, has transformed Guyana from a small, agriculture and services based economy into one of the world’s fastest-growing economies. From an annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent in 2019, when it first started producing oil, the country’s economy expanded by 43.5 per cent in the following year, 20.1 per cent in 2021, 63.3 per cent in 2022, 33.8 per cent in 2023, 43.8 per cent in 2024 and 19.3 per cent in 2025, International Monetary Fund data shows. The country's GDP is projected to grow by 16.2 per cent this year, the highest rate globally, as oil revenue continues to increase due to higher production and rising crude prices. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, is currently trading at about $100 per barrel. "The economic outlook [for Guyana] remains highly favourable," the IMF said in July. "Oil production is expected to continue expanding, and the non-oil economy is projected to grow by about 7 per cent on average over the next five years as the government continues its ambitious plans to address infrastructure and developmental needs." Data analysis and visualisation by Isaac Arroyo.

title: Louvre Abu Dhabi names Souraya Noujaim new director ahead of 10th anniversary
description: Islamic art specialist returns to Saadiyat Island museum after helping shape its curatorial vision
content: Souraya Noujaim has been appointed director of Louvre Abu Dhabi , returning to the museum where she spent five years overseeing its curatorial and collections work. The Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi announced the appointment as the museum prepares to mark its 10th anniversary in 2027. Noujaim takes over from Manuel Rabate , who led Louvre Abu Dhabi since 2016 and oversaw its opening the following year. Rabate's departure from the museum was announced in February. An art historian and curator specialising in Islamic art history and archaeology, Noujaim most recently served as director of the Department of Islamic Arts at the Louvre Museum in Paris and chief of the French Grand Department of Islamic Art Heritage. In Paris, she oversaw a collection of 18,000 Islamic artworks. But her relationship with Louvre Abu Dhabi stretches back to before the museum opened on Saadiyat Island in November 2017. Noujaim helped develop its intellectual and curatorial vision and returned in February 2018 as the museum's first scientific, curatorial and collections management director, a position she held until April 2023. During that period, she oversaw curatorial, scientific and collections activities, helped develop the museum's collection through acquisitions and was involved in establishing initiatives, including Art Here , the annual exhibition and prize for contemporary artists. As director, she will oversee Louvre Abu Dhabi's collection, exhibitions, research, conservation, education, public programmes and visitor experience, as well as its broader institutional strategy. “Louvre Abu Dhabi holds a special place in my professional and personal journey,” Noujaim said in a statement announcing her appointment. “Having had the privilege of contributing to the museum's development over many years, I am honoured to return to Abu Dhabi and lead this remarkable institution into its next chapter.” She said she planned to build on the museum's legacy, deepen its engagement with audiences and continue expanding its collection. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of DCT Abu Dhabi, said Noujaim's appointment continues a long-standing relationship. “As the first universal museum in the Arab world, Louvre Abu Dhabi is a powerful reflection of our belief in culture as a bridge between people, ideas and societies. Since 2017, it has contributed greatly to the emirate’s status as a global cultural capital. "Dr Noujaim has been part of the museum’s journey from its earliest stages, helping shape its collection, scholarly foundations and distinctive universal narrative. We are confident that Dr Noujaim’s international expertise and deep understanding of what makes Louvre Abu Dhabi unique will contribute to the museum’s role as a leading cultural institution in the region and on the global stage.” Noujaim takes over as Louvre Abu Dhabi prepares for a significant milestone. Since opening in November 2017, the Jean Nouvel-designed museum has welcomed more than eight million visitors and staged 22 temporary exhibitions. It has also held five editions of Art Here and six exhibitions at its Children's Museum , alongside educational, research, conservation and scholarship programmes. The makeup of its permanent galleries has also changed considerably. When Louvre Abu Dhabi opened, about 30 per cent of the works displayed were from its own collection, with about 70 per cent borrowed from French museums and regional lenders. While the overall number of works on display has remained broadly consistent, nearly two-thirds of those now shown across the museum's four chronological sections belong to Louvre Abu Dhabi. The change reflects the expansion of a permanent collection that spans thousands of years, from prehistoric objects and religious artefacts to paintings and contemporary art. The museum was established under an intergovernmental agreement between the UAE and France and remains the first universal museum in the Arab world. Noujaim will now oversee its transition into its second decade, including the continued development of its permanent collection and its role as a centre for research, conservation and cultural exchange.

title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman gives blood to launch country's donation drive
description: More than 900,000 people donated in Saudi Arabia in 2025
content: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has donated blood, launching the kingdom’s annual national donation campaign for this year, Saudi state media has reported. The campaign aims to promote regular voluntary blood donation and increase public awareness of its importance, while helping secure sufficient supplies of blood and blood products for patients, including those with cancer, blood disorders and critical or emergency medical conditions, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Tuesday. More than 900,000 people donated blood in Saudi Arabia in 2025, according to the news agency, as the kingdom seeks to increase voluntary donations and maintain a sustainable national blood supply. Last year’s campaign, also launched by Prince Mohammed , helped quadruple the number of donors and recorded more than 65,000, the highest figure in the history of Saudi blood banks, according to authorities. All donations recorded during the campaign were voluntary, with more than 85 per cent coming from first-time donors. The blood collected supported more than 63,000 patients, while platelet and plasma donations each benefited about 10,000 people, the SPA said.

title: Paris Fashion Week: The shows that defined spring/summer 2027
description: From Louis Vuitton and Chanel to Valentino and Balenciaga, designers revisit house codes and embrace craftsmanship
content: Paris Fashion Week is often a battle for attention, but this season’s strongest collections were less concerned with spectacle than with identity. Across the spring/summer 2027 shows, designers engaged with the codes that make their houses distinctive, whether through couture craftsmanship, archival references, eccentric styling or a renewed focus on clothes people might actually want to wear. That meant lightness at Hermes and Dior, romanticism at Elie Saab, everyday couture at Balenciaga and a celebration of individuality at Valentino and Dries Van Noten. Elsewhere, Schiaparelli explored a more practical side, Saint Laurent doubled down on unapologetic glamour and Matieres Fecales turned the runway into a platform for social commentary. The approaches differed, but the question running through Paris was much the same: what should a fashion house stand for now? Nicolas Ghesquiere has spent much of his career making clothes that look ready to take flight. For spring/summer 2027 at Louis Vuitton, he pushed the idea closer to literal, expressing futurism through weightless, fluid clothes engineered to move. Days after receiving the Chevalier de la Legion d’honneur from Emmanuel Macron, Ghesquiere stripped his architectural codes back to their lightest form. Beneath a suspended traffic jam of futuristic cars, dresses, coats and tailoring skimmed the body in scarf-weight silks, jersey, cashmere and fabrics lighter than chiffon. Clothes floated, bounced and shifted with the wearer, while tailoring was deconstructed and silhouettes recalibrated around the moving body. It was a distinctly Vuitton proposition: less baggage, more freedom. Ghesquiere’s future was not something to wear, but something to move through. Being a creative director at a heritage house means, sooner or later, talking to ghosts. At Chanel, that conversation is almost unavoidable, with Gabrielle Chanel’s presence remaining unusually tangible. For this spring/summer collection, Matthieu Blazy once again made the founder an active character. The collection unfolded like a history of the house. Sheer ivory knit slips were pinned with feather corsages; fringed cardigans softened the silhouette before raw-edged tailoring and reworked Charvet shirts introduced a more masculine note. Voluminous tutu skirts brought a touch of mischief, while cloud-printed organza, beaded plaids and delicate floral mesh added increasingly decorative flourishes. The staple tweed jacket remained the essential building block, sometimes cropped, sometimes sharpened with piping or crystal collars, or even as sleeveless iterations with playful card-suit buttons. A new stretchy tweed, made from re-embroidered organza and silk, loosened the formality of the house signature. Accessories followed suit: pearl drops, layered shells and beads, and quilted chain bags. The show was opened and closed by a model carrying an original 2.55 bag from the archives, as a neat reminder of where this new Chanel began. At Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez combined their New England upbringing with Spanish history, mixing American pragmatism with Andalusian drama. Polos appeared backwards, checked blazers and boat shoes avoided preppy clichés, while basketball jerseys inspired chiffon slip dresses with beaded fringing. Material and proportion made familiar pieces strange. Sunglass resin formed sculptural collars on knits and trench coats, while oversized buckles and bows transformed footwear. Shell jackets and anoraks sat alongside sheer dresses, leather minis and bright stripes and florals. Presented inside the Château de Vincennes, the collection placed the audience unusually close to the clothes, with a mazelike runway bringing models within arm’s reach. It suited a collection concerned with intimacy: how fabric feels against skin, how familiar clothes move and how recognisable pieces can be made strange through proportion or material. The finale brought bouclé mini dresses and hotpants fringed with floral embroidery. It captured the designers’ approach at Loewe: taking familiar clothes apart and rebuilding them through unexpected fabric, scale and colour. At Hermes , Nadège Vanhée embraced lightness for spring/summer. Taking her cue from the long, rectangular blades of ceiling fans, she worked swooping pleats into a black leather blazer, a chocolate-suede skirt lined in yellow silk and an orange dress cinched with a double-buckle belt. Sporty dresses made from narrow strips of leather laid over silk mesh brought further graphic lightness. Airiness ran throughout the collection. Perforated suede jackets and open-knit dresses, some resembling fishing nets, revealed flashes of skin and were layered over statement underwear. Wide-leg trousers and jackets in featherweight denim and printed silk kept silhouettes loose and breezy. Accessories were equally pared back: flat leather boots with delicate side stitching, barely-there strappy sandals, small bucket bags with fishnet details, cross-body styles and slim leather clutches. This season, Elie Saab looked to the languid glamour of 1930s film star Jean Harlow, mixing it with the house’s early-2000s codes. Sheer layers, intricate embroidery and soft shades of blush, powder blue, sage and sand came together in a deeply romantic collection of slip dresses, featuring appliqué flowers and delicate straps slipping from shoulders. Familiar floating silhouettes, bustiers and floral embellishments returned with a lighter, more contemporary hand. Backstage, Saab said the team had been exploring the house archive held at the Elie Saab Foundation in Beirut. The brand will also bring its couture-inflected codes to a younger audience this month with the launch of its H&M collaboration . Michael Rider’s Celine has a knack for making clothes feel considered yet unforced and this collection resisted fashion’s usual grandstanding. The clothes were relaxed: creamy whites, hay tones and tomato red; collarless leather capes, off-the-shoulder tops, delicate knits and slouchy trousers cinched at the ankle. A floor-length sundial-print dress brought a flower child element, while beaded knitwear and satin shirts added artisanal polish. Rider’s strength lies in the details. A skinny belt, oversized bangle, awkward fit or scuffed sneaker can push an otherwise polished look somewhere more interesting. His Celine moves between Parisian chic, sportswear and bohemia without settling into any one of them. The result feels spontaneous, but never accidental. At Balenciaga, Pierpaolo Piccioli applied atelier techniques to decidedly more democratic clothes: T-shirts, jeans and leather jackets. Craftsmanship was deliberately visible. Stitching used to structure couture corsets appeared externally on ready-to-wear, shaping shoulders, narrowing waists and exaggerating hips. Jeans were cut on the bias for a slouchier fit, tailoring lost its rigidity, and handbags were draped, twisted and knotted by hand. A pale-pink taffeta ballgown worn over jeans captured the idea best: on closer inspection, it was an enormous T-shirt. Piccioli’s proposition was clear: couture need not remain behind glass. At Balenciaga, it can be worn, altered and taken on to the street. After spending the summer driving around the US East Coast with social media deleted, Daniel Roseberry returned to essentials for Schiaparelli’s spring collection: sharp separates, a largely monochrome palette and the house’s unmistakable appetite for drama. A backward tuxedo dress opened the show, reshaped with hourglass boning. Elsewhere, bodysuits plunged dramatically, frills framed little black dresses and oversized tuxedo shirts were softened with moulded satin bibs. A laminated-jersey top could be paired with a skirt or dressed down with trousers. Roseberry also broadened Schiaparelli beyond its gilded occasionwear. Broderie anglaise and spiral knits brought warmer-weather ease, while final jackets nodded to Elsa Schiaparelli through archival embroidery. The result remained unmistakably Schiaparelli, but with enough practicality to suggest clothes intended to be worn. Alessandro Michele turned Valentino’s spring show into a celebration of books beneath the iron arches of Paris’s Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve. Guests were asked to donate a book, while Michele created a fictional library of imagined titles and authors, inspired by the “antilibrary” – books that remain unread, but whose potential still matters. Michele rarely settles for the obvious. Double-pleated jeans, plaid shirts and baseball caps offered glimpses of everyday dressing amid fuchsia satin, oversized rosettes, lace cycling shorts, jewel-toned bustiers and embroidered skirts. His unease with technology added another layer. He has spoken about preserving the human impulse behind fashion rather than reducing it to numbers, reflected here in deliberately improbable combinations: mohair with knobbly wool, harem trousers with sequins and gold-tipped shoes. In an increasingly algorithmic world, eccentricity may be one of fashion’s last human signatures. Haider Ackermann loosened the metaphorical tie at Tom Ford. For spring/summer 2027, the designer introduced racy swimwear to the runway, setting barely-there pieces against the house’s familiar armoury of sharp tailoring, cashmere, leather and silk. The mood was about freedom, he said, with a dash of danger and decadence, and the unabashed glamour of Tom Ford’s own era. Suits came in baby blue, black, olive and white, worn bare-chested or with plunging swimsuits, bras and open shirts. Sultry evening dresses slipped off the shoulder to reveal leather or satin bras, while silk robes and bathrobe-style trench coats nodded to Hugh Hefner. Ackermann has clearly understood that at Tom Ford, seduction is not a historical footnote; it is the house code. Stella McCartney took her spring/summer 2027 collection to the sea, opening with David Attenborough’s voice reminding us that the ocean, covering 70 per cent of the planet, is more than a backdrop to human life. Her childhood fascination with marine life surfaced in dolphin graphics, wave motifs and a rock-pool palette of washed greens, coral, cream and deep brown. Clear fishing line ran through knitwear, edges curled like oyster shells and recycled denim glittered with crystals. Drawstring-waist jackets, sheer-legged trousers, pastel windbreakers and utility pieces kept things sporty. Deadstock fabrics, recycled polyester, lab-grown wool and protein-based materials challenged others to rethink their supply chains. Fresh from launching her Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition, McCartney is in a fighting mood. Her talent lies in making that argument desirable, bringing wearability to planet-friendly dressing. A dolphin T-shirt may be nostalgic, but it also asks what we choose to protect – and what we will do to protect it. A year into his role at Balmain, creative director Antonin Tron unearthed Mark Shaw’s backstage photographs from 1954, recasting their mid-century silhouette as something darker, glossier and more louche. For his second show, animal prints, eel skin, snakeskin-effect leather, viscose and silk lamé exuded cinematic elegance. His strong-shouldered pilot jacket returned, while corsetry, garter belts, plunging necklines and cocktail dresses, barely more substantial than swimsuits, kept silhouettes close to the body. The setting was the Left Bank mansion once occupied by Karl Lagerfeld, a Balmain apprentice in the 1950s. Sunglasses, wet-look fabrics and clinging silhouettes gave the house fresh bite, charged with sensual, unapologetic glamour. For Julian Klausner, glamour lies in the pleasure of dressing for yourself. His spring/summer 2027 collection for Dries Van Noten imagined an actress leaving the set and slipping back into her everyday clothes. Taxi horns and sirens accompanied models in looks that captured the peculiar logic of a wardrobe assembled over time. A sequinned blouse sat over a casual button-down, a slinky cocktail dress over a rugby shirt, and a plunging silk dress over a graphic T-shirt. Nothing was quite where you expected it. Mismatched jewellery, an enamel brooch, a flouncy sheer skirt and, wonderfully, a single hot-pink racing glove added to the eccentricity. Bright red lipstick seemed as plausible at noon as after dark. Personal, slightly strange and instinctive, Klausner’s glamour requires no particular occasion. Having just given his final show for Diesel, creative director Glen Martens is now focused solely on Maison Margiela and, for this latest collection, took a more commercial turn. While earlier shows established just how far he was willing to push the house’s theatrical codes, this time the exercise was more forensic and focused on stripping Margiela back to the contradictions on which it was founded in the 1980s. The result was familiar yet disrupted. Contrasting hard and soft, 1960s-style brocades became column skirts tied with Margiela’s signature cotton ribbon, and tailoring arrived with concertina-like construction, with knife-edge lapels folding inward or out for a more conventional silhouette. Trenches, T-shirts and jersey dresses, meanwhile, were given rigid, balcony-like inserts. There was an appealing return to Margiela’s secret language of quietly intelligent clothes as well: a stiff-fronted white coat, checked shirt and high-waisted tailored ski trousers. But opulence remains his instinct, seen in elaborate metal-fronted gowns, crushed silver and baroque draping. For spring/summer 2027, Jonathan Anderson looked to something lighter at Dior – quite literally. Air became a material in its own right, worked through lace, silk mousseline and organza, while tailoring softened into fluid, almost weightless forms. Transparency drifted between sheer and opaque, giving the collection a sense of constant movement. The Dior ateliers supplied technical virtuosity, with pleats layered upon pleats, asymmetric florals, voluminous hems and a softer evolution of last season’s Marie Antoinette-inspired tutus. Anderson’s signatures were becoming clearer, too, via flowerlike silhouettes, iridescence, cropped proportions and deliberately off-kilter details. Long scarves, cascading earrings and draped fabrics reinforced the collection’s interest in asymmetry. Accessories supplied the wit. Flower photographs appeared on square-toe heels; the new Dior Bow Sandal and petal-soled Cigale played with familiar codes, while bags moved from updated Double and Initial Hobo shapes to a biker-inspired Cannage style. Most playful was a silver minaudiere shaped like the wenwan walnut featured on the invitation. After a year of historical references, Anderson’s Dior is beginning to speak in its own unmistakable language. It seems the rumours swirling around Saint Laurent are, in fact, true and that after a decade leading the brand, Anthony Vaccarello is leaving. He presented an extraordinary, gilded collection, steeped in the house’s history and charged with the atmosphere of a finale where Charlotte Gainsbourg performed, the song chorused with the words “You are so much, Yves Saint Laurent.” If this was a farewell, it was impeccably orchestrated. Under giant golden chandeliers, most looks were gilt, a deliberate reference to Yves Saint Laurent’s 1991 Rive Gauche collection, whose finale was entirely gilded. Metallic trenches, cocktail dresses, gilt brocades and metal-thread lace caught the light, while mousseline scarves in absinthe, amber and cognac added colour. There were enormous earrings, vertiginous stilettos and snake-shaped heels, but interestingly, not a single handbag. The Eiffel Tower glittered as the show began and ended, reinforcing the sense of occasion. Vaccarello has always resisted fashion’s drift towards accessibility and trend-chasing. Here, he made a case for something rarer, for glamour with no interest in apology. Designers Hannah Rose Dalton and Steven Raj Bhaskaran staged a deeply political outing. For their biggest show to date, the Matieres Fecales founders took over Place de la Republique – a symbolic site of protest – for a show called The 99 Per Cent, and the second chapter of a story that began last season with a collection focused on the world’s wealthiest one per cent. The Canadian duo has since moved further into the mainstream, dressing the likes of Demi Moore and Zendaya on the red carpet, and attracting Rihanna, who held up proceedings by arriving to the show over an hour late. This season, Dalton and Bhaskaran sent out 99 looks on 99 models of colour, drawing on Bhaskaran’s journey from poverty to the upper reaches of Paris fashion. The message was explicit: if the one per cent represented the villains of the previous chapter, the 99 per cent were now its heroes. It was activism translated into fashion spectacle – provocative, theatrical and deliberately difficult to ignore. The question is no longer whether Matieres Fecales can attract attention, but what it chooses to do with it.
