title: Who is Mayssa Baha, the 15-year-old Moroccan rewriting Barcelona's record books?
description: The youngest player to represent Barca - male or female - comes from a good sporting pedigree
content: It’s been quite the month for Mayssa Baha, the 15-year-old Moroccan international who became the youngest player to start for Barcelona’s Femeni team on September 26. Mayssa started the league match against Logrono, scoring her first senior goal. She is the youngest player to score for a Barcelona senior side, male or female, breaking a record set by Lamine Yamal . She is also the youngest player to score in Spain’s Liga F. In the preceding weeks, the forward had been coming on as a substitute for a side that win every week. European champions in three of the past four seasons and Spain’s champions in each of the past seven, Barca won 29 of their 30 league games last season and defeated Real Madrid 7-0 on Sunday in front of 40,000 fans. Mayssa was a substitute alongside the world’s best player, Aitana Bonmarti. She won’t be old enough to play in the Uefa Champions League until she turns 16 in January. She was born in Malaga, Spain, in 2011, while her father, the former Morocco international Nabil Baha, was at the club. She started playing football at FUS Rabat when her father played there from 2014 to 2016. She then returned to Malaga, where she and her brother Ziyad continued to play youth football. Mayssa played in teams two or three years up from her age group. Her brother, Ziyad, now 17, is in Olympique Marseille’s youth side and Morocco’s under-17 men’s team, where his father is head coach. Mayssa already plays for Morocco’s under-17 women's team, having made her debut aged just 12, another record. At last year’s Under-17 World Cup, she was the youngest player in the tournament. She could still choose to play for Spain when she is an adult. The siblings’ mother is Spanish-Moroccan model Farah Farabian, who spends much of her time watching her children play football. “People wonder why I quit my job for my kids like I had no life left,” Farabian recently wrote. “But today, my life is also accompanying them in theirs. Every weekend I travel miles between Barcelona and Marseille to share their matches, joys and progress. It's not a sacrifice; it's my choice, my happiness. “A career can wait, but their childhood and adolescence will never come back. So, yes, I choose them and I would do it a thousand times over. Because seeing them grow and reach their dreams is also my greatest achievement.” Mayssa joined Barcelona at age 13, living at La Masia academy and moving quickly through the ranks with the C team last season. She started this season with the B team, but during pre-season she was invited to train with the first team at a camp in Andorra and kept her place among some of the best players in the world. Rated the top player in the world for her age, she’s mentally and physically mature. She’s strong, confident, powerful and fast, but, at 15, she has much to learn about the game. Right now, she’s playing in the best possible place to advance her career.

title: UAE's 'very powerful' cyber defences can repel attacks, says Mistral AI boss
description: French company also open to investing in data centres in the Emirates
content: The UAE 's “very powerful” cyber defences enable it to defend against threats, especially during geopolitical instability, the chief executive of French company Mistral AI said. The UAE's pursuit of technological sovereignty will help it establish reliable and secure cyber capabilities, Arthur Mensch told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi . “The UAE is under pressure, in particular, on the defence side,” he said. “Cyber capabilities are a must-have when it comes to having capable defence systems. “Sovereignty matters in that. It's important to be able to wield defence systems without having to ask for permission.” Mr Mensch's comments come after UAE authorities reported an increasing number of cyber attacks. Last month, the UAE's cyber security chief, Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, said the country is continuing to contend with daily online threats, with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps behind many of the attacks. Mr Al Kuwaiti said the country faced about 640,000 attacks on September 15 and that Iran remains “one of the main players” in the high-tech offensive, which is being exacerbated by the rise of AI. “Having very powerful cyber models deployed here in Abu Dhabi in a way where the deployment is fully under Abu Dhabi control is going to be quite important,” Mr Mensch said. Mr Mensch said Mistral AI would consider investing in UAE data centres, a move that would further solidify its co-operation with Abu Dhabi and boost the country's AI ambitions. “We may [invest in UAE data centres]. It's an interesting place for our AI buildout that is currently under way in this part of the world,” he said. On Abu Dhabi's efforts at data sovereignty, Mr Mensch said authorities and the wider industry had “very early on decided” that this aspect will be crucial for the deployment of AI. Data sovereignty is becoming vital for nations as it gives them legal control over the data within their jurisdictions. The most notable project to achieve this is the planned Stargate UAE data centre campus, a 5GW development valued at $30 billion . Mistral AI met more local organisations and companies at the summit, trying to “get a sense of what Abu Dhabi needs to build with AI ... [and] go in depth into the technological aspect of the asks”, said Mr Mensch, adding that the company has worked “extensively” with the oil and gas industry. Mistral AI has already forged partnerships with Abu Dhabi organisations , including AI major G42, to develop advanced platforms and infrastructure, and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence for research and development in AI foundation models, talent development and real-world AI solutions. In June, the company teamed up with UAE AI investment firm MGX and lender Bpifrance for the planned expansion of Campus AI in France, which aims to build a capacity of 3GW across Europe's third-biggest economy. “There is more that can be done ... on being able to have a compute capacity under full Abu Dhabi control; that's something where as a company we can help,” he added. Fresh debacles have been hitting the AI industry, most notably AI models, supposedly in secure environments and built by names including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Anthropic and Google, going rogue and infiltrating external sites. Mr Mensch was clear on where the responsibility should fall. At the same time, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman made a plea at the recent UN General Assembly for governments to do more to rein in AI. “Accountability for AI deployments, when they are hosted by AI companies, falls on the AI companies. This should be very, very clear. There's no way in which the accountability of what we're doing should be offset to governments,” Mr Mensch said. Governments, though, “are accountable for the adoption of the technology, and they should be accountable for how it's being used in the government itself”, he said. Mr Mensch also called for a tempered tone on the call for deceleration – or even acceleration – of the development of AI, as recent events have shown the potential disruption the technology can bring. “I'm very cautious about those warnings [to slow development down] because they serve their own interests very clearly,” he said. “The world we don't want to live in, which would be an extremely dangerous world, is the world where you have a duopoly of companies operated from the US serving the rest of the world,” he said, referring to the strength of the US AI industry, led by OpenAI and Anthropic, which is widely viewed as a counter to China's growing influence in the sector. On Tuesday, at AI Everything, Mistral AI launched its latest Mistral Large 4 AI model, which, it says, is among the fastest in the world and rivals the best open-source models from China. “We see no sign of slowing down when we look at how our model is being improved by the day,” Mr Mensch said.

title: Iran war energy price shock large but contained so far, IMF chief says
description: Kristalina Georgieva says AI revolution and geopolitical instability are pulling global economy in two directions
content: The head of the International Monetary Fund has said the energy price shock driven by the US- Iran war has so far been “large but contained”, but warned that energy demand could lead to further pressure. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. This year's gathering, held in Bangkok, comes as supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East pile on to inflationary pressures, potentially leading to higher interest rates for advanced economies. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank have already begun to raise their key rates, with the Bank of England expected to join them next month. Higher energy prices and rising debt levels have also driven global borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, traded at 5.307 per cent as recently on Monday, its highest level since 2002. That pressure has also spread to markets in other advanced economies including in Japan, France, Germany and the UK. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to the markets. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline , which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through the East-West Pipeline . The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship tracking firm Kpler. The latest figures included transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Ms Georgieva had credited the Gulf Co-operation Council's efforts to reroute energy supplies for preventing a larger shock to the global economy during a meeting with the bloc's finance ministers and central bankers in Bahrain last week. She also said the IMF anticipates the GCC economy will contract this year, adding that the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping. A separate report from the World Bank released on Tuesday said GCC economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in liquefied natural gas will hit buyers in Europe and Asia particularly hard, Ms Georgieva said, noting price pressures could further build with winter approaching and reserves dwindling. In her address, the IMF chief also used her address to urge governments to embark on policies to unlock the productive gains under artificial intelligence . Ms Georgieva described the global economy as one being pulled in two directions, with the positive demand shock from AI partially offsetting the economic fallout from the US-Iran conflict. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. In the US, the AI buildout is shaping up to become the largest investment drive in the country's history. Analysts at Brookings anticipate AI investment in data centres, infrastructure, chips and other equipment will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or an average of 3.63 per cent of US GDP per year. The broad S&P 500 hit a fresh record-high of 7,800 on Tuesday driven by renewed AI enthusiasm. But with fears of an AI bubble also fomenting, Ms Georgieva said countries should adopt regulation and supervision as a “first line of defence” to prevent a far-reaching shock if AI earnings fall short. The Trump administration has recently adopted a defensive posture of AI amid a growing domestic backlash against the data centre buildout ahead of November’s midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has taken a light regulatory touch on AI advancement and repeatedly expressed his desire to beat China in the global AI race. Countries in the Gulf are seeking to advance large-scale acceleration of AI. The UAE targets to have AI contribute 20 per cent of its non-oil GDP by 2031. Ms Georgieva said AI could deliver up to a half percentage point of additional world growth – or “adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy” – annually. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

title: Countdown to new-look Abu Dhabi T10 begins with strong Pakistan and Caribbean cohorts
description: Star names selected via player draft as league prepares for fresh start under new ownership structure from November 7
content: The countdown to Abu Dhabi T10 ’s relaunch has started with five new team owners and a roster full of star players from across the world gearing up for what is effectively a second innings for the league, beginning November 7. The T10 tournament has undergone a significant transformation this year, with the Abu Dhabi Cricket & Sports Hub (ADCSH) assuming complete ownership of the league, with support from the Abu Dhabi Sports Council (ADSC) and the Emirates Cricket Board (ECB). With the new ownership structure in place and an emphasis on long-term partnerships, clear and predictable team structures, and organic growth, T10 is aiming to move away from the disjointed efforts of previous seasons. Five new team owners were announced for the 2026 season, with UAE Bulls, who had been with the league since its inception in 2017, continuing their association with Abu Dhabi T10 . Among the new inductees are Yas Lions, owned by UAE-based venture capitalist Jeetu Kataria, and Royal Desert Champions, helmed by former banker Amit Narang. Other teams in the league are Arabian Aces, Emirates Eagles and United Tigers. Last week, all stakeholders gathered in Abu Dhabi to complete the biggest task for any franchise tournament – player selection. A draft was held at Yas Island, where some of the most in-demand short-format players were allocated to the six teams. The ‘icon’ players had already been selected ahead of the draft. West Indies players were the most sought-after, led by Kieron Pollard (UAE Bulls 'icon' player), Jason Holder (Yas Lions), Nicolas Pooran (Royal Desert Champions) and Rovman Powell (Emirates Eagles). Moeen Ali (Arabian Aces) and Fakhar Zaman (United Tigers) are the only non-Caribbean 'icons' in T10 2026. With the Abu Dhabi T10 sharing November with another UAE-based franchise tournament – the DP World ILT20 – there was some overlap of players. However, one key difference was the composition of the squads. While the 2026 ILT20 put particular emphasis on Afghanistan players while restricting Pakistan stars largely to one team – ostensibly due to Indian ownership of other franchises - the Abu Dhabi T10 saw Pakistan names scattered across all franchises, barring one. In all, 15 Pakistan players have found a home in T10, including superstars such as Naseem Shah and Fakhar Zaman , compared to just five in ILT20. Left-arm pacer Mohammad Amir is the 16th Pakistan cricketer in T10, but he now qualifies as an England cricketer. For Matt Boucher, CEO of ADCSH and Abu Dhabi T10, the foundation has been laid for a new cricket structure. “The changes this season are about putting the right foundations in place to build Abu Dhabi T10 into a stronger and more sustainable global cricket property,” Boucher told The National . “We have six franchises for the 2026 season. UAE Bulls provide continuity from the previous era, while the other franchises are part of the new ownership and identity structure. "The focus is on having owners who share our long-term vision and are committed to building strong franchise identities and genuine connections with fans.” Boucher said the onus of growing the fan base and popularity of the league falls on both the T10 management and team owners. “The key difference is the long-term approach. We want franchises to grow beyond the tournament window, develop their own identities and fanbases, and become sustainable sporting brands. Stronger franchises will ultimately help us build a stronger Abu Dhabi T10,” he added. For Boucher, the presence of Pakistan players across the teams is encouraging, as is the presence of international and UAE stars. “Having Pakistan stars such as Naseem Shah, Mohammed Amir, Shadab Khan, Fakhar Zaman and Iftikhar Ahmed certainly adds quality and significant fan interest. But the strength of the league is its overall international mix, alongside a strong UAE presence with players such as Muhammad Waseem, Alishan Sharafu, Aayan Afzal Khan and Vriitya Aravind.” UAE star batter Waseem will undoubtedly have the spotlight on him when the Abu Dhabi T10 starts on November 7 at the Zayed Cricket Stadium, having secured a record $210,000 contract for the ILT20, which begins two days after the T10 tournament concludes on November 20.

title: Michelin Guide Dubai 2026: Closed restaurants retain stars as new winners emerge
description: Orfali Bros moves up to two stars as Birch and Kigo earn their first, with 20 restaurants receiving the coveted distinctions
content: Dubai's latest Michelin stars have been revealed, with two restaurants joining the prestigious list and another promoted to two stars – even as some of the city's award-winning dining rooms remain temporarily closed. The Michelin Guide Dubai 2026 was unveiled at a ceremony at Atlantis The Royal on Tuesday night, with 20 restaurants receiving at least one star. FZN by Bjorn Frantzen, which blends Scandinavian and Asian influences, and Tresind Studio , known for its modern Indian cuisine, remain at the top of Dubai's dining scene, retaining the three stars they received last year. Orfali Bros was one of the biggest winners of the night, promoted from one to two stars. Run by Syrian brothers Mohammad, Wassim and Omar Orfali, the home-grown restaurant serves contemporary Middle Eastern cuisine, drawing on their Syrian roots as well as Turkish and Armenian influences. Michelin noted the restaurant's evolution "from a brilliant neighbourhood bistro into a flagship of Middle Eastern gastronomy". "Rooted in the brothers' Aleppian, Armenian and Turkish heritage, its signature dishes and Voyage menu reveal cooking of increasing refinement, depth and personality," it said. Meanwhile, Birch and Kigo entered the guide with one star each. Birch, led by chef Arslan Berdiev, serves contemporary cuisine shaped by his travels and Turkmen heritage, while Kigo is a Japanese fine-dining restaurant offering sushi omakase and kaiseki menus. The latest awards come after a challenging period for Dubai's restaurant industry, with several high-profile venues temporarily pausing operations amid softer demand and disruption to tourism following the Iran war . Among the restaurants retaining Michelin stars for 2026 are Al Muntaha , Dinner by Heston Blumenthal , Ossiano and Smoked Room , which are currently temporarily closed . Several other restaurants in the wider Michelin Guide Dubai 2026 selection are also temporarily closed. Michelin has acknowledged the unusual situation after Dubai food writer Samantha Wood , founder of FooDiva, questioned why at least 10 restaurants across the guide's various lists were included despite currently being closed. In a statement provided to The National , Michelin said it was “fully aware” that a number of restaurants were currently closed “due to the current circumstances”. “We remain in close contact with their teams and are monitoring closely when they might reopen in the near future,” Michelin said. “As with all restaurants in the selection, they will be revisited and re-evaluated by our inspectors once they reopen to ensure they continue to meet the standards associated with their distinctions.” There are 20 Michelin-starred restaurants in Dubai in the 2026 guide, with two holding three stars, four holding two stars and 14 holding one. Beyond the starred restaurants, the 2026 guide includes 122 establishments representing 38 types of cuisine, up from 119 restaurants last year. There are 19 new additions across the guide, including two new one-star restaurants, four new Bib Gourmands and 13 restaurants added to the Michelin Selected category. The Bib Gourmand list features 22 restaurants this year, while another 80 restaurants appear in the Michelin Selected category, including 13 newcomers. “The selection has grown significantly since its inception and now features nearly twice as many establishments as it did when it was first launched,” said Gwendal Poullennec , international director of the Michelin Guides. “This year's combination of home-grown talent and international arrivals reflects a city that is developing its own culinary identity while embracing traditions from around the world.” The Bib Gourmand distinction recognises restaurants offering good-quality food at good value. There are 22 in the 2026 Dubai guide, including four new additions. Five individual and restaurant awards were also announced during Tuesday night's ceremony. Remy Marquignon, executive chef of Ossiano, received the Young Chef Award despite the restaurant being temporarily closed. Ninad Jani of avatara received the Sommelier Award, while Kigo's Akinori Tanigawa and his team received the Service Award. Zahra Erfanian Azmoodeh of Carbone Dubai received the Exceptional Cocktails Award, while Gonzalo Platero and Window were given the Opening of the Year Award.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed congratulates Saudi Arabia on Arabian Gulf Cup triumph over UAE
description: Sportsmanship of finalists and tournament organisers commended
content: President Sheikh Mohamed hailed the "high level of sportsmanship" on display after Saudi Arabia defeated the UAE in the Arabian Gulf Cup final on Tuesday. Sheikh Mohamed offered his congratulations after the Green Falcons secured a 2-0 victory in front of more than 60,000 fans in Jeddah. It was Saudi Arabia's first Arabian Gulf Cup crown for 22 years, and further extended the UAE's wait for their third title in the regional competition. "Sincere congratulations to the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques King Salman bin Abdulaziz, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and the Saudi people on winning the Arabian Gulf Cup," President Sheikh Mohamed wrote on X. "I also commend the high level of sportsmanship shown by both the Saudi and UAE teams during the final. "I commend the successful organisation of the tournament and wish Saudi Arabia continued success in future sporting competitions." More than 12,000 Emirati fans travelled to Jeddah in the hope of seeing their side continue their unbeaten start under new coach Zlatko Dalic. The UAE Football Association had chartered six aircraft to fly supporters to the final at King Abdullah Sport City Stadium.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo not retiring, wants punishment and says Portugal boss twice 'broke his word'
description: Portugal captain releases lengthy statement of his account of why he walked out on national team
content: Cristiano Ronaldo said he is not retiring from international football and that he deserved to be punished for walking out on Portugal last week, while also accusing national team boss Jorge Jesus of twice breaking his word to him. Ronaldo, 41, walked out of Portugal's training camp ahead of a Uefa Nations League match in Denmark last week after being unhappy at being an unused substitute in Portugal's previous match against Norway. Jesus then said his captain would not start the game in Copenhagen, prompting Ronaldo to pack up and leave. In a lengthy statement that ran to nearly 2,000 words, Ronaldo gave his account of the dispute and said he remained available for selection and that he should be held accountable for his actions. "The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said. "I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences." In the statement, the Al Nassr striker accused Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust". The five-time Ballon d'Or winner said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of ⁠the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes. "Everyone ​knows the ⁠rest. I warmed up from ‌half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said. "The manager ​had broken his word to me." Portugal's captain and all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al Nassr's sporting director Simao Coutinho, produced an agreement that the coach would clarify events at his next press conference. According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying that he had never demanded playing time, that he had respected Jesus' decisions, and that the coach's asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion. "The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting," Ronaldo explained. "I heard expressions and an aggressiveness I believe I did not deserve, a 'high-and-mighty' attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before. "It was the second time he had broken his word to me," Ronaldo added. "I decided to leave ​the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises." The ‌statement provided Ronaldo's account, but on ⁠Sunday, after Portugal's win over Norway, Jesus ​denied he had made any agreement with the player but left the ​door open ‌for his return. Ronaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway match and ⁠for leaving his teammates, accepting that his captaincy made his conduct more serious. "The consequences of my actions must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation," he said. Despite the rupture, Ronaldo said he was not limiting his international ambitions to a ​farewell appearance. "If I'm physically fit, playing for my club – scoring goals, I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I'll be available, as I've always been until now, to compete and win for our national team," he added. Portugal won the matches against Norway and Denmark without Ronaldo in the side, and are back in action in November in their final Nations League group games against the Danes and Wales. Some have questioned the timing of Ronaldo's revelation, coming just hours before Lionel Messi, his great rival, played his final international match with Argentina in Buenos Aires. Ronaldo had considered retiring from international football after this summer's World Cup following Portugal's exit at the last-16 stage. He was persuaded to reconsider after speaking with FPF president Pedro Proenca.

title: Capital Group secures ADGM licence to expand Middle East operations
description: US-based firm, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, adds to rising number of global investment firms in Abu Dhabi
content: Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager and expand operations across the region. The development comes after the company announced plans to set up its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi in May, with Capital Group relocating associates from North America, Europe and Asia to support clients in the region. The company will now be able to conduct trading, investment management and distribution activities within Abu Dhabi's financial centre, it said in a statement on Wednesday. “Establishing a regulated presence in Abu Dhabi brings us closer to our clients and to the investment opportunities across the Middle East, a region where we have been active for many years,” said Benno Klingenberg-Timm, head of Abu Dhabi office and head of institutional for Europe and Asia at Capital Group. “From day one, we will have a meaningful presence, with on-the-ground investment, operational and client-facing capabilities,” he added. The move reflects “our confidence in the region’s long-term growth”, Mr Klingenberg-Timm said. Capital Group’s expansion adds to the growing number of global investment firms setting up in Abu Dhabi. ADGM , the largest international financial centre in the Middle East and Africa by number of active licences, has continued to attract global institutions, despite the Iran war. New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said on Tuesday it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East. Founded in 1999, New Mountain has about $60 billion in assets under management across its private equity, credit and net lease investment strategies. “We have been privileged to work with many leading investors in the region for years and establishing a local presence will allow us to deepen those relationships while building new partnerships over time,” said Adam Weinstein, president and chief operating officer. Last week, Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, opened an office in ADGM . Global private markets firm Pantheon last week opened its first Abu Dhabi office in ADGM to expand its presence in the Middle East and tap growing demand from investors across the Gulf. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management. Capital Group’s “decision reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s financial ecosystem and ADGM’s growing position as a leading international financial centre for global institutions seeking long-term opportunities across the region”, said Ahmed Al Zaabi, chairman of ADGM.

title: Three killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports
description: King Khalid and Abha airports are attacked by Yemeni rebels
content: Three people have been killed in Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia , it was announced late on Wednesday. The kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said 36 others were injured in the strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south. Yemen 's Houthi rebels claimed responsibility for attacking both airports, saying drones hit the Riyadh airport while ballistic missiles and drones were used against the Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait airbase. At Abha airport, two women, one Moroccan and one Algerian, were killed, while 28 people were injured, including Saudi citizens and people from Bangladesh and the Philippines. At King Khalid International Airport, a Sudanese person was killed and eight people were injured: five Saudi citizens, two Egyptian residents and a Pakistani resident. The Saudi authority said the injuries ranged from minor to serious. It said the attacks caused "some material damage" that was being assessed. The Houthis also claimed strikes on government-held areas of Yemen at dawn on Wednesday, in an escalation of attacks around airports, military positions and other infrastructure. Saudi authorities separately reported attacks by Houthi rebels on Riyadh, Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran. The US embassy in Riyadh urged "heightened vigilance" and said the conflict could lead to flight cancellations. In the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the Transport Ministry said two ballistic missiles and several explosive-laden drones were fired at the international airport around daybreak, forcing a Cairo-to-Aden flight to divert to Jeddah. The ministry said one missile landed near the runway minutes before Yemenia Airways flight 603 from Cairo was due to land. Authorities evacuated passengers and airport staff and moved two Yemenia and Aden Airways aircraft away from the danger zone, the ministry said. The ministry said drones continued flying over Aden as authorities cleared the terminal. No casualties were reported following the attack. The local authority in Aden described the attack as an assault on a civilian facility and its surroundings. In a statement, the Houthi military said it had struck Saudi military supplies that had arrived at Badr camp near Aden airport with ballistic missiles. It claimed the attack killed and wounded a number of Saudi officers at Badr camp. "We warn the enemy against using Aden civilian airport for any military purposes," the group added. Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree claimed the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at three Saudi military camps in the Jazan and Asir regions. He said the strikes killed and wounded dozens of Saudi soldiers and officers and set fire to weapons depots. None of the Houthi casualty or damage claims could be independently verified. Videos circulating online showed flashes and explosions near Aden International Airport, with blasts heard across parts of the city, according to local reports. Journalist Ali Al Sakani, citing sources, said CCTV footage showed ballistic missiles being launched towards Aden, reportedly from the direction of Al Oud and Al Hasha districts. He reported no casualties or damage in the city. Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree separately claimed the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at three Saudi military camps in Jizan and Asir. Brig Gen Saree said the strikes killed and wounded dozens of Saudi soldiers and officers, and set fire to weapons depots. Those casualty and damage claims could not be independently verified. Saudi state television said the Saudi-led coalition intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait, in the south-west of the kingdom. The coalition also reported intercepting Houthi missiles and drones around Khamis Mushait and Jazan, and said it continued operations against missile launch sites. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said on Tuesday that coalition forces had destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Sanaa and a missile storage facility in Saada. The Aden attack comes amid renewed fighting after Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive supported by coalition air strikes. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, both near the Yemeni border, had been attacked. Aviation tracking platform Flightradar24 said flights to and from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were halted for more than an hour on Wednesday morning, after being put on hold for a few hours on Tuesday. The airport's website could not be accessed for a second successive day. Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah television later reported Saudi strikes on Ibb and Taiz. The coalition did not immediately confirm those reports. Yemen’s Minister of Legal Affairs, Eshraq Al Maqtari, said Houthi shelling in Taiz province killed six civilians and wounded 18 others, with most of the casualties women and children. In a post on X on Wednesday morning, Ms Al Maqtari said casualties were recorded across several districts. She said they include the deaths of a woman and child in Al Mawasit and five members of one family, including children, in Al Misrakh, while others were wounded by shelling and sniper fire.

title: Abu Dhabi lifts 80kph speed limit cap after morning fog alert
description: Motorists urged to exercise caution amid hazardous weather conditions
content: Police in Abu Dhabi have lifted a temporary 80kph speed limit cap introduced on Wednesday morning after parts of the capital were blanketed by thick fog. Motorists were urged to be vigilant during the hazardous weather conditions, which are expected to persist for several days. The speed-reduction measures were in place on stretches of the E11 - the main transport link between Dubai and Abu Dhabi - Abu Dhabi-Al Ain Road and Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road as well as routes including Sheikh Salem bint Buti Road and Ahmed Khamis Al-Hamli Road. Abu Dhabi Police said normal speed limits had been restored on affected routes, in a message on social media shortly before 10am. Drivers had received safety alerts on their mobile phones on the morning commute, notifying them of the 80kph speed cap and advising them to exercise caution during the dense fog. The National Centre of Meteorology issued a yellow alert for fog - calling on the public to expect areas of fog formation and mist for large parts of the county. A more severe red alert - covering parts of Abu Dhabi and the Northern Emirates - is also in place, cautioning that visibility would fall below 1km. Both fog warnings were in place until 9am. The NCM's latest five-day weather bulletin predicts that further fog and mist will roll in over internal and coastal areas until at least Sunday. Abu Dhabi Police began to enforce the 80kph speed limit during bad weather – such as heavy rain, sandstorms and fog – in April 2019 . Temporary speed limits are posted on electronic signboards on roads, sent to phone users and announced on social media. The force also posts messages on its social media channels to alert motorists when the temporary speed limits on roads are lifted. The strategy aims to encourage motorists to take care behind the wheel and to slow down during periods of challenging weather. Motorists who flout the safety rules can face fines of Dh300 ($81.6) when exceeding speed limits by up to 10kph. This fine is doubled for those breaking the speed limit by no more than 20kph. Penalties increase in line with the severity of the breach of traffic regulations.

title: 'Not coming anymore is going to hurt a lot': Messi's emotional message to Argentina on farewell appearance
description: Messi signs off 21-year international career with a goal as fans flock to Monumental to give national hero a fitting send-off
content: Lionel Messi delivered one last master class for Argentina to bring the curtain down on ​his illustrious 21-year international career by scoring one ⁠goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly ⁠win over Benin in Buenos Aires. More than 85,000 fans crammed into Monumental stadium to give Messi a final send-off in the famous blue-and-white shirt. The result mattered little. This was more a national ⁠celebration of Messi's service to La Albiceleste. Landmarks across the capital glowed with the national team's colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans poured their hearts into a rendition ⁠of Argentina's national anthem. "It's hard to talk," said Messi , 39, whose family watched proudly from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of 1978, 1986 and 2022. "There are a lot of emotions, a lot of things going through my head. ​The first thing I think about is my old man," he added, referring to the recent death of his father , Jorge. "It was a huge source of pride for me to wear this shirt all this time, more than 20 years. "Not coming anymore is going to hurt a lot. I swear, I'd love to keep coming my whole life, because playing for Argentina is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you." Hours earlier, a massive No 10 shirt emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's hometown. As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route. When the teams took the pitch, Benin's captain looked lost for words as he handed Messi a gift and a letter during the pre-match handshake. After a goalless first half, Messi supplied ​the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home Argentina's opener. Otamendi spent 17 years with Messi in the national team, including four World Cups, and was also ending his international career. Messi then set up Nico Paz, one of the players seen ​as a potential ‌successor for Argentina's No 10 shirt, to score the second goal. In a fairy-tale ending, Messi converted a penalty for ⁠3-0, his 126th international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd. At the ⁠final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky. Argentine singer Soledad Pastorutti, known as "La Sole", then sang her signature Brindis as part of a tribute to Messi and his journey with the national team. Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) ​and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international stage into a story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs. For years, Argentina asked Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say 'Thank You'.

title: Caravan Hatta by Our Habitas review: A different kind of Dubai escape
description: Retreat offers mountain views, outdoor living and peaceful surroundings
content: The journey towards Hatta is a scenic one, as towering skyscrapers gradually give way to rugged mountains and winding roads. Nestled in the Hajar Mountains overlooking Hatta Dam , Caravan Hatta by Our Habitas is a luxury retreat that marks the hospitality brand’s UAE debut. The property features 50 Airstream caravans, each with its own outdoor space overlooking the surrounding landscape. Inspired by the nomadic caravans that once travelled across the region, the concept swaps the UAE’s polished beach resorts and five-star hotels for hiking trails, open skies and a stay centred on nature, adventure and community. I checked in during the opening weekend to see whether this simpler approach to luxury is worth leaving the city for. After a two-and-a-half hour drive from Abu Dhabi , my partner and I reach the property as the sun begins to set. We leave our car in the guest car park, where a 4x4 is waiting to drive us the final stretch to reception. Check-in is smooth, with welcome drinks served as we hand over our Emirates IDs. Before being shown to our caravan, however, there is one more step: a small ritual involving frankincense and bakhoor. We are each given a piece of frankincense and asked to close our eyes and make a wish as the bakhoor burns in front of us. We then add the frankincense to the burner, with the promise that our wishes will come true, and are given bracelets to wear. It is a lovely, positive way to begin our stay – and sets the tone for a weekend designed to feel a little removed from everyday life. There are 50 caravans on the property – 13 Ridge Caravans and 37 larger Peak Caravans. Both come with an exterior deck, although the Peak Caravans also have a pergola, with views either towards the mountains or towards Hatta Dam. None directly face one another, offering welcome privacy. We stay in caravan 32, a Peak Caravan conveniently close to the restaurant and infinity pool. At 21.5 square metres, the interior is compact but cleverly laid out, with a queen-sized bed on a raised platform and a small living area with a sofa, coffee table and colourful patterned rug at one end. At the other end there is a surprisingly spacious bathroom with a walk-in shower. Although the curved metallic walls and ceiling are a reminder that this is a caravan, warm wood, earthy tones and soft furnishings make it feel surprisingly cosy. Glass doors lead to an 18.8-square-metre outdoor living space, effectively extending the room beyond its relatively small footprint. We have a view of the Hajar Mountains, with little between our deck and the rocky peaks. There is only one restaurant on site, Madar, which takes its name from the Arabic word for “orbit”. The idea is that, much like things being drawn into an orbit, food can bring people together and spark conversation. The menu is Emirati-influenced, with dishes prepared using traditional techniques including open-fire and underground cooking. The menu is relatively small, something my partner and I appreciate as we sometimes get decision fatigue when faced with too many choices. We start with a beet and halloumi salad (Dh54), with surprisingly gooey cheese, followed by the spinach and feta samboussek (Dh48), served piping hot, and the fatah Khaleej lahm (Dh62), a creative interpretation of the traditional flatbread dish. For mains, we order the lamb shoulder (Dh128) and claypot chicken biryani (Dh84). Both impress. My partner comments on how freshly prepared the biryani tastes, with tender chicken and fluffy rice. The lamb is tender with hints of spice, although we would have preferred a little more flavour. We finish with the toffee pudding and chocolate forest marquise, satisfying our sweet tooth without feeling overly heavy. Another detail we appreciate is the positioning of the tables. Rather than directly facing neighbouring diners, they are angled to give each table a little more privacy, which works particularly well in the retreat’s intimate setting. Thuraya Wellness is a small and simple spa with two rooms offering massages and other treatments. I opt for the 60-minute signature massage and find it so relaxing that I drift off. By the end, my body has all but forgotten the long drive from Abu Dhabi. There is also a small barrel sauna and two cold plunges outside the spa, which are available for guests even if they are not booked in for a treatment. The wider wellness programme includes activities such as sound healing and restorative yoga, with booking required. In addition to the spa, there is an outdoor “jungle gym”, where much of the equipment has been created using natural materials, in keeping with the retreat’s sustainability focus. Wooden weight plates replace conventional metal ones, while the open-air setting means workouts come with impressive views of the surrounding mountains. Those same rugged peaks provide the backdrop to the infinity pool, one of the most picturesque spots on the property. With the water appearing to blend into the mountainous horizon, it is an inviting place to swim, relax or simply take in the scenery. Unsurprisingly, given the setting, the pool area fills up quickly as the day goes on. In the evening, we head up to a dedicated observatory deck near the restaurant. Although the telescope isn't properly set up yet, we still get a lovely view of the stars. Despite the privacy, attentive service is never far away, particularly from the dining team. When I wake up with a sore throat one morning, I’m quickly made a lemon, ginger and honey tea to help soothe it – just one of the small gestures that make us feel well looked after. Quiet, private and surrounded by spectacular mountain scenery, Caravan Hatta by Our Habitas is an easy place to switch off. Its compact caravans encourage you to spend more time outdoors and reconnect, whether with your family or friends by the pool, exploring the surrounding landscape or simply sitting on the deck taking in the view. Room rates start at Dh1,040 per night. Check-in is from 3pm and check-out is at noon. This review was conducted at the invitation of the hotel and reflects standards during this time.

title: Abu Dhabi to upgrade Tamm app as it pursues AI-native government goal
description: Platform will be designed to be more proactive, personalised and trusted, DGE director general says
content: Abu Dhabi plans to launch the latest version of the Tamm app in December as it pursues its goal of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government, a senior executive has said. The refreshed Tamm 5.0 app, which would be introduced at the Gitex Global technology exhibition in Dubai, promises "increasingly intelligent" services, Department of Government Enablement director general Ruba Al Hassan told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Those services are to also be more "proactive and personalised", but they still have to remain "simple and trusted", said Ms Al Hassan, who oversees strategic affairs and future foresight at the department. Tamm currently has about 4.7 million users, having grown by more than 1.5 million in just a year. About 90 per cent of its transactions are finalised within a day, the latest data from the DGE shows. Tamm 5.0 would be "another step" in the evolution from a digital government to an AI-native government, "moving towards a model where government increasingly understands context ... anticipates needs and helps people achieve things more easily", Ms Al Hassan said. The DGE did not reveal the specific changes to Tamm or new services that are to be introduced. "It’s time for the next phase, which is about making the experience even more seamless and reducing the effort required from residents, businesses and visitors," she added. The DGE remains "focused" on its goal of transforming the capital's government services into a fully AI-native platform by next year, Ms Al Hassan said. The agency is "moving with urgency, but building responsibly", she added. "We are already seeing that tangible progress across government, not only through individual AI applications, but through the foundations that make AI-native government possible," she said, referring to data, infrastructure, digital services, workforce capability and governance. "The question is not whether we can deploy AI faster, it’s whether we can create lasting value at scale, so we believe we are on the right path to do that." Abu Dhabi is boosting tech use across the emirate under its digital strategy, which focuses on five key enablers – one of them being the use of AI across public services. Despite the persisting challenges – especially issues involving AI models going rogue and compromising other websites – the DGE is seeking to ensure the safety and reliability of such systems. "We’re seeing a lot of noise in the global AI conversation. New models are constantly coming out, capabilities are getting better quickly and everyone’s focused on what might happen in the future," Ms Al Hassan said. "Our focus is slightly different. We’re interested in where AI delivers practical value today ... we also believe trust is critical. People need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with clear human accountability." Educating users is also a key part of the DGE's mandate, she said. "As AI improves, the value of human judgment actually also increases. People need to know how to work effectively with AI, challenge AI outputs and make better decisions," she said. "When it comes to AI, the skill won’t be coding, it will be maintaining judgment." Meanwhile, Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, described the present generation as the "most powerful in human history", while calling for more responsible use of AI. "The reason ... is because you have the intelligence of every single generation, every single human that has lived, that has actually produced something that has lasted ... the content and knowledge are at your fingertips," he told the conference. "And you don't just have raw knowledge. You're actually able to leverage intelligence to do something with it through agentic AI," he added, referring to the class designed to make autonomous decisions and act with minimal human supervision. "This is the time for a new ambitious generation ... people might not believe in your ideas, to wield these tools to create something that others can't see or don't believe is possible. It's a calling."

title: Gaza and the choice ahead for Palestinians and Israelis
description: Three years after October 7, Palestinians and Israelis have a chance to break with the past
content: Three years ago, families in southern Israel woke to a nightmare. Parents held safe-room doors shut while their children hid behind them. Young people fleeing a music festival were hunted across open fields. In the Hamas-led attack, about 1,200 people were massacred and 251 taken hostage into Gaza. October 7 changed Israel profoundly. It shattered assumptions about security and left wounds that remain open to this day. No serious observer should expect Israelis to think about the future as though that day never happened. The war that followed brought devastation to Gaza on a scale that will shape Palestinian society for years. Tens of thousands of Palestinians lost their lives. Children grew up knowing displacement, and hunger and fear became part of everyday life. Across Gaza, grief settled into homes, schools and neighbourhoods. Having spent much of my professional life working on this conflict, I have become wary of anniversaries. They encourage remembrance but rarely reflection. Every year we repeat familiar arguments, revisit familiar grievances and reaffirm familiar loyalties. Then we move on, leaving unresolved the very questions that produced the tragedy in the first place. Yet one truth remains difficult to escape: grief has no nationality. A mother in Nir Oz and a mother in Khan Younis may never meet, and they may hold radically different views about this conflict and its causes, but neither needs a lesson in loss. The question before Israelis, Palestinians and the wider region is not whose suffering matters more. It is whether enough has been learnt to prevent a continuation of the cycle of pain and suffering. A year ago, the parties accepted a framework intended to move Gaza away from full-scale war. It established a path towards demilitarisation, deradicalistaion, transitional Palestinian governance, Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction. But the hardest part is not agreeing on the destination. It is turning those commitments into realities. Today there are essentially three possible futures for Gaza. The first is a return to the familiar and painful cycle. Hamas rebuilds its military capabilities. Israel prepares for the next confrontation. Another ceasefire eventually follows another round of violence, leaving the underlying reality unchanged. We have seen this many times before. Every round of fighting was meant to restore deterrence. Every truce was presented as a new beginning. Yet the conflict returned because the conditions that produced it never fundamentally changed. The second future may appear more stable but is ultimately no more promising. Gaza remains suspended in a state of permanent uncertainty. Humanitarian assistance attempts to replace governance. Reconstruction advances slowly, if at all. The world gradually loses interest. There are no dramatic headlines, but there is no meaningful progress either. History offers little reason to believe that such arrangements endure. Political vacuums rarely remain empty. Despair is a poor foundation for peace and an excellent recruiting tool for extremism. The third future is more difficult. It is also the only one that offers a genuine path forward . Its premise offers the best foundation for peace: verified decommissioning of weapons, deradicalisation, accountable Palestinian civilian governance, phased Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction. The future of Gaza must ultimately be determined by accountable Palestinian civilian institutions, not competing armed factions. Under US President Donald Trump’s Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict , security must be exercised through lawful structures that answer to a civilian transitional authority. Reconstruction must proceed in an environment where weapons have been permanently decommissioned and military infrastructure dismantled, and where investors, donors and ordinary families can have confidence that war is not simply being postponed. That is not simply a technical requirement, it is a political one. To Israelis, I would offer one observation. I understand why many hear proposals for withdrawal or transitional administration and think of the failings of the past. The lesson I draw is that withdrawal without durable security and governance arrangement inside Gaza was insufficient. The fundamental question of who legitimately controls force inside Gaza was never properly resolved. The answer cannot be blind trust. Security arrangements must be verified and enforced. Yet Israelis should also confront an uncomfortable reality. Walls, buffer zones and recurring military operations cannot deliver lasting security if Gaza remains permanently unstable and under the control of armed factions. A strategy built entirely around managing the next war is not, in the long run, a strategy for peace. To Palestinians, and to Arabs across the region, I would offer a similarly candid observation. The destruction of Gaza has generated understandable anger. Many Palestinians also view international initiatives with suspicion. But there is another question that deserves an honest answer. Has the dominance of armed factions brought Palestinians closer to statehood, prosperity or freedom? Societies become stronger when institutions function, when schools educate children, when hospitals care for patients and when accountable governance provides services to people. They do not become stronger when decisions about war and peace are concentrated in the hands of armed groups. Nor can Gaza build a different future without confronting the ideologies and narratives that have normalised violence and extremism. Change cannot be imposed from outside; it must come through education, functioning institutions, economic opportunity and a political horizon that gives young people an alternative to militancy. The Palestinians of Gaza have paid an intolerable price. They deserve a future that demands more from politics than just aid or calls to sacrifice. The region and the international community also have responsibilities. Gaza cannot make this transition through declarations alone. Security guarantees must be credible, reconstruction must be supported and Palestinian transitional institutions must be given the means to succeed. Commitments made in conference rooms must ultimately translate into change on the ground. Implementing President Trump’s comprehensive plan, endorsed by UN Security Council resolution 2803, will not be easy. Agreements alone change very little. What matters is implementation, political courage and sustained commitment long after international attention moves elsewhere. The framework exists. Regional partners are engaged. Technical expertise is available. Financial resources can be mobilised. The question is whether the political will exists. There will always be those who resist change because new arrangements challenge familiar interests and established sources of influence. Building something new is invariably harder than defending what already exists. Yet leadership is measured precisely by the willingness to choose the harder path. For generations, this conflict has imposed costs on the entire region. Palestinians and Israelis have borne by far the greatest burden. While the dead deserve remembrance, the living deserve a future . We can preserve the conditions that repeatedly produce war, or we can begin building the conditions for peace. There is no neutral ground between those alternatives.

title: The Middle East needs a different answer to the failures exposed by October 7
description: This means a political future in which Israeli security and Palestinian self-determination are no longer treated as contradictory
content: Today is the third anniversary of the Hamas -led October 7 attacks on Israel . For the families of the Israelis killed or kidnapped by the militants, this will be an especially heartbreaking date to mark. Meanwhile, the families of the many thousands of Palestinians killed and many more injured and displaced in the subsequent Israeli offensive on Gaza continue to endure great suffering. October 7 was a significant moment for the wider Middle East , but it is also important to remember that the Palestinian-Israeli conflict did not begin that day. Certainly, the sight of Palestinian gunmen roaming through Israeli bases and communities signalled a profound rupture, but it was also a catalyst for dynamics that had been building across the region for years. The attacks that originated from a besieged and impoverished Gaza Strip shattered Israel’s sense of security. They also exposed the flawed assumption that had come to underpin Israeli policy, namely that the Palestinian occupation could be managed rather than ended. The hurt inflicted on ordinary Israelis, the leaving of Gaza’s Palestinians defenceless to Israeli retaliation and the political boost given to Israel’s nationalist extremes are additional outcomes of that fateful day. The response to October 7 now extends well beyond Gaza. Israel has launched or supported military action against targets linked to Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Syria and Iran itself. It also attacked Hamas figures based in Qatar in September last year. What began as a response to one attack has become part of a much wider regional confrontation. That should not obscure Hamas’s crimes against civilians. Nevertheless, “security” cannot become a permanent justification for open-ended war. If military action alone could produce lasting security, three years of conflict would have brought the region closer to it. Instead, the geography of the violence has expanded. The main lesson of October 7 should be that the old assumptions were wrong. The Palestinian question cannot be indefinitely postponed, and the occupation must end. Gaza cannot simply be managed. Regional stability cannot be built on an expectation that adversaries and their grievances can be contained forever. In the end, real security requires not permanent displays of military strength but political arrangements that make another October 7 attack less likely. That means a process that eventually fulfils Palestinians’ right to a credible future of their own, free from occupation. Israel’s coming election offers that country’s society an opportunity to debate this question. The central issue should not be how to prevent the next attack, but what a genuinely secure Israel looks like in 10, 20 or 30 years. A realistic pathway to such a future leads to political negotiations, not war without end. Meanwhile, the need for Palestinian elections becomes ever greater. Remembering October 7 means remembering its victims. But honouring those lives should also mean refusing to accept that the suffering that followed is inevitable. The Middle East needs a different answer to the failures exposed by that day; that means a political future in which security and Palestinian self-determination are no longer treated as contradictory goals.

title: Could an Arab writer win the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature? Nine names to know
description: From Adonis to Hoda Barakat, these are the writers with some of the strongest claims to become the first Arab literature laureate since Naguib Mahfouz
content: With the Nobel Prize in Literature set to be announced on Thursday, attention is turning to the writers who could receive one of the world’s most prestigious literary honours. Ahead of the announcement, there is little firm information to work with. Candidates are nominated by eligible figures including literary academy members, university professors, previous laureates and representatives of recognised writers’ organisations. The Nobel Committee for Literature assesses the nominations before the Swedish Academy selects the winner. The names remain confidential for 50 years, so any list of favourites is necessarily speculative. Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz became the first Arab writer to win the prize in 1988 and remains its only Arab laureate. Nearly four decades later, several writers from across the region have strong claims to follow him. If there is one Arab writer whose name has become almost permanently attached to Nobel speculation, it is Adonis. Born Ali Ahmad Said Esber in Syria in 1930, he helped transform modern Arabic poetry through both his writing and his role in co-founding the influential journal Shi’r . His poetry broke sharply with inherited forms and drew on mythology, politics and history in ways that reshaped the possibilities of Arabic poetry. The Goethe Prize in 2011 and the PEN/Nabokov Award in 2017 only reinforced a reputation that had already been decades in the making. The Sahara is the great recurring presence in Ibrahim Al Koni’s work. The Libyan Tuareg novelist has spent decades turning the desert into a space of myth, spirituality, memory and survival, drawing on a cultural inheritance rarely represented on such a scale in modern fiction. He has written more than 80 books, with translations appearing in more than 35 languages, and was a finalist for the 2015 Man Booker International Prize. What distinguishes Al Koni is not simply his subject matter, but the completeness of the literary world he has built around it. Amin Maalouf ’s strongest claim may lie in the breadth of the territory his work covers. Across novels, essays and historical writing, the Lebanese-born author has returned repeatedly to questions of migration, identity and the meeting of civilisations. Leo Africanus and The Crusades Through Arab Eyes remain among his best-known works, while The Rock of Tanios won the Prix Goncourt in 1993. Maalouf has since become a central figure in French literary life. He joined the Academie Francaise in 2011 and has served as its permanent secretary since 2023. War is rarely distant in Hoda Barakat ’s fiction. Its consequences seep into memory, relationships and the private lives of her characters. The Lebanese novelist’s major works include The Stone of Laughter, The Tiller of Waters and Voices of the Lost , each marked by an interest in people living through rupture and displacement. Barakat was a finalist for the 2015 Man Booker International Prize and won the International Prize for Arabic Fiction in 2019. Her case rests less on scale than on precision: a sustained body of work that examines conflict without reducing its characters to symbols. Few writers on this list have moved as comfortably between literary cultures as Tahar Ben Jelloun. The Moroccan novelist, poet and essayist writes primarily in French, but much of his work remains rooted in questions of Moroccan identity, migration and political repression. The Sand Child and The Sacred Night established his international reputation, with the latter winning the Prix Goncourt in 1987. This Blinding Absence of Light later became one of his most acclaimed works. His membership of the Academie Goncourt reflects a career that has long straddled North African and French literary traditions. Faith sits at the centre of Leila Aboulela’s fiction in a way that remains unusual in contemporary English-language literature. The Sudanese novelist has explored belief, migration and belonging through works including The Translator, Minaret and River Spirit. Her characters often negotiate more than geography. They move between cultures, languages and expectations while trying to maintain a coherent sense of self. Aboulela became the first winner of the Caine Prize for African Writing in 2000. Since then, she has built a body of work that places Sudanese and Muslim experiences firmly within contemporary literary fiction. Samar Yazbek ’s career cannot be separated from the upheaval in Syria. Her writing has moved between journalism, memoir, literary testimony and fiction, often circling the same questions from different angles. The Crossing documented her journeys into opposition-held Syria, while Planet of Clay and Where the Wind Calls Home transformed the experience of war into fiction. The latter was a finalist for the 2024 National Book Award for Translated Literature. Yazbek has also won the PEN Pinter Prize and the Tucholsky Prize, recognition of a body of work shaped by exile, conflict and witness. What Have You Left Behind? begins with a simple but devastating premise: to record the people killed in Yemen’s war as lives rather than numbers. Bushra Al Maqtari built the work from interviews with families who had lost relatives, creating a form that sits between testimony, reportage and literature. That approach has become central to her writing, which repeatedly returns to political violence and its human consequences. The Yemeni novelist and journalist received the Tucholsky Prize in 2024, bringing greater attention to work that has documented a conflict often treated internationally through statistics and geopolitical shorthand. Salim Barakat is perhaps the least straightforward candidate here, and that is part of what makes him interesting. The Kurdish-Syrian writer is known for pushing the Arabic language towards its limits, using dense imagery, unusual vocabulary and highly experimental structures across poetry, fiction and autobiography. His books include The Iron Grasshopper and The Universe, All at Once , and his career was closely connected to Mahmoud Darwish and the Palestinian literary journal Al-Karmel . Barakat’s readership is smaller than that of several names on this list, but his influence rests on the radical originality of his prose and poetry.

title: Blood test could help avoid rise in mixed prescriptions for the elderly
description: Research could tackle rising polypharmacy where patients take up to 10 pills a day
content: A new blood test could help doctors to determine the safest and most effective medications for elderly patients who are prescribed several pills daily. Polypharmacy, defined as being prescribed at least five different medications to manage different health problems, is on the rise among older Emirati adults, including substantial use of non-prescribed medicines and supplements. A study by the Ras Al Khaimah College of Nursing found that of the 200 patients over the age of 60 surveyed in the emirate's primary care centres, 60 per cent took at least five different medications, with 40 per cent taking 10 or more. Millions of older people around the world already take anticholinergics – a class of medicines used to treat psychiatric disorders, bladder and stomach problems or lung conditions – but research has shown that mixing anticholinergics raises the risk of dementia. Also, as medications accumulate and interact, the body reacts differently than it does when the medicine is taken alone. But a £3 million ($3.9 million) UK research programme funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) will explore how a blood test to see what drugs elderly patients may have adverse reactions to could form part of routine prescription. Dr Arya Ayyappan, a specialist in internal medicine at NMC Royal Hospital Abu Dhabi, said polypharmacy was a big issue in seniors. “This is common, particularly in those with diabetes, hypertension or cardiac issues,” she said. “Elderly patients will keep seeing different doctors, and each one will add on different medicines for certain ailments.” As the global population ages, the number of people aged 60 and over is projected to almost double by 2050, rising to 22 per cent of the world’s population. Dr Yasmeen Ajaz, a consultant endocrinologist at Medcare Al Safa, said problems arise when the overall combination becomes difficult to manage, medicine is duplicated, or the risks and side-effects outweigh the benefits. “As the number of medicines increases, so does the possibility of drug interactions, dosing errors and unwanted side effects,” he said. “This is why regular medication reviews are particularly important for older adults and anyone taking several long-term medicines. “Older people can be more vulnerable because the body processes medicines differently with age, and kidney and liver function may gradually change. “The answer is not necessarily to reduce the number of medicines, but to make sure every medicine is appropriate, necessary and monitored.” Prof Diana Baralle, co-director at the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre, said the research into the blood test was an important step towards bringing the benefits of genomic medicine into everyday healthcare. It aims to avoid adverse effects such as dizziness, nausea, or more serious problems that become dangerous in the elderly and lead to fall-related fractures. Zenia Noronha, who is a pharmacist living in Dubai, said her mother, Margaret d’Souza, 85, was prescribed several medications. “We have tried to move my mum away from allopathy into alternative medicine because I know the ill effects of over-prescribing,” she said. “Recently we travelled to Canada for my niece's wedding, and mum was quite anxious and took ill before leaving. “The doctor was very quick to prescribe her with an asthmatic inhaler as she had developed a minor cough and cold, despite her existing medications for diabetes and blood pressure. “When we visit the doctor, they usually write a prescription and that also affects the insurance. There should be a regular review of what someone is taking.” Technology is also helping doctors to avoid prescribing medicine that may have negative interactions. Malaffi is the region’s first Health Information Exchange platform, a centralised database of unified patient records. It safely and securely connects public and private healthcare providers in Abu Dhabi to enable real-time exchange of important patient health information. “Plenty of other patients take over-the-counter medications, even vitamins, supplements or homeopathic medicines,” said Dr Ayyappan. “We should understand that they can also impact the patient's day-to-day life as well.”

title: UAE aims to take camel milk global in quest to turn product into new superfood
description: Al Ain Farms Group unveils plans to bring camel milk brand to China and Europe
content: Matcha was on the menu at a signing ceremony during Global Food Week on Tuesday, an unusual sight at a formal event. But this matcha is no ordinary drink – it was brewed with camel milk. Al Ain Farms Group announced that it was taking its camel milk brand, Camelait , to the global market, with ambitions to turn the traditional product into a superfood. In partnership with international companies, Al Ain Farms will begin exporting camel milk products to China and European countries and aims to take the brand global over the next few years. “What Al Ain is doing is a whole transformation. It's not only trying to sell camel milk in Europe, it's also managing the whole supply chain from A to Z, from production all the way to R&D [research and development] and experimenting to improve and enhance the quality of camel milk and camel production,” Tareq Al Hosani, chairman of Al Ain Farms Group, told The National . The company aims to produce high-quality camel milk in the UAE and ship the powder to Germany and China. The two countries will then act as regional hubs – Germany for the rest of Europe and China for East Asia. Mr Al Hosani said the company had high ambitions for the coming years. “Our target is to share the benefit of camel milk globally, to have camel milk on every table,” he said. “To be able to do that, we need partners.” The camel milk market is predicted to reach $24 billion worldwide by 2030. Currently, camel milk accounts for just 0.4 per cent of global milk production , while the company produces two million litres annually. “Local manufacturing is a long-term commitment to the Chinese market and gives Camelait the flexibility to respond as demand develops and consumer preferences evolve,” said Rick Chen, general manager at Suzhou Biology Healthy. “This partnership is an investment in the category’s future, with long-life products widening its appeal and making camel milk a more familiar choice for Chinese households.” The UAE recently launched the world’s first international standard for pasteurised camel milk, which the Codex Alimentarius Commission has since approved. Codex is the food standards body established by the Food and Agriculture Organisation and the World Health Organisation. “The significance of Codex cannot be underestimated,” said Minister of Foreign Trade Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi at Global Food Week. He said the globally recognised food standard improved market access and was “central to our vision of open rule-based trade and our ability to connect scientific research to commercial impact”. Mr Al Hosani believes camel milk has worldwide potential, particularly for young children, because of its health benefits. “What I hope is that in five years, the majority of market share when it comes to children and baby food will be camel milk-based. Baby and children’s food is where camel milk is the most beneficial, but that will be the latest development because of the regulations and the level of assurances that the government will want before they allow it,” the chairman said. A new collaboration with Khalifa University and Khalifa University Enterprises Company will also advance research into camel milk and its potential applications. When asked whether the world was ready to embrace the Emirati beverage, Mr Al Hosani was confident. “They are ready to drink more than 20 different flavours of camel milk and more camel products coming soon, inshallah. Al Ain is betting big on this, but that’s the way we are. We dream big and we deliver big,” he said. The new chapter will put another UAE product on shelves around the world. “Success stories such as this reinforce the UAE’s position as a global hub for trade and business, and a launch pad for Emirati brands in markets worldwide,” said Dr Al Zeyoudi. Global Food Week started on Tuesday at Abu Dhabi's Adnec. The largest edition yet is showcasing food and agriculture companies from the UAE and abroad.

title: Egypt archaeology: Great Sphinx rocks reveal new species of ancient crocodile
description: Egyptian species, identified from fossil missing tip of its snout, shares more than just a home with Giza Sphinx
content: Fossils recovered a century ago in the rocks that make up the 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation in Egypt have revealed a new species of crocodile. The rocks, used to build the Great Sphinx , contained the skull of a crocodile, missing only the tip of its snout. It has been named Herugavialis cairensis. “Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru, who was possibly the inspiration for this iconic monument,” said Prof Philip Mannion of University College London, who co-led the study published in the Royal Society Open Science journal.
