It was thought the fossil belonged to the Tomistoma schlegelii species of freshwater crocodiles, but it has now been reclassified owing to analytical advances in palaeontology. A CT scan was used to look inside the skull, allowing an international team of researchers to identify several differences between the fossil and Tomistoma. They belong to a group of crocodiles known as gavials, which are today found only on the Indian subcontinent and in South-East Asia. But the fossil record of gavials documents a near-global distribution, spanning more than 100 million years. Herugavialis was not the only crocodile in Egypt at the time. The shallow marine environments that covered much of the region were also home to at least two other species of gavials. “Throughout much of the last 50 million years, the Mediterranean region hosted a high diversity of crocodiles, including gavials,” said Dr Paul Burke, a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm and lead author of the study. “However, this diversity fluctuated over time, seemingly corresponding to changes in global temperature and sea level, before the loss of all crocodiles in this region as a result of the drying of the Mediterranean approximately six million years ago.” The Great Sphynx – with the head of a human and the body of a lion – lies on the west bank of the Nile in Giza. It was sculpted from the limestone rock of the Mokattam Foundation about 5,000 years ago and is 20 metres tall.

title: UAE fall short as Saudi Arabia win Arabian Gulf Cup final
description: National team lose 2-0 in Jeddah as new coach Zlatko Dalic suffers first defeat
content: The UAE had their hopes of a third Arabian Gulf Cup title extinguished as they were soundly beaten by Saudi Arabia in Jeddah. Early goals from Hammam Al Hammami, the outstanding young winger, and Feras Albrikan in the final were enough to give the hosts the trophy. It was a first defeat for Zlatko Dalic as coach of the UAE. For a tournament that is nominally about local bragging rights, the Gulf Cup final almost always creates a major frenzy. The King Abdullah Sport City Stadium was rocking way ahead of kickoff. The 12,000 or so travelling UAE fans were in their seats hours before the start. When the players arrived and took their acclimatisation walk around the pitch, they looked spellbound by the away support. Most whipped out their phones to video the scene for posterity. By the time of kick-off, all the stands were teeming, packed to their 60,000 capacity, and the home faithful were by then drowning out their counterparts. It was hostile stuff. Khalid Essa, the UAE captain, was visibly agitated by the cacophony of jeers overpowering the national anthem. Despite that, it was the national team who settled fastest. In the third minute, they carved out the first opening of the game when Guilherme Bala found Nicolas Gimenez in the box. Gimenez, the Al Wasl playmaker, has been in fine form in front of goal in this competition. But his improvised overhead-kick flew over the bar. It scarcely quietened the crowd. Within moments, the game was stopped as the field was engulfed with smoke from the fans’ pyrotechnics. Once they had restarted, it was the hosts who asserted authority, and they struck with a quick-fire double-strike. First, Al Hammami’s deflected shot found its way past a despairing Essa, after the UAE had failed to clear a corner. Almost immediately after, they doubled their lead through Albrikan, the striker who had struck in the same net earlier this year to make Al Ahli Saudi champions of Asia at club level. The UAE were shellshocked. They were clinging on, and lucky the game wasn’t completely gone moments later when Saleh Abu Alshamat hit the post when he really should have made it 3-0 for Saudi Arabia. In a wild start to the game, the UAE struck the post themselves when they, too, should have scored. This time Gimenez smashed his shot against the left-hand post when put through by a neat through ball by Mamadou Coulibaly. To compound the problem, Gimenez then saw another chance to pull one back taken away from him. He had the ball on the penalty spot, only for VAR intervention to overrule a decision to award a foul on Bruno de Oliveira in the box. On viewing the monitor, the referee agreed the UAE forward had gone down too easily in the presence of Hassan Al Tambakti, the Saudi Arabia centre back. Dalic shuffled his pack to try to find a way back into the game after the break – as well as quell the threat of Al Hammami on the wing. The UAE did see more of the ball and halt the onslaught, but they found little joy going forward. Late on, substitute Fabio de Lima came closest when he crashed a shot against the crossbar, then saw the follow up effort saved. Other than that late flourish, Saudi Arabia were able to keep them at arm’s length, and closed out the win with relative ease. And in the bad-tempered ending, Khaled Al Dhanhani, an unused UAE substitute, was shown a red card for disputing a decision.

title: Google backs 'existing nuclear plants' as data centres strain US energy grid
description: Tech company announces power-purchase agreement with Constellation
content: Google has said that its data centre growth , fuelled by the artificial intelligence boom, led the company to reach a power-purchase agreement involving the upgrade of six nuclear plants in the US. An essay posted to Google's corporate news detailed the agreement made with Constellation , which operates the "largest fleet of nuclear facilities in the US". Through the PPA, Google says it is essentially enabling more than "1.5GW of new nuclear capacity for the US energy system from increasing the power output of existing reactors and bringing dormant facilities back online". Technology companies continue to come under criticism in the US over the rise in data centre construction. The centres cause energy demand to surge in some areas and lead to an increase in electricity prices for consumers. "As our data centre investments in the US continue, so does our commitment to revitalise the nation’s energy supply, support local jobs and economic opportunity, and bring new reliable electricity capacity to strengthen US grids at no cost to other ratepayers," Google said. The company said that as part of the PPA, Constellation had agreed to use the technology company's agentic AI "workflows across its core operations to accelerate uprate planning, streamline construction and optimise plant output". Google is the latest among Big Tech firms to support nuclear reactors in the US, although the moves have not always been welcomed. Critics say that many of the reactor deals include large loans from the US government, meaning citizens are paying for nuclear energy centres. On Monday, the US Department of Energy announced the latest such deal "of up to $4.2 billion" to modernise nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania. "By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, round-the-clock energy for American families and businesses," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. There are also concerns about safety. Constellation's PPA with Microsoft in 2024 involved the rehabilitation of one of the Three Mile Island reactors in Middletown, Pennsylvania. In March 1979, the core of TMI Unit 2 was partially exposed, prompting a temporary partial evacuation of the area and a lengthy clean-up around Middletown that continues to this day. Although it is Unit 1 of TMI, closed in 2019, that is being rehabilitated, energy safety groups have continued to express concern. And in Covert, Michigan, efforts to restart the Palisades nuclear reactor, which closed in 2022, are also under way. The owners of Palisades, Holtec International , had hoped to restart the reactor by this year, but a series of incidents have cast doubt on that goal. In September, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that it was investigating an incident related to a "tipped fuel assembly" that occurred while the reactor was being fuelled. On Tuesday, however, Google did not appear concerned about the potential for opposition as it promoted its endeavour with Constellation. "This builds a more affordable energy future for everyone," the company said. It said it was providing guaranteed revenue that Constellation "needs to invest in upgrades for 11 of their nuclear reactors, while ensuring other grid customers bear none of the associated costs".

title: California Governor Newsom says Trump's remarks on Iran striking Los Angeles and San Diego were 'disgusting'
description: Gavin Newsom directs State Threat Assessment Centre to monitor situation after President's remarks
content: California Governor Gavin Newsom said on Tuesday that US President Donald Trump 's comments about a possible Iranian attack on Los Angeles or San Diego were "disgusting and disqualifying". Clips have spread on social media of Mr Trump at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, in which he appeared to encourage Iran to "take out" the major cities in the Democratic-leaning state. "Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs," Mr Newsom said in a post on X. "I am directing the State Threat Assessment Centre to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California." The FBI warned this year that Iran could attempt to strike California in a drone attack. "The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X. But the White House said that Mr Trump's comments were taken out of context, and were actually about petrol prices . "The media freak-out over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality," White House spokesman Steven Cheung said. "He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President." During the rally, Mr Trump said that a "tremendous victory" in the coming elections would verify all of the actions his administration has taken. He and his Republicans are facing increasing pressure before the midterm elections in November, as petrol prices and those of other necessities remain high, and the war with Iran, although muted, continues. "And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial. It's a little bit high. It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego," Mr Trump said to applause and cheers. "This is a very small price to pay and it's going to be over very soon. It's essentially almost over with." Mr Trump and Mr Newsom have been publicly critical of each other's policies. Last year, Mr Trump sent the National Guard to Los Angeles to control immigration-related protests. In response, Mr Newsom filed a lawsuit against the administration. Mr Newsom also claimed in June that Mr Trump ordered a criminal investigation into him and his wife.

title: US senator accuses Pentagon of blocking Qatar base visit
description: Democrat Chris Murphy also visited drone-damaged US embassy in Riyadh
content: ​Democratic ​US Senator ​Chris Murphy on Tuesday said the Pentagon stopped him from visiting Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar on his visit to the Middle East, describing it as an attempt to conceal the effects of the Iran war. Al Udeid ​is ⁠the largest US ‌base in the region and has repeatedly been attacked ​by Iran during the war launched by the US and Israel in February. “This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort under way to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people,” Mr Murphy told journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip, according to Reuters. A US official told The National that Mr Murphy’s office was informed before his trip to the Middle East that he would not receive Pentagon support for access to Al Udeid Air Base. This was "consistent with [Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's] directive on travel restrictions in the region", the official said. Mr Murphy also said that the Pentagon refused to set up a briefing for him on the war while ​he was in the region. “I've never ‌encountered anything like ⁠this in my time in ​the Senate and it's part of a deliberate ​campaign ‌of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an ⁠end to,” he said. The Connecticut Senator has posted several updates on his trip to the Middle East and said he is the first Democrat to visit the region since the war began. Mr Murphy said that while he was in Riyadh, he heard alerts set off by incoming Houthi missiles. “This is now a full-blown regional war – just as every expert predicted if the US attacked Iran,” he posted on X. Mr Murphy said he had visited the US embassy in Riyadh to see damage from a drone attack early in the war. “If the attack had happened during the day, it would have been a mass-casualty event,” he wrote on X. Despite his criticism of the Pentagon, Mr Murphy said that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had enabled his visit, including arranging meetings with diplomats. During his trip, he met Qatari ​Emir Sheikh Tamim, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other senior Gulf officials.

title: Hackers steal 1.5 million files from Saudi construction firm, cybersecurity group says
description: Group claims to have breached 'main contractor' for 2034 Fifa World Cup
content: Hackers have stolen more than 1.5 million files from a construction company in Saudi Arabia commissioned to build facilities for the 2034 Fifa World Cup, a cyber threat monitoring group has reported. About 17 terabytes' worth of documents, contracts, payment information, stadium designs and personal data of 150,000 employees at the China Railway Railway Construction Corporation /Sama Construction consortium is said to have been compromised on October 3. Hackmanac, a cybersecurity analysis firm based in the UAE , attributed the attack to a group commonly known as WallStreet. It described the consortium as the “main contractor for Jeddah Central Stadium, a planned 2034 Fifa World Cup venue”. Hackmanac classified the CRCC hack as one of the most severe it has seen. CRCC has not yet responded to The National 's requests for comment. In an email, the Saudi Arabia National Cybersecurity Council confirmed that it had received The National 's inquiry about the alleged hack, but did not provide comment. According to cybersecurity analysis firm SOCRadar, WallStreet first gained prominence this year. “They utilise double-extortion tactics, targeting various sectors with sensitive data breaches to pressure victims into compliance,” SOCRadar's ransomware group profile definition reads. The group “operates internationally, with notable activity in the United States and Ecuador”, it adds. SOCRadar says the hacking group has claimed responsibility for at least 32 attacks across the world. Saudi Arabia was chosen as the sole host nation of 2034 World Cup two years ago. The country tentatively plans to host the tournament in 15 stadiums across five cities, including eight in the capital, Riyadh. Eleven of those are to be built for the tournament – including the proposed 92,000-seat King Salman Stadium. Saudi Arabian Football Federation president Yasser Al Misehal has said host cities will be connected by “state-of-the-art facilities to guarantee an amazing fan experience”.

title: Abu Dhabi's Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council meets to review AI progress
description: Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed sets out Abu Dhabi's ambitions for AI
content: Abu Dhabi's top artificial intelligence body has convened to assess progress on the emirate's ambition to become a global leader in AI technology. Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, Deputy Ruler of Abu Dhabi, National Security Adviser and Chairman of the Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council, chaired the meeting on Tuesday, held in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Vice Chairman of the council. The council reviewed progress in several key priorities, including the UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi, advances in AI research, the development of specialised talent and open AI models, and the Abu Dhabi government's drive to become the world's first fully AI-native administration by 2027. Sheikh Tahnoon said Abu Dhabi's ambitions go beyond merely adopting AI, extending to developing underlying technology and shaping the economy around it. He stressed the importance of directing investment, research and international partnerships towards building a lasting scientific and technological base in the emirate, enabling its people and institutions to establish new industries and develop a model of government with AI at its core. The Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Technology Council serves as Abu Dhabi's supreme authority for AI and advanced technology projects, investment and research. It is responsible for setting policies, strategies and priorities across the emirate. In July, the UAE and US agreed to create a bilateral task force to speed up the development of AI tools for military purposes. Task Force Talon Synapse is to be based in Abu Dhabi and will be made up of about 20 US and Emirati personnel specialising in AI , data and cybersecurity.

title: Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed calls for innovation and resilience to boost world's food security
description: Vice President made comments on opening day of Global Food Security Summit in Abu Dhabi
content: Sheikh Mans our bin Zayed , Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, has pledged the UAE will continue collaborating to find innovative ways to strengthen global food security, as an international summit opened in Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Mansour said creating food systems capable of withstanding future challenges was crucial to long-term development throughout the world. “As Abu Dhabi hosts the Global Food Security Summit, the UAE continues to work with partners around the world to develop innovative solutions that strengthen and sustain food security,” he said in a statement on X. “Our aim is to build a more resilient and efficient food system that preserves resources and adapts to emerging challenges. Food security is a cornerstone of development and prosperity.” Last month, Khalifa Al Marar, Minister of State, warned threats to global supply chains could push tens of millions into acute food insecurity. Mr Al Marar was speaking at an Arria-formula meeting on September 17 on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly session in New York. He stressed that securing supply chains, trade routes and energy flows was essential to maintaining international peace and stability. He warned that disruption to these networks directly affects food security and the availability of fertilisers critical to global agriculture. The second Global Food Security Summit opened at Adnec on Tuesday as part of Global Food Week, which runs until Thursday. The summit brings together governments, international organisations, investors, researchers and food industry leaders to examine ways to protect supplies amid pressures including climate change, geopolitical tension, supply-chain disruption and rising costs. Discussions are focusing on international co-operation to make food systems more resilient, as well as the role of artificial intelligence, sustainable water management and technology. Global Food Week is being held under the patronage of Sheikh Mansour and has attracted participants from 92 countries, with speakers from 30 nations taking part in the Food Security Summit.

title: Energy forum seeks to rescue supply disrupted by US-Iran war
description: Rising output, resilience of export lines and increase in storage are shared ambitions
content: Energy market insiders who gathered in a vast underground ballroom in central London this week were united in support of a new emphasis on resilience in the oil industry. The duration of the US-Iran war has changed the industry from "a just-in-time to a just-in-case" sector, TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanne told the Energy Intelligence Forum. Amin Nasser, chief executive of Aramco, said that throughout the crisis conditions, the producer has not cancelled one committed delivery, thanks to a number of routes to market and, in the case of the East-West pipeline , a vast capacity. This comes despite the supply problems caused by the blockades in the Strait of Hormuz and, more recently, the Bab Al Mandeb strait. “It [the pipeline] has multiple lines with a lot of redundancy and flexibility built in and, because of that, all our customers are getting all their shipments required,” he said. “When this crisis happened, we said, “OK, we have three routes. Is that enough?” Mr Nasser added. “Maybe not for the future. And this is the responsibility of the current generation, to think of a fourth and a fifth export way out.” Sheikh Nawaf Al Sabah, chief executive of Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC), pointed out the value of having its own tanker fleet, which dates back to the 1990s. “I think there is a major difference that we are able to accomplish through our tankers by having these tankers owned by us,” Mr Al Sabah said. “We control where they go and the crews are our own crews. They, of course, all have the discretion of deciding whether they want to go through a passage or not.” An emerging picture of new codes of conduct from the US-Iran war stretches across customers, consuming nations, producers and product classes. Vaclav Bartuška, the Czech ambassador to the UK, said the long-term forces of change bear some resemblance to calculations last seen between the US and former Soviet Union. “We are relearning the escalation ladder, which was the basis of the Cold War for 40 years,” he told The National . “You know the level to which you escalate, that you deter, but also don't cause too much pain into the other side. “The Soviet Union and the United States developed a code, a language of how to hit each other without actually having open war between them. [They] managed to spend 40 years in a Cold War without killing the world. They had proxy wars. They had plenty of conflicts. They managed not to have a direct escalation among themselves. This could be a very long confrontation. It could also end the next day,” he said. During the gas dispute between Russia and Ukraine in January 2009, Mr Bartuska was involved in negotiations with Russian, Ukrainian and European Union leadership, when the Czech Republic held the EU Presidency. He also served as the Czech Republic's ambassador-at-large for energy security. Ichiro Takahara, chairman and chief executive of Japan's strategic reserves specialist operator, Jogmec, said diversification to avoid “chokepoints” was one priority in the country's stockpiling policy. He added that relations with resilient suppliers, such as Aramco and KPC, would include co-operation to build storage depots closer to customers in places such as Japan. Another Japanese executive, Takayuki Ueda, president of Inpex, said buyers now had wider considerations concerning diversification as well as resilience. “What matters for our buyers is security of supply,” he said. “They usually point out diversification of supply sources is important. However, they also emphasise the security and resilience of entire supply chain.” Countries with differing strengths must work together to boost supply undertakings, said Kevin Gallagher, managing director of Australian company Santos. “There's a real clarity and understanding with policymakers in Australia that more pragmatic rather than ideological policies when it comes to energy development and energy supply going forward is what was required,” he said. Mr Gallagher predicted Australia would “take its foot off the hose” that has restricted oil and gas exploration in recent years. The Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led European legislators to seek new energy deals in the Gulf – but the current war has narrowed those options. Mr Bartuška said European governments were likely to pursue a diversification of suppliers. “This is not a crisis yet. We have been through much worse, and European countries didn't start this conflict and are not taking direct part in it,” he said. Rising oil and gas prices would make some previously marginal projects more economically viable. “There are quite a few projects around the world which were basically on the threshold between being relevant and not,” Mr Bartuška said. “I think higher prices will make them sustainable economically. From Latin America, from African countries and projects in Asia, Australia or the US. There are quite a few resources which are not yet reserves, or they are becoming reserves, which means economically viable, thanks to the situation now.” “I think, in general, the European perception of war changed in 2022 with the start of the Russian war against Ukraine, and we now see huge attacks by drones and missiles very regularly,” he said. “There are also plenty of hybrid or hidden warfare and hidden attacks or deniable attacks against our installations. We are much more careful about what's happening in our countries, trying to deter another attack [while at] the same time, not to escalate too much.” He said western misconception of Iran was driving the inability to reach a truce – as well as a desire from the US and Iran sides to keep the war going. “I don't know if both sides actually want the end of confrontation. I'm not sure of that. It's been going on since the end of February. It's now October,” he said.

title: India condemns strike on oil tanker owned by Dubai company in Strait of Hormuz
description: Twelve crew members injured after MT On Peace was struck
content: The Indian government has condemned an attack in which an oil-tanker owned by Dubai shipping company Onex was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz . There were 12 crew members of the MT On Peace injured in the attack, including 11 Indians, according to a statement from the Indian Ministry of External Affairs. Of the 19-strong crew, 17 were Indians. The ship sails under a Panamanian flag, according to the ministry. "With the assistance of Omani authorities, the injured crew have since been evacuated and are receiving medical treatment in Khasab, Oman. We thank the Omani authorities for their valuable support," read the statement, released on Tuesday. "The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern for India. We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region." The attacks on commercial shipping, sailors and civilian infrastructure in the region must end, and navigation and commerce through international waterways must be restored as soon as possible, the statement said. Over the past weeks, nine commercial vessels were attacked close to the strait, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal . The UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday that an oil tanker crossing outbound from the Strait of Hormuz was hit by a projectile. Earlier on Tuesday, the UKMTO posted on X that "an oil tanker has been struck above the waterline by an unknown projection". The National contacted Onex for a statement but has yet to receive a response.

title: Rise expected in UAE's inflation figures, S&P Global says
description: Businesses last month increased prices at highest rate in 15 years
content: The steep increase in selling prices of non-oil businesses in September is an indication of a higher UAE inflation number for the third quarter of this year, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. The rising rate of inflation in selling prices by businesses is being partly driven by an increase in demand conditions in the UAE's non-oil private sector , David Owen, principal economist at the company, told The National . S&P Global Market Intelligence on Monday said non-oil private sector businesses in the country last month reported the steepest jump in sales prices since May 2011. “Out of the firms monitored in the survey, 13 per cent reported an increase in their selling prices since the previous month, compared to 5 per cent that noted a decline,” Mr Owen said. “The indicated rate of inflation was strong in the context of the survey history, as past data has often signalled a relatively cautious approach to price hikes among non-oil companies.” The rise in selling prices is also being driven by higher costs for materials, labour and energy amid the Iran war and will reflect in the pace of annual increase in consumer prices, Mr Owen said. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index for September, however, remained steady at 55.3, the same as the previous month and well above the 50-mark that indicates growth in economic activity. With the non-oil economy having shrugged off the mid-year slowdown linked to the war, businesses have started to pass on the higher cost of inputs to their customers. “The seasonally adjusted Output Prices Index has a strong historical relationship with consumer price inflation, as the measure captures changes in business charges, which has strong implications for overall consumer prices,” Mr Owen said. “The latest index reading points to consumer prices rising sharply at the end of the third quarter, with the annual pace of inflation accelerating notably.” Consumer prices have been affected by the sharp rise in fuel prices this year. Petrol prices in the UAE are about 80 per cent higher than in February, before the Iran war started. The disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has affected supply chains severely, pushing up the costs of materials and inputs. Inflation figures for the third quarter of the year have not yet been revealed. Since 2009, S&P Global Markets Intelligence has been compiling the S&P Global UAE PMI Index, a composite indicator designed to give an overview of operating conditions in the non-oil private sector. The company index is derived from responses sent by purchasing managers in a panel of around 1,000 non-energy private sector companies. The panel represents sectors including manufacturing, construction, wholesale, retail and services. The September survey data signalled that input cost pressures had been above the long-run trend in each month since March 2026 and the stronger increase in selling prices last month was “broad-based across the sectors of the non-oil private sector economy”, Mr Owen said.

title: Paramount completes Warner Bros merger in historic media deal to create Skydance
description: New company combines two major Hollywood film studios, covering franchises such as Harry Potter and Mission Impossible
content: Paramount Skydance closed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery on Tuesday, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time after engaging in a bruising battle for control with Netflix and fending off antitrust lawsuits. The new company, which is to be called Skydance, combines two of the five largest Hollywood film studios, covering major franchises such as Harry Potter and Mission Impossible. It will be home to dozens of TV networks, from CBS to TNT, and two major subscription streaming services, Paramount+ and HBO Max. David Ellison, who completed the merger of his Skydance Media film production company with Paramount in 2025, has become one of Hollywood’s biggest moguls. He appointed Ynon Kreiz, formerly chief executive of Mattel, to share oversight of Skydance as co-chief executive. Mr Kreiz will manage day-to-day operations, while Mr Ellison maintains the creative vision and handles relationships with talent. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Mr Ellison said in a statement. After pulling off two mega-mergers of century-old Hollywood companies in little more than a year, he now faces the significant challenge of making it all work . That means eliminating overlapping businesses and jobs without fanning the ire of Hollywood, which is suffering through a downturn and has opposed the consolidation from the start. Skydance also will need to manage nearly $80 billion in debt while adhering to a strict calendar of theatrical releases as stipulated by the lawsuit settlement. The path to closing the merger was often rocky and at times seemed likely to derail the endeavour. But Mr Ellison deemed the deal to be essential if he was to compete with the likes of Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Apple. “They’re starting off at a great place,” Michael Wolf, chief executive of management consulting firm Activate Strategy, told Bloomberg TV on Monday. “The logic makes sense. Scale puts them in the right position. Now they have to deliver against scale.” Paramount agreed to acquire Warner Bros in February after a months-long bidding war against Netflix, which had previously committed to purchasing Warner Bros’ studios and streaming business, but not its cable channels. Mr Ellison clinched the deal by sweetening the offer price and bringing his father, Larry Ellison, in to personally guarantee funding. Paramount paid a $2.8 billion break-up fee to Netflix on behalf of Warner Bros and said it would be able to close its own deal quickly, promising to pay fees to Warner Bros' shareholders of $7 million a day if the deal was not finalised by September 30. While Paramount managed to secure antitrust approval from the US Department of Justice, the EU and other jurisdictions, it was delayed by a pair of lawsuits brought by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, which were concerned about the threat of higher prices for consumers and fewer jobs. Thousands of actors, directors, writers and producers signed a letter protesting against the deal. Much of that fear stemmed from Paramount’s pledge to extract more than $6 billion in annual synergies within three years of closing the merger. Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners, a Paramount investor, said there were other ways to cut costs and operate more efficiently than reducing jobs. A company would not spend billions of dollars a year making movies “and figure your entire premise of your business plan is to fire everybody in Hollywood", he said at the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last week. “It’s just the opposite.” Skydance’s debt load will continue to weigh on the company, however. Its interest bills are much higher now than if it had issued debt just a few months earlier, since inflation concerns have lifted global borrowing costs. Paramount sold $52 billion of loans and bonds in only a week, a tight timeline for any debt deal – particularly for one of the largest financings in recent history. As part of a negotiated settlement with the states, whose case was led by California's attorney general Rob Bonta, Paramount vowed to release at least 30 films a year in theatres and keep them there for 45 days, before making them available for viewing at home. The company also agreed to create an editorial independence board for its news organisations, CBS and CNN, an effort to address concerns that the Ellison family’s close ties with US President Donald Trump would cause them to try to influence coverage. Mr Ellison has so far agreed to keep CBS and CNN separate and under different leadership. In announcing a new executive team on Monday, he said CNN chief executive Mark Thompson would remain in his role and Bari Weiss would keep her title as editor-in-chief of CBS News. While acknowledging “trepidations about this moment", Mr Thompson said in a letter to staff that he had “real confidence” that the Skydance leadership understood “and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for". Dana Goldberg, a long-time Skydance Media executive who developed and produced films including Top Gun: Maverick , and Josh Greenstein, a former president of Sony Pictures’ Motion Picture Group, will jointly oversee the new Skydance Motion Picture Group. James Gunn and Peter Safran, the co-chiefs of DC Studios, will continue in their roles at Skydance. Casey Bloys, who has ushered in hits for HBO including Game of Thrones spin-off House of the Dragon , will be in charge of Skydance’s streaming division, overseeing HBO Max and Paramount+ programming. George Cheeks, who joined Paramount in 2020, is to manage a newly formed TV division, encompassing a mix of Paramount and Warner Bros studios, networks, sports and cable brands. JB Perrette, who led the global introduction of the HBO Max streaming service at Warner Bros, will work as co-chairman and chief business officer of Skydance TV and Skydance streaming. While Mr Kreiz’s appointment came as a surprise to many on Wall Street, his experience complements Mr Ellison’s, bringing years of oversight of a large public company and more than three decades in entertainment. During his tenure at Mattel, Mr Kreiz was instrumental in pushing the toy company to capitalise on its beloved brands, such as Barbie and Hot Wheels, turning them into franchises that could span movies, TV and games. One executive who will not be part of the new team at Skydance is David Zaslav. The president and chief executive of Warner Bros is to take his leave along with potentially more than $667 million in cash severance and stock awards triggered by the sale.

title: The Phantom of the Opera is coming to Abu Dhabi
description: Longest-running show in Broadway history taking over Etihad Arena for three-week run
content: The Phantom of the Opera, one of the world's longest-running musicals , is coming to Abu Dhabi. The Andrew Lloyd Webber production will take over Etihad Arena for a three-week run from March 10 to 28 next year, with performances scheduled on 13 dates. Audiences will have more opportunities to catch the show at weekends, with afternoon and evening performances taking place on Saturdays and Sundays. Etihad Arena began teasing the arrival of the musical on Tuesday, sharing a short video on its social media channels. “After 40 years of haunting stages, he is coming to Abu Dhabi,” reads the video, set against a dark, swirling backdrop. “More to be revealed soon,” it adds. The venue shared the clip on Instagram with the caption: “09.10.26. Stay tuned, Abu Dhabi,” pointing to an official announcement on Friday. However, the identity of the mystery production appears to have already been revealed. Pre-sale emails for The Phantom of the Opera were sent to some customers on Tuesday, confirming the musical is heading to the capital. Tickets start at Dh240. The Abu Dhabi dates come as The Phantom of the Opera marks 40 years since its world premiere at Her Majesty's Theatre in London's West End on October 9, 1986. Based on Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel of the same name, the musical tells the story of a mysterious masked figure who lives beneath the Paris Opera House and becomes obsessed with young soprano Christine Daae. Featuring music by Lloyd Webber, the production includes some of musical theatre's best-known songs, including The Music of the Night , All I Ask of You and the title track. The production made its Broadway debut in 1988 and went on to become the longest-running show in Broadway history, playing almost 14,000 performances before closing in April 2023. The London production continues to run in the West End. The musical has been staged around the world and seen by more than 160 million people in dozens of countries. Further details about the Abu Dhabi production, including casting and general ticket sales, are expected to be announced on Friday.

title: UAE introduces new salt, sugar and fat limits with penalties of up to Dh500,000
description: Rule applies to packaged foods, whether manufactured locally or imported
content: The UAE has begun a nationwide push to cut the amount of salt, sugar and fat in some packaged foods to help improve their nutritional value , as well as tackling obesity and other conditions linked to an unhealthy diet . The Ministry of Health and Prevention said it would introduce the caps in phases, with the final limits due to take effect by December 31, 2030. The resolution, approved on Tuesday, is to apply to packaged foods, whether manufactured locally or imported, as well as establishments in the UAE that handle those products, including free zone companies. The move does not apply to food products manufactured or imported for direct export or onward export from the UAE, unless they are traded in the country. Companies that fail to comply with the resolution could face administrative penalties. They include a warning; an administrative fine of between Dh5,000 and Dh500,000 ($1,360 to $136,147); the closure of the establishment for up to six months; and cancellation of its licence or approval. Federal and local health authorities, along with other agencies, are in charge of enforcing the provisions and ensuring companies comply. They must also supply the ministry with the data and information needed to implement the caps. The ministry has adopted a phased compliance system based on each food product. That is aimed at enabling manufacturers and businesses to reformulate their products and adjust their operations to meet the requirements. Products manufactured or placed on the UAE market before the new requirements take effect can remain on sale for up to one year, or until their expiry date, whichever comes first. The resolution sets maximum levels for salt, sugar and fat for every 100g of each product over two phases. For leavened bread, the first phase allows a maximum of 444 milligrams of sodium, 6 grams of total sugars and 8.4 grams of total fat. These limits are to be reduced in the second phase to 370mg of sodium, 5g of total sugars and 7g of total fat. For flatbread, the first phase limits are 384mg of sodium, 6g of total sugars and 8.4g of total fat. That will later drop to 320mg of sodium, 5g of total sugars and 7g of total fat. For sweetened milk drinks, including milk alternatives, total sugars are to be limited to 9.6g in the first phase, before dropping to 8g. For sweetened or flavoured yoghurt and laban, the total sugar limit is 12g per 100g in the first phase, before dropping to 10g in the final phase. The health push will also apply to salty snacks. The sodium limit for salted crackers is to fall from 696mg per 100g in the first phase to 580mg in the final phase. For salted nuts and seeds, the limit will fall from 336mg to 280mg. For pretzels, the sodium limit will drop from 912mg to 760mg, while the limit for snacks made from potatoes, sweet potatoes, vegetables or grains will fall from 564mg to 470mg. A second group of products to be affected includes processed cheese. For spreadable cheese, the sodium limit will fall from 864mg for every 100g in the first phase to 720mg in the final phase. For other processed cheeses, the limit will drop from 1.2g to 1g. Businesses handling products in the first group of products will have up to nine months to meet the first-phase limits. They must then continue reducing levels of salt, sugar and fat to meet the final limits by December 31, 2030. Companies handling the second group of products will have up to two years and three months to meet the first-phase limits. But they must also meet the final limits by December 31, 2030. The resolution allows businesses to apply for an exception to the first-phase limits if they would require a targeted ingredient to be reduced by more than 20 per cent. Businesses must submit applications within 30 days of the resolution taking effect. They must include technical information, the product's registered nutrition label and test results from an accredited lab. Businesses must also commit to reducing the targeted ingredient by at least 20 per cent during the first phase. An approved exception does not remove the requirement to meet the maximum limits by December 31, 2030.

title: Human in the loop: teachers remain vital to learning in the age of AI, says Education Minister
description: Technology and artificial intelligence are tools that will not replace classroom interactions, says Sarah Al Amiri
content: Teachers have a crucial role to play in schools despite the rapid advance of artificial intelligence, the Minister of Education said. Sarah Al Amiri , at the Education First Forum in Abu Dhabi, said that AI will be used purposefully but it cannot replace human interaction. “Technology and artificial intelligence are tools we employ consciously, ensuring they do not come at the expense of independent thought or human interaction,” Ms Al Amiri said. “No educational transformation can be achieved without a highly capable teacher. It is the teacher who transforms the curriculum into a learning experience, discovers students' talents, builds their confidence, instils values ​​in them, and teaches them how to think, learn and relearn. “Therefore, educational development begins with investing in teachers – in their capabilities, their professional growth pathways and the tools that empower them to perform their roles optimally.” Senior figures from the country's education sector explained how AI will be used in the future of learning. Prof Ahmed Ali Alraeesi, vice chancellor of United Arab Emirates University, said the role of AI in education was being constantly re-evaluated. “We started to have a compulsory [AI] course required by every student before graduation in all colleges,” Mr Alraeesi told The National. “We refined all academic programmes to align with the job market and global trends in order to equip our students with the needed skills. If we wait, I think we will not be able to catch the changes.” Prof David Pedder, dean of Emirates College for Advanced Education (ECAE), which specialises in teacher training, told The National that the college prioritises AI in human-centric ways – and as a tool rather than a crutch. “Our basic approach to using AI is as a source of personalised formative and summative feedback on learners and teachers developing ideas,” he said. “Our approaches and methodologies for integrating AI in every context of learning, teaching and leading need to be human-centric, with the human learner at the centre of the enterprise. At ECAE, professors are expected to use AI to lessen their load, provide input on lesson plans and give feedback to students. “Because AI can draw on a truly global range of knowledge, it is a very rich source of ideas – a plan for a lesson, or a plan for a series of lessons,” he said. “It is also a source for informing how these lessons and sequences of lessons are to be taught. Teachers can test out the lesson plans, get feedback and open themselves to new ideas that they hadn't thought of by themselves.” At the forum, Prof Pedder announced the Nama'a initiative, which puts families at the heart of learning and well-being, to further this “ecosystem approach”. “We recognise that complex educational challenges need the full range of expertise that exists in that ecosystem,” he said. “We need the expertise of strategic stakeholders and their voices – parents, children and young people, policymakers, educators in schools, teachers, leaders, educational psychologists, classroom assistants. “The entire community needs to be mobilised to address complex educational challenges and this collaborative enterprise is really at the heart of the initiative.”

title: Why has war returned to Ethiopia?
description: A fragile peace deal, an alliance of former enemies and deepening rivalries with neighbouring states have brought fighting back to the north
content: Nearly four years after a peace deal ended one of this century’s deadliest wars, fighting has broken out in Ethiopia 's northern Tigray region once again. But the battle lines have shifted this time, with former enemies joining forces against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Tigrayan factions fighting on opposing sides. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Tigray Defence Forces launched a major offensive on September 23, seizing the airports at Mekelle, Aksum and Shire. Federal forces and allied fighters counter-attacked, entering the region's capital Mekelle on Saturday and declaring full control of the city by the following day. The TPLF acknowledged its retreat in a statement on Sunday, saying its regional government would be “temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else”. However, the war is not over. Humanitarian sources reported air strikes and artillery exchanges overnight into Monday. One aid bulletin said air attacks killed at least 17 people in the towns of Adwa and Sheraro. Addis Ababa accuses Egypt, Eritrea and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) of backing the rebellion. All three deny it but their quarrels with Ethiopia threaten to turn an unfinished domestic conflict into a wider regional confrontation. Tigray is Ethiopia’s northernmost region, bordering Eritrea and Sudan. Its population is predominantly Tigrayan and speaks Tigrinya, a language also spoken across the Eritrean border. Ethiopia’s regions are organised largely around ethnic and linguistic identities, with their own administrations and substantial autonomy. This “ethnic federalism” recognises the country’s diversity, but makes disputes over boundaries, political representation and central authority particularly combustible. The TPLF dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition for nearly three decades before Mr Abiy came to power in 2018. Its leaders retreated to Tigray as relations with the federal government unravelled after they refused to join Mr Abiy's new party. Civil war broke out in November 2020 after Tigrayan forces attacked federal army bases, an operation they described as pre-emptive. Ethiopia’s army fought alongside forces from Tigray's neighbouring Amhara region, Fano militias and Eritrean troops. The fighting spread to Amhara and Afar, killing hundreds of thousands through violence, hunger and the collapse of essential services. An African Union-brokered agreement signed in Pretoria in November 2022 stopped the major fighting. The TPLF promised to disarm, and Tigray was to receive an interim administration acceptable to both sides. But the settlement did not address territorial disputes and notably excluded Eritrea, a major participant in the war. The status of contested territory that Amhara forces had taken control of remained unresolved, leaving many Tigrayans in displacement camps. The TPLF regarded the Pretoria settlement as lopsided, while the federal government accused it of failing to disarm as per the terms of the deal. A split within the TPLF further weakened the peace. Getachew Reda, a former party spokesman who led the postwar interim Tigray administration, favoured engagement with Addis Ababa. An opposing faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael, who had previously led Tigray through the 2020-22 war, accused his administration of compromising Tigrayan interests. The TPLF expelled Mr Getachew in 2024 and pushed him out of the interim administration in early 2025. In April 2025, Mr Abiy made him an adviser with ministerial rank in the federal government. The TPLF then revived Tigray’s prewar regional council and installed its chairman, Mr Debretsion, as regional president. The Addis Ababa-backed interim government rejected the takeover as illegal. The TPLF also stepped up military conscription and signalled it wanted to remove Mr Abiy. Addis Ababa, already withholding federal funds and restricting fuel to Tigray, began occasional drone strikes in the region. On September 20, seven organisations formed the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival and pledged to overthrow Mr Abiy. Two days later, the government launched a major drone attack against an apparent concentration of Tigrayan forces. While the TPLF describes its campaign as defensive, the International Crisis Group attributes the large-scale ground offensive primarily to the TPLF and its allies. The federal army is supported by allied formations, including the Tigray Peace Forces, an anti-TPLF Tigrayan armed group. Its participation makes the previous war's “Ethiopia against Tigray” tagline an inadequate description this time around. The opposition alliance includes the TPLF, Amhara Fano National Movement, Oromo Liberation Army, Ogaden National Liberation Front, Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement and Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. The Amhara Fano National Movement represents the biggest reversal in positions. Its fighters helped Mr Abiy against the TPLF during the previous war, then began their own insurgency against Addis Ababa in August 2023 after his government moved to dismantle their regional security forces. Many Amharas feared the reform would leave them vulnerable and jeopardise their hold on territory seized from Tigray. So, the new alliance is based less on a shared blueprint for Ethiopia and more on facing a common opponent. But co-operation does not erase rival territorial claims among its members, nor guarantee agreement over what follows Mr Abiy's government. The alliance’s sharpest fault line is over territory in western and southern Tigray, which Amhara forces seized during the previous war. Tigrayan leaders demand its return, while Amharas claim it as historically theirs. Eritrea's original intervention grew out of decades of hostility towards the TPLF, which led Ethiopia during the 1998-2000 border war. The two governments then backed each other's opponents for years. That makes Eritrea's new alignment with the TPLF all the more striking. Mr Abiy's rapprochement with Eritrea in 2018 gave both an opportunity to confront their shared enemy. Asmara wanted the TPLF decisively defeated and resented the Pretoria deal for stopping short of that. Relations subsequently soured over Ethiopia’s pursuit of access to the Red Sea. Eritrea fears Ethiopian designs on its Assab port, although Mr Abiy says he will seek access peacefully. Crisis Group says Eritrea is now “quietly aligned with its former enemy the TPLF”. Diplomats and analysts told Reuters that Mr Isaias is giving the rebels access to the coast. In the last war, Tigray was cut off on all sides. Eritrea denies helping the rebels. However, ties broke down last Thursday after Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats. Eritrea responded cutting diplomatic relations. Over the past few years, Eritrean officials have increasingly portrayed the Addis Ababa government, rather than the TPLF, as the principal threat to their security. Last week, Eritrea’s Foreign Ministry accused Ethiopia of seeking its ports and coastal territory through force, and of training armed groups to destabilise its government. Crisis Group says SAF hosts thousands of Tigrayan fighters, many of whom have fought alongside it against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. It also reports alleged Ethiopian assistance to the RSF, which Addis Ababa denies. Ethiopia’s army chief accused Sudan, Egypt and other powers of supplying the rebels in late September, without presenting public evidence. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty rejected the claim, saying Cairo had nothing to do with events inside Ethiopia. The Nile dispute remains central to their rivalry. On Monday, President Abdel Fattah El Sisi reaffirmed Egypt’s water rights and pledged to defend them through international law. A day earlier, he hosted Eritrean, Sudanese and Somali leaders in New Alamein. Their declaration rejected unilateral measures affecting Egyptian and Sudanese water use, reserved Red Sea governance for coastal states, and opposed recognition of Somaliland, Ethiopia’s prospective sea-access partner. The summit demonstrated shared objections to Ethiopian policies, not evidence that its participants are arming rebels. Ethiopia's renewed war grew from an unfinished peace. Its neighbours’ rivalries now make it harder to contain.

title: Three Iranians 'spied on dissident journalists and plotted violent attack' in London
description: Trio accused of carrying out surveillance on Iran International
content: Three Iranians spied on UK-based dissident journalists on behalf of their country’s foreign intelligence service in preparation for an attack on one of them, a court was told. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, ⁠46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, are accused of carrying out surveillance on Iran International , a Farsi-language television channel that is critical of the Iranian regime. Mr Sepahvand is also accused of one count of preparing to commit serious violence, while the other two are accused of assisting him. One of the targets of the group was Kambiz Hosseini, a prominent Iranian satirist and critic who hosts London -based Iran International’s nightly show The Program . Mr Hosseini was monitored by Mr Noori and Mr Manesh as the group sought to gather information about his movements. The prosecution alleges that this intelligence gathering was done to help prepare for a violent attack against the journalist that would be carried out by Mr Sepahvand. “These defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” prosecutor William Emlyn Jones told Woolwich Crown Court in London. “Their ultimate objective was that one or more than one of their targets would be subjected to serious violence – no doubt as retribution for their criticism of the Iranian regime. Eliminating hostile or critical voices has effectively become a staple policy of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” The men are alleged to have watched London addresses and used open-source intelligence to gain information related to journalists working for Iran International. The news organisation has come under particular attack from the regime due to its support for opposition parties and its criticism of the Islamic republic, the jury was told. Mr Hosseini’s “family had suffered threats and intimidation from the authorities in Iran and in the end his siblings had to flee Iran”, Mr Jones told the jury. Mr Sepahvand is alleged to have carried out the work in return for money and to have had a series of accusations of theft against him in Iran withdrawn. The three accused are alleged to have carried out surveillance of another Iran International journalist, Mojtaba Pour Mohsen. Mr Sepahvand had briefing documents on his phone containing information about the activities and lives of Mr Pour Mohsen and Mr Hosseini in London, including the name of the latter’s dog, the court heard. The accused have each denied ​two ⁠charges under Britain's National Security ‌Act , brought in to give the authorities new powers to ​target threats from foreign state.

title: British Airways to launch world’s biggest business class cabin
description: First upgraded double-decker due to enter service in coming months, airline chief Sean Doyle says
content: British Airways will introduce what it describes as the world’s biggest business class on its upgraded double-decker Airbus SE A380 jets , targeting premium passengers as airlines rush to cash in on upscale travel . The IAG SA-owned airline will update its fleet of a dozen A380s with a 106-seat business class cabin spanning the entire upper deck of the aircraft, the airline said at an event in London. The first upgraded A380 is due to enter service in the coming months. The carrier said it would also upgrade its first-class seating with dividers that fold away , enabling the conversion of middle seats into larger cabins for passengers travelling together. The changes will reduce the number of seats on the A380 by 11 per cent, from 469 seats to 417, with the bulk of the reduction coming from the economy-class cabin. Economy berths will be reduced by about 30 per cent to 215 seats. “This is the largest single investment that any airline has ever made in reconfiguring an aircraft stretching from nose to tail and touching every single aspect of the experience on board,” British Airways chief executive Sean Doyle said on Monday. Retrofitting one aircraft takes about 100 days, he said. British Airways' decision to spend millions on transforming its fleet of A380s makes the carrier an industry outlier while rivals around the world are phasing out the four-engine behemoth for smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engined jets. Slot constraints at London’s Heathrow airport mean it cannot easily replace the super jumbo with smaller aircraft. US and European carriers have been pouring money into first and business-class seating to target well-heeled passengers who are a resilient source of income at a time when the Iran war has caused jet fuel prices to soar, driving up costs. Air France-KLM’s La Premiere recently won an award for the world’s best first-class in Skytrax’s annual airline rankings and has plans to expand the service to more US cities. Emirates, which operates the world’s biggest A380 fleet, has as many as 76 berths in business class. However, it will still have a party trick that British Airways’ upgraded jets will lack – a shower for first-class flyers . The airline is also spending heavily to upgrade its fleet, including reconfigured premium-economy cabins and new business-class cabins. Across the Atlantic, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines Holdings have generated most of the industry’s profitability by catering to premium customers. British Airways unveiled its plans for the new A380 first-class seating in November 2024, and had planned to launch the product in the middle of this year.

title: Trump’s anti-Muslim immigration policies weaken America’s Middle East bargain
description: They are exposing the transactional foundations of Pax Americana in the region
content: On September 30, the official White House rapid response account on X reproduced research from the libertarian Cato Institute showing that legal immigration from majority-Muslim nations was cut by 96 per cent after US President Donald Trump took office. Nineteen of the countries included Arab countries, countries in the broader Middle East and North Africa, and Arab League member states in East Africa, such as Somalia, Sudan and Djibouti. By highlighting this information, the Trump administration clearly regarded such a figure as a sign of success – an effort to implement Mr Trump’s failed “Muslim ban” of 2017, but this time directed against legal immigrants, not all Muslim travellers to the US. That the administration could take pride in keeping Muslims out of the country, most of them citizens of states with which the US has close political relations, was revealing. It showed that Mr Trump still regards Muslims as legitimate and popular targets for what increasingly appears to be his brand of ethno-nationalism, at a time when the American public remains highly polarised on the issue of Muslims and Muslim immigration. According to a Pew Research Centre poll conducted in spring this year, 43 per cent of US adults said Muslims were less patriotic than other Americans, against only four per cent who said they were more patriotic; 42 per cent said Muslim Americans were having a negative impact on the country, against only 17 per cent who said they were having a positive impact. Recently, the journalist Rozina Ali published a highly regarded book on Islamophobia in the US , in which she examined it through the lens of four families. While she was caustic about the extent of discrimination that Muslims have faced, especially since the 9/11 attacks , she closed her book on a fair-minded conclusion. While Islamophobia endured in America, she wrote, “it is also true that it is met with a refusal to accept it”. Indeed, the White House’s tweet received rapid pushback. David Biers of Cato, whose research led to the figures mentioned by the White House, responded by saying: “Thanks for citing my work. You are violating the law and harming Americans while making the country less safe, less free and less prosperous.” Mr Biers went on to point out that “Immigrants from majority-Muslim countries are more highly educated, work in higher-skilled occupations, and have reduced federal, state and local deficits by $1.1 trillion over the last 30 years”. Such attitudes raise questions about a matter that may seem distinct from Islamophobia in the US, namely the durability and strength of the US-dominated geopolitical order in the Middle East. The notion that American attitudes towards Muslims at home should affect whether Pax Americana in the region can endure is not evident. US security connections are about interests; immigration is about perceived social compatibility. The two need not be linked. They need not be linked, but usually are. The great strength of the Nato alliance was that the US anchored it in shared values with the countries of Western Europe. These endured even after the alliance lost much of its impetus and was declared “brain dead” by French President Emmanuel Macron. Similarly, the EU has been built around common principles, as has the Aukus security partnership of the US, UK and Australia. In the Middle East, this has never been the case. Other than Israel, which many Americans regard as an “exceptional” nation, in the words of the late writer Amy Kaplan – “a moral community of both concentration camp survivors and heroic warriors … a state both vulnerable and indomitable, an invincible victim” – there has been little US identification with the values (or states) of the region; or little regional identification with the US. The security relationship that the US has maintained with Middle Eastern states has never been underpinned by more than transactional reasoning. The problem, however, is that when ties are merely transactional , their foundations immediately buckle when one side fails to fulfil its end of the bargain. That is where we are today. With the US security umbrella having taken a major blow in the conflict with Iran, some countries in the region are looking for alternative paths to security, for example the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. Yet even when pragmatic ties come up short, inter-state relations can be prolonged when the public remains attached to an alliance. The Egyptians suffered a debacle in the June 1967 war with Israel, but many Arab societies remained emotionally committed to Egypt and its leader Gamal Abdel Nasser afterwards. This allowed the Egyptians to retain regional sympathy for years, adding an element of soft power more effective than their hard power. Pax Americana in the Middle East has no such appeal, and probably never did. For many people in the region, the insulting way a surprising number of US public figures speak of Muslims only adds to a broader perception that Americans are unconcerned about the well-being of the majority of the region’s inhabitants – which US actions in Gaza had already anchored in the minds of people. If a political relationship offers few practical benefits for Arab societies, and is accompanied by public disdain directed at them and what they consider important, there is little impetus to defend such an arrangement. As the Trump administration takes pride in barring immigrants from majority-Muslim countries, the message is clear: We may be friends, but we really don’t much care for you. Pax Americana cannot sustain itself on such fragile foundations when the more practical expectations of political ties have also come up short.

title: Russia tells WHO there are no plague cases as Rubio calls for more information on lab worker's death
description: Worker at plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances
content: Russian authorities told the World Health Organisation on Tuesday that there were no cases of plague ​in the Siberian city of Irkutsk, where a laboratory worker at a plague research institute died last week. Moscow had previously told the WHO that authorities were investigating whether pneumonic plague had caused her death. “No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk,” Russian authorities said in an official response to a WHO request, read out by Christian Lindmeier, a spokesman for the ​ UN health agency, at a Geneva press briefing. Russian authorities also told the WHO that they had identified the ​people in contact with the ‌dead laboratory worker and that ⁠test results for dangerous infectious ​pathogens were negative. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russia should reveal more about the laboratory worker's death. “I think it's incumbent upon Russia ​to ⁠obviously share ‌more information with the world,” Mr Rubio ​told reporters in Iceland. “We're watching it very closely, hour by hour.” He ​said the US ‌had “measures” available ⁠to help Russia ​if the situation turned out to ​be ‌more serious than has so far ⁠been acknowledged, but it needed to know ⁠more before it could step in. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the US would help, and added that the outbreak was a “big problem for Russia.” The ​WHO has previously said that the risk of plague to the general population appeared to be low.

title: Saudi Crown Prince meets Syria's President Al Shara in Riyadh
description: Visit comes as ⁠hostilities between kingdom ​and Yemen's ⁠Houthis escalate
content: Syrian ​President ⁠ Ahmad Al Shara met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ​in Riyadh during ‌an ​official visit ⁠on ​Tuesday. The Saudi Press Agency said they discussed bilateral relations and "promising opportunities for developing these relations in various fields". They also discussed the latest developments in the region. Several senior Saudi officials including Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman attended the meeting. Mr Al Shara was accompanied by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani and was first received by the Governor of the Riyadh region, Prince Faisal bin Bandar, Syria's Sana ⁠news ​agency ​reported. The visit comes as ⁠hostilities between the kingdom ​and Yemen's ⁠Iran-backed Houthis escalate, with Saudi Arabia announcing that ⁠airports in Jizan and ⁠Najran had been attacked, injuring ⁠three people and causing limited damage. The attacks came as ​Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pressed a major offensive to retake territory from the Houthis after weeks of rebel advances, with the kingdom increasing strikes in support of the campaign. The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, including ​airports, oil facilities ‌and military sites. Mr Al Shara and Prince Mohammed discussed the "latest regional developments and a number of issues of common concern, aiming to support security and stability in the region", Sana said. The Syrian President also visited Saudi Arabia in April this year and met Prince Mohammed in Jeddah, where they discussed developments in the region and efforts to strengthen bilateral relations. They also discussed economic and investment ties and "regional connectivity projects". Saudi Arabia has positioned itself as one of the major investors in Syria since Mr Al Shara took power in 2024, after leading a rebel offensive that ousted the regime of former president Bashar Al Assad .

title: DP World to invest $90m to upgrade Angola's Port of Luanda
description: Operator has been granted 10-year extension to its licence at African port terminal
content: Global ports operator DP World has been granted a 10-year extension to its concession to operate the multipurpose terminal at the Port of Luanda in Angola, as the company continues to expand in Africa. The Dubai-based firm will also be investing $90 million in the next two years to upgrade infrastructure at the terminal, DP World said on Tuesday. As part of the new investment, the ports operator will expand the terminal's capacity to more than 1.2 million twenty-foot equivalent units from the current 500,000 TEU. Under the expansion, the terminal’s quay will be extended by 222 metres and the operating area by 10 hectares. The acquisition of three ship-to-shore cranes and 12 semi-automated gantry cranes will enable the terminal to accommodate two “Post-Panamax” ships simultaneously. These are wide vessels that exceed the maximum limit of the Panama Canal's original locks. “The expansion of DP World Luanda is an important milestone both for Angola and for the wider region,” said Mohammed Akoojee, chief executive and managing director for Africa at DP World. “The ability to handle larger vessels will support new shipping services and strengthen the terminal’s potential as a gateway for West and Central Africa.” Since commencing operations in Angola in 2021, DP World said it has invested more than $260 million in upgrading and modernising the Luanda terminal. “Having our concession extended to 2051 demonstrates our long-term commitment to Angola and its future as a leading regional trade gateway,” said Paco Pinzon, chief executive of DP World Luanda. The expansion of the port will benefit the entire logistics ecosystem to help strengthen regional connectivity and support economic growth in Angola, he added. DP World operates ports and terminals in 10 locations and has 35 freight forwarding offices, employing 34,000 people across Africa. Globally, it operates in six continents with a workforce of more than 125,000. The company in August revealed plans to invest $3 billion to expand its operations in Asia, Africa and the UAE. In the Emirates, it is developing two new deepwater terminals in Fujairah to help vessels bypass the Strait of Hormuz as the key waterway in the Arabian Gulf remains virtually closed amid the Iran war. The project is to be developed in phases, within a 30-month time frame. DP World is also investing in the Democratic Republic of Congo, India and Saudi Arabia as part of its expansion plans. Last week, the company said it was exploring two major port and economic zone projects in Nigeria spanning 10,000 hectares that are expected to create 50,000 jobs.

title: Dubai Police arrest two over Dh11.8m phone scams
description: Fraudsters duped residents into transferring money and selling gold
content: Two people have been arrested in Dubai in connection with phone scams that netted more than Dh11.8 million ($3.2 million) from their victims. Dubai Police's Anti-Fraud Centre carried out the arrests after investigators uncovered scams in which the suspects allegedly impersonated employees of official and international organisations to deceive residents and steal from them. Police said the victims were contacted by phone and convinced that they were named in legal cases outside the country. The fraudsters sought to intimidate their victims by warning them of legal consequences and demanded they transfer funds to bank accounts outside the UAE. Victims were told the transfers were necessary to verify the legitimacy of their funds. The suspects allegedly promised to return the money once the verification process was complete. Investigations found some victims were asked to sell their gold jewellery and transfer the money, claiming the funds previously transferred were insufficient to complete the verification procedures. The scammers also told residents to book hotel rooms and cut off contact with others until they received confirmation that they were not involved in the fictitious cases. That tactic was intended to isolate the victims, tighten control and continue the fraud. After receiving reports of the scams, Dubai Police formed a task force from the Anti-Fraud Centre to analyse data and trace the stolen money. The investigations enabled authorities to identify and arrest the two suspects, with legal proceedings initiated against them. The suspects reportedly admitted their involvement in the phone fraud. They told investigators they been recruited through social media by an entity outside the country. They received the victims' data and instructions on how to communicate with them through an app. Phones seized from the suspects were examined and authorities uncovered the victims' data and conversations linked to the fraud operation. Dubai Police urged residents to exercise caution when receiving suspicious calls or messages from people claiming to represent government bodies, international groups or other official entities. People should always verify the source of communications through official channels, the force added. Dubai Police emphasised it was working to tackle all forms of fraud and would pursue those involved in scams. They also called on the public to report any fraud attempts through the eCrime platform or the 901 call centre.

title: Louvre Abu Dhabi announces six artists shortlisted for 2026 Richard Mille Art Prize
description: Finalists will create works for Art Here, which returns in November
content: Six artists have been shortlisted for the 2026 Richard Mille Art Prize, with their works set to be exhibited at Louvre Abu Dhabi from November. Saudi artist Ahaad Alamoudi, Emirati painter Almaha Jaralla and Dubai-based Malaysian artist and designer Muhammad Shamin Sahrum have been selected alongside Indian artists Ravikumar Kashi, Reena Kallat and Vivek Vilasini. More than 300 proposals were submitted for the sixth Louvre Abu Dhabi Art Here and the Richard Mille Art Prize . The competition was open to GCC citizens and residents, as well as Indian nationals – who were included for the first time this year. The six artists will develop their proposals into works to be presented beneath the museum’s dome at Art Here 2026, which runs from November 11 to February 28, 2027. Curated by Kamini Sawhney, former founding director of the Museum of Art and Photography in Bengaluru, the exhibition centres on the theme Confluences. It explores connections between India and the Gulf, shaped by centuries of trade, migration, and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Alamoudi’s practice explores history, representation and changing ideas of cultural identity in Saudi Arabia, while Jaralla works primarily with textiles and pigment, examining memory, movement and inherited histories across the Arabian Peninsula and Indian Ocean. Sahrum focuses on the visual language of everyday urban life and the shared experiences that emerge through movement, migration and community. Kashi works across a range of media in an interdisciplinary practice, while Kallat examines political and social borders and their effects on land, people and nature. Vilasini works across digital and sculptural media, exploring politics, identity and systems of knowledge. Sawhney also sits on the jury alongside Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan bin Khalifa, an art collector and patron; Guilhem Andre, director of scientific, curatorial and collections management at Louvre Abu Dhabi; and Maya Allison , founding executive director of the art galleries and chief curator at New York University Abu Dhabi. “Arriving at a final selection was a challenge but equally a privilege,” Sawhney said. “The six artists impressed the jury with their willingness to innovate – from fragile assemblage to immersive installation. “Each practice brings distinct perspectives that both stand alone and resonate together.
