The exhibition will, I hope, provide the platform for a lively, if unexpected dialogue between these diverse works, in a spectacular museum setting under the dome, inviting audiences to consider the meeting points where knowledge, histories and materials converge.” Art Here and the Richard Mille Art Prize were launched in 2021, initially for UAE-based artists, before expanding their geographical scope in subsequent editions. North African artists became eligible in 2024, while Japan was included for the first time last year. The six shortlisted artists will now develop their works before the exhibition opening and the winner of the Richard Mille Art Prize will receive $60,000 later in the season.

title: Abu Dhabi unveils hundreds of luxury taxis to boost airport transport links
description: Expansion of fleet will help meet demand during peak travel periods
content: Abu Dhabi has added 800 new taxis to its fleet in a drive to boost access to Zayed International Airport and expand its public transport network. The Integrated Transport Centre (ITC) – also known as Abu Dhabi Mobility – has joined forces with Abu Dhabi Airports to push forward with plans to improve connectivity across the capital . The ITC on Tuesday said 500 luxury taxis dedicated to serving airport passengers would be introduced under the scheme to help meet demand during peak periods. Another 300 have already hit the roads to support public transport options and keep pace with the needs of a growing population. The launch of additional taxis is in support of a broader push to bolster links with the airport, which attracted a record 32.5 million passengers last year. Last month, Etihad Airways and Etihad Rail unveiled plans to provide shuttle services between Mohamed bin Zayed City Station and the airport. “Through this partnership with Etihad Rail, we will explore new opportunities to link air travel with destinations across the UAE, supporting tourism growth, creating greater convenience for travellers and contributing to Abu Dhabi’s long-term economic development,” Arik De, chief revenue and commercial officer at Etihad Airways, said at the time. The agreement will also include the exploration of “integrated air and rail booking experiences [and] station-based passenger services, creating a more seamless end-to-end travel experience from the point of departure to the final destination”.

title: UK threatens tit-for-tat after Israel rebuffs plea on closure of Jerusalem consulate
description: National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell failed to secure a deal to keep mission open
content: The UK 's top national security official visited Israel last week in a futile bid to prevent the closure of the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which was ordered by the Israeli government last month. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell held talks with Israeli officials but failed to reach an agreement to keep the mission open. The Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office said it would not comment on live discussions, or on the National Security Adviser's mission, which also included a visit to Jordan to meet with King Abdullah II. The pair discussed Israel's “dangerous violations” in the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem, as well as security needs in Lebanon and Syria, parts of which are also under Israeli occupation, a statement from Al Husseiniya Palace said. The UK is said to be considering the expulsion of Israeli diplomats from Britain should the closure go ahead, according to Reuters. Around 30 British staff are attached to the Consulate , which opened in 1838. Asked about Mr Powell's visit and talks with London over the consulate, a representative of Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the diplomatic mission would close on Thursday as announced. Mr Powell has long-standing connections in the Middle East due to his work as a mediator before his appointment to the Downing Street role. The UK's current Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty was appointed to the role last week. Israel ordered the closure of the British Consulate General in Jerusalem in response to the UK’s announcement of a new sanctions package targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which many deem illegal. The Israeli government has repeatedly accused UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced the sanctions on September 8, of damaging relations between the two countries. Emily Thornberry, the veteran Labour MP who heads the Foreign Affairs Committee, said the UK must do what it can to prevent the closure. “Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem – occupied Palestinian territory – is not in Israel’s prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution. It is illegal, and the UK must resist it,” she wrote on X on Monday. The consulate is in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem and the mission was first established more than a century before the State of Israel. It handles the country’s relations with Palestinians in the city, as well as the West Bank and Gaza, while also providing consular services to Palestinians. Last week, Dominic Grieve KC, who was the government’s senior legal adviser from 2010 to 2014, said the closure was “an unlawful assertion of Israeli sovereignty over occupied East Jerusalem ”. He wrote to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office to argue that Israel was furthering its agenda to annex East Jerusalem by closing the British consulate. “The UK’s settlement sanctions are an excuse; sovereignty over Jerusalem is the object,” Mr Grieve wrote in an advisory paper commissioned by the Britain Palestine Project, a charity that advocates a British peacemaking role in the conflict. “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers out with those permitted to an occupier.” European countries that recognise Palestinian statehood have long sought to protect their consulates in Jerusalem. Their continued presence is important in protecting British and European Union policies of rejecting the annexation of East Jerusalem and Israeli claims to the entire city as its capital. Israel has yet to respond to French and Spanish restrictions on trade with illegal settlements but there is concern over the status of their consulates.

title: Qatar and Turkey in race to host 2036 Olympics
description: Germany, India, Hungary, South Africa and South Korea also in preliminary talks with IOC
content: Qatar and Turkey are among seven countries who have expressed their interest in hosting the 2036 Summer Olympics, the International Olympic Committee revealed on Tuesday. Germany, India, Hungary, South Africa and South Korea are also among the nations who are in preliminary talks with the IOC. Qatar will be hoping the successful hosting of the 2022 Fifa World Cup will work in its favour as it aims to become the first Muslim-majority nation to host the biggest sporting event in the world. A shortlist will be drawn up in ⁠March next year. Preferred hosts will ​be named after ‌discussion in 2028 and a final decision is expected in mid-2029. “Wherever the ​Games ⁠take place, one thing must ‌never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do ,” ​IOC president Kirsty Coventry said. “That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.” Turkey has attempted to host the Olympics five times before, while South Africa is hoping to become the first African host of the ​Olympics. The African nation has experience of hosting a large scale tournament; it hosted the 2010 Fifa World Cup . India too is looking to host its first Olympics, having last held the Commonwealth Games in 2010. Hungary most recently bid for the 2024 Olympics , while Germany is looking for its second Games after the 1972 Olympics. South ⁠Korea, meanwhile, has one of the strongest candidatures, having staged both the summer and winter ​Olympics in Seoul in 1988 and Pyeongchang in 2018, and also the 2022 Fifa World Cup alongside Japan. Bidding rules changed under Coventry this year, with the addition of the strategic dialogue stage. It is also likely that more than one country ​will be named as preferred hosts, unlike in past where just one bidder was put forward by the IOC executive board. Los Angeles will stage the 2028 Olympics and Australia's Brisbane will host the Games four years later. The IOC said that hosting the Olympics will benefit the host nation, stating that Paris 2024 is set to bring an estimated net contribution of €9-11 billion to the French economy by 2034.

title: Iraqi businessman denied entry to UK blames US interrogation nearly 20 years ago
description: Visa for 72-year-old to visit son refused on national security grounds
content: An Iraqi businessman believes he was refused entry to Britain to visit his son because he was detained by US forces in 2007, a court has heard. The 72-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons and is referred to by the initials DNM, applied for a visa but it was refused in March 2025 on the grounds that his presence in the UK would not be “conducive to the public good”. He is described as owning a business and property in Iraq and has three grown-up children, one of whom is married with children in the UK. DNM applied to the Special Immigration Appeals Commission and was represented by his son, who the court praised for “his clear and well directed representations”, although it is not clear whether he is a lawyer. The commission has now sent the case back to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to be reconsidered after it found that her officials did not follow their own guidance when making the decision. In its written decision, SIAC says that Ms Mahmood did not set out the reasons for deciding DNM's presence would not be “conducive to the public good” and is not required by law to do so. But DNM’s “conclusion could only rest on the fact” that the decision was based on his having been detained by US forces in April 2007 and then held for 11 months. His detention was during the time the administration of president George W Bush embarked on its “surge” policy that saw the number of US combat troops in Iraq increase in a bid to tackle violence within the country. DNM's son told the SIAC that the questioning of his father by the US military was “short-lived and superficial” and he was “not subject to extended interrogation”. After being released, he did not face charges in Iraqi courts. The businessman was one of “thousands of Iraqis” who were held by the US and its allies in the multinational force during what was a chaotic period of sectarian conflict as the country approached a state of civil war, his son said. Sometimes people were detained on the “basis of false accusations made by people who wanted to settle scores or who might think there was some advantage to be gained from a person's absence”. DNM’s detention had been “traumatic for the whole family and that it was further distressing for that now to be a reason why DNM could not visit the United Kingdom”, his son told SIAC. His father had never had connections to any terrorists or terrorist group and his uncle, DNM’s brother, was a policeman who was killed in a terrorist bombing, he said. SIAC said the substantive reasons given for the refusal of the Iraqi’s visa were contained in evidence that could not be revealed for national security reasons. But the commission highlighted that the guidance for refusal includes a provision on assessing whether the person poses a threat to the UK public. This includes consideration of the nature and seriousness of the behaviour, the level of difficulty that the UK might encounter as a result of admitting a person, and the frequency of the behaviour. SIAC said “the decision to refuse the visa application was not reached consistently with the requirements in the guidance”. “That guidance requires a thorough and methodical approach. Our conclusion is that the material available to the Secretary of State in this case was not considered in the way the guidance requires.” SIAC sent the decision back to Ms Mahmood for her officials to reconsider whether to grant DNM a visa and was scathing about the lack of rigour in the initial refusal. “This decision, like decisions on many visa applications, was a difficult decision to take. The evidence we have of this decision does not suggest that the difficulties were faced head on,” it said.

title: Saudi Arabia restores East-West pipeline flows to 5.8 million bpd, energy minister says
description: Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman addressed event in Bahrain, at which Gulf officials call for greater co-operation in manufacturing
content: Saudi Arabia had restored oil flows through its East-West pipeline, which had come under Houthi attacks, to 5.8 million barrels per day by Tuesday morning, its Energy Minister said. Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the Made in GCC Forum in Bahrain: “The East-West pipeline that was heavily attacked is operational now. Today around 5.8 million barrels of oil [flows] through the pipeline.” Operations were halted at the kingdom's main cross-country pipeline, which has a capacity of up to seven million bpd, after an attack last month. But engineers have managed to restore the flow to replenish global supplies disrupted by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . Prince Abdulaziz stressed the importance of resilience, preparedness and developing the skills needed to support future industries. “Gulf countries have witnessed many issues since [the] Iraq-Iran war and the invasion of Kuwait until today. The most important lesson is the supply and logistics chains,” he said. He said one of the most important lessons was the need to rely on Gulf capabilities to meet energy, medicine and food demand. “The development of industries and the transformation of the raw materials available to us into products to meet our needs should go hand in hand with innovation,” he added. “Without it, we risk becoming consumers of technologies rather than producing it.” Prince Abdulaziz said 70 per cent of the workforce in the kingdom's vital sectors are Saudis. “Localisation gives us greater flexibility and ability to withstand disruptions. Having multiple logistical options was one of the key factors that enabled us to deal with the crisis.” The Gulf states are seeking to turn the economic vulnerability exposed by the Iran war into a push for deeper industrial integration, with officials calling for enhanced production within the region and greater co-operation across supply chains. Also speaking at the inaugural Made in GCC Forum was Abdulla bin Fakhro, Bahrain's Minister of Industry and Commerce, who said the test for the Gulf was not simply to recover from the energy crisis but to use the experience to strengthen its economic base. “The GCC region has faced exceptional significant security challenges this year as our countries were subjected to a fierce Iranian aggression but we proved that we can protect our countries and overcome the challenges,” he said at the three-day event, being held at Exhibition World Bahrain from October 6 to 8. The Gulf now has an opportunity to capture a greater share of the goods it currently imports, he added. Gulf countries import more than $600 billion worth of goods a year, while the combined economy of the six states is worth about $2.4 trillion, he said. Intra-GCC merchandise trade, however, stands at only about $46 billion. “How many of the products, components and intermediate materials we import today can we manufacture here in the Gulf?” Mr Bin Fakhro said. A focus on domestic production would lead to new factories, investment and the creation of skilled jobs, while strengthening the region's ability to withstand future shocks. “We want to move from successful national industries towards an integrated Gulf industrial ecosystem,” Mr Bin Fakhro added. “We want it [Made in GCC] to become a Gulf economic and industrial identity representing quality, reliability and innovation.” Meanwhile, GCC Secretary General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said the bloc already has a substantial industrial base, with more than 22,000 factories employing about 1.7 million workers. Gulf industries contribute about 3 per cent of the region's GDP, he said, but called for the six member countries to move beyond separate national industrial strategies towards a more integrated manufacturing system. “When we integrate our industrial capabilities and align our policies, we can achieve greater prosperity for all our countries,” Mr Albudaiwi said. The GCC is developing 20 joint industrial investment opportunities, he added, with the first package already approved by its Industrial Co-operation Committee.

title: President Sheikh Mohamed and Jordan's King Abdullah discuss $2.5 billion UAE-Jordan railway project in call
description: UAE and Jordan leaders speak by phone to strengthen ties and back new rail infrastructure
content: President Sheikh Mohamed and King Abdullah of Jordan have spoken by phone to discuss the $2.5 billion landmark railway project. The UAE President and the Jordanian monarch reviewed relations between the nations and explored ways to deepen co-operation across developmental and economic fields, state news agency Wam reported on Tuesday. Central to their discussions was the Aqaba-Al-Shidiya-Maan Railway Project. The project is being developed by the Jordanian-Emirati Railway Company and is regarded as a cornerstone of the two countries' long-term development agenda. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of Abu Dhabi Executive Council, and King Abdullah attended the project's ground-breaking ceremony on Monday in the Jordanian port city of Aqaba. Sheikh Mohamed and King Abdullah praised the significance of the railway initiative, describing it as a reflection of their shared vision for a sustainable and extended development partnership. The project is expected to strengthen economic connectivity between the UAE and Jordan and support their mutual interests while delivering broader prosperity for their people. The two leaders also exchanged views on regional matters, with developments across the Middle East featuring prominently in their talks. They stressed their commitment to continued fraternal consultation and co-ordination on significant issues affecting the region. Sheikh Mohamed and King Abdullah reaffirmed their determination to support efforts to consolidate the foundations of security, stability and peace across the Middle East, underscoring that such efforts served the interests of all people in the region. The UAE is involved in several national and cross-border rail initiatives, including the Etihad Rail network , a 1,200km flagship railway spanning all seven emirates for heavy freight and passenger services. The UAE is also co-developing the Hafeet Rail (Oman-UAE Rail) link connecting Abu Dhabi to Sohar Port. The UAE is a key signatory in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. The multinational transport framework is designed to link India to Europe via a combined ship-to-rail transit network traversing the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel.

title: Iran politician files impeachment motion against Araghchi over US contacts
description: Foreign Minister facing criticism over reported interaction with US envoy Steve Witkoff during UN General Assembly
content: Iranian politician Amirhossein Sabeti has filed an impeachment motion against Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over contact with US officials during last month’s UN General Assembly in New York, alleging he acted without authorisation. Mr Sabeti said he had registered the motion in parliament’s electronic system and asked Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf to refer it to Iran 's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission. The motion says Mr Araghchi’s meeting with American officials was among actions carried out “without permission from the leader”, according to the text published by state media. It asks the commission to examine the allegations with Mr Araghchi and the legislators seeking his impeachment, citing Iran’s constitution and parliament’s internal regulations. Mr Sabeti specifically identified Mr Araghchi’s contact with US officials during his New York trip as the latest example of actions taken without consultation with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The move follows previous criticism of Mr Araghchi’s reported interaction with US envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the General Assembly on September 22. Citing information one of its reporters had obtained, Tasnim news agency said the contact with Mr Witkoff occurred without co-ordination or approval from Iran’s policy-making bodies, including the Supreme National Security Council. The dispute centres on whether Mr Araghchi was authorised to engage directly with US officials or had been instructed only to communicate Tehran’s conditions through intermediaries. Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei said Iran’s seven conditions were to be conveyed again to “mediators”, which Tasnim interpreted as evidence Mr Araghchi had no mandate to go beyond indirect contacts. State television, however, said the meeting followed repeated US requests and that Mr Araghchi accepted so he could convey Tehran’s conditions. Inside parliament, Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, demanded Mr Araghchi explain “under which authorisation and policy” the contact took place. But fellow committee member Mojtaba Zarei said Mr Araghchi had received the necessary authorisation from Iran’s governing structures and was implementing their decisions. As of Tuesday, Tasnim reported that the impeachment request had been entered into parliament’s system but had yet to be referred to the presiding board.

title: French warships ‘ready to go now’ for Gulf deployment, says admiral
description: France preparing minehunters and fleet of sea drones for potential Hormuz mission
content: French warships and minehunter drones are at “a very high readiness” for deployment to the Arabian Gulf , a French admiral has told The National. Rear Admiral Remi Thomas said France already had mine-countermeasure vessels and autonomous systems “ready to go now” for operations in the Middle East. French sea drones are already aboard the British Royal Fleet Auxiliary Lyme Bay, which has been converted into a mother ship for unmanned minehunting systems. “We have two minehunters ready to not only be deployed but ready to operate in the Middle East, and we have also drones embarked on board Lyme Bay,” said RAdm Thomas, who also acts as the French navy’s chief of staff for plans and programmes. RAdm Thomas was speaking before the Euronaval exhibition taking place in Paris next month and as the Iran war has shown few signs of ending. France has also positioned frigates in the Middle East and is prepared to maintain a permanent naval presence when the US and Iran have found a workable peace agreement, he said. Iran is said to have laid dozens of mines during the conflict, while merchant shipping remains vulnerable to missiles, drones and fast-boat attacks. It will also be announced in the coming days that the French navy has launched a tender to charter two vessels to serve as mother ships for its growing number of surface and submarine drones. Brig Gen Francois Watteau, who is in charge of international naval projects at the defence procurement agency, said France would order an additional 12 unmanned surface vessels to help with mine-clearing operations. “What we are currently facing is a need in very quick time for a solution for mine warfare,” he said. The officer described the system as a mine countermeasure “toolbox” developed with Britain and similar to the Lyme Bay system, which will be operational for up to 10 years with deployments to the Middle East. The security situation around the Strait of Hormuz remains volatile. Despite the return of commercial traffic in recent months, there have been seven attacks on commercial vessels in the past week. The minesweeping force could be used to help clear any mines planted in the Red Sea with the rebel Houthis said to have the potential to lay the devices. The fleet will also operate in the Arabian Sea off Oman on the approach to the Strait of Hormuz that is currently heavily used by oil tankers. Britain and France have also formed a “coalition of the willing” to build a multinational mission to support freedom of navigation and clear mines. In May, 38 countries gave political backing to the proposed operation. RFA Lyme Bay has already been sent to the Middle East with more than 270 sailors, including more than 100 Royal Navy mine-warfare and explosive-ordnance specialists. The Type-45 destroyer HMS Dragon is also in the Indian Ocean to assist with air defences and reassure commercial traffic when the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens. Working together, the Anglo-French Maritime Mine Counter Measures programme has developed a system where unmanned surface vessels tow high-resolution sonar systems to search for mines. Once discovered, they deploy remotely operated vehicles to identify and destroy them. At least 10 European Nato countries will contribute to the mission, including Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium. Each has traditional mine-sweeping ships that will be deployed when there is a “permissive environment” in the waters.

title: UAE citizens 'most satisfied' globally with digital government services
description: These are expected to lay a 'strong foundation' for the next phase of AI-powered services, BCG survey finds
content: The UAE has been ranked top globally in a new study on citizen satisfaction with digital government services, which are expected to lay a “strong foundation” for the next phase of services powered by artificial intelligence . Nearly 90 per cent of respondents to the Boston Consulting Group survey rated those services “highly” in the Emirates to outperform 43 other countries, the US consultancy said after the poll results were released on the sidelines of the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. The survey was based on about 48,500 responses. The UAE was also rated first for the use of digital government services, at 53 per cent, with more than three quarters claiming their latest online government transaction “delivered a better experience” than their typical private-sector interaction, it said. That is reflected in the Gulf – represented by the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar in the survey – as it was the only region surveyed in which a majority of citizens rated government services as better than the private sector, BCG said. “The UAE’s strong digital government experience reflects years of investment in making public services more accessible, seamless and responsive to citizens’ needs,” said Rami Mourtada, a partner and director at BCG. Gulf citizens are becoming increasingly neutral towards the use of artificial intelligence, with 53 per cent of respondents in the UAE saying AI's benefits outweigh its risks. Saudi Arabia and Qatar posted 50 per cent and 46 per cent, to bring the Gulf average to 49 per cent. That is markedly higher than the 27 per cent in Europe, 30 per cent in North America, 37 per cent in the Asia-Pacific and 36 per cent globally. Additionally, the report pointed out that the Gulf is the most “AI-receptive” region in the world, with almost 80 per cent of citizens open to government interactions that are powered by AI, compared with 66 per cent globally. “Governments have an opportunity to build on this foundation, with more AI-enabled experiences and process re-engineering to continue focusing on quality and convenience,” Mr Mourtada said. “This next phase will be about deploying AI where it creates clear value, while maintaining human expertise for more complex citizen needs.” The adoption of AI and related technology have become a priority for the UAE, the Arab world's second-biggest economy, as it prepares for the future. Part of its strategy is to ensure seamless government services backed by reliable and secure AI to save time and costs. The Emirates has encouraged entrepreneurship and is attracting investment to accelerate its AI agenda. On Monday, a report from data science firm Dataiku found UAE companies and organisations have some of the highest rates of agentic AI adoption in the world. “As citizens become more familiar with AI, building literacy and trust will be critical to sustained adoption,” said Lars Littig, managing director and senior partner at BCG. “The opportunity is to move forward with AI in ways that reflect how citizens want to engage, expanding automation and agentic capabilities where they create value, while retaining human judgment and embedding responsible safeguards where they matter most.”

title: UAE becomes first Arab nation to join Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research
description: Membership to create opportunities to work with global scientists to assess Antarctica's role in climate systems
content: The UAE has become the first Arab country to join the international Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research. Membership will help connect the UAE 's polar research to a global network of scientists and institutions, working to further understand Antarctica and its impact on the global climate system. Last December, The National reported the UAE was the first Arab nation to commit to scientific research under the Antarctic Treaty System, which reserves the continent for peaceful purposes and guarantees freedom of scientific investigation. Central to this quest is the Emirates Polar Programme, launched by President Sheikh Mohamed in 2023, which puts Emirati scientists at the forefront of international research in Antarctica and the Arctic. “ The UAE’s membership in [the committee] marks an important milestone for the Emirates Polar Programme and the development of our national capabilities in polar science,” said Mariam Almheiri, head of the International Affairs Office at the Presidential Court and chairwoman of the Emirates Polar Programme Steering Committee. “Scientific progress in the polar regions is built on international co-operation, shared knowledge and long-term partnerships. Through Scar, we are creating new pathways for Emirati scientists to contribute to international research, work alongside leading scientific institutions and build the expertise that will support the UAE’s growing role in polar science.” The UAE's involvement will be delivered through the Emirates Polar Programme and Polar Research Centre at Khalifa University, where researchers are developing expertise and working with established polar programmes on environmental monitoring and field research in Antarctica. Much of Antarctica sits more than 500 metres above sea level, making it the coldest and highest continent on the planet, where temperatures can fall below minus 60°C in winter. Antarctica has no permanent human population and supports only the most minimal form of terrestrial life. Yet it holds nearly 70 per cent of the world’s freshwater, preserved in ice built up over millions of years. As global temperatures rise, changes in this ice are already reshaping oceans and coastlines far beyond the poles. “Through Scar, we look forward to contributing to shared scientific priorities and building partnerships across nations in the co-operative spirit that defines Antarctica,” said Dr Aisha Al Suwaidi, professor of Earth science at Khalifa University. “Alongside this scientific endeavour, we are committed to bringing artists and storytellers alongside scientists, so that Antarctica’s story reaches our society as well as our laboratories.” UAE researchers will now be able to take part in Scar’s international research and expert groups, which assemble specialists across disciplines including ice-sheet dynamics, Southern Ocean change, permafrost and geological history. This membership will also open opportunities for early-career Emirati scientists to access committee fellowships, research placements and international scientific exchanges. “The Emirates Polar Programme already has several strong Antarctic research programmes, and we look forward to including Emirates researchers across the Scar Research programme and building collaborative research efforts to address globally important challenges,” said committee president Gary Wilson.

title: ‘Don’t sleep please, we need you,’ dentist told flydubai pilot as he battled to save him
description: Shota Musaev recounts 45 minutes of terror on board Dubai-Tel Aviv flight
content: The dentist who helped save the life of flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar said he feared time was running out when a group of passengers and reserve pilots took control of Flight FZ1073 and foiled a suspected terrorist attack. Dr Shota Musaev, 47, spoke to The National about the terrifying 45 minutes in which he struggled to control the blood gushing from stab wounds on Capt Machchhar’s head and hands, and of the post-traumatic stress he had suffered since the ordeal. The UAE’s Attorney General Hamad Al Shamsi has said investigations are continuing into “an attempted terrorist attack” on September 30, in which the co-pilot was said to have used an emergency crash axe in the cockpit to attack the captain and attempted to control the aircraft, before it was landed in Saudi Arabia. Dr Musaev and his wife Sigalit had been settling into a connecting flight from China via Dubai to take them home to Israel when he heard screams and later shouts for a doctor. He then rushed forward to help the stricken captain. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National from Holon, a city south of Tel Aviv. “I used T-shirts to press the wounds but it [the bleeding] didn’t stop so I asked the stewards for ice. “He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.” The doctor was crouched in the narrow space near the aircraft exit as he administered emergency aid and kept the badly wounded captain conscious. “I told him, ‘Please don’t sleep, we need you.’ I asked how many children he had, their names. I kept telling him, 'Don't be afraid, you will go back to your family, we are landing soon,'” Dr Musaev said. Capt Machchhar gave his name and age, said he lived in Dubai and was from India, and asked for help to ease his pain. “He said, ‘Please help me.' He said, 'My God is with me. I want to live. I don’t want to die here.' Every time we spoke, he said, 'I have pain in my head; it’s hurting.' “He was cut badly and would say, 'I’m feeling hot on my hands.' I kept telling him that he would be OK,” Dr Musaev said. He then propped up Capt Machchhar’s feet when his vital signs deteriorated. “At one time, his pulse was too low, so I put his feet up and the pulse came back,” Dr Musaev said. “When I saw his lips were blue, I told the steward, 'We need to land quickly. He doesn’t have much more time'.” In videos shared, Capt Machchhar can be heard asking for painkillers. Dr Musaev gave him small sips of water and decided against administering pills because of the heavy bleeding. “He was lying on his back and I hesitated to lift him because I didn’t want re-bleeding. It was dangerous to move him or give him medicines. The stewards wanted to give him medicine but I didn’t agree.” He constantly monitored Capt Machchhar’s vital signs to keep him alive. “If he talks, does not sleep, his pulse, the colour of lips, these were the indicators I had,” Dr Musaev said. While helping a passenger tie up the co-pilot with headphone cables, the doctor learnt the assailant had damaged the cockpit console. He saw two standby pilots enter the cockpit with a passenger to steady the plane as a small group of passengers kept a close watch on other passengers, fearing more terrorists were on board. “We were at the plane exit, in front of the cockpit, and every time we scanned the area, we were worried there may be more terrorists on the plane. A small group was scanning and checking until we landed in Saudi Arabia.” Once in Saudi Arabia, Dr Musaev handed the captain over to doctors on the ground in Tabuk with a quick farewell: “Good luck my friend. Everything will be good.” But he said he and his wife had suffered post-traumatic stress in the days following. “My wife and I sleep two hours in the night. My weight has gone down three kilograms in the last three days. The post-trauma will start now as we understand what happened to us.” He said each passenger had played a role in turning around what could have been a catastrophe, from a woman passenger who raised the alarm to those who handed him T-shirts to slow the severe bleeding. “Smit saved our lives. Smit is a hero and I thank him for everything he did to save my family, all the passengers. It's karma, he saved our lives and we saved his life. “Everyone in the plane is a hero, the woman who heard something wrong in the cockpit and shouted, she is a hero, too. Everyone on this flight has hero status,” the dentist said. “Without medical help, Smit would not have lived because of the bleeding. But I did not do something special, I just stopped the bleeding and stabilised his pulse, that’s it.”

title: How Iran gets away with it: The struggle to bring 'architects of atrocities' to trial
description: Abuses in Syria and Ukraine being investigated in Europe, but Iran is a different story
content: When Zhino Babamiri gets a call from Urmieh Central Prison in Iran , she stops everything to pick up the phone. Her father is on the other end, and she doesn’t know when he will be able to contact her again. “I just drop everything and take the call because sometimes when it doesn't go through, it could take a couple more weeks,” the 26-year-old told The National from her home in Norway. Sometimes there have been weekly calls of five or 10 minutes. “But sometimes it has been weeks until he has managed to do another one.” The father, Rezgar Beigzadeh Babamiri, 48, was arrested in April 2023 and accused of providing medical assistance to demonstrators in the Women, Life, Freedom movement . The protests had erupted the previous year after 22-year-old Jina Mahsa Amini died in police custody, having been arrested for allegedly violating hijab rules. Mr Babamiri was handed three death sentences after being tortured during interrogation. He was subjected to mock executions, waterboarding and electrocutions, according to a letter he wrote from prison last year. The phone calls are a lifeline for Zhino, who was not able to speak to him for more than two years following his detention. “Some weeks he's very good. He's very hopeful,” said Zhino, a Kurdish-Iranian Norwegian citizen. “He spends most of the time right now reading, but sometimes he's very stressed as well because the vibe of the prison gets so intense. When someone gets executed, they all lose hope.” Mr Babamiri’s death sentences are currently being reviewed following a Supreme Court order for a retrial. But his case is just one example of thousands of people who have suffered at the hands of the Iranian state for their involvement in anti-government protests. Hundreds of people were killed and tens of thousands arrested during the Women, Life, Freedom movement, according to campaigners. Like Mr Babamiri, some remain in prison to this day, and Iran continues to issue death sentences for demonstrators: two men, Mehrab Abdollahzade and Aref Khoshkar, were executed this year over their involvement. Amnesty International says Iranian officials should be investigated for crimes against humanity during the protests, including murder, torture, enforced disappearances and rape. The UN’s Fact Finding Mission on Iran said recently that Iranian security personnel had also committed crimes against humanity when suppressing protests in January 2026 . Activists outside Iran say the death toll was at least 8,000, and the unrest represented the largest popular challenge to Iran’s clerical leadership since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. But activists trying to bring the perpetrators to justice face several barriers, top lawyers told The National . They include bureaucracy, a push by US President Donald Trump to weaken the International Criminal Court, and a lack of political will and resources. That is the case even among European nations that advocate for human rights and whose own laws allow for crimes committed abroad to be investigated, the interviewees said. “We live in an age where the rules-based international order seems to be in the gutter,” Kaveh Moussavi, a human rights lawyer in the UK, told The National in a rare interview. Mr Moussavi prepared the criminal complaint that led to the arrest in 2019 of Hamid Nouri , a former Iranian prison official who had travelled to Sweden. He was later found guilty of war crimes in connection with mass executions of political prisoners in Iran in 1988, and sentenced to life in prison, but was returned to Iran in a prisoner swap deal in 2024. “I think there is certainly a case for arraigning, indicting, arresting and putting on trial the culprits,” Mr Moussavi said of the January violence. “But after Hamid Nouri, they don't travel any more.” That does not have to be a barrier to starting investigations, but foreign prosecutors still appear reluctant to open files on Iran. In February, Germany's prosecutor general turned down a request filed under the principle of universal jurisdiction from lawyers at the European Centre for Constitutional and Human Rights for an investigation into the recent unrest in Iran. Universal jurisdiction allows countries to open investigations into the most serious crimes regardless of where they were committed. Some states, such as Germany and Sweden, allow for a “structural investigation” that does not require a suspect to be present but looks into patterns of wrongdoing and identifies chains of command – essentially laying the groundwork for future criminal investigations. Alexander Schwarz, an ECCHR director for international crimes and accountability, said the German prosecutor told the applicants that an investigation into Iran "is currently not considered necessary." The prosecutor's reasoning, Mr Schwarz said, was the lack of a concrete link to Germany, limited access to evidence, and the fact that the UN or others could collect evidence without opening formal proceedings. The prosecutor’s arguments were “not convincing,” Mr Schwarz told The National. He said German prosecutors had a “distinct responsibility” to secure evidence and reconstruct the chain of command. “Waiting until a suspected perpetrator enters Germany risks losing evidence that could and should be secured now,” he said. The German prosecutor general's office did not respond to a request for comment. Amnesty International’s recent report, Architects of Atrocities , added to the voices calling for foreign investigations into Iran, as has been done for other countries. “This is something that has been done for Syria and Ukraine in Germany, and there is no clear explanation as to why it hasn't yet been done for Iran,” Raha Bahreini, an Amnesty researcher on Iran, told The National . She said there could be hundreds of witnesses and survivors living in Europe. Countries that call for accountability in UN meetings need to go “beyond toothless statements and find a pathway for that accountability to come,” she added. Amnesty has identified 87 Iranian officials it would like to see investigated over the women's rights movement. This would have to happen abroad because the Iranian judiciary is part of the regime and has no interest in accountability, it said. Among Amnesty's demands are posthumous investigations into the late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and former military chief Mohammad Bagheri, both killed in Israeli strikes. They also include Ahmed Vahidi, who was interior minister in 2022 and has since been promoted to lead the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The list also includes provincial IRGC and police commanders and governors. That includes West Azerbaijan province, where Mr Babamiri was arrested; he says he was tortured. Human rights lawyers believe prosecutors in Europe would have enough evidence to act. The Berlin organisation Mnemonic is preserving 1.3 million pieces of digital information related to the 2022 protests in the hope of supporting investigations. This evidence “can be a very valuable source of information for atrocity crimes units in different countries and the prosecutors there,” Gissou Nia, a lawyer focused on international criminal and human rights law, told The National. There are human witnesses too. “Certainly, there's enough Iranian victims, both of the Women, Life, Freedom movement and of other spates of violence in the country, to open up a structural investigation in Germany,” Ms Nia said. The benefit of this type of investigation is that it would prepare the ground so that if a suspect does enter German territory, an arrest warrant could quickly be issued, she added. Yet another hurdle stands in the way of arresting Iranian officials abroad. Iran’s willingness to seize foreign nationals as retaliation leads to caution among European attorneys general considering an arrest warrant, Mr Moussavi said. An attorney general is a government’s top legal adviser and a political appointee. “With the possible exception of Switzerland, I cannot conceive of any circumstances in which any European country would permit the prosecutors to go ahead with arresting a travelling peripatetic itinerant Iranian official, because they would seize immediate hostages in Iran,” Mr Moussavi said. In the case of Hamid Nouri, Sweden handed the convict back to Iran in a prisoner swap with Swedish nationals Johan Floderus and Saeed Azizi, who had been detained in 2022 and 2023 respectively. In an email to The National , Reena Devgun, team leader for Sweden’s war crimes prosecutors, declined to comment on whether the Swedish Prosecution Authority had opened any investigations following Amnesty International’s plea. “We can still in such matters assist in order to help other national prosecutions or UN fact-finding missions if they identify a link to Sweden in their investigations,” she added. Zhino Babamiri believes countries that attempt to remain neutral on Iran are missing the point. “I don't think this would be neutral if you close your eyes on humans dying,” she said. Countries that are “all about human rights and equality” must act. “I really love living in Norway, but I really hope these countries do not stay silent and hold each of these people who make these decisions accountable.” Norwegian public prosecutor Marit Formo told The National in an email that the country had not opened any investigations into the situation in Iran. “We are currently prioritising other continuing investigations into international crimes, where the suspects are residing in Norway,” Ms Formo said. Zhino’s father’s treatment at the hands of the Iranian security services compels her to keep speaking up about violations in Iran, in the hope that perpetrators will one day be brought to justice. “There has been definitely a lot of IRGC members who have who have tortured my dad and who have treated him very bad,” she said. When Rezgar Babamiri told Iranian judge Reza Najafzadeh about the torture he had experienced in detention, the response was telling of a system that human rights organisations say is designed to maintain impunity. “My father said, ‘These are the things they did to me,’” Zhino said. “He [Judge Reza Najafzadeh] just laughed and said, ‘Did you expect to be served with kebab?’”. Investigations should instil in Iranian officials the idea that “they don't get the privilege of just going wherever they want in the world,” should the Islamic Republic one day collapse, she added. Investigations in Europe become all the more important because of paralysis at the UN institutions designed to maintain peace and security. Activists, politicians and Iranian opposition groups have urged the UN Security Council to refer Iran to the International Criminal Court. The court in The Hague tries the gravest crimes, such as genocide and crimes against humanity. A UN referral would be necessary because Iran has never ratified the ICC's founding document, the Rome Statute. Yet any referral could be vetoed by Russia and China, which are friendlier towards Tehran. In the US, the Trump administration’s attack on the ICC is also a barrier to referring Iran to the ICC. The US Treasury Department has imposed sanctions on judges at the ICC, which President Trump called “evil” and “a rogue institution” at the UN General Assembly. While Israel is Iran’s arch enemy, it is no friend of the ICC either, due to the international arrest warrant issued against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the war in Gaza. “There is more chance of a snowball surviving in the fires of hell than the UN Security Council referring the matter to the ICC on any Iranians who happen to be travelling outside Iran,” Mr Moussavi said. “That won't happen, not while Trump is there.” If a referral is a non-starter, Amnesty believes the UN General Assembly could act instead by setting up a special mechanism to investigate crimes against humanity in Iran. This could happen in one of two ways, according to Raha Bahreini of Amnesty International. Countries could ask the UN Secretary General to study the options and then choose the best path. This has been done before in Cambodia, although the government there co-operated — something unlikely to happen in Iran. Alternatively, the assembly could create a tribunal via its own resolution. “This would be unprecedented, but it doesn't mean that the UN General Assembly cannot do it,” Ms Bahreini said. Again, political will may be lacking at the assembly. The war in Gaza and the US-Israeli campaign against Iran have lessened the willingness of some nations to take a stand against Tehran, Mr Moussavi said. Some may prefer to side with Iran against Israel, which stands widely accused of genocide in Gaza, rather than support a mechanism to hold Iran accountable. “I cannot believe that there'll be a consensus around that topic against any Iranian officials yet – yet. Much depends on resolving the Palestine issue right now,” Mr Moussavi said. Any route to justice depends on the will of the international community, while a failure to act could lead to further crackdowns in Iran because the perpetrators see they can get away with such actions, human rights defenders believe. “We need governments to hear our central message that people in Iran are at real risk of further protest massacres, and impunity is a key driver of these successive cycles of protest bloodshed in Iran,” Ms Bahreini of Amnesty said. The organisation believes that eyes glazing over at the news of more mass killings in Iran is another driver of inaction. “Our assessment is that mass protest killings in Iran have become sadly normalised,” she added. Mr Moussavi believes the arc of history bends in the right direction, even with the current crisis facing international accountability mechanisms. “History has an uncanny habit of calling to account people who commit these things,” he said. And regardless of the status of formal prosecutors’ investigations, Zhino says she will continue to speak up about the plight of her own father and other Iranian prisoners and victims so that the perpetrators’ alleged crimes become infamous. “I will do my best so that the world hears what you're doing,” she said.

title: US envoy in rare meeting with Sudan's army chief in Egypt
description: Massad Boulos says Washington committed to political solution as fighting intensifies in Kordofan
content: US President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, has met Sudanese army chief and de facto leader Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan in Egypt as Washington steps up efforts to end the country’s three-year war. Mr Boulos said on Monday that he had attended a lunch hosted by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi in New Alamein at the weekend alongside Gen Al Burhan. The rare publicly announced encounter took place on the sidelines of the African Union ’s eighth midyear co-ordination meeting. Mr Boulos did not describe the encounter as a formal bilateral meeting, but used the occasion to reaffirm US support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity. “The United States stands ready to support all efforts leading to a comprehensive dialogue among the Sudanese political forces, leading to a preliminary road map of the future of the Sudan ,” Mr Boulos said in a post on X. “We encourage the Sudanese to be inclusive and to engage actively with regional and international stakeholders to co-ordinate views.” The encounter came less than two weeks after Washington withheld a visa for Gen Al Burhan before the UN General Assembly in New York. The move was reportedly linked to Sudan’s army-led administration resisting a US proposal for a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire, followed by political negotiations to end the war and revive a transition towards civilian rule. Sudan has claimed it did not reject the US ceasefire proposal, but instead submitted comments on it. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, nor their leaders, represented legitimate constitutional government for Sudan. The US has nevertheless continued to press for a negotiated settlement. Mr Boulos said the US was working with Egypt and other regional and international partners to end the fighting and ease the humanitarian crisis, in line with Mr Trump’s calls for a political solution. Mr Boulos added that the US aimed ultimately to help Sudan restore security, begin reconstruction and move towards a civilian-led government through an “inclusive, Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led” national dialogue. The war broke out in April 2023 after a power struggle between the army and the RSF over the transition to civilian rule and the planned integration of the rival forces. Repeated diplomatic initiatives have failed to secure a lasting ceasefire. The conflict has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, according to the UN World Food Programme . A strike on two World Food Programme lorries in Sudan’s South Kordofan state at the weekend killed one of their drivers, the WFP said. The agency did not attribute responsibility for the attack and called for an impartial investigation. The UAE on Tuesday condemned the attack on the two lorries. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs "stressed the need to protect humanitarian and relief personnel and emphasised that humanitarian assistance must not be politicised or weaponised". Mr Boulos also condemned the attack on the WFP lorries in a post on X following his encounter with Gen Al Burhan, saying it was part of a “clear and dangerous pattern” of assaults on humanitarian operations. Fighting is intensifying in Kordofan, a strategically important region where Sudan's army and the RSF are battling for territory. Both the SAF and the RSF have been accused by the UN of war crimes and human rights violations. The UN Human Rights Council on Monday condemned indiscriminate attacks on civilians and aerial bombardments and drone strikes that have caused civilian deaths and damaged critical infrastructure. Drone warfare has escalated sharply. UN figures show that about 1,100 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and June this year, accounting for most of the roughly 1,400 civilian deaths documented by the UN during that period.

title: El Sisi says Egypt's share of Nile water is 'historical and legal' right
description: President says his country will defend its allocation from river
content: Egypt's share of the Nile's water is a “historical and legal” right that cannot be negotiated or touched, President Abdel Fattah El Sisi has said in the latest sabre-rattling in Cairo's water dispute with Ethiopia. Addressing the nation in a televised speech, the Egyptian leader said: “Let me say very clearly and decisively that the Nile is Egypt's lifeline and has for thousands of years been the foundation of its very existence. “Egypt's water share is an enshrined historical and legal right that cannot be reduced or touched,” he said. While Egypt was ready to co-operate with fellow Nile basin countries, “it will not tolerate any action that touches its water security and continue to defend these rights by all means provided under international law”, he added. Egypt , which depends on the Nile for nearly all its freshwater needs, has a share of 55.5 billion cubic metres of the river's water under a 1959 agreement with fellow downstream country Sudan. The agreement is dismissed by Ethiopia as invalid and outdated. The question of Egypt's share of the Nile's water came to the fore when Ethiopia began building a dam on the Blue Nile, the river's largest tributary that accounts for more than 80 per cent of the water reaching Egypt. While filling the water reservoir behind the dam had little impact on Egypt, thanks to plentiful rain in Ethiopia, Egypt is alarmed that its share will be reduced during a prolonged drought. Egypt and Sudan have been pressing Ethiopia during a decade of negotiations to accept a legally binding deal that allows the two allies to have a say in the operation of the dam, a demand rejected by Addis Ababa as an infringement on its sovereignty. Relations between Egypt and Ethiopia have deteriorated sharply in recent days, with Addis Ababa accusing Cairo along with Sudan and Eritrea of aiding an anti-government rebellion. The three countries have denied the charge. The Egyptian leader's address came just hours after Ethiopia's foreign ministry issued a defiant statement reasserting the country's control of the Blue Nile and the “legitimate” right of the landlocked Horn of Africa nation to the Red Sea, which it lost when Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1992. Turning to the issue of access to the Red Sea, the ministry said Ethiopia was geographically and historically connected to the strategic waterway despite the change of political boundaries. “Accordingly, any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia's legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea,” it said. The comments on the Red Sea appeared to be in response to a statement issued after Mr El Sisi and the leaders of Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan met in Egypt on Sunday. The four, whose countries control an uninterrupted Red Sea coastline that stretches from Egypt to the Horn of Africa, vowed to keep the governance of the Red Sea exclusively in the hands of littoral states.

title: Domestic worker in hospital after falling into open well in Fujairah
description: Child also rescued but in good condition
content: A child and a domestic worker were rescued after accidentally falling into an open indoor well at their home in Fujairah, prompting authorities to issue a safety warning to the public. Colonel Khalid Rabie Al Hamoudi, Deputy Director of Fujairah Civil Defence, visited the family to check on the child's health and also visited the domestic worker recovering at Fujairah Hospital. On Monday, the authority issued an urgent warning to property owners, farmers, and landowners to cover and seal all wells securely. Owners should install protective barriers with clear warning signs around wells to prevent similar accidents. Fujairah Police emphasised that wells must never be left uncovered or without fences, as it poses a serious risk to children and adults and could lead to tragic accidents. Residents, farmers, and commercial property owners who wish to dig or drill a private water well in Fujairah must obtain a permit from the Fujairah Environment Authority. This service applies to all individuals and entities seeking to construct a groundwater well. The approval process ensures compliance with environmental standards and requirements. Digging groundwater wells without a permit from the relevant authorities in the northern emirate may result in fines ranging from Dh2,000 to Dh10,000. Fines may increase depending on the nature of the violation.

title: 'We are abandoned': French youths move to street protests after weeks of school clashes
description: Interior Minister backs 'proportionate' police response as young people stage more nationwide rallies
content: Tens of thousands of young people took to the streets of France on Tuesday as protests persisted across the country following weeks of violent clashes near schools. Protesters spoke of anxiety about the future, fear of worsening social inequality and a feeling of being ignored by a generation of politicians that benefitted from the post-Second World War economic boom. “We are neglected. We are abandoned,” 18-year-old Elisha told The National in Paris. “We are a generation facing war, conflict , and precariousness, with no safety net to fall back on.” Organised demonstrations were largely peaceful by midafternoon in Paris, Marseille, Nantes and Toulouse. Scenes in Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes turned far more violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles. An estimated 200,000 people took part in protest marches around the country on Tuesday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. An afternoon protest in Paris attracted 56,000 participants. Speaking to France Inter radio earlier in the day, Mr Nunez described the recent clashes as “urban violence” and backed the police's tough response which he described as “proportionate” in the vast majority of cases. The view from a central square in Paris was that school pupils students had the right to demand change. Elisha, a student at Pantheon-Sorbonne University, criticised politicians who had access to cheap housing and easy access to the labour market and failed to understand her generation's anger. “They’re cutting our housing benefits – which are going to be frozen – and taking away our scholarships. Young people no longer have access to anything. It’s a disaster.” Juliette, 17, lambasted a political class more preoccupied about France's reputational standing in the world than young people's future. “No one else is doing anything, so we’re stepping up and taking action because things need to change,” she said. Referring to France's ballooning debt crisis, her friend Mai-Lan, deplored that “young people are inheriting an indebted France”. Both girls attend Lycee Victor Hugo high school in the upmarket third arrondissement of Paris. “We are privileged but we're also here to defend students from less privileged areas in the suburbs,” Mai-Lan said. The street demonstrations, organised by student unions and teachers after weeks of protests at schools, were dubbed “Black Tuesday”. The High School Students Union said ​more than ⁠half of France's secondary schools were blockaded or would close ‌for the day. Some local education authorities tried to move classes online. The protests started in a Paris suburb in mid-September in solidarity with a teachers' strike over a lack of staff and resources. They rapidly spread to schools across the country, with pupils complaining about dilapidated infrastructure and overcrowded classrooms. The level of violence during some clashes with the police has shocked sections of the French public and divided opinion. Masked people, including adults, have attacked teachers and school employees and set buildings ablaze. A 15 year old lost his hand and at least two other 16 year olds have suffered permanent eye damage apparently due to the police response and control methods. Mr Nunez said the teenager losing his hand was a “tragedy” but added the police response has been overwhelmingly proportionate. “It is only natural that police officers and gendarmes have access to the full range of intermediate weapons at their disposal – provided they use them within a legal framework,” he said. Ten separate investigations have been launched by the National Police Inspection Service, suggesting suspicion of excessive force by officers in some cases. About 6,000 protesters have been arrested since the protests started, and around 715 police personnel have been injured.

title: Iraqi police officer killed in ISIS attack near Kirkuk
description: First reported assault since withdrawal of US-led coalition
content: At least one federal officer was killed when ISIS targeted an Iraqi police site near Kirkuk, the interior ministry has said, in the first reported attack since the withdrawal of the US-led coalition last week. Bakr Majid Mohammed Al Lami was killed on Monday while confronting a group of ISIS members who attempted to attack his guard post in the Al Barghaliyah area, the ministry statement said. There was no claim of responsibility. The attackers used semi-automatic machineguns and sniper fire against the federal police post, two security sources told Reuters. It is the first reported ISIS assault against Iraqi security forces since the US-led coalition left Iraq on September 30. The military mission was formed in 2014 to support Iraqi forces in the fight against the group, which included efforts to prevent them from regrouping. Iraqi forces are now responsible for the country's security and for suppressing ISIS remnants, though the US has said it would continue to provide training and intelligence support. Just days before the withdrawal, Iraqi security forces killed two suspected ISIS suicide bombers in the northern province of Kirkuk. Since the territorial defeat of ISIS in Iraq in late 2017, remnants have continued to operate in small cells in remote areas, mainly in deserts or valleys, and it is unusual for clashes with militant fighters to break out in urban areas. The government of Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi and its supporters, including the Co-ordination Framework, say Iraqi forces are capable of maintaining security independently and that ending the foreign combat presence restores full sovereignty. Opponents, including some Sunni and Kurdish politicians as well as security analysts, have expressed concerns about the capabilities of Iraqi forces to contain ISIS without coalition air power, intelligence and logistical support.

title: Rory McIlroy confirmed for DP World Tour Championship as he chases Race to Dubai record
description: Northern Irishman to join Patrick Reed for the November 12-15 event at Jumeirah Golf Estates
content: Seven-time Race to Dubai champion Rory McIlroy has been confirmed for the season-ending DP World Tour Championship next month. McIlroy is the latest big name to be confirmed for the November 12-15 event at Jumeirah Golf Estates. The Northern Irishman will bid to draw level with Colin Montgomerie's record haul of eight Harry Vardon Trophies. The reigning European No 1 sits second in the Race to Dubai rankings, with leader Patrick Reed , who is also confirmed in the world-class field bound for Dubai, firmly in his sights. McIlroy more than halved the gap to the American at last month's BMW PGA Championship, where a closing 68 at Wentworth Club earned him a share of second place. Last week, the World No 2 confirmed his participation at the DP World Tour's penultimate tournament in Abu Dhab i, to be held at Yas Links the week before. McIlroy returns to Dubai on the back of a historic Masters defence earlier this year. Having completed the career Grand Slam at Augusta National last year, he successfully defended the Green Jacket in April to become only the fourth back-to-back Masters champion, after Jack Nicklaus, Nick Faldo and Tiger Woods. The 37-year-old also boasts a formidable record on the Earth Course, having won the DP World Tour Championship on three occasions in 2012, 2015 and 2024. “I’ve always loved coming to Dubai and I’ve had some great days on the Earth Course, so I’m really looking forward to being back for the DP World Tour Championship,” said McIlroy, a 21-time winner on the DP World Tour. “Getting to eight and drawing level with Monty would mean a lot. He was an amazing player to watch when I was growing up, and the Race to Dubai is something I’ve always taken a lot of pride in. To have the opportunity to win it again, and potentially match Monty’s record, would be a pretty special way to finish the season.” McIlroy is attempting to win the race for the fifth year in a row. To do so, he will have to climb above Reed, who currently leads the rankings by around 300 points. The duo have been familiar foes on courses around the world. Their matches in the Ryder Cup have been some of the most compelling in the recent history of that match, while they have also duelled for major crowns. The UAE has also witnessed their rivalry up close. McIlroy won the 2023 Dubai Desert Classic while embroiled in a sour feud with his American counterpart . The season culminates with the Play-off Series over two weeks in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Reed would become only the second American to be crowned European No 1, following Collin Morikawa, who claimed the title in 2021 . That was the last time McIlroy was denied the Order of Merit title. Reed will be making his eighth appearance at the DP World Tour Championship when the tournament.

title: Saudi airports attacked as Yemen's west coast battle intensifies
description: Two attacks on southern airports cause three injuries, General Authority of Civil Aviation says
content: Two airports in Saudi Arabia have been attacked as battles between the Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces intensified along the western coast overlooking the Red Sea and the strategic Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Tuesday that the attacks targeted King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jizan and Najran International Airport in the south of the kingdom, close to the Yemeni border. On Tuesday evening Saudi air defences also intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Khamis Mushait in the south of the kingdom, coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said. The Saudi cabinet meanwhile vowed to give "full support" to the Yemeni government in its campaign against the Houthis. At a meeting chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, ministers said the rebel group "has chosen military escalation as an alternative to peace", state media reported. Both the Yemeni government and the Houthis were trying to prevent each other from reinforcing their numbers. Rashad Al Alimi, the head of the government's Presidential Leadership Council, was briefed on Houthi "attempts to send more recruits to the battlefronts", state media said. Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said "enemy reinforcements" were advancing towards the Bab Al Mandeb strait. The attacks on the airports caused three "minor injuries" and material damage, the Saudi authority said. It added that it was "assessing the damage and taking measures to ensure the safety of passengers and staff and maintain the security of the kingdom’s civil aviation system". The Iran-backed Houthis had claimed on Monday night to have attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha International Airport and ⁠the Khamis Mushait military base. Those attacks could not be immediately verified. Aviation monitoring platform FlightRadar24 said flights to and from Riyadh were put "on hold" for a few hours on Tuesday. The airport's website could not be accessed. Two Saudis in Riyadh told The National on Monday that they heard explosions in the early evening, as the US mission in the kingdom encouraged all American citizens to "remain vigilant" amid the "ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia and the potential for aerial drone or missile attacks". On Monday, Turkey and Pakistan agreed to provide "military forces and capabilities" to Saudi Arabia as it faced attacks from the Houthis. Ministers and military commanders from the three countries gathered in Riyadh for talks on the Makkah defence pact . The committee established by the three allies "decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom", a joint statement said. The parliaments of both Pakistan and Turkey must approve the pact before each country's leaders can ratify it. Attacks by the Houthis come as battles with Yemeni government forces continue on the western coast, with the Saudi-led coalition offering aerial support and attacking Houthi positions in the capital Sanaa and Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said its forces "destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in the capital, Sanaa, and a ballistic missile storage facility at a mountainous site in Saada containing 20 ballistic missiles". He added that coalition naval forces carried out an operation in Hodeidah that destroyed "legitimate military targets belonging to the terrorist Houthi militia" and "thwarting a plot for imminent attacks targeting waterways" in the southern Red Sea, and "destroying weapons depots, storage facilities for explosive-laden boats, and naval mines". Yemeni government forces on Monday claimed that they secured control of the Bab Al Mandeb strait , the Dhubab area overlooking the sea lane, and the strategic port city of Mokha. The Houthis denied losing control of those areas. The strait is the southern exit passage for the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The waterway has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed since the outbreak of the Iran war.

title: Dubai Ride 2026 guide: Date, registration, bib collection and more
description: City gears up for cycling event as Dubai Fitness Challenge marks 10th anniversary
content: Registration is now open for Dubai Ride , the city's biggest community cycling event and a highlight of the Dubai Fitness Challenge. The free-to-attend race is to be held in the early hours of November 1, when it will once again take over the 14-lane Sheikh Zayed Road. It is open to cyclists of all ages and fitness levels. Launched in 2017 by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, the Dubai Fitness Challenge encourages the public to pursue a healthier lifestyle. This year marks the 10th anniversary of the initiative, which is to run from October 31 to November 29. Also known as the 30x30 challenge, it aims to get people to exercise for at least 30 minutes for 30 consecutive days. Many venues support the drive by offering free or subsidised classes and fitness sessions, in addition to a packed calendar of community-led activities. Dubai Ride drew a record 40,327 cyclists last year and organisers expect participation to be higher this year. Dubai Ride offers two routes – 4km and 12km – and will begin at the break of dawn from five places. The starting routes are at the Museum of the Future , Al Satwa, Coca-Cola Arena, Business Bay and Lower Financial Street. Those interested in taking part can register at www.dubairide.com. All participants will also receive a free T-shirt. The 4km Downtown family route follows Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Boulevard and goes past Dubai Mall, Dubai Opera and Burj Khalifa. It is a flat route suitable for cyclists of all ages and abilities. The 12km Sheikh Zayed Road route runs from Dubai World Trade Centre – passing landmarks including the Museum of the Future and Coca-Cola Arena – to Safa Park and back. It includes a climb over Dubai Canal Bridge and is suitable for more experienced cyclists. People of determination will also have a dedicated starting area. Participants should email PoD@linkviva.com for more information. Participants are advised to arrive between 4am and 6am. There are five starting points for the Sheikh Zayed Road route, and one for the Downtown family route. These rides begin at 6.15am, with gates closing at 7.30am. All roads will reopen for traffic at 8.15am. Participants are advised to finish their rides at the same gate they start from, so they can return home easily. All participants must bring their own bike and wear a helmet. E-bikes are allowed, but scooters are not permitted. All participants must wear numbered bibs. The collection point this year is at Dubai Municipality 30 x 30 Fitness Village at Zabeel Park. It is open from October 28 to 31. The collection times will be announced at registration. Participants must bring their registration QR codes to collect their bibs.

title: Saudi Arabia warns against filming or sharing missile and drone interceptions
description: Iran-backed Yemeni rebels claim military operations on locations across kingdom
content: Saudi Arabia has warned the public against filming, publishing or sharing images of missile and drone interceptions, as Yemen’s Houthis intensify attacks on the kingdom. The warning came hours after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed to have carried out military operations targeting several locations in Saudi Arabia. “Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability,” Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry said in a statement. Maj Gen Turki Al Malki, spokesman for a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, said the alliance was providing round-the-clock air support to Yemeni forces on the ground and air cover for the Bab Al Mandeb strait, with operations against moving targets continuing. The Yemen conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the internationally recognised government. The Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, which is also recognised by the United Nations, has since the Houthi takeover controlled parts of the south and east of the country, while its government is based in the southern city of Aden.

title: UAE weather: Speed limit caps lifted in Abu Dhabi after morning fog reduced visibility
description: More foggy weather is expected to roll in across the Emirates over the coming days
content: Temporary speed limit caps imposed on a number of Abu Dhabi roads were lifted shortly after 8am on Tuesday morning after dense fog had shrouded skies in the capital. Abu Dhabi Police moved to reduce speed limits to 80kph on key routes as a safety measure after foggy conditions reduced visibility. The National Centre of Meteorology had issued an alert over the challenging weather conditions, urging people to exercise caution. "Speed limits on all the external roads of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi are now back to normal," Abu Dhabi Police said in a social media message at 8.15am. In its latest five-day weather bulletin, the NCM said further mist and fog formations were in prospect until at least Saturday. The UAE has contended with several bouts of fog - particularly in low-lying areas - over recent weeks, prompting safety warnings from authorities.
