Abu Dhabi Police began to enforce the 80kph speed limit during bad weather – such as heavy rain, sandstorms and fog – in April 2019 . Temporary speed limits are posted on electronic signboards on roads and announced on social media to alert road users. The scheme was introduced after the Department of Transport's traffic safety committee approved a plan to reduce speeds during poor weather. Motorists who fail to stick to the revised speed limits face penalties. Police impose fines of Dh300 ($81.6) for drivers who exceed speed limits by up to 10kph. This fine is doubled for those breaking the speed limit by no more than 20kph. Penalties increase in line with the severity of the breach of traffic regulations. Drivers caught exceeding the speed limit by more than 80kph will be hit with a Dh3,000 fine and have their vehicle seized for 60 days.

title: UAE's e& returns to its original Etisalat name as it focuses on AI growth
description: Move comes as telecoms group celebrates 50 years of operations, with services expanding around world
content: UAE telecoms group e& is to return to its original Etisalat name, four years after it changed the company's name, as it looks to boost growth in the artificial intelligence era. “Etisalat is the name we are taking forward – a name that reflects our heritage, our strategy and our ambition for the AI era,” the company said on Tuesday in a filing to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. The move was announced in the presence of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court. It was revealed as the Abu Dhabi-based company marks 50 years since its formation. Etisalat was rebranded as e& in 2022 amid plans for the company to transform into a global technology investment conglomerate. “Etisalat means connection. For 50 years, that purpose has guided what we build and the role we play,” the company said. “Today, it carries even greater significance as we bring connectivity, digital capabilities and infrastructure together to enable new opportunities.” The telecoms company is pushing for AI-led growth, with the launch of a strategic project to develop and expand digital infrastructure capacity within the UAE and abroad. The project includes plans to expand international connectivity capacity to more than 500 terabits per second by 2030 – more than 25 times the current capacity – in addition to developing diverse routes to enhance connectivity efficiency and reliability, delivering advanced, low-latency performance, it said in a statement. The move comes after the company reported a 9 per cent increase in its second-quarter revenue, as it expanded its customer base across international markets despite uncertainty caused by the Iran war. Revenue in the quarter rose to Dh19.2 billion ($5.2 billion) year-on-year, with its overall customer base increasing by nearly a third to hit 251.5 million. In July, the company also agreed to sell its entire stake in Vodafone Group for $5.95 billion as it refocuses on its core businesses.

title: Saudi Arabia to legalise status of Yemenis living without proper authority in kingdom
description: Move would improve access to formal employment and financial services
content: Saudi Arabia has said it will begin procedures to legalise the residency status of Yemenis living in the kingdom without proper authority, following a request from the Yemen Presidential Council. The move was ordered by King Salman in response to the request from Rashad Al Alimi, the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, the Saudi Interior Ministry said in a statement. The announcement, which came a day after Mr Alimi declared all-out war on Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels , could have implications beyond the legal status of those affected. Saudi Arabia is home to an estimated 1.9 million Yemenis. The kingdom accounts for about 62 per cent of remittances sent to Yemen, making it by far the most important source of income sent home by Yemenis abroad. Legal status could give irregular residents greater access to formal employment and financial services, potentially making it easier to send money to relatives in Yemen , while also reinforcing Saudi Arabia’s standing among a population with close family and economic ties to the kingdom. The Interior Ministry said the process would be carried out with the Foreign Ministry, the Human Resources Ministry and the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority. Yemenis seeking to benefit from the measure must hold a valid Yemeni passport, the ministry said. It added that the date for starting the process and the applicable rules would be announced through official accounts of the General Directorate of Passports and other relevant authorities. Ahmed Obaid bin Dagher, chairman of Yemen’s Shura Council, welcomed the decision, saying it would have a significant effect on thousands of Yemenis and their families. “The leadership of the Shura Council and its members welcomed the generous directives of Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud,” Mr Bin Dagher said in a statement. He said the council expressed “deep thanks and appreciation to the kingdom and its leadership for this fraternal and humanitarian gesture”. He said the move reflected Saudi Arabia’s “continued commitment to alleviating” the hardships faced by the Yemeni people and supporting them. “These generous directives will have a significant impact on the lives of thousands of Yemenis and their families,” said Mr Bin Dagher. He described the decision as an extension of what he called Saudi Arabia’s “steadfast fraternal positions and its continued support for Yemen and its people”. The Saudi announcement also comes as the kingdom mounts nationwide enforcement campaigns targeting violations of residency, labour and border-security rules. Saudi authorities recorded 11,819 such violations between September 24 and 30, including 5,793 residency violations. On Sunday, Mr Al Alimi announced the start of military operations to retake territory held by the Houthi rebels. The move to regularise the status of Yemenis in Saudi Arabia echoes a similar programme introduced in 2015, at the start of the kingdom’s intervention in Yemen.

title: Why Jeffrey Archer kept coming back to the UAE
description: For decades, the bestselling British novelist travelled the world to meet the people who read his books – and found an enthusiastic audience in the Emirates
content: Bestselling British author Jeffrey Archer was a regular visitor to the UAE, returning several times to meet fans at literary festivals in Dubai and Sharjah during his five-decade career. Archer, whose novels sold more than 300 million copies worldwide, died suddenly and peacefully at his home on Monday aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins said. He died “between writing sessions”, a day before the publication of Adam and Eve . While Archer's career took him around the world, the UAE became a recurring stop. He appeared several times at the Emirates Airline Festival of Literature in Dubai, including in 2013, 2017 and 2023, and was a guest at the Sharjah International Book Fair in 2013. In 2017, when Archer was 76 and had already sold hundreds of millions of books, he admitted he was not particularly fond of travelling. But there was one thing that kept drawing him back to literary festivals. “I do it for things like this. To go out and meet the fans,” he told The National that year on the sidelines of the Emirates Airline Festival of Literature. “Every festival I attend, the room is full with hundreds and sometimes thousands of people. This is all such a privilege.” Archer's said he considered storytelling, rather than literary acclaim, to be his greatest strength. Speaking to The National in Dubai in 2013 , he said it was ultimately readers who determined whether an author could tell a compelling story. “The public will tell you. Not the critics or the clever talkers. The public can always tell who is the storyteller,” he said. “Being a storyteller is like being a ballet dancer, a concert pianist or an opera singer. Of course, you have to work very hard but you need the gift.” That same year, during a visit to the Sharjah International Book Fair , he reflected on how unexpectedly that gift had turned into a career. “I've always been a raconteur, but I didn't really believe, until I wrote Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less , that people would pay you for telling stories,” he told The National . “The storytelling, frankly, is a God-given gift.” His 1976 debut was followed three years later by Kane and Abel , the novel that became one of his best-known works and helped establish an international readership that would eventually stretch across 119 countries. At the Sharjah International Book Fair in 2013, he spoke about the particularly large following he had developed in India, recalling the lengths some readers would go to meet him during his visits to the country. "It was a shock," he said of the legions of fans he encountered on his first trip. "They were all young women, 16 to 20, very ­enthusiastic. "One fan had taken three days to cross India to get to me and he just wanted to say thank you and then he went. I chased after him but I lost him. I felt so guilty about the fact that he'd come all that way." Even after decades of bestselling books, Archer told The National that success had not made him complacent. “The worst fear after 16 number ones in a row, is number 2,” he said. “I am always competing with myself. “I can now be lazy for three or four books and make millions. But I don't need the money. I don't need anything, actually. But I want to get better each time and that's what drives me.” That work ethic continued well into his 80s. HarperCollins described him following his death as “the master storyteller and an editor's dream”. His death came only a day after he appeared with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at a sold-out event at London's Leicester Square Theatre, where he met readers and signed hundreds of books. Archer's appearances in the UAE also came after some dramatic chapters in his life. Before becoming a novelist, he had been a Conservative MP and later served as deputy chairman of the Conservative Party under Margaret Thatcher. His political career was eventually overshadowed by scandal. In 2001, he was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice after lying during a libel case he had brought against the Daily Star . He was sentenced to four years in prison and served two. Archer later turned that experience into material for his writing, publishing three volumes of A Prison Diary . Speaking to The National in 2011 , he said writing had helped him deal with his time behind bars. “I handled it by writing, really. It was a coping mechanism: I was killing time because prison is so boring. Such a waste of time.” His conviction did not end his publishing career. Archer returned to fiction and continued producing bestselling novels and short stories for more than two decades. “I've had a hell of a life,” he said. “Fortunately, I'm able to get a lot of it into books.” When he returned to the Emirates Airline Festival of Literature in 2023, as the event celebrated its 15th anniversary, Archer was in his 80s but remained as passionate about storytelling as ever. During the festival, he spoke to The National 's Books of My Life podcast about the books that had shaped him and the craft behind a writing career spanning almost five decades. Archer's final novel, Adam and Eve , is being published on Tuesday. He had also been due to appear at the Cheltenham Literature Festival this weekend to discuss his final novel.

title: UAE cricketers set for ILT20 earnings hit as USA’s Milind Kumar extends ODI world record
description: Batter strikes brilliant ton in Cricket World Cup League Two to edge further ahead of Virat Kohli, while UAE players face scheduling clash after latest defeat
content: Leading UAE players are set to have their ILT20 windfalls snatched away as a scheduling clash is now almost inevitable. Twenty-seven domestic players landed deals for a combined total of over a million dollars when the ILT20 auction took place last week. Six of those were watching on from the other side of the world as part of the UAE squad that had just touched down in the United States. The national team are in Dallas, where they are playing their penultimate tri-series in Cricket World Cup League Two. The eight-team competition is part of the exhaustive qualifying process for next year’s ODI World Cup in southern Africa. While the top four teams in it advance directly to the global qualifier, the bottom four will look to progress via the Qualifier Play-off. The UAE’s one-day international status will also be at stake in that tournament. Their hopes of making the top four are unrealistic. After losing by six wickets to the United States on Monday, they remain rooted to the bottom of the CWCL2 table. With six games still to play and 12 points still available, it is possible the UAE could match fourth-placed Oman’s total of 31 points. However, that would be dependent on Oman losing all eight of their own remaining games, and the UAE winning all six of theirs, while overhauling a huge net run-rate deficit. Although the dates for the play-off have yet to be officially announced, teams have been told it will take place from December 1 to 21. Season 5 of the ILT20 is from November 22 to December 20. With travel and acclimatisation ahead of the play-off, it means UAE’s ODI squad members will be unavailable for all but a few days of the competition. While the league’s rules allow for franchises to replace players, there is no clarity over lost earnings for players who are called up for national duty. As such, players could miss out on substantial pay days. Franchises were aware of the situation before the auction . As such, they largely steered clear of players who might have otherwise been attractive signings, like Harpreet Bhatia, the UAE captain, Adeeb Usmani and Sohaib Khan. Some were too good to overlook altogether, though. The six players signed were Aayan Khan (who earned a $95,000 deal), Khuzaima Tanveer ($75,000), Ibrar Ahmed ($46,000), Ali Naseer ($40,000), Mohammed Arfan ($10,000) and Tanish Suri ($10,000). A number of others who could potentially find themselves in the reckoning for the play-off also find themselves in the odd position of potentially hoping not to get picked. They are the likes of Alishan Sharafu (who earned a $110,000 bid from Abu Dhabi Knight Riders), Haider Ali ($36,000), Dhruv Parashar ($10,000) and Junaid Siddique ($10,000). While the national team sustained their 19th loss in 30 matches in the CWCL2 against the United States, they showed further signs of the progress they have made lately against a side who are set to win the title. Mohammed Shahdad hit his maiden ODI century as the UAE posted 330-8 in their 50 overs. And Tanish, the 21-year-old opener, showed why he attracted the interest of Sharjah Warriorz in the ILT20 with a sparkling, run-a-ball 78 at the top of the innings. The UAE appeared well placed to defend that as they had the league leaders at 172-4 with 19.3 overs remaining. Milind Kumar then set about an extraordinary chase in which he and Shubham Ranjane knocked off the remaining 159 runs in just 110 balls. Given what the UAE have seen from Milind in this competition, is seems odd he was overlooked at the ILT20 auction. He had played a similar counter-attacking innings when the sides met in Dubai earlier in the league, and his ODI batting average is a world record. His 84-ball 116 not out in Dallas means his average in his 30-match ODI career is now 70. That is better than the next best in the format, Ryan ten Doeschate (67), as well as Shubman Gill (64.01) and Virat Kohli (58.78).

title: World Bank says Middle East economy to contract 2.1% in 2026 due to Iran war
description: Economists anticipate UAE economy to contract by 1.6% while Qatar's GDP set for worst performance in five decades
content: The World Bank on Tuesday lowered its 2026 forecast for the economies in the Middle East , saying the region's overall GDP will contract by 2.1 per cent for this year. The revision was the latest downgrade the World Bank has forecast for the region as the Iran war continues to constrain energy supplies. Economists had previously lowered their 2026 forecasts from 3.6 per cent in January to 2.1 per cent in April. Global growth, meanwhile, is projected to slow to 2.5 per cent this year, the World Bank had said in June. The seven-month conflict has affected a wide variety of sectors as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz initially choked off much of the region's energy supplies. This also led to setbacks in tourism, aviation and logistics, with uncertainty in financial markets, the World Bank said in its latest Economic Update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menaap). “This conflict is very painful and it has concentrated the losses of the conflict in our region while the global economy and other regions are upgrading their forecasts, and we are downgrading significantly,” Roberta Gatti, Menaap chief economist at the World Bank, said in an interview. Economies in the Gulf Co-operation Council are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue. Economies in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are set to slow from 6.2 and 4.6 per cent in 2025 to minus 1.6 and minus 2 per cent in 2026, respectively, the World Bank said. Qatar is forecast to have its weakest economic performance in five decades, slowing from 1.8 per cent growth in 2025 to minus 20.9 per cent this year after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Kuwait's economy is forecast to contract by 14.6 per cent, a downwards revision of 8.2 percentage points from April. The war has hit oil exporters particularly hard, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks across the region. Oil production in the Gulf dropped from its prewar average of 26 million barrels a day to about 16 million in March, the World Bank said. The IMF's PortWatch monitor showed just three tankers moved through the strait in the seven-day moving average ending September 27. “It's a volume story. It's a quantity story for us. It's a price story for the world,” Ms Gatti said. Oman, which is less reliant on the Strait of Hormuz, is the only GCC member projected to experience positive growth this year, at 3.1 per cent. Iraq 's growth prospects also faced a downwards revision of 3.8 percentage points since April with a negative growth rate of 12.4 per cent. Iraq, which is Opec's second-largest producer, depends on oil for about 90 per cent of its government revenue. Iran's economy also expected to shrink by 7.7 per cent in 2026. The World Bank report works on the assumption that the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen beginning on December 31. Under this scenario, economic activity in 2027 for the UAE will rebound to 8 per cent, Saudi Arabia by 6.1 per cent, Qatar by 25 per cent, Kuwait by 20.5 per cent and the GCC as a whole by 8.6 per cent. The UAE has embarked on a “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy to diversify its supply chains, while Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West Pipeline to move oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. Oil prices have swung wildly since the onset of the war on February 28, with global benchmark Brent crude trading at about $118 a barrel in March and in May. Saudi Aramco chief Amin Nasser credited the East-West Pipeline for keeping oil prices at about $100 a barrel. Mr Nasser also warned it could take up to two years to refill global inventories that were reduced under emergency measures. He was speaking at an energy conference in London on Monday. Oil importers, by contrast, are expected to fare better in what Ms Gatti described as a “reversal of fortunes” compared to the 2022 energy shock after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The World Bank anticipates Egypt's economic activity to pick up at a 5.1 per cent pace after growing by 4.4 per cent last year. It also raised its 2026 forecast for Morocco by 0.2 percentage points to 4.4 per cent, and 0.7 percentage points for Pakistan at 3.7 per cent. Its projection for Jordan remained unchanged at 2.7 per cent, while Tunisia received a slight downgrade of 2.3 per cent growth, 0.2 percentage points lower than its April forecast. Ms Gatti said the Iran war is placing a compounding effect on economies already mired in conflict, harming recovery prospects and contributing to long-term economic pain. Renewed hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah are reversing Lebanon's economic recovery of 4.2 per cent growth in 2025 to a contraction of 6.4 per cent this year. Forecasts for growth in Afghanistan and Yemen were also lowered to 3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively, while the World Bank anticipates Syria's economy to pick up between 8 and 10 per cent this year. The World Bank estimates GDP growth in the West Bank and Gaza will slow from 4.3 per cent in 2025 to 1.5 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 3 percentage points compared to April. The poverty rate in the area remains an estimated 41.9 per cent. It also said Gaza's economy is still in a state of “near-total collapse” despite the October 2025 ceasefire, owing to flare-ups in tensions, continued restrictions and stalled reconstruction preventing recovery efforts. “There were ongoing fragilities and now we see less humanitarian aid. We see a need to keep the attention,” Ms Gatti said. She said the economic costs of fragility were being compounded by the conflict, with reduced humanitarian aid making it important to maintain attention and investment in affected countries to prevent the consequences from being felt by future generations. The report also said that, despite the conflict, artificial intelligence remains a key avenue for opportunity in the region. Economists said it could boost the productivity of up to 20 per cent of the region's jobs. The World Bank has previously urged developing countries to quickly adopt AI or risk falling behind on the economic gains it can deliver. It said developing economies can avoid mistakes by adopting available tools, adapting them to local conditions and advancing towards frontier AI development. “Some of the complements that are needed to fit the benefits of AI might not require money, but they require political will and vision. You need regulation and ethical regulation for AI to operate well,” Ms Gatti said.

title: The Gulf’s next industrial revolution should be made across borders
description: It is time to make the GCC one industrial marketplace
content: This week, ministers, manufacturers and investors from across the Gulf gather in Bahrain for the inaugural Made in GCC Forum. The discussions range from artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing to financing, regional value chains and supply-chain resilience . Yet, perhaps the most important question is contained in the forum’s name, but what does it really mean for something to be “Made in the GCC”? For the past two decades, Gulf countries have built increasingly ambitious national industrial strategies, and the results are visible from advanced manufacturing in the UAE and Saudi Arabia to petrochemicals in Qatar, aluminium in Bahrain and new minerals and logistics investments in Oman. However, the region is not living to its full potential, and the opportunity is to connect these strengths. The economic case is compelling. The Gulf’s combined gross domestic product reached $2.3 trillion in 2024, which would make it the world’s ninth-largest economy if treated as one, ahead of Canada, Brazil and Russia. Its 61.5 million people generate an average GDP per capita of about $38,000. Its commercial banks hold $3.9 trillion in assets, while 13 GCC sovereign wealth funds collectively manage more than an estimated $4.5 trillion. That is considerable economic firepower. Yet its real potential becomes clearer when we look beyond the aggregate numbers and consider what the six economies can offer one another. Saudi Arabia brings scale: the largest domestic market, an expanding industrial base and enormous demand generated by its transformation programmes. The UAE brings world-class logistics, technology, finance, aviation and access to international markets. Qatar adds formidable gas , energy and petrochemical capabilities. Oman combines minerals and industrial land with ports facing directly onto the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean. Bahrain has developed specialised manufacturing, particularly in aluminium, alongside a sophisticated financial sector, while Kuwait brings substantial capital, energy capabilities and one of the world’s oldest sovereign investment institutions. Put those assets together and the Gulf becomes something fundamentally different. I call this the GCC Full Potential. Geography makes the proposition even more interesting. The Gulf sits between Asia, Africa and Europe, but unlike many economic blocs, it has maritime access in several directions. Ports on the Arabian Gulf connect it eastwards towards Asia; Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports provide access towards Africa, the Mediterranean and Europe; and Oman’s ports on the Arabian Sea provide direct access to the Indian Ocean without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. In a world increasingly concerned about chokepoints, supply-chain disruption and geopolitical risk, this now requires an integrated investment in land transport networks. The lesson from the disruptions of recent years should therefore not be that every Gulf country must become self-sufficient. Six countries attempting to reproduce the same factories, warehouses, data centres and strategic inventories would be an extraordinarily expensive definition of resilience. Resilience through integration is more powerful than resilience through duplication. Imagine instead an industrial product whose minerals originate in Oman, whose energy-intensive components are produced in Saudi Arabia or Qatar, whose advanced manufacturing and technology are provided in the UAE or Bahrain, and which can be exported through whichever Gulf, Red Sea or Arabian Sea port provides the most resilient route to its destination. That is what “Made across the GCC” could mean. There is evidence that this type of integration produces disproportionately large economic returns. An International Monetary Fund study based on more than 13,000 investment transactions found that more than a quarter of investment into Gulf economies already originates elsewhere in the region. More strikingly, the medium-term effect of inward cross-border investment on real non-hydrocarbon GDP was estimated to be about three times greater than that of equivalent domestic investment. Capital, in other words, becomes more productive when it crosses borders. The same principle applies to talent. A regional industrial economy of 61.5 million people can create deeper pools of engineers, researchers, entrepreneurs and specialist workers than six separate labour markets. Infrastructure can work the same way. The Gulf has already demonstrated this principle through electricity. A regional super-grid connects the member states and allows electricity and reserve capacity to move across borders. The industrial equivalent should naturally follow. AI makes this far more achievable than it would have been a decade ago. A Gulf-wide industrial platform could map what the region imports, identify where production capacity exists, forecast demand, expose supply-chain vulnerabilities, match buyers with Gulf suppliers and reroute orders when disruption occurs. Governments would gain something close to a real-time map of the Gulf’s industrial metabolism. The objective should not be to decide administratively that one country makes one product, and another makes something else. Markets remain better at discovering competitive advantage. Government’s role should be to make the Gulf function increasingly like one industrial marketplace through common standards, interoperable regulation, connected infrastructure, open procurement and easier movement of capital, goods, data and specialist talent. The most important exhibits in Bahrain this week may therefore not be the products already carrying a national “Made in” label. They are the products that do not yet exist. The ones that will eventually say: Made across the GCC.

title: Lionel Messi set for 'Last Tango' with Argentina as Cristiano Ronaldo pouts on Portugal sidelines
description: While one veteran attacking superstar is calling it quits on the international stage, another is in the middle of an undignified row with his country's coach
content: Expect tears in Buenos Aires on Tuesday night as Lionel Messi bids what is sure to be an emotional farewell to the Argentina national team. The 39-year-old will be winning his 208th and final cap for La Albiceleste when they take on Benin in a friendly at Monumental Stadium, bringing the curtain down on a career that has seen him score 125 goals and provide 68 assists for his country. From 2021 to 2024, Messi captained the side to back-to-back Copa America triumphs, World Cup glory in Qatar and the relaunched Finalissima , ending his international trophy drought in spectacular style. All 85,018 tickets for the Benin game – dubbed 'The Last Tango' – were reported to have sold out within two hours, with fans desperate to pay their respects to their hero and Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player. The team will wear a bespoke one-off kit for the occasion while all of the 2022 World Cup-winning squad – and their families – have been invited to join Messi for the celebrations. “I imagine Tuesday's match will be very emotional for everyone, including Leo,” said Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni after Saturday's 7-0 friendly demolition of Burkina Faso, in which Messi did not feature. “It will be an unforgettable day. It will be his day, and his teammates' day, who also gave him his greatest footballing joy ... I imagine that if there were five Monumental Stadiums, they would be packed.” Messi missed out on successive World Cup wins in the summer after Argentina lost in the final to Spain . That was quickly followed by the death of his father , Jorge, 68, following a long illness. He announced his international retirement soon after. “I swear I always gave everything, not only in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too,” Messi said in a post on Instagram. “I love, I loved, and I will always love being part of the national team. I gave everything I had, and I don’t have anything more to give.” It had not been all plain sailing for Messi in his country's colours. He was sent off on his Argentina debut just 47 seconds after coming off the bench in a friendly against Hungary for elbowing an opponent in the face. The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner also retired from international football once before after losing the 2016 Copa America final to Chile, where he missed a penalty in the shoot-out. That had been Argentina's third final defeat in as many years. But he was back in the fold in time for the 2018 World Cup in Russia and, three years later, Argentina's 28-year trophy drought was over as Messi's team defeated Brazil in the Copa America final. With a post-Messi Argentina era about to begin, Scaloni made clear what his absence will mean. “The feeling of having him on the pitch is unique,” he said. “That is what I would like people to understand: what he transmits on a football field. “To everyone, to the opponent, to the teammate, to the rival fan, to his own. I haven’t seen it in anyone else. That is what we are going to miss the most. The Argentine national team will continue to exist, but logically it won’t be the same.” While Messi heads for the international exit, his old rival Cristiano Ronaldo is currently in the middle of an undignified fallout with his national team manager. The arrival of Jorge Jesus, his Saudi Pro League-winning manager at Al Nassr , as Portugal coach, appeared to be the perfect appointment as Ronaldo chases his 1,000th career goal and third Uefa Nations League crown with Portugal. But the cracks between captain and manager formed almost immediately as Ronaldo stormed out of the team's training camp ahead of last week's game against Denmark. Reports of a rift with Jesus came after Ronaldo was an unused substitute in Portugal's 2-1 win in Norway. “In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave,” the 41-year-old wrote on Instagram. While Ronaldo's prickly and substantial ego is widely known, Jesus is no shrinking violet on that front. “I’m in charge. People have to obey my decisions, even if it makes them nauseous. I can buy them tablets for that,” said Jesus during his reign at Portuguese club Sporting. In response to Ronaldo's apparent unhappiness at not coming off the bench against Norway, Jesus made his message clear. “It won’t be Cristiano, or any other player, who changes my ideas as a coach. Never. Neither him nor anyone else. Not even a president. Never. Zero,” he said. Following Sunday's win over Norway in the Nations League return game at the Estadio do Dragao, Jesus said the door was still open for Ronaldo to return. “If he wants to be in the national team and he’s playing, why not? There’s no resentment, because this was a misunderstanding,” he said. “I think it’s easy to resolve.” Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) president Pedro Proenca described the incident as a “misunderstanding” that will be “resolved internally”. “We are talking about the greatest player of all time, a player who has given more than two decades to Portuguese soccer,” Proenca said. “He will always be part of this squad if he is technically fit to play. Cristiano knows this.” As it turned out, Portugal won all three games without Ronaldo. The player picked ahead of him, Goncalo Ramos, scored in all of them. It will now be down to whether Ronaldo – who has scored a staggering 146 goals in 234 games for Portugal (both world-record totals) – and Jesus can repair relations before the next round of Nations League games in November. And as Messi basks in the adulation of his country on Tuesday, talk continues back in Portugal as to whether it is time for their own talisman to pass the baton on to the country's next generation of attacking talent.

title: ‘I’m Alex, who still fights’: Volkanovski returns to Abu Dhabi as UFC champion – and a changed man
description: After a difficult period that forced him to confront his mental health, the Australian has found a new balance through family, downtime and his passion for cooking
content: Alexander Volkanovski makes his Abu Dhabi return on October 24 as the headline bout of UFC 333. He returns as champion, putting his featherweight title on the line against Movsar Evloev , the Russian who boasts a perfect 20-0 record in professional MMA. “I've had a nice long camp; dieting hard, training hard. It's going to be a great card. Obviously, it's a stacked card, so I can see why everyone's getting excited for it. I cannot wait to get out there and do my thing,” Volkanovski tells The National from his base in Wollongong, New South Wales. This will be Volkanovski's fourth visit to Abu Dhabi during a 32-fight career (28-4). The second of his three fights with Max Holloway took place here, albeit behind closed doors, as Abu Dhabi hosted UFC 251 during the coronavirus pandemic. He has fond memories of the place. “Yeah, I've been there a few times now … Always get a good reception, always treated very well over there. It's gonna be good to be over there and do our thing, you know, put on a show for everyone.” There are some not-so-fond ones too. His last visit to the UAE capital three years ago was memorable for the wrong reasons. He took a rematch with Islam Makhachev on short notice. He got the call after Makhachev's original opponent for UFC 294, Charles Oliveira, withdrew due to injury . Volkanovski later revealed he had to shed 26.5lbs in 11 days to make the 155lb lightweight limit. It proved a mountain too high for the Australian. The fight was over inside the first round as the Dagestani executed a high kick that altered Volkanovski's equilibrium before the referee spared him any more punishment. Does he have any regrets about taking the fight on such short notice? “Nah, man, not really. I don't regret it. That's a part of who I am, you know? If I take that back, I'm taking a big chunk of myself back, and I wouldn't be the fighter or the champion I am if I didn't have that,” he says. “[Being] That guy that isn't scared of nobody, that'll take on any challenges, the same guy that turns up in the gym every single time, every single day. So that's my mindset. That's my mentality, and that's what's brought me to where I am today. So I wouldn't change a thing.” Volkanovski gave an emotional speech in his post-fight press conference, saying he “needed a fight” to help him deal with his mental struggles. It was hard not to feel for Volkanovski that night. When you have a warrior's mentality, making yourself vulnerable in the most macho of endeavours is one few are brave enough to do. Reflecting on that loss, Volkanovski said it was important for fighters to talk about their struggles. For him, opening up was ultimately a positive experience and one that helped him better understand himself. I asked him if perhaps the two are symbiotic, that to take care of his mental well-being, Volkanovski needed to be in constant fight mode, whether in camp or in the octagon. “People talk about the fighter's identity, right? Like, so when you're just that dialled in, you just got this tunnel vision of, you know, being the best fighter you can," he said. "Even though I just didn't know how to handle it at the time, now I do. Now I end up having the big break after [fights], and then I got to work a lot on myself, and you know, be Alex again.” How does he feel now? “Now I feel like I'm Alex, who still fights,” he said. “It was just a sort of a vulnerable time, which I'm glad people have seen. I think it's important. "It's important for young athletes to understand that, you know? If you want to sacrifice everything and be disciplined and you have that tunnel vision to achieve those goals, you might lose a little bit of yourself through that process, but you'll be all right at the end of the day. “At the end, as long as we can understand that, it's like 'All right, this is normal.' Maybe while you're going through that process, be a little careful. Make sure we still got some time for this and that.” Following that defeat to Makhachev, Volkanovski put his featherweight championship on the line against the division's rising star, Ilia Topuria, just four months later. He ended up on the receiving end of a lethal combination that ended his title reign. Many had written him off, believing back-to-back brutal knockouts would only diminish Volkanovski’s durability and mental acuity. This time, though, Volkanovski listened to his body and his inner voice. The 14 months off were well spent. A reset saw him return to the octagon with two flawless performances against Diego Lopes. The first saw him reclaim the featherweight title. The second saw him defend it. Both fights went the five-round distance. Volkanovski displayed his mastery of striking, distance management, his ability to engage, unload, and move out of danger. He looked back to his best. Given his previous admission about struggling when not competing, I ask Volkanovski how he managed his downtime between losing to Topuria and beating Lopes. “Spend a lot of time with the family, watching the kids' sports. I love doing that. That's actually real good downtime for me,” he said. “The break was unreal. Like I said, it was not only good for me to recover properly, but even for me to, you know, find myself again, be myself, be Alex for a while. And then that comes with so many good experiences: quality time with the family … so I feel like having that time off was very good in all aspects for everything, for my fighting, and then for just me personally.” Downtime also means spending time indulging in another of his passions: cooking. Volkanovski is a man who loves his food. His channel “Cookin' with Volk” has over 2.25 million subscribers across Instagram and YouTube. As you would expect of any self-respecting Aussie, Volk loves to grill. “Pretty much anything on the barbecue, especially on the charcoal outside on an open fire. Because it's not just the food; it's the experience that comes with it,” he said. “You're usually with friends and family … when you get nice seasoned meats or whatever you're cooking on that grill, it's always impressive. It's always a good experience that comes with it.” Fighter, champion and now aspiring chef. “Some of the stuff we do when we are cooking can sometimes feel a little bit like work, but not really,” he added. “But then I get to enjoy a lot of it as well. I get to go and hang out with chefs, and they teach you how to eat and prepare some really good food. So that's cool. "I'm still building my brand, and you could still look at it as work, but it doesn't feel like work. It feels like downtime, pretty much. So I'm pretty lucky to be in that position.” The position Volkanovski is perhaps most familiar with is having his hand raised in victory. His bout against Evloev will be his sixth title defence across his two reigns as champion. Evloev, an elite wrestler, opted to change tack in his last fight, electing to fight Lerone Murphy on the feet for the most part. The Russian was deducted a point in Round 4, but still did enough to take a majority decision. Was Volkanovski surprised by the change of Evloev's approach? “I guess it didn't surprise me,” he said. “I could see that he probably felt the pressure of trying to be more exciting. So he tried to stand. “He was able to get the win anyway, but you could clearly see that if he wanted to go the normal path and grapple, he would have had a lot of success and made that fight a lot easier for him. “But he clearly showed he was a better fighter. I said straight after that fight, 'Look, don't try to be exciting. You just make sure you bring your best game.' I don't want excuses if things don't go your way, like I should have wrestled more and this and that. You don't need to worry about that. We'll make this fight exciting. People want to see how I handle that wrestling anyway. I think that's a part of the story.” For Volkanovski, the challenge now is to prove that the fighter who returns to Abu Dhabi is not simply the same man who left it three years ago. He is a champion again, more comfortable with who he is away from the octagon and, at 38, perhaps more complete than ever.

title: Jeffrey Archer, whose books sold 300 million copies, dies aged 86
description: British novelist and former politician was also a regular guest at literary events in the UAE
content: Bestselling British author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86, his publisher HarperCollins has announced. Archer, whose novels sold more than 300 million copies worldwide, died suddenly and peacefully at his home on Monday “between writing sessions”, the publisher said. Kate Elton, chief executive of HarperCollins UK and Archer's editor, paid tribute to the author, describing him as “the master storyteller and an editor's dream”. “We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers – and a true friend,” she said. Archer was best known for novels including Kane and Abel , published in 1979, and his 1976 debut Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less . His books were sold in 119 countries and he spent a combined five and a half years on The New York Times bestseller lists, according to HarperCollins. His final novel, Adam and Eve , is being published on Tuesday, a day after his death. He had been due to discuss the book at the Cheltenham Literature Festival this weekend. Archer was also a familiar figure to readers in the UAE, having appeared several times at the Emirates Airline Festival of Literature in Dubai as well as the Sharjah International Book Fair. Before becoming a bestselling novelist, Archer had a prominent political career. He became a Conservative MP in 1969 and later served as deputy chairman of the Conservative Party under Margaret Thatcher. His political career was ultimately overshadowed by scandal. In 2001, he was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice after lying during a libel case he had brought against the Daily Star . He was sentenced to four years in prison and served two. Archer continued writing following his release, producing novels, short stories and A Prison Diary , which chronicled his time behind bars. Only a day before his death, he appeared with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at a sold-out event at London's Leicester Square Theatre, where he met hundreds of readers. Archer is survived by his wife Mary and their two sons.

title: 'Can I be in the UAE after overstaying my visit visa?'
description: What overstayers need to know about fines and finding a new job
content: Question : Can a telecoms company impose a travel ban over an unpaid bill? I owe a telecoms company money and haven't paid it for months. I have been sent a message saying that I owe Dh2,930 and that my account is now 190 days overdue. It also said: “We hereby inform you that legal proceedings may be initiated to recover the outstanding amount.” The message was from a credit management company. Can they make a case against me and put a travel ban on me for this? Is there any other action they can take? JC, Abu Dhabi Answer : For an unpaid telecom debt of Dh2,930, a full court case is unlikely, but JC can still face consequences. The account has probably already been cut off, and the company will follow up as he owes it money. Companies can pursue debts in court but, for in this case litigation costs would be disproportionate relative to the amount owed. A travel ban will not happen. Under Article 324 of the UAE Civil Procedure Law (Federal Decree Law No 42 of 2022), a creditor – a person or company that is owed money – can only apply for a travel ban against a debtor if the debt is Dh10,000 or more. Below that threshold, a civil travel ban cannot be issued, regardless of the risk of a person leaving the country without settling their debts. It is common for UAE companies to hand over small debts to collection agencies. That will lead to regular telephone calls, emails and even WhatsApp messages. These companies are licensed and regulated, and there are rules that they must follow. The agency must not overstep by making repeated calls designed to intimidate rather than to communicate, as that constitutes harassment under UAE law. They are only allowed to make contact between 9am and 8pm, and must not disclose information to any third party. That includes calling a place of work and telling anyone the call is about a debt. If the collection agency breaks these guidelines, a complaint can be made, first to the telecoms company, but if that doesn’t stop it, then to the Central Bank of the UAE. JC needs to start making repayments in order to stop follow-up calls and messages. Non-payment of any debt will affect a person’s UAE credit record . This will affect a person's ability to borrow and open financial accounts. Since the change in legislation this year, landlords can now ask for confirmation of a credit score, which can also affect a person's ability to rent a home. Q : I have overstayed my visit visa after my employer failed to arrange a work permit. What can I do? I have a question about overstaying a visit visa. I came to work for a company, and although the team promised me a visa, it never happened. I don’t have a contract, and they have now said they do not want me to work for them any more. What can I do about this? I want to find another job and stay in the UAE. Will I get in trouble or have to pay a fine? MP, Dubai A : The important point here is that MP has been working illegally since arriving in the UAE. From the outset, the employer should have given MP a proper offer of employment and a labour contract, and applied for a residence visa and a work permit. As this did not happen, the company has been employing MP illegally, so she has been working illegally. Sadly, this means that she has no protection under UAE law. This means that MP is unable to make a legal complaint against the company, even if it has broken the law. No doubt the employer will know that this is not permitted, but the company can be reported for breaking the law. Any company that takes on staff without a visa can be fined up to Dh50,000 and may have difficulty obtaining visas in the future. As MP has been in the UAE without a valid visa, MP will have overstay fines. Since February 2026, the UAE has unified overstay fines across all visa types and emirates. They are now the same for all visas, whether tourist, visit or residence visas, and there is no variation by emirate. The fine is Dh50 per day. If an overstay exceeds 30 days, an additional exit permit, known as an “outpass”, at a cost of Dh250 to Dh300, including base and service fees, is required before leaving the country. It is possible to pay the overstay fines and stay in the UAE without leaving the country, provided a new employer initiates the visa process immediately. If not, MP will need to leave and return on an employment entry permit from a new employer. MP should visit an Amer centre, a division of the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs, for advice and to find out how much MP owes. Once the overstay fine has been settled, MP can find a new job and be employed with a visa in order to stay legally in the UAE. Contact Keren Bobker at keren@holbornassets.com or at www.financialuae.com . The advice provided in our columns does not constitute legal advice and is provided for information only

title: Turning down the temperature in the Horn of Africa is good for the Middle East too
description: Mediation and serious diplomatic efforts can help at a moment when tensions are rising sharply
content: The importance of diplomacy in an increasingly volatile world may seem axiomatic. Nevertheless, when confronted by a regional neighbourhood in danger of unravelling – such as today’s Horn of Africa – it is worth highlighting how talking remains more critical than ever. This part of Africa, with its deep ties to neighbouring countries as well as the Middle East , cannot sustain further conflict. In its current state, old rivalries, shifting alliances, the nefarious presence of non-state actors as well as unresolved disputes threaten to once again turn it into a scene of confrontation. Mistrust is deep after years of conflict and national interests are colliding. Ethiopia 's renewed fighting with a rebel alliance comes four years after the 2022 Pretoria Agreement helped end a devastating war in Tigray. This newest conflict risks entangling neighbouring countries, with Addis Ababa accusing Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea of supporting armed groups – allegations they deny. Meanwhile, Sudan is now in the fourth year of a ruinous civil war between two rival generals accused of war crimes, while Somalia continues to confront the persistent threat posed by armed radicals and inherent state weakness. This north-eastern corner of the African continent increasingly resembles a patchwork of geopolitical zones of influence and competing factions. The latter is particularly destabilising given how armed groups can become instruments in wider power struggles. Rebel movements and militias ultimately weaken the institutions of the countries in which they operate. In addition, armed factions do not respect borders as neatly as states do, meaning that instability rarely remains confined to one country. The seizure of more territory by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels is a case in point. There is also a more basic cost. Constant armed rivalry consumes resources and attention that could instead be directed towards roads, ports, schools, health care, trade and jobs. The Horn of Africa and adjoining countries have enormous economic potential, sitting as they do on some of the world's most important maritime routes and strategic positioning. Conflict makes that potential impossible to realise. Peace, by contrast, pays dividends. Stable borders encourage investment, open trade creates jobs and governments are freed up to spend more on development and less on their militaries. Communities afflicted by displacement and insecurity can begin to rebuild. Averting the cumulative effect of interlinked crises in the Horn of Africa is vital not only for that region but the wider Middle East too. A four-way summit held on Sunday in Alamein that brought together leading figures from Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan is recognition of the seriousness of the situation. But diplomacy matters most when it includes parties from opposing sides. Egypt and Ethiopia remain deeply divided over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Other regional governments have legitimate and sometimes competing security interests. Mediation and serious diplomatic efforts can help bring the temperature down at a moment when tensions are rising sharply. For millions of people across this part of Africa, that is now essential to avoid further bloodletting and opportunity loss.

title: From Interstellar to Project Hail Mary: Eight space films that imagine a better future
description: These movies look beyond Earth and find hope in exploration, science and what humanity might become
content: As World Space Week celebrates humanity's achievements beyond Earth, cinema offers its own versions of where that journey might lead. Science fiction has often looked to space and found something to fear. The genre is full of abandoned ships, hostile planets, predatory aliens and futures in which humanity has carried its worst instincts beyond Earth. Yet some of the most enduring space films look upwards and see possibility. In these stories, scientific progress is paramount, difficult problems can still be solved and encounters with the unknown can broaden rather than diminish our sense of ourselves. Space becomes somewhere humanity might become more curious, more co-operative and, in some cases, more humane. Not all of these films depict utopias. Some begin with environmental collapse, extinction or profound uncertainty. What connects them is a refusal to imagine humanity's future solely in terms of decline. To mark World Space Week, which runs from until October 10, here are eight films that suggest the future beyond Earth might be worth looking forward to. The most moving thing about Interstellar 's future may be that humanity almost gives up on having one. Christopher Nolan 's film begins on Earth, where crops are failing, dust storms are worsening, and even the idea of space exploration has become unfashionable. Schools teach that the Apollo missions were propaganda. Former Nasa pilot Cooper has become a farmer. The film then spends nearly three hours pushing in the opposite direction. A mission through a wormhole becomes an attempt to recover not only humanity's future but its ambition. Cooper loses decades with his children, missions fail and the planets awaiting exploration are hardly welcoming. Yet the ending transforms the film's opening pessimism. Humans live aboard vast rotating habitats, civilisation has survived and another world lies ahead. Interstellar argues that exploration is not a luxury reserved for prosperous times. Sometimes it is what prevents decline from becoming permanent. There is something almost radical now about how little Star Trek: The Motion Picture seems interested in turning the unknown into an enemy. A vast entity called V'Ger is approaching Earth, and the USS Enterprise is dispatched to intercept it. Yet Robert Wise's film spends much of its running time not preparing for battle, but looking. The camera lingers on the Enterprise, on V'Ger and on the immensity of the space separating them. That approach suits Star Trek 's most enduring idea: humanity has matured. By the 23rd century, Earth is part of a wider federation and exploration is driven by curiosity. The film's climax follows the same philosophy. What appears threatening at first is eventually revealed to be something that needs to be understood. Its future is attractive because humanity has seemingly learnt to meet the unfamiliar with inquiry rather than destruction. Mark Watney's greatest weapon on Mars is not a laser, a secret technology or a convenient science-fiction miracle. It is competence. Ridley Scott's The Martian finds enormous pleasure in watching people be good at their jobs. Watney calculates, grows food and repairs equipment. Nasa engineers test ideas. Orbital mechanics become dramatic. Even the film's jokes often come from someone finding an unexpectedly practical solution to an impossible problem. That gives The Martian a different kind of optimism than grander space films have. Its future is only slightly ahead of ours and feels attainable. Humanity has reached Mars, but doing so still requires huge amounts of work, money and international effort. The eventual involvement of the China National Space Administration widens the story further. One stranded astronaut becomes a problem that people around the world decide is worth solving. There are few visions of the future more hopeful than one in which catastrophe is met with expertise rather than panic. What happens when humanity finally learns it is not alone? Contact's answer is wonderfully uncinematic: scientists listen. Robert Zemeckis's adaptation of Carl Sagan 's novel centres on astronomer Ellie Arroway, whose search for extraterrestrial intelligence is rewarded when a signal arrives from Vega. Hidden within it are plans for a machine whose purpose no one initially understands. The discovery causes political, religious and philosophical upheaval, but the film never loses sight of the wonder beneath all that noise. Contact is less interested in extraterrestrials themselves than in what their existence might do to us. Suddenly, national rivalries and ideological divisions appear provincial. The universe has become larger overnight. Even the machine is built through collective effort, turning contact into a scientific project on a planetary scale. The film leaves many questions unanswered. That is part of its appeal. A better future begins with humanity becoming curious enough to admit how much it still does not know. Mission to Mars belongs to a kind of science fiction that Hollywood rarely makes any more: completely sincere space exploration. Brian De Palma's 2000 film has no interest in making astronauts cynical about what they do. The possibility that humanity might finally answer questions about its own origins is treated with genuine awe. The story follows a rescue mission after the first crewed expedition to Mars encounters a mysterious structure. What initially resembles a disaster movie gradually becomes something stranger. Its central revelation connects humanity to a far older extraterrestrial civilisation, reframing the journey to Mars as more than exploration. Humanity is, in a sense, discovering part of its own history. There is a charming earnestness to all of this. Mission to Mars imagines scientific progress leading to one of the oldest questions imaginable: where did we come from? Its answer naturally leads to the next one: where do we go now? Before HAL 9000 turns murderous, 2001: A Space Odyssey gives us something remarkable: space travel as routine. A man dozes aboard a commercial flight. He makes a video call home. Scientists gather at a lunar base. Humanity has moved beyond Earth sufficiently that some of its most extraordinary achievements have become mundane. Stanley Kubrick presents that future without constantly announcing how futuristic it is. There is, of course, something much larger happening. The mysterious monolith connects humanity's distant past with an unknowable future. From the first tool used by early humans to the spacecraft orbiting Earth, technological progress becomes part of a continuous evolutionary process. That process does not end with spaceships. The film's famous final passages suggest humanity may eventually become something it cannot yet comprehend. 2001 's optimism is therefore unusual. It does not promise comfort. It promises that humanity is unfinished. Project Hail Mary begins with extinction looming, yet its real subject is the possibility that intelligence and co-operation can overcome almost anything. Ryan Gosling plays science teacher Ryland Grace, who wakes alone aboard a spacecraft light years from Earth with no memory of why he is there. Gradually, he discovers that his mission is to find a solution to a phenomenon threatening the Sun and, with it, life on Earth. The film, directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller and adapted from Andy Weir's novel, shares some DNA with The Martian . Problems are broken down, tested and solved through science rather than spectacle alone. What pushes it further is Grace's encounter with another intelligent species facing a similar crisis. That relationship gives the film its most hopeful idea. Humanity's future does not have to be secured alone. Somewhere beyond Earth, another civilisation might be confronting the same problems and reaching towards us for the same reason. Long before the Enterprise began exploring strange new worlds, the crew of Ikarie XB-1 were already living together on their way to Alpha Centauri. The 1963 Czechoslovak film seems striking today because it makes interstellar travel seem ordinary. There are meals, romances, exercise sessions, celebrations and disagreements. People dance. A crew member worries about ageing relatives back on Earth. The spacecraft feels like a small travelling community. That was an unusually sophisticated way to imagine the future in the early 1960s. Director Jindrich Polak was interested in what human life might look like once travelling between stars was possible. The ship is devoted to scientific exploration and its multinational crew suggests that humanity has moved beyond at least some of the divisions of the 20th century. The film's optimism lies in the everyday details: the future has not made people less human, it has simply given them much further to go.

title: Envision to end operations and stop product development if it can't find partner
description: App uses phone camera to read signs, menus and other things, making life easier for visually impaired users
content: Envision , a Netherlands-based start-up that made hardware and software tools for the visually impaired , will be stopping product development at the end of the year unless it can find a partner. In a statement posted to the company's website on Monday, founder Karthik Mahadevan and Karthik Kannan said that despite efforts towards a successful business model, the company has been unable to yield profitable results. "We reached the conclusion that we have given it our all and brought Envision as far as we could with our nimble efforts," they wrote. "There’s still so much potential for this product and business to grow, but realising it needs someone who can take it in a new direction, whether that's a new audience or a different business model." Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said they were in talks with a few possible partners who might be able to keep the company going. They were also open to speaking with others who may have ideas as to how to keep it alive. In 2024, Envision's founders spoke with The National about the company's aspirations. Its journey to selling smart glasses for the visually impaired started in 2017, when the start-up's smartphone app, Envision AI, began to gain popularity. The app uses a phone camera to identify and read signs, objects, menus, books or other material in real time, making life easier for visually impaired users. The popularity of the app's free version, according to Mr Kannan at the time, fuelled Envision's desire to improve the user experience based on feedback from customers. “If you're a low-vision person and you have to have a phone in one hand and a cane in the other, that can be cumbersome,” he said. “So we started looking for something that might be sleek and modern-looking to implement.” Part of enhancing the experience, Mr Kannan said, was to take the best aspects of the Envision app and use it in the glasses. Envision's app won a Google Play Award in 2019 in the category of “best accessibility experience”, and Mr Kannan said it could come to an agreement with Google and eventually use the company's largely defunct Google Glass technology for its product. The glasses, priced from $1,899 to $3,499, were introduced in 2020 and underwent various improvements amid the AI boom. In the announcement on Monday, the founders outlined plans to wind down operations and promised there would be a final update, with hopes of keeping the app and some offerings operational for as long as possible "offline”. Mr Mahadevan and Mr Kannan said the ultimate problem was scaling Envision's business model to something sustainable given the competition from Apple and Meta , and the current economy. "On paper, 300 million blind and low-vision people is a big market, but for the majority of them, the problems that come first are ones technology can't solve yet: poverty, lack of basic access, unemployment," Envision’s founders wrote. "That's why even products that are cheap or free struggle to get past that million mark, and paying users are a much much smaller slice of that." In 2024, Envision told The National of the intention to turn the company's focus to Arabic . "As our user base in the Middle East grew and we built up a community of users, we've started to bring a lot more of those efforts in-house,” Mr Kannan said. “As a result, we now have more control over how the AI works when translating documents that are scanned and how it works if there's written text on a blackboard.”

title: Polish embassy in US expresses outrage over Tucker Carlson comments on Second World War
description: Journalist 'justified' Germany's invasion of Poland and questioned why UK became involved in conflict
content: The Polish embassy in Washington on Monday expressed outrage over media personality Tucker Carlson 's comments about Poland , Adolf Hitler and the Second World War. Bogdan Klich, charge d'affaires for the embassy, called Carlson's comments at the weekend "false" and "deeply troubling", and demanded he retract them. "As an American journalist who enjoys the democratic right to the freedom of speech, you have now become an apologist for Adolf Hitler ," Mr Klich said of the comments, which came in an interview with a British politician. "In doing so, you resort to lies, completely falsifying the documented historical record." He said in the statement, which was posted on X, that Carlson had justified Nazi Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939 – which caused France and the UK to declare war on the Third Reich – by saying it was "German territory with Germans in it". "This statement constitutes a colossal insult to the millions of victims of Nazism, including hundreds of thousands of American soldiers who had been killed or wounded while liberating Europe from the occupation of the Third Reich," Mr Klich said. During the interview with Jacob Rees-Mogg , released at the weekend, Carlson asked why the UK been involved in the Second World War, as Hitler had had no quarrel with England. "Otherwise, we’d be speaking German,” Mr Rees-Mogg answered. Carlson replied: “Who cares? There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English. So it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.” Mr Rees-Mogg said that Carlson appeared to be on the verge of defending Hitler. Carlson has in the past expressed support for Russian President Vladimir Putin , whose excuse for invading Ukraine in 2022 was to come to the aid of Russian-speaking people living in the eastern part of the country. Carlson has frequently been accused of echoing Russian talking points, and has blamed the invasion on Nato and the West.

title: UAE among global leaders in AI agent adoption, analysis shows
description: Study compared technology acceptance among eight countries
content: UAE companies and organisations have some of the highest rates of agentic artificial intelligence adoption in the world, a survey has shown. The report – 2026 Global AI Confessions Report, CIO Edition – was commissioned by data science and AI platform company Dataiku and is based on the responses from 685 chief information officers in the UAE, US, UK, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea and Singapore. It found that 62 per cent of UAE chief information officers say their companies have more than 50 AI agents working in the organisation, while 15 per cent say they operate more than 500 agents. "That's the highest proportion across the eight markets surveyed, and substantially higher than the 9 per cent global average," the report said. In recent years, AI agents – digital personal assistants powered by artificial intelligence to carry out repetitive tasks – have become increasingly prevalent across various sectors. Technology companies have claimed that AI agents can match and often outperform humans in many functions, freeing employees to do other tasks. Dataiku's analysis also showed that businesses and organisations in the UAE were continuing to embrace agentic AI. "Among CIOs whose organisations are creating or planning embedded roles for AI experts or forward engineers, 22 per cent expect to recruit more than 10 people over the coming year, the highest compared to other countries in the study," it said. The analysis also highlighted areas in which UAE businesses and organisations can improve how AI agents are monitored. This comes after incidents in which AI models escaped containment and compromised the digital infrastructure of outside entities. "Only 5 per cent of UAE CIOs say their organisation could reliably identify and contain a problematic agent across environments within one to two hours, among the lowest results in the study and half the worldwide figure of 10 per cent," the survey read. The poll also indicated that 27 per cent of the UAE chief information officers surveyed said that they could intervene later in the day to address a hypothetical issue with a rogue AI agent, meaning that two thirds of those surveyed felt they "could not contain the agent on the same day". Kurt Muehmel, head of AI strategy at Dataiku, said that perspective is needed in looking at the results from the survey. "UAE organisations already do one important part of this well, with 80 per cent of UAE CIOs having seen an agent act against business intent or policy while still operating within its technical parameters, but 62 per cent say they caught the problem before it caused harm, the best result globally," Mr Muehmel said. The results of the survey can provide a road map for making the UAE's approach to AI more robust. "Keep one inventory of every agent, whoever built it and whatever platform it runs on," Mr Muehmel said, when asked for steps that can be taken by businesses and organisations in the UAE. He said an owner should be designated for every agent and that a decision must be made in advance about who would have the authority to stop it. "Standardise how agents are tested, changed and retired ... and practise containment the way you practise a cyber security incident response." Sid Bhatia, Dataiku 's vice president for the Middle East, Turkey and Africa, said that overall, the latest analysis bodes well for the UAE's push to be a leader in AI and making use of AI agents. "The UAE has established a strong foundation for agentic AI, with enterprises deploying at scale, investing in specialist expertise, and preventing a high proportion of agent incidents from causing real-world harm," Mr Bhatia said.

title: UAE aviation authority completes passenger transfers after flydubai Tel Aviv suspension
description: GCAA says 7,479 passengers were transferred on 37 flights after flydubai temporarily suspended Tel Aviv services
content: The UAE's General Civil Aviation Authority has completed the transfer of nearly 7,500 stranded passengers to Tel Aviv after the temporary suspension of flydubai flights to the Israeli city. The UAE's Attorney General , Hamad Al Shamsi, said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to flight FZ1073 last Wednesday , which was forced to land in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the pilot was attacked by his co-pilot in an "attempted terrorist attack". The GCAA said 37 flights were operated from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion Airport between Friday, October 2, and Monday, October 5, carrying 7,479 passengers. As part of measures to ease the disruption caused by the suspension of flydubai's scheduled services, authorities granted permits to Israeli carriers to operate flights to Dubai. These flights operated alongside services run by Etihad Airways, which continued to fly to Tel Aviv on its regular schedule throughout the period. The GCAA confirmed that co-ordination for the return of passengers whose flights were disrupted and who had been left stranded had been completed, with all affected travellers returned to their destinations. The authority said Etihad Airways would continue to operate its scheduled flights to Tel Aviv, increasing the travel options available to passengers in the absence of flydubai's regular services on the route.

title: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi to feature Frank Gehry exhibition in opening programme
description: Original sketches, hand-built models and archive materials will trace the development of the architect’s design for the museum
content: An exhibition exploring Frank Gehry’s design for Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will form part of the inaugural programme at the museum, which opens on December 11. Original sketches, early hand-built models and archival materials will trace the development of the late architect’s vision, showing how the building took shape in response to Abu Dhabi’s landscape, culture and ambitions for the arts, according to the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi. “ Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is an expression of Frank Gehry’s love for Abu Dhabi and his deep respect for its vision, courage and patience,” said Meaghan Lloyd, a partner at Gehry Partners. “From the first, he was inspired by the scale of the Saadiyat Island Cultural District and by Abu Dhabi’s strategic investment in culture as a way to drive progress and shape the future of the country. “Frank was always mindful of the faith Abu Dhabi’s leaders had placed in him, and of the responsibility that came with a project of this importance.” Gehry and his team undertook extensive site visits and research into how people gather, move around and experience Abu Dhabi. That work informed a design connecting galleries with shaded courtyards, terraces and outdoor spaces for art. The museum’s position beside the sea influenced the orientation of the building, the routes through it and the arrangement of public spaces, connecting the museum to its coastal setting and the wider Saadiyat Cultural District. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of DCT Abu Dhabi, said: “From the very beginning, Frank Gehry understood that this building had to be inspired by the emirate, being shaped by Abu Dhabi’s light, its climate, its coastline and its traditions. “What he has given us is a museum that draws from its surroundings, a building that carries the forms of this region into something entirely new. Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is a work of art in its own right.” The museum has 11,600 square metres of interior gallery space and 23,000 square metres of outdoor exhibition space. Its galleries vary in size and configuration, giving artists room to develop commissions and exhibitions in different media and at different scales. Gehry Partners explored those possibilities through physical models and design studies, considering how the architecture could accommodate artists’ work alongside the visitor’s journey through interconnected galleries, exhibition spaces and outdoor installations. Ten monumental cones are among the museum’s most distinctive features. Nine are clad in stainless steel mesh, with the remaining cone in onyx and glass. The cones also help shade public spaces and ventilate courtyards and terraces. By drawing warm air upwards and directing cooling breezes below, they are designed to make the outdoor spaces more comfortable for visitors. Developed in partnership with the Solomon R Guggenheim Foundation, the museum will focus on modern and contemporary art from the 1960s to the present. Its collection spans painting, sculpture, installation, photography, moving image and new media, with displays connecting artists across different periods and parts of the world. Tickets went on sale in September , with standard adult admission priced at Dh70 ($19). Bookings are available through the museum’s website.

title: Dubai's Golden Visa scheme rewards outstanding educators on World Teachers' Day
description: Hundreds of private schoolteachers apply for residency scheme launched to retain top teaching talent in the emirate
content: Hundreds of educators across private schools and universities in Dubai are benefiting from a Golden Visa drive recognising exceptional teaching. The annual programme, which was launched under the directive of Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, grants long-term residency to high-performing teachers and educators working in private early-childhood centres, schools and higher-education institutions. Since its launch on October 5, 2024, to coincide with World Teachers' Day, the visa initiative has attracted more than 835 applicants. Candidates are assessed through a comprehensive professional evaluation that considers academic qualifications, outstanding achievements, contributions to the education sector and wider community, and positive feedback from parents, pupils and students. The scheme forms part of Dubai's Education 33 strategy, which aims to attract and retain skilled teachers, tutors and lecturers whose expertise strengthens students and pupils' learning experiences and bolsters the emirate's regional and international competitiveness. To be eligible, applicants must work in a private educational institution and demonstrate outstanding academic achievements or creative contributions to education, a proven record of improving educational quality and a tangible positive effect within learning. Significant contributions to improving student outcomes – including academic progress and the attainment of accredited qualifications – are also among the criteria. Further details on eligibility requirements and the application process are available on the Knowledge and Human Development Authority website.

title: Lebanese army to hold joint drills with Britain
description: Pegasus Cedar 2026 is first UK-Lebanon exercise since regional conflict began three years ago
