content: Lebanon and Britain are to hold three weeks of military drills beginning on Tuesday, as European countries try to build the Lebanese army into a cornerstone of peace with Israel . The exercise, known as Pegasus Cedar 2026, will see troops from the Royal Regiment of Scotland train with an air assault team from the Lebanese Armed Forces. The drills will include reconnaissance, and urban warfare training, helicopter operations, and mortar fire exercises, the Lebanese army said. Six other countries including the US , Qatar and Jordan will also be involved. The British troops have been posted in a base in Cyprus for the first such drills since the Hamas attack on Israel sparked a regional war in 2023. Lebanon has repeatedly been caught up in the war due to Hezbollah and Israel exchanging fire on its soil. Israeli troops occupy a large part of southern Lebanon after ordering its residents to leave and demolishing homes and villages. A US-backed peace process calls for the Lebanese army to gradually reassert control and disarm Hezbollah in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal. But there are doubts whether the poorly funded and equipped Lebanese army is up to the task. The British forces “will train with their Lebanese counterparts to hone skills and exchange military expertise", said the UK's ambassador to Lebanon, Hamish Cowell. “British military training teams continue to work alongside all branches of the Lebanese military – army, navy and air force – to support them in their essential roles and building the Lebanese Armed Forces’ capabilities as the sole legitimate defender of Lebanon.” Lt Gen Charles Collins, Britain's deputy chief of the defence staff, also visited Beirut for talks on the security situation in southern Lebanon. He met Lebanese army chief Gen Rodolphe Haykal. There are several European efforts planned to assist the Lebanese army. France hosted a meeting of European, Arab and US military officials in Paris last month, where Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, a former general, called for a “long-term partnership”. Mr Aoun is also pushing for a replacement for the UN peacekeeping force Unifil, the mandate of which expires this year. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told The National last week that his country was involved in preparations for a new force.

title: Saudi Arabia has right to defend itself from Houthis, Marco Rubio says
description: US Secretary of State pledges to honour defence and security agreement with Riyadh
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Saudi Arabia has a right to defend itself against attacks by Yemen's Houthis. Before a trip to Iceland and mainland Europe, Mr Rubio also said Washington would honour its defence and security agreement with the kingdom, as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched an offensive against Iran-aligned Houthi fighters. Yemeni government forces on Monday said they had secured control of the Bab Al Mandeb strait , the Dhubab area overlooking the sea lane and the strategic port city of Mokha, as the Saudi-led coalition provided aerial support and carried out air strikes on Houthi targets. “Obviously the Saudis have come under Houthi attack and see the threat that that poses, and they have a right to defend themselves,” Mr Rubio said. “And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from.” He was asked if the US would provide air support for the Saudis, or if Washington had helped to co-ordinate the counter-offensive to retake Houthi territory. “The United States has a defence and security agreement with Saudi Arabia and we intend to live by it,” Mr Rubio said, without elaborating. President Donald Trump earlier rebuffed requests for direct US military action from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said the US can do a lot without becoming actively engaged in military combat. "It is likely already providing intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance support on missile and drone launch sites, Houthi leadership movements, maritime activity, command and control nodes [and] active threats," said Ms Dent, who was previously the Pentagon’s director for the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula, overseeing US defence relations with Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Washington may also be providing more assistance for air and missile defence through interceptors and radar coverage, as well as logistics and sustainment operations. "The US is also likely co-ordinating with the Saudi-led maritime coalition and may be providing targeting information for Saudi strikes," Ms Dent added. Mr Rubio confirmed senior US officials had met at Camp David, 100km from Washington, last week for an unannounced meeting. Axios reported Yemen was among the topics discussed when Mr Rubio joined Vice President JD Vance, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, CIA director John Ratcliffe, special envoy Steve Witkoff and other senior officials. “We’re constantly meeting for long-term strategic planning and things of this nature,” Mr Rubio said. The National Security Council regularly brings together senior officials to consider issues “six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road”, he added. Later on Monday, Mr Trump spoke briefly about developments in Yemen. "It'll all work out very well," he told reporters. During Prince Mohammed's visit to Washington last November, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a Strategic Defence Agreement major and Mr Trump declared Riyadh to be a major non-Nato ally . The designation will make it easier for the US to share military technology with Saudi Arabia and increase security co-operation. The Yemen conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year with a campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the rebel group. Since the Houthi takeover, the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, also ‌recognised by the UN, has controlled the ⁠south and east of the country and is based in the southern city of Aden. The Houthis have more recently launched attacks on Saudi Arabia and on commercial and military shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. Beyond reducing the Houthis' ability to threaten the Bab Al Mandeb strait, Saudi Arabia's broader objective is to alter the strategic balance in Yemen and ultimately create the conditions for a more favourable political settlement for Riyadh, Ms Dent said.

title: 'I was deceived': French ISIS recruit on trial in Iraq says he regrets joining group
description: Mehdi Ismail Mohammed one of 11 French citizens of North African origin brought before judge in Baghdad
content: A French man admitted on Monday in a court in Iraq to joining ISIS after claiming that he was lured on social media into helping Muslims in Syria during its gruelling civil war. He pleaded for mercy. Mehdi Ismail Mohammed, 33, is one of 11 French citizens of Algerian and Tunisian origin brought before a judge in Baghdad. They are accused of joining ISIS during its rule over much of Iraq and Syria from mid-2014 until its defeat in Iraq in 2017 and Syria in 2019. They are among 47 French fighters handed over to Iraq last year by the Syrian Democratic Forces militia, which had held thousands of suspected ISIS members and their families in overcrowded prisons and camps since the extremists lost their last bastion in Baghouz. The trials, which opened in Baghdad last month, expose Europe's unresolved dilemma over its ISIS fighters eight years almost a decade on. With no international tribunal in place, and European countries reluctant to take them back, Iraq has in effect become the courtroom for Europe's extremists. Monday was Mohammed's second appearance before the court. The judge had appointed a defence lawyer for him when he was unable to secure a French counsel. He told the court his story in a frail voice. As a student in France in 2013, he was troubled by the war in Syria, he said. After meeting a man known as Abu Mohammed Al Faransi on social media, he left France for Algeria, where he stayed for six months. Then in late 2013 he flew to Turkey and crossed into Syria with the help of smugglers. “He convinced me to come to Syria and to join the revolution to support them because they are Muslims,” Mohammed told the judge, with his hands clasped to his back and his head shaved. “It was never my intention to join the Islamic State. I was convinced that we as Muslims should help the Syrians.” He claimed he initially lived with his recruiter for three months when he knew he belonged to ISIS. “At first I refused to join ISIS because I did not come to fight,” Mohammed said. Eventually, he said, he agreed to join in a non-combat role: giving religious teaching to civilians and children and leading prayers in a mosque in Manbij, every day except Friday, while working as an accountant handing out salaries and aid to imams. In 2016, as the US-led coalition tightened its offensive, he moved to Raqqa, the group's capital, where he worked in the Diwan Al Zakat – the department that collected Islamic taxes from farmers and herders, which was a key revenue stream for the putative state. By 2018, with the caliphate collapsing, Mohammed said life became impossible. “Life became very difficult and I tried to leave the organisation,” he said. He said he paid a smuggler, took his two wives and four children and tried to flee to Turkey, planning to surrender to the French or Algerian embassy. Instead, he was arrested by the SDF. Inside ISIS he had used the names Abu Jawad Al Faransi, then Abu Musab Al Fransi. “The work I did was civilian. When I came to Syria I had no relationship with the party and I did not want to interfere in it, and when I discovered the group's violations and its heinous acts … I deeply regret it,” he said. Mohammed's court-appointed lawyer, Abbas Al Kinani, asked for acquittal or leniency, arguing his client confessed, was deceived online and had committed no proven crimes on Iraqi soil. Judge Mohammed Salman set October 27 as the date for the verdict. The trials for the other 10 defendants were adjourned until later this month. The judge gave them more time to arrange French lawyers or accept one appointed by the court. All 11 defendants face the same charge, according to Mr Salman – “belonging to the terrorist organisation ISIS and participating in terrorist acts threatening public peace and security and endangering people's lives”. Iraq has tried thousands of its own citizens for ISIS membership under its sweeping anti-terrorism law, which carries the death penalty for belonging to a terrorist group. Foreigners have received the same treatment, a policy that has drawn criticism from human rights groups, but which Baghdad defends as a matter of sovereignty and deterrence. Iraq is also preparing to put on trial 5,704 ISIS prisoners who were transferred from Syria early this year. They comprise 67 nationalities, according to the Supreme Judiciary Council . There are 16 Arab, 19 European and 32 other nationalities, the council said. The breakdown includes 474 Iraqis and 3,497 Syrians.

title: Daniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open after hitting spectator in face with ball
description: Russian's semi-final against Novak Djokovic ended after moment of frustration in Beijing
content: World No 5 Daniil Medvedev has been disqualified from the China ​Open after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball during his semi-final against Novak Djokovic. The Russian was 7-5, 5-3 down on Monday when Djokovic hit a winner with the ball ricocheting off the back of the court resulting in Medvedev swinging a backhand in frustration. But the ball flew into the crowd hitting a spectator who was sitting in the front row of the stand who was left clutching his eye and still appeared in pain as he walked out of the gallery, assisted by stadium staff. After speaking with umpire Mohamed Lahyani and an ATP official, Medvedev went to the net to shake hands with his Serbian opponent at the National Tennis Centre in Beijing. “Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all,” Medvedev said, who made no protest as the umpire's decision. “I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels. “I just hope he's OK. That's the most important. I just really care about him right now. “The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation.” The situation would have brought bad memories flooding back to the 24-time Grand Slam winner who was kicked out of the 2020 US Open after hitting a line judge in the throat with a ball. The then world No 1 was playing in the opening set of his first round match against Spain's Pablo Carreno Busta but saw his tournament brought to an abrupt end. “It's a bit of a shock to be honest. I hope that person is not badly injured,” said Djokovic, who will face Alex de Minaur in Tuesday's final. “I also feel sorry for Daniil. I know exactly how he feels to be disqualified in a big match. I am sure that Daniil did not want to do this intentionally.” Both semi-finals ended ​prematurely in Beijing as Hubert Hurkacz retired with an adductor injury earlier ‌in the day. Djokovic has a 33-0 record at the tournament, having been champion six times. Australian De Minaur was ⁠leading the first semi 6-4 3-2 when his Polish ​opponent, who had struggled with movement throughout the match, retired. It is far from the first time Medvedev's temper has got him into trouble on the tennis court. At last year's US Open, he suffered a complete meltdown when a photographer walked on court during his first-round defeat by Benjamin Bonzi. Earlier in 2025, his behaviour cost him a $42,500 fine and he was also fined a total of $76,000 for his antics at the Australian Open where he destroyed a net camera with his racquet in the first-round five-set win over Kasidit Samrej. In his second-round loss in Melbourne to American teenager Learner Tien, Medvedev picked up further punishments for throwing his racquet and then failing to attend a post-match news conference. In April, the 30-year-old smashed a racquet to pieces on his way to the first 6-0, 6-0 loss of his career against Matteo Berrettini in Monte Carlo. He was fined $7,000 for unsportsmanlike conduct. At the start of 2026, Medvedev ended a run of three successive first-round exits at majors – and a morale-sapping 370 day wait for a Grand Slam victory – by winning his opening match against Jesper de Jong at Melbourne Park.

title: Kuwaiti jailed for life in UK after failed Israeli embassy attack
description: Abdullah Sabah Albadri came to Britain by small boat and began his terror plot 12 days later
content: A Kuwaiti who attempted to break into the Israeli embassy in London armed with two knives to carry out a terrorist attack has been sentenced to life in jail. Abdullah Sabah Albadri, 34, was arrested by armed diplomatic protection police who prevented him from climbing over the gates at the embassy building. Body-camera footage of his arrest showed him telling officers he had “weapons” and wanted to “make a crime ” inside the building. Albadri was convicted of preparing terrorist acts and possessing two knives following a trial at the Old Bailey in London in April. He has now been given a life sentence and will serve a minimum of 20 years. “The significant prison sentence he has received reflects the danger he posed on the day and the lack of remorse he has shown since he was arrested,” said Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London. Ms Flanagan praised the officers who arrested Albadri for their “incredible bravery and professionalism, which, remarkably, resulted in nobody being seriously injured – despite being confronted by a man armed with knives, intent on carrying out a terrorist attack”. Albadri first entered Britain on a small boat from France in 2021 and again in April 2025. Only 12 days after arriving in the country, he searched online for the location of the Israeli embassy. Following his arrest, detectives found that Albadri had wanted to attack the embassy as an act of revenge for Israeli government’s military actions in Gaza . Albadri also had a note on him when he was arrested that said he intended to die. Officers found he had searched online for several Arabic terms related to suicide attacks during the five days leading up to his arrest. These internet searches strengthened the case that he had been planning to carry out a terrorist attack, London's Metropolitan Police said. On the day of the incident, CCTV footage recovered by police showed Albadri walking from Kilburn in north-west London to the embassy in Kensington. He was wearing a red-and-white scarf wrapped around his head and mouth, and sunglasses. Albadri told his trial he was born into the stateless Arabian Bedouin tribe on Iraqi-Kuwaiti border and had no human rights or passport in Kuwait. He said his father, a police officer, had paid for his education until he was 18 and that he later became a human-rights activist.

title: Sheikh Khaled and King Abdullah launch $2.5 billion Jordan rail link
description: Project connects Port of Aqaba with mining centres in Al Shidiya and Ghor Al Safi
content: Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of Abu Dhabi Executive Council, and King Abdullah II of Jordan attended the ground-breaking ceremony for the Aqaba-Al-Shidiya-Maan Railway Project on Monday. The project entails building a 403-kilometre $2.5 billion transport network connecting the Port of Aqaba with major mining centres in Al Shidiya and Ghor Al Safi in Jordan. The investment is expected to boost the mining sector by providing a direct connection between mines and ports, reducing transport costs and improving supply efficiency. The UAE signed the project in July, with Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, in attendance. Monday's ground-breaking is a step forward in regional transport infrastructure, developed by the Jordanian-Emirati Railways Company. Sheikh Khaled was received by King Abdullah at King Hussein International Airport in Aqaba, alongside several senior officials. The Crown Prince also met officials involved in the project. He said the project reflected the two countries’ commitment to further strengthening their bilateral partnership across key sectors. Dr Mohammad Thneibat, chairman of the Jordan-UAE Railway Company, said the ground-breaking marked the beginning of a new chapter in the Jordan-UAE partnership. “It reflects the vision of the leadership of both countries to translate co-operation and mutual trust into development and investment projects with tangible impact,” he said. “The significance of this project lies in its ability to connect production centres with the ports of Aqaba and regional and global markets, enhance the efficiency of the transport and logistics ecosystem, strengthen the competitiveness of national exports and create long-term value for the economy and society, thereby reinforcing Jordan’s position in regional and international trade.” In addition to the rail tracks, about 55 bridges, six tunnels and associated engineering structures will be built. Designed to carry about 16 million tonnes of phosphate and potash annually, the line aims to slash transport costs and streamline export logistics from Jordan's mining hubs directly to shipping terminals in Aqaba. The new railway will replace a congested road from Ghor Al Safi, in the Jordan Valley, to Aqaba, where potash is currently transported by lorry, and an old rail line that moved phosphate export cargo from Al Shidiya, in the south, to the port. The project’s economic impact will extend across the various sectors and regions it serves. It is expected to create about 5,000 jobs in southern Jordan and reduce mineral transportation costs by around $40 million annually, enhancing the competitiveness of Jordan’s mining sector. The project will also create broader opportunities for companies in engineering, construction, maintenance, logistics, technology and supporting industries, while boosting economic activity and supporting development across Jordan's southern governorates. Developed and operated through the UAE-Jordan Railway Company, the construction project is a 50-50 joint venture between UAE sovereign investment company L'imad Holding and a consortium from the kingdom, consisting of Jordan Phosphate Mining Company, Arab Potash Company, the investment management company Musahamat and the Social Security Fund, Petra news agency reported. Construction is expected to take five years. The UAE is involved in several national and cross-border rail initiatives, including the Etihad Rail network , a 1,200km flagship railway spanning all seven emirates for heavy freight and passenger services. The UAE is also co-developing the Hafeet Rail (Oman-UAE Rail) link connecting Abu Dhabi to Sohar Port. The UAE is also a key signatory in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. The multinational transport framework is designed to link India to Europe via a combined ship-to-rail transit network traversing the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel. This multibillion-dollar rail and shipping corridor would “significantly enhance connectivity and integration between participating countries”, Wam reported.

title: Teenager's hand blown off as French school protests enter third week
description: Students call national day ​of ​demonstrations on Tuesday
content: A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot ⁠police in northern France on Monday, on the ​eve of a national demonstration by the pupils' union against underfunding, overcrowding and dilapidation. The 15-year-old lost his hand ⁠and part of his lower arm after picking up a police stun grenade, which detonated, in the northern town of Lens as the wave of school protests entered its third week, local media said. Francois-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact circumstances, saying about 200 to 250 protesters had been hurling objects at police officers. Six ⁠months before an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron, his government and the far-right National Rally – headed by presidential front-runner Marine Le ​Pen – have accused ⁠hard-left France Unbowed politicians and mayors of stoking the ‌protests. The LFI denies the accusation. Rights groups have accused police of using heavy-handed tactics ​including batons, tear gas and flash-ball guns against minors. Among several investigations into police methods, authorities are examining the case of a 16-year-old who suffered an eye injury after police fired rubber bullets into a crowd of protesters, according to his friends. The LFI, headed by presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, denies encouraging violence and accuses the government of politicising the issue and neglecting pupils' interests. The protests have put more pressure on a government trying to narrow a budget deficit. Investors' growing concerns about state finances briefly pushed the yield on France's 10-year bonds to a 24-year high above 5 per cent last week, raising the likely cost of future borrowing. Between 400 and 500 high schools were closed or partially closed as demonstrations and blockades showed no sign of abating before Tuesday's nationwide protest. The protests began in September in Paris, focusing on the deprived suburbs, before spreading nationwide. The government says they have been hijacked and morphed into urban violence. “Our priority is to restore order,” government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told CNews television. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 teaching staff had been injured in the demonstrations. On Monday, BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille in northern France, tear ‌gas being used in Toulouse in the south-west, and ⁠a fire being lit as people tried to break into a school ​in central Paris. Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris, said it had been attacked by a “very ​determined” group wearing hoods ‌and masks who had tried to break through the entrance door and then lit a fire, forcing the school to be evacuated and classes suspended. “It was ⁠very violent and happened very quickly,” she said, adding that she did not believe the attackers were from the school. Since last ⁠Monday, 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them teenagers, have been arrested and dozens injured. Teachers and members of the public have been attacked, while damage to property is estimated in the millions of euros. Ms Bregeon said the government would fast-track a bill on October 27 to make young people found to have damaged property, or their parents, financially liable. Security officials fear that Tuesday's organised protests in central Paris, in particular, could bring further ​violence amid concern that far-left and anarchist groups could try to take them over. Sophie Binet, head of the CGT labour union, told TF1 television on Monday that her members would attend Tuesday's demonstrations to protect the students. “We've been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised,” Ms Binet said.

title: Israel building military line in occupied Syrian territory, Damascus says
description: Jordan and Qatar also voice alarm at creation of Sufa 53 Line
content: Syria has accused Israel of building major military fortifications in Syrian territory along the occupied Golan Heights, a move that could entrench a new territorial takeover and undermine a US drive for peace. The Syrian Foreign Ministry said that Israel was working to complete its “Sufa 53 Line”, in “flagrant violation” of a 1974 disengagement of forces agreement brokered by US secretary of state Henry Kissinger. The agreement followed Syria's failed war in 1973 to regain the Golan, a strategic plateau occupied by Israel since 1967. Building the line continues the “aggressive approach of the Israeli occupation, along with its attacks and field incursions”, the ministry said on Sunday. Qatar, a major backer of the post-Assad order in Syria, and Jordan, issued similar condemnation and called for an end to Israeli occupation of Syrian territory. There was no immediate reaction from Israel. If the Sufa Line is completed, the 1974 ceasefire line negotiated by Mr Kissinger would move east, entrenching old and new occupation of Syrian territory. An Israeli armoured brigade known as Sufa (storm) played a main role in foiling Syrian operations in the 1973 war. The areas near the occupied Golan Heights have been the scene of an increasing number of Israeli incursions this year. Israeli troops crossed into southern Syria and areas west of Damascus, and occupied parts of those regions, soon after rebel forces led by current President Ahmad Al Shara ousted the regime of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024. A security source based in Amman said Israel started work on the Sufa 53 Line in 2022 to counter infiltration by Hezbollah and other militant groups supported by Iran. The groups had expanded into the Syrian-controlled side of the Golan Heights during Assad's rule. “We are talking about a major military line running from west Damascus to the border of Jordan,” the source said. It comprises a north-south road and major barriers, observation posts and firing positions that “would give the Israelis flexibility” and make it easier to defend the Golan positions. “They will be more comfortable,” the source said. The line would run two to three kilometres parallel to the main 1974 armistice line, starting near the Syrian town of Hader in Quneitra governorate, about 40km south-west of Damascus. It would end in the Yarmouk river basin in Deraa governorate, near the border with Jordan , according to the source. It does not appear to encompass highly populated Syrian areas but would run through farms and other Syrian properties. After the 2023 Gaza war broke out, those areas became a launch pad for Iranian-supplied rockets fired at Israeli troops in the Golan Heights. However, Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Syria vastly weakened Hezbollah and, by the end of 2024, the group had withdrawn most of its forces from Syria, setting the stage for the Assad regime's fall. Last week, Syrian authorities said that security forces arrested three members of a cell linked to Hezbollah and dismantled rocket launchers in their possession in the southern Yarmouk river basin. This followed remarks by Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz that the Israeli army was mounting “daily activity” across the Golan to “thwart threats, to eliminate remnants of the old regime, to prevent dangerous consolidation of the new regime” and “protect our communities and our border”. The security source said the Sufa Line signals the “breakdown of trust” that the US tried to build between the two sides. “They look at Damascus and see a militant regime supported by Turkey, although Al Shara himself would love to strike a deal,” the source said. Turkey, the source said, had been pressuring Mr Al Shara to talk to Hezbollah. Reuters reported this month that Hezbollah and Syrian government officials had met in Turkey to calm tensions. The US, which backs Syria's current rulers, has supervised several meetings between Israeli and Syrian officials in an effort to negotiate a peace deal between the two countries. They discussed halting Israeli attacks on Syria and the return of Israeli forces to the 1974 armistice line adjacent to the Golan Heights. Early on Monday, Israeli forces killed a man at an undisclosed location in southern Syria. The military described him as an infiltrator. Syrian state news agency Sana reported extensive Israeli land-clearing operations in the Quneitra governorate.

title: Gulf family businesses face new succession test as women prepare to take on bigger roles
description: Leadership and AI emerge as key issues looking ahead
content: Gulf family businesses are entering a period of generational transition that could give women a bigger role in ownership, investment and executive decision-making, experts have said. The question facing family enterprises is no longer simply who will lead them next, but “who will receive the preparation, responsibility and trust to lead them forward”, Abdullah Jefri, division director for the Gulf at the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank 's private investment arm, said at an event in Dubai on Monday. “Across the GCC [Gulf Co-operation Council], a new generation of highly educated women is ready to lead and many are already doing so with distinction,” Mr Jefri said. He said women play important roles in family enterprises but the opportunity was to broaden those positions to include leading business units, guiding investment decisions and serving on family councils and boards. “For family enterprises, women's leadership is not only a matter of inclusion, it is a matter of competitiveness, continuity and legacy,” he said. Mr Jefri highlighted the UAE ’s efforts to advance women’s economic empowerment, including its Gender Balance Centre for Excellence and Knowledge Exchange, established with the World Bank in 2022. But barriers remain. Women remain underrepresented on corporate boards across the Gulf. A 2026 GCC Board Gender Index found that women held 7 per cent of board seats at listed companies across the region, although the UAE led with 15 per cent. Speaking at the same event, Haifa Al Kaylani , founder and president of the Arab International Women’s Forum, said women were bringing new perspectives to leadership, governance and intergenerational stewardship, including greater attention to innovation, sustainability and talent development. She said the ability of family businesses to remain competitive in a global economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence would depend on women participating as owners, investors, innovators, successors and executives. Discussions also highlighted how technology is changing the way family businesses operate. Raja Al Gurg, chairperson of the Easa Saleh Al Gurg Group, said the company was deploying AI agents across the business, including for a sales co-ordination system that allows employees to obtain immediate reports and information without relying on individual staff members. An AI-enabled human resources system is also being used to answer employees’ questions about company policies and procedures. The company is prioritising AI applications that can demonstrate measurable value through higher revenue, improved cash conversion, lower costs or greater efficiency, Ms Al Gurg said.

title: Abu Dhabi’s Eagle Hills to develop residential and tourism projects in Syria
description: New developments in Damascus and Latakia expected to create 40,000 jobs
content: Abu Dhabi-based Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria including a residential and tourism development as part of a framework agreement the company has signed with the Syrian government. Total investment in the two projects in Damascus and Latakia has not been disclosed but Syria 's Arab News Agency reported they will create more 40,000 jobs. The agreement was signed on Monday at the People’s Palace in Damascus in the presence of Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara by Eagle Hills and Syria’s ministries of Public Works, and Housing and Tourism. It covers two projects: the Tadamun Towers development in Damascus and the Eco Life tourism project in Latakia. The developments will combine housing, services and employment opportunities, while involving Syrian companies and skilled professionals, Mohamed Alabbar , founder and chairman of Eagle Hills, said during the signing ceremony. “We hope these projects will become communities where people can find suitable homes, good services, job opportunities and a decent life,” he said. He also called on Syrians living inside and outside the country to invest in Syria and take part in its reconstruction, saying domestic expertise would be important to the development of the projects. Mr Alabbar previously said he is looking to invest as much as $18 billion in Syria, with projects worth between $5 billion and $7 billion on the Syrian coast, and up to $11 billion in Damascus and its surroundings. The new projects are also expected to encourage Syrians living both inside and outside the country to invest in Syria and take part in their implementation, Mr Alabbar added. Demand for housing remains strong in Syria as it focuses on rebuilding its economy and attracting more investment. Syria aims to build or rehabilitate two million homes by 2035 to address housing shortages in the country. It plans to fund projects through a mix of government investment, private capital, new partnerships and foreign investment. The country is expected to provide land owned by the General Housing Establishment while private investors will develop projects and infrastructure to help increase housing supply. More than 1.7 million Syrians are estimated to have returned to Syria between December 2024 and April 2026 following the overthrow of Bashar Al Assad's regime nearly two years ago, according to the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR. UAE-based Arada also plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Syria in phases over 10 years. The new project in the west of Damascus will have 11,000 homes, including residential apartments, villas and town houses, branded residences, 500 hotel rooms and 1,000 serviced apartments. Two schools as well as a hospital, offices and retail units will also be built as part of the development. There is strong demand for “good-quality homes” in Syria, driven by residents and foreign citizens living abroad, Ahmed Alkhoshaibi, group chief executive of Arada, told The National . “You have the local current demand, which is very strong for good communities. And you also have Syrians living outside, who want to invest, or have a home or holiday home in the country. So that demand will continue to grow,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said.

title: UK loses £120bn as super-wealthy flee
description: Worsening tax picture blamed for billionaires choosing to live elsewhere
content: The exodus of super-rich individuals from Britain since Labour came to power has left a £120 billion ($160 billion) hole, according to a wealth index analysis. More than a dozen individuals with multibillion-pound fortunes have left or loosened ties with the country in favour of more favourable tax regimes, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index showed. It equates to more than half the wealth on the index. A series of tax changes by the Labour government since it returned to power two years ago has resulted in some of Britain’s richest individuals departing, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and telecoms investor Shravin Bharti Mittal. The UAE has been the preferred destination for many of the billionaires, along with Monaco, Switzerland and Italy. Hedge-fund tycoon and philanthropist Chris Rokos , founder of Rokos Capital Management, who was Britain’s third-biggest taxpayer last year has, has also relocated abroad . In 2025, he paid £330 million in tax, placing him near the top of the Sunday Times Tax List. The £120 billion figure does not include David Reuben, who was reported at the weekend to have relocated to Monaco, taking his £9.9 billion fortune with him. His brother Simon has been based there for around 40 years. David Lesperance, a lawyer and former non-dom who describes his job as integrated tax and migration adviser, told The National the key damage being done to the UK tax take was down to the departure of billionaires, rather than millionaires. "The simplest way of thinking about the impact of these super golden geese is that a billionaire contributes the same number of golden eggs as 1,000 millionaires in Income/Capital Gains Tax, VAT, property tax, consumer spending, direct and indirect employment, philanthropy," Mr Lesperance said. "With David Reuben joining Chris Rokos and the list of prior departures in leaving the UK, the loss of their prior annual contribution to the Treasury will put a permanent dent in monies available for social services." He said the many tax changes, including the taxation of international assets means the UK does not have a viable pipeline to attract the next generation of incoming super wealthy. "We are now weeks away from the Autumn Statement. Will the Chancellor accelerate the departure with an exit tax? Or will he bring in policies to bring back departed Golden Geese, keep current ones from leaving and open the spigot for new ones to come to the UK?" The UK government has toughened its tax policy as it tries to balance the books while the economy stutters. It scrapped the non-dom tax status, which allowed those with earnings abroad to keep them out of reach. There have also been changes to capital gains tax, property taxes and national insurance contributions, with further changes expected in the budget at the end of the month.

title: Withdrawal of US bombers from UK base signals 'success' for Iran
description: Experts fear British military bases can 'no longer be considered entirely secure'
content: The withdrawal of US bombers from UK military base RAF Fairford will be seen as a “success by Iran”, amid a series of security threats to Britain, former British diplomats have said. The US Air Force pulled its B-1 bombers out of Fairford on Sunday and redeployed them at bases in America. The move followed the arrests and release of six people by police investigating a suspected terror plot involving the airbase. US President Donald Trump said they were moved due to a threat. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy," he said. "But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." His message was at odds with comments earlier from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said denied suggestions the withdrawal was linked to the suspected terror attack. “The Department of War is constantly reallocating resources where they need to be. There's regular rotations that happen as well,” he said. “We've documented what happened last week. I wouldn't directly tie that to the move that was made.” He added that British officials “couldn't be more co-operative” about the incident last week. Former diplomat Edmund Fitton-Brown said Iran could interpret the withdrawal as a weakening of the US deterrent and its alliance with Britain. “From the Iranian point of view, its already a win if they’re driving a wedge between two Nato allies. They might think we need to do more of this,” he told The National . The withdrawal showed the “weakening of a US defence position by removing assets from a strategically significant base”, Mr Fitton-Brown said. Peter Ricketts, who served as the UK’s first national security adviser between 2010 and 2012, said: “I think it's hard to conclude anything other than that this will be seen as a success by Iran. “Whether it was the intention or whether it's the inadvertent outcome, it is certainly the outcome that they have now forced the US into a public bring-back of their forces from one of their allies,” Lord Ricketts told the BBC. “That what we thought were secure areas in the UK can no longer be considered entirely secure.” Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken of “strong indications” that Iran could be linked to the security incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire two weeks ago. But the investigation last week was mired in confusion . A 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London on Thursday last week in relation to the incident, with police searching two properties in the area. He was later bailed. Five British men were arrested after vehicles were seen driving near the base in the early hours of September 27, and released on bail the following day. One of the men dialled 999 himself, while a farmer living near the base also alerted police to a “large group” of masked men. Mr Fitton-Brown said the UK’s next steps would be to reassure the Americans that it can handle terrorist threats on British soil, or that the threat represented in this instance was low. Military analysts have disclosed that the $400 million aircraft, used extensively to bomb Iran this year, did not have any protective cover at the airbase and that plane spotters reported some have been “bombed up” – fully armed – within 20 metres of the base’s wire perimeter fence during the Iran war. It appears that there was a hurried departure, with the first of four waves of B1s departing just before 9am on Sunday and the last at some point after 1pm, including one jet that had arrived from the US only six days earlier, according to open-source aircraft tracking data. Other open-source data shows that four KC-135 tankers based around 200km away at RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk took off at the same time as the B-1s. There are reports that some bombers were not fully fuelled and might have rendezvoused with the tankers mid-Atlantic. While the B-1 has a reported 12,000km range, its most distant base in Texas was 7,700 miles away, and with weather and safety considerations, would probably have required a top-up. “If this was driven by specific security threats then this could be considered a win for Iran,” said military analyst Francis Tusa. “The fact that they were scrambled to get out of there fast does look strange.” Mr Tusa, editor of Defence Eye , suggested that another consideration could be that the Pentagon wanted the bombers back for maintenance, with some repair machinery only available at their US bases. “Someone in the Pentagon likely said ‘let’s get them all back, stand them down and put the crews on leave’. Then they will wait until after midterms and some point next month six B-1s could well arrive back at Fairford.” But Reuters has reported that Nato military sources believe Iran still presents an “acute threat” to US assets in Britain. US airbases in the Middle East have been heavily hit, making the air force wary about attacks. They will also be aware of the Ukrainian Operation Spider's Web in which lorries filled with kamikaze drones were driven to airbases to take out a substantial number of Russian bombers. The USAF has about 44 operational B-1s, with majority being used to bomb Iran. Iran has been accused of hiring petty criminals and organised criminal networks in the UK and across Europe to conduct attacks on Iranian dissidents, Jewish organisations and Israel-linked businesses. Last month, Sweden expelled an Iranian diplomat found to have undertaken “activities not in according with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations”. A Swedish government minister accused Iran of working with criminal networks to conduct attacks in Sweden. In the UK, there have been several attacks against Iranian opposition groups and Jewish organisations that police have linked to Iran. The Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati – a critic of the regime – was stabbed outside his home in London two years ago. British counter-terrorism police arrested two people in London on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in a case linked to Iran last week.

title: Dubai Police seize more than 400 e-scooters, e-bikes and bicycles in road safety campaign
description: Safety equipment distributed to workers in Naif area as part of initiative
content: Dubai Police confiscated more than 400 e-scooters, e-bikes and bicycles for unsafe riding and breaches of traffic rules during a road safety campaign in the city's Gold Souq area. Police said the riders faced legal action as part of efforts to reduce the risk of accidents and injuries. The campaign led to the seizure of 300 e-scooters, 50 e-bikes and 58 bicycles after riders breached traffic rules, officials at Naif Police Station said on Monday. The initiative also focused on educating riders about traffic regulations, the importance of using the proper paths and the need to wear protective equipment. Brig Omar Ashour, director of Naif Police Station, said officers in Dubai placed a strong emphasis on traffic awareness as part of wider efforts to reduce accidents. Dubai Police distributed safety equipment and supplies to workers in the area, with an estimated 932 people benefitting from the campaign. Brig Ashour warned that riding in areas that were not meant for scooters and bikes could increase the risk of accidents. Last month, Dubai Police said 13,657 e-scooters had been confiscated so far this year for dangerous riding , including travelling at speeds exceeding 60kph on public roads. E-scooters are limited to 20kph on designated routes and riders must be at least 16 years old. Data from the Ministry of Interior revealed that in 2025 there was a 97 per cent increase in major e-scooter accidents compared with the previous year – a jump from 61 to 120. Alongside those figures, Al Wathba Insurance and RoadSafetyUAE conducted an e-scooter perception study and found that 93 per cent of UAE residents witnessed e-scooter riders behaving unsafely or recklessly, while 90 per cent felt unsafe because of how e-scooters were used. In Dubai, riders must hold a permit issued by the Roads and Transport Authority. Permit holders may ride in designated areas, including Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Boulevard, Jumeirah Lakes Towers, Dubai Internet City, Al Rigga, City Walk, Palm Jumeirah and Karama.

title: From Iranian proxies to Giants Brigades: Who's who in Yemen conflict
description: Fighting pits Saudi-backed Yemeni government against Iran-sponsored Houthis
content: The renewed civil war in Yemen pits an exiled government backed by Saudi Arabia and several armed factions against the Iran -backed Houthi rebels. After a lull since 2022, fighting has burst back into the open in recent weeks as the Houthis seized control of Yemen's Red Sea coast, prompting a counter-offensive from the government. Although backed by the air power of a Saudi-led coalition, the Yemeni government also faces internal divisions and has failed in previous attempts to drive the Houthis out of their territory. Here is a guide to the key players: Based in Aden, Yemen's internationally recognised government has been unable to operate from Sanaa since the Houthis captured the capital in 2015. On Sunday it announced a new push to reclaim territory from the Houthis . The Saudi-backed government is run by an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council headed by Rashad Al Alimi. A factional struggle in December led to some members who favoured secession for southern Yemen being removed. Mr Al Alimi has declared a general mobilisation to beat back the latest Houthi advances, with a declared aim to “reclaim the remaining territories of the republic”. Pro-government forces have about 122,000 troops to their name as well as armoured vehicles, anti-tank rockets and air defence guns, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies. However, it says the government has “limited control” over some of the factions involved. Saudi Arabia has led the anti-Houthi alliance since 2015. On Monday the coalition said 100 fighter jets were taking part in the new government offensive and providing air cover on the Bab Al Mandeb strait. The kingdom has advanced warplanes and had a military budget of 272 billion riyals ($72.6 billion) last year. It also has a new defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan , who were holding a meeting in Riyadh on Monday. The UAE was part of the coalition until 2019. A small number of remaining counter-terrorism specialists were withdrawn late last year. The Iran-backed Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have occupied large parts of Yemen throughout the civil war. With a range of missiles and drones, they have also attacked shipping in the Red Sea and launched occasional strikes on Israel . Having largely sat out the first round of this year's regional war, they launched an offensive in September to seize Yemen's Red Sea coast and claim unrivalled control over the sensitive Bab Al Mandeb strait. The National revealed last month how Iran had played a role in the Houthi offensive , with an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative known as “Shadow Man” among those helping to use Yemen as a new pressure point in the wider war. Military experts say Iran is a key supplier of drones, missiles and other equipment to the rebels but that the Houthis have also experimented with their own weapons development . Led by Abdul-Malik Al Houthi, the group has also carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia, causing outrage by targeting the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah. The Yemeni government said two loyalist factions, the Giants Brigades and Nation’s Shield Forces, were helping to run a flanking manoeuvre around the Houthis on Monday. The Giants Brigades are a southern faction whose numbers have been estimated at between 15,000 and 30,000. They have previously taken action on the Bab Al Mandeb strait to intercept alleged weapons shipments to the Houthis. The Saudi Arabia-aligned Nation's Shields Forces helped to restore government control over the south after skirmishes late last year. Mr Al Alimi also said last month he “placed great hope” in Yemeni tribes siding with the government. Some anti-Houthi fighters are part of the National Resistance Forces, a coalition led by Gen Tariq Saleh – the nephew of Yemen's former billionaire president Ali Abdullah Saleh . There are rivalries within the anti-Houthi movement. The Hadhrami Elite Forces, a group loyal to the southern secessionists, last year seized oilfields in the south of Yemen before Saudi-backed forces restored government control.

title: The UK has failed to recognise the scale of Iran’s covert threat
description: The country has become a fertile ground for Tehran’s operations
content: What people fail to appreciate about Iran’s infiltration of the US and its western allies is that Tehran has developed a template that works – and has put it into practice. The Iranian regime might consider the US’s recent withdrawal of its bombers from the UK’s RAF Fairford as a success. Reporting from the US indicates that a bizarre escapade on the Fairford perimeter, involving three vans with contraband or stolen fuel and detected at midnight, was in fact a wider plot to swarm the base to inflict damage on American strategic assets. Answering the inevitable question of how Iran can mete out damage thousands of kilometres away is something that should have been done a long time ago. For the UK, the sense of emergency remains entirely absent. Whitehall has for decades viewed the Iran file as a diplomatic challenge rather than a security threat. This possibly stems from an attitude among officials to “understand a little more and condemn a little less”. As a result, however, the UK has long been paying the price – and today its humiliation is freshly clear. The Iranian gameplan is a developed capability that stretches across a number of countries, including the US . But it is the UK where Tehran appears to have found the biggest pool of willing recruits and dupes who are engaged effectively as foot soldiers. Where I think Tehran is underestimated is that its plots are fully fledged scripted exercises. Think of the Iranians orchestrating these events with the same approach as the writer or producer of a Netflix drama. The intelligence officials who do the plotting and recruitment from Tehran are not just dabbling in the lower reaches of gaming chat forums and messaging channels. There is methodology behind its recruitment and mobilisations. The UK courts are facing multiple cases of people who have been arrested for allegedly targeting Jewish communities and Iranian dissidents in the country. There have been a few convictions, too, with more likely to come out. Given the long lead times of the court process in the UK, there is much more to be revealed, but this will be too late to boost deterrence among the public. Part of the reason is a lot of the Iranian methodology remains hidden because of the rhythm of the courts. In cases where the defendants plead guilty, the facts that are shared in the public domain amount to fewer details than we would expect. We also have slower release because the courts can take up to two years to go to trial. Nonetheless, it is crucial that authorities in the UK demonstrate a grip on the scope and scale of the Iranian threat. This means recognising the sophistication with which Tehran has built up its operational footprint in countries that should be distanced from the regime’s threat. Iran has benefitted from the lack of preventive policing in post-Cold War European countries. Russia allegedly hired two people to attack the home of Keir Starmer when the then-British prime minister was living in Downing Street. The prosecution statement after the trial was mechanical and bland, relating how the investigation demonstrated that the pair had conducted reconnaissance and later returned to photograph the damage. This alone strengthened the prosecution’s claim that the offences were planned rather than spontaneous. “The prosecution made clear that the case did not depend on proving political or ideological motivation, nor on whether the defendants knew the properties were linked to the Prime Minister,” the Crown Prosecution Service statement said after the conviction. I quote this because it demonstrates to me the studied neutrality of the system and its inability to take on the wider security challenge. Yes, the prosecutors were able to get a conviction on the basis of the criminality of the offences. In narrow terms, they succeeded in their job. But this is the sort of flawed and self-limited response that has seen the UK hamstrung in its response to the spread of targeted hostile activity across the country. Iran has exploited Britain’s porous borders to filter its own nationals into the country, using the wave of migration across the English Channel among other routes. It has also been able to tap into divisions in the diaspora, with dual nationals suspected of conducting activities on its behalf. For wider recruitment, it has used connections with criminal gangs, including the Swedish Foxtrot network, to use lethal force in Europe. And it has tapped a cadre of lower-level criminal or sub-criminal gangs for hire to seed the ground for its operations. The reason these plots work as scripted operations is that method allows Iran to compose its threat from a matrix of established contacts. The costs of assembling these networks are not very high. Technology is an enabler that allows encrypted communications and payment by cryptocurrency . The UK has upgraded its laws with new offences targeted at those who work on behalf of a foreign power, even unknowingly. US President Donald Trump said that the UK was successful in the case of RAF Fairford, in disrupting whatever was planned, even if the vans were merely in the wrong place at a time of high alert. The wider challenge for Washington is that the more exposed the US grows, the more it pulls back from its former strongholds. Iran has found a formula that exploits these gaps, and the rest of the West is well past the point of reading every incident as a wake-up call.

title: Dubai schools tighten photo and video rules to protect pupil privacy
description: Parents back stronger measures set out in KHDA guidelines
content: Schools in Dubai have reminded parents to avoid taking photos or videos that capture children other than their own, or staff, without their consent on campus. The guidance applies to classrooms, corridors, playgrounds, assemblies, and school drop-off and pick-up areas. Parents are also asked not to share images or videos featuring other pupils on social media, WhatsApp groups or other online platforms without permission. The measures are aimed at protecting children's privacy while still allowing families to capture important school moments. A circular issued to a Dubai private school, seen by The National, told parents that photography will continue to be allowed at designated events but clearer guidance would be provided on when and where images could be taken. Official school photography will continue under existing consent and safeguarding procedures. The school said it understands parents want to capture their children's achievements and will, where possible, provide opportunities for families to do so safely. “Thank you for helping us keep our school community safe, respectful and protective of every child's privacy,” the circular said. Under federal law, personal data cannot be processed without consent , except in specific circumstances set out in the legislation, which also sets requirements around the confidentiality, security and protection of personal information. Dubai private schools are also required under the emirate's regulatory framework to safeguard and preserve pupils' rights and take necessary measures to protect them. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority guidance also treats photography as a privacy issue. Its current protocols for private schools state that photographing pupils in vulnerable situations is a violation of their privacy and that taking photos during emergencies is prohibited. The National spoke to parents in Dubai who broadly said they support tighter rules, particularly because images can be easily shared online. Jenita Clara, whose child attends Gems Legacy School, said parents should be mindful when taking photographs or videos in which other children could feature. “Everyone has a right to privacy and not everyone may be comfortable appearing in photos or videos that could later be shared online,” she said. She said the ease with which images can be posted on social media or sent through messaging groups makes clearer guidance important. “Photos and videos can easily be shared on social media or messaging groups without the knowledge or consent of those involved.” She suggested designated photography areas or specific opportunities for parents to take pictures of their own children. “I believe the right balance is to allow parents to capture memories of their own children while respecting the privacy and safeguarding needs of others,” she said. Verkha Bhatia, whose child attends Dubai British School, also supported the measures to protect pupils. “It's important to respect other parents' choice of not having their child's photos taken,” she said. She said schools already used consent forms to establish whether parents were comfortable with their children being photographed by the school but added that completely preventing other pupils from appearing in photographs could be difficult at large events. “This is something that cannot be controlled and it is not realistic, very hard to control,” said Ms Bhatia. “Measures are taken, for sure, but how successful they are to attain is difficult in a busy event environment.” She said some schools already limit photography or make certain events camera-free. However, she said a blanket ban could be difficult for parents who want to preserve memories of their children. “It cannot be completely prohibited. Only measures can be put in place, which most schools do already,” she said.

title: Adnoc signs Thai LNG deal after Iran war disrupts Gulf supply
description: Deliveries to begin in 2027 as Bangkok seeks to diversify sources of imported gas
content: Adnoc has agreed to supply about two million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to Thailand ’s Gulf Development, boosting the country's access to the fuel as the Iran war disrupts supplies from the Middle East. Deliveries under the multi-year sales and purchase agreement are to start in 2027, Adnoc said on Monday. The company did not disclose prices, the length of the contract or where the cargoes will be sourced from. The agreement builds on a first LNG supply deal between the companies signed in 2025. The latest deal comes as Thailand seeks to diversify its LNG supplies after the war sharply curtailed shipments from the Gulf. Natural gas accounts for more than 60 per cent of the country’s power generation, while about 24 per cent of its LNG imports – about 2.2 million tonnes a year – normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz, almost all from Qatar, according to Thailand-based Krungsri Research. State-controlled PTT has been exploring alternative supplies, including from Oman, Mexico and Canada. The regional war has upended a global LNG market that was already heading into a period of tighter seasonal demand. The strait, through which about a fifth of global crude and LNG flowed before the war began in late February, remains largely shut. QatarEnergy declared force majeure in early March, while an Iranian missile strike on the Ras Laffan complex on March 18 knocked out about 17 per cent of Qatar's LNG production capacity. Cargo cancellations to some Asian buyers have since been extended through November, helping push prices in Asia and Europe towards their highest levels since late 2022. Gulf LNG exports remain far below their prewar pace of about three shipments a day. “This agreement builds on our first LNG supply agreement with Gulf Group and reinforces Adnoc’s commitment to ensuring reliable energy supplies to Thailand and our Asian customers,” said Nasser Al Muhairi, acting chief executive of Adnoc downstream industry, marketing and trading. Gulf Development chief executive Sarath Ratanavadi said the agreement would help to build a “diversified, resilient LNG portfolio” and gave the company greater flexibility to meet demand. The supplies will be delivered through Adnoc Trading and its LNG marketing and trading platform , launched in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM in July. Adnoc is targeting 47 million tonnes a year of marketable LNG beyond 2030 as it expands its portfolio and trading operations.

title: UAE 'ready for the moment' as they face Saudi Arabia in Arabian Gulf Cup final
description: New coach Dalic confident his team can win the title for a third time against the hosts in Jeddah
content: Zlatko Dalic has urged his UAE players to enjoy the challenge when they face hosts Saudi Arabia in the Arabian Gulf Cup final. The Croatian coach has enjoyed a fine start since taking over the national team at the start of this season. The Gulf Cup is his first assignment. His side have played with great panache in progressing to the final, scoring nine goals in four games to this point, and conceding just once. They will face a significant step up in terms of the standard of opposition in Tuesday night’s title-decider. Saudi Arabia are the highest ranked side in the eight-team competition, with the UAE giving away 10 places in the Fifa standings. Over the course of history, the UAE have won just seven matches against their neighbour, to 23 won by Saudi Arabia. They will also be backed by a vociferous home support at the 62,000-capacity King Abdullah Sports City Stadium in Jeddah . Despite that, Dalic insists the game will be the “easiest” for his players to prepare for in the competition, simply because they know what is at stake. “Tomorrow will be the easiest game for us because it is a final,” Dalic said. “We have reached the final and I want my team to enjoy the game. We are here to enjoy playing, and I hope the fans will get to see an amazing game. “I know we will play against a very, very strong team who have been the best team so far in the tournament. They are playing in front of their people, their fans, and it will be a full stadium, but we are ready. “We are ready for this moment. We have been working hard for the past 20 days. Saudi Arabia are a really good team, with a really good coach, but, as always, I am an optimist and I believe in my team.” The UAE have won the biennial competition just twice before. They beat Oman in the final on home soil in Abu Dhabi in 2007, and claimed a second title six years later when they beat Iraq in Bahrain. Dalic’s remit is broader than the narrow confines of a tournament whose prize is essentially local bragging rights. He was brought in to help the UAE challenge for the Asian Cup, which will also be held in Saudi Arabia at the start of next year. Beyond that is the hope he can build a side that will be capable of qualifying for the World Cup for the first time since 1990. That said, a Gulf Cup title would be a huge boost so early in his tenure, especially given how difficult they have proved to win for the national team in the past. “I’ll give everything I have for the UAE national team,” Dalic said. “I hope to begin my journey here by winning this title.” While they will clearly be outnumbered in Jeddah, the UAE will still have a sizeable presence in the stands for the final. The UAE Football Association initially laid on six planes to transport supporters from the Emirates to Jeddah. They subsequently doubled the number of flights to 12, such was the appetite from supporters. They have also underwritten the price of tickets for the game, with around 6,000 UAE supporters expected to be present – so around a 10th of the stadium. Dalic and Khalid Essa, the UAE captain, both praised the role the supporters have played in the team’s progress to this point, with Essa terming them the side's “prime motivator”. Essa said his side are aware of the challenge facing them, but he is confident they will be better off for the string of near-misses they have had in big matches of late. “We expect a tough match as it’s a big derby between two of the Gulf’s most established national teams,” Essa said. “We’ve been through many challenges in recent times and came close on previous occasions, so we hope this will be the moment we reap the rewards.”

title: Fadel Chaker to hold first concert in 14 years at Riyadh Season
description: Lebanese singer set to perform in Saudi Arabia for first time amid military court case in Beirut
content: Fadel Chaker will perform his first concert for 14 years at Riyadh Season this month. The Lebanese singer's first concert in Saudi Arabia is to take place at Abu Bakr Salem Theatre in Riyadh's Boulevard City on October 22. Titled Awdat Al Ghayeb, or Return of the Absent, the show takes its name from Ya Ghayeb , one of his best-known songs. Tickets are to go on sale on Wednesday. Chaker is to perform three months after Lebanon's military court approved his release on bail while legal proceedings linked to his former association with radical cleric Ahmed Al Assir remain unresolved. Chaker, who has repeatedly denied taking part in 2013 clashes between Al Assir's supporters and the Lebanese army in Sidon, is due to appear before Lebanon's Permanent Military Court on October 21 – a day before the Riyadh concert. A September 23 hearing was postponed after his lawyer, Amata Mubarak, presented a medical excuse. Chaker was tried in his absence in 2020 and sentenced to a total of 22 years in prison over his support for Al Assir's armed group. After about 12 years in Ain Al Hilweh Palestinian refugee camp, near Sidon, he surrendered to Lebanese authorities in October last year. He turned himself in after reaching a deal in which the convictions issued in his absence were vacated and a new trial ordered. In May, a Beirut criminal court acquitted Chaker and Al Assir in a separate case over an alleged attempt to kill Hilal Hammoud, a cleric aligned with Hezbollah, in 2013. Chaker still faces proceedings before the military court over the Sidon clashes. He continued to make music while living in Ain Al Hilweh. His first attempt to return to the mainstream came in 2018 with Shab'an Min Al Tamtheel . The song was intended for Egyptian Ramadan drama Ladayna Iqwal Ukhra , but production company AG Group removed it following criticism over his legal situation in Lebanon. In a 2018 interview with Arabic Post , he described having musical arrangements recorded abroad and sent to him before adding his vocals and returning the files to be mixed and mastered. His 2025 releases included Ahla Rasma , Elhob W Bass , Hawa Aljnoub , Rouh El Baher and Kifek A Fira’i . By June, Ahla Rasma had passed 40 million views on YouTube. Released on July 7, Kifek A Fira’i , a duet with his son Mohamed , was included in The National 's 50 best Arabic songs of 2025 . The ballad about separation and loss was described as “a fine piece of balladry” and potentially “one of the defining Arabic songs of the year”. More releases followed, including Sahak El Shouq , which won Favourite Song at the Joy Awards in Riyadh this year, while Chaker was named Favourite Artist. Chaker's career took off in the late 1990s, with songs including Baya El Qolob , Aash Mn Shafak , Ma'oul , Law Ala Albi and Ya Ghayeb establishing him as a star act across the region. He also recorded collaborations with Sherine Abdelwahab, Yara and Elissa, including Al Aam Al Jadid , Khidni Maak and Gowa El Rouh . Chaker was still performing major concerts in 2012, including the closing concert of Abu Dhabi Festival at Emirates Palace. One of his last major public performances before withdrawing came weeks later at Morocco's Mawazine festival on May 19. He stepped back from mainstream music later that year.

title: UAE foils 14 drug smuggling attempts, seizing 300kg of narcotics at airports
description: Joint operations between security agencies intercept drugs hidden in baggage and transit consignments
content: UAE security authorities have foiled 14 attempts to smuggle narcotics through airports across the country, seizing more than 300kg of drugs in less than two months. The operations were carried out jointly by the National Anti-Narcotics Agency and the Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs and Port Security, through its General Directorate of Port Security, state news agency Wam reported. Several suspected smugglers from countries in Europe and Asia were arrested as a result of the operations. Intelligence on suspicious consignments and travel routes was exchanged before their arrival at airports in the UAE , enabling specialist teams to act immediately after the flights and shipments arrived. UAE Customs said the country used advanced technical detection systems and smart screening technology to identify suspicious substances concealed within baggage and transit consignments with a high degree of accuracy and speed. In many cases, this happened without the need for manual inspections. The authority said the systems had contributed to reducing inspection times while increasing detection rates for smuggling attempts involving sophisticated methods of concealment. Last week, The National reported how UAE Customs foiled an attempt to smuggle 16.2kg of crystal meth into the country after the drugs were found inside a vehicle's tyre at a border crossing.

title: Makkah pact countries plan 'rapid deployment of capabilities' in Saudi Arabia
description: High-level officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan discuss defence alliance
content: Turkey and Pakistan have agreed to provide "military forces and capabilities" to Saudi Arabia as it comes under attack by the Houthis. Ministers and military commanders from the three countries gathered in Riyadh on Monday for talks on the Makkah defence pact . The committee "decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom," a joint statement said. It said retired Pakistani Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood had been appointed secretary general of the alliance. Defence and foreign ministers as well as army chiefs attended the meeting of the Makkah pact’s strategic political and defence committee, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi officials or state media. Pakistan had said its officials would be meeting “counterparts” from the kingdom in its capital. The talks come as the war between Iran, the US and Israel drags on, and as Iran-backed Houthi rebels continue to launch ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on energy infrastructure. “The meeting's focus would definitely be Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia,” a Pakistani Foreign Ministry official briefed on the talks told The National . Monday’s meeting was to discuss “the stage reached in the alliance’s institutionalisation efforts”, the Turkish statement said, following the committee’s inaugural meeting in Istanbul in August. Pakistan’s participation indicates the country’s resolve “to continue contributing towards regional peace and stability”, the statement from Islamabad said. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August in an attempt to strengthen regional security as conflicts continued across the Middle East. The kingdom backs the internationally recognised government in Yemen, which is battling the Houthis. Rashad Al Alimi, head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, on Sunday announced the start of military operations to reclaim territory held by the rebel group, which in the past few weeks has captured the Bab Al Mandeb strait and about 150km of Red Sea coastline, increasing its leverage over a vital international shipping route. The text of the Makkah pact has not been made public but a joint statement from the three countries at the time of its signing said it was intended to strengthen collective deterrence. Similar to Nato's Article 5 on collective defence, an attack on one country would be considered an attack on all. Nuclear-armed Pakistan and major oil exporter Saudi Arabia already have a bilateral defence agreement but the three countries together represent a stronger alliance. Nato member Turkey is seeking opportunities for military co-operation as it builds out a burgeoning domestic defence manufacturing industry. Pakistan has an executive system of government and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's signing of the agreement is sufficient to move it forward. "There is no question of not taking any stakeholders into consultation," a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson told journalists after the pact was signed in August. Parliament can get involved in troop deployments if legislation is required, but its approval is not a constitutional requirement. In Turkey, parliament must approve the pact before President Recep Tayyip Erdogan can ratify it. The constitution allows for troop deployment without parliamentary approval if demanded by an international treaty to which Turkey is party. Ismail Numan Telci, director of the Centre for Gulf Studies and Global Policy at Istanbul's Ibn Haldun University, told The National he was expecting the Turkish parliament to ratify the pact swiftly, after it reopened last Thursday. The President can also act without parliamentary approval, but his actions “have limits" without it, Mr Telci said. "Whatever Turkey would do now before the ratification, can take place in the formula of defence collaboration. But this would be bilateral support as it can be done without parliament approval.” This could include provision of weapons or technical assistance, he added. He cited previous examples of Turkey providing military support to allies, including its deployment to Libya and its military presence in Azerbaijan in 2020.
